question: Abigail Adams ran the family farm at Braintree alone in the spring of 1776, while her husband John helped draft a new nation's laws at the Continental Congress. That March she wrote begging him to 'Remember the Ladies.' She did not ask out of mere kindness. What warning did she give him about the power husbands held over their wives?
answer: 'Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could.'
choices: 'Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could.'
'A wife's duty is obedience in all things.'
'Let the churches decide what is owed to women.'
'The colonies need every able hand at the loom.'
context: Abigail Adams pressed a natural-rights argument straight at the men writing the founding documents: do not put 'such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands.' It is the most famous documented founding-era argument over women's place in the new republic, and it survives in her own handwriting. Source: Massachusetts Historical Society, Adams Family Papers, Letter from Abigail Adams to John Adams, 31 March–5 April 1776 (masshist.org/digitaladams/archive/doc?id=L17760331aa).

question: John Adams was in Philadelphia in the spring of 1776, helping draft the laws of a new United States, when Abigail wrote to him from their Massachusetts farm. She asked him to 'Remember the Ladies' in the new code of laws, and she warned that women would 'foment a Rebellion' if the lawmakers gave them no voice. John wrote back in April. How did he answer her?
answer: He laughed it off as the 'Despotism of the Peticoat.'
choices: He laughed it off as the 'Despotism of the Peticoat.'
He promised to raise it at the next session.
He warned her never to write of it again.
He copied her argument straight into a speech.
context: John Adams replied, 'As to your extraordinary Code of Laws, I cannot but laugh,' joking that men only held 'the Name of Masters' and that rather than yield power 'to the Despotism of the Peticoat' he hoped 'General Washington, and all our brave Heroes would fight.' Abigail had turned the founding's own 'no taxation without representation' logic on the founders themselves. Source: Massachusetts Historical Society, Adams Family Papers, Letter from John Adams to Abigail Adams, 14 April 1776 (masshist.org/digitaladams/archive/doc?id=L17760414ja).

question: Josiah Wedgwood, the potter, made a small medallion in 1787 for the campaign against the slave trade. On it an African man knelt in chains, lifting his hands to the sky and asking one question. Supporters wore it as jewellery. What did he ask?
answer: "Am I Not a Man and a Brother?"
choices: "Am I Not a Man and a Brother?"
"Will No One Set Me Free?"
"Have I No Soul to Save?"
"Why Must I Wear These Chains?"
context: Wedgwood made the design the seal of the Abolition Society and produced it as fashionable jasperware cameos. Middle-class women wore it as pendants, hairpins and snuffbox inlays, and he even mailed a few of the cameos to Benjamin Franklin in Philadelphia in early 1788, carrying the British emblem across the Atlantic. It became the most recognizable piece of antislavery imagery the movement ever produced. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedgwood_anti-slavery_medallion; vam.ac.uk; blog.philamuseum.org)

question: John Newton captained slave ships. After a storm nearly drowned him, he found faith, quit the trade and became a pastor; in old age he helped William Wilberforce fight it. Newton wrote a hymn, still sung today, about a lost man saved. What is it?
answer: "Amazing Grace"
choices: "Amazing Grace"
"How Great Thou Art"
"Rock of Ages"
"Abide With Me"
context: It was a long conversation with Newton in 1787 that helped steel the young MP William Wilberforce to take up the abolition cause. The ex-slaver who wrote 'Amazing Grace' had seen the trade from the inside. (christianhistoryinstitute.org; docslib.org/doc/572237)

question: Thomas Clarkson rode across Britain in the 1780s gathering evidence against the slave trade, and he brought a wooden chest to show Parliament that Africa could trade in goods, not people. One side held ivory, cloth, spices and palm oil. What did he keep on the other side?
answer: Iron handcuffs, leg-shackles, thumbscrews and branding irons
choices: Iron handcuffs, leg-shackles, thumbscrews and branding irons
Maps, ledgers and signed merchant contracts
Bags of West Indian sugar and rum
Portraits of the captains who ran the ships
context: Clarkson rode roughly 35,000 miles on horseback and interviewed around 20,000 sailors to assemble his evidence; the chest also held devices made to force a captive's jaws open. The two sides — instruments of torture beside honest trade goods — were the whole argument in one box. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Clarkson; ageofrevolution.org)

question: A British woman in 1791 could not vote, but she did her family's shopping. That year the abolitionists asked British women to stop buying one product grown by slaves, and about 300,000 families joined in; some shops sold only Indian goods 'not made by slaves.' What did those families give up?
answer: Slave-grown West Indian sugar
choices: Slave-grown West Indian sugar
Tea from the East India Company
Tobacco from Virginia
Cotton cloth from the mills
context: Sugar was the great cash crop of the Caribbean slave plantations, so a family that gave it up was hitting the trade where it hurt. The boycott handed ordinary people — especially women shut out of the vote — a way to fight slavery from the kitchen. (theconversation.com; shropshirearchives.org.uk)

question: God had set before him 'two great objects,' William Wilberforce wrote in his diary one Sunday in October 1787, when he was a 28-year-old Member of Parliament. The first was suppressing the slave trade. He named a second great object beside it. What did he call that second great object?
answer: The Reformation of Manners
choices: The Reformation of Manners
The reform of Parliament
The relief of the poor
The spread of the gospel abroad
context: 'God Almighty has set before me two great objects, the suppression of the Slave Trade and the Reformation of Manners.' The diary entry came soon after a long talk with John Newton, the ex-slave-ship captain. Wilberforce framed both fights as one moral mission. (docslib.org/doc/572237; christianhistoryinstitute.org)

question: Thomas Clarkson's Quaker allies printed 7,000 copies of a poster in London in 1789. It showed the slave ship Brookes seen from above, with 482 tiny bodies drawn side by side on her decks like cargo. The number 482 was not chosen for effect. Where did the artists get it?
answer: The maximum the law allowed that ship to carry
choices: The maximum the law allowed that ship to carry
The number who died on her last voyage
The crew the ship signed on for the trip
The price in pounds the owners paid per captive
context: The 1788 Regulated Slave Trade Act capped the Brookes at 482 people — so the diagram drew the LEGAL limit and let viewers see that even the law's 'humane' maximum was monstrous. The Plymouth chapter printed it first in 1788. (loc.gov/pictures/item/98504459; archives.history.ac.uk)

question: Olaudah Equiano wrote a book in London in 1789 that became a huge British bestseller. It went through nine printings, and he toured the country to sell it. What made his story different from every pamphlet the white abolitionists were printing?
answer: He had survived the slave ships and bought his own freedom
choices: He had survived the slave ships and bought his own freedom
He was a Quaker merchant who had never left England
He was a Royal Navy officer who patrolled the African coast
He was a Member of Parliament writing under a false name
context: 'The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano' was the testimony of a man who had lived it and then purchased his liberty — a formerly enslaved African making the case in his own voice, not a sympathizer speaking for him. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Interesting_Narrative_of_the_Life_of_Olaudah_Equiano; britannica.com)

question: William Wilberforce had led the fight against the slave trade in the Commons for twenty years, losing vote after vote. On 23 February 1807, after a ten-hour debate, the House voted 283 to 16 to abolish it. When Samuel Romilly paid tribute to his struggle, the House rose to salute him. What did Wilberforce do?
answer: He bowed his head and wept
choices: He bowed his head and wept
He stood and gave a triumphant speech
He knelt and led the House in prayer
He quietly slipped out of the chamber
context: Wilberforce had brought abolition bills to Parliament year after year and lost again and again before this night. He sat overcome as Parliament saluted two decades of defeats finally turned to victory. Royal assent followed on 25 March 1807, making the Slave Trade Act law; it outlawed the trade in human beings throughout the Empire, though slavery itself in the colonies would not be abolished until 1833. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_Trade_Act_1807; historyofparliamentonline.org; historyskills.com 'William Wilberforce')

question: The Commons was about to pass the act freeing some 800,000 enslaved people across the British Empire when William Wilberforce heard the news in July 1833. Three days later, on 29 July, he died. Britain honoured the man who had fought the slave trade for forty years with a tribute it almost never granted a private citizen. What was it?
answer: The Lords and Commons walked in procession and carried his coffin into Westminster Abbey
choices: The Lords and Commons walked in procession and carried his coffin into Westminster Abbey
The Royal Navy fired a sixty-gun salute over his Yorkshire grave
The King knighted him on his deathbed and gave him a state funeral
His statue was raised in Trafalgar Square the following spring
context: Wilberforce lived just long enough to win, then was buried in Westminster Abbey near his friend William Pitt. Both Houses of Parliament, led by the Lord Chancellor and the Speaker, walked in solemn procession from their chambers and carried him 'to his fitting place among the mighty dead'; he had no title or office of his own. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wilberforce; westminster-abbey.org; christian.org.uk)

question: Parliament ended slavery across the British Empire in 1833 and set about 800,000 people free. Freedom came with a bill: Parliament paid out £20 million in compensation, a huge sum that ate a big share of the national budget. Who received the £20 million?
answer: The slave-owners, not the freed people
choices: The slave-owners, not the freed people
The freed people, as a fresh start
The African kingdoms that had lost their people
The Royal Navy crews who hunted the slavers
context: The money went to the planters for the loss of their 'property,' and the freed were made to serve years as unpaid 'apprentices' until that system finally ended in 1838. Britain led the world in abolition — and still paid the masters, not the enslaved. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833; nationalarchives.gov.uk)

question: At 6 feet 4 inches, Abraham Lincoln had to stoop through most doorways, and in a crowded room he stood a full head above nearly everyone. What distinction does that height still earn him among all the men who have served as U.S. president?
answer: The tallest U.S. president ever
choices: The tallest U.S. president ever
The second-tallest U.S. president ever
The tallest president only of the 1800s
Tied for tallest with George Washington
context: At 6'4", Lincoln is still the tallest president in American history. He had less than a year of formal schooling in his whole life and taught himself at night by the light of the fireplace. Source: Miller Center, life-before-the-presidency; National Geographic Kids, 'Abraham Lincoln'.

question: As a poor teenager on the frontier in Indiana and Illinois, Abraham Lincoln swung an axe for money, chopping logs into long fence pieces. When he ran for president in 1860, that picture of him with an axe became his campaign nickname. What was it?
answer: The Rail-Splitter
choices: The Rail-Splitter
The Backwoodsman
The Frontier Ploughman
The Prairie Woodsman
context: Republicans turned 'the Rail-Splitter' into Lincoln's 1860 campaign image, carrying fence rails in parades to show their candidate had risen from hard frontier labor. Source: CBC Radio, 'A bet landed Abraham Lincoln in the Wrestling Hall of Fame'; Britannica, 'Was Abraham Lincoln a Wrestler'.

question: In the Illinois village of New Salem, young Abraham Lincoln clerked in a general store, and his honesty there earned him the name 'Honest Abe.' One evening, with the store shut for the night, the story goes, he realised he had charged a customer about six cents too much. What did he do about it?
answer: He walked several miles after closing to return the change
choices: He walked several miles after closing to return the change
He left the extra coins in the till and forgot about it
He gave the customer free goods the very next morning
He told his boss and quietly split the difference with him
context: Another time, having shorted a woman a quarter-pound of tea, Lincoln weighed out the rest and delivered it before breakfast. The honesty stories are cherished frontier legend. Source: Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal, 'How Lincoln Became Known as Honest Abe'; teacher.depaul.edu, 'Honest Abe'.

question: Grace Bedell, eleven years old, wrote to Abraham Lincoln in 1860 telling him to grow whiskers, because his face was 'so thin.' He grew his famous beard soon after. On his train ride to Washington, what did the new president do when he reached her town of Westfield?
answer: He stopped the train, found Grace, and showed her his new whiskers
choices: He stopped the train, found Grace, and showed her his new whiskers
He sent a brief note from the train thanking her for the advice
He had a photographer take a picture of the two of them together
He arranged a federal job for Grace's father as a way of saying thanks
context: Lincoln told her, 'Gracie, look at my whiskers. I have been growing them for you.' His iconic bearded look began with a child's letter. Source: Abraham Lincoln Online, 'Letter to Grace Bedell'; Wikipedia, 'Grace Bedell'.

question: The Clary's Grove Boys put up their champion, Jack Armstrong, against young Abraham Lincoln, a wrestler who by legend lost only one match in about a dozen years. Lincoln said Armstrong was impossible to throw. What animal did Lincoln compare him to?
answer: A Russian bear
choices: A Russian bear
A bull moose
A timber wolf
A wild stallion
context: After the grueling bout, Lincoln won the rough crowd's respect and Jack Armstrong's lifelong friendship. In 1992 Lincoln was posthumously inducted into the National Wrestling Hall of Fame in Stillwater, Oklahoma. Source: Mr. Lincoln and Friends, 'Jack Armstrong'; CBC Radio, Under the Influence.  (Legend.)

question: Mechanical puzzles fascinated Abraham Lincoln, a lawyer on the Illinois frontier, and in 1849 he won Patent No. 6,469 for an invention of his own. He remains the only U.S. president ever to hold a patent. What was the invention designed to do?
answer: Lift a boat up and over shallow river shoals
choices: Lift a boat up and over shallow river shoals
Pump rising water out of a leaking hull
Guide a boat through rocky rapids after dark
Warn nearby boats during thick river fog
context: Lincoln dreamed up a system of inflatable bellows to buoy vessels over shoals after his own boats kept getting hung up on river obstructions. No president before or since has held a patent. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Abraham Lincoln Is the Only President Ever to Have a Patent'; Google Patents US6469A.

question: A witness at an 1858 murder trial swore he had clearly seen the young defendant commit the killing by bright moonlight. Abraham Lincoln, defending the young man, set out to prove the night had been too dark for any such sighting, and he pulled out one ordinary book and read from it. What book won the acquittal?
answer: An almanac
choices: An almanac
A family Bible
A railroad timetable
A county surveyor's map
context: The almanac showed the moon was low and gave almost no light that night, shredding the witness's story. The young defendant was Duff Armstrong, son of the wrestler Jack Armstrong — Lincoln was repaying the family that had sheltered him as a poor young man. Source: Mr. Lincoln and Friends, 'Jack Armstrong'.

question: Stephen Douglas kept his Illinois Senate seat in 1858 after seven famous three-hour debates with Abraham Lincoln, when the state legislature re-elected him. Yet that defeat helped carry Lincoln to the presidency. What did Lincoln do with the seven debates that turned his loss into national fame?
answer: He edited and published them as a popular book
choices: He edited and published them as a popular book
He reprinted them as newspaper ads across the South
He delivered them again as a two-year stump speech
He submitted them to Congress as a formal petition
context: The published debates made Lincoln a national antislavery figure and helped him win the 1860 Republican presidential nomination. Stephen Douglas had won the seat 54-46 in the legislature — but Lincoln won the bigger prize. Source: Britannica, 'Lincoln-Douglas debates'; Wikipedia (citing Allen Guelzo).

question: Abraham Lincoln was a little-known frontier lawyer from Illinois when he rose to speak at the Cooper Union hall in New York on the cold night of February 27, 1860. In a speech of over 7,000 words he argued against letting slavery spread into the western territories, quoting the Founding Fathers one after another. Many say the speech made him president that November. Which ringing line closed it?
answer: Let us have faith that right makes might
choices: Let us have faith that right makes might
A house divided against itself cannot stand
Government of the people, by the people, for the people
Let us strive on to finish the work we are in
context: Lincoln's full closing: 'LET US HAVE FAITH THAT RIGHT MAKES MIGHT, AND IN THAT FAITH, LET US, TO THE END, DARE TO DO OUR DUTY AS WE UNDERSTAND IT.' Source: Abraham Lincoln Online, 'Cooper Union Address'; Wikipedia, 'Cooper Union speech'.

question: Victory in the Civil War was near when Abraham Lincoln delivered his Second Inaugural Address on March 4, 1865, only weeks before his assassination. He did not gloat over the South's coming defeat. Instead he spoke a line now carved inside the Lincoln Memorial. What words lie at the heart of that speech?
answer: With malice toward none, with charity for all
choices: With malice toward none, with charity for all
Four score and seven years ago
A house divided against itself cannot stand
Government of the people, by the people, for the people
context: Lincoln went on: '...let us strive on to finish the work we are in, to bind up the nation's wounds ... to do all which may achieve and cherish a just and lasting peace.' He chose reconciliation over vengeance. Source: Avalon Project (Yale), 'Second Inaugural Address of Abraham Lincoln'; Miller Center.

question: A lone untrained worker, Adam Smith wrote in The Wealth of Nations, could barely make a single pin in a day. Ten workers who split the job into about eighteen steps did far better. How many pins could the ten make in a day?
answer: Upwards of 48,000 pins
choices: Upwards of 48,000 pins
Around 500 pins
Roughly 2,000 pins
Close to 10,000 pins
context: From barely one pin per man to 48,000 among ten — Smith's pin factory is his proof of the division of labour: split a job into specialized steps and output explodes. (The Wealth of Nations, Book I, Ch. 1, 1776; adamsmithworks.org/documents/chapter-1-of-the-division-of-labour)

question: The butcher, the brewer and the baker put dinner on a great city's tables every morning, and Adam Smith asked how that happened. Not out of kindness, he wrote in his 1776 book, The Wealth of Nations. What, according to Smith, did they care about?
answer: Their own self-interest
choices: Their own self-interest
Their sense of duty
Their good reputation
The wishes of the king
context: 'It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.' The seed of the whole book: self-interest, not charity, coordinates a market. (The Wealth of Nations, Book I, Ch. 2, 1776; oll.libertyfund.org/quotes/adam-smith-butcher-brewer-baker)

question: Someone snatched Adam Smith when he was about four years old, playing near his home in the seaside town of Kirkcaldy in Scotland. His uncle gathered a posse and gave chase, and the kidnappers dropped the boy and fled. Who had grabbed the future 'father of economics'?
answer: A band of passing gypsies
choices: A band of passing gypsies
A crew of coastal smugglers
A naval press-gang
A troop of king's soldiers
context: His biographer John Rae quipped of the rescued child: 'He would have made, I fear, a poor gipsy.' (britannica.com/biography/Adam-Smith)

question: Lost in conversation at breakfast one morning, the famously absent-minded Adam Smith rolled something up without thinking, dropped it into his teapot and brewed it. He tasted a cup and called it 'the worst tea he had ever met with.' What had he brewed?
answer: Bread and butter
choices: Bread and butter
A wad of letters
His pipe tobacco
A spoonful of jam
context: The great economist, deep in thought, brewed his breakfast bread and butter into a pot of tea. (encyclopaediaoftrivia.blogspot.com/2018/02/adam-smith.html)

question: Plain and unfashionable in almost every way, Adam Smith never married and lived most of his adult life quietly with his mother in the little Scottish town of Kirkcaldy. He allowed himself one indulgence. Of it he liked to joke, 'I am a beau in nothing but my' what?
answer: Books
choices: Books
Manners
Letters
Garden
context: A 'beau' was a dandy obsessed with fashion; Smith was a dandy only about his books — and he owned the finest private library in Edinburgh. (panmurehouse.org/adam-smith/biography/later-years-1778-1790)

question: A merchant who chased nothing but his own profit, Adam Smith wrote, was led by an invisible hand to help the whole society without meaning to. The phrase became the most famous in economics, and The Wealth of Nations filled roughly a thousand pages of tightly argued print. How many times did Smith use the words 'invisible hand' in all those pages?
answer: Just once
choices: Just once
A dozen times
Dozens of times
Hundreds of times
context: It appears one time, in Book IV, Ch. 2: a merchant 'intends only his own gain, and he is in this... led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention.' The most famous metaphor in the field was almost a throwaway line. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wealth_of_Nations)

question: A London printer brought out Adam Smith's enormous book, The Wealth of Nations, in March 1776. It explained how free trade, the division of labour and ordinary self-interest could quietly build a nation's prosperity, and it sold out in only six months. That same year, across the Atlantic in Philadelphia, another famous paper was signed. Which one?
answer: The American Declaration of Independence
choices: The American Declaration of Independence
The French Declaration of the Rights of Man
The English Bill of Rights
The Treaty of Paris
context: 1776: the founding text of the free market and the founding text of American liberty, in the same year. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wealth_of_Nations)

question: Out of curiosity, Adam Smith checked the government's list of banned foreign goods against his own wardrobe after he took a well-paid job as a Commissioner of Customs in Edinburgh in 1778. He was a fierce critic of trade barriers, and nearly every scarf and handkerchief he owned turned out to be illegal to wear in Britain. What did he decide to do?
answer: Burn them all to set an example
choices: Burn them all to set an example
Quietly keep wearing them
Give them to his servants
Petition Parliament to change the law
context: 'I wished to set an example and burnt them all.' (Letter to William Eden, 3 Jan 1780; fee.org/articles/why-adam-smith-burned-his-clothes)

question: Long before he wrote a word about economics, Adam Smith taught moral philosophy. His first book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, came out in 1759. In it he argued that a person judges his own behaviour by imagining how a calm, disinterested stranger would see it. What did Smith call this inner judge?
answer: The impartial spectator
choices: The impartial spectator
The hidden conscience
The silent witness
The inner sovereign
context: From the same author: free markets AND virtue. Smith held that markets rest on 'sympathy' and on this 'impartial spectator' — we check our conduct against how a fair-minded stranger would judge it. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Moral_Sentiments)

question: Dying in Edinburgh in July 1790, Adam Smith called in his two friends Joseph Black and James Hutton and gave them one strange last order, to be carried out in front of him. They fed sixteen volumes into the fire and destroyed them forever. What did Smith make them burn?
answer: His unpublished manuscripts
choices: His unpublished manuscripts
His personal letters
His entire library
His handwritten will
context: Sixteen volumes of unpublished writing, thought to include a history of law and government and a study of literature, destroyed days before he died on 17 July 1790. He is buried in Canongate Kirkyard. (maxwell.syr.edu/research/article/adam-smith-and-the-death-of-david-hume)

question: Adam Smith never set foot inside a pin factory, yet he opened The Wealth of Nations with one, to explain what he called the division of labour: a job split into small steps, each done by a different worker. That pin factory became the first great picture of modern industry. Where did Smith really get his example?
answer: From a description in Diderot's French Encyclopedie
choices: From a description in Diderot's French Encyclopedie
From a Scottish pin-makers' guild pamphlet
From a traveler's letter he received
From figures in a Glasgow newspaper article
context: The founder of the study of industry built his founding example from a book, not a factory floor. (panmurehouse.org/perspectives/articles/adam-smith-and-the-pin-factory)

question: David Hume lay dying, cheerful and openly unbelieving, and joked that he could find no good excuse to give Charon, the ferryman of the dead: no house left to finish, no daughter to provide for, no enemy left to crush. He was Adam Smith's closest friend. After Hume died, Smith did something that scandalized all of Britain. What was it?
answer: He published a public letter praising Hume's serene, godless death
choices: He published a public letter praising Hume's serene, godless death
He destroyed Hume's final manuscripts unread
He refused to attend the funeral
He recanted his friendship in print
context: Smith's open letter to William Strahan described his unbelieving friend dying calm and content — and pious Britain was outraged that he praised it. (econlib.org/book-chapters/chapter-letter-from-adam-smith-l-l-d-to-william-strahan-esq)

question: Italian soldiers held a fort at Mekelle in northern Ethiopia in January 1896 when Empress Taytu Betul sent about 900 men against them. Her men did not storm the walls; they took the one thing the fort could not live without, and days later the Italian commander gave up. What did they cut off?
answer: The garrison's water supply
choices: The garrison's water supply
The fort's main gunpowder store
The road carrying their food
The bridge behind the fort
context: At the Siege of Mekelle, Empress Taytu Betul ordered her contingent (about 900 men) to capture and cut off the Italians' water supply at the Enda Yesus fort. With his men dying of thirst, Major Galliano surrendered on 19 January 1896. Taytu went on to fight at Adwa weeks later. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Mekelle and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taytu_Betul

question: Menelik II, emperor of Ethiopia, signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy in 1889 as a pact between equals. Then Italy announced to the courts of Europe that Ethiopia had become its protectorate, and that Menelik must route all his foreign dealings through Rome. Menelik, who had agreed to no such thing, rejected the treaty, and war followed. What turned out to be the whole basis of Italy's claim?
answer: A single mistranslated verb in one article
choices: A single mistranslated verb in one article
A secret clause hidden from Menelik
A forged signature on the Italian copy
A map drawn with the wrong borders
context: Article 17 of the 1889 Treaty of Wuchale differed by one verb: Amharic 'can use' (optional) versus Italian 'must' route all foreign affairs through Italy (a protectorate). Menelik II denounced the treaty, and the dispute led to the war that ended at the Battle of Adwa in 1896. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Wuchale

question: In one of Aesop's fables, a speedy runner challenges a plodding rival to a race. The fast one, sure of winning, stops for a long nap partway through, and his rival plods steadily past him to the finish line. What is the fable called?
answer: The Tortoise and the Hare
choices: The Tortoise and the Hare
The Fox and the Stork
The Dog and the Bone
The Wolf and the Crane
context: The fable gave English the proverb 'Slow and steady wins the race.' Source: americanliterature.com/author/aesop/short-story/the-tortoise-and-the-hare.

question: A mighty lion pins a tiny mouse under his paw in one of Aesop's fables, but he spares the mouse rather than crush him. Some days later the lion is caught in a hunter's net and cannot break free, however he roars and strains. How does the little mouse repay the lion's mercy?
answer: He gnaws through the ropes with his teeth
choices: He gnaws through the ropes with his teeth
He frightens the hunters away
He fetches the other animals for help
He chews a hole in the hunter's sack
context: The fable's moral: no one is too small to be useful, and a kindness is repaid. Source: americanliterature.com/author/aesop/short-story/the-lion-and-the-mouse.

question: A thirsty crow finds water sitting at the bottom of a tall clay pitcher, too low for its beak to reach, in Aesop's fable 'The Crow and the Pitcher.' The heavy pitcher will not tip over, however hard the bird pushes. How does the clever crow raise the water high enough to drink?
answer: It drops pebbles in one by one
choices: It drops pebbles in one by one
It pecks a hole in the pitcher's side
It tips the pitcher onto its side
It calls other crows to lift it
context: The moral is 'Necessity is the mother of invention.' Cambridge researchers later showed real rooks can solve this exact puzzle. Source: americanliterature.com/author/aesop/short-story/the-crow-and-the-pitcher; cam.ac.uk/news/aesops-fable-the-crow-and-the-pitcher-more-fact-than-fiction.

question: Portuguese traders bought what they wanted in the kingdom of Benin, in present-day southern Nigeria, with manillas: horseshoe-shaped bracelets used as money. The kingdom's Edo metalworkers never mined the metal for their famous bronzes. What did they do with all that European money?
answer: Melted it down and recast it into the plaques
choices: Melted it down and recast it into the plaques
Traded it onward to inland kingdoms for gold
Buried it under the palace as a royal treasury
Hammered it flat into coins stamped with the Oba
context: The brass manillas have been traced to the Rhineland in Germany. The Edo melted European money and recast it into images of their own kings and court — a striking reversal of who was using whom. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benin_Bronzes

question: Oba Esigie of Benin wore a small ivory mask at his hip for ceremonies. Carved early in the 1500s, it showed the face of his mother, Queen Mother Iyoba Idia, beneath a carved crown. What tiny figures circled that crown?
answer: A row of tiny Portuguese heads
choices: A row of tiny Portuguese heads
A row of tiny leopards, the royal beast
A row of tiny coral beads of office
A row of tiny mudfish, sign of the Oba
context: Nigeria chose this mask of Iyoba Idia as the official emblem of FESTAC '77, the great Black-and-African arts festival held in Lagos. The ring of carved Portuguese heads marks the bearded foreigners who had just arrived by sea. Source: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/318622

question: Under Kwame Nkrumah, the Gold Coast broke free of Britain in 1957, the first land in sub-Saharan Africa to throw off European rule after the Second World War. Nkrumah dropped the colonial name for one borrowed from a medieval African empire. What did he call it?
answer: Ghana
choices: Ghana
Liberia
Nigeria
Mali
context: On 6 March 1957 the Gold Coast became independent and took the name Ghana, the first sub-Saharan African nation to throw off European colonial rule. Source: https://sahistory.org.za/place/ghana

question: Kwame Nkrumah refused to keep the name Gold Coast when his country won its freedom in 1957. It only marked a coast where Europeans bought slaves and metal, so he named the new nation after an old West African empire instead. What was that empire famous for?
answer: Arab traders called it 'the land of gold'
choices: Arab traders called it 'the land of gold'
It built the great mud mosque at Djenne
It crowned the richest pilgrim ever to cross to Mecca
It carved giant stone heads in the jungle
context: Nkrumah named the country after the ancient Ghana Empire, a powerful medieval West African kingdom that sat astride the trans-Saharan gold trade. Arab writers from the 9th century called it 'the land of gold,' and the word 'Ghana' itself was tied to gold and kingship. Choosing it broke from 'Gold Coast,' which only named the trading shore. Source: https://www.ghanaweb.com/GhanaHomePage/NewsArchive/How-Ghana-Got-its-Name-The-history-and-meaning-behind-it-1974653; ushistory.org/civ/7a.asp

question: White caps marked 'P.G.' sat on the heads of Kwame Nkrumah and his ministers at their country's independence ceremony in 1957. The men had paid a hard price in the struggle against British rule, and they wore the letters as a badge of pride. What did 'P.G.' stand for?
answer: Prison Graduates
choices: Prison Graduates
Provisional Government
People of Ghana
Proud Gold Coast
context: Nkrumah and ministers Kojo Botsio, Komla Gbedemah, Archie Casely Hayford, and Krobo Edusei wore caps marked 'PG' for 'Prison Graduates,' a proud title because the British had jailed them in the freedom struggle. Source: https://indepthnews.net/nkrumah-s-prison-cap-left-an-indelible-memory-with-mlk/

question: Half a million people heard Kwame Nkrumah declare his country free at midnight on 6 March 1957. He did not stop at his own nation. He told the roaring crowd that its freedom was meaningless on its own, and he named the one thing it had to be linked with. What did Nkrumah say independence had to be tied to?
answer: the total liberation of all Africa
choices: the total liberation of all Africa
the unity of all Africa under one government
driving every European power off the continent
the building of a single pan-African army
context: Nkrumah declared, 'Our independence is meaningless unless it is linked up with the total liberation of Africa' — he saw Ghana's freedom as the first step toward freeing the whole continent. Source: https://panafricanquotes.wordpress.com/speeches/independence-speech-kwame-nkrumah-march-6-1957-accra-ghana/

question: Unarmed Second World War veterans of the Gold Coast Regiment marched on Christiansborg Castle in Accra in February 1948. They had come to ask the British governor for the war pay they were owed. The British police chief met them at the castle. What did he do?
answer: ordered his men to open fire, killing three veterans
choices: ordered his men to open fire, killing three veterans
had the marchers' leaders arrested on the spot
ordered the heavy castle gates barred against them
sent the veterans home with a written promise
context: The police chief opened fire, killing Sergeant Cornelius Adjetey, Corporal Attipoe, and Private Odartey Lamptey, which triggered the Accra riots that set Ghana on the road to independence. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Accra_riots

question: Seventeen African nations won their freedom in one stunning year, most of them former French colonies, and together they joined the United Nations, giving the continent a much bigger voice at the world's table. Nkrumah's country had led the way in 1957. What is 1960 remembered as?
answer: the Year of Africa
choices: the Year of Africa
the Year of Empire
the Year of the Colonies
the Year of the United Nations
context: In 1960, seventeen African nations won independence (14 from France, 2 from Britain, 1 — Congo — from Belgium), and the year is remembered as the 'Year of Africa.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_Africa

question: Harold Macmillan, Britain's prime minister, spoke to South Africa's all-white parliament in Cape Town in February 1960. He was the first major Western leader to tell the apartheid government to its face that African self-rule could no longer be stopped. He pictured it as an unstoppable force sweeping the continent. What phrase did he use?
answer: the wind of change
choices: the wind of change
the tide of empire
the dawn of nations
the storm of freedom
context: Macmillan told South Africa's parliament that 'the wind of change is blowing through this continent,' the first time a senior Western leader openly told the apartheid government that African self-rule was unstoppable. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_of_Change_(speech)

question: Adolf Hitler sent German troops back into the Rhineland, the strip of German land along the French border, on March 7, 1936. The Treaty of Versailles allowed no soldiers or forts there, and his force was tiny next to France's huge army. So he gave his commanders one secret order in case the French tried to stop them. What was it?
answer: Turn around and retreat back across the Rhine
choices: Turn around and retreat back across the Rhine
Blow up the bridges behind them and hold
Surrender their weapons to the French at once
Dig in at the cathedral and fight to the end
context: Hitler deliberately picked a weekend, betting Britain's leaders would be off in the country and slow to react. His Rhineland force was only about 19 army battalions against a French army that could field roughly 100 divisions, so the commanders carried written orders to turn around and run if the French resisted. France, worried about money and an election and unwilling to act without Britain, never marched, and the remilitarization stood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remilitarisation_of_the_Rhineland

question: Adwa was the first prize Benito Mussolini made sure to take when his army invaded Ethiopia in 1935. There, in 1896, an Ethiopian army had crushed an Italian force, and Italy had burned over that loss for forty years. What made the defeat at Adwa so special?
answer: An African army had destroyed a European colonial force and forced Italy to recognize Ethiopia's independence
choices: An African army had destroyed a European colonial force and forced Italy to recognize Ethiopia's independence
It was the bloodiest single day in the whole history of the Italian army
The Italian king himself had been captured on the field
Italy had lost its entire navy in the same week
context: At the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896, Emperor Menelik II's army crushed an invading Italian force, the first time in the colonial era an African power decisively defeated a European one; by the Treaty of Addis Ababa, Italy abandoned its claim to Ethiopia. So when General Emilio De Bono's troops took Adwa on 6 October 1935, it was deliberate symbolic revenge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Italo-Ethiopian_War; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Adwa

question: German tanks rolled across the border into Austria on March 12, 1938, into the land where Adolf Hitler had been born and where many people spoke German. Hitler would soon proclaim the Anschluss, Austria's union with Germany. What met the soldiers in the Austrian towns?
answer: Cheering crowds throwing flowers
choices: Cheering crowds throwing flowers
Silent streets with shutters drawn
Stones and jeers from angry mobs
Church bells rung in mourning
context: The troops crossed around 5 a.m. and met no shots, only 'cheers and flowers.' Hitler rode in triumph first to his old hometown of Linz and then to Vienna, where he proclaimed Austria part of the German Reich to a roaring crowd at the Heldenplatz. Austria's chancellor Kurt von Schuschnigg had resigned on the radio the night before and told the army not to resist. Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/nazi-territorial-aggression-the-anschluss

question: Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia rose to speak to the League of Nations in Geneva on June 30, 1936, the first head of state ever to address it in person. He had come to accuse Italy of taking his country with poison gas. Italian reporters packed the gallery. What did they do as he rose?
answer: Whistled and jeered until guards threw them out
choices: Whistled and jeered until guards threw them out
Stood and saluted him with their arms raised
Walked out of the hall in a planned protest
Pelted the emperor with crumpled paper notes
context: The Italian journalists whistled and jeered at Haile Selassie until they were thrown out of the hall, and he then delivered his speech in his own language, Amharic. He warned the delegates that abandoning Ethiopia threatened everyone, saying 'It is international morality that is at stake,' and ended by asking 'What reply shall I have to take back to my people?' and telling them 'God and history will remember your judgment.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Selassie's_speech_to_the_League_of_Nations_(1936)

question: Paul Schmidt, Adolf Hitler's interpreter, heard him confess how close a call the Rhineland had been in March 1936. France could have fielded about a hundred divisions against his handful of battalions, but it never marched. Hitler called those first two days the most nerve-racking of his life. How did he say it would have ended if the French had marched in?
answer: Germany would have had to withdraw with its tail between its legs
choices: Germany would have had to withdraw with its tail between its legs
Germany would have crushed the French in a single day
The German people would have risen up and overthrown him
Britain would have rushed in to fight beside the Germans
context: Recorded by his interpreter Paul Schmidt, Hitler said: 'The forty-eight hours after the march into the Rhineland were the most nerve-racking in my life. If the French had then marched into the Rhineland we would have had to withdraw with our tails between our legs, for the military resources at our disposal would have been wholly inadequate for even a moderate resistance.' It was the last moment he could have been stopped cheaply. Source: Paul Schmidt, in Zachary Shore, 'What Hitler Knew'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remilitarisation_of_the_Rhineland

question: Nazis and mocking crowds turned on Vienna's Jews in the open street within days of the Anschluss in March 1938. A rigged vote soon claimed that 99 percent of Austrians approved the union, yet hundreds of thousands of people, including Jews and Roma, had been forbidden to vote at all. What did the Nazis and the crowds force Vienna's Jews to do?
answer: Scrub the pavements on their hands and knees
choices: Scrub the pavements on their hands and knees
March out of the city carrying white flags
Hand over their house keys at the town hall
Wear painted signs around their own necks
context: In Vienna's 'scrubbing parties,' Jews were dragged into the streets and forced on their knees to scrub the pavement while crowds mocked them. Hitler's April 10, 1938 vote reported about 99 percent approval for the union, but between 300,000 and 400,000 Austrians had been barred from voting at all. The Rhineland bluff (1936), the conquest of Ethiopia (1935-36), and the Anschluss (1938) formed a step-by-step slide the League ignored, each unpunished move making the next easier; six months later came the Munich crisis over Czechoslovakia. Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/nazi-territorial-aggression-the-anschluss

question: A brilliant musician arrived in Cordoba, in Muslim Spain, from Baghdad around 822. People called him 'the Blackbird' for his dark skin and beautiful voice. He changed how the city ate, dressed and made music, and he added a fifth string to the lute, which later grew into the guitar. What was his name?
answer: Ziryab
choices: Ziryab
Hasdai
Maimonides
Al-Hakam
context: Ziryab ('the Blackbird') reached Cordoba around 822 and transformed daily life: he added a fifth string to the lute, traded the wooden plectrum for an eagle's quill, introduced an early toothpaste, and invented the idea of changing clothing by season. Source: muslimheritage.com/ziryab-the-musician/ ; spainthenandnow.com/spanish-culture/spanish-food-ziryab-789-857

question: Cordoba, the capital of Muslim Spain, was a city where a person could walk safely for miles after dark in the 900s, chroniclers said, while by night most of northern Europe fell into pitch darkness. What did its main streets have that made this possible?
answer: Rows of oil lamps lining the streets
choices: Rows of oil lamps lining the streets
Guards posted at every corner
Bonfires burned in open squares
Painted markers along the walls
context: Chroniclers said the lamps were fixed to the outer doors and corners of houses, so a person could reportedly walk for miles by lamplight. Routine municipal street lighting did not reach many European cities until centuries later. Source: muslimheritage.com/cordoba-jewel-middle-ages/ ; sloughislamictrust.org.uk/dictionary/meaning/cordoba-street-lighting-history/

question: Caliph Al-Hakam II of Cordoba sent agents to Baghdad, Cairo, and Constantinople to buy rare books. His royal library grew so huge that the biggest Christian libraries in Europe held only hundreds of books next to it. Just the list of his library's titles was so long that it filled how much on its own?
answer: A catalogue of 44 volumes
choices: A catalogue of 44 volumes
A single bound ledger
A scroll one hundred feet long
A small shelf of notebooks
context: The catalogue of titles alone was said to fill 44 volumes; accounts claim the library itself held on the order of 400,000 books (some say 600,000). Cordoba became the greatest book market in the western world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Hakam_II

question: Lubna of Cordoba started life as an enslaved girl who copied books in the royal library. She knew Latin, Greek and Hebrew and was trained in math, and her skill with books changed her future. She was freed and rose to a high post. What position did she hold at the caliph's side?
answer: The caliph's personal secretary
choices: The caliph's personal secretary
The caliph's master of horses
The caliph's chief physician
The caliph's royal taster
context: Lubna of Cordoba rose from enslaved copyist to Al-Hakam II's personal secretary. Chronicles say more than 170 female scribes were copying manuscripts in Cordoba alone during this period. Source: muslimheritage.com/people/scholars/labana-of-cordoba/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Hakam_II

question: Al-Maqqari, the chronicler, wrote of a domed hall at the palace of Madinat al-Zahra with a basin at its centre. Servants would stir it to amaze guests, and it sent bright flashes of sunlight rippling across the room. Diggers have never found the basin, so the tale rests on the writer alone. What did he say it held?
answer: A pool of liquid mercury
choices: A pool of liquid mercury
A fountain of perfumed wine
A ring of polished gold mirrors
A basin of floating candles
context: Al-Maqqari described a pool of liquid mercury (quicksilver); stirred, the sunlight rippling off it flooded the room with flashing light. No archaeologist has located the basin, so the detail rests on his chronicle alone. Told here as legend, not forensic fact. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madinat_al-Zahra

question: Three faiths shared the streets of Cordoba under its Muslim rulers, a coexistence historians call the convivencia. They describe it as real but unequal, because its Christians and Jews were dhimmis, with a protected but lesser legal status. What, according to these historians, did that status most concretely require of them?
answer: Paying a special tax called the jizya
choices: Paying a special tax called the jizya
Wearing only the color black in public
Leaving the city walls each night
Surrendering one child to the court
context: Historians describe convivencia as real but limited: as dhimmis, Christians and Jews paid the jizya tax and could not hold the highest offices, build new churches, bear arms, or testify against a Muslim. The coexistence also broke down violently at times. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convivencia ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1066_Granada_massacre

question: Albrecht Durer made a rhinoceros woodcut in 1515, though he had never seen one; he worked only from a letter and a rough sketch sent from Lisbon. His picture stood as Europe's idea of the rhino for more than 200 years. What did he give his rhino that no real one has?
answer: Riveted plates of armor and an invented second horn
choices: Riveted plates of armor and an invented second horn
A long mane and cloven hooves like a horse
Folded leathery wings along its back
A coiled trunk and a pair of curved tusks
context: Working blind from a letter, Durer covered the beast in riveted plate armor with a gorget at the throat and scaly legs, and added a small twisted second horn on its shoulder. The print was accepted across Europe as the 'accurate' rhino until the late 18th century, when the living rhino Clara toured Europe in the 1740s-50s and finally showed people what one really looked like. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCrer's_Rhinoceros

question: Facing straight out at the viewer, with long hair and one hand raised near his chest, Albrecht Durer painted himself in 1500. Painters kept that head-on, matching-sides pose almost only for one kind of holy image. Who was Durer making himself look like, on purpose?
answer: Christ, the divine Creator
choices: Christ, the divine Creator
A Roman emperor on a coin
A saint shown with his halo
A king enthroned in his crown
context: The frontal, symmetric pose was almost exclusively used for images of Christ, so Durer composed his self-portrait to look like the divine Creator — a bold statement about the artist as a maker in his own right. He even signed it 'Albertus Durerus Noricus... at the age of 28,' placing the year 1500 above his 'A.D.' monogram so the initials also read 'Anno Domini.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-Portrait_(D%C3%BCrer,_Munich)

question: As a boy in Scotland, Alexander Graham Bell tried an experiment on the family dog. His father studied how mouths and throats shape speech. While the dog held a low growl, young Alec shaped its mouth and throat by hand. What did the dog seem to do?
answer: Say the words "How are you, grandmama?"
choices: Say the words "How are you, grandmama?"
Howl along to a tune he hummed
Fetch a ball without being told
Bark exactly ten times on command
context: Bell manipulated the dog's mouth and throat while it growled, shaping the growl into recognizable speech-like sounds. This early fascination with how voices are made ran straight through his life's work. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Graham_Bell

question: Alexander Graham Bell was working late in his Boston workshop on 10 March 1876. He spoke into his new machine's mouthpiece, and in the next room, at the far end of a wire, his assistant heard every word. What were the first words ever sent by telephone?
answer: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."
choices: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."
"Watson, the wire is working at last."
"Can you hear me on the other side?"
"Come quickly, the experiment is done."
context: The assistant was Thomas Watson. He heard the words clearly in the next room and wrote them down in his notebook (now in the Library of Congress Bell Papers). A popular story says Bell had just spilled acid on himself, but that is a myth: no spilled acid appears in Bell's lab notes, his letter to his father that night, or Watson's own notes. Sources: https://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/ahoy-alexander-graham-bell-and-first-telephone-call; https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/march-10/speech-transmitted-by-telephone

question: Dom Pedro II, the emperor of Brazil, pressed Alexander Graham Bell's receiver to his ear at the great Philadelphia fair of 1876. Far across the hall, Bell spoke into the wire to prove it could carry a human voice. Which famous lines did he choose to say?
answer: "To be, or not to be — that is the question"
choices: "To be, or not to be — that is the question"
"Mary had a little lamb"
"We hold these truths to be self-evident"
"Now is the winter of our discontent"
context: Bell recited Hamlet's soliloquy into the transmitter; judge William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) testified he heard the faint words 'to be or not to be' and 'there's the rub.' The 'My God, it talks!' line often pinned on Dom Pedro is only 'so legend has it.' Source: antiquetelephonehistory.com, 'Bell's Centennial Transmitter Telephone' (Kelvin's testimony); infostory.com, 'My God, it Talks!'

question: Alexander Graham Bell wanted everyone who picked up his strange new telephone to start with a bold sailor's cry: 'Ahoy.' A rival inventor working on a telephone of his own pushed a different greeting, and that word stuck for good. Which greeting beat 'Ahoy,' and who pushed it?
answer: "Hello," pushed by Thomas Edison
choices: "Hello," pushed by Thomas Edison
"Greetings," pushed by Elisha Gray
"Speak," pushed by Thomas Watson
"Yes," pushed by Mabel Hubbard
context: Bell's preferred "Ahoy" lost out to Thomas Edison's "Hello," which is why we still answer the phone that way today. Source: https://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/ahoy-alexander-graham-bell-and-first-telephone-call

question: Elisha Gray, a rival inventor, reached the U.S. Patent Office on 14 February 1876, the very same day as Alexander Graham Bell. It was nearly a dead heat, yet Bell walked away with the telephone patent, No. 174,465, issued on 7 March. Why did Bell's claim win out over Gray's?
answer: Gray filed only a preliminary notice while Bell filed a full application
choices: Gray filed only a preliminary notice while Bell filed a full application
Gray arrived a full week after Bell had already filed
Gray's drawings were rejected as too incomplete to judge
Gray withdrew his claim before the office could rule
context: Gray filed a caveat — a preliminary notice of intent — while Bell filed a complete patent application the same day, February 14, 1876. That difference is why Bell's name is on the telephone. The priority race is part of the honest record. Source: https://www.ericsson.com/en/about-us/history/communication/early-developments/bell-gray-and-the-invention-of-the-telephone

question: A penniless orphan from the Caribbean island of Nevis reached New York in his teens with nothing and grew up to design America's whole system of money and credit. His face is on circulating U.S. money today, and apart from Benjamin Franklin he is the only man there who was never president. Which founder is he?
answer: Alexander Hamilton
choices: Alexander Hamilton
Thomas Jefferson
Patrick Henry
Samuel Adams
context: Hamilton is on the modern ten-dollar bill — one of only two non-presidents (with Franklin) on circulating American money, and the only one born outside what is now the United States. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_ten-dollar_bill

question: Alexander Hamilton was a poor teenager on St. Croix, with no money and no way off the island, when a huge hurricane tore it apart in August 1772. What he did after the storm so amazed the local leaders that they took up a collection to send him to school in North America. What did he do?
answer: He wrote a vivid published account of the hurricane
choices: He wrote a vivid published account of the hurricane
He rebuilt the harbor warehouses by hand
He led survivors to shelter through the floodwaters
He nursed the injured back to health for weeks
context: After the August 31, 1772 hurricane, the teenage Hamilton's published essay about the storm so impressed local leaders that they paid his passage to North America — the essay that launched his American life. https://storyoftheweek.loa.org/2017/09/account-of-hurricane.html

question: Alexander Hamilton, the first Treasury Secretary, wanted the federal government to shoulder the war debts the states had run up in the Revolution. Virginia and the other Southern states, which had mostly paid their own, blocked him in Congress. Over a private dinner Jefferson hosted in June 1790, Hamilton and Madison struck a deal. In exchange for letting the debt plan pass, what did the South win?
answer: The permanent national capital, built on the Potomac
choices: The permanent national capital, built on the Potomac
A repeal of all federal taxes on tobacco
Control of the new national bank's headquarters
A guarantee that slavery could never be taxed
context: The 'dinner table bargain' of 20 June 1790, the Compromise of 1790: Madison let Hamilton's debt-assumption plan pass, and in return the permanent capital was placed on the Potomac River, which is why Washington, D.C. sits where it does. Jefferson later wrote that assumption was 'a bitter pill' for the South, so moving the seat of government there 'was a just measure.' Sources: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/compromise-1790; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compromise_of_1790

question: Alexander Hamilton faced his opponent across a rocky ledge at Weehawken, New Jersey, on 11 July 1804, for a duel with pistols. The ball that hit him ripped through his liver and stuck in his spine; he died the next day. What made the killing so shocking was the office the man who fired held at that very moment. Who fired the shot?
answer: Aaron Burr, the sitting Vice President
choices: Aaron Burr, the sitting Vice President
John Adams, the former president
James Madison, the Secretary of State
Thomas Jefferson, the sitting President
context: Hamilton was killed by sitting Vice President Aaron Burr, whose career Hamilton had helped wreck — costing Burr the 1800 presidency and the 1804 New York governorship. Burr's ball tore through Hamilton's liver and lodged in his spine. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burr%E2%80%93Hamilton_duel

question: Thomas Jefferson called the national bank Alexander Hamilton wanted plainly unconstitutional. The Constitution listed the government's powers, he argued; those powers 'can all be carried into execution without a bank,' and the Tenth Amendment kept the rest for the states. Hamilton's reply won Washington over and still shapes how the Constitution is read. What was his core argument?
answer: The Constitution grants implied powers, so the Necessary-and-Proper Clause lets Congress charter a bank
choices: The Constitution grants implied powers, so the Necessary-and-Proper Clause lets Congress charter a bank
A wartime emergency let the president act without Congress
The states had already surrendered all money powers to Congress
Any law a majority of Congress passes is automatically constitutional
context: This is the 'loose construction' doctrine: Hamilton argued the Constitution carries 'implied, as well as express powers,' so a bank was a reasonable means to a legitimate end. Washington sided with him on February 23, 1791. Jefferson's 'strict construction' held 'necessary' meant indispensable. https://billofrightsinstitute.org/essays/alexander-hamilton-and-the-national-bank/

question: Alexander the Great, still a boy, watched his father King Philip's big black horse buck and rear at every rider. Alexander noticed that the horse was scared of its own moving shadow. What clever thing did he do to calm it before climbing on?
answer: Turned it to face the sun
choices: Turned it to face the sun
Blindfolded it with his cloak
Sang to it until it grew still
Fed it apples from his hand
context: Alexander turned the stallion to face the sun so it could no longer see the shadow that frightened it, then quietly mounted and rode it. He named the horse Bucephalus — 'ox-head' — for a white mark on its brow, and rode it for decades. Source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander (via Livius.org); World History Encyclopedia 'Bucephalus'.

question: A Persian noble's blade split Alexander the Great's helmet and cut his head beside the Granicus River in 334 BC, in his first big battle against Persia. As the young king swayed, another Persian raised a sword to strike him from behind. What saved Alexander's life at that instant?
answer: Cleitus the Black sliced off the man's arm
choices: Cleitus the Black sliced off the man's arm
His bodyguards locked shields around him
Bucephalus reared and trampled the attacker
He twisted aside and the blow missed
context: Alexander's officer Cleitus 'the Black' sheared off the attacker's arm — sword and all — with a single stroke, saving the king's life. Alexander was only about 22. Source: History Hit '334 BC Battle of Granicus'; World History Encyclopedia 'Battle of the Granicus'.

question: Porus, a king in India, faced Alexander the Great at the Hydaspes River in 326 BC with a terrifying line of war elephants, and lost. Brought before Alexander wounded and in chains, he was asked how he wished to be treated. What did Porus say?
answer: Treat me as a king treats a king
choices: Treat me as a king treats a king
Spare my people and take my life
Kill me, for I will not serve you
Let me keep only my elephants
context: Porus answered, 'Treat me as a king would treat another king.' Impressed by his pride and bearing, Alexander not only spared him but gave him back his kingdom to rule. Source: Wikipedia 'Battle of the Hydaspes'; Britannica 'Battle of the Hydaspes'.

question: Philip of Macedon watched his young son Alexander ride a wild stallion that the king's grooms had given up on. Philip wept for joy, kissed the boy, and spoke words that sounded almost like a prophecy. What did Philip say to his son?
answer: Macedonia is too small for you, my son
choices: Macedonia is too small for you, my son
You will be the finest horseman in Greece
The horse is yours, you have won our wager
No other man will ever ride that beast
context: Philip told him: 'O my son, look thee out a kingdom equal to and worthy of thyself, for Macedonia is too little for thee.' The boy had wagered the horse's full price of thirteen talents that he could ride it — and won. Source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander (Livius.org translation).

question: Thebes rose against Alexander the Great in 335 BC, and he crushed the rebellion: he burned the city to the ground, killed about 6,000 Thebans and sold 30,000 more into slavery. But he gave a strict order to spare one single house, the home of one long-dead man. Whose house did Alexander save?
answer: The house of the poet Pindar
choices: The house of the poet Pindar
The house of the city's high priest
The house of the Theban king
The house of the army's general
context: Alexander spared the temples, the citadel, and the home of the long-dead poet Pindar, reportedly posting the order: 'Set not on fire the roof of Pindar, maker of song' — in gratitude for Pindar's verses praising one of Alexander's own ancestors. The destruction of Thebes was a real and brutal cost of his campaigns. Source: Wikipedia 'Battle of Thebes'; TheCollector 'Alexander's Destruction of Thebes'.

question: Sisygambis, the mother of the Persian king Darius III, fell into Alexander the Great's hands after his victory at Issus in 333 BC, along with Darius's wife and daughters. A beaten enemy's family could expect to be hurt or killed. Instead, how did Sisygambis come to feel about Alexander?
answer: She came to love him as her own son
choices: She came to love him as her own son
She begged him to spare Darius's life
She cursed him to his face as a tyrant
She took poison rather than be a captive
context: Alexander treated the captured royal women with conspicuous respect and let them keep their royal honors. Sisygambis came to regard him as a son — a striking act of magnanimity toward the family of the enemy king he was hunting. Source: Wikipedia 'Battle of Issus'; Britannica 'Battle of Issus'.

question: Alexander the Great founded the city of Alexandria in Egypt. He then crossed 300 miles of desert to the oracle at Siwa. There the priest hailed him as the son of the god Zeus-Ammon. Alexander took it so much to heart that he changed how he was shown on his coins. What did his coins now show him wearing?
answer: Ram's horns curling from his head
choices: Ram's horns curling from his head
A lion's mane around his face
A crown of golden sun-rays
An eagle perched on his helm
context: The god Ammon was pictured with a ram's horns, so after Siwa hailed him as Ammon's son, Alexander's coins showed him wearing the ram's horns. Alexandria became the most famous of the many cities he named after himself. Source: World History Encyclopedia 'Alexander the Great'; TheCollector 'Alexander at the Oracle of Siwa'.

question: Darius III's enormous Persian host faced Alexander the Great's smaller army at Gaugamela in 331 BC, and Alexander drove straight at its heart. The battle that decided the fate of the whole Persian Empire turned on a single act. What did Darius do that made his entire huge army collapse?
answer: Darius turned and fled first
choices: Darius turned and fled first
Darius was killed by a spear
Darius surrendered his crown
Darius charged at Alexander himself
context: Darius was the first man to break and run; when the Persians saw their own king flee, the whole line collapsed. It was the decisive blow that ended the Achaemenid Empire. Darius escaped east but was soon murdered in 330 BC by his own satrap Bessus, who hoped to seize power — robbing Alexander of the final victory over his rival. Source: Wikipedia 'Battle of Gaugamela'; Britannica 'Battle of Gaugamela'.

question: The island fortress of Tyre defied Alexander the Great for seven months in 332 BC. To reach its walls he built a vast causeway out into the sea and rolled tall siege towers along it toward the city. The Tyrians struck back with one devastating weapon to destroy those towers. What did the Tyrians launch against them?
answer: A burning fireship rammed into the towers
choices: A burning fireship rammed into the towers
A tunnel dug beneath the causeway
Divers who cut the towers loose
Boulders hurled from the city walls
context: The Tyrians packed an old transport ship with pitch, sulphur, and dried branches, hung cauldrons of oil from its masts, then rammed it blazing into Alexander's siege towers and set them on fire. Tyre's months-long resistance made it one of the most punishing sieges of the whole campaign. Source: World History Encyclopedia 'Alexander's Siege of Tyre, 332 BCE'; Wikipedia 'Siege of Tyre (332 BC)'.

question: A drunken victory banquet at Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of Persia, ended in flames in 330 BC, when Alexander the Great and his men set fire to the great palace of Xerxes itself. Ancient accounts say that the first person after the king to hurl a blazing torch into the palace was not one of his generals at all. Who threw that first torch?
answer: Thais, an Athenian dancing-girl
choices: Thais, an Athenian dancing-girl
Parmenion, his oldest general
Hephaestion, his dearest friend
Ptolemy, a trusted commander
context: The courtesan Thais urged the drunken company on and, the accounts say, was the first after Alexander to throw a torch into Xerxes's palace — as revenge for Xerxes burning the temples of Athens 150 years earlier, in 480 BC. The burning of Persepolis was a real and lasting loss. Source: World History Encyclopedia 'Alexander the Great & the Burning of Persepolis'; Penelope/UChicago 'Thais and Persepolis'.

question: Alexander the Great's army reached the Hyphasis River in India in 326 BC after eight years of war and thousands of miles of marching, and there, for the first time in his life, the king was forced to turn back. He had never lost a battle. What finally halted the undefeated conqueror at the edge of the known world?
answer: His own soldiers refused to march on
choices: His own soldiers refused to march on
A vast Indian army blocked the way
A plague swept through his camp
His supplies and money ran out
context: Alexander's exhausted, homesick troops mutinied and refused to go a single step farther east. Despite his pleas, he finally gave way and turned back — his eastward conquests ended not by any enemy, but by his own men's refusal to go on. Source: World History Encyclopedia 'The Hyphasis Mutiny'; Wikipedia 'Indian campaign of Alexander the Great'.

question: Alexander the Great led his army home across the Gedrosian Desert through terrible thirst and heat, and up to a third of his column may have died. He was parched too when scouts brought him a helmet holding enough water for one man. In full view of his thirsty army, what did he do with it?
answer: Poured it out onto the sand untouched
choices: Poured it out onto the sand untouched
Drank it down in a single gulp
Shared it among his officers
Gave it to the sickest soldier
context: Rather than drink while his men went without, Alexander tipped the helmet over and poured the water onto the sand where the whole army could see — refusing any comfort his soldiers could not share. (Arrian notes some sources placed this scene in a different desert crossing.) Source: Historyskills 'Gedrosian Desert'; Arrian, Anabasis 6.26 (via Livius.org).

question: Alexander the Great lay dying of fever at Babylon in 323 BC, just 32 years old, master of a vast empire and never once beaten in battle. He was asked who should inherit it all. According to the ancient accounts, what did he reply?
answer: To the strongest
choices: To the strongest
To my unborn son
To Perdiccas alone
Let the gods decide
context: Alexander reportedly answered 'to the strongest' (toi kratistoi) and handed his signet ring to his general Perdiccas. His death came soon after that of his closest companion, Hephaestion. With no clear heir, his generals tore the empire apart in decades of war. Source: Wikipedia 'Death of Alexander the Great'; labrujulaverde 'Crateros and the succession'.

question: Alexander the Great's generals argued for days over what to do with his body after a fever killed him at Babylon in June 323 BC, while the embalmers waited outside the royal chamber. When the embalmers were at last allowed in, they were astonished. According to the ancient reports, what was strange about the body?
answer: It showed no signs of decay
choices: It showed no signs of decay
It had turned the color of gold
It had already crumbled to bones
It glowed with a faint light
context: The embalmers reportedly said the body showed no decay and still looked lifelike. Alexander's corpse was eventually carried to Egypt and entombed at Memphis and then Alexandria, where his tomb became a famous shrine for centuries before it was lost to history in late antiquity — its location still unknown today. This marvel survives only as ancient testimony. Source: Wikipedia 'Death of Alexander the Great'.  (Legend.)

question: Douglas MacArthur slipped away in March 1942 from the doomed American defense of the Philippines, on President Roosevelt's orders. At a railway station in Australia he made reporters a promise that became famous. What did he promise?
answer: "I shall return."
choices: "I shall return."
"We will fight on."
"The line still holds."
"Remember the fallen."
context: MacArthur said it at the Terowie railway station in South Australia on March 20, 1942. Ordered to escape by President Roosevelt, he refused to soften the pledge to "we shall return" — he meant it as his personal word. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_MacArthur's_escape_from_the_Philippines

question: George Patton carried two famous revolvers with ivory grips. When a reporter wrote that the grips were 'pearl-handled,' Patton exploded: they were ivory, not pearl. What kind of person, Patton said, carries a pearl-handled pistol?
answer: "A pimp from a cheap New Orleans whorehouse"
choices: "A pimp from a cheap New Orleans whorehouse"
"A gambler who never fired a shot in anger"
"A general who polishes medals he never earned"
"A coward who hides behind his own staff"
context: Patton bought the ivory-gripped Colt .45 Single Action Army in 1916 and notched it after killing a man in Mexico; he also carried a .357 Smith & Wesson. The pearl-handled insult is one of his most-quoted lines. https://www.wearethemighty.com/mighty-history/the-history-of-general-pattons-ivory-handled-revolvers/

question: Douglas MacArthur, the theatrical commander of the Pacific war, waded through the surf onto a beach at Leyte on 20 October 1944. He did not wait for dry ground: right at the water's edge he spoke into a radio microphone. What words did he open with?
answer: "People of the Philippines, I have returned!"
choices: "People of the Philippines, I have returned!"
"Soldiers of America, the hour has come!"
"Today the enemy learns our strength!"
"From the sea we strike again!"
context: He fulfilled the exact vow he'd made in March 1942. The image of MacArthur striding through the surf at Leyte became one of the iconic photographs of the Pacific war. https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/macarthur-returns-philippines

question: Dwight Eisenhower handwrote a short note the night before D-Day, to be released only if the Normandy invasion failed. It said the troops had done all that bravery could do, and then it turned to the question of who was at fault. How did Eisenhower assign the blame in that note?
answer: He wrote that any blame "is mine alone."
choices: He wrote that any blame "is mine alone."
He blamed the unpredictable Channel weather.
He blamed faulty intelligence reports.
He left the question of blame unanswered.
context: His exact line: "If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone." In his only slip of nerves he mis-dated it July 5 instead of June 5; he pocketed it after the landings succeeded, and an aide later rescued it from the trash. https://www.archives.gov/exhibits/american_originals_iv/images/d_day/eisenhower_note.html

question: Arthur Zimmermann, Germany's foreign minister, wired a secret coded offer to Mexico in January 1917. It urged Mexico to attack the United States, and in return Germany promised to help Mexico take back the 'lost territory' it had ceded to the U.S. in 1848. Which three American states did the telegram name as Mexico's prize?
answer: Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona
choices: Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona
California, Nevada, and Utah
Texas, Louisiana, and Oklahoma
Arizona, Colorado, and Kansas
context: The decoded telegram read that 'Mexico is to reconquer her lost territory of New Mexico, Texas and Arizona.' Naming the three states by name is what made it feel so brazen to Americans. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimmermann_telegram; National WWI Museum, theworldwar.org/learn/about-wwi/zimmermann-telegram

question: A German U-boat lurking off the coast of Ireland in May 1915 torpedoed a giant British passenger liner without warning. The great ship rolled over and sank, and about 1,198 people drowned, 128 of them Americans. The sinking turned Americans sharply against Germany's submarine war. Which famous ship went down?
answer: the Lusitania
choices: the Lusitania
the Sussex
the Titanic
the Maine
context: The Lusitania sank on May 7, 1915. Germany later resumed sinking merchant and passenger ships without warning on February 1, 1917, breaking its own 'Sussex Pledge' of 1916 — and that, with the Zimmermann Telegram, pushed America off neutrality. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_the_RMS_Lusitania; britannica.com/topic/Sussex-pledge

question: Lloyd W. Williams, a captain of the 5th Marines, reached a thick French forest called Belleau Wood in June 1918, as Germany made its last great push toward Paris. Weary French soldiers falling back told the newly arrived Americans they had better retreat too. What did Williams fire back?
answer: "Retreat? Hell, we just got here."
choices: "Retreat? Hell, we just got here."
"We will hold this line or die on it."
"The Marines do not know how to retreat."
"Tell your general we are staying."
context: The Marines held. Belleau Wood changed hands repeatedly and was assaulted six times before the Germans were finally cleared on June 26, 1918. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Belleau_Wood; army.mil/article/207683

question: John J. Pershing's infantry chased bandits along the Mexican border in 1916. By the best-loved story, the mounted troopers riding with them teased the foot soldiers, and the teasing gave America's World War I soldiers their nickname, 'doughboys.' What did the riders mock them for?
answer: White adobe dust caked them, so riders called them 'adobes'
choices: White adobe dust caked them, so riders called them 'adobes'
Doughy biscuits they baked nightly in the camp ovens
Pale flour they rubbed on their belts for parade
Soft bread rations issued in place of hardtack crackers
context: Pershing's infantry got coated in white adobe dust, so mounted troopers called them 'adobes' or 'dobies' — which slurred into 'doughboys.' They were also called Sammies and Yanks. The exact origin is debated, so this is the leading tradition rather than proven fact. Source: theworldwar.org/learn/about-wwi/doughboys  (Legend.)

question: Charles E. Stanton, an aide to General Pershing, laid a wreath at the Paris tomb of the Marquis de Lafayette on 4 July 1917, just after the first American troops reached France. Lafayette was the Frenchman who had aided America's own revolution. Standing there, Stanton spoke four words that repaid that old debt. What did he say?
answer: "Lafayette, we are here!"
choices: "Lafayette, we are here!"
"France, America has come!"
"We repay our debt today."
"Old friend, we remember you."
context: General John J. Pershing led the American Expeditionary Force; he and the first 14,000 troops had landed at Saint-Nazaire on June 26, 1917. Stanton, Pershing's aide, made the declaration at Lafayette's tomb — a nod to France's help in the American Revolution. Source: pritzkermilitary.org; theworldwar.org/learn/about-wwi/doughboys

question: Dan Daly, a stocky Irish-American first sergeant who had already won the Medal of Honor twice, once in China and once in Haiti, led his Marines up out of cover at Belleau Wood in June 1918. Ahead of them lay a waist-high wheat field and the roaring German machine guns. What did he shout to drive them forward?
answer: "Come on, you sons of bitches, do you want to live forever?"
choices: "Come on, you sons of bitches, do you want to live forever?"
"Up and at them, Marines, the wood is ours!"
"On your feet, men, we take that field now!"
"Follow me through, and never mind the guns!"
context: The Marines advanced in lines straight into the guns. June 6 alone cost the Marine brigade 1,087 casualties — the bloodiest day in Marine Corps history up to that point. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Belleau_Wood
