question: Alvin York, a deeply religious corporal from Tennessee, had asked to skip combat. Yet in one fight in October 1918 he killed more than 20 Germans and marched a whole column back as prisoners. A general told him, 'I hear you have captured the whole German army.' How did York answer?
answer: "No sir. I got only 132."
choices: "No sir. I got only 132."
"Just the ones who surrendered, sir."
"More than I could rightly count, sir."
"Only a small part of it, General."
context: York led the capture of 132 prisoners and earned the Medal of Honor. He had wrestled with his faith before deciding he could fight. Source: history.com/this-day-in-history/october-8; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_York

question: German troops faced the U.S. Marines at Belleau Wood in June 1918, and tradition says the Marines' ferocity so unnerved them that they gave the Marines a fearsome nickname, one the Corps still proudly uses today. What name did the Germans supposedly give them?
answer: Devil Dogs ('Teufel Hunden')
choices: Devil Dogs ('Teufel Hunden')
Iron Wolves ('Eisen Wolfe')
Storm Devils ('Sturm Teufel')
Ghost Riders ('Geister Reiter')
context: Historians note the German term is unconfirmed in the records, so 'Teufel Hunden' may be legend. Afterward the French officially renamed the wood 'Bois de la Brigade de Marine' in the Marines' honor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Belleau_Wood

question: William Bayard Hale, a reporter, asked Arthur Zimmermann point-blank on 3 March 1917 whether the story of his leaked telegram to Mexico was true. Zimmermann could have called it a British forgery, and most people expected him to do just that. What startling reply did he give?
answer: "I cannot deny it. It is true."
choices: "I cannot deny it. It is true."
"I sent it only as a precaution."
"It was meant only for the event of war."
"Germany seeks only peace with America."
context: Almost everyone assumed Zimmermann would call the leaked telegram a fake — instead he admitted it. His confession destroyed any remaining doubt and inflamed American opinion. The U.S. declared war on Germany on April 6, 1917. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimmermann_telegram; constitutingamerica.org

question: Nigel de Grey, a codebreaker in the Admiralty's hushed Room 40, went to work on a coded German telegram in January 1917. It came from the foreign minister, Arthur Zimmermann, and de Grey cracked most of it within a day. When he saw Germany's offer to bring Mexico into the war against the United States, he turned pale and looked up at his chief. What stunned question did he ask?
answer: "Do you want to bring America into the war?"
choices: "Do you want to bring America into the war?"
"Shall we hand this to the Americans?"
"Has Germany truly gone this far?"
"Can we be certain of the wording?"
context: De Grey saw at once that the telegram could drag the still-neutral United States into the conflict. Room 40 was the Admiralty's secret cipher office, and its codebreaking is remembered as a feat of ordinary ingenuity. Source: history.com/articles/the-secret-history-of-the-zimmermann-telegram; history.blog.gov.uk

question: Eddie Rickenbacker, a former race-car driver, flew with the 94th Aero Squadron and became America's top flying ace, with 26 victories in the air. His squadron painted a homemade emblem on its planes, born of an officer's quip on the day America finally joined the fight. What was on that emblem?
answer: Uncle Sam's stovepipe hat tossed inside a ring
choices: Uncle Sam's stovepipe hat tossed inside a ring
A winged horse rearing over crossed swords
A diving eagle clutching a lightning bolt
A red devil straddling a spinning propeller
context: The emblem gave the squadron its nickname, the 'Hat-in-the-Ring Gang' — born when an officer quipped, 'Well, I guess our hat is in the ring now!' Rickenbacker, who had raced cars before the war, won the Medal of Honor for his 26 victories. Source: nationalmuseum.af.mil; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Rickenbacker

question: Arthur Zimmermann sent his secret coded telegram to Mexico in January 1917, inviting Mexico to attack the United States. Germany believed the code kept the message safe from every enemy eye. Yet for part of its long journey across the Atlantic Ocean, the telegram actually traveled over which line?
answer: A U.S. State Department cable Washington had lent Germany for diplomacy
choices: A U.S. State Department cable Washington had lent Germany for diplomacy
A Mexican government wire running direct from Berlin to Mexico City
A private German cable laid secretly across the Atlantic floor
A Swedish telegraph route Berlin was sure no enemy could tap
context: Neutral Washington had let Germany use a U.S. State Department cable for peace and diplomatic messages — and Britain had secretly been reading those transatlantic lines all along. So Germany's plot to set Mexico against America traveled on America's own wire. To hide that they were reading both German and American traffic, the British later invented a cover story blaming a spy in Mexico City. Source: history.com/articles/the-secret-history-of-the-zimmermann-telegram

question: Germany began shifting dozens of divisions west after a revolution in 1917 knocked one great power out of the war, racing to land a knockout blow before American troops could arrive in strength. Which power's collapse set off that race?
answer: Russia's
choices: Russia's
Italy's
France's
Austria-Hungary's
context: Revolution knocked Russia out of the war, so Germany raced to win in the west before American numbers could land — and lost that race. Germany had gambled America was too unready to matter (the U.S. Regular Army held only about 128,000 men in 1917), but after the draft, doughboys reached France at roughly 10,000 a day, over 2 million by the Armistice. Source: worldhistory.org/article/2823; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_entry_into_World_War_I

question: Edward Hopper painted Nighthawks in 1942: four people inside a brightly lit late-night diner, sealed behind one big curved sheet of glass. A viewer who looks hard at that diner notices something missing that every real diner has. What did Hopper leave out?
answer: Any visible door to get in or out
choices: Any visible door to get in or out
A clock on the wall above the counter
A single empty seat at the counter
The name of the diner over the entrance
context: There is no entrance into or out of the Nighthawks diner at all — the glass is one seamless wedge, shutting the viewer out of the scene. Hopper finished it on January 21, 1942. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nighthawks_(Hopper)

question: Andy Warhol painted a whole row of Campbell's soup cans for his 1962 show, each on a canvas of its own. The gallery director Irving Blum asked him why on earth he had made so many separate canvases. What was Warhol's flat little reason?
answer: "There are 32 varieties."
choices: "There are 32 varieties."
"I liked the color of the labels."
"My mother told me to."
"They sold well at the store."
context: There are exactly 32 canvases — one for each of the 32 soup flavors Campbell's sold then. MoMA bought all 32 together in 1996 and hangs them in four rows of eight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campbell%27s_Soup_Cans

question: Jackson Pollock turned his back on the upright easel that other painters stood at. 'I feel nearer, more part of the painting,' he explained in 1947; he wanted to 'literally be in the painting.' How did Pollock actually make his paintings?
answer: He spread the canvas flat and poured paint while walking around it
choices: He spread the canvas flat and poured paint while walking around it
He hung the canvas and dabbed it with tiny brushes
He propped the canvas up and sprayed it from across the room
He folded the canvas and pressed wet paint between the halves
context: Pollock laid the canvas flat on the studio floor and poured and flung house paint from sticks, trowels, and stiff dried brushes — almost never touching brush to cloth in the old easel way. Source: https://www.moma.org/collection/works/78699

question: Andy Warhol painted Campbell's soup cans over and over, and critics read them as a cold joke about advertising. Warhol said his real reason was far simpler than that. Why did Warhol paint that soup?
answer: He really ate it every day, the lunch his mother Julia made him
choices: He really ate it every day, the lunch his mother Julia made him
He found an old crate of cans in his studio
A company paid him to advertise the soup
He thought it was the ugliest label he could find
context: Warhol ate the same Campbell's soup lunch for about twenty years; his mother Julia made it for him. Source: https://www.thetakeout.com/2141649/andy-warhol-campbells-soup-lunch-twenty-years/

question: Jackson Pollock made his name by dripping and flinging house paint off sticks and trowels. In 1956 Time magazine pinned a mocking nickname on him, and it stuck to him for good. What did Time call Pollock?
answer: "Jack the Dripper"
choices: "Jack the Dripper"
"The Paint Wrangler"
"The Floor Master"
"Splatter Jack of the Hamptons"
context: "Jack the Dripper" punned on his drip-painting style. Pollock died months later, on August 11, 1956, at 44, speeding drunk in his Oldsmobile near East Hampton, New York. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Pollock

question: British soldiers sang 'Yankee Doodle' to mock the American colonists as country bumpkins. The joke turned on one word: a 'doodle' was a fool who thought sticking a single feather in his cap made him a 'macaroni.' In the 1760s, what was a macaroni?
answer: A flashy, over-dressed young English dandy
choices: A flashy, over-dressed young English dandy
A simple country farmer from the colonies
A foot soldier marching in the British army
A wandering musician who sang for coins
context: A 'macaroni' was a young Englishman of the 1760s who dressed in outrageously fashionable style, topped with a towering powdered wig. The insult: a backwoods colonial 'doodle' figured one feather made him that stylish. The Americans flipped the mockery and proudly adopted 'Yankee Doodle' as their own song of defiance. Source: HISTORY.com, 'Why Did Yankee Doodle Call a Feather Macaroni?'; Britannica, 'Yankee Doodle'.

question: Francis Scott Key, an American lawyer, watched British warships bombard Fort McHenry through a September night in 1814. Seeing the American flag still flying at dawn, he wrote a poem and set it to a tune Americans already knew, 'To Anacreon in Heaven.' Words and tune together became the national anthem in 1931. What had the tune begun life as?
answer: The theme song of a London gentlemen's drinking club
choices: The theme song of a London gentlemen's drinking club
A battle march played by the British army
A hymn sung in English country churches
A lullaby carried over by colonial settlers
context: 'To Anacreon in Heaven' was the theme song of a London club devoted to wine and music, honoring Anacreon — an ancient Greek poet famous as a lover of wine. Key's words rode that drinking-club tune, and 'The Star-Spangled Banner' didn't officially become the U.S. national anthem until 1931. Source: NPR, 'Star-Spangled Banner Born From A Drinking Song 200 Years Ago'; Library of Congress, Patriotic Melodies.

question: Martin Waldseemüller, a German mapmaker, printed a great world map in 1507 and gave the new lands a Latin name taken from the Italian navigator Amerigo Vespucci. Oddly, it does not come from Vespucci's family name at all, though two whole continents carry it today. Which part of his name did the mapmaker use?
answer: His first name, Amerigo
choices: His first name, Amerigo
His family name, Vespucci
His father's name
His birth city's name
context: America comes from Amerigo Vespucci's GIVEN name, not his surname — making it the rare case where two continents carry a man's first name rather than his family name. The Latin form of Amerigo is Americus, feminized to America. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_the_Americas

question: Christopher Columbus reached the western lands first, yet the continents bear Amerigo Vespucci's name instead. Columbus went to his grave insisting he had reached the eastern edge of Asia. What did Vespucci do that won him the honor?
answer: He argued in print the land was an entirely new continent, not Asia
choices: He argued in print the land was an entirely new continent, not Asia
He sailed farther west than Columbus ever did
He drew the first map of the coastline
He paid the mapmakers to use his name
context: In his printed letter 'Mundus Novus' (New World, c.1503), Vespucci was first in print to declare the western lands an entirely separate landmass — a whole new continent — rather than part of Asia as Columbus claimed. The continents are named for the man who first grasped what they were. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World

question: The Ancestral Puebloans built great stone towns in the Southwest's Four Corners and moved away around 1300. Outsiders long knew them as the Anasazi, but the word is not theirs: it comes from the Navajo, a neighboring people. Roughly, what does the Navajo word mean?
answer: ancient enemies
choices: ancient enemies
cliff people
star watchers
desert kings
context: 'Anasazi' comes from the Navajo (from ana'i, enemy or foreigner) and means roughly 'ancient enemies.' Because it is an outsiders' label, modern Pueblo people prefer 'Ancestral Puebloans' for their own ancestors. (indianpueblo.org/what-does-anasazi-mean-and-why-is-it-controversial)

question: Ancestral Puebloan builders cut a small hole into the floor of each kiva, the round ceremonial room they sank into the ground. To them that hole, called the sipapu, was no ordinary hole but a portal. What did they believe happened at that spot?
answer: their ancestors first emerged into this world
choices: their ancestors first emerged into this world
the dead descended to the underworld
rain was summoned in dry years
the sun was reborn each winter
context: Each kiva had a small floor hole called a sipapu, believed to be the very portal through which the people's ancestors first emerged into this world. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sipapu)

question: At Chaco Canyon, the Ancestral Puebloans raised Pueblo Bonito, a great house of about 800 rooms rising four to five stories. To roof it they needed more than 240,000 logs -- but they lived in a near-treeless desert and had to bring every beam from mountains over 50 miles away. By what means did all that timber make the journey?
answer: carried on foot by people
choices: carried on foot by people
floated on flood channels
dragged by teams of oxen
rolled on log sledges
context: Chaco's builders worked in a nearly treeless desert and hauled more than 240,000 roof-beam logs on foot from mountains over 75 km (about 50 miles) away, with no wheels, carts, or pack animals. (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1514272112)

question: Archaeologists digging inside Pueblo Bonito at Chaco Canyon uncovered the bones of creatures that had been brought to that dry canyon from more than 1,000 miles away as early as AD 900, proof of trade with distant Mexico. What were these creatures?
answer: scarlet macaws
choices: scarlet macaws
jaguar pelts
sea turtles
desert tortoises
context: Scarlet macaws -- tropical parrots native only to rainforests over 1,000 miles south -- were found at Pueblo Bonito (30 of 35 Chaco macaws), traded north as early as AD 900, proof of long-distance contact with Mexico. (pnas.org/content/112/27/8238)

question: King Wu Ding of the Shang wanted advice from his dead ancestors. His diviner scraped and polished an ox shoulder blade or a turtle's belly shell until it was perfectly smooth. To get the ancestors' answer, what did the diviner do next to the prepared bone?
answer: Pressed a red-hot rod into it until it cracked, and read the crack.
choices: Pressed a red-hot rod into it until it cracked, and read the crack.
Threw it on the fire and read the picture in the rising smoke.
Cast it like dice and read whichever side landed face up.
Soaked it in river water and read which way the bone bent.
context: The crack snaked across the front with a sharp 'pok,' and the diviner read its shape and direction as the ancestors' verdict, then carved the question and the outcome right beside it on the bone. (World History Encyclopedia, 'Oracle Bones'; Smarthistory, 'Oracle Bone, Shang Dynasty')

question: Shang diviners carved questions to the ancestors into turtle shells and ox bones more than 3,000 years ago, and later scratched the outcome beside each one. No older Chinese writing has ever been found. On those bones the sun appears as a dotted circle and the moon as a crescent. What happened to that script over the 3,000 years since?
answer: Today's Chinese characters descend straight from it, still recognizable.
choices: Today's Chinese characters descend straight from it, still recognizable.
A brand-new writing system replaced it completely long ago.
The Shang had borrowed it from a foreign people, who kept it.
A few signs survive as decoration, but the system itself died out.
context: On the bones the sun was a circle with a dot (日) and the moon a crescent (月), and a reader who knows modern Chinese can still recognize them. That unbroken line from Shang oracle bones to the characters used today, over 3,000 years, is the real wonder. (Wikipedia, 'Oracle bone script'; New World Encyclopedia, 'Oracle Bone Script')

question: Scribes of the Shang court carved the word bu, 'to divine,' onto their oracle bones in its earliest written form. Scholars think the character began as a tiny picture, and that even its sound carries a memory of the ritual. What do they believe the character shows, and what does its sound echo?
answer: A picture of the divination crack, said aloud to echo the 'pok' of the splitting bone.
choices: A picture of the divination crack, said aloud to echo the 'pok' of the splitting bone.
A picture of the diviner's hand, said aloud to echo a whispered prayer.
A picture of the ox whose bone was used, said aloud to echo its low bellow.
A picture of three stacked lines, said aloud to echo three drumbeats.
context: 卜 is thought to be a pictogram of a divination crack, a vertical line with a short branch, and its sound may imitate the 'pok' the heated bone made when it split. The Shang named the practice after the very noise and shape of breaking bone. (Wikipedia, 'Oracle bone')

question: Wu Ding, a Shang king, once read the cracks of an oracle bone about the coming childbirth of his consort, Lady Hao, and made a confident prophecy: if she gave birth on a lucky ding-day, there would be long good fortune. Later a scribe carved what actually happened, right onto the same bone. What did that carving record?
answer: The baby came late, on an unlucky day, and was a girl.
choices: The baby came late, on an unlucky day, and was a girl.
The baby came right on the ding-day, exactly as the king had foretold.
The consort and the baby both died before the lucky day arrived.
The scribe scraped the failed prophecy away to spare the king shame.
context: The verification reads: 'After thirty-one days... on day jiayin (day 51), she gave birth; it was not good; it was a girl.' The baby arrived on an unlucky day and was a daughter, not the wanted son. The king's reading was wrong, and the Shang carved the failure down anyway. (Facts and Details, 'Oracle Bone Inscriptions'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Oracle Bones')

question: A sore tooth sent one Shang king to his diviners with a question: who was causing the pain? Many Shang questions were homely ones like that, such as whether it would rain the next day, or whether three oxen or five made the right offering. Who did the bone blame for the toothache?
answer: A dead ancestor, 'father Yi,' reaching from beyond to cause it.
choices: A dead ancestor, 'father Yi,' reaching from beyond to cause it.
A rival king's curse, cast in secret across the border.
A bad spirit hiding in the well the king drank from.
An enemy soldier who had struck him in the jaw.
context: The inscription asks of the sick tooth, 'Is it not father Yi who is causing it?', pinning a toothache on a dead ancestor. Many oracle-bone questions were strikingly ordinary, the same worries any family has. (Facts and Details, 'Oracle Bone Inscriptions'; chinasage.info, 'Early Chinese writing on Oracle bones')

question: Wang Yirong, a scholar, was dosing his own malaria in 1899 with 'dragon bones,' the powder Chinese healers had long sold as a fever cure. He looked closely at some pieces that had not yet been ground up. What did he see on them that no one else had noticed?
answer: Lines of ancient writing carved across them.
choices: Lines of ancient writing carved across them.
Tiny holes drilled in neat rows across their backs.
Streaks of red paint along their cracked edges.
The fossil shapes of long-extinct animals pressed inside.
context: Wang Yirong realized the script on the 'dragon bones' was Chinese writing far older than any then known, pushing recorded Chinese history back more than a thousand years. Apothecaries had been selling the bones, ground to powder, as fever medicine. (Shandong/China Daily, 'Wang Yirong: discoverer of jiaguwen'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Oracle Bones')

question: Wang Yirong took a hopeless command as foreign troops fought their way into Beijing during the Boxer Rebellion in August 1900, only a year after his find among the dragon bones. The city fell. What did he do rather than be captured?
answer: Took his own life, together with his wife and daughter-in-law.
choices: Took his own life, together with his wife and daughter-in-law.
Slipped out of the city in disguise and vanished from history.
Surrendered his sword and was led away by the foreign troops.
Burned his collection of bones so no enemy could seize it.
context: When Beijing fell, Wang Yirong took his own life along with his wife and daughter-in-law rather than be captured, only a year after he had unlocked the oracle bones. (Wikipedia, 'Wang Yirong'; Shandong/China Daily, 'Wang Yirong: discoverer of jiaguwen')

question: Fu Hao, a consort of the Shang king Wu Ding, appears on about 200 cracked oracle bones from some 3,200 years ago, far more than any other Shang queen or princess. Strangely, the bones do not show her praying or weaving. What do they record her doing?
answer: Leading armies into battle as a Shang general.
choices: Leading armies into battle as a Shang general.
Ruling the whole kingdom alone after the old king died.
Reading the cracks herself as the realm's chief diviner.
Casting the bronze cauldrons used in the royal temple.
context: Fu Hao led 13,000 soldiers into battle, the largest Shang force on record. When her tomb was found intact at Yinxu in 1976 (the only unlooted Shang royal tomb ever discovered), it held 468 bronze vessels, 755 jade objects, 6,900 cowrie shells used as money, and 16 humans sacrificed to accompany her. (Smarthistory, 'War and Sacrifice: The Tomb of Fu Hao'; Lit Hub, 'The Woman With the Axe: On Fu Hao')

question: The Huang He rolls across the plain of northern China where Chinese civilization was born, and its water really is the color of straw and mustard. That is why it is better known in English as the Yellow River. What turns the water so yellow?
answer: Fine yellow soil, called loess, that it scoops up as it flows.
choices: Fine yellow soil, called loess, that it scoops up as it flows.
The yellow sky it mirrors at sunrise and sunset.
Great schools of golden-yellow fish in its waters.
Yellow desert sand blown across it in dust storms.
context: The river carries so much powdery yellow loess that the water turns yellow, and the same silt earns it a grimmer nickname, 'China's Sorrow,' because the mud piles up on the riverbed and people must build the dikes ever higher. (WorldAtlas, 'Yellow River (Huang He)'; WorldAtlas, 'Which River Is Called China's Sorrow And Why?')

question: China's Yellow River dumps thick yellow silt on its own bed every flood season, lifting the bed a little higher each time. To keep the water from bursting out and drowning the farmland, villagers pile the dikes ever higher. In the worst stretches, what has that endless race done to the river?
answer: The river now runs higher than the rooftops and fields beside it.
choices: The river now runs higher than the rooftops and fields beside it.
The river sank beneath the silt and now runs underground.
The river split into a hundred shallow streams on the plain.
The river froze into a solid road of ice most of the year.
context: In its worst stretches the Yellow River runs ABOVE the surrounding land, a 'perched river,' flowing between dikes higher than the rooftops of the plain below. So when a dike breaks, the river pours DOWN onto the countryside instead of staying in its channel, which is why its floods are so deadly. (factsanddetails.com, 'Yellow River' / '1887 Yellow River flood')

question: The Yellow River burst its dikes near Zhengzhou in late September 1887, and its water spread across some 50,000 square miles of the northern Chinese plain. Villagers had built those dikes ever higher to hold the river in. What did that one flood do?
answer: Drowned close to a million people across northern China.
choices: Drowned close to a million people across northern China.
Drowned a few thousand before crews patched the breach.
Wiped out Zhengzhou but stopped at the foothills beyond.
Forced a million from their homes yet killed surprisingly few.
context: The 1887 Yellow River flood killed at least about 930,000 people, with some estimates running to one or two million, and left some two million homeless, one of the deadliest disasters humanity has ever recorded. (Wikipedia, '1887 Yellow River flood')

question: The Yangtze, which the Chinese call Chang Jiang, pours down from the high Tibetan mountains and runs all the way to the sea at Shanghai, far to the south of the Yellow River. One fact about it puts the Yangtze among the most famous rivers on Earth. Which is true of the Yangtze?
answer: It is the longest river in Asia and the third-longest on Earth.
choices: It is the longest river in Asia and the third-longest on Earth.
It is the longest river on Earth, even ahead of the Nile.
It is the only river that crosses all of China twice.
It carries more water to the sea than any river in Asia.
context: The Yangtze (about 6,300 km) is the longest river in Asia and the third-longest in the world, behind only the Amazon and the Nile. The Yellow River (about 5,464 km) to its north is the shorter of the two, but it is the cradle of Chinese civilization and the Shang heartland. (Wikipedia, 'List of longest rivers of Asia'; topchinatravel.com, 'Yangtze River VS Yellow River')

question: Yu the Great, the legendary founder of the Xia dynasty, battled the flooding Yellow River for thirteen years, the story goes. Where his father had tried to dam the water, Yu dug channels to lead it out to the sea, and he gave himself so completely to the work that he did one remarkable thing. What does the legend say he did?
answer: Passed the door of his own home three times without ever going in.
choices: Passed the door of his own home three times without ever going in.
Carried every single basket of river mud upon his own back.
Went thirteen years without once sleeping beneath a roof.
Finished the last canal on the very day his father died.
context: The legend says Yu the Great succeeded where his father had failed: instead of damming the floods he dredged them, digging channels to lead the water to the sea, and he was so devoted that he passed his own door three times without going in. He is remembered as the founder of the Xia dynasty. (travelchinaguide.com, 'Yu the Great, Dayu'; The China Project, 'Yu the Great, tamer of China's greatest floods')

question: Inside Angkor Wat, the great Khmer temple in Cambodia, one long stone wall shows a cosmic tug-of-war. Gods and demons heave against each other. They churn a sea of milk to pull out the drink of everlasting life. What did the two sides use as their rope?
answer: A giant serpent wrapped around a mountain
choices: A giant serpent wrapped around a mountain
A river of fire poured from the sky
A chain forged by the gods themselves
A bridge of stone across the ocean
context: The east-gallery panel depicts the 'Churning of the Ocean of Milk': gods and demons pull a giant serpent coiled around a mountain, spinning it to churn the sea and draw out the elixir of immortality. https://sea.lib.niu.edu/islandora/object/SEAImages%3ASRAW42

question: Suryavarman II, a Khmer king, built Angkor Wat in what is now Cambodia in the early 1100s: the largest religious building on Earth, ringed by a wide moat and covered in stone carvings. Most Khmer temples face east toward the rising sun, but Angkor Wat's main entrance faces west, the direction of death in Khmer belief. What do many scholars believe the king meant it to be as well?
answer: His own funerary temple, a tomb for his death
choices: His own funerary temple, a tomb for his death
A fortress guarding the empire's western road
A market square for the capital's traders
A school for the kingdom's young priests
context: Unlike most Khmer temples, which face east, Angkor Wat opens to the west — the direction associated with death — leading many scholars to argue Suryavarman II built it as his own funerary temple. The west-facing-tomb reading is a scholarly inference, not certain fact. https://angkorwatinhistory.wordpress.com/2017/11/15/construction-of-angkor-wat/  (Legend.)

question: Anne Frank, a Jewish girl in Nazi-occupied Amsterdam, turned thirteen on 12 June 1942. The day before her birthday she walked through a bookshop with her father, Otto, and pointed at the present she wanted more than any other. What did she choose?
answer: A small diary with a red-checkered cover
choices: A small diary with a red-checkered cover
A leather satchel for school
A box of colored drawing pencils
A camera in a brown case
context: The diary was a little autograph book with a red-and-white checkered cloth cover and a clasp. Anne had spotted it the day before while browsing with her father, and got it on her 13th birthday, 12 June 1942 — the diary that would make her famous. Source: Anne Frank House, 'The red-checked diary.'

question: Anne Frank did not simply jot down events in her diary. She wrote it as a series of letters to a friend she invented, opening each entry by greeting her by name. What name did Anne give the make-believe friend she poured her heart out to?
answer: Kitty
choices: Kitty
Lotte
Emmy
Greta
context: Anne began her entries 'Dear Kitty.' She borrowed the name from a character in a series of Dutch novels by Cissy van Marxveldt that she was reading at the time. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Diary of a Young Girl'; Anne Frank House.

question: Eight people went into hiding in 1942 in a Secret Annex at the back of Otto Frank's office building in Amsterdam, among them his wife Edith and his daughters Anne and Margot. Anyone walking the hall saw only a plain wall, because the doorway was cleverly disguised. What hid it?
answer: A swinging bookcase
choices: A swinging bookcase
A sliding wall panel
A heavy oak wardrobe
A bricked-up archway
context: The hiding place was behind Otto Frank's office at Prinsengracht 263 in Amsterdam. A bookcase that swung aside like a door hid the entrance, so no one would suspect rooms lay behind it. Source: Anne Frank House, 'The Secret Annex.'

question: Anne Frank brightened her cramped, bare room in the annex herself, pasting things up 'with a pot of glue and a brush' until, she wrote, she had turned 'the entire room into one big picture.' The faded originals still hang on those walls today. What did she cover her walls with?
answer: Postcards and pictures of movie stars
choices: Postcards and pictures of movie stars
Maps of faraway countries
Pages torn from her schoolbooks
Drawings she had made of her family
context: Anne had been collecting picture-cards of movie stars since before the war — around 800 of them by 1939. Her father carried the collection into the annex ahead of time so she could decorate her wall. Source: Anne Frank House, 'The picture walls in the Secret Annex.'

question: Seagulls flashed silver past the attic window in February 1944, and Anne Frank, sitting there with her diary, wrote about them and about the dew. She also wrote about one tall thing outside that window, which she had already written about three times before. What was it?
answer: A chestnut tree
choices: A chestnut tree
A clock tower
A windmill
A drawbridge
context: The attic had the one window the hiders had not blacked out. Through it Anne could see the sky, the birds, and a tall chestnut tree she returned to again and again in her diary. Source: Anne Frank House, 'The chestnut tree.'

question: Miep Gies, one of the office helpers, biked over to the hidden annex nearly every day for two years, bringing meat, vegetables and library books to Anne Frank's family. If the Nazis had caught her helping Jews in hiding, what would her penalty have been?
answer: Death or being sent to a concentration camp
choices: Death or being sent to a concentration camp
A large fine and loss of ration books
House arrest for the rest of the war
Forced labor in a German factory
context: Miep Gies risked her life carrying supplies to the annex nearly every day for over two years. Anne's 'pack mule' line captures how much the hiders depended on her. Source: Anne Frank House, 'Miep Gies.'

question: All day long the eight people in the Secret Annex had to be silent. They could not run water, flush the toilet, or speak above a whisper. They could move around only after dark. Who were they so afraid would hear them?
answer: Warehouse workers in the rooms below
choices: Warehouse workers in the rooms below
German soldiers searching the building
Neighbors in the house next door
Police patrolling the canal outside
context: Ordinary workers filled the warehouse beneath the annex by day and had no idea anyone was hiding above them. One creak or flush could have given everything away, so the hiders froze in silence until the workers went home. Source: Anne Frank House, 'The Secret Annex.'

question: Anne Frank, hidden from the Nazis in the Secret Annex, dreamed of becoming a writer and journalist once the war was over. On 5 April 1944 she wrote in her diary that she knew she truly could write, and then set down a single line about her deepest hope. What did she write that she wanted?
answer: 'I want to go on living even after my death'
choices: 'I want to go on living even after my death'
'I want my name known in every land'
'I want to write a hundred great books'
'I want to be remembered for my courage'
context: Anne believed her writing could survive her — and it did. That same entry holds the line 'I want to become a journalist... I know I can write.' Source: Wikipedia, Anne Frank (5 April 1944 entry).

question: Gerrit Bolkestein, the exiled Dutch minister, spoke on the radio in the spring of 1944 and urged the Dutch to keep their wartime diaries and letters so the world could read them afterward. In the hidden annex Anne Frank heard him, and the idea seized her. What did she at once begin to do?
answer: Rewrite her whole diary to publish as a book
choices: Rewrite her whole diary to publish as a book
Hide her diary inside the attic wall
Mail her diary to the minister in London
Sew her diary into the lining of her coat
context: The minister was Gerrit Bolkestein. Inspired, Anne started copying her diary onto loose sheets, polishing it for a book she meant to call 'Het Achterhuis' (The Secret Annex) — a title she chose herself. Source: Wikipedia, Anne Frank; Anne Frank House.

question: Karl Josef Silberbauer, an SS officer, led a sudden police raid on the annex on the morning of 4 August 1944 and arrested all eight people hidden there, after more than two years in hiding. People have combed the records for decades since. What haunting question about that day has never been answered?
answer: Who tipped off the police has never been proven
choices: Who tipped off the police has never been proven
Where the family's money was hidden was never found
Why the raid came on that exact date stays unknown
How long the officer had watched them is unrecorded
context: The raid was led by SS officer Karl Josef Silberbauer; helpers Victor Kugler and Johannes Kleiman were arrested too. Who betrayed the annex remains an unsolved mystery to this day. Source: Wikipedia, Miep Gies; Anne Frank House.

question: Typhus raged through Bergen-Belsen, a freezing, lice-ridden camp in northern Germany, after Anne Frank and her older sister Margot were moved there in November 1944. Both girls caught it and died within days of each other in February 1945. How close had they come to surviving?
answer: British troops freed the camp just weeks later
choices: British troops freed the camp just weeks later
The war in Europe ended the very next day
Allied bombers had already cut the railways nearby
A rescue list had carried both their names
context: Margot died first, then Anne — only a few weeks before British troops liberated Bergen-Belsen in April 1945. They had come heartbreakingly close. Source: Anne Frank House timeline; PBS News.

question: Anne Frank wrote her most famous words on 15 July 1944, only three weeks before the raid, and they are now carved on memorials around the world. In the very same passage she wrote, 'I hear the ever approaching thunder, which will destroy us too.' What hopeful line did she set beside that dread?
answer: 'In spite of everything I still believe that people are really good at heart'
choices: 'In spite of everything I still believe that people are really good at heart'
'No matter how dark the night, I trust the morning will surely come'
'I refuse to let my fear take away the hope still inside me'
'Even in this hidden place, the world still feels full of beauty'
context: Anne wrote hope and dread side by side. The line is beloved precisely because she wrote it knowing the danger closing in — three weeks before the arrest. Source: Wikiquote, Anne Frank; FlaglerLive (15 July 1944 entry).

question: Miep Gies climbed into the emptied annex after the eight were arrested and taken away, and found Anne Frank's diary and loose pages scattered across the floor. She gathered them up and locked them away unread in her desk drawer, meaning to hand them back to Anne someday. Why did she later say it was lucky she had never read them?
answer: They named the helpers, so she'd have had to burn them
choices: They named the helpers, so she'd have had to burn them
She would have been too heartbroken to keep working
Reading them would have broken a promise to Otto
The police could have traced her own handwriting
context: Miep and Bep Voskuijl found the papers together. The diary named all five helpers and the black-market suppliers — had Miep read it, she said, she'd have been forced to destroy it to protect them all. Source: Anne Frank House, 'Miep Gies'; Smithsonian, 'A Small Light.'

question: Miep Gies handed the diary she had saved to the one person from the Secret Annex who came back to Amsterdam after the war. Of the eight hidden there, he alone survived, and in 1947 he had the diary published; it has since been printed in about 70 languages. Which of the eight was the lone survivor?
answer: Otto Frank, Anne's father
choices: Otto Frank, Anne's father
Peter van Pels, the neighbors' son
Fritz Pfeffer, the dentist
Hermann van Pels, Peter's father
context: Miep gave Otto the saved diary on 5 July 1945, after learning Anne had died. He published it in 1947; it has since sold more than 30 million copies. The father who survived gave his daughter's voice to the world. Source: Anne Frank House, 'The publication of the diary.'

question: Barton W. Mitchell, a Union corporal crossing a field in Maryland in September 1862, spotted three cigars in the grass. They were wrapped in a sheet of paper, and that paper turned out to be one of the luckiest finds of the war. What was written on it?
answer: General Lee's secret battle plan
choices: General Lee's secret battle plan
President Lincoln's travel schedule
A map of the Richmond defenses
A roster of a Virginia regiment
context: On Sept 13, 1862, Corporal Barton W. Mitchell of the 27th Indiana found the cigars wrapped in a lost copy of Lee's Special Orders No. 191, which revealed Lee had split his army into four separate parts. A Union officer, Samuel Pittman, proved it was genuine by recognizing the handwriting of Lee's chief of staff, an old banking colleague. Source: American Battlefield Trust, 'Special Order 191: Lost and Found'.

question: At Antietam, Confederate soldiers crowded into a worn-down farm road that worked like a natural trench, and fired into one Union charge after another for more than three hours. So many men fell along it that soldiers gave the road a grim new name. What did they call it?
answer: Bloody Lane
choices: Bloody Lane
The Devil's Den
The Hornet's Nest
The Slaughter Pen
context: The Sunken Road became 'Bloody Lane' after roughly 5,000 men fell there. The Irish Brigade under General Thomas Francis Meagher, carrying green emerald flags, charged it and lost around 60 percent of its men in about an hour. Source: American Battlefield Trust, Antietam Sunken Road; The Wild Geese, 'The Deadliest Day'.

question: Clara Barton brought a wagon of bandages to Antietam just as army surgeons ran out and were dressing wounds with corn husks. As she lifted a wounded soldier to give him water, a bullet passed between her arm and her body and killed the man in her arms. A grateful surgeon then gave her a name that stuck for the rest of her life. What was it?
answer: The Angel of the Battlefield
choices: The Angel of the Battlefield
The Maid of Maryland
The Mother of the Wounded
The Heroine of Sharpsburg
context: Surgeon Dr. James Dunn wrote that 'General McClellan, with all his laurels, sinks into insignificance beside the true heroine of the age, the angel of the battlefield.' Barton said the bullet cut through the soldier 'from shoulder to shoulder,' and she never mended the hole it left in her sleeve. Source: NPS Antietam, 'Clara Barton at Antietam'.

question: At dawn the battle of Antietam tore through a farmer's 24-acre field of tall corn, and the fighting was so fierce the field changed hands again and again. Union General Joseph Hooker later described the corn itself. What did he say the gunfire had done to it?
answer: Cut every stalk as cleanly as with a knife
choices: Cut every stalk as cleanly as with a knife
Torn it to shreds and left it smoking
Flattened every row flat to the ground
Riddled the ears until they burst apart
context: Hooker reported that 'every stalk of corn in the northern and greater part of the field was cut as closely as could have been done with a knife, and the slain lay in rows precisely as they had stood in their ranks a few moments before.' The Cornfield changed hands at least six times in three to four hours. Source: NPS Antietam, 'The Cornfield'.

question: On the south end of the Antietam battlefield, a few hundred Georgia riflemen on a high bluff held off Ambrose Burnside's force of more than 12,000 Union men for about four hours. The Union troops kept funneling onto one narrow stone bridge and were shot down in the open as they crossed. What could those men have done instead of crowding onto the bridge?
answer: Simply waded across the creek at shallow fords nearby
choices: Simply waded across the creek at shallow fords nearby
Waited for nightfall and slipped across unseen
Brought up cannon to blast the Georgians off the bluff
Marched miles upstream to a larger, safer bridge
context: Antietam Creek could be waded at several fords, yet thousands funneled toward the 125-foot stone crossing still called Burnside's Bridge and were cut down for a creek shallow enough to walk through. About 450 to 500 Georgians under Robert Toombs and Henry Benning held the bluff. Source: Wikipedia, 'Burnside's Bridge'; American Battlefield Trust.

question: Abraham Lincoln had been holding back a decision for months, telling his Cabinet he would wait for a battlefield win before announcing it. Antietam was enough of a Union victory to give him one. Five days after the battle, what did Lincoln announce?
answer: The Emancipation Proclamation, freeing the enslaved in the rebel states
choices: The Emancipation Proclamation, freeing the enslaved in the rebel states
A nationwide draft to force men into the Union army
A full naval blockade to choke off the Confederate ports
A peace offer to let the Southern states leave quietly
context: On September 22, 1862, Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, declaring enslaved people in the rebelling states would be free as of January 1, 1863. Lee had crossed into Maryland hoping a Northern victory would win European recognition for the Confederacy, and Antietam ended that hope. Source: Library of Congress, 'Today in History - September 22'; National Archives.

question: Cleopatra and Mark Antony met Octavian's fleet off the Greek coast at Actium in 31 BC, with the whole Roman world at stake. The battle still hung in doubt when Cleopatra suddenly turned her sixty ships and fled under sail. What did Antony do the moment he saw her go?
answer: He abandoned his own fighting fleet and chased after her
choices: He abandoned his own fighting fleet and chased after her
He ordered his archers to fire on her fleeing ships
He rallied his captains and pressed the attack harder
He ran his flagship aground to make a last stand
context: At the Battle of Actium (September 2, 31 BC), Cleopatra broke for open water with her 60 Egyptian ships, and Antony left his own warships mid-fight to follow her; his remaining fleet surrendered and Octavian became master of Rome. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Battle_of_Actium/ ; Britannica, Battle of Actium; History.com, 'This Day in History: Battle of Actium.'

question: Rather than be dragged through Rome in chains, Cleopatra, the last queen of Egypt, chose to end her own life. She had backed the losing side in Rome's civil war, and her lover Mark Antony had already killed himself in defeat. By the ancient legend, which creature did she let bite her?
answer: An asp
choices: An asp
A scorpion
A spider
A viper-fish
context: Plutarch records that Cleopatra died from the bite of an asp (a small venomous snake). Framed as legend: when the Romans found her dead, no snake was ever discovered, only tiny puncture marks on her arm. Source: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/encyclopaedia_romana/miscellanea/cleopatra/rixens.html

question: At the prow of a ship sailing away from Actium, Mark Antony stayed alone for three days after the battle. He was so ashamed that he could not bring himself to face Cleopatra. What did he do there all that time?
answer: He sat with his head in his hands
choices: He sat with his head in his hands
He refused all food and water
He wrote out his final will
He prayed aloud to the gods of war
context: Antony sat alone at the prow for three days, head in his hands, too ashamed to face Cleopatra after abandoning his fleet. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Battle_of_Actium/

question: Mark Antony brought the bigger fleet to Actium — about 500 ships, with a flagship named the Antonia that carried his war chests of gold. Yet Octavian's admiral Marcus Agrippa beat those huge, slow warships with a secret weapon. What was Agrippa's device that sank fifteen of Antony's ships?
answer: The harpax, an iron harpoon fired on a rope to reel ships in
choices: The harpax, an iron harpoon fired on a rope to reel ships in
A fleet of fire-ships steered into the enemy line
A ram tipped with Greek fire that burned on contact
A floating boom of chains that trapped the ships
context: Agrippa's harpax was an iron-cased wooden harpoon shot on a rope; it grappled Antony's vessels and reeled them in, sinking 15 of them. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Battle_of_Actium/

question: Trapped in Alexandria a year after Actium, Mark Antony heard a false report that Cleopatra was already dead, and he stabbed himself with his own sword. The wound did not kill him at once. How did the dying Antony reach Cleopatra to die in her arms?
answer: His men hauled his body up through an upper window of her sealed mausoleum

He was carried in secret past the Roman guards at the gate
He crawled through a tunnel beneath the palace floor
He was rowed across the harbor to her tomb at night
context: Cleopatra had sealed herself in her mausoleum, so Antony's men hoisted his dying body up through an upper window, where he died in her arms. Source: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/encyclopaedia_romana/miscellanea/cleopatra/rixens.html

question: Octavian beat Mark Antony and Cleopatra in the sea battle of Actium in 31 BC, and he wanted the queen taken alive. He meant to march her in chains through Rome in his triumph, the great victory parade that was the peak honor for any Roman conqueror. She took her own life instead and cheated him of his prize. What did he put in the parade in her place?
answer: An image of her with the asp
choices: An image of her with the asp
Her golden couch and royal robes
A captive playing the dead queen
The sword that had killed Antony
context: Robbed of the living queen, Octavian paraded a made image of Cleopatra with the asp. The win made him master of the Roman world and, by 27 BC, its first emperor. Source: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/encyclopaedia_romana/miscellanea/cleopatra/rixens.html

question: A policeman in apartheid South Africa could arrest any Black adult on the spot for not carrying one hated paper. It carried its holder's photograph, fingerprints and stamps setting out which parts of the country he or she could enter. What was it called?
answer: A passbook called the dompas
choices: A passbook called the dompas
A work permit called the reispas
A ration book called the koepon
An identity card called the kennkaart
context: Black South Africans called it the 'dompas' (roughly 'dumb pass'). It controlled where they could live, work, and travel in their own country, and produced millions of arrests. Source: EBSCO Research Starters, 'Sharpeville Massacre Focuses Global Awareness on Apartheid'; South African History Online, 'Pass Laws and Sharpeville Massacre'.

question: Nelson Mandela walked free in 1990, and four years later South Africa made him its first Black president. People of every background across the country grew to love him so much that they called him not 'Mandela' but by his clan name, as though he were their own kin. What was that name?
answer: Madiba
choices: Madiba
Dalibunga
Ngangelizwe
Mthembu
context: He was born Rolihlahla Mandela in 1918 into the Thembu royal house; 'Madiba' is his clan name, used affectionately by South Africans of every background. In 1961 he co-founded the ANC's armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe ('Spear of the Nation'). Source: Britannica, 'Nelson Mandela'; South African History Online biography of Nelson Mandela.

question: Robben Island's prison, off Cape Town, took in Nelson Mandela, a lawyer sentenced to life for opposing apartheid, in 1964. Years later the number on his prison uniform gave its name to a global charity he founded to fight poverty and AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome). What was his prison number?
context: It meant he was the 466th prisoner taken to Robben Island in 1964. He kept 466/64 until 1982, when he was moved to Pollsmoor Prison and renumbered 220/82. Source: Nelson Mandela Foundation, 'Prisoner 466/64'; Al Jazeera, 'How Mandela prison number became a brand'.

question: At the 1995 Rugby World Cup final against New Zealand, Nelson Mandela walked onto the field in the green Springbok jersey. For decades the Springboks had been an all-white symbol that most Black South Africans loathed. On his back was the number of one player. Whose number did Mandela wear?
answer: Captain Francois Pienaar's number 6
choices: Captain Francois Pienaar's number 6
Winger Chester Williams' number 11
Fly-half Joel Stransky's number 10
Lock Kobus Wiese's number 4
context: Wearing the captain's jersey, Mandela told the white Afrikaner team and crowd they belonged in the new South Africa too. South Africa beat New Zealand 15-12 in the final. Source: World Rugby, 'On this day in 1995: Mandela, Williams and Pienaar help unite South Africa'.

question: A roaring crowd watched Nelson Mandela walk out of Victor Verster Prison a free man on 11 February 1990, his fist raised, his wife Winnie beside him. He had spent the whole prime of his adult life locked away. How long had his imprisonment lasted in all?
answer: 27 years
choices: 27 years
18 years
33 years
21 years
context: Twenty-seven years — most of it on Robben Island — and he emerged preaching reconciliation, not revenge. Four years later he would be president. Source: South African History Online, 'Nelson Mandela released from prison, 11 February 1990'.

question: Police at Sharpeville opened fire on 21 March 1960 on a peaceful crowd that had gathered to protest the laws forcing Black South Africans to carry papers everywhere. They killed 69 people, among them women and children. How were many of the 69 shot?
answer: In the back, as they fled
choices: In the back, as they fled
In the legs, to scatter them
In the chest, as they advanced
In the air, over their heads
context: Many victims were shot in the back while running away — proof the crowd posed no threat. The Sharpeville massacre horrified the world; March 21 is now the UN International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. Source: Britannica, 'Sharpeville massacre'.

question: Thousands of Black schoolchildren marched through Soweto on 16 June 1976, and police opened fire on them; twelve-year-old Hector Pieterson was among the first to be killed. The children were furious about a new rule forced on their classrooms. What were the Soweto students protesting?
answer: Being forced to take their lessons in Afrikaans
choices: Being forced to take their lessons in Afrikaans
Being forced to carry passbooks to school
Being forced to pay new school fees
Being forced to attend classes on Sundays
context: Afrikaans was seen as the language of the oppressor. Sam Nzima's photograph of Hector Pieterson's body being carried away, his sister running alongside, shocked the world. June 16 is now Youth Day in South Africa. Source: Britannica, 'Hector Pieterson'; TIME, 'Soweto Uprising: How a Photo Helped End Apartheid'.

question: A glaring white limestone pit on Robben Island was where Nelson Mandela broke rock for thirteen years, and the glare hurt his eyes for good. But the prisoners taught each other reading, history and politics in secret, slipping lessons past the guards. They gave their prison a proud nickname. What did they call it?
answer: The University of Robben Island
choices: The University of Robben Island
The Freedom College
The Robben Island Reading Room
The Stone Quarry School
context: Prisoners with educations tutored those without, smuggling lessons past the guards. They emerged better read than when they went in — and Mandela came out ready to lead a nation. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'A Visit to Robben Island'.

question: Some 60,000 white Afrikaners, the very people whose government had jailed Nelson Mandela, packed the stadium for the 1995 Rugby World Cup final against New Zealand. They watched him walk out in the Springbok jersey, and then the crowd began to chant. What did they chant?
answer: "Nelson! Nelson! Nelson!"
choices: "Nelson! Nelson! Nelson!"
"Madiba! Madiba!"
"Viva, Mandela, viva!"
"Amandla! Awethu!"
context: The crowd that had once backed the regime that imprisoned him roared his first name in joy. Mandela's gamble — to honor the symbol his own people hated, in order to win over his former enemies — had worked. Source: History.com, 'How Nelson Mandela Used Rugby as a Symbol of South African Unity'; Wikipedia, '1995 Rugby World Cup final'.

question: In the dock at the 1964 Rivonia Trial, Nelson Mandela and his fellow leaders faced a charge of plotting sabotage against the white-minority government, and they might hang for it. Mandela did not plead for mercy. He spoke for three hours about a free, democratic South Africa where Black and white could live together, then closed with one defiant sentence. How did he end his speech?
answer: "It is an ideal for which I am prepared to die."
choices: "It is an ideal for which I am prepared to die."
"The struggle is now my whole life."
"You may jail me, but never my country."
"Let freedom reign in this land at last."
context: His full closing words: 'I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination... it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.' He was spared the noose but given life imprisonment. Source: Famous-Trials.com, 'I Am Prepared To Die'; South African History Online archive.

question: At night in his cell on Robben Island, Nelson Mandela wrote page by page, on smuggled paper, the manuscript of what would become his autobiography, Long Walk to Freedom. If the guards had found it, they would have destroyed it and doubled his punishment. When the pages were finished, where did he hide them?
answer: In cocoa tins, in the prison garden
choices: In cocoa tins, in the prison garden
In a hollow brick, in his cell wall
Inside the stuffing of his mattress
Behind a loose tile, under his bed
context: He sealed the pages in cocoa containers using tools made by fellow prisoner Jeff Masemola. Guards later found a copy while building a wall; Mandela, Sisulu and Kathrada lost study privileges for four years. The smuggled text became the 1994 book 'Long Walk to Freedom.' Source: Nelson Mandela Foundation, 'A Prisoner in the Garden'; BBC News Magazine, 'How a secret manuscript became a global bestseller'.

question: Percy Yutar, the prosecutor at the Rivonia Trial, had pushed for Nelson Mandela to be hanged. Decades later, as president, Mandela reached out to the old man who had once tried to send him to the gallows, and he did something that left Yutar marvelling. What did Mandela do?
answer: Invited Yutar to a private lunch
choices: Invited Yutar to a private lunch
Sent Yutar a letter of forgiveness
Pardoned Yutar on national television
Shook Yutar's hand at the trial site
context: Mandela said Yutar had 'only been doing his job.' Yutar marveled: 'I wonder in what other country would the head of government invite someone to lunch who prosecuted him thirty years ago.' Choosing reconciliation over revenge was Mandela's deliberate path — to be a victor over the system, not just over his enemies. Source: UPI Archives, 'Mandela lunches with man who prosecuted him'; IBTimes, 'Four Acts of Forgiveness'.

question: Neil Armstrong crawled through the hatch of the Apollo 11 lander on 20 July 1969 and climbed slowly down its ladder. As his boot pressed into the powdery grey dust of the Moon, he spoke a line still famous today. What did he say?
answer: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."
choices: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."
"Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed."
"For all the people on this Earth we are truly one."
"We came in peace for all mankind, July 1969."
context: Armstrong always insisted he actually said 'one small step for A man,' but the 'a' is inaudible in the recording. Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Neil_Armstrong

question: Two pairs of boots pressed clear footprints into the grey dust of the Moon in July 1969, Neil Armstrong's and Buzz Aldrin's, the first humans to walk there. The Moon has no wind, no rain and no air. What will happen to those prints?
answer: They will still be there, sharp-edged, for millions of years.
choices: They will still be there, sharp-edged, for millions of years.
They will fade as moondust slowly drifts back over them.
They will be erased by the next shower of meteorites.
They will blur as the lunar surface bakes in the Sun.
context: The Moon has no wind, rain, or atmosphere to erode them, so the prints at Tranquility Base are expected to stay as crisp as the moment they were made. Source: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/lunar/apollo_11_30th.html

question: Little black-and-white televisions flickered in homes on 20 July 1969 as Neil Armstrong stepped off the Apollo 11 lander and became the first human being to walk on the Moon. About how many people watched him do it live?
answer: Roughly 600 million people, about a fifth of everyone alive.
choices: Roughly 600 million people, about a fifth of everyone alive.
Roughly 5 million people, mostly inside the United States.
Roughly 90 million people, about half of all Americans.
Roughly 50 thousand people, gathered at Kennedy Space Center.
context: An estimated 600-650 million watched live, the largest television audience in history to that point. Source: https://www.nasa.gov/history/55-years-ago-apollo-11s-one-small-step-one-giant-leap/

question: The spidery lander dropped from lunar orbit with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin aboard on 20 July 1969, while Michael Collins waited above in the command ship. The moment its footpads settled onto a broad, flat plain of the Moon, Armstrong radioed Mission Control with words that became famous at once. What did he say?
answer: "Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed."
choices: "Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed."
"Houston, we have touched the magnificent desolation."
"Houston, the Columbia has reached the far side."
"Houston, three billion are watching us tonight."
context: The landing site in the Sea of Tranquility was named Tranquility Base in that very transmission. The lander was named Eagle; the command module orbiting overhead, flown by Michael Collins, was Columbia. Source: https://www.archives.gov/files/social-media/transcripts/transcript-eagle-has-landed-1969-45017.pdf

question: Apollo 11 left its launch pad in Florida on 16 July 1969 on top of a Saturn V, the tallest and most powerful rocket that had ever flown. Measured against a city skyscraper, how tall was the Saturn V?
answer: Taller than a 36-story building.
choices: Taller than a 36-story building.
About a 10-story tower.
Roughly a 5-story school.
Around a 20-story block.
context: The Saturn V stood 363 feet tall, and its five first-stage F-1 engines produced about 7.5 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. Source: https://airandspace.si.edu/explore/stories/apollo-11-launch-vehicle-and-spacecraft

question: Buzz Aldrin climbed back into the lander after the first moonwalk and saw that his bulky backpack had broken off a small circuit breaker. That switch armed the engine that would lift them off the Moon, there was no spare, and metal in a live circuit was dangerous. How did Aldrin get the switch working again?
answer: He pushed the broken breaker back in with the plastic tip of a felt-tip pen.
choices: He pushed the broken breaker back in with the plastic tip of a felt-tip pen.
He rewired the breaker using a strip of wire from his glove.
He jammed a metal screwdriver into the open switch.
He radioed Houston, who reset the breaker remotely from Earth.
context: Aldrin avoided putting metal into a live circuit by using the pen's plastic tip, which carries no current, and the ascent engine fired, letting them leave the Moon. Source: https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/50-years-pen-saved-apollo-11/story?id=64228723

question: The lander's guidance computer flashed a 1202 alarm in the last minute of the descent: it had been handed more tasks than it could finish. In Houston, Jack Garman, an engineer of 24, had seconds to decide what the crew should be told. What was his call?
answer: He said the alarm was harmless and gave a 'Go' to keep landing.

He ordered an immediate abort to save the astronauts.
He told the crew to shut the computer down and fly blind.
He held the decision and waited for the alarm to clear itself.
context: The '1202' (and later '1201') alarm meant 'executive overflow': the computer was swamped with too many tasks. Garman had memorized which alarms were survivable, knew it was not dangerous, and his 'Go' saved the landing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11

question: While Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked the surface, Michael Collins stayed behind, orbiting the Moon alone in the command module Columbia. On every orbit his path carried him behind the Moon, and during those passes something happened to his link with everyone else. What was it?
answer: He lost all radio contact for about 47 minutes each time.
choices: He lost all radio contact for about 47 minutes each time.
He drifted out of the Moon's gravity and had to fire his thrusters.
He fell into shadow so dark he could not read his instruments.
He overheard Houston talking to the surface crew on a crossed line.
context: With the whole Moon between him and Earth, Collins was completely cut off from every other human being for about 47 minutes per orbit. Source: https://airandspace.si.edu/amp-stories/dark-side-of-the-moon/index.html

question: Michael Collins circled the Moon alone in the command module Columbia while Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface below, and on every orbit he swung round the far side. Years later he summed up his solitude with a famous tally of who was on each side of the Moon. How did he put it?
answer: "Three billion plus two over on the other side, and one plus God-knows-what on this side."
choices: "Three billion plus two over on the other side, and one plus God-knows-what on this side."
"One man awake while the whole sleeping world turned slowly beneath me."
"Two friends below, three billion above, and the cold dark between us."
"Alone with the Moon, and the Moon alone with me, for forty-seven minutes."
context: Collins counted himself, plus 'God-knows-what,' against the rest of humanity on the far side of the Moon. Source: https://airandspace.si.edu/amp-stories/dark-side-of-the-moon/index.html

question: Buzz Aldrin, the second man to walk on the Moon, followed Neil Armstrong down the ladder in July 1969. He looked over grey, airless dust to a horizon with no trees, no clouds and no life. Which two words did he choose for the view?
answer: Magnificent desolation
choices: Magnificent desolation
Endless quicksilver
Frozen wasteland
Beautiful nothingness
context: Apollo 11, July 1969. Buzz Aldrin's first impression of the lunar surface was 'magnificent desolation': magnificent for the achievement, desolate for the empty view; it captured both the beauty and the utter emptiness of the surface, and he later titled his memoir with the phrase. Source: https://www.nasa.gov/history/55-years-ago-apollo-11s-one-small-step-one-giant-leap/

question: Neil Armstrong stepped off the ladder onto the Moon and at once made a safety move. If the crew had to blast off in an emergency, he wanted to be sure they did not go home empty-handed. What did he do before anything else?
answer: Scooped some Moon soil into his pocket
choices: Scooped some Moon soil into his pocket
Snapped a photo of his bootprint
Planted the American flag
Saluted back toward Earth
context: It was called the 'contingency sample' — grab a piece of the Moon immediately, so even an emergency liftoff would bring something home. Source: https://www.nasa.gov/history/55-years-ago-apollo-11s-one-small-step-one-giant-leap/

question: Eagle dropped toward the Moon as Neil Armstrong hunted for safe ground, and in Houston Charlie Duke, the Capsule Communicator, read the crew their fuel as it ran down: sixty seconds left, then thirty. Armstrong was still searching. How close did Eagle come to running dry?
answer: Eagle touched down with only seconds of flying time left in the tank.
choices: Eagle touched down with only seconds of flying time left in the tank.
Eagle landed with enough fuel left to take off and try again.
Eagle ran completely dry and dropped the last few feet.
Eagle aborted once, climbed away, and came back down.
context: Eagle landed with only about 216 pounds of usable fuel left, roughly 25 seconds before Mission Control's mandatory-abort point; estimates of the margin ranged from roughly 25 to 50 seconds of flying time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11

question: The instant the Eagle settled onto the Moon, Mission Control erupted. The Capsule Communicator (CAPCOM) Charlie Duke keyed his mic to answer, and was so wound up he tripped on the word 'Tranquility,' blurting 'Twang' first. When he got the words out, how did Duke describe the men in Houston?
answer: 'A bunch of guys about to turn blue. We're breathing again.'
choices: 'A bunch of guys about to turn blue. We're breathing again.'
'The proudest men on the planet tonight.'
'Cheering so loud we can't hear ourselves.'
'Shaking hands and wiping away tears.'
context: They'd been holding their breath through the white-knuckle descent. Duke: 'You've got a bunch of guys about to turn blue. We're breathing again. Thanks a lot.' Source: https://www.archives.gov/files/social-media/transcripts/transcript-eagle-has-landed-1969-45017.pdf

question: Through his small triangular window, in the final seconds of the descent, Neil Armstrong saw that the autopilot was steering Eagle straight into a crater ringed with boulders the size of cars. Every extra second of hovering burned precious fuel. What did he do?
answer: Took manual control and flew level past the rocks
choices: Took manual control and flew level past the rocks
Aborted and fired the engine to climb back up
Let the computer pick its own safe spot
Dropped straight down between two boulders
context: Armstrong grabbed the controls, skimmed the lander past the boulder field around the 300-foot-wide West crater, and hunted for clear ground while Aldrin called out the altitude, which is why Eagle landed 'long,' well past the planned spot. Source: https://blog.sciencemuseum.org.uk/apollo-11-moon-landing-the-most-difficult-moments/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11

question: A small package of science instruments stayed behind on the Moon when Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin climbed back into Eagle. Every night observatories on Earth still use one of those devices to pin down the distance between Earth and Moon to within a few inches. What did the astronauts leave behind?
answer: A mirror array that reflects lasers back to Earth
choices: A mirror array that reflects lasers back to Earth
A nuclear-powered radio beacon
A telescope aimed back at our planet
A buried time capsule of recordings
context: The laser retroreflector — a panel of mirrors. Fire a laser at it from Earth, time the bounce, and you get the Earth–Moon distance to within inches. They also left a seismometer to detect moonquakes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11

question: Inside Eagle, before he and Neil Armstrong stepped out onto the Sea of Tranquility, Buzz Aldrin quietly did something private. In one-sixth gravity he watched the liquid curl 'slowly and gracefully up the side of the cup.' What was Aldrin doing?
answer: Taking Holy Communion with bread and wine
choices: Taking Holy Communion with bread and wine
Toasting the crew with a sip of brandy
Testing how water behaves in low gravity
Eating the first meal from a ration pack
context: Aldrin ate bread and drank wine from a tiny silver chalice. NASA asked him to keep it off the air: the agency was being sued by atheist activist Madalyn Murray O'Hair after the Apollo 8 crew read from Genesis on Christmas Eve 1968. So on the radio he only invited listeners to 'give thanks in his own individual way.' Source: https://www.history.com/articles/buzz-aldrin-communion-apollo-11-nasa

question: Apollo crews planted six American flags on the Moon between 1969 and 1972, and photographs taken from lunar orbit decades later showed five of them still standing, but not the first, planted by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin. Aldrin had seen with his own eyes what happened to it. What happened to that first flag?
answer: The ascent engine's blast knocked it flat
choices: The ascent engine's blast knocked it flat
Sunlight bleached it until it crumbled
A micrometeorite tore it off the pole
Astronauts folded it and brought it home
context: It had been planted too close to the lander; the liftoff blast blew it over. Aldrin watched it fall, and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photos decades later confirmed he was right. Source: https://lroc.im-ldi.com/images/537

question: Michael Collins circled the Moon alone in the command module, and on every pass behind it he heard nothing from Earth for 47 minutes at a stretch. A NASA voice called him the loneliest man since Adam. When Collins later wrote about those hours, what did he say about them?
answer: He never actually felt lonely out there
choices: He never actually felt lonely out there
He had been terrified the whole time
He nearly lost radio contact for good
He wished he had walked on the Moon too
context: Cut off from all of humanity for stretches of each orbit, Collins was arguably the most isolated person in history — yet he insisted he never felt lonely. Source: https://airandspace.si.edu/amp-stories/dark-side-of-the-moon/index.html

question: Neville Chamberlain stood outside 10 Downing Street on 30 September 1938, home from meeting Hitler at Munich, and waved a signed paper. He told the cheering crowd to go home and sleep quietly in their beds. What did he promise the paper had won?
answer: Peace for our time
choices: Peace for our time
Peace for a generation
An honourable lasting peace
Peace across all Europe

His full line: 'for the second time in our history a British Prime Minister has returned from Germany bringing peace with honour. I believe it is peace for our time.' Within a year Britain was at war. (ushmm.org; speakola.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_for_our_time)

question: Czechoslovakia lost its border lands to Hitler at Munich in September 1938, and Czechs still call the deal the Munich Betrayal. How many Czechoslovaks sat at the table when it was signed?
answer: None — not one Czechoslovak was at the table
choices: None — not one Czechoslovak was at the table
One — only its president was allowed to sign
Two — its president and foreign minister
Three — a small Czech delegation took part
context: Czechoslovakia's fate was decided entirely by Germany, Britain, France, and Italy. Its two envoys, Vojtech Mastny and Hubert Masarik, were not in the room; they were kept waiting nearby and learned their country's fate only after the four powers had decided. Czechs still call it the 'Munich Betrayal' and sum it up as 'About us, without us.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Agreement; radio.cz)

question: Desperate to avoid another war over Czechoslovakia, the 69-year-old Neville Chamberlain went to Germany three times in September 1938 to plead with Adolf Hitler in person. Every trip meant doing something he had never done before in his life. What was Chamberlain doing for the very first time?
answer: Flying in an airplane
choices: Flying in an airplane
Sailing across the Channel
Speaking on the radio
Visiting Germany
context: Chamberlain made three flights to Germany in September 1938 — his first time ever in the air — yet at each meeting Hitler simply raised his demands rather than settling. (Wikipedia: Heston Aerodrome; foreignpolicy.com)

question: Adolf Hitler's troops rolled into Prague in March 1939, six months after Munich, and swallowed what was left of Czechoslovakia. Hitler gave the seized Czech lands a new official name inside his Reich. What did he call them?
answer: The Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia
choices: The Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia
The General Government of Poland
The Reichskommissariat of Ukraine
The Reichskommissariat Ostland
context: On 15 March 1939 Hitler tore up his Munich pledges, seized the rest of Czechoslovakia, and reorganized the Czech lands as the 'Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia.' Britain abandoned appeasement, guaranteed Poland, and when Germany invaded Poland that September the world war began. (Britannica; nationalww2museum.org)

question: Jan Masaryk, Czechoslovakia's foreign minister, saw Munich differently from the men who signed it. He watched the great powers slice up his homeland, and he answered with one savage image for what they had done to a living nation. What did he call it?
answer: An experiment in vivisection
choices: An experiment in vivisection
A funeral without a corpse
A trial without a judge
A theft without a thief
context: Masaryk protested that the victim 'was not even heard in its own defence,' though Czechoslovakia had already granted every concession demanded. Vivisection is the cutting open of a living creature — the country was still alive as they carved it. (radio.cz)

question: Like much of Britain, Neville Chamberlain carried a fresh, terrible memory that made him want to avoid another bloodletting at almost any cost. He and the other appeasers truly thought they were saving a whole generation from it. What horror haunted the men who signed away Czechoslovakia?
answer: The horror of the trenches
choices: The horror of the trenches
The misery of the Depression
The fall of the Russian throne
The terror of the Spanish flu
context: Britain's cabinet argued it would be wrong 'to plunge into a certain catastrophe in order to avoid a future danger.' Chamberlain genuinely believed he was sparing a generation the horror of the trenches — the case the appeasers could honestly make for themselves. (nationalww2museum.org)

question: Along the mountain border of the Sudetenland ran the Benes Line, Czechoslovakia's defences: hundreds of heavy gun blockhouses and over ten thousand pillboxes, built to stop just this kind of invasion. What happened to that fortress line when the Sudetenland was handed over at Munich?
answer: It was given up without a single shot fired
choices: It was given up without a single shot fired
It was blown apart in a week of fighting
It was secretly kept by the Czech army
It was bought back the following year
context: The Benes Line had 264 heavy artillery blockhouses and roughly 10,014 light pillboxes. Handed over at Munich, it was abandoned to the Germans without resistance; with it Czechoslovakia lost about 70% of its iron and steel industry and some 3 million people. (Wikipedia: Czechoslovak border fortifications; globalsecurity.org)

question: Benito Mussolini broke a tense deadlock at Munich by presenting a compromise he called his own neutral plan, one that Chamberlain and Daladier could accept without seeming to give in to Germany. In fact outsiders, not Italians, had written it for him the day before. Whose hands had really written it?
answer: Goring and the German Foreign Office
choices: Goring and the German Foreign Office
Ribbentrop and his personal staff
Mussolini's own delegation in Rome
Hitler, dictating it himself
context: The plan was drafted by Goring, Neurath and Weizsacker — who deliberately cut out Ribbentrop — then translated into French and phoned to Mussolini in Rome before he set off. The 'Italian plan' was German all along. (Shirer, Rise and Fall of the Third Reich; worldhistory.org)

question: Adolf Hitler signed a short peace pledge for Neville Chamberlain on the morning of the Munich deal, and it was this scrap of paper, not the treaty itself, that Chamberlain proudly waved in London. Later a worried Ribbentrop raised it with Hitler. How did Hitler describe the paper, according to his interpreter?
answer: Of no further significance whatever
choices: Of no further significance whatever
A clever trap for the British
The proudest day of his life
