A promise he meant to keep
context: When Ribbentrop objected to him signing, Hitler said (per interpreter Paul Schmidt): 'Oh, don't take it so seriously. That piece of paper is of no further significance whatever.' (nationalww2museum.org; historylearning.com)

question: 'Peace with honour' was Neville Chamberlain's boast: for the second time in British history, he said, a prime minister had brought it home. He was reaching for the glory of a Victorian prime minister who had come back from the 1878 Congress of Berlin and said the same words in Downing Street. Which statesman was Chamberlain trying to echo, only to see the echo turn against him?
answer: Benjamin Disraeli
choices: Benjamin Disraeli
Robert Peel
William Gladstone
Lord Palmerston
context: Disraeli told the crowd in 1878, 'I have returned ... bringing you peace, but a peace, I hope, with honour.' Chamberlain hoped to be a second Disraeli; instead history made the echo a rebuke. (winstonchurchill.org; Wikipedia: Peace for our time)

question: "You were given the choice between war and dishonour; you chose dishonour, and you will have war." Winston Churchill came to be famous for that verdict on Munich. Historians who set it beside what he actually said in the Commons on 5 October 1938 noticed something about its exact wording. What was the truth about the quotation?
answer: A later paraphrase of his actual words
choices: A later paraphrase of his actual words
A line he shouted across the chamber
A sentence Chamberlain wrote in reply
A quote he never spoke at all
context: Churchill's real 5 October speech used 'total and unmitigated defeat' and warned of 'the first sip ... of a bitter cup.' The smoother 'war and dishonour' wording was attached to his Munich criticism afterward and circulates in several versions — the idea is genuinely his, the exact sentence is not from that speech. (Wikipedia: A total and unmitigated defeat; libquotes.com)  (Legend.)

question: Wilmer McLean's farm at Manassas lay in the path of Bull Run, the Civil War's first great battle, and a shell crashed down his kitchen chimney. He moved to Appomattox Court House to escape the war, and in 1865 Lee surrendered to Grant in McLean's house. What did McLean say about the war?
answer: "The war began in my front yard and ended in my parlor."
choices: "The war began in my front yard and ended in my parlor."
"Two great armies camped on my land and left me nothing at all."
"I moved my family a hundred miles, and still the guns found us."
"I gave up one farm to the cannon and a second to the generals."
context: Wilmer McLean's farm at Manassas hosted the First Battle of Bull Run in July 1861 (a shell came down his kitchen chimney); he relocated ~120 miles to Appomattox Court House, where Lee surrendered to Grant in his parlor on Palm Sunday, April 9, 1865. Source: U.S. National Archives, prologue.blogs.archives.gov/2010/11/10/the-peculiar-story-of-wilmer-mclean; nps.gov/apco/mclean-house.htm.

question: Union officers rushed in for trophies the moment Lee and Grant left the McLean house. One snatched a family keepsake and tossed it to a friend, and the Moore family kept that trophy for more than a century before giving it back to the park in 1992. What was this 'Silent Witness' to the surrender?
answer: Lula McLean's homemade rag doll
choices: Lula McLean's homemade rag doll
An inkwell from the surrender table
A small carved chess piece
A glass paperweight from the mantel
context: Lula McLean's homemade rag doll (rag-bag body, stuffed potato-shaped head, painted face) was thrown by a Union officer to Capt. Thomas W. C. Moore of Sheridan's staff as a 'war trophy.' Nicknamed the 'Silent Witness,' it returned to the park in December 1992. Source: National Park Service, nps.gov/apco/kids-rag-doll.htm and nps.gov/apco/silent-witness.htm.

question: Ulysses S. Grant knew that most of the men Lee had just surrendered to him at Appomattox were small farmers, and the war had stripped their land bare. Without help they would go home to fields they could not plant. What did Grant's written terms let every Confederate soldier do?
answer: Take his own horse or mule home to plant a spring crop
choices: Take his own horse or mule home to plant a spring crop
Collect a cash payment for the property he had lost
Draw a wagon and supplies from the Union army stores
Claim a parcel of farmland once the armies disbanded
context: Grant ordered that 'every man of the Confederate army who claimed to own a horse or mule take the animal to his home' to put in a spring crop; Lee said this 'would have a happy effect.' The army horses were officially government property, so this was Grant's deliberate generosity. Source: Personal Memoirs of U.S. Grant, Ch. LXVII (americanliterature.com).

question: Robert E. Lee admitted to Grant at Appomattox that his surrendered men were starving: they had marched and fought for days with almost nothing to eat. Grant asked how many of them needed feeding, and Lee answered, 'about twenty-five thousand.' What did the victorious Grant do at once?
answer: Ordered rations from his own army sent over to feed Lee's men
choices: Ordered rations from his own army sent over to feed Lee's men
Told Lee his men must forage for their own food on the march
Held the food back until every Confederate had signed a parole
Sent the hungry soldiers straight to the nearest Union prison camp
context: Grant authorized 25,000 rations sent from Appomattox Station to feed the surrendered Confederate army. He later wrote that he felt 'sad and depressed... like anything rather than rejoicing at the downfall of a foe who had fought so long and valiantly.' Source: Personal Memoirs of U.S. Grant, Ch. LXVII (americanliterature.com).

question: Joshua Chamberlain, a Union general, ordered his troops to 'carry arms' on April 12, 1865, as the defeated Confederates came forward to stack their weapons: a marching salute of honor for the men they had beaten. John B. Gordon, the Confederate general riding at the front of the column, saw the gesture. How did Gordon return honor for honor?
answer: Wheeled his horse, made it bow its head, and dipped his swordpoint to his toe
choices: Wheeled his horse, made it bow its head, and dipped his swordpoint to his toe
Halted the entire column and ordered three cheers for the Union men
Rode down the line and shook the hand of every Union officer present
Lowered the last Confederate battle flag and laid it across his saddle
context: Chamberlain called it the 'last salute of the Army of Northern Virginia'; Gordon wheeled his horse, made it bow, and 'dropped his swordpoint to his toe in salutation.' About 27,000 stands of arms and roughly 100 battle flags were surrendered that day. Source: Chamberlain's own account, American Battlefield Trust, battlefields.org/learn/primary-sources/last-salute-army-northern-virginia; nps.gov/places/chamberlain-gordon-salute.htm.

question: At Appomattox, the story goes, Robert E. Lee drew his fine dress sword in defeat and offered it to Grant, and Grant graciously handed it back, a perfect picture of honor between enemies. Years later Grant read the tellings of that moment and answered them in his memoirs. What did he write about the sword?
answer: That it never happened and was 'the purest romance'
choices: That it never happened and was 'the purest romance'
That he handed the sword back as a sign of respect for Lee
That he kept Lee's sword and sash as personal souvenirs
That he firmly refused the sword when Lee tried to offer it
context: Grant wrote: 'The much talked of surrendering of Lee's sword and my handing it back... is the purest romance. The word sword or side arms was not mentioned by either of us until I wrote it in the terms.' The terms did let officers keep their side-arms — so no sword was ever surrendered to hand back. Source: Personal Memoirs of U.S. Grant, Ch. LXVII (americanliterature.com).

question: Soldiers marched south out of Rome on a new road begun in 312 BC to fight the Samnites, and in time it stretched to Brundisium, the port on the heel of Italy. Romans were so proud of it that they gave it a royal nickname, the Queen of Roads. What was the road called?
answer: The Appian Way
choices: The Appian Way
The Flaminian Way
The Aurelian Way
The Salt Road
context: The Romans called it the regina viarum, 'Queen of Roads.' The censor Appius Claudius Caecus began it in 312 BC, the same year he built Rome's first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia. Long stretches of its original polygonal basalt paving stones can still be walked on today. Source: https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/article/via-appia-queen-of-roads/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian_Way

question: Augustus set up a single bronze-covered column in the middle of the Roman Forum around 20 BC. Every mile of Roman road, from Britain to Egypt, was measured back to that one point, so the old saying that all roads lead to Rome pointed at a real object. What was the column called?
answer: the Golden Milestone
choices: the Golden Milestone
the Eternal Column
the Stone of Augustus
the Pillar of Roads
context: The Milliarium Aureum, the 'Golden Milestone,' was the zero-point of the whole Roman road network, inscribed with the distances from Rome to the great cities of the empire; because all distances were measured from it, it is the origin of the saying 'all roads lead to Rome.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_roads_lead_to_Rome ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milliarium_Aureum

question: Roman aqueducts carried water for dozens of miles on a slope so gentle that it dropped only inches per mile. The channel feeding the city of Nimes ran 50 kilometres from its spring and fell only about 12 metres over the whole distance. What single force moved all that water?
answer: gravity alone
choices: gravity alone
steam pressure
wind power
water wheels
context: The Nimes aqueduct averaged a drop of about 24 cm per kilometer, roughly one inch every 400 feet. No pumps, no machines, just a perfect downhill slope. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pont_du_Gard

question: Roman engineers carried the channel to Nimes across a river gorge on a stone bridge, three tiers of arches rising 48.8 metres, its blocks cut so precisely that no mortar held them. It poured about 11 million gallons a day into the city, and no Roman aqueduct bridge ever stood taller. What is it called?
answer: the Pont du Gard
choices: the Pont du Gard
the Aqua Marcia
the Arch of Nimes
the Trajan Span
context: The Pont du Gard crosses the Gard river and carried water toward Nimes. It has 6 arches on the bottom tier, 11 in the middle, and 35 small ones on top. Its stone blocks, some weighing up to 6 tons, were cut so precisely they hold together by friction with no mortar. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pont_du_Gard

question: Frontinus, a retired general, became Rome's water commissioner in AD 97 when the emperor Nerva gave him the job. He wrote a detailed first-hand report on the city's aqueducts, and his investigation uncovered a huge scandal. What was going on?
answer: Wealthy Romans were secretly siphoning public water into their homes
choices: Wealthy Romans were secretly siphoning public water into their homes
The aqueducts were about to collapse from earthquake damage
Slaves who maintained the pipes had all fled the city
The Tiber River had been poisoned by nearby mines
context: Frontinus's De aquaeductu is a rare insider account of how Rome managed its water. He recorded the channels, their sources, and even the fraud of people tapping the lines illegally. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_aquaeductu

question: The Romans laid each highway like a layer cake, in four layers, with big flat stones underneath, broken stone and concrete above them, and tight-fitting paving on top. Ditches ran beside it to catch the rain. What did the Romans do to the road's shape to send the water into them?
answer: crowned it higher in the middle
choices: crowned it higher in the middle
sloped it down to one side
cut grooves along its length
raised stone curbs on the edges
context: The four layers were the statumen, rudus, nucleus, and summum dorsum. Crowning the road so the center sat higher than the edges meant rain ran straight off into the drainage ditches, keeping the surface dry and durable. Source: https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/curiosities/cross-section-of-roman-road/amp/

question: Francisco de Vitoria never wrote a single book of his own, though he held the top chair of theology at Salamanca, then the greatest university in Europe, and lectured on the gravest questions of his age, from the rights of the peoples of the New World to the rules of a just war. How have his ideas survived?
answer: from notes his students wrote down at his lectures
choices: from notes his students wrote down at his lectures
from letters he mailed to scholars across Europe
from a book his brother finished after his death
from sermons copied out by parish priests
context: Everything we have of Vitoria survives only as student notes from his end-of-term lectures, the 'relectiones,' first printed in 1557, after he died. Source: Wikipedia, Francisco de Vitoria; universityhistoryarchive.org.

question: Charles V ruled Spain, Austria, the Netherlands and much of the New World, the most powerful man in Europe, yet when he faced a hard question of Christian conscience he did not put it to a bishop or a cardinal. He sent to Salamanca for the friar Francisco de Vitoria, a theologian famous for straight answers even to kings. Which royal marriage crisis did Charles ask him about?
answer: Henry VIII's break with Catherine of Aragon
choices: Henry VIII's break with Catherine of Aragon
Louis VII's break with Eleanor of Aquitaine
Philip II's match with Mary Tudor
Ferdinand's match with Isabella of Castile
context: Charles V consulted Vitoria on the gravest matters of the day, including the legality of the Spanish conquests and Henry VIII's divorce from Catherine of Aragon. Source: acton.org, 'In the Liberal Tradition: Francisco de Vitoria'; universityhistoryarchive.org.

question: Francisco Suarez, a Jesuit, wrote a book answering King James I of England, who was forcing an oath of allegiance on Catholics. James, a scholar-king himself, was so enraged by the reply that he had the book destroyed in the most humiliating way he could, on the steps of St Paul's Cathedral in London. How did he have it destroyed?
answer: burned by the common hangman
choices: burned by the common hangman
shredded by the royal guard
sunk in the Thames by the navy
smashed by the king's masons
context: The book was Suarez's 'Defensio Fidei' (1613); it was burned again the next year in the courtyard of the Paris Parliament. The pope had titled Suarez 'Doctor Eximius et Pius' — the Exceptional and Pious Doctor. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francisco Suarez'; iep.utm.edu, 'Suarez.'

question: Thomas Aquinas wrote in his vast Summa Theologiae that one rule is woven into every human mind. No one has to be taught it, everyone already reasons from it, and every other rule of right and wrong follows from it. What did he say that first command was?
answer: Good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided
choices: Good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided
Treat others only as you would have them treat you
Render to each person whatever is due
Obey the lawful ruler unless he commands a sin
context: Aquinas held that the first precept of natural law, the bedrock from which all others flow, is that 'good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided' (in Latin, 'bonum est faciendum et prosequendum, et malum vitandum'; Summa Theologiae, Prima Secundae, Q. 94, A. 2). Natural law is the moral order reason can read off the world on its own, no scripture needed. Source: Wikipedia, Treatise on Law; newadvent.org/summa/2094.htm.

question: Martin Luther King Jr. sat in a Birmingham jail cell and wrote a defense of breaking certain laws, and he reached back to a short verdict from Augustine of Hippo, quoting it word for word. The line became a rallying cry of natural-law thinkers. What was Augustine's blunt verdict?
answer: "An unjust law is no law at all"
choices: "An unjust law is no law at all"
"Let justice be done though the heavens fall"
"The safety of the people is the supreme law"
"Render unto Caesar what is Caesar's"
context: King wrote: 'I would agree with St. Augustine that an unjust law is no law at all.' The maxim 'lex iniusta non est lex' traces to Augustine's De Libero Arbitrio; King separately paraphrased Aquinas as an unjust law being 'not rooted in eternal law and natural law.' Source: Wikipedia, 'An unjust law is no law at all'; King, Letter from Birmingham Jail (letterfromjail.com).

question: In a celebrated lecture at Salamanca in 1539, Francisco de Vitoria asked what right Spain had to rule the peoples of the New World. Conquistadors had claimed the Americas for Spain, and Vitoria thought the claim through with care. Though the native peoples were not Christians, what did he conclude they truly held?
answer: real ownership and rule that neither Pope nor Emperor could take
choices: real ownership and rule that neither Pope nor Emperor could take
their goods, while their land belonged to whoever first discovered it
rule of themselves only after a Christian king first granted it
personal freedom, though the Emperor still owned all their land
context: In 'De Indis' Vitoria said the native peoples 'undoubtedly had true dominion in both public and private matters, just like Christians' (he called them 'veri domini,' true owners): real ownership and real political authority that neither the Pope nor Emperor Charles V could lawfully strip away. He went on to argue that mere unbelief 'does not render it lawful to make war on them.' Source: Wikipedia, Francisco de Vitoria; unr.edu/nevada-today.

question: Francisco de Vitoria taught his students at Salamanca that every people on earth, Christian or not, belonged to one moral community, and that the whole world was in some sense one republic. Even mighty kings and emperors, he held, were bound by shared duties that no state could override. For pioneering that idea, what honorary title did later scholars give him?
answer: the father of international law
choices: the father of international law
the father of the law of war
the father of the just-war tradition
the father of human rights
context: Vitoria's phrase was 'totus orbis, qui aliquo modo est una respublica' — the whole world is in some sense one republic — bound by a common 'ius gentium,' the law of nations. Source: U. of Valencia, 'El totus orbis y el ius gentium en Francisco de Vitoria'; avemarialaw.edu; e-ir.info.

question: Thomas Jefferson wrote rights into the Declaration of Independence that no government may take away. He did not invent the idea: he had it from John Locke, and Locke had it from the Dutch thinker Hugo Grotius, among others. Whose earlier account of an unchanging moral order stood behind them all?
answer: the medieval Catholic natural-law tradition
choices: the medieval Catholic natural-law tradition
the pagan philosophy of Greece and Rome
the Protestant Reformation's break from Rome
the secular thought of the later Enlightenment
context: The chain runs Salamanca (Vitoria, Suarez) to Grotius to Pufendorf to Locke to Jefferson. Locke quoted 'the judicious Hooker,' an English follower of Aquinas, roughly 13-16 times in his 'Second Treatise of Government' (1689) to ground natural rights; Aquinas's reason-grasped natural law is the seed that grows into the 'self-evident' rights the Founders wrote into the Declaration. Source: Wikipedia, Hugo Grotius; nlnrac.org, 'Richard Hooker'; https://www.nlnrac.org/classical/aquinas.html

question: Fibonacci, an Italian merchant's son, urged Europe's bankers to drop clumsy Roman numerals like XIV for the far quicker digits 0 to 9. Arab mathematicians had carried those digits west, and English calls them Arabic numerals. But the Arabs had learned them from someone else first. Where were the ten symbols really invented?
answer: India
choices: India
Egypt
Greece
China
context: Because the Arabs only carried the digits rather than invented them, the honest name historians use is "Hindu-Arabic numerals" - the chain runs from India, through the Arab world, to Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Hindu%E2%80%93Arabic_numeral_system

question: A Baghdad mathematician wrote a book around 825 explaining a new system of counting with ten digits, and when it was put into Latin his own name was mangled on the cover. That mangled name became the English word 'algorithm,' a step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. What was the mathematician's name?
answer: al-Khwarizmi
choices: al-Khwarizmi
Brahmagupta
Pythagoras
Archimedes
context: His name was Latinized to "Algoritmi" in the title "Algoritmi de numero Indorum" (Algoritmi on the numbers of the Indians), and over time "Algoritmi" became the plain English word "algorithm." Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_ibn_Musa_al-Khwarizmi

question: Archimedes was lowering himself into a bath when he saw how to test King Hiero's gold crown for hidden silver without melting it. The story says he leapt out and ran naked through the streets, shouting one word. What did he shout?
answer: Eureka!
choices: Eureka!
Hosanna!
Bravo!
Hurrah!
context: 'Eureka' is Greek for 'I have found it!' The tale comes from the Roman writer Vitruvius (De Architectura, Book IX), writing about 200 years after Archimedes lived.

question: King Hiero of Syracuse feared a goldsmith had hidden cheap silver in his gold crown. He asked Archimedes to catch the trick without melting the crown. Archimedes found a way to test it by measuring one thing about the crown and a lump of pure gold. What did he measure?
answer: how much water each one pushed out of a tub
choices: how much water each one pushed out of a tub
how much each one weighed on a balance scale
how brightly each one shone in the sunlight
how loudly each one rang when it was struck
context: Silver is bulkier than gold for the same weight, so a crown with silver hidden in it shoves out more water than the same weight of pure gold. (Vitruvius, De Architectura, Book IX)

question: With the right levers and pulleys, Archimedes told King Hiero, he could move any weight, however heavy. To prove it was no joke, he sat at a rig of compound pulleys, took hold of the rope, and with a single gentle tug set a huge loaded weight moving. Hiero was so amazed he said Archimedes should be believed in all he said. What had Archimedes moved by himself?
answer: a fully loaded three-masted ship
choices: a fully loaded three-masted ship
a wagon stacked with marble blocks
a cart piled high with bronze shields
a chariot loaded with sacks of grain
context: Plutarch says the merchant ship 'glided through the water' as if moving by itself while Archimedes sat still and worked a system of compound pulleys. (Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 14)

question: Marcellus brought a Roman fleet against Syracuse in 214 BC, and Archimedes turned the city's sea walls into a weapon. His most feared machine stood on the harbor wall, and the Romans called it the Claw. What did it do to their ships?
answer: lifted them clear of the water and dropped them
choices: lifted them clear of the water and dropped them
set them on fire with flaming arrows
rammed and split them below the waterline
blew them off course with great gusts of wind
context: Plutarch describes cranes with iron hands and beaks that seized ships by the prow, hauled them straight up into the air, then dropped them stern-first -- sinking them or smashing them on the cliffs. (Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 15)

question: The Romans laid siege to Syracuse, where Archimedes built war machines to defend his city. A legend first told long after his death says he set the whole Roman fleet on fire by himself as it lay in the harbor. Serious historians do not believe the story. How does the legend say he did it?
answer: with mirrors that focused the sun into a burning beam
choices: with mirrors that focused the sun into a burning beam
with flaming arrows shot from the city walls
with clay pots of burning oil hurled by catapults
with rafts of blazing pitch pushed out to sea
context: The earliest mention is Lucian (2nd century AD); burning-glasses were named by Anthemius of Tralles around 500 AD. No contemporary historian (Polybius, Livy, Plutarch) mentions any mirror, so most scholars treat it as later legend. (Wikipedia: Archimedes' heat ray)

question: When Syracuse fell to the Romans, a soldier found the old Archimedes and told him to come along. But Archimedes was so lost in his work that he refused to budge until he had finished. The angry soldier killed him. What was he so wrapped up in that it cost him his life?
answer: a geometry problem he was drawing in the sand
choices: a geometry problem he was drawing in the sand
a letter he was writing to King Hiero
a new war-machine he was building
a map of escape routes out of the city
context: Archimedes was about 75 when Syracuse fell in 212 BC. He was so absorbed in a diagram that he never noticed the city had been taken. (Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 19)

question: Archimedes cared more for pure mathematics than for any of his war machines, and he asked that the result he loved best be carved on his tomb. About 137 years after Archimedes died, Cicero found the grave under brambles and thorns and knew it at once by that carving. What did it show?
answer: a sphere sitting inside a cylinder
choices: a sphere sitting inside a cylinder
a lever raising a heavy boulder
a screw lifting water up a tube
a crown weighed against pure gold
context: He had proved that a sphere is exactly two-thirds of the cylinder that encloses it -- in both volume and surface area -- and treasured this result above all others. (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations V.64-66)

question: Cicero, a young Roman lawyer, was working in Sicily around 75 BC, more than a century after Archimedes died, when he set out to hunt down the great man's grave. He believed it lay near an old gate outside Syracuse. He asked the people of the city where their greatest citizen was buried. What did they tell him?
answer: that no such tomb existed at all
choices: that no such tomb existed at all
that it had been moved to Rome long ago
that only priests were allowed to see it
that the Romans had smashed it in the war
context: Serving as quaestor in 75 BC (about 137 years later), Cicero found the grave anyway -- choked in brambles and thorns near the Agrigentine Gate -- and recognized it by a small carved column, even though the locals had sworn no such tomb existed. (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations V.64-66)

question: Archimedes set himself a puzzle in Syracuse: to find pi, the number linking a circle's width to the distance around its rim, more exactly than anyone before him. He worked long before calculators existed, yet his answer stood as the world's best for nearly 400 years. How did he pin pi down?
answer: he trapped the circle between many-sided shapes
choices: he trapped the circle between many-sided shapes
he weighed a round disk against a square one
he rolled a wheel and measured the track it left
he counted the grains of sand laid around its rim
context: Archimedes drew 96-sided polygons inside and outside a circle, proving pi lies between 223/71 and 22/7 (about 3.1408 to 3.1429). It was the best estimate of pi for roughly 400 years. (Archimedes, Measurement of a Circle, Prop. 3)

question: Archimedes is credited with a spiral sealed inside a tube that bears his name. Cranked by its handle, the spiral does something to river water that looks impossible, and farms still use it today. What does Archimedes' screw do to the water as it turns?
answer: It lifts water uphill against gravity
choices: It lifts water uphill against gravity
It freezes the water into solid ice
It splits the water into air and salt
It crushes grain caught inside the tube
context: As the spiral rotates, each turn scoops up a pocket of water and walks it up the slope of the tube. Archimedes is credited with it for irrigating fields; over 2,000 years later the same design still pumps water in wastewater plants and drains the low-lying Nile delta. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedes'_screw; greekreporter.com.

question: Archimedes understood how a lever turns a small push on its long arm into an enormous lift. He was so sure of it that he is said to have boasted: 'Give me a place to stand, and I will move...' What did Archimedes claim he could move?
answer: The Earth itself
choices: The Earth itself
The walls of Syracuse
A mountain in Sicily
The fleet of Rome
context: The popular form is 'Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.' Plutarch's wording is even bolder: Archimedes said that 'if there were another world, and he could go to it, he could move this' one. Source: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus ch.14; Pappus of Alexandria.

question: A Roman soldier found the old Archimedes crouched over a shape he had drawn in the sand when Syracuse fell in 212 BC, the story goes, and Archimedes would not leave until he had finished. His most famous last words, a later paraphrase, were one sharp command. What is he said to have demanded?
answer: Do not disturb my circles!
choices: Do not disturb my circles!
Spare me, I am only a scholar!
Strike, and end an old man's work!
Take me to your general at once!
context: In Latin: 'Noli turbare circulos meos.' The enraged soldier ran him through. Treat it as legend: the earliest detailed account, by Plutarch, has no 'circles' line — it only says Archimedes refused to leave until he had finished his demonstration, 'whereupon the soldier flew into a passion, drew his sword, and dispatched him.' The memorable phrasing is a much later embellishment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noli_turbare_circulos_meos; Plutarch, Life of Marcellus ch.19.

question: Plutarch tells how the Romans besieging Syracuse came to dread the very walls where Archimedes had mounted claws, catapults and huge stone-throwers. Even a plain rope or a stick of wood poking over the top was enough. How did they react to it?
answer: They cried 'There it is!' and turned and fled
choices: They cried 'There it is!' and turned and fled
They cheered, thinking the machines were broken
They hurled their spears blindly at the wall
They knelt and prayed to their war gods
context: Convinced Archimedes was about to aim some new engine at them, the Romans bolted at the sight of any object on the wall. It's one of history's great pictures of one mind terrifying an entire army. Source: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus ch.17.

question: Marcellus, the Roman general, had given his troops one strict order before they broke into Syracuse in 212 BC: take Archimedes alive. In the chaos of the sack a soldier killed the old man anyway, and Marcellus gave him no reward. How did Marcellus treat the killer, and Archimedes' family?
answer: He shunned the killer as polluted and honored Archimedes' kin
choices: He shunned the killer as polluted and honored Archimedes' kin
He executed the killer and burned the body
He promoted the killer and ignored the family
He freed the killer but jailed Archimedes' kin
context: Plutarch says Marcellus 'turned away from his slayer as from a polluted person, and sought out the kindred of Archimedes and paid them honour.' A conquering general mourning the enemy's greatest mind. Source: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus ch.19.

question: Archimedes built the Claw, the catapults and the other engines that held off the Roman fleet at Syracuse for years. Yet Plutarch says he looked down on engineering, and on every craft that serves everyday needs, as unworthy of a real thinker. What did Archimedes do about those machines?
answer: He left no written instructions for any of them
choices: He left no written instructions for any of them
He sold the designs to King Hieron for gold
He smashed them himself before the Romans landed
He demanded the credit go to his students
context: Plutarch says Archimedes regarded the work of an engineer 'and every art that ministers to the needs of life as ignoble and vulgar.' He left no written instructions for his war machines and cared only for pure geometry — so when the engines were gone, the secret of how they worked was gone with him. Source: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus ch.17.

question: Archimedes set himself an absurd-sounding challenge in a work called The Sand Reckoner: to count how many grains of sand it would take to fill the whole universe. Before he could finish the job, he had to invent something first. What was it?
answer: A brand-new system for naming gigantic numbers
choices: A brand-new system for naming gigantic numbers
A telescope to measure the distant stars
A scale precise enough to weigh one grain
A map dividing the universe into squares
context: With nothing bigger than 'myriad' to work with, Archimedes built a fresh notation for naming numbers far past anything the Greeks had words for, and used it to reach an answer of roughly 8 followed by 63 zeros (8 x 10^63) grains. He was doing it to show that even unimaginable quantities can be pinned down by reasoning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sand_Reckoner.

question: Archimedes squeezed the true value of pi between two numbers he could calculate, while people before him had found it only by measuring round objects and eyeballing the ratio. What could Archimedes now claim about pi that no one could before?
answer: Its exact value could be nailed down by proof
choices: Its exact value could be nailed down by proof
Its exact value was a tidy whole fraction
Its exact value matched a square's diagonal
Its exact value shrank as a circle grew
context: The inside polygon's edge is a bit too small and the outside one a bit too big, so the true circle is squeezed between them. Archimedes proved pi lies between 3 + 10/71 and 3 + 1/7 — about 3.1408 to 3.1429 — the first time pi was pinned down by proof rather than by tape measure. Source: Measurement of a Circle, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurement_of_a_Circle.

question: J. L. Heiberg, a Danish scholar, bent over an old prayer book in 1906, magnifying glass in hand. Around 1229 a monk had scrubbed its parchment clean and written prayers over the top, but Heiberg could read the faint text underneath: The Method, a lost book of Archimedes. Why did it stun mathematicians?
answer: In it Archimedes anticipated calculus about 1,900 years early
choices: In it Archimedes anticipated calculus about 1,900 years early
In it Archimedes claimed the Earth circled the Sun
In it Archimedes confessed his machines were fakes
In it Archimedes recorded the date of his own death
context: 'The Method of Mechanical Theorems' showed Archimedes using ideas resembling the calculus that Newton and Leibniz would not formalize until the late 1600s — roughly 1,900 years later. The faded prayer-book overwriting nearly erased one of the most advanced texts of the ancient world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedes_Palimpsest; The Method of Mechanical Theorems.

question: Whales and dolphins swim in the sea among the fish, yet Aristotle watched them closely and insisted that they are no fish at all. He pointed to two things about them that set them apart. What did Aristotle notice?
answer: They breathe air and bear live young
choices: They breathe air and bear live young
They have leathery shells over their skin
They are cold-blooded but build nests
They hatch from eggs hidden in the sand
context: Aristotle was right: whales and dolphins are mammals that surface to breathe and give birth to live calves. Many of his sea observations were dismissed as fanciful and only confirmed in the 1800s. (Wikipedia: History of Animals; iep.utm.edu/aristotle-biology)

question: On the shores of Lesbos, Aristotle studied sea creatures, and he wrote that the mouth of one of them looked 'like a horn lantern with the panes of horn left out.' Zoologists still call that mouth Aristotle's lantern. Which sea creature has it?
answer: a sea urchin
choices: a sea urchin
a sea sponge
a starfish
a jellyfish
context: A sea urchin's mouth has five teeth meeting in the middle, which reminded Aristotle of the five panes of a candle lantern of his day. The name 'Aristotle's lantern' is still used by scientists. (Wikipedia: Aristotle's lantern; britannica.com/science/Aristotles-lantern)

question: Aristotle wrote one of the first serious books on animals, from what they ate to how they were built inside, and he did not just copy other writers. He checked his findings with the working people who handled animals every day. Which three kinds of workers did Aristotle question?
answer: beekeepers, fishermen, and sponge divers
choices: beekeepers, fishermen, and sponge divers
hunters, herdsmen, and bird-catchers
farmers, butchers, and snail-gatherers
shepherds, falconers, and horse-breakers
context: Aristotle treated firsthand testimony as evidence, cross-checking his own dissections against the knowledge of people who worked with bees, fish, and sponges. (neelburton.com/2025/05/13/aristotles-biology-on-lesbos; plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-biology)

question: Aristotle told his students at the Lyceum to study every kind of animal, even the small, ugly and lowly ones that seemed too humble to bother with. A careful eye, he promised, would always be rewarded, however mean the creature. What did he promise every animal would show them?
answer: something natural and something beautiful
choices: something natural and something beautiful
something useful and something profitable
something strange and something frightening
something simple and something dull
context: His full words: 'We should venture on the study of every kind of animal without distaste; for each and all will reveal to us something natural and something beautiful.' (neelburton.com/2025/05/13/aristotles-biology-on-lesbos; plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-biology)

question: Aristotle observed that a bee colony had workers, drones and a single ruler that all the others served, and he called that ruler the 'king bee.' Centuries later, in 1586, a Spaniard named Luis Mendez de Torres showed that Aristotle had the ruler's most basic fact wrong. What was the truth about the 'king bee'?
answer: the ruler was actually a queen, a female
choices: the ruler was actually a queen, a female
the ruler was actually two rival kings
the ruler was just an ordinary worker
the colony actually had no ruler at all
context: Aristotle's era assumed that leadership and reproduction were male, so he naturally read the ruler as a king. The 'king bee' is really an egg-laying queen, as de Torres showed in 1586. (aleteia.org/2018/01/24/why-queen-bees-were-once-king-bees)

question: Aristotle watched the Moon go dark during a lunar eclipse and found in it one of his strongest proofs that the Earth is a ball, not flat, long before anyone had sailed around the world. What did he point to during the eclipse as his proof?
answer: Earth always casts a round shadow on the Moon
choices: Earth always casts a round shadow on the Moon
the curved edge of the Moon flattens out
a straight band of darkness crosses the Moon
the Moon's whole face dims to an even grey
context: During an eclipse the Earth passes between Sun and Moon; the shadow it throws is always curved -- only a ball casts a round shadow from every angle. Aristotle added that ships' hulls vanish over the horizon before their masts, and that travelers see new stars as they move north or south. (spark.iop.org/greek-evidence-earths-shape-and-spin)

question: Georges Cuvier found a loose arm inside a female octopus in 1829, just as Aristotle had described: a mating arm that can break off and stay inside her. The thing baffled Cuvier so much that he gave it the wrong kind of name. What did he first take it to be?
answer: a parasitic worm
choices: a parasitic worm
a new kind of eel
a piece of seaweed
an unhatched egg
context: The detachable mating arm is real -- it is called the hectocotylus. Aristotle's account was dismissed as a fishermen's tale until Cuvier described it in 1817, and in 1829 he mistook a detached one inside a paper-nautilus for a worm, naming it 'Hectocotyle.' (Wikipedia: History of Animals; Wikipedia: Hectocotylus)

question: Eels stumped Aristotle, who studied every animal he could catch. He never found an eel egg, a baby eel or any eel parents anywhere. He decided that eels must have no parents at all and simply arise from something else. Where did Aristotle say eels came from?
answer: from the mud and 'guts of the earth'
choices: from the mud and 'guts of the earth'
from the foam of breaking waves
from rotting fish left in the sun
from raindrops falling on the river
context: This 'spontaneous generation' was wrong but understandable: eels breed far out in the Sargasso Sea, so no one in the ancient world ever saw them spawn. Their true reproduction was not pinned down until Carlo Mondini found eel ovaries in 1777. (smithsonianmag.com -- the search for the origin of eels; Wikipedia: Spontaneous generation)

question: Aristotle cracked open a hen's egg day by day and watched the tiny chick take shape inside, in one of the world's first experiments in embryology, the study of how babies grow before birth. One organ appeared before any other, the first spark of the new bird. Which organ did Aristotle see form first?
answer: the heart
choices: the heart
the brain
the eyes
the wings
context: Aristotle wrote that 'the heart is first to be differentiated in actuality,' and that it was also the first to begin beating. This true observation convinced him that the heart, as the body's first and most central organ, must also be the seat of life and thought. (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-biology; Wikipedia: Aristotle's biology)

question: Aristotle taught that human intelligence, feeling and the soul itself did not live in the brain at all. To him the brain looked pale, bloodless and dull, so he gave it a small, humble job instead. What job did Aristotle assign to the brain?
answer: to cool the overheated heart
choices: to cool the overheated heart
to store up the day's memories
to pump blood out to the body
to keep the senses working
context: Aristotle treated the brain as a kind of radiator for the hot, ever-beating heart -- he reasoned this partly from noticing that when the heart stops, the whole body goes cold. Medical students were taught a heart-centered body until the 1500s. (Wikipedia: Cardiocentric hypothesis; Wikipedia: Aristotle's biology)

question: Aristotle pictured the whole universe as a set of giant clear spheres nested one inside another like Russian dolls, with a motionless Earth at the very center. The Moon, the Sun, and each planet rode its own sphere -- but he had to put all the countless stars somewhere too. Where did Aristotle place all of the stars?
answer: all together on the single outermost sphere
choices: all together on the single outermost sphere
each one on its own little sphere
on a sphere nearer than the Moon's
drifting loose between the planets' spheres
context: Aristotle borrowed these nested 'crystalline spheres' from Eudoxus, with the stars pinned to the outermost shell of all. This Earth-centered picture ruled astronomy for centuries, until Copernicus moved the Sun to the center. (cabinet.ox.ac.uk -- celestial sphere; teachastronomy.com -- Aristotle and geocentric cosmology)

question: Aristotle set the whole of nature in a single fixed order: bare rock at the bottom, then plants, then animals, and human beings at the top. His ranking shaped how the West saw nature for 2,000 years. What famous name did later ages give it?
answer: the Great Chain of Being
choices: the Great Chain of Being
the Ladder of Souls
the Stair of Ranks
the Order of Forms
context: Aristotle called it the scala naturae ('ladder of nature'); plants had a 'vegetative' soul, animals a 'sensitive' soul, and humans a 'rational' soul at the top. It became known as the Great Chain of Being and shaped Western biology for two millennia. (Wikipedia: Aristotle's biology; neelburton.com/2025/05/13/aristotles-biology-on-lesbos)

question: Charles Darwin was reading Aristotle's Parts of Animals, freshly translated, early in 1882, only weeks before he died. In a letter he set his own two scientific gods, Linnaeus and Cuvier, beside the old Greek. What did he write about the two of them next to Aristotle?
answer: they were mere schoolboys to old Aristotle
choices: they were mere schoolboys to old Aristotle
they were the true equals of old Aristotle
they had borrowed all their ideas from him
they had never once read his work
context: Darwin wrote: 'Linnaeus and Cuvier have been my two gods... but they were mere schoolboys to old Aristotle.' He penned it after reading a new translation of Aristotle's 'Parts of Animals.' (libquotes.com/charles-darwin; link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1004404206298)

question: Aristotle opened a school of his own in Athens around 335 BC, the Lyceum, in a grove sacred to the god Apollo. His followers came to be called the Peripatetics, after one odd habit of their teacher's. How did Aristotle teach?
answer: He walked about as he taught, never sitting down
choices: He walked about as he taught, never sitting down
He lectured from a high marble throne
He taught only by candlelight at midnight
He made students memorize in total silence
context: The school was nicknamed the Peripatos, 'the walkway,' and his followers were called Peripatetics, 'the walkers,' because lessons happened while strolling the covered colonnades. Source: Britannica, 'Lyceum (Greek philosophical school)'; philopedia.org Peripatetic School.

question: King Philip of Macedon needed a tutor for his 13-year-old heir in 343 BC, and he paid Aristotle to teach the boy at a royal country estate called Mieza. For three years Aristotle drilled him in Homer, science and rhetoric. The prince grew up to be the greatest conqueror of the ancient world. Who was he?
answer: Alexander the Great
choices: Alexander the Great
Julius Caesar
Hannibal of Carthage
Leonidas of Sparta
context: The lessons were held at Mieza, the 'shrine of the Nymphs,' whose Nymphaeum still survives as a two-story arcade of Ionic columns among natural caves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle; GreekReporter, 'Mieza: The School Where Aristotle Tutored Alexander.'

question: Plutarch tells of a jewelled casket taken from the tent of the Persian king Darius after his defeat in 331 BC. The young Macedonian who won it, Aristotle's old pupil, kept inside it the thing he treasured most, and at night it lay under his pillow, next to his dagger. What was in the casket?
answer: A copy of Homer's Iliad corrected by Aristotle
choices: A copy of Homer's Iliad corrected by Aristotle
A lock of his mother Olympias's hair
The crown he took from Darius
A map of every land left to conquer
context: Nicknamed 'the casket copy,' Alexander called it 'a perfect portable treasure of all military virtue.' Aristotle had personally corrected the text for him. (Legend via Plutarch.) Source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 8 & 26 (Livius.org / classics.mit.edu).

question: Aristotle spent three years, from around 343 BC, tutoring a teenage Macedonian prince at Mieza, a royal country estate. Nearly four centuries later, Plutarch wrote that visitors to the estate could still see traces of those lessons. What could they see?
answer: Aristotle's stone seats and his shady garden walks
choices: Aristotle's stone seats and his shady garden walks
His original lesson scrolls and lecture notes
A marble statue and golden altar to Aristotle
The dagger and shield Alexander trained with
context: Plutarch wrote that visitors could still see 'Aristotle's stone seats, and the shady walks which he was wont to frequent' — the actual benches where the philosopher taught the future world-conqueror. Source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 7 (via Livius.org, Dryden/Clough translation).

question: Beside a lagoon on the island of Lesbos, Aristotle spent about two years cutting open sea creatures, and one of his strangest finds concerned the dogfish, a small shark. How does a mother dogfish nourish her pup before it is born?
answer: By feeding it through a cord and a placenta, like a mammal
choices: By feeding it through a cord and a placenta, like a mammal
By spitting a stream of food into the water for it
By tucking the eggs into a pouch on its belly
By warming the eggs inside its own mouth
context: Aristotle described how a dogfish nourishes its embryo through a cord attached to something like a mammalian placenta — an account so precise the anatomist Johannes Peter Muller re-investigated and confirmed it in 1842, over 2,000 years later. He worked in the Pyrrha lagoon, today the Gulf of Kalloni. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle's_biology; EMBRC, 'Aristotle, the first marine biologist.'

question: At his Lyceum, Aristotle kept an organised collection of things for his students to examine, so that they learned from real objects and not only from words. Scholars see it as the ancestor of two kinds of places people still visit today. Which two?
answer: The research library and the museum
choices: The research library and the museum
The hospital and the pharmacy
The courthouse and the senate
The bank and the marketplace
context: At the Lyceum Aristotle assembled what may be the first research library and museum — manuscripts, maps, and 'museum objects' (biological specimens) gathered for study — pioneering learning from a collected reference set of real things rather than from texts alone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle.

question: Aristotle once reported something tender about a river catfish. He said the father fish guarded the eggs for six or seven weeks, scaring off intruders and even making a murmuring sound. People laughed it off for centuries, until Louis Agassiz, a Swiss naturalist, proved him right in the 1850s. What official name did Agassiz give the fish?
answer: He named it Silurus aristotelis, 'Aristotle's catfish'
choices: He named it Silurus aristotelis, 'Aristotle's catfish'
He named it Silurus platoni, after the teacher Plato
He named it Silurus lesbiacus, after the isle of Lesbos
He named it Silurus macedonicus, after Alexander's homeland
context: After confirming the long-doubted observation in 1856-57, Agassiz named the species Silurus aristotelis — 'Aristotle's catfish' — after him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle's_biology; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle's_catfish; GBIF Silurus aristotelis (Agassiz, 1857).

question: Plato had taught at his Academy on private, walled grounds in Athens. When his old student Aristotle opened a rival school, the Lyceum, it had to meet on public land and teach anyone who came, for free. One plain fact about Aristotle himself explains why he could not simply buy grounds of his own. What was it?
answer: He was a foreigner, not an Athenian citizen
choices: He was a foreigner, not an Athenian citizen
He had sworn a philosopher's vow of poverty
Philip of Macedon forbade him to own land
Plato's Academy held the rights to all teaching land
context: Aristotle was not an Athenian citizen, so by law he could not own property in Athens; that is why his Lyceum met on public grounds and lectured openly, free of charge, unlike Plato's private Academy. Source: Britannica, 'Lyceum'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle.

question: 'All Athenians are Greek; all Greeks are human; so all Athenians are human.' Aristotle, who invented formal logic, set out patterns of argument like this one. A reader who knows nothing at all about Athens or the Greeks can still see that it holds. Why must the conclusion follow?
answer: Because the shape of the argument alone forces the conclusion
choices: Because the shape of the argument alone forces the conclusion
Because Athens was the most famous city in the ancient world
Because Aristotle himself was Greek and knew the facts
Because most people already agree that Athenians are human
context: In his Prior Analytics, Aristotle defined the syllogism as 'a discourse in which, certain things being stated, something other than what is stated follows of necessity from them.' The first-figure pattern 'All A are B; all B are C; so all A are C' is traditionally nicknamed Barbara. Source: Aristotle, Prior Analytics; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prior_Analytics; plato.stanford.edu, 'Aristotle's Logic.'

question: Aristotle described a feature of the male octopus so bizarre that naturalists laughed it off as a fisherman's tall tale for more than two thousand years, until zoologists of the nineteenth century proved the old philosopher right. What had Aristotle claimed?
answer: One of the male's arms breaks off inside the female during mating
choices: One of the male's arms breaks off inside the female during mating
The octopus changes color to match any human's mood
The octopus can live for a year out of the water
The male octopus sings to lure the female closer
context: The specialized arm is called the hectocotylus; it transfers sperm and can snap off. Cuvier confirmed Aristotle's account in his 1817 'Le Regne Animal.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle's_biology.

question: Aristotle wrote in the Politics that the human being is a political animal, made by nature to live in a community. A person who could truly live wholly outside any community at all, he argued, must be one of two extremes. Which two?
answer: Either a beast or a god
choices: Either a beast or a god
Either a slave or a king
Either a child or a fool
Either a soldier or a priest
context: The Greek phrase is zoon politikon. Aristotle meant humans are made for the polis (the city); anyone needing no community is below humanity (a beast) or above it (a god). Source: Aristotle, Politics I.2, 1253a (antiquitatem.com; oll.libertyfund.org).

question: Athens accused Aristotle of impiety, the same charge that had sent Socrates to his death, and he fled the city rather than stand trial. He explained his escape with a pointed line. What did he say he would not let the Athenians do?
answer: Sin twice against philosophy
choices: Sin twice against philosophy
Burn his library to ashes
Forget the name of Alexander
Make him drink as Socrates did
context: Aristotle fled to Chalcis declaring he would not let the Athenians 'sin twice against philosophy' (the first 'sin' being the execution of Socrates). He died at Chalcis the next year, 322 BCE. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle (citing ancient tradition).

question: Talaat Pasha, the Ottoman Interior Minister, ordered the first mass arrests of Armenians in Constantinople on 24 April 1915, by night. He did not start with soldiers or with rebels; he began with a different group. Which Armenians did he have seized first?
answer: The doctors, lawyers, teachers and poets — the community's educated leaders
choices: The doctors, lawyers, teachers and poets — the community's educated leaders
The soldiers and officers — the men serving at the war front
The bankers and traders — the community's wealthiest men
The farmers and laborers — the people of the villages
context: Armenians call that night 'Red Sunday' (Karmir Kiraki) and still mark April 24 as Genocide Remembrance Day. The first wave seized roughly 235 to 270 community leaders; later waves brought the total to about 2,345 notables, sent to the holding towns of Cankiri and Ayas, and most were later murdered. Striking down a people's leadership first is a hallmark of killing organized from the top. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deportation_of_Armenian_intellectuals_on_24_April_1915

question: Starving Armenian refugees lay scattered around Deir ez-Zor, a desert town on the Euphrates River, where the death marches ended. One foreign official kept count of the dying and reported about 150,000 of them around the town. Who was this witness keeping the tally?
answer: The American consul in the city of Aleppo
choices: The American consul in the city of Aleppo
The Russian consul in the city of Tiflis
The British consul in the city of Baghdad
The German consul in the city of Mosul
context: He was Jesse B. Jackson, the United States vice-consul at Aleppo, who funneled relief to survivors and documented the catastrophe. Deir ez-Zor, on the Euphrates, was the terminal point of the death marches; historians estimate roughly 192,000 Armenians perished in that area alone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deir_ez-Zor_camps

question: American schoolchildren sent their pennies to feed 'the starving Armenians' an ocean away. Near East Relief saved more than a million refugees and raised 132,000 orphans, and one rallying phrase became tied to its mission. What was the phrase?
answer: They Shall Not Perish
choices: They Shall Not Perish
Lest We Forget Them
Bread For The Nations
Mercy Knows No Border
context: Founded in 1915 at Ambassador Morgenthau's urging, Near East Relief raised more than $116 million and cared for Armenian, Greek, and Assyrian orphans alike — one of the first great humanitarian campaigns in history. Source: https://neareast.org/our-history/

question: Raphael Lemkin, a Polish-Jewish law student, was haunted by the Ottoman destruction of the Armenians, a crime that no law existed to punish. In 1944 he gave a name to the deliberate destruction of a whole people, and he fought to get it into the Nuremberg case. What name did he give it?
answer: genocide
choices: genocide
holocaust
pogrom
extermination
context: Lemkin built it from the Greek 'genos' (race or tribe) and the Latin '-cide' (killing). He later said the Armenian case was directly on his mind when he made the word, and he was the first person ever to write the phrase 'Armenian Genocide.' Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/coining-a-word-and-championing-a-cause-the-story-of-raphael-lemkin

question: Aurora Mardiganian, a teenage Armenian survivor, escaped to America after a forced march of more than 1,400 miles; she had seen her family killed and had been sold in Turkish slave markets. A Hollywood silent film told her story in 1919. What did she do that almost no survivor ever does?
answer: She starred in it, playing herself on screen
choices: She starred in it, playing herself on screen
She refused to watch it and walked out
She sued the studio that had made it
She wrote the music score for it
context: The film was 'Ravished Armenia' (also called 'Auction of Souls'). Mardiganian testified she had seen sixteen young Armenian girls crucified, and the film depicted it; her tour helped raise enormous sums for Armenian relief. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora_Mardiganian

question: Soghomon Tehlirian, a young Armenian survivor, shot and killed the exiled Talaat Pasha on a Berlin street in 1921. Talaat had directed the killing of the Armenians, and Tehlirian had lost dozens of relatives in the slaughter. Germany put him on trial. What became of him?
answer: The German jury heard the genocide evidence and acquitted him
choices: The German jury heard the genocide evidence and acquitted him
He was hanged within a week of the shooting
He was sentenced to life in a Prussian prison
He escaped Berlin before the trial could begin
context: Nemesis was the Greek goddess of retribution. Because the men who ordered the killings were never tried, survivors set out to deliver justice themselves; Tehlirian used a Luger pistol and shot Talaat once in the back of the neck. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soghomon_Tehlirian

question: Komitas, a priest and composer, had saved Armenia's folk music by writing down thousands of its village songs. He was among those seized in Talaat's arrests of 24 April 1915, and friends who included the American ambassador got him freed. But he had already witnessed the slaughter. What became of the man who saved Armenia's songs?
answer: He broke down and lived his last 20 years silent in an asylum
choices: He broke down and lived his last 20 years silent in an asylum
He fled to Paris and composed there into old age
He led survivors across the Syrian desert to safety
He went home and rebuilt the national choir
context: Among those who intervened to free Komitas was the U.S. ambassador, Henry Morgenthau. Having witnessed the killing, Komitas suffered a complete mental breakdown and spent his final two decades in psychiatric asylums, silent, until his death in 1935. The man who saved his nation's music was broken by watching its people die. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komitas

question: Henry Morgenthau, America's ambassador in Constantinople, begged Talaat Pasha again and again in 1915 to stop the killing, while the Ottoman government marched whole Armenian villages into the Syrian desert to die of thirst, hunger and massacre. Talaat gave one short, cold answer and treated the matter as closed. What did he say?
answer: There are no more Armenians.
choices: There are no more Armenians.
The matter is out of my hands.
They will be returned after the war.
We did only what Russia forced on us.
context: His full reply, recorded in Vahakn Dadrian's History of the Armenian Genocide, was: 'What on earth do you want? The question is settled. There are no more Armenians.' The flat finality of that line captures the intent behind the killing better than any statistic. Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Mehmed_Talat

question: Watching the Armenian deportations with his own eyes, Henry Morgenthau, the United States ambassador in the Ottoman capital, Constantinople, cabled Washington on 16 July 1915. His message named exactly what he believed was happening to the Armenian people. What phrase did he use?
answer: a campaign of race extermination is in progress
choices: a campaign of race extermination is in progress
a tragic famine has gripped the eastern provinces
a wartime disorder threatens the Christian population
a forced migration of doubtful necessity is underway
context: Morgenthau confronted the Ottoman leaders to their faces and later published what he saw in his 1918 book 'Ambassador Morgenthau's Story.' An American diplomat in the capital naming it 'race extermination' as it happened is among the clearest proofs that the killing was intended, not wartime chaos. Source: https://www.armenian-genocide.org/morgenthau.html

question: The Ottoman government gave its slaughter of the Armenians a legal disguise in May 1915. Its decree framed the round-ups not as murder but as a routine, lawful wartime measure, though the Syrian desert soon told the truth. What did the decree claim the Armenians were merely undergoing?
answer: a temporary relocation for safety
choices: a temporary relocation for safety
an emergency military draft
a tax on enemy property
a quarantine against disease
context: The decree, passed May 29, 1915, is known as the Tehcir Law, or Temporary Deportation Law. Dressing genocide in the language of an orderly 'resettlement' is the trick later regimes copied: the paperwork said relocation, the desert held the truth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide

question: In a Berlin courtroom, Soghomon Tehlirian admitted that he had shot the exiled Talaat Pasha dead. Instead of denying the killing, his lawyers put the genocide itself on trial, parading the evidence of the massacres before the world. Asked to speak, Tehlirian gave the court one unforgettable sentence. What did he say?
answer: I have killed a man, but I am not a murderer.
choices: I have killed a man, but I am not a murderer.
I only did what your courts refused to do.
Judge me as you judged my whole people.
I acted alone and I regret nothing at all.
context: The twelve-man German jury deliberated barely over an hour and acquitted him; the not-guilty verdict made headlines around the world and is part of what drew Raphael Lemkin to study the case. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soghomon_Tehlirian

question: Adolf Hitler's generals feared in August 1939 that the world would punish mass murder, and Hitler, days before he invaded Poland, is said to have waved their worry away. He pointed to an earlier slaughter the world had already forgotten. The exact wording is disputed, but the lesson stands: a forgotten genocide invites the next. Which killing is he reported to have named?
answer: the annihilation of the Armenians
choices: the annihilation of the Armenians
the famine in Soviet Ukraine
the massacres of the American Indians
the slaughter in the Belgian Congo
context: The line comes from a contested transcript, the 'L-3 document' handed to the Nuremberg prosecutors by the journalist Louis Lochner; some historians doubt its precise wording, which is why it is treated as testimony rather than verified record. Reported words: 'Who, after all, speaks today of the annihilation of the Armenians?' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hitler's_reference_to_the_Armenian_genocide  (Legend.)

question: The roaring guns finally went silent on the Western Front in 1918, ending a war that had killed millions. Officers said the moment was easy to remember, because it was built from a single number said three times over. What was that famous pattern?
answer: The eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month
choices: The eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month
The seventh hour of the seventh day of the seventh month
The ninth hour of the ninth day of the ninth month
The first hour of the first day of the first month
context: 11:00 a.m. on the 11th day of the 11th month, 1918 — three elevens — is why the moment is so easy to remember. November 11 became Armistice Day, first marked in 1919, and is honored today as Veterans Day in the United States and Remembrance Day in the Commonwealth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_11_November_1918

question: Marshal Ferdinand Foch set out the Allied terms to the German delegates in 1918 inside his own railway carriage, parked on a hidden siding in the Compiegne forest. Twenty-two years later, in June 1940, the carriage had one more part to play. What happened to it?
answer: Adolf Hitler had it hauled out so he could force a beaten France to surrender in it
choices: Adolf Hitler had it hauled out so he could force a beaten France to surrender in it
French soldiers hid it underwater in a flooded tunnel to keep it safe
It was given to the United States and put on display in Washington
It was rebuilt into a moving hospital train for wounded soldiers
context: In June 1940 Hitler had the carriage dragged from its museum back to the same forest clearing and made defeated France surrender inside it — even deliberately sitting in Marshal Foch's old chair before storming out early. The carriage was later taken to Germany and destroyed near the end of WWII in 1945, reportedly burned or blown up by the SS as American troops closed in; an identical sister car stands in its place at Compiègne today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compi%C3%A8gne_Wagon

question: Private Henry Gunther, an American soldier, charged a German machine-gun nest on the Western Front in 1918, while the German gunners rose to their feet, waving at him to stop. Commanders already knew the ceasefire was coming. Gunther kept charging and fired, so the gunners shot back. When was he killed?
answer: At 10:59 a.m., one minute before the war ended
choices: At 10:59 a.m., one minute before the war ended
Three days after the armistice was already signed
The night before, in a raid that started early
At noon, an hour after the guns had fallen silent
context: Private Henry Gunther is considered the last soldier of any nation killed in World War I, shot at 10:59 a.m. — sixty seconds before the 11:00 ceasefire. He was one of about 2,738 men killed on that final day, even though commanders already knew the armistice had been signed before dawn (between roughly 5:00 and 5:45 a.m.) and had simply set the ceasefire six hours later. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Gunther and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_11_November_1918

question: Marcel Duchamp bought a plain porcelain urinal from a New York plumbing showroom in 1917, turned it on its back and signed it with the false name R. Mutt. He entered it in an art exhibition as a serious sculpture, mocking the whole idea of fine art. What one-word title did he give it?
answer: Fountain
choices: Fountain
Cascade
Monument
Spring
context: Marcel Duchamp signed the urinal "R. Mutt 1917" and titled it Fountain, submitting it to the 1917 Society of Independent Artists exhibition in New York. The Society had promised to show any work by any artist who paid the fee — yet they rejected Fountain an hour before the show opened. Duchamp was secretly on the board himself and resigned in protest over his own anonymous urinal being thrown out. It became the most famous example of Dada "anti-art." Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fountain_(Duchamp)

question: Congress begged the states for $3,800,000 in its last appeal before the Constitution took the place of the Articles of Confederation. Under the Articles it could not tax a single person; it could only ask each state to chip in, a plea called a requisition. How much did the states actually pay in?
context: Out of $3.8 million requested, the states sent a grand total of $663 — they treated the demands, in a phrase of the era, as 'mere recommendations' and 'pompous petitions for charity.' A government that can beg but not collect cannot pay its soldiers or its debts; this is the central reason the Constitution gave Congress the power to tax directly. Source: Constitution Annotated, Library of Congress (constitution.congress.gov, ALDE_00013388).

question: New Jersey had no great seaport of its own, and under the Articles of Confederation it was caught between New York's port to the north and Philadelphia's to the south, which drained its trade while the states taxed one another's goods like foreign rivals. Benjamin Franklin mocked its plight with one homely image. What was it?
answer: a barrel tapped at both ends
choices: a barrel tapped at both ends
a sheep penned between two wolves
a coin worn smooth by two hands
a candle burned at both ends
context: Franklin likened New Jersey to a barrel tapped at both ends, its trade drained into New York and Philadelphia at once; the line is preserved in Abram Browning's 1876 Centennial speech. New Jersey struck back by taxing a New York-owned lighthouse on Sandy Hook. Source: libquotes.com (Franklin, via Browning 1876); Project MUSE, 'A Barrel Tapped at Both Ends.'

question: Vedic priests composed the Rigveda in ancient India, more than a thousand sacred hymns in Sanskrit that are still chanted today. Its very first hymn does not praise the king of the gods or the sun. Which god do its opening words name?
answer: Agni, the god of sacred fire
choices: Agni, the god of sacred fire
Indra, the dragon-slaying warrior
Soma, the sacred pressed potion
Savitr, the shining sun-god
context: The first word of the entire Rigveda is 'Agni' — the fire god. Hymn 1.1 opens by praising him, and roughly 200 of the Rigveda's 1,028 hymns are addressed to Agni, making him the most-invoked god after the warrior Indra. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigveda.

question: Priests pressed the juice of a holy plant and filtered it for the Vedic sacrifice, and one of the Rigveda's three chief gods was the god of that plant. The Rigveda's ninth book, all 114 of its hymns, is his from start to finish. Which god gets a whole book to himself?
answer: Soma
choices: Soma
Agni
Indra
Varuna
context: The 9th mandala — the 'Soma Mandala' — is made up entirely of 114 hymns sung as the soma juice was strained and purified. Soma is one of the Rigveda's three chief gods alongside Indra and Agni. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigveda; wisdomlib.org 'The Ninth Mandala of Rigveda'.

question: The Rigveda's poets composed the Gayatri mantra, a short prayer to Savitr, the sun-god, and Hindus still chant it every day some three thousand years later. For almost all of that long history, how was the prayer passed from one age to the next?
answer: Memorized and chanted aloud, never written down
choices: Memorized and chanted aloud, never written down
Carved onto stone temple walls across India
Copied by scribes onto palm-leaf manuscripts
Printed in the world's first religious book
context: The Gayatri Mantra (Rigveda 3.62.10), a prayer to the sun-god Savitr, is traditionally credited to the sage Vishvamitra and is preceded by the 'great utterance' om bhur bhuvah svah. It is still chanted daily by Hindus today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gayatri_Mantra.

question: Reciters of the Rigveda guarded against any slip by weaving its verses into braided patterns and chanting them even backwards; the hardest pattern, called the bell, swung the words to and fro. The backward check works because of one striking feature of Sanskrit. What is it?
answer: Reversing Sanskrit words doesn't change their meaning
choices: Reversing Sanskrit words doesn't change their meaning
The backward version is a separate sacred hymn
Only priests were allowed to hear the forward version
The words rhyme the same forwards and backwards
context: Reciters used elaborate cross-checking patterns: jata-patha 'braids' words forwards-and-backwards, and the hardest, ghana-patha or 'bell' mode, repeats them in bell-shaped back-and-forth sequences. Backward recitation works as an error-check because reversing Sanskrit words doesn't alter their meaning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_chant.

question: The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) honored Vedic chant in 2008 as a masterpiece of humanity's heritage. It called the chant 'a perfect canon,' kept unchanged in word and even in the exact sounds. What sweeping claim did UNESCO make about the tradition?
answer: It may be the oldest unbroken oral tradition in existence
choices: It may be the oldest unbroken oral tradition in existence
It is the most widely performed chant on Earth today
It is the longest single hymn ever composed by anyone
It is the only chant memorized by an entire people
context: UNESCO named Vedic chant a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity on Nov 7, 2008, calling it possibly 'the oldest unbroken oral tradition in existence' and 'a perfect canon not just in terms of unaltered word order but also in terms of sound.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_chant.

question: Carl Sagan admired the Rigveda's Hymn of Creation, the Nasadiya Sukta, which asks how the universe began and will not give a sure answer. It ends by saying that even the god who watches creation from highest heaven 'knows, or maybe even he does not know.' What did Sagan praise the hymn for showing about ancient India?
answer: A tradition of skeptical questioning
choices: A tradition of skeptical questioning
A hymn of pure praise to the creator
A poem matching later Greek philosophy
The oldest written cosmology on record
context: The Nasadiya Sukta (Rigveda 10.129) opens 'Then even non-existence was not there, nor existence...' and ends not with an answer but a shrug. Carl Sagan praised it as evidence of ancient India's 'tradition of skeptical questioning.' Translation by A.L. Basham, The Wonder That Was India (1954). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasadiya_Sukta.

question: The Hittite king and the king of Mitanni sealed a peace treaty in northern Syria around 1380 BC, and the two kings swore their oaths by Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatya twins. Why did this treaty astonish later scholars?
answer: Those are the same gods praised in the Rigveda, found far west of India
choices: Those are the same gods praised in the Rigveda, found far west of India
The treaty was written in flawless Sanskrit script
It named gods no other ancient people ever worshipped
It was the first treaty ever signed between two kingdoms
context: The Mitanni-Hittite treaty (c. 1380 BC) swore oaths by Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatya twins — Vedic deities — making it one of the earliest references to these gods anywhere, and turning up in Syria, far west of India. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Mitanni.

question: Kikkuli, who trained horses for the kingdom of Mitanni, left a training manual on Hittite clay tablets that counts the horses' laps with words like aika, tera, panza, satta and na. Scholars seized on those counting words as hard evidence. What did they reveal about the Mitanni elite?
answer: They were Indo-Aryan speakers, since the words match Sanskrit numbers
choices: They were Indo-Aryan speakers, since the words match Sanskrit numbers
They were Hurrian speakers who hired Indo-Aryan horsemen
The counting words were really Old Persian, not Sanskrit
The numbers were a secret jargon invented just for trainers
context: Kikkuli's lap-counts — aika (eka, one), tera (tri, three), panza (pancha, five), satta (sapta, seven), na (nava, nine) — are almost identical to Sanskrit numbers, hard evidence of an Indo-Aryan elite in the ancient Near East. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Mitanni.

question: Steppe people buried the oldest spoked-wheel chariots yet found in graves of about 1950 BC, along with the first known bridle-bits. Scholars link them to the ancestors of the Vedic Indo-Aryans, though that reconstruction is still debated. Who left these graves?
answer: The Sintashta culture
choices: The Sintashta culture
The Mitanni kingdom
The Hittite empire
The Harappan cities
context: The Sintashta culture's graves in the southern Urals of Russia (c. 1950-1880 BC) hold the oldest spoked-wheel chariots ever found, buried with the first known bridles and bits. These Proto-Indo-Iranian steppe peoples are linked by scholars to the ancestors of the Vedic Indo-Aryans. The leading model holds that Indo-Aryan speakers moved into northern India around 1500 BC from the Central Asian steppes — a contested reconstruction from language, archaeology and genetics, not a settled date. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chariot; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Aryan_migrations.

question: Nedeljko Cabrinovic stepped out of the crowd by the river in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 and hurled a hand grenade at the open car of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary. What did the grenade do?
answer: It bounced off the car's folded roof and blew up under the next car in line
choices: It bounced off the car's folded roof and blew up under the next car in line
It exploded in mid-air directly above the Archduke's head
It landed in the Archduke's lap and he calmly threw it back
It rolled under the seat and failed to go off at all
context: The grenade had a 10-second fuse; it skipped off the convertible's folded-back roof, rolled into the street, and detonated under the following car, wounding roughly 16-20 people but leaving Franz Ferdinand completely unhurt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: Archduke Franz Ferdinand escaped unhurt when a plotter threw a bomb at his car in Sarajevo on the morning of 28 June 1914. Later that morning the Archduke turned up on the very street where another plotter, Gavrilo Princip, was standing. What brought him there?
answer: The driver took a wrong turn and stopped right in front of Princip
choices: The driver took a wrong turn and stopped right in front of Princip
Princip chased the motorcade for miles on foot
The Archduke insisted on giving a speech in the main square
Austrian police mistakenly guided the car past the assassins
