context: Princip fired an FN Model 1910 in .380 caliber from about 1.5 metres away. The car itself was a 1911 Graf & Stift open-top Double Phaeton. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: Gavrilo Princip stepped up to Archduke Franz Ferdinand's open car in Sarajevo and fired at point-blank range, and one bullet struck the Archduke in the neck. Bleeding to death in the back seat, he did not speak of himself. He spoke to his wounded wife Sophie, slumped beside him. What did he say?
answer: "Sophie, Sophie! Don't die! Live for our children!"
choices: "Sophie, Sophie! Don't die! Live for our children!"
"Drive on, the show must go on as planned."
"Now they have what they wanted from us."
"Tell the Emperor I did my duty to the end."
context: He then repeated 'It is nothing' six or seven times before a violent choking from the hemorrhage. Both he and Sophie were dead by about 11:30 a.m. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/gavrilo-princips-sandwich-79480741/

question: Princip's judges in Austria-Hungary could not send him to the gallows, though his two shots in Sarajevo had set off the First World War. Austrian law hanged no one under twenty, and he had been born just 27 days too late. What sentence did the court give him instead?
answer: The maximum prison term of 20 years
choices: The maximum prison term of 20 years
Hard labor for life in a fortress
A 15-year term cut short by his health
Banishment for life to a penal colony
context: Habsburg law set 20 as the minimum age for execution, and Princip was still 19 by less than a month, so he received the maximum 20-year sentence instead of the rope. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavrilo_Princip

question: Leopold Lojka, the Archduke's driver, hit the brakes when the governor shouted at him, and tried to back the car up. In doing so he made one fatal slip that left the open car dead in the road. What happened?
answer: He accidentally stalled the engine
choices: He accidentally stalled the engine
He backed into the car behind and jammed both
He turned the wheel and hit a lamppost
He flooded the brakes and rolled forward instead
context: The car came to a dead stop in front of Moritz Schiller's delicatessen, the exact spot where Princip happened to be. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/gavrilo-princips-sandwich-79480741/

question: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, shaken but unhurt after the grenade, wanted to see the people it had wounded in the city hospital, and the governor, Potiorek, chose a safer road along the river. Yet the cars still swung onto the old street. Why did the drivers take that route?
answer: No one had told the drivers the route was changed
choices: No one had told the drivers the route was changed
The new route was blocked by the bomb wreckage
The Archduke personally ordered the old turn
A crowd forced the cars off the safer road
context: Potiorek changed the plan but never passed it to the chauffeurs, so Leopold Lojka simply followed the cars ahead onto Franz Joseph Street, straight toward Princip. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: Having missed the Archduke with his grenade, Nedeljko Cabrinovic swallowed a cyanide capsule and jumped into the Miljacka River to die before he could be caught. Both attempts failed, and he was pulled out and arrested. Why did they fail?
answer: The old cyanide only made him vomit and the river was barely ankle-deep
choices: The old cyanide only made him vomit and the river was barely ankle-deep
The capsule was a fake and police nets had been strung across the water
He lost his nerve and spat out the poison before reaching the bank
Bystanders pulled him back and forced an antidote down his throat
context: The cyanide had gone stale, and that dry summer the Miljacka was only about 13 cm (4-5 inches) deep, so Cabrinovic survived to be arrested. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: At Schiller's delicatessen, a famous story says, Gavrilo Princip was eating a sandwich when the Archduke's car appeared right in front of him. Historians find no trace of it in the court records. Where does the sandwich story actually come from?
answer: A 2001 Brazilian novel and a 2003 documentary
choices: A 2001 Brazilian novel and a 2003 documentary
A 1990s History Channel segment on the war
A 1920s newspaper interview with Princip himself
A Sarajevo cafe owner's memoir from the 1930s
context: LEGEND, not history: the shooting was around 10:55 a.m., too early for lunch, and sandwiches weren't a Sarajevo custom. The real cool fact is the wrong turn and the stalled engine, not a sandwich. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/gavrilo-princips-sandwich-79480741/

question: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia a month after Princip's shots, to punish it for the Archduke's murder. Each of Europe's great powers had promised to fight for another, and now those promises came due. What happened over the next week?
answer: Germany, Russia, France, Belgium, and Britain were all dragged into the fighting
choices: Germany, Russia, France, Belgium, and Britain were all dragged into the fighting
Russia and France mobilized briefly, then both backed down and stood aside
Britain, Germany, and Italy brokered a settlement that kept the war between two nations
Serbia quickly surrendered and the great powers stayed out of the quarrel
context: The web of alliances meant Austria's declaration against Serbia dragged in the great powers within about a week, turning two gunshots into the First World War. Germany, Russia, France, Belgium, Montenegro, and Great Britain were all pulled in. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/the-assassination-of-archduke-franz-ferdinand

question: The young plotters who killed Franz Ferdinand chose 28 June on purpose: it fell on Vidovdan, St Vitus Day, the most sacred anniversary on the Serbian calendar. Every Serbian child grew up knowing what had happened on that date more than 500 years earlier, in 1389. What did the day remember?
answer: The Battle of Kosovo, where Prince Lazar fell to the Ottomans
choices: The Battle of Kosovo, where Prince Lazar fell to the Ottomans
The coronation of Stefan Dusan as the first Serbian emperor
The treaty by which Serbia broke free of the Habsburg crown
The founding of the Serbian church under the monk Saint Sava
context: Vidovdan marked the 1389 defeat where Prince Lazar died fighting the Ottomans; the date carried enormous symbolic weight for the assassins. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavrilo_Princip

question: Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijevic, code-named Apis, ran Serbia's military intelligence. He also led a secret society, and the young Sarajevo plotters' pistols, bombs and training all came from it rather than from the boys themselves. What was that secret society called?
answer: The Black Hand
choices: The Black Hand
The Young Bosnians
The Carbonari
The People's Will
context: The Black Hand's agent Major Vojislav Tankosic supplied the FN pistols and bombs and trained the assassins. Apis himself was executed by firing squad in 1917. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: On trial for the killings in Sarajevo, Gavrilo Princip told his judges that he was a Yugoslav nationalist who wanted to unite all the South Slavs and free them from Austria. When the court asked by what method he meant to achieve it, what did he answer?
answer: "By means of terror."
choices: "By means of terror."
"Through honest persuasion."
"With a Russian army at our backs."
"By the will of God alone."
context: Princip stated his aim was 'the unification of all Yugoslavs... it must be free from Austria,' and named his method as terror. His co-conspirator Trifko Grabez testified he would never have taken part had he known it would lead to a European war. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand

question: Athens grew rich on trade, but Sparta wanted no trade, no merchants and no greed. So the story goes that Spartans used money so bulky and worthless that storing a small fortune took a whole room and a team of oxen to haul it. What was Spartan money made of?
answer: Bars of iron
choices: Bars of iron
Tablets of clay
Shells from the sea
Coins of silver
context: Sparta supposedly used heavy iron bars instead of gold or silver, on purpose, so that wealth was too cumbersome to pile up or trade with — killing greed and commerce in one stroke. (Plutarch credits the lawgiver Lycurgus, but the story is part legend; a real later law banning Spartans from owning gold and silver coins is genuinely attested.) Source: http://kiwihellenist.blogspot.com/2018/02/paying-iron-price-spartan-money.html

question: Pericles stood over the bodies of the Athenian war dead and gave the most famous speech in his city's history, praising everything that made Athens special. One boast was about how Athens treated strangers from other lands. Which boast did he make?
answer: "We throw our city open to all the world"
choices: "We throw our city open to all the world"
"We let no foreigner set foot inside our walls"
"We make the stranger swear to our gods or leave"
"We take the outsider's gold but never his counsel"
context: Pericles boasted Athens 'throws open the city to the world and never by alien acts excludes a foreigner' — the open city. The other choices describe closed-city policies; Sparta really did expel foreigners (a practice called 'xenelasia'), the opposite of what Pericles celebrated. He also called Athens 'the school of Hellas [Greece].' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pericles's_Funeral_Oration

question: The citizens of Athens met in their Assembly on a bare hill called the Pnyx more than forty times a year, to debate and vote on the city's laws. An ordinary Athenian farmer wanted a say in a new law. What did he do at the Assembly?
answer: He climbed a platform and argued before the whole Assembly
choices: He climbed a platform and argued before the whole Assembly
He elected a representative to cast the votes for him
He mailed a written petition to a council of old nobles
He whispered his view to a city magistrate once a year
context: Athenian democracy was DIRECT, not representative: any adult male citizen could mount the speaker's platform (the 'bema') on the Pnyx and address the entire Assembly in person — no go-betweens. (Women, slaves, and foreigners, about three-quarters of the people there, had no vote.) Source: https://www.history.com/articles/ancient-greece-democracy

question: An Athenian citizen who could not read handed his pottery shard to a stranger on the day of a banishment vote and asked him to scratch on the name Aristides. He did not know the stranger was Aristides himself. Athenians could send any man away for ten years this way, with no crime charged. Why did this man want Aristides gone?
answer: He was simply tired of hearing him called "the Just"
choices: He was simply tired of hearing him called "the Just"
He blamed him for a harsh tax that had ruined him
He had lost an important lawsuit that Aristides judged
He bitterly envied Aristides for his famous riches
context: The man didn't even know Aristides by sight — he just said he was sick of everyone forever calling the fellow 'the Just.' Aristides quietly wrote his own name on the shard, handed it back, and was banished. This banishment-by-pottery is where our word 'ostracism' comes from. Source: https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:abo:tlg,0007,024:7

question: Ordinary citizens, not nobles or judges, ran the courts of Athens, on juries of 500 and sometimes 2,500. In the courthouse stood the kleroterion, a stone slab with slots for citizens' bronze name-tickets and a tube that dropped black and white balls. What was this stone machine for?
answer: It picked the day's jurors purely at random
choices: It picked the day's jurors purely at random
It tallied the votes the jurors cast at a trial
It decided guilt on its own once evidence was heard
It chose which rich citizens would pay for a trial
context: The kleroterion chose jurors purely by chance: citizens slotted in bronze name-tickets, and a white ball meant a whole row served that day. Random selection meant no bribe could pick a friendly jury — radical trust in ordinary citizens, the opposite of Sparta's rule by a council of elders. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dikasterion

question: Sparta's army was unbeatable on land and Athens had the mightiest navy in Greece when the two finally fought a brutal war of 27 years, 431 to 404 BC. Sparta could not break Athens until it did one thing. How did land-power Sparta beat sea-power Athens?
answer: It took Persian gold to build a fleet and beat Athens at sea
choices: It took Persian gold to build a fleet and beat Athens at sea
It marched a huge army over the mountains in deep winter
It burned every farm in the Athenian countryside to starve them
It bribed the Athenian generals into surrendering the city
context: To beat Athens, Sparta had to fight at sea — so it took GOLD from Persia, the very empire Greeks had united to defeat, and built a navy. The Spartan admiral Lysander then destroyed 168 Athenian ships at Aegospotami in 405 BC and starved Athens into surrender. (Burning the Athenian farmland really happened early in the war, but didn't win it.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloponnesian_War

question: Gaius Octavius was a teenager when Brutus and Cassius killed his great-uncle, Julius Caesar, on 15 March 44 BC. Caesar's will stunned everyone: it adopted the boy as his son and made him chief heir, and he at once seized the one inheritance that mattered most. What did he take?
answer: Caesar's name
choices: Caesar's name
Caesar's villa
Caesar's sword
Caesar's crown
context: He became 'Caesar' overnight, the most powerful name in Rome handed to a teenager, along with the fortune. That name carried him to supreme power and outlived him as a title for emperors. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus

question: Rome's first emperor first held the consulship in the month the Romans called Sextilis, and in that same month he later took Egypt and ended the civil wars. In 8 BC the Senate renamed the month after him. What is that month called today?
answer: August
choices: August
March
October
January
context: Sextilis became 'Augustus.' His victories are literally written into the calendar every year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextilis

question: 'Whatever is done well enough is done quickly enough,' Augustus liked to say, and he packed the thought into a tidy two-word Latin motto that seemed to contradict itself. What was his famous motto?
answer: 'Make haste slowly'
choices: 'Make haste slowly'
'Conquer by yielding'
'Win by losing'
'Rest, then strike'
context: 'Festina lente' means 'make haste slowly.' Suetonius records the emperor's fondness for the phrase and his saying that whatever is done well enough is done quickly enough. Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Augustus

question: Suetonius, the historian, wrote down the most famous boast Augustus ever made about rebuilding Rome. Augustus had taken a shabby, flood-prone capital, he said, and he had left it a capital fit for an empire. How did he sum up that change?
answer: 'I found Rome brick and left it marble'
choices: 'I found Rome brick and left it marble'
'I found Rome poor and left it rich'
'I found Rome small and left it vast'
'I found Rome weak and left it armed'
context: 'I found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.' In Latin, 'Marmoream relinquo, quam latericiam accepi.' Suetonius adds the boast was 'not without reason,' since Augustus had transformed a city of mud-brick liable to floods and fires. Source: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 28 (perseus.tufts.edu).

question: Octavian took a title on 16 January 27 BC that no Roman had ever borne before, granted to him by the Senate: Augustus. It was not a family name or a place but an ordinary word, lifted into a man's title for the very first time. What did that word mean?
answer: 'the revered one'
choices: 'the revered one'
'the unconquered one'
'the firstborn one'
'the golden one'
context: 'Augustus' meant 'the revered' or 'consecrated one,' a word of religious awe hinting he was edging toward the divine. Granted 16 January 27 BC, the coined word marks the birth of the Empire. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reign_of_Augustus

question: Dying at seventy-five in AD 14, Augustus called for a mirror and had his hair combed. Then, Suetonius says, he asked his gathered friends a strange question about how he had handled his whole long life, summing it up in one surprising image. How did he describe his life at the very end?
answer: as a part played in a comedy
choices: as a part played in a comedy
as a battle hard fought
as a long road now ended
as a debt at last repaid
context: He asked if he had 'played the part well in the comedy of life,' then quoted Greek comedy: 'clap your hands and send us off with applause.' His true last words were to his wife: 'Livia, live mindful of our marriage; and now, farewell.' Source: Suetonius, Augustus (penelope.uchicago.edu).

question: Augustus carefully avoided the one Roman word that could get a man killed: rex, king, a word Romans had hated ever since they threw out their kings. He quietly held all the armies, yet in the Res Gestae, the record of his deeds that stood in bronze at his tomb, he gives himself one plain title and no other. Which title did he choose?
answer: princeps, 'first citizen'
choices: princeps, 'first citizen'
imperator, 'supreme commander'
dictator, 'absolute ruler'
tribunus, 'champion of the people'
context: 'Princeps,' meaning 'first citizen,' is why his system is called the Principate. The careful word let a king avoid being called a king. He also took 'Pater Patriae,' Father of his Country. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principate

question: Augustus boasted that he had shut the double doors of a small shrine in the Roman Forum three times. Those doors stood open in wartime and were closed only when the whole empire was at peace, and in seven centuries before him they had been shut just twice. By the name of which god were they known?
answer: the Gates of Janus
choices: the Gates of Janus
the Gates of Jupiter
the Gates of Mars
the Gates of Saturn
context: The Gates of Janus (the 'Gates of War') were shut three times under Augustus, in 29, 25, and 13 BC, the vivid symbol of the Pax Romana. Janus was the two-faced god of doorways and beginnings. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/augustus-res-gestae/

question: Brutus and Cassius, the killers of Julius Caesar, waited for his adopted son Augustus at Philippi in 42 BC, and before the battle Augustus vowed a temple to a god if he were granted vengeance. He won. Years later he crowned his grand new Forum in Rome with that temple, honoring the god with a new title, the Avenger. Which god did he honor?
answer: Mars the Avenger
choices: Mars the Avenger
Bellona the Avenger
Victoria the Avenger
Quirinus the Avenger
context: The Temple of Mars Ultor ('Mars the Avenger') crowned the Forum of Augustus, fulfilling his vow at Philippi to avenge Caesar's murder. Source: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 29 (perseus.tufts.edu).

question: Augustus kept the Senate, the consuls and the elections, all the old forms of the Republic, while he quietly controlled the armies. In the record of his deeds he gave away the secret in one honest sentence: in the formal powers of his office he was no greater than his fellow magistrates, yet in one other quality he towered over them all. What did he have more of than anyone?
answer: authority, not legal power
choices: authority, not legal power
respect, not high office
fame, not armed force
honor, not the vote
context: Res Gestae 34: he 'surpassed all in authority (auctoritas), but had no more power (potestas) than the others.' Auctoritas was personal weight and influence; potestas was the formal legal power of an office. The honest trade in one sentence: the real control without the king's title. Source: https://www.judaism-and-rome.org/printpdf/res-gestae-divi-augusti-chapter-34

question: Rome enjoyed forty years of peace and stability under Augustus, but at a price the old Republic had fought for centuries to prevent. When he died in AD 14, power did not return to the Senate and the people; it passed on to one chosen successor. What did the Republic lose for good in that handover?
answer: its elected leaders, replaced by family succession
choices: its elected leaders, replaced by family succession
its trade routes, replaced by foreign tribute
its old gods, replaced by emperor worship
its standing army, replaced by hired troops
context: Power passed to his stepson Tiberius, setting the pattern that rule would pass within a family, the very thing the Republic had fought to prevent. The Senate declared the dead Augustus a god (divus). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus

question: Germany invaded its eastern neighbor in September 1939, and outside the small town of Oswiecim the SS later built Auschwitz, the largest of the Nazi death camps. German guards ran the gas chambers there, yet the camp did not stand on German soil. In which country did it stand?
answer: Poland
choices: Poland
Germany
Austria
Czechoslovakia
context: Auschwitz stood about 40 miles west of Krakow, in German-occupied Poland. The original camp, Auschwitz I, opened on May 20, 1940 with its first 30 prisoners. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Auschwitz'.

question: Prisoner metalworkers, on SS orders, forged the iron sign over the main gate of Auschwitz, reading 'Arbeit macht frei,' 'work sets you free': a cruel lie to people being worked to death. As they made it, the prisoners slipped in one silent act of defiance the guards never caught. What did they do?
answer: Welded the letter B upside down
choices: Welded the letter B upside down
Spelled one whole word wrong
Hid their initials underneath
Bent the whole frame crooked
context: The upside-down B in 'ARBEIT' is still visible today - a small protest hidden in plain sight above the gate. Source: Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum; auschwitz-guide.com, 'The Arbeit Macht Frei Gate'.

question: The SS sorted the new arrivals at Auschwitz, sending some straight to the gas chambers and keeping others alive for slave labor. Of all the Nazi camps, only Auschwitz did one thing to the prisoners it spared, a permanent mark that stayed on them for life. What did the SS do to them?
answer: Tattooed a serial number on the forearm
choices: Tattooed a serial number on the forearm
Branded a triangle on the shoulder
Stamped a number on a metal collar
Shaved a wide stripe through the hair
context: Auschwitz was the only Nazi camp that tattooed prisoners with serial numbers, on the left forearm. SS doctors ran 'selections' on the arrival ramp: those judged fit were tattooed and sent to labor; the elderly, the sick, and most mothers with young children were sent straight to the gas chambers. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Auschwitz Camp Complex'.

question: Guards at Auschwitz dropped pellets of a poison called Zyklon B into the gas chambers. It had not been invented as a weapon: before the war, ordinary farmers and shopkeepers bought the same chemical off the shelf. What was Zyklon B normally used for?
answer: Killing insects and rats
choices: Killing insects and rats
Fueling farm tractors
Cleaning factory floors
Preserving canned food
context: Zyklon B was a commercial pesticide - pellets of hydrogen cyanide. An SS man dropped the pellets through openings in the chamber roof, and the gas killed by asphyxiation. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Nazi Gas Chambers / Gassing Operations'.

question: Soldiers of an advancing Allied army reached Auschwitz from the east on 27 January 1945 and freed about 7,000 prisoners, most of them so starved and sick they could barely stand. The world now marks that date as International Holocaust Remembrance Day. Whose army opened the gates?
answer: The Soviet Red Army
choices: The Soviet Red Army
The American Army
The British Army
The Polish Home Army
context: Soldiers of the Soviet Red Army entered the camp on January 27, 1945. Most of the prisoners able to walk had already been driven away days earlier; those left behind were the ones too weak to move. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Soviet Forces Liberate Auschwitz'.

question: The SS ran Auschwitz as three camps: the main camp, a slave-labor camp for a rubber factory, and Birkenau, a killing center with gas chambers and crematoria. About how many people did the SS murder at Birkenau in under five years?
answer: Over 1 million people, most of them Jews
choices: Over 1 million people, most of them Jews
About 50,000, mostly Soviet prisoners of war
About 200,000, mostly Polish political prisoners
About 500,000, mostly disabled Germans
context: Birkenau, begun in October 1941, was the killing center. Auschwitz III-Monowitz served the I.G. Farben synthetic-rubber factory from October 1942. By spring 1943 four large gas-chamber-and-crematorium complexes were running at Birkenau. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Auschwitz'.

question: Adolf Eichmann rushed one country's Jews to Auschwitz in the spring and summer of 1944, with the war all but lost: about 426,000 people in barely ten weeks, most of them gassed within hours of arriving. From which country had they been taken?
answer: Hungary
choices: Hungary
Poland
Greece
the Netherlands
context: The deportation of the Hungarian Jews, from late April to early July 1944, was the single largest to Auschwitz. At the peak of the killing an average of about 6,000 Jews were gassed every day at Birkenau. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Auschwitz'.

question: The SS marched the people picked to die at Birkenau into a sealed underground room. To keep them calm and moving in an orderly line, the guards told them a gentle, ordinary lie about what was about to happen. What did the guards say the people were going to do?
answer: Take a shower
choices: Take a shower
Get a hot meal
Move to a new camp
Line up for new clothes
context: The victims were told they were going to take a shower; instead the doors were sealed and the Zyklon B was dropped in. The deception kept thousands moving quietly to their deaths. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Auschwitz / Gassing Operations'.

question: Rudolf Vrba broke out of Auschwitz with Alfred Wetzler in April 1944, and the two young Slovak Jews hid for three days inside a hollow woodpile while the SS and their tracking dogs hunted them. They had prepared one clever trick to beat the dogs' noses. What was the trick?
answer: Scattered tobacco soaked in gasoline
choices: Scattered tobacco soaked in gasoline
Rubbed mud and ash on their skin
Waded a mile down an icy stream
Smeared themselves with raw onion
context: The gasoline-soaked tobacco threw the search dogs off the scent. Once free, the two men dictated the 'Vrba-Wetzler Report' - the first detailed eyewitness account of the gas chambers, complete with maps - sent to warn the world. Source: Britannica, 'Rudolf Vrba'; Wikipedia, 'Vrba-Wetzler report'.

question: Josef Mengele, an SS doctor, stood on the Auschwitz arrival ramp and, with a flick of his hand, sent some new prisoners to the right and others to the left, and the left meant the gas chamber. The prisoners gave him a grim nickname for it. What did they call him?
answer: the Angel of Death
choices: the Angel of Death
the Butcher of Birkenau
the White Wolf
the Iron Surgeon
context: Mengele took part in at least 74 ramp selections between May 1943 and November 1944. He singled out twins for cruel experiments - drawing their blood and operating on them, often with no anesthetic. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Josef Mengele'.

question: When soldiers reached Auschwitz in January 1945, the SS had fled, leaving warehouses still piled with the belongings of the murdered, among them thousands of suitcases. One detail on many of the cases made them almost unbearable to look at. What was it?
answer: Their owners' names
choices: Their owners' names
A yellow cloth star
A red warning stamp
The SS skull badge
context: About 3,800 suitcases were found, roughly 2,100 still painted with their owners' names - people who had packed expecting to start a new life. The same warehouses held about 7,000 kg of human hair and around 110,000 shoes. Source: Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum, Historical Collection.

question: The Jewish prisoners whom the SS forced to work the Birkenau crematoria rose up in revolt on 7 October 1944. Women slave-laborers had smuggled them gunpowder a pinch at a time from a nearby munitions factory. Before the SS crushed the rising, what did the rebels manage to do with it?
answer: Blew up one of the crematoria
choices: Blew up one of the crematoria
Shot the camp commandant dead
Opened the gate for an escape
Burned down the Kanada warehouses
context: The Sonderkommando rebels destroyed Crematorium IV and killed several SS guards before being overwhelmed. In early January 1945 the SS publicly hanged four young women - including Roza Robota - for supplying the gunpowder. Source: National WWII Museum, 'The Sonderkommando Uprising'.

question: Rudolf Hoss, the commandant of Auschwitz, faced a question at the Nuremberg trials: how did the guards know when the people locked in a gas chamber had finally died? He gave a flat, matter-of-fact answer that became one of the most chilling lines of the whole trial. How did he say they knew?
answer: The screaming stopped
choices: The screaming stopped
The guards checked pulses
A clock simply ran out
A doctor peered through glass
context: In his testimony Hoss said the Zyklon B took three to fifteen minutes, and that 'we knew when the people were dead because they stopped screaming.' He even boasted he had improved on the camp at Treblinka. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf Hoss', citing his Nuremberg testimony and memoir.

question: Hanns Alexander, a Nazi-hunter, tracked down Rudolf Hoss, who had run Auschwitz longer than any other commandant and had lived since the war under the false name Franz Lang. A Polish court sentenced Hoss to hang in 1947. Of all the places the gallows could have stood, where was he hanged?
answer: At Auschwitz, beside the crematorium
choices: At Auschwitz, beside the crematorium
At a prison yard in Warsaw
At Nuremberg, with the others
At an army base in Berlin
context: Hoss was hanged on April 16, 1947 on a small gallows next to the Auschwitz I crematorium - at the very place he had run. The German-Jewish Nazi-hunter Hanns Alexander had found him in 1946. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf Hoss'.

question: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, wrote the Canon of Medicine, a five-book encyclopedia of more than a million words. Universities such as Padua and Bologna were still teaching from it in the 1600s. Doctors put such faith in the book that they gave it a nickname. What did they call it?
answer: The Medical Bible
choices: The Medical Bible
The Doctor's Mirror
The Book of Cures
The Healer's Almanac
context: Avicenna's al-Qanun fi al-tibb was translated into Latin in the 12th century and remained a standard medical textbook in European universities for about 600 years, in use as late as 1650 — earning the nickname the 'Medical Bible.' A book written in the Islamic world taught Europe's doctors for six centuries. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna ; https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Avicenna

question: Young Ibn Sina boasted that he had mastered every science by eighteen, but one book defeated him. He read Aristotle's Metaphysics forty times until he nearly knew it by heart, yet still could not understand it, and he fell into despair. What finally broke the riddle open for him?
answer: a cheap little commentary a bookseller talked him into buying
choices: a cheap little commentary a bookseller talked him into buying
a fresh translation a fellow scholar lent him
a vision of Aristotle that came to him in prayer
a debate he won against a famous rival scholar
context: After 40 readings left him stuck, a bookseller talked Ibn Sina into buying al-Farabi's short commentary on the Metaphysics for just three dirhams — and suddenly it all made sense. He was so overjoyed that he gave thanks to God and handed out alms to the poor. The greatest mind of the age was unlocked by a throwaway booklet he almost refused to buy. Sources: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Avicenna ; https://iep.utm.edu/avicenna-ibn-sina/

question: Ahuitzotl, who conquered more than any other Aztec ruler, rededicated the rebuilt Templo Mayor in 1487. He took his name from a creature of legend, and like every Aztec ruler he had a name-glyph, a small picture that spelled out what his name meant. What did Ahuitzotl's glyph show?
answer: A water-beast with a human hand at the end of its tail
choices: A water-beast with a human hand at the end of its tail
An eagle clutching a writhing serpent in its beak
A jaguar with a obsidian blade for each claw
A feathered serpent swallowing the evening sun
context: The 'ahuizotl' was a mythical aquatic monster said to lurk at the bottom of a lake and grab creatures that came to the water's edge; Ahuitzotl was the 8th Aztec ruler (reigned 1486-1502). Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Ahuitzotl'.  (Legend.)

question: Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec war god, sprang from his mother's womb fully grown and armed, the myth says, and struck down his sister, the goddess Coyolxauhqui. A huge carved stone at the foot of the Templo Mayor pictured her broken body. What became of her head?
answer: It was flung into the sky and became the moon
choices: It was flung into the sky and became the moon
It was buried under the temple as an offering
It was turned to stone and became a mountain
It was carried off by her four hundred brothers
context: The Coyolxauhqui Stone is over 11 ft across and shows the goddess naked, beheaded, with arms and legs cut off; the chance find in 1978 sparked the INAH excavation of the buried Templo Mayor. In the myth, Huitzilopochtli sprang fully armed from Coatlicue's womb and struck Coyolxauhqui down, and her severed head was tossed into the sky and became the moon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coyolxauhqui Stone'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Coyolxauhqui' and 'Templo Mayor.'

question: At the dedication of the Templo Mayor in 1487, priests sacrificed captives for four days on its summit, about 180 feet above Tenochtitlan's market. Two shrines stood side by side on that summit, each painted its own color for its own god. Which two gods shared the top of the Great Temple?
answer: Huitzilopochtli, god of war and sun, and Tlaloc, god of rain
choices: Huitzilopochtli, god of war and sun, and Tlaloc, god of rain
Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent, and Xipe Totec, the flayed one
Coatlicue, the earth mother, and Coyolxauhqui, the moon
Mictlantecuhtli, lord of the dead, and Tezcatlipoca, the smoking mirror
context: The red shrine honored Huitzilopochtli (war and sun); the blue shrine honored Tlaloc (rain). A double flight of steps climbed the western face of the four-tiered pyramid. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Templo Mayor'.

question: Four priests pinned each victim on his back across a stone block atop the Templo Mayor, and a fifth cut open his chest below the ribs with a blade of flint or obsidian. What did the fifth priest do next, the act the whole rite was for?
answer: Tore out the still-beating heart and held it up to the sun
choices: Tore out the still-beating heart and held it up to the sun
Pressed a jade bead onto the victim's tongue
Painted the victim's face blue for the rain god
Read the future in the pattern of the spilled blood
context: The knife was the 'tecpatl' (obsidian or flint); the slab was the 'techcatl'. After the heart was offered to the sun, the body was flung down the temple stairs. Source: Wikipedia, 'Human sacrifice in Aztec culture'; 'Tecpatl'.

question: Mexican archaeologists digging beside the Templo Mayor uncovered the Huey Tzompantli, the great skull rack built in Ahuitzotl's day. Spanish chroniclers had described such racks, and some modern historians had dismissed their stories as propaganda for the conquest. What did the dig prove?
answer: That the mass skull racks were real, not Spanish invention
choices: That the mass skull racks were real, not Spanish invention
That the Spanish had built the racks to frame the Aztecs
That the skulls came from a single plague, not sacrifice
That the racks held only carved stone heads, never real ones
context: Built around 1485-1502 in Ahuitzotl's era, the Huey Tzompantli was about 112 ft long, its hundreds of real skulls coated in lime and cemented into a tower — forensic confirmation of the practice. Source: Smithsonian Magazine (2017); NPR (2017).

question: The Aztecs built the Templo Mayor to stand for Coatepec, the Snake Mountain where, in their myth, the newborn war god Huitzilopochtli sprang up fully armed. Bodies thrown down the temple steps landed on a giant carved stone at its base. What did each falling body act out?
answer: The moon-goddess Coyolxauhqui being hurled down the mountain
choices: The moon-goddess Coyolxauhqui being hurled down the mountain
The drowning of an enemy king beneath the sacred lake
The flooding of the world before the rain god relented
The first sunrise climbing over the eastern horizon
context: The carved disk at the temple foot showed Coyolxauhqui dismembered; every body flung down the stairs replayed Huitzilopochtli's defeat of his sister. Source: Smarthistory, 'The Templo Mayor and the Coyolxauhqui Stone'; Wikipedia, 'Coyolxauhqui Stone'.  (Legend.)

question: Scientists measured each skull from the Huey Tzompantli tower and studied the growth of its teeth, expecting to find captured warriors. What they found led the anthropologist Rodrigo Bolaños to call it a first. Whose remains turned up in the tower besides warriors'?
answer: Women and at least three small children
choices: Women and at least three small children
Elderly priests of the rain god
Spanish soldiers killed in the conquest
Foreign kings sent as royal tribute
context: Bolanos said, 'Something is happening that we have no record of, and this is really new, a first in the Huey Tzompantli.' The find showed sacrifice reached beyond captured fighters. Source: NPR (2017); Smithsonian Magazine (2017).

question: Diego Durán, a Spanish friar, wrote that 80,400 captives were killed at the Templo Mayor's dedication in 1487. That would mean about fourteen deaths a minute, day and night, for four days, and most historians reject the figure as impossible. The Aztecs believed that human blood repaid a debt and kept the sun moving in its endless war against darkness. What do historians estimate the real toll was closer to?
answer: About 20,000
choices: About 20,000
About 250,000
About 500
context: Duran's 80,400 and the Spanish eyewitness claim of 100,000-plus skulls are treated as wild exaggerations; one Aztec source, the Codex Telleriano-Remensis, gives about 4,000. Even the lower estimates describe an enormous death toll. Source: Wikipedia, 'Human sacrifice in Aztec culture'; History.com.

question: Tlaloc, the Aztec rain god, kept his shrine on the summit of the Templo Mayor dressed in blue and white, the colors of water and life. Beside it, on the great pyramid of Tenochtitlan, stood the shrine of the war god Huitzilopochtli. What color was the war god's shrine painted?
answer: Red, the color of blood
choices: Red, the color of blood
White, the color of bone
Green, the color of jade
Gold, the color of the sun
context: The twin shrines split the Aztec world in two: Tlaloc's blue-and-white half for water and life, Huitzilopochtli's red half for blood and war, atop a pyramid about 60 m (180 ft) high. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Templo_Mayor.

question: The Aztecs built the Templo Mayor as the sacred hill of their myths, the place where their war god was born and crushed his enemies. Carved stone heads of one creature ran up the whole length of its great stairway. What animal's heads lined the stairs?
answer: Serpents
choices: Serpents
Jaguars
Eagles
Wolves
context: The hill was Coatepec, 'Snake Mountain,' where Huitzilopochtli was born and defeated his foes, so its stairway was lined with carved serpent heads — worshippers were climbing a man-made sacred mountain. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Templo_Mayor.

question: An Aztec priest cut open a victim's chest atop the great pyramid at Tenochtitlan with a ritual knife called a tecpatl, whose edge was finer than a modern scalpel's. What stone was the knife chipped from?
answer: Obsidian
choices: Obsidian
Marble
Chert
Granite
context: The tecpatl was knapped from obsidian (volcanic glass), or sometimes flint, to an edge sharper than a modern scalpel. Source: Human sacrifice in Aztec culture / Tecpatl, en.wikipedia.org.

question: At Teotihuacan, in the Aztec story of creation, a humble little god covered in sores named Nanahuatzin threw himself into a sacred blaze and became the Fifth Sun. But the new sun stood still on the horizon and would not move. What did the Aztecs believe finally set it moving across the sky?
answer: The gods feeding it their own blood
choices: The gods feeding it their own blood
A great wind sent by Tlaloc
The beating of a giant drum
The prayers of the first people
context: The sun moved only because the other gods sacrificed themselves to feed it; human sacrifice was understood as repaying that debt to keep the sun moving. Legend, from the Leyenda de los Soles (1558). Source: Five Suns, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Suns.

question: In the standard rite, four priests held the victim spread-eagled over a stone block while a fifth cut open the chest and tore out the still-beating heart to offer to the sun. The Aztecs gave that heart a beautiful name. What did they call it?
answer: 'Precious eagle-cactus fruit'
choices: 'Precious eagle-cactus fruit'
'The red dawn-flower'
'The sun's own bread'
'The gift of warm rain'
context: The heart was the 'precious eagle-cactus fruit' and was placed in a carved stone bowl called a cuauhxicalli, the 'eagle vessel.' Source: Human sacrifice in Aztec culture, en.wikipedia.org.

question: When drought struck, Aztec priests gave small children to Tlaloc, the rain god, and on the road to the altar they made sure each child wept. Excavators uncovered at least 42 such children at the Templo Mayor, sacrificed during a drought that lasted from 1452 to 1454. Why did the priests want the children to cry?
answer: A child's tears were believed to call down rain
choices: A child's tears were believed to call down rain
Crying drove out the evil spirit of the drought
Tears were the only payment Tlaloc would take
A silent child was thought to anger the gods
context: Excavation of 'Offering 48' at the Templo Mayor (1980-81) found at least 42 children, mostly boys aged 2-7, sacrificed during the drought of 1452-1454; many showed signs of anemia and malnutrition. Source: Ancient Origins / La Brujula Verde.

question: Xipe Totec's priests put something over their own bodies at the spring festival of Tlacaxipehualiztli and wore it for twenty days. Then they shed it, like the husk a sprouting maize seed throws off, to stand for the new green growth of spring. What did the priests put on and wear?
answer: The flayed skins of sacrificed victims
choices: The flayed skins of sacrificed victims
Cloaks woven from green maize leaves
Masks carved from human skulls
Robes dyed with sacrificial blood
context: Xipe Totec's name means 'Our Lord the Flayed One'; the rotting skins were shed after 20 days to mirror a maize seed shedding its husk, then sealed in containers under the temple to trap the smell. Source: Britannica, britannica.com/topic/Xipe-Totec.

question: Elite Eagle and Jaguar warriors, fully armed, fought a lone captive at the Aztec spring festival, in the duel called the gladiatorial sacrifice. He was tied by one ankle to a round stone, and the fight was set up so he could not win. What was he given to fight with?
answer: A war club edged with feathers instead of blades
choices: A war club edged with feathers instead of blades
A short spear with no shield to guard himself
Only his bare hands and the rope at his ankle
A blunt wooden club used to train young boys
context: The captive's club (a macuahuitl) had its obsidian blades replaced with feathers; survivors of the tlahuahuanaliztli were rare. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Xipe_Totec.

question: For the festival of Toxcatl, the Aztecs chose one flawless young captive to live for a whole year as the god Tezcatlipoca made flesh. He wore gold and turquoise, and people knelt to kiss the earth as he passed. How did that golden year end for him?
answer: He climbed the temple steps and his heart was cut out
choices: He climbed the temple steps and his heart was cut out
He was set free to wander the land as a holy beggar
He led the army into the next war and fell in battle
He was walled up alive inside the temple as a guardian
context: On the feast day he climbed the steps alone, breaking one clay flute on each step, before the priests seized him and cut out his heart. The captive was the ixiptla, the god's living image. Source: Toxcatl, en.wikipedia.org; Sahagun, Florentine Codex Book 2.

question: Atop the Hill of the Star, once every 52 years, Aztec priests waited for the Pleiades to cross overhead at midnight. Every fire in the land was out, and people dreaded that the sun might not come up again. At that moment the priests sacrificed a man and kindled a brand-new flame, and runners carried it to every hearth. In what unlikely place did they kindle it?
answer: Inside the open chest of the victim
choices: Inside the open chest of the victim
On the summit of a high volcano
Inside the great palace of the emperor
On a reed raft out on the lake
context: This was the New Fire Ceremony; priests on the Hill of the Star kindled the flame inside the victim's open chest cavity, and runners carried it out to relight every hearth in the empire. The last such ceremony was in 1507 under Motecuhzoma II. Source: New Fire ceremony, en.wikipedia.org.

question: Tlacaelel, the Aztec priest-statesman, pushed a strange kind of war on neighbours such as Tlaxcala during the famine of the 1450s. These Flower Wars were not fought to kill the enemy in the field or to seize his land. What were the Aztec warriors sent out to do?
answer: Capture enemy warriors alive to be sacrificed
choices: Capture enemy warriors alive to be sacrificed
Burn the enemy's temples down to the ground
Steal the enemy's grain during the famine
Win honor in a fight where no one was hurt
context: Diego Duran reports Tlacaelel expanded the xochiyaoyotl and human sacrifice during the famine, keeping Tlaxcala unconquered as a permanent 'farm' for captives. Source: Flower war / Tlacaelel, en.wikipedia.org.

question: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, a Spanish soldier, heard the great snakeskin drum of the Templo Mayor boom so loud that it carried for miles. He saw 62 of his comrades, taken prisoner, dragged up the temple steps to the altar. He wrote that one dread stayed with him every single day. What was it?
answer: That he would be dragged up those same steps next
choices: That he would be dragged up those same steps next
That the drum was calling the war god down in person
That his ground-up bones would go into the temple walls
That his trapped soul would never leave Snake Mountain
context: Bernal Diaz watched 62 captured comrades have their chests struck open and hearts torn out, and wrote that he feared every day the Aztecs would do the same to him. Source: Bernal Diaz, The History of the Conquest of New Spain.

question: Nebuchadnezzar II faced Babylon's northern entrance, the Ishtar Gate, with brick glazed a deep blue, and across it he set rows of golden beasts that seemed to glow, each one sacred to a god. Which three creatures marched across the face of the Ishtar Gate?
answer: A lion, a bull, and a dragon-snake
choices: A lion, a bull, and a dragon-snake
A lion, a horse, and an eagle
A lion, a bull, and a winged bull
A lion, a ram, and a serpent
context: Each beast belonged to a god: the lion to Ishtar, goddess of love and war; the bull to the storm god Adad; and the scaly dragon-snake, the mushhushshu, to Marduk, chief god of Babylon. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ishtar_Gate/

question: Amytis, the story goes, pined in Babylon for the land where she grew up, and her husband, King Nebuchadnezzar, raised one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world for her. No Babylonian writing ever names her. What did she miss?
answer: The green forested mountains of her home
choices: The green forested mountains of her home
The salt sea that ringed her old city
The marble palaces of her childhood
The vast deserts she had crossed as a girl
context: The story is legend more than record: no Babylonian text mentions any queen named Amytis at all. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon/

question: Priests carried the statues of Babylon's gods along the Processional Way to the blue Ishtar Gate at every New Year. On both sides of the road, more than 120 figures of the same golden beast in bright glazed brick strode beside them. Which beast was it?
answer: Lions
choices: Lions
Horses
Bulls
Eagles
context: At New Year, priests carried the statues of the gods down the Processional Way past the watching brick lions. The lion was sacred to Ishtar, whom the gate was named for. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ishtar_Gate/

question: Robert Koldewey shipped the broken glazed bricks of Nebuchadnezzar's Ishtar Gate out of Babylon, nearly 800 crates of them, and the pieces were cleaned and fitted back together over many years. The blue gate stands again, though not in Iraq. In which city can visitors walk through it now?
answer: In a museum in Berlin
choices: In a museum in Berlin
In a museum in London
In a museum in Munich
In a museum in Paris
context: The German archaeologist Robert Koldewey shipped the fragments to Germany, where over decades they were desalted, cleaned, and reassembled into the towering gate now standing in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. Source: https://isaw.nyu.edu/publications/newsletters/025/ishtar

question: Diodorus, a Greek historian, described the Hanging Gardens of Babylon some two thousand years ago, centuries after they were said to stand and without ever having seen them. He called them a green mountain made by human hands, about 20 metres high. How did Diodorus say its planted terraces were arranged?
answer: Sloping up like the seats of a theatre
choices: Sloping up like the seats of a theatre
Spinning slowly on a great stone wheel
Floating on barges in the river
Hanging from chains off the palace roof
context: Diodorus never saw the gardens himself and wrote centuries after they supposedly stood, so this is a passed-down description, not an eyewitness one. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon/  (Legend.)

question: Belshazzar of Babylon held a wild feast on the night his city fell, the Bible says, drinking from golden cups carried off from Jerusalem. In the middle of the party, something terrifying took place that still gives English a famous saying. What happened?
answer: A hand appeared and wrote on the wall
choices: A hand appeared and wrote on the wall
A statue stepped down from its pedestal
A star fell burning into the hall
A voice thundered from an empty throne
context: A disembodied hand wrote glowing words on the wall, which is where we get the phrase 'the writing on the wall.' That same night the city was taken and Belshazzar was killed. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/fall-babylon  (Legend.)

question: Soldiers of Nebuchadnezzar stormed Jerusalem in 587 BC and led thousands of its people away into exile in Babylon. Before they marched the captives off, they burned one great building of the city to the ground. Which building did they burn?
answer: The Temple of Solomon
choices: The Temple of Solomon
The royal palace of the city
The great granaries by the gate
The library of the old kings
context: Nebuchadnezzar's men carried off the Temple's gold and silver vessels along with the people. Half a century later, in 538 BC, the Persian king Cyrus let the exiles go home. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Nebuchadnezzar-II

question: Archaeologists dug through the ruins of Babylon for decades, hunting for the green mountain of the Hanging Gardens that Berossus the priest, Diodorus the historian and Strabo the geographer had all described so vividly. They turned up one startling result. What did they find of the gardens?
answer: Nothing at all, not a single trace
choices: Nothing at all, not a single trace
The cracked stone steps of the terraces
The clay pipes that once watered the trees
The carved sign that named the garden
context: Of all Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, the Hanging Gardens are the only one no archaeologist has ever found a trace of, and not one Babylonian text or dug-up brick mentions them. The greatest wonder may be that they might never have stood in Babylon at all. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon/

question: Stephanie Dalley, a British scholar, argues that the Hanging Gardens were real, only in a different city, built a hundred years earlier by another king. That king boasted in his inscriptions of a great park of trees planted by his palace, and stone carvings from his city picture trees growing on stepped, arched terraces. Her case is still debated. Where, and by whom, does Dalley say the gardens were built?
answer: At Nineveh, built by the Assyrian king Sennacherib
choices: At Nineveh, built by the Assyrian king Sennacherib
At Nineveh, built by the Egyptian pharaoh Necho
At Ur, built by the Sumerian king Gilgamesh
At Babylon, built by the queen Semiramis
context: Sennacherib boasted he planted 'a great park beside the palace... with all kinds of herbs and fruit trees,' and stone carvings from Nineveh actually show trees growing on tiered, arched terraces. This is Dalley's argued case, still debated. Source: https://www.biblicalarchaeology.org/daily/news/hanging-gardens-of-babylon-in-assyrian-nineveh/

question: Strabo, the Greek geographer, claimed that something in the Hanging Gardens raised river water against gravity to the topmost terraces, so that the trees up there stayed green. Trees stacked that high would need water without pause. What did Strabo say did the lifting?
answer: A hidden machine of screws pumping water upward
choices: A hidden machine of screws pumping water upward
A chain of slaves hauling buckets up the steps
A network of clay pipes fed only by rainfall
A deep stone well dug beneath the terraces
context: Strabo described screws inside the gardens drawing water up from the river to keep the high terraces green, an ancient water-lifting machine working against gravity. Like the rest of the gardens, it survives only in such written accounts. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon/  (Legend.)

question: Bach loved the fugue above every other form: a piece in which one voice stated a short theme alone and each new voice took up the same theme in turn while the earlier ones wove on around it. Its name came from the Latin word 'fuga.' What did 'fuga' mean?
answer: To flee or chase
choices: To flee or chase
To sing in unison
To repeat note for note
To slowly grow louder
context: 'Fuga' = to flee or to chase: the subject is stated, then 'chased' by each entering voice, which is why a fugue feels like music pursuing itself. Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'Fugue' (newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Fugue); San Francisco Bach Choir (sfbach.org/what-is-a-fugue).

question: Maria Barbara, Johann Sebastian Bach's cousin and first wife, and after her death the singer Anna Magdalena bore him twenty children between them. Only about ten lived to grow up. What did four of Bach's surviving sons become?
answer: Four became famous composers
choices: Four became famous composers
Four became court painters
Four became sea captains
Four became Lutheran priests
context: Wilhelm Friedemann, Carl Philipp Emanuel, Johann Christoph Friedrich, and Johann Christian Bach all became noted composers in their own right. Source: Classic FM, Bach's children (classicfm.com/composers/bach/guides/children); Britannica, 'Johann Sebastian Bach'.

question: A twenty-year-old conducted Bach's St Matthew Passion in Berlin in 1829, the first great performance of it in some eighty years. Since Bach's death the work had gone unheard, dismissed as old-fashioned, and that performance relaunched his fame. Who was the young conductor?
answer: Felix Mendelssohn
choices: Felix Mendelssohn
Joseph Haydn
Johannes Brahms
Wolfgang Mozart
context: Felix Mendelssohn, only 20, conducted the St. Matthew Passion in Berlin on 11 March 1829, the first major performance in some 80 years, and essentially revived Bach's reputation. Source: Classical Music, 'How Mendelssohn helped bring back the St. Matthew Passion'; Library of Congress, Mendelssohn reviving Bach.

question: Bach made a fair copy of his St Matthew Passion, a huge sacred work that retells the Gospel story of Jesus's arrest and death. He inked most notes in ordinary brown-black but switched to deep red for certain words, so that they would stand out. Which words did Bach write in red?
answer: The words of Jesus
choices: The words of Jesus
The name of the king
His own signature
The title at the top
context: Bach inked the words of Jesus and the Gospel text in red and everything else in brown-black, so the sacred words literally stand out on the page. Source: Plough, Marianne Wright, 'Bach's Saint Matthew Passion'; Interlude (interlude.hk).

question: St Thomas's church in Leipzig had two organ lofts, and Bach placed two groups of singers and players in them for his St Matthew Passion, so that they could call back and forth across the nave like two crowds answering each other. Bach wrote for far more than a single ensemble. What did he write the Passion for?
answer: Two full choirs and two orchestras
choices: Two full choirs and two orchestras
Two boys' choirs and two organs
Two brass bands and two drummers
Two solo singers and two lutes
context: Bach scored the St. Matthew Passion for two full choirs and two orchestras at once, using the church's two organ lofts so the ensembles could answer each other across the space. Source: Wikipedia, 'St Matthew Passion'; LA Opera blog, Bach and the St. Matthew Passion.

question: Johann Sebastian Bach wanted to show off a new way of tuning a keyboard, in an age when the usual tuning made many keys sound sour and most music kept to a few safe ones. He wrote a huge collection of matched preludes and fugues and called it 'The Well-Tempered Clavier.' How many keys did it cover?
answer: All 24 keys, major and minor
choices: All 24 keys, major and minor
Only the 12 major keys
Only the 12 minor keys
Only the 7 easiest keys
context: Bach wrote a prelude and fugue in all 24 keys, every major and every minor, to prove a keyboard could be tuned so music sounded good in ANY key. Source: Britannica, 'The Well-Tempered Clavier, BWV 846-893'; Wikipedia, 'The Well-Tempered Clavier'.

question: Count Keyserlingk, a famous legend says, could not sleep, and Bach wrote the gentle, looping Goldberg Variations for the count's young harpsichordist, Johann Goldberg, to play through those long nights. Scholars doubt most of the tale. In the legend, what did the grateful count give Bach?
answer: A gold goblet of 100 coins
choices: A gold goblet of 100 coins
A silver crown of jewels
A velvet purse of pearls
A carved chest of silks
context: Legend: a golden goblet filled with 100 gold coins. Scholars now think the insomnia tale is mostly a charming myth. Source: Interlude, 'Sleep Gently, Count Keyserlingk' (interlude.hk); Wikipedia, 'Goldberg Variations'.

question: Frederick the Great played the flute and kept the newest keyboards in his palace at Potsdam, and in 1747 the ageing Bach came to visit. The king sat him down at one, gave him a long, winding tune he had composed himself, and challenged him to build a complex fugue on it. What did Bach do at the keyboard?
answer: Improvised a fugue on the spot
choices: Improvised a fugue on the spot
Refused and left the palace
Copied one from a songbook
Asked for a week to prepare
context: Bach improvised the fugue on the spot, then went home and built a whole work, 'The Musical Offering,' from the king's theme, labeling it RICERCAR, an acrostic for a Latin phrase meaning 'the theme given by the king, worked out in canon.' Source: Wikipedia, 'The Musical Offering'; Oxford Frederick the Great project (frederick.mml.ox.ac.uk).

question: Bach could spell his own name in music, because in the German note-names of his day B stood for B-flat and H for B-natural, so B-flat, A, C, B-natural read as B-A-C-H. He wove those four notes in as a theme near the end of one of his last works, in a closing piece he never finished. Which work was it?
answer: The Art of Fugue
choices: The Art of Fugue
The Well-Tempered Clavier
The Goldberg Variations
The Musical Offering
context: Bach worked the B-A-C-H motif (B-flat, A, C, B-natural) into the last fugue of 'The Art of Fugue,' hiding his own name in the notes. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Art of Fugue'; Medium, 'The Bach Motif'.

question: Bach wrote one piece of his Musical Offering for two players reading the same line at once, one from the first note forward and the other from the last note backward, and the two parts fit together perfectly. What animal nickname did the canon get?
answer: The Crab Canon
choices: The Crab Canon
The Spider Canon
The Eagle Canon
The Serpent Canon
context: It is called the Crab Canon (canon cancrizans) because crabs move backwards, just as the second player plays the line in reverse, making it a musical palindrome. Source: Wikipedia, 'Crab canon'; kottke.org, Bach's crab canon.

question: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach wrote a note on the manuscript of his father's last, unfinished fugue, at the spot where it stopped dead in the middle of a phrase, just after the four-note B-A-C-H signature had entered. What did the son write had happened there?
answer: That his father died while writing it
choices: That his father died while writing it
That the rest was lost in a fire
That a pupil completed it later
That the ink had run dry
context: C.P.E. Bach wrote that 'where the name BACH was placed in the countersubject, the author died.' Modern scholars doubt Bach literally died mid-note, but the broken-off page is real. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Art of Fugue' (quoting C.P.E. Bach); Slate, 2008, on The Art of Fugue.

question: A. B. Marx, a critic, reported a tale that the score of the St Matthew Passion was nearly lost for good, because a Berlin shop was using pages torn from it to wrap what it sold, until Carl Friedrich Zelter, a Berlin music teacher, got hold of a copy. Scholars think the story is at least exaggerated. What did the shop sell?
answer: Cheese
choices: Cheese
Fish
Bread
Soap
context: The legend says the pages wrapped cheese in a Berlin cheese shop. Scholars think the cheese-shop story is at least exaggerated. Source: Robert Greenberg on Medium (quoting A. B. Marx); skepticism noted at Wikipedia Talk, 'Johann Sebastian Bach'.

question: Bartolomé de las Casas sailed to the Caribbean about 1502 as a young colonist, and the Spanish crown granted him an encomienda: land worked by Indians forced to labour for him. Around 1514, after years of watching how the Indians were beaten, starved and worked to death, Las Casas decided the whole system was unjust. What did he do?
answer: He handed his Indians back to the governor and became the system's fiercest enemy
choices: He handed his Indians back to the governor and became the system's fiercest enemy
He sold his Indians to a wealthier planter and sailed back home to Spain
He doubled his landholding and drove the Indians to mine for gold
He kept his Indians but vowed to the governor to work them gently
context: Las Casas had owned forced laborers on Hispaniola and Cuba before he turned on the encomienda system and spent the rest of his life fighting it — the colonist who became its deadliest enemy. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/Bartolome_de_las_Casas); Wikipedia 'Bartolomé de las Casas'; Britannica.

question: Charles V brought Spain's conquests in the Americas to a halt in 1550 and called theologians to Valladolid to judge them. There Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda called the Indians barbarians and natural slaves, by Aristotle's rule fit only to be ruled by others. What was Bartolomé de las Casas's answer?
answer: That the Indians were fully rational humans, able to govern themselves, so no people are 'natural slaves'
choices: That the Indians were fully rational humans, able to govern themselves, so no people are 'natural slaves'
That the Indians could be conquered, but only by Spanish soldiers who had first been baptized
That the Indians should be left wholly alone, with no Spanish priest or settler ever sent
That the Indians owed Spain nothing until the Pope himself had formally ruled on it
context: Answering Sepúlveda point by point, Las Casas held that 'All the World is Human' — the Indians had reason and could rule themselves, so the category of 'natural slave' was a lie. The judges named no winner and both men claimed victory, but it stands as history's first formal debate over the rights of an indigenous people, and a root of the natural-rights tradition. Source: Gilder Lehrman Institute 'Las Casas debates the subjugation of the Indians, 1550'; History Today 'The Valladolid Debate'.

question: Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488 with three small ships, the first European known to do it, after his ships were driven far from the coast. He gave the headland a name of his own. What did Dias call it?
answer: Cabo das Tormentas, the 'Cape of Storms'
choices: Cabo das Tormentas, the 'Cape of Storms'
Cabo da Boa Esperanca, the 'Cape of Good Hope'
Cabo Verde, the 'Green Cape'
Cabo do Fim, the 'Cape of the End'
context: Dias named the southern tip Cabo das Tormentas in 1488 for the storms and currents that battered his ships. Portugal's King John II later renamed it the Cape of Good Hope, because rounding it opened the long-sought sea route toward India. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/bartolomeu-dias

question: Three small Portuguese ships under Bartolomeu Dias sailed past the southern tip of Africa in 1488 and proved that a sea route around Africa toward India could be sailed. Dias wanted to press on and reach India itself, but his sailors had been at sea for months and were nearly out of food and water. How did the voyage end?
answer: His crew refused to go on, forcing Dias to turn back
choices: His crew refused to go on, forcing Dias to turn back
Dias pressed on alone and reached the coast of India
A rival Portuguese fleet ordered him home
Dias sailed onward and circled the whole continent
context: Dias appointed a council that agreed he could sail just three more days, then he had to turn for home. He returned to Lisbon in December 1488 after an absence of sixteen months and seventeen days. It would be Vasco da Gama, years later, who finished the route to India. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/bartolomeu-dias

question: Frédéric Bastiat wrote a mock petition in which the candle and lamp makers of France pleaded with the government for protection from an unfair foreign rival, one who poured light into the country so cheaply that no candlemaker could compete. Bastiat's joke lay in who that unbeatable rival was. Who was it?
answer: The sun
choices: The sun
The Dutch
The English
The moon
context: In Bastiat's satirical 'Petition of the Candlemakers,' the makers demand a law shutting every window, skylight, shutter and curtain so the free light of the sun cannot enter, forcing France to buy candles by day. He used the absurdity to mock protectionist tariffs that punish cheap competition. Bastiat, 'Petition of the Candlemakers' (in Economic Sophisms, 1845). https://monadnock.net/bastiat/petition.html

question: A shopkeeper's careless son broke a shop window, in a parable by Frédéric Bastiat, and onlookers cheered that it was good for trade, since the glazier would now earn six francs. Bastiat argued that the town was no richer at all, because everyone forgot one thing the shopkeeper could no longer do with those six francs. What was it?
answer: Buy new shoes or another book
choices: Buy new shoes or another book
Pay the glazier
Repair the window
Hire the careless boy
context: This is Bastiat's 'seen versus unseen': the SEEN is the glazier's six-franc job; the UNSEEN is that the same six francs would have bought the shopkeeper new shoes or another book for his library. The money is only moved, not created, so destruction never enriches a society. Bastiat, 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen' (1850), his last published work. https://www.econlib.org/library/Bastiat/basEss1.html

question: Japan's army swept into the American-held Philippines in December 1941, days after the Pearl Harbor attack, and its defenders, Americans and Filipinos, retreated into the jungle of the Bataan Peninsula. Japan's planners gave themselves 50 days to take it. Cut off from any supply ship and on quarter rations of rice, the defenders held on. How many days did they last before Bataan surrendered?
answer: 99 days
choices: 99 days
52 days
75 days
120 days
context: The defenders held Bataan for 99 days before Major General Edward King surrendered on April 9, 1942. Historians link the brutal treatment that followed partly to Japanese commanders being enraged by the unexpectedly long fight and unprepared for tens of thousands more prisoners than they had planned for. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/battle-bataan-death-march

question: Masaharu Homma commanded the Japanese 14th Army in the Philippines in 1942, when his men drove about 76,000 surrendered American and Filipino prisoners some 65 miles north on the Bataan Death March. The guards beat, bayoneted or shot stragglers, and some seven to ten thousand prisoners died on the march. After the war Homma faced 43 charges and was held answerable for his troops' conduct. What was his fate?
answer: Executed by firing squad
choices: Executed by firing squad
Imprisoned for life
Acquitted of all counts
Released after ten years
context: Homma was sentenced to death and executed by firing squad on April 3, 1946. He was held responsible not for atrocities he personally committed but for failing to control the soldiers under his command. Colonel Masanobu Tsuji, blamed for ordering the Pantingan River massacre of 350-400 captured Filipinos, escaped prosecution entirely and vanished in Laos in 1961. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bataan_Death_March

question: Fighter pilots of the Royal Air Force rose day after day through the summer of 1940 to hold off the German air force over southern England. Winston Churchill gave them a name that has stuck to them ever since. By what name are these pilots remembered?
answer: the Few
choices: the Few
the Brave
the Eagles
the Aces
context: Churchill coined it in his 20 August 1940 speech to the House of Commons. Ever since, the RAF pilots who fought the Battle of Britain have been known simply as 'the Few.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never_was_so_much_owed_by_so_many_to_so_few

question: Adolf Hitler had conquered France by June 1940, but before his army could cross the English Channel, his Luftwaffe had to sweep the Royal Air Force from the sky. From July to October, British fighters met the German raiders over southern England. What made that fight a first in the history of war?
answer: It was the first major battle decided entirely in the air.
choices: It was the first major battle decided entirely in the air.
It was the first major battle fought entirely at night.
It was the first major battle decided by aircraft carriers.
It was the first major battle won by tanks alone.
context: No armies clashed on land and no fleets met at sea. After France fell in June 1940, Britain stood as the only major power in Western Europe still fighting Nazi Germany, and the whole campaign was decided overhead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain

question: Two British fighters rose to meet the German air force in the summer of 1940. The sleek, glamorous Supermarine Spitfire took the fame, but a plainer, tougher fighter brought down some 60 percent of the German planes destroyed, more than every other British defence put together. Which fighter did most of the real work?
answer: The Hawker Hurricane
choices: The Hawker Hurricane
The Bristol Blenheim
The Boulton Paul Defiant
The Gloster Gladiator
context: The unglamorous Hurricane shot down about 60 percent of all enemy aircraft destroyed in the battle. In tactics, Spitfires were sent high to tangle with the German fighter screen while Hurricanes tore into the bomber formations. Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/why-the-hurricane-was-a-vital-aircraft-in-the-second-world-war

question: The Royal Air Force watched for German bombers in 1940 from a line of tall towers along Britain's south and east coasts, which could spot the raiders up to 200 miles away, while they were still climbing over France. What new invention let the towers see that far?
answer: Radar
choices: Radar
Sonar
Searchlights
Spotter balloons
context: This was Chain Home, the world's first early-warning radar network. Its weakness: the towers faced out to sea, so once raiders crossed the coast the human-staffed Observer Corps had to track them inland by eye and ear. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_Home

question: Stuka dive-bombers screamed down on Hitler's enemies in 1939 and 1940, and the siren-wail of their dive terrified Europe. Then, in August 1940, the slow Junkers Ju 87 Stuka met Britain's fighters over the English Channel and southern England. What happened to the Stuka in those skies?
answer: British fighters shot it down so easily it was withdrawn.
choices: British fighters shot it down so easily it was withdrawn.
It smashed the airfields and broke Fighter Command.
It switched to sinking ships in the English Channel.
It was grounded by the autumn storms over France.
context: Over 20 percent of the whole Stuka force was lost between 8 and 18 August 1940, so the Luftwaffe pulled it out of the battle to save it. Its myth of invincibility was shattered over the Channel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junkers_Ju_87

question: Pilots of No. 303 Squadron had fled when German armies conquered their homeland, and they joined the Battle of Britain two months late. Nearly one pilot in five in the battle was not British, yet this squadron finished with more German planes to its name than any other in Fighter Command. Which country's pilots flew it?
answer: Poland
choices: Poland
New Zealand
Canada
France
context: About 595 of roughly 3,000 aircrew came from abroad, including 145 Poles and 88 Czechoslovaks. No. 303 Squadron joined two months late yet became the top-scoring RAF fighter unit, claiming 126 German aircraft in 42 days. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._303_Squadron_RAF

question: Under Hugh Dowding, Fighter Command tied its coastal stations, ground observers, telephone lines, map rooms and radio into one network that shared everything they saw, the first air defence of its kind in the world. Why did this system let a smaller Royal Air Force beat a much larger German air force?
answer: British planes didn't waste fuel patrolling empty sky
choices: British planes didn't waste fuel patrolling empty sky
British planes were much faster than any German fighter
British pilots were the only ones with radar in their cockpits
German bombers had to fly at night to hit their targets
context: It was named after Air Chief Marshal Sir Hugh Dowding. By scrambling fighters only against confirmed raids, it spared fuel, pilots and planes, the heart of how an outnumbered force kept winning. Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/what-was-the-dowding-system

question: From a gallery at Bentley Priory, Fighter Command's controllers watched the whole Battle of Britain unfold on a giant map table below them. Operators with long wooden rods slid coloured counters across the map to show each German formation's position, height and strength. Who were the operators moving the counters?
answer: Women of the WAAF
choices: Women of the WAAF
Off-duty fighter pilots
Royal Navy sailors
Army signalmen
context: The plotters were members of the WAAF, the Women's Auxiliary Air Force. A wall clock divided into red, blue and yellow five-minute segments matched the counters, so anyone could see at a glance how fresh, or how stale, each plot was. Source: https://bentleypriorymuseum.org.uk/bentley-priory-and-the-battle-of-britain/the-many/

question: Hermann Göring's airmen believed by early September 1940 that Fighter Command was nearly finished. Then, after British bombers raided Berlin, Göring changed the Luftwaffe's target, a switch historians count among the great blunders of the war, and it let the worn-out British fighter squadrons rebuild. What did the Luftwaffe do?
answer: It stopped hitting the airfields and bombed London instead.
choices: It stopped hitting the airfields and bombed London instead.
It gave up daylight raids and attacked only by night.
It pulled its bombers back to France to refit.
It turned its full weight onto the Royal Navy.
context: The switch began on 7 September 1940, the first day of the Blitz on London. By taking the pressure off the airfields and radar stations, it gave Fighter Command exactly the time it needed to rebuild. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain

question: Fighter Command's controllers guided British fighters onto about nine incoming raids in ten in 1940, with reports from coastal stations and ground observers routed through filter rooms. Before the war, commanders had expected fighters to catch only a third to a half of any raid. What did this do to Fighter Command's effective strength?
answer: It roughly tripled it
choices: It roughly tripled it
It roughly doubled it
It barely changed it
It cut it in half
context: The system lifted the interception rate to about 90 percent, against the 30-50 percent thought good before the war. In effect it tripled Fighter Command's strength, letting outnumbered British fighters keep beating larger German formations to the punch. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowding_system

question: Trafford Leigh-Mallory and Douglas Bader, the ace on artificial legs, wanted British fighters sent up in huge massed wings, and the Big Wing feud raged among the air chiefs. Hugh Dowding, who had built Britain's system of air defence, and Keith Park had beaten the Luftwaffe with quick scrambles, one squadron at a time. What became of Dowding in November 1940?
answer: He was sacked from Fighter Command.
choices: He was sacked from Fighter Command.
He was promoted to head the whole RAF.
He was knighted by the King for the victory.
He retired quietly to write his memoirs.
