context: In a striking twist, the man who built the winning system was relieved of Fighter Command within weeks of victory, partly over the Big Wing feud led by Leigh-Mallory and Bader, who wanted mass wings rather than the fast squadron scrambles Dowding and Park preferred. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Dowding

question: Alexander the Great met the vast Persian army of King Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BC, on a dusty plain in what is now northern Iraq, with a smaller, superbly drilled army of his own. When the Persian line split open, Alexander massed his elite Companion cavalry and drove them straight at Darius. What shape did he drive at the enemy?
answer: A giant wedge, with Alexander at its tip
choices: A giant wedge, with Alexander at its tip
A long thin crescent curling around the flank
A hollow square bristling with spears
A double column splitting left and right
context: Alexander packed his Companion cavalry into a giant wedge with himself at the very point and drove it straight through the gap, aimed directly at King Darius III. When the wedge burst toward him, Darius turned and fled the field in his chariot; the moment his soldiers saw their king run, the Persian army collapsed. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/108/the-battle-of-gaugamela-331-bce/

question: Darius III had his soldiers smooth out the plain of Gaugamela before the battle, so that his horsemen and some 200 scythed chariots would have a clear run at the enemy. The preparation backfired. Why did the level ground end up helping Alexander instead?
answer: The flat ground was ideal footing for Alexander's tight phalanx formation
choices: The flat ground was ideal footing for Alexander's tight phalanx formation
The dust kicked up blinded only the Persian archers
The cleared field left the Persians no walls to retreat behind
The level surface let Greek scouts count the Persian host exactly
context: Darius deliberately had the plain leveled smooth for his cavalry and roughly 200 scythed chariots, but the flat ground turned out to be perfect for Alexander's tightly packed phalanx. Alexander's light troops shot the chariot drivers and grabbed the reins, and the phalanx opened lanes to let the rest rumble harmlessly through, then closed up again. Source: https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/gaugamela-331-bce/

question: William of Normandy won the English crown in 1066, and the Bayeux Tapestry, made in the late 1000s, told the story in 58 scenes nearly 70 metres long. Despite its name, it was never a tapestry at all. What kind of object was it really?
answer: A long strip of embroidered wool stitched onto linen
choices: A long strip of embroidered wool stitched onto linen
A woven wool-and-silk tapestry hung on a wall
A painted mural spread across wet plaster
A carved stone frieze set above a doorway
context: A true tapestry is woven on a loom; the Bayeux Tapestry is embroidery — coloured wool thread stitched onto bleached linen, like a 70-metre medieval comic strip. It survives today in a museum in Bayeux, Normandy, France. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayeux_Tapestry

question: After his victory at Hastings in 1066, William the Conqueror built Battle Abbey right on the battlefield. By tradition, the abbey's high altar stood on the very spot where one event of the fighting took place. Which spot did the altar mark?
answer: Where King Harold was killed
choices: Where King Harold was killed
Where William was crowned king
Where the blazing comet first appeared
Where the English line first formed up
context: The battle was fought on 14 October 1066, not at Hastings itself but about 7 miles inland near the town now literally called Battle, in East Sussex. William placed the altar of Battle Abbey where Harold is said to have fallen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: Harold Godwinson's army crushed a Viking invasion led by Harald Hardrada of Norway at Stamford Bridge, in northern England, on 25 September 1066. Three days later Duke William of Normandy's fleet landed on the south coast near Hastings. What did Harold's exhausted English army have to do next?
answer: Force-march roughly 200 miles south
choices: Force-march roughly 200 miles south
Rest and regroup for a full month
Sail the long way round the coast
Wait in London for fresh reinforcements
context: Harold's men had beaten the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada and Harold's own treacherous brother Tostig at Stamford Bridge on 25 Sept 1066, then had to march the length of England to meet William — arriving exhausted. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stamford_Bridge ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: The English held their ground near Hastings on 14 October 1066 from dawn until late afternoon, against everything William of Normandy and his invaders could throw at them. How did Harold Godwinson's English army fight?
answer: Entirely on foot behind a wall of shields
choices: Entirely on foot behind a wall of shields
Mounted on horseback with heavy lances
From small boats along the nearby river
Hidden among the trees of a thick forest
context: Harold's housecarls stood in mail wielding two-handed Danish battle-axes, locked shoulder to shoulder. William's advantage was exactly what Harold lacked: heavy cavalry on horseback and ranks of archers. Harold had to hold the high ground; William had to break it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: The Norse invaders had crossed the sea to England in about 300 ships, and Harold Godwinson's victory over them at Stamford Bridge was so complete that the survivors needed only a small part of that fleet to sail home. About how many ships carried them back?
answer: About 24
choices: About 24
About 70
About 130
About 220
context: Around 300 Norse ships came; survivors needed only 24 to sail home — a measure of how many men never left. Both leaders, Harald Hardrada and the traitor Tostig, were killed. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stamford_Bridge ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: A fiery star blazed across the English sky in the spring of 1066, and people took it as an omen of doom for King Harold. The Bayeux Tapestry pictured it above a row of frightened onlookers, with the Latin caption 'These men marvel at the star.' It was the first known picture of what?
answer: Halley's Comet
choices: Halley's Comet
A total solar eclipse
An exploding supernova
The planet Venus blazing
context: The same comet returns about every 76 years, but nobody knew that in 1066. Centuries later the British astronomer Edmond Halley worked out its orbit and predicted its return, so it took his name — and the Bayeux Tapestry holds its earliest known image. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayeux_Tapestry ; https://www.physics.unlv.edu/~jeffery/astro/art/bayeux_tapestry.html

question: Mounted knights charged the English line at Hastings again and again, and all day it would not break. The chronicler William of Poitiers wrote that the Normans finally cracked it with a single trick, which they used twice, though some historians suspect the story was polished later. What was the trick?
answer: They pretended to flee, then wheeled around on the chasers
choices: They pretended to flee, then wheeled around on the chasers
They dug tunnels under the English-held hill
They set the dry grass ablaze before the line
They simply waited the English out through the night
context: The 'feigned retreat': horsemen faked a panicked flight, luring English troops to chase them downhill — then turned and cut the scattered pursuers to pieces. Some historians suspect the story was polished later to disguise a real Norman rout. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: Norman soldiers began to break and run in the middle of the battle at Hastings, after a rumour tore through their ranks that Duke William had been killed. William rode along his lines to stop the panic, and as he went he did one bold thing. What did he do?
answer: Tore off his helmet to show his bare face
choices: Tore off his helmet to show his bare face
Charged out alone straight at King Harold
Called down a fresh storm of arrows
Sounded the horns to retreat and regroup
context: William ripped off his helmet, rode along the line showing everyone he was alive, and shouted that he still lived — turning the panic into a counter-charge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: Harald Hardrada, the towering Viking king of Norway, had invaded England from the north, and before the battle at Stamford Bridge he demanded that Harold of England hand over some land. Legend says an English messenger gave him an answer. What did the messenger offer?
answer: Six feet of ground, or a little more
choices: Six feet of ground, or a little more
A rich earldom in the north
A chest of silver and gold
Half of England to rule
context: The full reply, from Snorri Sturluson's saga: Hardrada would get 'six feet of ground, or as much more as he needs, as he is taller than most men' — meaning a grave. Hours later Hardrada was dead. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stamford_Bridge

question: A lone Norman named Taillefer, the story goes, galloped out ahead of William's whole army at Hastings toward the English line, and he became the first man to die there that day. What did he do as he closed on the enemy?
answer: Rode out singing aloud and juggling his sword in the air
choices: Rode out singing aloud and juggling his sword in the air
Knelt to bless the whole army with holy water
Read out William's claim to the crown for all to hear
Planted the Pope's banner on the open hillside
context: The minstrel was named Taillefer. He rode out singing the 'Song of Roland' and tossing his sword, killed an Englishman who charged him, then plunged alone into the English line and was cut down — the first man to die at Hastings. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taillefer

question: Writing within months of the battle, the author of the Carmen de Hastingae Proelio told of King Harold's death at Hastings with no arrow in his eye at all, though that arrow is the death most people picture. Even the arrow on the Bayeux Tapestry may be a later repair. How did the Carmen say Harold was killed?
answer: Four knights cut him down with lance and blade
choices: Four knights cut him down with lance and blade
A single arrow struck him through the eye
A crossbowman shot him from his horse
William himself ran him through with a spear
context: Per the Carmen, four knights set on Harold: one ran him through with a lance, the second cut off his head, the third speared his entrails, the fourth carried off his thigh. The arrow in the famous Bayeux Tapestry scene may itself be an 1800s repair — eighteenth-century drawings of the same figure show a plain shaft, not a fletched arrow. Some scholars think the real arrow-death belonged to Harald Hardrada (shot through the throat weeks earlier) and got transplanted onto Harold over time. Source: https://www.medievalists.net/2022/10/arrow-king-harold-eye/

question: Harold had once sworn to support William's claim to England, the Normans said, with his hands laid on something, so his taking of the crown became a sacred crime and earned William a banner from the Pope. What had Harold supposedly sworn on?
answer: A chest of holy relics
choices: A chest of holy relics
A great stack of gold
The old king's own crown
A Bible held out by William
context: Because Harold was said to have sworn on holy relics and then broken it, William won the backing of the Pope, who (per William of Poitiers) sent a consecrated papal banner to carry into the invasion. Sources: https://www.readingmuseum.org.uk/harold-makes-solemn-oath ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hastings

question: Rebels in the north of England rose against William the Conqueror in 1069 and 1070, and William crushed them by burning and starving whole villages. Sixteen years later, William's great survey of the kingdom still marked estate after estate in those lands with one grim word. What was that word?
answer: Waste
choices: Waste
Burned
Empty
Cursed
context: The campaign is remembered as the 'Harrying of the North,' and the Domesday Book (1086) marked the ruined estates as 'waste.' By then only about 8% of England's land was still held by English owners — roughly 92% had passed to Normans. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrying_of_the_North ; https://www.thecollector.com/what-domesday-book-tell-norman-conquest/

question: Iwo Jima lay right on the bomber route to Tokyo, and United States Marines stormed it in February 1945. The island's Japanese name, Iōtō, told exactly what the island was made of. What did Iōtō mean?
answer: Sulfur Island
choices: Sulfur Island
Iron Island
Ash Island
Storm Island
context: Iōtō means 'Sulfur Island,' and the name was no exaggeration — the volcanic air on Iwo Jima actually stank of sulfur. The island mattered because it lay about 650 miles from Tokyo with airfields right on the route Allied bombers flew to Japan. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwo_Jima ; National WWII Museum, nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/battle-iwo-jima

question: The ground itself fought the Marines who stormed the beaches of Iwo Jima in February 1945. The slopes were piled up to fifteen feet deep in a loose material that swallowed boots and vehicles, and the men could not dig a proper foxhole in it. What were the beaches made of?
answer: Black volcanic ash
choices: Black volcanic ash
Thick gray mud
Loose river gravel
Crushed coral sand
context: The beaches were soft black volcanic ash — men slid backward with every step and vehicles bogged down. It did have one mercy: the deep ash helped smother the blast of incoming Japanese shells. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Iwo_Jima

question: American planners expected the fight for Iwo Jima to be over in about five days. But General Tadamichi Kuribayashi had dug 11 miles of tunnels through the island's rock, and his men fought from underground. How long did the battle really last?
answer: 36 days
choices: 36 days
19 days
12 days
21 days
context: The Marines expected about 5 days; the Japanese held out for 36 (19 February – 26 March 1945). The American codename for the assault was Operation Detachment. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Iwo_Jima ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadamichi_Kuribayashi

question: Joe Rosenthal, a photographer for the Associated Press, was on top of Mount Suribachi on 23 February 1945 when six Marines heaved a flag aloft on a length of pipe. How did he take what became America's most famous war photograph?
answer: He fired the shutter without even looking through the viewfinder
choices: He fired the shutter without even looking through the viewfinder
He posed the Marines and took three careful frames
He waited for the smoke to clear and zoomed in close
He climbed a ladder to shoot down from above them
context: Rosenthal swung his bulky Speed Graphic camera up and fired blind — he almost missed the shot entirely. That single frame won the 1945 Pulitzer Prize for Photography, the only photo ever to win in the same year it was taken. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_the_Flag_on_Iwo_Jima ; Pulitzer Prizes, pulitzer.org/article/joe-rosenthal-and-flag-raising-iwo-jima

question: Chandler Johnson, the battalion commander, sent for a second flag to fly over Mount Suribachi after an officer asked to keep the first one as a souvenir. The second flag was the one Joe Rosenthal photographed. What were Johnson's orders about the new flag?
answer: "Make it a bigger one"
choices: "Make it a bigger one"
"Raise it before nightfall"
"Guard it with your lives"
"Fly it at half-staff"
context: Johnson said "And make it a bigger one," so troops fighting on the far side of Suribachi could see it. The little first flag measured 54x28 inches; the big replacement was 96x56 inches and came from the ship USS LST-779. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_the_Flag_on_Iwo_Jima ; military.com/history/story-behind-two-flag-raisings-battle-of-iwo-jima.html

question: Chester Nimitz, commander of the United States Pacific Fleet, read the casualty lists from Iwo Jima, where nearly 7,000 Americans had died fighting Japanese defenders dug into the rock. He summed up the men who served there in one sentence, later cut into the stone of the Marine Corps War Memorial. What did Nimitz say about them?
answer: "Uncommon valor was a common virtue"
choices: "Uncommon valor was a common virtue"
"They died so that freedom might live"
"No finer fighting men ever drew breath"
"Their courage outlasted the longest night"
context: Nimitz's line — "Among those who served on Iwo Jima, uncommon valor was a common virtue" — is now engraved on the Marine Corps War Memorial in Arlington. Sources: National Museum of the Marine Corps, usmcmuseum.com/blog/uncommon-valor-was-a-common-virtue ; defensemedianetwork.com

question: A damaged B-29 bomber set down safely on Iwo Jima's runway on 4 March 1945, while Marines were still fighting for the island. It was the first of about 2,400 bombers in trouble to land on the island, and an estimated 27,000 airmen were saved that way. What name was painted on that first bomber?
answer: "Dinah Might"
choices: "Dinah Might"
"Enola Gay"
"Bockscar"
"Memphis Belle"
context: The B-29 'Dinah Might' (a pun on 'dynamite') was the first of roughly 2,400 American bombers in trouble that would make emergency landings on Iwo Jima — saving an estimated 27,000 airmen who might otherwise have ditched in the sea. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Iwo_Jima ; National WWII Museum, nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/iwo-jima-sacrifice-and-sanctuary

question: Jack Lucas, a seventeen-year-old private first class, was in a trench on Iwo Jima when two enemy grenades landed among his comrades. There was no time to throw them back. What he did next made him the youngest Marine ever to receive the Medal of Honor. What did Jack Lucas do?
answer: He threw himself on top of both grenades
choices: He threw himself on top of both grenades
He kicked them into a flooded shell hole
He hurled his helmet over the nearest one
He shoved his buddies out of the trench
context: Lucas pushed one grenade as deep as he could into the soft black ash; one failed to go off, the other blew up under him. His buddies thought he was dead and left him — but he lived. He had faked his way into the Marines at 14 by forging his mother's signature and stowed away to reach the battle; the blast left 250+ pieces of shrapnel in his body and he endured 26 operations. Truman pinned on his medal on 5 October 1945. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacklyn_H._Lucas ; nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/incredible-story-jack-lucas-youngest-medal-honor-recipient-world-war-ii

question: John Basilone had won the Medal of Honor at Guadalcanal and was already a national hero, yet he insisted on going back into combat. On the very first day at Iwo Jima he pushed his machine-gun team toward the airfield. What happened to him?
answer: He was killed by a bursting mortar shell
choices: He was killed by a bursting mortar shell
He was captured leading the assault
He was wounded and shipped home again
He was promoted on the battlefield
context: Basilone was killed on the first day on Red Beach by a bursting mortar shell and was awarded the Navy Cross posthumously — a Medal of Honor hero from one battle, killed in the opening hours of another. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Basilone ; usmcu.edu/Research/Marine-Corps-History-Division

question: Marines found copies of the Courageous Battle Vows inside captured Japanese pillboxes on Iwo Jima. Tadamichi Kuribayashi had written them for every defender of the island, and he had banned wasteful banzai charges. How did his last vow order each man to fight?
answer: Kill ten of the enemy before dying
choices: Kill ten of the enemy before dying
Hold the beach until reinforcements come
Surrender only on his direct command
Fall back to the northern caves
context: The last of the vows read: "Each man will make it his duty to kill ten of the enemy before dying." Kuribayashi forbade the wasteful 'banzai' charges other commanders used and instead made his men sell every yard dearly — which is why this tiny island cost so much. Sources: Issuu/Faircount USMC Iwo Jima 75, issuu.com/faircountmedia/docs/iwo_jima_75_marines ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadamichi_Kuribayashi

question: As a young officer, Tadamichi Kuribayashi spent time in the United States, at Harvard and the University of Michigan, years before he would defend Iwo Jima to the death. Having seen American factories and American power up close, what did he keep warning his family?
answer: "America is the last country in the world Japan should fight"
choices: "America is the last country in the world Japan should fight"
"America will soon tire of war and seek peace"
"America's soldiers have no stomach for losses"
"America can be beaten if Japan strikes first"
context: Kuribayashi knew American industrial might firsthand and told his family America was the last country Japan should ever take on. He was probably killed leading a final attack in the early morning of 26 March 1945 — and held that grim conviction as he defended the island. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadamichi_Kuribayashi

question: Tadamichi Kuribayashi most likely died leading one last attack on Iwo Jima, yet the Americans could never identify his body, and it has never been found. Why could they not identify the general who had cost them so dearly?
answer: He had stripped off all his officer's insignia
choices: He had stripped off all his officer's insignia
He had burned his own face beyond recognition
He had switched uniforms with a dead private
He had been buried by his men beforehand
context: Kuribayashi deliberately removed every badge of his rank before that final charge, so no enemy could ever identify the commander who had cost them so dearly. His body was never recovered. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadamichi_Kuribayashi

question: Hitler opened Operation Citadel in July 1943, his final great attack in the East, meant to cut off the Soviet salient around Kursk in western Russia with Panther and Tiger tanks. But the Soviets had dug in for weeks behind mines and gun lines placed just where the German pincers would strike, because Moscow already knew the plan. How had Moscow learned it?
answer: The 'Lucy' spy ring in Switzerland and British Ultra decrypts of German radio traffic
choices: A captured German general gave up the whole plan under interrogation
The 'Lucy' spy ring in Switzerland and British Ultra decrypts of German radio traffic
A double agent inside Hitler's bunker smuggled out the orders by courier
Soviet scouts photographed the German maps from a downed reconnaissance plane
context: Moscow learned of Operation Citadel almost as soon as Hitler approved it on 15 April 1943, thanks to Rudolf Roessler's 'Lucy' ring in Switzerland feeding precise German intentions, plus British Ultra decrypts of Enigma traffic. The Soviets fortified exactly where the pincers would strike. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Operation_Citadel; Wikipedia, Battle of Kursk.

question: Pavel Rotmistrov's tanks took brutal losses at Prokhorovka on 12 July 1943, yet he claimed to Stalin that his crews had destroyed 400 German tanks, including 70 Tigers, ramming them in a heroic charge. The historian Ben Wheatley later examined the Luftwaffe's aerial photographs of the battlefield. What did they actually show?
answer: The Germans lost only about five tanks while the Soviets lost roughly 250 or more
choices: Rotmistrov had undercounted — the Germans lost closer to 600 tanks
The Germans lost only about five tanks while the Soviets lost roughly 250 or more
Both sides lost almost exactly the same number, about 200 tanks each
The famous battlefield was empty — the clash happened miles away
context: The legend of T-34 crews ramming Tigers was largely invented by Rotmistrov himself to explain his catastrophic losses to Stalin. Many of his T-34s had charged downhill into ground they had not scouted and tumbled into a 4.5-meter anti-tank ditch dug by their own side, exposing their flanks. Aerial-photo study ('Shattered Myths: The Tank Battle at Prokhorovka') put German losses at roughly five. Framed as legend: Rotmistrov's ramming account is testimony, not forensic fact. Source: the-past.com/feature/prokhorovka-the-greatest-tank-battle-in-history/.

question: A 23-year-old Greek named Spyridon Louis won the marathon at the first modern Olympic Games, in Athens in 1896, and became a national hero overnight, cheered by the king and the whole stadium. Before that day, what humble job did he do for a living?
answer: He was a water-carrier
choices: He was a water-carrier
He was a goat-herd
He was a fisherman
He was a stonemason
context: Spyridon Louis hauled his father's mineral water into Athens, a city with no central water supply. He won by over seven minutes before about 100,000 spectators and ran the final lap flanked by two Greek princes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyridon_Louis

question: The army of Athens beat a much larger Persian force on the plain of Marathon in 490 BC, and 192 of its soldiers fell. They were cremated and buried on the very spot where they died. What still marks their grave, over 2,500 years later?
answer: A great earthen mound
choices: A great earthen mound
A row of marble pillars
A bronze statue
A stone temple
context: The mound is called the Soros, a roughly 9-meter-high earthwork still standing on the Marathon plain. Herodotus put the dead at 192 Athenians and 11 Plataeans, against 6,400 Persians counted on the field. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: Darius I sent a Persian army across the Aegean in 490 BC to Marathon, only 26 miles from Athens. The Athenians sent their runner Pheidippides racing over the mountains to beg the greatest warrior city in Greece for help. Which city did he run to?
answer: Sparta
choices: Sparta
Thebes
Corinth
Argos
context: Herodotus says Pheidippides covered the roughly 150 miles to Sparta in about two days, then ran back. In Herodotus this Sparta run is the ONLY run Pheidippides makes; the famous Marathon-to-Athens death run is not in Herodotus at all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheidippides

question: The Spartans agreed to help Athens against the Persian army that had landed at Marathon, but they would not march yet, and they reached the field only after the battle was over. What were the Spartans waiting for before their army could set out?
answer: For the moon to grow full
choices: For the moon to grow full
For new shields to be forged
For an oracle to be consulted
For the spring floods to fall
context: Spartan religious law forbade marching until the full moon, and it was only the ninth day of the month. They arrived after the battle was over, toured the field, and praised the Athenian dead. Athens essentially won Marathon without them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: Pheidippides came home from his long run over the mountains with a strange story. High in the hills of Arcadia, he said, a god had stopped him, called him by name and grumbled that the Athenians had been ignoring him. Which god did Pheidippides claim to have met?
answer: The god Pan
choices: The god Pan
The god Hermes
The god Apollo
The god Zeus
context: Pheidippides reported that Pan complained the Athenians neglected him despite his friendliness and past help. After the war the grateful Athenians built Pan a shrine in a cave below the Acropolis. Herodotus relays this as Pheidippides's own testimony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheidippides  (Legend.)

question: Runners at the first modern Olympic marathon, in Athens in 1896, raced a round 40 kilometres or so, yet the race later became an oddly exact 26 miles 385 yards. The strange extra distance was added at a later Olympic Games in Europe. What stretched the course to that precise length?
answer: Moving the finish to a royal box
choices: Moving the finish to a royal box
Matching the old run to Athens
A surveyor's measuring error
A rule copied from ancient Greece
context: At the 1908 London Games the course was extended to start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box, making it 26 miles 385 yards (42.195 km). That distance became the official standard in 1921. Source: https://www.britannica.com/sports/Why-Is-a-Marathon-26-2-Miles

question: Robert Browning, the English poet, wrote a dramatic poem in 1879 called 'Pheidippides,' about the Greek runner who, in legend, carried news of victory with the cry 'Rejoice, we conquer!' and then died. What did Browning's poem directly inspire?
answer: A new Olympic race
choices: A new Olympic race
A famous oil painting
A children's adventure novel
A military marching song
context: Frenchman Michel Breal, moved by Browning's poem 'Pheidippides,' proposed a 'marathon' race for the very first modern Olympics in Athens in 1896. The poem, not the ancient record, gave the race its battle-cry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheidippides  (Legend.)

question: Miltiades, the Athenian general at Marathon, had too few hoplites to match the wide Persian battle line at full depth all along the front, yet his line had to stretch just as far without breaking. How did Miltiades arrange his hoplite formation?
answer: He thinned the center and kept the wings strong
choices: He thinned the center and kept the wings strong
He stacked every rank evenly across the line
He held most men back in a deep reserve
He spread the strongest fighters in the center
context: Miltiades cut his center to only four ranks deep instead of the usual eight. The center buckled on purpose while the strong wings wheeled inward and surrounded the Persians, a double envelopment. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: The Athenians at Marathon sprinted about a mile of open ground straight at the Persian line, though they had no horsemen or archers of their own. No Greek army had ever been recorded charging at a run before. How did the Persians read the charge?
answer: They thought the Athenians had gone mad
choices: They thought the Athenians had gone mad
They mistook it for a surrender
They assumed it was a feint
They believed reinforcements had come
context: Herodotus says this was the first time a Greek army is recorded running into battle. The sprint cut their losses to Persian arrows and shocked the enemy, who could not believe men would charge an empire with no horsemen or bowmen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: Cynaegirus, whose brother was the playwright Aeschylus, seized the stern of a Persian ship with his bare hands as the beaten Persians fled to their boats at Marathon, trying to hold it back. What did a Persian do to him for it?
answer: Hacked off his hand with an axe
choices: Hacked off his hand with an axe
Ran him through with a spear
Dragged him under the waves
Struck him down with an arrow
context: Cynaegirus died this famous death gripping the ship. Also killed that day was Callimachus, the war-archon (polemarch) who had cast the deciding vote to attack in the first place. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: The beaten Persians took to their ships after Marathon and rowed south around Cape Sounion, making for Athens itself while no army guarded the city. What did the tired Athenian hoplites, the heavy-armoured citizen soldiers, do next to save their city?
answer: Force-marched the army back to Athens
choices: Force-marched the army back to Athens
Sent a single runner ahead to warn the city
Sailed a captured Persian ship home
Lit warning fires along the coast
context: The just-victorious hoplites marched roughly 25 miles straight back and lined the shore, so when the Persian ships arrived they gave up and sailed home. THIS desperate march by a whole army, not one runner, is the real 'marathon.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon

question: Herodotus wrote the earliest account of the Battle of Marathon, and in it no messenger ran back to Athens, cried that the Athenians had won and dropped dead. Robert Browning's poem later retold that story. Where did the drop-dead version first appear?
answer: In Lucian, writing 600 years later
choices: In Lucian, writing 600 years later
In a Spartan war monument
In Herodotus's own footnotes
In an Athenian victory hymn
context: The satirist Lucian (2nd century AD) has a runner named 'Philippides' cry 'Nenikekamen' ('We have won!') and die on the spot. Lucian is the only ancient source with every element of the modern legend; over the centuries Herodotus's Pheidippides, Plutarch's Eucles, and Lucian's Philippides got merged into one hero. Source: https://sententiaeantiquae.com/2015/12/06/myths-of-marathons-herodotus-lucian-plutarch-and-us/

question: Japan's navy steamed toward the tiny American base at Midway atoll in June 1942, six months after Pearl Harbor, meaning to draw out the American carriers and destroy them. Until then Japan had been winning almost everywhere in the Pacific. Instead, on 4 June, American dive-bombers sank all four of its fleet carriers in a single day. What did that day do to the war?
answer: It turned the tide of the Pacific War
choices: It turned the tide of the Pacific War
It forced Japan to surrender within weeks
It ended all fighting in the Pacific
It captured the Japanese home islands
context: The four sunk carriers were Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, and Hiryu. Japan had used these same ships to attack Pearl Harbor; losing all four in one day cost it the heart of its carrier striking force. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway)

question: Joseph Rochefort's codebreakers in Hawaii kept decoding Japanese orders to attack a target named by only two letters, but they had no proof the target was Midway. So Captain Wilfred Holmes had Midway radio a false message, in plain language, about a sudden shortage. A day later the Japanese sent a coded report naming the same shortage at their target. What was the fake shortage that baited the trap?
answer: A shortage of fresh water
choices: A shortage of fresh water
A shortage of aircraft fuel
A shortage of ammunition
A shortage of medical supplies
context: Holmes had Midway radio that its fresh-water purification plant had broken down. Within about 24 hours HYPO intercepted a Japanese message reporting that "AF is short of fresh water" -- proving AF was Midway and letting the Americans set their ambush. The codebreaking effort was led by Commander Joseph Rochefort. (nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/battle-midway)

question: Torpedo Squadron 8 flew off the carrier Hornet in slow, out-of-date Devastator torpedo planes with no fighter escort, and Japanese Zeros shot down all fifteen before a single torpedo could hit anything. Ensign George Gay, the only one of the squadron's thirty aircrew to live, floated wounded in the open sea for about thirty hours until a flying boat found him. What kept him afloat and hidden?
answer: A floating seat cushion from his downed plane
choices: A floating seat cushion from his downed plane
A wooden crate of rations from a sunk ship
An empty fuel drum that drifted past him
A life raft dropped by a passing bomber
context: Gay hid under the black rubber seat cushion partly to shelter from the sun and partly to avoid being spotted by Japanese ships; he watched the carriers burn from the water. He was the only aircrew survivor of Torpedo Squadron 8. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._Gay_Jr.)

question: Chester Nimitz wanted every carrier he could get for Midway, but the Yorktown had been badly mauled at the Coral Sea a month before, and engineers first estimated months of repairs. Shipyard crews at Pearl Harbor patched her up in about 72 hours. What were the workmen still doing when the Yorktown sailed for Midway?
answer: Still aboard and working as she put to sea
choices: Still aboard and working as she put to sea
Still waiting on parts that never arrived
Still arguing she was unfit to sail
Still painting her new hull number on
context: The around-the-clock repair brought a third American carrier to the battle that the Japanese believed had already been sunk at Coral Sea -- a surprise that helped even the odds. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway)

question: Dauntless dive-bombers plunged out of the high sky almost unopposed from about 10:22 on the morning of 4 June 1942, after hours of failed American attacks on the Japanese carrier fleet. In roughly five minutes they wrecked three of the four carriers, the Akagi, Kaga and Soryu. Why did a few hits turn those ships into floating infernos so fast?
answer: Their decks were crammed with armed, fueled planes
choices: Their decks were crammed with armed, fueled planes
Their crews had already abandoned the ships
Their fuel tanks had been drained for safety
Their fighters were still parked below decks
context: Caught in the middle of re-arming and refueling, each carrier's deck was packed with bombs, torpedoes, and fuel hoses; a few hits set off chain explosions. Naval historians call this stretch "the five fateful minutes." (usni.org/magazines/proceedings/1955/june/five-fateful-minutes-midway)

question: Wade McClusky led the Enterprise's dive-bombers to the spot where the Japanese fleet was supposed to be and found nothing but empty ocean. Though his fuel was running low, he kept looking instead of turning back, and he caught sight of a single Japanese destroyer, the Arashi, racing north all alone. McClusky gambled on what she was doing and followed her. What did he bet the Arashi was doing?
answer: Hurrying to rejoin the main carrier fleet
choices: Hurrying to rejoin the main carrier fleet
Fleeing the battle after being damaged
Laying a smoke screen to hide the fleet
Scouting ahead for an American attack
context: Admiral Nimitz later wrote that McClusky's decision to keep searching and his judgment of where the enemy lay "decided the fate of our carrier task force and our forces at Midway." (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Wade_McClusky)

question: Dick Best dived almost straight down on the carrier Akagi on the morning of 4 June and put his bomb into her. That same afternoon he flew a second mission. By nightfall Best had done something that no other pilot in the entire war would ever match. What did he alone accomplish?
answer: He helped sink two enemy carriers in one day
choices: He helped sink two enemy carriers in one day
He sank an enemy battleship with one bomb
He shot down five enemy fighters in one day
He led three separate strikes in one day
context: Best's morning bomb helped doom Akagi; that afternoon his bomb was among those that finished off the last Japanese carrier still fighting, the Hiryu. No other pilot in the war helped sink two carriers in a single day. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Halsey_Best)

question: Tamon Yamaguchi, one of Japan's finest carrier commanders, was aboard the Hiryu, the last of the four Japanese carriers still fighting, when American dive-bombers from the Enterprise and Yorktown left her burning and doomed. He was offered the chance to leave the ship and save himself for the war ahead. What did he choose to do?
answer: Go down with his ship and her captain
choices: Go down with his ship and her captain
Transfer his flag to a nearby cruiser
Order the survivors to ram an American ship
Escape by destroyer to report the defeat
context: Yamaguchi stayed aboard the sinking Hiryu alongside her captain, Tomeo Kaku, rather than be rescued. Japan lost not just four carriers at Midway but many of its most skilled commanders and aircrews. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamon_Yamaguchi)

question: Japanese Zeros cut the slow American torpedo planes at Midway to pieces, almost to the last man, and not one of their torpedoes struck a carrier. Minutes later the American dive-bombers arrived high overhead and found the sky above the carriers wide open, with no fighters to stop them. How had the doomed torpedo attacks, though they hit nothing, set up the dive-bombers' success?
answer: They pulled the defending Zeros down to wave-top level
choices: They pulled the defending Zeros down to wave-top level
They knocked out the carriers' anti-aircraft guns
They forced the carriers to scatter out of formation
They used up the last of the Zeros' ammunition
context: To chase the low torpedo planes, the Japanese fighters dove to sea level -- leaving no one to guard the high altitude when the Dauntless dive-bombers tipped over into their attack. The sacrifice bought the decisive opening. (nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/battle-of-midway)

question: The destroyer Arashi was alone that morning, far behind the rest of the Japanese fleet, when Wade McClusky's dive-bombers spotted her and followed her wake. She had been held back by a task that had nothing to do with McClusky. Why had the Arashi fallen behind the fleet?
answer: She had stayed behind to hunt an American submarine
choices: She had stayed behind to hunt an American submarine
She had stopped to pick up downed Japanese pilots
She had broken down and made hasty repairs
She had been scouting eastward for the American fleet
context: The Arashi had been depth-charging the U.S. submarine Nautilus (Lt. Cdr. William Brockman), which was harassing the carriers; her dash back to rejoin drew the wake McClusky followed. So an American submarine indirectly led the dive-bombers to their targets -- skill and luck braided together. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Nautilus_(SS-168))

question: Chuichi Nagumo, commanding the Japanese carriers at Midway, had his reserve planes armed with bombs to strike the island again, then switched them to torpedoes when his scouts reported American ships nearby. Then he made one more choice that left his carriers exposed at the worst possible moment. What did Nagumo do that doomed them?
answer: He delayed launching to first recover his returning strike
choices: He delayed launching to first recover his returning strike
He launched his half-armed planes into a storm
He turned the fleet away and split it in two
He ordered all aircraft below to refuel at once
context: Rather than launch a hasty attack, Nagumo waited to land his returning Midway strike planes first, leaving the flight decks jammed with fueled, armed aircraft exactly when the American dive-bombers struck. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway)

question: Isoroku Yamamoto sent the largest fleet Japan ever built against Midway, the giant battleship Yamato among it, and on paper it outgunned the three American carriers many times over. Yet when the carriers fought, only Chuichi Nagumo's four took part, and the Yamato never fired a shot. What had Yamamoto done with his fleet to throw away his lead?
answer: He split it into groups too far apart to help each other
choices: He split it into groups too far apart to help each other
He held it all back to bombard the island first
He sent the carriers in without any escorts
He launched the attack before the fleet was ready
context: Yamamoto spread his ships across diversions and separate forces, so his battleships and the Yamato were hundreds of miles from the carrier fight. Only the four carriers were in range -- and they were the ones that were lost. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway_order_of_battle)

question: Andrew Jackson's mixed army of regulars, militia, frontier riflemen, Choctaw warriors, free men of colour and pirates shattered a British assault outside New Orleans on 8 January 1815, in about half an hour of fighting. It was the greatest American land victory of the War of 1812. Yet no soldier on the field that morning knew one thing about the war itself. What was it?
answer: The peace treaty ending the war had already been signed two weeks earlier
choices: The peace treaty ending the war had already been signed two weeks earlier
The British had already captured and burned the city of New Orleans
Jackson had secretly been ordered to surrender the city without a fight
The American government had already declared the war a lost cause
context: The Treaty of Ghent was signed in Europe on December 24, 1814 — but news couldn't cross the Atlantic faster than a wooden sailing ship, so the armies fought a battle for a war that was technically already over. The U.S. wouldn't even ratify the treaty until February 16, 1815, over a month after the battle. The pointless victory still made Jackson 'Old Hickory' a national hero and put him on the road to the presidency. Source: battlefields.org/learn/war-1812/battles/new-orleans; history.com.

question: Jean Lafitte ran a pirate base in the swamps south of New Orleans, and before the battle of January 1815 the British wrote to him offering $30,000 and a captain's rank in the Royal Navy if he would help them take the city. Andrew Jackson had once called his men 'hellish banditti.' Lafitte did not take the bribe. What did he do instead?
answer: He handed the British letters to the Americans and joined Jackson for a pardon
choices: He handed the British letters to the Americans and joined Jackson for a pardon
He fled the region with his ships and stayed out of the fighting entirely
He pocketed the money and then quietly betrayed the British plans to no one
He demanded twice the sum and a fleet before agreeing to help the British
context: Jackson had once called Lafitte's Baratarian privateers 'hellish banditti' — but he took the deal. About 50 of Lafitte's men worked the cannons in Jackson's defense. The defending army was a wild mix: Tennessee and Kentucky frontier marksmen, Louisiana militia, New Orleans free Men of Color, Choctaw warriors under leaders like Pushmataha, U.S. regulars, sailors, marines, and the pirates. Source: britannica.com/biography/Jean-Laffite; nps.gov.

question: Japan ordered the Yamato, the biggest battleship ever constructed, to sail for Okinawa in April 1945, while American soldiers and Marines were fighting for the island, on a mission she was never meant to survive. Her orders were not to win a sea battle. What was she supposed to do once she reached Okinawa?
answer: Run herself aground on the beach and fight until destroyed
choices: Run herself aground on the beach and fight until destroyed
Slip past the fleet and bombard the American landing zones
Ferry reinforcements ashore under cover of darkness
Lure the carriers into a trap for the waiting submarines
context: The Yamato never reached Okinawa. On April 7, 1945, American carrier planes hit her with about a dozen bombs and many torpedoes; she rolled over and exploded, taking roughly 2,498 of her crew down with her. Sources: history.com/this-day-in-history/april-7/japanese-battleship-yamato-is-sunk-by-allied-forces; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_battleship_Yamato

question: Soldiers and Marines of the United States fought for Okinawa for 82 days in 1945, and more than 12,000 Americans died, along with roughly 90,000 to 110,000 Japanese soldiers and some 94,000 to 150,000 Okinawan civilians. American war planners studied that toll for one purpose. What did they use it to do?
answer: Estimate the cost of invading mainland Japan, weighing the atomic-bomb decision
choices: Estimate the cost of invading mainland Japan, weighing the atomic-bomb decision
Negotiate a ceasefire with the Japanese high command
Redraw the postwar borders of the Ryukyu Islands
Calculate pensions owed to the families of the fallen
context: With civilian and military dead together topping 200,000 on a single island, Okinawa became the bloody preview of what invading the Japanese home islands might cost, a calculation that directly weighed on the decision to drop the atomic bombs instead. Sources: nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/battle-of-okinawa; britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Okinawa

question: Amompharetus, a Spartan officer at Plataea in 479 BC, refused his commander Pausanias's order to pull the army back from the Persians. He picked something up, laid it before Pausanias, and declared that with it he cast his vote against running from the strangers. What did he set down?
answer: A large stone
choices: A large stone
His broken spear
His own helmet
A handful of soil
context: Herodotus reports his words: "With this pebble I give my vote not to run away from the strangers." In a Spartan assembly men voted by casting pebbles, so a soldier laying down a boulder-sized 'pebble' was a defiant joke and a vote rolled into one. Source: Herodotus, Histories Book 9.55 (Rawlinson translation).

question: Pausanias, the Spartan regent, crushed the Persians at Plataea in 479 BC and then ordered the cooks of the dead Persian general Mardonius to serve up the rich feast they had been making for their master. Beside it he had a plain Spartan supper set out. Then he laughed and made one joke about the two meals. What was his joke?
answer: A man who ate this well was a fool to invade poor Greece to rob it
choices: A man who ate this well was a fool to invade poor Greece to rob it
Spartan food would make the Persians too soft to fight
The gods favored whichever side ate the simpler meal
Greek cooks could never match such Persian splendor
context: Herodotus quotes Pausanias: he summoned the Greeks "to show you the folly of this Median captain, who, when he enjoyed such fare as this, must needs come here to rob us of our penury" (our poverty). The joke is the irony: Mardonius left luxury to conquer a land that had little worth taking. Source: Herodotus, Histories Book 9.82 (Rawlinson translation).

question: Xerxes of Persia led perhaps 600 to 800 warships into Greek waters in 480 BC. The Greek fleet at Salamis, under Themistocles, had only about 370, and the Greeks knew they could never win a fair fight in open water. What did they do instead?
answer: Lured the huge fleet into a narrow strait where its numbers could not be used
choices: Lured the huge fleet into a narrow strait where its numbers could not be used
Sailed straight out to meet the larger fleet in open water
Split their ships into many tiny squadrons across the coast
Burned half their own triremes to lighten the line
context: Roughly 370-380 Greek triremes (Athens supplied about 180, the largest contingent) faced perhaps 600-800 Persian ships. The Greeks chose the cramped strait precisely so the giant fleet could not bring its numbers to bear. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/671); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Salamis.

question: Xerxes did not fight aboard a ship at Salamis. He had a throne carried up the slopes of Mount Aegaleus, high over the water, and sat there in full view of both fleets. What did he keep beside him as he watched?
answer: Scribes ready to write down the names of captains who fought bravely
choices: Scribes ready to write down the names of captains who fought bravely
A cage of war hounds to loose on shipwrecked sailors
A herd of horses saddled for a charge across the water
A chest of gold to throw to the first ship that rammed an enemy
context: Herodotus says Xerxes watched from his throne on Mount Aegaleus with scribes at his side, recording the names of brave captains so they could be rewarded. He expected to be recording a victory. Source: Herodotus, Histories 8.90; World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/671).

question: Themistocles set a trap for the Persian fleet on the night before the battle of Salamis. He secretly sent his sons' Persian tutor, Sicinnus, across the water to Xerxes with a lie. What lie did Sicinnus tell the king?
answer: That the Greeks were about to flee, so Xerxes should block the exits.
choices: That the Greeks were about to flee, so Xerxes should block the exits.
That the Greek crews had mutinied and would switch sides.
That a great storm was coming that would wreck the Greek fleet.
That Athens had already surrendered to the king in secret.
context: Themistocles sent Sicinnus, the Persian tutor of his own children, with the bluff that the Greeks were breaking apart and would flee. Xerxes believed it and sealed the exits, trapping his own oversized fleet in waters too cramped to maneuver; Herodotus says roughly 300 Persian ships were lost to about 40 Greek.

question: Themistocles won Athens over with his reading of an oracle. The Delphic oracle had warned that only a 'wooden wall' would save Athens, and some Athenians took it to mean a thorn hedge around the Acropolis. What did Themistocles tell the Athenians the wooden wall really was?
answer: Their fleet of ships
choices: Their fleet of ships
A new palisade around the harbor
The wooden gates of the Acropolis
A bridge of rafts across the strait
context: Themistocles insisted the 'wooden wall' meant Athens' triremes. He even pointed out that the oracle called the island 'divine Salamis,' not 'hateful Salamis,' so the deaths it foretold must be the enemy's, not Athens'. The Athenians abandoned their city and staked its survival on the fleet.

question: Queen Artemisia of Caria, the only woman commanding a ship in Xerxes's fleet, had an Athenian trireme on her tail at Salamis. She escaped by ramming and sinking a ship of her own side. Xerxes, watching from the shore, believed she had sunk an enemy. What did he exclaim?
answer: 'My men have become women, and my women men'
choices: 'My men have become women, and my women men'
'Even the gods now fight on the side of Greece'
'Bring me her name, that all Persia may honor it'
'No captain of mine has shown such loyalty today'
context: Artemisia rammed a friendly ship to shake off her pursuer; Xerxes, watching from Mount Aegaleus, assumed she had sunk a Greek and exclaimed that his men had become women and his women men. He never realized the rammed ship was on his own side: her 'brave' act was sinking one of his own.

question: Hitler's armies drove toward a city on the Volga in 1942. Its old name was Tsaritsyn, but in 1925 it took the name of the Soviet Union's rising leader, so holding it became a matter of personal pride for him. Who was that leader?
answer: Joseph Stalin
choices: Joseph Stalin
Vladimir Lenin
Leon Trotsky
Nikita Khrushchev
context: Renamed Stalingrad, the city carried Stalin's own name, so holding or taking it became a prestige contest for both Stalin and Hitler on top of its value controlling Volga shipping. The battle there (17 July 1942 to 2 February 1943) is often called the deadliest single battle in human history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stalingrad

question: German and Soviet soldiers fought through Stalingrad's bombed-out ruins for single rooms, cellars and stairwells, and the same building changed hands again and again. The Germans gave this grinding fight a grim nickname. What did they call it?
answer: the War of the Rats
choices: the War of the Rats
the Iron Harvest
the Meat Grinder
the Devil's Anvil
context: In German it was 'Rattenkrieg.' Streets, single buildings, and even individual floors of one building were lost and retaken over and over in the rubble. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stalingrad

question: A Soviet platoon of about 25 to 30 men seized a four-story apartment building in central Stalingrad. They ringed it with barbed wire and mines, fired down on German tanks from the roof, and held it for roughly two months. The building took the name of the sergeant who led them. What is it called?
answer: Pavlov's House
choices: Pavlov's House
Rodimtsev's House
Lyudnikov's House
Gorishny's House
context: Sergeant Yakov Pavlov led the defense, so the building took his name. Soviet general Vasily Chuikov later boasted the Germans lost more men trying to take Pavlov's House than they did capturing all of Paris, though that vivid claim has no support in the military archives. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavlov%27s_House

question: Vasily Zaitsev, the Red Army's most celebrated sniper at Stalingrad, had about 225 kills to his credit in roughly five weeks, eleven of them enemy snipers. His deadly aim came from the way he grew up in the Ural Mountains. What had the young Zaitsev done there?
answer: hunted deer and wolves
choices: hunted deer and wolves
herded reindeer
trapped sable for furs
fished the cold rivers
context: Zaitsev was a former deer and wolf hunter who killed his first wolf at age 12; the 225 confirmed kills were tallied between 10 November and 17 December 1942. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Zaitsev_(sniper)

question: A tiny Soviet force held a giant grain elevator, a tower of steel and concrete at the southern edge of Stalingrad, against three full German divisions. The two sides fought through it floor by floor. About how many defenders held the tower?
answer: about 50 men
choices: about 50 men
about 500 men
about 2,000 men
about 10,000 men
context: The elevator was roughly 90 meters long and 35 meters high, and the fighting inside was so close the two sides battled level by level. Source: https://stalingradtours.com/en/sights/articul/stalingrad_grain_elevator

question: Armed men of the blocking detachments waited behind the Red Army's own front lines, posted there by Stalin's Order No. 227. In their first three months they sent 24,000 soldiers to penal battalions. What were they ordered to do to Red Army men who retreated without orders?
answer: shoot them on the spot
choices: shoot them on the spot
strip them of all rank
march them home in chains
force them to clear minefields
context: The blocking detachments (zagraditelnye otryady) executed about 1,000 of their own troops in those first three months. Soviet soldiers fought heroically and were driven forward by a murderous regime; both are part of the honest record. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_No._227

question: The German Sixth Army had pushed deep into Stalingrad by November 1942, but weaker allied armies guarded its long flanks. The Soviets launched Operation Uranus on 19 November: instead of hitting the Germans head-on, their pincers smashed through one ally's lines and met near the town of Kalach, encircling about 290,000 Axis troops. Whose troops did the pincers tear through?
answer: Romania's
choices: Romania's
Italy's
Hungary's
Bulgaria's
context: The pincers broke the Romanian armies holding the flanks and met near Kalach on 22 November, sealing the 6th Army inside the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Uranus

question: Hermann Goering made a promise to Hitler with the German Sixth Army trapped inside Stalingrad: the Luftwaffe would supply the army entirely by air, at 300 tons of cargo every day. The airlift went on for 71 days. What did it really average each day?
answer: about 120 tons a day
choices: about 60 tons a day
about 120 tons a day
about 200 tons a day
about 280 tons a day
context: The airlift averaged only about 117 tons daily, less than half what Goering promised, while losing more than 266 Junkers Ju 52 transport planes, a crippling blow to German air power. Source: https://www.ospreypublishing.com/ca/osprey-blog/2023/the-luftwaffe-s-stalingrad-airlift-the-transport-fleet-that-failed/

question: Adolf Hitler promoted Friedrich Paulus to field marshal on 30 January 1943, with the Sixth Army doomed inside Stalingrad, and pointedly noted that no German field marshal had ever surrendered. It was a coded order for Paulus to shoot himself. Paulus surrendered the next morning instead. What did his aide record him saying about killing himself?
answer: I'm not going to do them such a favour.
choices: I'm not going to do them such a favour.
A soldier dies, he does not beg.
Let history judge this defeat.
I serve Germany, not one man.
context: Paulus's surrender made the 6th Army the first of Hitler's field armies ever to capitulate. Of roughly 91,000 frozen, starving Germans taken prisoner, only about 5,000 to 6,000 ever returned home. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Paulus

question: Antony Beevor, a historian, went through the Russian Defence Ministry archives to test a famous story about Vasily Zaitsev: a legendary duel with a German marksman supposedly sent to Stalingrad just to hunt him down. The tale was later turned into several films. What did Beevor conclude about the duel?
answer: It never happened, a Soviet propaganda invention.
choices: It never happened, a Soviet propaganda invention.
It happened, but Zaitsev embellished the range.
It happened on a quieter stretch of front.
The truth was lost when the archives burned.
context: Beevor judged the duel a propaganda invention because the Defence Ministry archives contradict it; the dramatic version lives on mainly through films. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Zaitsev_(sniper)  (Legend.)

question: Friedrich Paulus turned against the Nazi regime as a prisoner after Stalingrad, and he testified for the prosecution at the Nuremberg war-crimes trials. He refused to call Adolf Hitler by his title and used a contemptuous nickname instead. What did Paulus call him?
answer: the Bohemian corporal
choices: the Bohemian corporal
the Austrian house-painter
the Berlin butcher
the trench-runner
context: Paulus said he had 'no intention of shooting myself for this Bohemian corporal,' then joined a Soviet-backed anti-Nazi committee and testified at Nuremberg. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Paulus

question: Writing his war memoirs afterwards, Winston Churchill confessed that while Britain fought to keep its Atlantic supply line open against Germany's submarines, only one danger had ever really frightened him. Which danger did he name?
answer: The U-boat peril
choices: The U-boat peril
The London Blitz
The fall of France
The threat of invasion
context: Churchill feared the U-boats could cut the Atlantic lifeline and starve Britain into surrender. The Battle of the Atlantic ran from the first day of the war, 3 September 1939, to Germany's surrender in May 1945 — the longest campaign of WWII. Source: Imperial War Museum, 'What you need to know about the Battle of the Atlantic'; Churchill, The Second World War.

question: German U-boats hunted the Allied merchant ships that carried food, weapons and troops across the Atlantic from America to Britain. To live through the attacks, the merchant ships did not sail alone: they packed together by the dozens, up to about sixty in columns of five, with Allied warships ringed around them. What was this guarded grouping called?
answer: A convoy
choices: A convoy
A flotilla
A blockade
A picket line
context: Safety came from sailing together, not alone — the escorts could only guard ships that stayed bunched in the box. The Germans answered the convoy with their 'Wolfpack' tactic, gathering many U-boats to swarm one convoy at night. Source: Imperial War Museum, 'What you need to know about the Battle of the Atlantic'.

question: Günther Prien threaded the submarine U-47 past sunken blockships at slack tide, through the narrow Kirk Sound, into Scapa Flow, the Royal Navy's main home base, on the night of 13 to 14 October 1939. Once inside, what did he sink in just thirteen minutes?
answer: The battleship HMS Royal Oak
choices: The battleship HMS Royal Oak
An ammunition depot on shore
The base's main fuel tanks
A line of moored destroyers
context: Hitler sent his personal plane to fly Prien's crew to Berlin; Prien became the first U-boat captain to win the Knight's Cross and was nicknamed 'the Bull of Scapa Flow.' Less than 17 months later, on about 8 March 1941, Prien and all 45 of his crew vanished with U-47 attacking a convoy — the sub was never found. Source: Navy History (AU); Osprey Publishing.

question: Allied merchant ships crossing the Atlantic met their worst danger in a band of open ocean about 500 miles across, in the middle of the crossing. It lay so far from any airfield that no Allied aircraft could reach it to guard them, and German U-boats hunted hardest there. What did the crews and the Allies call this deadly stretch?
answer: The Black Pit
choices: The Black Pit
The Cold Reach
The Devil's Trench
The Iron Triangle
context: Also called the Mid-Atlantic Air Gap, the Black Pit was finally closed in May 1943 when Very-Long-Range Liberator bombers and escort carriers could at last cover the whole crossing — a turning point in the battle. Source: Mid-Atlantic gap references; Canadian Nautical Research Society.

question: British escorts forced the submarine U-110 to the surface on 9 May 1941, and its crew abandoned ship. David Balme, a sub-lieutenant, led a boarding party down into the dark, possibly sinking hull. What did his men carry out that soon proved priceless to Britain?
answer: Its intact Enigma cipher machine and codebooks
choices: Its intact Enigma cipher machine and codebooks
A complete map of the convoy routes
A list of every U-boat captain
The submarine's secret fuel reserves
context: U-110's captain Fritz-Julius Lemp had jumped into the sea to swim back and scuttle the boat, but it was too late. Reading this traffic ('Ultra') let the Allies steer convoys around waiting wolfpacks — and German intelligence kept assuring Admiral Dönitz that Enigma was unbreakable. The genuine 'science wins wars' thread linking the Atlantic to Bletchley. Source: ForcesNews; WW2Today.

question: Hitler's armies tore into the snowbound Ardennes forest of Belgium in December 1944, and on the war maps the ground they seized pushed deep into the Allied front line. American soldiers named the fight after that shape. What did they call it?
answer: the Battle of the Bulge
choices: the Battle of the Bulge
the Battle of the Dent
the Battle of the Breakthrough
the Battle of the Wedge
context: The German breakthrough on December 16, 1944 pushed a huge dent into the Allied front line — the bulge that gave the battle its nickname. Over 600,000 American troops were eventually drawn in, making it the largest battle the U.S. Army has ever fought. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/battle-of-the-bulge

question: Anthony McAuliffe and his American paratroopers were surrounded in the Belgian town of Bastogne in December 1944. The Germans sent in a written demand for an 'honorable surrender,' sure the trapped men would give up. McAuliffe typed his whole reply as a single word. What was that word?
answer: NUTS!
choices: NUTS!
RETREAT
NEVER
SURRENDER
context: On December 22, 1944, McAuliffe's full typed note read: 'To the German Commander, / N U T S ! / The American Commander.' When the German envoy didn't understand the slang, Col. Joseph 'Bud' Harper explained it meant 'Go to hell.' Source: https://www.army.mil/article/92856/the_story_of_the_nuts_reply

question: Adolf Hitler launched a surprise winter attack through the snowy Ardennes Forest on 16 December 1944, codenamed 'Wacht am Rhein,' Watch on the Rhine. He meant to smash through Belgium and capture one great prize, a target that would cut the Allied armies in two. What was the objective Hitler was driving for?
answer: the port of Antwerp
choices: the port of Antwerp
the city of Paris
the Rhine bridges
the beaches of Normandy
context: Taking the deep-water port of Antwerp would have choked Allied supplies and split the British and American armies. The Ardennes was chosen precisely because it was lightly defended and thought too rugged for a winter offensive. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Bulge

question: Otto Skorzeny's English-speaking German commandos put on captured American uniforms and drove American jeeps behind the lines. At checkpoints the guards could not tell friend from spy by sight, so they grilled each other with questions a real American would know cold but a disguised German might miss. What did the GIs quiz each other about?
answer: American pop culture, like Mickey Mouse's girlfriend
choices: American pop culture, like Mickey Mouse's girlfriend
the day's secret password
their home addresses and birthdays
the names of their officers
context: GIs asked things like who Mickey Mouse's girlfriend was, which baseball team played where, or state capitals — trivia a homegrown American absorbed by osmosis. Otto Skorzeny led the operation; only about 10 of his men spoke flawless American slang. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/operation-greif-secret-mission-sow-chaos-us-army

question: George Patton needed his planes in the air, with the 101st Airborne trapped at Bastogne, but fog and rain kept them on the ground. He ordered his Third Army chaplain, James O'Neill, to write a prayer for clear skies and had it printed on cards for the troops. The skies cleared on 23 December 1944 and the planes flew. How did Patton reward the chaplain?
answer: Pinned a Bronze Star on him
choices: Pinned a Bronze Star on him
Promoted him to colonel
Gave him his own ivory pistol
Named a tank in his honor
context: Patton reportedly said, 'God damn! That O'Neill sure did some potent praying,' and pinned a Bronze Star on the chaplain. The clear weather let Allied planes fly and drop supplies to the besieged defenders, and the Third Army wheeled north to relieve the 101st Airborne at Bastogne. Sources: https://www.wwiimemorialfriends.org/blog/pattons-prayer; https://www.warhistoryonline.com/instant-articles/battle-of-the-bulge-patton-ordered-the-priest-to-pray-for-clear-weather-the-weather-subsequently-cleared.html

question: Joachim Peiper's Waffen-SS troops captured a group of unarmed American prisoners at the Baugnez crossroads near Malmedy, Belgium, on 17 December 1944 and machine-gunned them in a field: about 84 men, the largest massacre of U.S. soldiers in Europe during the war. How did more than 50 of the captured Americans manage to survive the shooting?
answer: they fell down playing dead, then ran
choices: they fell down playing dead, then ran
they hid in a nearby barn
they were ransomed back by officers
a German soldier let them go
context: On December 17, 1944, more than 50 GIs survived by dropping as if killed and then running once the SS men moved on. After the war Peiper was sentenced to death for the massacre, but his sentence was commuted and he was released in 1956; in 1976 his house in France was firebombed and he was killed. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/malmedy-massacre

question: George Patton stunned a room full of generals on 19 December 1944, with the 101st Airborne trapped at Bastogne, by promising to counterattack within 48 hours. To keep that promise he pulled off a maneuver generals usually call impossible, in the dead of winter. What did Patton actually do with his 250,000 men and hundreds of tanks?
answer: wheeled them 90 degrees from facing east to driving north
choices: wheeled them 90 degrees from facing east to driving north
dug them into a defensive line and waited
loaded them onto trains heading west
split them into small raiding parties
context: Patton wheeled 250,000 men and hundreds of tanks 90 degrees — from facing east to driving north — through the worst winter in 50 years. His tanks broke the siege and relieved Bastogne on December 26, 1944. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Bulge

question: American and Japanese fleets fought for five days in the Coral Sea, north of Australia, in May 1942, in one of the largest sea battles in history. Yet the ships of the two sides never traded a single shot directly at one another. How was that possible?
answer: The whole battle was fought by carrier aircraft striking ships far over the horizon
choices: The whole battle was fought by carrier aircraft striking ships far over the horizon
The two fleets agreed to a truce and only bombed empty islands
Thick fog hid the ships so completely that no guns could be aimed
The ships fired only at submarines hidden deep beneath the waves
context: Coral Sea (4-8 May 1942) was the first naval battle in history in which the opposing fleets never sighted or fired on each other directly. Aircraft launched from carriers did all the fighting, hitting ships miles away over the horizon. It changed naval warfare forever: the aircraft carrier, not the big-gun battleship, was now the deciding weapon at sea. Source: Naval History and Heritage Command, history.navy.mil.

question: Robert Dixon, a lieutenant commander, led the Lexington's dive-bombers down onto the Japanese carrier Shoho at the Coral Sea on 7 May 1942 and helped sink her. She was the first enemy aircraft carrier the United States destroyed in the war. Dixon radioed back a jubilant message that became famous. What did he say?
answer: "Scratch one flat top!"
choices: "Scratch one flat top!"
"The carrier is going down!"
"We have struck the enemy!"
"First blood is ours today!"
context: Lt. Cmdr. Robert E. Dixon's radio call, 'Scratch one flat top!', announced the first Japanese aircraft carrier ever sunk in the war. Shoho was hit by an avalanche of bombs and torpedoes and went down just four minutes after the abandon-ship order at 11:31 on 7 May 1942. Source: Wikipedia, Robert E. Dixon; Wikipedia, Japanese aircraft carrier Shoho.

question: Sir Douglas Haig launched the Battle of the Somme on 1 July 1916, and that day the British Army lost about 57,470 men killed and wounded, the worst day in its history. Many of those killed came from units raised on a promise that friends from the same town, factory or street could enlist and serve side by side. What were these units called?
answer: The Pals battalions
choices: The Pals battalions
The Iron Brigades
The Home Companies
The Kitchener Lancers
context: Because Pals battalions kept neighbours together, a single bad morning could wipe out the young men of an entire community at once — the Accrington Pals sent about 720 men against the village of Serre and took 585 casualties in roughly half an hour. Source: https://www.historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofBritain/Battle-of-the-Somme/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accrington_Pals

question: British tunnellers set off the Lochnagar mine two minutes before the infantry climbed out of their trenches on 1 July 1916: 60,000 pounds of explosive packed beneath the German strongpoint at La Boisselle. The blast threw earth thousands of feet into the air and tore open a hole 330 feet across and 70 feet deep. What record was that explosion said to have set?
answer: The loudest man-made sound in history to that point
choices: The loudest man-made sound in history to that point
The first shot fired in the First World War
The deepest tunnel ever dug under a city
The first use of poison gas on the Western Front
context: The crater the Lochnagar mine left is still the largest ever made by warfare, and it survives in the French countryside today as a memorial. Source: https://www.lochnagarcrater.org/history/statistics/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lochnagar_mine

question: Charles, mayor of the palace of the Franks, met a Muslim army pushing north into Gaul near Tours in 732 and turned it back. Chroniclers gave him a nickname, and it stuck. What did they call him?
answer: Charles the Hammer
choices: Charles the Hammer
Charles the Bald
Charles the Fat
Charles the Simple
context: 'Martel' (from the Latin Martellus) is not a family name but an epithet, 'the Hammer,' given to Charles Martel for hammering back the Umayyad advance at Tours in 732. His family, the Carolingians, took their name from him; his son Pepin the Short became the first Carolingian king in 751, and his grandson Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800.

question: The foot soldiers of Charles, leader of the Franks, had held their ground all day at Tours in 732 against the Umayyad cavalry of Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi. Then a rumor tore through the Muslim camp, and the battle line suddenly came apart. What did the rumor claim was happening?
answer: Frankish troops were ransacking their baggage and plunder
choices: Frankish troops were ransacking their baggage and plunder
A second Frankish army was marching up from the south
Their commander al-Ghafiqi had already been slain
A river crossing behind them had been cut off
context: Word spread that Franks were looting the Umayyad baggage train -- the army's accumulated plunder -- and so many men broke off to defend the camp that the line collapsed. Al-Ghafiqi was killed trying to rally his fleeing men. Arab sources call the battle Balat al-Shuhada, the 'Pavement of the Martyrs.' Source: worldhistory.org/article/1809; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tours

question: Philippe Pétain led the French defence of Verdun in 1916, as German shells rained down on the ring of old forts. His defenders, determined to stop the German advance no matter the cost, took up a short rallying cry that became the spirit of the whole battle. What did they vow?
answer: "They shall not pass!"
choices: "They shall not pass!"
"We will hold the line!"
"France will never kneel!"
"Hold or die here!"
context: "Ils ne passeront pas!" became the watchword of Verdun, associated with General Philippe Petain, who ordered the front line to hold fast. Source: firstworldwar.com/battles/verdun.htm

question: French and German armies ground through ten months of slaughter at Verdun in 1916, and the rail lines into the town were cut. France kept the whole battle supplied along a single narrow road out of Bar-le-Duc, soon called the Voie Sacrée, the Sacred Way. At its peak in June, how relentless was the traffic on that one road?
answer: A truck rolled past every 14 seconds
choices: A truck rolled past every 14 seconds
A truck rolled past every 4 minutes
A convoy crossed twice a day
A single train ran each night
context: Up to 12,000 vehicles a day formed an unbroken stream hauling men and shells to the front, since the rail lines were cut and this road was Verdun's only lifeline. Source: worldhistory.org/article/2878/battle-of-verdun/

question: Sylvain Raynal, the French major commanding Fort Vaux, fought the Germans corridor by corridor through its tunnels in June 1916, his men dying of thirst under gas attacks with every telephone line cut. To get one last message out, Raynal turned to an unusual messenger. What did he send?
answer: His last carrier pigeon
choices: His last carrier pigeon
A runner through the sewers
A signal mirror at dawn
A swimmer down the moat
context: The pigeon, named Le Vaillant, carried a message ending 'This is my last pigeon' and delivered it though mortally gassed; it was later awarded the Legion of Honour. Raynal surrendered on 7 June and was honored even by his captors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Vaillant

question: German soldiers took Fort Douaumont, the mightiest of France's forts at Verdun, on 25 February 1916, only the fifth day of the battle, in a way that shocked all of France. The fort guarded Verdun behind thick concrete and steel. How did it fall?
answer: Without a shot being fired
choices: Without a shot being fired
Under a week-long siege
To a massive flamethrower assault
After its magazine exploded
context: A tiny German raiding party of the 24th Brandenburg Infantry Regiment slipped in through an unguarded passage and captured the surprised garrison of about 57 territorials. The French would not retake the fort until 24 October 1916. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Douaumont

question: Erich von Falkenhayn, chief of the German army, chose to attack Verdun knowing that French national pride would force France to defend it to the last man. He was not really aiming to capture the town at all. How did he sum up his grim purpose?
answer: To 'bleed France white'
choices: To 'bleed France white'
To 'break the French spirit'
To 'win by sheer numbers'
To 'starve France of guns'
