context: Falkenhayn's aim was attrition itself, compelling the French to throw in every man they had. The battle cost both sides roughly 700,000 casualties, with around 300,000 dead. Source: britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Verdun and worldhistory.org/article/2878/battle-of-verdun/

question: Beethoven was so deaf when his Ninth Symphony was first played in 1824 that he had no idea the crowd behind him was on its feet, cheering and waving handkerchiefs. The singer Caroline Unger stepped over so he would know. What did she do?
answer: Turned him around to face the cheering crowd
choices: Turned him around to face the cheering crowd
Handed him a written note of praise
Led him gently offstage by the arm
Placed the finished score back in his hands
context: Unger, the contralto soloist, physically turned the deaf composer toward the hall so he could SEE the ovation he could not hear. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_(Beethoven); thevintagenews.com/2016/09/10/premiere-symphony-no-9-beethoven-physically-turned-around-see-audience-applaud-even-waved-handkerchiefs/

question: Ludwig van Beethoven finished his Fifth Symphony in Vienna in 1808. It opens with four notes so striking that many people call them the most famous four notes in all of music. How do those four opening notes go?
answer: Short-short-short-LONG (da-da-da-DUM)
choices: Short-short-short-LONG (da-da-da-DUM)
Long-long-short-short (DUM-DUM-da-da)
Short-long-short-long (da-DUM-da-DUM)
Long-short-long-short (DUM-da-DUM-da)
context: Those four notes, in C minor, open the Fifth and are arguably the most recognizable phrase in Western music. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_(Beethoven)

question: Beethoven gave the world one of its most beloved melodies in the Ninth Symphony that Vienna first heard in 1824: the tune known as the Ode to Joy. A great union of nations later adopted it as its official anthem. Which union?
answer: The European Union
choices: The European Union
The United Nations
The British Commonwealth
The International Red Cross
context: The choral finale sets Friedrich Schiller's poem 'An die Freude' ('Ode to Joy'); its melody is today the official anthem of the European Union. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_(Beethoven)

question: Beethoven broke with tradition in the last movement of his Ninth, first played in Vienna in 1824. Until then a symphony was played by an orchestra alone: strings, brass, woodwinds and drums. He added something no major symphony had ever used, and it stunned the first crowds. What did he add?
answer: A full singing chorus
choices: A full singing chorus
A solo church organ
A band of hunting horns
A military marching drum corps
context: The Ninth was the first major symphony to fold a singing chorus into the music itself, in the choral finale built on Schiller's words. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_(Beethoven)

question: Michael Umlauf, the real conductor at the premiere of the Ninth on 7 May 1824, had told the players to ignore the composer and follow him instead. Beethoven stood on stage flinging his arms about and shouting tempos, though he could not hear a note. How did his beat compare to the actual music?
answer: He had fallen several bars behind it
choices: He had fallen several bars behind it
He stayed perfectly in step with it
He raced several bars ahead of it
He stopped beating partway through it
context: Eyewitnesses said Beethoven seemed to play every instrument and sing every chorus part, and by the end was several bars behind the music the orchestra was actually playing under Umlauf. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_(Beethoven); history.com/this-day-in-history/may-7/beethoven-ninth-symphony-debuts-vienna

question: The British Broadcasting Corporation sent four notes from Beethoven's Fifth over the air during the Second World War. Their rhythm matched dot-dot-dot-dash in Morse code, and they became the signal of a famous wartime campaign. Which campaign?
answer: The 'V for Victory' campaign
choices: The 'V for Victory' campaign
The 'Dig for Victory' campaign
The 'Keep Calm and Carry On' campaign
The 'Lend and Lease' campaign
context: Dot-dot-dot-dash is Morse for the letter V, matching the Fifth's opening rhythm, so the BBC used the four notes as the audio signal for the Allied 'V for Victory' campaign. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_(Beethoven)

question: Terrified of losing music itself as he went nearly deaf in his forties, Beethoven found a strange trick to keep 'hearing' his piano. He pressed one end of a wooden rod against its soundboard and held the other end in one particular spot on his body, feeling the music through vibration. Where did he hold the rod?
answer: Clenched between his teeth
choices: Clenched between his teeth
Pressed flat against his ear
Held tight against his chest
Cupped in both of his hands
context: By biting a rod pressed to the piano, Beethoven felt the vibrations carry through his jawbone. (The tale that he sawed off his piano's legs to feel the floor is widely repeated but disputed.) mso.com.au/the-blog/2022-how-did-beethoven-write-one-of-his-greatest-compositions-while-deaf; hearinghealthmatters.org/hearing-international/2023/hearing-beethoven-part-ii-the-medical-conclusion/

question: At Heiligenstadt, a village outside Vienna, Beethoven, then 31, poured his despair into a letter to his brothers in 1802, terrified that his growing deafness was destroying everything he was. He never sent it, and it turned up only after he died. In it he confessed he had come close to ending his own life, and named the one thing that had held him back. What was it?
answer: His art — the music he still felt called to write
choices: His art — the music he still felt called to write
His faith in God and a life to come
His duty to look after his younger brothers
His hope that a doctor would yet cure him
context: In the Heiligenstadt Testament (6 October 1802) Beethoven wrote that 'only art it was that withheld me... it seemed impossible to leave the world until I had produced all that I felt called upon me to produce.' lvbeethoven.com/biography/the-heiligenstadt-testament/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heiligenstadt_Testament

question: Anton Schindler, Beethoven's secretary and first biographer, reported that the composer called the four-note opening of his Fifth Symphony 'Fate knocking at the door.' Almost everyone has heard the line, yet historians now doubt Beethoven ever said it. Why has the quotation fallen under suspicion?
answer: The man who reported it forged entries in Beethoven's notebooks
choices: The man who reported it forged entries in Beethoven's notebooks
The man who reported it admitted he had made the line up
The man who reported it had never actually met Beethoven
The man who reported it was a rival composer with a grudge
context: The phrase comes from Beethoven's secretary Anton Schindler, now known to have forged entries in Beethoven's notebooks, so scholars treat 'Fate knocking' as almost certainly invented rather than the composer's own words. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_(Beethoven); classical-music.com/features/works/beethoven-fifth-symphony  (Legend.)

question: Beethoven lay dying in Vienna in March 1827 when word came that a long-awaited case of fine wine had arrived as a gift from his London publisher. Those at his bedside said his reply was his last words. What did the dying composer say?
answer: 'Pity, pity — too late!'
choices: 'Pity, pity — too late!'
'At last, my dear old friend.'
'Pour it out, and let me rest.'
'Tell them all I forgive them.'
context: Beethoven died on 26 March 1827, aged 56; his documented last words, on hearing of the wine, were reportedly 'Pity, pity — too late!' en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Ludwig_van_Beethoven; popularbeethoven.com/what-were-beethovens-last-words/

question: Anselm Hüttenbrenner, a friend at Beethoven's deathbed, flatly denied in 1860 a romantic legend about the composer's final words: a Latin farewell, 'Applaud, friends, the comedy is over.' On what grounds did Hüttenbrenner reject the story?
answer: He had not been in the room for the rite the line refers to
choices: He had not been in the room for the rite the line refers to
He had never once heard Beethoven speak any Latin
He swore Beethoven had been unconscious for days before
He claimed a rival had invented it to mock the church
context: Huttenbrenner denied the 'comedy is over' line because he was not even present for the religious rite the remark would have followed, so historians treat it as legend, not record. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Ludwig_van_Beethoven; libquotes.com/ludwig-van-beethoven/quote/lbv0f1d

question: Geneticists read Beethoven's DNA in 2023 from verified locks of his hair, granting his old wish that his illnesses be studied after his death. Along with a strong inherited risk of disease, they found an infection from his final months that, with his heavy drinking, most likely killed him. Which infection did the hair reveal?
answer: Hepatitis B
choices: Hepatitis B
Tuberculosis
Typhoid fever
Malaria
context: The 2023 genome study of five genetically-matched hair locks found a hepatitis B infection plus a genetic risk for liver disease; it also debunked an older 'lead poisoning' claim because that earlier 'Beethoven hair' was not actually his. cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(23)00181-1; phys.org/news/2023-03-dna-beethoven-hair-poor-healthand.html

question: Thomas Edison ran his lab like a factory. He promised a small invention every ten days and a big one every six months, and the newspapers, dazzled, gave him a nickname. What was it?
answer: The Wizard of Menlo Park
choices: The Wizard of Menlo Park
The Sage of New Jersey
The Lord of Lightning
The Genius of Greenfield
context: Menlo Park, New Jersey, was the site of his famous lab. Edison's name ended up on 1,093 U.S. patents, still among the most by any single person. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Edison

question: Thomas Edison did not think great inventions came from sudden flashes of genius. To him they came from trying, failing and trying again, and he packed that belief into one famous line, which he confirmed in a 1927 letter. What did he say invention really was?
answer: "One percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration."
choices: "One percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration."
"A thousand failures for every single success."
"Equal parts imagination and stubborn hard work."
"Mostly luck, and a little bit of cleverness."
context: The line captures Edison's whole method: test 1,600 materials if that's what it takes. https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Thomas_Edison

question: George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla backed a kind of electricity that could be pushed for miles over thin wires. Thomas Edison, their rival in the War of the Currents, championed direct current (DC), which was safe but grew weak after a short distance. The rival to DC won, and it still flows from every wall socket today. What kind of current was it?
answer: Alternating current (AC)
choices: Alternating current (AC)
Stronger direct current (DC)
Static electric charge
Stored battery current
context: Alternating current reverses direction many times a second, which let transformers boost it to high voltage for long trips and then lower it again for safe use in homes. https://www.history.com/articles/what-was-the-war-of-the-currents

question: Thomas Edison's camp wanted Americans to dread his rivals' current as a killer. So they made up a creepy new verb meaning 'to execute someone with electricity,' built from the surname of the industrialist who put his money behind that current. What was the made-up word?
answer: "Westinghoused"
choices: "Westinghoused"
"Edisoned"
"Teslated"
"Currented"
context: George Westinghouse was the businessman backing AC, so Edison's camp turned his name into the verb, tying him personally to death by electricity. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/edison-vs-westinghouse-a-shocking-rivalry-102146036/

question: George Westinghouse used Nikola Tesla's alternating current to switch on more than 100,000 light bulbs at once at the Chicago World's Fair of 1893, more electric light than most people had ever seen in one place. What glittering nickname did the glowing fairgrounds earn?
answer: The White City
choices: The White City
The Crystal Court
The Golden Mile
The Silver Fair
context: Westinghouse had won the lighting contract by underbidding Edison's people, $399,000 to $554,000. The dazzling display proved AC was safe and practical to the public. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World%27s_Columbian_Exposition

question: Harold Brown, Thomas Edison's man, staged a grim demonstration at Columbia College on 30 July 1888, before a hall of electricians and reporters. He shocked the same dog first with Edison's direct current and then with alternating current. What happened to the dog?
answer: It survived 1,000 volts of DC but died at just 330 volts of AC.
choices: It survived 1,000 volts of DC but died at just 330 volts of AC.
It shrugged off 700 volts of DC but died at 700 volts of AC.
It survived 500 volts of AC but died at 1,400 volts of DC.
It died at 250 volts of AC and 250 volts of DC alike.
context: The rigged demo was meant to brand AC as a killer even at low voltage, helping Edison's campaign against Westinghouse. https://www.discovermagazine.com/technology/the-cruel-animal-testing-behind-thomas-edisons-quest-to-show-dangers-of-ac

question: George Westinghouse had fought to keep his alternating current out of executions. Yet it powered the first electric chair, and on 6 August 1890 the execution of William Kemmler went horribly wrong: after the first jolt he was still breathing, and a witness screamed, "Great God! He's alive!" What did Westinghouse say afterward?
answer: "They could have done better with an ax."
choices: "They could have done better with an ax."
"No machine of mine was ever meant for this."
"The fault lies with the men, not the wires."
"This is murder dressed up as science."
context: Westinghouse had fought to keep his AC out of executions, and the gruesome failure horrified him. The first jolt of about 700 volts ran 17 seconds and failed; a second of over 1,000 volts ran two minutes. Edison's camp had used AC in the chair to smear Westinghouse's technology. Sources: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/edison-vs-westinghouse-a-shocking-rivalry-102146036/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kemmler

question: Thomas Edison, a popular story goes, electrocuted Topsy, a working circus elephant, in order to scare the public away from Nikola Tesla's rival alternating current. Historians say that version is false. What really happened to Topsy?
answer: Topsy died at Coney Island in 1903, after Edison had left his electric company, which only filmed it.
choices: Topsy died at Coney Island in 1903, after Edison had left his electric company, which only filmed it.
Topsy died of old age at the Bronx Zoo in 1910, and Edison's film crew staged a re-enactment afterward.
Topsy was put down by her own circus handlers in 1908, and no film of her death was ever made at all.
Topsy died at Coney Island in 1903, but it was George Westinghouse's company, not Edison's, that filmed it.
context: The War of the Currents was effectively over by the mid-1890s, when AC at Niagara Falls sent power 26 miles to Buffalo. Topsy died on January 4, 1903, ten years after the current war ended; Edison's film company merely recorded it in a short titled 'Electrocuting an Elephant' and did not stage it as anti-AC propaganda. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topsy_(elephant)

question: Benedict Arnold, one of the boldest generals in Washington's army, took a bad leg wound leading a charge at Saratoga. Yet slights from Congress embittered him, and he was buried in debt. He secretly agreed to betray the Americans for British money and a British command. What did he plot to hand over to the enemy?
answer: West Point, the fort guarding the Hudson River
choices: West Point, the fort guarding the Hudson River
George Washington's personal battle plans
the Continental Army's main gunpowder stores
the harbor defenses of New York City
context: Arnold negotiated 20,000 British pounds and a generalship for surrendering West Point, the fort that controlled the Hudson River. After the plot collapsed he received only about 6,000 of the promised 20,000 pounds. His name became the American synonym for traitor; he died unpopular in London in 1801. Source: history.com, 'Benedict Arnold commits treason' / '9 things you may not know about Benedict Arnold'.

question: Three militiamen stopped a British courier near Tarrytown, New York: John Andre, a major carrying the secret plans of Benedict Arnold's plot. Andre tried to bluff his way past, but the men searched him and found the papers in an unexpected hiding place. Where were the plans hidden?
answer: folded inside his boot
choices: folded inside his boot
sewn into his saddle
rolled in his pistol barrel
tucked under his hat
context: Three ordinary militiamen, John Paulding, Isaac Van Wart, and David Williams, caught Andre and found the plans hidden in his boot/stocking. Andre offered them a bribe to let him go; they refused. He asked to die a soldier's death by firing squad rather than the gallows; the request was denied and he was hanged at Tappan, New York on October 2, 1780, at age 29. Source: metmuseum.org collection record; allthingsliberty.com, 'Major Andre's Captors Revisited'; westminster-abbey.org, 'John Andre'.

question: Benedict of Nursia wrote a rule around 529 for monks living together in a community, and it shaped Christian monasteries for a thousand years. His followers summed up its way of life in two Latin words, a motto that gave a monk's day its balance. What did the motto say?
answer: Pray and work
choices: Pray and work
Watch and fast
Read and obey
Give and serve
context: 'Ora et labora' — 'pray and work.' Benedict split a monk's day roughly into thirds: about eight hours of prayer, eight of work, and eight of sleep, so a man was ruled by neither prayer alone nor labor alone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ora_et_labora

question: On the mountaintop of Monte Cassino, Benedict wrote a Rule of 73 chapters on how monks should live together in a monastery. He opened the whole book with a single quiet command from the master to the monk. What was its very first word?
answer: Listen
choices: Listen
Obey
Kneel
Pray
context: The Rule opens: 'Listen carefully, my child, to the master's instructions, and incline the ear of your heart.' The Latin is 'Obsculta' / 'Ausculta.' A whole rulebook for the disciplined life begins by telling the monk simply to listen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_Saint_Benedict

question: Benedict told his monks in chapter 53 of his Rule exactly how to treat any traveller who knocked at the monastery gate, rich or poor, friend or stranger. According to Benedict, every guest who arrived was to be received as whom?
answer: Christ himself
choices: Christ himself
royal envoy
lost brother
wandering angel
context: 'Let all guests who arrive be received like Christ, for He is going to say: I was a stranger and you welcomed me.' Every traveler at the gate, however poor, was to be greeted as if Christ Himself had come. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_Saint_Benedict

question: Romanus, a monk from a monastery above, kept the young Benedict alive for three years while he lived as a hermit in a cave in the cliffs at Subiaco, seeking God far from the city. In Pope Gregory the Great's account, Romanus lowered one thing to him on a rope. What was it?
answer: Bread
choices: Bread
Water
Firewood
Clothing
context: Romanus secretly lowered bread on a rope from the monastery above. The story is told by Pope Gregory the Great in Book II of his 'Dialogues' (c. 593) — the only real biography of Benedict, and the origin point of Western monasticism. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Benedict-of-Nursia  (Legend.)

question: Benedict's monks hunched over desks in the scriptorium, the writing-room, copying books by hand one letter at a time. For nearly a thousand years they were Europe's librarians, and besides the Bible they saved a whole body of writing that the Church might have let die. What did they copy out?
answer: The classical works of Greece and Rome
choices: The classical works of Greece and Rome
The laws of the Frankish kings
The songs of traveling minstrels
The trade records of merchants
context: In the scriptorium, monks copied scripture and the Church Fathers — and crucially the pagan classics of Greece and Rome. Almost everything written that survived to the age of the printing press passed through their hands. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scriptorium

question: Benedict ordered his monks to spend set hours of every day at hard manual labour and other set hours at sacred reading. In chapter 48 of the Rule he gave his blunt reason: one thing, he wrote, was the enemy of the soul. What did Benedict call the enemy of the soul?
answer: Idleness
choices: Idleness
Pride
Greed
Doubt
context: 'Idleness is the enemy of the soul' (Rule, ch. 48). It is the reason Benedict filled the monastic day with labor and reading rather than leaving any hours empty. Source: https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-geneseo-humanities1-1/chapter/the-rule-of-st-benedict-chapters-26-50/

question: High on a mountaintop in southern Italy, around 529, Benedict founded his greatest monastery, Monte Cassino, which became the home of all Benedictine monks. The summit was not empty when he came, and before he could build he tore down what already stood there. What did he tear down?
answer: A pagan temple to Apollo
choices: A pagan temple to Apollo
A fort built by Caesar
A shrine to the goddess Vesta
A palace of the Lombard kings
context: Monte Cassino was raised on the site of an old pagan temple to Apollo, which Benedict tore down. It became the cradle of Benedictine monasticism. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Benedict-of-Nursia

question: An English scribe of the eleventh century, worn out by copying books by hand, scribbled a short four-word prayer in Old English into a margin. One monk complained that such work dimmed the eyes, ached the back and knit the chest and belly together. What did the weary scribe write?
answer: 'God help my hands'
choices: 'God help my hands'
'God grant me sleep'
'God spare my eyes'
'God end this book'
context: An 11th-century English scribe wrote, in Old English, 'God helpe minum handum' — 'God help my hands.' Other real margin-notes: 'Three fingers write, but the whole body labours,' and 'While the fingers write, the rest of the body hardly rests.' Source: https://thijsporck.com/2017/06/12/scribal-complaints/

question: Benedict of Nursia was humane rather than harsh with his monks over one drink. He admitted he had read that it 'is not at all proper for monks,' yet he allowed each monk a fixed daily ration of it, with somewhat more in hot weather or after heavy work. How much did he permit each monk per day?
answer: Half a pint of wine
choices: Half a pint of wine
A quart of ale
A cup of milk
A jug of cider
context: Each monk was allowed about a 'hemina' of wine — roughly a quarter-litre, or half a pint — even though Benedict admitted 'we read that wine is not at all proper for monks.' On hot days or for hard work the abbot could allow more. The moderation is what made the Rule humane. Source: https://ccel.org/ccel/benedict/rule/rule.xlii.html

question: Dom Pierre Perignon, a Benedictine monk, worked on the wines of the Champagne region in the 1600s. A beloved story has him cry out on first tasting sparkling champagne, 'Come quickly, I am drinking the stars!' Historians say Perignon never said it, was blind in old age, and did not even invent champagne. Where did the line first appear?
answer: In a 19th-century advertisement
choices: In a 19th-century advertisement
In a medieval monk's chronicle
In a French royal decree
In an old drinking song
context: The beloved 'drinking the stars' line is a fiction, invented in a 19th-century advertisement long after Perignon's death. The real Dom Perignon did pioneering work on Champagne wines at Hautvillers Abbey but did not invent sparkling champagne. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dom_P%C3%A9rignon_(monk)  (Legend.)

question: Scientists studying the skeleton of a medieval nun buried in Germany around the year 1100 found over a hundred specks of brilliant blue in the hardened tartar on her teeth in 2019. The blue was ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli carried all the way from Afghanistan and costlier than gold. How did the precious blue get into her mouth?
answer: She licked her paintbrush to a fine point
choices: She licked her paintbrush to a fine point
She chewed the raw stone as medicine
She drank from a blue-glazed cup
She kissed a painted holy book
context: She had repeatedly licked her ultramarine-loaded brush to a fine point while illuminating manuscripts. Her blue-stained teeth are some of the only physical proof that women, too, painted and decorated medieval books. Source: https://www.york.ac.uk/news-and-events/news/2019/research/ultramarine-pigment-reveal-forgotten-female-scribe/

question: Monks guarded their hand-copied books with written curses against anyone who might steal them. One curse, copied into a German Bible around 1172, called down a whole storm of torments on the thief. What was one of the fates it wished on him?
answer: That he be roasted in a frying pan
choices: That he be roasted in a frying pan
That his hands wither to the bone
That his name be struck from all books
That wolves devour him by night
context: The real curse: 'may he die, may he be roasted in a frying pan, may the falling sickness and fever attack him, and may he be broken on the wheel and hanged. Amen.' Another, shorter, simply spat: 'Out with his eyes, out with his eyes!' Source: https://www.openculture.com/2021/08/medieval-scribes-discouraged-theft-of-manuscripts (Marc Drogin, 'Anathema!')

question: In chapter 7 of his Rule, Benedict set out twelve steps of humility that a monk had to climb like the rungs of a ladder, each a harder discipline than the one before. The ninth told a monk not to speak until he was spoken to, and the tenth forbade a very ordinary, human thing. What was a humble monk not to be quick to do?
answer: Laugh
choices: Laugh
Eat
Sleep
Weep
context: The tenth step of humility is that a monk 'should not be quick to laugh' (the ninth being that he should not speak until spoken to). The twelve steps run from fearing God and surrendering one's own will all the way up to a settled, quiet humility of bearing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_Saint_Benedict

question: Benjamin Franklin walked off the boat into Philadelphia in October 1723, seventeen, broke and hungry. He bought three puffy rolls and had no bag to hold them. Deborah Read, the girl he would one day marry, laughed at the sight from her father's doorway. How did he carry the rolls?
answer: With a roll under each arm, eating the third
choices: With a roll under each arm, eating the third
Balanced in a stack on top of his head
Wrapped in his coat slung over his shoulder
Stuffed two in his hat and ate the third
context: Franklin tells the story in his Autobiography: he arrived broke and famished, bought three great rolls, and marched up Market Street 'with a Roll under each Arm, & eating the third.' Deborah Read, watching from her father's doorway, thought he looked absurd, and later married him. Source: Franklin, Autobiography (ushistory.org/franklin/autobiography; Founders Online); Penn Today, 'An inauspicious arrival for the ambitious Benjamin Franklin'.

question: Benjamin Franklin printed a best-selling almanac every year from 1732 to 1758, packed with sayings still quoted today, such as 'A penny saved is a penny earned.' He never signed his own name to it. Instead he made up a folksy character to 'write' it. What was that author's name?
answer: Poor Richard Saunders
choices: Poor Richard Saunders
Honest Abel Trueman
Plain Tom Tickler
Simple Simon Pry
context: Franklin wrote as 'Richard Saunders' — 'Poor Richard' — and the book became Poor Richard's Almanack, one of the best-selling things in the colonies. Many of its sayings are still everyday English. Source: americanliterature.com, 'Poor Richard's Almanack'; worldhistoryedu.com, 'Poor Richard's Almanack'.

question: Benjamin Franklin printed the first American political cartoon in 1754, as the colonies went to war with the French. It showed a snake cut into eight pieces, each marked with a colony's initials. By an old belief, a snake cut apart could come back to life if rejoined before sunset. What caption ran beneath it?
answer: JOIN, or DIE
choices: JOIN, or DIE
UNITE OR FALL
DON'T TREAD ON ME
LIBERTY OR DEATH
context: Franklin drew on a folk belief that a snake cut in pieces could come back to life if its pieces were joined before sunset: so the divided colonies, like the divided snake, would die unless they united, and a united America would live. The 'Join, or Die' snake was revived years later during the Revolution. Source: Join, or Die (Wikipedia); National Constitution Center, constitutioncenter.org/blog/the-story-behind-the-join-or-die-snake-cartoon.

question: Benjamin Franklin grew tired of swapping between his reading glasses and his distance glasses. So he had the lenses cut and fitted together into a single frame. What are glasses made his way called today?
answer: Bifocals
choices: Bifocals
Trifocals
Monocles
Binoculars
context: Franklin's 'double spectacles' are what we now call bifocals: one pair does two jobs, so the wearer looks up to see across a room and glances down to read, exactly how bifocals still work. Like his other inventions, he never patented them. Source: The Franklin Institute, 'Benjamin Franklin's Inventions' (fi.edu); History.com; science.howstuffworks.com, '10 Ben Franklin Inventions'.

question: Mozart and Beethoven both wrote music for a strange instrument Benjamin Franklin built in 1761: a row of 37 nested glass bowls, spun on a rod by a foot pedal and played by touching wet fingertips to the turning rims. What did Franklin name his instrument?
answer: The armonica
choices: The armonica
The clavier
The seraphine
The melodeon
context: Franklin called it the glass armonica (from the Italian word for harmony). Spinning glass bowls touched by wet fingers gave it a haunting tone that fascinated Europe's greatest composers. Source: The Franklin Institute, 'Benjamin Franklin's Glass Armonica' (fi.edu); Glass harmonica — Wikipedia.

question: Benjamin Franklin invented a tall, pointed metal rod for rooftops around 1750, so that a building could survive a direct lightning strike instead of burning down. Independence Hall wore some of the first. When lightning hits the rod, what does the rod do with all that electricity?
answer: It carries the electricity safely down into the ground
choices: It carries the electricity safely down into the ground
It hurls the electricity back up at the clouds
It locks the electricity away inside itself
It changes the electricity into harmless light
context: This is the lightning rod. The pointed rod catches the strike and a wire runs the electricity harmlessly into the earth, so it never sets the building ablaze. Franklin invented it soon after his electricity experiments. Source: The Franklin Institute, 'Benjamin Franklin's Inventions' (fi.edu); constitutioncenter.org, 'Ben Franklin's best inventions'.

question: The French treated Benjamin Franklin like a star when he arrived in Paris as America's envoy. A French gentleman was expected to wear a fancy powdered wig, but Franklin went about in something plain and homespun that the French found charming. What did he wear on his head?
answer: A plain fur cap
choices: A plain fur cap
A simple straw hat
A tall silk hat
A red liberty cap
context: The fur cap made Franklin a sensation — fashionable French women piled their hair into a tall style they called the 'coiffure a la Franklin' to imitate it, and his face turned up on snuffboxes and medallions all over France. Source: history.com, 'Ben Franklin in Paris'; benjamin-franklin-history.org, 'Ambassador to France'.

question: Benjamin Franklin could have grown rich on his inventions, from the lightning rod to the Franklin stove. Yet he refused to take out a patent on a single one. In his Autobiography, what reason did he give for letting everyone use his inventions for free?
answer: Since we enjoy others' inventions, we should gladly serve others with ours
choices: Since we enjoy others' inventions, we should gladly serve others with ours
A gentleman should never stoop to selling his clever ideas for coin
An inventor who hoards his ideas insults the God who inspired them
Patents only invite endless lawsuits that he had no time for
context: Franklin wrote that 'as we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others, we should be glad of an opportunity to serve others by any invention of ours; and this we should do freely and generously.' He wanted his ideas used by everyone, not locked up for profit. Source: Franklin, Autobiography, quoted by constitutioncenter.org, 'Ben Franklin's best inventions'; The Franklin Institute (fi.edu).

question: Benjamin Franklin persuaded France to sign a treaty of alliance with the struggling young United States on 6 February 1778, his greatest win as a diplomat. Even a jealous John Adams admitted that Paris treated Franklin like a star. What did the alliance give the American cause that made winning the Revolution possible?
answer: Money, weapons, and a powerful navy
choices: Money, weapons, and a powerful navy
Maps, spies, and a promise of secrecy
Settlers, farm tools, and seeds for the frontier
Gold, silk, and fine wine for the generals
context: France's cash, guns, and especially its fleet tipped the war toward American victory; without the French alliance Franklin secured, independence might have failed. Source: history.state.gov, 'Benjamin Franklin: First American Diplomat'; history.com, 'Ben Franklin in Paris'.

question: George Washington presided over the Constitutional Convention of 1787 from a chair with a half-sun carved on its back, and through the long, uncertain debates Benjamin Franklin sat staring at it. He could never tell, he said, whether it was rising or setting. As the delegates signed the finished Constitution, what did Franklin at last declare it to be?
answer: A rising sun, not a setting one
choices: A rising sun, not a setting one
A setting sun, sinking at last
A noon sun, fixed in place
A clouded sun, its fate unclear
context: James Madison's convention notes record Franklin saying he had often looked at that half-sun unsure if it was rising or setting, 'but now at length I have the happiness to know that it is a rising and not a setting Sun', taking the carving as a sign of hope for the new republic. That very chair, with its half-sun, still survives. Source: James Madison's notes, via teachingamericanhistory.org, 'Benjamin Franklin's Final Remark'; National Park Service, 'September 17, 1787: A Republic, If You Can Keep It'.

question: Benjamin Franklin loved to swim, and at about 11 years old he made his very first invention to go faster in the water. He cut two flat oval pieces of wood with holes for his thumbs and strapped them to his hands. What had he built?
answer: Swim paddles for his hands
choices: Swim paddles for his hands
A wooden diving mask
A pair of webbed wooden flippers
An inflatable leather float
context: The oval paddles were about 10 by 6 inches; Franklin recalled they sped him up by letting him push more water, but they tired out his wrists. He stayed a strong swimmer his whole life. Source: The Franklin Institute, fi.edu/en/science-and-education/benjamin-franklin/inventions; History.com.

question: Benjamin Franklin sent a silk kite aloft in 1752, and the test proved his point. He soon turned the discovery into a practical invention, and before long it was found all over the colonies. Which of his inventions grew out of that kite?
answer: The lightning rod
choices: The lightning rod
The Franklin stove
The glass armonica
Bifocal spectacles
context: The pointed iron rod carries the charge safely down a wire into the ground instead of letting it blast through the roof — a direct payoff from Franklin's kite work, and still standard on tall buildings today. Source: The Franklin Institute, fi.edu/en/science-and-education/benjamin-franklin/inventions; History.com.

question: Benjamin Franklin flew a silk kite into a thunderstorm in June 1752, with his son William, to prove that lightning was electricity. A metal key hung from the wet string, and Franklin held a dry silk ribbon, kept under shelter. As the storm passed, he brought his knuckle close to the key. What happened?
answer: A spark jumped from the key
choices: A spark jumped from the key
The kite caught fire
The key melted in his fingers
The whole string glowed blue
context: A spark leaping to his knuckle showed the storm cloud had charged the key: lightning really was electricity, the same thing as the spark from a laboratory. He also noticed the loose threads of the wet twine standing straight up, repelling each other. His own Pennsylvania Gazette instructions (19 October 1752) told readers that once the rain wet the kite and twine, the electric fire 'will stream out plentifully from the Key on the Approach of your Knuckle.' Source: The Franklin Institute, 'Kite-Key Experiment' (fi.edu); Franklin's 19 Oct 1752 letter to Peter Collinson; Kite experiment (Wikipedia).

question: Benjamin Franklin's kite hung in the storm clouds, quietly soaking up electric charge, and no forked bolt ever struck it, whatever the paintings show. Historians say that picture is flat wrong. If a real bolt had hit the kite, why would that have been a catastrophe?
answer: It would almost certainly have killed him
choices: It would almost certainly have killed him
It would have burned the silk kite to ash
It would have shattered the metal key
It would have flung him across the field
context: A direct strike carries enough energy to kill instantly, which is why Franklin was careful to draw charge slowly, not catch a bolt. The danger was real: in 1753 Georg Wilhelm Richmann tried a similar experiment and was killed, reportedly by ball lightning. Source: The Franklin Institute, fi.edu; History.com.

question: James Franklin printed fourteen letters in his newspaper, the New-England Courant, in 1722. Then he learned that his sixteen-year-old brother Benjamin had written them in disguised handwriting and slipped them under the print-shop door at night. Benjamin, kept out of the paper, had invented a fake author. Who was the made-up writer?
answer: A middle-aged widow named Silence Dogood
choices: A middle-aged widow named Silence Dogood
An almanac-maker named Poor Richard
A country preacher named Father Abraham
A busybody named Anthony Afterwit
context: 'Silence Dogood' was a sharp-tongued widow with strong opinions, and her letters were a hit — until James discovered his teenage kid brother was the real author and was furious. Source: Massachusetts Historical Society, masshist.org/online/silence_dogood; ushistory.org/franklin/courant.

question: Benjamin Franklin gave the world a pointed rod to guard rooftops in storms, spectacles with split lenses, an iron stove that heated a room better than an open fire, and a strange instrument of glass bowls, spun and played with wet fingers. Late in life he said one of them had 'given me the greatest personal satisfaction.' Which invention did he mean?
answer: The glass armonica
choices: The glass armonica
The lightning rod
Bifocal spectacles
The Franklin stove
context: The glass armonica was a musical instrument: 37 nested glass bowls spun on an iron spindle by a foot pedal, played by touching the wet rims to make 'incomparably sweet' notes. Mozart and Beethoven later wrote music for it. Source: The Franklin Institute, fi.edu; History.com.

question: Pennsylvania's governor offered Benjamin Franklin a patent on the new iron fireplace he designed in the 1740s, the Franklin stove, which heated a room far better than an open hearth and sold well. The patent would let him collect a fee from everyone who copied the design, a guaranteed stream of money for years. What did Franklin do?
answer: Refused it, so anyone could copy it free
choices: Refused it, so anyone could copy it free
Accepted it and made a fortune in fees
Sold it to the governor for a lump sum
Patented it quietly under a false name
context: Franklin never patented any of his inventions. He wrote that 'as we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others, we should be glad of an opportunity to serve others by any invention of ours.' Source: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, ushistory.org/franklin/autobiography/page55.htm; c4sif.org.

question: Benjamin Franklin made up plain English words for what he was finding about electricity. His electrical work won him the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1753, and his words are still in use. Which set of words did Franklin coin?
answer: battery, charge, conductor, positive, negative
choices: battery, charge, conductor, positive, negative
volt, watt, ohm, ampere, hertz
atom, molecule, electron, proton, neutron
current, circuit, voltage, resistance, wattage
context: Franklin needed new vocabulary to describe what he was discovering, so he named it, and the words stuck: positive and negative (plus and minus) for the two kinds of charge, battery for stored charge, conductor and charge. The volt, watt, ohm, ampere and hertz came later, each named after a different scientist. Source: Library of Congress, loc.gov/exhibits/franklin/franklin-scientist.html; Founders Online (Copley Medal award); https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/benjamin-franklin-and-lightning-rods

question: Timothy Folger, a whaler, solved a puzzle for his cousin Benjamin Franklin, then the colonial postmaster: why did British mail ships take two weeks longer to cross the Atlantic than American ones? The British captains, Folger explained, were sailing straight against a powerful warm current. Franklin charted it and named it. What is it called?
answer: The Gulf Stream
choices: The Gulf Stream
The Sargasso Sea
The Humboldt Current
The Labrador Current
context: Franklin published his chart in 1769 and later measured the current with a thermometer, noting it 'is always warmer than the sea on each side of it.' Whalers knew its path because they followed it to find whales. Source: NOAA, oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/bfranklin.html; Smithsonian.

question: Turgot, a French statesman, summed up Benjamin Franklin's whole life in a single Latin line, later carved on busts and engravings. It praised Franklin for taming lightning with his rod and for helping to topple a king. The line said Franklin had snatched two things away. Which two?
answer: The thunderbolt from heaven and the scepter from tyrants
choices: The thunderbolt from heaven and the scepter from tyrants
The fire from the gods and the crown from kings
The lightning from the sky and the throne from emperors
The storm from the clouds and the scepter from Rome
context: The Latin reads 'Eripuit caelo fulmen sceptrumque tyrannis.' It casts Franklin as a kind of Prometheus — stealing fire from the sky — who also helped strip power from a monarch. Source: Oxford Reference, oxfordreference.com; Journal of the American Revolution, allthingsliberty.com.

question: Benjamin Franklin owned enslaved people as a younger man and ran slave-sale ads in his Pennsylvania Gazette. Late in life he turned against slavery, and in 1787 he became president of the Pennsylvania abolition society. A few weeks before he died in April 1790, the 84-year-old made his very last public act. What was it?
answer: Signing a petition asking the first Congress to abolish slavery
choices: Signing a petition asking the first Congress to abolish slavery
Freeing the last people he had enslaved
Delivering a speech to Congress against slavery
Leaving his estate to the abolition society
context: The man who once sold enslaved people made ending slavery his dying cause. The Pennsylvania Abolition Society's petition, which he signed as its president, asked Congress to end slavery and the slave trade and to 'devise means for removing the Inconsistency from the Character of the American People.' He died a few weeks later. In those last weeks he also published a hoax as 'Historicus', a fake speech by an Algerian, Sidi Mehemet Ibrahim, defending the enslavement of Christians, mirroring a Georgia congressman's defence of American slavery to expose it as absurd. Source: National Archives, 'Benjamin Franklin's Anti-Slavery Petitions to Congress' (archives.gov); Bill of Rights Institute.

question: A crowd of hungry German children stood watching the planes at the fence of a Berlin airfield in 1948 when Gail Halvorsen, an American pilot, walked over. All he had to offer them was two sticks of chewing gum. What did the children do that amazed him?
answer: Shared the gum and asked about his plane
choices: Shared the gum and asked about his plane
Fought each other for the first piece
Refused it and demanded real bread
Ran off to tell the Soviet guards
context: Instead of fighting over the gum, the children split it and just wanted to hear about his aircraft. That moment moved Halvorsen so much that he started the famous candy drops. Source: hersheyland.com 'The Berlin Candy Bomber'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Halvorsen.

question: Gail Halvorsen promised the Berlin children at the airfield fence that he would drop them sweets, and they wanted to tell his plane apart from the hundreds of others coming in each day. So he told them of a signal he would give from the cockpit as he made his approach. What was the signal?
answer: He would wiggle his wings
choices: He would wiggle his wings
He would flash his landing lights
He would dip his nose down twice
He would circle the field once
context: Wiggling his wings earned Halvorsen the German nickname 'Onkel Wackelflugel' -- Uncle Wiggly Wings. Source: hersheyland.com 'The Berlin Candy Bomber'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Halvorsen.

question: American and British pilots flew supplies into blockaded West Berlin around the clock in 1948. The British called their share Operation Plainfare. The American code name was not grand or warlike. What did the Americans call their operation?
answer: Operation Vittles
choices: Operation Vittles
Operation Lifeline
Operation Stockpile
Operation Freedom Road
context: 'Vittles' is folksy slang for grub or food -- a humble name for the first time in history a whole city would be fed entirely from the sky. Source: history.state.gov 'Berlin Airlift'; amcmuseum.org 'Operation Vittles'.

question: Gail Halvorsen and his crew wanted to get chocolate and gum down to the Berlin children without the sweets smashing apart as they fell from a moving plane. They tied them to something small that the children could chase across the rubble. What did they tie the candy to?
answer: Tiny parachutes sewn from handkerchiefs
choices: Tiny parachutes sewn from handkerchiefs
Wooden crates packed with straw
Cloth sacks weighted with sand
Paper kites strung with ribbon
context: They pushed the little candy parachutes out the plane's flare chute as they came in to land. The candy-drop project was officially named 'Operation Little Vittles.' Source: airandspace.si.edu 'Friends Forever'; hersheyland.com 'The Berlin Candy Bomber'.

question: Joseph Stalin moved on 24 June 1948 to choke West Berlin into surrender: two million people stranded deep inside the Soviet zone of a Germany the victors had carved into American, British, French and Soviet parts. His forces never fired a shot at the city. What did they do to it?
answer: Cut every road, rail line, and canal into it
choices: Cut every road, rail line, and canal into it
Shut off its electricity and water mains
Closed its banks and froze its money
Halted all its mail and telephone lines
context: With every land and water route sealed, West Berlin had only about 36 days of food and roughly six weeks of coal left. Source: history.com 'Soviets Blockade West Berlin'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Blockade.

question: The Western Allies faced two grim choices once Stalin's blockade closed around West Berlin in 1948: shoot their way in by land, or abandon two million people to him. They rejected both and chose a third path no one had tried on such a scale. What did they decide to do?
answer: Feed the entire city from the air
choices: Feed the entire city from the air
Tunnel supplies in underground
Smuggle food past the checkpoints
Trade away territory for the city
context: Supplying a city of two million entirely by air had never been done before -- the Allies bet they could outlast the blockade plane-load by plane-load. Source: history.state.gov 'Berlin Airlift'; amcmuseum.org 'Operation Vittles'.

question: Allied pilots brought loaded supply planes down on West Berlin's runways day and night at the height of the airlift. A busy peacetime airport might land one plane every minute or two; the airlift packed them in far tighter. About how often did a fully loaded plane touch down?
answer: Every 45 seconds
choices: Every 45 seconds
Every 10 seconds
Every 3 minutes
Every 8 minutes
context: At the peak a loaded plane landed roughly every 45 seconds, and in the busiest spring-1949 stretch the cadence tightened to about one every 30 seconds. Source: history.state.gov 'Berlin Airlift'; historyfacts.com '5 Astonishing Facts About the Berlin Airlift'.

question: Mercedes Simon, a Berlin girl, could never reach the crowds where Gail Halvorsen's candy came down. So she wrote him a letter with directions to her home near Tempelhof, telling him to look for a landmark in her own yard and drop the candy there. What landmark did she tell him to find?
answer: Her family's white chickens
choices: Her family's white chickens
The tall church steeple
A red roof on the corner
The big oak by the gate
context: Her letter read, 'When you see the white chickens please drop it there, all will be OK.' He never spotted them, so he mailed candy straight to her house -- and when he returned to Berlin in 1972, Mercedes invited him to dinner. Source: airandspaceforces.com '0313halvorsen'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Halvorsen.

question: Airlift pilots had to fly at least 4,500 tons of supplies into West Berlin every day just to keep its two million people alive. Food, though, was the smaller share of that weight. What made up the larger share of the cargo the city needed?
answer: Coal for heat and power
choices: Coal for heat and power
Water in sealed drums
Ammunition for the troops
Timber and cement
context: Of the daily minimum, roughly 3,475 tons was coal versus about 1,500 tons of food -- keeping the lights and furnaces on mattered as much as eating. Source: airandspace.si.edu 'Supplying a City by Air'; historyfacts.com '5 Astonishing Facts About the Berlin Airlift'.

question: William Tunner had just taken command of the airlift when a cloudburst over Tempelhof turned it into chaos on 13 August 1948, a day remembered as Black Friday. One plane crashed, another blew its tires and a third skidded off the runway, while the rest stacked up blind in the clouds with Tunner trapped overhead. His answer fixed the airlift for good. What rule did he impose on every pilot?
answer: One shot at each landing, with no second try
choices: One shot at each landing, with no second try
Half the planes flying at twice the spacing
Night-only flights to dodge bad weather
A backup runway built at every field
context: Tunner rebuilt the airlift around rigid assembly-line timing: fixed slots, one approach, and a botched landing meant flying home, not circling. Source: historynet.com 'Berlin Airlift Anniversary'; amcmuseum.org 'Operation Vittles'.

question: Jean Ganeval, the French general in Berlin, had two tall Soviet-run radio towers blown up in December 1948 because they blocked the approach to the brand-new Tegel airport. As the story is told, a furious Soviet officer demanded to know how he could possibly have done it. How did Ganeval reportedly answer?
answer: 'With dynamite!'
choices: 'With dynamite!'
'Very carefully.'
'I lit the fuse myself.'
'The same way you built them.'
context: This famous one-line reply, dated to December 16, 1948, is told as legend -- a great story that may be polished in the retelling. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin-Tegel_radio_transmitter; billdownscbs.com '1948 French Destroy Soviet-Controlled'.

question: The airlift's commanders staged the Easter Parade over 15 and 16 April 1949, a furious 24-hour blitz that flew nearly 13,000 tons into West Berlin in a single day, about 600 railcars of coal, without one crash. After a feat like that, what could Stalin no longer believe?
answer: That his blockade could ever starve the city out
choices: That his blockade could ever starve the city out
That the Allies would defend Berlin by force
That the airlift planes would run short of fuel
That winter weather would soon ground the flights
context: The Easter Parade proved the planes could outlast the blockade indefinitely; Stalin lifted it on May 12, 1949. The free world had fed a whole city from the sky for nearly a year. Source: globalsecurity.org 'Berlin Airlift'; history.state.gov 'Berlin Airlift'.

question: Ronald Reagan stood at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin on 12 June 1987 before a crowd of more than 20,000, two panes of bulletproof glass shielding him from snipers in the communist East. He aimed his words at the Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev. What ringing demand did Reagan make?
answer: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"
choices: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"
"Mr. Gorbachev, recall your missiles!"
"Mr. Gorbachev, free your prisoners!"
"Mr. Gorbachev, leave Afghanistan now!"
context: Reagan built to it: "General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace... Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" He spoke about 100 yards from the Wall with the Gate at his back. The Soviet news agency branded the speech "openly provocative" and "war-mongering"; the barrier itself did not fall until November 9, 1989, two and a half years later.

question: Howard Baker, Ronald Reagan's chief of staff, called the most defiant line of the Brandenburg Gate speech of 1987 'unpresidential.' Reagan's own State Department and National Security Council handed him seven rewrites with the challenge to Gorbachev stripped out, for fear it would embarrass the Soviet leader. How did Reagan settle the fight?
answer: He overruled them all and kept the line.
choices: He overruled them all and kept the line.
He cut the line to spare Gorbachev.
He let his advisors rewrite the ending.
He softened it into a polite request.
context: On May 18, 1987, Reagan told his speechwriters simply, "I think we'll leave it in." In the limousine to the gate he grinned at aide Ken Duberstein: "It's gonna drive the State Department boys crazy, but I'm gonna leave it in." Deputy National Security Advisor Colin Powell had sided with Baker against the line. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tear down this wall!'; Stanford Report, 2019, 'Reagan's Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall was almost left unsaid.'

question: Gian Lorenzo Bernini carved Apollo and Daphne from a single block of marble between 1622 and 1625. He caught the instant the nymph Daphne was transformed as she fled the god Apollo, and he made her change burst right out of the stone at her fingertips. What did he make sprout from the ends of her marble fingers?
answer: Delicate laurel leaves and twigs
choices: Delicate laurel leaves and twigs
A spray of carved seawater
A cluster of golden grapes
A nest of small songbirds
context: Bernini carved real-looking, paper-thin laurel leaves and twigs growing straight out of Daphne's fingertips at the exact moment she becomes a tree. He made the work in his early twenties, between 1622 and 1625, pausing partway to carve his famous David. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_and_Daphne_(Bernini)

question: Teresa of Avila, a Spanish mystic, described in her own writings a vision of a smiling angel holding a golden arrow. Gian Lorenzo Bernini carved that vision in white marble for the small Cornaro Chapel in Rome between 1647 and 1652. To make the marble seem to glow from heaven itself, he built one hidden feature into the chapel above the statue. What was it?
answer: A concealed window letting real daylight pour down
choices: A concealed window letting real daylight pour down
A ring of flickering oil lamps
A ceiling painted with a golden sunburst
A polished silver mirror behind the angel
context: Bernini hid a real window above the Cornaro Chapel so daylight streams down onto gilded bronze rays behind the figures, making the marble appear lit from heaven. The group was carved from white Carrara marble between 1647 and 1652. He was illustrating Teresa of Avila's own written vision of the angel and the spear of gold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecstasy_of_Saint_Teresa

question: Henry Bessemer wanted to blow cold air straight up through a vat of glowing molten iron. His workers swore the blast would chill the metal and freeze it into a useless solid lump. Instead the iron grew even hotter, and a roaring flame shot up. What material was actually catching fire to push the temperature higher?
answer: The carbon and silicon already dissolved in the iron
choices: The carbon and silicon already dissolved in the iron
The cold air itself igniting on contact
The clay lining of the vat melting away
Extra coal the workers shoveled in
context: The cold blast burned out the carbon and silicon mixed into the iron, and those elements caught fire and burned as fuel — so the air didn't cool the metal, it turned the whole vessel into a self-heating reaction. Bessemer described the apparatus becoming 'a veritable volcano.' Source: thechemicalengineer.com 'Henry Bessemer – Man of Steel'; HowStuffWorks Bessemer Process.

question: The same trains rolled over a stretch of English track where, from 1862, one rail of Bessemer's cheap new steel lay beside ordinary iron rails. The soft iron rails wore out and had to be replaced, while the steel rail just sat there unworn. By the time the steel rail finally needed replacing, how many times had the iron rails been swapped out?
answer: Eighteen times over
choices: Eighteen times over
Just twice over
Not even once
Exactly once over
context: The single Bessemer steel rail outlasted eighteen replacements of the iron rails next to it. In hard-worn spots, iron rails sometimes wore out in under six months; steel rails carried heavier locomotives and longer trains and lasted for decades — which is why cheap steel rapidly replaced iron across the railroads. Source: cprr.org/Museum/Iron_and_Steel_Rails.html; trains.com 'Rail' / ABCs of Railroading.

question: Betsy Ross, a Philadelphia flag-maker, was shown a plan for the new nation's flag with six-pointed stars, or so the story goes. She folded a scrap of paper and made a single snip with her scissors. What shape did she open out to surprise her visitors?
answer: A perfect five-pointed star
choices: A perfect five-pointed star
A ring of thirteen stripes
A curled red ribbon
A small blue square
context: The one-snip five-pointed star is the most beloved detail of the Betsy Ross story, and the committee is said to have chosen it for the new flag. It's a treasured national folk-tale, first told publicly by Ross's grandson decades later rather than firmly documented at the time. (ushistory.org/betsy/flagtale.html; historicphiladelphia.org)  (Legend.)

question: A small group of visitors came to the Philadelphia sewing shop of a young widow named Betsy Ross in June 1776, an old American story says, and asked her to stitch the very first flag of the new United States: thirteen stripes and a ring of stars. Which famous American leader supposedly came along?
answer: General George Washington
choices: General George Washington
King George the Third
Captain John Smith
Governor William Penn
context: In the tale, Washington came with financier Robert Morris and Colonel George Ross (the uncle of Betsy's late husband). The story even says Ross knew Washington already — their church pews at Christ Church sat side by side. A beloved folk-tale, not firmly documented. (ushistory.org/betsy/flagtale.html)  (Legend.)

question: When James Madison wrote the First Amendment, the first of the ten that made up the Bill of Rights of 1791, he packed five freedoms into a single sentence. It opens, 'Congress shall make no law...' Which five freedoms went into it?
answer: Religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition
choices: Religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition
Voting, trial, property, travel, and privacy
Speech, voting, marriage, property, and protest
Religion, arms, trial, voting, and a free press
context: All five ride in one sentence: '...prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.' Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript.

question: James Madison put a ban on unreasonable searches and seizures into the Fourth Amendment, part of the Bill of Rights of 1791. It keeps the government from tearing through a citizen's home and papers on a whim. Because of it, what must a government agent usually get before entering a house to search it?
answer: A warrant signed by a judge
choices: A warrant signed by a judge
A signed note from the mayor
A majority vote of the town council
A written order from the President
context: The amendment bars 'unreasonable searches and seizures,' which is why agents normally need a judge's warrant, based on cause, to come in. Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript.

question: In the Eighth Amendment, the shortest of the ten in the Bill of Rights, James Madison banned three things in a single sentence. Two of the three are excessive bail and excessive fines. What is the third thing the Eighth Amendment forbids?
answer: Cruel and unusual punishments
choices: Cruel and unusual punishments
Trials held in total secret
Imprisonment with no trial at all
Banishment out of the country
context: The whole amendment reads: 'Excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted.' Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript.

question: James Madison made a promise to every witness in the Bill of Rights: the government cannot force him to testify against himself and so talk his way into a prison cell. A famous expression grew out of that right, used by anyone refusing to answer a question that might incriminate him. What is the expression?
answer: Pleading the Fifth
choices: Pleading the Fifth
Taking the stand
Throwing the book
Reading the charges
context: This right against self-incrimination lives in the Fifth Amendment, which also promises 'due process of law' and a grand jury for serious crimes — but its most quoted line is the one that gave us 'pleading the Fifth.' Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript.

question: Clarence Earl Gideon, a poor man, faced his trial alone, so from his prison cell he wrote a five-page plea to the Supreme Court by hand, in pencil, on prison stationery. In Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) the Court ruled unanimously in his favor. What did the justices say states must now provide to any defendant who cannot pay?
answer: A lawyer paid for by the state
choices: A lawyer paid for by the state
A faster date for the trial
A transcript of the whole case
A jury drawn from his neighbors
context: Gideon's penciled petition turned the Sixth Amendment's promise of counsel into a real right for the poor: if you cannot afford a lawyer, one must be provided. Source: Wikipedia, Gideon v. Wainwright; U.S. Courts case summary.

question: Mary Beth Tinker, 13, her brother John and their friend Christopher Eckhardt protested the Vietnam War at their Des Moines schools in December 1965, and they were suspended for it. They sued, and in Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) the Supreme Court sided with them 7 to 2. What had the students done to get suspended?
answer: Worn black armbands to school
choices: Worn black armbands to school
Walked out of their classes
Refused to say the Pledge
Handed out anti-war leaflets
context: The Court declared that students do not 'shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate' — making the armbands one of the most famous acts of student free speech in American history. Source: Wikipedia, Tinker v. Des Moines; U.S. Courts case summary.

question: George Mason of Virginia refused to sign the new Constitution in 1787 because it contained no bill of rights. He swore he would rather do something terrible than put his name to the document as it stood. What did Mason say he would rather do?
answer: Chop off his own right hand
choices: Chop off his own right hand
Never set foot in Virginia again
Burn down his own great house
Give away his entire fortune
context: Mason said he 'would sooner chop off his right hand than put it to the Constitution as it now stands.' He was one of only three delegates present at the end of the Convention who refused to sign. Source: Wikipedia, George Mason; National Archives 'Pieces of History' blog.

question: George Washington had 14 handwritten copies of the Bill of Rights made, one for the new federal government and one for each state. A Union soldier carried off North Carolina's copy in 1865, and it vanished for 138 years. How did federal agents finally get it back in 2003?
answer: They posed as buyers in a sting operation
choices: They posed as buyers in a sting operation
They traced an old letter back to his family
They spotted it hanging in a public museum
They followed a tip from a retired soldier
context: The soldier who first took it had sold it for $5; in 2003 a dealer tried to sell the same document for $5 million, and the FBI sting recovered it for North Carolina. Source: TIME, 'Bill of Rights History: FBI Sting Operation'; NC DNCR.

question: Franklin Roosevelt proclaimed a Bill of Rights Day to mark the 150th anniversary of the Bill of Rights, and he chose 15 December 1941 for it. That first observance fell in the shadow of a national catastrophe just eight days earlier. What had happened on 7 December 1941?
answer: The attack on Pearl Harbor
choices: The attack on Pearl Harbor
The great stock-market crash
The sinking of the Lusitania
The assassination of a president
context: Roosevelt's proclamation of the 150th anniversary collided with the Pearl Harbor attack of December 7, 1941, that pulled the United States into World War II — so the first Bill of Rights Day passed almost unnoticed. Source: National Archives, 'Bill of Rights Day'; Proclamation 2524.

question: John Hancock and Samuel Adams worked out the Massachusetts Compromise during the fight to ratify the Constitution: ratify now, amend at once. It became the template for one faction that made written protections for individual rights the price of its votes. Which faction demanded a bill of rights as its price?
answer: The Anti-Federalists
choices: The Anti-Federalists
The Democratic-Republicans
The Federalists
The Sons of Liberty
context: Several states ratified only on the promise that protections would be added at once — the Massachusetts Compromise was the model. Georgia alone thought a bill of rights so pointless it refused to ratify. Source: Wikipedia, United States Bill of Rights; Library of Congress, 'Demand for a Bill of Rights.'

question: James Madison wrote the Bill of Rights and drove it through Congress, yet at first he had argued against having one at all. He dismissed written guarantees with a scornful phrase, saying angry majorities had trampled them in every state. What did Madison call written rights?
answer: 'parchment barriers'
choices: 'parchment barriers'
'parchment promises'
'parchment shadows'
'parchment fences'
context: Madison called written rights mere 'parchment barriers' against overbearing majorities — then changed his mind to win ratification, having pledged amendments to beat James Monroe for a seat in the House. Source: Madison to Jefferson, 17 Oct 1788, Founders Online; Wikipedia, United States Bill of Rights.

question: Gregory Watson, a University of Texas student, wrote a paper in 1982 about a forgotten amendment that Madison had proposed in 1789 to stop Congress from voting itself a raise before the next election. His professor gave the paper a C and called the idea a dead letter. Furious, Watson spent about six thousand dollars of his own money writing to state lawmakers. What did he end up pulling off?
answer: He got the amendment ratified as the 27th
choices: He got the amendment ratified as the 27th
He had the professor fired by the university
He won a seat in Congress for himself
He rewrote the whole Bill of Rights
context: Watson's 1789 amendment was finally ratified as the 27th Amendment in 1992 — about 203 years after Madison proposed it, the longest gap in U.S. constitutional history. In 2017 the University of Texas went back and changed his grade to an A. Source: National Constitution Center; NPR, 'The Bad Grade That Changed The U.S. Constitution.'

question: 'Congress shall make no law,' James Madison wrote at the head of the Bill of Rights, and into the clauses after it he put 'shall not be infringed,' 'shall not be violated' and 'No Soldier shall.' What kind of list did he write?
answer: A list of things the government may NOT do
choices: A list of things the government may NOT do
A list of crimes the people may not commit
A list of powers handed to Congress
A list of gifts the government gives the people
context: Every key clause opens with a prohibition aimed at the new federal government, marking where its power must stop — these are negative rights, telling the government what it may not do rather than gifts it bestows. Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript.

question: James Madison feared a danger in any written list of rights: people might think the government held every power and right left off the list. The Ninth Amendment keeps unlisted rights 'retained by the people.' What does the Tenth say about powers not given to the federal government?
answer: They are reserved to the states and the people
choices: They are reserved to the states and the people
They belong to the President to use as needed
They pass to the Supreme Court to decide
They are surrendered until Congress claims them
context: The Tenth reserves undelegated powers 'to the States respectively, or to the people.' Together the Ninth and Tenth answer the fear that a written list of rights could shrink the rights and powers the people kept. Source: National Archives, Bill of Rights Transcript; Constitution Center, Ninth & Tenth Amendment interpretations.

question: Athenian voters gathered to banish a too-powerful man from the city for ten years, each one scratching the man's name onto a bit of scrap and dropping it on the pile. What everyday object did an Athenian scratch the name onto?
answer: A broken piece of pottery
choices: A broken piece of pottery
A wax writing tablet
A strip of papyrus
A clay drinking cup
context: The broken potsherd was called an ostrakon -- free, throwaway scrap, used like scrap paper. That is why a vote into exile is called 'ostracism.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostracism

question: The citizens of Athens climbed the Pnyx hill above their city around 500 BC and voted on their own laws by a show of hands, the first people to try such a thing seriously. They named the practice with two Greek words joined together. What does 'democracy' literally mean?
answer: People-power
choices: People-power
Council-rule
City-law
Noble-voice
context: Demos ('the people') + kratos ('power/rule') = 'people-power.' Eligible citizens met on the Pnyx hill west of the Acropolis and voted by a simple show of hands. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_democracy; https://www.worldhistory.org/Athenian_Democracy/

question: Draco, an early lawgiver of Athens, set penalties so savage that even stealing a cabbage could cost a man his life. Demades, an orator of a later age, summed up Draco's code in one cutting line about what it seemed to be written with. How did Demades say Draco's laws were written?
answer: Not in ink but in blood
choices: Not in ink but in blood
Not on stone but on sand
Not by men but by gods
Not with care but in haste
context: Draco's code made death the penalty for even minor crimes. When Solon reformed Athens he scrapped all of Draco's laws except the one on murder. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draco_(legislator)

question: Solon set free the Athenian citizens who had been sold into slavery for their debts, around 594 BC, and he banned ever again using a person's own body as security for a loan. Athenians remembered the rescue by a single Greek name. What did that name mean?
answer: The shaking-off of burdens
choices: The shaking-off of burdens
The breaking of the chains
The gift of the poor
The mending of the city
context: The law was the seisachtheia -- literally 'the shaking off of burdens.' It ended Athenian debt-slavery before democracy was even born. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seisachtheia

question: The Athenians chose Solon, the poet and lawgiver, around 594 BC to save poor farmers whose debts were selling them into slavery. He ripped up the horoi, the mortgage marker-stones they had been forced to plant in every field they owed money on, and later boasted of it in a poem. What did his line say the ripping had done to the land?
answer: Freed the black earth
choices: Freed the black earth
Opened the closed gate
Lit the dark hills
Filled the empty barn
context: Solon's line ran: 'Before, Earth was in bondage, now she is free.' Tearing up the debt-marker stones literally 'freed the black earth.' Sources: Plutarch, Life of Solon (Fragment 36); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solon

question: Solon made the citizens of Athens swear a binding oath to leave his new laws unchanged for ten full years. Then he did something drastic so that no one could talk him into softening them. What did Solon do right after the Athenians took the oath?
answer: Sailed away on a long voyage
choices: Sailed away on a long voyage
Burned his only copy of the laws
Handed himself over to a rival
Locked himself inside a temple
context: Solon left Athens for years rather than stay and be begged to change his laws, hoping the city would grow used to ruling itself before he came home. Source: Plutarch, Life of Solon (Perrin trans.)

question: A citizen who could not read walked up to Aristides, the Athenian statesman nicknamed the Just, on the day of a banishment vote. Not knowing who he was, the man asked him to scratch the name Aristides on his ballot. According to Plutarch, what did Aristides do?
answer: Wrote his own name and handed it back
choices: Wrote his own name and handed it back
Tore it in half and walked away
Refused and reported the man
Begged the man to change his vote
context: Told as a famous legend by Plutarch. The man said: 'None whatever, I don't even know the fellow, but I am tired of hearing him everywhere called The Just.' Aristides calmly inscribed his own name. Source: Plutarch, Life of Aristides, ch. 7.

question: To smash the grip of the old noble clans on Athenian politics, Cleisthenes re-sorted every citizen around 508 BC. Instead of grouping men by their ancestral families, he grouped them by one different measure, so that no single noble family could control a voting bloc. What did Cleisthenes group citizens by instead?
answer: Where each man lived
choices: Where each man lived
How old each man was
Which trade each man worked
How rich each man was
context: Cleisthenes junked the four ancestral tribes and built ten new ones, each deliberately mixing people from the city, the coast, and the inland so no region or clan could dominate. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleisthenes; https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Greece/The-reforms-of-Cleisthenes

question: Cleisthenes created a Council of 500, the boule, to run the daily business of Athens, drawn from across his new tribes. He filled its seats in a way that meant an ordinary farmer, not just a wealthy noble, could end up helping to govern the city. How were the 500 councilmen chosen?
answer: Picked by lot
choices: Picked by lot
Elected by vote
Named by the nobles
Chosen by wealth
context: Fifty men from each of the ten tribes were selected by lot, not election -- so governing was open to ordinary citizens. Cleisthenes called the whole system isonomia, 'equality before the law,' not yet 'democracy.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleisthenes

question: Isagoras, the rival of Cleisthenes, called in King Cleomenes of Sparta, who drove out 700 Athenian families and tried to break up the new council. Athens's self-rule was nearly strangled in its cradle, but the ordinary Athenians rose up. What did they do to Cleomenes and Isagoras?
answer: Besieged them on the Acropolis until they surrendered
choices: Besieged them on the Acropolis until they surrendered
Bribed them with gold to sail home quietly
Put them on public trial before the Assembly
Begged the other Greek cities to drive them out
context: The Athenians trapped Cleomenes and Isagoras on the Acropolis and, after two days, forced them to surrender and leave. Cleisthenes was recalled in triumph. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleomenes_I; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleisthenes

question: Archaeologists digging a well near the Acropolis found a buried cache of 190 banishment ballots, every one scratched with the name Themistocles, as if 190 separate voters wanted him gone. Studying the handwriting exposed a fraud: far fewer people had written them. About how many different hands wrote all 190?
answer: About 14 hands
choices: About 14 hands
About 25 hands
About 45 hands
About 70 hands
context: Roughly 14 hands producing 190 ready-to-vote sherds means someone mass-produced ballots in advance -- ancient evidence of ballot-stuffing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostracism

question: Only free adult male citizens raised their hands to vote on the Pnyx in democratic Athens; women, enslaved people and resident foreigners had no say at all, so the first democracy was narrower than its name suggests. Out of perhaps a few hundred thousand people living in Attica, roughly how many held the vote?
answer: Around 30,000 to 40,000 men
choices: Around 30,000 to 40,000 men
Around 3,000 to 4,000 men
Around 100,000 to 150,000 men
Around 250,000 to 300,000 men
context: Only free adult male citizens voted -- women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners (metics) were excluded. The first democracy was genuine but narrow. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_democracy; https://www.worldhistory.org/Athenian_Democracy/

question: Percy Brooks, editor of the British magazine Melody Maker, greeted Louis Armstrong in England and accidentally squashed one of the boyhood nicknames that mocked his huge mouth into a single new word. Armstrong kept it for the rest of his life. What was it?
answer: Satchmo
choices: Satchmo
Gatemouth
Dippermouth
Slidehorn
context: Percy Brooks, editor of the British magazine Melody Maker, accidentally contracted 'Satchelmouth' into 'Satchmo' when greeting him in England.
