'Gatemouth' and 'Dippermouth' were two of Armstrong's real earlier nicknames, all of which mocked the size of his mouth. Source: Louis Armstrong House Museum FAQ, 'How did Louis Armstrong get the nickname Satchmo?' (louisarmstronghouse.org).

question: The Colored Waif's Home for Boys in New Orleans took in eleven-year-old Louis Armstrong after he fired his stepfather's pistol into the air on New Year's Eve 1912 and was arrested on the spot. What happened to him inside the home?
answer: The home's bandmaster taught him to play the cornet
choices: The home's bandmaster taught him to play the cornet
A wealthy visitor adopted him and paid for his schooling
A riverboat captain hired him on as a deckhand
He escaped over the wall and rode the rails north
context: Bandmaster Peter Davis taught Armstrong the cornet at the Colored Waif's Home for Boys, the spark that turned the arrested boy into a musician. He was released in 1914. Source: Biography.com 'Louis Armstrong'; Louis Armstrong House Museum biography (louisarmstronghouse.org/biography).

question: The Karnofskys, a Jewish immigrant family in New Orleans, hired Louis Armstrong at about seven to haul coal and junk, fed him at their own table, and even lent him money toward his first cornet. Armstrong never forgot their kindness. How did he honour them for the rest of his life?
answer: He wore a Star of David around his neck
choices: He wore a Star of David around his neck
He named his first band after them
He learned Yiddish and sang it on records
He sent them money from every concert he played
context: Morris Karnofsky lent young Louis two dollars toward the five-dollar pawnshop cornet, which Louis paid off at fifty cents a week. Armstrong wrote, 'It was the Jewish Family who instilled in me singing from the heart,' and wore a Star of David for the rest of his life. Source: Louis Armstrong, 'Louis Armstrong + the Jewish Family in New Orleans, La., the Year of 1907' (memoir); Aish.com; National Park Service, Karnofsky Tailor Shop (nps.gov).

question: Louis Armstrong was recording a song called 'Heebie Jeebies' in Chicago in 1926 when, as the story goes, his lyric sheet fluttered to the floor mid-take. Rather than stop, he kept singing, and with no words left he made up a stream of wordless syllables on the spot. What is that style of singing called?
answer: scat singing
choices: scat singing
crooning
yodeling
the blues holler
context: Armstrong popularized scat singing on 'Heebie Jeebies' (recorded February 26, 1926, in Chicago). Bandmates Kid Ory and Johnny St. Cyr confirmed he dropped the sheet, but scat already existed in New Orleans, so he did not invent it, only made it a sensation. Source: Wikipedia 'Heebie Jeebies (composition)'; Library of Congress NRPB Hot Five/Seven essay; Louis Armstrong House Museum exhibit '100 Years of Heebie Jeebies'.  (Legend.)

question: Doug Ramsey, a jazz historian, wrote about the opening of Louis Armstrong's 1928 recording of West End Blues, a soaring trumpet solo of about nine bars with no other instrument behind it. Ramsey said three of the greatest classical composers who ever lived would have been grateful to have written it. Which three did he name?
answer: Mozart, Bartok, and Stravinsky
choices: Mozart, Bartok, and Stravinsky
Bach, Beethoven, and Brahms
Handel, Haydn, and Schubert
Chopin, Liszt, and Wagner
context: The unaccompanied opening cadenza of 'West End Blues' (recorded June 28, 1928) announced that jazz could be art at the highest level. Doug Ramsey wrote that 'Mozart, Bartok, or Stravinsky would have been grateful for the inspiration to compose' it. Source: uDiscoverMusic 'The Day Jazz Changed Forever'; Library of Congress NRPB Hot Five/Seven essay (Doug Ramsey quotation).

question: Ludwig Boltzmann set out to explain why a smashed egg never puts itself back together, and why heat always flows from hot to cold, never back. No law forbids the reverse, he said. Why does the egg stay smashed?
answer: There are vastly more ways to be a mess than to be whole
choices: There are vastly more ways to be a mess than to be whole
A hidden law of physics forbids broken things from mending
The egg loses weight as it breaks, so it cannot rebuild
Time pushes on objects with a small but constant force
context: This is the heart of Boltzmann's entropy: disordered, jumbled arrangements outnumber tidy ones so overwhelmingly that the orderly outcome essentially never happens by chance. It is also why time seems to have a direction — the universe drifts toward the states there are more ways to be in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H-theorem ; academic.oup.com/book/34859/chapter/298194940

question: Ludwig Boltzmann lies buried in Vienna beneath a marble wall, raised in 1933 and carved with the one short equation that sums up his life's work, his definition of entropy. What formula is engraved above his name?
answer: S = k log W
choices: S = k log W
E = m c squared
F = m times a
P V = n R T
context: S is entropy, k is the Boltzmann constant, and W counts how many microscopic arrangements look the same from the outside. The bust and inscribed marble wall were made by sculptor Gustinus Ambrosi and unveiled in 1933, decades after Boltzmann died — the formula was added as a memorial. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann%27s_entropy_formula ; visitingvienna.com/sights/zentralfriedhoffamousgraves

question: Ludwig Boltzmann never wrote the short equation carved above his grave in that tidy form, though it sums up his work. Another physicist squeezed his ideas into it around 1900 as he worked on the glow of hot objects. Who was he?
answer: Max Planck
choices: Max Planck
Albert Einstein
Ernst Mach
Wilhelm Ostwald
context: Boltzmann developed the underlying idea between 1872 and 1875, but Max Planck put it into the terse form S = k log W around 1900–1901 while working out black-body radiation. The grave honors Boltzmann with a sentence written by someone else. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann%27s_entropy_formula

question: Ernst Mach and other powerful colleagues insisted that atoms were a convenient fiction, and Ludwig Boltzmann's whole theory of heat depended on their being real. Worn down and convinced the deniers had won, Boltzmann took his own life in 1906. What happened just two years later?
answer: Jean Perrin measured Brownian motion and proved atoms are real
choices: Jean Perrin measured Brownian motion and proved atoms are real
Ernst Mach published a final book denying atoms once more
The Vienna academy quietly removed Boltzmann's name from its rolls
A rival theory of continuous matter swept across the universities
context: Perrin's 1908 experiments on Brownian motion gave decisive proof that atoms exist, vindicating Boltzmann right after he died believing he had failed. Even Ostwald eventually conceded; Planck and Einstein carried Boltzmann's ideas to victory. Source: kroneckerwallis.com/ludwig-boltzmann-the-physicist-who-proved-atoms-exist-through-statistics ; plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-Boltzmann

question: The Sailendra dynasty raised Borobudur, the largest Buddhist temple in the world, on the island of Java around 800 AD. Pilgrims climb its nine stone platforms, stacked into a giant mandala, level by level, and the climb carries a meaning drawn from the Buddhist path. What is a pilgrim's walk up Borobudur meant to represent?
answer: The journey from worldly desire up toward Nirvana
choices: The journey from worldly desire up toward Nirvana
The voyage of a trader from India home to China
The march of an army up to besiege a hill fort
The flight of a soul up through nine starry heavens
context: Borobudur's tiers map the stages of the Buddhist path: Kamadhatu, the realm of desire, at the hidden base; Rupadhatu, the realm of form, on the square terraces; and Arupadhatu, the formless realm, on the bare circular terraces at the top. So climbing the monument is walking from worldly desire toward Nirvana. Built around 800 AD by the Sailendra dynasty from roughly 2 million andesite blocks fitted without mortar. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur; UNESCO World Heritage #592.

question: The Sailendra builders crowned Borobudur, on Java, with three round terraces crowded with 72 bell-shaped stone stupas, each pierced with diamond-shaped holes like stone latticework. A visitor who peers through the gaps in one of these stone bells gets a surprise. What is sealed inside, looking back out through the holes?
answer: A seated stone Buddha
choices: A seated stone Buddha
A bowl of temple ashes
A coiled stone serpent
A casket of royal bones
context: Each of the 72 perforated stupas on the upper circular terraces hides a seated stone Buddha, visible only as a shape glimpsed through the latticework. The whole temple holds 2,672 relief panels and once held 504 Buddha statues. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur; UNESCO #592.

question: A Boston crowd pelted British soldiers with snowballs, ice and rocks outside the Custom House on the night of 5 March 1770, and the soldiers fired into the mob, killing five colonists. The first to fall was a sailor of African and Wampanoag descent who had escaped slavery, remembered as the first man to die for the American Revolution. Who was he?
answer: Crispus Attucks
choices: Crispus Attucks
Samuel Maverick
James Caldwell
Patrick Carr
context: Crispus Attucks fell first on King Street. A 1750 newspaper ad had once offered a 10-pound reward for a runaway named 'Crispas,' about 6 feet 2 inches tall; he later worked as a sailor and ropemaker and had just returned from the Bahamas. The other four who died that night were Samuel Gray, James Caldwell, 17-year-old Samuel Maverick (who died the next morning), and Patrick Carr (who died of his wounds nearly two weeks later). Sources: nps.gov/articles/000/boston-massacre-trial.htm; historyhit.com/who-was-crispus-attucks.

question: Thomas Preston, a British captain, and eight of his soldiers faced trial for the killings in a town that wanted them hanged, and no lawyer would take their case. Then a fierce patriot stunned Boston by agreeing to defend them. 'Facts are stubborn things,' he told the jury, and he won acquittals for Preston and six of the eight. Which patriot was he?
answer: John Adams
choices: John Adams
Paul Revere
Samuel Adams
John Hancock
context: John Adams, a future U.S. president, believed all accused people deserved counsel even in a free country that hated them. Captain Thomas Preston and six soldiers were acquitted; only Hugh Montgomery and Matthew Kilroy were convicted of manslaughter and, instead of hanging, had their thumbs branded under 'benefit of clergy.' A free Black witness, Newton Prince, testified Preston stood in front of his men and never ordered them to fire. Sources: nps.gov/articles/000/boston-massacre-trial.htm; masshist.org/features/massacre1770-2020/trials.

question: Boston's Sons of Liberty climbed aboard three British tea ships after dark on 16 December 1773 to tip the tea overboard. They did not go as themselves: they smeared their faces with soot and wrapped up in blankets. Who were they dressed as?
answer: Mohawk warriors
choices: Mohawk warriors
British redcoats
Spanish sailors
French traders
context: The raiders disguised themselves as Mohawk warriors, smearing their faces with soot and lampblack. The costume partly hid their identities, but it also sent a message: they saw themselves as Americans of this land, not British subjects. Source: American Battlefield Trust, battlefields.org/learn/topics/boston-tea-party; americanrevolution.org/boston-tea-party/

question: The raiders tipping British tea into Boston Harbor on 16 December 1773 caught one of their own men quietly stuffing tea into his coat to keep for himself. They turned on him hard. What did they do to him?
answer: Made him run a gauntlet, every person kicking him
choices: Made him run a gauntlet, every person kicking him
Tossed him overboard into the icy harbor
Locked him in the ship's hold overnight
Painted his face and marched him home
context: Stealing the tea instead of destroying it was treated as a betrayal of the whole protest, so the raiders made the thief run a gauntlet through the crowd on the wharf, every person kicking him as he passed. The point was destruction as principle, not personal profit. Source: bostonteapartyship.com/the-destruction-of-the-tea; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Robert_Twelves_Hewes

question: Boston's Sons of Liberty tipped the East India Company's tea into the harbor in December 1773. That same year Parliament had passed the Tea Act to help the struggling Company. What had the new law done to the tea's price?
answer: Lowered it, so it would undersell smuggled Dutch tea
choices: Lowered it, so it would undersell smuggled Dutch tea
Doubled it overnight with a steep new duty
Frozen it at the old smugglers' rate
Tied it to the price of British wool
context: The Tea Act cut duties so East India Company tea would actually be cheaper than smuggled Dutch tea. Colonists protested anyway, because the cheap tea was a trap to get them to accept Parliament's right to tax them without their consent. The fight was over the principle of the tax, not its cost. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Act; americanrevolution.org/tea-act/

question: Sandro Botticelli painted the Roman goddess of love coming ashore in his Birth of Venus, around 1485. She arrives already grown, drifting in from the sea, her long red-gold hair blowing sideways in the wind. What is she standing on?
answer: A giant scallop shell
choices: A giant scallop shell
A small wooden raft
A leaping dolphin's back
A bed of floating reeds
context: In Botticelli's 'The Birth of Venus' (mid-1480s) the goddess floats ashore on a giant scallop shell, blown to land by the wind-god Zephyr; Botticelli paints the shell 'as pure and as perfect as a pearl.' The painting hangs today in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence.

question: Zephyrus, the blue wind god, swoops in from the right edge of Botticelli's Primavera, Italian for Spring, and grabs the wood nymph Chloris as she runs. Beside them she is changing into Flora, the goddess of flowers and spring. How did Botticelli paint that change?
answer: Real flowers spill out of her open mouth
choices: Real flowers spill out of her open mouth
Green vines wrap and bind her wrists
Her bare feet sink and root into the soil
A gold light bursts from her chest
context: As Zephyrus catches Chloris, blossoms pour from her lips — she becomes Flora before the viewer's eyes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primavera_(Botticelli)

question: Botticelli hid a signature in the orange trees behind the figures of his Primavera. Their round gold fruit echoes the gold balls on a famous coat of arms, the badge of the family that paid for the work. Which family was he honoring?
answer: The Medici family
choices: The Medici family
The Borgia family
The Sforza family
The Visconti family
context: The golden oranges echo the gold balls — the 'palle' — on the Medici coat of arms; both Primavera and the Birth of Venus were Medici works. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primavera_(Botticelli)

question: The Florentines had been building their cathedral for over a century by 1418, yet a huge eight-sided hole still yawned over it. No builder alive knew how to close it. Long before, the ancient Romans had raised domes over vast buildings. Why could no one copy them?
answer: The secret of how the Romans built giant domes had been lost
choices: The secret of how the Romans built giant domes had been lost
The Pope had forbidden anyone to build a dome that tall
No quarry in Tuscany could supply enough white marble
The original architect had died before drawing the plans
context: After Rome fell, the know-how for vast concrete domes like the Pantheon's vanished for a thousand years. In 1418 nobody knew how to roof the octagonal opening at Santa Maria del Fiore. Source: worldhistory.org/Filippo_Brunelleschi; arsartisticadventureofmankind.wordpress.com.

question: Before he dared to design the dome, Filippo Brunelleschi went down to Rome with his friend, the sculptor Donatello. For years he spent his days there doing one thing over and over. What was it?
answer: He crawled over the ruins measuring the Pantheon
choices: He crawled over the ruins measuring the Pantheon
He prayed at the tomb of Saint Peter for guidance
He bought every Roman statue he could carry home
He copied the frescoes on the old basilica walls
context: Brunelleschi and Donatello clambered over Rome's ruins for years, and he measured the Pantheon again and again, determined to work out how its ancient dome stayed up. Source: worldhistory.org/Filippo_Brunelleschi.

question: Suppose you climb the 463 steps that visitors take today to the top of Filippo Brunelleschi's dome in Florence, up to the lantern that crowns it. Which way do the steps take you up?
answer: You walk up the curved gap between two domes, one inside the other
choices: You walk up the curved gap between two domes, one inside the other
You ride a wooden cage pulled up the outside by ropes
You climb a straight iron ladder bolted to the inner wall
You wind up a stone tower built against the cathedral side
context: It is a double dome — a shell within a shell — and the 463-step climb spirals up the hollow gap between them. Source: brunelleschi.imss.fi.it (TheDomeOfSantaMariaFiore); duomo.firenze.it.

question: Andrea del Verrocchio's workshop hoisted a gilded copper ball, eight feet across, onto the lantern of Brunelleschi's dome in 1471, and there it stayed for 130 years, high above Florence. Then in January 1601 it came crashing down into the square below. What brought it down?
answer: A lightning bolt knocked it clean off the top
choices: A lightning bolt knocked it clean off the top
A flock of birds slowly pecked the gold leaf away
An earthquake cracked it loose from the lantern
A careless workman dropped it during a repair
context: Lightning struck the golden ball on 27 January 1601 and knocked it clean off; it crashed into the square and was rebuilt in 1602. A marble disc still marks the spot where it landed. Source: duomo.firenze.it (Verrocchio's golden ball); guidedflorencetours.com.

question: For his dome to hold up its own weight as it rose, Brunelleschi needed every new ring of bricks to grip the one below. So he set more than four million bricks at angles, in a self-locking pattern. What is that pattern called?
answer: Herringbone
choices: Herringbone
Basketweave
Honeycomb
Pinwheel
context: The herringbone (Italian spina-pesce, 'fish-spine') brickwork let each ring grip the last, so the dome supported itself with no centring scaffold beneath it. Brunelleschi laid over four million bricks this way.

question: To lift millions of bricks and stones hundreds of feet up to his rising dome, Brunelleschi invented a hoist driven by a team of oxen walking in a circle. What was the cleverest feature of his machine?
answer: A reversible hoist that could raise or lower without turning the oxen around
choices: A reversible hoist that could raise or lower without turning the oxen around
A water wheel on the river that wound the ropes by current
A spiral ramp the oxen themselves walked up to the rooftop
A counterweight of sand that dropped to lift each load
context: His ox-powered hoist had a gear that reversed the load between rising and lowering without un-hitching the animals. Decades later the young Leonardo da Vinci sketched these machines. Source: bdml.stanford.edu/BrunelleschiNotes; brunelleschi.imss.fi.it.

question: Rival masters demanded to see Brunelleschi's plan for the dome before they would back him. The story goes that he dared them instead to stand an egg upright on a marble table, and every one of them failed. When they scoffed at his trick, he said they could have built the dome too, had they seen his design. How did he make the egg stand?
answer: He cracked the egg flat on its base so it stood upright
choices: He cracked the egg flat on its base so it stood upright
He spun the egg fast so it balanced like a top
He nestled the egg in a ring of soft wax
He leaned the egg against a coin on edge
context: In Vasari's tale Brunelleschi tapped the egg's bottom flat on the marble so it stood; when the masters scoffed 'we could have done that,' he answered they could likewise build his dome if he showed them how. He won the commission. Told as legend.

question: High on the rising dome, Brunelleschi's men worked on platforms hung hundreds of feet above the ground, where a man could freeze with fear or fall. Besides fitting railings to the platforms, Brunelleschi made one change his workers grumbled about, to keep them steady and clear-headed. What was it?
answer: Watered down the workers wine so they stayed steady up high
choices: Watered down the workers wine so they stayed steady up high
Tied every worker to a rope fixed at the lantern above
Sent the workers home whenever the wind began to gust
Made the workers climb blindfolded so they felt no fear
context: Brunelleschi watered the men's wine (to grumbling) and added parapets to the suspended platforms so they wouldn't fall or freeze looking down. Source: througheternity.com; firenzemadeintuscany.com.

question: A teenage apprentice from Andrea del Verrocchio's workshop helped hoist a gilded copper ball, eight feet across, to the top of Brunelleschi's dome on 27 May 1471. The workshop had made the ball to crown the lantern. Who was that apprentice?
answer: Leonardo da Vinci
choices: Leonardo da Vinci
Sandro Botticelli
Donatello
Lorenzo Ghiberti
context: The golden ball was made in Andrea del Verrocchio's workshop and hoisted up on 27 May 1471, with the teenage apprentice Leonardo da Vinci helping. Source: duomo.firenze.it (Verrocchio's golden ball); guidedflorencetours.com.

question: Filippo Brunelleschi took on a job in 1420 that had beaten every builder in Florence for a century: closing the vast eight-sided hole above the cathedral. Yet he had never been trained to design buildings at all. What had he trained as before he took on the dome?
answer: He was a trained goldsmith and clockmaker, not an architect
choices: He was a trained goldsmith and clockmaker, not an architect
He had built three smaller cathedrals in northern Italy
He had studied dome-building under a master in Rome
He had spent his youth as a stonemason in the quarries
context: Brunelleschi trained as a goldsmith and clockmaker. In 1401 he even lost the famous competition for Florence's bronze Baptistery doors to his lifelong rival Lorenzo Ghiberti — yet it was Brunelleschi who solved the dome. Source: worldhistory.org/Filippo_Brunelleschi.

question: Lorenzo Ghiberti, Brunelleschi's lifelong rival, shared command of the dome with him by order of the city, and Ghiberti took the credit without understanding the engineering. At the most critical moment, the story goes, Brunelleschi exposed him with a trick. What did he do?
answer: He pretended to be sick and stayed home until work ground to a halt
choices: He pretended to be sick and stayed home until work ground to a halt
He tore up the building plans in front of the whole guild
He challenged the rival to a public building contest
He bribed the workers to follow only his orders
context: As the tale is told, Brunelleschi faked an illness and stayed home; with Ghiberti unable to direct the work, it stalled — proving who the real engineer was. Brunelleschi then 'recovered' and took sole charge. Told as legend. Source: britannica.com/biography/Filippo-Brunelleschi; worldhistory.org.

question: Brunelleschi finished his dome over Florence's cathedral in 1436, after sixteen years of work. In the nearly six centuries since, engineers have learned to build with steel and reinforced concrete, yet one claim about his dome has held all along. What is still true of it today?
answer: It is still the largest brick-and-stone dome ever built
choices: It is still the largest brick-and-stone dome ever built
It was the tallest building in the world for a year
It is the only cathedral dome shaped like an egg
It was the first dome ever raised over a church
context: Nearly 600 years on, it remains the largest masonry dome ever built — over 4 million bricks and an estimated 37,000 tons, raised without any centring scaffold. Source: brunelleschi.imss.fi.it (TheDomeOfSantaMariaFiore).

question: Filippo Brunelleschi began raising Florence's cathedral dome in 1420, the widest brick dome anyone had ever attempted, and the judges feared it would crumble before its mortar set. Every builder believed a dome that size needed one thing to hold it up while it was being built. What did Brunelleschi do without?
answer: Any wooden scaffolding rising from the ground to hold the dome up as it rose
choices: Any wooden scaffolding rising from the ground to hold the dome up as it rose
Any iron chain wrapped around the base to stop it spreading
Any central stone pillar inside to carry the weight
Any smaller practice dome built first to test the design
context: No one in 1418 knew it was possible to raise a dome that wide with nothing supporting it from below. More than 600 years later it is still the largest masonry (brick-and-stone) dome ever built. (Museo Galileo / IMSS Brunelleschi archive: 'the biggest dome ever built without using centring to support the masonry'; ArchDaily, 'How Did Filippo Brunelleschi Construct the World's Largest Masonry Dome?')

question: The Buddha told his followers that their goal was nirvana, or nibbana in Pali: a perfect peace that could come while a person still lived, once craving was gone. The word is not the name of a heavenly place but a plain, homely picture. What does nirvana literally describe?
answer: A flame being blown out
choices: A flame being blown out
A river reaching the sea
A bird let out of a cage
A lamp carried into a dark room
context: Nirvana (Pali nibbana) literally means 'to be blown out' or 'extinguished,' like a flame going out. It is not a place but the state reached when the fires of greed, aversion, and delusion are snuffed out -- a perfect peace that can arrive even while one is still alive, once craving ends. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana_(Buddhism)

question: In the Sallatha Sutta the Buddha taught that physical pain cannot be avoided, but that much misery is something extra a person piles on himself. When an untrained man is hurt, the Buddha said, he is struck not once but twice: first by the hurt itself, then by his own grief, resentment and brooding over it. In the Buddha's own image, what is that second blow?
answer: A second arrow we shoot into ourselves
choices: A second arrow we shoot into ourselves
A wound that never finishes healing
A debt we can never finish paying
A shadow that follows us everywhere
context: In the Sallatha Sutta the Buddha used the image of 'two arrows.' When something hurts, an untrained person is struck twice -- first by the physical pain (the first arrow), then by self-made grief, resentment, and storytelling about it (the second arrow), feeling two pains. The trained disciple feels the first arrow but not the second: 'he feels one pain: physical, but not mental.' Source: https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/sn/sn36/sn36.006.than.html

question: Opening his very first sermon, the Buddha warned against two opposite dead ends: chasing sensual pleasure, and torturing the body with extreme self-denial. Between them he set the Middle Way, and he spoke of both dead ends as roads he had walked himself. What had he done before he found the Middle Way?
answer: He had lived as a pampered prince and then nearly starved himself as an ascetic
choices: He had lived as a pampered prince and then nearly starved himself as an ascetic
He had reigned as a great king and then begged for alms in rags
He had led armies in war and then lived alone in a forest
He had mastered the old scriptures and then debated rival teachers
context: The Buddha opened his first sermon by naming two extremes to avoid: devotion to sensual pleasure ('base, vulgar, common, ignoble, unprofitable') and devotion to self-affliction ('painful, ignoble, unprofitable'). The Middle Way between them was the discovery of a man who had tried both -- he had lived as a pampered prince and then nearly starved himself as an ascetic before finding the road in the middle. Source: https://www.dhammatalks.org/suttas/SN/SN56_11.html

question: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, named the cause of suffering in his Second Noble Truth with a Pali word, tanha, and he listed three forms of it: craving for pleasure, craving to keep on existing, and even craving to be wiped out of existence. Tanha is an ordinary bodily word that turns craving into a raw physical urge. What does it literally mean?
answer: Thirst
choices: Thirst
Hunger
Fever
Itch
context: The Second Noble Truth pins the cause of suffering on tanha, a Pali word that literally means 'thirst.' The Buddha named three thirsts: craving for sensual pleasure (kama-tanha), craving to keep existing or becoming (bhava-tanha), and craving for non-existence or self-annihilation (vibhava-tanha). Suffering is not random; it is produced by a graspingness that always wants more or wants out. Source: https://inthewordsofbuddha.wordpress.com/2013/12/24/the-second-noble-truth-the-noble-truth-on-the-cause-of-suffering/

question: American militiamen dug in on the Charlestown peninsula, across from Boston, were short of gunpowder when the British attacked on 17 June 1775. Legend says they were told to hold their fire until the redcoats were almost on top of them, to make every shot count. What were they to wait to see before shooting?
answer: The whites of their eyes
choices: The whites of their eyes
The buttons on their coats
The mud on their boots
The fear on their faces
context: 'Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes' is attributed to Colonel William Prescott and/or General Israel Putnam, but most historians think the line is apocryphal. With little powder, holding fire until the British were close meant no shot was wasted. Source: nps.gov/articles/000/the-battle-of-bunker-hill.htm; armyhistory.org  (Legend.)

question: British redcoats charged up Breed's Hill, beside Bunker Hill on the Charlestown peninsula, on 17 June 1775, and the Americans dug in on top threw them back twice. The redcoats carried the hill only at the third attempt, after the Americans' powder ran out. They won the day, yet the battle proved the Americans would stand and fight. Why did the victory prove it?
answer: The British lost over 1,000 men taking the hill
choices: The British lost over 1,000 men taking the hill
The colonists never actually retreated
The British surrendered their cannon afterward
The fighting lasted for three straight days
context: About 1,054 British casualties (including 89 officers killed or wounded) versus roughly 450 American. The colonists threw back the first two charges with close-range musket fire; the British only stormed the redoubt on the third assault, when the defenders ran out of powder. A victory that bloody showed Britain the colonists would stand and fight. Source: nps.gov/articles/000/the-battle-of-bunker-hill.htm; britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Bunker-Hill

question: The emperors in Constantinople kept ruling for nearly a thousand years after the western half of their empire fell in 476. Historians gave their realm the name Byzantine only long afterwards. What did its own people call themselves?
answer: Romans
choices: Romans
Greeks
Hellenes
Trojans
context: They called themselves Romaioi — 'Romans.' To them, the Roman Empire had never fallen; it simply ruled from a new capital. The word 'Byzantine' was invented by outsiders centuries later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire

question: Justinian was a peasant boy from the village of Tauresium whom his uncle, Justin I, adopted and raised to power. Justin had started life lower still, in a humble trade, then climbed to palace guardsman and at last to emperor. What work had Justin done at the start?
answer: He had kept pigs
choices: He had kept pigs
He had mined silver
He had rowed galleys
He had baked bread
context: Justin I began life as a swineherd. He brought his nephew Justinian — likely the last Roman emperor to speak Latin as his native tongue — from a village called Tauresium to Constantinople. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I

question: Two condemned rioters, one a Blue and one a Green, stood on the scaffold in Constantinople in January 532, while the rival chariot-racing gangs looked on as bitter enemies. Then something went wrong at the hanging that united the two gangs, for once, against Justinian. What happened?
answer: The gallows broke and two men survived
choices: The gallows broke and two men survived
The executioner fled before the crowd
A sudden fire scattered the guards
The emperor's pardon arrived too late
context: The scaffold failed and the two survivors were spirited to a church for sanctuary. The Blues and Greens, normally enemies, united against Justinian and the rebellion began. Source: https://roman-empire.net/constantinople/nika-riots

question: The Nika rioters had burned half of Constantinople and crowned a rival emperor, but Justinian stayed. He sent the eunuch Narses, by himself, into the crowded Hippodrome where the rebels had gathered. How did Narses break the Blues and the Greens apart?
answer: He paid the Blues to abandon the Greens
choices: He paid the Blues to abandon the Greens
He freed prisoners to start a brawl
He promised the Greens their own emperor
He set the wooden stands ablaze
context: Narses bribed the Blue faction's leaders to walk out, splitting the alliance. The generals Belisarius and Mundus then sealed the exits; Procopius reports some 30,000 dead in a day, and the rival emperor Hypatius was executed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nika_riots

question: Within weeks of the riot that burned the old church, Justinian began building a new Hagia Sophia. To design its great dome he chose two men from an unexpected line of work, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. What were they by training?
answer: Mathematicians
choices: Mathematicians
Shipwrights
Sculptors
Bishops
context: Anthemius was a geometer and Isidore a fellow mathematician. Over 10,000 workers raised the church in 5 years and 10 months, dedicated 27 December 537. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia

question: Procopius, who saw Justinian's reign at first hand, wrote glowing books about the emperor's wars and buildings. He also wrote a venomous tell-all savaging Justinian and Theodora, a book that came out only after Procopius had died. What is it called?
answer: The Secret History
choices: The Secret History
The Roman Confessions
The Imperial Annals
The Book of Shadows
context: The Secret History (Greek 'Anekdota,' meaning 'unpublished things') is Procopius's poisonous private account, the dark twin of his official praise. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/history-famous-people/theodora-humble-beginnings-powerful-empress-who-changed-history-002368

question: The mosaic-makers of Byzantium pressed a sheet of real gold leaf between two thin skins of glass to make each tiny gold tile. As they set the tiles into a church wall, they tilted each one at a slightly different angle. In flickering candlelight, what did that trick make the gold wall seem to do as a worshiper walked past?
answer: Shimmer and ripple, as if the wall itself is moving
choices: Shimmer and ripple, as if the wall itself is moving
Stay a flat, even sheet of unchanging color
Cast colored shadows of red and blue onto the floor
Slowly fade from gold to silver and back again
context: Because every tessera faces a slightly different way, each one catches the candle flame at a different instant, so light seems to chase across the gold as the viewer moves. The gold-leaf-between-glass tile and the angled setting are both deliberate. The gold ground was meant as a window into eternity, not mere decoration. Source: mosaicartstudio.us 'Byzantine Mosaic Art: Detailed Guide'; Smarthistory, San Vitale.

question: A painter of the 500s made the oldest surviving icon of Christ, working in colors mixed into hot wax, and it is still kept at Saint Catherine's monastery in the Sinai desert. He gave the two halves of the face different expressions on purpose. Which two faces of Christ did he paint into one portrait?
answer: One half a stern judge, the other half a calm, merciful savior
choices: One half a stern judge, the other half a calm, merciful savior
One half a young man, the other half a white-bearded elder
One half awake with open eyes, the other half asleep
One half lit by sun, the other half lost in shadow
context: Cover one side, then the other, and you see two different men: the judge who sees all, and the savior who blesses. The icon was painted in encaustic (pigment in hot wax), a technique that grew rare after the icon-smashing fights. It survived only because remote Sinai sat far from the Byzantine emperors destroying images. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Pantocrator_(Sinai); mused.com.

question: Sophocles wrote about 120 plays for the great theater of Dionysus in Athens and won first prize more often than any playwright of his day. Long before printing, a play lasted only as long as scribes went on copying it by hand; when the final copy fell apart, it was lost forever. How many of Sophocles's plays still survive?
context: Just 7 of Sophocles's ~120 plays survive; of Aeschylus's ~90 only 7, and of Euripides's ~80 only about 18. A work vanished the instant the last copy crumbled and no one had made a new one, which is why the thousand-year labor of hand-copyists is the reason any ancient Greek books reached us at all. Source: talesoftimesforgotten.com 'If You Like Ancient Greek Texts, Thank the Byzantines'; potentialdifference.org.uk on the lost Greek tragedies.

question: Gemistos Plethon, an aged Byzantine scholar, lectured in Florence in 1438, while his own empire was dying. Moved by him, Cosimo de' Medici founded a new school and lent the young Marsilio Ficino his Greek manuscripts to translate. Which ancient Greek thinker did Plethon's lectures put at the heart of the Italian Renaissance?
answer: Plato
choices: Plato
Homer
Aristotle
Archimedes
context: The Florentines were so dazzled they called Plethon 'the second Plato.' Cosimo de' Medici's new Platonic Academy lent the young scholar Marsilio Ficino its Greek manuscripts of Plato to translate, so the Renaissance's love of Plato was in a real sense a parting gift from a dying empire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemistos_Plethon; encyclopedia.com 'Florentine Academy'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platonic_Academy_(Florence).

question: At the heart of Cahokia, near modern St. Louis, its people heaped up a flat-topped pyramid of packed earth, now called Monks Mound. It rises about 100 feet, on a base of about 1,000 by 800 feet. How does it compare with every mound and pyramid raised across the Americas, north and south?
answer: the biggest earthen mound anywhere in the Americas
choices: the biggest earthen mound anywhere in the Americas
smaller only than the stone pyramids of Mexico
about equal to several other great American mounds
the biggest in the north but small beside Peru's
context: Monks Mound is the largest earthwork in the Americas and the biggest pyramid north of Mexico — roughly 100 feet tall with a base about 1,000 by 800 feet, a footprint broader than the Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Monks-Mound

question: Melvin Fowler, an archaeologist digging into Mound 72 at Cahokia, uncovered a powerful man laid to rest on a bed of over 10,000 polished shell beads. The beads had not been scattered at random but laid out in one great shape beneath his body. What shape was it?
answer: a falcon, a bird of prey, with outspread wings
choices: a falcon, a bird of prey, with outspread wings
a serpent, a great snake, with a coiling body
a panther, a big cat, with a long tail
a turtle, a river creature, with a broad shell
context: In Mound 72, Melvin Fowler (digging from 1967) found the man on more than 10,000 cut marine-shell beads shaped like a falcon — its head beneath his head, its wings and tail under his arms and legs. He is known as the 'Birdman'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_72

question: Crowds at Cahokia gathered around a long, smooth court to watch their favorite sport. One player rolled a polished stone disc skidding across the ground, and the moment it slowed the others hurled their spears, each trying to land closest to where the disc would stop. What was this game called?
answer: chunkey
choices: chunkey
lacrosse
atlatl
shinny
context: Chunkey was Cahokia's signature sport, and the city spread it across the South and Great Plains. Crowds bet so heavily that, by some accounts, ruined losers killed themselves rather than face their debts. A famous stone figurine shows a kneeling chunkey player, disc in one hand and sticks in the other. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Chunkey/

question: Without wheels, horses, oxen or metal tools, the builders of Cahokia raised about 120 earthen mounds beside the Mississippi, one of them a hundred feet tall, moving about 55 million cubic feet of soil. How did they move that mountain of earth?
answer: by hand, hauling it basket by basket on their backs
choices: by hand, hauling it basket by basket on their backs
by floating it downriver on great wooden rafts
by dragging it on stone sledges pulled by dogs
by washing it into place through dug canals
context: Workers dug earth from 'borrow pits' and carried it in woven baskets, moving an estimated 55 million cubic feet over decades — one basket-load at a time, with no wheels, draft animals, or metal tools. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia

question: Mississippian Native Americans built their great city of Cahokia beside the Mississippi, near modern St. Louis, long before Europeans reached the Americas. Around 1100 perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people lived there, among miles of earthen mounds and plazas. How did that crowd compare with the cities of Europe at the time?
answer: It held more people than London or Paris did then.
choices: It held more people than London or Paris did then.
It rivaled the world's greatest city, Constantinople.
It was about the size of a small European market town.
It held a few hundred souls, like a country village.
context: Around 1100 Cahokia held roughly 15,000-20,000 people, probably more than London or Paris at the same moment. No city in what is now the United States would grow larger until Philadelphia passed 40,000 in the 1780s. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia

question: A community of monks settled near the empty city of Cahokia in the early 1800s, centuries after its builders had gone, and the city's great earthen pyramid, about 100 feet high, is named after them: Monks Mound. Who were they?
answer: Trappist monks who later gardened on one of its terraces
choices: Trappist monks who later gardened on one of its terraces
French priests who first dug into the mound for treasure
Spanish friars who built a chapel on its summit
English monks who mapped the ruins for a king
context: The mound is named for a group of Trappist monks who lived nearby and gardened its first terrace in the early 1800s. They never lived on the great mound itself, and the city's true builders had been gone for centuries. Source: https://cahokiamounds.org/mound/mound-38-monks-mound/

question: Warren Wittry, an archaeologist digging at Cahokia in the 1960s, kept finding rings of holes where tall wooden posts had once stood. When he worked out that the posts had followed the sun's rising and setting, he nicknamed the place after a famous monument in England. What did he call it?
answer: Woodhenge
choices: Woodhenge
Timberhenge
Cedarhenge
Posthenge
context: Wittry found the post-hole rings during 1960s salvage digging and realized they tracked the sun, nicknaming them 'Woodhenge' after Stonehenge. The main ring was about 410 feet across with 48 tall posts of red cedar, likely painted red with ochre. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia_Woodhenge

question: The builders of Cahokia set their great ring of cedar posts so that, at the spring and fall equinoxes, anyone standing at its center saw the rising sun seem to climb straight out of one spot half a mile away. What did the sun seem to rise from?
answer: the front of Monks Mound, the city's great pyramid
choices: the front of Monks Mound, the city's great pyramid
the river, glinting along the Mississippi's bend
a gap notched between two distant hills
the tallest post on the ring's far side
context: At the equinoxes, the sun rose as if emerging from the front of Monks Mound, half a mile away — and the builders kept that alignment even as they raised the mound taller over time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia_Woodhenge

question: Diggers opening one grave at Cahokia found about 700 finely made arrowheads. Testing the stone traced it to four far-apart regions: Tennessee, Wisconsin, southern Illinois and Oklahoma. Which explanation for that haul do scholars favor?
answer: trade networks that reached across half a continent into Cahokia
choices: trade networks that reached across half a continent into Cahokia
Cahokia's war parties had raided each of the four regions in turn
Cahokia's own traders had travelled out to all four regions themselves
pilgrims had carried points from their home regions as offerings
context: The roughly 700 arrowheads were sourced to four distant regions — Tennessee, southern Illinois, Wisconsin, and the Oklahoma Caddo — proof of trade networks reaching across half a continent into Cahokia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_72

question: Cahokia's founders, who raised the largest city of ancient North America near modern St. Louis, left no writing behind, so their own name for it is lost. The name it carries today came much later. Where did it come from?
answer: a much later, unrelated people who moved into the area after the city fell
choices: a much later, unrelated people who moved into the area after the city fell
the French missionaries who built a chapel among the ruined mounds
an American army surveyor sent to map the strange earthen mounds
Spanish explorers who came up the river valley hunting for gold
context: The builders left no writing, so we do not know what they called their city or themselves. The name 'Cahokia' actually belongs to a much later, unrelated Illiniwek (Illini) people who lived in the area centuries after the city was abandoned. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia

question: Archaeologists digging Mound 72 at Cahokia found about 272 people buried there over roughly a century. One pit held 53 young women, all about 15 to 30 years old, set out in neat rows in two layers. What did the archaeologists conclude about how the women died?
answer: they had been strangled and buried as sacrifices
choices: they had been strangled and buried as sacrifices
they had been a chief's wives, buried to follow him in death
they had been warriors fallen in a great battle
they had been travelers lost to a winter storm
context: Mound 72 held about 272 people buried over roughly a century, and scholars estimate nearly 62 percent were sacrificial victims — evidence that Cahokia's rulers held the power of life and death. The 53 young women, ages about 15 to 30, were laid in two layers separated by matting and showed signs of strangulation. A separate pit held 39 people killed violently, with fractured skulls and partial decapitations; some seemed to have been trying to climb out as they were buried. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_72

question: Caitlin Rankin, an archaeologist, dug into the old creek beds beside Cahokia in 2021 and read their layers of soil. She was testing the most popular idea of why the city stood empty by about 1350: that its people had felled so many trees that the bared hillsides washed mud down and ruined their farmland in floods. What did she find?
answer: no real evidence the tree-cutting caused any flooding
choices: no real evidence the tree-cutting caused any flooding
the logging really had triggered the ruinous floods after all
the floods had come, but from far upstream rains, not local logging
the creeks had dried to dust, killing the crops with drought
context: Cahokia was abandoned by about 1350, and why is still a mystery. The 2021 Washington University study led by Caitlin Rankin found no evidence the people caused flooding by overcutting trees, challenging the popular 'deforestation' story and leaving the collapse genuinely unsolved. Source: https://source.washu.edu/2021/04/study-scant-evidence-that-wood-overuse-at-cahokia-caused-collapse/

question: Michelangelo Merisi, called Caravaggio, made the figures in his paintings loom out of near-total blackness, lit as if by a single spotlight on a dark stage. Rubens and Rembrandt were among the painters who learned from that dramatic light. What is his technique called?
answer: Tenebrism
choices: Tenebrism
Sfumato
Pointillism
Impasto
context: Tenebrism comes from the Italian 'tenebroso,' meaning gloomy or dark. It is an extreme form of chiaroscuro (Italian for 'light-dark'): instead of gently shading figures, Caravaggio drowned everything but his lit subjects in black, so they seem caught in a single shaft of theatrical light. Sources: britannica.com/art/tenebrism; thecollector.com/caravaggio-use-light-baroque-art/

question: Caravaggio killed a man with his sword in a fight in 1606 and ran from Rome with a death sentence on his head. While still on the run he painted the boy David gripping the severed head of the giant Goliath, and sent the picture toward the papal court as a plea for a pardon. Whose face did he give the dead giant?
answer: His own
choices: His own
The murdered man's
A rival knight's
The pope's
context: Caravaggio painted his OWN face onto Goliath's severed, bleeding head, casting himself as the defeated villain begging for mercy. The sword in the painting carries the inscription 'H-AS OS,' read as the Latin 'humilitas occidit superbiam' -- 'humility kills pride.' Sources: galleriaborgheseroma.it (David and Goliath); blog.ricksteves.com/blog/caravaggios-david-with-the-head-of-goliath/

question: Christopher Columbus left Palos, in Spain, in August 1492 with three ships. Two were small, fast caravels, the Pinta and the Nina; his flagship was a heavier, slower carrack, a cargo ship. What was the flagship's name?
answer: The Santa Maria
choices: The Santa Maria
The Trinidad
The Esperanza
The San Antonio
context: Columbus's flagship, the Santa Maria, was a larger and slower carrack (a 'nau', a cargo ship of about 110 tons), not a caravel. The two caravels that sailed with her, the Pinta and the Nina, were the nimble ones.

question: The authors of a Chinese army manual of the 1040s, in the Song dynasty, told how to float a magnetized iron fish in a dish of water so it would swing round and show the way in the dark. They did not call its pointing end the north end. Which way did they say it pointed?
answer: South
choices: South
East
West
Down
context: The Chinese called it the 'south-pointing fish' (or south-pointing needle), not north-pointing. The 1040s manual describes a magnetized iron fish floated in water to find direction 'in the obscurity of the night.' (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_compass)

question: Portuguese and Spanish sailors with square sails could run only with the wind behind them, and a captain who ran a long way down the African coast could find himself stuck, unable to beat home against the wind. The caravel solved it with one piece of gear that let it sail close to the wind and tack its way back. What was it?
answer: A triangular lateen sail
choices: A triangular lateen sail
A deeper iron keel
A second steering oar
A taller mainmast
context: The triangular lateen sail let a caravel point as close as about 55-60 degrees off the wind and tack (zig-zag) toward a goal that lay directly upwind. This is the one trick that let ships explore a coast and still get home against the prevailing wind. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravel)

question: Out on the open ocean with no land in sight, Portuguese and Spanish navigators still worked out their latitude with a mariner's astrolabe. At night they measured one particular star's angle above the horizon, and by day the noon sun's. Which star did they measure?
answer: Polaris, the North Star
choices: Polaris, the North Star
The planet Venus
The red star Mars
The Dog Star, Sirius
context: Polaris stays within about 1 degree of true north, so its height above the horizon basically equals your latitude. A sailor sighted it at night through the two pinholes of his astrolabe and read the angle off the rim. By day he used the noon sun instead. (Source: exploration.marinersmuseum.org/object/astrolabe/)

question: The makers of the mariner's astrolabe cut large open spokes through its brass or bronze disc so that the wind would blow straight through. They also made it thick and heavy on purpose. Why did they want it heavy?
answer: A heavy disc hung steadier on a rolling deck
choices: A heavy disc hung steadier on a rolling deck
Heavy metal held the sun's heat to glow at night
The weight let it double as an anchor in a calm
Extra metal stopped the brass from rusting at sea
context: The weight was a feature, not a bug: a heavy disc dangled by its ring hung steadier on a pitching, rolling deck, so the angle could be read. Even so, in high seas it still swung enough to throw a ship off course. (Source: exploration.marinersmuseum.org/object/astrolabe/)

question: Divers pulled a bronze disc from the wreck of the Esmeralda in 2014, a Portuguese ship lost off Oman in 1503, but its surface looked blank and smooth. A laser scan then revealed faint marks too worn for the eye to see, proving it the world's oldest known mariner's astrolabe. What did the scan show on the disc?
answer: Degree markings cut every five degrees
choices: Degree markings cut every five degrees
A captain's name scratched into the rim
A map of the African coastline
A row of holes for sighting the stars
context: The laser scan of the 'Sodre astrolabe' revealed degree markings every 5 degrees, too worn to see by eye, plus the Portuguese royal coat of arms and the armillary sphere of King Manuel I. Made between 1496 and 1501 and certified by Guinness World Records as the oldest known mariner's astrolabe. (Source: smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/mariners-astrolabe-recovered-shipwreck-worlds-oldest-180971761/)

question: Baldassare Castiglione, a diplomat at the court of Urbino, coined a brand-new word in The Book of the Courtier, published in 1528, for a gentleman's master skill: making hard things look completely effortless, with every trace of practice hidden. What word did he invent?
answer: Sprezzatura
choices: Sprezzatura
Magnificenza
Disinvoltura
Cortesia
context: Castiglione defined it as 'a certain nonchalance, so as to conceal all art and make whatever one does or says appear to be without effort.' The term first appears in The Book of the Courtier (1528). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprezzatura

question: Count Ludovico da Canossa, one of the speakers in Castiglione's Book of the Courtier, laid down a 'one universal rule' for the perfect courtier: he must hide every trace of the study and practice behind what he does. What did Canossa say happens to the courtier's grace the moment people glimpse the effort?
answer: The grace is destroyed, because true art is the kind that does not look like art
choices: The grace is destroyed, because true art is the kind that does not look like art
The grace is doubled, because the audience admires the labor
The grace is unchanged, since skill speaks for itself
The grace is delayed, until the courtier rests and tries again
context: Canossa urges the courtier 'to avoid affectation to the uttermost' and 'to conceal art, for if it is discovered, it quite destroys our credit' — 'we may call that art true art which does not seem to be art.' Source: https://publicdomainreview.org/collection/baldassare-castiglione-the-book-of-the-courtier/

question: Raphael, Castiglione's close friend, painted him around 1514, in a portrait that hangs today in the Louvre. At an Amsterdam auction of the painting in 1639, a Dutch master sketched it, and its pose echoed through his own self-portraits for decades. Who was he?
answer: Rembrandt
choices: Rembrandt
Vermeer
Titian
Caravaggio
context: Rembrandt sketched Raphael's Portrait of Baldassare Castiglione (c. 1514-15) at the 1639 auction; Rubens also painted a copy, now at the Courtauld. Castiglione and Raphael had been close friends since about 1504 at Urbino. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_Baldassare_Castiglione

question: England's Edward I laid siege to Stirling Castle in 1304 and ordered the biggest siege engine ever built, a huge trebuchet made to throw boulders and crack open the Scottish castle's walls. He gave it a dreaded name. What was it called?
answer: Warwolf
choices: Warwolf
Stormcrow
Wolfsbane
Ironclaw
context: Warwolf (also called Loup-de-Guerre or Ludgar) took five master carpenters and about fifty workmen roughly three months to build, and when taken apart it was said to fill around 30 wagons. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwolf; blog.historicenvironment.scot/2024/04/the-war-wolf-at-stirling-castle/

question: Castle defenders slammed their gates shut in an instant with a portcullis, a heavy grille of oak and iron that dropped on chains. The strongest gatehouses in Europe had two, one behind the other. What was the second one for?
answer: To trap attackers in the killing space between the two
choices: To trap attackers in the killing space between the two
To double the gate's weight against a battering ram
To give defenders a spare if the first grille jammed
To block arrows shot in through the open gateway
context: Defenders slammed down the inner grille first, then the outer one, sealing attackers in the deadly space between them with no way forward and no way back. Source: medievalchronicles.com/medieval-castles/medieval-castle-parts/castle-portcullis/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portcullis

question: The Normans under William the Conqueror needed forts in a hurry after they seized England in 1066. Their answer was a castle so quick and cheap that a small one went up in mere weeks: a wooden tower on a great mound of earth, over a yard fenced with timber and ringed by a ditch. What is this kind of castle called?
answer: A motte-and-bailey
choices: A motte-and-bailey
A moat-and-mound
A keep-and-ward
A ring-and-tower
context: William and his barons threw up an estimated 500 to 600 of these motte-and-bailey castles across England between 1066 and 1087, later rebuilding many in stone. The Bayeux Tapestry even shows men shovelling up such a mound. Source: exploring-castles.com/castle_designs/motte_and_bailey/; worldhistory.org/image/8757/

question: King John's miners dug a tunnel under one corner of the stone keep at Rochester Castle in 1215 and held up its roof with wooden props. To bring the tower down they had to burn the props away, so John sent to London for forty of the fattest of one farm animal. Which animal did he send for?
answer: Pigs
choices: Pigs
Oxen
Sheep
Goats
context: John's order asked for 'forty of the fattest pigs, the sort least good for eating.' Their burning fat collapsed the mine, and one whole corner tower of Rochester's keep came crashing down. The starving defenders, by then reduced to eating their horses, surrendered on 30 November 1215. Source: exploring-castles.com/uk/england/rochester_castle/; english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/rochester-castle/history/

question: The thirty or so men holding Stirling Castle in 1304 tried to give up before Edward I had even finished building the huge siege engine meant to batter their walls. Edward said no and made them wait. What was his reason?
answer: He wanted to fire his monster engine at them first
choices: He wanted to fire his monster engine at them first
He suspected their surrender was a hidden trap
He demanded a far heavier ransom in gold
He was waiting for more soldiers to arrive
context: Edward I made the garrison wait until his great engine had been tested as a public show of power, accepting the surrender only on 24 July 1304. To feed his thirteen siege engines he even ordered Scottish churches stripped of the lead on their roofs — 22 cartloads came from St Andrews alone. Source: blog.historicenvironment.scot/2024/04/the-war-wolf-at-stirling-castle/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Stirling_Castle_(1304)

question: Defenders in the gatehouses of European castles really did strike at enemies through murder holes, gaps in the ceiling of the gate passage, but movie scenes of boiling oil pouring through them are mostly invented. Why did real defenders almost never use oil?
answer: Oil was far too scarce and costly to waste
choices: Oil was far too scarce and costly to waste
Oil could not be made hot enough to burn
The murder holes were too narrow for oil
Their faith forbade burning enemies alive
context: Through murder holes defenders really did drop stones or pour boiling WATER, heated sand, or quicklime — but oil was too precious to pour away. With the gate sealed behind them, attackers packed into the gatehouse had nowhere to flee. Source: exploring-castles.com/castle_designs/machicolations/; medievalchronicles.com/medieval-castles/medieval-castle-parts/murder-holes/

question: Besiegers of medieval castles across Europe built trebuchets, huge wooden machines with a long throwing arm that could send a stone weighing as much as 350 pounds crashing into a castle wall. What single, simple force gave the machine all its throwing power?
answer: A heavy falling weight
choices: A heavy falling weight
A tightly twisted rope
A bent wooden arm
A charge of gunpowder
context: Earlier catapults stored their punch in twisted ropes or bent wood, but the trebuchet used only gravity — a heavy counterweight box on the short arm falling a little way while the long sling-end whipped around, hurling the stone fast enough to break a wall. Source: history.howstuffworks.com/european-history/trebuchet.htm; medievalchronicles.com/medieval-weapons/castle-siege-weapons/trebuchet-siege-weapon/

question: Castle builders across Europe began swapping their square towers for round ones in the 1100s and 1200s, and not for looks. They were answering one dreaded attack: enemy miners would dig under a tower's base, prop it with wooden posts, then burn the posts so the stone above caved in. Why did a round tower stand up to this better?
answer: It had no corner to undermine and collapse
choices: It had no corner to undermine and collapse
Its curved wall was always far thicker
Its smooth face gave miners nowhere to dig
Its round weight crushed the tunnel shut
context: A square tower has corners that crumble when one is mined out; a round tower has none, so there is no weak point to bring it down. Defenders also fought back by countermining — digging their own tunnels to break into the attackers' mine for a brutal fight in the dark. Source: medievalchronicles.com/medieval-castles/castle-siege/; templarknightstours.com/templar-blog/beneath-the-walls-medieval-sappers-and-the-secret-tactics-of-siege-warfare

question: Edward I laid out Beaumaris Castle in Wales as a castle inside a castle: one full ring of walls circled by a second, lower one, with the inner wall built taller than the outer. What deadly advantage did that taller inner wall give the defenders?
answer: Archers on both walls could fire at the same time
choices: Archers on both walls could fire at the same time
The inner keep stayed hidden from outside view
Rocks dropped from it gathered far more speed
Sentries could spot enemies much farther away
context: Because the inner archers stand higher, they fire right over the heads of the outer archers, so anyone caught in the gap between the two walls faces arrows from both at once. Edward I's Beaumaris Castle in Wales, laid out in near-perfect symmetry, is the finest concentric design ever planned — though it was never even finished. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentric_castle; worldhistory.org/Beaumaris_Castle/

question: Attackers of European castles learned to huddle right at the foot of the wall, where defenders leaning over the battlements could not hit them. Builders answered with stone galleries that jutted out past the wall's top, with holes in their floors, so that stones dropped through fell straight onto the men below. What is each of these galleries called?
answer: A machicolation
choices: A machicolation
A barbican
A crenellation
A casemate
context: Before stone machicolations, castles used wooden HOARDINGS — galleries bolted onto the wall in wartime — but being timber they could be set alight. Stone machicolations replaced them precisely because masonry will not burn. Source: exploring-castles.com/castle_designs/machicolations/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoarding_(castle)

question: The Knights Hospitaller held Krak des Chevaliers in Syria, a fortress that almost no enemy ever took by force, and in 1271 Baibars, the Mamluk sultan, besieged it for a month without breaking in. In the traditional story, what trick lured the knights out?
answer: A forged letter faking their commander's surrender order
choices: A forged letter faking their commander's surrender order
A secret tunnel dug beneath the chapel floor
A traitor who unbarred the gate one night
A sickness that emptied the fortress of men
context: The forged message pretended to come from the knights' own Grand Master, ordering them to give up; they obeyed and were spared. Historians treat the tale as a traditional story rather than proven fact. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krak_des_Chevaliers; worldhistory.org/Krak_Des_Chevaliers/  (Legend.)

question: Che Guevara took charge of the revolutionary tribunals at La Cabaña, the old Spanish fortress in Havana, in January 1959, and the men they condemned were shot in its floodlit moat. One was Jesús Sosa Blanco, an officer of Batista's, charged with 108 killings. By one account, as the firing squad took aim, what did Sosa Blanco do?
answer: He shouted the squad's own commands at them — "Atención! Apunte! Fuego!" — ordering his own death
choices: He shouted the squad's own commands at them — "Atención! Apunte! Fuego!" — ordering his own death
He fell to his knees and begged the young soldiers to spare his life
He read aloud a list of judges he swore would die after him
He stayed silent and refused the blindfold the guards offered him
context: By the recounting, Sosa Blanco — charged with 108 murders — cried out the firing-squad's own orders ('Pelotón, atención! Prepare! Apunte! Fuego!'), commanding the volley that killed him. La Cabaña's condemned were shot in the fortress's dry, floodlit moat, beneath a giant lit statue of Christ; Che Guevara had been placed in command of the tribunals on January 3, 1959. https://magazine.atavist.com/2021/the-butcher-of-havana-cuba-che-castro-aclu

question: A group of Cubans hijacked an old tugboat, the 13 de Marzo, on 13 July 1994 and made a run for the United States. Seven miles off Havana, Cuban government boats caught them and sank the tug, drowning 41 of the 72 people aboard, 10 of them children. What did the government boats use to sink it?
answer: High-pressure water hoses, aimed at the people on deck
choices: High-pressure water hoses, aimed at the people on deck
Mounted machine guns firing across the water
Depth charges dropped beneath the hull
Tow cables that dragged it back to port
context: Cuban government boats rammed the hijacked 13 de Marzo and blasted it with high-pressure water hoses until it sank; 41 of the 72 aboard drowned, 10 of them children. The sinking became the defining tragedy of the 1994 'balsero' (rafter) crisis, when tens of thousands of Cubans fled on homemade rafts of inner tubes and planks. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_tugboat_13_de_Marzo

question: Armies fought the Second World War from 1939 to 1945, and in China from 1937, and 70 to 85 million people died, about one in every thirty then alive. No war in history has killed more. Who made up the majority of the dead?
answer: Civilians, who died in about double the numbers of the soldiers killed
choices: Civilians, who died in about double the numbers of the soldiers killed
Front-line soldiers, who died in about double the numbers of civilians killed
Sailors and airmen, who died in about double the numbers of foot soldiers
Prisoners of war, who died in about double the numbers of civilians killed
context: Civilian deaths totaled roughly 50-55 million while military deaths from all causes were about 21-25 million -- so for every soldier who died, roughly two ordinary people did, killed by bombing, famine, disease, and massacre. Source: Wikipedia, World War II casualties.

question: Joseph Stalin watched German armies drive deep into Russia in the summer of 1942. On 28 July he issued an order that placed special units behind his own front lines, with orders to shoot any soldier who tried to retreat. By what number and short slogan is that order remembered?
answer: Order No. 227, 'Not one step back!'
choices: Order No. 227, 'Not one step back!'
Order No. 270, 'Surrender means treason!'
Order No. 88, 'Hold the motherland!'
Order No. 145, 'Forward without fear!'
context: Order No. 227's blocking detachments shot retreating troops; archives suggest as many as 158,000 Soviet soldiers were executed by their own side over the war, including about 15,000 in a couple of weeks at Stalingrad. A real share of the USSR's enormous losses traces to Stalin's own conduct, not the Germans alone. Source: Wikipedia, Order No. 227; ww2today.com.

question: Alexander Stephens, the new Confederacy's vice president, rose to speak at Savannah in March 1861. He boasted that his government was the first in the history of the world founded on one 'great truth,' its 'corner-stone.' What did Stephens claim that truth was?
answer: That the negro is not equal to the white man
choices: That the negro is not equal to the white man
That each state could govern its own affairs
That Northern tariffs were crushing the South
That the North had broken the Constitution
context: Stephens's exact words: the cornerstone 'rests, upon the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man; that slavery -- subordination to the superior race -- is his natural and normal condition.' This is now called the Cornerstone Speech. (American Battlefield Trust, Cornerstone Speech primary source.)

question: Mississippi's convention voted to leave the Union in January 1861 and set out its reasons in a Declaration of the Immediate Causes. Its very first sentence pinned the state's whole stance on one thing, 'the greatest material interest of the world.' What did that opening line name?
answer: Slavery
choices: Slavery
Cotton shipping
Free trade
Plantation banking
context: Mississippi's first line: 'Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery -- the greatest material interest of the world.' It added: 'a blow at slavery is a blow at commerce and civilization.' (American Battlefield Trust; National Constitution Center, Mississippi Declaration of the Immediate Causes.)

question: South Carolina's leaders took their state out of the Union in December 1860, the first to go. Their Declaration of Causes objected that the North had just put a man in the presidency whose views, it said, were 'hostile to slavery,' before he had even taken office. Whose election did they mean?
answer: Abraham Lincoln
choices: Abraham Lincoln
Stephen Douglas
John Brown
Roger Taney
context: South Carolina objected that the North had 'united in the election of a man to the high office of President of the United States, whose opinions and purposes are hostile to slavery.' That man was Abraham Lincoln, who had won weeks earlier but had not yet even taken office. (Avalon Project, Yale Law School, South Carolina Declaration of Causes.)

question: Mississippi's 100 delegates met in January 1861 to decide whether to leave the United States and join the new Confederacy. Slavery was the burning question in the room, and the men voting on it were hardly neutral judges. How many of the 100 owned slaves themselves?
answer: 84 of the 100 delegates
choices: 84 of the 100 delegates
51 of the 100 delegates
39 of the 100 delegates
22 of the 100 delegates
context: 84 of the 100 convention delegates owned slaves, and the ordinance to leave the Union passed 84 to 15. Slavery was no abstraction in Mississippi: enslaved people were roughly 55% of the state's 1860 population, an outright majority. (Wikipedia, Mississippi Secession Convention.)

question: In the Cornerstone Speech, Alexander Stephens did not dance around what had split the country. He named it. He said the new Confederate constitution had 'put at rest, forever, all the agitating questions relating to our peculiar institution.' He called that same thing 'the immediate cause of the late rupture and present revolution.' What was the 'peculiar institution' he meant?
answer: Slavery
choices: Slavery
Tariffs
Federal courts
States' rights
context: Stephens, the Confederacy's own vice president, used the era's polite phrase 'our peculiar institution' for slavery, and called it 'the immediate cause of the late rupture and present revolution' while the war was just beginning. (American Battlefield Trust, Cornerstone Speech.)

question: Mississippi's leaders tried to pass slavery off as a fact of nature, not a human choice, in the declaration of causes they issued in January 1861. Their crops, they wrote, grew only in a climate close to the tropics, and 'by an imperious law of nature' only one kind of person could work under that sun. Who alone, they claimed, could 'bear exposure to the tropical sun'?
answer: None but the black race
choices: None but the black race
Only the native-born Southerner
Only the experienced plantation hand
Only those raised in the lowland heat
context: Mississippi dressed up slavery as biology: 'by an imperious law of nature, none but the black race can bear exposure to the tropical sun.' The declaration ended that the state's only options were 'submission to the mandates of abolition, or a dissolution of the Union.' (American Battlefield Trust, Declaration of Causes of the Seceding States.)

question: Texas quit the Union in February 1861, and its leaders wrote out a list of what they called 'undeniable truths.' American governments, they declared, were 'established exclusively by the white race,' and the African race was 'rightfully held and regarded as an inferior and dependent race.' What did the same Texas declaration call the slavery it was defending?
answer: The beneficent and patriarchal system of African slavery
choices: The beneficent and patriarchal system of African slavery
A sacred trust handed down from their forefathers
A Christian guardianship over a dependent people
The firm foundation of Southern peace and prosperity
context: Texas praised slavery in glowing terms, calling it 'the beneficent and patriarchal system of African slavery,' and condemned the idea of racial equality as 'a doctrine at war with nature.' (Texas State Library, Declaration of Causes, Feb 2, 1861.)

question: The Confederacy's leaders adopted a new constitution in March 1861, and in it they tied the hands of their own lawmakers. The Confederate Congress could never pass one kind of law, no matter what later Southerners might want. Which law was the Congress barred from ever passing?
answer: A law abolishing slavery
choices: A law abolishing slavery
A law raising tariffs on imports
A law granting the president a second term
A law admitting a free state to the Confederacy
context: The Confederate Constitution barred the Confederate Congress from ever passing 'any law denying or impairing the right of property in negro slaves' (Art. I, Sec. 9) and required that slavery 'be recognized and protected' in all new territories (Art. IV) -- making it legally impossible for the Confederacy to end slavery itself. (Avalon Project, Yale Law School, Constitution of the Confederate States.)

question: At Savannah, Alexander Stephens squared off against the American founders themselves. The framers, he admitted, had believed slavery 'wrong in principle, socially, morally, and politically.' He did not leave that belief unanswered. What verdict did Stephens pass on the founders' view that slavery was wrong?
answer: That their ideas were 'fundamentally wrong' and rested on 'an error'
choices: That their ideas were 'fundamentally wrong' and rested on 'an error'
That their ideas were noble but impossible for any nation to live up to
That their ideas had been honored by the South better than by the North
That their ideas applied only to white men and never to any other race
context: Stephens broke openly with the founders: 'Those ideas, however, were fundamentally wrong. They rested upon the assumption of the equality of races. This was an error.' He was rejecting the equality principle on purpose, by name. (American Battlefield Trust, Cornerstone Speech.)

question: So sure was Alexander Stephens of his 'great truth' that he likened it to ideas the world had once scorned before it came round to them. He named Galileo first, then Adam Smith. Third on his list came a 17th-century English doctor. Which scientist did Stephens name third?
answer: William Harvey
choices: William Harvey
Isaac Newton
Charles Darwin
Louis Pasteur
context: Stephens: 'It was so with the principles announced by Galileo -- it was so with Adam Smith... It was so with Harvey, and his theory of the circulation of the blood.' He genuinely expected his racial 'truth' to be proven right by history. It was not. (American Battlefield Trust, Cornerstone Speech.)

question: After the Confederacy lost, Alexander Stephens tried to rewrite history. In an 1868 book he claimed the war had really been about constitutional questions, not slavery, and that newspaper reporters had simply misquoted his famous 1861 speech. But Stephens did one thing that quietly destroyed his own excuse. What did Stephens do that undercut his claim of being misquoted?
answer: He reprinted the speech in full in his own authorized biography
choices: He reprinted the speech in full in his own authorized biography
He repeated the same racial claims in a later public address
He kept private letters that praised the original speech
He paid the reporters who had first written it down
context: Stephens could not credibly cry 'misquote': he let the entire Cornerstone Speech be reprinted in his own authorized biography. The story that the war was 'really about states' rights' collapses against the secessionists' own published words. (Wikipedia, Cornerstone Speech.)

question: Riding across La Mancha, Don Quixote spots thirty or forty windmills standing in a row. He tells his squire that he means to charge them and kill every one. What does the knight insist the windmills really are?
answer: Monstrous giants he must fight
choices: Monstrous giants he must fight
A castle of an evil king
A camp of enemy soldiers
A herd of wild bulls
context: Don Quixote calls them 'thirty or more monstrous giants' and charges with his lance lowered, while Sancho protests they are only windmills. Source: Don Quixote, Vol.1 Ch.8 (Ormsby trans.), en.wikisource.org/wiki/Don_Quixote_(Cervantes/Ormsby)/Volume_1/Chapter_8.
