question: Don Quixote has read so many tales of chivalry that he believes he is a knight, and he lowers his lance to charge a row of windmills. His loyal companion tells him flatly that they are windmills and nothing more. What is this down-to-earth squire's name?
answer: Sancho Panza
choices: Sancho Panza
Rocinante
Friston
Alonso Quijano
context: Sancho Panza is Don Quixote's earthy, sensible squire, who sees plain windmills where his master sees giants. (Rocinante is the horse; Friston the imagined enchanter; Alonso Quijano the knight's real name.) Source: Don Quixote, Vol.1 Ch.8 (Ormsby trans.), en.wikisource.org/wiki/Don_Quixote_(Cervantes/Ormsby)/Volume_1/Chapter_8.

question: Don Quixote jams a barber's brass shaving-basin onto his head before he rides to battle, and nothing will shake his belief that it is a famous treasure from his books of chivalry. What does he call the shaving-basin?
answer: The helmet of Mambrino
choices: The helmet of Mambrino
The crown of La Mancha
The shield of Rocinante
The sword of Friston
context: His real name is Alonso Quijano; convinced he is a knight-errant, he treats a barber's brass basin as 'the helmet of Mambrino.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Quixote.

question: Like every knight in his beloved stories, Don Quixote needs a noble lady to whom he can dedicate his brave deeds. So he dreams one up, names her Dulcinea del Toboso, and sings her praises without end. Who is this 'lady' really?
answer: A sturdy local farm girl he has barely spoken to
choices: A sturdy local farm girl he has barely spoken to
A queen he served as a young soldier
A princess he rescued from a castle
His late wife he still mourns
context: Dulcinea is a noble name Don Quixote invented for Aldonza Lorenzo, a robust farm girl; he never sees her as she really is. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Quixote.

question: When Don Quixote drives his lance into a turning windmill, the sail whirls round with such force that it shatters the lance and sweeps both horse and rider rolling across the plain. Knocked flat, Don Quixote refuses to admit he was wrong. How does he explain his defeat?
answer: An evil enchanter turned the giants into mills
choices: An evil enchanter turned the giants into mills
His horse Rocinante stumbled and threw him
The wind itself was a demon sent against him
He had been tricked by Sancho Panza
context: He blames 'that same sage Friston,' claiming the enchanter turned the giants into mills to rob him of glory. This scene gave English the phrase 'tilting at windmills' -- fighting imaginary enemies. Source: Don Quixote, Vol.1 Ch.8 (Ormsby trans.).

question: Long before he wrote about a mad old knight, Miguel de Cervantes fought as a soldier. In 1571, in a great sea battle where a Christian fleet crushed the Ottoman navy off Greece, he fought on though burning with fever and was struck by three bullets. What proud nickname did he give himself ever after?
answer: El manco de Lepanto -- the one-handed man of Lepanto
choices: El manco de Lepanto -- the one-handed man of Lepanto
El Cid -- the lord of the sea
The captain of La Mancha
The iron knight of Spain
context: Cervantes wore the maiming of his left hand at Lepanto (Oct 7, 1571) as a badge of honor, calling himself 'el manco de Lepanto.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes; britannica.com/biography/Miguel-de-Cervantes.

question: Sailing home from war in 1575, Miguel de Cervantes was captured by Barbary corsairs and enslaved in Algiers for five years. After one of his four failed escape plots, he was dragged before the viceroy Hassan Pasha and threatened with death. What did Cervantes do when he stood before the viceroy?
answer: Took all the blame on himself to shield the others
choices: Took all the blame on himself to shield the others
Betrayed the names of his fellow plotters
Begged on his knees for his own life
Offered the viceroy a secret ransom
context: Cervantes shouldered the entire blame to protect his fellow captives; his bold bearing won a reprieve, and he was finally ransomed in 1580. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes; excellence-in-literature.com/miguel-de-cervantes-biography/.

question: Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote in January 1605, when he was about 57, poor and worn down by life. It was an instant sensation across Europe. Why does the book hold a landmark place in the history of literature?
answer: It is called the first modern novel
choices: It is called the first modern novel
It was the first book ever printed in Spanish
It was the first story written about a king
It was the first book read aloud in churches
context: Don Quixote's instant fame is why it is called the first modern novel; today it is among the most-translated books on earth, with over 500 million copies. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Quixote.

question: A rival writing under the false name 'Avellaneda' put out a fake, unauthorized Part Two of Don Quixote in 1614, stealing the very characters that had made Miguel de Cervantes famous across Europe. How did Cervantes answer that insult?
answer: He finished his own genuine Part Two in 1615
choices: He finished his own genuine Part Two in 1615
He sued the impostor in the king's court
He abandoned the story in disgust
He paid the rival to stop printing it
context: The insult of Avellaneda's fake spurred Cervantes to complete his authentic Part Two in 1615. He died on April 22, 1616 -- the date tradition also links to Shakespeare's death, now marked as World Book Day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes.

question: Anna Sofaer, an artist, discovered the Sun Dagger high on Fajada Butte in Chaco Canyon in 1977: three leaning stone slabs that let a thin blade of sunlight fall onto a spiral carved into the rock. At about 11:15 in the morning on the summer solstice, what does that blade of light do to the spiral?
answer: It pierces straight through the center of the spiral
choices: It pierces straight through the center of the spiral
It traces the full outline of the spiral's curve
It splits into a ring of small bright dots
It slowly fades from the top of the spiral down
context: The Sun Dagger on Fajada Butte marks the summer solstice when a single dagger of light cuts the center of the carved spiral around 11:15 a.m.; at the winter solstice TWO daggers frame the spiral's outer edges, and the equinox gets its own mark. Artist Anna Sofaer spotted it in 1977 while recording rock art, and on a later visit watched the light split the spiral. Around 1989 visitor foot traffic shifted one slab and broke the alignment forever. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Dagger

question: At Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon, scientists tested the residue inside tall cylinder-shaped jars and found theobromine. That single chemical proved the Chacoans were doing something no one expected of a desert people. What were they doing?
answer: Drinking chocolate carried over 1,200 miles from Mesoamerica
choices: Drinking chocolate carried over 1,200 miles from Mesoamerica
Brewing a bitter tea from a local desert shrub
Trading dried beans they grew in the canyon floor
Grinding seeds into a paint for the great-house walls
context: The cylinder jars from Pueblo Bonito tested positive for theobromine, the signature of cacao, meaning chocolate had traveled more than 1,200 miles up from Mesoamerica. The same long-distance trade brought scarlet macaws and copper bells from far to the south. Source: https://www.sciencenews.org/article/pueblo-traded-chocolate-big-time + https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pueblo_Bonito

question: Pope Leo III set a crown on Charlemagne's head as he knelt in Old St Peter's on Christmas Day 800, and the crowd cheered him three times by a title no Western ruler had borne in over 300 years. What title did they cry out?
answer: Emperor of the Romans
choices: Emperor of the Romans
King of the Franks
Duke of Aachen
Consul of Gaul
context: The crowd shouted three times: 'To Charles, Augustus, crowned by God, great and pacifying emperor of the Romans, life and victory!' It was the first imperial coronation in the West in over 300 years. (Royal Frankish Annals c.801; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlemagne)

question: Charlemagne made Aachen his capital for its hot springs. Einhard, who wrote his life, says nobody could beat him in the water, and that he loved company there so much a whole crowd sometimes joined him at once. Roughly how many shared his bath?
answer: A hundred or more men
choices: A hundred or more men
Around a dozen friends
Just three or four guards
Only his two brothers
context: Einhard wrote that Charlemagne was so strong a swimmer that none could surpass him, and that 'a hundred or more persons sometimes bathed with him.' (Einhard, Life of Charlemagne ch.22; Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook)

question: Einhard, Charlemagne's biographer, reveals a surprise about the king behind the greatest revival of learning Europe had seen in ages. Charlemagne practised one skill in his spare hours, keeping what he needed under his pillow, but he had started too late and never did it well. What was he struggling to learn?
answer: Form his letters and write
choices: Form his letters and write
Pray in proper Latin
Play the harp like David
Speak the Greek tongue
context: Einhard says Charlemagne kept 'tablets and blanks in bed under his pillow, that at leisure hours he might accustom his hand to form the letters; however... they met with ill success.' The near-illiterate king still drove a learning revival. (Life of Charlemagne ch.25; Fordham)

question: Enemies of Pope Leo III set upon him during a street procession in Rome in April 799, meaning to leave him too maimed ever to serve as pope again. Leo survived and fled to Charlemagne. According to the chronicles, which two parts of Leo did the attackers go for?
answer: His tongue and his eyes
choices: His tongue and his eyes
His right hand and ear
His feet and his knees
His teeth and his nose
context: The attackers tried to cut out Leo's tongue and tear out his eyes; he survived the 25 April 799 attack, fled north to Charlemagne at Paderborn, and a year later crowned him emperor. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_III; Britannica 'Saint Leo III')

question: Basque warriors fell on the rearguard of Charlemagne's army in a mountain pass in the Pyrenees in August 778, wiped it out and looted its baggage of Spanish gold. Among the dead, Einhard names a governor of the Breton March whose name later swelled into the most famous knight's legend in French literature. Who was he?
answer: Roland
choices: Roland
Alcuin
Widukind
Eggihard
context: Einhard lists Eggihard the steward, Count Palatine Anselm, and 'Roland, Governor of the March of Brittany' among the fallen of 15 August 778. The small real defeat became one of history's most famous legends. (Life of Charlemagne ch.9; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Roncevaux_Pass)

question: French poets turned the ambush of 778 into a vast battle three centuries later, in the oldest great epic of French literature. In the poem the proud hero refused to sound the alarm for rescue until far too late, then blew his great war-horn so desperately hard that his temples split. What name did the poem give his ivory horn?
answer: The olifant
choices: The olifant
The Gjallarhorn
The Sackbut
The Buisine
context: In the 11th-century poem the few Basques become 400,000 Saracens; Roland blows the ivory olifant too late, then dies beside his friend Oliver after trying to shatter his sword Durendal on the rocks. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Roncevaux_Pass, Song of Roland section)  (Legend.)

question: Alcuin of York, an English scholar, ran Charlemagne's palace school, where scribes worked out a clean new style of handwriting. Renaissance printers later copied it, mistaking it for genuine ancient Roman script, and so one everyday feature of modern writing descends straight from those scribes. Which feature did their script introduce?
answer: The lowercase letters
choices: The lowercase letters
The Roman numerals
The printing press
The exclamation mark
context: The script, Carolingian minuscule, introduced lowercase letters and spaces between words. Renaissance humanists revived it as 'roman' type, thinking it ancient. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_minuscule; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcuin)

question: Charlemagne fixed money across his empire around 793 on one silver penny: 12 pennies to a shilling, 240 to a pound. Britain kept that pounds, shillings and pence system for nearly twelve centuries, until 15 February 1971, when it switched to a pound worth 100 new pence. What did Britons call the day of the switch?
answer: Decimal Day
choices: Decimal Day
Sterling Day
Coronation Day
Empire Day
context: The L/s/d system (the d standing for the Roman denarius) survived in Britain until decimalisation in 1971 -- almost 1,200 years after Charlemagne set it. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_monetary_system)

question: Scientists tested an old boast against one of Charlemagne's own bones, kept in Aachen Cathedral, in 2010. Einhard had written that the king stood 'seven times the length of his own foot,' and for a thousand years everyone assumed that was flattery. The scientists found he really had towered over almost everyone of his age. Which bone did they measure?
answer: His shinbone
choices: His shinbone
His skull
His jawbone
His kneecap
context: Measuring his tibia (shinbone), a 2010 study put Charlemagne near 1.84 m -- taller than about 99% of men of his day. The flattering legend turned out literally true. (Ruhli, Blumich & Henneberg, Economics & Human Biology, 2010; Medievalists.net)

question: Saxon rebels wiped out a Frankish army in 782, and Charlemagne struck back at Verden. The Frankish annals report that he had some 4,500 Saxon prisoners killed in a single day, by a method chosen because it was the old Roman penalty for oath-breakers. How were the captives put to death?
answer: Beheaded
choices: Beheaded
Burned alive
Hanged
Drowned
context: At Verden, where the Aller meets the Weser, about 4,500 Saxons were beheaded -- the Roman punishment for oath-breakers. It remains the darkest episode of his reign. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_Verden; Royal Frankish Annals 782)

question: Charles Lindbergh lifted off from Long Island alone in May 1927 and flew nonstop across the Atlantic to Paris, the first person ever to make that crossing solo. His small single-engine plane carried a famous name. What was it called?
answer: The Spirit of St. Louis
choices: The Spirit of St. Louis
The Pride of New York
The Atlantic Arrow
The Paris Comet
context: Lindbergh named the silver monoplane the Spirit of St. Louis after the city whose businessmen helped pay for it. He flew it from New York to Paris on May 20-21, 1927 -- the first solo nonstop crossing of the Atlantic. (Source: britannica.com/topic/Spirit-of-Saint-Louis)

question: Charles Lindbergh had his plane stripped down to save weight and loaded with extra fuel, so much that a gas tank sat right where a front window would normally go. With no windshield, he could not see straight ahead at all. How did Lindbergh watch where he was flying?
answer: He peered through a small periscope on the plane's side
choices: He peered through a small periscope on the plane's side
He flew with his head out the side window the whole way
He steered only by watching his compass needle
He trusted a second pilot to call out the way
context: With a fuel tank filling the nose, the Spirit of St. Louis had no front windshield, so Lindbergh watched the way ahead through a small periscope mounted on the side -- or by banking the plane to peek out a side window. He flew the whole 3,600 miles alone, with no co-pilot. (Source: airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/stories-inside-spirit-st-louis)

question: Geoffrey Chaucer, a courtier of the late 1300s, moved among lords who spoke French and churchmen who wrote their books in Latin. Then he set his own pilgrims on the road to Canterbury in a long story, told in a language of his choosing, with a famous beginning. Which line opens his Canterbury Tales?
answer: Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote
choices: Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote
Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita
In principio erat verbum
En l'an de grace mil trois cent
context: Chaucer wrote the Canterbury Tales in Middle English, the spoken language of ordinary people, while the court used French and the Church used Latin. Its opening line, 'Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote' (When April with its sweet showers), is one of the most famous beginnings in English and helped earn him the title 'Father of English literature.' The other lines are Dante's Italian, the Latin Vulgate, and courtly French. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Canterbury_Tales; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Prologue

question: Chaucer's Pardoner, one of the Canterbury pilgrims, preached that greed was the root of all evil, then sold fake holy relics to his listeners. He carried a brass cross studded with fake jewels and a pillowcase he swore was the Virgin Mary's veil. His most brazen fake was a glass jar of relics he swore had belonged to a saint. What was in the jar?
answer: the bones of a pig
choices: the bones of a pig
a splinter of the True Cross
a lock of an angel's hair
a vial of holy water
context: The Pardoner sells pig bones in a glass jar as saints' bones, along with a fake-jeweled brass cross and a pillowcase he calls Mary's veil -- all while preaching the Latin text 'Radix malorum est cupiditas' (greed is the root of all evil), the very sin he commits. Source: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/the-canterbury-tales/the-pardoner-s-tale and https://www.shmoop.com/study-guides/literature/pardoners-tale/analysis/relics-and-pardons

question: Pilgrims who came to Chavin de Huantar in the Peruvian Andes made their way through a maze of dark stone galleries to a cramped cross-shaped chamber at its heart. There, in near-total darkness, they met the Lanzon, a fifteen-foot granite idol shaped as a fanged man-jaguar god. What were the god's hair and eyebrows carved as?
answer: Coiled snakes
choices: Coiled snakes
Bird feathers
Curling flames
Twisting vines
context: The Lanzon's hair and eyebrows are carved as snakes, one hand pointing up and the other down, in a cramped cross-shaped chamber at the very heart of the temple labyrinth. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/ancient-places-americas/lanzon-0015725

question: Antonio Raimondi recorded a carved slab at Chavin de Huantar, the old temple centre in the high Andes of Peru, in 1873. Its Staff God gripped a staff in either hand, but the carving hid a second picture that appeared only when the slab was turned upside down. What did the god's tall headdress become?
answer: A stack of grinning fanged faces
choices: A stack of grinning fanged faces
A field of blooming flowers
A circle of dancing condors
A pair of crossed staffs
context: Flipped over, the Raimondi Stele's headdress becomes a stack of grinning fanged faces and the god's face becomes a smiling reptile. The 1.98 m stele packs in 10 sets of eyes, 11 mouths, and 50 snakes; Antonio Raimondi documented it in 1873. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raimondi_Stele

question: Sarah Gooder, eight years old, told inspectors that she worked in a coal pit without a light, and that she was scared. Her job, like that of children as young as five, was to sit alone and pull a rope to open a wooden air door every time a coal cart rumbled past. What were these children called?
answer: Trappers
choices: Trappers
Sweepers
Stokers
Carters
context: Eight-year-old Sarah Gooder, a trapper in the Gawber pit, told the 1842 Royal Commission: 'I have to trap without a light and I'm scared.' The door she worked controlled the air flow that kept the mine from filling with deadly gas. (Ashley's Mines Commission, 1842; victorianweb.org/history/ashley.html)

question: A frightened climbing boy froze partway up a sooty British chimney, in a flue that might be only seven inches across, and would not climb any higher. His master, a sweep who had bought the orphan to brush the soot loose, wanted him moving. What did the master do to drive the boy on?
answer: Lit a fire of straw beneath his bare feet
choices: Lit a fire of straw beneath his bare feet
Rang a loud bell to startle him upward
Lowered a rope for him to grab and climb
Sent a second boy up to guide him out
context: Masters lit a fire or jabbed pins at the boy's feet to force him up. The flues could be only seven inches wide; elbows and knees were rubbed raw, and boys could get stuck and suffocate in the dark. (historic-uk.com, History of the Boy Chimney Sweep; daily.jstor.org/chimney-sweeps)

question: Mill owners in Britain's early industrial age set the smallest children, some only six or seven, to work as 'scavengers' beside their great cotton and flax spinning machines. A scavenger worked while the machines still ran at full speed, and one slip could mean a crushed hand. What was a scavenger's job?
answer: Crawl beneath the running machines to sweep up loose cotton
choices: Crawl beneath the running machines to sweep up loose cotton
Carry heavy buckets of water up to the spinning floor
Stand at the great door and count the finished cloth
Climb the rafters to free threads snagged up high
context: One slip meant a crushed hand or worse. Older children worked as 'piecers,' leaning across the machine to retie snapped threads on their feet 12 to 14 hours a day. (courses.lumenlearning.com, Child Labor; Factory Acts)

question: In the coal fields of Pennsylvania, 'breaker boys' as young as eight sat hunched over chutes of coal thundering past, snatching out chunks of slate by hand all day long. The sharp coal sliced their fingers bloody -- yet the bosses forbade them to wear gloves. Why were gloves banned?
answer: So the boys could feel the rock by touch and pick faster
choices: So the boys could feel the rock by touch and pick faster
Because gloves were far too costly to buy in bulk
So the boys could not hide stolen coal inside them
Because the breaker rules demanded bare hands
context: Breaker boys breathed coal dust all day, and sulphuric acid washed off the wet coal burned and cracked their hands. A boy who slipped could be pulled into the gears. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breaker_boy; wynninghistory.com)

question: Deep in Britain's coal pits, the older children worked as hurriers, crawling through passages too low to stand in as they dragged heavy coal carts called corves. A chain pulled each cart along behind its hurrier. How was the chain fastened to the hurrier's body?
answer: It ran between the legs to a belt buckled round the waist
choices: It ran between the legs to a belt buckled round the waist
It was looped twice over both of the shoulders
It was gripped tightly in the teeth while crawling
It was tied around one ankle and dragged behind
context: Patience Kershaw, a 17-year-old hurrier near Halifax, said she pushed corves a mile and more underground, hauling eleven of them a day. (speakingwhilefemale.co, Patience Kershaw 1842; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_in_coal_mines)

question: Patience Kershaw was seventeen and hauled coal carts deep under Halifax. When she was brought before the 1842 Commission, the gentlemen could not stop staring at one strange mark on her body: a bald patch worn clean across the top of her head. How had years of underground labor rubbed her scalp bare?
answer: From shoving the loaded carts forward with her head
choices: From shoving the loaded carts forward with her head
From a leather strap she wore tight over her hair
From baskets of coal balanced upon her crown
From the low rock ceiling scraping her as she crawled
context: 'The bald place upon my head is made by thrusting the corves,' she testified. Day after day she had pushed the loaded wagons forward with her skull. (speakingwhilefemale.co, Patience Kershaw; sniff.numachi.com, Testimony 1841)

question: Elizabeth Bentley first went to work in a Leeds flax mill at six years old. In the busy season, she told a committee of Parliament in 1832, she stood at the machines from five in the morning until nine at night. Out of that whole sixteen-hour day, how much time was she given to rest and eat?
answer: Forty minutes for all the day's meals
choices: Forty minutes for all the day's meals
Two full hours spread across the day
One long hour at the noon bell
A half-day of rest each Saturday
context: Asked if she was ever 'strapped' -- hit with a leather strap to keep her working -- Bentley answered, 'Yes, severely,' and said the girls were strapped as well as the boys. (history.hanover.edu, Sadler Committee 1832, Elizabeth Bentley testimony)

question: Children at work in the Huskar pit, near Silkstone in Yorkshire, scrambled to escape up the mine drift in 1838 as a flood swept through the workings, and twenty-six of them drowned, eleven girls and fifteen boys. What had let the water loose into the pit?
answer: A thunderstorm bursting on the surface above
choices: A thunderstorm bursting on the surface above
A pump that broke down during the night
An underground spring the diggers had struck
A canal wall that gave way nearby
context: Eleven girls aged 8 to 16 and fifteen boys aged 9 to 12 drowned when the storm water poured down the drift. The newly crowned Queen Victoria heard of it; an inquiry followed, and the disaster helped push Parliament toward the Mines Act. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mines_and_Collieries_Act_1842)

question: Mill owners had simply ignored the earlier laws against child labor, so those laws failed. When Parliament passed the Factory Act of 1833, barring children under nine from the textile mills, it added one thing no factory law had ever had before. What did the 1833 Act add?
answer: Paid government inspectors sent into the mills
choices: Paid government inspectors sent into the mills
A printed notice nailed to every factory wall
A yearly oath sworn by each mill owner
A reward paid to children who reported abuse
context: The 1833 Act limited 9-to-13-year-olds to eight hours a day and, for the first time, sent salaried Factory Inspectors to enforce the rules -- because owners could not be trusted to obey on their own. (parliament.uk, Factory Act; britannica.com/event/Factory-Act-United-Kingdom-1833)

question: Respectable Victorians who opened the great 1842 report on the mines found page after page of dry testimony, yet something else in it set off an uproar that drove Parliament to act that same year. What in the report struck its readers harder than any words?
answer: Engravings of small children chained to coal carts
choices: Engravings of small children chained to coal carts
A grim county-by-county list of the pit dead
Signed letters of protest from the mine owners
A folding map of every working pit in Britain
context: The pictures of women and small children harnessed to wagons deep underground shocked the public into outrage. The Mines and Collieries Act followed that same year. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mines_and_Collieries_Act_1842, Children's Employment Commission illustrations)

question: Lord Ashley pushed the Mines Act through Parliament in 1842, keeping all women and girls, and boys under ten, out of the pits. A devout Christian who stood in the line of William Wilberforce, he spent decades fighting powerful mine and factory owners on behalf of ordinary working families. What nickname did working people give him?
answer: 'The Poor Man's Earl'
choices: 'The Poor Man's Earl'
'The Iron Lord'
'The Mill Baron'
'The People's Knight'
context: Shaftesbury took up the cause, he said, 'after meditation and prayer,' and acted at real political cost. His 1842 Act banned all women and girls from working underground and set a minimum age of ten for boys. (britannica.com, Shaftesbury; christianity.org.uk/article/lord-shaftesbury)

question: Percivall Pott, a London surgeon, noticed in 1775 that grown men who had been chimney climbing boys kept dying of the same rare cancer, which they called 'soot-wart.' Pott suspected the chimney soot was to blame and set out to prove it. What did Pott establish for the very first time?
answer: That a person's job could cause cancer
choices: That a person's job could cause cancer
That washing the skin could prevent the cancer
That soot was poisonous to breathe in
That the cancer ran in sweeps' families
context: Pott traced the soot-wart to the chimney soot ground into the boys' skin in childhood. His finding launched the science of occupational medicine and helped pass the first Chimney Sweepers Act of 1788, setting a minimum age of eight. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percivall_Pott; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimney_sweeps'_carcinoma)

question: The ancient Hebrews counted the burning of children among Canaan's worst evils, and their Bible tells of such burnings in a valley at the edge of Jerusalem, the Valley of Hinnom. The valley's Hebrew name, Ge-Hinnom, grew so hateful that it passed into Greek as the New Testament's word for hell. What is that word?
answer: Gehenna
choices: Gehenna
Tartarus
Hades
Sheol
context: Ge-Hinnom (Valley of Hinnom) became the Greek 'Gehenna' (Geenna), the word Jesus uses in the New Testament as an image for hell. The valley held the Tophet, the burning-ground where the rite was carried out. A real cursed place outside Jerusalem became the language's name for hell itself. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gehenna ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tophet

question: Hebrew scribes who wrote down the name of the god of child sacrifice refused to spell it plainly. They started from melekh, 'king,' but gave it the vowels of another word, so that the name itself read as an insult to anyone who knew Hebrew. Which word lent its vowels to the god's name?
answer: boshet, meaning 'shame'
choices: boshet, meaning 'shame'
sheker, meaning 'lie'
tame, meaning 'unclean'
ra, meaning 'evil'
context: The name Moloch (Molech) is widely understood as melekh, 'king,' deliberately given the vowels of boshet, 'shame' — so the god's own name was rigged to read 'the shameful king.' The scribes built their verdict on the cult right into its spelling. Sources: jewishvirtuallibrary.org/the-cult-of-moloch ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tophet

question: Aztec farmers worked long green strips of cropland on the shallow waters of Lake Xochimilco around the year 1500. The Spanish took them for 'floating gardens,' yet a chinampa never floated at all. How did the farmers really build one?
answer: They packed layers of lake mud and rotting plants between staked reeds until solid ground rose above the water
choices: They packed layers of lake mud and rotting plants between staked reeds until solid ground rose above the water
They lashed hollow reed rafts together so the beds rode loose on the lake's surface
They quarried stone blocks and sank them to make islands that broke the waterline
They let mats of tangled waterweed drift until enough silt collected to plant on
context: Farmers staked out a rectangle of shallow lakebed, wove reeds and branches between the stakes, and piled in alternating layers of mud and decaying vegetation until the bed sat solid and rooted to the bottom. "Floating gardens" is a charming mistake. Sources: worldhistory.org/Chinampas/; anthrome.wordpress.com/2011/04/24/chinampa-raised-bed-hydrological-agriculture/

question: Aztec farmers in the Valley of Mexico had to anchor the edges of every chinampa, because loose soil beside open water washes away easily. Along each plot's border grew one particular tree whose roots gripped the soil and stopped it eroding, while its leaves kept the crops in shade. Which tree held the islands together?
answer: The ahuejote willow, grown straight from the construction stakes
choices: The ahuejote willow, grown straight from the construction stakes
The Montezuma cypress, planted in rings around each plot
The mangrove, whose stilt roots gripped the lakebed
The mesquite, set deep to anchor the bank
context: The stakes farmers drove in to build the plot sprouted into ahuejote willows (Salix bonplandiana). Their roots bound the soil against erosion while their canopy shaded the crops and cut evaporation. The willows quite literally held the islands together. Sources: worldhistory.org/Chinampas/; hilo.hawaii.edu/nihopeku/2018/02/02/chinampa-an-ancient-agricultural-system/

question: Foreign traders carried the world's finest tableware away from the Chinese town of Changnan, now called Jingdezhen, for more than a thousand years. A popular account holds that on their tongues the town's old name wore down into a short English word still in use. Which word did Changnan become?
answer: China
choices: China
Silk
Jade
Ivory
context: Porcelain was so bound up with the land that one word, 'china', came to mean both the country and any fine ceramic dish. The town was renamed Jingde in 1004 CE after the emperor's reign-name; he prized its ceramics as tribute. Source: MudandLeaves, 'Jingdezhen Porcelain and the name China'; WildChina, 'Jingdezhen: City of Porcelain'.

question: A Chinese master of shan shui, the 'mountain-water' landscape, left wide stretches of his silk bare on purpose, giving the blank gaps as much thought as his brushwork. Some things in the picture he painted with the brush; others he left to the bare silk. Which three did the bare silk stand for?
answer: The mist, the water, and the sky
choices: The mist, the water, and the sky
The cliffs, the pines, and the rocks
The bridges, the boats, and the huts
The herders, the mules, and the carts
context: The empty, unpainted silk IS the mist, the water, and the sky — painters 'paid as much attention to the unpainted areas of their compositions as they did to the detailed sections.' Song masters Ma Yuan ('One-Corner Ma') and Xia Gui ('One-Side Xia') pushed all the detail into one corner and left the rest as open mist. Source: Princeton University Art Museum, 'Chinese Landscape Painting during the Song Dynasty'; Shan shui, New World Encyclopedia.

question: Fan Kuan painted 'Travelers Among Mountains and Streams' around the year 1000, and he hid his own signature in it so well that no one noticed for centuries. Not until 1958 did the scholar Li Lincan finally spot the two-character name in the lower right of the silk. Where in the painting had Fan Kuan hidden his name?
answer: Among the leaves of a tree
choices: Among the leaves of a tree
Beneath the tiny travelers' feet
Inside a red seal in the corner
Along the bottom edge of the silk
context: Fan Kuan disguised his name among the leaves of a lower-right tree, made to look like a drooping branch, and it went unnoticed for roughly 900 years. In the same painting a single towering mountain fills nearly two-thirds of the picture, while a mule caravan led by two herders is so tiny you can barely find it. Source: China Online Museum / DailyArt Magazine, citing Li Lincan, National Palace Museum Taipei, August 1958.

question: An ink painter ground his ink stick with water, loaded a soft brush and set it to the silk to paint a mountain. Ink on silk worked unlike a Western oil painting in one strict way. What could the painter never do to a brush mark once it had landed?
answer: Erase a stroke once it's down
choices: Erase a stroke once it's down
Darken a stroke by retracing it
Nudge a stroke while it's still wet
Soften a stroke's edge with water
context: A brush stroke cannot be erased or painted over — the moment the brush touches the silk, the mark is permanent, so the painter must commit with full intention and no hesitation. The same brush, ink, and silk carry the 'Three Perfections' — poetry, calligraphy, and painting together; painting itself was called 'silent poetry'. Source: National Gallery of Victoria, 'Three Perfections: Poetry, Calligraphy and Painting'; ink-and-brush.com.

question: Wang Xizhi sat at a riverside drinking party in 353, brush in hand, and dashed off the 'Orchid Pavilion Preface' while drunk. It came to be honored as the most famous piece of calligraphy ever written. One common character appeared in it twenty times. What did Wang Xizhi do with that character each of the twenty times?
answer: Wrote it a different way all 20 times
choices: Wrote it a different way all 20 times
Wrote it bigger each of the 20 times
Left it out and drew a dot instead
Wrote all 20 copies in one breath
context: The character was 'zhi' (之), and Wang Xizhi formed it differently every single time. When he sobered up and tried to rewrite the preface, he could never recapture the same beauty; he is honored as the 'Sage of Calligraphy.' The party itself: 42 scholars along a winding stream, cups of wine floated down the water, and whoever the cup stopped before had to compose a poem or drink. Source: Lantingji Xu, Wikipedia.

question: Francois Xavier d'Entrecolles, a French Jesuit, studied the great kilns of Jingdezhen in 1712, helped by Christian workers there, at a time when Europe still could not make true porcelain. He pulled off one of the earliest acts of industrial spying. What did d'Entrecolles send back to France?
answer: The secret recipe for porcelain
choices: The secret recipe for porcelain
The location of China's finest clay
The names of the kiln masters
The price charged for each vase
context: d'Entrecolles mailed China's closely-guarded porcelain method home to France — one of the earliest cases of industrial espionage. When his letters were published in 1716 they caused a sensation, and Europeans began hunting for kaolin clay of their own. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'One of the Earliest Industrial Spies Was a French Missionary'; Francois Xavier d'Entrecolles, Wikipedia.

question: Chinese parents bound their young daughters' feet for about a thousand years, starting when a girl was as young as five, folding her four small toes beneath the foot and pressing until the bones snapped. They aimed for a foot no longer than three Chinese inches, about ten centimetres, prized as the height of a woman's beauty. What poetic name did such a foot carry?
answer: The golden lotus
choices: The golden lotus
The silver lotus
The iron lotus
The jade lotus
context: The 'golden lotus' (jin lian) was a foot of no more than three Chinese inches, about 10 cm. A pair under four cun were merely 'silver lotuses,' and anything larger was dismissed as an 'iron lotus.' Girls' binding began as young as five, when the four small toes were curled under and pressed until the bones broke. Sources: worldhistory.org/Foot-Binding and chinahighlights.com/shanghai/article-discover-foot-binding.htm.

question: John MacGowan, a missionary, stood at the head of about sixty Christian women in the city of Xiamen in 1875 when they took one of the first stands against foot binding, a custom that had crippled women for a thousand years. They named their group for the kind of foot they defended. What was their society called?
answer: The Natural Foot Society
choices: The Natural Foot Society
The Bound Daughters League
The Lotus Mercy Mission
The Golden Foot Sisterhood
context: They called it the 'Natural Foot' or 'Heavenly Foot' Society (Tianzu Hui) -- a name defending the unbroken, unbound foot. The Chinese reformer Kang Youwei later built on this: in the 1898 Hundred Days' Reform he sent the throne a memorial titled 'Plea to Forbid Female Foot Binding,' arguing the custom had to end for China to modernize. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavenly_Foot_Society and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_Emancipation_Society.

question: Cai Lun, a Han court official, invented paper around the year 105. Chinese books had been written on heavier stuff before that, and a long one took up a great deal of room. What could a single long book fill?
answer: A whole wagon-load of bamboo slips
choices: A whole wagon-load of bamboo slips
A whole cart of carved stone tablets
A whole chest of heavy clay bricks
A whole crate of folded silk bolts
context: Chinese writing went on bamboo and wooden tablets that were heavy, bulky, and awkward to store — a single long book could fill a whole cart of bamboo slips. Cai Lun's paper replaced all of it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cai_Lun.

question: Daoist alchemists in China mixed saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal about a thousand years ago, hoping to brew an elixir of eternal life. What they made instead was gunpowder. Its Chinese name, huo yao, is still in use today. What does huo yao mean, word for word?
answer: Fire medicine
choices: Fire medicine
Black sand
War dust
Dragon ash
context: Gunpowder was a happy accident of immortality-seeking alchemists. The Chinese name huo yao (火药) literally means 'fire medicine' and is still used today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gunpowder; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elixir_of_life.

question: Wise men in China, more than two thousand years ago, carved the first compass from lodestone, a natural rock that quietly pulls on iron, and called it the si nan. The spoon-shaped stone spun on a smooth bronze plate until it slowed and settled. Which way did the si nan always come to rest pointing?
answer: Pointing south
choices: Pointing south
Pointing north
Pointing east
Pointing toward water
context: The si nan, or 'south-pointing spoon,' was carved from lodestone and spun on a bronze plate. By tradition Chinese compasses point south, not north like the ones we use today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_compass; ancient-origins.net.

question: Francis Bacon counted printing among three inventions that had remade the world, around 1620, but China had printed books long before. The oldest of them that carries a date was pressed from carved wooden blocks in 868, on seven sheets joined into a single roll about sixteen feet long, some 600 years before Gutenberg. What is this Buddhist scroll called?
answer: The Diamond Sutra
choices: The Diamond Sutra
The Dream Pool Essays
The Lotus Scroll
The Book of Changes
context: The Diamond Sutra of 868 AD was printed roughly 600 years before Gutenberg's Bible. Its end note says a man named Wang Jie had it made 'for universal free distribution' to honor his two parents. Source: idp.bl.uk/blog/the-diamond-sutra (British Library); smithsonianmag.com.

question: Craftsmen in ancient China found that a lodestone compass needle settles along the earth's unseen magnetic pull. Yet for hundreds of years afterwards no one in China used it to find the way across land or sea. What did the Chinese use it for instead?
answer: Feng shui and fortune-telling
choices: Feng shui and fortune-telling
Healing and medicine
Music and ceremony
Astronomy and stargazing
context: Only later did the compass go to sea. For centuries it lined up houses, graves, and fields with the Earth's magnetic force for feng shui and fortune-telling. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_compass; encyclopedia.com.

question: Cai Lun, the Han official who invented paper, later passed along a slander at court that helped bring about a death. In 121 he was ordered to prison to stand trial for it. Rather than face the trial, what did Cai Lun do?
answer: He put on his finest robes and drank poison
choices: He put on his finest robes and drank poison
He fled north in disguise and vanished for good
He confessed and begged the emperor for a pardon
He burned his workshop down and turned himself in
context: Cai Lun had passed along a slander that helped cause the death of a consort, the emperor's grandmother. Ordered to prison in 121 AD, he bathed, dressed in his finest formal robes, and chose a dignified death over trial. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cai_Lun (Hou Hanshu).

question: Chinese printers made a Buddhist scroll from carved wooden blocks in 868, and in time it ended up sealed in a cave near Dunhuang along with tens of thousands of other manuscripts. There it lay for about 900 years. How did the hidden library come to light again around 1900?
answer: By chance, when a monk was clearing drifted sand
choices: By chance, when a monk was clearing drifted sand
By an emperor's officials on a grand treasure hunt
By a farmer breaking in to dig a well
By archaeologists who had searched for it for years
context: The Mogao caves near Dunhuang had been walled up for centuries. Around 1900 the Daoist caretaker-monk Wang Yuanlu uncovered the sealed Library Cave by chance while clearing drifted sand; the explorer Aurel Stein later carried off much of the hoard. Source: idp.bl.uk/blog/the-diamond-sutra; openculture.com.

question: Bi Sheng, a commoner, invented movable type between 1039 and 1048, so that a printer could set a page from single pieces and use them again. Yet for centuries after him, Chinese printers kept carving each whole page as one solid woodblock. Why did movable type struggle to catch on in China?
answer: Written Chinese needs thousands of separate characters
choices: Written Chinese needs thousands of separate characters
The emperor had banned all clay type
Carved woodblocks outlasted fragile clay type
Woodblocks alone could print in color
context: Cutting a full set of type for thousands of characters cost far more than carving one page as a single block, so woodblock printing stayed dominant. Centuries later the same idea met Europe's roughly 26-letter alphabet and exploded. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bi_Sheng; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_printing_in_East_Asia.

question: Mao Zedong stood atop the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing on 1 October 1949 and proclaimed the People's Republic of China. As cannon boomed out a 21-gun salute, a brand-new national flag rose over the square for the first time. What did that red flag carry in its corner?
answer: Five gold stars
choices: Five gold stars
A gold hammer and sickle
A coiled gold dragon
A rising gold sun
context: The five-starred red flag was hoisted for the first time during Mao's proclamation on 1 October 1949, to a 21-gun salute. The one big star with four smaller ones is still China's flag today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China

question: Chiang Kai-shek, leader of the Nationalists, refused to surrender when the Communists won China's civil war in 1949. He fled across the sea with roughly two million refugees and most of the country's gold reserves. Which island did Chiang make his last stronghold?
answer: Taiwan
choices: Taiwan
Hainan
Hong Kong
Okinawa
context: Chiang Kai-shek and the Nationalists fled across the strait to Taiwan with about two million refugees and most of China's gold, which became the backing for the New Taiwan dollar. Source: https://factsanddetails.com/southeast-asia/Taiwan/sub5_1a/entry-3800.html

question: With the Communists closing in, Chiang Kai-shek's men quietly emptied the Shanghai vaults of the Bank of China after dark on 1 December 1948. A British journalist watching from a hotel saw a line of figures filing through the dark across the waterfront. What did he see the men carrying the gold on?
answer: Long poles slung over their shoulders
choices: Long poles slung over their shoulders
Armored bank trucks
Steel handcarts
Mule-drawn wagons
context: The reporter described 'men with long poles carrying heavy boxes' filing across Shanghai's Bund waterfront to a customs vessel. The first shipment was about 2 million of the 4.6 million taels in the treasury. Source: https://www.scmp.com/article/716329/how-chiang-spirited-chinas-gold-away-reds

question: The Red Army marched out of Jiangxi in the southeast in 1934, about 86,000 strong, on the retreat that made Mao Zedong a legend: the Long March. The troops trudged some 6,000 miles over snow-capped mountains to Shaanxi in the far northwest. Of the 86,000 who started, roughly how many reached the end?
answer: A few thousand
choices: A few thousand
About sixty thousand
About forty thousand
Almost all of them
context: Of roughly 86,000 troops who set out, only about 4,000-8,000 reached Shaanxi after 368 days, 24 rivers, and 18 mountain ranges. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/october-20/maos-long-march-concludes

question: Mao Zedong gave China a slogan in 1949 that every Chinese child still learns: 'The Chinese people have stood up.' Most picture him roaring it from the Gate of Heavenly Peace as he proclaimed the People's Republic on 1 October. Yet his proclamation that day contains no such line. Where did the words come from?
answer: A different speech ten days earlier
choices: A different speech ten days earlier
A poster pasted up after the parade
A song the crowd sang that night
A letter Mao wrote from prison
context: 'The Chinese people have stood up' was the title of a speech Mao gave on 21 September 1949 to the Political Consultative Conference, not part of the October 1 proclamation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China

question: Communist armies destroyed about 550,000 American-armed Nationalist troops around Xuzhou in the Huaihai Campaign, fought across 1948 and 1949, the largest battle of China's civil war. They had almost no trucks of their own to face that motorized army, yet over two million ordinary people kept them fed and armed all the way to the front. Who hauled those supplies?
answer: Peasants pushing wheelbarrows
choices: Peasants pushing wheelbarrows
Mule and camel caravans
River junks poled upstream
Lines of conscripted porters
context: Over 2 million peasants pushing wooden wheelbarrows hauled supplies to the Huaihai front, a peasant supply line that helped crush an American-equipped mechanized army. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huaihai_campaign

question: Edgar Snow, a journalist, wrote about the Long March's most famous episode, the fight at Luding Bridge in 1935. In his telling, the bridge's wooden planks over the boiling Dadu River had been ripped out, leaving a deadly gap 50 feet above the water, yet a handful of Communist commandos seized the far side under machine-gun fire. How, Snow wrote, did they get across?
answer: Swung hand-over-hand along the iron chains
choices: Swung hand-over-hand along the iron chains
Swam the icy river at night
Floated across on bamboo rafts
Built a new rope bridge under fire
context: Edgar Snow wrote that 22 commandos swung hand-over-hand across the bare chains under machine-gun fire and burning planks; he called it 'the most crucial single incident of the Long March.' This is the legendary telling, not settled fact. Source: https://thechinaproject.com/2023/05/31/what-really-happened-at-the-battle-of-luding-bridge/

question: Deng Xiaoping, who later led China, admitted to the American adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski that Luding Bridge, Communist China's proudest war story, had really been 'a very easy fight,' not the version the propaganda told. According to Deng, what were the warlord soldiers on the far bank armed with?
answer: Old muskets
choices: Old muskets
Rusty bolt-action rifles
Belt-fed machine guns
Bamboo spears and swords
context: Deng Xiaoping told Brzezinski the defenders were warlord troops 'armed with old muskets' and that the heroic crossing was 'a very easy military operation' -- 'that is how our propaganda presents it.' Jung Chang and Jon Halliday wrote 'there was no battle at the Dadu Bridge,' citing a witness and Nationalist plans showing the guards had already withdrawn. Source: https://thechinaproject.com/2023/05/31/what-really-happened-at-the-battle-of-luding-bridge/

question: Jung Chang and Jon Halliday published 'Mao: The Unknown Story' in 2005, a biography of the man who ruled a quarter of the world's people. Its very first sentence makes a charge about Mao Zedong: that in peacetime he was responsible for more deaths than any other leader of the twentieth century. What toll did that opening line put on him?
answer: Well over 70 million
choices: Well over 70 million
About 5 million
Around 20 million
Nearly 200 million
context: Chang and Halliday's opening line states Mao was 'responsible for well over 70 million deaths in peacetime, more than any other twentieth-century leader.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao:_The_Unknown_Story

question: Sophie Scholl and her brother Hans slipped into the empty main hall of the University of Munich one February morning in 1943 with a case of banned anti-Nazi leaflets. As students were about to pour out of the lecture rooms, one last batch was left over. What did Sophie do with it?
answer: Pushed the stack off the top-floor railing onto the students below
choices: Pushed the stack off the top-floor railing onto the students below
Handed them out at the main doors as the students left
Pinned them one by one on the campus boards
Stacked them on the benches by the lecture halls
context: She sent them fluttering down into the atrium. A custodian, Jakob Schmid, saw her do it, locked the doors, and held her and Hans until the Gestapo came. The White Rose leaflets had declared, 'We will not be silent. We are your bad conscience,' and one had named the crime outright: 'three hundred thousand Jews have been murdered in this country in the most bestial way... a crime against human dignity.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakob_Schmid ; encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/white-rose

question: Roland Freisler, a Nazi judge, condemned Sophie Scholl to death for helping the White Rose spread leaflets against Hitler. Minutes before she went to the guillotine on 22 February 1943, the 21-year-old student looked up at the sky and spoke a few quiet words that are still remembered. What did Sophie say?
answer: The sun is still shining.
choices: The sun is still shining.
The sky has never looked clearer.
Let them see I was not afraid.
I would do it all again.
context: 'Die Sonne scheint noch.' She added, 'What does my death matter, if through us thousands of people are awakened and stirred to action?' She, Hans, and Christoph Probst were tried before the screaming Nazi judge Roland Freisler and guillotined the same day, 22 February 1943. Sources: theepochtimes.com/bright/the-suns-still-shining-the-courage-of-sophie-scholl-3665966 ; en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Sophie_Scholl

question: Hans Scholl followed his sister Sophie to the guillotine minutes after her, in February 1943. The two Munich students had been caught spreading leaflets against Adolf Hitler for their small resistance group, the White Rose. As the blade was about to fall, Hans shouted words that echoed through the whole prison. What did he cry out?
answer: Long live freedom!
choices: Long live freedom!
God will judge you all!
You cannot kill the truth!
Remember our names!
context: 'Es lebe die Freiheit!' Hans and Sophie were medical and philosophy students who, with their friends, had written and mailed six secret leaflets to cities from Hamburg to Vienna. Sources: womenshistorynetwork.org/sophie-scholl ; executedtoday.com/2009/02/22/1943-sophie-scholl-of-the-white-rose

question: Christoph Probst, a 23-year-old medical student with three small children, went to the guillotine on the same day as his friends Hans and Sophie Scholl of the White Rose. In the minutes before his death, a Catholic priest came to his cell. What did Probst receive from the priest?
answer: Baptism into the church and his first communion
choices: Baptism into the church and his first communion
A blessing and absolution for his sins
A psalm read over him and a wooden cross
The last rites and prayers for the dying
context: Probst had no church baptism, but at the threshold of death he asked for it, and the priest baptized him and gave him communion minutes before he was beheaded. Sources: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Christoph_Probst ; aleteia.org/2018/12/07/this-friend-of-sophie-scholl-became-catholic-moments-before-his-martyrdom

question: As Hitler's crimes grew, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a Lutheran pastor who had once leaned close to pacifism and believed a Christian should not kill, decided that his faith now demanded action. He joined a secret group plotting one particular deed. What had the pastor signed on to do?
answer: Assassinate Adolf Hitler
choices: Assassinate Adolf Hitler
Kidnap Heinrich Himmler
Blow up the Reichstag building
Smuggle weapons to the Allies
context: Bonhoeffer used a job in the Abwehr (military intelligence) as cover; under the code name 'Operation 7' he had already helped smuggle a group of Jews into Switzerland. After the failed 20 July 1944 bomb plot was traced to his circle, Hitler personally ordered the conspirators killed. The SS hanged Bonhoeffer at Flossenburg on 9 April 1945, just two weeks before US troops liberated the camp. Sources: history.com/this-day-in-history/april-9/defiant-theologian-dietrich-bonhoeffer-is-hanged ; gedenkstaette-flossenbuerg.de/en/history/prisoners/dietrich-bonhoeffer

question: Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a book in 1937 attacking what he called 'cheap grace': forgiveness offered with no repentance and no cross, religion made easy. Against it he set a demanding opposite, the grace that claims a person's whole life. What did Bonhoeffer name that opposite?
answer: Costly grace
choices: Costly grace
Saving grace
Hard grace
Pure grace
context: In 'The Cost of Discipleship,' Bonhoeffer wrote that costly grace is the grace that costs a disciple's very life, the call to follow no matter the price. His own death under Hitler became the test of those words. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cost_of_Discipleship ; thegospelcoalition.org/article/great-books-friday-bonhoeffer-cost-of-discipleship

question: Romans whispered that their emperor Nero had set the fire that swept through the city for days in July 64, to clear land for a grand new palace. To turn the crowd's anger away from himself, what did Nero do?
answer: He blamed the city's Christians and had them killed
choices: He blamed the city's Christians and had them killed
He blamed the Senate and had them exiled
He blamed the Jewish priests and closed their temple
He blamed foreign sailors and banned them from the port
context: The Roman historian Tacitus (Annals 15.44) is the sole source linking the fire directly to this first persecution; Nero wanted the land for his Domus Aurea, his 'Golden House.' Source: https://brians.wsu.edu/2016/11/14/tacitus-neros-persecution-of-the-christians/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_Rome

question: Roman Christians scratched a secret sign to recognize one another in the dangerous early years, when openly showing a cross could get a believer arrested. The Greek word for the sign spelled out a hidden phrase: 'Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.' What simple creature was it?
answer: A fish
choices: A fish
A lion
An eagle
A serpent
context: The Greek word ICHTHYS ('fish') worked as an acrostic for the phrase; Christians also carved an anchor as a disguised cross. Both appear on tombs in the Catacomb of Callixtus from the early 2nd century. Source: https://www.ewtn.com/catholicism/library/symbolism-of-the-fish-10733 ; https://www.catacombesancallisto.it/en/simboli-cristiani.php

question: Christians dug a maze of tunnels beneath Rome, more than fifty sites and about 150 km of passages, some four levels deep. Legend says they dug them as secret hideouts from the persecutors, but historians call that story mostly a myth, since the tunnels' locations were well known. Why did the Christians really dig them?
answer: To bury their dead, because they believed the body would rise again
choices: To bury their dead, because they believed the body would rise again
To stay hidden from Roman soldiers during the persecutions
To hold secret church services away from the emperor's spies
To store the church's gold where thieves could not reach it
context: Believing in bodily resurrection, Christians buried their dead rather than cremating them like most Romans. The tunnels were dug and sold by gravediggers called fossors; bodies were slid into wall shelves called loculi. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs_of_Rome ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacomb_of_Callixtus

question: Ignatius, the bishop of Antioch, sentenced to die by the wild beasts of Rome's arena around 107, knew that the Christians of the city had the connections to try to save his life. He wrote ahead to them, but not to ask for rescue. What did Ignatius beg them to do?
answer: To let him be ground by the beasts like wheat into the pure bread of Christ
choices: To let him be ground by the beasts like wheat into the pure bread of Christ
To care for the poor of Antioch once he was gone
To send word of his death to every church in the East
To bury his bones in the catacombs beside the other martyrs
context: His exact words to the Roman Christians: 'I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ' (Epistle to the Romans 4). Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Ignatius-of-Antioch ; https://www.franciscanmedia.org/saint-of-the-day/saint-ignatius-of-antioch/

question: A Roman proconsul offered Polycarp, the aged bishop of Smyrna, his life around 155 if he would swear by Caesar and curse Christ. Polycarp refused with a single sentence about how long he had followed his King. What did the old man say?
answer: Eighty and six years I have served Him, and He has done me no wrong
choices: Eighty and six years I have served Him, and He has done me no wrong
I was born a Christian and a Christian I will die
Caesar rules my body, but my soul belongs to another
Do your worst, for tomorrow I dine in heaven
context: He added, 'How then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?' The 'Martyrdom of Polycarp' is the earliest detailed account of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycarp ; https://www.earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html

question: Vibia Perpetua, a noblewoman of about 22 with a baby still at her breast, kept a diary in prison at Carthage in 203, one of the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman. In it she described a striking dream of how she would reach heaven. What did she write that she saw?
answer: A ladder hung with swords, guarded by a serpent at its foot
choices: A ladder hung with swords, guarded by a serpent at its foot
A river of fire that her enemies could not cross
A white horse waiting to carry her over the city walls
A golden door that opened only when she spoke her name
context: Perpetua's prison diary records several visions before her death; she climbed the bladed ladder past the serpent in the dream. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Passion_of_Saints_Perpetua_and_Felicity ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Perpetua-Christian-martyr

question: Felicity, Perpetua's pregnant slave, faced death in the arena at Carthage beside her mistress. As the day drew near she grew afraid, not of dying, but of being left behind to miss it. What stood between Felicity and the martyrdom she wanted?
answer: Roman law forbade executing a pregnant woman
choices: Roman law forbade executing a pregnant woman
Her owner could pay a fine to free her at the last moment
Slaves were sold off rather than sent to the arena
The governor had pardoned all the women in her cell
context: Felicity gave birth to a daughter in prison just days before the games, and so was allowed to die alongside Perpetua. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Passion_of_Saints_Perpetua_and_Felicity ; https://orthodoxwiki.org/Perpetua_and_Felicitas

question: In the arena at Carthage in 203, a nervous young gladiator stepped up to finish Perpetua, a young Christian noblewoman who had refused to sacrifice to the Roman gods. His first stroke struck bone and only made her cry out in pain. What did the badly wounded Perpetua do next?
answer: She took his shaking hand and guided the blade to her own throat
choices: She took his shaking hand and guided the blade to her own throat
She knelt and prayed aloud until he found the courage to strike
She forgave him before the crowd and asked that he be spared
She seized his sword and turned it against the watching guards
context: Her last words to the watching catechumens were: 'Stand fast in the faith, and love one another, and be not offended at my sufferings.' She and Felicity had first risen to give each other the kiss of peace. Source: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm (Passion of Perpetua, ch. 21)

question: Ordered to hand over the Church's wealth, Lawrence, a deacon of Rome, gathered the city's poor instead and called them its treasures. Tradition says he was martyred in 258 by roasting on an iron gridiron, and that even there he managed a grim joke. What is he said to have told his executioners?
answer: Turn me over; I am done on this side
choices: Turn me over; I am done on this side
Your fire is cold next to the love of God
I thank you for the warmth on this cold night
Caesar's gold burns hotter than these coals
context: LEGEND: ancient accounts disagree on the details of Lawrence's death, so the gridiron quip is traditional rather than firmly attested fact. His line that the poor were 'the treasures of the Church' is the better-documented part of the story. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Lawrence ; https://missions.ewtn.com/seasonsandfeastdays/stlawrence/

question: Tertullian, a Christian writer in North Africa, argued around 197 that Rome's public killings were backfiring: every believer killed in the arena won the faith more converts, not fewer. He summed up the idea in one line still quoted today. What did Tertullian write?
answer: The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church
choices: The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church
Rome may kill the body but never the truth
Each death in the arena lights a hundred candles
What the sword cuts down, faith grows back twofold
context: From Tertullian's Apologeticus; the literal Latin reads 'semen est sanguis Christianorum' — 'the blood of Christians is seed.' Tertullian was also an early source of the dramatic lions imagery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apologeticus ; https://earlychurchtexts.com/public/tertullian_blood_christians_seed.htm

question: Perpetua and her companions faced a boar, a bear, a leopard and a wild cow in the arena at Carthage, not lions. Being 'sent to the beasts' was a punishment for condemned criminals of every kind, and it rarely meant lions at all. What do modern historians say about the Colosseum in Rome?
answer: There is no solid evidence any Christian was martyred there
choices: There is no solid evidence any Christian was martyred there
Only nobles, not commoners, were sent to die there
It was reserved for gladiators and never used for executions
The lions there were too valuable to risk on prisoners
context: 'Damnatio ad bestias' was used on many criminals, not just Christians, and rarely specified lions; despite the long tradition, there is no firm evidence of a Christian martyrdom in the Colosseum specifically. Source: https://www.badancient.com/claims/lions-christians/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damnatio_ad_bestias

question: Officials of the emperor Diocletian opened the last and fiercest persecution of the Christians on 23 February 303, and they did not begin with arrests. They began in Nicomedia, in full public view. What did they do first?
answer: They razed the church and burned the Christians' scriptures
choices: They razed the church and burned the Christians' scriptures
They marched every bishop of the East off to the mines
They crucified the clergy along the road into the city
They melted down the empire's coins bearing Christian signs
context: The Diocletianic or 'Great Persecution' opened with razing the Nicomedia church, burning scriptures, and seizing church treasures; later edicts ordered everyone in the empire to sacrifice to the Roman gods. It ended in stages — Galerius's Edict of Toleration (311) and the Edict of Milan (313). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletianic_Persecution ; https://www.historytoday.com/archive/months-past/diocletians-great-persecution

question: Mark Antony's soldiers hunted down Cicero, Rome's greatest orator, in 43 BC, after he had attacked Antony in fourteen fierce speeches, the Philippics. The killers cut off his head and nailed it up in the Forum on the Rostra, the stand where orators spoke. What else of Cicero's did they cut off and nail beside it?
answer: His hands
choices: His hands
His feet
His ears
His eyes
context: Antony ordered Cicero's hands cut off along with his head — the hands that wrote the Philippics — and both were nailed to the Rostra, the very platform where Cicero had given his greatest speeches. Plutarch, Life of Cicero 48; Ancient World Magazine, 'Resigned to fate: the death of Cicero.'

question: Fulvia, Mark Antony's wife, is said to have taken Cicero's severed head into her lap when it was brought to her husband, and to have pulled the pins from her hair. She was bent on revenge against the orator whose words had savaged Antony. In the tale Cassius Dio tells, what did Fulvia stab with those hairpins?
answer: Cicero's tongue
choices: Cicero's tongue
Cicero's eyes
Cicero's nose
Cicero's lips
context: Legend recorded by Cassius Dio: Fulvia jabbed her hairpins into the dead orator's tongue — final revenge for the speeches it had spoken against Antony. Marked as legend (ancient testimony, not forensic fact). Imperium Romanum, 'Death of Cicero.'

question: An army of the Aequi trapped a Roman force in the hills southeast of Rome in 458 BC, and it looked sure to be wiped out. The Senate chose a former consul, Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus, to rule as dictator with full emergency power, and sent messengers to find him. Where did they find him?
answer: Plowing a field on his small farm
choices: Plowing a field on his small farm
Lounging at his villa by the sea
Speaking on the floor of the Senate
Drilling soldiers out on the frontier
context: Cincinnatus was working a tiny plot of about four iugera (a few acres) across the Tiber, called the Quintian Meadows. Livy says the messengers found him 'either pushing upon a stake in a ditch, or busy plowing,' and asked him to put on his toga so they could deliver the Senate's command. Source: Livy, History of Rome 3.26 (elfinspell.com/PrimarySourceCincinnatus.html); worldhistory.org/Cincinnatus.

question: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus took absolute command of Rome for a term of six months in 458 BC. He raised an army, marched through the night and beat the Aequi, forcing them to stoop beneath a yoke of spears. How long did he keep that power before he laid it down and walked back to his plow?
answer: About sixteen days
choices: About sixteen days
About four months
The full six months
A little over a year
context: Livy says Cincinnatus 'laid down his dictatorship on the sixteenth day, although he had received it for six months' (some retellings say fifteen). Handed absolute power to save Rome, he beat the Aequi, made their whole army stoop one by one 'under the yoke' of three spears, then gave the power straight back and returned to farming. Source: Livy 3.27-3.29 (elfinspell.com/PrimarySourceCincinnatus.html); worldhistory.org/Cincinnatus.

question: Benjamin West, the painter, told King George III during the American Revolution that George Washington meant to give up his power and go back to farming if he won the war. Washington did just that in 1783, laying down his command and going home to Mount Vernon, as Cincinnatus had gone back to his plow. What had the King replied?
answer: If he does that, he will be the greatest man in the world
choices: If he does that, he will be the greatest man in the world
Then America will have found itself a king instead
No man alive gives up such power willingly
I shall believe that on the day I see it
context: Washington did exactly that on December 23, 1783, surrendering his commission as commander-in-chief at the Maryland State House in Annapolis and riding home to Mount Vernon. His officers named the Society of the Cincinnati after the same Roman, with Washington as its first president general; the city of Cincinnati, Ohio was renamed for the Society in 1790. Source: americanrevolutioninstitute.org/the-american-cincinnatus; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington's_resignation_as_commander-in-chief.

question: Locked out of her own palace in Alexandria by her brother's soldiers in 48 BC, the twenty-one-year-old Cleopatra wanted to reach the Roman general Julius Caesar, who was inside. With the help of one loyal servant, how did she get in to see him?
answer: Rolled up and carried in past the guards inside a bed-sack
choices: Rolled up and carried in past the guards inside a bed-sack
Disguised herself in the armor of a Roman soldier
Was lowered over the palace wall on a rope at night
Bribed the guards with a chest of Egyptian gold
context: Plutarch says her servant Apollodorus smuggled her in rolled inside a bed-sack (often retold as a carpet); she tumbled out at Caesar's feet, and her sheer audacity won him over — they became allies and lovers. Source: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 49; History.com, '10 Little-Known Facts About Cleopatra.'

question: Alexander the Great's general Ptolemy seized Egypt when Alexander died, and his family ruled it for almost three hundred years. Legend made Cleopatra, the last of that line, an Egyptian queen, but her family were outsiders in the land they ruled. By blood, what was she?
answer: Greek
choices: Greek
Egyptian
Persian
Phoenician
context: Cleopatra was a Macedonian Greek of the Ptolemaic dynasty, descended from Ptolemy I Soter — not an Egyptian by blood at all. Her real power was political brilliance, not exotic mystery. Source: History.com, '10 Little-Known Facts About Cleopatra'; Britannica, Cleopatra.

question: Cleopatra broke a habit her family had kept for almost three centuries. The Ptolemy kings ruled Egypt from Alexandria without once reaching out in one basic way to the ordinary Egyptians they governed. What did she become the first of her royal family to do?
answer: Learned to speak Egyptian
choices: Learned to speak Egyptian
Worshipped at Egypt's temples as a native pharaoh would
Took an Egyptian commoner as her husband
Moved her court out of Greek Alexandria
context: Plutarch notes the Ptolemy kings before her 'had not even made an effort to learn the native language'; Cleopatra was the first of her line to learn Egyptian. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 27; ASOR, 'Cleopatra's Languages.'

question: Octavian meant to lead Cleopatra through Rome as a captive in his victory parade once her ally Mark Antony was beaten, but she chose to die instead. In the famous tale, the means of her death was smuggled past her palace guards hidden inside a very ordinary object. What was it hidden in?
answer: A basket of figs
choices: A basket of figs
The lining of her gown
A sealed jar of wine
A box of her jewels
context: The legend says an asp (an Egyptian cobra) was smuggled to her in a basket of figs; she was found dead on a golden couch in full royal robes. Plutarch passes this on as the famous story, not proven fact. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 85-86; Wikipedia, Death of Cleopatra.

question: Plutarch marvelled that Cleopatra could deal face to face with envoys of the Ethiopians, Arabs, Hebrews, Medes and Parthians, rarely needing an interpreter. She reportedly spoke about nine languages. Plutarch likened her tongue to one kind of object. What did he compare it to?
answer: An instrument of many strings
choices: An instrument of many strings
A coin stamped with many faces
A river fed by many streams
A key that opened many doors
context: Plutarch wrote that her tongue was 'like an instrument of many strings,' switching to whatever language she pleased — she reportedly commanded around nine. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 27.

question: Mark Antony summoned Cleopatra to Tarsus in 41 BC to answer for backing his enemies. She came on a magnificent barge with purple sails, a stern of gold and silver oars keeping time to flutes, and she was dressed to overwhelm him at first sight as one goddess. Which goddess was she made up to be?
answer: Venus, goddess of love
choices: Venus, goddess of love
Isis, goddess of magic
Athena, goddess of war
Diana, goddess of the hunt
context: Dressed as Venus (the Greek Aphrodite) with purple sails overhead, she made such a spectacle that word spread 'Aphrodite had come to revel with Dionysus' — and Antony was won. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 26; National Geographic, Antony & Cleopatra.

question: Cleopatra bet Mark Antony over who could throw the costliest banquet. To win, she called for one of the two largest pearls in the world, plus a simple cup of vinegar. In the story recorded by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder, what did she then do with that priceless pearl?
answer: Dissolved it in the vinegar and drank it down
choices: Dissolved it in the vinegar and drank it down
Ground it to powder and stirred it into wine
Tossed it into the harbor before the guests
Crushed it over a roasted peacock as seasoning
context: Pliny says the pearl-and-vinegar meal was worth ten million sesterces; the judge Lucius Plancus stopped her before she could destroy the second pearl and declared Antony the loser. It is a famous tale, likely exaggerated. Source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 9.119-121.  (Legend.)

question: Coins struck in Alexandria during Cleopatra's reign carried her portrait in profile, before legend turned her into the most beautiful woman in the world. Some of those coins survive today. What sort of nose did they give her?
answer: A strong hooked nose
choices: A strong hooked nose
A small upturned nose
A broad flat nose
A long straight nose
context: Her coins show a sharp, hooked-nosed profile with a jutting chin — no great beauty. Plutarch agreed her looks were 'not altogether incomparable,' crediting instead her charm, wit, and a 'mellifluous' voice. Source: History.com, '10 Little-Known Facts About Cleopatra'; Plutarch, Life of Antony 27.

question: Antony and Cleopatra sat on golden thrones at the Donations of Alexandria, a grand ceremony in 34 BC, and handed out Rome's eastern lands to her children. They declared her son Caesarion, fathered by Julius Caesar himself, to be Caesar's true heir, and crowned him with a title borrowed from the great emperors of the East. What was the title?
answer: King of Kings
choices: King of Kings
Pharaoh of Egypt
Son of the Divine
Great King of Asia
context: Proclaiming Caesarion 'King of Kings' and Caesar's real heir was a direct challenge to Octavian (Caesar's adopted heir) and helped trigger the final war of the Roman Republic. Source: Wikipedia, Donations of Alexandria; World History Encyclopedia, Cleopatra & Antony.

question: Charmion, Cleopatra's maid, was straightening her dead queen's crown when Octavian's soldiers burst into the tomb. Cleopatra lay dead in her royal robes, and her other maid lay dying beside her. A guard angrily demanded whether this was a fitting end for her lady. What did Charmion answer before she fell dead?
answer: 'Extremely well, and as became the descendant of so many kings.'
choices: 'Extremely well, and as became the descendant of so many kings.'
'She has cheated your master of his triumph in Rome.'
'Ask the gods, soldier, for I will not answer you.'
'Better a queen's death than a Roman's chains.'
context: Charmion was straightening the dead Cleopatra's crown when the Romans burst in; asked if this was fitting, she replied that it was extremely well done, as became the descendant of so many kings, and fell dead. Her last words, pride in Cleopatra's royal Ptolemaic line, are recorded by Plutarch. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 85 (Dryden); Wikipedia, Charmion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charmion_(servant_to_Cleopatra)
