question: Arius Didymus, a scholar who stood at Octavian's side after Cleopatra's death, urged him to have her son Caesarion hunted down and killed. Caesarion, about seventeen, was Julius Caesar's one true son, and Octavian wanted no rival left alive. Arius pressed his case with a grim joke that twisted a line of the poet Homer. What did he say?
answer: 'It is not good to have too many Caesars.'
choices: 'It is not good to have too many Caesars.'
'Two suns cannot share a single sky.'
'A dead lion no longer bites.'
'Rome has room for only one heir.'
context: Arius Didymus punned on Homer to justify the killing; with about-17-year-old Caesarion's death ended the last claim of Caesar's true blood-heir. His murder closed the Ptolemaic line and roughly 3,000 years of Egyptian pharaohs as Egypt became a Roman province. Source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 81-82; Wikipedia, Caesarion and Arius Didymus.

question: Two cowboys hunting stray cattle along a canyon rim in Colorado spotted something huge across the gorge through falling snow in December 1888. No one had lived there for hundreds of years. What did they see tucked under a single sandstone overhang?
answer: A stone village of about 150 rooms
choices: A stone village of about 150 rooms
A wooden fort ringed by a tall palisade
A mine shaft cut deep into the rock
A row of painted burial caves
context: They named it Cliff Palace -- the largest cliff dwelling in North America, built by the Ancestral Puebloans and packed with about 150 rooms under one overhang. Source: coloradoencyclopedia.org/article/cliff-palace

question: Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason, two cowboys, climbed down a rough ladder into the silent ruins of Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde and found pottery and human bones inside. No one had lived there for about 600 years, yet one tool looked as if its owner had only just set it down. What was it?
answer: A stone axe still lashed to its wooden handle
choices: A stone axe still lashed to its wooden handle
A loaded bow with its string still drawn
An iron sword resting in a leather sheath
A bronze knife wrapped in woven cloth
context: The Ancestral Puebloans had no metal tools -- the axe head was shaped stone bound to a wooden handle, abandoned with the village around the 1280s. Source: coloradoencyclopedia.org/article/cliff-palace

question: Ridgely Whiteman, a 19-year-old, found long stone spear points near Clovis, New Mexico, in 1929, and points of their kind have carried the town's name ever since. One signature trait let hunters fit a Clovis point onto a wooden spear shaft, and no later style copies it. What is that trait?
answer: A long flute channeled up from the base
choices: A long flute channeled up from the base
A hooked barb notched along each edge
A hollow socket drilled through the center
A serrated saw-edge ground into the tip
context: The 'flute' is the channel flake struck off the base of the point. It is the single trait that distinguishes a Clovis point from every later style. The culture is named for Clovis, New Mexico, where in February 1929 a 19-year-old named Ridgely Whiteman spotted such fluted points lying among the bones of Columbian mammoths at Blackwater Draw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_culture

question: Archaeologists working in a dry streambed in Arizona uncovered a Columbian mammoth that Ice Age hunters had butchered some 12,000 years ago, at a place called Naco. The kill lay exactly as the hunters had left it, frozen mid-hunt. What did they find with the kill?
answer: Eight stone spear points still among its ribs
choices: Eight stone spear points still among its ribs
A clay pot buried beneath its skull
A painted handprint left on a nearby wall
A necklace of carved teeth around its neck
context: Eight Clovis points lay in and among the rib cage of the one butchered mammoth at Naco, caught mid-hunt about 12,000 years ago. The site came to light after a local man, Marc Navarrete, found points while his father dug fossil bones out of Greenbush Draw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naco_Mammoth_Kill_Site

question: The Maya left their great jungle cities in the southern lowlands one by one in the 800s, as the building stopped and their god-kings lost their power. Many say the Maya mysteriously 'vanished.' But the people did not disappear. What is true of the Maya today?
answer: About seven million people still speak Mayan languages in Mesoamerica
choices: About seven million people still speak Mayan languages in Mesoamerica
Their language survives only in carvings no living person can read
A single elderly speaker of Mayan remained when Spain arrived
Every Maya community was wiped out within a century of the collapse
context: It was the great Classic-era CITIES that emptied, not the people. Around 800-900 CE the southern lowland cities went quiet one after another until roughly 60,000 square miles of jungle held only deserted pyramids. But millions of Maya descendants still live in the Yucatan, Guatemala, and southern Mexico, and about seven million people speak Mayan languages today. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'The Classic Maya Collapse' (worldhistory.org/article/759).

question: The Maya carved Long Count dates into their monuments for some 700 years, but the carving trailed off as the southern cities emptied: they finished some forty a year around 750, only ten a year by 800. Monument 101 at Tonina carries one from January 909. What became of the 700-year tradition after that carving?
answer: No Maya city ever carved a Long Count date again
choices: No Maya city ever carved a Long Count date again
Northern cities revived it and carved Long Count dates for centuries more
The Spanish recorded it from Maya scribes in the 1500s
It shifted from stone monuments onto painted pottery
context: Monument 101 at Tonina, dated 10.4.0.0.0 (January 909 CE), bears the last Long Count date the Maya ever carved; the 700-year tradition simply stopped. The fall is visible in the numbers: the Maya carved about 40 dated monuments a year around 750 CE, but the count dropped to ten by 800 and to zero by 900. Tikal's last dated stela went up in 869 CE. Sources: Encyclopedia.com 'Tonina'; Wikipedia 'Classic Maya collapse'; American Scientist, 'Climate and the Collapse of Maya Civilization'.

question: Scientists drilled long cores of mud from the bottom of Lake Chichancanab in the Yucatan and read in them a chemical record of the 800s, the century when the southern Maya cities were dying. Scholars still argue over why the cities emptied, and the lake gave one clue. What did its mud reveal about those years?
answer: A drought so severe that yearly rainfall fell by half or more
choices: A drought so severe that yearly rainfall fell by half or more
A run of floods that drowned the lowland cornfields
A sudden cold snap that froze the tropical lowlands
A layer of volcanic ash that buried the farmland
context: Sediment cores from Lake Chichancanab (Hodell, Curtis & Brenner, 1995), later refined by gypsum-hydrate analysis (Evans et al., 2018, Science), showed the 9th century suffered drought so severe that annual rainfall dropped 41-54%, and at the worst peaks fell by up to 70%. Drought is only one suspect, though: scholars also blame relentless warfare between rival city-states and soil exhaustion from overpopulation and deforestation, and most now see a chain reaction rather than a single cause. Sources: American Scientist, 'Climate and the Collapse of Maya Civilization'; Eos, 'Severe Drought May Have Helped Hasten Ancient Maya's Collapse'.

question: The red hammer-and-sickle flag came down over the Kremlin in Moscow for the last time on the night of 25 December 1991, and the Soviet Union ended with it. As crowds watched, a different flag rose in its place. Which flag was raised?
answer: The pre-revolutionary white-blue-red Russian tricolor
choices: The pre-revolutionary white-blue-red Russian tricolor
A plain white flag of surrender
The blue-and-yellow flag of Ukraine
A new flag with a golden two-headed eagle
context: At 7:32 p.m. the Soviet flag was lowered and the old Russian tricolor — the white-blue-red banner from before the 1917 revolution — was raised in its place. The empire that built the Gulag was gone; the flag it had buried came back. Source: https://history.state.gov/milestones/1989-1992/collapse-soviet-union

question: Tanks rolled into Moscow on 19 August 1991, sent by hardliners grabbing for power, and Boris Yeltsin, whom Russia had just elected its president, stepped out of the parliament building. What he did next became the symbol of the coup's defeat. What did Yeltsin do?
answer: Climbed on top of one of the tanks to speak to the crowd
choices: Climbed on top of one of the tanks to speak to the crowd
Surrendered himself to the soldiers to spare the city
Ordered Russian jets to bomb the advancing column
Fled Moscow by helicopter to set up a government in exile
context: Yeltsin climbed onto tank No. 110 of the elite Taman Division, outside the Russian White House, and read a defiant decree to the crowd. The photograph went around the world and became the image of the coup collapsing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Soviet_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt

question: Gennady Yanayev, the coup's stand-in president, faced the television cameras after the plotters seized power in August 1991, to show that they were in command. A reporter asked him whether this was a coup. One thing the watching public saw convinced them the plotters had already lost control. What did viewers notice about Yanayev?
answer: His hands would not stop shaking
choices: His hands would not stop shaking
He could not name a single fellow plotter
He admitted on air that Gorbachev was dead
He read his answers from a child's notebook
context: On live television Yanayev's hands trembled visibly and his voice wavered. Soviet viewers read it instantly: the men who claimed to be in charge were terrified. The coup unraveled within days. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/1991-Soviet-coup-attempt

question: Hardline Communist officials tried to overthrow Mikhail Gorbachev in August 1991 to stop his reforms. While their coup lasted, Soviet state television dropped its normal programs and played the same thing over and over, a trick older viewers knew meant the leaders were hiding a crisis. What did it play?
answer: Tchaikovsky's ballet Swan Lake
choices: Tchaikovsky's ballet Swan Lake
The national anthem over a still photo of Lenin
Old newsreels of the Red Army's victory parade
A test pattern with a steady warning tone
context: State TV looped Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake. Russians had seen this trick before during secret crises, so the graceful ballet itself told them something was being concealed at the very top. Source: https://web.viu.ca/davies/H102/CNN.coup.1991.htm

question: Tom Johnson, president of the Cable News Network (CNN), stood by as Mikhail Gorbachev took his seat before the live television cameras on 25 December 1991 to sign his resignation as Soviet president. Gorbachev's Soviet-made pen would not write, so Johnson handed him a replacement. What kind of pen was it?
answer: A Montblanc pen
choices: A Montblanc pen
A Parker pen
A Waterman pen
A gold Kremlin pen
context: Gorbachev asked if the pen was American; told it was European, he used it. The Montblanc — a gift from Johnson's wife — later went on display at the Newseum in Washington, D.C. The USSR ended on a borrowed Western pen. Source: https://www.cjr.org/the_media_today/soviet_union_thirty_years_media.php

question: The eight hardliners who launched the August 1991 coup knew they could not act while Mikhail Gorbachev was free, since he led the country. Gorbachev was on holiday at his seaside dacha in Foros, in Crimea, when they moved against him. What did the plotters do to Gorbachev there?
answer: Held him prisoner in the dacha and cut off all his phone lines
choices: Held him prisoner in the dacha and cut off all his phone lines
Flew him to Moscow and forced him to read their demands on TV
Quietly let him keep governing while they ran things in his name
Put him on trial before a military tribunal in Sevastopol
context: The 'Gang of Eight' — including KGB chief Vladimir Kryuchkov and Defense Minister Dmitry Yazov — sealed Gorbachev inside his own vacation house and severed every communication line, leaving the leader of a superpower cut off from his own country. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Soviet_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt

question: Unarmed Muscovites by the tens of thousands ringed Russia's parliament in August 1991 against the coup's tanks and secret police, a clash that could have become a massacre. In the end the confrontation took lives in just one place, a single road tunnel under the Garden Ring. How many people were killed?
answer: Three
choices: Three
Roughly two hundred
About fifty
More than a thousand
context: Only three young defenders died — Dmitry Komar, Vladimir Usov, and Ilya Krichevsky — crushed trying to stop armored vehicles in the Sadovoye Koltso tunnel. They were the coup's only deaths and were honored as heroes. Source: https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2019/08/19/otd-aug-19-coup-attempt-a66922

question: Boris Yeltsin and two fellow presidents met in secret on 8 December 1991 and signed an accord declaring that the Soviet Union was ceasing to exist. Those men had effectively dissolved a superpower, and they did it not in any capital city but inside one of Europe's last ancient forests. In which forest did they sign it?
answer: The Belovezha Forest of Belarus
choices: The Belovezha Forest of Belarus
The Black Forest of Germany
The Ardennes of Belgium
Sherwood Forest of England
context: Yeltsin (Russia), Kravchuk (Ukraine), and Shushkevich (Belarus) met at the Viskuli lodge deep in the Belovezha Forest — the last primeval woodland on the Belarus–Poland border. Their Belovezha Accords pronounced the Soviet Union finished, signed not in a capital, but among the trees. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belovezha_Accords

question: Mikhail Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president on 25 December 1991, and power passed to Boris Yeltsin, leader of the new Russia. Even before his farewell speech went out on the air, Gorbachev quietly passed one object straight to Yeltsin. What did he hand over?
answer: The briefcase controlling the nuclear missiles
choices: The briefcase controlling the nuclear missiles
The keys to the Kremlin gates
His Communist Party membership card
The Soviet Union's gold reserves
context: Gorbachev handed the nuclear-command briefcase to Yeltsin even earlier than planned, before his resignation speech aired. Control of the world's largest nuclear arsenal changed hands quietly, without a shot. Source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1991/12/25/Gorbachev-resigns/6282693637200/

question: When the August 1991 coup collapsed and arrests began, several of its organizers chose not to face trial. Interior Minister Boris Pugo and Marshal Sergey Akhromeyev, a military adviser who had backed the plot, both met the same end rather than be taken into custody. What did these coup figures do?
answer: They took their own lives
choices: They took their own lives
They fled across the border into China
They begged Gorbachev for a public pardon
They burned the committee's records and vanished
context: Pugo shot himself; Akhromeyev hanged himself in his Kremlin office. They were among three coup-linked figures who died by suicide in the aftermath rather than answer for the failed seizure of power. Source: https://www.rferl.org/a/what-happened-to-the-august-1991-coup-plotters/27933729.html

question: Boris Yeltsin reached for the phone on 8 December 1991, right after he secretly signed the accord that dissolved the Soviet Union. Before he told Gorbachev, still the Soviet president, he called a Cold War rival and said, 'I couldn't even wait ten minutes to call you.' Whom did Yeltsin phone first?
answer: U.S. President George H.W. Bush
choices: U.S. President George H.W. Bush
British Prime Minister John Major
The UN Secretary-General
The leader of Communist China
context: Yeltsin read the agreement aloud to President Bush before telling his own Soviet president it was over. The man who ran the closed empire's chief rival learned of its end first — a small sign of which side had won. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belovezha_Accords

question: Moscow paid for its Cold War arms race largely by selling oil abroad. Then, in September 1985, one country dropped its production limits and pumped roughly five times as much; world oil prices crashed, and the Soviet Union was starved of the hard currency it needed. Which country flooded the oil market?
answer: Saudi Arabia
choices: Saudi Arabia
The United States
Iran
Norway
context: When Saudi Arabia opened the taps and oil prices collapsed, the oil-export-dependent USSR lost the revenue that kept its military competitive and its shelves stocked. Many argue economic exhaustion, not any battle, broke the closed system. Source: https://www.energycrisis.com/reynolds/SovietDecline.htm

question: Lookouts on Columbus's ships sighted an island before dawn on 12 October 1492. Columbus was sure he had sailed all the way to the Indies, near Asia. Because of that belief, what did he call the people who lived there?
answer: Indians
choices: Indians
Asians
Saracens
Cathayans
context: Columbus named the island San Salvador; its Taino people called it Guanahani. He had not reached the Indies at all, but the name 'Indians' stuck for the peoples of the Americas. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus

question: Columbus's sailors, heading west in search of a shortcut to Asia, had been out of sight of land for weeks in September 1492 when their ships entered a strange stretch of ocean carpeted with floating brown weed. What did the frightened men believe the weed would do?
answer: Trap their ships and drag them to the bottom
choices: Trap their ships and drag them to the bottom
Poison anyone who touched the water
Hide sea monsters waiting beneath it
Mark the edge of the flat world
context: This was the Sargasso Sea, named for its floating sargassum weed. The crew feared being snared in shallows and sunk -- but the weed is far too flimsy to snag any vessel. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/the-sargasso-sea-62459984/

question: The men aboard Christopher Columbus's three small ships were on the edge of mutiny by 10 October 1492, after more than a month sailing west across the empty Atlantic with no land in sight. To calm them, what bargain did Columbus strike?
answer: He would turn back if no land appeared within three days
choices: He would turn back if no land appeared within three days
He would share all the gold equally with the crew
He would free any sailor who wished to leave at the next port
He would sail north toward known fishing waters
context: It was a desperate gamble -- and it paid off. Just two days later, on October 12, the lookouts sighted land. Source: https://www.the-map-as-history.com/Age-of-Discovery/christopher-columbus-first-voyage-1492-1493

question: Rodrigo de Triana, a sailor on the Pinta, was the first to cry 'Tierra!', 'Land!', at about 2 a.m. on 12 October 1492. Ferdinand and Isabella had promised a yearly pension of 10,000 maravedis to whoever first sighted land, yet Rodrigo never received it. Why not?
answer: Columbus claimed the reward for himself, saying he had seen a dim light the night before
choices: Columbus claimed the reward for himself, saying he had seen a dim light the night before
The crown ruled that a sighting at night did not count
Rodrigo drowned before the ships returned to Spain
The captain of the Pinta took the prize instead
context: The promised reward was 10,000 maravedis a year (plus a silk doublet). Columbus insisted he had glimpsed a faint light the previous evening, and took the pension himself. Rodrigo de Triana got nothing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_de_Triana

question: Columbus handed his steel swords to the Taino to look at when he first met them on the islands, and he wrote down in his journal what happened next. What did the Taino do with the swords?
answer: They grasped the swords by the blades and cut themselves
choices: They grasped the swords by the blades and cut themselves
They bowed down and worshipped the swords
They refused to touch the cold iron
They traded gold for them on the spot
context: Columbus wrote on October 12, 1492: 'I showed them swords, which they grasped by the blades, and cut themselves.' The Taino had no metal weapons of their own. He also noted some wore little bits of gold in their noses. Source: https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/columbus1.asp

question: Samuel Eliot Morison, a historian, called one famous scene of the Columbus story pure moonshine: Columbus bravely arguing that the Earth was round while everyone else feared it was flat. Learned Europeans had known the Earth was a sphere since ancient Greece. Where did the flat-Earth showdown come from?
answer: An American author, Washington Irving, invented it in an 1828 biography
choices: An American author, Washington Irving, invented it in an 1828 biography
Spanish priests spread it to discredit Columbus's rivals
Columbus himself put it in his own journal
It was carved on a monument built centuries later
context: Washington Irving dramatized a flat-Earth showdown in his 1828 life of Columbus. Historian Samuel Eliot Morison called that scene 'pure moonshine.' Source: https://www.history.com/articles/christopher-columbus-never-set-out-to-prove-the-earth-was-round

question: A storm off the Azores nearly sank the Nina in February 1493, as Columbus sailed home with news of his discovery. Afraid the news would die with him, he wanted word of it to reach land even if he drowned. What did he do?
answer: Sealed a report in a waxed cask and threw it into the sea
choices: Sealed a report in a waxed cask and threw it into the sea
Carved his account into the ship's mast
Sent a sailor ahead in a small boat
Burned a signal to passing ships
context: He wrapped the report in waxed cloth, sealed it in a cask, and cast it overboard, hoping it might drift ashore. The crew survived the storm, and Columbus delivered the news himself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus's_letter_on_the_first_voyage

question: Columbus linked the Old World and the Americas, and with them two worlds of germs: smallpox, measles and flu struck native peoples who had no immunity to them at all. In the century and a half after 1492, roughly what share of those peoples died?
answer: Roughly 80 to 95 percent
choices: Roughly 80 to 95 percent
Roughly 10 to 15 percent
Roughly 25 to 30 percent
Roughly 50 to 55 percent
context: Historians estimate that disease killed about 80-95% of the Americas' Indigenous population in the 150 years after 1492 -- a demographic catastrophe of tens of millions of deaths, driven by germs against which they had no defense. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/columbian-exchange-impact-diseases

question: On Hispaniola, which he ruled in 1495, Columbus ordered every Taino older than fourteen to bring him a set amount of gold every three months. The island had little gold, and those who failed to pay ran into the mountains. Bartolome de las Casas, a priest, later wrote down what came next. What did Columbus's men do when they hunted the runaways down?
answer: slaughtered them like sheep penned in a corral
choices: slaughtered them like sheep penned in a corral
marched them in chains to the gold mines
burned every village they had fled from
shipped them across the sea to be sold
context: Las Casas wrote that to crush the resistance Columbus's men formed squadrons, pursued the fleeing Taino, and 'pitilessly slaughtered everyone like sheep in a corral.' (The popular 'hands cut off for a missing token' tale is not in Las Casas's account of the tribute and is judged a later embellishment.) Source: Las Casas, History of the Indies, quoted at Zinn Education Project, 'Columbus: No Monuments for Murderers.'

question: Columbus knelt on a Caribbean beach on 12 October 1492, after five weeks at sea, and claimed the island for the monarchs of Spain. The Lucayan people who lived there called it Guanahani. What new name did Columbus give it?
answer: San Salvador
choices: San Salvador
Hispaniola
Fernandina
Isabela
context: San Salvador means 'Holy Savior.' Hispaniola, Fernandina, and Isabela were OTHER islands Columbus also named on the voyage (Isabela and Fernandina after Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand). Source: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/columbus-makes-landfall-caribbean/

question: Columbus met the Taino on their Caribbean islands in 1492, and several of their words later passed into English, among them names for things from their own world. Which English word for a kind of storm did the Taino give the language?
answer: hurricane
choices: hurricane
tornado
monsoon
blizzard
context: Several Taino words crossed into English: canoe, hammock, barbecue, tobacco, and hurricane. Their chiefs were called caciques. (Tornado, monsoon, and blizzard come from other languages.) Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/who-were-taino-original-inhabitants-columbus-island-73824867/

question: Columbus's sailors stepped ashore in October 1492 and met the Taino, who offered them parrots, balls of cotton thread and food. Neither side could speak the other's language, so gifts did the talking. What did Columbus hand the Taino in return?
answer: red caps and glass beads
choices: red caps and glass beads
gold coins and silver
muskets and gunpowder
silk robes and spices
context: Columbus handed out red caps, glass beads, and small trinkets. He noticed some of the Taino wore tiny pieces of gold in their noses, which set his mind on finding more. Source: https://www.americanyawp.com/reader/the-new-world/journal-of-christopher-columbus/

question: A cabin boy held the steering tiller late on 24 December 1492 while Columbus slept, and his flagship drifted onto a reef off Hispaniola and could not be saved. Columbus used her timbers to build a little fort and left 39 men behind in it. What did he name the fort?
answer: La Navidad
choices: La Navidad
San Salvador
La Isabela
Santo Domingo
context: La Navidad means 'Christmas' in Spanish: Columbus named the fort for the night the flagship wrecked. It was the first European settlement in the Americas, and the garrison left there did not survive.

question: Columbus sailed west to reach Asia, and when he landed on the Caribbean islands he was certain he had done it: he had arrived, he believed, in the Indies, the rich lands near China and Japan. In truth he had found two continents no European knew. How long did Columbus go on believing he had reached Asia?
answer: for the rest of his life
choices: for the rest of his life
for only about a year
until his second voyage returned
until he reached the mainland coast
context: Columbus never realized what he had found. He kept insisting he had touched the edge of Asia right up to his death in 1506. Source: https://www.arcadiapublishing.com/blogs/news/columbus-day-a-history-of-myth-misunderstanding-and-indigenous-perspectives

question: Five weeks out of sight of land on the open Atlantic, Columbus feared his men would panic, so on the crossing he secretly kept two logbooks at once, one of them to read aloud to the crew. How did that public logbook differ from his private one?
answer: it listed shorter daily distances to hide how far they had sailed
choices: it listed shorter daily distances to hide how far they had sailed
it was written in a code only Columbus could read
it left out the islands they had passed
it recorded the sailors' daily complaints
context: Columbus read the crew the smaller, fake distances so they would not panic. The irony: his 'fake' shorter numbers turned out to be closer to the true distance than the 'real' ones in his private log. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/history-famous-people/columbuss-captains-log-0017037

question: By his reckoning, Columbus expected Japan to lie only about 3,000 miles beyond his starting islands; the real distance is more than 7,000. Learned critics, who knew as well as he did that the Earth is round, doubted his figures, and they were right. What basic mistake had Columbus made?
answer: he had badly underestimated the size of the Earth
choices: he had badly underestimated the size of the Earth
he had been handed a faulty compass
he had ignored the ocean's trade winds
he had miscounted the days at sea
context: Columbus made two errors at once: he undercounted Earth's circumference by about 25 percent (using the wrong 'mile'), and, following Marco Polo and Toscanelli, he overestimated how far east Asia stretched. Together they made the world seem far smaller than it is. The doubters were correct: Asia really was too far to reach.

question: Columbus's 39 men stayed behind in the little fort built from his wrecked flagship when he sailed home early in 1493. He came back later that year to see how they had fared. What did he find?
answer: the fort burned to the ground and all 39 men dead
choices: the fort burned to the ground and all 39 men dead
the men thriving in a growing town
the men gone, having sailed home without him
the fort empty but standing undamaged
context: The men Columbus left had abused the local Taino, who struck back; the chief Caonabo is blamed in the accounts. The first European settlement in the Americas lasted less than a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Navidad

question: Hunting for gold on the island of Hispaniola, Columbus set up a harsh tribute system. Every Taino aged about fourteen and older was ordered to hand over a set amount of gold every three months, or face punishment. How much gold was each person forced to deliver each time?
answer: a thimbleful, enough to fill a small hawk's-bell
choices: a thimbleful, enough to fill a small hawk's-bell
a heavy leather sackful of nuggets
a fist-sized golden lump
a wagon-load shared by each village
context: Even a hawk's-bell of gold dust was an impossible quota, because there was very little gold to be found; those who failed were brutally punished. The eyewitness friar Bartolome de las Casas later documented and condemned the cruelty, and the Taino population collapsed catastrophically. Source: https://latinamericanstudies.org/taino/taino-conquest.htm

question: In his journal for 14 October 1492, two days after the Taino had welcomed him ashore, Columbus wrote that they 'should be good servants' and could 'easily be made Christians.' Then he set down how many men it would take to subjugate them all. How many did he say?
answer: fifty men
choices: fifty men
two hundred men
a thousand men
five thousand men
context: On October 14, 1492, Columbus wrote that 'with fifty men they can all be subjugated and made to do what is required of them.' On his very first day he had already seized several Taino to carry back to Spain as captives. Source: https://www.americanyawp.com/reader/the-new-world/journal-of-christopher-columbus/

question: Commodore Matthew Perry led four American warships into Edo Bay, the harbour of Japan's capital, on 8 July 1853. Their hulls were painted black, and their funnels poured black smoke from burning coal. The astonished Japanese gave the strange vessels a nickname. What did they call them?
answer: The Black Ships
choices: The Black Ships
The Iron Whales
The Smoke Dragons
The Storm Riders
context: 'Kurofune' -- the Black Ships -- named for their black-painted hulls and the black coal smoke from their funnels. Japanese who had never seen ships move without sails were stunned. (history.state.gov/milestones/1830-1860/opening-to-japan; nippon.com, Black Ships Shock)

question: Japanese watchers crowded the shore in 1853 as two of Commodore Perry's warships came in, the coal-burning steam frigates Susquehanna and Mississippi, which needed no sails at all. To them the two ships seemed to work sorcery. What did the steamships do that no sailing vessel could?
answer: Sailed straight into the wind
choices: Sailed straight into the wind
Floated without touching water
Glowed red after dark
Split apart and rejoined
context: The steam frigates could sail directly INTO the wind, towing the smaller sloops Saratoga and Plymouth behind them. To people who had only ever seen wind-driven ships, vessels moving against the wind looked like magic. (japantoday.com; ebsco.com Perry Expedition)

question: Commodore Perry came back to Japan in February 1854 for an answer to America's demands, and he brought gifts to dazzle his hosts. Among them was a little working steam locomotive that circled a loop of track near Yokohama. Its car 'could hardly carry a child of six.' How did dignified Japanese officials ride it?
answer: They climbed onto the roof and rode it
choices: They climbed onto the roof and rode it
They harnessed it to a horse
They carried it on their shoulders
They watched and refused to board
context: It was a quarter-scale Norris Works locomotive, the first railway ever built in the Far East. Officials rode around perched on the ROOF with their ceremonial robes flying in the wind. (nippon.com/en/nipponblog/m00123; library.brown.edu/cds/perry)

question: The Tokugawa shoguns held Japan almost shut against the world for about 250 years before Commodore Perry came, under a policy called sakoku, the closed country. A Japanese who left could be put to death, and nearly every foreigner was barred. One small crack stayed open: a single foreign trading post. Who ran it?
answer: Dutch merchants on the island of Dejima
choices: Dutch merchants on the island of Dejima
Portuguese priests in Edo harbor
Chinese envoys at Kyoto
Russian whalers near Hokkaido
context: Under sakoku, only a small Dutch trading post on the artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki was permitted. Perry's four ships cracked that 250-year isolation open. (history.state.gov; ebsco.com Perry Expedition)

question: The Japanese turned the panic over Commodore Perry's warships into satire. One comic poem, a kyoka, seemed only to grumble about a potent tea named Jokisen. But every word of it carried a hidden second meaning. What was the poem secretly saying?
answer: Four steamships rob the country of its peaceful sleep
choices: Four steamships rob the country of its peaceful sleep
The shogun has secretly fled the capital
Foreign tea will poison the people
The emperor alone can save Japan
context: 'Jokisen' means both the tea and 'steamships'; 'four cups' also means 'four vessels.' So the poem secretly reads: the steamships shatter the peaceful sleep of the Pacific -- just four boats rob us of sleep. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Ships; japanesewiki.com/culture/Jokisen)

question: Colonists in taverns heard Common Sense read aloud after Thomas Paine, an English corset-maker, published his fiery pamphlet of barely fifty pages in January 1776. Only about 2.5 million people lived in the colonies. By the end of the war, by Paine's own count, roughly how many copies were in circulation?
answer: About 500,000 copies
choices: About 12,000 copies
About 60,000 copies
About 200,000 copies
About 500,000 copies
context: By the end of the Revolution roughly 500,000 copies were said to be in circulation — a half-million copies of a ~50-page pamphlet in a population of only ~2.5 million, read aloud in taverns to people who couldn't read it themselves. Honest caveat: the famous '120,000 copies in three months' and '500,000' figures come from Paine himself; almost no print or sales records survive, and Paine had every reason to inflate his impact, so historians treat these as claims, not verified counts. Sources: American Battlefield Trust, battlefields.org/learn/articles/common-sense; ushistory.org/us/10f.asp; Journal of the American Revolution, 'Thomas Paine's Inflated Numbers,' allthingsliberty.com/2013/03/thomas-paines-inflated-numbers/

question: Thomas Paine would not call George III the king of America. In Common Sense he wrote that America's true king reigned in heaven and did no harm to mankind, unlike the man who ruled the colonies from across the ocean. Few writers of 1776 dared to mock a reigning monarch in print. What scornful name did Paine give George III?
answer: the Royal Brute of Britain
choices: the Tyrant of the Thames
the Crowned Beast of London
the Pharaoh of England
the Royal Brute of Britain
context: Paine wrote: 'where, says some, is the King of America? I'll tell you, friend, he reigns above... and doth not make havoc of mankind like the Royal Brute of Britain.' He had landed in Philadelphia barely 14 months earlier and published the pamphlet anonymously, signed only 'Written by an Englishman' — yet branding the actual reigning king a 'Royal Brute' helped turn fence-sitting colonists toward independence. Source: ushistory.org primary text, ushistory.org/paine/commonsense/sense4.htm; American Battlefield Trust, battlefields.org/learn/articles/common-sense

question: Kong Qiu taught in Lu, a small Chinese state, around 500 BC, and his own people called him Kongzi or Kong Fuzi, Master Kong. The Latin name Confucius, by which the West came to know him, was one his people never used. Who invented it?
answer: European Jesuit missionaries
choices: European Jesuit missionaries
His earliest Chinese students
Travelers on the Silk Road
Scribes in the emperor's court
context: Jesuit missionaries first translated his works into Latin, published in Paris in 1687 as 'Confucius Sinarum Philosophus' -- "Confucius, the Philosopher of China." The name the whole English-speaking world uses is a 17th-century European invention. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucius; plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/.

question: The students of Confucius gathered the sayings they remembered into the Analects after he died, for he wrote no book of his own. They began its short passages again and again with the same three words. What were those words?
answer: "The Master said"
choices: "The Master said"
"Long ago it happened"
"Heaven has decreed"
"Hear and obey"
context: The Analects (Lunyu) is built of short fragments, many opening with the formula "The Master said," taking shape within about a century after Confucius died. It is a collection of remembered conversations, not a book he authored. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/.

question: Zigong, a student of Confucius, once asked him for a single word a person could live by for a whole lifetime. Confucius gave him one, reciprocity, and then the rule that goes with it, centuries before the famous Western versions. What was the rule?
answer: "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others"
choices: "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others"
"Repay every kindness, and answer every injury with justice"
"Honor your father and your mother above all other people"
"Speak only the truth, even when the truth will cost you"
context: Analects 15.23 (James Legge translation). The word Confucius gave was shu -- reciprocity. This negative form of the Golden Rule predates its famous Western phrasings by centuries. Source: en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Chinese_Classics/Volume_1/Confucian_Analects/XV.

question: Yan Hui, the student Confucius loved best, lived in a mean, narrow lane, yet he was so cheerful that his teacher cried 'Admirable indeed!' To show how little the young man had, Confucius named the only two things at his meals. What were they?
answer: A bamboo dish of rice and a gourd of water
choices: A bamboo dish of rice and a gourd of water
A wooden bowl and a worn straw mat
A single candle and a borrowed book
A clay cup and a handful of millet
context: Analects 6.9/6.11 (Legge): "With a single bamboo dish of rice, a single gourd dish of drink... he did not allow his joy to be affected by it." Confucius prized Yan Hui because poverty never touched his contentment. Source: en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Chinese_Classics/Volume_1/Confucian_Analects/VI.

question: Confucius never lost his temper, as his students remembered him in the Analects, and he taught with calm and measure. But when Yan Hui, his favourite student, died young, his composure broke completely. What did the grieving teacher cry out?
answer: "Heaven is destroying me! Heaven is destroying me!"
choices: "Heaven is destroying me! Heaven is destroying me!"
"The world has gone dark and will not brighten"
"I have failed him, and the fault is mine alone"
"Let no one speak to me of joy again"
context: Analects 11.8 (Legge). When disciples said his grief was excessive, he answered, "If I am not to mourn bitterly for this man, for whom should I mourn?" (11.9). It is the most emotionally raw moment in the entire Analects. Source: en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Chinese_Classics/Volume_1/Confucian_Analects/XI.

question: Confucius took to the road around 498 BC and wandered for some fourteen years through the states of Wei, Song, Chen and Chu, meeting mostly indifference. By an old Chinese belief, a truly virtuous man was bound to win power, and Confucius had every gift for governing well. What was he searching for all that time?
answer: A ruler who would put his ideas into practice
choices: A ruler who would put his ideas into practice
A quiet province in which to retire
An army strong enough to seize the throne
A library that held the lost ancient texts
context: From about 498 BCE Confucius wandered, hoping to find a prince who would govern by virtue. He became the tragic counterexample to his own civilization's theory -- worthy to rule, yet dying with no ruler willing to use him. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/.

question: Confucius idolized the Duke of Zhou, a sage who lived centuries before him, and he modeled himself on the great rulers of the past. He once summed up his whole life's work in a single line about the old wisdom and anything new. What did he say?
answer: "I transmit but do not create"
choices: "I transmit but do not create"
"I create what the ancients only dreamed"
"I both transmit and create anew"
"I correct what the ancients got wrong"
context: Analects 7.1: "I transmit but do not create; I am faithful to and love the ancients." He saw himself as a conservator of older wisdom, not an original genius -- and in old age lamented, "It has been so long since I dreamed of the Duke of Zhou" (7.5). Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/.

question: Duke Jing of Qi asked Confucius, the wandering teacher, how a country should be governed. Confucius answered with one short phrase built on repetition. His whole idea was that a country stays whole only if everyone does the duty of his own place. What was his answer?
answer: "Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son"
choices: "Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son"
"Let the strong serve the strong, the wise teach the wise, the rich feed the rich, the poor obey the poor"
"Let the soldier be a farmer, the farmer a scholar, the scholar a priest, the priest a king"
"Let the wise rule the strong, the strong guard the rich, the rich feed the poor, the poor serve them all"
context: Analects 12.11. This expresses what Confucius called the "rectification of names" (zhengming): if names are not made to match reality, language goes wrong, and then nothing -- rites, music, punishments -- comes out right (13.3). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectification_of_names.

question: Confucius held one virtue above all the rest, ren, and he said a gentleman would sooner die than betray it. Asked for a definition of this highest virtue, he gave a strikingly plain answer. What did Confucius say ren is?
answer: Caring for others
choices: Caring for others
Mastering the old texts
Obeying every ritual
Serving the ruler
context: Analects 12.22 defines ren simply as "caring for others"; 15.9 says a gentleman would rather die than compromise it. Its root, Confucius taught, is filial piety -- devotion to one's parents and family -- the soil from which all other goodness grows (1.2). Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/.

question: Confucius once summed up his entire life as a ladder of moral growth: at fifteen he set his heart on learning, at thirty he took his stand, at forty he was free of doubt. Describing his seventieth year, he claimed a freedom he had spent a lifetime earning. What could he finally do at seventy?
answer: Follow his heart's desire without ever overstepping what was right
choices: Follow his heart's desire without ever overstepping what was right
Recite every one of the ancient classics from memory
Persuade any ruler in the land to follow his counsel
Live in complete solitude without longing for company
context: Analects 2.4 (Annping Chin translation): "At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired without overstepping the line." After a lifetime of discipline, doing right had become effortless -- desire and duty finally one. Source: thetedkarchive.com/library/confucius-annping-chin-the-analects.

question: Wu, the Han emperor, made the teaching of Confucius the official doctrine of the empire in 136 BC, long after Confucius had died a disappointed man. His words became the core of one institution that chose China's officials right up until 1905. What was it?
answer: The imperial civil-service examination
choices: The imperial civil-service examination
A hereditary council of noble families
The personal court of the reigning emperor
A standing army of scholar-generals
context: Urged on by the scholar Dong Zhongshu, Emperor Wu established a state university for the Confucian Classics, which became the basis of the exam every aspiring official had to pass -- abolished only in 1905. The failed wanderer's words ran the empire for two thousand years, and are why education is still so revered in Chinese culture. Source: britannica.com/topic/Chinese-examination-system.

question: Mencius, a follower of Confucius, set out the tradition's Five Relationships in full, beginning with ruler and subject. Subjects owed their ruler loyalty, but the bond was not meant to run one way only. What did the ruler owe his people in return?
answer: Genuine care and good government
choices: Genuine care and good government
Firm command and nothing more
Only what Heaven required of him
Strict laws and harsh punishment
context: The bonds are reciprocal, not one-way: a ruler owes real duties to his subjects just as they owe loyalty to him. The clean five-fold list (the wulun) was actually formulated by Mencius, a follower born about 150 years after Confucius died, who paired each bond with its virtue -- affection, righteousness, distinction, proper order, and trustworthiness (Mencius 3A:4). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Fundamental_Bonds_and_Five_Constant_Virtues.

question: An aide grew alarmed as Constantine paced out the walls of his new Roman capital on the Bosporus, the legend says, trailing a spear to mark the ground and walking on far past all sense. At last the aide asked how far the emperor meant to go. What did Constantine answer?
answer: "I shall go on until He who leads me stops."
choices: "I shall go on until He who leads me stops."
"The walls of Rome were never wide enough."
"A city is measured by its emperor, not its men."
"Let no enemy ever find a gate to enter."
context: As he walked, Constantine dragged a spear along the ground to mark the boundary, and said an unseen guide was leading him onward. The city he founded in 330 AD, on the site of the old Greek town of Byzantium, he declared 'New Rome' (Nova Roma) -- though everyone soon called it Constantinople, 'the city of Constantine.' [Legend.] Source: OUPblog 'Constantine dedicates Constantinople' + EBSCO Research Starter 'Constantinople Is Founded'.

question: The Greeks had cast a bronze trophy from captured Persian shields after their victory at Plataea in 479 BC. Centuries later Constantine set it up in the Hippodrome of Constantinople, the great chariot-racing track, among the treasures he stripped from across the empire. What did the trophy show?
answer: Three intertwined snakes
choices: Three intertwined snakes
A laurel-crowned emperor on horseback
A pair of wrestling athletes
A winged goddess of victory
context: The Serpent Column had stood for over 800 years at the temple of Apollo at Delphi before Constantine moved it. Part of it still stands in Istanbul's Hippodrome today. Source: EBSCO Research Starter 'Constantinople Is Founded'.

question: Constantine raised a towering column of purple porphyry stone in the forum of Constantinople, the new capital he dedicated in 330. On top he set a bronze statue of himself, made over in the image of a god and crowned with a ring of metal rays. Which god was the emperor's statue made over as?
answer: The sun-god Apollo, or Helios
choices: The sun-god Apollo, or Helios
The sky-father Jupiter
The war-god Mars
The messenger Mercury
context: The column rose roughly 40 meters from seven colossal drums of porphyry, each weighing about 60 tons and banded with carved laurel wreaths. Legend held that the statue's sun-rays were forged from the nails of Christ's crucifixion. Source: TheByzantineLegacy 'Column of Constantine'.

question: Constantine was marching on Rome in 312 when, as he later told the historian Eusebius, he looked up about midday and saw a cross of light above the sun, with words that his whole army saw too. What did the words command?
answer: By this sign, conquer
choices: By this sign, conquer
Rome favors the bold
Fear no mortal foe
March on to glory
context: In Greek 'En toutoi nika,' in Latin 'In hoc signo vinces' -- 'in this sign you will conquer.' Eusebius says he heard the story from the emperor himself. (Eusebius, Life of Constantine I.28)

question: Constantine had his soldiers paint a sign on their shields before the battle at the Milvian Bridge in 312, after the vision he said he had seen on the march to Rome. The sign was a monogram of two overlapping Greek letters, chi and rho, the opening of a single name. Whose name did it begin?
answer: Christ
choices: Christ
Constantine
Caesar
Apollo
context: The Chi-Rho overlaps X (chi) and P (rho), the first two letters of the Greek 'CHRISTOS' -- so the soldiers carried the start of Christ's name into battle. (Wikipedia 'Chi Rho')

question: The army of Maxentius broke at the Milvian Bridge in 312, in his fight with Constantine for the Roman Empire, and it fled over a makeshift bridge of boats on the Tiber, which gave way beneath it. How did Maxentius himself die?
answer: He drowned in the Tiber under his armor
choices: He drowned in the Tiber under his armor
He was cut down in a last charge
He escaped to Rome and was never seen
He fell on his own sword in defeat
context: Weighed down by his armor, Maxentius drowned; his body was later pulled from the Tiber and beheaded. (Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors 44; Wikipedia 'Battle of the Milvian Bridge')

question: Eusebius reports that after his vision Constantine ordered a new battle standard. It was a tall gilded spear crossed by a bar and topped with a jewelled golden wreath around the Chi-Rho, and from it hung a banner showing the emperor with his children. What is this standard called?
answer: the labarum
choices: the labarum
the aquila
the vexillum
the signum
context: The labarum became the Christian battle-standard of the later Roman army. (Eusebius, Life of Constantine I.31)

question: Maxentius, inside Rome, turned to the Sibylline Books as Constantine marched on the city in 312. They foretold that on 28 October an enemy of the Romans would perish. Certain it meant Constantine, what fateful choice did Maxentius make?
answer: He left the safety of Rome's walls to give battle
choices: He left the safety of Rome's walls to give battle
He sealed the gates and prepared for a siege
He sent envoys to make peace with Constantine
He sacrificed to the gods and waited in Rome
context: The grim irony: it was Maxentius himself, not Constantine, who perished that 28 October. (Wikipedia 'Battle of the Milvian Bridge'; ancient-origins.net Ponte Milvio)

question: Theodoret the historian tells how Constantine came face to face at Nicaea with bishops whom the persecutors had blinded and maimed, and greeted these scarred confessors in a way no one expected of a Roman emperor. What does the story say Constantine did?
answer: He kissed their wounds and empty eye-sockets
choices: He kissed their wounds and empty eye-sockets
He knelt and washed their feet
He gave each of them a province
He had their torturers hunted down
context: Rufinus says Constantine especially honored Bishop Paphnutius of Egypt, whose right eye had been gouged out, kissing the scarred socket. Recorded as pious tradition. (Theodoret and Rufinus; Wikipedia 'Paphnutius of Thebes')  (Legend.)

question: Nicholas of Myra, the bishop who became Santa Claus, grew angry at the priest Arius during the Council of Nicaea, or so a legend says. The tale first appeared about a thousand years later, and the council's lists did not include Nicholas. What does the legend say Nicholas did to Arius?
answer: He struck Arius across the face
choices: He struck Arius across the face
He shouted Arius down before all
He tore Arius's books to pieces
He turned his back on Arius
context: The legend says the bishops jailed Nicholas and stripped his vestments, but a vision of Jesus and Mary restored them. It first appears about 1,000 years later -- legend, not history. (St. Nicholas Center 'Bishop Nicholas Loses His Cool')

question: Arius, a priest from Alexandria in Egypt, taught something about the Son of God that outraged the bishops of the Church. Constantine summoned them to Nicaea in 325 to settle the fierce quarrel. What did Arius claim about the Son?
answer: There was a time when the Son was not
choices: There was a time when the Son was not
The Son was lesser than the Father in glory
The Son had never truly suffered or died
The Son would return to earth within a year
context: Arius held the Son was created, not eternal. The council rejected this and declared the Son 'homoousios' -- of one substance with the Father. (Britannica 'First Council of Nicaea')

question: Constantine gathered the bishops at Nicaea in 325, and fewer than 318 of them signed the council's lists. Yet later Christians named it the Council of 318 Fathers, treasuring that exact number because it echoed something famous. What did the number 318 echo?
answer: The 318 servants Abraham led to rescue Lot
choices: The 318 servants Abraham led to rescue Lot
The 318 days the council sat in debate
The 318 cities that sent their bishops
The 318 psalms sung when it closed
context: In Genesis 14, Abraham leads 318 servants to rescue his nephew Lot -- a number later writers cherished, even though the actual attendance was nearer 250 to 318. (Wikipedia 'First Council of Nicaea')

question: Constantine favoured the Christians from his victory over Maxentius in 312 onward, and in 325 he summoned the great council of bishops at Nicaea. When the emperor lay dying in 337, he was at last baptized, by Bishop Eusebius of Nicomedia. Which movement did that bishop follow?
answer: The Arian movement
choices: The Arian movement
The Donatist movement
The Montanist movement
The Manichaean movement
context: Constantine was baptized by an Arian -- the very party Nicaea had condemned -- and is said to have died wearing the white robes of the newly baptized. He had delayed baptism to wash away a lifetime of sin at the end. (Wikipedia 'Eusebius of Nicomedia')

question: Constantine had beaten Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge, and in 315 the Roman Senate dedicated an arch to his victory, carving on it that he had won 'by divine inspiration.' When it came to naming that divinity, what did the inscription pointedly do?
answer: It never said which god
choices: It never said which god
It named the sun-god Sol
It credited Constantine's genius alone
It thanked the Roman Senate itself
context: The wording left it ambiguous between the Christian God and the pagan gods -- a careful political tightrope. (Wikipedia 'Arch of Constantine'; World History Encyclopedia)

question: Eusebius and Lactantius, the two earliest writers on Constantine's heavenly sign, told the story in two different ways. Eusebius described a blazing cross in the daytime sky, seen by the entire army. Lactantius, who wrote earlier, told it otherwise. How does Lactantius's version differ?
answer: He says it came to Constantine in a dream
choices: He says it came to Constantine in a dream
He says it appeared on the enemy's shields
He says it was seen only after the battle
He says no sign appeared at all
context: Lactantius says Constantine was warned in a dream to mark the 'heavenly sign of God' on his soldiers' shields. The two oldest sources thus disagree on whether it was a daytime sky-vision or a dream. (Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors 44)

question: Benjamin Franklin, 81 years old, could barely walk the summer the Constitutional Convention met. Gout kept him from covering even the short way from his house to the State House, so every day he rode there in a sedan chair. Who carried it?
answer: Four prisoners from the city jail
choices: Four prisoners from the city jail
Four soldiers of the city guard
Four servants from his own household
Four porters hired down at the docks
context: Four inmates from the Walnut Street jail bore Franklin's sedan chair on their shoulders each day. The chair itself had been brought back from Paris. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Benjamin Franklin at the Constitutional Convention'; Mental Floss, '21 Things You May Not Know About the U.S. Constitution.'

question: Delegates from twelve states sweated through the Philadelphia summer of 1787 in heavy wool suits, drafting a new plan of government for the United States. The delegates wanted not one word of their debates to get out. What drastic thing did they do to their meeting room?
answer: Nailed the meeting-room windows shut
choices: Nailed the meeting-room windows shut
Hung heavy curtains over the windows
Met only after dark each night
Moved down into a windowless cellar
context: With the windows nailed shut and sentries posted at the doors, the delegates roasted all summer rather than risk a single word leaking out. Source: Gilder Lehrman Institute, 'Philadelphia and the Constitutional Convention Heat Up'; National Archives, 'How Did It Happen.'

question: Benjamin Franklin walked out of the State House as the Constitutional Convention ended. A woman named Elizabeth Powel stopped him and asked what kind of government the delegates had made, a republic or a monarchy. James McHenry's diary records Franklin's answer. What was it?
answer: A republic, if you can keep it
choices: A republic, if you can keep it
A monarchy, if the people allow it
A democracy, if the states agree
A new empire, if it can be defended
context: The exchange survives only in McHenry's diary, so it is remembered as legend rather than proven word-for-word — but 'A republic, if you can keep it' became one of the most quoted lines in American history. Source: National Park Service, 'September 17, 1787' (citing McHenry's diary).

question: Jonathan Dayton of New Jersey put his name to the Constitution in 1787 and became the youngest man ever to sign it. Benjamin Franklin, the oldest delegate, was 81, and the average delegate was only about 42. How old was Dayton?
answer: Just 26 years old
choices: Just 26 years old
Just 31 years old
Just 35 years old
Just 38 years old
context: Jonathan Dayton was only 26 when he signed — a full 55 years younger than Franklin. Source: Constitution Center, 'Jonathan Dayton'; Britannica, 'Jonathan Dayton.'

question: Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth of Connecticut faced a convention stuck fast in July 1787. The big states wanted seats in Congress handed out by population, so a state with more people got more votes; the small states demanded an equal vote for every state, whatever its size. What was the two men's fix?
answer: Two houses: one by population, one equal per state
choices: Two houses: one by population, one equal per state
One house: each state casting a single equal vote
One house: seats split by each state's wealth
One council: state governors sharing a rotating chair
context: The Great (Connecticut) Compromise created a two-chamber Congress: a House of Representatives by population and a Senate giving every state two votes regardless of size. That bicameral split is exactly how Congress still works. Source: Britannica, 'Connecticut Compromise'; Connecticut History, 'The Connecticut Compromise.'

question: Rhode Island alone refused to send a single delegate to Philadelphia in 1787, so suspicious of a strong central government that it boycotted the whole meeting. Its opponents threw an insulting nickname at it. What did they call Rhode Island?
answer: Rogue Island
choices: Rogue Island
the Renegade State
Traitor's Cove
Fool's Harbor
context: Mocked as 'Rogue Island,' Rhode Island held out the longest of all — it became the last of the thirteen states to ratify the Constitution on May 29, 1790, more than a year after Washington was already president. Source: 'Constitutional Convention (United States)' — Wikipedia; RISD Constitution Day.

question: Patrick Henry, the Virginian who had once declared 'Give me liberty, or give me death,' flatly refused in 1787 to go to the secret Philadelphia meeting that became the Constitutional Convention, though he had been picked to represent his state. What memorable reason did he give for staying home?
answer: He smelt a rat in Philadelphia
choices: He smelt a rat in Philadelphia
He had no time to leave Virginia
He could not afford the long journey
He thought the meeting would fail
context: Henry declared he 'smelt a rat in Philadelphia, tending toward the monarchy.' He later became a leading voice against ratifying the Constitution. Source: History.com, '7 Things You May Not Know About the Constitutional Convention.'

question: Gouverneur Morris of Pennsylvania, who spoke more often than any other delegate and did it on a wooden peg leg, took up the Constitution's first draft. It opened by listing the states one by one: 'We the People of the States of New Hampshire, Massachusetts...' and so on. Morris turned that clunky opening into a single ringing phrase. What did he write?
answer: We the People of the United States
choices: We the People of the United States
We the thirteen States of America
We the free Citizens of the Republic
We the United Colonies of America
context: Madison later said 'the finish given to the style and arrangement of the Constitution fairly belongs to the pen of Mr. Morris.' Morris had lost his real leg in a carriage accident at 28 and gave 173 speeches at the Convention — more than anyone. Source: Heritage Foundation, 'Gouverneur Morris: Penman of the Constitution'; Constitution Center (Madison's 1831 letter quoted).

question: James Wilson and Charles Pinckney pushed through the Convention's worst bargain, a rule for deciding how many House seats and how much tax each state got. It set how a state's enslaved people would be counted toward its population. How many of a state's enslaved people did the rule count?
answer: Three-fifths of them were counted
choices: Three-fifths of them were counted
Every one of them was counted in full
Half of them were counted
None of them were counted at all
context: The Three-Fifths Compromise counted three of every five enslaved people toward a state's population for representation and taxes. James Wilson, who helped introduce it, later came to disavow his own clause. Source: 'Three-fifths Compromise' — Wikipedia; Britannica, 'Three-fifths compromise'; Montpelier ConText.

question: James Madison of Virginia walked into the Convention better prepared than anyone alive. Thomas Jefferson had shipped him two whole trunks of books from Paris, and Madison had studied the ancient Greek, Roman, Swiss and Dutch confederacies. He arrived with his own population-based blueprint already drawn up, and he took notes at every session. What nickname did this earn him?
answer: Father of the Constitution
choices: Father of the Constitution
Pen of the Revolution
Sage of Philadelphia
Architect of Liberty
context: Madison's preparation — plus the nightly shorthand notes he took without missing a single session — earned him the title 'Father of the Constitution.' His Notes remain the most complete record of what was said in that closed room. Source: Monticello, 'James Madison'; Library of Congress, 'James Madison and the Federal Constitutional Convention of 1787.'

question: The delegates at Philadelphia handed every state the same two votes in the Senate, tiny Delaware as many as giant Virginia. Then, in Article V, they treated that one deal in a way they treated no other part of the Constitution. What did they do to it?
answer: Made it the one rule that can never be amended away
choices: Made it the one rule that can never be amended away
Set it to expire automatically after twenty years
Left it for the states to revisit every decade
Made it changeable by a simple majority vote
context: Article V declares that 'no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate' — making equal Senate representation essentially the only thing in the Constitution that can never be amended away. Source: U.S. Constitution, Article V (quoted in 'Connecticut Compromise' — Wikipedia).

question: A mob stormed the palace in Muslim Granada on 30 December 1066, killed the Jewish vizier Joseph ibn Naghrela, and turned on the city's Jews. The coexistence of Muslims, Christians and Jews in Moorish Spain was real but unequal, and here it turned deadly. According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, how many Jewish lives did the mob take in that single day?
answer: About 4,000 people
choices: About 4,000 people
About 40 people
About 400 people
About 400,000 people
context: The 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia records that about 1,500 Jewish families, some 4,000 people, fell in a single day; Joseph ibn Naghrela was found hiding in a coal-pit with his face blackened, then crucified. The episode is a check against romanticizing convivencia: non-Muslims lived as dhimmis, a protected but subordinate class who paid the jizya head-tax, and the older tolerance was later ended outright when the fundamentalist Almohads ordered Jews and Christians to convert, flee, or die — driving the philosopher Maimonides into exile from Cordoba. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1066_Granada_massacre

question: Calvin Coolidge said in a 1925 speech that the business of America was business, or so the famous soundbite goes. Right after that line, in the same speech, he said something the soundbite leaves out. What did Coolidge say America really was?
answer: A nation of idealists
choices: A nation of idealists
A republic of farmers
A land of inventors
A people of soldiers
context: In his January 17, 1925 address 'The Press Under a Free Government,' Coolidge followed 'the chief business of the American people is business' with 'The chief ideal of the American people is idealism. I cannot repeat too often that America is a nation of idealists' — arguing wealth should serve schools, knowledge, and culture. The popular soundbite cuts out this half, making it a famously unfair misquote. Source: thisdayinquotes.com; presidency.ucsb.edu.

question: Andrew Mellon, Treasury Secretary under Calvin Coolidge, wrote that steep tax rates did not always bring in big revenue, an idea that sounds backwards. He cut the top rate of income tax from 73 percent to 25 percent. According to Cato Institute figures, what happened to federal income-tax revenue after those cuts?
answer: Revenue rose, surpassing the old 1920 level
choices: Revenue rose, surpassing the old 1920 level
Revenue collapsed by roughly half
Revenue barely changed for a decade
Revenue vanished, forcing new borrowing
context: Mellon — Treasury Secretary under Harding, Coolidge, and Hoover (1921-1932) — wrote in his 1924 book 'Taxation: The People's Business' that 'high rates of taxation do not necessarily mean large revenue.' After the cuts, by 1928 federal revenues surpassed the 1920 level, the budget ran surpluses, and the national debt was paid down from about $24-26 billion to $16-17 billion. Real GNP grew about 4.7% a year (1922-1929) and unemployment fell to 3.2%. Source: cato.org; coolidgereview.com.

question: The Moon slid across Aldebaran, the red star at the bull's eye in Taurus, and hid it one night in 1497, while Copernicus, a student at Bologna, watched. He worked out his Sun-centred heavens before anyone built a telescope. How did Copernicus study the sky?
answer: With only his naked eyes and mathematics, since the telescope did not yet exist
choices: With only his naked eyes and mathematics, since the telescope did not yet exist
With a giant brass telescope he built himself in his cathedral tower
With a set of mirrors that magnified the planets a hundred times
With a crystal lens ground for him by the finest glassmakers in Italy
context: The telescope would not be invented until about 65 years after Copernicus died. He reasoned his way to a Sun-centered cosmos using naked-eye observations and math alone. Source: Britannica summary (britannica.com/summary/Nicolaus-Copernicus); History.com 'Copernicus born'.

question: Copernicus set the solid Earth spinning and racing round the Sun, against everything common sense seemed to say. His critics objected that if the ground were really rushing through space, everyone standing on it would feel it move. How did Copernicus answer them?
answer: The Earth only looks still because we ride along with it as it moves
choices: The Earth only looks still because we ride along with it as it moves
The Earth moves so slowly that no human could ever notice the motion
The Earth is held perfectly steady while only the Sun and stars drift
The motion stops and starts so gently that our bodies smooth it out
context: This was Copernicus's key insight: a spinning, orbiting Earth LOOKS still because we travel along with it. Source: Britannica, Nicolaus Copernicus (britannica.com/biography/Nicolaus-Copernicus); Commentariolus postulate 5 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commentariolus).

question: Copernicus spent his last thirty years in the service of Frombork Cathedral in Poland, fitting his star-watching around his church duties. He turned one building at the cathedral into his own observatory. Which one?
answer: A defensive tower built into the cathedral's wall
choices: A defensive tower built into the cathedral's wall
The cathedral's tall bell tower
A loft in the bishop's palace nearby
The flat roof above the cathedral nave
context: Copernicus served as a canon (a cathedral official) at Frombork from 1497 until his death; for his observations he is traditionally tied to a tower in the cathedral's defensive wall, still called the Copernicus Tower and now a museum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus; New World Encyclopedia, Nicolaus Copernicus; Astronomical Heritage, 'Copernicus observing site in Frauenburg/Frombork.'

question: Copernicus set down a brief sketch of his Sun-centred idea around 1514, long before his great book appeared. He never printed it: he gave a few handwritten copies to trusted friends, and it passed quietly from hand to hand for decades. By what name is the little sketch known?
answer: The Commentariolus, the 'Little Commentary'
choices: The Commentariolus, the 'Little Commentary'
The Almagest, the 'Great Treatise'
The Narratio, the 'First Account'
The Tabulae, the 'New Tables'
context: 'Commentariolus' is Latin for 'Little Commentary.' Copernicus never printed it but passed handwritten copies to trusted friends, and it circulated quietly for decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commentariolus; peterschulte.org, Copernicus and the Commentariolus.

question: Rheticus, a young Lutheran from Wittenberg, came to visit Copernicus, who had held his great book back for years. The old Catholic astronomer took him on as his only pupil, and the two lived together for about two years. What did Rheticus finally get Copernicus to do?
answer: Publish his sun-centered theory of the heavens
choices: Publish his sun-centered theory of the heavens
Move away from Poland to a Protestant city
Convert from Catholicism to Lutheranism
Give up astronomy for good
context: Rheticus, a young Lutheran from Wittenberg, became Copernicus's only student and in 1540 wrote the first published account of the theory, the 'Narratio Prima.' Source: Britannica, Narratio prima; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narratio_Prima; Oregon State, Lutherans' Reading of Copernicus.

question: Copernicus first saw his great book in print on 24 May 1543, a famous legend says, though historians call the story dramatic. What does the legend say happened to him that day?
answer: He woke from a stroke-induced coma, saw his printed book, and died that same day
choices: He woke from a stroke-induced coma, saw his printed book, and died that same day
He read his book aloud to a crowd of students gathered around his bed
He burned his only copy in fear before the Church could ever seize it
He signed the last page with a trembling hand and lived on for many years
context: By tradition Copernicus saw his printed book for the first and only time as he woke from a coma on the day he died. Historians call this a dramatic legend; the manuscript reached the printer about two years before his death. Source: History for Atheists, 'The Great Myths 6: Copernicus' Deathbed Publication'; historyofinformation.com #3729.

question: In the most beautiful line of his great book, Copernicus pictured the Sun in one glowing image. He asked who would set such a light anywhere other than the middle, from where it could light the whole at once. What did he compare the Sun to?
answer: A lamp set at the heart of a temple
choices: A lamp set at the heart of a temple
A king riding to war on a white horse
A pearl resting at the bottom of the sea
A torch carried through a darkened forest
context: The line reads: 'In this most beautiful temple, who would place this lamp in another or better position than that from which it can light up the whole thing at the same time?' Source: De Revolutionibus Bk 1 Ch 10, translation at webexhibits.org/calendars/year-text-Copernicus.html.

question: As an adviser on money, Copernicus watched debased coins passing from hand to hand beside full-weight ones around 1519; he was a trained doctor and an astronomer too. He set down a rule in one short sentence, a rule that later took the name Gresham's Law. What did Copernicus say happens between the two kinds of coin?
answer: Bad money drives out good money
choices: Bad money drives out good money
Borrowed gold always returns to its owner
Coins lose their value the moment they are buried
Silver and gold can never circulate together
context: Around 1517 Copernicus worked out an early quantity theory of money, and by 1519 the principle later named Gresham's Law: bad money drives out good. In 1526 he wrote a treatise on coinage, 'Monetae cudendae ratio.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus; Mises Institute, 'Copernicus and the Quantity Theory of Money'.

question: Archaeologists digging beneath the floor of Frombork Cathedral in 2005 found a skeleton they suspected was Copernicus's, whose grave had been lost for centuries. To prove it, scientists matched its DNA to a sample left inside a book of his, kept today at Uppsala University in Sweden. What was that telltale sample?
answer: Strands of his hair
choices: Strands of his hair
Drops of dried ink
Flakes of his fingernail
A smear of old blood
context: Scientists matched the skeleton's DNA to hairs still tucked inside one of Copernicus's books, now kept at Uppsala University. The forensic skull also bore a broken nose and a scar above the left eye, matching his old self-portrait. Source: Space.com, 'The strange story of the grave of Copernicus'; Discover Magazine.

question: For his own tomb Copernicus chose humble words, though he had dared to set the Earth in motion. He did not ask God for the grace that Saint Paul received, nor for Saint Peter's pardon, but for one smaller mercy from the Gospels. Which forgiveness did he ask for?
answer: The forgiveness granted to the robber crucified beside Jesus
choices: The forgiveness granted to the robber crucified beside Jesus
The forgiveness granted to the crowd that mocked Jesus
The forgiveness granted to the soldier who pierced Jesus
The forgiveness granted to the judge who condemned Jesus
context: Copernicus asked only for 'that forgiveness which Thou didst grant to the robber' (the thief crucified beside Jesus), not the grace of St. Paul nor the pardon of St. Peter. Source: The Spectator Archive, 'The Epitaph on Copernicus' (20 Sep 1890); inyourpocket.com, Copernicus' Grave.

question: Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish churchman, published a famous book in 1543 that took the Earth out of the centre of the heavens and put the Sun there instead, a huge shift in how people pictured the universe. What was the book called?
answer: On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres
choices: On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres
On the Structure of the Human Body
Dialogue on the Two Great World Systems
Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy
context: 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium,' printed in Nuremberg by Johannes Petreius in 1543. This is the very book where the word 'revolution' began its journey from meaning a turning sphere to meaning an overturning of ideas. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_revolutionibus_orbium_coelestium

question: Lucas Watzenrode, a bishop and the uncle of Copernicus, got the young man a paid church post at Frombork in 1497 that covered his bills and that he held for life. Copernicus watched the stars only in his spare hours, and he earned a doctorate in the law of the Church. What was his day job?
answer: A cathedral canon
choices: A cathedral canon
A bishop's secretary
A monastery scribe
A choir music teacher
context: Copernicus was a canon at Frombork (Frauenburg) cathedral, a salaried administrative post his uncle Bishop Lucas Watzenrode secured for him in 1497 and which he held for life. Scholars (notably Edward Rosen) think he was probably never even ordained a priest — a canon ran the cathedral's affairs. The man who moved the Earth was a churchman, not the Church's enemy. Source: hao.ucar.edu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus

question: Copernicus lay dying in 1543, and legend says a finished copy of his great book was rushed to his bedside. The printers, though, had not quite completed their work. What did Copernicus most likely hold at the very end?
answer: The final printed pages of his book
choices: The final printed pages of his book
A finished leather-bound copy
A letter of praise from the Pope
His original handwritten manuscript
context: Legend (so framed): the story says a printed copy reached his deathbed and he died the same day, 24 May 1543, aged 70. The romantic version is exaggerated — the manuscript had been with the printer almost two years, and what he likely held were the final printed front pages (the front matter), not a finished bound book. Either way, he never lived to fight for his idea. Source: scientus.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus
