question: Georg Joachim Rheticus, a young Lutheran mathematician, came to Frombork in 1539 and stayed two years as the aging Copernicus's only pupil. In 1540 he published his First Account, the Narratio Prima, the earliest book to announce a bold new idea. What did it announce?
answer: Copernicus's sun-centered theory of the heavens
choices: Copernicus's sun-centered theory of the heavens
The three laws of planetary motion
The discovery of Jupiter's four moons
The invention of the reflecting telescope
context: Georg Joachim Rheticus, a Lutheran, sought Copernicus out, stayed two years, and in 1540 published 'Narratio Prima' (First Account) — the first printed word of the new astronomy. Across the religious divide of the day, a young Protestant talked the elderly Catholic canon into going public. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Joachim_Rheticus; britannica.com

question: Copernicus opened his great book with a warm dedication to one of the most powerful men in Europe. He admitted that he had held the work back for fear of scorn, and he hoped that this reader, a lover of mathematics himself, would judge it fairly. To whom did Copernicus dedicate the book?
answer: Pope Paul III
choices: Pope Paul III
King Sigismund of Poland
Emperor Charles V
Bishop Lucas Watzenrode
context: Copernicus dedicated his masterwork to Pope Paul III himself, admitting he had held the work back for fear it would be 'scorned' for its novelty and torn apart by the 'peripatetics and theologians.' The book that supposedly defied the Church opens with a letter to the Pope. Source: hti.osu.edu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_revolutionibus_orbium_coelestium

question: Polish scientists identified the bones of Copernicus, who taught that the Sun sits at the centre of the heavens, centuries after he was buried in an unmarked grave. In 2010 he was reburied as a national hero in Frombork Cathedral, and a carving was cut into his new black granite tombstone. What does the carving show?
answer: A golden Sun circled by six planets
choices: A golden Sun circled by six planets
A cross above an open book
A globe held in two hands
An angel pointing at the stars
context: After his bones were identified, Copernicus was reburied in 2010 as a national hero under the same cathedral floor. The tombstone shows a golden Sun ringed by six planets — his own model marking his grave. Source: nbcnews.com; cbsnews.com

question: Andreas Osiander, a Lutheran clergyman, oversaw the printing of Copernicus's great book in Germany as the old astronomer lay dying in 1543. Nervous about the trouble the book's bold idea might cause, Osiander secretly slipped an unsigned note into the front of the book without the author's permission. What did the note claim?
answer: That the moving Earth was just a calculating trick, not the truth
choices: That the moving Earth was just a calculating trick, not the truth
That the author had recanted everything on his deathbed
That the Pope had personally approved every page
That a rival had stolen the ideas from an older book
context: Osiander secretly inserted an unsigned preface ('Ad lectorem') claiming the moving Earth was merely a device for calculation, not physical reality. Because it was unsigned, readers for decades wrongly assumed Copernicus himself had written this watered-down disclaimer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_revolutionibus_orbium_coelestium; lindahall.org

question: Rheticus learned that when his master's great book went to press in Germany in 1543, the man overseeing the printing had slipped in a fake preface without permission. The note was unsigned, so readers would take it for Copernicus's own words. How did his loyal pupil react?
answer: He flew into a furious rage and demanded a reprint
choices: He flew into a furious rage and demanded a reprint
He calmly added a correction to the next edition
He thanked the printer for protecting the author
He quietly hid every copy he could find
context: By Maestlin's account Rheticus got into 'a very bitter wrangle with the printer' and reportedly threatened violence. He and Copernicus's friends demanded the book be reprinted without the fake preface — but the printer refused. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_revolutionibus_orbium_coelestium; scientus.org

question: Copernicus published his book putting the Sun at the centre of the heavens, and many people suppose the Church made war on it at once. In fact the Church put the book on its Index of Forbidden Books only on 5 March 1616. How long after publication did the ban come?
answer: More than seventy years later
choices: More than seventy years later
Within a year of publication
About ten years later
Within his own lifetime
context: The book was published and dedicated to a Pope in 1543; it wasn't banned until 1616 — over 70 years later — and stayed on the Index until Pope Benedict XIV had it removed in 1758. The supposed clash with the Church came generations after the man was dead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_revolutionibus_orbium_coelestium

question: Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish churchman, overturned in 1543 what Europeans had believed since ancient times: an unmoving Earth in the middle of everything. His book made the Earth just one more planet in motion. What did Copernicus put at the centre instead?
answer: The Sun
choices: The Sun
The Moon
The North Star
Jupiter
context: This idea is called heliocentrism: the Earth is just one of the planets orbiting the Sun. The book was printed in Nuremberg in 1543 by Johannes Petreius. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_revolutionibus_orbium_coelestium

question: Galileo Galilei, 69 years old, stood before the Inquisition in Rome in 1633. The court found him 'strongly suspect of heresy' for teaching that the Earth moves, and it forced him to take that teaching back. What sentence did it pass on the old man?
answer: House arrest for life
choices: House arrest for life
Burning at the stake
Banishment from Italy
Ten years in prison
context: On June 22, 1633, Galileo was made to 'abjure, curse, and detest' the moving Earth and sentenced to house arrest for the rest of his life at his villa in Arcetri near Florence. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_affair

question: Johannes Kepler was working out the laws of the planets as the emperor's own mathematician when his elderly mother, Katharina, was arrested for witchcraft after a quarrel with a neighbour. She sat in jail for over a year, and she was even shown the instruments of torture to frighten a confession out of her. How did Kepler save her?
answer: He wrote a long legal defense
choices: He wrote a long legal defense
He paid a heavy ransom
He smuggled her abroad
He appealed to the Pope
context: Katharina Kepler spent 405 days in prison (1620). Kepler wrote a roughly 50-folio legal brief tearing each accusation apart with the same rigor he used on the planets, and won her acquittal. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katharina_Kepler

question: Galileo Galilei was fond of quoting a churchman's witty saying about what the Bible was meant to teach and what it was not. A devout Catholic, he argued that faith and science answered different questions. By that saying, the Holy Spirit teaches how one goes to heaven, but not what?
answer: How the heavens go
choices: How the heavens go
How the Earth was made
How the stars were named
How time began
context: The full line Galileo quoted was 'The intention of the Holy Spirit is to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go.' He argued faith and science answer different questions rather than opposing each other. https://christianscholars.com/god-and-galileo-what-a-400-year-old-letter-teaches-us-about-faith-and-science/

question: An enslaved Nahua woman, sold away as a girl, became Hernan Cortes's voice among the Aztecs. She knew both Nahuatl and Maya and learned Spanish so quickly that she stood between him and the Aztec world. 'After God,' Cortes said, 'we owe this conquest to her.' By what name did the Spanish know her?
answer: Dona Marina, the one they called La Malinche
choices: Dona Marina, the one they called La Malinche
Isabella, the noblewoman of the Mexica court
Sister Catalina, the convert from Cempoala
Tecuichpo, the captive princess of Tacuba
context: Malinalli ('grass'), baptized Dona Marina and remembered as La Malinche, first relayed Maya to a Spanish priest, then learned Spanish herself. Cortes credited the conquest to her after God. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Was La Malinche a Traitor'; Wikipedia, La Malinche.

question: Moctezuma met Hernan Cortes on the causeway into Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519 and welcomed him with gifts, among them a great disc of gold and a great disc of silver, each a crafted treasure. What did Cortes end up doing with the two discs?
answer: Melted them down for the value of the metal
choices: Melted them down for the value of the metal
Hung them in a cathedral back in Spain
Returned them to Moctezuma as a gesture of peace
Buried them beneath his camp for safekeeping
context: Moctezuma greeted Cortes, in the Aztec account, 'You have come to sit on your throne... which I have kept for a while for you.' Cortes melted the gold and silver discs down for their metal. Source: AHA, 'Mexica Accounts of Moctezuma Meeting Cortes'; Wikipedia, Moctezuma II.

question: Tenochtitlan was starving when it fell on 13 August 1521, after a siege of about 93 days: its canals were full of the dead, and its survivors were eating bark and lizards. As the Spanish closed in, they took the last Aztec emperor, Cuauhtemoc. How was he captured?
answer: Trying to escape across the lake by canoe
choices: Trying to escape across the lake by canoe
Hiding in the cellar beneath his own palace
Slipping out disguised as a common porter
Trying to swim a canal under cover of smoke
context: Cuauhtemoc was taken on the open water as he tried to slip away by canoe; with his capture the empire's resistance ended. By then an estimated tens of thousands of bodies floated in the canals. Source: Britannica, 'Battle of Tenochtitlan'; Wikipedia, Fall of Tenochtitlan.

question: Hernan Cortes came ashore in Mexico in 1519 with eleven ships, and soon he feared that his nervous men would seize them and sail back to the safety of Cuba. He had to make retreat impossible before he marched inland against the Aztecs. What did Cortes actually do to his ships?
answer: Secretly had men bore holes to sink them, then blamed it on shipworms
choices: Secretly had men bore holes to sink them, then blamed it on shipworms
Set them all ablaze on the beach in front of his whole assembled army
Sailed them back home to Cuba himself to fetch fresh reinforcements
Handed the whole fleet over to his new native allies as a parting gift
context: In 1519 Cortes had loyal men quietly bore holes in ten of his eleven ships at night to scuttle them, then blamed the damage on shipworms, so no one could retreat. The famous 'burned his ships' tale is a myth that first appeared in 1558, borrowed from the Greek tyrant Agathocles. Source: Word & Sorcery, 'Cortes Didn't Burn His Ships'; National Geographic.

question: Hernan Cortes tried to slip out of Tenochtitlan along a causeway on the night of 30 June 1520, the Night of Sorrows, and he let each man carry off all the Aztec gold he could hold. Then the alarm went up, and the Aztecs attacked on the narrow causeway. What doomed many of the fleeing soldiers?
answer: Weighed down by the gold, they fell off the causeway and drowned
choices: Weighed down by the gold, they fell off the causeway and drowned
Trapped against the water, they were trampled by their own war-horses
Lost in the dark and surrounded, they laid down their arms at dawn
Cut off on a small island, they slowly starved until they surrendered
context: The alarm was raised by a woman drawing water and a priest atop the temple. Soldiers stuffed with looted gold lost their footing on the causeway, fell into the lake, and drowned. Source: Wikipedia, La Noche Triste; History.com.

question: Narvaez's relief expedition carried an infected man, and with him the deadliest force of the conquest, a sickness the Americas had never seen and one the Spanish never meant to bring. In 1520 it swept through Tenochtitlan, killing much of the Aztec army and a quarter to half of the city's people. What was it?
answer: Smallpox
choices: Smallpox
The bubonic plague
Yellow fever
Cholera
context: Smallpox, unknown in the Americas, killed roughly a quarter to a half of the population and gutted the Aztec army before the final siege. Moctezuma's successor Cuitlahuac died of it after a reign of only 80 days. Source: Ancient Origins, '80 Days of Cuitlahuac'; Britannica, Cuitlahuac.

question: The Tlaxcalans kept their city free, though Aztec lands surrounded it, and they had every reason to hate the Aztecs. The Aztecs forced the peoples they conquered to send their own young men to Tenochtitlan as tribute. What became of those young men there?
answer: They were given up to the priests to be sacrificed
choices: They were given up to the priests to be sacrificed
They were shipped down the coast to row in galleys
They were held for ransom and traded for gold and cacao
They were resettled as bonded farmers on conquered land
context: Subject peoples sent their own to be sacrificed at Tenochtitlan, so Tlaxcala and rivals like Texcoco and Cempoala gladly allied with Cortes against the Aztecs. Source: TheCollector, 'Traitors or Survivors? The Tlaxcalans'; HistorySkills, Aztec Flower Wars.

question: Hernan Cortes landed in Mexico in 1519 with only about 630 men and 16 horses, and the popular story says that a few hundred Spaniards toppled the Aztec Empire. That story leaves out most of the army that took Tenochtitlan. Who made up the bulk of it?
answer: Tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other native warriors
choices: Tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other native warriors
Fresh regiments of Spanish soldiers shipped over from Spain
Hired European mercenaries with cannon and gunpowder crews
A fleet of armored knights sent across the sea by the king
context: Tlaxcala alone is estimated to have fielded 80,000 to 200,000 warriors. The Spanish were a minority of the army; indigenous allies who hated Aztec rule, plus smallpox, brought the city down. Source: Wikipedia, Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire.

question: Hernan Cortes needed warships to take Tenochtitlan, an island city in the middle of Lake Texcoco. In 1521 his shipwright Martin Lopez built him thirteen small ones far inland, up in the mountains and nowhere near the water. How did Cortes get the finished ships down to the lake?
answer: Carried them in pieces over the mountains and rebuilt them
choices: Carried them in pieces over the mountains and rebuilt them
Floated them the whole way down a long winding river to the shore
Dragged them across the open plain on rolling logs by ox-team
Seized the Aztecs' own war-canoes and rearmed them with cannon
context: The 13 brigantines, each carrying 25 men, were built inland, taken apart, hauled piece by piece over the mountains, and reassembled. About 40,000 native laborers then dug a canal roughly 12 feet wide and over 9,000 feet long to launch them. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'The Fall of Tenochtitlan.'

question: The Aztecs captured groups of Spaniards alive during the siege of 1521 and made an example of them where their comrades could see. To the beat of drums and the blast of conch shells, they marched the prisoners up the pyramid at Tlatelolco. What did the watching Spanish soldiers, powerless to stop it, see done to their comrades?
answer: Their hearts were cut out on the altar at the top
choices: Their hearts were cut out on the altar at the top
They were hurled down from the temple steps into the lake
They were branded on the face and sent back across as slaves
They were shut in wooden cages and starved along the causeway
context: One account names about 50 to 70 Spanish prisoners sacrificed at the altar in full view of Cortes's men. The Aztec sacrifice regime was real, not mere Spanish propaganda. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'The Fall of Tenochtitlan'; Wikipedia, Fall of Tenochtitlan.

question: Hernan Cortes's men hunted for Aztec gold after Tenochtitlan fell, and they burned the oiled feet of the captured emperor Cuauhtemoc over a fire. Beside him the lord of Tacuba groaned for relief. According to the story long remembered, how did Cuauhtemoc answer that groan?
answer: 'Do you think I am in a bath for pleasure?'
choices: 'Do you think I am in a bath for pleasure?'
'The gold lies where you will never find it.'
'Strike me down and be done with it.'
'My people will avenge this fire.'
context: Cuauhtemoc is remembered to have answered his fellow captive's groan with these words. The Spanish found almost no treasure; most of the fabled 'Aztec gold' was a myth. Told as remembered testimony, not a verified transcript. Source: Encyclopedia.com, Cuauhtemoc; New World Encyclopedia, Cuauhtemoc.  (Legend.)

question: David Ben-Gurion rose in a museum hall in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948 and read out a paper founding a new country in the ancient Jewish homeland. He ended the meeting with a few bold words. What did he say?
answer: "The State of Israel is established! This meeting is adjourned!"
choices: "The State of Israel is established! This meeting is adjourned!"
"Let every nation now witness the birth of our people."
"We have come home at last, and here we will remain."
"From this day the long exile of our people is over."
context: Ben-Gurion read the whole Declaration of Independence aloud in just 16 minutes and ended with this line. When he first struck his gavel to open, the guests spontaneously began singing the anthem Hatikvah. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Declaration_of_Independence

question: Guests in a Tel Aviv museum burst into the anthem Hatikvah on 14 May 1948, when David Ben-Gurion first struck his gavel at the meeting where he proclaimed a new Jewish state. The state was barely a day old when it faced its first test. What happened to it on 15 May?
answer: The armies of five neighboring Arab countries invaded it
choices: The armies of five neighboring Arab countries invaded it
Britain returned and reoccupied the new state's cities
The United Nations voted to cancel the new state
A rival Jewish government declared itself in Jerusalem
context: On May 15, 1948 the armies of Egypt, Syria, Jordan, Iraq, and Lebanon invaded the one-day-old state, beginning the 1948 Arab-Israeli War, which Israel calls its War of Independence. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/1948-Arab-Israeli-War

question: David Ben-Gurion proclaimed a new Jewish state in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948. One major world power moved fastest: only eleven minutes after his declaration, it became the first country in the world to recognise the new state. Which country was it?
answer: The United States
choices: The United States
The Soviet Union
France
Britain
context: President Harry Truman recognized Israel just eleven minutes after the declaration, over the strong objection of his own Secretary of State, George Marshall, who feared alienating the Arab world. Source: https://www.trumanlibrary.gov/education/presidential-inquiries/recognition-israel

question: Crowds danced in the streets of Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948, when David Ben-Gurion declared the founding of Israel, a Jewish homeland born in the shadow of the Holocaust, in which six million Jews had just been murdered in Europe. But that night, in his private diary, Ben-Gurion wrote a strikingly sombre line. What did he write?
answer: "I mourn among the joyful."
choices: "I mourn among the joyful."
"Today the dead are avenged at last."
"We have only begun the harder fight."
"The world will never forgive us this."
context: Israel's Declaration explicitly invokes the Nazi catastrophe as the reason for an urgent Jewish homeland. Amid the public celebration, Ben-Gurion privately recorded his grief that the homeland came too late for the murdered millions. Source: https://www.timesofisrael.com/ben-gurion-diary-entries-on-day-of-independence-revealed-i-mourn-among-the-joyful/

question: David Ben-Gurion stood before the newsreel cameras in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948 and seemed to read Israel's Declaration of Independence from a grand ceremonial scroll. The scroll looked magnificent in the pictures, but it hid a secret. What was really true of the scroll he read from?
answer: It was largely blank, so he really read from handwritten notes
choices: It was largely blank, so he really read from handwritten notes
It was written in the wrong language and had to be hidden
It was a copy, while the original stayed locked in Jerusalem
It listed a different country name that had to be covered up
context: The calligrapher Otte Wallish had finished only the bottom portion of the parchment, so Ben-Gurion read from handwritten notes; the scroll itself was not fully completed until June. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Declaration_of_Independence

question: Israel's founders settled on the name Israel on 12 May 1948, only two days before the declaration. They rejected two other names, Judea and Zion, and gave one concrete reason for dropping those two in particular. What was the objection to Judea and Zion?
answer: They named places, like Jerusalem, that lay outside the new state's borders
choices: They named places, like Jerusalem, that lay outside the new state's borders
They were too closely tied to a single ancient royal dynasty
They had already been claimed by rival settlement movements
They could not be easily pronounced in the world's main languages
context: Ben-Gurion proposed 'Israel' on May 12, 1948; it was received coolly and won with seven votes. Judea and Zion were dropped because they named places, such as Jerusalem, that were not inside the new state's borders; another rejected option was Ever. Source: https://martinkramer.org/2020/04/27/1948-why-the-name-israel/

question: Alfred Tennyson heard the news of a doomed British cavalry charge at Balaclava in 1854, and weeks later he wrote a poem to fix the disaster in memory. Its galloping refrain names the place where the riders charged. What is that refrain?
answer: "Into the valley of Death / Rode the six hundred"
choices: "Into the valley of Death / Rode the six hundred"
"Across the field of glory / Rode the gallant men"
"Down to the gates of ruin / Rode the doomed brigade"
"Through the storm of cannon / Rode the king's own horse"
context: Tennyson wrote 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' on 2 December 1854 and it was published a week later (9 December 1854, in The Examiner). The same poem hammers home the crossfire: 'Cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them, / Cannon in front of them.' Source: https://poemanalysis.com/alfred-tennyson/the-charge-of-the-light-brigade/

question: Lord Raglan wanted his cavalry at Balaclava in 1854 to recover some captured guns up on the heights. When Lord Lucan demanded to know which guns, Captain Louis Nolan, who carried the order, flung out his arm and pointed, but not at the heights. Where did Nolan point, sending about 670 horsemen the wrong way?
answer: Down the valley at the massed Russian battery
choices: Down the valley at the massed Russian battery
Up the heights at the captured British guns
Back toward the British camp at Balaclava
Across the river at the Russian infantry
context: Nolan snapped, 'There, my lord, is your enemy; there are your guns!' He had written a book on cavalry tactics — yet he became the very first man killed in the charge he misdirected, struck in the chest by a shell splinter in the first minute. The brigade lost about 110-118 killed of roughly 670, and achieved nothing. The French general Bosquet watched and said, 'It is magnificent, but it is not war.' Source: https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/their-own-words-captain-louis-nolan

question: Major Richard Heyser took a U-2 spy plane on a high pass over Cuba on 14 October 1962, at the height of the Cold War, and the sharp photographs he brought back terrified President Kennedy and his advisers. The Soviets had been secretly building something on Cuban soil, only 90 miles from Florida. What did the photographs show?
answer: Nuclear missile launch sites
choices: Nuclear missile launch sites
A new naval shipyard
A radio broadcast tower
An underground bunker city
context: Major Richard Heyser piloted the flight; the photos showed Soviet SS-4 medium-range ballistic missiles being assembled on Cuban soil — the first hard proof. Source: jfklibrary.org; history.state.gov.

question: John F. Kennedy decided, after seeing the U-2 photographs, that the navy would stop and turn back any ship carrying weapons to Cuba. Stopping a country's shipping with warships was legally an act of war, so to avoid declaring one, Kennedy chose a gentler word. What did he call the operation?
answer: A quarantine
choices: A quarantine
A blockade
An embargo
A siege
context: Calling it a 'quarantine' rather than a 'blockade' let Kennedy avoid declaring war. The line was drawn 500 nautical miles out from the eastern tip of Cuba. Source: history.state.gov.

question: John F. Kennedy went on live television in October 1962 to tell a frightened public what the Soviets were secretly doing in Cuba, only 90 miles off Florida. Then he drew a line. What did he warn would happen if a nuclear missile were fired from Cuba at any country in the Americas?
answer: The U.S. would treat it as a Soviet attack requiring full retaliation
choices: The U.S. would treat it as a Soviet attack requiring full retaliation
The U.S. would file a complaint at the United Nations
The U.S. would impose new trade sanctions on Cuba
The U.S. would withdraw its ambassador from Moscow
context: Kennedy's televised line drew the brightest possible red line: any launch from Cuba would mean nuclear war with the Soviet Union itself. Source: jfklibrary.org.

question: Kennedy's most trusted advisers met in secret at the White House from 16 October 1962, after he saw the U-2 photographs taken over Cuba. The group was nicknamed ExComm, short for Executive Committee, and for days it debated two main ways to answer what the photographs showed. What were the two choices on the table?
answer: Bomb-and-invade the island, or ring it with warships
choices: Bomb-and-invade the island, or ring it with warships
Surrender Berlin, or break off relations with Moscow
Launch a first strike, or do nothing and wait
Recall the army from Europe, or ask the UN to vote
context: ExComm (the Executive Committee) debated air strikes plus invasion versus the naval ring. Kennedy chose the ring of ships. Source: jfklibrary.org.

question: Adlai Stevenson, the American ambassador, cornered the Soviet ambassador Valerian Zorin before the whole United Nations Security Council on 25 October 1962 and demanded that he admit the missiles were in Cuba. When Zorin stalled, what did Stevenson do to prove his case right there in the chamber?
answer: Unveiled large U-2 photographs of the missile sites
choices: Unveiled large U-2 photographs of the missile sites
Played a tape of a Soviet general's orders
Produced a defecting Soviet officer as a witness
Read out the missiles' exact map coordinates
context: Stevenson had aides reveal blown-up spy-plane photos of the missile sites for the world to see — the visual proof that Zorin could not deny. Source: cfr.org.

question: Major Rudolf Anderson flew his U-2 spy plane over Cuba on Black Saturday, 27 October 1962, and a Soviet missile shot him down. He was the only American killed in combat in the whole crisis. One fact about that mission sets his death apart. What was it?
answer: He had not even been scheduled to fly — he lobbied hard for the mission
choices: He had not even been scheduled to fly — he lobbied hard for the mission
He had been ordered to turn back minutes before he was hit
He was flying his very first mission over Cuba that day
He had spotted the missile crews and radioed home before he fell
context: Anderson was downed by a Soviet SA-2 surface-to-air missile, the crisis's only combat death. Kennedy posthumously awarded him the Distinguished Service Medal. His death pushed Kennedy harder toward a peaceful settlement. Source: defensemedianetwork.com; jfklibrary.org.

question: Dean Rusk, Kennedy's Secretary of State, was waiting on 24 October 1962 for news from the sea around Cuba. When he heard that Soviet ships had halted short of the American navy's line, he leaned over to McGeorge Bundy and whispered what became the most famous line of the crisis. What did Rusk say?
answer: "We're eyeball to eyeball, and I think the other fellow just blinked"
choices: "We're eyeball to eyeball, and I think the other fellow just blinked"
"The hour of maximum danger is upon us tonight"
"We will not be the first to fire, but we will be the last"
"Pray that this cup may pass from us"
context: Rusk whispered it to McGeorge Bundy. The line captured the showdown's nerve so perfectly it outlived the crisis itself. Source: cfr.org.

question: Nikita Khrushchev wrote to Kennedy on 26 October 1962 and reached for a vivid image of how the standoff might end in catastrophe. Both sides, he warned, were pulling on the ends of a rope, and the harder each pulled, the worse it got. What did Khrushchev say they had tied into that rope?
answer: The knot of war
choices: The knot of war
The noose of the world
The chain of war
The cord of doom
context: Khrushchev wrote that the harder both pulled, the tighter the 'knot of war' grew — until it might have to be cut, unleashing 'terrible forces.' He urged both to stop pulling. Source: jfklibrary.org.

question: Nikita Khrushchev sent Kennedy a second, tougher letter on 27 October 1962, the day later nicknamed Black Saturday, the tensest of the whole crisis. It raised the price of peace with a new demand on the United States. What did the letter now insist the United States must also do?
answer: Remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey
choices: Remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey
Pull all its troops out of West Berlin
Recognize Cuba's government formally
Hand back its naval base at Guantanamo
context: The Turkey demand made Black Saturday the crisis's knife-edge: a new condition that could have wrecked any deal. Source: jfklibrary.org; atomicarchive.com.

question: Dean Rusk whispered the crisis's most famous remark on 24 October 1962, about a stand-off at sea between Soviet ships and the American navy, and as the legend goes, that was the moment the United States stared down the Soviet fleet. Historians who later checked the records found that the showdown never happened. Why not?
answer: The Soviet missile ships had already turned back the day before, hundreds of miles away
choices: The Soviet missile ships had already turned back the day before, hundreds of miles away
The quarantine line had secretly been moved much closer to Cuba
Rusk had confused two different days of the crisis
The American ships had been ordered to hold their position out of range
context: The missile-carrying ships had reversed course on October 23 and were about 500 miles away, heading home, when Rusk spoke. The most famous moment of the crisis was a confrontation that wasn't. Source: washingtonpost.com; nsarchive.gwu.edu.

question: Kennedy's ExComm advisers faced two very different letters from Nikita Khrushchev late in October 1962. On Friday came a softer letter; on Saturday came a much harder one with a new demand. The advisers found a clever escape they nicknamed the 'Trollope ploy.' What did they do?
answer: Publicly answered only the softer Friday letter, ignoring the Turkey demand
choices: Publicly answered only the softer Friday letter, ignoring the Turkey demand
Leaked both letters to the press to embarrass Khrushchev
Sent a fake reply to stall while the navy prepared
Demanded Khrushchev choose between his own two letters
context: ExComm accepted the Friday letter's terms as if the Turkey demand had never been made. Privately, Robert Kennedy told Soviet Ambassador Dobrynin the U.S. would quietly remove the Jupiter missiles from Turkey too — a concession kept secret for years. Source: jfklibrary.org.

question: Vasili Arkhipov was a senior officer aboard the Soviet submarine B-59 on 27 October 1962, deep underwater and cut off from Moscow, as American depth charges pounded the hull. The crew thought war had already begun, and Captain Savitsky ordered the sub's nuclear torpedo readied to fire. Arkhipov would not agree, because he had realised what the Americans were really doing. What had he figured out?
answer: They were dropping signaling charges to force the sub to surface, not to sink it
choices: They were dropping signaling charges to force the sub to surface, not to sink it
They had already located and were about to ram the sub
They were Soviet ships mistaken for Americans in the dark
They had lost the sub's trail and were dropping charges at random
context: Launching the nuclear torpedo needed all three senior officers to agree; Arkhipov, the brigade chief of staff who happened to be aboard, calmed Savitsky, and the B-59 surfaced and turned home — the torpedo never fired. In 2002 the U.S. National Security Archive's Thomas Blanton called him 'the man who saved the world.' Source: nsarchive.gwu.edu; en.wikipedia.org.

question: Nikita Khrushchev, the Soviet leader, spoke over Radio Moscow on 28 October 1962, after thirteen days in which the world came closer to nuclear war than ever before. What did he say the Soviet Union would do with its missiles in Cuba?
answer: Dismantle the missiles and ship them back to the USSR
choices: Dismantle the missiles and ship them back to the USSR
Place the missiles under United Nations control
Trade the missiles for control of West Berlin
Keep the missiles but promise never to arm them
context: In return, the U.S. publicly pledged not to invade Cuba (and, secretly, to remove its missiles from Turkey). The world stepped back from the edge. Source: history.state.gov; atomicarchive.com.

question: Fidel Castro sailed from Mexico for Cuba late in 1956 with 82 fighters, set on overthrowing Cuba's American-backed dictator, Fulgencio Batista. Their boat was a little pleasure yacht meant to carry only 25 people, so it was dangerously overloaded, and only about 20 of the men survived the landing. What was the yacht called?
answer: Granma
choices: Granma
Corrina
Aurora
Santa Ana
context: The yacht Granma (named for a previous owner's grandmother) launched the revolution. Its name became so iconic in Cuba that the regime later named its official state newspaper Granma after it. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Revolution; history.com/articles/cuban-revolution

question: Che Guevara had only about 300 fighters outside Santa Clara late in 1958, in the last months of the Cuban revolution. The dictator Fulgencio Batista rushed an armored train there with 3,500 fresh soldiers and heavy guns. Che had a captured bulldozer and some dynamite. What did his band do to the train?
answer: Tore up the tracks and derailed it, then seized its weapons
choices: Tore up the tracks and derailed it, then seized its weapons
Loaded it with explosives and blew it off a high bridge
Set it ablaze and drove the troops out into open fields
Sealed the tunnel ahead so it sat trapped in the dark
context: Che's men ripped up the railway with the bulldozer, derailed the armored reinforcement train, and captured the soldiers along with all their guns. Santa Clara fell, and within hours Batista decided to flee Cuba. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Santa_Clara; worldpolitics.substack.com/p/battle-santa-clara-che-guevara-fidel-castro-cuba-revolution

question: Fidel Castro, a young lawyer, led about 160 rebels in an attack on the Moncada army barracks in Santiago de Cuba on 26 July 1953, and the attack failed. Put on trial, he acted as his own defense lawyer and kept talking for nearly four hours. He closed with one defiant line that became the slogan of his whole revolution. How did he end the speech?
answer: Condemn me, it does not matter; history will absolve me.
choices: Condemn me, it does not matter; history will absolve me.
Strike me down now; my words will outlast every one of you.
Judge me as you wish; the people have already judged you.
Kill the man before you; you can never kill the idea behind him.
context: "History Will Absolve Me" became the manifesto of Castro's cause. He was sentenced to 15 years but freed after just 22 months under public pressure (May 1955). Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_Will_Absolve_Me; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Revolution

question: Fidel Castro took power in Cuba in 1959 and for two years dodged the word 'communist,' promising only a national revolution. Then, on live television in December 1961, he settled the question with a statement about his own beliefs. What did Castro declare?
answer: I am a Marxist-Leninist, and shall be one until the end of my life.
choices: I am a Marxist-Leninist, and shall be one until the end of my life.
I am a revolutionary first, and a follower of Marx only second.
I am a socialist, and Cuba will gladly walk the Soviet road.
I am a communist in deed, though I march under no party's name.
context: With that sentence Castro confirmed the revolution had become communist, turning Cuba into the first and only one-party communist state in the Western Hemisphere, about 90 miles off the coast of Florida. Sources: history.com/this-day-in-history/december-2/castro-declares-himself-a-marxist-leninist; newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Fidel_Castro

question: Che Guevara, the young Argentine doctor whose face became a romantic icon on countless T-shirts, set down in 1967 exactly what he believed a true revolutionary had to become. He wrote it in his own words, in his 'Message to the Tricontinental.' Which phrase did he use?
answer: A cold-blooded, violent, selective killing machine
choices: A cold-blooded, violent, selective killing machine
A patient, humble, tireless teacher of the people
A gentle, selfless servant of the poor and the landless
A fearless, loyal, sleepless soldier for the cause
context: Castro had earlier put Che in charge of the La Cabana fortress in Havana, where revolutionary tribunals sent condemned men to the firing squad; the prison chaplain Javier Arzuaga said Che 'never overturned a sentence.' Researcher Armando Lago documented 179 names executed there. Sources: independent.org/article/2005/07/11/the-killing-machine/; en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Che_Guevara

question: Fidel Castro faced a crowd of thousands packed into the Peruvian embassy in Havana in April 1980, all of them Cubans desperate to escape his rule. His answer startled everyone: he opened a single port and told all who were unhappy that they were free to leave. Over the next five months, what happened through that one port?
answer: About 125,000 Cubans crossed the sea to Florida by boat.
choices: About 125,000 Cubans crossed the sea to Florida by boat.
About 9,000 Cubans crossed before Castro sealed it shut again.
About 40,000 Cubans crossed, most of them riding homemade rafts.
About 250,000 Cubans crossed in one frantic opening week.
context: They were nicknamed 'Marielitos' after the port of Mariel and sailed the 90-mile crossing to Key West in some 1,700 boats. The exodus never really stopped: 35,000 more 'balseros' fled on rafts in 1994, and since 1959 roughly 2.9 million Cubans have emigrated, most settling around Miami. Sources: history.com/articles/mariel-boatlift-castro-carter-cold-war; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_post-revolution_exodus

question: Sumer's scribes, in what is now southern Iraq, began pressing signs into small, soft tablets of clay around 3200 BC. That was the world's first writing, cuneiform, and every one of its signs is built from one tiny shape, repeated over and over. What is that shape?
answer: A wedge
choices: A wedge
A circle
A star
A cross
context: The very name says so: 'cuneiform' comes from the Latin cuneus, meaning 'wedge.' Every sign is built from little wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay. Source: worldhistory.org/cuneiform/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform

question: Scribes in Sumer wrote cuneiform, the world's first script, around 3200 BC, on slabs of soft, damp clay with a stylus. They made every tiny wedge-shaped mark the same way, one after another, across each tablet. To make each mark, what did a scribe do with the stylus?
answer: Pressed it straight down and lifted it back out
choices: Pressed it straight down and lifted it back out
Dragged it across the surface like a pen
Scratched thin lines with a sharp point
Dabbed the marks on with wet ink
context: Each straight-down press left one little wedge; the scribe lifted the stylus and pressed again for the next mark. The clay was then dried or baked hard. Source: cdli.ox.ac.uk cuneiform_writing_techniques ; britishmuseum.org/blog/how-write-cuneiform

question: Mesopotamian scribes, writing cuneiform in soft clay between the Tigris and the Euphrates, needed a stylus that was cheap, sharp-edged and easy to find. One plant grew thick in the rivers and marshes all around them. What did they make the stylus from?
answer: Reed
choices: Reed
Bone
Bronze
Bamboo
context: The prized species was Arundo donax, the giant reed of the marshes; the Sumerian word for the stylus literally meant 'tablet-reed.' You can sometimes still see the reed's fiber traces inside the wedge marks. Source: cdli.ox.ac.uk cuneiform_writing_techniques

question: The Sumerians and their neighbors in Mesopotamia wrote on little tablets of wet clay from about 3200 BC onward. Paper rots and leather crumbles, so most writing from that far back is long gone. Yet one common disaster that wrecks other records is exactly what preserved these tablets by the hundreds of thousands. What disaster?
answer: A fire that baked them rock-hard
choices: A fire that baked them rock-hard
A flood that swept over them
An earthquake that buried them deep
A long frost that sealed them
context: Fire that would burn a scroll to ash instead bakes wet clay into something like pottery. That is why an estimated half a million cuneiform tablets still survive in museums today — most of them ordinary receipts and ledgers. Source: loc.gov/collections/cuneiform-tablets

question: Nanni, a merchant of Ur, sent a furious letter on a small clay tablet to the dealer Ea-nasir around 1750 BC. It is the oldest customer complaint anyone has found, some 3,700 years old, and archaeologists dug it up long after both men were dust. What was Nanni so angry about?
answer: The copper he was sent was bad quality
choices: The copper he was sent was bad quality
The grain he bought was short-weighted
A promised marriage was called off
A loan he made was never repaid
context: Nanni wrote, 'What do you take me for, that you treat somebody like me with such contempt?' Other tablets found in Ea-nasir's house show he annoyed his other customers too — one wrote he was 'tired of receiving bad copper.' The tablet is now in the British Museum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complaint_tablet_to_Ea-nasir

question: Archaeologists digging at Uruk, the great Sumerian city that holds the oldest writing yet found, turned up clay tablets from around 3200 BC. The first scribes might have set down myths of the gods, hymns of praise or a king's boasts of victory. Yet about 85 percent of the very oldest tablets turned out to be one far plainer kind of thing. What was it?
answer: Records of who owed grain and beer
choices: Hymns sung to the temple gods
Boasts of a king's victories
Records of who owed grain and beer
Letters between distant families
context: The first scribes were essentially temple accountants. As the Metropolitan Museum puts it, 'this is how not poets or artists or philosophers, but rather middle managers brought about the birth of writing.' Source: metmuseum.org/essays/the-origins-of-writing ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-cuneiform

question: Someone in the Sumerian city of Uruk wrote a man's name on a small clay tablet about 5,300 years ago: Kushim. It is the oldest personal name that survives in any writing anywhere on Earth, and it did not belong to a king. What was Kushim?
answer: An accountant tracking a brewery's barley
choices: An accountant tracking a brewery's barley
A priest serving the temple of the gods
A king uniting the warring cities
A soldier guarding the high city walls
context: One Kushim tablet records 135,000 liters of barley to be delivered over 37 months for the brewery at the Temple of Inanna; his records cover nine cereals used to make eight kinds of beer. His name (signs KU + SHIM) is signed off like a clerk initialing a ledger — the first named human was tracking the beer supply. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kushim_(Uruk_period) ; metmuseum.org/essays/the-origins-of-writing

question: Sumerian scribes drew their first signs, around 3200 BC, as little pictures of the very things they were counting: a stalk of grain, a fish, a jar of beer. One sign meant 'to eat,' and it kept track of who had received a food ration. What little picture did the scribes draw for it?
answer: A head tipped toward a bowl
choices: A head tipped toward a bowl
Two hands around a round loaf
An open mouth beside a fish
A man seated at a low table
context: The earliest signs literally drew what they counted, so 'to eat' was a human head bent toward a bowl. Source: smarthistory.org/cuneiform/ ; archaeology.org/collection/the-worlds-oldest-writing/

question: Boys training to be scribes in Sumer, around 2000 BC, spent years in a strict school the Sumerians called the edubba, or House of Tablets. Day after day they copied their teacher's words onto wet clay until they knew hundreds of signs by heart. A Sumerian poem called 'Schooldays' tells what happened to a pupil who made sloppy marks. What was it?
answer: He was caned with a stout stick
choices: He was caned with a stout stick
He was fined a measure of grain
He was sent home in shame
He lost his daily bread ration
context: Break a rule or make careless marks and you got beaten with a stick. The Sumerian satire 'Schooldays' survives in 21-plus copies, which is how we know the scribal school's harsh routine. Source: worldhistory.org/article/2144/schooldays-sumerian-satire--the-scribal-life/

question: Traders in Sumer counted goods with little clay tokens long before writing: a cone for grain, an ovoid for a jar of oil. A trader sealed a shipment's tokens in a hollow clay ball, first pressing each into its wet outer skin so the contents could be read without breaking it. Then a clerk noticed the marks outside already said what was inside. What did the clerks do next?
answer: Threw the tokens away and kept the marks
choices: Threw the tokens away and kept the marks
Sealed even more tokens inside the ball
Baked the clay ball until it cracked open
Drew the tokens onto a strip of leather
context: Writing was 'invented' the day people realized the impressed marks made the tokens inside pointless — so they ditched the tokens and kept the marks on a flat tablet. A 3-D counter had become a 2-D sign. This is Denise Schmandt-Besserat's token-to-cuneiform theory; the hollow ball is called a bulla. Source: sites.utexas.edu/dsb/tokens/the-evolution-of-writing/

question: The scribes of Sumer hit a wall with their first picture-signs, in which a drawing of a fish stood for 'fish' and a jar stood for 'jar': no one can draw an idea like 'life' or 'to give.' Around 3000 BC they found a way past it, and cuneiform could suddenly record almost anything a person could say. How did a scribe write a word that could not be drawn?
answer: Borrowed a picture that sounded the same
choices: Borrowed a picture that sounded the same
Drew the idea in smaller pictures
Invented a brand-new sign for it
Left an empty space for it
context: This is the rebus trick — a picture used for its SOUND, not its meaning. The sign for an arrow, pronounced 'ti,' got reused to write 'til,' the word for 'life,' because they sounded alike. Now scribes could finally write anything you could say. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TI_(cuneiform) ; worldhistory.org/cuneiform/

question: Henry Rawlinson, a British army officer, set out in the 1830s and 1840s to crack cuneiform, a script no one alive had been able to read for about 1,500 years. The text he needed was King Darius's giant boast, carved in three languages. How did Rawlinson get a copy of that three-language text?
answer: Scaled a sheer cliff to copy a royal inscription
choices: Scaled a sheer cliff to copy a royal inscription
Dug up a buried library of clay tablets
Bought an old scribe's practice textbook
Found a bilingual coin in a market
context: Rawlinson climbed the Behistun cliff himself and had a local boy rig ropes to take papier-mache casts of the signs high on the rock face. Those copies let him finally decipher the script. Source: worldhistory.org/Behistun_Inscription/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decipherment_of_cuneiform

question: Cyril, a Byzantine monk, travelled north from Constantinople to Great Moravia in 863, sent by Emperor Michael III at the request of Prince Rastislav. Rastislav wanted the Slavs of his land to hear Scripture in their own tongue, but Slavic had never been written down, and there were no letters at all for its sounds. What did Cyril do so the Slavs could read Scripture?
answer: He invented a brand-new alphabet from scratch, the oldest known Slavic script
choices: He invented a brand-new alphabet from scratch, the oldest known Slavic script
He borrowed the Hebrew letters and read them backwards
He carved word-pictures into wood the way the Egyptians did
He wrote the Slavic sounds using only Latin letters
context: Cyril created the Glagolitic alphabet, the oldest known Slavic script, with 41 letters. Its very first letter, azu, was shaped like a cross, marking the script as a Christian creation. The name Glagolitic comes from the Old Church Slavonic word glagol, meaning 'word' or 'to utter.' Source: Wikipedia, Glagolitic script.

question: Cyril, the Byzantine monk who brought Scripture to the Slavs in their own tongue, never made the alphabet that is named for him, though hundreds of millions of people now write Russian, Bulgarian and Serbian in it. Who created the Cyrillic alphabet?
answer: His own disciples, at a literary school in the Bulgarian Empire
choices: His own disciples, at a literary school in the Bulgarian Empire
Cyril's older brother Methodius, alone in a German prison
The Emperor Michael III, who had sent the brothers out
Pope Adrian II, who had blessed their Slavic mission
context: Cyril's followers built the Cyrillic script later at the Preslav Literary School in the First Bulgarian Empire, building on his earlier Glagolitic work. Naming it 'Cyrillic' was an act of homage to their teacher, not a record of who wrote it. Source: Wikipedia, Cyrillic script; wordopedia.org Cyrillic guide.

question: Cyrus Field's crew set out in 1858 to do something no one had ever done: string a telegraph cable clear across the Atlantic seabed. Two warships, Niagara of the American navy and Agamemnon of the British, met in the middle of the open ocean, and there their crews joined the two ends of their cable. What did the two ships do next?
answer: Steamed off in opposite directions, one toward Ireland and one toward Newfoundland
choices: Steamed off in opposite directions, one toward Ireland and one toward Newfoundland
Sailed side by side together all the way to the coast of Newfoundland
Towed the spliced cable back to the harbor they had started from
Anchored in place and waited for a third ship to finish the crossing
context: With the two cable ends spliced in mid-Atlantic, USS Niagara steamed west toward Newfoundland and HMS Agamemnon east toward Ireland, unreeling cable behind them so the line met in the middle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transatlantic_telegraph_cable.

question: New Yorkers threw a wild celebration in August 1858, when the first telegraph message ever to cross the Atlantic came through, with a huge parade and fireworks over the city's main government building. The party got so out of hand that the fireworks did something nobody had planned. What happened?
answer: The fireworks set the dome of City Hall on fire
choices: The fireworks set the dome of City Hall on fire
The fireworks were rained out before they could begin
The fireworks frightened the parade horses into a stampede
The fireworks were banned by the mayor partway through
context: New York's 1858 cable celebration grew so wild that the fireworks ignited the dome of City Hall itself. Source: spectrum.ieee.org/the-first-transatlantic-telegraph-cable-was-a-bold-beautiful-failure.

question: Cyrus the Great began as the king of Anshan, a small realm in today's southern Iran. In roughly twenty years he built something no one had built before. What had Cyrus built by the time he died in 530 BC?
answer: The largest empire the world had yet seen
choices: The largest empire the world had yet seen
The first city ever built of solid stone
A wall stretching across the whole of Asia
The oldest library in the ancient world
context: Cyrus reigned 559-530 BC and founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire, the biggest the world had yet seen, going from a minor king to a superpower ruler in about two decades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_the_Great

question: Cyrus the Great marched into Babylon around 539 BC and toppled its empire, and inside the city he found the Jews, captives whom King Nebuchadnezzar had dragged from Jerusalem decades earlier. Instead of keeping them enslaved the way other kings had, Cyrus issued a decree, and the Book of Ezra records it. What did his decree let the captives do?
answer: Return to Jerusalem and rebuild their Temple
choices: Return to Jerusalem and rebuild their Temple
Serve as soldiers in his royal army
Settle new farmland along the Indus River
Build a great palace for him at Babylon
context: The Edict of Cyrus, recorded in the biblical Book of Ezra, ended decades of the Babylonian Captivity and launched the building of the Second Temple in Jerusalem. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Cyrus

question: Babylon stood behind walls far too strong to storm when Cyrus the Great came against it in 539 BC. The great Euphrates, though, flowed right through the middle of the city, passing in under its towering walls, and Cyrus's engineers used the river itself to take Babylon with hardly a battle. What did they do to the Euphrates?
answer: Lowered it and walked up the bare riverbed under the walls
choices: Lowered it and walked up the bare riverbed under the walls
Dammed it into a lake to flood the whole city out
Poisoned it to sicken the city's defenders within
Filled it with burning oil and set it alight upstream
context: Greek and Babylonian accounts say the Persians dropped the level of the Euphrates and waded along the exposed riverbed, in under the walls, while the gates stood open. Cyrus's general Gobryas (Ugbaru) marched in, and Cyrus's own cylinder boasts that the god Marduk 'made him enter his city Babylon without fighting or battle.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Babylon ; https://www.livius.org/sources/content/cyrus-cylinder/cyrus-cylinder-translation/

question: Cyrus the Great marched against Croesus of Lydia, whose horse-mounted cavalry was the most feared in the region. On a general's advice, Cyrus lined up his shaggy baggage camels at the very front of his army. What happened when the Lydian cavalry charged?
answer: Their horses panicked at the camels and bolted
choices: Their horses panicked at the camels and bolted
Their arrows bounced off the camels' hide
Their riders dismounted to fight on foot
Their commander surrendered on the spot
context: Horses panic at the smell and sight of camels. The trick came from the Mede general Harpagus, and it broke the dreaded Lydian cavalry at the Battle of Thymbra around 546 BC. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/Battle_of_Thymbra/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Thymbra

question: Cyrus the Great had his triumph at Babylon written on a clay cylinder, and on it he piled up grand titles: 'king of the world, great king, mighty king, king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad.' He crowned the list with one ancient Mesopotamian phrase that meant ruler of absolutely everything. How did Cyrus style himself?
answer: King of the four quarters
choices: King of the four quarters
Lord of the rising sun
Shepherd of the seven seas
Master of a thousand cities
context: 'King of the four quarters [of the world]' was the old Mesopotamian phrase for ruler of everything. It appears on the Cyrus Cylinder, a barrel-shaped clay object dug up at Babylon in 1879 and now in the British Museum. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/cyrus-cylinder/cyrus-cylinder-translation/ (lines 20-21)

question: Herodotus tells how Cyrus the Great captured Croesus, the richest king in the world, and set him atop a burning pyre. As the flames climbed, Croesus cried out one name over and over: a wise Athenian who had once warned him to 'count no man happy until he is dead.' Whose name did Croesus cry from the fire?
answer: Solon
choices: Solon
Homer
Midas
Apollo
context: Intrigued by the name, Cyrus ordered the fire quenched (in the Lydian version a sudden rainstorm put it out), and he kept Croesus as a trusted advisor for the rest of his life. Legend, told by Herodotus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croesus

question: Tomyris, queen of the nomadic Massagetae far to the northeast, faced Cyrus the Great in his last war. By Herodotus's account, Cyrus had killed her son with a wine-soaked banquet trap, and the grieving queen swore a terrible vow. After she defeated and killed Cyrus, what did Tomyris do to keep her vow?
answer: Dipped his head in a skin full of blood
choices: Dipped his head in a skin full of blood
Sealed his crown inside a block of ice
Scattered his ashes across the open steppe
Hung his banner from her own saddle
context: Tomyris had vowed 'I will give you your fill of blood'; finding Cyrus's body, she dipped his severed head into a blood-filled skin and said 'I give you your fill of blood.' Legend, told by Herodotus. Sources: https://www.cais-soas.com/CAIS/History/hakhamaneshian/herod_tomyr.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomyris

question: Alexander the Great marched into Pasargadae about two hundred years after Cyrus the Great died, and went to see the tomb of the Persian king he had admired all his life. He found it broken into, the golden coffin pried open and the body flung out. What did Alexander order done about it?
answer: Restore the tomb and punish the robbers
choices: Restore the tomb and punish the robbers
Carry Cyrus's bones back to Macedon
Seal the ruins and leave them forever
Build a new tomb beside his own
context: The historian Arrian, using an eyewitness who marched with Alexander, records that the tomb had held a golden coffin and couch, purple Median robes, scimitars, and jeweled earrings. The tomb still stands in Iran today. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/arrian/anabasis/alexander-and-the-tomb-of-cyrus/

question: In the book of the prophet Isaiah, God spoke straight to Cyrus the Great, the Persian conqueror, and gave him a sacred Hebrew title that the Bible gives no other non-Jew. God also said Cyrus would set the exiles free 'not for a price or reward.' What title did Isaiah give Cyrus?
answer: The Lord's anointed
choices: The Lord's anointed
The lion of Judah
The shield of Abraham
The voice in the wilderness
context: The Hebrew word in Isaiah 45:1 is 'mashiach' (messiah), meaning anointed one. Cyrus, a Persian who let the exiles go home after he took Babylon in 539 BC, is the only non-Jew ever given that title in the Bible.

question: Babylon's priests welcomed Cyrus the Great when he took their city, for he did not tear down their gods. His cylinder even claims that Babylon's own chief god had chosen him, calling out his name and, in its words, taking 'a righteous king, his favourite, by the hand.' Which god did Cyrus say had picked him to rule Babylon?
answer: Marduk
choices: Marduk
Ahura Mazda
Baal
Osiris
context: By presenting himself as the rescuer of Babylon's own religion rather than imposing Persian gods, Cyrus won over the Babylonian priesthood, who welcomed him. Marduk was Babylon's chief god; Ahura Mazda was the Persians' own. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/cyrus-cylinder/cyrus-cylinder-translation/ (lines 11-12)

question: Xenophon, a Greek soldier and writer, admired Cyrus the Great so deeply that he wrote an entire book holding the Persian king up as the model of the perfect ruler. It went on to become a favorite handbook of Western statesmen, and one American founder kept two copies of it in his library. Which founder?
answer: Thomas Jefferson
choices: Thomas Jefferson
Benjamin Franklin
Alexander Hamilton
John Adams
context: A Persian king became a textbook for Western statesmen. Thomas Jefferson owned two copies of the Cyropaedia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_the_Great

question: Dwight Eisenhower launched D-Day against German-occupied France on 6 June 1944 with nearly 160,000 American, British and Canadian troops. What record does D-Day still hold?
answer: the largest seaborne invasion in history
choices: the largest seaborne invasion in history
the longest siege in all of history
the first naval battle in history
the costliest air raid in history
context: D-Day, June 6, 1944, remains the largest seaborne invasion ever attempted. Nearly 160,000 Allied troops landed along about 50 miles of the Normandy coast in occupied France on that one day. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/media/press-releases/d-day-fact-sheet-0

question: The invasion's planners split the Normandy coast into five code-named beaches for D-Day, 6 June 1944, when Allied troops would storm ashore to break Nazi Germany's grip on Europe. Two of the beaches went to the Americans, two to the British and one to the Canadians. Which two did the American troops take?
answer: Utah and Omaha
choices: Utah and Omaha
Gold and Sword
Juno and Sword
Gold and Juno
context: The five code-named beaches: the Americans landed at Utah and Omaha, the British at Gold and Sword, and the Canadians at Juno. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/media/press-releases/d-day-fact-sheet-0

question: Andrew Higgins, a stubborn small-time boat maker from New Orleans, built the landing boats that dropped Allied soldiers onto the Normandy sand on D-Day, 36 at a time, under German fire. After the war Dwight Eisenhower, who had run the invasion, said a startling thing about him. What did Eisenhower call Higgins?
answer: the man who won the war for us
choices: the man who won the war for us
the man who never lost a bet
the man who saved the British
the man who built the fastest boat
context: These were the 'Higgins boats' (LCVPs), plywood landing craft holding 36 men. Eisenhower said Andrew Higgins 'is the man who won the war for us' — over 23,000 of the boats were built. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LCVP_(United_States)

question: The first waves of American soldiers on D-Day came ashore on a beach where steep cliffs rose over a bare, open tidal flat with no cover at all. They were cut down there, and the toll on that one beach came to about 2,400 men killed or wounded. What grim nickname did the beach earn?
answer: Bloody Omaha
choices: Bloody Omaha
Hell's Half-Acre
the Devil's Gate
the Iron Coast
context: Omaha Beach earned the name 'Bloody Omaha.' Steep bluffs rose behind a bare tidal flat; Company A of the 116th Infantry was nearly wiped out in the first waves, and Omaha alone cost roughly 2,400 Allied casualties. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaha_Beach

question: John Steele, an American paratrooper, dropped in the darkness before dawn and drifted down onto the village of Sainte-Mère-Église, where his parachute snagged on the church steeple. Wounded and dangling above the firefight below, what did Steele do for the next two hours?
answer: hung limp and played dead
choices: hung limp and played dead
cut his lines and dropped
climbed onto the bell tower
called out for the medics
context: John Steele's chute snagged on the church steeple at Sainte-Mère-Église. Wounded in the foot, he hung there feigning death for about two hours as the firefight raged below. An effigy of him still hangs from the church today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Steele_(paratrooper)

question: Bill Millin, a Scottish piper, marched up and down the open sand of Sword Beach while men fell around him, carrying no weapon at all, only his bagpipes, on which he played 'Highland Laddie.' German snipers, captured later, were asked why they had never shot him. What did they say?
answer: they thought he had gone mad
choices: they thought he had gone mad
they had run clean out of bullets
they had been ordered to surrender
they could not hear him coming
context: On Sword Beach, piper Bill Millin marched along the sand unarmed, playing 'Highland Laddie' as men fell around him. Captured German snipers later said they didn't shoot him because they thought he'd gone mad. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Millin

question: James Stagg, a Group Captain and the weatherman for the invasion, watched a storm sweep the English Channel until he spotted one brief break in it. Dwight Eisenhower put the landings off by a day, then launched the whole invasion with three plain words. What did he say?
answer: "OK, we'll go."
choices: "OK, we'll go."
"God help us."
"Open the gates."
"Begin the assault."
context: Whether D-Day happened at all came down to one forecast. Group Captain James Stagg spotted a brief break in a Channel storm; Eisenhower postponed one day, then gave the go-order with the words 'OK, we'll go.' Source: https://www.archives.gov/publications/prologue/2014/spring/d-day-ok-well-go

question: James Rudder, a lieutenant colonel, had to get his American Rangers up 100-foot sheer cliffs at Pointe du Hoc on D-Day, under German machine-gun fire, to reach a battery of huge coastal guns at the top. Alongside their grapnels and ropes, they hauled one very unlikely piece of equipment. What did the Rangers use to scale the cliff face?
answer: extension ladders from the London Fire Brigade
choices: extension ladders from the London Fire Brigade
folding bridges flown in from America
iron spikes hammered into the rock
scaffolding towers built on the beach
context: At Pointe du Hoc, Lt. Col. James Rudder's 2nd Ranger Battalion scaled 100-foot cliffs under fire to knock out a German gun battery, using grapnels, ropes, and 100-foot extension ladders borrowed from the London Fire Brigade and mounted on amphibious DUKW trucks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointe_du_Hoc

question: The Allies tricked the Germans before D-Day into guarding the wrong stretch of French coast. In southeast England, across the water from Calais, they staged a phantom army, put the famous American general George Patton in fake command of it, and let German spy planes photograph its camps from the air. What was this ghost army actually made of?
answer: inflatable rubber tanks and dummy landing craft
choices: inflatable rubber tanks and dummy landing craft
wooden forts and painted cannon
empty tents and idle trucks
cardboard planes and straw soldiers
context: The deception was Operation Fortitude — a fake army (FUSAG) under General Patton in southeast England, built from inflatable rubber tanks and dummy landing craft that looked real from the air. Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/d-days-parachuting-dummies-and-inflatable-tanks

question: British and American engineers faced a hard problem after the Normandy landings of 6 June 1944: the Allies had seized no working French port, and an invading army cannot be fed, fuelled and armed across open beaches for long. Instead of waiting weeks to capture a port, what did the Allies do to land their supplies?
answer: towed two whole artificial harbours across the Channel
choices: towed two whole artificial harbours across the Channel
laid a floating railway bridge across the Channel
parachuted every crate of supplies from the air
pumped fuel and food through an undersea pipeline
context: Having no captured port, the Allies brought their own: two huge artificial 'Mulberry' harbours towed across the Channel in pieces — concrete caissons called Phoenix, floating roadways called Whales, and breakwaters of scuttled old ships called Gooseberries. Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/how-the-mulberry-harbours-kept-d-day-afloat

question: Allied planners hoped their phantom army would fool Hitler for two weeks, convincing him that the real invasion would strike far to the north, at the Pas-de-Calais, and buying the landings a little time. How long did Hitler actually hold his reinforcements back from Normandy?
answer: about seven weeks
choices: about seven weeks
about three days
about two weeks
about one year
context: The deception worked beyond all hope: Hitler was so sure the real invasion would land at the Pas-de-Calais that he held back reinforcements from Normandy for about seven weeks. The Allies had only hoped to buy two. Source: https://www.history.co.uk/article/operation-fortitude-the-d-day-deception-campaign-that-fooled-the-nazis

question: Dwight Eisenhower wrote a short note before D-Day, to be released only if the landings failed. Drafting it, he crossed out a line written in the passive voice, 'the troops have been withdrawn,' and rewrote it so that the responsibility fell squarely on him. How did the rewritten line read?
answer: "I have withdrawn the troops."
choices: "I have withdrawn the troops."
"I must answer for this loss."
"I alone gave the final order."
"I accept the blame in full."
context: Eisenhower handwrote a note to release if the invasion failed, taking sole blame: 'If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone' — he underlined 'mine alone.' He crossed out the passive 'the troops have been withdrawn' and rewrote it in the active voice, 'I have withdrawn the troops,' so responsibility landed on himself. He kept the note in his wallet. Sources: https://veteransbreakfastclub.org/ikes-d-day-failure-message/ ; https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna55329990

question: Dahomey's kings killed war captives and condemned criminals at a yearly festival in their capital, Abomey, so that the victims' spirits could serve the dead kings in the next world. King Agaja made it a royal custom around 1730, and the Fon called it the 'yearly head business.' What grim nickname did English explorers give the festival?
answer: the Watering of the Graves
choices: the Watering of the Graves
the Feast of Returning Kings
the Gathering of the Shades
the Night of Open Doors
context: The Fon name was 'xwetanu' ('yearly head business'); the English translated it as the 'Annual Customs' and also called it the 'Watering of the Graves,' because its central rite was killing victims to honor and serve Dahomey's dead kings. The rite was formalized around 1730 by King Agaja and continued until France conquered Dahomey in the 1890s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annual_Customs_of_Dahomey; face2faceafrica.com.

question: The Fon of Dahomey believed their departed rulers still held court in a spirit world the living could not see, and sometimes the living king needed to send them a message. At the yearly Customs, he whispered it to a condemned prisoner. According to European eyewitnesses, what happened to the prisoner then?
answer: He was sent with a knife across the throat to carry the words to the dead kings
choices: He was sent with a knife across the throat to carry the words to the dead kings
He was sealed alive inside an old king's tomb to deliver the words below
He was set loose to climb the sacred hill and shout the words to the sky
He was burned at the festival fire so the smoke would lift the words upward
context: The Fon held that the visible world was only part of a larger reality. At the Customs the king dispatched 'messengers' to the council of dead kings: the message was whispered to a condemned prisoner, who was then killed with a knife across the throat so he could carry the words to the ancestors. The British explorer Richard Francis Burton was sent to King Gelele in 1863-64 to protest the killings and wrote them up in 'A Mission to Gelele, King of Dahome' (1864). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annual_Customs_of_Dahomey.

question: British troops entered Benin City in February 1897 and found, in the Oba's palace, raised platforms holding rows of the cast heads now famous in museums as the Benin Bronzes, each fitted with a tall carved ivory tusk. These were sacrificial altars, and the heads and tusks were not clean. According to the expedition surgeon, Dr. Felix Norman Roth, what covered them?
answer: a thick crust of dried human blood
choices: a thick crust of dried human blood
a layer of beaten gold leaf
a wash of bright red palm oil
a coating of pale river chalk
context: Dr. Felix Norman Roth recorded that the celebrated Benin bronze heads and ivory altar-tusks were caked over with dried human blood; sacrificed bodies lay around the palace 'in various stages of evisceration.' Reporters who marched with the expedition wrote that the city 'reeked of human blood,' and Commander R.H. Bacon titled his 1897 book 'Benin: The City of Blood.' The same royal court that produced the celebrated artwork used these altars for blood sacrifice — both are part of one honest record. Source: culturalpropertynews.org (citing Felix Norman Roth); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benin_Expedition_of_1897.

question: Dante Alighieri imagined himself walking down into Hell in his great poem, the Divine Comedy, with the long-dead Roman poet Virgil as his guide. A grim warning stood over the gate of Hell, ending in its most famous words. What did it tell all who entered?
answer: 'Abandon all hope, you who enter here.'
choices: 'Turn back, for the dead alone may pass.'
'Abandon all hope, you who enter here.'
'Weep now, for tears are forbidden within.'
'Forget your name, you who enter here.'
context: The full inscription says the gate was built by divine Power, highest Wisdom, and primal Love, and that it is eternal; it ends 'Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate.' Source: Wikiquote: Divine Comedy / CliffsNotes Inferno Canto III / WIST Quotations (Hollander translation).

question: Satan stood at the very bottom of Dante's Hell, locked in ice up to his waist, a three-faced giant chewing a famous traitor in each of his mouths. Dante crammed the worst traitor of all in head-first, with only his kicking legs left sticking out. Who was it?
answer: Judas Iscariot
choices: Marcus Brutus
Judas Iscariot
Gaius Cassius
Pontius Pilate
context: Judas, who betrayed Jesus, is the central mouth's victim, head-first. From the other two mouths, Brutus and Cassius -- who killed Julius Caesar -- dangle by their legs. Source: Wikipedia: Dante's Satan / SparkNotes Inferno Canto XXXIV / CliffsNotes Canto XXXIV.

question: Dante wrote his masterpiece not in Latin, the language of all serious learning in his day, but in the everyday Tuscan speech of ordinary people, so that they could read it. That daring choice won him an honorary title that has stuck ever since. What is it?
answer: the Father of the Italian Language
choices: the Tongue of the Old Romans
the Father of the Italian Language
the Voice of Old Florence
the Last of the Roman Poets
context: His Tuscan vernacular became the basis of modern standard Italian, which is why he is called the Father of the Italian Language. Source: FIRSTonline 'The Divine Comedy and its consequences on the language' / Wikipedia: Dante Alighieri.

question: Virgil, the long-dead Roman poet, guided Dante through Hell and up most of Purgatory, but at the border of Paradise he had to stop and turn back: as a virtuous pagan, he was barred from Heaven. Dante made Virgil stand for a power that could lead a soul right to the door of the divine, but no further. What power was it?
answer: human reason
choices: blind fate
human reason
noble courage
mortal fear
context: Virgil represents human reason: it can carry Dante through Hell and up Purgatory, but reason alone cannot enter Heaven, so a new guide takes over at the gate of Paradise. Source: Study.com 'Virgil in Dante's Inferno' / University of Leeds Discover Dante: Purgatorio / Britannica: The Divine Comedy.

question: The dead Pope Nicholas III, stuffed head-down in a burning pit of Dante's Hell, heard footsteps and took the newcomer for his foretold successor. Dante set his journey at Easter 1300, when Pope Boniface VIII was still alive, but wrote the poem from about 1308 to 1321, and he used the gap to damn Boniface among the simonists, those who bought and sold holy office. What did Nicholas cry out?
answer: 'Are you standing there already, Boniface?'
choices: 'Have you come to take my place, Boniface?'
'Are you standing there already, Boniface?'
'Why have they sent you here, Boniface?'
'Do you repent at last, Boniface?'
context: Boniface VIII had been Dante's enemy in the feud that got the poet exiled from Florence. By having Nicholas III mistake the visitor for Boniface, Dante condemns a still-living pope to Hell. Source: Shmoop 'Pope Boniface VIII in Inferno' / CliffsNotes Inferno Canto XIX / New World Encyclopedia: Boniface VIII.

question: Li Er, tradition says, was the real name of the sage who taught the Way of Daoism in China in the 500s BC. He comes down to us instead as Laozi, one of the most famous names in all of Chinese thought, yet that is a title of respect, not a personal name. What does Laozi mean?
answer: Old Master
choices: Old Master
Heavenly Sage
the Nameless One
the First Teacher
context: Tradition says his family name was Li and his given name Er (also called Dan). 'Laozi' (Lao = old, zi = master/child) is a title of respect, not a birth name. Source: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/laozi/

question: Laozi, the sage who by tradition founded Daoism in China in the 500s BC, did not live as a wandering hermit or as a warlord. Tradition says he held a humble post at the court of the Zhou kings instead. What was his job there?
answer: Keeper of the royal archives
choices: Keeper of the royal archives
Commander of the king's army
The court's chief astrologer
Collector of the royal taxes
context: He was, in effect, the royal librarian — minding the king's records and books. The image of the great sage as a humble archivist is part of his charm. Source: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/laozi/

question: As the Zhou kingdom rotted from within, the legend says, the old sage Laozi turned his back on it and rode west, never to return. At the Hangu Pass a gatekeeper stopped him and would not let him go on. What does the legend say Laozi did before he passed through, never to be seen again?
answer: He wrote the whole Tao Te Ching on the spot, then rode on
choices: He wrote the whole Tao Te Ching on the spot, then rode on
He turned back toward the capital and was lost to history
He handed the gatekeeper a single jade tablet and left
He stayed and taught the gatekeeper for ten long years
context: The legend (in the Inward Training tradition retold at iep.utm.edu) says the gatekeeper Yin Xi recognized a sage and would not let him pass until he set down his wisdom — so Laozi wrote the roughly 5,000-character book then disappeared westward forever. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/laozi/

question: Laozi, the Chinese sage said to have written the Tao Te Ching more than two thousand years ago, fitted his whole book into only about 5,000 characters.
