context: These figures are called shabti (or ushabti). The spell made them answer 'Here I am!' and march off to work so their owner could enjoy paradise in peace. Source: Egypt Fun Tours, https://egyptfuntours.com/blog/egyptian-shabti-meaning-afterlife-servants/  (Legend.)

question: Karl Richard Lepsius, a German Egyptologist, named the Egyptians' scrolls of afterlife spells in 1842, calling them the Book of the Dead. Some of those spells were more than 4,000 years old, and the Egyptians had never called them by his title. What did the Egyptians call them?
answer: The Spells of Coming Forth by Day
choices: The Spells of Coming Forth by Day
The Litany of the Setting Sun
The Scroll of the Two Lands
The Words of the Silent Ones
context: In Egyptian it is 'rw nw prt m hrw' — the Spells of Coming Forth by Day. Its oldest spells trace back through the Coffin Texts and Pyramid Texts and are over 4,000 years old. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_the_Dead

question: One Theban took to his grave, around 1250 BC, the finest copy of the Book of the Dead known: a scroll some 78 feet long that the British Museum bought in 1888. He was no pharaoh and no king. Who was he?
answer: Ani, a royal scribe
choices: Ani, a royal scribe
Imhotep, a temple architect
Sinuhe, a palace guard
Hesy-Ra, a court dentist
context: It is called the Papyrus of Ani, made around 1250 BCE for Ani, a royal scribe of Thebes — proof that even a working scribe, not just royalty, could be sent into the afterlife with the full book of spells. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papyrus_of_Ani

question: Arthur Sasse, a photographer, begged one more picture from Albert Einstein, who was leaving a party on his 72nd birthday in 1951. Tired of smiling for cameras all day, the old man pulled a face at the lens. What was Einstein doing in the photo?
answer: Sticking out his tongue
choices: Sticking out his tongue
Crossing both his eyes
Covering up his face
Puffing out his cheeks
context: UPI photographer Arthur Sasse snapped it on March 14, 1951; Einstein loved the shot so much he ordered nine prints for friends. Source: https://rarehistoricalphotos.com/albert-einstein-tongue-1951/

question: Albert Einstein wrote down E = mc² in 1905, and people have recited it ever since. Its meaning is stranger than it looks: it says that two things everyone thinks of as separate are really one thing wearing two different disguises. What did Einstein's equation claim?
answer: Mass and energy are the same thing
choices: Mass and energy are the same thing
Light and sound travel together
Gravity and magnetism are equal
Time and distance never change
context: Because you multiply by the speed of light (about 186,000 miles per second) squared, even a pinch of matter holds enormous energy -- the principle behind both the Sun's furnace and the atomic bomb. Source: https://www.discovermagazine.com/the-sciences/e-mc2-what-does-einsteins-most-famous-equation-mean

question: Albert Einstein was a 26-year-old patent clerk in Bern, ranked 'Technical Expert, Third Class,' when he wrote four scientific papers in his spare time in 1905. Each one rewrote a corner of physics. What do scientists call that year of his?
answer: Einstein's 'miracle year'
choices: Einstein's 'miracle year'
Einstein's 'patent year'
Einstein's 'Bern lectures'
Einstein's 'first theory'
context: In Latin it is the 'annus mirabilis.' No other scientist has matched four field-changing papers in twelve months -- and he did it as a junior clerk, not a professor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: Arthur Eddington, a British astronomer, sailed to the island of Principe off West Africa in May 1919 to photograph a total eclipse of the Sun. He meant to test Einstein's bold claim about the Sun's pull on starlight. What had happened to the light of the stars near the Sun in his photographs?
answer: The starlight bent off its straight path
choices: The starlight bent off its straight path
The starlight faded almost to nothing
The starlight turned a deep red
The starlight split into two beams
context: Eddington's result matched Einstein's prediction exactly and made Einstein the most famous scientist in the world almost overnight. Source: https://earthsky.org/human-world/may-29-1919-solar-eclipse-einstein-relativity/

question: Albert Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, but not for relativity, the theory that had made him famous: the committee felt it was still too new and too debated to honor. Its citation named a different discovery of his. Which discovery did the Nobel committee cite?
answer: The law of the photoelectric effect
choices: The law of the photoelectric effect
The motion of atoms inside fluids
The theory of special relativity
The equation linking mass and energy
context: The official citation read 'for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect' -- not for relativity, which the committee thought too contested. At the 1923 ceremony Einstein lectured on relativity anyway. Source: https://www.advancedsciencenews.com/the-dramatic-story-behind-general-relativitys-nobel-prize-snub/

question: Thomas Harvey, a pathologist, carried out the autopsy on Albert Einstein when the physicist who had rewritten space and time died in 1955. During it Harvey did something the family had never allowed, and he kept quiet about it. What did Harvey do?
answer: He secretly kept the brain
choices: He secretly kept the brain
He photographed the whole body
He preserved the heart in a jar
He embalmed the body for display
context: Harvey removed Einstein's brain, sliced it into about 170 pieces, and stored them in jars for over forty years before finally returning them to a Princeton hospital in 1998. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Stoltz_Harvey

question: Albert Einstein said the 'happiest thought of my life' struck him in 1907 while he sat in his chair at the patent office. It was a simple picture of an ordinary person, and from it he reasoned that gravity and acceleration are one and the same, the seed of general relativity. What was the thought?
answer: A falling person feels no weight
choices: A falling person feels no weight
A running person feels no air
A spinning person sees no stars
A sleeping person hears no sound
context: If you fall freely, you don't feel your own weight at all -- so Einstein realized that 'gravity' and simply 'accelerating' must be two names for one thing. That insight grew into general relativity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%27s_thought_experiments

question: One twin rockets away at nearly the speed of light, travels far and comes home, while the other stays on Earth the whole time. Einstein's relativity says that time itself can run at different speeds. When the two stand side by side again, what does relativity say has happened to them?
answer: The twin who traveled is younger
choices: The twin who traveled is younger
The twin who stayed is younger
The twins have switched bodies
The twins are exactly the same age
context: Time runs slower for whoever is moving fast (time dilation), so the rocket twin ages less. This 'twin paradox' is the most famous thought experiment in relativity. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/time-and-the-twin-paradox-2006-02/

question: The young state of Israel asked Albert Einstein in 1952 to take one of the highest jobs a country can give a person, not a prize or a medal. Einstein turned it down, saying he lacked the knack for dealing with people. What had Israel asked him to become?
answer: Its president
choices: Its president
Its chief rabbi
Its army general
Its court inventor
context: Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion had privately worried, 'But if he accepts, we are in trouble.' Einstein declined, citing his lack of 'the natural aptitude and the experience to deal properly with people.' Source: https://www.britannica.com/story/the-time-albert-einstein-was-asked-to-be-president-of-israel

question: Engineers who run the GPS satellites have to correct their clocks every day, because those clocks run about 38 millionths of a second a day faster than clocks on the ground, just as Einstein's relativity predicts. If the engineers ever stopped, a phone's place on the map would slide further off each day. About how far off would it be after just one day?
answer: Several miles
choices: Several miles
Only a few inches
About one single foot
A few hundred feet
context: The satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day (45 from weaker gravity up high, minus 7 from their speed). Ignore that, and GPS positions would drift off by several miles every single day. Source: https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/pogge.1/Ast162/Unit5/gps.html

question: Two bolts of lightning struck a railway track at the same instant in one of Einstein's thought experiments, one far ahead and one far behind, for a man watching from the embankment. A passenger raced past on a fast train at that very moment. Einstein worked out that the passenger would not see the timing the watcher saw. For the passenger, when did the two bolts strike?
answer: One clearly struck before the other
choices: One clearly struck before the other
Both struck at the exact same instant
Both struck just after the train passed
Both struck the instant the train stopped
context: Two events that are simultaneous for one observer are NOT simultaneous for another who is moving -- whether two things happen 'at the same time' depends on who is moving. This is the relativity of simultaneity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%27s_thought_experiments

question: Einstein argued that gravity is no invisible rope pulling things downward. His general relativity predicted that even a beam of light, which has no weight for any rope to grab, will swerve as it passes a heavy object like the Sun. In his theory, what bends the light's path?
answer: The Sun's mass curves the space around it
choices: The Sun's mass curves the space around it
The Sun's heat shoves the beam aside
The Sun's magnetism pulls the beam inward
The Sun's brightness drags the beam along
context: Physicist John Wheeler put it in one line: 'Matter tells spacetime how to curve; spacetime tells matter how to move.' Gravity isn't a pull -- mass bends spacetime, and objects (and even light) simply follow the curves. Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/John_Archibald_Wheeler

question: Joseph Nicholson, a congressman from Maryland, was so sick in February 1801 that he could barely stand, yet the House of Representatives was balloting day after day to choose the next president, Thomas Jefferson or Aaron Burr. Maryland's vote hung on him. How did Nicholson keep casting his vote for Jefferson?
answer: He had himself carried into the Capitol on a stretcher to cast each ballot
choices: He had himself carried into the Capitol on a stretcher to cast each ballot
He mailed in a signed ballot from his sickbed every morning
He sent his wife to the Capitol to vote in his place
He had a doctor declare him healthy so he could attend
context: Joseph Hopper Nicholson was gravely ill in February 1801 but had himself carried on a stretcher to the Capitol to keep casting his ballots for Jefferson. Without his sickbed vote, Maryland's delegation would have flipped to Burr. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Hopper_Nicholson (citing John Ferling, Adams vs. Jefferson, p.187).

question: Thomas Jefferson and Aaron Burr, his own running mate, tied at 73 electoral votes each in 1800, and the choice fell to the House of Representatives, voting state by state. The chamber jammed for 35 ballots over six days, and partisans spoke openly of settling the matter by force. Delaware's single congressman, James Bayard, controlled his entire state's vote by himself. What did he do on the 36th ballot?
answer: He switched from voting for Burr to abstaining, ending the deadlock
choices: He switched from voting for Burr to abstaining, ending the deadlock
He convinced two other states to change their votes overnight
He proposed a coin flip to settle the contest fairly
He demanded a brand-new election be held that spring
context: James Bayard of Delaware, the lone representative from his state, controlled an entire state's vote; after seeking assurances from a Jefferson ally, he switched from voting for Burr to abstaining on the 36th ballot, collapsing the deadlock and giving Jefferson the presidency. Two states had put their militia on alert, raising the real prospect of armed conflict — yet power passed by ballot, the first U.S. transfer from one party to its bitter rival. Source: smithsonianmag.com/history/thomas-jefferson-aaron-burr-and-the-election-of-1800-131082359.

question: Eli Whitney, a Yankee tinkerer fresh from Yale, built a cotton gin on a Georgia plantation in 1793 that pulled the seeds out of raw cotton far faster than any pair of hands, and it remade the economy of the South. Yet Whitney himself barely earned a cent from his invention. What ruined him?
answer: Planters and blacksmiths simply built their own copies
choices: Planters and blacksmiths simply built their own copies
The machine turned out not to work in humid weather
He gave the design away for free to help poor farmers
A factory fire destroyed his entire first shipment
context: The gin was so simple that planters and blacksmiths built their own copies, many improved, rather than pay Whitney's fees; before he could even deliver his machines the South was already awash with illegal replications. He had as many as sixty infringement suits pending at once and still came away with practically nothing. Source: New Georgia Encyclopedia, georgiaencyclopedia.org; History.com, history.com/articles/cotton-gin-and-eli-whitney.

question: Eli Whitney stood before President John Adams and his officials in January 1801 and assembled musket locks from a pile of mixed-up parts, to prove that the parts were interchangeable. Modern historians say the show was staged. What gave it away?
answer: The surviving muskets bear secret matching marks on each part
choices: The surviving muskets bear secret matching marks on each part
Whitney confessed the trick years later in a letter
The parts were all stamped with the very same date
No two of his muskets have ever been found since
context: Historian Merritt Roe Smith concluded Whitney 'purposely duped government authorities' with specimens specially prepared for the occasion. Surviving Whitney muskets carry engraved matching marks pairing each part to one specific lock, marks that would be needed ONLY if the parts were not truly interchangeable. Source: American Heritage 'Eli Whitney's Other Talent', americanheritage.com/eli-whitneys-other-talent (quoting Merritt Roe Smith).

question: Honoré Blanc, a French gunsmith, took fifty musket locks apart in 1785, jumbled the pieces together and put working locks back together at random, sixteen years before Eli Whitney's famous show. One American watched him do it and later praised Whitney's version. Who was he?
answer: Thomas Jefferson
choices: Thomas Jefferson
Benjamin Franklin
John Adams
Alexander Hamilton
context: Jefferson, then U.S. ambassador to France, witnessed Blanc's July 8, 1785 demonstration in the courtyard of the Chateau de Vincennes and tried unsuccessfully to bring Blanc to America. Years later the same Jefferson marveled that Whitney's parts were 'so exactly equal' they could be 'put together as well by taking the first pieces which come to hand.' Source: Wikipedia 'Interchangeable parts' and 'Honore Blanc', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interchangeable_parts; American Heritage, americanheritage.com/eli-whitneys-other-talent.

question: Eli Whitney said that no one he knew could pick the sticky green seeds from more than a pound of short-staple cotton a day by hand. On a Georgia plantation in 1793 he built a small hand-cranked gin, worked by one person, to do the job. About how much could it clean in a day?
answer: About fifty pounds
choices: About fifty pounds
About five pounds
About fifteen pounds
About two hundred pounds
context: Whitney's gin cleaned roughly fifty times what a person could do by hand — about a pound a day became about fifty. A revolving cylinder studded with hundreds of short wire hooks dragged the fiber through slots too narrow for the seeds. Source: https://www.eliwhitney.org/cotton-gin-and-its-legacies and https://eh.net/encyclopedia/cotton-gin/

question: Eli Whitney, like many Americans, hoped slavery would slowly fade away, since tobacco was wearing out the soil and paying less each year. Then his gin made upland cotton, which grew all over the inland South, fast and cheap to clean. What happened to slavery instead?
answer: The demand for enslaved labor grew enormously as cotton spread west
choices: The demand for enslaved labor grew enormously as cotton spread west
Slavery shrank to the coast where smooth-seeded cotton grew
Plantations replaced enslaved field hands with the new machines
The South turned away from cotton back to tobacco
context: The gin reversed expectations: with cleaning suddenly fast and profitable, the cotton South expanded and the demand for enslaved labor exploded. The number of enslaved people in the U.S. rose from about 700,000 in 1790 to over three million by 1850, and raw-cotton output jumped from about 3,138 bales in 1790 to roughly 3.8 million by 1860. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/aia/part3/3h1522.html and https://courses.lumenlearning.com/wm-ushistory1/chapter/the-cotton-revolution/

question: Courtiers begged Elizabeth I again and again to take a husband and give the realm an heir, for she ruled England alone. She refused every suitor and told them she was already married, though not to any man. To what did she say she was wedded?
answer: the kingdom of England
choices: the kingdom of England
the Protestant faith
the sea and her navy
the ancient city of London
context: Elizabeth I told pressing courtiers, 'I am already bound unto a husband, which is the kingdom of England' — and never married, earning the nickname the Virgin Queen. Source: Unofficial Royalty 'Queen Elizabeth I of England'; Historic UK 'Queen Elizabeth I'.

question: Sir Walter Raleigh sent ships in 1585 to found England's first colony in North America, on its east coast, and he named the land in honour of his queen, Elizabeth I, who famously never married. What name did he give it?
answer: Virginia
choices: Virginia
Carolina
Georgia
Maryland
context: Raleigh named the land 'Virginia' for Elizabeth, the Virgin Queen. (The famous tale that he laid his cloak over a puddle so she would not muddy her shoes is unverified folklore.) Source: Mariners' Museum 'Walter Raleigh'; Biography.com 'Sir Walter Raleigh'.

question: Francis Drake sailed from Plymouth in 1577 with five ships on a secret voyage for Queen Elizabeth I, raided Spain's ports in the Americas and crossed the Pacific. He limped home in 1580 with only one ship left, the Golden Hind. What did the voyage make Drake the first Englishman to do?
answer: sail all the way around the world
choices: sail all the way around the world
cross the whole Atlantic Ocean
reach the far coast of India
map the entire shore of Africa
context: Drake was the first Englishman to circumnavigate the globe; the Golden Hind's plunder reportedly repaid its investors a return of around 4,700–5,000 percent. Source: Wikipedia 'Francis Drake's circumnavigation'; goldenhinde.co.uk 'The circumnavigation 1577–1580'.

question: Soldiers rowed Princess Elizabeth to the Tower of London in 1554 as a suspected traitor, on the orders of her half-sister, Queen Mary. By tradition, she froze at the water-gate and would not step ashore. What had happened to her mother, Anne Boleyn, inside that same fortress?
answer: she had been beheaded there
choices: she had been beheaded there
she had been crowned there
she had been married there
she had died of fever there
context: Princess Elizabeth was taken to the Tower as a suspect in Wyatt's Rebellion; tradition says she balked at the water-gate (later called Traitors' Gate) — the same fortress where her mother, Anne Boleyn, had been beheaded. Source: Tudor Society 'Elizabeth is taken to the Tower' 18 March 1554; Wikipedia 'Traitors' Gate'.  (Legend.)

question: Elizabeth I rode out in a silver breastplate to her army's camp at Tilbury in 1588, while the Spanish Armada of about 130 warships sailed up the Channel to invade Protestant England. She told her soldiers not to fear. Though she had the body of a weak and feeble woman, she said, she had something more. What did she say she had?
answer: the heart and stomach of a king
choices: the heart and stomach of a king
the courage of ten thousand men
the soul of a soldier of Christ
the fierce blood of old King Harry
context: Elizabeth's Tilbury speech: 'I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman, but I have the heart and stomach of a king — and of a King of England too.' Source: Royal Museums Greenwich 'Queen Elizabeth I's speech to the troops at Tilbury'; Speakola Tilbury 1588.

question: King Philip II of Spain lost dozens of ships at anchor in the harbour of Cádiz in April 1587, when Francis Drake slipped in and set them ablaze, delaying the invasion of England by a year. Drake summed up the raid with a cheeky boast about the Spanish king himself. What did he say he had done?
answer: he had singed the King of Spain's beard
choices: he had singed the King of Spain's beard
he had clipped the Spanish lion's claws
he had bloodied Spain's own proud nose
he had plucked the crown off King Philip
context: Drake stormed Cádiz, burned dozens of ships, seized the rich carrack São Filipe, and boasted he had 'singed the King of Spain's beard' — delaying the Armada by about a year. Source: Wikipedia 'Singeing the King of Spain's Beard'; Historic UK 'Drake and the Singeing of King of Spain's Beard'.

question: A rider brought word to Plymouth Hoe on 19 July 1588, the legend goes, that the Spanish Armada had been sighted, sailing to invade England. Francis Drake was up there playing bowls with his officers and would not hurry down to his ship. What did he say there was still time enough to do?
answer: finish the game and beat the Spaniards too
choices: finish the game and beat the Spaniards too
say his prayers and then arm his men
drink his ale and then board his ship
raise the fleet and pray for a wind
context: The story that Drake finished his game of bowls — 'time enough to finish the game and beat the Spaniards too' — is famous but has no contemporary evidence. Source: Historic UK 'Drake and the Singeing of King of Spain's Beard'; britishbattles.com 'The Spanish Armada'.  (Legend.)

question: Mary, Queen of Scots, knelt at the block at Fotheringhay Castle in 1587, and the nervous headsman needed three separate blows to sever her head. When attendants finally lifted her heavy skirts to move the body, they found a small living animal hiding in them, refusing to leave her. What creature was it?
answer: her little dog
choices: her little dog
her pet songbird
a small white kitten
her tame brown hare
context: The executioner needed three blows — the first struck the back of her head — and Mary's little dog was found hiding in her skirts, refusing to leave her. Source: Wikipedia 'Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots'; allthatsinteresting.com 'Mary Queen of Scots Execution'.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Francis Walsingham, Queen Elizabeth's spymaster, let the imprisoned Mary, Queen of Scots, smuggle coded letters out to her plotters, so that his own codebreakers could intercept and read every one, and the letters later trapped her in a plot to murder Elizabeth. In what everyday object were the letters hidden?
answer: the bung of a beer barrel
choices: the bung of a beer barrel
the heel of a leather boot
the collar of a fast courier
a hollow loaf of fresh bread
context: Mary's letters were smuggled in the bung of a beer barrel — a sting that trapped her in the 1586 Babington plot to murder Elizabeth. Source: Wikipedia 'Babington Plot'; British Library 'The Gallows Letter'.

question: Elizabeth I took the throne in 1558 after years in which Catholic and Protestant rulers alike had burned their enemies for wrong belief. She set out to end the bloodshed with a compromise: everyone had to attend the official Church of England on Sunday, but she would not hunt heretics or punish quiet Catholics. She said she had no wish to do one thing to men's souls. What was it?
answer: make windows into men's souls
choices: make windows into men's souls
pry open the doors of men's souls
read the secret pages of men's souls
hold a bright candle to men's souls
context: Elizabeth's 1559 religious settlement was a deliberate 'middle way' — outward conformity without prying into belief — captured in the line that she had no wish to 'make windows into men's souls.' Source: elizabethi.org 'The Elizabethan Religious Settlement (1559)'; America Magazine 'Windows into Men's Souls'.  (Legend.)

question: Elizabeth I tortured herself over ordering the death of Mary, Queen of Scots, a crowned queen and her own cousin. She finally signed the warrant in 1587. Then she claimed she had never meant it sent, and blamed her secretary, William Davison, who had carried the warrant to the executioners. What did Elizabeth do to Davison?
answer: fined him and threw him in the Tower
choices: fined him and threw him in the Tower
stripped his lands and banished him
forgave him and kept him at court
rewarded him with a quiet knighthood
context: Elizabeth signed Mary's warrant on 1 February 1587, then blamed secretary William Davison for sending it — having him fined and imprisoned in the Tower after Mary's head fell. Source: Wikipedia 'Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots'; Unofficial Royalty 'Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots (1587)'.

question: The painter of the Rainbow Portrait showed the ageing Elizabeth I gripping a rainbow beneath the motto 'No rainbow without the sun,' and covered her golden cloak with a repeating pattern that carried a warning to her subjects. What images covered the cloak?
answer: eyes and ears
choices: eyes and ears
serpents and crowns
stars and golden suns
swords and iron keys
context: In the Rainbow Portrait Elizabeth grasps a rainbow under 'Non sine sole iris' — 'No rainbow without the sun' — and her cloak is covered in eyes and ears, signalling that the queen sees and hears everything in her realm. Source: World History Encyclopedia 'Elizabeth I & the Power of Image'; Tudors Dynasty 'Symbolism in Elizabeth's Portraits'.

question: Miners in the lands south of the Sahara dug up gold in plenty while Ghana's kings ruled the desert trade, yet they had none of one ordinary thing. Traders from the north brought it south, and in some places it fetched its own weight in gold. What was it?
answer: Salt
choices: Salt
Iron
Ivory
Amber
context: Salt was scarce in the gold-rich southern forests, so it could be worth its own weight in gold. Sources: brewminate.com/the-salt-trade-of-ancient-west-africa/; worldhistory.org/article/1342/the-salt-trade-of-ancient-west-africa/

question: Foreign traders who crossed the Sahara heard the Soninke speak of their ghana, their warrior king, and named the whole land after his title. The Soninke never called their kingdom Ghana at all. What was their own name for it?
answer: Wagadu
choices: Wagadu
Taghaza
Al-Ghaba
Koumbi
context: 'Ghana' was the rulers' title (warrior king); the kingdom's own name was Wagadu. Later traders heard the title and named the whole land after it. Sources: britannica.com/place/Ghana-historical-West-African-empire; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Empire

question: Northern merchants on Ghana's trade routes laid out their goods, beat a drum and walked off. The gold people then came, set gold beside the goods they wanted and left again; the two sides never met, and the mines stayed secret. What is this way of trading called?
answer: Silent barter
choices: Silent barter
Tribute payment
Sacred bargain
Drum auction
context: In silent barter (the 'silent trade'), the two sides never met, which kept the gold mines' location a secret for generations. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_trade; brewminate.com/the-medieval-west-african-trading-empire-of-ghana/

question: The king of Ghana kept gold scarce by law, as al-Bakri, the Arab geographer, recorded in 1068. The merchants and common people were allowed to keep one kind of gold from the king's mines, and the crown took the other kind for itself. What did the king keep?
answer: Every solid gold nugget
choices: Every solid gold nugget
Every nugget over a set weight
A fixed share of every gold load
The single richest gold mine
context: Al-Bakri wrote that 'the nuggets found in all the mines of his country are reserved for the king, only the gold dust being left for the people' - a deliberate way to keep gold scarce and prices high. Sources: jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/history/worldspring09/paperdemo/albakri.html; al-Bakri (1068)

question: Mourners in Ghana raised a great timber dome over a dead king, al-Bakri wrote in 1068, and laid him inside on carpets with his weapons and jewels, his food and his drink. Then they turned to the servants who had carried the king his meals. What did they do with those servants before they heaped earth over the dome?
answer: Sealed them in alive beside the king
choices: Sealed them in alive beside the king
Made them guard the mound for life
Handed them to the new king as slaves
Strangled them at the dome's door
context: Al-Bakri recorded that the men who served the king's meals were placed alive inside the tomb before the dome was sealed and covered with earth. Sources: al-Bakri (1068), via ebsco.com/research-starters/history/ancient-ghana-emerges; face2faceafrica.com

question: Ghana's kings never handed the crown to their own sons, al-Bakri noted in 1068. The Soninke wanted an heir whose share of the royal blood no one could ever doubt. To whom did the kingship pass?
answer: The king's sister's son
choices: The king's sister's son
The king's eldest daughter
The king's chosen general
The king's youngest brother
context: This is matrilineal succession: al-Bakri explained the throne went to the sister's son because the people could always be sure he shared the royal blood. Sources: worldhistory.org/Ghana_Empire/; newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Ghana_Empire

question: The Soninke told a legend of where their land's gold came from. A great black snake named Bida lived in a deep well, and every year the people gave him the one gift he demanded, so that he would shower the land with gold. What, by the legend, did they give the snake each year?
answer: Their most beautiful young woman
choices: Their most beautiful young woman
Their finest war-horse
A dome of carved wood
A donkey-load of salt
context: Legend: each year the Soninke sacrificed their most beautiful virgin to the serpent Bida, who in return made gold rain on Wagadu. (Told as Soninke legend, not history.) Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Soninke_people; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinga_(ruler)

question: A priest in medieval England blessed a deep pool, and an accused man, tied to a rope so that he could not drown, was let down into it for the ordeal of cold water. The whole crowd watched for one thing: did he sink or float? Which result proved him innocent?
answer: Sinking, because the holy water accepted the body
choices: Sinking, because the holy water accepted the body
Floating, because the holy water rejected the body
Sinking, because the cold numbed the body
Floating, because guilt made the body lighter
context: It feels backwards to us: sinking saved you. The priest had consecrated the water, so if it 'accepted' your body and you sank, you were judged innocent; if the holy water 'rejected' you and you floated, you were guilty. A rope kept the innocent from drowning. Sources: https://hls.harvard.edu/today/the-veiled-history-of-the-english-jury-trial/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_by_ordeal

question: An accused man in medieval England gripped a red-hot iron bar and carried it three paces for the ordeal of hot iron, badly burning his hand. The burnt hand was then bound up and left to heal. How did the court decide whether he was innocent or guilty?
answer: His bandage was unwrapped three days later and the wound judged
choices: His bandage was unwrapped three days later and the wound judged
His confession was taken the moment the iron seared him
His iron was carefully reweighed by the priest after the walk
His fate was put to a vote of twelve local neighbours
context: The verdict came from the burn itself. Exactly three days later a priest unwrapped the hand: a clean, healing wound meant God had declared him innocent; a festering, infected one meant guilty. The accused walked about nine feet (three paces) carrying the glowing iron. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_by_ordeal ; https://hls.harvard.edu/today/the-veiled-history-of-the-english-jury-trial/

question: Old Giles Corey of Salem would not plead to the charge against him in 1692, and without a plea the law could not try him. So his tormentors laid him on his back and piled heavy stones on him to make him speak. He held out for two days, and each time they demanded his plea, he gave the same answer. What was it?
answer: More weight
choices: More weight
I am innocent
God will judge
Take them off
context: 'More weight' is what Giles Corey is said to have growled as the stones piled on. He chose to be pressed to death rather than plead, because a man who died WITHOUT a verdict kept his estate for his heirs, while a convicted felon's property was forfeited to the crown. 'Peine forte et dure' is Law-French for 'hard and forceful punishment.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giles_Corey ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/peine-forte-et-dure

question: Henry II of England issued the Assize of Clarendon in 1166, one of the earliest ancestors of the modern jury. The sheriff of every district had to summon twelve trusted men of the neighbourhood, and when the king's new circuit of travelling judges rode into town, the twelve swore a solemn oath before them. What did that oath bind them to do?
answer: Name aloud anyone they suspected of robbery, murder, or theft
choices: Name aloud anyone they suspected of robbery, murder, or theft
Decide the guilt of anyone the sheriff had already jailed
Carry out the hangings the king’s travelling judges ordered
Collect the king’s taxes from every household in the district
context: These twelve were sworn ACCUSERS, not judges — they reported the names of suspected robbers, murderers, and thieves to the king's roving judges. This 'jury of presentment' is the direct ancestor of the modern grand jury, which still decides whom to charge. The Assize also drew in four lawful men from every township. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/event/Assize-of-Clarendon ; https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/law/law/grand-jury

question: Pope Innocent III issued one rule at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, and within a few years it brought down the trial by ordeal that English courts had used for centuries to settle their hardest cases. What did the pope's rule forbid?
answer: Priests from blessing the iron or the water
choices: Priests from blessing the iron or the water
Kings from sentencing any man to lose a limb
Judges from travelling between the country districts
Sheriffs from seizing the goods of a convicted man
context: The priest's blessing was the secret ingredient — it was what supposedly called down God's judgment. Canon 18 of the Fourth Lateran Council barred priests from blessing the iron or the water, and without that the ordeal was 'just torture' and meaningless. England then had to invent a replacement: letting twelve men weigh the evidence. Sources: https://academic.oup.com/ojls/article-abstract/26/3/473/1452002 ; https://hls.harvard.edu/today/the-veiled-history-of-the-english-jury-trial/

question: England's barons made King John put his seal to Magna Carta in 1215. Clause 39 held that no free man would be seized or imprisoned 'except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land.' Centuries later those words passed into American law. Which American text carried that promise into its own wording?
answer: The Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments' due-process guarantees
choices: The Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments' due-process guarantees
The Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel and unusual punishment
The Declaration of Independence's list of royal abuses
The Northwest Ordinance's guarantee of trial by jury
context: An 800-year-old line from an English charter is load-bearing in American law: Magna Carta's 'judgment of his peers' and 'law of the land' were copied straight into the due-process guarantees of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. Clause 40 added a companion promise — 'To no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay, right or justice.' Sources: https://magnacarta.cmp.uea.ac.uk/read/magna_carta_1215/Clause_39 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presumption_of_innocence

question: Johannes Monachus, a French church lawyer, argued around 1300 about how a fair judge must act, and he found his answer in the first judgment in the Bible: God meeting Adam after Adam had eaten the forbidden fruit. According to Monachus, what did God do when He faced Adam?
answer: He questioned Adam first, holding a kind of trial
choices: He questioned Adam first, holding a kind of trial
He cursed the serpent before turning to Adam
He banished Adam from Eden before a word was spoken
He demanded Adam name who was at fault
context: Monachus's point: even God did not simply condemn — He held a kind of trial, asking 'Where are you?' and 'Who told you that you were naked?' before judging. If even God presumed Adam innocent and heard him first, Monachus argued, no earthly judge may do less. This is where the maxim 'everyone is presumed innocent until proven guilty' was first put into crisp Latin, around 1300 — people often think it was in Magna Carta, but it was not. Sources: Kenneth Pennington, 'Innocent Until Proven Guilty: The Origins of a Legal Maxim' (scholarship.law.edu) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presumption_of_innocence

question: Alan Turing, a mathematician breaking Nazi Germany's Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park, suffered badly from hay fever. Each June he cycled the country lanes to work wearing one strange thing to keep the pollen out of his lungs. What did Turing wear for the ride?
answer: A military gas mask
choices: A military gas mask
A beekeeper's veil
A woollen scarf
A doctor's surgical mask
context: Turing cycled to Bletchley Park in a military gas mask during the first week of June each year to block hay-fever pollen. The same eccentric chained his tea mug to a radiator pipe so no one could steal it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing

question: Afraid that his paper money would lose its value if Britain lost the war, Alan Turing changed his savings into a pair of heavy silver bars and hid them in the ground in the woods near Bletchley. After the war he went back for his fortune and never got it back. What had gone wrong?
answer: He had hidden the location in a code he could no longer crack
choices: He had hidden the location in a code he could no longer crack
A neighbour had dug them up and sold them
A wartime bomb had cratered the whole field
He had forgotten which town he buried them in
context: The man who broke the German Enigma cipher hid his own buried silver in a code even he could never solve again, and lost the bars for good. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing

question: Bletchley's Wrens, some 700 of them, took turns at Bletchley Park's noisy code-breaking machines while the codebreakers worked on Nazi Germany's Enigma messages. About 9,000 people worked there at the peak, and most of them were not the men later films remember. Out of every four Bletchley workers, about how many were women?
answer: Three
choices: Three
One
Two
Four
context: Roughly three of every four Bletchley workers were women, including some 700 Wrens who ran the noisy bombe machines in shifts. All had signed the Official Secrets Act and stayed silent for decades, even from one another. Source: https://www.bletchleypark.org.uk/our-story/6-facts-about-the-bombe/

question: Signing off almost every message the same way, German Enigma operators handed Bletchley Park free clues. The codebreakers could safely guess those letters at the end of the text, a known scrap they called a crib. Which sign-off gave Bletchley its ready-made guess?
answer: 'Heil Hitler'
choices: 'Heil Hitler'
'Sieg Heil'
'Auf Wiedersehen'
'Ende der Nachricht'
context: A guessed scrap of known plaintext was called a 'crib.' The predictable 'Heil Hitler' sign-off and the daily weather report were two of the most reliable cribs Bletchley relied on. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptanalysis_of_the_Enigma

question: Codebreakers of the Polish Cipher Bureau met British and French officers in a forest south of Warsaw on 25 July 1939, with the war just five weeks away. There they handed over something Britain had been stuck without, the base of all Bletchley Park's later work. What did the Poles hand over?
answer: Replica Enigma machines and their breaking methods
choices: Replica Enigma machines and their breaking methods
A captured German invasion timetable
A list of every German spy in Britain
The blueprints for a new Polish tank
context: At Pyry the Poles gave Dilly Knox and Alastair Denniston working Enigma replicas plus their methods. Britain had been beaten by the cipher until then; the Polish gift was the foundation of the entire Bletchley effort. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_Rejewski

question: Bletchley's codebreakers faced an Enigma machine that could be set up in about 159 quintillion ways a day. Yet most of that strength did not come from its spinning rotors. One other part of the machine, on its own, added more security than a fourth rotor ever could have. Which part was it?
answer: The plugboard
choices: The plugboard
The reflector
The keyboard
The lampboard
context: Enigma's 158,962,555,217,826,360,000 settings — about 159 quintillion — drew most of their strength from the plugboard, which scrambled letter-pairs and beat adding another rotor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_machine

question: Bletchley's codebreakers turned one fatal flaw in Enigma's design against it. A mirror-like part inside the machine bounced every electrical signal back through the rotors. Because of it, Enigma could never produce one particular result, whatever its settings, and the codebreakers could throw out impossible line-ups of a guessed word at once. What could Enigma never do?
answer: Encrypt any letter as itself
choices: Encrypt any letter as itself
Repeat the same setting two days running
Encrypt a message longer than 250 letters
Light two lamps at once
context: Enigma's reflector guaranteed a letter could never be enciphered as itself. Codebreakers slid a guessed phrase along the ciphertext and threw out any position where a letter lined up with its own match. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptanalysis_of_the_Enigma

question: Codebreakers at Bletchley Park fed Alan Turing's bombe a guessed scrap of plain text to start each run. The machine raced through Enigma's 17,576 rotor positions in about twenty minutes, throwing out the wrong ones wherever it found a contradiction. What was the bombe's job?
answer: Finding the day's Enigma settings
choices: Finding the day's Enigma settings
Printing out the German plaintext
Jamming German radio signals
Building new codes for the Allies
context: The bombe hunted for the day's key, not the message itself. Once it found the settings by eliminating trillions of wrong ones through logic, human operators could read every Enigma signal of that day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombe

question: Cipher Deavours, a cryptologist, gave a grand nickname to one theorem that Marian Rejewski had leaned on to crack Enigma. Rejewski had used no stolen secrets, only permutation group theory, which studies how symbols can be shuffled. What did Deavours call the theorem?
answer: 'The theorem that won World War II'
choices: 'The theorem that won World War II'
'The Warsaw conjecture'
'The unbreakable lemma'
'The Enigma equation'
context: The theorem — that two permutations are conjugate exactly when they share the same cycle structure — let Rejewski reconstruct Enigma's wiring. Deavours called it 'the theorem that won World War II': abstract algebra, not spycraft, cracked the machine. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_Rejewski

question: Sir Harry Hinsley, the official historian of Britain's wartime intelligence, gave his verdict on how much Bletchley's secret code-breaking, known as Ultra, had changed the war. Without Ultra, he judged, the fighting would have dragged on longer. By Hinsley's reckoning, how much longer?
answer: About two years longer
choices: About two years longer
About six months longer
About five years longer
Roughly a decade longer
context: Hinsley judged the war would have run 'something like two years longer, perhaps three years longer, possibly four years longer' without Ultra. Secret mathematics shortened the deadliest war in history by years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_(cryptography)

question: Frederick the Great of Prussia built a low, one-storey summer palace at Potsdam where he could play his flute, talk philosophy and escape the business of ruling. He gave it a French name. What did he call it?
answer: Sanssouci, meaning 'without care'
choices: Sanssouci, meaning 'without care'
Versailles, meaning 'the turning'
Fontainebleau, meaning 'fine spring'
Malmaison, meaning 'the bad house'
context: Sanssouci ('without care' / carefree) was Frederick's retreat; he asked to be buried there beside his greyhounds, and his grave sits on its grounds to this day. Source: AP via US News (2025-07-02); National Geographic, 'What's So Great About Frederick?'

question: Voltaire, the most famous intellectual in Europe, came to live at Frederick the Great's court in 1750, but the friendship soon soured. Voltaire griped that the king made him wash his dirty linen by fixing his clumsy French verse. How did Frederick belittle his worn-out guest in return?
answer: He said one squeezes the orange and throws away the peel
choices: He said one squeezes the orange and throws away the peel
He said a borrowed lamp is returned once it is dim
He said a guest, like fish, begins to stink on the third day
He said the bee is welcome only until the honey is taken
context: Voltaire fled Prussia in 1753, and Frederick had him briefly detained at Frankfurt. The break had blown up over Voltaire's pamphlet savaging Maupertuis, head of Frederick's Berlin Academy. Source: National Geographic, 'Frederick the Great, King of Prussia.'

question: Visitors to Frederick the Great's grave still leave raw potatoes on it. German tradition calls him the Potato King, who set guards on a royal potato field to make the crop look precious, so that peasants would steal it and plant it themselves. What do historians say about the beloved tale?
answer: He likely never even ate potatoes, and the legend has beaten the truth
choices: He likely never even ate potatoes, and the legend has beaten the truth
He grew them only as cattle feed, never meaning them for people
He banned the potato outright as a poisonous foreign weed
He paid a French chemist to invent the recipe from scratch
context: Legend, not fact: Frederick preferred Italian food and French wine, and Germans had grown potatoes since 1647. As one account puts it, 'the legend has beaten the truth.' Source: AP via US News (2025-07-02); berlinexperiences.com.

question: Denis Diderot, the philosopher, was drowning in debt when Catherine the Great of Russia, who liked to bankroll the French Enlightenment in person, came to his rescue. She bought his entire library, let him keep the books and named him their paid librarian. How far ahead did she pay his salary?
answer: Fifty years in advance
choices: Fifty years in advance
One year in advance
For the rest of that decade
Until the books were catalogued
context: A grateful Diderot travelled to St. Petersburg in 1773 and stayed five months as Catherine's guest. Source: Los Angeles Review of Books on Zaretsky's 'Catherine & Diderot'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: Joseph II of Austria poured out about 6,000 imperial decrees in a single decade, setting serfs free and ordering religious toleration. Then Hungary's nobles made him undo almost every reform before he died. He composed his own epitaph. What did it say?
answer: That he meant well but failed in everything he tried
choices: That he meant well but failed in everything he tried
That his enemies would answer to history's judgment
That a kinder age would finish what he began
That he ruled longer than his works would last
context: Joseph's self-written epitaph ran: 'Here lies a ruler who, despite his best intentions, was unsuccessful in all his endeavors.' Only his toleration edict and the end of serfdom survived him. Source: EBSCO Research Starters; Britannica, 'Joseph II.'

question: Catherine the Great issued her Nakaz, or Instruction, in 1767, drawing on Montesquieu and Beccaria to speak against torture and even to question serfdom, and Europe hailed her as an enlightened ruler. Yet serfdom spread under her, and after Pugachev's revolt she tightened the nobles' grip on their serfs instead. Historians see a basic flaw here in reform handed down by a monarch. What is it?
answer: Reform a ruler grants, a ruler can simply withdraw
choices: Reform a ruler grants, a ruler can simply withdraw
Reform always arrives too slowly to matter
Reform copied from foreigners can never take root
Reform announced abroad must be hidden at home
context: The contrast historians draw is with rights a people secure for themselves, as in the American case — those don't vanish at a monarch's whim. Catherine's Nakaz produced no actual law code and was banned from the French public even as it won her fame. Source: Britannica, 'Instruction of Catherine the Great'; thecollector.com.

question: Benjamin Franklin took up his pen over the first draft of the Declaration of Independence in June 1776, where the opening line read, 'We hold these truths to be sacred and undeniable.' He struck out the last two words and put in a single immortal phrase. What did Franklin make the line?
answer: We hold these truths to be self-evident
choices: We hold these truths to be self-evident
We hold these truths to be God-given
We hold these truths to be ours alone
We hold these truths to be beyond doubt
context: Franklin's edit turned a claim of faith ('sacred & undeniable') into a claim of reason ('self-evident') -- truths any thinking person can see. Source: https://veteransbreakfastclub.org/self-evident-truths-franklin-jefferson-and-the-editing-of-the-declaration-of-independence/

question: Thomas Jefferson kept a copy of Virginia's new Declaration of Rights at his side as he drafted the Declaration of Independence, which came three weeks after Virginia's. The Virginia paper promised men the right to seek happiness and safety, and Jefferson followed its wording closely. Who drafted the Virginia paper Jefferson leaned on?
answer: George Mason
choices: George Mason
Patrick Henry
George Washington
James Madison
context: Mason's wording came first, and Jefferson followed it closely. Historian John Ferling: 'Nothing influenced Jefferson more than the draft of Virginia's Declaration of Rights.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Declaration_of_Rights

question: John Locke had written that 'the necessity of pursuing happiness is the foundation of liberty,' long before the Declaration of Independence set 'the pursuit of Happiness' in place of Locke's 'property.' Yet that line of Locke's did not come from his political book on government. Which kind of Locke work did it appear in?
answer: his book on how the human mind knows things
choices: his book on how the human mind knows things
his pamphlet defending religious toleration
his letters on raising and educating children
his treatise on the origins of money
context: The 'pursuit of happiness' line is from Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding -- a book about knowledge and the mind -- not the Second Treatise of Government, where his 'life, liberty, and property' triad lives. Source: https://historynewsnetwork.org/article/46460

question: While staying at a friend's house in London in 1509, the Dutch scholar Erasmus dashed off In Praise of Folly, a witty little book that pokes fun at the vanities of his age. Its Latin title hid a sly pun on the name of the very friend who was hosting him. Who was that friend?
answer: Thomas More
choices: Thomas More
Thomas Cromwell
Thomas Wolsey
William Tyndale
context: The Latin title Moriae Encomium puns on More's Latinized name, Morus — so it can be read 'In Praise of More.' Erasmus wrote it in about a week at More's house; in it the goddess Folly herself stands up in a jester's cap and praises herself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Praise_of_Folly

question: Martin Luther broke away from the Church that Erasmus had hoped to mend from within, and the critics of Erasmus jeered: 'Erasmus laid the egg, and Luther hatched it.' Erasmus shot back with his own twist on the egg. What was his retort?
answer: He had laid a hen's egg, but Luther had hatched a very different bird.
choices: He had laid a hen's egg, but Luther had hatched a very different bird.
He had laid the egg, but another hand had cracked it open.
He had laid a sparrow's egg, but Luther had raised an eagle.
He had laid the egg, but God alone decided what hatched.
context: In 1523 Erasmus said he 'had laid a hen's egg, but Luther had hatched a bird of quite a different breed.' He sought to reform the church from within and was dismayed by Luther's break with it. Source: https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/ch-145-dyk-erasmus

question: Erasmus of Rotterdam urged in 1516 that the Bible be turned out of Latin into every common tongue, so that ordinary working people could read it for themselves. To picture his dream, he imagined one humble worker singing Scripture aloud as he laboured. Which worker did Erasmus picture?
answer: A farmer singing it behind his plow.
choices: A farmer singing it behind his plow.
A blacksmith reciting it over his anvil.
A shepherd chanting it on the hillside.
A fisherman humming it in his boat.
context: In his Paraclesis (1516), Erasmus wished 'that the farmer sing some portion of them at the plow, the weaver hum some parts to the movement of his shuttle, the traveler lighten the weariness of the journey' — and that even 'the Turks' might read them. This 'plowboy' vision was later echoed by William Tyndale. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plowboy_trope

question: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam worked like a textual detective, comparing old handwritten copies of ancient books with one another. In 1516 he did something with the New Testament that no printer had ever done before him. What was this first?
answer: He printed the New Testament in its Greek, beside his own fresh Latin.
choices: He printed the New Testament in its Greek, beside his own fresh Latin.
He printed the New Testament with a painted picture beside every chapter.
He printed the New Testament small enough to tuck inside a coat pocket.
He printed the New Testament set as rhyming verse for singing.
context: Erasmus's Novum Instrumentum omne ('A Whole New Instrument'), printed by Johann Froben in Basel in 1516, set the Greek text in one column and Erasmus's own new Latin translation beside it — the first Greek New Testament ever published. A believing scholar was applying humanist textual scholarship straight to Scripture. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novum_Instrumentum_omne

question: When Erasmus prepared his printed Greek New Testament, he left out one short verse that was prized as proof of the Trinity, since he could find it in no Greek manuscript at all. Critics howled. Then something happened that led him to put the verse in after all. What was it?
answer: A lone Greek manuscript containing the verse suddenly turned up.
choices: A lone Greek manuscript containing the verse suddenly turned up.
An older, more trusted Greek manuscript was found in Rome.
The Pope commanded him to restore the missing verse.
A friend talked him into adding the verse for peace.
context: The verse was 1 John 5:7, the 'Comma Johanneum.' A manuscript (the Codex Montfortianus), evidently copied by a friar from the Latin Vulgate, conveniently appeared; Erasmus added the verse to his third edition (1522) but wrote in his notes that he still doubted it was genuine. The old story that he made a formal 'promise' to include it is now considered a fabrication. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novum_Instrumentum_omne

question: Erasmus and Martin Luther circled each other warily for years: Erasmus admired Luther's fire, yet he refused to leave the Catholic Church. In 1524 Erasmus finally drew his sword in a book, and Luther answered with a book of his own. What great question split them?
answer: Whether a person's will is free to choose or reject God's grace.
choices: Whether a person's will is free to choose or reject God's grace.
Whether priests and monks ought to be free to marry.
Whether the bread at communion truly becomes Christ's body.
Whether the Pope at Rome holds authority over all churches.
context: Erasmus published On Free Will (De libero arbitrio, 1524), arguing the will can still choose to accept or resist grace; Luther fired back with On the Bondage of the Will (1525), insisting the will is enslaved to sin and saved by grace alone. Erasmus stayed a Catholic to the end, seeking reform from within. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_libero_arbitrio_diatribe_sive_collatio

question: Eratosthenes, who ran the great Library of Alexandria, set out to measure the whole Earth with nothing but sunlight and geometry. He began from one strange fact about the town of Syene, today called Aswan, at noon on the summer solstice. What did the sunlight do there at that moment?
answer: It shone straight down a deep well and lit the water at the very bottom, casting no shadow at all
choices: It shone straight down a deep well and lit the water at the very bottom, casting no shadow at all
It bent sideways through the desert haze and split into a faint band of colors over the river
It dimmed to a deep red as a thin veil of dust rolled in off the surrounding sand dunes
It glared off the temple's polished bronze gates and blinded the priests gathered to watch
context: At noon on the summer solstice the sun stood directly overhead at Syene, so it lit the bottom of a deep well and a vertical stick cast no shadow — proof the sun was straight up. Eratosthenes (c. 245 BC) ran the Library of Alexandria and tutored Pharaoh Ptolemy III's children. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Eratosthenes/

question: Eratosthenes measured a stick's noon shadow in Alexandria on the summer solstice and found it leaning about 7.2 degrees. He set that beside what the sun did at the same hour at Syene, far to the south, and saw that this one number was the whole trick. What did 7.2 degrees tell him about the two cities?
answer: They sat exactly 1/50 of a full circle apart, so the road between them was 1/50 of the whole Earth
choices: They sat exactly 1/50 of a full circle apart, so the road between them was 1/50 of the whole Earth
They lay on two different meridians, so the sun reached them a little under half an hour apart
They differed in height above the sea by the same fraction the shadow leaned from straight up
They were close enough that the sun's rays reached them bent at slightly different sideways angles
context: 7.2 degrees is exactly 1/50 of a 360-degree circle, so Syene and Alexandria were 1/50 of the Earth apart. Royal surveyors called bematists had paced the distance at 5,000 stadia; 5,000 x 50 gives about 250,000 stadia — roughly 40,000 km, within a few percent of the true circumference, found with a stick, a shadow, and geometry. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2006/06/eratosthenes-measures-earth

question: Eratosthenes, head of the great Library at Alexandria, measured the Earth around 240 BC with nothing more than a stick, two shadows and some geometry. What did the educated Greeks of his day already take for granted about the Earth?
answer: That the Earth was a sphere, and he was measuring how big the ball was
choices: That the Earth was a sphere, and he was measuring how big the ball was
That the Earth was flat, and he was the first to prove it was round
That the Earth was flat, and his shadow result was rejected as nonsense
That the Earth's true shape could never be known by anyone
context: This kills the flat-earth myth: educated ancient Greeks already KNEW the Earth was a sphere and roughly how big -- Eratosthenes was measuring a ball, not discovering one. The differing shadows at Syene (where the noon sun cast NO shadow down a well) and Alexandria only made sense on a curved Earth, which is exactly why his method worked. Sources: oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_geodesy/geo02_hist.html; worldhistory.org/Eratosthenes

question: King Ptolemy I of Egypt was learning geometry from Euclid himself, and he grew tired of the long chain of proofs in the Elements. He asked his teacher for a quicker, easier way into the subject. According to the philosopher Proclus, who told the story some seven centuries later, what did Euclid tell the king?
answer: "There is no royal road to geometry."
choices: "There is no royal road to geometry."
"A king need not stoop to such labor."
"Begin again from the first proof."
"Geometry rewards only the patient."
context: Legend, recorded by the philosopher Proclus around 450 AD, centuries after Euclid lived. The point: even a king cannot skip the step-by-step proofs; everyone must walk the same road. Source: mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Euclid/ (citing Proclus); en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Euclid

question: Euclid built his Elements on five starting rules. Four felt clean and obvious, but the fifth was clumsy: through a point, only one line can run parallel to a given line. For over 2,000 years mathematicians tried to prove it from the other four and failed, until Lobachevsky, Bolyai and Gauss found a way nobody expected. What did they discover could be done with the fifth rule?
answer: DENY it and still build a consistent geometry
choices: DENY it and still build a consistent geometry
Prove it cleanly using only the first four
Replace it with a simpler equivalent rule
Remove it without changing any theorem
context: Denying the parallel postulate created non-Euclidean geometry, which later helped Einstein describe curved space. The lesson: a rule unprovable from the others wasn't a flaw but a choice. Source: mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Non-Euclidean_geometry/

question: Euclid proved a famous fact about the prime numbers in Book IX of the Elements, with a trick still taught today. Suppose you had a finite list of every prime. Multiply them all together and add 1. What did Euclid show must be true of this brand-new number?
answer: It has a prime factor missing from your list
choices: It has a prime factor missing from your list
It is always divisible by the largest prime
It must itself be an even number
It equals the sum of the primes you listed
context: Proposition 20 of Book IX. The new number is either prime itself or has a prime factor not on your list, so no finite list can ever hold them all. Source: mathcs.clarku.edu/~djoyce/java/elements/bookIX/propIX20.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's_theorem

question: Joachim Roenneberg and a few Norwegian commandos skied through the snowbound mountains to the Vemork plant in Nazi-held Norway one night in February 1943. They blew up the plant's store of one rare liquid the Germans needed for an atomic bomb, without firing a shot. What did Roenneberg and his men destroy?
answer: The plant's only supply of heavy water
choices: The plant's only supply of heavy water
The plant's stockpile of enriched uranium
The plant's reserves of liquid oxygen
The plant's tanks of synthetic fuel
context: Operation Gunnerside, the night of 27-28 February 1943. Vemork was the only factory in occupied Europe making 'heavy water' for a German atomic-bomb program. Roenneberg's team destroyed about 500 kg of it without firing a shot or losing a single man, then he skied more than 200 miles to neutral Sweden and not one of the team was killed or captured. The British later called it 'the most successful sabotage mission of the war.' Source: https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/operation-gunnerside/

question: Georg Duckwitz, a German diplomat, secretly warned Denmark's resistance in 1943 that the Germans planned to round up the country's Jews at the Jewish New Year. Over three weeks that October, fishermen, priests, doctors and police officers helped about 7,200 Jews escape to neutral Sweden, rescuing more than 95 percent of them. How did the Danes move so many people across the water?
answer: By smuggling them across the strait in fishing boats
choices: By smuggling them across the strait in fishing boats
By forging exit visas through the city port
By hiding them in cellars until the war ended
By marching them over a guarded land border
context: A German diplomat, Georg Duckwitz, secretly tipped off the resistance to the planned Rosh Hashanah roundup. Among the rescuers, 19-year-old Henny Sinding used the lighthouse-service boat Gerda III to ferry roughly 300 Jews across; estimates suggest about 50 Danes helped for every Jew saved. Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/timeline-event/holocaust/1942-1945/danish-jews-escape

question: Robert Kalina, an Austrian artist, won the Europe-wide contest to draw the euro notes in the late 1990s, and he put a bridge on the back of every note. People long took them for real European bridges, but Kalina had made up every one. Why did he draw imaginary bridges instead of famous real ones?
answer: So no country's landmark would be favoured and none offended
choices: So no country's landmark would be favoured and none offended
So the notes would be cheaper and faster to print
So forgers could not copy a real photograph
So each bridge could be a famous wartime ruin
context: Kalina designed seven fictional bridges in Classical, Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, 19th-century iron-and-glass, and modern 20th-century styles, precisely so no real nation's bridge would be picked over another's. Later a Dutch artist, Robin Stam, built all seven for real in coloured concrete in the town of Spijkenisse near Rotterdam. Source: https://99percentinvisible.org/article/fact-follows-fiction-real-bridges-based-euro-banknote-artwork/

question: Bankers in Frankfurt, at the European Central Bank, set one borrowing cost for all twenty countries that use the euro, Germany, France, Italy and Spain among them. Each of those countries still runs its own budget, its own taxes and its own pensions. What deep problem do economists say this setup creates?
answer: One interest rate cannot fit every country's economy at once
choices: One interest rate cannot fit every country's economy at once
Each country secretly prints its own extra euros
The shared currency forces every country to share one budget
Interest rates change too fast for banks to keep up
context: This is the 'monetary union without fiscal union' tension: a single monetary policy is one-size-fits-all, but economies differ, so it can fit no one exactly. The euro was created under the Maastricht Treaty (signed 7 February 1992); it launched as an invisible accounting currency on 1 January 1999 for over 300 million people, three years before coins and notes reached wallets on 1 January 2002. Source: https://www.imf.org/en/blogs/articles/2018/02/21/the-euro-area-needs-a-fiscal-union

question: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay stood on the summit of Mount Everest, the highest point on Earth, on 29 May 1953, and stayed only about fifteen minutes. Tenzing, a Buddhist, scooped a small hollow in the snow and left a gift for the mountain gods. What did he bury there?
answer: Sweets, a chocolate bar, and biscuits
choices: Sweets, a chocolate bar, and biscuits
A handful of Himalayan wildflowers
A lock of his own hair
A coin from his home village
context: Tenzing Norgay, a Buddhist, dug the hollow and buried sweets, a chocolate bar, and biscuits as an offering. Beside him, Hillary dug a second hole and buried a small crucifix that expedition leader John Hunt had handed him before the climb. https://www.discoveryworldtrekking.com/blog/conquering-everest-the-story-of-tenzing-norgay-sherpa-and-edmund-hillary

question: Reporters crowded around Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay after the two came down from the top of Everest in 1953, asking again and again which of them had set foot on the summit first. The climbers and their leader, John Hunt, had already made a pact. What was it?
answer: They agreed never to reveal who stepped first
choices: They agreed never to reveal who stepped first
They agreed Tenzing would always be named first
They agreed to let a coin toss decide the credit
They agreed to ask the newspapers to keep it secret
context: The three men treated the summit as a shared team achievement. Hillary said, 'To a mountaineer, it's of no great consequence who actually sets foot first.' Only years later, in Tenzing's autobiography, did it come out that Hillary had stepped first. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/sir-edmund-hillary-tenzing-norgay-1953

question: Aksum's king, Ezana, became a Christian around 340, and his own money shows the change. His early coins bore the disc and crescent of the moon-god Almaqah; later ones carried a new symbol in their place, possibly the first of its kind on any coin anywhere. What replaced the crescent?
answer: A Christian cross
choices: A Christian cross
A lion of Judah
A royal crown
A laurel wreath
context: Ezana's coins are the most concrete sign of his conversion: the pagan disc-and-crescent of the moon-god Almaqah vanished and a cross took its place, possibly the first use of the cross on any coin anywhere in the world. Ezana made Aksum one of the world's first Christian states — Africa was Christian centuries before most of Europe. Source: smarthistory.org/aksumite-coins/ ; coinweek.com/the-coinage-of-aksum/

question: Ezana of Aksum called himself the son of a god in his early royal inscriptions, before he became a Christian. His kingdom, in the highlands of what is now Ethiopia, grew rich on Red Sea trade. Which god did Ezana claim as his father?
answer: The war-god Mahrem
choices: The war-god Mahrem
The sea-god Beher
The sun-god Astar
The earth-god Medr
context: Ezana's pagan inscriptions name him son of Mahrem, the Aksumite war-god (their version of Ares); he also worshipped Astar, Beher and Medr. After his conversion, a later inscription drops the old gods entirely to invoke 'the Lord of Heaven who in the sky and on earth holds power over all beings.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezana_of_Axum ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezana_Stone

question: The historian Rufinus said Christianity reached Aksum by shipwreck. Raiders fell on a merchant ship from Tyre in an Aksumite harbour and left only two boys alive. One of them, Frumentius, was taken to the royal court, where he tutored the young prince Ezana and later helped convert him. Ethiopians honour Frumentius as Abba Salama. What does that title mean?
answer: Father of Peace
choices: Father of Peace
Father of Lions
Apostle of the Sea
Apostle of the Cross
context: Frumentius was one of two shipwrecked boys spared at the Aksumite court (Rufinus' account, told as early-church tradition). He tutored Ezana, traveled to Alexandria to be consecrated first bishop of Aksum by Athanasius, and is honored as 'Abba Salama,' Father of Peace, founder of the Ethiopian church. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frumentius ; britannica.com/biography/Saint-Frumentius ; dacb.org/stories/ethiopia/frumentius/  (Legend.)

question: Soviet soldiers were closing in on 30 April 1945 when Hitler shot himself in his Berlin bunker. The Soviets razed the Chancellery above it, and East Germany left the site unmarked for decades, afraid it might become a Nazi shrine. What covers the site now?
answer: A parking lot
choices: A parking lot
A grand war memorial
A glass museum
A statue of a Soviet soldier
context: The Fuhrerbunker site off In den Ministergarten is a plain apartment-block car park. Kept unmarked on purpose so it would not draw neo-Nazi pilgrims, it got only a single small information board in 2006. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%BChrerbunker.

question: Adolf Hitler climbed out into the wrecked garden of the Chancellery on 20 April 1945, his 56th birthday, the last time he ever saw daylight. There he pinned Iron Crosses on a line of defenders who were about to be thrown against Soviet tanks. Who were the defenders he decorated?
answer: Hitler Youth boys, some only 12
choices: Hitler Youth boys, some only 12
His personal SS bodyguards
Veteran panzer commanders
Captured enemy officers
context: It was the last time Hitler ever saw daylight; he was dead within ten days. By the end the regime was sending children to die for it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%BChrerbunker.

question: Joseph Goebbels and Martin Bormann stood witness in a cramped bunker room in the first minutes of 29 April 1945, as Adolf Hitler married Eva Braun, his companion of many years. The Red Army was fighting only blocks away. How long did the marriage last before the newlyweds were both dead?
answer: Fewer than two days
choices: Fewer than two days
About six months
Nearly a year
Over three years
context: They were husband and wife for fewer than 40 hours before killing themselves on 30 April. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eva_Braun.

question: Werner Haase, Hitler's personal doctor, tested one of Hitler's cyanide capsules down in the bunker on 29 April 1945. Hitler did not trust that the capsules were real poison and not a harmless fake slipped to him by traitors. On what living thing did Haase test the poison?
answer: Hitler's dog, Blondi
choices: Hitler's dog, Blondi
A captured Soviet prisoner
A condemned SS guard
A caged laboratory rat
context: The German shepherd Blondi died, proving the cyanide was lethal. The next day Hitler used the same poison on Eva Braun. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Adolf_Hitler.

question: Eva Braun bit a cyanide capsule in the bunker in the afternoon of 30 April 1945, and Hitler shot himself with a pistol. His aides then had to carry out a standing order he had given about the two bodies, out in the Chancellery garden while Soviet shells crashed down around them. What did they do with the bodies?
answer: Soaked them in petrol and burned them
choices: Soaked them in petrol and burned them
Sealed them in a steel coffin
Buried them deep under the bunker
Smuggled them out of the city
context: The fire burned from roughly 16:00 to 18:30 but left only charred bone fragments, never a whole body. That missing corpse fed decades of rumors that Hitler had escaped. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Adolf_Hitler.

question: A band of Red Army soldiers battled up onto the roof of the Reichstag late one night in April 1945 and ran up their flag, the sign of Nazi Germany's fall. What was still going on in the building beneath them at that moment?
answer: German troops still held the floors below
choices: German troops still held the floors below
The building stood completely empty
Berlin had already officially surrendered
Hitler was still alive inside it
context: The first flag went up around 22:40 while the Reichstag was still being fought through room by room. The banner flew over a building the defenders had not yet given up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_a_Flag_over_the_Reichstag.

question: Magda Goebbels gave her six children morphine in the Berlin bunker the day after Hitler's death, and then cyanide as they slept. Witnesses later told what she did in the minutes that followed. According to them, what did Magda do?
answer: Sat down and played a game of solitaire
choices: Sat down and played a game of solitaire
Ran screaming through the bunker
Tried to surrender to the Soviets
Wrote a long letter to Hitler
context: The six children were all given names beginning with H (Helga, Hilde, Helmut, Holde, Hedda, Heide), ages 4 to 12. After the killings Magda reportedly played solitaire before she and Joseph Goebbels took their own lives. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magda_Goebbels.

question: Yevgeny Khaldei staged the famous photograph of a Soviet soldier raising the flag over the Reichstag in May 1945, using a flag his uncle had sewn from a tablecloth. Before the picture ran, Khaldei scratched something off one soldier's arm. What did he remove, and why?
answer: A second wristwatch, hiding that troops had looted
choices: A second wristwatch, hiding that troops had looted
A bloodstain, hiding that he was wounded
A swastika armband, hiding a captured trophy
A rifle strap, hiding that he was armed
context: A soldier wearing a watch on each wrist would have shown the world that Red Army men had been plundering, so Khaldei retouched one away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_a_Flag_over_the_Reichstag; Bronx Documentary Center, 'Altered Images.'

question: Felix Steiner, an SS general, never launched the relief attack Adolf Hitler was counting on, and on 22 April 1945 Hitler learned of it. He flew into a screaming, tearful rage and admitted aloud for the first time that the war was lost. In his last days, what did Hitler keep doing at his map table?
answer: Moving flags for armies that no longer existed
choices: Moving flags for armies that no longer existed
Drafting a plan to flee to Argentina
Writing letters begging the Allies for terms
Recording radio speeches to the German people
context: Even after admitting defeat, Hitler kept shuffling little unit flags across his map for divisions that had already been destroyed, directing phantom forces. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Detachment_Steiner.

question: Walther Wenck's 12th Army was Adolf Hitler's last hope: Hitler ordered it to turn its back on the Americans and fight its way east to break the siege of Berlin. Wenck's worn-out army never reached the city. What did it manage to do instead, before it surrendered to the Americans?
answer: Held open an escape corridor for fleeing civilians
choices: Held open an escape corridor for fleeing civilians
Captured a Soviet marshal
Retook the Reichstag for a day
Reached the bunker minutes too late
context: Wenck quietly disobeyed the suicidal spirit of the order: instead of dying to reach Hitler, his army kept a route open so civilians and soldiers could flee west, then surrendered to the Americans. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Detachment_Steiner.

question: Georgy Zhukov opened the final push on Berlin at 05:00 on 16 April 1945 by switching on 143 giant anti-aircraft searchlights, one every 200 yards, meaning to dazzle and blind the German defenders on the Seelow Heights. The beams bounced off the smoke and mist instead. What did his searchlights actually do?
answer: Silhouetted his own attacking soldiers as targets
choices: Silhouetted his own attacking soldiers as targets
Set the German trenches on fire
Guided German bombers onto the Soviet lines
