Burned out and plunged the field into darkness
context: The light scattered off the haze and lit up the advancing Red Army from behind, outlining the men as easy marks for the German gunners. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Seelow_Heights.

question: Kathe Heusermann, who had assisted Hitler's dentist, gave the Soviets their proof of his death in May 1945, though almost nothing of his body was left to identify. From memory she described one unusual feature, and it matched the remains they had found. What identified Hitler?
answer: His distinctive gold dental bridge
choices: His distinctive gold dental bridge
A scar on his recovered jawbone
The serial number on his pistol
A signet ring on his hand
context: Heusermann and a dental technician described Hitler's unusual gold bridgework from memory, and it matched fragments the Soviets recovered, for years the only physically identified part of Hitler ever found. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Adolf_Hitler.

question: Writing from the Berlin bunker in her last days to her grown stepson, Magda Goebbels explained why she meant to kill her six children rather than let them live on. How did she describe the world that would come after Hitler and National Socialism?
answer: 'Not worth living in' after the regime fell
choices: 'Not worth living in' after the regime fell
Too poor and starving to survive
Too dangerous from Allied revenge
Too shameful after Germany's defeat
context: Magda wrote that the coming world was 'too good, too lovely' and that the children could not bear to live in one without National Socialism. She killed them rather than let them grow up free of the ideology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magda_Goebbels.

question: Antony Beevor, the historian, combed Soviet files opened after the Cold War to measure a crime that came with the fall of Berlin: Red Army soldiers carried out mass rape across the occupied city. How many women did Beevor estimate were raped in Berlin alone?
answer: At least 100,000 women
choices: At least 100,000 women
Around 5,000 women
Several hundred women
Roughly 1,000 women
context: Beevor estimated at least 100,000 women raped in Berlin and perhaps 2 million across the whole Soviet occupation zone. The conquest of the city opened a new chapter of brutality for the German East. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape_during_the_occupation_of_Germany.

question: Josef Stalin kept his army in place after Red Army soldiers stormed Berlin in 1945 and ended Hitler's Third Reich. Crushing Hitler did not give the eastern half of Germany a happy ending. What became of it in the years right after 1945?
answer: It was sealed behind the Iron Curtain under communist rule
choices: It was sealed behind the Iron Curtain under communist rule
It was rebuilt as a free democracy at once
It was handed back to a neutral German government
It was split evenly among all four Allied powers forever
context: Berlin and the East passed under Soviet control, and within a few years the Iron Curtain closed over them. The defeat of Hitler delivered eastern Germans straight into a second tyranny. Source: framing per HISTORY_FRAMEWORK 'honest about Soviet role'; Battle of Berlin / occupation context (Wikipedia; Beevor, 'Berlin: The Downfall 1945').

question: Mehmed II's army stormed Constantinople on 29 May 1453, when he was only twenty-one, and ended the Eastern Roman Empire. The Turks have called him Fatih ever since. What does Fatih mean?
answer: The Conqueror
choices: The Lawgiver
The Conqueror
The Magnificent
The Grim
context: In Turkish he became Mehmed 'Fatih' — the Conqueror. He made the captured city his new capital, replacing Edirne (old Adrianople). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehmed_II

question: A soldier of Mehmed II's army was prising up the marble floor of Hagia Sophia to loot it, just after Constantinople fell in 1453, when the sultan rode into the great domed church and caught him. Mehmed stopped the man with a single line about what in the city now belonged to him. What did Mehmed say was his?
answer: The buildings of the city are mine
choices: The buildings of the city are mine
The gold and the silver are mine
Every captive taken here is mine
All the lands of the earth are mine
context: Mehmed reportedly told the man the plunder and the captives belonged to the soldiers, but 'the buildings of the city belong to me' — then had a muezzin sound the call to prayer, turning the 900-year-old church into a mosque. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople

question: Mehmed II threw his army at the walls of Constantinople in three waves on the final night, 29 May 1453. The throwaway irregulars charged first and the Anatolian regulars after them; last came his best-armed household troops, sent to crush the tired defenders. What were these elite soldiers called?
answer: The Janissaries
choices: The Janissaries
The sipahi cavalry
The akinji raiders
The azab infantry
context: The elite Janissaries — perhaps 5,000 to 10,000 of them — formed the third and decisive wave that finally cracked the exhausted defense. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople

question: Giovanni Giustiniani, a Genoese captain, had brought 700 men of his own and fought for weeks on the land walls of Constantinople. Then, in the final assault, something happened to him that sent his Genoese running and broke the whole defence. What happened to Giustiniani?
answer: He was badly wounded and carried off the wall
choices: He was badly wounded and carried off the wall
He was captured alive by the Janissaries
He turned traitor and opened a city gate
He was killed by a blast of the giant cannon
context: Struck by shot or a bolt, Giustiniani had himself carried to a ship; seeing their commander leave, the Genoese followed and the line broke into panic. He died of the wound on 1 June and was buried on Chios. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Giustiniani

question: George Sphrantzes, a Byzantine court official, secretly counted every man inside the walls who could fight before Mehmed II's siege of Constantinople began in 1453. Outside waited an army of 50,000 to 80,000. Even with the Genoese and the other foreign volunteers added in, about how many defenders did the city have?
answer: About 7,000
choices: About 7,000
About 20,000
About 35,000
About 60,000
context: Sphrantzes counted only about 4,773 Greeks plus roughly 200 foreigners — fewer than 7,000 to hold miles of wall against a host more than ten times their size. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople

question: Cardinal Bessarion gathered some 800 Greek manuscripts and later gave them to Venice, while other scholars fleeing fallen Constantinople carried Greek books and learning west into Italy. What great European awakening did this tide of Greek books and teachers help to feed?
answer: The Renaissance
choices: The Renaissance
The Reformation
The Enlightenment
The Crusades
context: Bessarion alone gathered some 800 Greek manuscripts; refugee scholars taught Greek and the ancient texts in Italy, helping revive classical learning and feed the Renaissance. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_scholars_in_the_Renaissance

question: Nicolo Barbaro, a Venetian eyewitness inside Constantinople in 1453, wrote down a darker end for the last emperor, Constantine XI, than most accounts give. Most say he died sword in hand in the fighting. What did Barbaro claim happened to him?
answer: He hanged himself as the Turks broke through
choices: He hanged himself as the Turks broke through
He was beheaded and his head sent away
He drowned swimming for a rescue ship
He was burned alive in his own palace
context: Barbaro claimed the emperor hanged himself when the Turks forced the San Romano gate. Most other accounts have him dying sword-in-hand; his true fate remains unknown. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople

question: Walking through the half-empty ruins of the city he had just won, the 21-year-old Mehmed II did not boast. Instead, he is said to have recited a sad old Persian verse about how all empires fall. What image did the verse set in the old palace of the Caesars?
answer: A spider at the curtains, an owl on the towers
choices: A spider at the curtains, an owl on the towers
Wolves at the throne, ravens on the dome
Sand in the great halls, ivy on the gates
Frost on the marble, silence in the courts
context: The verse runs: 'The spider weaves the curtains in the palace of the Caesars; the owl calls the watches in the towers of Afrasiyab.' Mehmed cut the three-day sack short because little was left to take. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople

question: Doukas, a later chronicler, blamed the whole fall of Constantinople in 1453 on one small mistake at the walls, though he was not there and historians reject his tale. By his story, what let the first Turks slip inside the city?
answer: A small back gate was left standing open by accident
choices: A small back gate was left standing open by accident
A drunken night-watch was bribed to look away
A long section of wall had already collapsed
A drain beneath the wall was left unbarred
context: The chronicler Doukas wrote that a little postern called the Kerkoporta was left open, letting about 50 Ottomans in to raise their banner. Doukas was not present and wrote years later; no matching gate has been found, so historians treat it as legend. https://hispanatolia.com/en/the-mystery-of-the-kerkoporta-did-an-open-gate-cause-the-fall-of-constantinople/

question: Mehmed II brought his army against Constantinople in 1453 and faced a triple wall on the city's land side, fronted by a moat 60 feet wide. A Roman emperor of the fifth century had built it, and it was long thought unbreakable. What were these walls called, after the emperor who raised them?
answer: The Theodosian Walls
choices: The Aurelian Walls
The Servian Walls
The Antonine Walls
The Theodosian Walls
context: The Theodosian Walls were a triple line with a 60-foot-wide moat that had protected Constantinople for roughly 800 years and were long thought unbreachable. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople

question: Orban, a Hungarian gunsmith, built Mehmed II a bronze cannon about 27 feet long for the siege of Constantinople, a monster called the Basilica, and sixty oxen and more than 400 men were needed to haul it to the walls. Between firings, something startling could fit inside its barrel. What could?
answer: A grown man, who could crawl in
choices: A small wagon, wheels and all
A horse, standing upright
A cart of cannonballs at once
A grown man, who could crawl in
context: The Basilica was about 27 feet (8.2 m) long and hurled roughly 600-pound stone balls over a mile; its bronze barrel was wide enough for a man to crawl inside. It took 60 oxen and over 400 men to drag it to the walls. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople

question: Mehmed II could not get his warships past a huge iron chain floated across the entrance to the Golden Horn, Constantinople's harbour. Then one April morning in 1453 dozens of his ships suddenly showed up inside the harbour, behind the chain, and the shock crushed the defenders. How did he get them in?
answer: He dragged them overland on a road of greased logs
choices: He sailed them up a hidden river channel
He blasted a gap in the chain with his cannon
He bribed the harbor guards to let them slip past
He dragged them overland on a road of greased logs
context: Unable to break the chain, Mehmed had a road of greased logs built over the hill of Galata and dragged dozens of warships overland into the Golden Horn behind the chain. Ships suddenly appearing inside the 'safe' harbor shattered Byzantine morale. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople

question: Constantine XI, the last emperor, vanished as the city fell; no one ever found his body. The Greeks could not bear to believe he was simply gone. So they told a legend that promised he would return one day to win Constantinople back. What did the legend say had become of him?
answer: An angel turned him to stone and hid him to wake again
choices: He escaped by sea to found a new empire abroad
An angel turned him to stone and hid him to wake again
He was crowned in secret as a monk on a far mountain
He was carried up to heaven in a chariot of fire
context: LEGEND. Greek folklore turned the lost emperor into the 'Marble Emperor': an angel turned Constantine XI to marble and hid him beneath the city, where he sleeps until the day he rises to win Constantinople back. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1180/1453-the-fall-of-constantinople/

question: Doukas, a historian, quoted Loukas Notaras, a Byzantine official, as bitterly rejecting union with the Catholic West, though that union might have brought ships to save Constantinople. The line may have been made up. According to Doukas, what did Notaras say he preferred to see in the City?
answer: A Turkish turban rather than a Latin mitre
choices: A burning fleet rather than a foreign flag
An empty throne rather than a Western prince
A Turkish turban rather than a Latin mitre
A ruined wall rather than a papal crown
context: LEGEND / disputed. Loukas Notaras is quoted by the historian Doukas (the line may be apocryphal) as saying he would 'rather see a Turkish turban in the midst of the City than the Latin mitre,' rejecting the union with the Catholic West that might have brought rescue. The quarrel weakened the defense. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loukas_Notaras

question: French soldiers manned the Maginot Line, a row of massive concrete forts along the German border, built before the war to stop any invasion cold. When Germany attacked in May 1940, how did the German army beat this fortress wall?
answer: They marched around its end through Belgium, leaving the forts behind them
choices: They marched around its end through Belgium, leaving the forts behind them
They smashed it head-on with the largest artillery ever built
They tunneled beneath the forts and blew them up from below
They starved the garrisons out over a long winter siege
context: The Maginot Line was never actually broken through. The Germans simply went around its northern end through Belgium and the Ardennes, and France fell behind it - the fortress guns ended up facing the wrong way. Source: Warfare History Network, The French Maginot Line; Sedan 1940, Wikipedia.

question: The Germans did not send their panzers where the French expected when they struck France in May 1940, and within six weeks they had beaten an army that looked, on paper, the strongest in the West. Their main thrust drove through a region the French had barely defended. Which region did the Germans punch through?
answer: The Ardennes, a hilly forest the French called impassable to tanks
choices: The Ardennes, a hilly forest the French called impassable to tanks
The open wheat plains of Picardy north of Paris
The marshlands of the Rhine delta near the sea
The high alpine passes along the Italian border
context: The French were certain the dense Ardennes woods and the Meuse River made the region impregnable to tanks, so they barely defended it. The German panzers poured through exactly there, crossing the Meuse at Sedan on May 13. The strongest army in the West on paper was beaten in six weeks - doctrine failed, not courage. Source: Britannica, Battle of France; Manstein Plan, Wikipedia.

question: Erich von Manstein drew up the plan for Germany's invasion of France in May 1940, known as Sichelschnitt, the Sickle Cut. It rested on a battlefield deception the Germans called the matador's cloak. What was the trick at the heart of the plan?
answer: A fake heavy attack into Belgium and Holland to lure the best Allied armies north
choices: A fake heavy attack into Belgium and Holland to lure the best Allied armies north
A false radio campaign convincing France the blow would land in the Alps
A staged retreat that drew the French tanks deep into Germany
A bribed double agent who fed Paris the wrong invasion date
context: The 'matador's cloak' was a feint: a showy attack into Belgium and Holland drew the strongest Allied armies north, while the real blow swung behind them through the Ardennes like a scythe and cut them off from the sea. Source: Warhistory.org, Sickle Cut Through France; Manstein Plan, Wikipedia.

question: A huge crowd of East Berliners pressed up against the Berlin Wall on the night of 9 November 1989, wanting to be let through to the West. As they shoved at the checkpoints, what did they chant over and over?
answer: "Open the gate!"
choices: "Open the gate!"
"Down with walls!"
"We want bread!"
"Set us free!"
context: In German the chant was "Tor auf!" — literally "Gate open!" The wall had split the city for 28 years, and that night the crowd's roar finally won. Source: history.com/articles/berlin-wall; iwm.org.uk/history/cold-war/germany/berlin-wall.

question: Crowds swarmed the Berlin Wall with hammers and chisels in November 1989, days after it opened, chipping off painted chunks to keep. The endless tap-tap-tap of their tools earned them a nickname taken from a bird. What were they called?
answer: Wall woodpeckers
choices: Wall woodpeckers
Wall foxes
Wall beavers
Wall magpies
context: In German, "Mauerspechte" — wall woodpeckers. They knocked loose so many fragments that a brisk trade sprang up selling painted bits of the wall to tourists. Source: iwm.org.uk/history/cold-war/germany/berlin-wall/film; stiftung-berliner-mauer.de.

question: Günter Schabowski, the East German government spokesman, read out new travel rules on the evening of 9 November 1989, rules meant to start the next day. When a reporter asked when they took effect, his one-word answer sent crowds rushing to the border that night. What was the word?
answer: "Immediately"
choices: "Immediately"
"Tomorrow"
"Soon"
"Gradually"
context: "Das tritt nach meiner Kenntnis ... ist das sofort, unverzüglich" — "As far as I know ... that is effective immediately, without delay." The German word "sofort" is what cracked the wall. Source: chronik-der-mauer.de (Hertle account); 1989.rrchnm.org transcript.

question: A reporter shouted a question at Günter Schabowski during a live televised press conference on 9 November 1989: when would East Germany's new travel rules take effect? Schabowski had barely studied the paperwork himself, and millions of East Germans were watching. What did he do at that moment?
answer: He fumbled with his glasses, shuffled his papers, and guessed at an answer
choices: He fumbled with his glasses, shuffled his papers, and guessed at an answer
He confidently quoted the official start date from memory
He snapped that it was none of the reporter's business
He stepped aside and let an aide read the rules aloud
context: He had been handed a note about the new rules he hadn't read. Peering at his papers, he stammered that the change was effective "immediately, without delay" — the rules were really meant to begin the next day. Source: chronik-der-mauer.de (Hertle account, 9 Nov 1989 18:00).

question: Germans danced on top of the Berlin Wall at the Brandenburg Gate in November 1989 once word spread that it was open, and West Berliners handed out champagne, flowers and sweets. Over the weekend more than two million East Berliners poured into the West. What did one writer call the celebration?
answer: The greatest street party
choices: The greatest street party
The greatest peace march
The greatest harvest feast
The greatest victory parade
context: By midnight people were dancing on the wall itself; the weekend crossing of over 2 million was called "the greatest street party in the history of the world." Source: time.com/5720386/berlin-wall-fall; history.com/articles/berlin-wall.

question: Harald Jäger, an East German border officer who had never once broken an order in decades of service, was on his break at his checkpoint on the evening of 9 November 1989 when the radio carried Schabowski's announcement. Jäger was so stunned that he nearly choked. What did he nearly choke on?
answer: His sandwich
choices: His sandwich
His coffee
His cigarette
His own words
context: Jäger was eating a sandwich in the guards' break room when the announcement came over the radio and he "almost choked on his sandwich." He had served since 1961. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_J%C3%A4ger.

question: The Bornholmer Strasse checkpoint filled with crowds on the night of 9 November 1989. Harald Jäger had guarded the border for decades for a regime that shot anyone who tried to cross, and now he phoned his superiors again and again and got no orders. Then one of them sneered at him with a single contemptuous word. The insult broke Jäger, and he opened the gate. What was the word?
answer: A coward
choices: A coward
A traitor
A fool
A weakling
context: After three decades of obedience, the jab — "or is he simply a coward?" — was the last straw. Jäger asked his men, "Should we shoot all these people or should we open up?" then told his commander, "I am going to end all controls and let the people out." Source: history.com/articles/reasons-berlin-wall-fall (drawing on Mary Elise Sarotte's research).

question: Patrols and guard dogs watched over a wide corridor between the Berlin Wall's inner and outer barriers, lined with 302 watchtowers and roughly 55,000 land mines, to stop anyone trying to escape. What grim name did this no-man's-land carry?
answer: The death strip
choices: The death strip
The iron belt
The grey mile
The cold corridor
context: The wall ran about 96 miles (155 km), and its patrolled "death strip" is what made escape so deadly — at least 140 people were killed at the wall between 1961 and 1989. That toll is what made the night it fell so meaningful. Source: acton.org "5 facts about the Berlin Wall"; chronik-der-mauer.de/en/victims/.

question: Mstislav Rostropovich, the famous cellist, heard in Paris that the Berlin Wall had opened, and two days later he was there. He begged a friend with a private jet to fly him to Berlin, borrowed a chair, and sat down before a graffiti-covered slab of the falling wall in honour of the people killed trying to cross it. What did he play?
answer: Bach's cello suites
choices: Bach's cello suites
a Russian folk lament
his own farewell song
the East German anthem
context: On November 11, 1989, Rostropovich played the Sarabande from Bach's Cello Suite No. 2 against the broken wall — a quiet tribute to the dead. Source: thestrad.com "Rostropovich plays Bach at the Checkpoint Charlie"; classicfm.com.

question: A crowd of about a million people packed in around the Brandenburg Gate on 31 December 1989 for the first New Year's Eve party after the Wall opened. An American star was hoisted above them in a crane's cage, wearing a jacket strung with flashing lights, and belted out his hit 'Looking for Freedom.' Who was he?
answer: David Hasselhoff
choices: David Hasselhoff
Bruce Springsteen
Elton John
Billy Joel
context: "Looking for Freedom" was already a chart-topper in divided Germany, which made Hasselhoff's crane-cage performance above the crowd an instant legend. Source: time.com/5714602/david-hasselhoff-berlin-wall-fall; nbcnews.com.

question: East German guards tried a cruel trick called the valve solution before the gates fully opened on 9 November 1989. They let the loudest troublemakers out one at a time, secretly stamping each passport to cancel its owner's citizenship. What made the scheme collapse?
answer: Young parents pushed out realized they could never return to their children
choices: Young parents pushed out realized they could never return to their children
West German police refused to let the exiles cross the border
Schabowski went on the radio and ordered the guards to stop
The guards ran out of ink and could not stamp any more passports
context: The "Ventillösung" backfired when parents shoved through the gate understood the stamp meant they could never go home to their kids; the cruelty was so plain the scheme fell apart and the guards gave up. Source: history.com/articles/reasons-berlin-wall-fall; chronik-der-mauer.de (9:30 pm "Ventilösung").

question: Grigori Rasputin, a wandering holy man, told the weeping Tsarina Alexandra that her son Alexei, near death from a bleeding no doctor could stop, would live: 'God has seen your tears and heard your prayers. The Little One will not die.' The bleeding stopped. What did Alexandra come to believe?
answer: That Rasputin had been sent by God to save her son
choices: That Rasputin had been sent by God to save her son
That the doctors had been wrong about the disease
That Alexei would grow up to be a great warrior
That the palace itself was blessed and protected
context: Alexei had hemophilia; when his bleeding stopped after Rasputin's words, the Tsarina believed God had sent the peasant to save her son, and Rasputin gained enormous influence over the royal family. Source: discovermagazine.com 'Uncover the Myth of Rasputin'; rasputinarchive.com.

question: Prince Felix Yusupov lured Rasputin to a cellar room of the Yusupov Palace one night in December 1916 and fed him cakes and Madeira wine laced with cyanide, enough, the plotters thought, to kill several men. By Yusupov's own story, what happened next?
answer: The poison seemed to have no effect on him at all
choices: The poison seemed to have no effect on him at all
Rasputin collapsed within minutes and stopped breathing
Rasputin tasted the cyanide and refused to eat
Rasputin fell into a deep, motionless sleep
context: Yusupov claimed the cyanide-laced cakes and wine did nothing, fueling the legend that Rasputin could not be killed. The conspirators then shot him. Source: nationalgeographic.com 'How did Rasputin die'; rbth.com.

question: Grigori Rasputin, the shaggy, wild-eyed mystic, won his way into the court of Tsar Nicholas II before the First World War by claiming he could heal young Alexei's bleeding disease. Books and films have called him the Mad Monk ever since, but historians say the nickname is simply wrong. Why is it wrong?
answer: He was a self-taught peasant and was never ordained
choices: He was a self-taught peasant and was never ordained
He was actually a trained palace physician, not a holy man
He was a bishop, far higher in rank than a monk
He was a nobleman who only pretended to be poor
context: Rasputin was born in 1869 in the Siberian village of Pokrovskoye, became a wandering self-taught holy man, and was never ordained — so calling him a 'monk' was never accurate. Source: discovermagazine.com 'Uncover the Myth of Rasputin'.

question: Bolshevik gunmen opened fire on the Romanov family in the cellar of the Ipatiev House one night in July 1918, and their first bullets bounced off the four princesses, Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia. Why did the bullets bounce off the girls?
answer: Over a kilogram of diamonds was sewn into their corsets
choices: Over a kilogram of diamonds was sewn into their corsets
They were standing behind a heavy oak cabinet
They wore steel-lined hunting jackets for the journey
The cellar's stone walls deflected the ricocheting shots
context: The duchesses had more than a kilogram of diamonds and jewels sewn into their corsets and clothing; the bullets ricocheted off the hidden gems, and the executioners had to finish them with bayonets and point-blank shots. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Murder of the Romanov family'; thehistoryreader.com.

question: Doctors performed an autopsy on Grigori Rasputin after his murder in December 1916. Legend would make him the man who could not die, poisoned and shot and drowned at last under the river ice, but his body told a different story. What did the autopsy actually find in him?
answer: No trace of poison — only alcohol
choices: No trace of poison — only alcohol
Enough cyanide to have killed five men
Poison pooled in his stomach but not his blood
River water filling both of his lungs
context: The autopsy found no poison at all, only alcohol, plus three gunshot wounds — a close-range shot to the forehead was what actually killed him. The cyanide-and-icy-water survival saga is largely embellished myth. Source: nationalgeographic.com 'How did Rasputin die'; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38386172.

question: Anna Anderson insisted for decades that she was Grand Duchess Anastasia, the one Romanov child who had escaped the cellar alive. Hers was the most famous royal mystery of the century, until DNA testing in 1994 revealed who she really was. Who was she?
answer: Franziska Schanzkowska, a missing Polish factory worker
choices: Franziska Schanzkowska, a missing Polish factory worker
Eugenia Smith, a Russian émigré painter
Nadezhda Vasilyeva, a Siberian peasant woman
Tatiana Botkina, the family doctor's daughter
context: DNA proved Anna Anderson was no relation to the Romanovs but Franziska Schanzkowska, a missing Polish factory worker. The 2007 discovery of two more bodies near Yekaterinburg, DNA-matched to the family, proved no child escaped — Anastasia died in the cellar. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2652717; content.time.com.

question: A powerless boy sat on the throne of the Western Roman Empire as its very last emperor in 476. By coincidence his two names echoed two figures from the very start of Rome: the city's legendary founder and its first emperor. Which two names did the boy share?
answer: Romulus and Augustus
choices: Romulus and Augustus
Julius and Constantine
Aeneas and Tiberius
Remus and Caesar
context: Romulus was the legendary founder of the city of Rome; Augustus was its first emperor. By coincidence the boy who ended the Western Empire shared a name with both men who started it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus

question: Emperor Zeno still sat on the throne of the empire's other half in 476, the year the West lost its last emperor, and that half lived on for almost another thousand years. It was ruled from one great city until the Turks took that city in 1453. Which city was it?
answer: Constantinople
choices: Constantinople
Alexandria
Carthage
Jerusalem
context: The Eastern Roman Empire, which we call Byzantium, was ruled from Constantinople by Emperor Zeno in 476 and carried the Roman name onward until Constantinople fell in 1453 — almost a thousand years after the West ended. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/835/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire/

question: Romulus Augustulus lost his throne in 476 but not his life. The Germanic general who deposed him did not have him killed; he granted the boy a pension of 6,000 solidi a year and sent him away to live. Where did the boy go?
answer: To a seaside fortress-villa in Italy
choices: To a seaside fortress-villa in Italy
To a monastery in distant Gaul
To the imperial court in the East
To a prison cell beneath Ravenna
context: The boy was given the castellum Lucullanum, a fortress-villa on the coast of Campania near Naples, plus a yearly pension of 6,000 solidi — a fortune. He may have lived on there quietly for decades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus

question: Behind the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus, who held the western throne for less than a year, stood another man who made every big decision and ran what was left of the empire in the boy's name. Who was the man really in charge?
answer: His father, Orestes
choices: His father, Orestes
His uncle, Julius Nepos
The general Odoacer
The eastern emperor Zeno
context: Orestes installed his own son on the throne as a puppet, perhaps when the boy was only about fifteen, and ruled in his name. Orestes held the real power; the boy held only the title, for less than a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus

question: Orestes took Germanic soldiers into his pay, Heruli and Sciri among them, to fight for the Western Empire, and then refused to give them the reward they demanded. They rose up, killed him and toppled the last western emperor. What had the soldiers asked for?
answer: A third of all the land in Italy
choices: A third of all the land in Italy
A year of gold from the treasury
Command of the Roman navy
The freedom to sack the city
context: The mercenaries — Heruli, Sciri, and others — wanted one-third of the land of Italy as their payment to settle on. Orestes refused, and the empire fell over that single unkept bargain. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odoacer

question: Germanic soldiers rose in revolt, and on 4 September 476 their general stormed into Ravenna, the imperial capital, and pulled the boy Romulus Augustulus off the throne. Historians mark that day as the end of the Western Roman Empire. Who was the general who took down the last emperor?
answer: Odoacer
choices: Odoacer
Theodoric
Alaric
Attila
context: Odoacer, general of the revolting mercenaries, deposed Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna on 4 September 476. He then ruled Italy himself, governing from Ravenna and keeping the Roman Senate running. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odoacer

question: The Germanic general who overthrew the last western emperor in 476 let the boy live, though winners in those hard times usually killed a beaten rival. A Roman chronicle known as the Anonymus Valesianus gives a very personal reason for the mercy. What does it say moved the general to spare Romulus Augustulus?
answer: The boy's youth and good looks
choices: The boy's youth and good looks
A solemn oath sworn to Orestes
The pleading of the Roman Senate
A warning from the eastern emperor
context: The Anonymus Valesianus records that Odoacer 'was moved by Romulus's youth and his beauty' and spared his life rather than execute him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odoacer

question: Orestes, a Roman general in the last years of the Western Empire, had a startling past. Years earlier he had taken dictation as personal secretary to the most feared enemy Rome ever faced. Whose secretary had Orestes been?
answer: Attila the Hun
choices: Attila the Hun
Alaric the Visigoth
Genseric the Vandal
Theodoric the Ostrogoth
context: Before he handed the empire to his son, Orestes had served as notarius — personal secretary — to Attila the Hun. The man who had taken dictation for Rome's deadliest foe ended up father to Rome's last emperor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orestes_(father_of_Romulus_Augustulus)

question: Italy's new master after 476, the Germanic general who deposed the last western emperor, could easily have crowned himself emperor of the West. He refused, and with the imperial crown and the purple robes he did something that told the world the West needed no emperor of its own. What did he do with them?
answer: Shipped them across the Adriatic to Constantinople
choices: Shipped them across the Adriatic to Constantinople
Burned them publicly in the Roman Forum
Locked them away in his private treasury
Wore them at his own grand coronation
context: Odoacer sent the Western regalia to Emperor Zeno in Constantinople and took for himself only the humbler title 'rex,' King of Italy. The gesture declared the West no longer needed its own emperor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odoacer

question: Edward Gibbon and historians like him picked 476 as the year the Western Roman Empire fell, decades after Alaric had sacked Rome itself in 410. Yet Rome changed shape more than it died: its law grew into the root of Western law, and the Church took up its structure. Its everyday tongue never stopped being spoken either. Which living languages did Latin grow into?
answer: French, Italian, and Spanish
choices: French, Italian, and Spanish
English, German, and Dutch
Greek, Turkish, and Arabic
Irish, Welsh, and Breton
context: Latin lived on and slowly became French, Italian, and Spanish; Roman law became the foundation of Western law, and the Church took up Rome's organization. The empire transmuted rather than simply vanishing in 476. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historiography_of_the_fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire

question: Sergei Prokofiev gave every character in Peter and the Wolf an instrument of its own, to teach children the orchestra. To make the hungry wolf sound big and frightening, he gave him three of the same instrument playing together. Which instrument did the wolf get three of?
answer: French horns
choices: French horns
violins
flutes
drums
context: Prokofiev assigned each character its own instrument so children would learn the four families by story: the bird is a flute, the duck an oboe, the cat a clarinet, the grumpy grandfather a bassoon, and Peter himself is the whole string section. The wolf gets three French horns (a brass instrument, sounded by buzzing the lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece). Source: laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/552/peter-and-the-wolf

question: The hasty wolf in Prokofiev's Peter and the Wolf gulps the duck down whole and alive, too rushed to chew her. Listeners can still hear her quacking faintly inside his belly at the finish. Which instrument plays the duck's voice?
answer: the oboe
choices: the oboe
the flute
the clarinet
the bassoon
context: Each animal in the piece is voiced by a fixed instrument: the bird is the flute, the cat the clarinet, the grumpy grandfather the bassoon, and the duck is the oboe. Because the wolf swallowed her whole and alive, Prokofiev keeps the oboe quacking faintly at the end -- the duck is still down there. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_and_the_Wolf

question: Michael Faraday, a poor blacksmith's son from near London, left school at fourteen and never went to a university, yet he grew into one of the greatest experimenters of all. As a young apprentice with almost no money, how did he teach himself science?
answer: By reading the very books he was hired to bind
choices: By reading the very books he was hired to bind
By attending free evening lectures at Oxford
By copying out the notebooks of a rich tutor
By memorizing a single encyclopedia given to him
context: Faraday was apprenticed to a bookbinder at 14 and educated himself on the books passing through the shop, becoming one of history's greatest experimentalists without ever going to university. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: A self-taught experimenter at the Royal Institution unlocked the secrets of electricity in the 1830s with hands-on experiments, though he never learned advanced mathematics. Today a common unit, used to measure the electrical storage in every phone and computer, is named in his honour. Which unit is it?
answer: The farad
choices: The volt
The watt
The farad
The joule
context: The farad, the unit of electrical capacitance, honors Michael Faraday, the self-taught bookbinder who never learned advanced mathematics. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: James Clerk Maxwell was driving his family to distraction before he was three, asking how doors and locks, streams and bells worked. Which short question did the curious toddler keep repeating?
answer: "What's the go o' that?"
choices: "Where does it all go?"
"What's the go o' that?"
"Who made it move?"
"How can that be true?"
context: As a toddler Maxwell endlessly asked 'What's the go o' that?', demanding the workings of everything around him long before he grew into the century's greatest physicist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell

question: Queen Victoria offered Michael Faraday a knighthood once his experiments at the Royal Institution had made England the world capital of electrical science, and the Royal Society, Britain's most prestigious club of scientists, twice begged him to be its president. Faraday turned it all down. What did he insist on staying instead?
answer: "plain Mr Faraday to the end"
choices: "a free man of science"
"plain Mr Faraday to the end"
"a humble servant of God"
"only a poor bookbinder"
context: Faraday refused the knighthood and twice declined the Royal Society presidency, vowing to remain 'plain Mr Faraday to the end'; he also refused to help make poison gas for the Crimean War on ethical grounds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: Using a red, a green and a blue filter in turn, James Clerk Maxwell photographed one object three times in 1861, then combined the three pictures into the world's first true colour photograph. Which everyday object did he choose for it?
answer: A tartan ribbon
choices: A bowl of fresh fruit
A tartan ribbon
A garden of roses
A stained-glass window
context: Maxwell's three-filter method produced the first color photograph in 1861 using a tartan ribbon, proving any color could be built from red, green, and blue light. Source: https://www.historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=3666

question: Michael Faraday wound two separate coils of wire onto an iron ring in August 1831, with only the iron joining them. He turned the current on in the first coil and watched the meter fixed to the second, which had no battery of its own. What did he see happen in that second coil?
answer: Its meter needle twitched, showing a current
choices: Its meter needle twitched, showing a current
Its wire glowed red and began to smoke
Nothing at all, until the iron melted
Its coil flung itself off the ring
context: Switching current on in one coil made Faraday's galvanometer twitch in the other: moving magnetism had created electricity (electromagnetic induction), the principle behind every generator. That iron ring is still on display at the Royal Institution. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: Maxwell put his new equations of electricity and magnetism to work around 1862 to find how fast an invisible electric wave should travel through empty space. The number he calculated matched a speed scientists had already measured in a completely different way. What did it turn out to equal?
answer: The speed of light
choices: The speed of sound in air
The speed of light
The speed of the Earth's orbit
The speed of a falling object
context: Maxwell's electromagnetic wave speed equaled the measured speed of light, leading him to conclude light itself is an electromagnetic wave, uniting light, electricity, and magnetism as one phenomenon. Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Maxwell/

question: Heinrich Hertz, a German physicist, made Maxwell's invisible electric waves in his laboratory in 1887, after Maxwell had died, and reportedly shrugged that they were of no use whatsoever. Within a decade those useless waves had become a world-changing invention. Which one?
answer: Radio
choices: The telephone
Radio
The electric lightbulb
The X-ray machine
context: Hertz confirmed Maxwell's waves in 1887 and dismissed them as useless; within ten years they became radio. The 'of no use whatsoever' quote is widely retold but only loosely documented, so it is treated as legend. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Heinrich_Hertz

question: Franklin Roosevelt took office in March 1933 with the country at the bottom of the Great Depression, a quarter of its workers jobless and banks failing every day. In his first speech he tried to calm a frightened nation with one famous sentence. How did it go?
answer: "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself."
choices: "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself."
"Ask not what your country can do for you."
"We have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears, and sweat."
"Government of the people, by the people, for the people."
context: FDR's 1933 inaugural line — "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself — nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror" — is often credited to adviser Louis Howe, who added it to the draft. The other three quotes belong to John F. Kennedy, Winston Churchill, and Abraham Lincoln. Source: National Archives, FDR's First Inaugural Address (archives.gov); Yale Avalon Project (avalon.law.yale.edu).

question: Franklin Roosevelt hired almost 3 million young men without jobs for his Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s, paying each $30 a month to plant trees and build parks. The men did not get to keep most of that pay. What was the rule for the $30?
answer: $25 of it was sent straight home to their families.
choices: $25 of it was sent straight home to their families.
All of it was held back until they finished their service.
Half of it was taxed to pay for the camps' upkeep.
$25 of it was paid in scrip good only at the camp store.
context: Of the CCC's $30 monthly pay, $25 was mailed straight home to the worker's family. The Corps ran from 1933 to 1942 in camps organized like the Army, and its crews together planted more than 3 billion trees. Source: History.com, Civilian Conservation Corps (history.com); Britannica, Civilian Conservation Corps (britannica.com).

question: Terrified Americans were pulling out their savings and banks were collapsing every day when Franklin Roosevelt took office in March 1933. Two days later he made a startling first move to stop the panic. What did he order?
answer: He shut every bank in the country for several days.
choices: He shut every bank in the country for several days.
He seized the failing banks and ran them from Washington.
He sent federal troops to guard the largest banks.
He printed emergency cash to hand out at every bank.
context: FDR's Proclamation 2039 (March 6, 1933) declared a nationwide "bank holiday" that closed every bank, then Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act — the first law of his presidency — to reopen them under federal supervision. In his first radio "fireside chat" the night before they reopened, he told listeners it was safer to keep money in a reopened bank than under the mattress; that week Americans returned about $1 billion in hoarded cash. Source: Federal Reserve History (federalreservehistory.org); Library of Congress, 1933 Bank Holiday (guides.loc.gov).

question: Backcountry farm families in seven poor Southern states got something most of them had never had at home when Roosevelt's Tennessee Valley Authority built sixteen dams there in the 1930s. What did the dams bring them?
answer: Electric lights
choices: Electric lights
Running water
Telephones
Paved roads
context: TVA power lit up farms that had never had electricity. Its first dam, Norris Dam, was named for Senator George Norris of Nebraska, called "the father of TVA." The cost deserves telling honestly too: Norris Dam flooded the valley, forcing nearly 3,000 people from their homes and requiring the government to relocate some 5,200 graves. Source: History.com, Why the TVA Was the New Deal's Most Ambitious Program (history.com); TVA, Our History (tva.com).

question: Frances Perkins, Roosevelt's Labor Secretary, had pushed harder than anyone in Washington to get the Social Security Act passed, and in 1935 he handed her one of the pens he signed it with. She had already made history two years earlier, on the day she joined his cabinet. How?
answer: She was the first woman ever to serve in a U.S. Cabinet.
choices: She was the first woman ever to serve in a U.S. Cabinet.
She was the first Labor Secretary to rise from a union.
She was the youngest Cabinet member in the nation's history.
She was the first Cabinet member born outside the country.
context: Frances Perkins was the first woman ever to serve in a U.S. Cabinet, and she fought for the Social Security Act before receiving one of FDR's signing pens on August 14, 1935. Source: EBSCO Research Starters, Social Security Act of 1935 (ebsco.com); SSA History (ssa.gov/history).

question: Franklin Roosevelt hired 8.5 million Depression-era Americans through his Works Progress Administration to build roads and bridges, but the program also spent federal money on a kind of worker few people would picture on a New Deal jobs program. Who else did it put on the payroll?
answer: Out-of-work writers and artists
choices: Out-of-work writers and artists
Retired soldiers and sailors
Schoolchildren and students
Foreign engineers and architects
context: The WPA paid unemployed writers and artists: its Federal Art Project funded 2,566 murals, and its Federal Writers' Project produced the American Guide Series — 378 books and pamphlets describing every state, city, and village in the nation. In all the WPA ran 1.4 million projects from 1935 to 1943. Source: Britannica, Works Progress Administration (britannica.com); Wikipedia, Works Progress Administration (en.wikipedia.org).

question: Ida May Fuller, a retired Vermont schoolteacher, cashed the very first monthly Social Security check in 1940. Over three years she had put just $24.75 into the new payroll tax, and then she lived to 100. By the time she died, how much had Social Security paid her?
context: Ida May Fuller's first check (number 00-000-001, dated January 31, 1940) was for $22.54; against $24.75 in payroll taxes she ultimately collected $22,888.92 — 924 times what she paid in. FDR was candid that the payroll tax was political armor, telling aide Luther Gulick: "With those taxes in there, no damn politician can ever scrap my social security program... they're straight politics." Source: Social Security Administration History, Ida May Fuller and the Gulick Memorandum (ssa.gov/history).

question: The Schechter family, who sold food to local markets in Brooklyn, fought the federal rules of the National Industrial Recovery Act, the heart of Roosevelt's first New Deal, in 1935. They took their case all the way to the Supreme Court, and every justice voted to strike the whole act down. By what nickname is the case remembered?
answer: The Sick Chicken Case
choices: The Sick Chicken Case
The Bad Milk Case
The Rotten Meat Case
The Spoiled Egg Case
context: A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935), the "Sick Chicken Case," was decided unanimously; the Court ruled the NIRA had handed the President legislative power he could not constitutionally hold. Source: Cornell LII, Schechter Poultry (law.cornell.edu); Wikipedia, A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (en.wikipedia.org).

question: The nine justices of the Supreme Court struck down one New Deal law after another, and in February 1937 a furious Franklin Roosevelt sent Congress a bold plan to reshape the Court so it would stop blocking him. Critics quickly nicknamed the scheme court-packing. What exactly did his plan propose?
answer: Add one new justice for every sitting justice over age 70
choices: Add one new justice for every sitting justice over age 70
Force every justice over age 70 to retire at once
Let the President remove justices who voted against his laws
Send each major law to a public vote instead of the Court
context: Unveiled February 5, 1937, the plan would have let FDR appoint up to six extra justices, ballooning the bench from 9 to as many as 15. The conservative bloc that kept voting the New Deal down — Sutherland, Butler, McReynolds, and Van Devanter — was nicknamed "the Four Horsemen." The bill died in the Senate on July 22, 1937, opposed even by FDR's own Vice President, John Nance Garner; the Court has stayed at nine justices ever since. Source: Wikipedia, Judicial Procedures Reform Bill of 1937 (en.wikipedia.org); Federal Judicial Center (fjc.gov).

question: Owen Roberts, the Supreme Court's swing vote, had been striking down New Deal laws, but in March 1937, in the middle of the court-packing fight, he voted to uphold a state minimum-wage law. The humorist Cal Tinney gave his about-face a nickname that stuck. What was it?
answer: "The switch in time that saved nine"
choices: "The switch in time that saved nine"
"The one vote that kept them nine"
"The turn that spared the bench"
"The change of heart that held the line"
context: Humorist Cal Tinney coined "the switch in time that saved nine" (a pun on "a stitch in time saves nine") after Roberts joined the majority in West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish (March 29, 1937), upholding a state minimum-wage law. Historians debate whether the threat actually caused it: records show Roberts had already voted to uphold the law at the justices' private conference on December 19, 1936 — weeks before FDR announced his plan — so the timing may be coincidence, not capitulation. Source: Wikipedia, The switch in time that saved nine (en.wikipedia.org); Constitution Center (constitutioncenter.org).

question: Franklin Roosevelt told Americans in his yearly message to Congress in 1944 that political freedom means little to a hungry man, and that real freedom cannot exist without economic security. He proposed promising every American a job, a decent home, medical care and an education. What did Roosevelt call this sweeping list of guarantees?
answer: A Second Bill of Rights
choices: A Second Bill of Rights
The Four Freedoms
The Fair Deal
The Economic Charter
context: FDR's 1944 "Second Bill of Rights" reframed freedom around economic security — "Necessitous men are not free men" — listing rights to a job, a home, medical care, education, and protection from old age, sickness, and unemployment. Here this positive-rights case stands at full strength, with no verdict imposed. (The Four Freedoms was FDR's earlier 1941 idea; the Fair Deal was Truman's.) Source: FDR Presidential Library, 1944 State of the Union (fdrlibrary.org); Wikipedia, Second Bill of Rights (en.wikipedia.org).

question: Friedrich Hayek, an Austrian economist teaching in London, answered Roosevelt in 1944, the year the president called for economic security to be treated as a right. Big central plans wear away freedom even when their aims are good, Hayek warned: a guaranteed good is a claim on someone else, and a plan works only by silencing those who resist. What did he title his warning?
answer: The Road to Serfdom
choices: The Road to Serfdom
The End of Liberty
The Servile State
The Price of Security
context: F.A. Hayek published The Road to Serfdom in 1944 — the same year as FDR's Second Bill of Rights — arguing that the New Deal's kind of planning was exactly the transformation that erodes liberty. Here the FDR case and the Hayek case both stand at full strength, with no verdict on which is right. (The Servile State is a real 1912 book by Hilaire Belloc.) Source: Wikipedia, The Road to Serfdom (en.wikipedia.org); Future of Freedom Foundation (fff.org).

question: George Washington stepped down from the presidency in 1796 and began a tradition that every president after him followed. Franklin Roosevelt broke it. He won the presidency four times, in 1932, 1936, 1940 and 1944, and led the country through the Great Depression and most of the Second World War. What was the tradition?
answer: No president would serve more than two terms
choices: No president would serve more than two terms
No president would run during a war
No president would lead from a wheelchair
No president would leave the capital in wartime
context: FDR broke Washington's unwritten two-term tradition during the Depression and WWII. After he died, the 22nd Amendment (ratified 1951) made the two-term limit actual law, so no one could do it again. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/fdr-four-term-president-22-amendment

question: America would keep its soldiers at home, Franklin Roosevelt promised in a radio fireside chat in December 1940. The country would beat Hitler by out-building him instead, pouring American planes, ships and tanks into Britain and the Allies. What did he call the role America would play?
answer: The great arsenal of democracy
choices: The great arsenal of democracy
The shield of the free world
The workshop of the brave
The fortress of liberty
context: 'We must be the great arsenal of democracy' became the rallying idea: win the war by manufacturing, not by sending troops (yet). Source: https://millercenter.org/the-presidency/presidential-speeches/december-29-1940-fireside-chat-16-arsenal-democracy

question: Reporters came to a press meeting with Franklin Roosevelt at a hard time for Britain: by late 1940, it had no money left to buy American weapons. Roosevelt gave them a simple picture. Suppose you have a garden hose and your neighbour's house catches fire. What did he say you should do?
answer: Hand him the hose to fight the fire, no haggling over price
choices: Hand him the hose to fight the fire, no haggling over price
Sell him the hose for fifteen dollars cash up front
Call the fire brigade and wait on your own porch
Lock your hose away so the fire can't spread to you
context: You don't haggle '$15 for the hose' while the fire spreads — you lend it and he replaces it after. That image sold Lend-Lease, which by 1945 shipped about $36.5 billion in war supplies to Britain, the Soviet Union, and China. Source: https://www.fdrlibrary.org/lend-lease

question: Franklin Roosevelt lost the use of his legs to polio in 1921, and as president he kept it hidden so well that a biographer called it his 'splendid deception.' Gripping a cane and an aide's arm, he could swing himself forward a few steps on steel braces. The reporters who covered him agreed to one rule that helped keep the secret. What was it?
answer: Never to photograph him in his wheelchair
choices: Never to photograph him in his wheelchair
Never to mention his age in print
Never to report on his fireside chats
Never to film him giving a speech
context: Locking steel braces on his withered legs, FDR swung his hips forward a few agonizing steps. His own wheelchair was a homemade thing — an armless kitchen chair on a bicycle-wheeled frame — and reporters honored the no-photo agreement for years. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/inside-fdrs-lifelong-health-struggles-and-his-sudden-death

question: Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 on 19 February 1942, two months after Pearl Harbor. The order never named a single group, but in practice it was turned almost only against one group of Americans. What did it do to about 120,000 of them?
answer: Forced Japanese Americans from their West Coast homes into incarceration camps
choices: Forced Japanese Americans from their West Coast homes into incarceration camps
Drafted Japanese Americans into segregated combat units overseas
Barred German Americans from holding wartime factory jobs
Stripped Italian Americans of citizenship until the war ended
context: The order's words were neutral, but it was aimed almost entirely at people of Japanese descent — a dark mark on FDR's record that historians have judged harshly ever since. Source: https://www.fdrlibrary.org/executive-order-9066

question: James Madison, writing as Publius in Federalist No. 51, admitted that the men who run a government are far from perfect, so the government itself must still be kept from abusing its own power. What was Madison's mechanism for keeping each branch of it in check?
answer: Set each branch's ambition to fight the others, so 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition'
choices: Set each branch's ambition to fight the others, so 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition'
Let the people vote out any official who oversteps his constitutional bounds
Bind every officeholder by a sworn oath taken before taking up the post
Appoint a council of wise elders to overrule any branch that abused power
context: Federalist No. 51 (Madison, as 'Publius'): the famous design connects 'the interest of the man' to 'the constitutional rights of the place' — each branch is given both the means and the motive to resist the others, turning selfishness against itself. Source: https://billofrightsinstitute.org/primary-sources/federalist-no-51/

question: 'Liberty is to faction what air is to fire,' James Madison wrote in Federalist No. 10. Faction, rival groups each pushing its own interest, could not be stamped out without destroying the liberty that feeds it. What design did Madison argue was safest against any single faction seizing control?
answer: A republic spread wide over many people, so rival factions multiply and check each other
choices: A republic spread wide over many people, so rival factions multiply and check each other
A republic kept small and close-knit, where neighbors watch the public good together
A republic that bans political parties of any kind from forming at all
A republic guided by one virtuous leader standing above every faction
context: Federalist No. 10 (1787), James Madison: faction cannot be removed without ending liberty ('liberty is to faction what air is to fire'); the remedy is an extended republic where the multiplicity of factions prevents any single one from dominating.

question: A warrior in medieval Europe knelt before a great lord, bareheaded, with no sword or belt, to swear himself to him for land and protection in the ceremony called homage. He put his clasped hands inside the lord's, and the lord closed his fingers around them. What did that sign mean he had become?
answer: Wholly his lord's man
choices: Wholly his lord's man
A free citizen of the town
A sworn knight of the realm
An owner of his own land
context: The kneeling, weaponless, bareheaded posture showed submission; the enclosing hands signaled the lord's promise of protection. The man was now 'wholly his man.' Source: Britannica, 'Homage and fealty'; Littleton's Tenures c.1480.

question: The whole household looked on as a lord in medieval Europe took a vassal's oath of homage. The kneeling vassal put his clasped hands inside the lord's and swore loyalty and service. Then, before every witness, the lord did one last thing to make the oath a public bond. What did he do?
answer: Gave him a kiss on the mouth
choices: Gave him a kiss on the mouth
Handed him a written contract
Struck him on the shoulder with a sword
Poured wine over his clasped hands
context: The kiss on the mouth made the agreement public before witnesses, sealing the bond of homage. Source: Britannica, 'Homage and fealty'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Feudalism'.

question: A great lord in medieval Europe granted his warrior-vassal a piece of land. The vassal kept all its income, ruled the peasants on it and could pass it to his heirs; in return he owed the lord military service, usually riding to war as an armored knight on horseback. What was the granted land called?
answer: A fief
choices: A fief
A tithe
A guild
A charter
context: The fief (land-for-service) was the heart of feudalism. 'Vassal' itself comes from a Celtic word *wasso-, meaning 'young man, servant' (Welsh gwas, boy or servant). Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Feudalism'; Wiktionary/Etymonline 'vassal'.

question: An English knight received from his lord a knight's fee, the smallest standard grant of land, sized to keep one knight with his family, his servants, and his costly warhorses, armour and weapons. In return he owed his lord a fixed number of days of fighting each year, capped so that no noble stayed away from his own lands too long. How many days did he owe?
answer: 40 days a year
choices: 40 days a year
12 days a year
100 days a year
365 days a year
context: This unit was called a 'knight's fee.' The 40-day cap kept nobles from abandoning their own lands too long; when the lord called, the knight rode to war with his own arms and armour. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Feudalism'; Wikipedia 'Knight's fee'; Britannica 'Knight service'.

question: Henry II of England collected one payment from his knights seven times between 1157 and 1187, and with it he hired paid soldiers loyal only to him. A knight paid it instead of riding to war for his lord, and its name meant shield-money. What was the payment called?
answer: Scutage
choices: Scutage
Tithe
Wergild
Danegeld
context: Scutage ('shield-money') let kings swap unreliable feudal levies for cash-paid troops loyal to the crown alone, quietly weakening the old land-for-fighting bargain. Source: Wikipedia 'Scutage'; Britannica 'Scutage'.

question: Fulbert, the bishop of Chartres, wrote a famous letter in 1020 listing the duties a vassal owed his lord. Then he made the bond run both ways: a lord owed as much in return to his faithful vassal. What did Fulbert warn that a lord who failed his vassal would be considered guilty of?
answer: Bad faith
choices: Bad faith
High treason
Mortal sin
Petty theft
context: Fulbert wrote the lord 'ought to act toward his faithful vassal reciprocally in all these things. And if he does not... he will be justly considered guilty of bad faith.' Feudal loyalty was a two-way contract, not one-way servitude. Source: Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, 'Fulbert of Chartres: On Feudal Obligations, 1020'.

question: William the Conqueror summoned about 170 of his great landholders to Old Sarum on Lammas Day, 1 August 1086. There he had each of them swear loyalty directly to him as king, ahead of their own immediate lords. What is that event remembered as?
answer: The Oath of Salisbury
choices: The Oath of Salisbury
The Treaty of Sarum
The Domesday Charter
The Council of Clarendon
context: By making even his vassals' vassals swear personally to him, William bound the whole pyramid to the crown. It was finished the same month as the Domesday Book survey. Source: English Heritage, 'William the Conqueror and the Oath of Sarum'; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; Wikipedia 'Oath of Salisbury'.

question: A Fijian chief in a sacred tapu state took his place at a victory feast, where the victors ate the enemies they had slain. The feast followed strict rules for a man in that state, and attendants waited on him with an object made for no other use. What was it?
answer: A long-pronged wooden fork made only for feeding the chief human flesh
choices: A long-pronged wooden fork made only for feeding the chief human flesh
A clay bowl reserved for the chief's portion of the feast
A woven palm-leaf mat the chief had to kneel upon
A polished whale-tooth ornament worn around the chief's neck
context: The carved wooden fork was called the iculanibokola ('icula ni bakola' = the fork for the bakola, the human victim). Because a chief or priest in a tapu (taboo) state could not touch the flesh with his hands, attendants used it to feed him. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'The Fiji Cannibal Fork'; Finch & Co, 'Fijian Chief's Ritual Flesh or Cannibal Fork Icula Ni Bakola'.

question: James Calvert, a missionary, baptized the Fijian chief Seru Epenisa Cakobau in 1854. Cakobau had once eaten his enemies, and a year later, victorious at the Battle of Kaba, he stood over his captured foes. By the old custom, a winning chief would have killed and eaten them. What did Cakobau do instead?
answer: He pardoned his captured enemies on the battlefield and spared their lives
choices: He pardoned his captured enemies on the battlefield and spared their lives
He handed his captured enemies to a rival chief for the customary feast
He demanded a ransom in whale-teeth before releasing his captured enemies
He exiled his captured enemies to a distant island under guard
context: Cakobau (who took the Christian name Epenisa, 'Ebenezer') pardoning his captives reversed the old custom under which they would have become 'long pig'. His conversion prompted tens of thousands of Fijians to adopt Christianity, hastening the end of the practice. Source: Wikipedia, 'Seru Epenisa Cakobau'; Britannica, 'Cakobau'.

question: Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson sat in George Washington's own cabinet, Hamilton at the Treasury and Jefferson as Secretary of State, and their bitter feud gave birth to America's first two political parties. No election did it. What did the two men split over?
answer: How strong the central government should be
choices: How strong the central government should be
Whether to keep a standing peacetime army
Where to build the first federal courthouse
Which foreign language to use in treaties
context: Hamilton's Federalists wanted a strong central government, a commerce-and-manufacturing economy, and a 'loose' reading of the Constitution; Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans wanted stronger states, an agrarian economy, and a 'strict' reading where any power not explicitly granted stays with the states. The disagreement, not a campaign, created the parties. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Party_System

question: Thomas Jefferson and James Madison recruited the poet Philip Freneau to Philadelphia in 1791 to run the National Gazette, their answer to the Federalists' paper. Its attacks on the administration reached George Washington, who in private had his own name for the editor. How did Washington refer to Freneau?
answer: As 'that Rascal Freneau'
choices: As 'that Rascal Freneau'
As 'a most honest journalist'
As 'the conscience of the Republic'
As 'a harmless pamphleteer'
context: The Federalists had John Fenno's 'Gazette of the United States'; the Republicans answered with Freneau's 'National Gazette,' which hammered the administration. Washington fumed in private about 'that Rascal Freneau' — a sign that the party press had turned a cabinet feud into a public, nationwide fight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Party_System

question: Alexander Fleming came back from his summer holiday to his messy lab at St Mary's Hospital in London and found a blob of mould on one of his dishes of bacteria. All around the mould ran a clear ring. What had the mould done to the bacteria in that ring?
answer: Killed it off
choices: Killed it off
Made it glow
Frozen it solid
Turned it blue
context: 1928. Fleming realized the Penicillium mould was making something that killed germs around it — the clear ring was the first glimpse of the world's first antibiotic. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/alexander-fleming/

question: Alexander Fleming gave his discovery its name, penicillin, after the mould Penicillium, in March 1929. Until then he had no proper name for the liquid his mould made, so he called it by a plain, almost silly nickname. What did Fleming first call it?
answer: Mould juice
choices: Mould juice
Germ soap
Sick water
Bug killer
context: He only gave it the proper name 'penicillin' on 7 March 1929, after the mould Penicillium — mostly so he'd stop having to write out 'mould broth filtrate'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_penicillin

question: Scientists at Oxford turned their laboratory into a makeshift mould factory in the Second World War, when penicillin was in desperate demand for wounded soldiers but fiendishly hard to grow. The mould needed so much surface that they used every odd container they could scavenge around the hospital. What did they end up using?
answer: Biscuit tins and bedpans
choices: Biscuit tins and bedpans
Glass beakers and flasks
Wooden barrels and crates
Sealed steel drums
context: They grew it in biscuit tins, sheep-dip cans, pie dishes, bath tubs, milk churns and hospital bedpans. Gallons of mould broth yielded only a fingernail's worth of penicillin. Source: https://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/how-was-penicillin-developed

question: Sorting a stack of forgotten dishes in his cluttered lab in September 1928, Alexander Fleming spotted a patch of bluish mould on one of them. Legend says he spoke two quiet words to himself just then, a line that became one of the most famous in the history of science. What were they?
answer: "That's funny."
choices: "That's funny."
"At last!"
"How dreadful."
"Run for help!"
context: Remembered as legend, not a recording. Fleming also said, looking back: 'One sometimes finds what one is not looking for.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_penicillin

question: Alexander Fleming owed his great discovery of 1928 to a single rare mould spore that drifted through the air of St Mary's Hospital in London and settled on one of his dishes. Historians have since worked out where in the crowded old building that spore most likely came from. Where do they think it drifted in from?
answer: A mould expert's lab one floor below
choices: A mould expert's lab one floor below
An open window facing the street
A bakery across the road
A damp basement under the building
context: The spores most likely floated up from the lab of the Irish mycologist C.J. La Touche, working one floor below Fleming through an open door — the rare strain Penicillium notatum. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_penicillin

question: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, but he could not purify it or keep it stable, and his paper about it gathered dust for some ten years. Then two scientists at Oxford revived the work and turned penicillin into a real medicine. Who finished the job Fleming could not?
answer: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain
choices: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain
Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch
Marie Curie and Pierre Curie
Edward Jenner and Joseph Lister
context: Discovering penicillin was NOT enough to save anyone — Florey and Chain revived the work in 1939-1940 and made it a drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Fleming. Source: https://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/how-was-penicillin-developed

question: The Oxford team put penicillin to the test on 25 May 1940. They injected eight mice with deadly streptococci germs and then gave the drug to only four of them. When the scientists came back the next morning, what did they find?
answer: The four treated mice were alive; the four untreated were dead
choices: The four treated mice were alive; the four untreated were dead
All eight mice had survived the night
All eight mice had died despite the drug
Only one treated mouse had pulled through
context: By the next morning all four untreated mice were dead and the treated ones were alive and well — the proof that penicillin could save a living body, not just a lab dish. Source: https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v01/n05/peter-medawar/florey-story

question: Albert Alexander, a 43-year-old Oxford policeman, became the first person ever treated with penicillin on 12 February 1941. He had a bad face infection, so bad that one of his eyes had already been removed. Within 24 hours of his first shot, what happened?
answer: His fever dropped and his infection began to heal
choices: His fever dropped and his infection began to heal
His other eye had to be taken out too
He felt nothing different at all
He broke out in a worse new rash
context: The popular tale that he scratched himself on a rose thorn is doubted; the infection more likely began with wounds from a German bombing raid during the Blitz. Source: https://www.phc.ox.ac.uk/blog/on-this-site-penicillin-a-historic-first

question: Two Oxford scientists crossed to the United States in 1941 to get penicillin made in bulk, and Norman Heatley was one of them. If the Nazis invaded Britain, they feared, the precious mould might be lost for ever. What did the two men do with the mould's spores?
answer: Rubbed them into the linings of their coats
choices: Rubbed them into the linings of their coats
Swallowed them in sealed capsules
Sewed them inside their shoe heels
Mailed them ahead in a diplomatic bag
context: Even if everything else was lost, they could carry penicillin out hidden in their clothing. Biographer Eric Lax titled his book 'The Mold in Dr. Florey's Coat.' Source: https://www.acponline.org/about-acp/chapters-regions/united-states/tennessee-chapter/about-the-chapter/grand-rounds-in-literature/the-mold-in-dr-floreys-coat-by-eric-lax

question: Mary Hunt, nicknamed 'Moldy Mary,' worked at an American government laboratory in Peoria, Illinois, where scientists were hunting for a mould that made more penicillin than Fleming's weak original strain. She brought in the winner from a local market, where she found it growing on an everyday piece of food. What was the food?
answer: A mouldy cantaloupe
choices: A mouldy cantaloupe
A rotten potato
A spoiled loaf of bread
A bad wheel of cheese
context: Its strain (Penicillium rubens NRRL 1951) made far more penicillin than Fleming's and became the ancestor of mass-production mould — it is now the official state microbe of Illinois. Source: https://www.the-scientist.com/how-a-moldy-cantaloupe-took-fleming-s-penicillin-from-discovery-to-mass-production-72304

question: Doctors treating Albert Alexander in 1941 could not bear to waste a drop of penicillin, which was still desperately scarce. About 80 percent of the drug passed straight through his body and out in his urine. What did the doctors do to stretch the tiny supply?
answer: Collected his urine to recover the penicillin and re-injected it
choices: Collected his urine to recover the penicillin and re-injected it
Diluted each dose with ten times the water
Gave him only one injection a week
Switched him to a cheaper sister drug
context: Even so the supply ran out. After improving dramatically, Albert Alexander relapsed and died on 15 March 1941 — there simply wasn't enough penicillin yet to finish the cure. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Alexander_(police_officer)

question: Anne Miller was dying of blood poisoning in New Haven in March 1942 when penicillin saved her, the first patient the drug truly rescued. The dose flown in for her was only about a tablespoon, yet that small amount was a huge share of something. What was a tablespoon of penicillin roughly equal to?
answer: Half of all the penicillin then existing in the United States
choices: Half of all the penicillin then existing in the United States
A single week's output of one factory
The yearly dose for one small hospital
What a doctor's bag normally carried
context: That's how rare the drug still was in early 1942 — saving one woman took half the nation's entire supply. Source: https://medicine.yale.edu/news-article/who-saved-the-first-life-with-penicillin/

question: Accepting his Nobel Prize on 11 December 1945, Alexander Fleming used his speech to give the world a warning about his own discovery. He said that a careless person who took too little penicillin would expose germs to a weak dose and not kill them. According to Fleming, what would happen to those germs?
answer: They would become resistant to penicillin
choices: They would become resistant to penicillin
They would spread twice as fast
They would turn into a deadlier strain
They would hide inside the body for years
context: Fleming warned: 'the ignorant man may easily underdose himself and by exposing his microbes to non-lethal quantities of the drug make them resistant.' He foresaw antibiotic resistance the very year penicillin was celebrated. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/fleming-lecture.pdf

question: Norman Heatley found the methods and built the equipment that turned penicillin from a lab curiosity into a real drug. Yet when the 1945 Nobel Prize was awarded, he was left off it entirely because he was a chemist rather than a doctor. In 1990, Oxford University finally honored him with a startling gift for a man who had never trained in medicine. What did Oxford award Heatley?
answer: An honorary Doctorate of Medicine
choices: An honorary Doctorate of Medicine
An honorary chair in the chemistry department
A bronze bust in its medical school's entrance hall
A graduate scholarship established under his name
context: Per Oxford University and Eric Lax's 'The Mould in Dr Florey's Coat', in 1990 Oxford gave Heatley -- a chemist, not a medic -- an honorary Doctorate of Medicine, said to be the first such degree it had awarded a non-physician.

question: The wounded soldiers in the army hospital at Scutari watched Florence Nightingale walk the wards alone each night during the Crimean War, long after the surgeons had gone to bed. The grateful men named her after the thing she carried on those rounds. What did she carry?
answer: A small lamp
choices: A small lamp
A heavy hammer
A leather ledger
A basket of bread
context: The soldiers called her 'the Lady with the Lamp.'
