The Times described a 'ministering angel' with 'a little lamp in her hand,' and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow fixed the image forever in his 1857 poem 'Santa Filomena': 'A Lady with a lamp shall stand.' Her actual lamp (c.1856) survives in a museum collection. Sources: https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/florence-nightingale-lady-lamp ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Nightingale

question: Florence Nightingale was certain that filth and disease, rather than enemy bullets, had killed most of the British soldiers at the hospital at Scutari. She had to convince doubtful officials in Parliament, and she won them over with something she made that put the truth in plain view. What did she create?
answer: A colored statistical diagram
choices: A colored statistical diagram
A signed petition
A public newspaper letter
A stirring speech
context: She invented the 'coxcomb' or polar-area diagram — now called the 'Nightingale rose' — a circle of twelve wedges, one per month, with big blue areas for deaths from disease and red for battle wounds. The enormous blue swaths made it electrically clear that preventable disease was the real killer, and the chart shrinks dramatically after her sanitary reforms. In 1859 she became the first woman ever elected a Fellow of the Royal Statistical Society. Sources: https://cwfn.uoguelph.ca/short-papers-excerpts/nightingale-statistics-and-the-crimean-war/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Nightingale

question: The Marquis de Lafayette, a wealthy nineteen-year-old French nobleman, landed in America in July 1777, begging to fight for the young United States. The Continental Congress distrusted foreign officers, yet it made him a major general, partly because of an unusual offer he had made about how he would serve. What did he offer?
answer: To serve without any pay
choices: To serve without any pay
To command the navy at sea
To bring a regiment from France
To stay only one summer
context: The Marquis de Lafayette was only 19 when Congress commissioned him a major general on July 31, 1777, and his willingness to serve WITHOUT PAY helped win them over. Source: history.com/this-day-in-history/july-31/marquis-de-lafayette-becomes-a-major-general-without-pay

question: Baron Friedrich von Steuben, a Prussian officer, reached Valley Forge, George Washington's frozen winter camp, in February 1778 to drill the Continental Army. He was appalled. The soldiers barely knew how to use their bayonets, the long steel blades fixed to their muskets, for fighting; around camp they used them for something else entirely. What were they doing with their bayonets?
answer: Roasting their beefsteak over the fire
choices: Roasting their beefsteak over the fire
Digging trenches in the snow
Trading them to local farmers
Cleaning mud off their boots
context: Von Steuben was appalled that the men used their bayonets to roast beefsteak over the campfire — or left them behind entirely. He retrained the army to charge with the bayonet as a real weapon. Source: newenglandhistoricalsociety.com/baron-von-steuben-shows-the-army-a-bayonet-is-not-a-grilling-tool/

question: Lafayette fought beside George Washington through much of the American Revolution and came to love the older Virginian like a father. Back home in France, he gave his newborn son a name from his years in America. What did he name the boy?
answer: Georges Washington de Lafayette
choices: Georges Washington de Lafayette
Louis Capet de Lafayette
Jean Brandywine de Lafayette
Henri Yorktown de Lafayette
context: Lafayette loved Washington so much that he named his son Georges Washington de Lafayette. Source: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'Marquis de Lafayette' (mountvernon.org)

question: De Grasse, the six-foot-two French admiral, hosted George Washington at a victory dinner aboard his flagship when Yorktown fell in 1781, and Washington stood taller still. To everyone's amusement, de Grasse kept doing one thing to the American commander. What was it?
answer: Hugging him and calling him 'my little general'
choices: Hugging him and calling him 'my little general'
Saluting him as 'King of America'
Toasting him with twelve cannon volleys
Offering him command of the French navy
context: The 6-foot-2 Comte de Grasse repeatedly embraced the 6-foot-4 Washington aboard the Ville de Paris, calling him 'mon petit général' — my little general. Source: americanrevolution.org/degrasse.php

question: Benjamin Franklin sent Baron von Steuben over to America billed as a Prussian 'lieutenant general' who had served Frederick the Great, to get Congress excited about him. The grand title was largely invented. What had von Steuben's real top rank been?
answer: Captain and aide-de-camp
choices: Captain and aide-de-camp
Field marshal of cavalry
Colonel of the royal guard
Admiral of the Baltic fleet
context: Franklin padded the resume: von Steuben's true top rank had been captain and aide-de-camp to Frederick the Great, and even the 'Baron' title was inflated. He proved a brilliant drillmaster anyway. Source: smithsonianmag.com/history/underappreciated-true-story-prussian-military-office-whipped-patriots-into-shape-valley-forge-180987172/

question: Confederate gunners around Charleston Harbor opened fire on Fort Sumter on 12 April 1861, the first shots of the Civil War. They heated cannonballs in ovens until the iron glowed red, then fired them into the fort to set its wooden barracks on fire. What was this kind of shot called?
answer: Hot shot
choices: Hot shot
Grapeshot
Chain shot
Canister shot
context: Over the 34-hour bombardment beginning at 4:30 a.m. on April 12, 1861, the Confederates hurled more than 3,000 rounds at Sumter's brick walls, and the red-hot 'hot shot' set the fort's wooden barracks on fire. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/fort-sumter

question: Daniel Hough, a private in the Union garrison of Fort Sumter, came through 34 hours of Confederate bombardment in April 1861, and not one soldier on either side was killed in it. Yet Hough became the Civil War's very first dead man, after the fighting had already stopped. How did he die?
answer: An accidental cannon explosion during a salute to the flag
choices: An accidental cannon explosion during a salute to the flag
A Confederate cannonball that finally found its mark
A bullet to the chest while lowering the fort's flag
A fall from the rampart as the garrison evacuated
context: After Major Robert Anderson surrendered, his men fired a 100-gun salute to the U.S. flag. A spark set off a pile of cartridges, and the explosion killed Private Daniel Hough, the first soldier to die in the war that would kill hundreds of thousands more. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Sumter

question: Robert Anderson, the Union major, surrendered Fort Sumter in April 1861, but he lowered its 33-star flag and carried it north rather than leave it to the enemy. Four years later, with the war won and Charleston retaken, he came back to the ruined fort. What did he do there?
answer: Raised the very flag he had carried off in defeat
choices: Raised the very flag he had carried off in defeat
Buried the flag in the rubble where the fort stood
Cut the flag into pieces for his surviving soldiers
Donated the flag to a museum back in the North
context: On April 14, 1865, Robert Anderson hoisted the same flag over the recaptured Fort Sumter and broke down weeping, saying it had been 'the cherished wish of my heart' to restore it. Source: https://emergingcivilwar.com/2020/04/14/190026/

question: The Mexica told how their war god guided them south and ordered them to build their city where they saw an eagle sitting on a prickly cactus. By the story, they found that sign on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco and founded Tenochtitlan there. Where does the sign still appear today?
answer: On Mexico's national flag
choices: On Mexico's national flag
On the U.S. dollar bill
On the Olympic rings
On a Roman coin
context: The eagle on the prickly-pear cactus sits at the center of Mexico's flag and coat of arms, making the founding legend a living national symbol. (Legend element: the divine omen.) Source: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/tenochtitlan/

question: Aztec artists first drew the founding sign of Tenochtitlan as an eagle on a cactus, with no snake at all, as on the title page of the Codex Mendoza. The serpent the eagle grips in the image known today first appeared only around 1576, about fifty years after the Spanish conquest. Scholars think later artists misread a glyph drawn beside the eagle's beak. What was that glyph?
answer: A glyph of fire-and-water, the Aztec sign for sacred war
choices: A glyph of fire-and-water, the Aztec sign for sacred war
A glyph of falling rain the priests drew beside the eagle
A ribbon of speech, the Aztec sign for a god's command
A coiled rope the eagle stood on in the older drawings
context: The snake first appears in the Codex Aubin around 1576, roughly 50 years after the conquest. Scholars think it is a misread of the atl-tlachinolli glyph (water-and-fire, the sign of sacred war), which sits near the eagle's beak and looks similar. The famous serpent is a post-Conquest add-on. Source: https://www.mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/ask-us/eagle-and-the-snake

question: One of the Allied leaders of the Second World War came up with the name 'United Nations' himself, years before the organisation itself was founded. Twenty-six Allied countries fighting Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy and Imperial Japan signed a wartime pact under that name in Washington on 1 January 1942. Who coined it?
answer: President Franklin Roosevelt of the United States coined it
choices: President Franklin Roosevelt of the United States coined it
Prime Minister Winston Churchill of Britain coined it
Marshal Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union coined it
Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek of China coined it
context: Franklin Roosevelt coined "United Nations," and it first appeared in print in the Declaration by United Nations signed by 26 countries on January 1, 1942 — long before the UN itself was founded. Source: https://www.un.org/en/about-us/history-of-the-un/preparatory-years

question: Delegates of fifty Allied governments met in San Francisco in 1945 to write the charter of the United Nations, and they gave it a Security Council to keep the peace. Five of the winning powers, the United States, Britain, France, China and the Soviet Union, became its permanent members. The charter gave those five one special power no other member got. What was it?
answer: A single "no" from any one of them blocks any resolution
choices: A single "no" from any one of them blocks any resolution
A guaranteed seat for one of their generals on every mission
The right to host every Security Council meeting in turn
Permanent exemption from paying any UN membership dues
context: Each of the five permanent members got a veto: one "no" blocks a resolution no matter how many other nations agree. This "Yalta formula" was settled by the great powers at the Yalta Conference in early 1945. The great powers had refused to join any body they could be forced to act against — that was the price of getting them to join at all. Source: https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/un-security-council-working-methods/the-veto.php

question: Soviet tanks rolled into Czechoslovakia in 1968 to crush the Prague Spring. Ten members of the United Nations Security Council voted for a resolution that condemned the invasion and told the troops to leave. With ten nations on one side, what happened to the resolution?
answer: The single Soviet veto killed it, and the tanks stayed
choices: The single Soviet veto killed it, and the tanks stayed
It passed, and Soviet troops withdrew within the week
It passed, but the Soviets simply ignored the order
It was tabled because China refused to take part in the vote
context: The Council voted 10-to-1, but one Soviet veto was enough to kill the resolution — exactly the limit built into the veto from the start. The same thing had happened in 1956, when the USSR vetoed action over its crushing of the Hungarian Revolution, calling it merely a "reactionary uprising," and the matter had to be pushed to the General Assembly, where no nation holds a veto. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_veto_power

question: Cai Lun, a Han court official, perfected paper around AD 105 from a pulp of everyday scraps. He drained the pulp thin across a screen and let it dry into smooth sheets, so cheap that paper could reach everyone. What scraps went into Cai Lun's pulp?
answer: Tree bark, hemp, old rags, and worn-out fishing nets
choices: Tree bark, hemp, old rags, and worn-out fishing nets
Reed stalks, clay, wax, and linen thread
Bamboo shavings, wool, sand, and tree sap
Sheep's wool, beeswax, animal fat, and dried reeds
context: Cai Lun mashed bark, hemp, rags, and ragged fishing nets into pulp and drained it on a cloth screen, c. 105 AD. Making paper from cheap scraps is exactly why it could spread to everyone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cai_Lun

question: Tang-dynasty alchemists, Daoists hunting a potion that would grant eternal life, stirred saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal together in their workshops around 850, believing they were brewing it. Instead of the immortality they hoped for, what did their mixture actually do?
answer: It exploded
choices: It exploded
It turned to gold
It froze solid
It glowed silver
context: The recipe for immortality turned out to be the recipe for gunpowder: instead of eternal life, the alchemists got fire and a blast. Source: https://www.chinaxiantour.com/xian-travel-blog/chinese-gunpowder-invention.html

question: Chinese soldiers at the siege of De'an in 1132 fought with a new weapon, centuries before Europe had cannons. They called the weapon the fire lance. In plain terms, what was a fire lance?
answer: A bamboo tube on a pole that blasted flame into the enemy's face
choices: A bamboo tube on a pole that blasted flame into the enemy's face
A giant crossbow that hurled a barrel of burning oil
An iron ball flung over the walls by a catapult
A spinning wheel of swords pushed at charging horses
context: The huo qiang was a bamboo (or paper) tube tied to a spear that shot out a roar of flame and smoke -- the direct ancestor of the gun. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gunpowder

question: Daoist alchemists of Tang China were mixing minerals in the 800s, still searching for an elixir of eternal life. The oldest known text about a gunpowder recipe comes from their world, and it is no weapon design: it warns alchemists never to combine sulfur, saltpeter and honey. By the text's account, what had the mixture done?
answer: It burned their hands, faces, and even their houses
choices: It burned their hands, faces, and even their houses
It crumbled away into useless gray ash
It gave off a silent and deadly poison gas
It hardened overnight into unbreakable stone
context: The Zhenyuan Miaodao Yaolue warns that 'smoke and flames result, so that their hands and faces have been burnt, and even the whole house burned down' -- the first gunpowder document is a safety warning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhenyuan_Miaodao_Yaolue

question: An Arab army of the Abbasid Caliphate defeated a Tang Chinese army beside the Talas River in Central Asia in 751. China had kept its paper-making a close secret for centuries. How did the victorious army walk away from Talas with it?
answer: It captured Chinese prisoners who knew the craft
choices: It captured Chinese prisoners who knew the craft
It found the recipe written inside a stolen sutra
It was handed the method as a gift for peace
It bought the formula from a wandering merchant
context: Prisoners taken at Talas could make paper, and the first paper mill in the Islamic world soon rose at Samarkand -- from there paper crossed to Europe. Source: https://www.computersmiths.com/chineseinvention/paper.htm

question: Wang Yuanlu, a Daoist monk at the Mogao caves of Dunhuang in China's western desert, came upon a door walled shut for centuries in one of the caves in 1900. Behind it, where a small forgotten shrine might have been expected, lay a lost library of ancient scrolls. Roughly how many manuscripts were inside?
context: The sealed Dunhuang cave hid about 40,000 manuscripts, including the printed Diamond Sutra. The archaeologist Aurel Stein bought the famous scroll from the monk in 1907. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/artifacts-ancient-writings/diamond-sutra-oldest-known-printed-book-world-006185

question: Bi Sheng, a commoner of Song China, built the world's first movable type around 1040, some four hundred years before Gutenberg. He made one small reusable piece for every character, set the pieces in a frame to print a page, then reset them for the next, and he chose his material because wood warped. What were Bi Sheng's type pieces made of?
answer: Baked clay
choices: Baked clay
Cast bronze
Carved jade
Polished bone
context: Bi Sheng carved each character into sticky clay 'as thin as the edge of a coin,' then fired it hard so it could be used again. He chose clay over wood because wood warped and stuck in the glue. Everything we know of him comes from Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bi_Sheng

question: Shen Kuo, a scholar of Song China, wrote out how to make a magnetic needle compass in his book the Dream Pool Essays, in 1088, the first clear account of one. Studying his needle closely, he spotted something about it that no one had ever recorded before. What did Shen Kuo notice?
answer: It pointed slightly east of due south, not dead on it
choices: It pointed slightly east of due south, not dead on it
It swung harder during a thunderstorm
It lost its pull after many years of use
It pointed the opposite way below the equator
context: Shen Kuo was the first known person to record magnetic declination -- that the compass needle leans a little off true north. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shen_Kuo

question: Napoleon III, emperor of France, was at war with Prussia in 1870, and on 1 September his army was caught in a valley at Sedan, ringed by hills the Germans had crowned with cannon. He raised a white flag, and the army laid down its arms. What made this surrender unheard of in modern Europe?
answer: A reigning emperor was captured on the battlefield with his whole army
choices: A reigning emperor was captured on the battlefield with his whole army
A king escaped in disguise and was never found by the enemy
A peace treaty was signed before the first shot was fired
A capital city surrendered without losing a single soldier
context: Roughly 104,000 French soldiers and 558 cannon were taken prisoner, along with Napoleon III himself — the first time in modern European history a reigning emperor was captured on the battlefield with his entire army. He was sent into comfortable captivity at Schloss Wilhelmshöhe, then exile in England, where he died in 1873. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sedan; Britannica summary (ebsco.com).

question: Otto von Bismarck, Prussia's chancellor, wanted a war that would unite the German states in a single empire with the Prussian king at its head, and in 1870 he got it: the Prussian armies crushed France within weeks. To crown the victory he had Wilhelm I proclaimed Kaiser on French soil in January 1871, at a showplace of France's old kings. Where did the Germans proclaim their empire?
answer: In the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles
choices: In the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles
In the throne room of the royal palace in Berlin
In the cathedral where French kings were crowned
In a captured fortress on the German border
context: On 18 January 1871 Bismarck, in a cuirassier uniform, read the proclamation in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles as Wilhelm I was hailed Kaiser on French soil. The Treaty of Frankfurt then stripped Alsace-Lorraine from France — the grievance that fed 1914 and 1919. Source: en.chateauversailles.fr/discover/history/key-dates/proclamation-german-empire-1871; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_German_Empire.

question: Like most children born into slavery, Frederick Douglass was never told his birthday, so once he was free he picked one for himself: 14 February, Valentine's Day. Why did he choose that day?
answer: His mother had called him her 'Little Valentine'
choices: His mother had called him her 'Little Valentine'
It was the day he finally escaped to freedom
It was the day he learned to read his first word
It was the day his first newspaper went to print
context: Douglass wrote in his 1845 Narrative, 'I have no accurate knowledge of my age, never having seen any authentic record containing it.' His enslaved mother had nicknamed him her Little Valentine, so he chose Feb 14. (Britannica, Frederick Douglass; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Douglass, citing his 1845 Narrative)

question: Hugh Auld, who held young Frederick Douglass as a slave in Baltimore, forbade anyone to teach the boy to read, saying it would spoil a slave. Frederick hatched a plan out on the streets. What did he do to keep getting reading lessons?
answer: Traded his own bread to poor white boys for lessons
choices: Traded his own bread to poor white boys for lessons
Hid a spelling book under the floorboards of the kitchen
Practiced writing letters in chalk on the ship timbers
Memorized the sermons the preacher gave each Sunday
context: Sophia Auld had begun teaching him until her husband Hugh forbade it. Douglass kept learning in secret, giving bread to hungry poor white boys on Philpot Street in exchange for lessons; he called it buying 'the bread of knowledge.' (frederick-douglass-heritage.org/biography-early-life; SparkNotes, Narrative ch. VII-IX)

question: With fifty cents saved from shining boots, Frederick Douglass, about twelve years old, bought a single schoolbook. Inside it, a 'Dialogue Between a Master and Slave,' in which a captured slave out-argues his owner until the owner frees him, gave the boy his first words for arguing his own freedom. What was the book?
answer: The Columbian Orator
choices: The Columbian Orator
The American Spelling Book
The Liberty Almanac
The Freedman's Reader
context: The Columbian Orator was a popular school reader of speeches and dialogues. Its master-and-slave dialogue, in which the slave's arguments win him his freedom, became a model for the young Douglass. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Columbian_Orator; frederickdouglasspapersproject.com, his Narrative ch. VII)

question: Nathan Johnson, an abolitionist in New Bedford, renamed the runaway Frederick Bailey to throw slave-catchers off his trail, and the name he chose was Douglass. Johnson borrowed it from one of his favourite stories. Where did the name come from?
answer: A hero in Sir Walter Scott's poem 'The Lady of the Lake'
choices: A hero in Sir Walter Scott's poem 'The Lady of the Lake'
A Baltimore deacon who had once hidden the runaway
The captain of the ship that carried him north
A verse the preacher read from the book of Exodus
context: Nathan Johnson was reading Scott's poem, which features the heroic clan of Douglas, and suggested the name. Frederick Bailey became Frederick Douglass — the name under which the runaway would become world-famous. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Douglass, citing Douglass's own account)

question: Slave-catchers watched every rail line and station for Black men without papers when Frederick Douglass, twenty years old, made his run for freedom from Baltimore on 3 September 1838. By train and then steamboat he reached New York in less than a day, slipping past them all. How did he get through?
answer: He disguised himself as a free Black sailor with borrowed seaman's papers
choices: He disguised himself as a free Black sailor with borrowed seaman's papers
He hid inside a wooden shipping crate nailed shut by a friend
He waited until a snowstorm and walked the rails on foot at night
He bribed a conductor to lock him alone in a baggage car
context: Douglass wore a red shirt, a sailor's hat, and a knotted black cravat, and carried a friend's 'seaman's protection papers.' His future wife Anna Murray, a free woman, had sewn the sailor outfit and sold her own featherbed to help fund the escape. (history.com/articles/frederick-douglass-escapes-slavery; smithsonianmag.com, 'The Hidden History of Anna Murray Douglass')

question: Edward Covey, a farmer paid to whip rebellious slaves into obedience, met his match in the sixteen-year-old Frederick Douglass, who had been hired out to him. One day Douglass refused to take another whipping and grappled with Covey for nearly two hours, and Covey never whipped him again. What did Douglass call that fight?
answer: 'The turning point in my career as a slave'
choices: 'The turning point in my career as a slave'
'The first free breath of my whole life'
'The bloodiest hour I ever lived through'
'The day I lost my fear of the lash'
context: Douglass wrote the fight with Covey 'revived within me a sense of my own manhood.' Beating the man hired to break him restored his will to be free. (essentialcivilwarcurriculum.com/frederick-douglass.html; cliffsnotes.com, Narrative ch. X, quoting his 1845 Narrative)

question: Frederick Douglass, himself a runaway from slavery in Maryland, launched his own weekly antislavery newspaper in Rochester, New York, in 1847. He named it after the one bright thing that escaping slaves followed through the night to freedom. What did he call the paper?
answer: The North Star
choices: The North Star
The Liberator
The Freeman's Torch
The Morning Bell
context: Runaways navigated north by the fixed North Star. The paper's masthead read: 'Right is of no Sex — Truth is of no Color — God is the Father of us all, and we are all Brethren.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Douglass; loc.gov Frederick Douglass Timeline)

question: Frederick Douglass posed for more than 160 portraits in his life, the most of any American of his century, Abraham Lincoln included. In almost every one he kept a stern, unsmiling face and looked straight into the lens, and he did it on purpose. Why did Douglass refuse to smile for the camera?
answer: He would not look like the grinning 'happy slave' of racist cartoons
choices: He would not look like the grinning 'happy slave' of racist cartoons
He thought a smile made a portrait look cheap and unserious
A childhood injury had left him unable to smile evenly
Photographers of the day told everyone to hold a blank face
context: Douglass deliberately used the brand-new technology of photography to broadcast Black dignity, refusing the caricature that pretended slaves were content. His 160-plus portraits beat Lincoln's 126 and Custer's 155. (npr.org/2015/12/13, 'Picture This: Frederick Douglass...'; nbcnews.com/news/nbcblk)

question: The citizens of Rochester, New York, invited Frederick Douglass in 1852 to give their town's yearly Fourth of July oration. Douglass agreed, but he made one pointed choice to protest a nation celebrating freedom while roughly three million Black people were still held in chains. What did he do?
answer: He gave the speech a day late, on July 5, refusing to honor the Fourth itself
choices: He gave the speech a day late, on July 5, refusing to honor the Fourth itself
He delivered it in total silence, holding up a chained man's irons
He spoke only the words of the Declaration and then walked off
He refused his fee and gave it to a fund for runaway slaves
context: On July 5, 1852, at Corinthian Hall, Douglass told the crowd: 'This Fourth of July is yours, not mine. You may rejoice, I must mourn.' He asked what the day meant to the slave and answered: 'your celebration is a sham... your shouts of liberty and equality, hollow mockery.' (constitutioncenter.org; nmaahc.si.edu, 'A Nation's Story'; americanyawp.com reader)

question: Police at the White House door turned Frederick Douglass away from Abraham Lincoln's reception after his second inauguration in March 1865, because he was Black. Douglass got word inside to the president. What did Lincoln do in front of the whole crowded room?
answer: Called out 'Here comes my friend Douglass' and asked his opinion of the speech
choices: Called out 'Here comes my friend Douglass' and asked his opinion of the speech
Quietly slipped out a side door to shake his hand in private
Sent an aide to apologize and pressed money into his hand
Pretended not to notice to spare Douglass any embarrassment
context: Lincoln told him, 'there is no man's opinion that I value more than yours,' and Douglass called the Second Inaugural 'a sacred effort.' After the assassination, Mary Todd Lincoln sent Douglass the president's own walking stick, still kept at the Frederick Douglass National Historic Site. (mrlincolnswhitehouse.org; whitehousehistory.org, 'Frederick Douglass and Abraham Lincoln')

question: William Lloyd Garrison, Frederick Douglass's old mentor, publicly set fire to a copy of the United States Constitution and called it 'a covenant with death,' a proslavery pact best destroyed. Douglass studied the document for himself and broke with Garrison over it. What did Douglass come to argue the Constitution was?
answer: Rightly read, a 'glorious liberty document' to be turned against slavery
choices: Rightly read, a 'glorious liberty document' to be turned against slavery
A wicked bargain that honest men were bound to burn
A dead letter with no force until slavery was abolished
A foreign British relic that free Americans should discard
context: Douglass broke with Garrison, arguing the founding document should be wielded for freedom, not surrendered to slaveholders. (reason.com/2015/07/04, 'Douglass on Liberty, Slavery, and the Fourth of July'; californialawreview.org, 'Frederick Douglass and the Two Constitutions')

question: Frederick Douglass, born a slave himself, rose before a Rochester crowd in 1852 to give the town's Fourth of July oration. He told them that the Fourth belonged to them and not to him. What did he urge his listeners to do with them?
answer: Stand by them 'against all foes, and at whatever cost'
choices: Stand by them 'against all foes, and at whatever cost'
Scrap them and start the whole nation over
Admit they had always been an empty boast
Keep them for white citizens only, as written
context: Douglass called the Declaration's principles 'saving principles' and demanded the nation live up to them rather than abandon them — the natural-rights argument that the country must keep its own promise. (billofrightsinstitute.org, Douglass July 5 1852 speech; loveman.sdsu.edu/docs/1852FrederickDouglass.pdf)

question: Galileo Galilei aimed his new telescope at Jupiter from a rooftop in Padua in January 1610. Night after night he watched tiny points of light beside the planet that shifted place and travelled along with it, and he counted four. What had Galileo found?
answer: Four moons orbiting Jupiter
choices: Four moons orbiting Jupiter
Four comets passing near Jupiter
Four new planets beyond Jupiter
Four bright stars behind Jupiter
context: They were the first moons ever found circling another world — today named Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, and still called the Galilean moons. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_moons

question: Grinding his own lenses, Galileo Galilei built telescopes far stronger than the Dutch spyglass he had heard of. In March 1610 he hurried his first discoveries into a slim Latin book, printed in Venice, the first book of science built on what a telescope showed. What is that book called?
answer: 'The Starry Messenger'
choices: 'The Starry Messenger'
'On the Revolutions'
'The Book of the Heavens'
'Letters on the Sun'
context: In Latin it was 'Sidereus Nuncius.' It made Galileo instantly famous across Europe. Source: Wikipedia, Sidereus Nuncius; Museo Galileo, Sidereus Nuncius facsimile.

question: Galileo Galilei named the four new lights he had found beside Jupiter in 1610 for the ruling family of Florence, hoping to win a rich and powerful patron, and he printed their name on his title page. The flattery worked: the Grand Duke made him court mathematician. Which family got the honour?
answer: The Medici family
choices: The Medici family
The Borgia family
The Sforza family
The Visconti family
context: He called them the 'Medicean Stars,' and the flattery worked: Grand Duke Cosimo II made Galileo his court Philosopher and Mathematician. https://www.lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/galileo-galilei-2/

question: Galileo Galilei turned his new telescope in 1610 on the faint, milky band that stretched across the night sky. People had long called it the Milky Way, but no one knew what it was made of. What did his lens show it to be?
answer: Countless faint stars
choices: Countless faint stars
One single huge bright star
Glowing dust between the stars
Frozen crystals of ice
context: He described it as 'innumerable stars grouped in clusters' — too faint and tightly packed for the naked eye to split apart. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidereus_Nuncius

question: With his naked eye, Galileo Galilei could count only about nine stars in Orion the hunter, one of the easiest constellations to find. Then he raised his telescope to the same patch of sky, and the number leapt. Roughly how many stars did he count in Orion through the lens?
answer: About 80
choices: About 80
About 15
About 30
About 200
context: The Pleiades did the same: 6 stars to the naked eye became about 35 through his lens. The sky was far fuller than anyone had imagined. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidereus_Nuncius

question: Galileo Galilei found Saturn strangely misshapen through his telescope in 1610, writing that it was 'not alone but composed of three which almost touch', as if it had a bump on each side. Two years later the bumps were gone. What part of Saturn had Galileo really glimpsed?
answer: Its rings
choices: Its rings
Its moons
Its storms
Its shadow
context: Galileo's telescope was too weak to resolve them, so the rings looked like 'ears'; when Earth crossed their plane in 1612 they turned edge-on and seemed to disappear. https://www.astronomy.com/today-in-the-history-of-astronomy/july-30-1610-galileo-sees-saturns-rings/

question: Venus waxed and waned through crescent, half and full, just as the Moon does, while Galileo Galilei watched it through his telescope night after night in 1610. Ptolemy's old system, with the Earth at the centre, could never show a full Venus at all. What did the phases prove?
answer: That Venus orbits the Sun
choices: That Venus orbits the Sun
That Venus is closer than the Moon
That Venus shines with its own light
That Venus is larger than the Earth
context: Galileo first hid the discovery in a Latin anagram, later decoded as 'The Mother of Love [Venus] imitates the shapes of Cynthia [the Moon].' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phases_of_Venus

question: The Inquisition made Galileo Galilei, ailing and about 69, kneel in a penitent's white gown at a Roman convent on 22 June 1633. Questioned under threat of torture and found vehemently suspect of heresy, he had to read aloud an oath about the moving Earth that everyone in the room knew the Church had forced from him. What did the oath make him swear?
answer: To curse and detest the idea Earth moves
choices: To curse and detest the idea Earth moves
To beg the Pope's forgiveness in writing
To praise the Earth-centered heavens
To deny he ever owned a telescope
context: He swore to 'abjure, curse, and detest' the belief that the Earth moves, at the convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. https://brunelleschi.imss.fi.it/itineraries/itinerary/TheAbjuration.html

question: An old friend asked Galileo Galilei to put his own favourite argument against a moving Earth into the great book Galileo published in 1632, a debate among three characters. Galileo gave the argument to Simplicio, the book's simpleton, who lost every debate, and the friend took it as mockery and never forgave him. Whose argument did Galileo hand to the fool?
answer: Pope Urban VIII's
choices: Pope Urban VIII's
Cardinal Bellarmine's
Ptolemy's
Aristotle's
context: Putting Pope Urban VIII's own anti-Copernican argument in the mouth of 'Simplicio' (literally 'Simpleton') turned a science book into a personal insult, and that wound helped trigger the trial as much as the doctrine did. Source: Wikipedia, Galileo affair; EBSCO Research Starters, Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems.

question: Isaac Newton would one day build on the last great work of Galileo Galilei. Condemned at his trial and going blind, Galileo finished it in his last years at his villa near Florence. What did that last book lay the foundations of?
answer: The science of motion
choices: The science of motion
The mapping of the stars
The grinding of lenses
The measuring of time
context: It was 'Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations Relating to Two New Sciences' (1638), smuggled out and printed abroad because his writings were forbidden at home. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_affair

question: The Doge of Venice and his senators climbed the bell tower of St Mark's with Galileo Galilei in August 1609, and Galileo handed them his new spyglass to look out over the lagoon. Through it they could spot something hours before anyone watching with the naked eye. What could they make out?
answer: Ships still far out at sea
choices: Ships still far out at sea
Storm clouds on the horizon
Fish swimming below the surface
Stars in the daytime sky
context: The grateful Venetian Senate rewarded the 8-power instrument with a lifetime professorship at Padua and doubled Galileo's salary to 1000 florins. Source: Italy On This Day, Galileo demonstrates telescope (Aug 1609); Design World, Galileo Demonstrates Telescope to Venetian Senate.

question: Galileo Galilei turned his new telescope on the Moon late in 1609. Scholars taught that it was a flawless, polished ball of pure heavenly stuff, but Galileo read its shifting shadows with a painter's eye. What did he see covering its surface?
answer: Mountains, valleys, and craters
choices: Mountains, valleys, and craters
Oceans of dark blue water
Forests of strange grey trees
A glassy, polished surface
context: Trained as a Renaissance artist in chiaroscuro (light-and-shadow shading), Galileo read the moving shadows along the terminator line as real peaks throwing shadows, proving the Moon was a rugged world like the Earth. Source: HISTORY, Galileo begins observing the moon, Nov 30 1609; Linda Hall Library, Mapping the Moon.

question: Admirers moved Galileo Galilei's body to a grand new tomb in Florence in 1737, nearly a century after he died, and cut pieces from it as relics. One of those keepsakes is still on show in Florence, sealed in a little gilded glass egg. What part of him is it?
answer: His middle finger
choices: His middle finger
His right ear
His left eye
His tongue
context: Admirers cut off three fingers, a tooth, and a vertebra, joking that they were taking the parts with which 'Galileo wrote so many beautiful things.' His mummified middle finger, pointing upward in a gilded glass egg, is still displayed at the Museo Galileo in Florence. Source: Wikipedia, Galileo's middle finger; Museo Galileo, Galilean iconography and relics.

question: Galileo Galilei tested his telescope on the Pleiades, the famous little cluster of stars where the naked eye can pick out just six. Through the lens a whole crowd of extra stars sprang into view around them. How many did the lens add?
answer: About forty more
choices: About forty more
About a dozen more
About a hundred more
About four hundred more
context: Orion told the same story, jumping from nine visible stars to about eighty through the lens. The universe was suddenly vastly more crowded than anyone had imagined. Source: Cloudy Nights, The Discoveries of Galileo Part 5; Sidereus Nuncius (Smithsonian Libraries digital edition).

question: Galileo Galilei saw four small moons circling Jupiter in January 1610, and the sight struck a quiet blow at the heavens as the scholars of his day understood them. It knocked down one long-held belief. Which belief did those four little moons overturn?
answer: That every heavenly body must circle the Earth
choices: That every heavenly body must circle the Earth
That nothing in the heavens ever moves at all
That only the Sun can hold moons of its own
That every planet shines with its own light
context: Here were four objects plainly orbiting Jupiter, not the Earth — so the claim that the Earth must be the one center around which everything turns could no longer hold. Source: Linda Hall Library, Galileo Galilei (Scientist of the Day); Britannica, Telescopic discoveries.

question: Sister Maria Celeste, the eldest daughter of Galileo Galilei, mixed medicines for her aging father in her convent near Florence and wrote to him again and again. Of her letters, 124 survive among his papers. What became of his side of the letters?
answer: All of his replies are lost
choices: All of his replies are lost
They were burned by the Inquisition
They were written in secret code
They were never written at all
context: Suor Maria Celeste's 124 letters (1623-1633) survive, but every one of Galileo's replies to his devoted daughter is gone. Source: Wikipedia, Maria Celeste; Harvard Magazine, Vita: Suor Maria Celeste.

question: Galileo Galilei made a new discovery in the autumn of 1610 and wanted to claim it without giving it away to his rivals. So he sent them a line of Latin with its letters deliberately jumbled. Put back in order, it announced his find in one poetic sentence. What did the hidden message say?
answer: That Venus imitates the shapes of the Moon
choices: That Venus imitates the shapes of the Moon
That the Moon borrows its light from Venus
That Venus burns brighter than any fixed star
That Venus and the Sun share one orbit
context: Galileo had discovered the phases of Venus. Unscrambled, his Latin read 'Cynthiae figuras aemulatur mater amorum' — 'The mother of love [Venus] imitates the shapes of Cynthia [the Moon].' Source: Rutgers Physics, Galileo Galilei's Anagram; The Renaissance Mathematicus, Phases of Venus.

question: Peering at Saturn through a lens too weak to show it clearly, Galileo Galilei took the bulge he saw on each side of the planet for two companions. He hid the find in a scrambled Latin anagram announcing a triple planet. What playful name did Galileo later give those two bulges?
answer: Its 'ears'
choices: Its 'ears'
Its 'horns'
Its 'wings'
Its 'twins'
context: Galileo thought Saturn was 'triple-bodied'; his anagram spelled 'Altissimum planetam tergeminum observavi.' Kepler misread the same anagram as 'Mars has two moons' — wrong, but by luck Mars really does. Source: Wikipedia, Rings of Saturn; ScienceBlogs/Uncertain Principles, Advent Calendar of Science Stories 10.

question: The Inquisition forced Galileo Galilei to kneel in 1633 and swear that the Earth does not move. The story goes that as he got up off his knees he muttered a few defiant words, though nothing written in his own time recorded them. What is he said to have muttered?
answer: 'And yet it moves'
choices: 'And yet it moves'
'Still the stars turn'
'God sees the truth'
'The light remains'
context: In Italian, 'Eppur si muove.' No contemporary evidence shows Galileo said it — but tellingly, a 1640s painting attributed to Murillo already shows the phrase scrawled on a dungeon wall behind him. Source: Wikipedia, Galileo affair ('Eppur si muove' legend, Murillo painting).

question: Old and nearly blind after his trial, Galileo Galilei finished one last book, Two New Sciences, though he was banned from printing anything at all. His friends had to do something risky with the manuscript to put it beyond the Inquisition's reach. What did they do?
answer: Smuggled it out of Italy to be printed abroad
choices: Smuggled it out of Italy to be printed abroad
Buried it until the Pope had died
Read it aloud in secret meetings
Hid it inside a religious prayer book
context: Friends smuggled the manuscript to Leiden, Holland, where the Elzevir Press printed it in 1638, beyond the reach of the Inquisition. Source: Wikipedia, Two New Sciences; High Altitude Observatory, Galileo Galilei.

question: Pope John Paul II stood up in public in 1992 and admitted that the churchmen who condemned Galileo Galilei had been wrong to demand a strictly literal reading of Scripture. The Church had left the case unsettled for centuries. How long had it taken to admit its error?
answer: 359 years
choices: 359 years
About 50 years
About 150 years
About 700 years
context: From the 1633 condemnation to the 1992 acknowledgment was 359 years. Pope John Paul II conceded that Galileo was right that the Sun, not the Earth, sits at the center. Source: Wikipedia, Galileo affair (1992 John Paul II acknowledgment).

question: William Scurry, an Australian corporal, rigged two kerosene tins one above the other in December 1915, as the Allies made ready to slip away from Gallipoli by night. Water trickled from the top tin into the lower one until its weight tugged a rifle's trigger, so the emptied trenches kept firing on their own. What was Scurry's device called?
answer: The drip rifle
choices: The drip rifle
The trench mortar
The smoke screen
The dummy sentry
context: Scurry's 'drip rifle' let abandoned trenches keep firing on their own after the men had crept away, helping screen the secret withdrawal. Source: https://www.awm.gov.au/articles/encyclopedia/gallipoli/drip_rifle

question: Mustafa Kemal, the Ottoman commander, threw his 57th Regiment straight at the Australian and New Zealand troops scrambling up the cliffs at Anzac Cove on 25 April 1915. He knew most of his men would not live. What did Kemal tell them he was ordering them to do?
answer: To die where they stood so reinforcements had time to arrive
choices: To die where they stood so reinforcements had time to arrive
To hold the ridge until the very last bullet was spent
To charge downhill and drive the invaders back into the sea
To dig in deep and wait for the enemy guns to fall silent
context: Kemal's order is remembered as: 'Men, I am not ordering you to attack. I am ordering you to die. In the time it takes us to die, other forces and commanders can come and take our place.' He later became Ataturk, founder of modern Turkey. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_at_Anzac_Cove

question: Mohandas Gandhi, 61 years old, walked some 240 miles in March 1930 in protest against a British law. It forbade Indians to gather or sell one cheap, everyday thing for themselves that every Indian needed. What was it?
answer: Salt
choices: Salt
Tea
Cloth
Sugar
context: Gandhi argued, 'Next to air and water, salt is perhaps the greatest necessity of life,' so a tax on it crushed the poorest Indians hardest. The British Salt Act made it illegal for Indians to gather or sell their own salt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March

question: Mohandas Gandhi told his followers to break unjust laws in the open, to never strike back, and to accept their punishment, and he insisted that in this way ordinary people could beat an empire without a single weapon. Gandhi called the method satyagraha, a word he made from two Sanskrit roots. What did the word literally mean?
answer: 'Holding firmly to truth'
choices: 'Holding firmly to truth'
'The patience of the poor'
'Rule by our own hands'
'Peace without surrender'
context: The word is satyagraha, often translated 'truth-force.' Gandhi built it himself from satya (truth) and agraha (firmness). Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/satyagraha-philosophy

question: Webb Miller, an American reporter, watched about 2,500 of Gandhi's followers march in rows on the works at Dharasana on 21 May 1930, and he saw the police club them to the ground. His account ran in some 1,350 newspapers, though British censors at first tried to block it. How did Miller describe the way the marchers fell?
answer: 'They went down like ten-pins'
choices: 'They went down like ten-pins'
'They fell as quietly as snow'
'They dropped like wheat before the scythe'
'They sank without a single cry'
context: Miller wrote, 'Not one of the marchers even raised an arm to fend off the blows. They went down like ten-pins.' British telegraph operators first censored his dispatch; he counted 2 dead and roughly 320 wounded, many with fractured skulls, none of whom fought back. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharasana_Satyagraha

question: Mohandas Gandhi led India's peaceful struggle against British rule in the early 1900s. Historians went hunting through his letters, speeches and books for one of the most repeated sayings credited to him: 'An eye for an eye leaves the whole world blind.' What did they find?
answer: No record of Gandhi ever saying or writing it has been found
choices: No record of Gandhi ever saying or writing it has been found
Gandhi first said it to the Viceroy before the Salt March
Gandhi borrowed it word-for-word from an ancient Sanskrit text
Gandhi wrote it in a letter from prison after Dharasana
context: The line seems to trace to biographer Louis Fischer paraphrasing Gandhi's philosophy, not to Gandhi himself — a teachable misattribution rather than a documented quote. Source: https://quoteinvestigator.com/2010/12/27/eye-for-eye-blind/  (Legend.)

question: Mohandas Gandhi left the Sabarmati Ashram on 12 March 1930 with just 78 followers, walking to the sea to break the salt law. Each night he stopped in a new village to speak against the salt tax, and more people joined. By the time he reached Dandi, 24 days later, what had his band become?
answer: A marching column more than two miles long
choices: A marching column more than two miles long
A handful who quietly turned back home
A few hundred guarded by armed soldiers
A crowd that waited at the shore instead of walking
context: The 24-day march (12 March to 6 April 1930) ran about 240 miles from the Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, roughly 10–12 miles a day. He started with 78 followers; by the sea the procession was more than three kilometres — nearly two miles — long, and the protest he triggered led to over 60,000 Indians being arrested. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March; britannica.com/event/Salt-March)

question: British officials ground the shore salt at Dandi into the sand to stop Mohandas Gandhi, but on 6 April 1930, after his march to the sea, he found a lump of salty mud anyway. He held it over his head before the crowd. What did Gandhi declare as he held it up?
answer: "With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire."
choices: "With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire."
"Today the sea itself has joined our struggle."
"Let the King come and take this salt from my hand."
"This grain of salt is worth more than English gold."
context: British officials had tried to cheat him by grinding the seashore salt back into the sand so he couldn't pick any up — but he easily found a salt-crusted lump and raised it in triumph. The protest he triggered led to over 60,000 Indians being arrested, Gandhi included. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March; history.com/articles/gandhi-salt-march-india-british-colonial-rule)

question: Police with steel-tipped clubs waited at the Dharasana Salt Works after Gandhi's arrest, and row after row of 2,500 unarmed marchers walked straight into the blows. Webb Miller, an American reporter who had covered twenty-two countries in eighteen years, had never seen anything like it, above all because of one thing not a single marcher did. What did not one marcher do?
answer: Raise an arm to block the blows
choices: Raise an arm to block the blows
Cry out for mercy
Break ranks and run
Shout back at the police
context: Miller wrote, 'I heard the sickening whacks of the clubs on unprotected skulls... They went down like ten-pins,' and counted 320 wounded and 2 dead with not one arm lifted to deflect a blow. The poet Sarojini Naidu had told the marchers beforehand: 'You will be beaten, but you must not resist; you must not even raise a hand to ward off the blows.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharasana_Satyagraha)

question: Lord Irwin, the Viceroy of India, sat down with Mohandas Gandhi in March 1931 and signed a pact with him as an equal, less than a year after the march to the sea. Winston Churchill was disgusted that Britain would bargain with Gandhi at all, and he sneered at him in a phrase that Indians then wore as a badge of honour. What did Churchill call Gandhi?
answer: A "half-naked fakir" striding up the Viceroy's steps
choices: A "half-naked fakir" striding up the Viceroy's steps
A "barefoot lawyer playing at saints"
A "spinning-wheel rebel" who fooled the crowds
A "penniless pilgrim" begging for an empire
context: Churchill called it 'the nauseating and humiliating spectacle of this one-time Inner Temple lawyer, now seditious fakir, striding half-naked up the steps of the Viceroy's palace... to parley on equal terms with the representative of the King-Emperor.' The Gandhi–Irwin Pact was signed 5 March 1931, and the 'half-naked fakir' insult became Gandhi's badge of honour. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gandhi%E2%80%93Irwin_Pact; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March)

question: Genghis Khan began life around 1162 in a felt tent on the Mongolian steppe, under another name. His father had named the baby after a Tatar enemy he had just beaten in battle, and the boy kept that name until he took the title of Khan in 1206. What was his birth name?
answer: Temujin
choices: Temujin
Subutai
Yesugei
Inalchuq
context: He was born Temujin (Temüjin) around 1162, named for a captured Tatar enemy. 'Genghis Khan' came only as a title in 1206. Source: worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan and britannica.com/biography/Genghis-Khan

question: Genghis Khan's sons and grandsons rode on after his death until their empire ran from the Sea of Japan in the east to the plains of eastern Europe in the west, about a fifth of the land on Earth. In one plain, measurable way it still beats every other empire. What record does it hold?
answer: The largest contiguous land empire ever
choices: The largest contiguous land empire ever
The first empire to circle the whole globe
The longest-lasting empire in history
The first empire with a written constitution
context: At its peak it covered about 9 million square miles (~23 million sq km) of unbroken territory — the largest contiguous land empire that has ever existed. Source: britannica.com/place/Mongol-empire and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_Empire  (Legend.)

question: The baby who would become Genghis Khan came into the world, Mongol legend says, with his tiny fist clenched tight around something. When his mother pried the hand open, the story goes, she found a sign of the conqueror he would grow into. What was the newborn holding?
answer: A clot of blood
choices: A clot of blood
A shard of bone
A lock of black hair
A scrap of gold cloth
context: The Secret History of the Mongols tradition says he was born clutching a blood clot — read as a sign he would shed blood and rule. Told here as legend, not fact. Source: worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan

question: Yesugei sat down to a meal with some Tatars on the road, and they poisoned him over an old grudge. His son, the future Genghis Khan, was about nine years old. With Yesugei dead, what did his own clan do to the widow and her young children?
answer: Abandoned them on the open steppe to die
choices: Abandoned them on the open steppe to die
Sold them into slavery to a rival tribe
Took them in and raised them as their own
Handed them over to the Tatars as hostages
context: After Tatars poisoned Yesugei, the clan deserted his widow and children, expecting them to perish. The future conqueror of the world grew up an outcast. Source: worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan and history.com/articles/genghis-khan

question: Merkit raiders swept down on Genghis Khan's camp early in his rise, long before he took that title, and carried off his wife Borte. Instead of accepting the loss, he did something that first made other men want to follow him. What did he do?
answer: Gathered allies and led a raid to rescue her
choices: Gathered allies and led a raid to rescue her
Paid the Merkits a ransom in horses and gold
Challenged the Merkit chief to single combat
Swore off marriage and vowed lifelong revenge
context: He rallied allies and struck back to recover Borte — a defining moment in his climb and the start of his reputation as a leader men would follow. Source: history.com/articles/genghis-khan and worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan

question: An enemy archer shot the horse out from under Genghis Khan in a battle in 1202. Captured later, the man did not deny it: he openly confessed that he had fired the arrow, and he offered to serve faithfully. What did Genghis Khan do with the archer who had nearly killed him?
answer: Made him one of his top generals
choices: Made him one of his top generals
Had him shot with arrows in return
Set him free but banished him forever
Kept him as a stable hand for life
context: Genghis spared the archer Jirqo'adai, renamed him Jebe ('the Arrow'), and made him a leading commander — he promoted men by ability, not birth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jebe

question: Genghis Khan sent envoys to the Sultan of Khwarezm to demand justice for some 450 Mongol merchants, whom a governor at Otrar had accused of spying and put to death in 1218. The Sultan's answer left no path but war. What did the Sultan do to the envoys?
answer: Beheaded the chief envoy and shaved the others' beards
choices: Beheaded the chief envoy and shaved the others' beards
Threw all of the envoys into a desert prison
Sent them home with chests of silver and apologies
Forced them to convert before releasing them
context: After the Otrar massacre, the Sultan beheaded the lead ambassador and shaved the beards of the rest — a deliberate insult that unleashed the invasion of Khwarezmia. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otrar_Catastrophe and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inalchuq

question: The terrified people of conquered Bukhara watched Genghis Khan climb into the pulpit of their great Friday mosque in February 1220, and they heard him speak. The Persian chronicler Juvayni recorded his words. How did Genghis Khan describe himself to them?
answer: As the punishment God had sent for their sins
choices: As the punishment God had sent for their sins
As a humble guest who came only to trade
As the rightful heir of their fallen Sultan
As a prophet bringing a new and final law
context: He told them: 'I am the punishment of God. If you had not committed great sins, God would not have sent a punishment like me upon you.' Recorded by Ata-Malik Juvayni. Source: en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Genghis_Khan and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Bukhara

question: A Mongol messenger swung from his tired horse onto a fresh one at a relay station and galloped on. Stations like it stood every 25 to 30 miles across the empire, so messengers could cover 120 to 190 miles in a single day, and at its height the network kept more than 50,000 horses. What was this horseback relay called?
answer: The yam
choices: The yam
The paiza
The kurultai
The Yassa
context: The yam relay let a rider hand off to a fresh mount every 25–30 miles, so news crossed the empire at up to ~190 miles a day. (Greatly expanded by Genghis's successor Ogedei from 1234.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yam_(route) and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Mongolica

question: Genghis Khan died on campaign against the Tangut kingdom in August 1227, and no one has ever found his grave. By Mongol legend, his funeral escort made sure that nobody could ever tell where it lay. What does the legend say they did?
answer: Killed everyone they met on the road to the grave
choices: Killed everyone they met on the road to the grave
Burned every map that showed the route
Took a vow of silence and were never seen again
Built a hundred false tombs to confuse searchers
context: Legend (no forensic proof) says the escort killed all they encountered and diverted a river over the grave; the Burkhan Khaldun region became 'Ikh Khorig,' the Great Taboo, sealed on pain of death. Told here as legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_place_of_Genghis_Khan

question: The people of one Persian town fought back against a Mongol army, and the army wiped them out; famine followed the killing. Every town that resisted met the same end, until a whole people collapsed. By one common count, Persia held 2,500,000 people before the conquest. About how many were left?
answer: About 250,000
choices: About 250,000
About 900,000
context: One cited estimate puts the fall at 2,500,000 down to 250,000 — a tenth — through massacre and famine (the Persia figures are contested). Overall Mongol-conquest death tolls run from ~30 million to 40–60 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_under_the_Mongol_Empire

question: Jebe and Subutai, two of Genghis Khan's generals, took one army on a scouting trip out of Central Asia, across northern Persia and through the Caucasus. They crushed an army of Rus' and Kipchak warriors at the Kalka River in 1223, then rode all the way home. About how far had that one ride carried them?
answer: More than 5,500 miles
choices: More than 5,500 miles
More than 1,200 miles
More than 800 miles
More than 3,000 miles
context: Jebe and Subutai rode over 5,500 miles in about three years, crushing the Rus'–Kipchak coalition at the Battle of the Kalka River on 31 May 1223 before returning home. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subutai and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Kalka_River

question: Zerjal and fellow geneticists studied men across a vast region of Asia and reported in 2003 that about 8 percent of them shared one Y-chromosome line. They proposed that it came down from Genghis Khan and his sons. Others think ordinary Mongol warriors may have spread it. Scaled to every man on Earth, about how many carry it?
answer: About 1 in 200 men
choices: About 1 in 200 men
About 1 in 10 men
About 1 in 5,000 men
About 1 in a million men
context: The lineage is carried by roughly 0.5% of all men on Earth — about 16 million people. Later researchers argue it may come from ordinary Mongol warriors rather than Genghis himself, so the direct link is debated. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_descent_from_Genghis_Khan

question: George Washington had led America to victory in the Revolutionary War, and by December 1783 no one in the new country was more powerful or more loved. He hurried home to Virginia and got there on Christmas Eve. What did he go home to become?
answer: a farmer working his own fields
choices: a farmer working his own fields
a king crowned by his officers
a general still leading the army
a governor ruling all Virginia
context: He spent Christmas as a private citizen tending his land rather than as a general. This image of the war hero choosing the plow over power became one of the most admired things about him. Source: Wikipedia, 'George Washington's resignation as commander-in-chief'; American Revolution Institute, 'The American Cincinnatus'.

question: Congress was sitting at Annapolis on 23 December 1783 when George Washington walked in, holding the most dangerous thing in the new country: command of its only army. The war was won. What did he do with that power?
answer: handed it back to Congress and went home
choices: handed it back to Congress and went home
used it to make himself the new king
kept the army under his own command
demanded that Congress pay him for it
context: He told Congress, 'Having now finished the work assigned me, I retire from the great theatre of Action,' surrendered his commission, and left as a private citizen. Generals who win wars almost never give the power back. Source: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'Resignation of Military Commission'; Wikipedia, 'George Washington's resignation as commander-in-chief'.

question: George Washington reminded his countrymen of a famous Roman of old. That Roman left his plough to lead Rome's army with a dictator's power, won the war, gave the power straight back and went home to his fields. What did Americans call Washington?
answer: the American Cincinnatus
choices: the American Cincinnatus
the American Caesar
the American Augustus
the American Hannibal
context: Cincinnatus was the Roman who took total power only to win a war, then handed it back the moment victory came. Washington's officers were so moved by the parallel that they founded the Society of the Cincinnati in his honor. Source: American Revolution Institute, 'The American Cincinnatus'.

question: Unpaid officers of the Continental Army gathered at Newburgh in March 1783, ready to turn on Congress, and George Washington came in person to talk them out of it. His prepared speech failed to move them. Then he did one small thing, and the hardened men broke down in tears and abandoned the plot. What did he do?
answer: put on a pair of reading glasses no one knew he needed
choices: put on a pair of reading glasses no one knew he needed
drew his sword and dared them to strike him down
tore off his war medals and flung them to the floor
read aloud the names of the men who had died
context: As he fumbled with the spectacles, Washington said, 'Gentlemen, you will permit me to put on my spectacles, for I have not only grown gray but almost blind in the service of my country.' Seeing this private weakness from their commander, the officers wept and abandoned the plot. Source: Wikipedia, 'Newburgh Conspiracy'; Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'Newburgh Address'.

question: Colonel Lewis Nicola wrote to George Washington in 1782, when the war was nearly won but the army had gone months without pay and Congress looked weak. Washington, he urged, should make himself king of America. Washington answered the same day. What did he tell Nicola to do with the idea?
answer: to banish such thoughts from his mind forever
choices: to banish such thoughts from his mind forever
to gather the officers and prepare a crown
to keep the plan secret until the time was right
to put the question before Congress instead
context: Washington said he must 'view with abhorrence, and reprehend with severity' the idea, calling it 'big with the greatest mischiefs that can befall my Country.' He flatly refused the crown. Source: Founders Online, 'From George Washington to Lewis Nicola, 22 May 1782'.

question: Electors of the young United States met in the winter of 1788 to 1789 to choose its first president, and met again in 1792. George Washington won both times, and both times he did what no president since has done. How did he win those two elections?
answer: unanimously, with every single elector voting for him
choices: unanimously, with every single elector voting for him
by a single electoral vote over his rival
only after the House broke a deadlock
by sweeping every state except his own
context: He took all 69 electoral votes in 1789 and all 132 in 1792. No one campaigned against him because everyone wanted him; he remains the only president ever elected unanimously by the Electoral College. Source: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'Presidential Election of 1789'; Britannica, 'United States presidential election of 1789'.

question: George Washington refused a third term as president in 1796, and every president who followed him did the same for almost 150 years; none served more than two terms. Through all those years, what actually held presidents to that limit?
answer: nothing but Washington's own example
choices: nothing but Washington's own example
a clause in the original Constitution
a law that Congress had passed
an oath sworn at each inauguration
context: No law required it. Washington simply declined a third term in his 1796 Farewell Address, and his example alone held for over a century and a half, until the two-term limit was finally written into the Constitution as the 22nd Amendment in 1951. Source: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'George Washington's Farewell Address'; U.S. State Department Office of the Historian, 'Washington's Farewell Address, 1796'.

question: Young George Washington, the story goes, chopped down his father's cherry tree with a little hatchet and confessed, 'I cannot tell a lie, I did it.' Historians and Washington's own home at Mount Vernon agree that it never happened. Where did the famous story come from?
answer: a preacher invented it to sell more biographies
choices: a preacher invented it to sell more biographies
Washington himself told it in his old age
his mother wrote it down in a family diary
British newspapers printed it to mock him
context: A traveling preacher and bookseller named Mason Locke 'Parson' Weems added the cherry-tree scene to the 5th edition of his Washington biography in 1806 to sell copies and teach children virtue. There is no evidence it ever happened. Source: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, 'Cherry Tree Myth'; National Park Service, 'George Washington and the Cherry Tree'.  (Legend.)

question: George Washington rode for hours across his farms through snow and sleet in December 1799 and came down with a violent throat infection. His doctors took about two-fifths of his blood, but nothing helped. Dying at Mount Vernon, he gave his secretary, Tobias Lear, one strange instruction about his body. What did he demand?
answer: that they wait three days before burying him
choices: that they wait three days before burying him
that his heart be buried beside his mother
that no doctor be allowed near him again
that he be buried in his old army uniform
context: Washington was terrified of being buried alive, so he told his secretary Tobias Lear to wait three days. His doctors had drained roughly 40 percent of his blood trying to cure what was likely epiglottitis, and his last words were 'Tis well.' Source: Mount Vernon, 'Death of George Washington' and '8 Facts About George Washington's Death'.

question: George Washington enslaved people at Mount Vernon his entire adult life, and in 1799 the estate held 317 enslaved men, women and children. He owned 123 of them himself, and with those he did something none of the other early presidents who held slaves did. What was it?
answer: ordered them freed in his will
choices: ordered them freed in his will
freed them the day he became president
sold them all before he died
left them to his nephews in his will
context: Washington directed that the 123 he owned be freed after Martha's death, making him the only slaveholding early president to free all of his own enslaved people. He could not legally free the other 153 'dower' slaves tied to the Custis estate. The virtue and this contradiction are part of the same honest record. Source: Mount Vernon, 'Ten Facts About Washington & Slavery' and 'A Decision to Free His Slaves'.

question: William Lee, called Billy, rode beside George Washington through the whole Revolutionary War as his enslaved valet. When Washington wrote his will, he singled Lee out from all the people he held in slavery. What did Lee alone receive under the will?
answer: his freedom at once and a yearly pension
choices: his freedom at once and a yearly pension
a parcel of land near Mount Vernon
a fine horse from the general's stable
a letter of thanks and nothing more
context: Lee was freed immediately and granted $30 a year for life 'as a testimony of my sense of his attachment to me, and for his faithful services during the Revolutionary War.' Source: Wikipedia, 'William Lee (valet)'; Mount Vernon, 'Slavery and George Washington's Will'.

question: Ona Judge, Martha Washington's skilled seamstress, and Hercules Posey, the household's cook, refused to wait for any master's permission to be free. Both won their freedom while George Washington was still alive and still the most powerful man in the country. How did they become free?
answer: they ran away and were never recaptured
choices: they ran away and were never recaptured
they bought their freedom with saved wages
they petitioned a court and won release
they were freed early in Washington's will
context: Ona Judge escaped in 1796 and Hercules Posey escaped in 1797. Despite Washington's efforts to recover them, both eluded recapture and lived out their lives free. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ona Judge'; Zinn Education Project, 'Hercules Escapes from Enslavement by George Washington'.

question: Otto von Bismarck set out in the 1860s to weld the scattered German kingdoms and duchies into one empire under Prussia. He did it with three short, sharp wars, one after another, each knocking out a rival to Prussian leadership. Which three countries did Prussia fight, in the order the wars came?
answer: Denmark, then Austria, then France
choices: Denmark, then Austria, then France
Poland, then Russia, then Britain
France, then Spain, then Italy
Austria, then Russia, then Turkey
context: Bismarck engineered the wars against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866), and France (1870-71) as a planned sequence, each designed to remove a rival to Prussian leadership of the German states. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Koniggratz ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War

question: Defending the king's army budget before Prussia's parliament in 1862, Bismarck warned that the great questions of the day would not be settled by speeches and majority votes. Something far harsher would. What two things did he say would settle them, in the pairing the world came to remember?
answer: Blood and iron
choices: Blood and iron
Faith and fire
Gold and steel
Sword and crown
context: Bismarck actually said 'iron and blood' (Eisen und Blut) on 30 September 1862, calling speeches and majority votes 'the great mistake of 1848 and 1849.' The catchier flipped order, 'blood and iron' (Blut und Eisen), is the version that stuck and earned him the nickname 'the Iron Chancellor.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_and_Iron_(speech)

question: Prussian infantrymen at Königgrätz in 1866 could fire ten to twelve rounds a minute lying flat on the ground, while Austrian soldiers had to stand up to ram each charge down the barrel. What gave the Prussians this edge of about five shots to one?
answer: The breech-loading 'needle gun'
choices: The breech-loading 'needle gun'
Heavier cavalry armor
Repeating revolver pistols
Steel-tipped bayonets
context: The Dreyse 'needle gun' loaded at the breech, so a Prussian soldier could fire lying down about five shots to every Austrian one. At Koniggraetz (3 July 1866) Austria lost about 45,000 men, Prussia fewer than 10,000. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreyse_needle_gun ; https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Koniggratz

question: Bismarck took a telegram his king had sent from Bad Ems in July 1870 and trimmed it until a polite report read like a curt snub to France's ambassador. The edited version, he told his dinner guests, would be 'a red rag upon the Gallic bull.' What did it bring about within six days?
answer: France declared war on Prussia
choices: France declared war on Prussia
Austria rejoined the German states
The French king abdicated his throne
Britain entered the war on Prussia's side
context: By shortening the Ems Dispatch, Bismarck made a parley sound like a challenge. Moltke said the edited version 'sounded before like a parley; now it is like a flourish in answer to a challenge.' France declared war six days later, exactly as Bismarck intended. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ems_dispatch

question: Wilhelm I, the Prussian king, wanted the grand title 'Emperor of Germany' when the new empire was proclaimed in 1871, a title claiming lordship over all German lands. Bismarck forced on him the humbler 'German Emperor,' first among equal princes, to avoid offending the southern kings. How did the slighted Wilhelm show his anger at the ceremony?
answer: He refused to shake Bismarck's hand
choices: He refused to shake Bismarck's hand
He tore up the proclamation document
He ordered Bismarck arrested on the spot
He cancelled the planned coronation feast
context: Bismarck insisted on 'German Emperor' (first among equals) over Wilhelm's preferred 'Emperor of Germany' to avoid offending the southern kings and Austria. The slighted Wilhelm stepped down from the dais, refused to shake Bismarck's hand, and snubbed him for several days. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_German_Empire

question: Robert E. Lee ordered about 12,500 Confederate soldiers against the Union line on Cemetery Ridge on 3 July 1863, the third day at Gettysburg, in the assault remembered as Pickett's Charge. They stepped off in parade-ground lines toward Union troops waiting behind stone walls. What did they have to cross to reach them?
answer: Nearly a mile of open, empty field
choices: Nearly a mile of open, empty field
A deep, fast-moving river crossing
A thick forest tangled with brush
A swamp full of mud and reeds
context: Pickett's Charge sent roughly 12,500 men across almost a mile of open ground with no cover, in full view of Union cannon and rifles the whole way. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/picketts-charge

question: George Meade's Union army and Robert E. Lee's Confederates fought for three days in July 1863 in the fields around the little town of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. By the time the guns fell silent, the battle had set a grim record. What was it?
answer: It caused about 50,000 casualties, the most of any battle in North America
choices: It caused about 50,000 casualties, the most of any battle in North America
It lasted longer than any other battle ever fought on the continent
It was the first battle in history to be photographed by cameras
It was the only Civil War battle fought during a heavy snowstorm
context: Three days of fighting, July 1-3, 1863, left roughly 50,000 men killed, wounded, or missing — the bloodiest battle ever fought in North America. Lee's army began retreating south on July 4 and never invaded the North again. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/civil-war/battles/gettysburg

question: John Buford's Union horsemen held the ridges outside Gettysburg early on 1 July 1863, a thin screen against what was coming. Buford knew Robert E. Lee's whole Confederate army was marching straight at him. When an officer asked how things looked, what was Buford's grim reply?
answer: "The devil's to pay!"
choices: "The devil's to pay!"
"Not one step backward, boys!"
"We shall hold or we shall fall!"
"God defend the right today!"
context: Buford understood the whole Confederate army was bearing down on his outnumbered cavalry, who had to hold the ridges until Union infantry came up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gettysburg,_first_day

question: Union troopers under John Buford were badly outnumbered on McPherson's Ridge at Gettysburg on 1 July 1863, so every fourth man held the horses while the rest fought on foot. What gave these dismounted troopers the edge that let them stall the Confederates until Union infantry arrived?
answer: Their breech-loading carbines fired faster than the enemy's muzzle-loaders
choices: Their breech-loading carbines fired faster than the enemy's muzzle-loaders
They had dug deep trenches across the whole ridge overnight
They were hidden behind a tall stone fort on the hilltop
They greatly outnumbered the Confederate troops attacking them
context: Each Union trooper carried a single-shot breech-loading carbine that reloaded faster than the Confederates' muzzle-loaders — enough of a head start to buy time for the infantry to reach the field. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gettysburg,_first_day
