question: Abraham Lincoln offered John Reynolds command of the whole Army of the Potomac after the Battle of Chancellorsville, and Reynolds did something startling with the offer. On 1 July 1863 he led the first Union infantry onto the field at Gettysburg, and minutes later a bullet killed him. What had he done with Lincoln's offer?
answer: He turned it down, refusing unless free of Washington's meddling
choices: He turned it down, refusing unless free of Washington's meddling
He accepted it and led the whole army into Gettysburg
He demanded a huge sum of money before he would agree
He passed it to his younger brother, also a general
context: Reynolds refused command unless he could run the army without interference from Washington, so the job went to Meade instead. Reynolds was the highest-ranking soldier on either side killed at Gettysburg. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/john-f-reynolds

question: Gouverneur K. Warren, a Union engineer, climbed Little Round Top at Gettysburg on 2 July 1863 and found the hill almost empty, held only by a small signal station. Looking southwest, he saw a sign that an entire enemy column was about to seize the high ground. What did he see?
answer: The glint of Confederate bayonets shining in the sun
choices: The glint of Confederate bayonets shining in the sun
A long row of campfires already burning on the hill
A signal flag waving the order to retreat
A cloud of smoke from a barn set ablaze
context: Warren spotted the sun flashing off enemy bayonets and realized a whole Confederate column was moving to grab the unguarded hill, so he raced off to find troops to defend it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Round_Top

question: Strong Vincent, a Union colonel, rushed his brigade up Little Round Top at Gettysburg on 2 July 1863 without waiting for orders. He placed Joshua Chamberlain's 20th Maine at the very end of the whole Union line and gave Chamberlain one fierce command. What did Vincent tell him?
answer: "You are to hold this ground at all costs!"
choices: "You are to hold this ground at all costs!"
"Fall back the moment they break through!"
"Wait here for the general's next order!"
"March around and strike them from behind!"
context: Vincent told Chamberlain this was the left of the entire Union line and it had to hold. Vincent was mortally wounded and given a deathbed promotion to brigadier general. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/defense-little-round-top

question: Joshua Chamberlain's 20th Maine beat back one Alabama assault after another on Little Round Top until the men ran out of ammunition. With the enemy only thirty yards off and his line about to be overrun, what did Chamberlain order?
answer: A downhill bayonet charge straight into the enemy
choices: A downhill bayonet charge straight into the enemy
A quiet retreat back over the crest of the hill
His men to lie flat and play dead until dark
A white flag raised to ask for a truce
context: Out of ammunition, Chamberlain ordered the bayonet; in his official report he wrote the word 'ran like fire along the line' and the charge swept up about 400 prisoners, mostly from the 15th and 47th Alabama. His regiment lost about 136 men, roughly 30 killed. Source: Chamberlain's official report, July 6 1863 (https://ironbrigader.com/2020/06/29/joshua-lawrence-chamberlains-report-on-the-20th-maine-at-gettysburg/)

question: Winfield Scott Hancock saw a gap open in the Union centre at Gettysburg on 2 July 1863, with only the small 1st Minnesota regiment, 262 men, on hand. He flung them at an oncoming Confederate brigade to buy five minutes. What was the cost of that charge?
answer: An 82% casualty rate, the worst of any Union regiment in one action
choices: An 82% casualty rate, the worst of any Union regiment in one action
A complete encirclement that captured the whole regiment alive
A long stalemate that pinned both sides down until nightfall
A quick victory that cost only a handful of wounded men
context: Colonel William Colvill led the charge that bought the five minutes Hancock needed; the 1st Minnesota suffered an 82% casualty rate — the highest of any Union regiment in a single action in the entire war. Hancock wrote, 'there is no more gallant deed recorded in history.' Source: https://www.civilwarmed.org/1st-minnesota-at-gettysburg/

question: James Longstreet was sure the attack planned for the third day at Gettysburg, 3 July 1863, was doomed. When George Pickett came to him and asked, 'General, shall I advance?', Longstreet gave the order that sent 12,500 men forward. By his own later account, how did he give it?
answer: He only nodded, unable to speak the command aloud
choices: He only nodded, unable to speak the command aloud
He shouted it eagerly to spur the men onward
He wrote it on paper and handed it over silently
He fired a single pistol shot as the signal
context: Longstreet wrote that 'the effort to speak the order failed, and I could only indicate it by an affirmative bow.' He believed the attack would fail but could not stop it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickett's_Charge

question: Lewis Armistead led his Virginians deeper into the Union line than any other attacker in Pickett's Charge, shouting, 'Come on, boys, we must give them the cold steel!' To keep his men following him through the smoke, he made himself easy to see. What did he do?
answer: He stuck his black hat on the tip of his sword and held it high
choices: He stuck his black hat on the tip of his sword and held it high
He tied a bright red sash around his waist as a banner
He climbed onto the shoulders of two of his soldiers
He carried the regiment's flag in his own two hands
context: Armistead crossed the stone wall at the Angle and laid his hand on a Union cannon — the deepest point of the whole assault — before he was mortally wounded. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/picketts-charge

question: As Lewis Armistead lay dying in Pickett's Charge, he asked that his regrets be sent to Winfield Scott Hancock, the Union general defending that very spot, who lay wounded nearby. What does the story say had once bound the two generals?
answer: They were dear old friends who had wept as they parted before the war
choices: They were dear old friends who had wept as they parted before the war
They were brothers who had not spoken in many long years
They had once dueled each other over a bitter insult
They had been rival suitors competing for the same woman
context: Story holds that Armistead and Hancock were close friends who parted in tears to 'Auld Lang Syne'; as Armistead lay dying he asked that his regrets be sent to Hancock, wounded nearby at almost the same moment. Armistead died on July 5. (Told as legend — the depth of the friendship is debated by historians.) Source: https://militaryhistorynow.com/2022/11/27/armistead-and-hancock-rethinking-the-storied-friendship-between-opposing-generals-at-gettysburg/

question: George Pickett's charge at Gettysburg collapsed in under an hour on 3 July 1863, costing roughly 6,555 casualties, about half his men. Years after the war a reporter asked Pickett why it had failed. What was his famously rueful answer?
answer: "I've always thought the Yankees had something to do with it."
choices: "I've always thought the Yankees had something to do with it."
"We were betrayed by a coward who fled the field."
"The good Lord simply willed us to lose that day."
"Our powder was wet and not a gun would fire."
context: About half the attacking force fell. As the survivors streamed back, Robert E. Lee rode among them taking the blame, repeating 'It's all my fault.' Pickett's dry answer years later became one of the most quoted lines of the war. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/picketts-charge

question: Giordano Bruno stood before his judges in Rome in February 1600, after seven years in the Inquisition's prisons, and heard them sentence him to be burned alive. He turned the moment back on them with one defiant line. What did Bruno say?
answer: "Perhaps you pronounce this sentence with greater fear than I receive it."
choices: "Perhaps you pronounce this sentence with greater fear than I receive it."
"You may burn my body, but my books will outlive every one of you."
"I have served the Church faithfully, and the Church has betrayed me."
"Strike, then, for I no longer fear the power of any man on Earth."
context: The eyewitness Caspar Schoppe recorded nearly the same words in a 1600 letter: "You who pronounce this sentence have more fear than I in hearing it." Bruno was burned at the stake in Rome's Campo de' Fiori on February 17, 1600. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giordano_Bruno; religionnews.com (2000); famous-trials.com/bruno/261-home.

question: Robert Bellarmine, a cardinal who would later confront Galileo, boiled Giordano Bruno's case down to eight heretical propositions before Bruno was burned in Rome in 1600. Bruno is remembered by many as a martyr for astronomy, yet his belief in countless worlds was only one of the eight. Which charges actually doomed him to the fire?
answer: Denying the Trinity, that Jesus was God, and the bread's change at Mass
choices: Denying the Trinity, that Jesus was God, and the bread's change at Mass
Forging papal letters, selling indulgences, and pocketing the Church's gold
Practicing alchemy, casting horoscopes, and conjuring spirits for hire
Leading an armed revolt of friars against the bishops of Naples
context: The charges that sealed his fate were theological: denying the Trinity, denying that Jesus was God made flesh, denying transubstantiation, and denying the perpetual virginity of Mary. Cardinal Robert Bellarmine — the same theologian who later confronted Galileo — boiled the case down to eight heretical propositions. Bruno was no modern scientist-saint; he was a Hermetic mystic who also believed in the transmigration of souls. Sources: scientificamerican.com ("Was Giordano Bruno Burned at the Stake for Believing in Exoplanets?"); famous-trials.com/bruno/261-home.

question: Charley Kline, a student, typed 'login' on 29 October 1969 to a computer at Stanford, over the early network that grew into the internet. Stanford's machine crashed before he finished, and only part of the word got through. What was the first message ever sent?
answer: 'LO'
choices: 'LO'
'LOG'
'LOGI'
'GO'
context: The Stanford machine crashed after just 'L' and 'O', so history's first network message was the unintended 'LO' — as in 'lo and behold'. The team fixed the bug and sent the full 'LOGIN' about an hour later. Source: icann.org / samueli.ucla.edu / cyberlaw.stanford.edu.

question: Malcolm McLean sent 58 steel boxes, each the size of a truck trailer, from New Jersey to Houston in April 1956. Loading them took under eight hours, where loose cargo took days. What were those 58 boxes the first true example of?
answer: The shipping container
choices: The shipping container
The oil supertanker
The cargo airplane
The railroad boxcar
context: Loose 'breakbulk' cargo had to be carried aboard sack by sack; McLean's 58 boxes loaded in under eight hours instead of days. Marc Levinson called his history of it 'The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger.' Source: porthouston.com / maritime-executive.com.

question: A colleague of Tim Berners-Lee at the European Organization for Nuclear Research stuck a red-ink warning on one black NeXT computer in 1991. The world's first website lived on that machine, and turning it off would have knocked the whole World Wide Web offline. What did the warning say?
answer: 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!'
choices: 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!'
'CRITICAL: live web server — DO NOT UNPLUG!'
'WARNING: powering this off kills the network!'
'STOP! Keep this machine running at all times!'
context: The whole World Wide Web lived on that one NeXT cube; the first website, info.cern.ch, went live in 1991. Source: home.cern 'The web spreads beyond CERN' / cds.cern.ch.

question: Tim Berners-Lee gave his boss, Sendall, a short paper in March 1989 about a way to link documents across many computers, the idea that grew into the World Wide Web. Sendall scrawled a three-word note at the top that let the project go ahead. What did it say?
answer: 'Vague, but exciting…'
choices: 'Vague, but exciting…'
'Brilliant — start now.'
'Strange, but worth trying.'
'Confusing, but promising.'
context: Sendall's 'Vague, but exciting…' note greenlit the project that became the Web. Berners-Lee gave it away free to the world rather than patenting it. Source: info.cern.ch/Proposal.html / home.cern.

question: Malcolm McLean, a young truck driver from North Carolina, sat on a dock for hours in 1937, watching dockworkers haul his cargo onto a ship one bale at a time. Staring at his fully loaded trailer, he made one frustrated wish. What did he wish he could simply do with it?
answer: Lift the entire trailer straight onto the ship
choices: Lift the entire trailer straight onto the ship
Drive the truck right onto the deck himself
Pay the dockworkers to hurry up
Mail the cargo in smaller parcels
context: That dock-side wish became containerization. McLean founded Sea-Land Service in 1960, and his containers later carried U.S. military supplies in the Vietnam War, proving the system at full scale. Source: maritime-executive.com / americanbusinesshistory.org.

question: Keith Tantlinger, an engineer, designed a twist-lock in the 1950s: a steel fitting at each corner, so that cranes could hoist any box and boxes could stack and lock together securely. When it came to the patent, he persuaded Malcolm McLean's company to make one particular decision. What did the company do with the patent?
answer: Released it royalty-free for anyone to use
choices: Released it royalty-free for anyone to use
Gave it free only to U.S. shipping lines
Published the design in an engineering journal
Donated the patent to the U.S. Navy
context: Because the twist-lock was free for everyone, a box from any port fits any ship, train, or truck — the standardized ISO container measured in 'TEU', the twenty-foot equivalent unit. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twistlock.

question: A crane driver in a busy port swung one more steel box onto a ship. As freight grew cheaper and trade barriers came down between 1990 and 2015, the world gained more than two billion people, yet nearly 1.2 billion fewer lived in extreme poverty. About how many people escaped it each day?
answer: About 130,000 a day
choices: About 130,000 a day
About 1,000 a day
About 12,000 a day
About 1 million a day
context: As a share of all humanity, extreme poverty fell from 36% in 1990 to 10% in 2015, and East Asia's rate collapsed from 62% to 2%. The ~130,000-a-day pace met the UN's goal of halving 1990 poverty more than five years early. Source: cato.org / worldbank.org press release 2018-09-19.

question: Mikhail Gorbachev launched a policy called glasnost in 1985, and Soviet newspapers began printing stories about empty shops, corruption and Stalin's crimes. What does the Russian word glasnost mean?
answer: Openness
choices: Openness
Rebuilding
Equality
Victory
context: Glasnost (literally 'publicity' or 'public voice') relaxed strict government censorship and allowed open public discussion of political and social problems for the first time in decades. Source: britannica.com/topic/glasnost ; time.com/5512665/mikhail-gorbachev-glasnost-perestroika/

question: Mikhail Gorbachev inherited a Soviet economy of empty shelves in 1985. He weakened the central planners in Moscow and allowed some private ownership again, and he called the reform perestroika. What does the word mean?
answer: Restructuring
choices: Restructuring
Openness
Brotherhood
Friendship
context: Perestroika means 'restructuring' or 'reconstruction' -- Gorbachev's plan to decentralize the economy: weakening the central planners in Moscow, allowing more local decisions, and permitting some private ownership for the first time since the 1920s. Source: alphahistory.com/coldwar/glasnost-and-perestroika/ ; history.com/articles/perestroika-and-glasnost

question: Sergei Gorbachev taught his teenage son Mikhail to drive a big machine on a state farm. The boy grew up in the poor peasant village of Privolnoye in southern Russia and would one day be the last leader of the Soviet Union. What did he learn to drive?
answer: A combine harvester
choices: A combine harvester
A threshing machine
A hay wagon
A tractor
context: Gorbachev was born March 2, 1931, in Privolnoye in the Stavropol region; as a teenager he drove a combine harvester at a state farm, a skill taught by his father Sergei. Source: notablebiographies.com/Gi-He/Gorbachev-Mikhail.html ; nobelprize.org/prizes/peace/1990/gorbachev/biographical/

question: Workers tore out vineyards across the Soviet Union on Mikhail Gorbachev's orders, part of the sweeping campaign against drinking that he launched in May 1985, two months after taking power. He also raised prices and cut production. Mocking citizens quickly gave him a teasing nickname. What did they call him?
answer: The mineral-water secretary
choices: The mineral-water secretary
The empty-bottle secretary
The lemonade secretary
The dry-throat secretary
context: Citizens nicknamed him the 'mineral-water secretary' (mineralny sekretar) instead of General Secretary (generalny sekretar), mocking the anti-alcohol drive. Source: rferl.org/a/russia-gorbachev-admits-botching-anti-alcohol-campaign/27018247.html ; soviethistory.msu.edu/1985/anti-alcohol-campaign/

question: Soviet officials tried at first to hide a catastrophe that struck Soviet Ukraine at 1:23 in the morning on 26 April 1986. Mikhail Gorbachev later called it the 'turning point' that opened the way to far greater freedom of expression, after which the old system 'could no longer continue.' Which catastrophe did he mean?
answer: The Chernobyl reactor explosion
choices: The Chernobyl reactor explosion
The Kyshtym nuclear disaster
The sinking of the submarine Komsomolets
The Spitak earthquake in Armenia
context: Gorbachev called Chernobyl -- the reactor that exploded at 1:23 a.m. on April 26, 1986, in northern Ukraine -- a 'turning point' that 'opened the possibility of much greater freedom of expression' so the old system 'could no longer continue.' (Kyshtym 1957, the Komsomolets sinking 1989, and the Spitak earthquake 1988 were other real Soviet catastrophes.) Source: gorby.ru/en/presscenter/2006/04/view-turning-point-at-chernobyl-mikhail-s-gorbachev-kopiya ; slate.com/technology/2013/01/chernobyl-and-the-fall-of-the-soviet-union

question: Mikhail Gorbachev visited East Berlin for a big anniversary in October 1989 and warned Erich Honecker, East Germany's hardline Communist boss, not to fight reform. Weeks later Honecker was forced out, and the Berlin Wall fell on 9 November. What grim line had Gorbachev given him?
answer: Life punishes those who come too late
choices: Life punishes those who come too late
The walls of empires fall from within
History forgives the bold and buries the slow
No throne outlasts the people's patience
context: Gorbachev's warning to Honecker -- 'Life punishes those who come too late' -- preceded Honecker's ouster and the fall of the Wall on Nov 9, 1989. Source: ecfr.eu/article/life-punishes-those-who-come-too-late/ ; blogs.loc.gov/international-collections/2019/11/the-rise-and-fall-of-the-berlin-wall/

question: Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev met at Reykjavik in October 1986 and came close to scrapping all their nuclear weapons; when Reagan floated the idea, Gorbachev answered, 'Let's eliminate them.' It fell apart only because Reagan would not confine the testing of one program to the laboratory. Which program?
answer: His Star Wars missile-defense program
choices: His Star Wars missile-defense program
His Pershing missiles in West Germany
His B-1 bomber fleet
His underground nuclear tests
context: The Reykjavik deal to abolish all nuclear weapons collapsed when Reagan would not confine his 'Star Wars' missile defense (SDI) testing to the laboratory. Source: nsarchive.gwu.edu/document/22397-document-2-transcript-gorbachev-reagan ; armscontrol.org/act/2011-09/features/reykjavik-when-abolition-was-within-reach

question: Gennadi Gerasimov, Mikhail Gorbachev's spokesman, joked in October 1989 that Moscow had traded the Brezhnev Doctrine for the Sinatra Doctrine. Under the old doctrine Moscow crushed protest in Eastern Europe with tanks, and Gorbachev had dropped that rule. Which Frank Sinatra song gave the joke its point?
answer: My Way
choices: My Way
New York, New York
Fly Me to the Moon
Strangers in the Night
context: Gerasimov dubbed the hands-off policy 'the Frank Sinatra Doctrine -- he has a song, My Way, so every country decides on its own which road to take,' replacing the Brezhnev Doctrine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinatra_Doctrine ; archive.macleans.ca/article/1989/11/6/the-sinatra-doctrine

question: Mikhail Gorbachev sat down on 25 December 1991 to sign the papers dissolving the Soviet Union, and his Soviet felt-tip pen ran dry. Tom Johnson, president of the Cable News Network, offered him another pen. Before he would use it, Gorbachev asked one wry question. What did he ask?
answer: Is it an American pen?
choices: Is it an American pen?
Is the camera still rolling?
Is this the final copy?
Is the whole world watching?
context: Gorbachev asked 'Is it an American pen?' and used the Mont Blanc only after being told it was French or German -- a last small refusal to end the USSR with an American pen. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Johnson_(journalist) ; quote.org/quote/is-it-an-american-pen-in-that-601911

question: Mikhail Gorbachev waged a campaign against drinking from 1985, and it carried a hidden trap. Vodka taxes had quietly supplied a huge share of the Soviet budget, and the campaign tore a hole in the government's income. To cover it, his government did something that helped wreck the economy in the years that followed. What did it do?
answer: Printed more money
choices: Printed more money
Raised income taxes sharply
Sold off the state gold reserves
Borrowed heavily from Western banks
context: Vodka taxes funded much of the state; with that revenue gone, the government printed more money, fueling the inflation that helped wreck the Soviet economy. Source: soviethistory.msu.edu/1985/anti-alcohol-campaign/ ; euronews.com/my-europe/2021/12/23/mikhail-gorbachev-tried-to-get-russia-on-the-wagon-he-failed

question: Mikhail Gorbachev used perestroika to dismantle the command economy, in which planners in Moscow had told Soviet factories what to make. But the reform left one fatal gap: inflation, empty shelves and long shortages followed, and the USSR dissolved in 1991. What did perestroika fail to do as it tore the old system down?
answer: Build a working market to replace central planning
choices: Build a working market to replace central planning
Free prices fast enough to refill the shelves
Let farmers freely sell their own grain
Keep the ruble from collapsing in value
context: Perestroika dismantled central planning without building a working market to replace it, producing inflation and empty shelves; a system that could not survive even partial honesty about itself unraveled, and the USSR dissolved in 1991. Source: courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-worldhistory/chapter/37-2-2-gorbachev-and-perestroika/ ; britannica.com/place/Russia/The-Gorbachev-era-perestroika-and-glasnost

question: Carpenters framing the roof of Notre-Dame de Paris in the 1200s cut down about 5,000 oak trees, and they nicknamed the web of timber they built 'the Forest.' What was special about each beam in it?
answer: Each beam came from a different oak tree.
choices: Each beam came from a different oak tree.
Each beam was painted with a saint's name.
Each beam was carved into a leafy shape.
Each beam was as old as the cathedral itself.
context: Builders cut roughly 5,000 oaks from 522 hectares of woodland to frame the roof, and because each timber came from its own tree, the carpenters called the whole structure 'the Forest.' The 2019 fire destroyed it almost entirely. Source: notredamedeparis.fr 'The roof structure'; woodcentral.com.au 'How Notre-Dame fully traced oaks for rebuild'.

question: Father Jean-Marc Fournier, the fire brigade's chaplain, ran into Notre-Dame de Paris late on 15 April 2019 as fire raced through it, and firefighters formed a human chain beside him. He was after the cathedral's most sacred relic. What did he carry out?
answer: The Crown of Thorns.
choices: The Crown of Thorns.
The bishop's golden mitre.
A jeweled silver chalice.
The high altar's gold cross.
context: Father Fournier led a human chain inside and brought out the Crown of Thorns, Notre-Dame's holiest relic, along with the Blessed Sacrament. Source: cbsnews.com 'Notre Dame heroes human chain crown of thorns'; cnn.com 'Notre Dame art saved'.

question: Workers sifting the charred wreckage of Notre-Dame after the 2019 fire found the copper rooster from the tip of the fallen spire, dented but whole. Something had been sealed inside the bird. What was it?
answer: Three holy relics.
choices: Three holy relics.
A builder's old coins.
A folded prayer card.
A lock of human hair.
context: Inside the rooster were three relics: a piece of the Crown of Thorns and bone fragments of Saint Denis and Saint Genevieve, the patron saints of Paris. The bird was dented but intact. Source: foxnews.com 'Notre Dame cathedral cross reinstalled'; onejourney.com 'Notre-Dame de Paris complete guide'.

question: A beekeeper kept some 180,000 bees in hives on a stone ledge of Notre-Dame, about 30 metres below the roof that burned in 2019. Once the smoke cleared, the keeper announced news about the bees. What was it?
answer: They were still alive.
choices: They were still alive.
They had flown to safety.
They had made extra honey.
They had moved to a new hive.
context: Because the hives sat about 30 meters below the burning roof, the colonies survived; the keeper announced, 'Our Lady's bees are still alive.' Source: cbsnews.com '180,000 bees were living on top of Notre Dame'; smithsonianmag.com 'Honey bees on Notre Dame's roof survived fire'.

question: Firefighters fought the blaze on Notre-Dame's roof that April night in 2019, and the spire fell through the vault. High in the walls below hung the cathedral's three giant rose windows, famous wheels of 13th-century glass. What had become of all three when the smoke cleared?
answer: All three survived intact.
choices: All three survived intact.
Two shattered, one held.
All three were badly cracked.
Their colors melted in the heat.
context: All three great rose windows came through the fire undamaged, sparing Notre-Dame's most famous artworks even as the roof collapsed below them. Source: catholicnewsagency.com 'Famous rose windows survive massive Notre Dame fire'; newsweek.com 'Notre Dame rose windows fire'.

question: The masons who raised Notre-Dame de Paris gave up the round Roman arch, which shoves hard against the walls that hold it, and changed the shape of their arches to a point. That one change redirected the weight. Where does a pointed arch send most of its load?
answer: Straight down its supports.
choices: Straight down its supports.
Outward against the walls.
Sideways along the roofline.
Up toward the arch's peak.
context: A pointed arch funnels weight steeply downward instead of pushing sideways, cutting the outward thrust; it can carry roughly three times the load of a round arch, letting builders raise far taller, thinner walls. Source: architecturecourses.org 'The pointed arch'; aramcoworld.com 'The point of the arch'.

question: The people of Chartres rebuilt their cathedral after the fire of 1194, and in the new floor they set a labyrinth whose one winding path runs for about 261 metres. Pilgrims who could never make a long, dangerous pilgrimage made it in miniature here. How did they travel the path?
answer: They shuffled to the center on their knees.
choices: They shuffled to the center on their knees.
They carried a lit candle around it.
They recited a psalm at each turn.
They walked it backward in silence.
context: The labyrinth is nearly 13 meters across with a path 261.5 meters long; pilgrims walked or shuffled on their knees to its center as a symbolic pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Source: worldhistory.org 'Chartres Cathedral'; labyrinthos.net 'Chartres FAQs'.

question: Louis IX of France built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris in the 1240s, a jewel-box chapel to house a holy relic. In its upper chapel he pushed the Gothic style to its limit. What are that chapel's walls almost entirely made of?
answer: Stained glass.
choices: Stained glass.
Carved oak.
Polished marble.
Gold leaf.
context: The upper chapel is almost solid glass: 15 windows about 15 meters tall holding 1,113 stained-glass panels, the flying-buttress idea taken to its extreme. Source: sainte-chapelle.fr 'A unique set of stained-glass windows'; sainte-chapelle.fr 'History of the Sainte-Chapelle'.

question: A medieval glassmaker gave a window of Chartres Cathedral its deep cobalt blue, a colour that has weathered better than the reds and greens beside it for some 800 years. A romantic story says its recipe was a secret, lost forever, that no modern glassmaker could copy. What do historians say about that lost secret?
answer: It is a myth; the recipes survive.
choices: It is a myth; the recipes survive.
It is true; the formula died out.
It is true, but only for the cobalt.
It is unknown; no records were kept.
context: The blue was made from sodium-based cobalt oxide, which proved unusually durable, but the tale of a lost, irreproducible secret is a romantic myth: medieval glass recipes actually survive. Told as legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Stained glass windows of Chartres Cathedral'; worldhistory.org 'The stained glass windows of Chartres Cathedral'.

question: The builders of Beauvais, in France, raised choir vaults about 48 metres tall, the highest anywhere, in the Gothic race to lift cathedrals ever higher. But they had reached too far. What became of their record-setting cathedral in the end?
answer: Its choir collapsed and it was never finished.
choices: Its choir collapsed and it was never finished.
Its bishop ran out of money to roof it.
Its design was copied all across Europe.
Its tower still stands as France's tallest.
context: Beauvais raised the tallest choir vaults in the world, but the choir collapsed in 1284 and its 153-meter tower fell in 1573; the cathedral was never completed. Source: mdpi.com (Heritage journal, Beauvais study); frenchmoments.eu 'Beauvais Cathedral'.

question: A mason on a scaffold high on a great cathedral, one like Notre-Dame in Paris or Cologne Cathedral, set a true gargoyle jutting far out from the roofline, a grotesque stone creature that seemed carved only to frighten. Yet such a gargoyle does a very practical job for the building. What does it do?
answer: Spouts rainwater out through its mouth
choices: Spouts rainwater out through its mouth
Holds the heavy roof up on its back
Frightens evil spirits from the church
Marks a buried saint down below it
context: A real gargoyle is a waterspout: rain runs through a trough in its back and pours out its open mouth, throwing the water clear of the walls. The name comes from the Old French 'gargouille', meaning throat or gullet - the same root as the word 'gurgle.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargoyle

question: Charles the Bald, a king and a grandson of Charlemagne, gave Chartres Cathedral its holiest treasure in 876, the Sancta Camisia. Pilgrims came hundreds of miles to see it, believing that Mary had worn it on the night she gave birth to Jesus. What kind of object was it?
answer: A veil of silk
choices: A veil of silk
A crown of gold
A robe of wool
A cloak of fur
context: King Charles the Bald, grandson of Charlemagne, gave the silk veil to Chartres in 876. It turned the town into one of medieval Europe's greatest pilgrimage destinations. During the French Revolution the veil was cut into pieces; the largest fragment is still displayed in a side chapel today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres_Cathedral

question: The craft guilds of Chartres, its shoemakers, tanners, butchers and money-changers, each paid for windows in the cathedral. What did the guilds have pictured in the lowest panels of those windows?
answer: Themselves at work in their trades
choices: Themselves at work in their trades
The kings who once ruled France
Angels blowing golden trumpets
The walls of the Holy City
context: In the lower 'donor panels' you can still find the shoemakers, the tanners, the butchers, and the money-changers shown plying their trades - the ordinary craftsmen who footed the bill, proudly pictured in the windows they paid for. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass_windows_of_Chartres_Cathedral

question: Napoleon Bonaparte came to Notre-Dame de Paris in December 1804 to be made Emperor of the French, and Pope Pius VII had travelled from Rome to crown him. At the high point of the ceremony, Napoleon did something startling with the crown. What did he do?
answer: Took the crown and crowned himself
choices: Took the crown and crowned himself
Knelt low and let the Pope crown him
Refused the crown and walked away
Passed the crown to his young son
context: By taking the crown from the Pope's hands and placing it on his own head, Napoleon signaled that his power came from himself and the people, not the Church. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre-Dame_de_Paris

question: Jean Texier, an architect, raised a lacy north spire, a burst of carved stone, at Chartres Cathedral beside a plain, square, heavy spire that had come through the great fire of 1194. The two spires of the west front still do not match. How far apart in time were they built?
answer: More than three centuries apart
choices: More than three centuries apart
Within the very same single year
Only about a decade apart
Roughly one generation apart
context: The plain south spire (about 105 m) was finished around 1160 in the older Romanesque style. The lacy north spire (about 113 m) was built in flamboyant Gothic by architect Jean Texier between 1507 and 1513 - over 340 years later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres_Cathedral

question: Priests at Chartres sheltered with their cathedral's holiest relic behind iron trapdoors in the crypt when fire swept through the church in June 1194. Most of the old cathedral burned, but the relic came out unharmed. How did the townspeople read its survival?
answer: A sign the Virgin wanted a grander church
choices: A sign the Virgin wanted a grander church
A punishment for the whole town's sins
Proof that the relic had been a forgery
A warning to abandon the ruined site
context: Belief that the Virgin herself willed a greater cathedral fueled an astonishing burst of rebuilding. The crypt, towers, and west facade had survived the fire; the rest rose new around them. Source: https://www.christianity.com/church/church-history/timeline/901-1200/chartres-burned-but-relic-survived-11629810.html

question: Builders at Chartres set an eleven-ring stone labyrinth into the cathedral floor around 1200, one winding path about 261 metres long. Believers too poor or too frail for a far, dangerous journey followed its path instead, as a stand-in for one particular pilgrimage. Which pilgrimage did it stand in for?
answer: A pilgrimage to Jerusalem
choices: A pilgrimage to Jerusalem
A pilgrimage to Rome
A pilgrimage to Compostela
A pilgrimage to the Jordan
context: Pilgrims called it the 'chemin de Jerusalem' - the road to Jerusalem - a symbolic pilgrimage to the Holy Land for those who could never make the real trip. The labyrinth is about 12.9 metres across. Source: https://www.discover-chartres.com/chartres-labyrinth.html

question: Bell-founders cast a giant bell for Notre-Dame de Paris in 1683, during the reign of Louis XIV, and it was named Emmanuel. The great bell weighed about 13 tonnes, and its clapper alone half a tonne. It rang out on only a handful of days each year. Which days called for it?
answer: The greatest feasts, like Christmas
choices: The greatest feasts, like Christmas
The funeral day of a French king
The day a new pope is chosen
The city's yearly founding day
context: Emmanuel rings for the greatest feasts and major national events - moments grave enough to deserve the deepest voice in Paris. Source: https://www.friendsofnotredamedeparis.org/cathedral/artifacts/bells/

question: A tourist high on Notre-Dame in Paris came face to face with Le Stryge, a winged stone monster with its chin propped on its hands among the cathedral's other horned, brooding chimeras. What is the truth about these creatures that most tourists never learn?
answer: Added in the 1800s, not the Middle Ages
choices: Added in the 1800s, not the Middle Ages
Carved by the cathedral's first bishop
Made of solid gold beneath the grime
Given as a gift by England's king
context: These brooding figures are 'chimeras' - pure decoration that drains no water, so not true gargoyles either. They were added during Eugene Viollet-le-Duc's 1844-1864 restoration. Le Stryge became famous through Charles Meryon's 1850s etching. Source: https://www.friendsofnotredamedeparis.org/cathedral/artifacts/grotesques/le-stryge/

question: Maurice de Sully, a bishop, began building the Gothic cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris in 1163, and it stood unfinished until about 1345, a span of roughly 182 years. What did that long span mean for the masons who laid the very first stones?
answer: Generations of them died before it was done
choices: Generations of them died before it was done
They finished early and left for other towns
One master oversaw it from start to finish
They rebuilt it twice after it collapsed
context: Building a great cathedral could swallow more than a century of labor, so the men who laid the first stones knew they would never see the towers rise. Notre-Dame's towers reach about 69 metres. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre-Dame_de_Paris

question: American gunners stood ready to shell Chartres Cathedral in August 1944, just after the town's liberation, because commanders feared German snipers were hiding in its towers. Colonel Welborn Barton Griffith Jr. stepped in to stop it. What did he do to save the cathedral?
answer: Climbed the towers himself, found them empty, and stopped the order
choices: Climbed the towers himself, found them empty, and stopped the order
Phoned the German commander and arranged a quiet local truce
Posted his own men to surround and guard the towers all night
Towed the heavy artillery guns far away under cover of darkness
context: Griffith and his driver climbed into the towers, found them empty of snipers, and had the shelling called off - saving the 800-year-old cathedral. Hours later, on 16 August 1944, Griffith was killed directing troops in the nearby town of Leves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welborn_Griffith

question: The masons of Notre-Dame in Paris leaned stone arms against its walls, each reaching from high on the wall across open air to a heavy pier standing apart. Those flying buttresses were the trick that let the walls turn into walls of glass. What does each stone arm do?
answer: Carries the roof's outward push to a pier, freeing the wall
choices: Carries the roof's outward push to a pier, freeing the wall
Adds heavy weight to the wall so it cannot sway in the wind
Funnels rainwater down from the high roof to the street
Hides iron chains that secretly tie the building together
context: The arched arm catches the roof's outward thrust high up and channels it across open air into a massive pier, which sends the force straight down into the ground. Freed from holding itself up, the wall can become a thin curtain pierced by enormous windows. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_buttress

question: Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, rebuilt his abbey church just north of Paris and dedicated it in 1144, and historians call it the birthplace of the Gothic style. He opened its walls with pointed arches and ribbed vaults, and he called the glow of the art that filled them lux nova, the new light. What was that art?
answer: Stained glass
choices: Stained glass
Mosaic tiles
Painted plaster
Frescoes
context: Abbot Suger called the glowing result 'lux nova' - new light. By combining the pointed arch, ribbed vault, and radiating chapels lit by large stained-glass windows, Saint-Denis set the template every later Gothic cathedral would follow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_of_Saint-Denis

question: Louis IX of France bought a famous relic from the broke emperor of Constantinople and then raised the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris as its home, a dazzling jewel-box chapel consecrated in 1248 after under seven years of work. Set against what he paid for the relic, what did the whole chapel cost him?
answer: Less than the relic itself had cost
choices: Less than the relic itself had cost
Roughly ten times the relic's price
About the same as one stained window
Nothing, since monks built it free
context: Louis paid more for the Crown of Thorns than the entire jewel-box chapel cost to build. Its upper chapel is almost all glass - 15 soaring windows holding 1,113 stained-glass scenes that wrap a visitor in colored light. Source: https://www.sainte-chapelle.fr/en/discover/history-of-the-sainte-chapelle

question: Francisco Goya, in his painting The Third of May 1808, set a poor labourer in a glowing white shirt on his knees before a French firing squad, arms flung wide like Christ on the cross. On the man's outstretched right hand, Goya added one small detail that drives the likeness home. What did he paint there?
answer: A dark mark like the nail-wound of the crucifixion
choices: A dark mark like the nail-wound of the crucifixion
A wedding ring he is twisting in fear
A scrap of bread he refused to drop
A rosary wound tightly around his fingers
context: The mark echoes the stigmata, the nail-wound of Christ's hand. Goya turned a Napoleonic firing-squad killing into a timeless image of sacrifice — the man's yellow-and-white clothing even matches the papal colors. Yet unlike a saint in old religious art, his face shows raw terror, not holy calm. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Third_of_May_1808 ; artincontext.org/the-third-of-may-1808-francisco-goya/

question: Francisco Goya, deaf, bitter and shut away from the world, bought a house outside Madrid already nicknamed the Quinta del Sordo, the Villa of the Deaf Man. Between 1820 and 1823 he made fourteen nightmare works there that he never meant anyone to see, Saturn Devouring His Son among them. What did he paint these Black Paintings onto?
answer: The bare plaster walls of his own house
choices: The bare plaster walls of his own house
Wooden panels he hid in his cellar
Tattered sheets stretched over his windows
Small canvases he locked away in a chest
context: Goya painted the Black Paintings straight onto his interior plaster walls between 1820 and 1823, for no eyes but his own. Decades after his death they were carefully peeled off the walls and transferred to canvas; they now hang in the Prado in Madrid. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Paintings

question: Emperor Yang of Sui toured his finished Grand Canal in 609 aboard a fleet of giant dragon-boats. By the old accounts, they moved in one solid row down the water. How far did that line of boats stretch from end to end?
answer: About 65 miles long
choices: About 65 miles long
About 7 miles long
About 20 miles long
About 40 miles long
context: The flotilla reportedly stretched about 105 km (65 miles) as it traveled from the north down to the southern capital — a column of boats longer than many countries are wide. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Canal_(China)

question: Emperor Yang of the Sui forced roughly five million people, including women and children, to dig the Grand Canal, and ancient records put the dead from overwork and disease at perhaps two million. That crushing cost, added to failed wars in Korea, sparked rebellions. What became of the Sui dynasty?
answer: Rebellions toppled it within one generation
choices: Rebellions toppled it within one generation
It ruled on peacefully for three more centuries
It abandoned the canal and moved the capital
It split the empire into rival northern and southern courts
context: The forced labor of the canal and other projects, piled onto failed wars against Goguryeo, ignited revolts that overthrew the Sui within a single generation of the canal's completion — the dynasty was destroyed by the very lifeline it built. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Canal_(China)

question: Irish farmers lifted their potatoes in 1845 and found them shrunken and rotting in their hands. Healthy green plants had turned to dark, oozing splotches almost overnight, and over the next years the blight would starve the poor who lived on potatoes. What caused the rot?
answer: A water mold that arrived from North America
choices: A water mold that arrived from North America
A swarm of beetles blown over from France
A frost that froze the fields three winters running
A fungus carried in by infected English seed
context: The blight was Phytophthora infestans, a water mold (not a true fungus) that crossed the Atlantic from North America in 1845. It blackened the leaves and rotted the tubers into slime. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytophthora_infestans ; history.com/articles/irish-potato-famine

question: Families across the Irish countryside watched the potato blight rot their main food year after year, from 1845 to 1852. Roughly a million Irish men, women and children died, of starvation itself and of diseases such as typhus that swept through the weakened villages. What happened to at least another million Irish people in those same years?
answer: They fled their homeland as refugees
choices: They fled their homeland as refugees
They were drafted into the British army
They moved into the cities to find factory work
They were resettled by the government on new farms
context: About one million died and at least another million emigrated. Ireland's population fell from 8,175,124 in the 1841 census to 6,552,385 by 1851 — a drop of over 1.5 million in a decade. Sources: history.com/articles/irish-potato-famine ; britannica.com/event/Great-Famine-Irish-history

question: Irish families could not bury their dead as fast as the dead piled up in 1847, the year hunger swept every county at once. It was the worst year of the Great Famine, and the Irish gave it a grim nickname that has stuck ever since. What did they call 1847?
answer: Black '47
choices: Black '47
The Hungry Forty-Seven
The Lost Harvest
The Great Mortality
context: 1847 was the worst year of the famine, remembered as 'Black '47.' Sources: smithsonianmag.com (Choctaw Nation's gift to the Irish, 2018)

question: Robert Peel, Britain's prime minister, secretly bought 100,000 pounds' worth of American maize in the winter of 1845-46 to sell cheaply to the starving Irish. The hard, gritty yellow grain was difficult to cook and digest, and the hungry gave it a bitter nickname. What did they call it?
answer: Peel's brimstone
choices: Peel's brimstone
Peel's penance
The yellow famine
Treasury gruel
context: The Irish nicknamed the imported Indian corn 'Peel's brimstone.' Peel also repealed the Corn Laws in 1846. Sources: historyhome.co.uk/peel/ireland/famine.htm ; rte.ie (Temporary Relief Commission)

question: Nicholas Cummins, a magistrate of Cork, carried bread into the village of Skibbereen in December 1846. Inside one hut he found six people on filthy straw, alive only by their soft moaning. His letter to the Duke of Wellington ran in The Times. What did he say happened the moment he stepped outside?
answer: He was surrounded by at least 200 such phantoms
choices: He was surrounded by at least 200 such phantoms
He found the village priest digging graves alone
He counted forty fresh coffins stacked in the lane
He watched a cart carry off the dead by lamplight
context: Cummins found 'six famished and ghastly skeletons' — four children, a woman, and what had once been a man — and wrote, 'In a few minutes I was surrounded by at least 200 such phantoms.' His letter to the Duke of Wellington was published in The Times. Sources: irishcentral.com (Great Famine workhouse) ; sites.evergreen.edu/ireland1617/texts/history/famine

question: Charles Trevelyan, who ran Britain's famine relief from the Treasury, shut down Robert Peel's food programs. He put the blame for the suffering on the Irish and their own character, and he received a knighthood for his relief work in 1848. How did Trevelyan describe the famine?
answer: As 'a direct stroke of an all-wise and all-merciful Providence'
choices: As 'a direct stroke of an all-wise and all-merciful Providence'
As 'a misfortune beyond any government's power to mend'
As 'the gravest trial ever laid upon the Crown'
As 'a debt the empire must labour to repay'
context: Trevelyan, Assistant Secretary to the Treasury (1840-1859), called the famine 'a direct stroke of an all-wise and all-merciful Providence' and 'the sharp but effectual remedy by which the cure is likely to be effected,' blaming 'the selfish, perverse, and turbulent character' of the Irish. He was knighted (KCB) on 27 April 1848 for his famine-relief services. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Charles_Trevelyan,_1st_Baronet ; legallegacy.wordpress.com

question: British troops often guarded the convoys of Irish wheat, oats, butter and nearly ten thousand calves bound for England in 1847, while Irish families starved. Historians such as Austin Bourke and Christine Kinealy still disagree about what that export record proves. What is the heart of their dispute?
answer: Whether scarcity alone, or also policy and profit, drove the death toll
choices: Whether scarcity alone, or also policy and profit, drove the death toll
Whether the exports were larger than Britain officially admitted
Whether the troops were guarding food or hunting rebels
Whether the calves were sold abroad or kept for breeding
context: Ireland exported roughly 39,000 tonnes of wheat, 98,000 tonnes of oats, about a million gallons of butter, and 9,992 calves to England in 1847. Austin Bourke argued grain imports exceeded exports by 1847; Christine Kinealy stresses the deadly 'starvation gap' of winter 1846-47 before imports arrived, and that merchant profit-seeking and laissez-faire ideology — not absolute scarcity alone — shaped the catastrophe. Sources: historyireland.com/food-exports-from-ireland-1846-47 ; usbornefamilytree.com/irishfoodexports.htm

question: An emigrant vessel packed with famine refugees left Ireland for Quebec in 1847, and its steerage passengers were let up on deck barely an hour a day. So many of the dead went over the side that sharks were said to trail such vessels, and over a tenth of the Irish bound for Quebec that year perished on the voyage or in quarantine. What were these vessels called?
answer: Coffin ships
choices: Coffin ships
Fever barques
Hunger packets
The grave fleet
context: At the Grosse Île quarantine station below Quebec, of 98,749 Irish who sailed for Quebec in 1847, 10,820 died at sea or in quarantine — about 11%, a rate on par with slave ships. Sources: amusingplanet.com/2017/11/the-coffin-ships ; rte.ie (Revisiting the coffin ships, 2023)

question: The people of one Native American nation in Oklahoma raised $170 for Ireland's starving poor in March 1847, half a world away. Only about fourteen years earlier they had been driven west on their own Trail of Tears. Which nation sent the gift, still honored between the two peoples today?
answer: The Choctaw Nation
choices: The Choctaw Nation
The Cherokee Nation
The Seminole Nation
The Chickasaw Nation
context: The Choctaw Nation raised $170 (worth several thousand dollars today) for Irish famine relief in 1847. The Irish repaid the kindness with donations to the Choctaw during the 2020 pandemic. Sources: choctawnation.com/about/history/irish-connection ; smithsonianmag.com (2018)

question: Builders in the 1500s carved a tall Christian nave right through the middle of the old prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, which had become a cathedral after Christian armies took the city. Charles V had approved the plan. When the emperor saw the finished work, what did he reportedly say?
answer: "You have built here what others might have built anywhere, but you have destroyed something unique in the world."
choices: "You have built here what others might have built anywhere, but you have destroyed something unique in the world."
"You have raised here the grandest house of worship that my whole empire has ever seen."
"You have repaired here a ruin that lay neglected, and given the city back its proud heart."
"You have matched here the great cathedrals of the north, stone for stone and arch for arch."
context: The emperor had approved the cathedral himself, then regretted it on seeing the result. The remark is recorded as testimony (legend), not a verbatim transcript. The mosque's prayer hall had been one of a kind; the inserted cathedral nave could have been built in any city. Source: https://www.emperorcharlesv.com/in-charles-footsteps/spain/cordoba/

question: The builders of Córdoba's Great Mosque salvaged columns from Roman and Visigothic ruins for the prayer hall, but the old columns were too short to hold a roof at the soaring height they wanted. Their fix turned the flaw into the hall's most famous sight, a striped red-and-white canopy that seems to march on forever. What did they do to gain the height?
answer: They stacked a second tier of arches on top of the first, doubling them up to reach the roof.
choices: They stacked a second tier of arches on top of the first, doubling them up to reach the roof.
They sank the floor of the hall well below ground level so the short columns would stand taller.
They carved fresh capitals from a single huge block and fitted them between every old column.
They bound the short columns together in clustered bundles to make each one count as taller.
context: At the Great Mosque of Cordoba (begun 785 under Abd al-Rahman I), the reused short columns were extended with a double-tier arcade: a second row of arches stacked atop the first, in alternating red brick and white stone (voussoirs), creating the famous striped two-level arches. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque-Cathedral_of_Cordoba.

question: Forebears of the Shona raised a great granite city in southern Africa in the Middle Ages, high on a plateau. Centuries later the modern country around its ruins took its name straight from them, borrowing a phrase in the Shona language: 'dzimba dza mabwe.' What does that phrase mean?
answer: Houses of stone
choices: Houses of stone
City of gold
Walls of the king
Land of the eagle
context: 'Dzimba dza mabwe' means 'houses of stone' (or 'large houses of stone'). When the modern nation became independent it named itself after the ancient stone city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; The Met (metmuseum.org/essays/great-zimbabwe).

question: Shona masons raised granite walls up to 11 meters high at Great Zimbabwe between roughly 1100 and 1450, as tall as a modern three-story building. What has stunned visitors for centuries is the way those huge stones stay in place. What holds the walls up?
answer: Their own weight, with no mortar at all
choices: Their own weight, with no mortar at all
Iron clamps driven between the blocks
Lime-and-sand mortar in every joint
Wooden pegs hidden inside the wall
context: The walls were built with no mortar at all. Each granite block was cut and stacked so precisely that the wall holds together by its own weight. This dry-stone fitting is the city's signature achievement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; PanAfroCore (panafrocore.com).

question: Craftsmen at Great Zimbabwe shaped eight tall figures out of soapstone and set each one on top of a stone column. One of them became the emblem of modern Zimbabwe, and it appears on the country's flag, coins and coat of arms. What does the figure show?
answer: A bird
choices: A bird
A lion
A crocodile
A spear and shield
context: The soapstone Zimbabwe Bird is the country's emblem, appearing on the flag, coat of arms, banknotes, coins, and the logos of over 100 organizations. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Bird.

question: Builders of the Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe, ancestors of the Shona, ran its curving granite wall about 250 meters around and raised it up to 11 meters high some 700 years ago. Among all the ancient stone buildings of Africa south of the Sahara, where does it rank in size?
answer: The largest of them all
choices: The largest of them all
About the tenth-largest
Roughly average-sized
One of the smallest known
context: The Great Enclosure is the largest ancient stone structure in sub-Saharan Africa. Its walls run about 250 meters (820 feet) around and rise up to 11 meters (36 feet). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: Modern archaeologists examined the Conical Tower inside the Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe, a rounded tower of fitted granite blocks about 9 meters tall and 5.5 meters across at its base. They looked closely at what lay within its walls. What did they find?
answer: It is completely solid -- no door, no room inside
choices: It is completely solid -- no door, no room inside
A spiral staircase climbing to the top
A burial chamber holding a king's bones
A hidden well shaft going deep underground
context: The Conical Tower has no entrance and no chamber: it is a solid mass of stone. What it was for is still unknown. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: Miners on Great Zimbabwe's high plateau, far inland and hundreds of kilometers from the sea, dug out one prized metal, and it was hauled down long trade routes to Swahili merchants on the Indian Ocean coast. That metal and huge herds of cattle made the royal court rich. Which metal was it?
answer: Gold
choices: Gold
Copper
Silver
Tin
context: Gold mined on the plateau was carried to the coastal port of Sofala, then north to the Swahili city of Kilwa, and out into the Indian Ocean. Cattle herds were the court's other great source of wealth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/Kilwa).

question: A family at Great Zimbabwe made its home behind the granite walls of a city laid out in three parts: the Hill Complex on a rocky outcrop, the great walled compound below it and the Valley Complex. Nobody lived in the walls themselves. What was the family's home built of?
answer: Packed earth and clay
choices: Packed earth and clay
Stacked granite blocks
Timber and thatch
Sun-dried mud brick
context: Inside the stone walls, people lived in 'daga' houses made of packed earth and clay. The three main parts are the Hill Complex (oldest), the Great Enclosure, and the Valley Complex. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: Masons quarrying stone for Great Zimbabwe had to split solid granite into brick-shaped slabs, with no iron tools to spare. They knew that granite tends to peel apart in flat layers, and they turned that to their advantage. What did they do to the rock?
answer: Heated it with fire until it cracked apart
choices: Heated it with fire until it cracked apart
Soaked it in vinegar to dissolve it
Froze water in its cracks overnight
Pounded it for days with wooden mallets
context: Workers quarried granite from local outcrops, then heated the rock with fire and cracked it into slabs -- using granite's natural tendency to peel in layers (called exfoliation) -- then shaped and selected each piece to fit. Source: MemoryCherish (memorycherish.com); Smarthistory.

question: Carvers at Great Zimbabwe gave their tall soapstone figures human lips in place of a hooked beak and five toes where talons should be, and they set each one high on a stone column. What does each figure most likely represent?
answer: A messenger eagle of God and the ancestors
choices: A messenger eagle of God and the ancestors
A guardian spirit set to watch over the dead king
A rain-god summoned to bring the harvest
A trophy from a great royal hunt by the king
context: The birds mix human and eagle features and likely depict the bateleur eagle, called 'chapungu' in Shona, believed to be a messenger from Mwari (God) and the ancestors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Bird.

question: Archaeologists digging in the ruins of Great Zimbabwe, far inland in southern Africa, turned up goods carried from thousands of miles away. Their finds proved that this inland city was part of long-distance trade. What did they pull from the ground?
answer: Chinese porcelain and a coin minted by a sultan of Kilwa
choices: Chinese porcelain and a coin minted by a sultan of Kilwa
Roman silver coins stamped with an emperor
Egyptian hieroglyphic tablets and gold masks
Viking silver arm-rings and amber beads
context: Excavations turned up Chinese porcelain (Longquan green-glazed and blue-and-white ware), Persian glass, beads, and a copper coin minted by a sultan of Kilwa -- proof the inland city was plugged into Indian Ocean trade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: Masons at Great Zimbabwe crowned the outer wall of the Great Enclosure with a long band of dark stone, still the city's most famous decoration. The stones run in one repeating pattern all along the crest. What pattern is it?
answer: A double-chevron zigzag, often read as a snake
choices: A double-chevron zigzag, often read as a snake
A row of carved human faces
A line of interlocking circles
A spiral coiling around the wall
context: The crest of the outer wall is decorated with a long double-chevron (zigzag) band of dark stone -- the city's most famous pattern, often read as a snake or as a symbol of fertility and continuity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; thedarkatlas.com.

question: Willi Posselt, a European hunter, came to the ruins of Great Zimbabwe in 1889 and wanted one of its carved soapstone figures for himself. He hacked it free from the top of its stone column and then dealt with the local chief. How did he get it from the chief?
answer: He paid with blankets and a few small goods
choices: He paid with blankets and a few small goods
He traded a rifle and ammunition for it
He won it in a wrestling contest
He bought it for a chest of gold coins
context: Posselt cut the soapstone bird from its column and paid a local chief in blankets and a few goods. The bird ended up at Cecil Rhodes's Cape Town estate, Groote Schuur; a piece of its column was sold to a Berlin museum in 1907. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Bird.

question: Builders at Great Zimbabwe raised the Conical Tower, some 9 meters of fitted granite, inside the Great Enclosure, and its purpose is still debated. Many scholars read the whole tower as a giant stone copy of an everyday Shona object. What object is it thought to copy?
answer: A grain bin (granary)
choices: A grain bin (granary)
A war drum
A king's crown
A cooking pot
context: Legend and scholarly reading: the tower is thought to be a giant stone copy of a Shona grain bin -- a symbol that the ruler, like a generous chief filling his granary, was the provider for his people. Others read it as a fertility symbol; its true purpose is debated. Source: Timbuktu Travel (timbuktutravel.com); AP Art History notes.

question: Vicente Pegado, a Portuguese captain, wrote the first European account of Great Zimbabwe in 1531. Of all he might have said about the towering granite city, he reached for one short phrase that has been quoted ever since. He called it a fortress built of stones of what?
answer: Marvelous size
choices: Marvelous size
Painted gold
Sacred fire
Royal blood
context: Pegado, the first European to write about the city, described 'a fortress built of stones of marvelous size, and there appears to be no mortar joining them.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: Karl Mauch, a German explorer, reached Great Zimbabwe in 1871 and refused to believe that Africans had built it. He cut a sliver from a fallen wooden door-beam, sniffed it, and convinced himself that it matched a familiar object in his own pocket. What did he compare the wood to?
answer: His cedar pencil
choices: His cedar pencil
His leather boot
His tobacco pipe
His brass compass
context: Mauch decided the lintel smelled and looked like his cedar pencil, declared it Lebanese cedar, and claimed Phoenicians had built the city for the Queen of Sheba as a copy of King Solomon's temple. Source: zimfieldguide.com (Karl Mauch); World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/1429).

question: Richard Nicklin Hall came to Great Zimbabwe in the days of Cecil Rhodes with orders to restore the ruins. Instead he dug out and dumped as much as two meters of buried earth, which he called the 'filth and decadence' of African occupation. What did Hall wipe out?
answer: The dated layers of soil that recorded who built it
choices: The dated layers of soil that recorded who built it
A hidden vault of the kingdom's gold
The foundations holding up the Great Enclosure walls
A library of written records kept by the kings
context: Hall removed up to two meters of archaeological deposits, erasing the dated evidence of who built Great Zimbabwe -- because he wanted to remove signs of African occupation. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/1429).

question: Gertrude Caton-Thompson, the British archaeologist, came to dig at Great Zimbabwe in 1929, after decades in which European settlers had refused to believe that Africans built it. She worked carefully beneath the walls and settled the long argument over the city's builders. What did her evidence show?
answer: Africans, ancestors of the Shona, built it in medieval times
choices: Africans, ancestors of the Shona, built it in medieval times
Phoenician sailors built it for the Queen of Sheba
Arab traders built it as a coastal trading fort
Portuguese settlers built it in the 1500s
context: Caton-Thompson wrote that the evidence produced 'not one single item that is not in accordance with the claim of Bantu origin and medieval date.' Great Zimbabwe was built by Africans, the ancestors of the Shona. Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/1429); Lady Science (ladyscience.com).

question: Paul Sinclair, an archaeologist, stated publicly that Black Africans had built Great Zimbabwe at a time when Rhodesia's white-minority government, in the 1960s and 70s, was pressing archaeologists to deny it. He later said he was threatened for telling the truth. What did the government threaten to do to him?
answer: Make him lose his job
choices: Make him lose his job
Put him in prison
Deport him from the country
Take away his excavation findings
context: Sinclair said he was threatened with losing his job for stating publicly that Black Africans built Great Zimbabwe. The government also censored radiocarbon dates and printed tourist guidebooks showing Africans bowing to imaginary white 'builders.' Source: World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/1429); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe.

question: Greek traders borrowed their letters from the Phoenicians, who called each letter by the name of something ordinary a person could point at. The first two, aleph and bet, became alpha and beta in Greek mouths, and the two names ran together into one word. Taken literally, what does the word 'alphabet' mean?
answer: Ox-house
choices: Ox-house
Sun-river
Hand-mouth
Bird-stone
context: Greek alpha and beta came from Phoenician aleph ('ox') and bet ('house'). The Phoenicians named their letters after common objects, so the very word 'alphabet' literally reads as 'ox-house.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleph; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bet_(letter); metmuseum.org Alphabet Origins.

question: The Greeks took over a writing system from the Phoenicians in the early 700s BC. It had served the Phoenicians well for centuries, but Greek set down in those letters would have been hopelessly hard to read. To make their own language clear on the page, the Greeks did one thing no writers before them had ever done. What was that breakthrough?
answer: They wrote down the vowels
choices: They wrote down the vowels
They wrote on papyrus scrolls
They carved letters into stone
They read the lines aloud
context: The Phoenician script was an 'abjad' (consonants only). By repurposing spare Phoenician consonants their tongue didn't need (aleph became alpha, He became epsilon, and so on), the Greeks gave every sound on the page a letter the first true alphabet. That line ran Phoenicians to Greeks to Etruscans to Romans, whose Latin letters we still write. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Greek_alphabet; worldhistory.org/Greek_Alphabet.

question: The Roman writer Vitruvius passed down a legend about the Greek sculptor Callimachus, who was walking past the grave of a young girl of Corinth when he saw there the shape for a new column capital, wrapped in curling leaves. What did Callimachus see growing on the grave?
answer: A spray of acanthus leaves curling out from under a roof tile set atop a basket
choices: A spray of acanthus leaves curling out from under a roof tile set atop a basket
A laurel wreath that a mourner had hung across the headstone that morning
A grapevine that had twisted itself around the marble grave marker
A bed of poppies that had bloomed in a ring around the burial mound
context: The girl's nurse had set a votive basket of the child's toys on the grave and laid a square roof tile on top as a lid. An acanthus plant grew up through the basket, and the tile forced its leaves to curl outward -- the exact shape Callimachus then carved into the Corinthian capital. Told as legend by Vitruvius. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinthian_order (citing Vitruvius).

question: The builders of the Erechtheion, a temple on the Acropolis of Athens, left out the usual stone columns on its south porch. Instead the heavy roof-beam rests directly on the heads of a row of carved figures. What are these six load-bearing figures?
answer: Six carved stone women standing as living pillars
choices: Six carved stone women standing as living pillars
Six carved lions seated on their haunches
Six carved warriors holding raised shields
Six carved horses rearing on their hind legs
context: They are called the Caryatids -- six stone women carrying the entablature on their heads, draped in carved robes. They are the best-known case of figures used in place of columns. Source: greektraveltellers.com/blog/caryatids and acropolis.athenstickets.org/erechtheion.

question: Byzantine sailors guarding Constantinople sprayed a stream of liquid flame at enemy fleets from siphons mounted at the bows of their warships. When the enemy crews tried to douse it, the fire kept burning right on top of the water until their wooden ships were ash. By what name does history know this weapon?
answer: Greek fire
choices: Greek fire
Persian oil
Roman pitch
Spartan tar
context: Greek fire was a Byzantine liquid weapon that kept burning even on water, so it could not be splashed out, and it tore through enemy wooden fleets at sea. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Greek_Fire/

question: Constantine VII, the emperor, warned his son and heir that an angel had revealed the recipe for the empire's secret liquid fire to Constantine the Great, as a gift never to be handed to foreigners. What became of the formula?
answer: It was lost and is still not fully known today
choices: It was lost and is still not fully known today
It was carved into the walls of Constantinople
It was sold to the Arab fleets after the siege
It was published in the emperor's own war manual
context: Constantine VII told his heir the weapon had been 'shown and revealed by an angel' to Constantine the Great and must never be given to foreigners (a legendary claim of divine origin). The secret was kept so well that the formula was eventually lost completely and is still not fully known. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_fire

question: In the Greek myths, Zeus and his family of gods feasted and quarrelled in a palace above the clouds. The Greeks set it on a true peak of northern Greece, the highest in the country and still climbed today. Which mountain was it?
answer: Mount Olympus
choices: Mount Olympus
Mount Parnassus
Mount Ida
Mount Pelion
context: Mount Olympus sits on the border of Thessaly and Macedonia; its highest peak, Mytikas ('the nose'), rises to 2,917 m (9,573 ft), the tallest in Greece, and the massif has 52 peaks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Olympus

question: Zeus, king of the gods in the Greek myths, would not stand for any mortal who defied him. Whenever he grew angry, he hurled his own signature weapon down from the sky at the offender. What was the weapon Zeus threw?
answer: a thunderbolt
choices: a thunderbolt
a warhammer
a longbow
a battleaxe
context: Zeus's symbols were the thunderbolt (his weapon), the eagle (his royal bird), the bull, and the oak tree. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeus

question: Hephaestus, the smith-god, swung his heavy axe at the skull of Zeus, the king of the gods, when Zeus begged him for relief from a terrible, splitting headache. Out of the cracked skull leapt the goddess Athena. What was startling about the way Athena was born?
answer: Fully grown, in armor, and shouting a war-cry
choices: Fully grown, in armor, and shouting a war-cry
As a baby who aged a year every day
As an owl that flew to the Acropolis
As a column of fire that spoke aloud
context: Zeus had earlier swallowed Athena's pregnant mother, the Titaness Metis, because of a prophecy that her child would surpass him, which is why Athena was born straight from his head. Legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/athena/

question: Athena and Poseidon each wanted to be the namesake of a new city, and by the myth the two gods held a contest before its king, Cecrops. Poseidon struck the Acropolis rock with his trident, and a spring of salt water gushed out. Athena offered another gift, which the people chose. What was her gift?
answer: the first olive tree
choices: the first olive tree
the first grapevine
the first fig tree
the first rose bush
context: The olive became the wealth of Athens, its oil prized across the ancient world. Legend. Source: https://www.greekmyths-greekmythology.com/athena-vs-poseidon-contest-name/

question: Poseidon, the sea-god, set the ground trembling in Greek myth, and the Greeks named him the 'Earth-Shaker.' The sea-god was also said to have created one particular animal. He shaped the very first one of its kind from the white foaming crests of the waves. Which animal did Poseidon make?
answer: the horse
choices: the horse
the dolphin
the bull
the eagle
context: Poseidon's chief epithet, Ennosigaios ('Earth-Shaker'), tied earthquakes to him; he was also god of horses. Legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poseidon

question: Athena carried a goatskin shield, the aegis, and at its center she fixed the snake-haired head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose stare turned men to stone. Athena had not killed the monster herself. A mortal hero cut off the head and gave it to her. Which hero gave Athena the Gorgon's head?
answer: Perseus
choices: Perseus
Heracles
Theseus
Achilles
context: The snake-fringed head on the aegis was called the Gorgoneion. Athena's other signature symbol was the owl, her bird of wisdom. Legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/athena/

question: The Cyclopes, three giant one-eyed smiths, owed their release from imprisonment to Zeus, and in gratitude they forged a signature weapon for each of the three ruling brothers. They armed Zeus and Poseidon first. What did they make for the third brother, Hades, who ruled the dead?
answer: a helm that turned its wearer invisible
choices: a helm that turned its wearer invisible
a sword that never missed its mark
a net that could trap any god
a shield that reflected any spell
context: The three Cyclopes were Brontes ('Thunder'), Steropes ('Lightning'), and Arges ('Bright'). Hades's gift was the Helm of Darkness, or Cap of Invisibility. Legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap_of_invisibility

question: In his forge beneath the volcanoes, Hephaestus, the limping smith-god, made golden servant-women to work beside him. He crafted wonders no other god could match, and these handmaidens were no ordinary golden statues. What could the golden handmaidens do?
answer: They could think, move, and speak on their own
choices: They could think, move, and speak on their own
They could turn lead into solid gold
They could fly the god across the sky
They could heal any wound with a touch
context: Because they could think and speak, these golden handmaidens are often called literature's first robots. Hephaestus also forged the wonder-worked shield of Achilles. Legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hephaistos/

question: Zeus, Poseidon and Hades overthrew the Titans together, and then the three brothers had to share out the whole world: the sky, the sea and the gloomy underworld. They did not let the eldest simply choose, and they did not fight over it. How did they decide which realm each would rule?
answer: They drew lots for it
choices: They drew lots for it
Zeus chose first and gave the orders
They settled it with a wrestling match
Their mother Rhea divided it up
context: Zeus drew the sky, Poseidon the sea, and Hades the underworld; in the Iliad, Poseidon says the earth and Olympus stayed common to all three. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hades

question: Cronus, the Titan king, had heard a prophecy that one of his own children would one day overthrow him. To stop it, he swallowed each of his babies whole the moment it was born. When her youngest, Zeus, was born, the mother Rhea hid the infant and handed Cronus something else to swallow in the baby's place. What did Rhea trick Cronus into swallowing instead of Zeus?
answer: A stone wrapped in baby clothes
choices: A stone wrapped in baby clothes
A goat dressed in royal robes
A clay doll painted to look real
A loaf of bread shaped like a child
context: Grown Zeus forced Cronus to vomit up his swallowed siblings and the stone; that stone was set up at Delphi as the Omphalos, the 'navel of the world.' Legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronus

question: One Greek poet, naming the twelve chief gods of Olympus, the Dodekatheon or 'Twelve Gods,' put Hestia, goddess of the home and hearth, in the twelfth place. Other poets and cities chose a different god, for no list was ever official. Who was the other claimant to that disputed twelfth seat?
answer: Dionysus, god of wine
choices: Dionysus, god of wine
Hades, god of the dead
Eros, god of love
Pan, god of the wild
context: Hades, though brother to Zeus and Poseidon, was never counted among the Twelve at all, because his realm lay far off in the underworld rather than on Olympus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_Olympians

question: Phidias sculpted a colossal seated Zeus for the temple at Olympia, plated in gold and ivory, some 12 meters tall and counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. The geographer Strabo summed up its size with a famous remark about what would happen if the statue ever moved. What did Strabo say the god would do if he stood up?
answer: He would smash through the roof of the temple
