choices: He would smash through the roof of the temple
He would crush the worshippers at his feet
He would tower higher than Mount Olympus
He would set the whole temple ablaze
context: Strabo wrote that 'if Zeus arose and stood erect he would unroof the temple.' The 12-metre (40-ft) statue held a small figure of Nike, goddess of victory, in one hand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia

question: Heracles faced the Nemean lion, a beast whose golden hide was so tough that arrows bounced off it, as the first of his twelve labors. No blade could cut its skin either. With every weapon useless, how did Heracles kill the lion?
answer: He strangled it with his bare arms
choices: He strangled it with his bare arms
He crushed it beneath a boulder
He starved it inside its own cave
He drowned it in a river
context: Because no weapon could harm the invulnerable hide, Heracles wrestled the lion and choked it to death. Apollodorus: 'putting his arm round its neck held it tight till he had choked it.' He later wore the lion's pelt as his signature armor. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.1 (Perseus Tufts).  (Legend.)

question: Ariadne, daughter of King Minos of Crete, fell in love with Theseus when he came to face the Minotaur in the Labyrinth. The maze twisted so cleverly that no one who entered had ever found the way out again. What did Ariadne give Theseus so he could escape?
answer: A ball of thread to unwind behind him
choices: A ball of thread to unwind behind him
A torch to light the dark passages
A trail of white pebbles to drop
A map scratched onto a clay tablet
context: Ariadne told Theseus to tie one end at the entrance and unwind the thread as he went, then follow it back out. Plutarch calls it a 'clue of thread' -- which is literally why the word 'clue' came to mean a hint that leads you to the answer. Source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus (classics.mit.edu).  (Legend.)

question: Young Prince Theseus watched his city, Athens, make ready to send seven youths and seven maidens to Crete as tribute, where they would be shut in the Labyrinth and eaten by the Minotaur. When the fourteen were being chosen, what did Theseus do?
answer: He volunteered to go as one of the fourteen
choices: He volunteered to go as one of the fourteen
He hid himself among the temple priests
He begged his father to stop the ships
He paid another man to take his place
context: The tribute was Athens' penalty for the death of Minos' son Androgeos. Theseus put himself among the fourteen on purpose, planning to kill the Minotaur and end the tribute forever. Source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus, and Apollodorus (ancient-greece.org).  (Legend.)

question: The Lernaean Hydra grew two new heads in place of every one that Heracles cut off, so the monster only got worse the more he struck. Heracles needed help from his nephew Iolaus to win. How did the two of them stop the heads from growing back?
answer: They burned each neck-stump with fire
choices: They burned each neck-stump with fire
They froze the necks in cold spring-water
They tied each stump shut with rope
They smeared the wounds with poison
context: As Heracles cut, Iolaus seared each stump with a flaming firebrand so no new heads could sprout. The one head that was immortal, Heracles buried under a heavy rock. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.2 (Perseus Tufts).  (Legend.)

question: Perseus went to fetch the head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose face turned anyone who looked straight at her to stone. The goddess Athena showed him how to get close enough to cut off her head without ever meeting her gaze. What was Athena's trick?
answer: He watched her reflection in his polished shield
choices: He watched her reflection in his polished shield
He fought her with his eyes shut tight
He attacked only after dark had fallen
He wore a blindfold woven by Athena
context: By striking while watching only Medusa's reflection in his bronze shield, Perseus never met her petrifying gaze. Medusa was the only one of the three Gorgon sisters who could be killed at all -- the other two were immortal. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.4.2; Wikipedia 'Medusa'.  (Legend.)

question: Daedalus built wings of feathers for himself and his son Icarus so that they could escape from Crete. Thrilled by flight, Icarus soared higher and higher toward the sun, ignoring his father's warning to keep a middle course, and his wings came apart. What did the sun's heat do to them?
answer: It melted the wax holding the feathers together
choices: It melted the wax holding the feathers together
It scorched the feathers down to bare ash
It dried the feathers until they cracked apart
It set the wooden frame of the wings alight
context: The feathers were fixed with wax; the sun's heat melted it, the feathers fell away, and Icarus dropped into the sea still crying his father's name. The water where he fell was named the Icarian Sea after him. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses Book 8 (web.sas.upenn.edu/discentes).  (Legend.)

question: Acrisius, king of Argos, heard an oracle warn that his own grandson would one day kill him, so he locked his daughter Danae away in a chamber of solid bronze. Yet the god Zeus still reached her, and she gave birth to the hero Perseus. How did Zeus get into the sealed chamber?
answer: He poured in as a shower of golden rain
choices: He poured in as a shower of golden rain
He slipped in disguised as a palace guard
He flew in through a crack as an eagle
He tunneled up through the chamber floor
context: Zeus reached Danae as a shower of golden rain pouring through the roof, and Perseus was born despite every precaution -- the prophecy could not be stopped. Source: Apollodorus, Library, and Theoi.com 'Danae'.  (Legend.)

question: Eurystheus, the king Heracles was bound to serve, ordered him to clean the stables of King Augeas in a single day, filthy pens that housed more than a thousand cattle and had gone uncleaned for years. No amount of shovelling could have done it in time. How did Heracles clean the stables in one day?
answer: He rerouted two rivers to flood through them
choices: He rerouted two rivers to flood through them
He hauled the dung out on a hundred carts
He set the soiled straw ablaze and burned it
He summoned a storm to rain the filth away
context: Heracles diverted the courses of the rivers Alpheus and Peneus and turned them through the yard, washing it clean in a day. Eurystheus refused to count this labor because the rivers had done the work. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.5 (Perseus Tufts).  (Legend.)

question: The three Graeae, sisters so ancient that they had only one eye and one tooth among them and passed them from hand to hand, refused to give Perseus the directions he needed on his way to the Gorgon Medusa. How did Perseus force them to reveal the way?
answer: He stole their single shared eye and held it hostage
choices: He stole their single shared eye and held it hostage
He threatened to smash their one shared tooth
He chained the three sisters to a great rock
He offered them a chest of gold for the directions
context: Perseus snatched the eye in the moment it was being passed between them and refused to return it until they revealed where to find the gear he needed -- the winged sandals, the cap of invisibility, and the kibisis bag. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.4.2; Theoi.com 'Graeae'.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus promised his father, King Aegeus, a signal before he sailed to fight the Minotaur: his ship would come home under a white sail if he had lived and a black one if he had died. Theseus won, but in his joy he forgot the promise and left the black sail flying. What did the heartbroken Aegeus do when he saw it?
answer: He threw himself off the cliff into the sea
choices: He threw himself off the cliff into the sea
He set the returning ship on fire
He sailed out alone to search for the body
He took his own life by the palace altar
context: Seeing the black sail, Aegeus believed his son was dead and hurled himself from the rocks into the water -- which is why that sea has been called the Aegean ever since. Source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus (classics.mit.edu).  (Legend.)

question: Only the Titan Atlas could pick the golden apples that Heracles needed, but Atlas was busy holding up the whole sky. Heracles bore the heavens himself as Atlas fetched the apples, and Atlas returned so pleased with his freedom that he refused the burden again. How did Heracles trick him into bearing it once more?
answer: He asked Atlas to take the sky back while he padded his shoulders
choices: He asked Atlas to take the sky back while he padded his shoulders
He challenged Atlas to a contest to see who could hold it longer
He promised Atlas a generous share of the golden apples
He pretended to be crushed and quietly slipped out from under it
context: Heracles pretended to agree to hold the sky forever, asking Atlas to take it back just for a moment so he could cushion his shoulders -- then picked up the apples and walked away, leaving Atlas stuck again. Source: standard Apollodorus/Pherecydes tradition (Wikipedia 'Labours of Hercules').  (Legend.)

question: Theseus went into the Labyrinth on Crete to face the beast the Greeks called the Minotaur, though that was only a nickname meaning 'the Bull of Minos.' The beast had a name of its own: Asterion. What does the name Asterion mean?
answer: The starry one
choices: The starry one
The bull-child
The maze-born
The man-eater
context: The beast's real given name was Asterion, which means 'the starry one'; 'Minotaur' simply means 'Bull of Minos.' It was the child of Minos' wife Pasiphae and a white bull sent by Poseidon. Source: Apollodorus, Library (Wikipedia 'Minotaur').  (Legend.)

question: Perseus competed at athletic games in Larissa long after an oracle had warned his grandfather, King Acrisius, that a grandson would kill him. Acrisius had done everything he could to escape that fate, but at the games it caught up with him by pure accident. How did Perseus end up killing his grandfather?
answer: A discus he threw flew wild and struck the old man
choices: A discus he threw flew wild and struck the old man
A javelin slipped from his hand and impaled a bystander
His chariot overturned and crushed a man in the stands
A wrestling throw flung an opponent into the crowd
context: At games in Larissa, a discus Perseus threw veered off course and struck an old spectator who happened to be Acrisius -- fulfilling the prophecy by pure accident, no matter how hard Acrisius had tried to dodge fate. Source: Apollodorus, Library 2.4.4 (Wikipedia 'Acrisius').  (Legend.)

question: Leucippus and his pupil Democritus reasoned, some 2,400 years before modern chemistry, that a lump of matter cut in half again and again must end at a bit of matter too small to divide. They named that smallest piece 'atomos,' the ancestor of our word 'atom.' What does the Greek word literally mean?
answer: Uncuttable
choices: Uncuttable
Unchanging
Unending
Unseen
context: 'Atomos' comes from a- ('not') + tomos ('cut') — literally 'uncuttable.' Leucippus and Democritus held that everything is built from these indivisible, eternal atoms. They were guessing 2,400 years before chemists confirmed matter is made of tiny particles, and our modern word 'atom' is their word handed down. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/atomism-ancient/

question: Democritus of Abdera taught that sweetness, bitterness, heat and colour are not really out there in the world but are merely how arrangements of atoms strike us. In a fragment that survives in his own words, he finished the thought: 'By convention sweet is sweet, by convention bitter is bitter... but in truth there are only atoms and the ____.' What else did Democritus count as real?
answer: the void
choices: the void
the gods
the elements
the heavens
context: Democritus and the atomists insisted reality is just two things: indivisible atoms and the empty 'void' they move through. They argued that even 'what is not' — empty space — must be real, because without void the atoms would have nowhere to move or rearrange. The famous fragment is preserved by Sextus Empiricus. Source: en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Democritus

question: The poet who won Athens' earliest drama contests is said to have carried home a live animal as his prize. The Greek word for a serious play, tragoidia, joined the word for 'song' with the name of that animal. The word 'tragedy' means the song of which creature?
answer: A goat
choices: A goat
A bull
A ram
A stag
context: 'Tragedy' = tragos ('goat') + oide ('song') — 'goat-song.' A goat was the original prize handed to the winning playwright at Athens' drama festival. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_ancient_Greece + Britannica 'Great Dionysia'.

question: An Athenian actor stepped out before thousands of spectators in an open-air theater, his face hidden behind a stiffened linen mask painted with a huge expression. The mask's mouth was made in one particular way. How was the mouth of the mask made?
answer: Flared open wide like a megaphone
choices: Flared open wide like a megaphone
Sewn shut into a thin line
Fitted with a bronze sound-tube
Carved into a wide grin
context: The masks were built with a flared, megaphone-shaped mouth to project the voice across the open-air theater, and painted with exaggerated expressions readable from the back rows. Source: europe.factsanddetails.com/article/entry-989 + thedramateacher.com 'Role of Masks in Greek Theatre'.

question: A singer in an Athenian chorus left his place around 534 BC and spoke lines alone, as a single character. No one had done it before, and he became the first true actor of Western theater. What are actors still called after him?
answer: Thespians
choices: Thespians
Choristers
Dramatists
Orators
context: Thespis (around 534 BC) was the first to step out of the chorus and speak as a character — the first actor. Performers have been called 'thespians' after him ever since. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_ancient_Greece + ebsco.com 'Thespis'.

question: The Athenians cut their great stone theater into a steep natural hillside above the city instead of building it on flat ground, so that its curving rows of seats could climb the slope. At its peak it held some 16,000 people. Into the side of which famous Athenian height was the theater carved?
answer: The south slope of the Acropolis
choices: The south slope of the Acropolis
The harbor wall of Piraeus
The summit of Mount Olympus
The marble quarry of Pentelicus
context: The Theater of Dionysus was cut into the south slope of the Acropolis hillside; at its peak under Lycurgus (around 330 BC) it held roughly 16,000–17,000 spectators. Source: worldhistory.org/article/814/theatre-of-dionysos-eleuthereus + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Dionysus.

question: Athenian citizens packed their hillside theater each spring to watch three poets compete, each staging three tragedies and then a satyr play, while judges chosen by lot named the winner. Serious plays like Oedipus Rex were part of a sacred festival, not mere entertainment. Which god did the festival honor?
answer: Dionysus, the god of wine
choices: Dionysus, the god of wine
Apollo, the god of light
Athena, the city's patron
Hephaestus, the smith god
context: The plays were a religious competition at the City Dionysia, a spring festival for Dionysus, god of wine. Three tragic poets each staged three tragedies plus a satyr play, judged by men chosen by lot. Source: britannica.com/topic/Great-Dionysia + artsedge.kennedy-center.org.

question: The chorus of an Athenian play sang and danced on a level circle of ground at the heart of the theater. The Greeks called that space the 'orchestra,' and to them the word had nothing to do with a band of musicians. What did the word literally mean?
answer: The dancing place
choices: The dancing place
The singing pit
The judges' ring
The actors' door
context: 'Orchestra' came from orcheisthai ('to dance') — it was the circular 'dancing place' at the theater's center where the chorus performed, not a group of musicians. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_ancient_Greece + greektheater8.weebly.com.

question: Honored men of Athens sat on 67 marble thrones across the front row of the city's great open-air theater, each throne carved with its owner's name. One stood grander than all the rest, set in the very center as the most honored seat in the house. To whom did that central throne belong?
answer: The priest of Dionysus
choices: The priest of Dionysus
The richest grain merchant
The winning playwright
The captain of the fleet
context: Among the 67 named marble thrones in the front row, the grandest central seat belonged to the priest of Dionysus — the most honored place in the theater. Source: worldhistory.org/article/814/theatre-of-dionysos-eleuthereus.

question: Sophocles, who wrote Oedipus the King and Antigone, made one small change to the stage of Athenian tragedy in the 400s BC, and that single change let a poet tell a far deeper and more tangled story than before. What did Sophocles add?
answer: A third actor
choices: A third actor
A second chorus
A trap door in the floor
A musicians' balcony
context: Sophocles' great innovation was adding a third actor (Aeschylus had used two), enabling three-way confrontations; he also pioneered painted scenery (skenographia) behind the action. Source: worldhistory.org/sophocles + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophocles.

question: Young Sophocles challenged Aeschylus, the old master of tragedy, at the drama contest of 468 BC, and feelings ran so high that the usual judges chosen by lot were set aside. A group of men already in the city was called in to decide instead. Who judged that contest?
answer: The general Cimon and his commanders
choices: The general Cimon and his commanders
The priests of the temple of Apollo
The elders of the Athenian council
The ten archons of Athens
context: Sophocles' first victory (468 BC) defeated Aeschylus. The contest was so charged that, instead of judges chosen by lot, the general Cimon and his fellow commanders — soldiers, not poetry experts — were called in to decide. Source: britannica.com/biography/Sophocles + Plutarch via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophocles.

question: Oedipus hunted, in Sophocles' Oedipus the King, for the man whose crime had cursed his city, and the trail led to the most devastating truth in Greek drama, about himself. Aristotle praised that moment of recognition as the perfect tragic reversal. What did Oedipus discover he had done?
answer: He had killed his own father and married his own mother
choices: He had killed his own father and married his own mother
He had stolen the sacred fire from the gods themselves
He had betrayed his own brother to win the throne
He had broken a vow sworn upon his children's lives
context: Oedipus realizes the stranger he killed was his own father and the queen he married is his own mother. Aristotle held up this recognition (anagnorisis) as the perfect example of tragic reversal. Source: britannica.com/biography/Sophocles + fiveable.me 'Aristotle Poetics'.

question: Stagehands in Athens swung an actor playing a god out over the stage on a crane called the mechane, when a poet's plot had grown too tangled for any human to fix. The god set everything right, and the trick gave later writers a famous phrase for an out-of-nowhere rescue. What is the phrase?
answer: Deus ex machina
choices: Deus ex machina
In medias res
Anagnorisis
Catharsis
context: A crane called the mechane hoisted the god-actor over the stage to resolve tangled plots — giving us 'deus ex machina,' Latin for 'god from the machine.' Euripides loved the device. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_ex_machina + helinika.com 'Greek Stage Machinery'.

question: Aristophanes mocked real, living Athenians by name, and in The Clouds, staged in 423 BC, he made one famous thinker a babbling fraud who taught young men to wriggle out of paying their debts. Years later that same man complained at his own trial that the play had turned the jurors against him. Whom did The Clouds mock?
answer: Socrates
choices: Socrates
Euripides
Cleon
Pericles
context: The Clouds (423 BC) ridiculed Socrates as a babbling fraud teaching students to dodge debts; Socrates later said the play helped poison the jury against him at his trial. Source: britannica.com/art/Old-Comedy + fiveable.me 'Aristophanes and Political Satire'.

question: Lord Byron, the most famous poet in Europe, sailed to the besieged Greek town of Missolonghi in 1824, hoping to die a soldier's death for Greek freedom. He never saw a real battle. He caught a fever at 36, yet the fever alone did not kill him. What did?
answer: His own doctors bled him over and over with leeches and a lancet
choices: His own doctors bled him over and over with leeches and a lancet
A Turkish sniper picked him off as he inspected the walls
His ship struck rocks and went down in a winter storm
A rival officer challenged him to a duel and shot him dead
context: Byron's doctors, believing bloodletting would break the fever, drained him repeatedly until he was too weak to recover. His reported last words were 'I must sleep now.' He had given the Greek cause both his fortune and his life. Source: https://www.bars.ac.uk/blog/?p=5192

question: Edward Codrington, a British admiral, led a British, French and Russian fleet into a bay on the Greek coast on 20 October 1827 and anchored alongside the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet. He meant only to intimidate the Turks, not to fight them, yet by nightfall about 60 Ottoman ships were sunk or burning. What turned the standoff into a slaughter?
answer: A single musket shot during a quarrel over an Ottoman fireship
choices: A single musket shot during a quarrel over an Ottoman fireship
A planned dawn assault the allied admirals had agreed on in advance
A Greek army attacking the Turkish camp on the shore at the same time
A formal ultimatum that expired at noon and triggered the bombardment
context: When a British boat rowed over to stop an Ottoman crew from lighting a fireship, muskets cracked, a shot rang out, and the anchored fleets erupted into point-blank carnage. Navarino was the last major naval battle fought entirely with wooden sailing ships, most of them blasting each other while still at anchor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Navarino

question: Guido of Arezzo, a monk who taught church singers, found a hymn around the year 1000 whose every line begins one note higher than the line before. He named the six climbing notes from the words that open each line. What did those six names become?
answer: The do-re-mi we still sing today
choices: The do-re-mi we still sing today
The A-B-C note letters
The loud-soft volume marks
The sharp and flat signs
context: The hymn was 'Ut queant laxis,' a song to St. John the Baptist; Guido (c. 991-1033) named the notes ut-re-mi-fa-sol-la, and centuries later 'ut' was changed to 'do,' giving the do-re-mi children still sing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ut_queant_laxis

question: Ernest King, the American admiral, pushed the Marines' landing on Guadalcanal forward in August 1942, though they went in badly short of supplies. The plan's official name was Operation Watchtower, America's first big offensive of the Pacific war. What bitter nickname did the Marines give the operation?
answer: Operation Shoestring
choices: Operation Shoestring
Operation Watchfire
Operation Lost Cause
Operation Empty Hand
context: Operation Watchtower began August 7, 1942 -- just six months after Pearl Harbor and the first major American ground offensive of the Pacific war. Admiral Ernest King had ordered the invasion forward 'even on a shoestring,' and the under-supplied Marines turned that phrase into a grim nickname for the whole campaign. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/war-shoestring-fight-guadalcanal

question: Merritt 'Red Mike' Edson, a Marine lieutenant colonel, dug in on a coral ridge guarding Henderson Field on Guadalcanal in September 1942, with roughly 800 Raiders and paratroopers. For three nights about 3,000 Japanese troops charged them, some reaching the edge of the runway, and the Marines lost about a hundred men, the Japanese 700 or more. What did the survivors name the ridge?
answer: Bloody Ridge
choices: Bloody Ridge
Shoestring Hill
Watchtower Heights
Henderson Ridge
context: The Battle of Edson's Ridge (Sept 12-14, 1942) was fought south of Henderson Field. During the night fighting Edson stood about 20 yards behind the firing line shouting 'Hold out just one more night,' and Major Kenneth Bailey physically shoved panicking men back into position. The Marines held, and the place was renamed Bloody Ridge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Edson%27s_Ridge

question: Abbas, the Safavid shah of Persia, tore down the old fortifications of Iran and built up a corps of artillery. Across the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal lands, huge siege cannon could now bring down in days stone walls that had held out for centuries, and historians argue the guns reshaped power there. What did the cannon do to royal power?
answer: It broke the castle nobles and let kings centralize huge empires
choices: It broke the castle nobles and let kings centralize huge empires
It made open-field cavalry charges the deciding force again
It pushed kings to share power with the castle-holding lords
It ended large land empires in favor of small trading cities
context: Because only wealthy central rulers could afford the giant guns, the old castle-holding nobility collapsed and kings built vast centralized land empires — the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal states. The Safavid Shah Abbas even tore down Iran's old fortifications and built an artillery corps answering to him alone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpowder_empires

question: A Gupta emperor had an iron column more than 7 meters tall raised some 1,600 years ago, and today it is in a courtyard in Delhi. Ordinary iron left out in rain and sun rusts away within a few years. After sixteen centuries in the open, what state is this pillar in?
answer: It has barely rusted at all
choices: It has barely rusted at all
It has rusted down to a thin stump
It has turned bright green like old copper
It has crumbled into reddish flakes
context: The Iron Pillar of Delhi weighs over 6 tonnes (about 13,000 lb) and is roughly 98% wrought iron, yet after ~1,600 years outdoors it has scarcely corroded — a metallurgical marvel of the Gupta age. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_pillar_of_Delhi

question: Aryabhata, an astronomer born in 476 near Patna, argued that the Earth spins, and he measured the sky with great accuracy. Nearly 1,500 years after his birth, in 1975, India found a fitting way to remember him. How did India honor Aryabhata?
answer: It named its very first satellite after him
choices: It named its very first satellite after him
It named its first university after him
It put his face on its first banknote
It built him a great marble tomb
context: India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named 'Aryabhata' after the astronomer born in 476 CE who wrote his masterwork at age 23. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryabhata

question: Samudragupta, the Gupta conqueror nicknamed the 'Indian Napoleon,' put his own image on his gold coins for his subjects to see. One well-known coin type shows him seated, absorbed in a favorite pastime. What is Samudragupta doing on that coin?
answer: Seated, playing the veena, a lute
choices: Seated, playing the veena, a lute
Seated, playing a board game
Seated, reading from a scroll
Seated, feeding a tame peacock
context: Despite conquests that earned him the 'Indian Napoleon' nickname, Samudragupta's gold coins also show him seated playing the veena — advertising a warrior-king who was also a musician. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samudragupta

question: Fa-Hien, a Chinese Buddhist monk, walked across Gupta India around 400 and wrote home amazed that the highways were safe and the death penalty hardly ever used. In the capital, Pataliputra, he found a place paid for entirely by donations, where anyone in need was taken in and helped without charge. What was this place?
answer: A free hospital
choices: A free hospital
A free library
A free granary
A free travelers' inn
context: Fa-Hien (Faxian) reported that Pataliputra had a free hospital, funded by donations, giving the poor and sick food, shelter, and medicine — in a land so peaceful that criminals were usually just fined. https://byjus.com/free-ias-prep/fa-hien-faxian-337ce-422ce/

question: Aryabhata's critics had a ready objection when he claimed, around 499, that the Earth itself spins and that the sky merely appears to turn: if the Earth were spinning, surely people would feel it whirl. Aryabhata answered them with an everyday picture. Which picture did he use?
answer: A man drifting downstream sees the still bank slide backward
choices: A man drifting downstream sees the still bank slide backward
A child on a spinning top feels pinned to its centre
A bird gliding feels the wind hold it perfectly still
A stone dropped from a tower lands far behind the thrower
context: Aryabhata wrote that just as a man in a moving boat sees the stationary shore drift backward, people on the spinning Earth see the still stars sweep toward the west. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryabhata

question: To rebuild a patient's lost nose, an Indian surgeon followed the steps of the Sushruta Samhita, a Sanskrit surgery book put into shape in Gupta times. Before cutting any skin, he had to size the replacement exactly right. What simple tool did he use to take that measurement?
answer: A leaf, held up to the face
choices: A leaf, held up to the face
A knotted length of string
A carved wooden mold
A lump of soft clay
context: The surgeon measured the missing nose with a leaf, then cut a matching flap of living skin from the patient's cheek or forehead and stitched it on, propping the new nostrils open with little castor-oil-plant tubes. https://hekint.org/2017/01/22/sushruta-the-ancient-indian-surgeon/

question: A surgeon of the Sushruta tradition, about to operate, turned to the Sushruta Samhita, a Sanskrit surgery book of Gupta times. The book did more than describe operations; it told him how to prepare the patient before the knife went in. According to that text, what should the patient be given first?
answer: Wine, to make him insensible to pain
choices: Wine, to make him insensible to pain
A leather strap, to bite down on
A priest's chant, to calm his fear
A cup of cold water, to wet his lips
context: Sushruta's text orders wine before an operation 'to produce insensibility to pain' — a form of anesthesia roughly 2,000 years before modern surgery. https://hekint.org/2017/01/22/sushruta-the-ancient-indian-surgeon/

question: Brahmagupta, an Indian mathematician, wrote down in 628 the earliest known rules for treating one quantity as a real number that could be added, subtracted and multiplied. Older thinkers had refused to call it a number at all, though Indian scholars had already built the place-value way of writing numbers used everywhere today. Which quantity was Brahmagupta taming?
answer: Zero
choices: Zero
Infinity
One half
The square root of two
context: In his Brahma-sphuta-siddhanta (628 CE), Brahmagupta wrote the first known rules for treating zero as a real number. The digit zero and the decimal place-value system both grew up in Gupta-era India. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahmagupta

question: Kalidasa, the Gupta court's greatest poet and later called 'the Shakespeare of India,' wrote a play in which a curse makes King Dushyanta utterly forget the woman he loves, Shakuntala. At the climax, a single small keepsake brings his memory back. What was the keepsake?
answer: A ring he had given her
choices: A ring he had given her
A lock of her hair
A song she once sang
A scar on her hand
context: Kalidasa's play 'Abhijnanashakuntalam' (The Recognition of Shakuntala) turns on a ring of recognition that restores King Dushyanta's cursed memory — still performed 1,500 years later. https://curiousindian.in/reign-of-chandragupta-ii-vikramaditya/

question: R. Balasubramaniam, a metallurgist at the Indian Institute of Technology in Kanpur, studied Delhi's 1,600-year-old Iron Pillar in the 1990s. He found one element in unusual abundance in its ancient iron, and across the centuries that element had grown a wafer-thin skin on the surface that locks the rust out. What was different about this iron?
answer: It held far more phosphorus than modern iron
choices: It held far more phosphorus than modern iron
It held far more carbon than modern iron
It held far more sulphur than modern iron
It held a hidden thread of pure silver
context: The pillar's iron carries about 0.25% phosphorus (versus under 0.05% in modern iron), which slowly formed a protective iron-phosphate film called 'misawite,' only about one-twentieth of a millimetre thick. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_pillar_of_Delhi

question: A surgeon of the Sushruta school bent over a patient whose intestine had been sliced, and he needed stitches that would still hold deep inside once the belly was sewn shut. Their answer used living creatures as the stitches themselves. What did these surgeons do?
answer: Let black ants bite across the cut, then snipped off their bodies
choices: Let black ants bite across the cut, then snipped off their bodies
Let leeches clamp the cut, then sealed them under hot wax
Held the cut shut with live beetles' pincers, then crushed their shells
Packed the cut with maggots, then bound it tight with silk
context: They let big black ants bite down across the wound with their pincer jaws, then cut off the bodies — leaving the locked heads in place as natural living stitches. https://www.gocuriousmind.com/2024/09/ancient-indian-medicine-live-ants-wound-sutures.html

question: Aryabhata gave a value for pi around 499, the number 3.1416, accurate enough to serve Indian astronomers for centuries. Yet he called it 'asanna,' meaning 'approaching' or 'approximate,' and scholars read that one careful word as a hint at a deep truth about pi. What was he hinting?
answer: That pi can never be written out exactly
choices: That pi can never be written out exactly
That pi changes from one circle to the next
That pi is exactly twenty-two sevenths
That pi had been copied from Greek books
context: Aryabhata gave pi as 62832/20000 = 3.1416 and called it 'asanna' — read by scholars as a hint that pi is irrational and can never be written out exactly. His value went unbeaten for about a thousand years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryabhata

question: Johannes Gutenberg spent years in Mainz perfecting an invention that let a single press do the work of dozens of hand-copying scribes, and around 1455 he finished the first major book ever printed in Europe with it. What was his great breakthrough?
answer: Casting hundreds of tiny metal letters that could be arranged into a page and then rearranged for the next
choices: Casting hundreds of tiny metal letters that could be arranged into a page and then rearranged for the next
Carving each whole page into a single wooden block that was inked and stamped
Teaching dozens of scribes to copy the same page at the same time
Pressing wet clay tablets against a stone master copy
context: This was movable metal type. Gutenberg cast hundreds of individual letters, locked them into a page, printed, then broke the page apart and reused the same letters for the next, instead of carving a brand-new block for every page, so one press replaced a roomful of hand-copyists. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Partway through printing his Latin Bible, Johannes Gutenberg squeezed more lines into each tall column than he had begun with, until every column held the same count. Collectors still name the book by that number. By what number is the finished Bible known?
answer: The 42-line Bible
choices: The 42-line Bible
The 40-line Bible
The 66-line Bible
The 100-line Bible
context: Each column ended up with exactly 42 lines, so collectors call it the '42-line Bible.' Gutenberg actually began printing with 40 lines per column, then tightened the spacing to squeeze in two more partway through — you can spot the switch, since the earliest pages have fewer, more open lines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Johannes Gutenberg, the German who first printed books in Europe with movable metal type, turned up in 1999 on a countdown by A&E, an American television network. What did A&E name him?
answer: The single most influential person of the millennium
choices: The single most influential person of the millennium
Inventor of the year for the 1450s
The richest man of medieval Germany
The first modern celebrity
context: A&E rated Gutenberg the most influential PERSON of the whole millennium — ahead of every king, scientist, and explorer — because cheap printed books spread knowledge to ordinary people for the first time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg

question: For the luxury copies of his Bible, Johannes Gutenberg passed over paper and printed on vellum, a fine parchment made from calfskin. He made roughly 180 copies in all at Mainz in the 1450s. How many calves gave their skins for the pages of just one of those vellum Bibles?
answer: about 170 calfskins
choices: about 170 calfskins
about 12 calfskins
about 40 calfskins
about 600 calfskins
context: About 170 calfskins went into a single vellum copy, an entire calf herd for one Bible. Of all the copies, only three complete vellum Gutenberg Bibles survive today. Source: https://www.history.com/news/7-things-you-may-not-know-about-the-gutenberg-bible

question: Vido Aras hid inside Harvard's Widener Library one night in 1969 until the doors closed, then stuffed both heavy volumes of its Gutenberg Bible into a knapsack. He tried to rope his way down the outside of the building. What happened to him on the way down?
answer: The heavy load dragged him off the wall and he fell six stories
choices: The heavy load dragged him off the wall and he fell six stories
Campus guards spotted his rope and caught him at the bottom
His rope snapped clean and he tumbled into the bushes unhurt
He froze halfway down and had to be talked back up by police
context: The two volumes weighed about 70 pounds — so heavy the load pulled Aras off the building. He plunged six stories and fractured his skull, but he survived, and so did the Bible, which went back on the shelf. Source: https://www.history.com/news/7-things-you-may-not-know-about-the-gutenberg-bible

question: For all his fame, Johannes Gutenberg was not the first to print with metal letters that could move. A Buddhist book called the Jikji had already been printed that way in 1377, in the Korean city of Cheongju. How long was that before Gutenberg's Bible?
answer: About 73 years earlier
choices: About 73 years earlier
About 5 years earlier
About 300 years earlier
About the same year
context: The Jikji, printed in Korea in 1377, beat Gutenberg by 73 years and survives as the oldest book printed with movable metal type — now held in Paris and listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World. Gutenberg's leap was building a whole system that flooded a continent with books. Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/689333-oldest-book-printed-using-movable-metal-type

question: Maruzen, a Tokyo firm, bought a single volume of the Doheny copy of the Gutenberg Bible at Christie's in New York in October 1987, at a price that set a world record for any printed book. About how much did that one volume bring?
answer: About $5.4 million
choices: About $5.4 million
About $90,000
About $250 million
context: The buyer, Maruzen of Tokyo, paid about $5.4 million for one volume — a record for any printed book at the time. Experts now estimate a complete two-volume copy would fetch over $35 million. Source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/10/23/Record-49-million-spent-on-Gutenberg-Bible/1356561960000/

question: Page by page, Johannes Gutenberg crammed the lines of his great Bible closer together, from 40 to a column, then 41, then 42, and the count gave the book its nickname, the 42-line Bible. Why did Gutenberg squeeze in those extra lines?
answer: To save costly paper
choices: To save costly paper
To finish the book faster
To copy a rival's design
To leave room for pictures
context: The first sheets had 40 lines (one page even has 41); Gutenberg then tightened the spacing to fit 42, most likely to save paper. Paper and vellum were the most expensive part of the job, so fitting more text on each page meant fewer sheets per Bible. The nickname records the squeeze: the 42-line Bible. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible)

question: Johannes Gutenberg brushed the thin, watery ink that scribes had used for a thousand years onto his smooth metal letters, and it beaded up and slid right off, leaving smears instead of print. To make an ink that would cling to metal, he borrowed a recipe from painters. What was the key ingredient he added?
answer: Oil
choices: Oil
Wax
Sap
Soot
context: Water-based scribal ink would not stick to metal, so Gutenberg made an oil-based ink, closer to a varnish, like the paints of oil painters; analysis shows it was rich in metals like copper, lead, and titanium. A whole new ink had to be invented just to make the press work. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible)

question: For his wealthy buyers, Johannes Gutenberg printed some of his roughly 180 Bibles on something far costlier than paper, which gave a smoother, more luxurious page. It was the same surface monks had long used for their grandest hand-copied books. What were the deluxe Gutenberg Bibles printed on?
answer: Fine animal skin
choices: Fine animal skin
Pressed silk cloth
Thin birch bark
Beaten copper sheets
context: Of roughly 180 copies, about 135 were on paper and 45 on the finer animal skin, called vellum -- fine parchment made from calfskin. The vellum copies are the rarest survivors today. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible)

question: While his Bible took about two years, Johannes Gutenberg kept his workshop paying by printing thousands of small slips for the Church, each with a blank for the buyer's name. For a fee, the Church promised that the heavenly punishment owed for the buyer's sins would be cancelled, and one batch around 1454 was sold to fund a crusade. What were these slips called?
answer: Indulgences
choices: Indulgences
Crusader maps
Cathedral tickets
Church tax bills
context: Gutenberg's shop printed thousands of paper indulgences for the Church, with blanks for the buyer's name, including Cypriot indulgences issued under Pope Calixtus III around 1454-1455 to fund a crusade: fast, profitable jobs next to the slow Bible. An indulgence known to exist by 22 October 1454 is the earliest work from his shop with a firm date. (https://www.mainz.de/en/microsite/gutenberg/zeit/zeitleiste_gutenberg)

question: To make his printed Bible look exactly like a monk's handwriting, where letters often join and shrink into shorthand, Johannes Gutenberg needed many more than the 26 letters of the alphabet. Copying every joined pair, every shorthand mark and both capitals and small letters, his Bible type held a startling number of different characters. About how many?
answer: About 290
choices: About 290
About 26
About 52
About 75
context: The B42 type had roughly 290 characters: 47 capitals, 63 lowercase, 92 abbreviations, 83 joined-letter ligatures, and 5 punctuation marks -- all to mimic a scribe's hand. (https://oldbookappreciator.com/libraryofhistoricaltype/exhibits/show/gutenbergsb42/b42type)

question: Johann Fust, a rich Mainz businessman, had lent Johannes Gutenberg a fortune to build his shop and print what Gutenberg called 'the Work of the Books.' In November 1455, just as the Bibles were ready to sell, Fust took him to the archbishop's court in Mainz and won. What did the verdict let Fust carry off?
answer: His press and the finished Bibles
choices: His press and the finished Bibles
His house and his goldsmith's tools
His store of fresh paper and ink
His chest of gold and silver coins
context: On 6 November 1455 Fust, who had lent Gutenberg about 1,600 guilders, sued in the archbishop of Mainz's court and won; he seized Gutenberg's press, equipment, and a share of the finished Bibles just as they were ready to sell, so Fust, not Gutenberg, reaped the profit. Fust then carried on the business with Gutenberg's assistant Peter Schoeffer. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Helmaspergersches-Notariatsinstrument)

question: Johann Fust and Peter Schoeffer, once Gutenberg's assistant, printed the Mainz Psalter in 1457, and on its very last page they added a short line, a first that printed books have copied ever since. Gutenberg had never put his own name anywhere in his great Bible. What did that line record?
answer: Who made it and when
choices: Who made it and when
How much it cost
A blessing for readers
A warning to copyists
context: The 1457 Mainz Psalter carried the first printed colophon -- a closing line naming the printers and the date -- plus the first printer's mark and printed colored initials. The names history records there are Fust and Schoeffer (Gutenberg's former assistant), not Gutenberg, whose press they had seized two years earlier. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainz_Psalter)

question: Johannes Gutenberg left no diary, no business books, not even a page signed in his own hand, for all his fame as the inventor of printing in Mainz in the 1450s. Nearly everything known about his workshop survives on a single piece of paper, kept today in the university library at Göttingen, Germany. What is that one precious source?
answer: The court record of Fust's lawsuit against him
choices: The court record of Fust's lawsuit against him
A city tax roll listing his Mainz workshop
An archbishop's account book of his pension
A goldsmiths' guild register bearing his name
context: The Helmasperger Notarial Instrument, recording the 1455 lawsuit, is the only contemporary account of Gutenberg's work -- so our knowledge of the printing revolution rests largely on the document that ruined its inventor. (https://www.mainz.de/en/microsite/gutenberg/zeit/zeitleiste_gutenberg)

question: Adolf von Nassau, an archbishop, took pity on the poor old Johannes Gutenberg in January 1465 and made him a courtier, with a yearly gift of grain, wine and clothing, all of it tax-free. Gutenberg died in Mainz three years later, in 1468, and left one gap that has never been filled. What has history never found of him?
answer: A genuine portrait of his face
choices: A genuine portrait of his face
A single copy of his Bible
The city records of his birth
Any printing by his rivals
context: Archbishop Adolf von Nassau gave the impoverished Gutenberg a tax-free pension of grain, wine, and clothing in 1465; he died on 3 February 1468. No genuine likeness of him survives -- every famous 'portrait' was imagined long after his death. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg)

question: A buyer in Mainz in the 1450s found a printed Gutenberg Bible a real bargain next to one copied by hand. Yet a finished copy still cost him about 30 gold florins, roughly 100 grams of gold. For an ordinary working man of that era, how much was 30 florins really worth?
answer: about three years' wages
choices: about three years' wages
about three weeks' wages
about three days' wages
about thirty years' wages
context: Thirty florins was about three years' pay for a clerk and equal to roughly 100 grams of gold — far cheaper than a hand-copied Bible, but still a small fortune for most people. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Johannes Gutenberg set his press in Mainz to printing Bibles in the 1450s. A lone scribe bent over his desk needed roughly a whole year to copy out just one by hand. In that same span, about how many copies did Gutenberg's press turn out?
answer: about 180
choices: about 180
about 12
about 3
about 40
context: Gutenberg printed the entire run of about 180 Bibles in roughly the time it would take one scribe to hand-copy a single one. That one comparison is the whole revolution. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Johannes Gutenberg hammered a steel punch, carved with a reversed letter, into a bar of soft copper to make a little mould called a matrix. He set the matrix in a hand mould and poured in molten metal, and seconds later out popped one finished letter. What did that single matrix let him do?
answer: make thousands of identical copies of that one letter
choices: make thousands of identical copies of that one letter
press that one letter straight onto the page
shape an entire page in a single pour
engrave a decorated capital by hand
context: One steel punch stamped one copper matrix, and that single matrix could be filled with molten metal again and again to cast thousands of identical reusable letters (each called a 'sort'), and each one cooled in seconds. That is what made mass printing possible. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movable_type

question: Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, a churchman who would one day be Pope Pius II, looked over pages of Gutenberg's new Bible on show at Frankfurt in March 1455. He wrote the earliest known eyewitness report of printing. What amazed him most about the pages?
answer: so clean and clear you could read it without glasses
choices: so clean and clear you could read it without glasses
so bright with gold paint it lit up the room
so sweet with perfume the whole hall smelled of it
so thin and light you could fold it into a pocket
context: In his letter of 12 March 1455 to Cardinal Carvajal, Piccolomini marveled that the lettering was so neat and correct it 'could be read effortlessly, even without glasses.' It is the first eyewitness account of printing. Source: https://www.historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=292

question: Gabriel Wells, a New York bookseller, owned an incomplete Gutenberg Bible in 1921 and did something that scandalized the rare-book world. He pulled the centuries-old book apart and sold its loose pages one at a time, each in its own leather case with a scholar's essay. What did he call these single sheets?
answer: "Noble Fragments"
choices: "Noble Fragments"
"Holy Leaves"
"Mainz Relics"
"Gutenberg Shards"
context: Wells sold the dismembered pages as 'Noble Fragments.' The rare-book world was scandalized — but he died rich, because the Bible turned out to be worth more in pieces than whole. Source: https://www.themorgan.org/incunables/145177

question: Martin Luther turned out short German pamphlets after his 95 Theses of 1517, and printers ran them off so fast that more than half a million copies had sold by 1525. Historians give Luther a title that no author had held before him. What is that title?
answer: the first bestselling author in history
choices: the first bestselling author in history
the first man to print a book
the first translator of the Bible
the first to write in German
context: Between 1517 and 1525 Luther published over half a million works — making him the first bestselling author of the modern age. His short German pamphlets were nicknamed Flugschriften, 'flying writings,' because they spread so fast; Luther called printing 'God's highest and extremest act of grace.' Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2039/the-printing-press--the-protestant-reformation/

question: Johannes Gutenberg began with one great Bible in Mainz around 1450. Just fifty years later, presses were running in about 282 European towns, and books printed before 1501 still carry the name incunabula, the Latin word for 'cradle.' Roughly how many books had Europe printed by 1500?
answer: over nine million
choices: over nine million
over ninety thousand
over nine hundred
over nine billion
context: By 1500 presses in about 282 towns across some 18 countries had produced over nine million books in just fifty years. Books printed before 1501 are called 'incunabula' — Latin for 'cradle' — and about 30,000 distinct editions are known. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incunable

question: Johannes Gutenberg spent years in Mainz quietly working on a press that printed with tiny metal letters, and he paid his bills in the meantime with the craft he had trained in. That trade had taught him how to melt, cast and shape fine metal, the very skills his letters would need. What was his trade?
answer: Goldsmith
choices: Goldsmith
Blacksmith
Locksmith
Bell-founder
context: As a goldsmith, Gutenberg had spent years cutting, casting and polishing metal by hand, and the trade taught him to cut steel punches and strike copper matrices, exactly the metalwork needed to mass-produce reusable type. The invention grew straight out of his craft. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg

question: Rhineland farmers cranked a heavy screw press down every autumn, and Johannes Gutenberg rebuilt one, keeping its great turning screw, to push paper firmly and evenly onto inked metal type. What was that press first built to squeeze?
answer: grapes, to make wine
choices: grapes, to make wine
olives, to make oil
apples, to make cider
barley, to make beer
context: Gutenberg's press was a converted wine press, the wooden screw press Rhineland vintners turned to crush grapes. He kept the big turning screw that crushed grapes and used it to push a flat plate (the platen) down onto the paper, pressing every letter evenly at once. The machine that made wine became the machine that made books. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press

question: Johannes Gutenberg finished printing the first big book Europe ever made with a press and reusable metal letters, at Mainz around 1455. He chose a book that almost every European household longed to own, 1,282 pages long. Which book was it?
answer: a Latin Bible
choices: a Latin Bible
a book of Greek myths
a royal law code
a book of love poems
context: The Gutenberg Bible, printed in Latin at Mainz in the 1450s, was the first major book in Europe made with mass-produced movable metal type, the work that launched the age of printed books in the West. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: A small crew worked Johannes Gutenberg's press in Mainz, and it outran every older way of making pages. A monk with a quill copied a few pages a day, and printers working from carved wooden blocks managed only about 40. About how many pages could one of his presses print in a day?
answer: about 3,600
choices: about 900
about 1,800
about 3,600
about 7,200
context: Roughly 3,600 pages a day, hundreds of times faster than a human copyist. For the first time, books could be made faster than people could hand-copy them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press

question: To cast his tiny letters, Johannes Gutenberg blended lead and tin with a third, cleverer metal. Where most metals contract as they cool, this one made the blend expand a touch as it hardened, so every letter filled its mould and came out razor-sharp. Printers used the recipe for centuries. What was the third metal?
answer: antimony
choices: antimony
copper
silver
iron
context: Type metal mixed lead, tin and antimony, soft enough to cast sharply and tough enough to survive thousands of pressings. The antimony was the clever part: most metals shrink as they cool, but antimony made the blend expand a touch when setting, so the letters filled the mould completely and came out crisp. The same recipe was still in use centuries later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_metal

question: When the pages came off his press, Johannes Gutenberg had left deliberate blank gaps where the big capital letters and chapter headings belonged, since the press printed only the black text. What went into those gaps is why almost no two surviving copies match. What was done in the blank spaces?
answer: artists hand-painted the initials in red and blue
choices: artists hand-painted the initials in red and blue
buyers wrote their own names in the gaps
Gutenberg pasted in small woodcut pictures
the spaces were filled with gold leaf
context: The press printed only black text. Afterwards artists painted the big red and blue initials and headings by hand (called rubrication); buyers paid the scribes and artists themselves, so richer buyers got fancier decoration. Because each painter worked a little differently, almost no two surviving Gutenberg Bibles look exactly alike. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible

question: Martin Luther wrote out his 95 Theses in 1517, a list of complaints against the Church meant only for his fellow scholars. Printers seized on them and ran off copies without asking him. Thanks to the press, how fast did Luther's 95 Theses spread?
answer: across Germany in about two weeks
choices: across Germany in about two weeks
across Germany in about two years
across Germany in about twenty years
across Germany in about two centuries
context: Within two weeks the Theses had spread across Germany, and within two months across Europe. Historians say bluntly, 'No printing press, no Reformation' — ideas could now multiply faster than any king or church could suppress them. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2039/the-printing-press--the-protestant-reformation/

question: A Roman soldier at Vindolanda, a fort on the northern frontier of Britain, got a parcel around AD 100 to help him through the cold British weather, and a thin wooden tablet listed what was in it. Along with two pairs of sandals and two pairs of underpants, what woolen item did the parcel include?
answer: Socks
choices: Socks
A cloak
Gloves
A scarf
context: Vindolanda Tablet 346 lists 'pairs of socks from Sattua, two pairs of sandals and two pairs of underpants' — a genuine Roman care package from the edge of empire. Hundreds of these tablets survived ~2,000 years in a waterlogged, oxygen-free rubbish heap and were voted the British Museum's top treasure from Roman Britain in 2003. Source: britishmuseum.org Vindolanda tablets; Antigone Journal.

question: Writing a report at Vindolanda, a Roman soldier sneered that the wretched Britons would not even climb onto their horses to throw javelins. In it he pinned a single mocking Latin word on them, a word found in no other surviving Latin writing. What was the insult?
answer: Brittunculi
choices: Brittunculi
Gallunculi
Barbarunculi
Germanunculi
context: Tab.Vindol. 164 (c. AD 97-105) is the only known use of 'Brittunculi' in all of surviving Latin — a contemptuous diminutive coined by a Roman on the frontier. The full line jeers that 'the cavalry do not use swords nor do the wretched Britons mount in order to throw javelins.' Source: romaninscriptionsofbritain.org TabVindol164; penelope.uchicago.edu.

question: Justinian finished a huge domed church in his capital, Constantinople, in 537, and gave it a Greek name of two words: Hagia Sophia. He did not name it for any saint called Sophia. What does the name mean?
answer: Holy Wisdom
choices: Holy Wisdom
Holy Cross
Sacred Heart
Blessed Mother
context: Hagia Sophia is Greek for 'Holy Wisdom' — it was dedicated to the Wisdom of God, not to any saint named Sophia. Source: britannica.com 'Hagia Sophia'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia.

question: Tradition tells how Justinian, on first stepping into his finished Hagia Sophia in 537, gazed up at its enormous dome and shouted a famous boast. What did he cry out?
answer: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
choices: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
"Babylon itself would envy me!"
"Behold, a second Eden!"
"Rome has never seen the like!"
context: King Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem was the most famous building in the Bible; Justinian's boast claimed he had outbuilt it. Told as tradition: the line is a later legend, not found in Procopius, who saw the church new.

question: When people later wanted to take down the eight giant calligraphy panels that hang high in Hagia Sophia, gold Arabic letters on black, each about 7.5 meters across, they hit one obstacle. What was it?
answer: They were too big to fit through the doors.
choices: They were too big to fit through the doors.
They were too holy to be moved.
They were bolted to the dome itself.
They were promised to stay forever.
context: Each roundel is about 7.5 meters across — among the largest pieces of calligraphy in the world — bearing the names of Allah, Muhammad, the first four caliphs, and Muhammad's two grandsons. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; thehagiasophia.com 'Medallions'.

question: Suppose you visit Hagia Sophia and stop at its wishing column, where you press your thumb into the hole worn through its bronze plate and slowly turn your hand. According to the old legend, what sign tells you your wish will come true?
answer: Your thumb comes out damp.
choices: Your thumb comes out damp.
Your thumb feels suddenly warm.
The hole hums very faintly.
The bronze turns slightly green.
context: Byzantines believed the moisture was the tears of the Virgin Mary, and legend says Justinian once cured a headache by leaning against the column. Told as legend. Source: atlasobscura.com 'Hagia Sophia wishing column'; ayasofyamuzesi.gov.tr 'Wishing Column'.

question: Rioters swept through Constantinople in January 532, in the furious uprising called the Nika Revolt, and set the old church on the site of Hagia Sophia ablaze. Justinian ordered a new one built at once. What had first set the riot off?
answer: A chariot race.
choices: A chariot race.
A new royal tax.
A shortage of bread.
A feud between bishops.
context: The Nika Revolt began as a brawl between chariot-racing factions in the Hippodrome, then exploded into a city-wide riot. Justinian ordered the new church rebuilt within weeks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nika_riots; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia.

question: A Norse warrior who guarded the Byzantine emperor, one of the Varangian Guard, carved runes into a stone railing high in the upper gallery of Hagia Sophia, centuries after the church was built. They were found again only in 1964. Roughly translated, what do they say?
answer: "Halfdan was here."
choices: "Halfdan was here."
"Olaf owns this seat."
"Glory to the emperor."
"God keep this hall."
context: It was carved by a member of the Varangian Guard, the Norse warriors who served the Byzantine emperor, and was only rediscovered in 1964. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runic_inscriptions_in_Hagia_Sophia; atlasobscura.com.

question: Mehmed II, the young Ottoman sultan, broke into Constantinople on 29 May 1453 and rode straight to Hagia Sophia, for some nine hundred years the greatest church in Christendom. That very day he gave an order about the great building. What did he order done with it?
answer: Turned into a mosque.
choices: Turned into a mosque.
Pulled down for its stone.
Sealed shut forever.
Made into his palace.
context: A scholar climbed the pulpit and recited the shahada, and Mehmed prayed the first Friday prayer there days later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia.

question: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, the builders of Hagia Sophia, had to set a round dome on top of a square hall. They solved it by filling the four upper corners with curved triangles of masonry, like sails of stone. What is each of those corner pieces called?
answer: A pendentive.
choices: A pendentive.
A buttress.
A keystone.
An archway.
context: Pendentives let a round dome sit smoothly on a square base — the breakthrough that made Hagia Sophia's vast dome possible. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; smarthistory.org 'Hagia Sophia, Istanbul'.

question: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, Turkey's first president, changed Hagia Sophia's purpose once more in 1934, after centuries as one of the world's grandest mosques, and opened it to people of every faith and nation. What did he turn it into?
answer: A public museum.
choices: A public museum.
A royal library.
A military fortress.
A national cathedral.
context: As a museum, its Byzantine Christian mosaics and Islamic calligraphy were displayed side by side, and it became Turkey's most-visited tourist site. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; middleeasteye.net.

question: Procopius, the historian, saw Hagia Sophia when it was brand new, with daylight pouring through the forty windows round the foot of its dome so that it seemed to float. He wrote that it did not rest on solid foundations but appeared to hang from heaven. What did he say it hung by?
answer: A golden chain.
choices: A golden chain.
A silver thread.
An iron rod.
A silken cord.
context: Procopius wrote that the dome 'seems not to rest upon solid masonry, but to cover the space as though suspended from heaven by a golden chain' — the 'dome of heaven' effect the architects wanted. Source: hagiasophia.com 'Hagia Sophia dome'; smarthistory.org.

question: Isidore the Younger, whose uncle had helped design Hagia Sophia, rebuilt the church's dome after earthquakes cracked Justinian's original and its eastern half collapsed in 558. The new dome has stood for more than 1,400 years. How did it differ from the one that fell?
answer: It was steeper and taller.
choices: It was steeper and taller.
It was wider and flatter.
It was thicker and heavier.
It was lower and rounder.
context: Isidore the Younger (nephew of the first Isidore) raised the rebuilt dome about 6.25 meters steeper and higher than Justinian's too-flat original. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; hagiasophia.com 'Hagia Sophia dome'.

question: Zoe, a Byzantine empress, married three emperors in her lifetime, and a gold mosaic in Hagia Sophia shows her standing beside her husband. Each time she remarried, workmen had to bring the picture up to date. How did they change it for the new emperor?
answer: They chiseled out the old face and set in the new one.
choices: They chiseled out the old face and set in the new one.
They added the new husband beside the old one.
They covered the whole panel with fresh paint.
They built a second mosaic on the far wall.
context: When Zoe swapped husbands, workmen cut out the previous emperor's face and name and inserted her new husband, Constantine IX Monomachos — even Christ's and Zoe's own faces were redone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia; byzantine-world.com 'Zoe Porphyrogenita'.

question: Jean-Jacques Dessalines took up the French tricolor of blue, white and red in May 1803, the flag of the very country his soldiers were beating, and made it the flag of a free Haiti. By tradition, it was his goddaughter Catherine Flon who did the needlework. What did they do to the tricolor?
answer: Tore out the white middle stripe and sewed the blue and red together
choices: Tore out the white middle stripe and sewed the blue and red together
Added a white star in the corner for each region they had freed
Turned the three stripes sideways and dyed the top one green
Stitched a golden lion across the center of the three stripes
context: The white middle stripe stood for the white colonists, so the leaders cut it out and joined the remaining blue and red. Tradition says Catherine Flon, goddaughter of the general Jean-Jacques Dessalines, sewed the two halves together in May 1803. (Source: Marxists.org, 'Dessalines, the Flag, and Independence'; Wikipedia, Catherine Flon.)

question: Toussaint Bréda, master strategist of the slave revolt that broke out in 1791 in Saint-Domingue, a French colony in the Caribbean, took a new surname around 1792. He chose the French word 'Louverture.' What does that word mean?
answer: 'The opening' — the one who opens the way
choices: 'The opening' — the one who opens the way
'The lion' — the one who knows no fear
'The free man' — the one born to no master
'The storm' — the one who never rests
context: 'Louverture' is French for 'the opening.' The name was said to mark his talent for breaking open the enemy's lines in battle. By 1801 this once-enslaved man was the de facto ruler of the whole island and issued a constitution making himself governor-general for life and permanently abolishing slavery. (Source: Wikipedia, Toussaint Louverture.)

question: Toussaint Louverture worked the reins as an enslaved coachman, so skilled with horses that his masters made him their own driver. He never went to school, yet he taught himself to read. Which writers did this self-taught man go on to study?
answer: The Stoic philosopher Epictetus and Machiavelli
choices: The Stoic philosopher Epictetus and Machiavelli
The poet Homer and the general Julius Caesar
The explorer Marco Polo and the artist Leonardo da Vinci
The scientist Isaac Newton and the king Louis XIV
context: Teaching himself to read, Toussaint studied the Stoic philosopher Epictetus and the political writer Machiavelli. He was freed around 1776 and even rented a coffee plantation of his own before the revolution — all before becoming the general who drove Napoleon's army out of the island. (Source: Wikipedia, Toussaint Louverture.)

question: Brunet, a French general, invited Toussaint Louverture to friendly talks in June 1802, then seized him by treachery and put him aboard a ship bound for prison in France. As he was taken aboard, Toussaint is said to have warned his captors. What did he tell them?
answer: "In overthrowing me you have cut down only the trunk of the tree of liberty; it will spring up again by the roots, for they are numerous and deep."
choices: "In overthrowing me you have cut down only the trunk of the tree of liberty; it will spring up again by the roots, for they are numerous and deep."
"You may chain my hands, but a hundred thousand free men will rise where I have fallen to finish what I began."
"Take me to your emperor, and let him look me in the eyes and say that one man may own another."
"The sea you sail me across is wide, but freedom has crossed it ahead of you to reach my island."
context: Toussaint died a prisoner on April 7, 1803, in the cold of Fort de Joux in the Jura Mountains, from illness and neglect — he never lived to see independence, which came less than a year later. His warning proved true: the fight went on without him. (Reported as his words; framed as legend. Source: Wikipedia, Toussaint Louverture; History Today.)

question: Napoleon Bonaparte poured a huge army into Saint-Domingue to win back the colony, but the rebels and yellow fever destroyed it. With his dream of an empire in the Americas in ruins, Napoleon made a sudden decision in 1803 that reshaped the map of North America. What did he do?
answer: Sold the entire Louisiana Territory to the United States, doubling its size
choices: Sold the entire Louisiana Territory to the United States, doubling its size
Invaded Canada to seize a fresh base from the British
Sent his fleet to burn the ports of the United States in revenge
Handed Saint-Domingue back to Spain in exchange for Florida
context: Because losing Saint-Domingue wrecked his plans for an American empire, Napoleon sold the whole Louisiana Territory to the United States in 1803 for about $15 million — doubling the size of the country. The slaves' fight for freedom indirectly reshaped the map of a continent. (Source: History.com, 'The Louisiana Purchase Was Driven by a Slave Rebellion.')

question: The enslaved people of Saint-Domingue won their freedom and founded Haiti in 1804, the only country ever created by a successful slave revolt, but France refused to recognize it. In 1825 France sent warships and set one staggering condition for its recognition. What did France force the Haitians to do?
answer: Pay 150 million francs to repay the former slave-owners for their lost slaves
choices: Pay 150 million francs to repay the former slave-owners for their lost slaves
Return all freed people to their former masters within ten years
Give back half the island's land to the French planters who had fled
Swear loyalty to the French king and fly his flag over their ports
context: France made the freed nation pay its former enslavers as the price of being recognized — a crushing 'independence debt' Haiti did not finish paying until 1910, generations later. (Source: Wikipedia, Haitian independence debt; NPR Planet Money, 'The Greatest Heist in History.')

question: Hammurabi had his 282 laws carved into a single upright black stone more than two meters tall, around 1754 BC, and set it up in public in Babylon so that anyone could come and hear the laws read aloud. Archaeologists have a special word for a tall carved pillar like this. What is it?
answer: a stele
choices: a stele
a tablet
a scroll
a ledger
context: The stele still stands today in the Louvre in Paris. The whole code (about 4,130 lines) is carved in cuneiform in the Old Babylonian dialect of Akkadian. It is the earliest famous written law code -- the deep root of the idea that the law is written down, public, and read aloud to all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi ; https://www.louvre.fr/en/the-code-of-hammurabi

question: Hammurabi of Babylon made the punishment mirror the crime in the most famous of his 282 laws, carved almost 4,000 years ago. A man who blinded a nobleman's eye had his own eye blinded in return. What is the Latin name for this 'eye for an eye' principle?
answer: lex talionis
choices: lex talionis
habeas corpus
casus belli
quid pro quo
context: Lex talionis means 'the law of retaliation.' Law 196 states it plainly: 'If a man has blinded the eye of a member of the awilum class, his eye will be blinded.' It is a real, nameable legal principle, not just a saying. Source: https://ehammurabi.org/law/196 ; https://www.louvre.fr/en/the-code-of-hammurabi

question: 'I am the ___ who brings peace, with a staff that is straight,' wrote Hammurabi of Babylon in the closing words of his law code. He did not call himself a warlord or a god, but chose a humble title for one who gently guards and guides his people. Which title fills the blank?
answer: shepherd
choices: shepherd
high priest
judge
father
context: Hammurabi calls himself 'the shepherd' of his people in the epilogue: 'I am the shepherd who brings peace, with a staff that is straight.' The shepherd-with-staff image for a just ruler is one of the oldest in recorded history. Source: https://ehammurabi.org/epilogue ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammurabi

question: Babylonians who looked up at the top of Hammurabi's black law stone saw the king on his feet before a seated god of justice, Shamash, lord of the sun, as if receiving the laws from him. Any of them would have known the god by one clear sign carved into the stone. What was it?
answer: flames rising from his shoulders
choices: flames rising from his shoulders
a crown of bright golden rays
a blazing torch in each hand
a glowing disk above his head
context: Shamash is identified by flames bursting from his shoulders and by a footrest shaped like the mountains over which he rises each morning. The relief is the famous 'Shamash handing Hammurabi the law' image. Source: https://www.louvre.fr/en/the-code-of-hammurabi ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi

question: Hammurabi, king of Babylon, began his 282 laws with justice in court. His Law 1 dealt with a man who accused another of murder but could not prove the charge, and it turned the punishment back on the accuser. What did the law say happened to him?
answer: the accuser was killed
choices: the accuser was killed
the accuser was fined
the accuser was branded
the accuser was exiled
context: Law 1: 'If a man accuses another man and charges him with homicide, but cannot bring proof against him, his accuser shall be killed.' Bringing a deadly charge you couldn't prove cost you your own life -- an early version of putting the burden of proof on the accuser. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi

question: Shutruk-Nahhunte, an Elamite king, sacked Babylon around 1158 BC and carried off a black stone more than two meters tall as a war trophy. Carved on it were 282 laws laid down centuries earlier by a famous Babylonian king, best known for the rule 'an eye for an eye.' What was that king's name?
answer: Hammurabi
choices: Hammurabi
Nebuchadnezzar
Sargon the Great
Gilgamesh
context: The Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte (reigned c. 1185-1160 BC) carried the stele off as plunder to his capital, Susa, in modern Iran. A French archaeological team under Jacques de Morgan rediscovered it there in 1901; the Louvre has displayed it since 1904. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi ; https://www.louvre.fr/en/the-code-of-hammurabi

question: Under Law 230, Hammurabi set a chillingly literal price for a builder whose shoddy house collapsed and crushed the homeowner's son to death. The builder paid in the most terrible way the law could find. What did Law 230 demand?
answer: the builder's own son was killed
choices: the builder's own son was killed
the builder himself was executed
the builder paid the owner in silver
the builder was sold into slavery
context: Law 230: 'If it has caused the death of the son of the owner of the house, they shall kill that builder's son.' The builder's innocent son died for the homeowner's son -- the eye-for-an-eye principle turned into a vendetta against a man's family. Source: https://ehammurabi.org/law/230 ; https://ehammurabi.org/law/229

question: With Law 218, Hammurabi put a surgeon's own body on the line for his skill. Babylonian surgeons operated with a real bronze blade called a lancet. If one of them cut open a nobleman and the patient died, what was done to the surgeon?
answer: his hand was cut off
choices: his hand was cut off
his eye was put out
his fee was seized
his tongue was cut out
context: Law 218: 'If a physician performs major surgery with a bronze lancet... and thus causes the awilum's death, or opens his temple and blinds his eye, they shall cut off his hand.' Yet by Law 215, a surgeon who succeeded with that same bronze lancet earned ten shekels of silver. Source: https://ehammurabi.org/law/218 ; https://sacred-texts.com/ane/ham/ham07.htm

question: In Law 2, Hammurabi let no human judge decide a charge of witchcraft. The accused man was flung into the Euphrates, and the river alone gave the verdict, a trial by ordeal. By the law's own logic, which outcome cleared him of the charge?
answer: surviving the plunge
choices: surviving the plunge
sinking to the bottom
floating to the top
being swept downstream
context: Law 2 prescribes trial by river ordeal: if the river drowned the accused, the accuser took their estate; but 'if the River has cleared that man and he has come out alright,' the false accuser was executed. The river itself delivered the verdict. Source: https://ehammurabi.org/law/2

question: By Law 202, Hammurabi ordered sixty blows, counted out in public before the whole assembly, for any commoner who slapped a man of higher rank across the cheek. The law even named the instrument for the beating. Which one did it name?
answer: an ox-hide whip
choices: an ox-hide whip
a heavy bronze rod
a sharp willow cane
a thick knotted rope
context: Law 202: 'If a man has struck the cheek of a man who is of higher rank than he, he will be struck with an ox whip sixty times in the assembly.' Punishment was public and tied to social rank. By Law 205, a slave who struck a free man had his ear cut off. Source: https://ehammurabi.org/law/202 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi

question: For the very same injury, Hammurabi set different punishments by the victim's class.
