A man who blinded a noble lost his own eye, but for putting out a commoner's eye, Law 198 did not call for blinding the attacker in return. It set a fixed price instead. What did Law 198 make the attacker pay?
answer: a mina of silver
choices: a mina of silver
a year of service
ten head of cattle
a plot of farmland
context: Same injury, three different prices by rank: a noble's eye for an eye (Law 196); a commoner's eye paid off with one mina of silver (Law 198); a slave's eye costing only 'half his value' in silver (Law 199). The famous 'eye for an eye' applied in full only between social equals. Source: https://ehammurabi.org/law/196 ; https://ehammurabi.org/law/198 ; https://ehammurabi.org/law/199

question: The Hebrews wrote down the law of Moses centuries after Hammurabi, and it shared his 'eye for an eye' rule, but it split from him sharply on rank. Where Hammurabi cut off a slave's ear for striking a free man, the law in Exodus did the opposite for a slave whose master knocked out his eye or tooth. What happened to that slave?
answer: the slave was set free
choices: the slave was set free
the slave was paid silver
the slave was given land
the slave was sent home
context: Honest contrast: lex talionis in Hammurabi's Code (~1754 BC) predates the Hebrew Torah versions by centuries. The key difference -- Hammurabi sorted punishments by class, while the Hebrew code posited one set of laws for the whole community, and where Hammurabi cut off a slave's hand, Exodus set the injured slave free (Exodus 21:26-27). Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Lex_talionis ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hebraic-law

question: Liu Bang founded a dynasty around 202 BC that went on to rule China for four centuries. Its name outlived every one of its emperors: well over a billion Chinese still use it for their ethnic group today. What do they call themselves?
answer: The Han people
choices: The Han people
The Qin people
The Tang people
The Zhou people
context: More people are named after the Han dynasty than after any other in history. The name traces to the Han River region, where the dynasty's founder first built his base. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Chinese and Britannica, Han dynasty.

question: When Liu Bang took the throne as Emperor Gaozu around 202 BC, after overthrowing the harsh Qin dynasty, he founded a line of emperors that would last four centuries. Historians ever since have marveled at one fact about who he was before he seized power. What was startling about where he came from?
answer: He was born a peasant commoner
choices: He was born a peasant commoner
He was a captured Qin prince
He was a wealthy Zhou nobleman
He was a foreign Xiongnu general
context: Liu Bang was a man of common birth with no royal blood who rose all the way to emperor, founding the dynasty that still gives the Han people their name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Chinese and Britannica, Han dynasty.

question: Zhang Qian set out west for Emperor Wu around 138 BC with about a hundred men, seeking allies against the Xiongnu, the steppe nomads to the north. The Xiongnu caught him and held him for about thirteen years before he escaped and struggled home. Of the hundred who set out, how many made it back?
answer: Two men
choices: Two men
Twelve men
Forty men
Ninety men
context: Only Zhang Qian and his loyal guide Ganfu survived the journey. During his captivity Zhang Qian married a Xiongnu wife and had a son, but he never abandoned the emperor's mission. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Qian.

question: Zhang Heng built a machine for the Han court in 132 that no one had seen before: a bronze urn circled by eight dragons, each gripping a ball in its mouth above an open-mouthed bronze toad. When a tremor from a distant earthquake reached the urn, a pendulum inside swung. What happened next?
answer: A dragon dropped its ball into a toad's mouth
choices: A dragon dropped its ball into a toad's mouth
A bell rang out from the center of the urn
A needle swung across a marked dial
A toad leapt toward the distant tremor
context: A tremor tipped an internal pendulum, and a single dragon released its ball with a loud clang into the toad below it, pointing toward the direction of the quake. The device was called the Houfeng Didong Yi. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/ancient-technology/incredible-earthquake-detector-invented-nearly-2000-years-ago-001377.

question: Zhang Qian, Emperor Wu's envoy, walked through a market in Bactria, a kingdom shaped by Greek culture thousands of miles from home, and was startled to find bamboo and cloth made in Sichuan, in southwest China. He had not carried them there himself. What did finding them reveal had existed all along?
answer: Trade roads already linked China to the wider world
choices: Trade roads already linked China to the wider world
Bactria had once been ruled by Chinese kings
Greek traders had recently visited Sichuan
Greek merchants had carried the goods from China themselves
context: Chinese goods had beaten Zhang Qian to Bactria along routes no Han official had mapped. His report of this to Emperor Wu is what opened the official Silk Road. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Qian.

question: Emperor Wu heard from his envoy Zhang Qian, back from Central Asia around 130 BC, of 'heavenly horses' from Dayuan, out in the Ferghana Valley: tall, powerful animals that looked as if they sweated blood and outmatched any horse in China. When Dayuan refused to sell them, how did Emperor Wu respond?
answer: He launched a war to seize the horses
choices: He launched a war to seize the horses
He offered Dayuan a royal marriage alliance
He banned all trade with Dayuan
He sent spies to steal the breeding stock
context: It became the War of the Heavenly Horses (104 and 102 BC). General Li Guangli's second expedition was enormous, and the Han came home with roughly 3,000 of the prized horses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Heavenly_Horses.

question: Court officials scoffed at Zhang Heng's earthquake machine, until one day it gave its signal in Luoyang, the capital, though no one in the city had felt the ground move at all. What arrived days later?
answer: A messenger arrived reporting a quake hundreds of miles away
choices: A messenger arrived reporting a quake hundreds of miles away
A second dragon released its ball moments later
A rival official accused him of faking the drop
An order from the emperor to destroy the device
context: The galloping messenger from the Long region (Gansu) reported an earthquake exactly where the dragon had pointed, far beyond where anyone in the capital could feel it. The doubters fell silent. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/ancient-technology/incredible-earthquake-detector-invented-nearly-2000-years-ago-001377.

question: Sima Qian was at work on China's first great history, the Shiji, when he made the mistake of defending a defeated general before Emperor Wu around 99 BC. The emperor sentenced him to death. He was offered one legal way out, at a shattering personal price, and he accepted it. What did Sima Qian choose, and why?
answer: Castration, so he could live to finish his history
choices: Castration, so he could live to finish his history
Exile, so he could escape the emperor's reach
Execution, so he could die with his honor intact
A heavy fine, so he could buy back his freedom
context: Sima Qian accepted castration and disgrace rather than die, so he could complete his father's life-work, the Shiji ('Records of the Grand Historian'), the foundational history of China that still records the Han. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sima_Qian and worldhistory.org/Sima_Qian.

question: Rich Roman women paraded through the forum in see-through gowns of Chinese silk, carried thousands of miles along the Silk Road, and Rome's moralists were alarmed. In AD 16, under the emperor Tiberius, the Senate answered with a formal ban. What did the Senate forbid?
answer: It barred men from wearing silk
choices: It barred men from wearing silk
It taxed all silk at half its value
It outlawed all trade with the silk people
It banned silk from the public games
context: To Rome, China was the land of the Seres, the 'silk people,' and the empire itself was called Daqin, 'Great Qin.' Pliny the Elder complained the eastern luxury trade drained Rome of about 100 million sesterces a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Roman_relations and https://www.unrv.com/economy/silk.php.

question: Ban Chao, a general, sent his envoy Gan Ying west in 97 to try to reach Rome itself. Gan Ying pushed as far as the Persian Gulf, farther west than any Chinese official had gone, and there Parthian sailors met him; the Parthians grew rich standing between the two empires. How did they turn him back?
answer: They scared him off with tales of a deadly two-year voyage
choices: They scared him off with tales of a deadly two-year voyage
They demanded a toll he could not possibly pay
They seized his ship and his entire crew
They offered to carry his message the rest of the way
context: The Parthians warned Gan Ying the sea crossing could take two years and that homesick sailors died on the way. He turned back, and China and Rome never met directly that day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Roman_relations.

question: Merchants, monks and worshippers of many faiths jostled through the wide grid of streets in Chang'an, today's Xi'an, the walled Tang capital at the eastern end of the Silk Road, in the 700s. Among all the cities on earth at that time, where did Chang'an rank in size?
answer: It was the largest city on earth, with about a million people
choices: It was the largest city on earth, with about a million people
It was the third-largest city, just behind Rome and Baghdad
It was the largest city in Asia but smaller than Constantinople
It was a mid-sized trading town that grew famous only later
context: Tang Chang'an held roughly one million people inside its packed-earth walls, with millions more in the suburbs — the biggest city in the world. Buddhists, Taoists, Zoroastrians, Nestorian Christians and Manichaeans all worshipped there at once. Source: worldhistory.org / Wikipedia (Tang dynasty).

question: Court skywatchers of the Song dynasty logged a 'guest star' on 4 July 1054, so brilliant that it shone in full daylight for 23 days before it faded from the sky. That star had blown itself apart, and astronomers still train telescopes on what it left behind. What did it leave?
answer: The Crab Nebula
choices: The Crab Nebula
The Ring Nebula
The Veil Nebula
A black hole at its center
context: That 1054 'guest star' was a supernova — a star blowing itself apart. It blazed in daylight for 23 days and stayed visible at night for about 21 months; its expanding cloud of debris is the Crab Nebula. Chinese court records (Song Shi / Song Huiyao) pinned down the date and brightness. Source: jila.colorado.edu / earthmagazine.org.

question: Soldiers in China had learned by the 900s to pack gunpowder into a bamboo or paper tube, lash it to a spear and light it, so that it shot a roaring jet of flame and shrapnel at the enemy. Historians of weapons see this fire-spitting spear, the fire lance, as the direct ancestor of one later invention. Which one?
answer: The gun
choices: The gun
The cannonball
The rocket
The land mine
context: The fire lance (huo qiang) is regarded as the ancestor of every firearm: a powder-filled tube on a pole that blasted flame and debris. Its earliest known image is a mid-10th-century Buddhist painting from Dunhuang showing an armored demon firing one. Lengthen and harden the tube, and you are on the road to the gun. Source: Wikipedia (History of the firearm) / military-history.fandom.com.

question: The London audience at the premiere of Handel's Messiah rose to its feet during the Hallelujah Chorus because of one man in the crowd, the story goes, and audiences still stand for it today. Who is said to have stood up first, so that everyone else stood too?
answer: King George II
choices: King George II
Handel himself
Charles Jennens
The Archbishop of Canterbury
context: By legend, King George II rose to his feet during the Hallelujah Chorus at the London premiere, and since no one stays seated while the king stands, the entire audience stood with him. The custom of standing has continued ever since. Historians actually doubt the story: there is no convincing evidence the king was even present, and the earliest written mention of the standing custom is a letter from 1756, years after the premiere. Source: https://floridaorchestra.org/messiah/

question: George Frideric Handel began Messiah in the summer of 1741: 259 pages of choruses, solos and full orchestration, a work that might take a composer the better part of a year. How long did it take Handel to write the whole score?
answer: 24 days
choices: 24 days
8 months
two years
a single night
context: Handel wrote all 259 pages of Messiah in just 24 days, working at his home on Brook Street in London. By accounts from the time, during those weeks he barely slept or ate; servants who brought his meals often found them untouched. He wrote only the music — the words were assembled by his librettist Charles Jennens from the King James Bible and the Book of Common Prayer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messiah_(Handel)

question: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and then went back into slave territory again and again, through slave-catcher country by night, to lead her family, her friends and total strangers out. Abolitionists gave her a nickname from the Hebrew Bible, the name of a leader who brought his people out of slavery. What did they call her?
answer: Moses
choices: Moses
Joshua
Deborah
Miriam
context: Just as Moses led the Israelites out of Egypt, Tubman led the enslaved out of bondage. Abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison is credited with popularizing the title. Source: National Women's History Museum, 'Harriet Tubman' (womenshistory.org); NPS, 'Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad' (nps.gov).

question: John Tubman, a free Black man, married an enslaved young woman around 1844, and from then on she went by Harriet, her mother's name. That was not the name she had been given at her birth in Maryland around 1822. What was she called as a girl?
answer: Araminta Ross, called 'Minty'
choices: Araminta Ross, called 'Minty'
Henrietta Greene, called 'Hattie'
Cassandra Ross, called 'Cassie'
Adeline Ross, called 'Addie'
context: She took the name Harriet, her mother's name, around 1844 when she married John Tubman, a free Black man. Source: Wikipedia, 'Harriet Tubman'; National Parks Conservation Association, '5 Facts You Might Not Know About Harriet Tubman' (npca.org).

question: An overseer hurled something at an enslaved person who was trying to run away, and it struck the teenage Harriet Tubman on the head instead. The blow cracked her skull and left her with seizures and sudden sleeping spells all her life. What had the overseer thrown?
answer: A two-pound iron weight
choices: A two-pound iron weight
A heavy wooden club
A sharp field hoe
A large river stone
context: She said it 'broke my skull.' She lay unconscious for about two days with no medical care. Source: Wikipedia, 'Harriet Tubman'; PMC/NIH, 'Harriet Tubman's Hypersomnia' (PMC10713879).

question: Harriet Tubman stood up at a suffrage convention for women in 1896 and looked back on her years guiding people north along the Underground Railroad, the hidden chain of safe houses and guides. She made one proud boast that most other conductors could never truthfully make. What was her boast?
answer: "I never ran my train off the track, and I never lost a passenger"
choices: "I never ran my train off the track, and I never lost a passenger"
"I freed more souls than any other man alive"
"I crossed that river more than a hundred times"
"I never once carried a weapon on the road"
context: She said this at an 1896 suffrage convention. 'Conductors' and 'passengers' were Underground Railroad code for guides and the people they led to freedom. Source: U.S. National Park Service, 'Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad' (nps.gov); NPS, 'Travel with Tubman'.

question: A frightened runaway in Harriet Tubman's party lost his nerve one night on the road north and demanded to turn back, a move that could get the whole group captured, whipped or killed. Tubman pulled out the loaded revolver she always carried, pointed it at his chest, and spoke. What did she say?
answer: "You'll be free or die"
choices: "You'll be free or die"
"Move now, or I leave you"
"Walk on, and don't look back"
"Be quiet, or we all hang"
context: Every person she warned went on. Days later, the same man reportedly crossed safely into Canada. Wikipedia renders the line as 'Go on or die.' Source: Sarah Hopkins Bradford, 'Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman' (1869); Wikipedia, 'Harriet Tubman'.

question: Fugitives waiting in a hiding place in the 1850s knew that Harriet Tubman had come to lead them north when they heard her sing. She used one particular spiritual as her coded signal that it was time to gather their bundles and go. Which song was it?
answer: "Go Down, Moses"
choices: "Go Down, Moses"
"Swing Low, Sweet Chariot"
"Steal Away to Jesus"
"Wade in the Water"
context: By her own account in Sarah Bradford's 1869 biography, this was one of two code songs she used. Source: Sarah Hopkins Bradford, 'Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman' (1869); Wikipedia, 'Songs of the Underground Railroad'.

question: On her final rescue, in 1860, Harriet Tubman led a party that had a baby from the Ennalls family in it. They had to creep for miles past slave patrols and bounty hunters, and one loud wail from the infant would have given them all away. How did Tubman and the fugitives keep the baby silent?
answer: They dosed it with paregoric, an opium-based sedative, to make it sleep
choices: They dosed it with paregoric, an opium-based sedative, to make it sleep
They gagged it gently with a strip of cloth
They left it behind with a trusted free family
They took turns nursing it through every night
context: The infant was a child of the Ennalls family, kept quiet with paregoric while slave patrols passed nearby. Source: Wikipedia, 'Harriet Tubman' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Tubman).

question: John Brown, the white abolitionist, was planning an armed raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, hoping to spark a slave uprising, when he turned to Harriet Tubman for help in 1858. He deeply respected her skill at leading people out of slave territory, so he gave her a military title whenever he spoke of her. What did he call her?
answer: "General Tubman"
choices: "General Tubman"
"Captain Minty"
"Colonel Moses"
"Major Ross"
context: Brown valued her tactical knowledge of the routes and the country. Source: Wikipedia, 'Harriet Tubman' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Tubman).

question: Three Union gunboats steamed up South Carolina's Combahee River in June 1863 with Harriet Tubman as their guide. Using intelligence she had gathered, she steered them past hidden Confederate mines, and the raid set more than 700 enslaved people free. Which first did the raid make her?
answer: The first woman to lead an armed U.S. military assault
choices: The first woman to lead an armed U.S. military assault
The first woman commissioned as a Union army officer
The first woman awarded a Civil War battlefield medal
The first woman to command her own naval gunboat
context: The three gunboats were the John Adams, the Harriet A. Weed, and the Sentinel. Source: HISTORY.com, 'After the Underground Railroad, Harriet Tubman Led a Brazen Civil War Raid'; National Museum of African American History & Culture, 'The Combahee Ferry Raid'.

question: A Boston surgeon opened Harriet Tubman's skull around 1898, at her own request, because her old head wound had brought on unbearable pain. She refused any anesthetic, and afterward she put on her bonnet and walked home. What did she bite down on during the operation?
answer: A bullet
choices: A bullet
A leather strap
A wooden dowel
A folded rag
context: She bit down on a bullet just as she had watched Union soldiers do during battlefield amputations. Source: National Parks Conservation Association, '5 Facts You Might Not Know About Harriet Tubman' (npca.org); NPS, 'Harriet Tubman's Boston: 1890s'; PMC/NIH PMC10713879.

question: Frederick Douglass wrote Harriet Tubman a tribute that set his own very public battle against slavery beside her secret, dangerous one. Except for John Brown, he wrote, no one he knew had faced more danger for the enslaved. How did he draw the contrast between his labors and hers?
answer: "I have wrought in the day; you in the night"
choices: "I have wrought in the day; you in the night"
"I spoke before crowds; you walked the roads alone"
"My words reached thousands; your hands freed hundreds"
"I fought with the pen; you fought with the gun"
context: Douglass added that, excepting John Brown, he knew of no one who had willingly faced more peril to serve the enslaved than she had. Source: Wikipedia, 'Harriet Tubman', quoting Douglass's 1868 letter.

question: Kate Clifford Larson, a historian, combed through bills of sale, court records and family letters in the 2000s to check the legend of Harriet Tubman: 19 daring trips into the slave South, more than 300 people freed and a $40,000 reward on her head. What does the documentary record show instead?
answer: About 13 trips, freeing roughly 70 people
choices: About 13 trips, freeing roughly 70 people
About 19 trips, freeing roughly 300 people
About 30 trips, freeing roughly 200 people
About 25 trips, freeing roughly 150 people
context: Her instructions helped 50-60 more escape on their own. No record of any $40,000 bounty exists; that figure first appeared in an 1867 plea supporting her pension. The smaller, documented number is no less heroic. Source: Wikipedia, 'Harriet Tubman' (reward-myth analysis); NPS, 'Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad'.  (Legend.)

question: Charlemagne received a living gift at his court in Aachen in July 802, sent by Harun al-Rashid from Baghdad to dazzle him. A Jewish envoy named Isaac had sailed it to Italy, then walked it over the Alps. What was the gift?
answer: A live elephant named Abul-Abbas
choices: A live elephant named Abul-Abbas
A white stallion named Tencendur
A trained falcon from the desert
A pair of roaring lions in a cage
context: Harun al-Rashid's elephant Abul-Abbas ("father of intelligence") was the only elephant in all of Western Europe. Isaac escorted it by ship to Porto Venere near Genoa in October 801, wintered it in Vercelli, then walked it over the Alps, reaching Charlemagne at Aachen on 20 July 802. It lived about eight years and died in 810 at Lippeham on the Rhine — and the Royal Frankish Annals, which normally recorded only kings, wars, and eclipses, paused to note the elephant's death. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abul-Abbas)

question: Harun al-Rashid sent Charlemagne a brass water clock that the Franks thought almost magic. Every hour, the Frankish royal annals reported, a ball fell onto a cymbal and twelve little figures came out through twelve windows, closing each one behind them. What were the twelve figures?
answer: Mechanical horsemen who rode out on the hour
choices: Mechanical horsemen who rode out on the hour
Singing brass birds that flapped their wings
Marching soldiers who beat little drums
Robed monks who bowed and rang bells
context: Per the Royal Frankish Annals, the clock chimed by dropping twelve brazen balls one per hour onto a cymbal, and twelve mechanical horsemen stepped out of twelve windows on the hour, closing the windows behind them. The Franks, who had no such machine, saw it as near-magical. The full gift caravan also included silks, ivory chessmen, perfumes, and a great many-colored tent. (laphamsquarterly.org; muslimheritage.com/baghdad-clock)

question: Antoine Galland, a French scholar, added Aladdin and Ali Baba to the Thousand and One Nights in the early 1700s. Those two tales, the most famous in the collection, have no old Arabic manuscript behind them at all. Where did Galland get the stories?
answer: From a Syrian storyteller, Hanna Diyab, who told them to him
choices: From a Syrian storyteller, Hanna Diyab, who told them to him
From a hidden manuscript he found in a Cairo library
From the personal diary of the caliph Harun al-Rashid
From an old Persian poem he translated himself
context: Aladdin, Ali Baba, and Sinbad's voyages are "orphan tales" with no original Arabic manuscript. Antoine Galland (translating 1704–1717) got Aladdin and Ali Baba from a Syrian storyteller named Hanna Diyab; Diyab's role was only firmly confirmed by scholars in 2015. The legendary caliph who wanders the Nights in disguise, Harun al-Rashid, was a real ruler (786–809) — but these particular famous tales were never part of the old Arabic core. (pookpress.co.uk; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aladdin)

question: Hatshepsut took the throne of Egypt for herself in the 1400s BC and reigned for about twenty years as a full pharaoh, a king and not a queen. Custom said a pharaoh must look like a man, so her carvings gave her a man's body and one piece of royal gear. What did they add?
answer: The ceremonial false beard of a pharaoh
choices: The ceremonial false beard of a pharaoh
The leopard-skin robe of a high priest
A crown carved in the shape of a falcon
A bronze war helmet
context: To rule as 'king' rather than 'queen,' Hatshepsut (reigned in the 1400s BCE) was depicted with a male body and the ceremonial false beard Egyptian tradition demanded of a pharaoh. She took full royal titles and called herself 'Lady of the Two Lands.' Source: nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/hatshepsut

question: Thutmose III had been a boy when his stepmother Hatshepsut governed for him and later made herself pharaoh. After she died around 1458 BC, he struck at her memory. To the Egyptians, what he did could destroy a person even in the afterlife. What did he order done?
answer: Her name and image were chiseled off the stone
choices: Her name and image were chiseled off the stone
Her golden statues were melted down for coins
Her great temple was torn down stone by stone
Her body was carried out and burned in the desert
context: Thutmose III had Hatshepsut's name and image chiseled off many monuments and left her off the official king lists; to the Egyptians, erasing a name wiped a person out even in the afterlife. He left the inside reliefs of her temple intact, and she was nearly forgotten until scholars decoded the hieroglyphs at Deir el-Bahri in the 1800s. Source: worldhistory.org/article/1100/the-temple-of-hatshepsut/

question: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady of the Japanese court, finished a long, deep story about a nobleman and his loves around the year 1000, centuries before anything like it was written in Europe. Because it came so early, what do scholars widely call her book?
answer: The world's first novel
choices: The world's first novel
The world's first poem
The world's first play
The world's first history
context: The book is The Tale of Genji, following the 'Shining Prince' Hikaru Genji. Murasaki wrote it in the Heian period (794-1185), centuries before the European novel form, which is why it is widely called the world's first novel. Sources: britannica.com/topic/The-Tale-of-Genji ; worldhistory.org/Tale_of_Genji/

question: The court lady who wrote The Tale of Genji went by names that were not her own, since Heian manners forbade using a person's real name, and her birth name is lost. History kept the nickname Murasaki, which means purple wisteria. Where did that nickname most likely come from?
answer: A heroine she invented in her own novel
choices: A heroine she invented in her own novel
A purple robe she wore at the empress's court
A wisteria garden outside her family home
A purple seal she pressed on her letters
context: 'Shikibu' came from her father's post at the Shikibu-sho (Ministry of Ceremonials); 'Murasaki' (purple wisteria) was likely given to her at court after the heroine she herself created in The Tale of Genji — so the author of the world's first novel ended up named after her own character. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murasaki_Shikibu ; newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Murasaki_Shikibu

question: Henry Ford sold his Model T in many colors when it first appeared in 1908. From about 1914 to 1925, though, he allowed only one, because that paint dried the fastest. Which color did every Model T wear in those years?
answer: Black
choices: Black
Green
Grey
Red
context: In his 1922 autobiography 'My Life and Work,' Ford wrote: 'Any customer can have a car painted any colour that he wants so long as it is black.' Black-only ran roughly 1914-1925 because black paint dried fastest on the fast-moving line. Source: Henry Ford, 'My Life and Work' (1922); pressreader.com 'Any colour - if it's black'.

question: Henry Ford set half-built Model Ts moving past his men on a line in October 1913, each man at one small job. Before that, putting one car together had taken more than 12 hours. How long did a Model T take once the moving line was running?
answer: About 1.5 hours
choices: About 1.5 hours
About 6 hours
About 9 hours
About 11 hours
context: The moving line cut a Model T from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes (1.5 hours), refined to roughly 93 man-minutes within a year. The famous line debuted October 7, 1913. Source: history.com 'Moving assembly line debuts at Ford factory'; corporate.ford.com 'Assembly Line Revolution'.

question: Henry Ford was turning out close to 10,000 cars a day in 1925. At the peak, finished Model Ts rolled off his line one hard on the heels of another, with hardly a pause between them. How often did a finished Model T come off the line?
answer: Every 24 seconds
choices: Every 24 seconds
Every 90 seconds
Every 240 seconds
Every 540 seconds
context: A finished Model T rolled off about every 24 seconds at peak, and Ford built close to 10,000 cars a day in 1925. Source: automotivehistory.org 'October 7, 1913 - Model T chassis moving assembly line'; bestsellingcarsblog.com.

question: Henry Ford was losing men from his moving line so fast in 1913 that his worker turnover hit about 380 percent; the work was that dull. On 5 January 1914 he answered with a new daily wage for eight hours' work, over twice the old minimum, meant to keep men on the job and let them buy the cars they built. What daily wage did Ford announce?
answer: $5 a day
choices: $5 a day
$4 a day
$6 a day
$7 a day
context: Ford's $5 day for an eight-hour shift more than doubled the old $2.34 nine-hour minimum, partly to fight monotony that drove ~380% turnover. The logic: pay workers enough to buy what they build. Source: EBSCO Research Starters 'Henry Ford Institutes the $5.00 a Day Minimum Wage'; thehenryford.org 'Ford's Five-Dollar Day'.

question: Henry Ford attached strings to his new high wage. To collect the full pay, a man had to live what Ford counted a proper life, and inspectors from a special company department visited workers' homes to check that each one stayed sober, kept his house clean and rented no rooms to lodgers. What was the department called?
answer: The Sociological Department
choices: The Sociological Department
The Inspection Bureau
The Welfare Office
The Conduct Committee
context: Ford's Sociological Department inspected workers' homes; a man who failed the 'proper life' test had his profit-sharing withheld for six months. Source: EBSCO Research Starters 'Henry Ford Institutes the $5.00 a Day Minimum Wage'; thehenryford.org 'Ford's Five-Dollar Day'.

question: Henry Hudson was hunting a sea passage to Asia when his half-starved crew, locked all winter in the ice of the bay later named for him, turned on him in June 1611. What did the mutineers do to him, his young son John and a few loyal and sick men?
answer: Cast them adrift in a tiny open boat, never to be seen again
choices: Cast them adrift in a tiny open boat, never to be seen again
Locked them in the hold and sailed them home to stand trial
Marooned them on a frozen island with a year of supplies
Handed them over to a rival Dutch captain for ransom
context: When the spring ice broke, Hudson wanted to press on to Asia while the exhausted crew wanted to go home; they set him, his son, and about seven men adrift in a small boat (a shallop) in Hudson Bay. They vanished. Source: https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/maritime-history/henry-hudson-north-west-passage-expedition-1610-11 ; https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/june-22/hudson-set-adrift-by-mutineers

question: Francisco Vázquez de Coronado led an enormous Spanish expedition north out of Mexico in 1540. He was chasing an old legend of Cibola, the Seven Cities of Gold, said to shine with treasure. When his men finally rode up to the first of the golden cities, what did they really find?
answer: Ordinary mud-and-stone Zuni villages, with no gold at all
choices: Ordinary mud-and-stone Zuni villages, with no gold at all
A walled fortress packed with Aztec treasure
A city already burned to the ground by rivals
A river of gold dust guarded by armored warriors
context: The fabled cities turned out to be plain Zuni Pueblo villages of mud and stone. The whole legend traced back to Fray Marcos de Niza, who relied on reports from the enslaved African scout Estevanico. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1754/cibola---the-seven-cities-of-gold--coronado/ ; https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/coronado-expedition

question: Samuel de Champlain and two other Frenchmen joined their native allies against about 200 Iroquois in July 1609, near the spot where Fort Ticonderoga later stood. A guide pointed out the three enemy chiefs. Champlain raised his arquebus, an early gun the Iroquois had never seen, and fired one shot. What happened?
answer: He killed two of the chiefs at once, and the rest fled in terror
choices: He killed two of the chiefs at once, and the rest fled in terror
The gun misfired and his allies had to drag him to safety
The shot missed but the noise alone scattered the warriors
He wounded one chief, who then surrendered the whole band
context: The Iroquois shields stopped arrows but not bullets; two chiefs fell to one shot and the terrified warriors fled. The moment ignited generations of French-Iroquois enmity. Source: https://minnstate.pressbooks.pub/ushistory1/chapter/lake-champlain-1609/ ; https://www.americanhistorycentral.com/entries/lake-champlain-battle-1609/

question: René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, canoed down the Mississippi to the sea in 1682, the first European to reach its mouth that way, and claimed all of Louisiana for France. On a later voyage by sea he overshot the river, lost his ships and was stranded in Texas. How did La Salle finally die there in 1687?
answer: His own frustrated, mutinous men ambushed and murdered him
choices: His own frustrated, mutinous men ambushed and murdered him
He drowned trying to swim back to find the lost river
A fever swept the camp and killed him within days
He was captured and executed by a Spanish patrol
context: Unable to find the Mississippi again, La Salle's exhausted men turned on him and shot him in an ambush on March 19, 1687. Source: https://www.humanitiestexas.org/programs/tx-originals/list/ren%C3%A9-robert-la-salle ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9-Robert_Cavelier,_Sieur_de_La_Salle

question: Francisco Vázquez de Coronado, hungry for gold, trusted a captive guide the Spaniards called El Turco. The guide swore that a far richer kingdom, Quivira, lay out on the plains. The trail led to what is now Kansas and ended among villages of grass huts. When Coronado pressed him for the truth, what did El Turco confess?
answer: The natives had invented Quivira to lure the Spanish out to die in the wilderness
choices: The natives had invented Quivira to lure the Spanish out to die in the wilderness
He had simply lost his bearings and led them the wrong direction
The gold of Quivira had been hidden by its people just before they arrived
He was a Spanish spy testing Coronado's loyalty to the crown
context: El Turco admitted his people had made up the golden kingdom to draw the Spanish deep into the plains to perish; Coronado had him strangled and returned to Mexico bankrupt and disgraced in 1542. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1754/cibola---the-seven-cities-of-gold--coronado/ ; https://www.desertusa.com/desert-trails/coronado-expedition-quivira.html

question: Henry VIII married six times in his hunt for a male heir. English schoolchildren still learn the fates of his queens with a rhyme in pairs. Its first half tells how Catherine of Aragon was cast aside, Anne Boleyn sent to the block and Jane Seymour lost after childbirth. How does the rhyme end?
answer: "...Divorced, Beheaded, Survived"
choices: "...Divorced, Beheaded, Survived"
"...Beheaded, Divorced, Survived"
"...Divorced, Died, Beheaded"
"...Survived, Beheaded, Divorced"
context: The full rhyme is "Divorced, Beheaded, Died; Divorced, Beheaded, Survived." In order the six wives were Catherine of Aragon (divorced), Anne Boleyn (beheaded), Jane Seymour (died), Anne of Cleves (divorced), Catherine Howard (beheaded), and Catherine Parr (survived). Source: https://www.historyhit.com/the-6-wives-of-henry-viii-in-order/

question: Henry VIII wrote a book in 1521, long before his break with Rome, that defended the seven sacraments of the Church and attacked Martin Luther. Pope Leo X, grateful, rewarded him with a Latin title, and British monarchs still carry it. What was the title?
answer: "Fidei Defensor" — Defender of the Faith
choices: "Fidei Defensor" — Defender of the Faith
"Rex Catholicus" — the Catholic King
"Vicarius Christi" — Vicar of Christ
"Sacrae Maiestas" — the Sacred Majesty
context: Pope Leo X granted the title on 11 October 1521 for Henry's book the 'Assertio Septem Sacramentorum' (Defence of the Seven Sacraments). The irony is that British monarchs still carry 'Defender of the Faith' today — even after Henry's own break with Rome, the very thing the title was meant to oppose. Source: https://www.tudorsociety.com/october-11-henry-viii-becomes-defender-of-the-faith/

question: Catherine of Aragon had been Henry VIII's wife for twenty years when he tried to set her aside at a church trial in 1529. Instead of arguing law, she crossed the courtroom, knelt before the king himself and pleaded with him. What did she insist about how she had treated him?
answer: That she had been a true, humble and obedient wife who never showed a spark of discontent
choices: That she had been a true, humble and obedient wife who never showed a spark of discontent
That she had borne him more sons than any other woman in his realm
That she had brought him the richest dowry in all of Christendom
That she alone had nursed him through every illness of his reign
context: At the Blackfriars trial on 21 June 1529 Catherine knelt and appealed directly to Henry: "I have been to you a true, humble and obedient wife... I never grudged in word or countenance, or showed a visage or spark of discontent." She then refused to recognize the court's authority. Source: https://thefreelancehistorywriter.com/2017/04/14/catherine-of-aragons-speech-at-blackfriars-june-1529/

question: Anne Boleyn, the queen Henry VIII had broken with Rome to marry, heard her death sentence in 1536. Told that the king had sent to Calais for a skilled French swordsman, who would kill more swiftly than an axe, she reportedly laughed and put her hands around her throat. What did she say?
answer: "I have a little neck"
choices: "I have a little neck"
"God keep my poor child"
"Strike now, and quickly"
"The king has been good to me"
context: Anne was executed on 19 May 1536. Told the executioner was skilled, she laughed and put her hands round her throat, saying "I have a little neck." The French swordsman took her head in a single stroke. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/anne-boleyn-beheaded-facts

question: Sir Thomas More, once Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor, would not swear that the king and not the pope was head of the Church in England, and in 1535 he climbed the scaffold. He joked with the man who helped him up the shaky steps, but his last words to the crowd named where his deepest loyalty lay. How did More describe himself as he died?
answer: The King's good servant, but God's first
choices: The King's good servant, but God's first
A loyal subject who chose silence over a lie
An old man who feared no king's anger
The last honest counselor in a faithless court
context: More was beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535. Climbing the rickety scaffold he joked, "See me safe up: for my coming down, I can shift for myself," then told the crowd he died "the King's good servant, but God's first." Source: https://www.executedtoday.com/2008/07/06/1535-saint-sir-thomas-more/

question: Pope Clement VII refused to annul Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon. A real point of Church law was at stake, since Catherine had first been the wife of Henry's late brother Arthur, but the deeper obstacle was a kinsman of hers whose armies had just sacked Rome itself, and no pope dared anger him. Who was this kinsman?
answer: Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor
choices: Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor
Francis I, the King of France
Suleiman, the Ottoman Sultan
Ferdinand, the King of Aragon
context: Catherine of Aragon was the aunt of Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor, whose troops had recently sacked Rome. The Pope dared not offend him, so the annulment was blocked. The break with Rome turned above all on this political deadlock — and led directly to the 1534 Act of Supremacy making Henry "Supreme Head of the Church of England." Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/act-supremacy

question: Herodotus of Halicarnassus travelled the ancient world in the 400s BC, gathering stories from Persians, Egyptians and Greeks about the great war their fathers had just fought. He named his book with a Greek word, historie, which English later turned into history. Yet to him the word did not mean a record of the past. What did it mean?
answer: Inquiry, or investigation
choices: Inquiry, or investigation
Memory of the dead
A tale told by elders
The will of the gods
context: Herodotus's word 'historie' (historia) literally meant 'inquiry' or 'investigation' — asking questions and checking, not just passing down myth. He prized 'autopsy' (seeing for himself) over 'akoe' (mere hearsay), traveling to Egypt and Babylon to look and to question locals. That shift from myth-telling to asking questions is why he is remembered as the first true historian. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/herodotus

question: Herodotus repeated a sailors' story that a Phoenician crew, sent by Pharaoh Necho II, spent three years sailing all the way around Africa. He flatly refused to believe one detail they reported. Yet that very impossible-sounding detail is exactly what any real crew rounding the far south of Africa would witness, which is why modern historians think the voyage actually happened. What was the detail he refused to believe?
answer: The sun stood on their right hand
choices: The sun stood on their right hand
The stars wheeled backward overhead
The sea boiled at the world's edge
The days grew longer than the nights
context: Rounding southern Africa, a crew sees the midday sun to the NORTH — on their right hand as they sail west. Herodotus reported this but wrote he did NOT believe it. Because no Greek of his day knew the Southern Hemisphere works this way, his very disbelief is treated as evidence the voyage really occurred. This shows his rule for sources: 'My duty is to report what is said, but it is not my duty to believe it all alike.' Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/herodotus/herodotus-on-the-first-circumnavigation-of-africa/

question: Napoleon's scholars gave a French name to the oval loop that Egyptian scribes always drew around a pharaoh's name, in the form of a knotted rope tied in a circle, to wrap the king's name in protection. Egyptologists still use their word. What is the loop called?
answer: A cartouche
choices: A cartouche
A pylon
A scarab
An obelisk
context: A cartouche is the oval loop drawn around a king's name in hieroglyphs. It represents a looped rope, and Egyptians believed it magically protected the royal name sealed inside it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartouche

question: A Greek traveller stood before an Egyptian temple wall crowded with tiny pictures of birds, eyes, feet and reeds. The Greeks gave the script a name of their own, hieroglyphs. What does that Greek name mean in plain words?
answer: Sacred carvings
choices: Sacred carvings
Merchant tallies
Star charts
Royal seals
context: 'Hieroglyph' is Greek for 'sacred carvings' (sacred carved letters). The Egyptians themselves called their script 'gods' words' — medu netjer. Source: suzannearnold.com/blog/egyptian-hieroglyphs-and-the-rosetta-stone

question: A stonecutter sealed a dead king's name inside a protective oval on his tomb wall, for in ancient Egypt a name mattered a great deal. Many Egyptians believed that for as long as a name was still spoken or read aloud by the living, one thing would keep happening for the person who bore it. What did keeping the name alive do?
answer: It kept the person's soul living in the afterlife
choices: It kept the person's soul living in the afterlife
It doubled the size of the royal harvest
It frightened away enemy armies at the border
It forced the Nile to flood on command
context: To Egyptians a name was sacred: many believed that as long as people's names were still spoken or read, their souls would keep living in the afterlife. That is why the cartouche was said to 'preserve their essence.' Source: egyptunitedtours.com/ancient-egyptian-cartouche

question: An Egyptian scribe at his work counted one god as his patron, the keeper of the sacred library of the gods. Egyptians believed this same god had given them writing itself. Which of the gods did they thank for that gift?
answer: Thoth, the ibis-headed god
choices: Thoth, the ibis-headed god
Anubis, the jackal-headed god
Horus, the falcon-headed god
Sobek, the crocodile-headed god
context: Thoth, the ibis-headed god, was the patron of scribes, and Egyptians credited him with inventing writing. A scribe's kit — a palette, a reed-pen case, and a water bag — was itself a single hieroglyph meaning 'scribe.' Source: ancientegyptonline.co.uk/thoth/

question: Esmet-Akhom, who served the goddess Isis as a priest, scratched an inscription in hieroglyphs on a wall of the Philae temple in AD 394, the last one anyone has found with a date. Christianity was spreading through Egypt. What became of the ancient script over the next fourteen hundred years?
answer: No one left on earth could read it
choices: No one left on earth could read it
Romans translated it into Latin schoolbooks
It was carved onto every new coin
Arab scholars taught it in their academies
context: The 'Graffito of Esmet-Akhom,' dated 24 August AD 394, is the last known hieroglyphic inscription. After it, for roughly 1,400 years, no one on earth could read hieroglyphs — the meaning was completely lost. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graffito_of_Esmet-Akhom

question: Hildegard of Bingen wrote a sung morality play, Ordo Virtutum, around 1151, in which the Virtues, the human Soul, and the Devil all appear on stage. Every single role is sung in plainchant except one: the Devil never sings a note, only yells and grunts. Why did Hildegard write him that way?
answer: She believed a creature of sin cannot produce divine harmony
choices: She believed a creature of sin cannot produce divine harmony
She had run out of melodies to give the final character
Audiences of the time forbade the Devil from being sung
The actor who played the Devil could not read music
context: Ordo Virtutum (c. 1151) is the earliest surviving morality play by more than a century, and the only medieval music-drama that survives with both its words AND its music attributed to one named author. The 16-17 sung Virtues triumph over the speechless Devil at the end. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordo_Virtutum

question: Hildegard of Bingen, a German abbess and composer of the 1100s, did something no one is known to have done before her: she made up a whole new language, giving it an alphabet of its own and some 1,000 new words. What is her invention called?
answer: The Lingua Ignota, her 'unknown language'
choices: The Lingua Ignota, her 'unknown language'
Gregorian chant, a way of singing prayers
The Symphonia, her cycle of sung visions
Causae et Curae, her book of medical cures
context: The Lingua Ignota ('unknown language') had its own alphabet, the Litterae ignotae, and about 1,000 invented nouns — possibly the first constructed language in recorded history. Hildegard was also a working healer and natural philosopher, writing Physica and Causae et Curae. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hildegard_of_Bingen

question: Arab scholars learned zero from Indian mathematicians, who called it shunya, and gave it an Arabic name of its own, sifr. That one word branched into two very different English words. One is zero; the other belongs to the world of spies and secret messages. What is that second word?
answer: Cipher
choices: Cipher
Riddle
Token
Symbol
context: 'Sifr' Latinized to 'zephirum' (via Fibonacci), then Italian 'zefiro', contracted to 'zero' -- while the same root traveled separately into 'cipher', a secret code. (etymonline.com/word/cipher; etymonline.com/word/zero; sciencefriday.com/articles/the-origin-of-the-word-zero/)

question: Brahma creates the universe and Vishnu keeps it in balance, Hindu tradition tells, while a third great god destroys each world so that a fresh one can begin. Which of the three is the destroyer?
answer: Shiva
choices: Shiva
Brahma
Vishnu
Krishna
context: The three together are the Trimurti ('three forms'): Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer. The three sounds of the sacred syllable Om (A-U-M) are said to stand for the same three acts — creation, preservation, and destruction. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimurti

question: Vishnu, the preserver, keeps the universe in balance, as Hindu tradition tells it. Whenever evil grows strong and the world starts to slide toward chaos, he sets things right, and he does not stay up in heaven and send help from above. What does he do?
answer: He is born on earth in a new bodily form
choices: He is born on earth in a new bodily form
He sends a lesser god to fight in his place
He floods the whole world and starts it over
He hands his powers to a chosen human king
context: Each of these earthly descents is an avatar; together they are the Dashavatara, Vishnu's ten avatars, each appearing in a different age: Matsya the fish, Kurma the tortoise, Varaha the boar, Narasimha the man-lion, Vamana the dwarf, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, Buddha, and Kalki, who is still to come. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashavatara

question: In the Hindu epic the Ramayana, the demon-king Ravana has stolen Rama's wife Sita. He has carried her over the sea to his island of Lanka. To reach her, Rama gets help from the monkey-god Hanuman and a whole army of monkeys. How does this monkey army get Rama's men over the water?
answer: They build a bridge across the sea
choices: They build a bridge across the sea
They turn themselves into a fleet of ships
They drink the channel dry
They fly the army over on Hanuman's back
context: Rama, Vishnu's seventh avatar, crosses the monkey-built bridge, kills the ten-headed Ravana, and frees Sita. https://www.britannica.com/topic/Rama-Hindu-deity  (Legend.)

question: Shiva has a third eye set in his forehead, kept shut except in moments of terrible anger. The young love-god Kamadeva once shot a flower-arrow at him to break his deep meditation, hoping to make him fall in love with the goddess Parvati. Furious, Shiva opened the eye on him. What happened to Kamadeva?
answer: He was burned to ashes on the spot
choices: He was burned to ashes on the spot
He was frozen solid where he stood
He was hurled to the far side of the world
He was turned into a stone statue
context: Shiva's right eye is said to be the sun, his left the moon, and the third eye fire — which is why opening it incinerated Kamadeva. https://isha.sadhguru.org/mahashivratri/shiva/shivas-third-eye-its-hidden-symbolism/  (Legend.)

question: Shiva, as Nataraja, the Lord of the Dance, dances on one leg inside a ring of fire with a drum in one hand. Beneath his raised foot he tramples a small crouching figure. Who is the dwarf that Shiva crushes as he dances?
answer: Apasmara, the demon of ignorance
choices: Apasmara, the demon of ignorance
Ravana, the ten-headed demon-king
Kamadeva, the love-god
Vasuki, the serpent-king
context: As Nataraja, Shiva performs the Ananda Tandava ('dance of bliss'): his upper hands hold the damaru drum and agni fire, a lower hand makes the abhaya mudra ('fear not'), and his foot pins Apasmara (Muyalaka), trampling ignorance underfoot. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nataraja

question: Brahma, the creator, looks out with four faces, one turned toward each direction of the compass. The faces are not only for seeing every way at once: each of his four mouths, Hindus say, recites one ancient work aloud, forever, without pause. Which of these is on Brahma's lips?
answer: One of the Vedas
choices: One of the Vedas
One of the Upanishads
One of the Hindu law-books
One of the epic poems
context: Brahma's four mouths recite the four Vedas — Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda, one to a mouth. He is pictured being born from a lotus that grows from the navel of Vishnu, who reclines on the cosmic ocean. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahma

question: The sacred river Ganga came crashing down out of heaven, Hindus say, and her torrent was violent enough to smash the earth to pieces where she landed. Shiva stepped in to soften the fall. How did he tame the falling river so that it reached the ground gently?
answer: He caught it in his matted hair and let it trickle down
choices: He caught it in his matted hair and let it trickle down
He swallowed it and breathed it out as mist
He dammed it behind a mountain range
He froze it into a ladder of ice
context: King Bhagiratha had won the river's release; Shiva catching her in his hair earned him the name Gangadhara, 'Bearer of the Ganga.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhagiratha  (Legend.)

question: Vishnu will come one final time, Hindus say, as his tenth avatar Kalki, to end the present dark age, wipe out evil and begin a new golden age. Kalki has not yet appeared, but the prophecy tells exactly how he will arrive. How is Kalki said to come?
answer: Riding a white horse with a flaming sword
choices: Riding a white horse with a flaming sword
Walking out of the sea as a giant fish
Falling from the sky in a chariot of fire
Rising from the earth as a man-lion
context: Kalki's white horse is named Devadatta. His arrival is prophesied to end the Kali Yuga (the iron age) and usher in a new Satya Yuga (golden age). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalki  (Legend.)

question: In a Hindu tale, the proud demon-king Bali rules the three worlds, and Vishnu comes to him disguised as Vamana, a small dwarf. Vamana humbly asks for only as much land as he can cover in three steps, and Bali laughs and grants it. Then Vamana swells into a cosmic giant. What do those three steps cover?
answer: The whole earth, the entire sky, and Bali's own head
choices: The whole earth, the entire sky, and Bali's own head
Three kingdoms, three oceans, and three mountains
The past, the present, and all of time to come
The earth, the underworld, and the realm of the gods
context: Grown into the giant Trivikrama ('three strides'), Vishnu covered the earth with one step and the sky with the next; with nowhere left for the third, Bali offered his own head, and Vamana pressed him down into the netherworld. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vamana  (Legend.)

question: Gods and demons once churned the Ocean of Milk together, the Hindu story goes, hoping to draw up the nectar of immortality. Before any treasure rose, up came Halahala, a poison so deadly it could wipe out all creation, and Shiva saved the world by dealing with it himself. What did Shiva do with the poison?
answer: He drank it and held it in his throat, which turned blue
choices: He drank it and held it in his throat, which turned blue
He sealed it inside a mountain forever
He hurled it into the empty void beyond the sky
He drained it into the deepest ocean trench
context: The blue-stained throat earned Shiva the name Neelakantha, 'the blue-throated one.' When the demons later seized the immortality-nectar, Vishnu took the form of the enchantress Mohini and tricked it back out of them for the gods. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samudra_manthan  (Legend.)

question: Brahma made the world, Hindu tradition holds, yet almost no temples anywhere in India are built for him, though temples to other great gods stand everywhere. The one famous exception stands at Pushkar in Rajasthan. By legend, why does the creator of the world have almost no temples?
answer: His own consort cursed him never to be worshipped
choices: His own consort cursed him never to be worshipped
He fell asleep and forgot to claim a temple
He gave up all worship to Vishnu and Shiva
He grew too proud and was banished from earth
context: The legend ties the curse to a quarrel at a ritual where the goddess Gayatri took his consort's place; the curse was later softened to allow worship at Pushkar alone. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahma_Temple,_Pushkar

question: The demon Hiranyakashipu wins a near-perfect boon in a Hindu legend: he cannot be killed by man or beast, by day or by night, indoors or outdoors, on the ground or in the air, or by any weapon. He believes himself unkillable, yet Vishnu, coming in one of his avatars, slays him without breaking a single clause. Which way of doing it threads every loophole at once?
answer: A man-lion, striking at twilight, on the threshold of a doorway
choices: A man-lion, striking at twilight, on the threshold of a doorway
A man-bird, striking at the eclipse, in the gate of the courtyard
A man-serpent, striking at dusk, on the sill of a window
A man-stag, striking at dawn, under the eaves of the porch
context: Each loophole is defeated at once: Narasimha is a man-lion (neither man nor beast); twilight is neither day nor night; a threshold is neither indoors nor out; he holds the demon on his lap (neither ground nor sky); and he kills with his claws (no weapon). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narasimha  (Legend.)

question: Hippocrates of Kos taught in the 400s BC that disease comes from natural causes, not from angry gods. Yet the young doctors who swore the oath in his name began by calling on the gods themselves. Which god did they swear by first?
answer: Apollo, the healer
choices: Apollo, the healer
Hades, lord of the dead
Ares, god of war
Poseidon, the earth-shaker
context: The Oath opens: 'I swear by Apollo Healer, by Asclepius, by Hygieia, by Panacea, and by all the gods and goddesses.' Asclepius was the god of medicine and Hygieia (root of 'hygiene') the goddess of health. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippocratic_Oath

question: A new doctor stood to swear the oath of Hippocrates, as sure as almost everyone else that it held the famous Latin command 'primum non nocere,' meaning 'first, do no harm.' Scholars searched the ancient text of the oath for those exact words. What did they find?
answer: Those words appear nowhere in it
choices: Those words appear nowhere in it
They form the Oath's closing line
Hippocrates carved them on his tree
They open the Oath's first sentence
context: The phrase is not in the Oath at all. The closest real Hippocratic line, from the 'Epidemics,' reads: 'either help the patient, or do not harm him.' The Latin tag was traced only to 1860 and linked to the 17th-century physician Thomas Sydenham. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primum_non_nocere

question: Colonel Paul Tibbets flew the B-29 bomber that dropped the first atomic bomb ever used in war, on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945. He had named the plane Enola Gay after someone close to him. Who was the plane named after?
answer: His mother
choices: His mother
His wife
His daughter
His sister
context: Tibbets named the B-29 for his mother, Enola Gay Tibbets. 'Little Boy' was a uranium gun-type bomb; it fell for 43 seconds and detonated about 1,968 feet over Hiroshima at 8:15 a.m. local time. Source: nps.gov/articles/000/the-atomic-bombings-of-hiroshima-and-nagasaki.htm

question: A B-29 crew bombed Hiroshima with a uranium bomb on 6 August 1945, and three days later another crew dropped a plutonium bomb on Nagasaki. The American crews gave each atomic bomb a grim nickname. What were the two bombs called?
answer: Little Boy and Fat Man
choices: Little Boy and Fat Man
Iron Mike and Big John
Slim Jim and Tall Paul
Grey Wolf and Red Fox
context: Hiroshima's uranium bomb was 'Little Boy'; Nagasaki's heavier, rounder plutonium bomb was 'Fat Man.' Fat Man, dropped from the B-29 Bockscar on Aug 9, yielded about 21 kilotons — roughly 40% more powerful than Little Boy. These remain the only two times atomic weapons have been used in war. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/bombing-nagasaki-august-9-1945

question: Sadako Sasaki was two years old when the bomb fell on Hiroshima, and at twelve she fell ill with leukemia. In her hospital bed a friend reminded her of an old Japanese legend, and Sadako began folding paper and did not stop. By the legend, what would win the folder a wish?
answer: Folding one thousand paper cranes
choices: Folding one thousand paper cranes
Folding one thousand paper lanterns
Folding one thousand paper boats
Folding one thousand paper flowers
context: The legend holds that anyone who folds 1,000 paper cranes is granted a wish. Sadako folded more than 1,300 before she died on Oct 25, 1955. Her classmates raised money for the Children's Peace Monument in Hiroshima Peace Park (unveiled 1958), where roughly 10 million folded cranes are left by visitors every year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_Peace_Monument

question: Emperor Hirohito went on the radio on 15 August 1945 to tell Japan it must stop fighting and endure 'the unendurable,' though he never once said the word 'surrender.' For millions of Japanese at home, what made simply hearing the broadcast such a shock?
answer: They were hearing their emperor's voice for the very first time
choices: They were hearing their emperor's voice for the very first time
They were ordered to bow toward the radio as he spoke
They heard him name the American president out loud
They were told the long war had in fact been won
context: It was the first time the Japanese public had ever heard their emperor's voice — the so-called 'Jewel Voice Broadcast.' Hirohito called for peace by 'enduring the unendurable and suffering what is insufferable,' citing 'a new and most cruel bomb.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirohito_surrender_broadcast

question: Hiroshima lay all but flattened for a mile around the bomb's burst on 6 August 1945, but one domed building, now called the A-Bomb Dome, kept its walls and the skeletal frame of its dome, though everyone inside died. The bomb had burst in the air only about 500 feet from it. Why did it survive when others nearby were swept flat?
answer: The blast was almost directly overhead, so its force pressed straight down through the building
choices: The blast was almost directly overhead, so its force pressed straight down through the building
Its copper-clad dome reflected away most of the bomb's heat
Deep underground vaults soaked up the force of the shock wave
Thick earthen walls had been packed around it as a bomb shelter
context: The bomb burst almost directly above the building, so the blast wave pushed straight down through its center, leaving the walls and metal dome intact. Designed by Czech architect Jan Letzel in 1915, the Genbaku (A-Bomb) Dome is now a UNESCO World Heritage site and the iconic ruin of Hiroshima. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial

question: Tsutomu Yamaguchi, a Mitsubishi engineer, was on a work trip to Hiroshima when the bomb fell about two miles from him on 6 August 1945, and it left him badly burned. He made it home to Nagasaki and reported back to work on 9 August. What was he doing as the second atomic bomb exploded over Nagasaki?
answer: Describing the Hiroshima blast to a supervisor who did not believe him
choices: Describing the Hiroshima blast to a supervisor who did not believe him
Riding a streetcar toward the Mitsubishi shipyard gates
Lying in a hospital bed recovering from his earlier burns
Boarding a train to take his family out of the city
context: Yamaguchi was about 3 km from both blasts. In 2009 Japan officially recognized him as the only 'double survivor' (double hibakusha). He said his record 'can tell the younger generation the horrifying history of the atomic bombings even after I die.' He died in 2010 at age 93. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsutomu_Yamaguchi

question: At a bank in Hiroshima, the bomb's flash was so intense that it bleached the pale stone of the front steps even whiter — except for one dark patch in the middle that the light never reached. Decades later the bank gave the steps to Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Museum. What had cast that one unbleached shadow onto the stone?
answer: A person who had been sitting on the steps
choices: A person who had been sitting on the steps
A bicycle that had been leaning on the steps
A stone lantern that had stood beside the steps
A wooden door that had fallen across the steps
context: The shadow, about 850 feet from the hypocenter, marks where a person sitting on the steps shielded the stone from the flash. That person almost certainly died in that instant and was never identified. In 1971 the Sumitomo Bank donated the steps to the museum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Shadow_Etched_in_Stone

question: The crew of the second atomic bomber made three runs over Kokura, the city they had been sent to bomb, on the morning of 9 August 1945, but smoke and haze hid it every time, so they flew on to their backup target, Nagasaki. The spared city never knew how close it had come. What do the Japanese still call that kind of narrow, unknowing escape?
answer: Kokura's luck
choices: Kokura's luck
Bomber's luck
Soldier's luck
Devil's luck
context: Smoke — partly from a firebombing raid on nearby Yahata the day before — covered about 70% of Kokura. Over Nagasaki, clouds also blocked the view until a hole opened at the end of the run and bombardier Capt. Kermit Beahan called out that he could see the target. 'Kokura's luck' came to mean a narrow escape from disaster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bockscar

question: A band of rebel army officers stormed the palace grounds in Tokyo late on 14 August 1945, determined to keep Japan in the war after Emperor Hirohito had decided to surrender. They searched the palace through the night. What were they trying to find and destroy?
answer: The phonograph recording of the surrender speech
choices: The phonograph recording of the surrender speech
The Emperor's official seal of state
The signed pages of the surrender order
The palace radio's only transmitter
context: The Emperor's words had already been recorded onto discs to be aired the next day. Palace staff hid the discs, the coup failed, and the broadcast went out on August 15. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirohito_surrender_broadcast

question: Believers in Nagasaki, long the heart of Japanese Christianity, searched the ruins of Urakami Cathedral after the atomic bomb burst only some 500 meters away and killed thousands of its worshippers. They found one of its two bells still whole and hung it from a wooden log. What did the survivors do with the bell?
answer: Rang it for a Christmas Eve Mass
choices: Rang it for a Christmas Eve Mass
Sealed it inside a shrine as a war memorial
Carried it in a march through the ruined streets
Buried it again with the cathedral's dead
context: Fat Man detonated only about 500 m from the Urakami Cathedral, killing roughly 8,500 of its 12,000 parishioners. Believers dug a surviving Angelus bell from the rubble, hung it from a log, and rang it for Christmas Eve Mass on December 24, 1945. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Conception_Cathedral,_Nagasaki

question: The crew of Bockscar, the B-29 that bombed Nagasaki, nearly failed to make it home. A stuck pump had trapped 640 gallons of fuel where the engines could not reach it, and the long detour over Kokura had burned through much of the rest. They barely reached Okinawa and landed hard. When the flight engineer checked the tanks, how much flying time did he reckon they had left?
answer: Less than five minutes of fuel
choices: Less than five minutes of fuel
About one hour of fuel
Around thirty minutes of fuel
Just over two hours of fuel
context: Between the stuck fuel-transfer pump and the Kokura delay, Bockscar limped to Okinawa with the flight engineer estimating under five minutes of fuel left in the tanks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bockscar

question: President Harry Truman's government was planning Operation Downfall in 1945, the invasion of Japan's home islands. On the island of Okinawa, about a third of the Americans who fought had just been killed or wounded. What did Truman say he hoped an invasion of Japan would not become?
answer: An Okinawa from one end of Japan to the other
choices: An Okinawa from one end of Japan to the other
A slaughter with no surrender ever in sight
A second front to rival the whole European war
A grave for a generation of young Americans
context: Okinawa's roughly 35% casualty rate was the grim model. Casualty forecasts for invading Japan ranged enormously — from a June 1945 estimate of about 40,000 US dead, to Truman's later claim of being warned of 250,000 to a million US casualties, with Japanese deaths projected in the millions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Downfall

question: Ward Wilson is one of the historians who point to a second blow that struck Japan on 8 August 1945, the day between the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombs, and he calls it the greater shock, though other historians put the bombs first. What happened that day?
answer: The Soviet Union declared war and invaded Japanese-held Manchuria
choices: The Soviet Union declared war and invaded Japanese-held Manchuria
The United States warned it would firebomb Tokyo next
Japan's navy lost its last carriers in a final sea battle
China's armies broke through into the Japanese home islands
context: On Aug 8 the USSR declared war on Japan; the next day over a million Soviet troops poured into Manchuria, crushing the Kwantung Army. Many historians argue the Soviet entry, alongside the atomic bombs, was a decisive shock; a minority (e.g. Ward Wilson) argue it was the bigger factor. This remains a genuinely debated question. Source: history.com/this-day-in-history/august-8/soviets-declare-war-on-japan-invade-manchuria

question: Adolf Hitler forced his way into a packed Munich beer hall late on 8 November 1923, backed by about 600 armed SA men. He jumped on a chair and shouted that the revolution had begun. What did he do to silence the crowd?
answer: Fired a pistol shot into the ceiling
choices: Fired a pistol shot into the ceiling
Smashed a beer stein on the floor
Threw a burning torch onto the stage
Hung a Nazi banner over the bar
context: Hitler jumped on a chair, fired into the ceiling, and yelled 'The national revolution has broken out! The hall is surrounded by six hundred men.' The takeover, later called the Beer Hall Putsch, collapsed within a day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_Hall_Putsch; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia.

question: Adolf Hitler sat in Landsberg prison in 1924 after his failed attempt to seize power in Munich. There he spoke his political ideas aloud to a devoted fellow prisoner, Rudolf Hess, who took them down. What book did the two of them produce?
answer: Mein Kampf
choices: Mein Kampf
The Communist Manifesto
The Prince
Das Kapital
context: So the book at the heart of Nazism was literally composed by a convicted coup-plotter sitting in a jail cell, dictated to Rudolf Hess. The title means 'My Struggle.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mein_Kampf; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landsberg_Prison.

question: Hitler's SA and SS men poured through Berlin in their tens of thousands on the night of 30 January 1933, the day he became chancellor of Germany. What did the marchers carry that made the night so famous and so frightening to watch?
answer: Flaming torches
choices: Flaming torches
Black coffins
Iron chains
Brass trumpets
context: The torchlight parades became the iconic image of the night a democracy lit the way for the man who would destroy it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler's_rise_to_power.

question: Berlin police rushed into the burning Reichstag, Germany's parliament, on the night of 27 February 1933, as flames gutted its grand glass dome. Inside they caught a 24-year-old man who confessed he had set the fire alone. Who was the man?
answer: A Dutch bricklayer named Marinus van der Lubbe
choices: A Dutch bricklayer named Marinus van der Lubbe
A German general named Erich Ludendorff
An Austrian painter named Adolf Hitler
A Russian agent named Georgi Dimitrov
context: Marinus van der Lubbe, a young Dutch ex-communist bricklayer, was caught inside the burning building and confessed to acting alone. The fire gutted the debating chamber and the gilded glass cupola. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reichstag_fire; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marinus_van_der_Lubbe.

question: Police at the Feldherrnhalle in Munich opened fire on some 2,000 marching Nazis the day after the failed Beer Hall Putsch of 1923, and sixteen marchers fell dead. One Nazi banner was soaked in the blood of the men who died beneath it. What did the movement turn that banner into?
answer: Its holiest relic, touched to every new flag
choices: Its holiest relic, touched to every new flag
A burial shroud laid over the fallen dead
A war trophy mailed to Berlin headquarters
A velvet curtain hung in Hitler's office
context: The blood-splattered banner became the movement's most sacred object, the 'Blutfahne' (Blood Flag). New SS and SA banners were 'consecrated' by being physically touched to it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_Hall_Putsch.

question: Hermann Göring, Hitler's loyal lieutenant, took a bullet in the groin when police opened fire at the Feldherrnhalle and ended the 1923 putsch. He was smuggled out of Germany to escape arrest, but the agony of that wound left him with a lifelong affliction. What was it?
answer: An addiction to morphine
choices: An addiction to morphine
A permanent limp
Blindness in one eye
A paralyzed arm
context: Goring was given morphine for the pain and became addicted to it for the rest of his life, a habit that dogged him to the Nuremberg trials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_Hall_Putsch.

question: President Hindenburg, aged and pressed by Hitler, signed the Reichstag Fire Decree the day after the parliament building burned in February 1933. It cancelled freedom of speech and of the press, the right to gather and the privacy of the mail. With those rights gone, what did the police do overnight, days before the election?
answer: Arrested thousands of Communists, including every KPD deputy
choices: Arrested thousands of Communists, including every KPD deputy
Shut every newspaper and radio station in the country
Seized all the gold in Germany's banks
Drafted every jobless man into the army
context: Police arrested thousands overnight, jailing every Communist (KPD) member of parliament and gutting the opposition before the 5 March 1933 vote. The Fire Decree was never lifted and became the permanent legal skeleton of the dictatorship. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org Reichstag Fire Decree article.

question: Adolf Hitler drew a hard lesson from his 1923 coup, which failed in a hail of police bullets: guns and barricades had landed him in prison and gotten his men killed. To take Germany, he decided to use a completely different weapon. What new strategy did he choose?
answer: Seizing power legally, through elections
choices: Seizing power legally, through elections
Fleeing Germany to lead the party from exile
Allying with the Communists to share power
Petitioning the French occupiers to back him
context: This 'path of legality' is the mechanism the whole story turns on: Hitler never won a majority at the ballot box, but he exploited the democratic system from the inside to dismantle it. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Beer Hall Putsch article.

question: Hitler's Nazis polled only about 800,000 votes in 1928, a fringe party. Then came the Great Depression, millions of Germans lost their jobs, and the Nazis rode that desperation into the election of July 1932. Roughly how far did their vote climb from that 800,000?
answer: About 14 million votes
choices: About 14 million votes
About 4 million votes
About 8 million votes
About 21 million votes
context: The Depression was the rocket fuel: as unemployment soared from about 8.5% to nearly 30% between 1929 and 1932, the Nazi vote leapt from 800,000 to roughly 14,000,000, making them the largest party in parliament. Source: britannica.com, Nazi Party; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_1932_German_federal_election.

question: Franz von Papen, a former chancellor, struck a backroom deal in January 1933. The Nazis had become the biggest party in the Reichstag with 37.4 percent of the vote the summer before, yet still lacked a majority, and Papen persuaded the aged President Hindenburg to make Hitler chancellor anyway, giving the Nazis just three of eleven cabinet seats. What did Papen convince Hindenburg that Hitler would be?
answer: A harmless puppet they could control
choices: A harmless puppet they could control
A loyal soldier for the army
A temporary caretaker until new elections
A unifying hero for all Germans
context: Papen persuaded the aged Hindenburg to appoint Hitler, certain he could be controlled; only 3 of the 11 cabinet seats went to Nazis. Papen took the Vice-Chancellorship for himself. Source: history.com, Hitler named Chancellor; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler's_rise_to_power.

question: Otto Wels, leader of the Social Democrats, rose to speak in a hall packed with SA and SS men on 23 March 1933, as the German parliament voted on the Enabling Act. He alone told Hitler to his face what the Nazis could never take from his party. What did Wels declare they could never take?
answer: Our honor
choices: Our honor
Our homeland
Our faith
Our children
context: Otto Wels told Hitler, 'Freedom and life can be taken from us, but not our honor.' His 94 Social Democrats cast the only No votes against the Enabling Act, and his speech was the last free speech in the German parliament for twelve years. Source: germanhistorydocs.org, Otto Wels speech, 23 March 1933.

question: Catholic Centre Party deputies gave Adolf Hitler the extra votes he needed for his Enabling Act on 23 March 1933, won over by his pledge to shield the Church, which he soon broke. What did the Act let Hitler do without needing the Reichstag's approval?
answer: Make his own laws
choices: Make his own laws
Command the army only in wartime
Appoint mayors of cities
Set tax rates
