context: The Centre (Catholic) Party voted 72 to 0 in favor after Hitler verbally promised to protect Catholic schools and civil liberties. Without their cooperation the two-thirds majority would have failed and the legal road to dictatorship would have closed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enabling_Act_of_1933.

question: Odysseus reaches home in Ithaca after twenty years, dressed as a ragged beggar. Before anyone in the palace sees through it, one old friend lying on a dung heap knows him at once, then dies. Who is the first to recognize him?
answer: His old hunting dog, Argos
choices: His old hunting dog, Argos
His childhood nurse, Eurycleia
His aging father, Laertes
His loyal swineherd, Eumaeus
context: Argos had waited twenty years just to see his master return; he wagged his tail one last time, and Odysseus -- unable to greet him without blowing his cover -- secretly wiped away a tear as the old dog died. Homer, Odyssey Book 17; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argos_(dog); cliffsnotes.com Odyssey Book 17

question: Odysseus must sail a narrow strait between Charybdis, a whirlpool that swallows whole ships, and Scylla, a monster with many heads who reaches down from a high cliff. Rather than risk the whirlpool, he steers close to Scylla. As his ship slips past, what does she do?
answer: Snatches and eats six of his men, one in each mouth
choices: Snatches and eats six of his men, one in each mouth
Drags the whole ship down beneath the waves
Wraps the mast in her coils and snaps it
Sings until half the crew leap overboard
context: Scylla had six heads, and her victims screamed his name as she devoured them, one per mouth. The phrase 'between Scylla and Charybdis' still means an impossible choice between two dangers. Homer, Odyssey Book 12; cliffsnotes.com / sparknotes.com Odyssey Book 12

question: Hector, prince of Troy, says goodbye to his wife at the city gate in the Iliad and reaches out to hold their baby son, Astyanax. The child suddenly shrieks and shrinks back in terror, hiding his face. What frightens him?
answer: The bronze helmet with its nodding horsehair crest
choices: The bronze helmet with its nodding horsehair crest
The great bronze shield strapped to his father's arm
The strangers crowding around the gate
The great war-horse stamping behind Hector
context: Hector laughed, lifted the gleaming helmet off his head, set it shining on the ground, and kissed his son -- a flash of gentleness from the war's greatest defender, who would soon die. Homer, Iliad Book 6 (poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Iliad6.php); litcharts.com The Iliad Book 6

question: The suitors in Odysseus's hall strain one by one at his mighty bow, even warming it at the fire to soften the wood, and every one fails to string it. Then a ragged beggar, Odysseus in disguise, asks for a turn. What does he do with the bow?
answer: He strings it easily and shoots an arrow through a row of axe-heads
choices: He strings it easily and shoots an arrow through a row of axe-heads
He braces it on the floor and snaps the string trying to bend it
He warms it longer at the fire until the wood finally gives way
He hands it back, unable to bend it any more than the suitors could
context: The 'beggar' was Odysseus himself, home at last. He bent the great bow as easily as a singer strings a lyre, sent his arrow clean through the long line of axe-heads set up in the hall, and then turned the bow on the suitors. Homer, Odyssey Book 21; litcharts.com / cliffsnotes.com Odyssey Book 21

question: Eurycleia, Odysseus's old nurse, kneels to wash the feet of a ragged stranger who has come to the palace. Suddenly she gasps and drops his foot, so the basin clangs and the water spills; she has almost cried out her master's name, not because she sees his face but because of one thing she has noticed on his leg. What gives him away?
answer: A scar from a wild boar's tusk
choices: A scar from a wild boar's tusk
A ring carved with his family's crest
A tattoo from his sailing days
A birthmark shaped like a star
context: The boar had gored him long ago while he hunted as a boy with his grandfather Autolycus. Odysseus seized Eurycleia's throat and hushed her so his secret would hold. Homer, Odyssey Book 19; sparknotes.com Odyssey Books 19-20; cliffsnotes.com Odyssey Book 19

question: Achilles refuses to fight at Troy after a quarrel. His dearest friend Patroclus marches out in Achilles' own armor to frighten the Trojans, but the god Apollo strikes him from behind and Hector finishes him off. When the news reaches Achilles, what does he do?
answer: He pours ashes over his head and lies face-down in the dust
choices: He pours ashes over his head and lies face-down in the dust
He arms instantly and charges the walls alone
He calls the Greek kings together to plan revenge
He sails out to beg his mother for new armor
context: Mad with grief, Achilles tore his hair and vowed to kill Hector -- the death that finally brought him roaring back into the war. Patroclus had even prophesied with his dying breath that Hector too would soon die. Homer, Iliad Books 16 & 18; standardebooks.org Iliad Book 18; americanliterature.com Iliad Book 16

question: Homer opened the Iliad on a single Greek word, menis: the rage of Achilles, which launched all 24 books of the poem. Everywhere else in his poems he saved that word for one kind of being, and never used it for ordinary human anger. Whose anger did Homer otherwise reserve the word for?
answer: The immortal gods
choices: The immortal gods
Kings and great generals
The dead in the underworld
Wild beasts and monsters
context: The Greek word menis opens the poem: 'Sing, goddess, the rage of Achilles, son of Peleus...' By giving a mortal man's anger the very word he reserves elsewhere for divine wrath, Homer frames Achilles' rage as almost more than human. Homer, Iliad Book I; poets.org Iliad Book I lines 1-16; sententiaeantiquae.com 'Beginning the Iliad'

question: The Trojan warrior Asteropaios hurls his spear at Achilles, the greatest of the Greeks, in Book 21 of Homer's Iliad, and its point finds Achilles' forearm, though legend makes Achilles almost proof against weapons. What does Homer say happens when the spear strikes him?
answer: Black blood spurts forth from the wound
choices: Black blood spurts forth from the wound
The spear shatters against his unscarred skin
It glances off him and leaves no mark
The cut closes over and heals at once
context: In Homer, Achilles is an ordinary mortal who can be cut and bleed -- 'black blood spurted forth.' The dipped-in-the-Styx, held-by-the-heel invulnerability tale first appears in the Roman poet Statius's Achilleid, written around AD 90 -- some 800 years after Homer. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achilles%27_heel; talesoftimesforgotten.com on Statius, Achilleid

question: A playwright in England, writing around 1590 a play about a man who sells his soul to the Devil, gave Helen of Troy her most famous line of praise: 'the face that launched a thousand ships.' The phrase sounds ancient, but it appears nowhere in Homer. Who wrote it?
answer: Christopher Marlowe
choices: Christopher Marlowe
Homer himself
Virgil of Rome
Geoffrey Chaucer
context: The line is from Marlowe's play Doctor Faustus: 'Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships, / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?' In Homer, a Greek fleet of about a thousand ships did sail for Troy to win Helen back after she left with the prince Paris. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_of_Troy; interestingliterature.com on Marlowe

question: Statius, a Roman poet, told a legend around AD 90 about the baby Achilles: his mother dipped him into a magic river while she held him by one spot, and the water never touched it. Years later at Troy, an arrow shot by the Trojan prince Paris struck him in that one place and killed him. Which part of his body was it?
answer: His heel
choices: His heel
His eye
His hand
His heart
context: The river Scamander's channels choked with corpses until the river-god flooded to drown Achilles; the goddess Hera saved him by sending Hephaistos, god of fire, whose flames boiled the river until it surrendered. Homer, Iliad Book 21; sparknotes.com The Iliad Books 21-22; etc.usf.edu Lit2Go Iliad Book 21

question: Homer set his Iliad in the ten-year Trojan War, yet he did not tell the whole war. He dropped his listeners into its last year and never narrated the wooden horse or the fall of the city at all. About how much of the war did Homer's 24 books take in?
answer: Only about fifty days
choices: Only about fifty days
All ten years from start to finish
Roughly the first five years
Exactly one year, day by day
context: The whole poem spans some fifty days near the war's end -- the bulk of it just four days and two nights of fighting -- and closes with Hector's funeral, BEFORE the Trojan Horse. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iliad; cliffsnotes.com 'About the Iliad' (E.V. Rieu)

question: Heinrich Schliemann, a businessman turned archaeologist, was sure the Iliad described a real city, and in the 1870s he dug into a mound at Hisarlik in Turkey and found buried ruins where Homer had set Troy. Digging at Mycenae in Greece in 1876, he lifted a golden death mask out of a grave. As the story goes, what did he announce?
answer: I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon
choices: I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon
I have found the tomb of Achilles
Here lie the walls of Troy itself
This is the helmet of great Hector
context: Schliemann claimed the gold 'Mask of Agamemnon,' though scholars now date it centuries before any Trojan War. He had proven a real city stood at Troy -- but his most famous mask belonged to no one from Homer. smithsonianmag.com on Schliemann; worldhistory.org 'Discovery of Troy'; archive.archaeology.org 'Behind the Mask of Agamemnon'

question: Odysseus, trapped in the cave of the Cyclops Polyphemus, gave the giant a false name, got him drunk and blinded his one eye. When the blinded giant howled to his neighbors for help, he bellowed that name. What name had Odysseus given?
answer: Nobody
choices: Nobody
Stranger
Captain
Hunter
context: In Greek the name was 'Outis' — 'Nobody.' So when the other Cyclopes asked who was hurting him, Polyphemus howled 'Nobody is killing me!' — and they just shrugged and walked away. (Legend.) Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outis; ancientworldmagazine.com/articles/blinding-polyphemus/

question: Odysseus had just blinded the giant Cyclops Polyphemus. Now the blind giant sat in the cave mouth. As each big woolly ram filed out to pasture, he ran his hands over its back. He wanted to catch any man riding on top. How did Odysseus and his men slip past those searching hands?
answer: They clung to the undersides of the rams
choices: They clung to the undersides of the rams
They drove the rams out ahead as a screen
They squeezed out one by one at a run
They tossed meat to lure the giant away
context: The men each hung beneath a ram's belly while Polyphemus felt only the wool on top — and never caught them. (Legend.) Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphemus; greekmyths-greekmythology.com/odysseus-and-cyclops-myth/

question: Penelope had waited twenty years for Odysseus, and now more than a hundred suitors crowded his palace, pressing her to marry one of them. She said she would choose the day she finished weaving a burial shroud, and she wove in plain sight for about three years. How did she keep it from ever being finished?
answer: She secretly unraveled her weaving each night
choices: She secretly unraveled her weaving each night
She used thread far too weak to hold
She demanded ever finer wool be brought
She wove in a hidden flaw and restarted
context: Penelope pulled out every day's work after dark, so the cloth never grew — until a servant gave away the trick. Her cunning matches her husband's. (Legend.) Sources: britannica.com/topic/Penelope-Greek-mythology; ebsco.com/research-starters

question: The Sirens sang so sweetly that passing sailors steered onto the rocks, and Odysseus wanted to hear them and live. He had his crew stop their ears with beeswax. What did he have the deaf crew do to him?
answer: Tie him to the mast and ignore his pleas
choices: Tie him to the mast and ignore his pleas
Lock him below deck behind the cargo
Bind his own hands to the steering oar
Lower him in a barrel over the side
context: With his ears open Odysseus heard the Sirens and begged to be freed; the deaf crew only roped him tighter until they were past. (Legend.) Sources: litcharts.com/lit/the-odyssey/book-12; sparknotes.com/lit/odyssey/section7/

question: Milman Parry, a scholar, studied the stock phrases that come back again and again in Homer's two epics, close to 28,000 lines of strictly measured verse: 'swift-footed Achilles,' 'rosy-fingered Dawn,' 'the wine-dark sea.' What did Parry argue those repeated phrases showed about how the poems were first made and kept?
answer: They were sung aloud from memory before being written down
choices: They were sung aloud from memory before being written down
They were copied by hand from a single master scroll
They were translated from an older Egyptian poem
They were written down slowly over several centuries
context: Parry argued that the stock phrases were memory-pegs that let a bard sing the poem live in its strict metre. For centuries no one wrote the epics down: they were composed and performed from memory and passed from singer to singer, not rigidly word for word but rebuilt each time from formula phrases the bards knew by heart.

question: Homer left the wooden horse and the burning of Troy out of his Iliad altogether. He closed the poem instead on a single event in the war's tenth year, with the city still standing. What did Homer end the Iliad with?
answer: The funeral of the Trojan prince Hector
choices: The funeral of the Trojan prince Hector
The death of the Greek hero Achilles
The burning and sack of the city
The Greeks sailing home from Troy
context: The Iliad ends not in triumph but in grief, with Hector's burial — Troy still standing, Achilles still alive. The famous sack of the city, and Achilles' own death, come only in later stories. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iliad

question: Achilles had killed the Trojan prince Hector and was dragging his body in the dust, refusing to give it back for burial. Then in the dead of night Hector's old father, King Priam, slipped alone and unarmed into the enemy camp and knelt before Achilles. What did the grieving Priam do that broke even Achilles?
answer: Kissed the hands that had killed his son
choices: Kissed the hands that had killed his son
Offered his own life in his son's place
Cursed the Greek gods to their faces
Drew a hidden blade against Achilles
context: Priam kissed the very hands that slew Hector; the two enemies wept together — Priam for his son, Achilles for his dead friend Patroclus — and Achilles gave the body back. The Iliad's most human moment. Sources: litcharts.com/lit/the-iliad/book-24; americanliterature.com

question: Heinrich Schliemann dug into a great mound called Hisarlik in Turkey in the 1870s and uncovered ruined city built upon ruined city, stacked in layers, along with a hoard of gold he proudly named Priam's Treasure. What turned out to be wrong with his prize gold?
answer: He had dug too deep, to gold far older than Troy
choices: He had dug too deep, to gold far older than Troy
The gold was a fake planted by a rival
The gold was Roman coins from centuries later
The hoard was actually made of painted bronze
context: The treasure was about 1,250 years too old for the Trojan War — Schliemann had cut straight past Homer's Troy to a far earlier city. Still, he had found the real buried site Homer sang about. Sources: smithsonianmag.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priam%27s_Treasure

question: Workers with blowtorches cut into Stalin's giant bronze statue in Budapest on 23 October 1956, while a crowd of about 200,000 Hungarians looked on. They looped a thick steel rope around its neck and pulled, and an hour later the towering figure crashed down. What part of the statue was still standing on the pedestal?
answer: Only his boots
choices: Only his boots
Only his head
Only his right arm
Only his bronze coat
context: The blowtorches and rope severed the figure at the ankles, leaving the giant bronze boots planted on the limestone base. Hungarians mockingly renamed the spot 'Boots Square.' The statue had stood about 25 meters (82 feet) tall, unveiled in 1951 as a 'gift' for Stalin's 70th birthday. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stalin_Monument_(Budapest)

question: Protesters gathered at Bem Square in Budapest on 23 October 1956, hating the communist emblem the government had stamped into the center of every Hungarian flag. What did they do to their flags, in a gesture that became the lasting sign of the uprising?
answer: They cut the communist seal out, leaving a hole
choices: They cut the communist seal out, leaving a hole
They dyed the whole flag a defiant blood red
They flew it upside down as a signal of distress
They burned it on the steps of the radio building
context: They snipped the red-star emblem out of the flag's middle with scissors, and the ragged 'flag with a hole' (Lyukas zaszlo) became the symbol of the revolution — still honored in Hungary today. Source: https://www.freedomfirst1956.com/the-1956-revolutions-symbol-the-hole-with-a-flag-in-the-center/

question: Imre Nagy, the reformer who became Hungary's prime minister in the 1956 uprising, took shelter in the Yugoslav embassy in Budapest when Soviet tanks rolled back in to crush the revolt. He came out only after he was handed a written promise of safe passage. What happened to him once he stepped outside?
answer: He was seized, secretly tried, and hanged
choices: He was seized, secretly tried, and hanged
He was exiled to live out his years abroad
He was pardoned and allowed to retire quietly
He escaped to the West and told his story
context: The safe-conduct was a trap: Nagy was arrested, deported to Romania, secretly tried for treason, and hanged on June 16, 1958 — the same day as Colonel Pal Maleter, who had been arrested while negotiating under a flag of truce. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Imre-Nagy

question: Ibn Battuta set out from Tangier in Morocco in 1325, aged 21, meaning to make one pilgrimage to Mecca, and he did not come home for 24 years. By then he had crossed three continents and gone far enough to circle the Earth three times. About how many miles had he travelled?
answer: About 75,000 miles
choices: About 75,000 miles
About 7,000 miles
About 25,000 miles
About 50,000 miles
context: Ibn Battuta covered roughly 75,000 miles (120,000 km) across some 40 countries and three continents over about 30 years -- around three times the distance of Marco Polo, making him the greatest traveler of the pre-modern world. He set out at 21 for a single hajj and stayed away 24 years. Source: Britannica biography (via worldhistory.org) and islamicity.org, '75,000 Miles of Travel by Ibn Battuta'; theconversation.com (Jan 2025).

question: Ibn Battuta left Tangier alone at twenty-one, bound for Mecca, and the loneliness hit him hard. Reaching the city of Tunis without a single friend to lift his spirits, he did something he later admitted to, until a stranger befriended him. What did he do?
answer: He wept bitterly from loneliness
choices: He wept bitterly from loneliness
He turned back toward Tangier
He sold his horse for passage
He prayed through the night
context: In Tunis he wrote that he 'wept bitterly' because he had 'neither fellow-traveller in whose companionship I might find cheer,' until a stranger befriended him. The greatest traveler in the world began in tears. Source: worldhistory.org/Ibn_Battuta/

question: On a bandit-haunted desert stretch on the road to Mecca, Ibn Battuta came down with a fever so violent he could barely stay upright in the saddle. Rather than stop and let the caravan leave him behind in dangerous country, he did something desperate to keep himself on his horse. What did he do?
answer: He tied himself to his saddle with a turban-cloth
choices: He tied himself to his saddle with a turban-cloth
He swallowed a handful of dried herbs
He paid a guard to hold him upright
He chained his wrists to the reins
context: Falling behind a caravan in bandit country could mean death, so the feverish Ibn Battuta lashed himself to the saddle with his turban-cloth to keep from collapsing off the horse. Source: history.com/articles/why-arab-scholar-ibn-battuta-is-the-greatest-explorer-of-all-time

question: Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq of Delhi picked Ibn Battuta to carry a huge gift to the emperor of China. It held about 200 slaves, singers and dancers, 100 horses, and heaps of cloth, dishes, and swords. The whole grand mission fell apart near the coast of Calicut, before Ibn Battuta had even sailed. What ruined it?
answer: A storm destroyed his ships in port
choices: A storm destroyed his ships in port
Pirates seized the treasure fleet
The emperor refused the envoy
Plague swept through the crew
context: A storm smashed his ships in the harbor near Calicut (Kozhikode), drowning companions and sinking the sultan's treasure-gifts. Ibn Battuta was left empty-handed and too afraid to return to the brutal sultan. Sources: britannica.com/biography/Ibn-Battuta/Time-in-India-and-later-journeys ; history.com

question: Ibn Battuta, too afraid of the brutal sultan of Delhi to go back without the gifts for China he had lost, drifted to the Maldive Islands. Their rulers were desperate for someone who could read Arabic and Islamic law, and they heaped pearls and gold on him. What did they do to keep this rare scholar from leaving?
answer: They refused to let his ship leave so he would stay as their judge
choices: They refused to let his ship leave so he would stay as their judge
They hid his maps and charts at sea
They jailed him until he swore loyalty
They burned the only ship in the harbor
context: Desperate for an Arabic-speaking Islamic judge, the Maldive rulers showered Ibn Battuta with pearls and gold and refused to let his ship depart so he would serve as their qadi (judge). Source: orias.berkeley.edu/resources-teachers/travels-ibn-battuta/journey/escape-delhi-maldive-islands-and-sri-lanka-1341-1344

question: Mansa Sulayman, whose brother was the famous Mansa Musa, ruled the rich empire of Mali when Ibn Battuta crossed the Sahara to his court. There the traveller watched the ruler's subjects show their submission: they groveled low, beat the ground with their elbows, and did one more thing to their own heads. What did they do?
answer: They threw dust and ashes over their heads
choices: They threw dust and ashes over their heads
They shaved their heads bald
They covered their heads with gold cloth
They struck their heads on stone
context: Ibn Battuta left the first eyewitness account by an outside traveler of a West African kingdom, the court of Mansa Sulayman (brother of the famous Mansa Musa). Subjects groveled, beat the ground with their elbows, and threw dust and ashes over their own heads in submission. Sources: orias.berkeley.edu ; faculty.buffalostate.edu Ibn Batuta on Mali

question: Iñigo of Loyola, a young Spanish soldier, was helping defend the fortress of Pamplona in 1521 when an enemy shot smashed into him, breaking one leg and tearing open the other. It ended his fighting days for good. What kind of weapon struck him down?
answer: A cannonball
choices: A cannonball
A crossbow bolt
A cavalry lance
A thrown spear
context: The wound left Ignatius of Loyola with a lifelong limp. Jesuits still celebrate 'Cannonball Day' because that single shot, on May 20, 1521, redirected his whole life from soldiering toward founding a religious order. Source: jesuits.org/stories/celebrating-cannonball-day; gonzaga.edu/about/our-mission-jesuit-values/gonzagas-history.

question: Stuck in bed to heal, Ignatius of Loyola asked for the knightly tales he loved, but the house held very different books. Before long he asked himself whether he could do what one man had done. Whose deeds did he dream of matching?
answer: Saint Francis
choices: Saint Francis
Charlemagne
Julius Caesar
King Arthur
context: Reading the only books on hand, Ignatius thought, 'What if I should do what St. Francis or St. Dominic did?' That daydream was the start of his conversion. Source: worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola; jesuits.org/stories/celebrating-cannonball-day.

question: Ignatius of Loyola hated what his healed leg looked like: it had set crooked, and a lump of bone stuck out below the knee and ruined the look of his tight stockings. With no painkiller to be had, he ordered the surgeons to do something he later called butchery, and he never cried out, only clenched his fists. What did he have them do?
answer: Saw off the protruding bone and stretch the leg straight
choices: Saw off the protruding bone and stretch the leg straight
Pack the wound in salt and ice for a week
Amputate the leg at the knee entirely
Bind the leg in iron splints for a year
context: Surgeons sawed off the bony lump and stretched the leg on traction, all while Ignatius was fully awake. He suffered it silently out of vanity about his appearance. Source: International Orthopaedics (2025), link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00264-025-06591-4; worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola.

question: Ignatius of Loyola kept an all-night vigil, as a knight would, before the Black Madonna's altar at the mountain abbey of Montserrat in 1522. At dawn he gave his fine clothes to a beggar and put on rough sackcloth. What did he hang by the altar as he walked away, to show he was done with war?
answer: His sword and dagger
choices: His sword and dagger
His war horse's saddle
His soldier's helmet
His captain's banner
context: Hanging his weapons by the Black Madonna's altar was Ignatius's deliberate surrender of the soldier's life. He left Montserrat dressed as a pilgrim in sackcloth. Source: covamanresa.cat/en/march-21-22-vigil-st-ignatius-montserrat-and-pilgrimage-manresa; worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola.

question: Riding toward Jerusalem, Ignatius of Loyola fell in with a Muslim traveler who insulted the Virgin Mary's purity. The old soldier in him itched to ride the man down and stab him, but he could not decide whether killing him would be right. Unable to choose, how did Ignatius settle whether to pursue and kill the man?
answer: He dropped the reins and let his mule pick the road at the fork
choices: He dropped the reins and let his mule pick the road at the fork
He drew his sword and prayed for a sign before striking
He challenged the traveler to a formal duel
He waited overnight to see if his anger would cool
context: Ignatius let the mule choose at a fork in the road; it took the path away from the man, and he was spared. The half-converted soldier still trusted a beast to decide a killing. Source: worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola; covamanresa.cat.

question: Alone in a cave at Manresa for nearly a year, Ignatius of Loyola fasted, let his hair and nails grow wild, and was at times so tormented by despair that he thought of suicide. Out of that ordeal he wrote a step-by-step program of guided meditations that Jesuits still lead people through on silent retreats today. What is this book called?
answer: The Spiritual Exercises
choices: The Spiritual Exercises
The Confessions
The Imitation of Christ
The Rule of Saint Benedict
context: In the cave at Manresa (1522-1523) Ignatius worked out the Spiritual Exercises, the meditation program at the heart of every Jesuit retreat to this day. Source: worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_Saint_Ignatius.

question: Francis Xavier, among the earliest Jesuits, came ashore in Japan in 1549, the first Catholic priest the country had ever seen. Hoping for an audience with Japan's rulers, he carried European marvels they had never seen. Which of these was among the wonders Xavier brought?
answer: A mechanical chiming clock
choices: A mechanical chiming clock
A printing press
A telescope
A steam-driven pump
context: Xavier, one of Ignatius's first six companions and the first Jesuit missionary east, dazzled Japanese rulers with European marvels including a chiming clock, a music box, a mirror, muskets, spectacles, and port wine. Source: ebsco.com/research-starters/history/father-xavier-introduces-christianity-japan; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: Sailors buried Francis Xavier in a chest packed with quicklime when death took him in 1552 on a tiny island within sight of China, meaning the lime to eat away his flesh for easier carrying. When the coffin was opened months later, what had become of his body?
answer: It was fresh and undecayed, as if newly dead
choices: It was fresh and undecayed, as if newly dead
It had turned entirely to white bone
It had been reduced to ash by the lime
It had been stolen and replaced with stones
context: The quicklime had not destroyed the body; it was found fresh and 'incorrupt,' reportedly sweet-smelling. Xavier's body still lies in a glass casket in the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Goa, India. Source: daily.jstor.org/the-incorruptible-body-of-francis-xavier; atlasobscura.com/places/body-st-francis-xavier.

question: The head of the Jesuit order decided in 1614 that one part of Francis Xavier's long-dead body deserved special honor: the right arm said to have baptized tens of thousands of people across Asia. He ordered it removed. What did he have done with Xavier's right forearm?
answer: Cut it off and sent it to Rome as a relic
choices: Cut it off and sent it to Rome as a relic
Buried it separately under the altar at Goa
Cast it in gold as a statue
Returned it to Xavier's family in Spain
context: The Jesuit superior had Xavier's forearm cut off at the elbow and carried to Rome, where it is still displayed in a silver reliquary in the Gesu, the Jesuit mother church. Source: liquisearch.com/francis_xavier/burials_and_relics; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: Eadfrith, a monk on the holy island of Lindisfarne off Northumbria who rose to be the island's bishop, made its gospel book, one of the most beautiful books of the Middle Ages, packed with painted birds, knots and color. How much of the Lindisfarne Gospels did Eadfrith do himself?
answer: He wrote and painted the entire book alone
choices: He wrote and painted the entire book alone
He painted the pictures but others wrote the words
He drew the outlines and apprentices colored them in
He copied the words and other monks added the pictures
context: A single scribe-artist, Eadfrith, produced the whole Lindisfarne Gospels by his own hand. He became Bishop of Lindisfarne in 698 and died in 721. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindisfarne_Gospels

question: Thieves broke into the stone church at Kells in Ireland one night in 1007 and stole the Book of Kells for its gold-and-jeweled cover. The Annals of Ulster record that two months and twenty nights later the book was found again. Where had it been left?
answer: Buried under a sod of earth with its gold cover ripped off
choices: Buried under a sod of earth with its gold cover ripped off
Floating in a river with its pages soaked through
Hidden in a hollow oak with its cover still on
Sold to a trader in a market across the sea
context: The thieves wanted the precious shrine, not the book itself, so they tore off the gold cover and abandoned the pages buried under a sod of earth. The Book of Kells survived; the gold did not. Source: https://ireland-calling.com/when-the-priceless-book-of-kells-was-discarded-under-a-sod/

question: A monk preparing paint for the Book of Kells ground orpiment, a pigment whose yellow glittered and shone like real gold on the page. There was a hidden danger in his work. What was the monk who ground orpiment really handling?
answer: Poison, because orpiment is made of arsenic
choices: Poison, because orpiment is made of arsenic
Crushed gold flakes, which were rare and costly
Burning lime, which scorched the fingers
Rotting plant dye, which carried disease
context: Orpiment is arsenic sulphide. It glittered like gold but was genuinely poisonous, so a monk grinding it to fake the look of gold was handling real poison. Source: https://www.tcd.ie/library/research-collections/book-of-kells.php

question: Irish monks painted the Book of Kells around the year 800 and hid tiny animals in its swirls. On the page given over to Christ's name, two cats pin two mice that nibble at a communion wafer, and one more creature lies on its back. Which creature is it, and what does it hold?
answer: An otter holding a fish
choices: An otter holding a fish
A raven holding a ring
A hound holding a bone
A serpent holding an egg
context: On the Chi-Rho page of the Book of Kells, hidden among the spirals, an otter lies on its back gripping a fish, while two cats pin the tails of two mice nibbling a wafer and two more mice ride on the cats' backs. The monks tucked a whole little zoo into a page about the name of Christ. Source: https://www.futurelearn.com/info/courses/book-of-kells/0/steps/50086

question: Gerald of Wales, a travelling writer also known as Giraldus Cambrensis, saw a gospel book in Ireland around 1185 whose pages were so crowded with spirals and interlace that they hardly seemed human work. His line of praise has clung to the Book of Kells ever since. What did he say the book looked like?
answer: The work of an angel, not of a man
choices: The work of an angel, not of a man
A garden grown from gold and ink
The dream of a sleeping saint
A window into the next world
context: Giraldus Cambrensis declared the book seemed 'the work of an angel, not of a man' — a line later attached to the Book of Kells, whose density still astonishes viewers. This is testimony, Giraldus's own awed reaction, not a forensic claim about who painted it. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Book_of_Kells/  (Legend.)

question: Louis Leroy, a critic, made fun of Claude Monet's hazy harbor painting after the rebel painters' first show in 1874, and he titled his sneering review 'The Exhibition of the Impressionists.' What did the painters do with that jeer?
answer: They adopted the insult and made it the name of their movement
choices: They adopted the insult and made it the name of their movement
They sued the critic and forced a printed apology
They painted over the picture he had mocked
They never exhibited their work in public again
context: Leroy coined the jeer in Le Charivari, April 25, 1874, riffing on Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise.' The rebels seized the slur and wore it as their banner. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impression,_Sunrise

question: Claude Monet painted the harbor of Le Havre in 1872 as a blur of gray, its ghostly ships and cranes fading into the mist. One blazing thing sits in the middle of all that gray, and the eye jumps straight to it. What is it?
answer: A small burning orange sun and its rippling reflection on the water
choices: A small burning orange sun and its rippling reflection on the water
A tall white lighthouse flashing above the docks
A red sail crossing in front of the harbor
A golden church spire rising over the rooftops
context: The little orange sun and its broken reflection streaking down the gray water are the heart of the picture, with everything else dissolved into fog. Source: https://www.claude-monet.com/impression-sunrise.jsp

question: John Goffe Rand patented a collapsible tin paint tube in 1841, and painting outdoors suddenly became easy. Before it, artists had no clean way to carry wet oil paint out into a field. What did they squeeze their oil paint out of before the tube?
answer: Tied-off pig's bladders that you pricked with a pin
choices: Tied-off pig's bladders that you pricked with a pin
Hollow cow horns stoppered with wax
Sealed clay jars dug into the ground
Folded squares of oiled leather
context: You pricked the bladder with a pin, squeezed, then tried to patch the hole; they leaked, burst, and dried out within a day or two. American artist John Goffe Rand's collapsible tin tube (patented 1841) fixed all of it. Source: https://uk.winsornewton.com/blogs/articles/winsor-newton-archive-pigs-bladders

question: Rejected again and again by the official Paris Salon, the rebel painters, Monet and Renoir among them, put on their own exhibition in the photographer Nadar's studio in April 1874. That same spring the Salon drew about 400,000 visitors. Roughly how many people came to the rebels' show?
answer: About 3,500
choices: About 3,500
About 90,000
About 200,000
About 500,000
context: Only about 3,500 came against the Salon's 400,000. The rebels' 'Anonymous Society of Painters, Sculptors and Engravers' lost money and was dissolved by December 1874 before the name caught on. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Impressionist_Exhibition

question: Camille Pissarro, like the other Impressionists, did not mix a smooth tone on his palette; he laid small dabs of pure color side by side on the canvas. From a few steps back, the dabs seemed to melt into shimmering light. Where did that final blending of the colors happen?
answer: In the viewer's own eye
choices: In the viewer's own eye
On the artist's palette
In the drying coat of varnish
Under the warm studio lamplight
context: This is the 'broken color' trick: the separate dabs of pure color combine in your eye as you step back, so the picture shimmers instead of going flat. The mixing happens in your eyeball, not on the palette. Source: https://www.jacksonsart.com/blog/2015/04/24/impressionist-painting-techniques/

question: Claude Monet kept painting from about 1912 even as cataracts clouded his eyes so badly that he could barely tell one color from another. To know which paint he was reaching for, what did the half-blind Monet have to do at his easel?
answer: Read the printed labels on his paint tubes
choices: Read the printed labels on his paint tubes
Have an assistant call out each color aloud
Arrange the tubes by smell instead of sight
Mix every color himself the night before
context: With his color vision gone, Monet relied on the labels to tell his tubes apart; his pictures from those years turned muddy red and brown until he finally had eye surgery in 1923. Source: https://hekint.org/2017/01/24/monet-and-his-cataracts/

question: Inca road builders carried the Qhapaq Ñan, a highway of stone, some 40,000 km (25,000 miles) through the mountains of what are now Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina. Laid end to end, that much road would be just about long enough to do what?
answer: Circle the whole Earth
choices: Circle the whole Earth
Reach partway to the Moon
Cross the Sahara Desert
Span the Atlantic Ocean
context: About 40,000 km is roughly the distance around the planet. The Inca built it with no iron, no wheeled vehicles, and only wooden, stone, and bronze tools, rivaling the Roman road network built a thousand years earlier. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_road_system; worldhistory.org/article/757/the-inca-road-system/

question: An Inca emperor sent a royal order from the coast, and within a single day it had reached deep into the high Andes, faster than any one person could ever have run it. How did the order travel so fast?
answer: Fresh runners each sprinted a short leg and handed it on
choices: Fresh runners each sprinted a short leg and handed it on
A single rider galloped through on a fast horse
Watchmen flashed it peak to peak with mirrors
Fast canoes rushed it up the rivers
context: These relay messengers were the chasquis, posted in small cabins only about 2.5 km apart. Each ran his short stretch flat-out, so a message could cover roughly 240 to 300 km a day. The Spanish historian Bernabe Cobo called the chasqui post 'one of the great accomplishments of the Inca kings.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasqui; worldhistory.org/article/757/the-inca-road-system/

question: A chasqui came pounding up an Inca road with a royal message for the runner waiting at the next hut, who had to be on the move already when the two met, so that no time was lost. How did the arriving chasqui signal him to set off?
answer: He blew a conch-shell trumpet
choices: He blew a conch-shell trumpet
He waved a burning torch
He rang a heavy bronze bell
He shouted out a secret password
context: The trumpet was a pututu, a sea-conch shell. The chasqui also wore a white feather headdress so he could be spotted coming from far off, and often carried a knotted-string record called a quipu. We can still see one drawn from life in Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala's 1615 manuscript. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasqui; trexperienceperu.com/blog/chasquis-ancient-messengers

question: At Moray, near Cusco, the Inca cut sunken rings of terraces that sink like giant bowls into the ground. From the top ring to the bottom the temperature can differ by as much as 15 degrees, giving the site about twenty different little climates. What do archaeologists think Moray was used for?
answer: A laboratory to test which crops grew best
choices: A laboratory to test which crops grew best
A temple for sun-worship ceremonies
A reservoir to store mountain rainwater
An arena to stage public games
context: The twenty mini-climates would let Inca farmers see which crops thrived at which altitude before planting them across the empire's terraced mountainsides, an open-air agricultural laboratory. Source: leadingperutravel.com/blog/moray-peru; mdpi.com/2571-9408/9/2/56

question: Knot-keepers trained to read the Inca quipus passed their skill from father to son, but Spanish colonists burned great numbers of the knotted strings, believing they hid pagan worship. Most quipus can no longer be read today. What was lost that leaves the knots silent?
answer: The spoken key, passed keeper to keeper, that explained each quipu
choices: The spoken key, passed keeper to keeper, that explained each quipu
The original cords, which all rotted away in the damp
The bright dyes that once colored every string
A master alphabet the Spanish carried back to Europe
context: The keepers were quipucamayocs, and the story explaining a quipu was passed father to son; a keeper whose count was wrong could be severely punished, even executed. Gary Urton's Harvard Khipu Database has catalogued more than 900, about 700 well-formed enough to study, yet most still cannot be read because the code died with its keepers. Source: worldhistory.org/Quipu/; atlasobscura.com/articles/khipus-inca-empire-harvard-university-colonialism

question: An Inca stonemason at Sacsayhuamán, the fortress above Cusco, shaped a block weighing many tons until it met its neighbors exactly, and set it with no mortar at all. Even today, at many of those joints, what can no visitor do?
answer: Slip a sheet of paper between two blocks
choices: Slip a sheet of paper between two blocks
Find where one block ends
Tell the wall is hundreds of years old
Hear an echo off the surface
context: Inca masons fitted their blocks so tightly, with no mortar, that not even a sheet of paper or a knife blade can slip into many of the joints, at Sacsayhuamán, in Cusco and at Machu Picchu alike.

question: Visitors to a street in Cusco still stop at one green block set into the wall of the ruler Inca Roca's old palace. Its edges were cut to lock into every neighboring stone, and no Spaniard ever managed to pry it out. What did its makers cut into it?
answer: Twelve angles, each matched to a neighbor
choices: Twelve angles, each matched to a neighbor
Four clean right-angle corners
A single curved, polished face
Seven shallow grooves for ropes
context: The Twelve-Angled Stone of Hatun Rumiyoc is a single green diorite block carved with twelve precisely matched corners that lock it into its neighbors with no mortar — so solid the Spanish could not pry it loose, and it stands intact after 500-plus years. Sources: peruforless.com/blog/twelve-angle-stone; ticketmachupicchu.com/stone-twelve-angles.

question: Spanish builders raised churches and mansions in Cusco on top of Inca foundations after the 1530s. When earthquakes struck, the newer Spanish work cracked and fell, while the older Inca walls beneath, set without a speck of mortar, stayed standing. What let the Inca walls ride out the quakes?
answer: The interlocking blocks shift and resettle, so the wall 'dances' instead of cracking
choices: The interlocking blocks shift and resettle, so the wall 'dances' instead of cracking
A hidden iron frame ran through the core of each wall
The stones were fused together by intense heat
Deep mortar channels absorbed the shaking
context: Because the mortarless blocks interlock like a 3-D jigsaw, they can shift slightly and resettle during a tremor — the walls 'dance' through earthquakes instead of cracking, surviving centuries of Andean quakes that toppled later Spanish buildings. Sources: peru-explorer.com (earthquake-resistant techniques); History.com/articles/machu-picchu-construction.

question: A farmer digging a field near Peshawar in 1881 turned up 70 fragile leaves of birch bark, now called the Bakhshali manuscript, which hold the oldest written zeros known. Oxford scientists later carbon-dated some leaves to the 200s or 300s AD, far older than anyone had guessed. The zero on them is not the round 0 of today. How does it appear?
answer: as small dots
choices: as small dots
as tiny crosses
as open squares
as short dashes
context: Oxford's 2017 carbon dating pushed parts of the Bakhshali manuscript back to roughly 224-383 AD, about 500 years earlier than scholars had thought. On its birch-bark leaves, zero is written as hundreds of little dots -- the symbol slowly rounding out into the '0' shape over later centuries. Source: https://www.glam.ox.ac.uk/article/carbon-dating-finds-bakhshali-manuscript-contains-oldest-recorded-origins-symbol-zero

question: Brahmagupta, an Indian mathematician, explained numbers less than nothing in 628 with an image borrowed from money. He gave positive and negative numbers two names, so that even a minus times a minus made plain sense. What pair of names did he choose?
answer: fortunes and debts
choices: fortunes and debts
profits and losses
riches and ransoms
savings and fines
context: In his Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 AD), Brahmagupta wrote the first rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers, calling positives 'fortunes' and negatives 'debts.' One rule, 'the product or quotient of two debts is one fortune,' is the ancient way of saying a minus times a minus makes a plus. Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Brahmagupta/

question: Builders on Java raised Borobudur around the year 800 from some two million blocks of volcanic stone, and it became the greatest Buddhist temple anywhere. What is surprising about how those two million blocks fit together?
answer: They used no mortar at all, locking the stones by shape alone
choices: They used no mortar at all, locking the stones by shape alone
They poured molten iron into channels between the stones
They glued the stones with rice paste and tree resin
They left every stone loose so the temple could be rebuilt
context: Borobudur (c. 780-850 AD, built under the Sailendra dynasty) was assembled from about 2 million stone blocks fitted together WITHOUT mortar. It also carries 2,672 carved relief panels - laid end to end nearly 6 km, the longest continuous stone narrative on Earth - and 504 Buddha statues. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/world-heritage/article/borobudur-temple

question: An Indian merchant sailed east for Southeast Asia, counting on the monsoon, the Indian Ocean's great seasonal wind, to carry him there and home again on one trip. Most ocean winds keep blowing one way, which can strand a ship far from home with no breeze to carry it back. What does the monsoon do?
answer: It flips direction with the seasons, blowing one way then the opposite way
choices: It flips direction with the seasons, blowing one way then the opposite way
It blows twice as hard one way, fast enough to outrun the return
It dies away completely each night so ships drift gently home
It curves ships around in a giant circle back to where they began
context: The southwest monsoon blows June-September from Africa/India toward Southeast Asia; the northeast monsoon blows back October-March. Sailors timed voyages to ride one wind out and the other home - going and returning on a single trip without ever rowing against the wind. https://www.britannica.com/place/Indian-Ocean/Trade-winds-zone

question: Gajah Mada, who served as chief minister of the Majapahit empire on Java, made a famous public vow, the Sumpah Palapa. By legend, he swore to give up one pleasure until he had joined the whole island chain under Majapahit rule. What did he swear to give up?
answer: Eating any food flavored with spices
choices: Eating any food flavored with spices
Sleeping under any roof made of wood
Speaking to his own family members
Riding any horse into battle
context: Legend: Gajah Mada, prime minister under King Hayam Wuruk (ruled 1350-1389), swore the Palapa Oath - to eat no spiced food until all of Nusantara (the archipelago) was united under Majapahit. The court poem Nagarakretagama (1365) claimed Majapahit's reach spanned 98 territories from Sumatra to New Guinea. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palapa_oath

question: Suryavarman II, a Khmer king, built Angkor Wat in Cambodia in the 1100s and dedicated it to one god, whose stories fill its long carved galleries; only later did it become a Buddhist temple. Which god was Angkor Wat first dedicated to?
answer: The god Vishnu
choices: The god Vishnu
The god Shiva
The god Brahma
The god Indra
context: Suryavarman II (1113-1150 AD) built Angkor Wat as a HINDU temple to Vishnu; its galleries carry carved scenes from the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. Only from the late 1200s did it gradually become the Buddhist temple it remains today - so the largest religious monument on Earth began as a Hindu, not a Buddhist, temple. https://www.worldhistory.org/Angkor_Wat/

question: A king of Funan took up Hindu and Buddhist gods, Sanskrit and Indian temple art, though no Indian army had ever marched into his land to impose them. Historians call this spread across Southeast Asia Indianization. How, they say, did it take hold?
answer: Indian merchants and holy men settled in ports, and local rulers invited them to court
choices: Indian merchants and holy men settled in ports, and local rulers invited them to court
Indian rulers paid the local chiefs tribute in gold to adopt their gods
Local rulers each sailed to India and copied whatever they saw there
An older shared religion already linked India and the islands beforehand
context: In 'Indianization,' Indian merchants settled in coastal ports bringing Brahmin priests and Buddhist monks; impressed local rulers invited these holy men to their courts, because a ruler surrounded by Indian gods, Sanskrit, and ceremony was seen as more powerful and legitimate. Culture carried by trade and prestige, not conquest. https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hinduism/The-spread-of-Hinduism-in-Southeast-Asia-and-the-Pacific

question: Johann Tetzel, a Dominican friar, toured the German lands in 1517 selling indulgences, and he promised buyers that each one could release a dead relative's soul from purgatory. To close a sale he chanted a short rhyme. How did it go?
answer: 'As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs'
choices: 'As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs'
'Lay a gold piece on the holy shrine, and lift a soul from purgatory's line'
'Drop a silver in the begging bowl, and purgatory frees a waiting soul'
'Give the friar a coin to ring, and from the fire a soul takes wing'
context: Tetzel's reported sales-jingle is often rendered "As soon as the gold in the casket rings, the rescued soul to heaven springs." The instant the buyer's money clinked into the secured metal chest — the famous "Tetzel chest" — he promised the dead loved one's soul shot out of purgatory. Sources: worldhistory.org/Johann_Tetzel; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Tetzel; reformation500.csl.edu/johannes-tetzel.

question: Pope Leo X was raising money in 1517 for the rebuilding of St Peter's in Rome, and Johann Tetzel sold indulgences across Germany to help pay for it. Tetzel believed every coin went to the new church, and so did his buyers. Yet a secret arrangement quietly sent half of the German takings elsewhere. Where did that half go?
answer: To repay a loan from the banker Jacob Fugger that had bought Albert of Mainz his archbishopric
choices: To repay a loan from the banker Jacob Fugger that had bought Albert of Mainz his archbishopric
To fund a new Crusade the Pope was quietly preparing against the Turks
To pay the wages of the Swiss Guard protecting the Pope in Rome
To purchase a private collection of relics for the papal treasury
context: Albert of Mainz had borrowed roughly 20,000 guilders from the banker Jacob Fugger to buy his archbishopric. By a secret arrangement, half the German indulgence money went to repay that Fugger loan while the other half went toward rebuilding St. Peter's. Sources: britannica.com/biography/Johann-Tetzel; christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/selling-forgiveness-sparked-protestant-reformation.

question: Local farmers kept turning up old objects in a lonely heap of ancient bricks, long before any archaeologist found the great Indus city buried beneath it. In their own Sindhi language they gave the place a name, Mohenjo-daro. What does the name mean?
answer: Mound of the Dead
choices: Mound of the Dead
City of the River
Hill of the Kings
Gate of the Sun
context: Locals named it 'Mound of the Dead' because they kept turning up human and animal bones along with old artifacts there, ages before anyone knew a Bronze-Age city was underneath. Source: World History Encyclopedia, https://www.worldhistory.org/Indus_Valley_Civilization/

question: An Indus artist cast a tiny bronze girl about 4,000 years ago, barely four inches tall, with one hand on her hip, her chin lifted and bangles stacked all the way up her left arm. By what nickname is the statue from Mohenjo-daro known?
answer: the Dancing Girl
choices: the Dancing Girl
the Snake Charmer
the Bangle Maiden
the River Maiden
context: The 'Dancing Girl,' about 10.5 cm tall, was cast by the lost-wax method (c. 2300-1750 BCE) and found by Ernest Mackay in 1926 -- one of the earliest metal castings ever made. She wears about 24-25 bangles on her left arm and only 4 on her right. Mortimer Wheeler said: 'She stands there with bangles all the way up her arm and nothing else on.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing_Girl_(prehistoric_sculpture) ; https://smarthistory.org/dancing-girl-mohenjodaro/

question: Archaeologists digging at the heart of Mohenjo-daro's raised citadel uncovered a watertight brick pool about 40 feet long, with wide staircases leading down into it at both ends. It was the oldest public water tank ever found. What do archaeologists call the pool?
answer: the Great Bath
choices: the Great Bath
the Royal Cistern
the Sun Temple
the Council Hall
context: The Great Bath is the oldest known public water tank in the world -- about 12 m by 7 m and 2.4 m deep (40 x 23 x 8 ft), reached by two wide brick staircases descending from the north and south ends. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Bath ; worldatlas.com Great Bath article

question: A child in Mohenjo-daro pushed a little clay bullock cart along on wheels that really turned. Diggers found the city's other toys too: clay animals that nodded their heads and bird-shaped whistles. One clay figure did a trick when a child pulled a string through it. What was the toy?
answer: a monkey that slid down it
choices: a monkey that slid down it
a snake that reared up
a bull that charged ahead
a bird that flew in circles
context: Among the Mohenjo-daro toys was a little monkey figurine posed to slide down a string like a vine, alongside terracotta bullock carts with detachable oxen and clay animals with movable nodding heads. Sources: https://www.amarchitrakatha.com/history_details/toys-of-indus-valley-civilization/ ; https://www.harappa.com/blog/toys-and-civilization

question: Whoever designed Mohenjo-daro and Harappa more than 4,500 years ago set out their streets in advance, so that no lane tangled like a maze, and made the main avenues double the width of the side lanes. How did the main streets run?
answer: in a strict grid, north-south and east-west
choices: in a strict grid, north-south and east-west
in winding rings around a hilltop
in spokes spreading from a harbor
in terraces climbing a hillside
context: Straight streets ran north-south and east-west, oriented to the compass, with main avenues twice the width of the side lanes -- among the earliest grid-planned cities ever built. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/Indus_Valley_Civilization/ ; https://www.thearchaeologist.org/blog/sanitation-of-the-indus-valley-civilisation

question: Engineers at Mohenjo-daro gave almost every house its own toilet more than 4,000 years ago, while in most cities of the age people threw their waste into the open street. What carried the waste away beneath Mohenjo-daro's streets?
answer: covered brick sewers
choices: covered brick sewers
hollow wooden pipes
open roadside gutters
a diverted stream
context: Household toilets drained into covered brick sewers running under the streets -- the world's first urban sanitation system. National Geographic called it the 'ancient world's best plumbing,' in some ways ahead of what Rome built two thousand years later. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitation_of_the_Indus_Valley_Civilisation ; https://humanprogress.org/centers-of-progress-pt-3-mohenjo-daro-2/

question: A craftsman of the Indus Valley pressed a small carved seal into clay and left the print of a single creature. For about 700 years the same beast, always facing right, appeared on roughly half of the thousands of seals the Indus people carved. No one can say for certain what real animal it was meant to be. What do scholars nickname it?
answer: the unicorn
choices: the unicorn
the griffin
the phoenix
the sphinx
context: The 'unicorn' -- a one-horned bull facing right with a ritual object before it -- appears on roughly half to 60% of the inscribed seals (thousands of them) across c. 2600-1900 BCE. The single horn gave it the nickname; scholars still argue over what real animal, if any, it represents. Sources: https://imp-art.org/perspectives/dispatches/the-unicorn-seals-an-indus-valley-mystery/ ; https://www.harappa.com/slide/unicorn-seal-0

question: A trader in Harappa and another in Mohenjo-daro, hundreds of miles apart, weighed their goods against matching little stone cubes, and no king's stamp forced the weights to agree. The weights climbed from small to large in one exact pattern. What was it?
answer: each weight double the one before (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...)
choices: each weight double the one before (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...)
each weight one more than the last (1, 2, 3, 4, 5...)
each weight ten times the last (1, 10, 100, 1000...)
each weight a square number (1, 4, 9, 16, 25...)
context: Indus traders used cubical chert weights cut to an exact binary doubling system -- 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 -- with a base unit of about 0.86 grams. A trader in Harappa and a trader in Mohenjo-daro weighed goods on the identical standard, with no king's stamp needed to enforce it. Sources: https://www.sizes.com/units/harappan_weights.htm ; https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/social-science/chapter-1-seals-script-weights-class-12-history-notes/

question: Excavators uncovered the huge Indus cities of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, which flourished in the same age as Egypt and Mesopotamia. Yet one thing that both of those lands left behind never turned up in the Indus cities. What did the diggers never find there?
answer: any palace, royal tomb, or name of a king
choices: any palace, royal tomb, or name of a king
any clay pot, bead, or bronze tool
any house, well, or workshop
any drain, brick, or doorway
context: Unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, the Indus cities left no palaces, no temples, no royal tombs, no giant statues of kings, and not one name of any ruler -- a vast civilization with no visible monarchy. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Indus_Valley_Civilization/

question: George Dales, an archaeologist, took a fresh look at the scattered skeletons of Mohenjo-daro. An old theory had offered them as proof that invaders stormed the city and massacred its people. What did Dales find that demolished the massacre story?
answer: the skeletons bore no wounds at all
choices: the skeletons bore no wounds at all
the skeletons were soldiers in armor
the skeletons came from a much later age
the skeletons belonged to wild animals
context: George Dales showed the skeletons once read as 'battle victims' had no wounds at all, demolishing the old 'Aryan invasion massacre' story. The Indus cities show almost no signs of war. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Indus_Valley_Civilization/

question: A traveller passing under the north gate of the Indus city of Dholavira looked up at a row of ten big white gypsum symbols set into a wooden plank, every one more than a foot high. Nobody can read a word of it today. What nickname has this line of writing earned?
answer: the world's oldest billboard
choices: the world's oldest billboard
the world's oldest sundial
the world's oldest milestone
the world's oldest tombstone
context: The Dholavira signboard -- 10 large signs about 37 cm tall, inlaid in a roughly 3 m board over the citadel's north gate -- has been called the world's oldest billboard. We can see it, but still cannot read a word of it. Sources: https://www.harappa.com/blog/dholavira-and-its-mysterious-sign-board ; https://atlasobscura.com/articles/oldest-billboard-in-world

question: M. K. Stalin, chief minister of the Indian state of Tamil Nadu, put up a reward in January 2025 for anyone who could read the Indus script, some 400 signs that have defeated a century of scholars because no Rosetta Stone was ever found to unlock them. How big was the prize?
answer: one million US dollars
choices: one million US dollars
one hundred thousand dollars
ten thousand dollars
one thousand dollars
context: In January 2025, on the centenary of the civilization's discovery, Tamil Nadu's chief minister M.K. Stalin offered a US $1 million prize to anyone who can decipher the Indus script. The script has a little over 400 distinct signs, written mostly right-to-left, with inscriptions averaging about 5 signs (none longer than 26) and no bilingual key -- still unread after 100 years. Sources: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/officials-are-offering-1-million-to-anyone-who-can-decode-this-ancient-script-180985922/ ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Indus_Script/

question: John Marshall, who excavated Mohenjo-daro, studied a small stone seal from the city showing a horned figure seated like a yogi, legs crossed, with an elephant, a tiger, a rhino and a buffalo around him. In 1931 he suggested the figure was an early form of a Hindu god, the Lord of Animals, though the reading is still debated. Which god did Marshall mean?
answer: Shiva
choices: Shiva
Vishnu
Brahma
Ganesha
context: On the 'Pashupati seal' (~3.5 cm square, found 1928-29), Marshall in 1931 called the cross-legged horned figure a 'proto-Shiva,' an ancestor of the Hindu Lord of Animals -- though that reading is still debated, not settled fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pashupati_seal  (Legend.)

question: James Hargreaves, a Lancashire weaver who could not read or write, built the spinning jenny in the mid-1760s to make thread faster. An old spinning wheel spun only one thread at a time. How many threads could one worker spin at once on Hargreaves's first jenny?
answer: Eight threads at once
choices: Eight threads at once
Two threads at once
Four threads at once
Sixteen threads at once
context: The spinning jenny (1764-65) was a metal frame holding eight wooden spindles, so one worker did the work of eight spinning wheels. Later versions pushed it to 120 spindles from a single operator. Source: britannica.com/biography/James-Hargreaves ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinning_jenny

question: Richard Arkwright set a water wheel turning the machines of his new mill at Cromford, on the River Derwent, in 1771. Some 200 workers there kept hours fixed by the clock, not by daylight. What title is Arkwright remembered by?
answer: The Father of the Factory System
choices: The Father of the Factory System
The Father of British Cotton
The Master of the Mills
The Father of the Spinning Frame
context: Cromford Mill (1771) was the world's first water-powered cotton spinning mill, employing about 200 people. It was one of the first workplaces where the working day was set by the CLOCK instead of by daylight. Source: scienceandindustrymuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/richard-arkwright ; britannica.com/biography/Richard-Arkwright

question: Machine-breakers across England began smashing the new textile machines in 1811, blaming them for their poverty, and they signed their threatening letters 'Ned Ludd', the name of the leader they claimed to follow. What do historians say about Ned Ludd?
answer: He almost certainly never existed
choices: He almost certainly never existed
He was secretly Lord Byron
He owned the largest mill in Nottingham
He was hanged at York in 1813
context: The machine-breakers became known as the Luddites, after the imaginary 'Ned Ludd' they signed their letters in the name of. They carried out at least 100 attacks and destroyed about 1,000 frames. Source: nationalarchives.gov.uk/explore-the-collection/stories/the-proclamation-of-ned-ludd/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ned_Ludd  (Legend.)

question: Members of Parliament passed the Frame Breaking Act in 1812 to stop the Luddites wrecking textile machines. It set one penalty for breaking a machine, even when no person had been harmed. What could a frame-breaker now be sentenced to?
answer: Death by hanging
choices: Death by hanging
A fine of five pounds
A year in prison
Banishment from England
context: Breaking a frame became a capital crime. At York in January 1813, 14 convicted Luddites were hanged in two batches of seven, and others were transported to Australia. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_Stocking_Frames,_etc._Act_1812 ; ludditebicentenary.blogspot.com

question: Lord Byron, the poet, stood up among the Lords in February 1812 for the first speech he ever made there, while Parliament debated a new law against Luddites who smashed textile machines. What did Byron argue in that maiden speech?
answer: That hunger, not hatred of machines, drove the men
choices: That hunger, not hatred of machines, drove the men
That every last machine-breaker fully deserved to hang
That England ought to ban all of the new spinning machines
That the king himself should personally tour the cotton mills
context: Byron's maiden speech (27 February 1812) defended the Luddites against the new hanging law. He told the Lords that in Nottingham 'not twelve hours elapsed without some fresh act of violence' — forty frames broken in a single evening. Source: ludditebicentenary.blogspot.com/2012/02/27th-february-1812-lord-byrons-maiden.html ; historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=4654

question: Surveyors walked into 143 water-powered textile mills across England and Scotland in 1788 to count who was working the machines. Two-thirds of the whole workforce, they found, belonged to one group, and the finding later moved Parliament toward the Factory Act of 1833. Who were they?
answer: Children
choices: Children
Whole families together
Skilled master weavers
Irish migrant workers
context: Children made up two-thirds of the workforce in the 1788 survey. The Factory Act of 1833 finally banned mill work under age 9 and created paid inspectors to actually enforce it. Source: britannica.com/event/Factory-Act-United-Kingdom-1833 ; galbithink.org/child.htm

question: Georges Lemaître, a Belgian physicist, used Einstein's own equations in 1927 to show that the whole universe is expanding, its far-off galaxies flying apart faster the farther away they are. He worked it out two full years before Edwin Hubble measured it. Lemaître had been ordained in 1923. What was he besides a physicist?
answer: a Catholic priest
choices: a Catholic priest
a Lutheran pastor
a Baptist preacher
an Anglican vicar
context: Georges Lemaître, ordained a Catholic priest in 1923, published the expanding-universe law in 1927, two years before Hubble's measurement — a priest at the root of what became the Big Bang. (Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Georges Lemaître,' britannica.com; University of Navarra Science, Reason and Faith, unav.edu)

question: Edwin Hubble photographed a faint star in the Andromeda nebula one October night in 1923 and marked his glass plate 'N' for a nova. Then he looked again, saw what the star really was, and scrawled a triumphant word in red ink. That star proved Andromeda a separate galaxy far beyond the Milky Way. What did Hubble write?
answer: VAR!
choices: VAR!
FAR!
NEW!
RED!
context: 'VAR!' marked it as a variable star — the kind whose brightness let Hubble measure distance and prove Andromeda lay far outside the Milky Way. The plate has been called 'the only scientific artifact I know of that shows human emotion.' (Live Science 'Edwin Hubble uncovers the vastness of the universe,' livescience.com; Carnegie Science 'Hubble's Famous M31 VAR! plate,' carnegiescience.edu)

question: Fred Hoyle, an astronomer, thought the idea that the universe burst out of one explosive start was nonsense, and he backed a rival Steady State universe instead. Yet he was the man who gave the idea its everyday name, on British Broadcasting Corporation radio in 1949. What did Hoyle call it?
answer: the Big Bang
choices: the Big Bang
the Cosmic Egg
the First Flash
the Great Burst
context: Fred Hoyle used 'Big Bang' on BBC radio on 28 March 1949 to describe an idea he rejected; the name stuck to the very theory he spent his career arguing against. (Popular Science 'The big bang got its name from a man who thought the theory was total nonsense,' popsci.com; BBC Radio 4 / SciHi Blog, scihi.org)

question: The old German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on the tiny Polish base at Westerplatte in Danzig at dawn on 1 September 1939, firing some of the first shots of World War II. Days earlier it had sailed into the harbour flying party flags, as if on a friendly visit. What was it really hiding?
answer: More than 200 German marines waiting below deck
choices: More than 200 German marines waiting below deck
A cargo of food aid for the starving city
A delegation of diplomats seeking peace talks
A shipment of coal bound for the harbor
context: The pre-dreadnought Schleswig-Holstein had arrived under cover of a WWI-anniversary courtesy visit, with the assault troops concealed aboard. At 04:45 its guns opened on the Westerplatte depot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Poland; polishhistory.pl 'The Defence of Westerplatte'.

question: Major Henryk Sucharski held the little Polish base at Westerplatte with about 200 men when the Germans attacked in September 1939. His orders were to last twelve hours until help arrived, but no help came, and some 3,400 Germans kept attacking. How long did his men actually hold out?
answer: For seven days, through thirteen assaults
choices: For seven days, through thirteen assaults
For about three hours, then they fled
For a single afternoon of fighting
For exactly the twelve hours ordered
context: Ordered to last 12 hours, the garrison repelled thirteen assaults and held until September 7. The German commander, General Friedrich Eberhardt, was so impressed he let Sucharski keep his Polish saber into captivity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Westerplatte.

question: German Stukas swept over the little Polish town of Wieluń at about 4:40 on 1 September 1939, the first morning of the war, and pounded it for hours, hitting the hospital first and wrecking most of the town centre. What set the raid on Wieluń apart?
answer: The town was undefended, with no guns and no soldiers
choices: The town was undefended, with no guns and no soldiers
The town had just surrendered the day before
The bombs were meant for a different city entirely
The pilots dropped leaflets warning people first
context: Wielun had no anti-aircraft guns and no garrison. About 90 percent of its center was destroyed in roughly nine hours; one of the first buildings hit was the hospital. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Wielu%C5%84.

question: Polish horsemen of the Wołyńska Cavalry Brigade fought the German Panzers at Mokra on the first day of the war in 1939, and they won. Their ally was an unusual weapon that rolled right up to the tanks and blasted them at point-blank range. What was it?
answer: An armored train, No. 53
choices: An armored train, No. 53
A captured German Panzer
A fleet of motorcycle scouts
A row of buried land mines
context: Armored Train No. 53 fired on the Panzers at point-blank range while the cavalry brigade held; together they inflicted about 800 casualties and forced the 4th Panzer Division back to its start line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mokra; nationalww2museum.org.

question: The 18th Pomeranian Uhlans, a Polish cavalry regiment, went into battle near the village of Krojanty on 1 September 1939. The famous old story of Polish riders attacking Panzers with lances is a myth. What did the Uhlans really do?
answer: They drew sabers and scattered German infantry resting on foot
choices: They drew sabers and scattered German infantry resting on foot
They galloped straight into a column of heavy tanks
They threw their lances at low-flying Stukas
They surrendered the moment the shooting started
context: The Uhlans routed German infantry on foot and were winning until armored cars arrived. Italian reporter Indro Montanelli later saw the dead horses, assumed they had charged tanks, and the lance-versus-tank legend was born. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charge_at_Krojanty.

question: A German Panzer crew punched through the Polish lines in September 1939, its radio keeping it in touch with every other unit, in a new way of fighting called Blitzkrieg, lightning war. The Ju 87 Stuka dive-bombers overhead had one special job to do for the tanks. What did the Stukas do for them?
answer: They served as flying artillery, smashing targets ahead of the tanks
choices: They served as flying artillery, smashing targets ahead of the tanks
They dropped supplies and fuel to the advancing tanks
They scouted quietly and reported enemy positions by radio
They evacuated wounded crews back behind the lines
context: Stukas dived near-vertically as precision 'flying artillery' clearing the way for the Panzers, while the Luftwaffe bombed rail lines, bridges and airfields so the Poles could never concentrate a defense. Source: nationalww2museum.org; historyskills.com.

question: Adolf Hitler wanted the world to see Germany as the victim, not the attacker, when he invaded Poland. So the night before the invasion, under the code name Himmler, German agents staged a fake attack and left a body behind as proof. What did they stage?
answer: SS men in Polish uniforms faked an assault on a German radio station
choices: SS men in Polish uniforms faked an assault on a German radio station
A Polish ship was reported sinking a German fishing boat
A bomb was set off in a crowded Berlin train station
A border guard was photographed tearing down a German flag
context: At Gleiwitz, SS men in Polish uniforms staged the attack and left a body in a Polish uniform as 'proof', giving Hitler his pretext to claim Germany was returning fire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Poland; nationalww2museum.org.

question: A Polish soldier was still fighting the Germans in the west on 17 September 1939 when more than 600,000 troops swept over Poland's border in the east. Britain and France had declared war on Germany two weeks before but sent no real help. Who launched this second invasion, from the east?
answer: The Soviet Union
choices: The Soviet Union
The kingdom of Hungary
The Czechoslovak army
The forces of Romania
context: Under the secret Molotov-Ribbentrop pact that had already carved Poland in two, the Red Army invaded from the east. Molotov claimed the Polish state 'had ceased to exist' and the Soviets were merely 'protecting' Ukrainians and Belarusians. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_invasion_of_Poland; ushmm.org.

question: General Guderian of the German army and Brigadier Krivoshein of the Red Army ate breakfast together on 22 September 1939 in the fortress of Brest-Litovsk, which the Germans had captured. Before the fortress changed hands, what did the two armies stage?
answer: A joint military parade
choices: A joint military parade
A signing of a peace treaty
A prisoner exchange ceremony
A funeral for the fallen
context: The Germans and Soviets held a joint parade in Brest-Litovsk before the Germans handed the fortress to the Red Army, a striking image of the two totalitarian powers cooperating to dismember Poland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German%E2%80%93Soviet_military_parade_in_Brest-Litovsk.

question: Soldiers of Stalin's Red Army took a Polish officer prisoner in 1939, one of as many as 450,000 Poles they captured. The ordinary troops were released in time, but thousands of officers like him, along with policemen and educated leaders, were never freed. What did Stalin's secret police, the People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs (NKVD), do to them in 1940?
answer: They shot about 22,000 of them at Katyn and other sites
choices: They shot about 22,000 of them at Katyn and other sites
They drafted them into the Soviet army by force
They put them on trial and then released most of them
They sent them home in exchange for grain shipments
context: The NKVD murdered roughly 22,000 Polish officers and elites at Katyn and elsewhere, then for decades the Soviets blamed the Germans. The eastern invasion fed directly into one of the war's great hidden massacres. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_invasion_of_Poland.

question: Henry IV, the German king, crossed the freezing Alps in January 1077 to Canossa castle, where Pope Gregory VII was staying. The pope had excommunicated him, and his nobles threatened to dethrone him. What did Henry do for three days to win forgiveness?
answer: Stood barefoot in the snow, wearing only rough wool
choices: Stood barefoot in the snow, wearing only rough wool
Was chained to the gate by his own soldiers
Crawled the final mile on his bare knees
Waited on horseback in full armor and his crown
context: Henry IV, the most powerful king in Europe, humbled himself completely. Pope Gregory VII later wrote that Henry, 'having laid aside all the belongings of royalty, wretchedly, with bare feet and clad in wool,' stood three days before the gate. This is the most famous penance in medieval history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_to_Canossa

question: Pope Gregory VII and Henry IV, the German king, fought in the late 1000s over who could install new bishops. Whoever handed a new bishop the two signs of his office, one marking his bond to his church, showed who outranked whom. Which two objects were they?
answer: A ring and a staff
choices: A ring and a staff
A crown and a sword
A scroll and a key
A chalice and a candle
context: The staff was called a crozier (shaped like a shepherd's crook), and the ring marked the bishop's bond to his church.
