The real quarrel was over who got to do the handing — king or pope — which meant a fight over who outranked whom. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Investiture-Controversy

question: Henry IV sent Pope Gregory VII a furious letter in 1076, a year before Canossa, and would not even call him pope: he addressed it to Hildebrand, Gregory's birth name, and called him a false monk. How did Henry end the letter?
answer: "Descend, descend, and be damned throughout the ages."
choices: "Descend, descend, and be damned throughout the ages."
"Kneel, kneel, and repent before your king."
"Be silent and obey the crown of Germany."
"Surrender your throne or perish in disgrace."
context: Henry's letter opened by calling Gregory 'not pope but FALSE MONK' and ordered him off the papal throne. Gregory's answer was to excommunicate Henry and release all Christians from their oaths of loyalty to him — which is exactly why Henry later had to crawl to Canossa. Source: https://historyofthegermans.com/2021/10/lettertogregory/

question: Otto von Bismarck, the German chancellor, took on the Catholic Church in a power struggle of his own in 1872. By then, to go to Canossa meant to humble oneself before an enemy, after Henry IV's penance there in 1077. What did Bismarck declare?
answer: "We will not go to Canossa!"
choices: "We will not go to Canossa!"
"Let them remember Canossa!"
"Berlin is not Canossa!"
"Canossa shall be avenged!"
context: The idiom is so deeply rooted that it survives in German, Dutch, Danish, Swedish, French, Italian, Hungarian, Hebrew, and Polish. Bismarck's full boast was 'We will not go to Canossa, neither in body nor in spirit' — 800 years after a king stood barefoot in the snow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_to_Canossa

question: Pope Gregory VII set out the Dictatus Papae in 1075, twenty-seven bold claims about a pope's powers, among them the right to depose an emperor. One clause spelled out the submission Gregory expected from every prince. What were all princes to do?
answer: Kiss the feet of the pope alone
choices: Kiss the feet of the pope alone
Send their crowns to Rome each year
Swear their oaths upon the pope's ring
Kneel before any bishop they met
context: The Dictatus Papae was a stunning assertion that spiritual authority outranked every king and emperor. The collision between this claim and royal power is a deep root of the Western distinction between sacred and secular authority — a separation the later tradition of liberty inherited. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictatus_papae

question: Gregory VII died far from Rome, at Salerno, in 1085, after Henry IV had marched on Rome with an army, driven the pope out and set up a rival in his place. What do the words later carved on Gregory's tomb have him say?
answer: "I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile."
choices: "I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile."
"Rome has fallen, but Heaven remembers her servant."
"Let no king ever again raise his hand against God."
"I forgive Henry, as I hope to be forgiven."
context: Gregory died at Salerno, exiled by the very king who had once knelt barefoot before him — so Canossa was a setback for Henry, not a true defeat. The defiant epitaph casts the dying pope as the righteous loser. Source: https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/06791c.htm

question: Winston Churchill, recently voted out as Britain's prime minister, spoke in Fulton, Missouri, in March 1946. 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic,' he warned, something had come down across Europe, walling the Soviet-held East off from the free West. What did he call it?
answer: An iron curtain
choices: An iron curtain
A steel wall
An iron gate
A stone barrier
context: Churchill titled the address 'The Sinews of Peace,' but history remembers it as the 'Iron Curtain Speech.' The line he drew — Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic — marked off the Soviet-controlled captives from the free West, naming a divide that would define the next forty years. Source: America's National Churchill Museum (nationalchurchillmuseum.org); Wikipedia 'Fulton Speech.'

question: Reporters in the hall at Fulton, Missouri, held printed copies of Winston Churchill's speech in March 1946 before he began. Yet afterwards the shorthand writers had to rebuild several of his best-remembered lines from their own notes, since those lines were nowhere in the printed text. How did the lines get into his speech?
answer: He ad-libbed them past his prepared text
choices: He ad-libbed them past his prepared text
He memorized them and recited from notes
An aide cued them to him from the wings
He read them from a hidden index card
context: Churchill spoke past his typed text, so the stenographers in the hall had to reconstruct his most famous lines from their shorthand notes — the words the whole world would quote were improvised on his feet and pieced back together afterward. Source: Wikipedia 'Fulton Speech.'

question: A farmer near Jos in Nigeria gave Bernard Fagg, a British archaeologist, a clay head in 1943 that had been sitting on top of a scarecrow among the farmer's yams. What did the scarecrow's head turn out to be?
answer: The namesake first find of the lost Nok culture
choices: The namesake first find of the lost Nok culture
A burial mask traded down from ancient Egypt
A toy carved by a bored colonial soldier
A medieval charm left by passing merchants
context: Named the Jemaa Head after the nearby village, it launched the study of the Nok culture of central Nigeria, whose terracottas are the oldest known figurative sculptures made south of the Sahara. Source: Archaeology Magazine, 'The Nok of Nigeria'.

question: A Nok artist in central Nigeria, some 2,500 years ago, pierced the nostrils, mouth and ears of a hollow clay head, drilled tiny holes through the pupils of its eyes, and then fired it. The holes did more than look striking. What else did they do?
answer: Let trapped heat escape so the figure wouldn't crack
choices: Let trapped heat escape so the figure wouldn't crack
Held strings so the heads could be worn as pendants
Drained rainwater so the clay would not rot
Whistled in the wind to scare birds from the field
context: The pierced nostrils, ears, and pupils doubled as air vents: as the hollow clay was fired, heat and steam escaped through them instead of building up and shattering the sculpture. Function and style in one move. Source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Nok Terracottas'; World History Encyclopedia, Nok Culture.

question: Archaeologists digging at Taruga in central Nigeria uncovered iron furnaces lying next to old flaked blades, and they dated the smelting to the fourth to second centuries BC. Much of the ancient world went from knapped flint to bronze and only later to iron. What did the Taruga finds show about the Nok?
answer: They skipped bronze entirely, jumping from stone tools straight to iron
choices: They skipped bronze entirely, jumping from stone tools straight to iron
They mastered bronze first, then slowly worked their way up to iron
They learned iron-smelting from Egyptian traders crossing the Sahara
They used bronze and iron side by side for hundreds of years
context: Charcoal from the Taruga furnaces radiocarbon-dates the smelting to the 4th-2nd centuries BCE, making the Nok among the earliest iron-smelters in sub-Saharan Africa. They jumped from stone tools straight to iron hoes, hand-axes, and cleavers, with no Bronze Age in between. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Nok Culture.

question: Hannah, Isaac Newton's mother, gave birth to him at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire on Christmas Day 1642. He came early and so tiny that no one expected him to live a week. She later said he could have fit inside one everyday thing. What was it?
answer: A quart mug
choices: A quart mug
A cooking pot
A wooden pail
A soldier's helmet
context: His mother Hannah Ayscough said the premature baby was so small he could have fit inside a quart mug; his father had died three months before he was born, at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton (also National Trust, Woolsthorpe Manor history).

question: A piece of fruit fell from a tree in the garden at Woolsthorpe while the young Isaac Newton, home from Cambridge, sat watching. It came straight down, not sideways and not up, and he asked himself why. What fruit set him thinking about gravity?
answer: An apple
choices: An apple
A pear
A plum
A cherry
context: The apple story is real and in Newton's own words: his friend William Stukeley recorded Newton saying the idea of gravity came to him 'occasion'd by the fall of an apple... Why should it not go sideways or upwards, but constantly to the earth's centre?' Source: William Stukeley, Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life (1752); https://blogs.royalsociety.org/history-of-science/2012/02/22/newtons-apple-tree/.

question: Isaac Newton asked himself in the 1660s whether the pull that brings falling things down to the ground might reach far beyond it, out into the sky. He came to believe that one force was doing two jobs, one on Earth and one in the heavens. What else did he say that pull was doing?
answer: Holding the Moon in its orbit around the Earth
choices: Holding the Moon in its orbit around the Earth
Streaming a comet's bright tail out behind it
Turning the whole sky of stars once a night
Pushing the clouds across the sky
context: This was the unification of the heavens and the earth: one law of universal gravitation governs both the falling apple and the orbiting Moon, set out in his 1687 book the Principia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophi%C3%A6_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica.

question: The 22-year-old Isaac Newton left Cambridge in the summer of 1665 and went home to the family farm at Woolsthorpe for nearly two years. A deadly outbreak, killing about one Londoner in four, had shut the university. What disease had closed it?
answer: The plague
choices: The plague
Cholera
Smallpox
Typhoid
context: Those years home from the plague (summer 1665 to spring 1667) became his 'year of wonders,' when he invented calculus, split sunlight with a prism, and began his theory of gravity. He later said, 'For in those days I was in the prime of my age for invention.' Source: https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/nottinghamshire-lincolnshire/woolsthorpe-manor/history-of-woolsthorpe-manor.

question: Edmond Halley, the astronomer, paid out of his own pocket to print Isaac Newton's Principia in 1687, or the book might never have appeared. The Royal Society could not pay, because it had just used up its funds on something else. What had the Society spent its money on?
answer: A lavish book about fish
choices: A lavish book about fish
A new telescope for the king
A grand banquet for its members
A voyage to chart the stars
context: When Halley visited in 1684 and asked what curve a planet follows under an inverse-square force, Newton instantly replied 'an ellipse.' Halley coaxed him to write it all up, then paid for printing himself because the Royal Society had run out of money after spending its budget on a book about fish. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophi%C3%A6_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica.

question: Isaac Newton found that the pull between two bodies falls off with the distance between them squared. When two bodies end up twice as far apart, the pull between them does not simply drop to a half. What fraction of the original pull is left?
answer: One quarter
choices: One quarter
One third
One eighth
One sixteenth
context: Universal gravitation is an inverse-square law: the force falls off with the square of the distance. Doubling the distance squares to four, so the pull drops to one-quarter. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophi%C3%A6_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica.

question: Robert Hooke insisted in public that the inverse-square law of gravity was his own idea, just as Isaac Newton was finishing the Principia, and he demanded the credit. What did the furious Newton do to his manuscript?
answer: Went through it deleting nearly every mention of Hooke
choices: Went through it deleting nearly every mention of Hooke
Burned the whole manuscript in a fit of rage
Added a page openly mocking Hooke by name
Refused to let it be published for ten years
context: Hooke conceded the mathematical proof was entirely Newton's, but Newton went through the manuscript striking out nearly every mention of Hooke's name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton-Hooke_priority_controversy_for_the_inverse_square_law.

question: Gottfried Leibniz, the German mathematician, and Isaac Newton both insisted they had invented calculus first, and their quarrel turned bitter. Newton, president of the Royal Society, had it name a committee to judge the dispute, and he filled the committee with his own supporters. What else did he secretly do to fix the outcome?
answer: He wrote the committee's verdict himself
choices: He wrote the committee's verdict himself
He bribed two of the committee members
He fed secret evidence to a chosen ally
He destroyed Leibniz's oldest letters
context: Newton stacked the supposedly impartial committee with his own supporters and anonymously wrote its 1713 verdict (the Commercium Epistolicum), ruling in his own favor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leibniz%E2%80%93Newton_calculus_controversy.

question: John Maynard Keynes, the economist, bought a hoard of Isaac Newton's private papers in 1936, expecting mathematics, and turned up roughly a million words on alchemy, with even more on religion. Newton was no first man of the age of reason, Keynes declared. What was he instead, in Keynes's words?
answer: The last of the magicians
choices: The last of the magicians
The last of the prophets
The last of the alchemists
The last of the philosophers
context: Of roughly 10 million words Newton left in manuscript, about a million are on alchemy and about half is religious writing. After buying these papers in 1936, Keynes declared, 'Newton was not the first of the age of reason. He was the last of the magicians.' Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Keynes_Newton/ (Keynes, 'Newton, the Man', 1936).

question: Shut out of Cambridge by the plague in 1665, young Isaac Newton went home to Woolsthorpe, where in under two years he began work on gravity, light and a new kind of mathematics. What Latin name do scholars give that stretch of his life?
answer: His annus mirabilis, or 'wonderful year'
choices: His annus mirabilis, or 'wonderful year'
His tempus fugit, or 'time that flies'
His terra incognita, or 'unknown land'
His casus belli, or 'cause for war'
context: With Cambridge shut for the plague (1665-1666), Newton at Woolsthorpe Manor laid the groundwork for gravity, optics, and calculus all at once -- the 'annus mirabilis.' Source: thonyc.wordpress.com 'Isaac and the Apple'; Linda Hall Library scientist-of-the-day.

question: In a room he had darkened, Isaac Newton let one beam of sunlight in through a hole in the shutter and passed it through a triangular glass prism. What did he see the beam become on the wall?
answer: A spread-out band of every rainbow colour
choices: A spread-out band of every rainbow colour
A single narrow beam of pure white light
One round, bright white spot of sunlight
Two thin beams of plain white light
context: The prism fanned white light into a band of colours -- Newton called this spreading 'dispersion.' Source: livescience.com on Newton's light experiments; testbook.com Newton's prism experiment.

question: William Stukeley took tea with the elderly Isaac Newton under some apple trees in 1726, and Newton told him how, long before, an apple had set him thinking about gravity. Cartoons later had the apple strike him on the head. What did Newton say really happened?
answer: He watched an apple fall straight to the ground
choices: He watched an apple fall straight to the ground
An apple struck him hard on the top of the head
He caught a falling apple in his open hand
He shook the tree until apples rained down
context: William Stukeley's 'Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life' (1752) records Newton saying a falling apple set him wondering about gravity; the apple-on-the-head version is later myth. Source: gethistories.com 'The Apple of His Eye'; amusingplanet.com on Newton's apple tree.

question: A storm blew flat the old Flower of Kent apple tree at Woolsthorpe early in the 1800s, the very tree said to have set Isaac Newton thinking about gravity. Yet the same tree went on living in the orchard. How did the fallen tree live on?
answer: Part of the toppled tree re-rooted and kept growing
choices: Part of the toppled tree re-rooted and kept growing
Gardeners propped it upright again with iron posts
New bark slowly grew over the cracked, fallen trunk
A cutting was replanted in the same spot
context: After the 1816 storm, part of the fallen 'Flower of Kent' re-rooted, so the same tree -- over 350 years old -- still grows in the orchard. Source: york.ac.uk on Newton's apple tree; amusingplanet.com.

question: Isaac Newton built a new kind of telescope in 1668, the first of its kind, because glass lenses blurred starlight with fringes of colour. The king, Charles II, was shown it. What did Newton put inside to gather the starlight?
answer: A curved polished mirror
choices: A curved polished mirror
A second, thicker glass lens
A hollow polished cone of brass
A spinning disc of clear quartz
context: Newton's reflecting telescope (1668) used a curved mirror instead of a lens to dodge the colour-smearing of glass; the Royal Society showed it to Charles II and elected Newton a Fellow in January 1672. Source: en.wikipedia.org, Newton's reflector.

question: A cannon lurched backward the instant it fired its ball, and Isaac Newton explained why with one of the three laws of motion he set out in the Principia. Which law explained the lurch?
answer: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
choices: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
A moving body keeps moving until some force stops it
The push on a body equals its mass times its speeding-up
Every body pulls every other body with the force of gravity
context: Newton's third law: 'To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction... directed to contrary parts.' (The other choices paraphrase his first and second laws and his law of gravity -- all real, but not the one behind recoil.) Source: en.wikipedia.org, Newton's laws of motion.

question: Edmond Halley called on Isaac Newton in 1684 with a puzzle that had stumped London's finest minds: what path would a planet follow if the Sun's pull grew weaker the farther away it went? Newton answered at once: an ellipse. Halley asked how he knew. What did Newton reply?
answer: That he had already calculated it years before
choices: That he had already calculated it years before
That he had read the answer in Kepler's books
That he had simply guessed the likeliest shape
That he would need many more years to find out
context: Per Abraham De Moivre's memorandum, Newton said 'I have calculated it' -- then couldn't find the paper and had to work it out again. Source: newtonproject.ox.ac.uk (De Moivre); pbs.org NOVA on the Principia.

question: Isaac Newton ran what he called his crucial experiment in 1666. He picked out a single colour of light with one prism and sent it alone through a second prism, and it came out exactly the same colour as before. What did Newton say this proved about white light?
answer: The colours were already hidden inside the white light
choices: The colours were already hidden inside the white light
The prism itself was painting fresh colours onto the light
Glass slowly stains any light that passes through it
White light has no real colours, only tricks of the eye
context: Because a single colour passed unchanged through a second prism, Newton argued the prism does not create colours -- they are already present in white light, and the prism only separates them. Source: testbook.com Newton's prism experiment; livescience.com.

question: Edmond Halley paid the whole printing bill for Isaac Newton's Principia in 1687, because the Royal Society had no money left. Later, when the Society fell behind on Halley's salary and still had no cash, it paid him in a very strange currency. What did the Society hand him?
answer: Leftover copies of its costly picture-book about fishes
choices: Leftover copies of its costly picture-book about fishes
A gold medal struck specially in his honour
A lifetime seat on the Society's ruling council
A share of every future copy of the Principia sold
context: The Society had blown its whole book budget on 'De Historia Piscium' (History of Fishes), a lavish flop, leaving nothing to print the Principia -- so Halley funded it, and was later 'paid' part of his salary in unsold fish books. Source: royalsociety.org 'the fishy blunder'; en.wikipedia.org, De Historia piscium.

question: Johannes Kepler worked out three separate rules of how the planets move, decades before Isaac Newton, one of them that every planet's path is an ellipse around the Sun. They looked like three unrelated facts of nature. What did Newton prove about them in the Principia?
answer: They all follow automatically from his one law of gravity
choices: They all follow automatically from his one law of gravity
They were wrong and had to be completely replaced
They applied only to Earth, not the other planets
They were three different forces, not one
context: Newton proved Kepler's laws are not separate rules but consequences of the single inverse-square law of gravity -- the planets obey Kepler because they obey Newton. Source: en.wikipedia.org, universal gravitation; britannica.com, Principia.

question: 'I seem to have been only like a boy playing on the seashore,' Isaac Newton is supposed to have said, 'finding a smoother pebble or a prettier shell, whilst the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me.' What do careful scholars say about the line?
answer: It is found nowhere in any of Newton's own writings
choices: It is found nowhere in any of Newton's own writings
A Victorian schoolbook editor first put the words in his mouth
It was actually a saying of the older scientist Robert Boyle
It first turns up in a biography written long after he died
context: LEGEND: the 'pebbles and shells on the seashore' humility quote is traditionally attributed to Newton but appears nowhere in his own writings -- it is fond tradition, not a documented saying. (The other choices are plausible-sounding stories, but the sourced truth is simply that it is absent from everything he wrote.) Source: todayinsci.com on Newton 'playing on the seashore.'

question: Abd al-Malik was caliph when builders finished a great shrine in Jerusalem around 691, the oldest Islamic building to stand to this day. They set a huge golden dome on an eight-sided base and raised the whole shrine around one thing at its very centre. What was it?
answer: A bare rock
choices: A bare rock
A golden coffin
A carved throne
A stone tablet
context: The Dome of the Rock was built under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik (691-692 CE), about 60 meters wide with a golden dome roughly 20 meters across, raised to shelter one bare stone. Three faiths hold that rock sacred: Muslims tie it to Muhammad's Night Journey, while Jewish and Christian tradition link it to Abraham's near-sacrifice and the ancient Temple. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome_of_the_Rock

question: Ibn Zamrak, court poet at the Alhambra in Granada, wrote verses for its walls in the voice of the rooms themselves, so that the palace would speak to everyone who entered. In the Hall of the Two Sisters, what did he have the room announce?
answer: "I am a garden adorned by beauty."
choices: "I am a garden adorned by beauty."
"I am the gate to paradise."
"I am the throne of kings."
"I am stronger than stone."
context: Ibn Zamrak (1333-1393) made the Alhambra's walls literally speak. On the lions' fountain he wrote of the water and marble that 'you cannot tell which of them is flowing,' and in the Hall of the Two Sisters the room declares itself a garden. Source: https://www.alhambradegranada.org/en/info/epigraphicpoems.asp

question: The Nasrid sultans, the last Muslim rulers of Granada, roofed the Hall of the Two Sisters in the Alhambra with a ceiling that seemed to hang overhead like the night sky: more than 5,000 tiny plaster cells dropping in tiers from a central star, like a honeycomb or hanging stalactites. What is this kind of plasterwork called?
answer: Muqarnas
choices: Muqarnas
Arabesque
Minaret
Mihrab
context: Muqarnas was invented around the 10th century in northeastern Iran or North Africa to solve a real engineering puzzle: how to fit a round dome on top of a square room. Stacks of small prism-like cells bridge the corners and hide the join, turning a structural problem into pure decoration. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muqarnas

question: The tile-cutters of the Alhambra, with only compass and ruler in hand, covered its walls with patterns that repeat without end. Centuries later mathematicians proved, in the 1890s, that such a pattern can repeat across a flat surface in only a fixed number of basic ways. The old craftsmen, it is famously said, used every one. How many of those patterns are said to be in the Alhambra?
answer: 17 of them
choices: 17 of them
9 of them
24 of them
40 of them
context: Mathematicians call them the 17 'wallpaper groups' (plane crystallographic groups) and proved in the 1890s that exactly 17 exist. The Nasrid artisans hit all 17 by eye, centuries earlier, using only compass, ruler, and medieval set-squares called cartabones. Source: https://euromathsoc.org/magazine/articles/246

question: Abd al-Malik, the caliph who built the Dome of the Rock, had his name set in its dedication, dated to the Islamic year 72. More than a century later the caliph al-Ma'mun had that name scraped away and his own carved in its place, but he left one detail untouched. What gives his forgery away?
answer: A date a century too early
choices: A date a century too early
A misspelling of his name
A crack down the gold dome
A verse quoted wrong
context: The Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun (early 800s) swapped in his own name but forgot to change the date, which still reads 'year 72' (692 CE), more than a century before his reign. That same inscription band, about 240 meters of Kufic script, carries some of the oldest surviving verses of the Quran anywhere. Source: https://www.islamic-awareness.org/history/islam/inscriptions/dotr

question: Craftsmen decorating a mosque left out pictures of people and animals, for fear such images might be worshipped as idols, though painters at the Persian and Mughal courts did paint them. One art came to stand above all the rest: to make it, or merely to look at it, was itself an act of worship. What was it?
answer: Beautiful Arabic calligraphy of the Quran's verses
choices: Beautiful Arabic calligraphy of the Quran's verses
Lifelike portraits of the prophets and caliphs
Stained-glass windows showing scenes from heaven
Carved marble statues of angels and guardians
context: With figural images off-limits in sacred settings (aniconism), writing itself became the highest art. Arabic calligraphy of Quranic verses is ranked above all other Islamic arts, and crafting or contemplating it counts as worship and meditation. Source: metmuseum.org/essays/geometric-patterns-in-islamic-art; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calligraphy

question: Tilemakers finished the walls of the Darb-i Imam shrine in Isfahan in 1453, building their design from just five shapes called girih tiles. In 2007 Peter Lu, a Harvard student, saw that they had made a kind of pattern Roger Penrose described in the West about 500 years later. What had the tilemakers built?
answer: A non-repeating 'quasicrystal' tiling
choices: A non-repeating 'quasicrystal' tiling
A perfectly symmetrical mirror grid
A spiral that shrinks toward its center
A repeating checkerboard of square tiles
context: In 2007 Harvard physics student Peter Lu recognized the Isfahan tiling as a near-perfect 'quasicrystal' — a pattern that fills space forever without ever repeating. He was so gripped he said he couldn't sleep for days and skipped Christmas break to study it. The craftsmen had anticipated Penrose's quasicrystal geometry by roughly five centuries. Source: sciencenews.org/article/ancient-islamic-penrose-tiles-0 (Lu & Steinhardt 2007)

question: Ibn Sina, the Persian scholar known in Europe as Avicenna, was already treating patients as a doctor in his teens. Years before that, by the age of ten, he had learned one enormous book by heart, word for word. Which book was it?
answer: The entire Quran
choices: The entire Quran
Aristotle's works
Euclid's Elements
Homer's Iliad
context: Avicenna had memorized the whole Quran by age 10 and was practicing as a physician by about 16–17. As a teenager he cured the Samanid ruler Nuh ibn Mansur when the royal doctors couldn't, and his reward was the run of the prince's magnificent library. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna.

question: Avicenna finished his Canon of Medicine around 1025, and doctors in both Islamic and Christian schools went on learning from it long after most textbooks would have been replaced. About how long did the Canon stay their standard medical textbook?
answer: About 600 years
choices: About 600 years
About 300 years
About 900 years
About 1,200 years
context: The Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, c.1025) was THE standard medical textbook in European universities until roughly 1650 — about 600 years as the doctor's bible across both the Islamic world and Christian Europe. It even argued, centuries before microscopes, that some diseases spread by tiny tainted particles, recommending a 40-day isolation — an early quarantine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna.

question: Ibn al-Haytham let a single pinpoint of light into a sealed, pitch-dark room in Cairo and watched an upside-down picture of the street outside glow on the far wall. He called such a room al-bayt al-muzlim, 'the dark room.' What name did the Arabic take in Latin?
answer: Camera obscura
choices: Camera obscura
Lucerna magica
Speculum solis
Vitrum opticum
context: Ibn al-Haytham (c.965–c.1040, known in Europe as Alhazen) called the darkened room 'Albait Almuzlim,' Latinized as CAMERA OBSCURA — the ancestor of the photographic camera. Through the pinhole he even watched an eclipsed sun appear as 'the form of a moonsickle.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_al-Haytham.

question: A scholar in the service of the Abbasid caliphs worked in one famous place in Baghdad around 820, turning Greek science into Arabic while others beside him did the same with Persian and Indian science. It was part library, part study hall and part observatory. What was it called?
answer: The House of Wisdom
choices: The House of Wisdom
The Hall of Mirrors
The Tower of Scholars
The Court of Stars
context: The House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) in Baghdad was a library, study center, and observatory rolled into one, where al-Khwarizmi himself worked under Caliph al-Ma'mun. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wisdom

question: An astronomer of the Islamic world turned the openwork map of the heavens on his flat brass disc until it matched the night sky, and the instrument told him the hour and his place. Its name comes from Greek. What does that name mean?
answer: Star-taker
choices: Star-taker
Sky-wheel
Sun-reader
Night-glass
context: From Greek astron (star) + lambanein (to take). The astrolabe has been called a 'mathematical jewel.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrolabe

question: Al-Khwarizmi set the Arabic word al-jabr into the title of his book around 820. Before it ever meant anything in mathematics, al-jabr was a medical word. What did it first mean?
answer: Setting broken bones
choices: Setting broken bones
Mixing healing potions
Reading the stars
Weighing gold coins
context: 'Al-jabr' meant the restoration or reuniting of broken parts — it was the word for bone-setting. Al-Khwarizmi borrowed it because his method 'restores' an equation by moving terms to make it whole again. Source: https://www.wnycstudios.org/podcasts/science-diction/articles/algebra-from-broken-bones-to-twitter-feuds

question: Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on the numerals of India, and Europeans came to read it. From him they took the round sign that holds an open place in a number, so that 105 is never mistaken for 15, and its Arabic name, sifr, which became the word zero. What did sifr mean?
answer: Empty
choices: Empty
Round
Hidden
Endless
context: 'Sifr' (empty) became Latin 'cifra,' then split into both 'cipher' (a secret code) and 'zero.' Al-Khwarizmi's book popularized this Hindu place-holder idea. Source: https://www.todayifoundout.com/index.php/2015/09/the-story-of-zero/

question: Ibn al-Haytham ran careful experiments on light in Cairo around 1020, and they overturned a theory of sight that Euclid and Ptolemy had taught for centuries. Their explanation, he showed, was simply wrong. What had the two Greeks believed the eye did when it looked at something?
answer: Shot out rays to feel distant objects
choices: Shot out rays to feel distant objects
Soaked up light reflected off objects
Caught thin films shed by objects
Stirred the air between itself and objects
context: Euclid and Ptolemy held that the eye sends out rays to 'feel' the world. Ibn al-Haytham proved the opposite — we see because light bounces OFF objects and travels INTO the eye. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_al-Haytham

question: A Muslim astronomer read the sun's height on his astrolabe and fixed from it the hour of one of the five daily prayers. The same instrument showed each worshipper which way to face while praying. Which direction did it find?
answer: The direction of Mecca
choices: The direction of Mecca
The direction of sunrise
The direction of the North Star
The direction of the nearest river
context: That direction is called the qibla. The 10th-century astronomer al-Sufi wrote a text of 386 chapters describing more than 1,000 uses for the astrolabe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrolabe

question: Mariam al-Astrulabi built astrolabes in Aleppo in the 900s for its ruler, Sayf al-Dawla, so cleverly made that she was one of the first women engineers whose names survive. A thousand years later, she received a fitting honour. What was named after her?
answer: An asteroid
choices: An asteroid
A university
A bridge
A festival
context: The main-belt asteroid 7060 Al-'Ijliya, discovered in 1990, is named for Mariam al-Astrulabi (al-'Ijliyya) — a fitting tribute to a maker of star-finding instruments. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-%CA%BBIjliyyah

question: Ibn al-Haytham, whom Europe would know as Alhazen, wrote the Book of Optics. He also set down one famous line about the attitude that a seeker after truth must take toward every book he studies. What, by that line, must the seeker make himself?
answer: The enemy of all that he reads
choices: The enemy of all that he reads
The servant of all that he reads
The mirror of all that he reads
The heir of all that he reads
context: Ibn al-Haytham wrote that a truth-seeker 'must make himself the enemy of all that he reads' — questioning every authority. His Book of Optics drew conclusions from controlled experiments centuries before the term 'scientific method' existed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_al-Haytham

question: Al-Hakim, the feared caliph of Egypt, summoned Ibn al-Haytham to dam the Nile after the scholar promised he could tame its yearly floods. At the river he saw it was far too great to tame, and failure meant death. By the famous story, how did he stay alive until al-Hakim died?
answer: He faked being insane
choices: He faked being insane
He fled across the desert
He bribed the caliph's guards
He swore a binding oath of secrecy
context: Legend holds that madness was legally protected, so Ibn al-Haytham pretended to lose his mind and was kept under house arrest for about ten years — and used that confinement to write his Book of Optics. Source: https://www.ibnalhaytham.com/discover/who-was-ibn-al-haytham/

question: American commanders in the Pacific jumped past the strongest Japanese island fortresses after 1942 and seized weaker islands nearby for airfields. The garrisons they left behind were cut off and bombed but never invaded. What did the Americans say would become of them?
answer: They would wither on the vine
choices: They would wither on the vine
They would melt into the sea
They would burn to the ground
They would sink without a trace
context: The leapfrogging strategy bypassed fortified islands and let their garrisons 'wither on the vine' — useless to Japan's war effort, cut off from supply and reinforcement. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/pacific-strategy-1941-1944 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leapfrogging_(strategy)

question: Willie Keeler, a baseball hitter of the old days, was famous for where he put the ball. American commanders in the Pacific borrowed his motto for their plan to skip past the strongest Japanese islands and take weaker ones. What was the motto?
answer: "Hit 'em where they ain't"
choices: "Hit 'em where they ain't"
"Keep your eye on the ball"
"Swing for the fences"
"Three strikes and you're out"
context: Willie Keeler's hitting motto became the commanders' shorthand for leapfrogging: the goal was speed and saving lives, not capturing every island for its own sake. Source: warhistory.org/article/island-hopping-and-leap-frogging-u-s-strategies-part-i ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leapfrogging_(strategy)

question: General Douglas MacArthur drove north up the New Guinea coast toward the Philippines in one of the two great American thrusts across the Pacific. Who led the other, the drive across the open Central Pacific through the Gilbert, Marshall and Mariana Islands?
answer: Admiral Chester Nimitz
choices: Admiral Chester Nimitz
General George Patton
Admiral William Halsey
General Omar Bradley
context: MacArthur and Nimitz ran two parallel drives — MacArthur up through New Guinea, Nimitz across the Central Pacific island chains — both aimed at Japan. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/pacific-strategy-1941-1944 ; macarthurmemorial.org Island Hopping Primary Resources

question: Allied bombers pounded Rabaul, Japan's mightiest base in the South Pacific, with its tens of thousands of troops, but no one ever stormed its beaches. The Allies isolated it and left it useless instead. How did the Allies finally take Rabaul in September 1945?
answer: They walked in to accept its surrender
choices: They walked in to accept its surrender
They stormed the beaches at dawn
They burned it with carrier fire-raids
They blew its harbor with submarines
context: Rabaul was never invaded. Its roughly 69,000 soldiers and 20,000 civilian workers were cut off from late 1943 to war's end, and the Allies simply accepted the surrender in September 1945. Source: history.com/topics/world-war-ii/battle-of-new-britain-rabaul ; historytools.org/stories/the-neutralisation-of-rabaul-a-turning-point-in-the-pacific-war

question: Marines charged head-on at the fortified islet of Betio, at Tarawa, in November 1943, and in 76 hours they suffered more than 3,000 casualties, a toll to rival the six-month Guadalcanal campaign. What lesson did later commanders take from it?
answer: Bypass the strongholds instead of charging them
choices: Bypass the strongholds instead of charging them
Land only after a week of bombing
Attack at night to hide the landing
Never assault an island without tanks
context: Tarawa cost 1,027 Marines killed and 2,292 wounded in 76 hours on tiny Betio. The slaughter is exactly why later commanders leapfrogged fortified islands rather than assaulting them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tarawa ; history.com/articles/battle-of-tarawa

question: Pilots from American aircraft carriers struck Truk Lagoon, the Japanese fleet's main forward base, in February 1944 and wrecked about 45 ships there in the two days of Operation Hailstone. Japanese commanders had called Truk the 'Gibraltar of the Pacific'. What did the American fleet do about Truk next?
answer: Sailed past it and left it to starve
choices: Sailed past it and left it to starve
Landed Marines to seize the lagoon
Towed away its damaged warships
Garrisoned it as a new airbase
context: Task Force 58 destroyed about 45 ships and 250–275 aircraft at Truk, then the fleet simply bypassed it. Its roughly 28,000-man garrison was left cut off until surrender. Source: the-past.com/feature/operation-hailstone-17-18-february-1944-the-task-force-58-raid-on-the-japanese-fortress-of-truk/

question: American fleets drove across the Central Pacific toward Saipan, Tinian and Guam, the Mariana Islands, the real prize of the whole island-hopping campaign. Lying on the road to Japan was only part of their worth. What made the Marianas so valuable?
answer: They put the new B-29 bombers in range of Japan
choices: They put the new B-29 bombers in range of Japan
They held Japan's largest oil refineries
They guarded the only route to the Philippines
They sheltered the deepest fleet anchorage
context: The Marianas were close enough to bring the new B-29 Superfortress bombers within range of the Japanese home islands — the leapfrog had a target, not just a direction. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/pacific-strategy-1941-1944

question: Japanese troops stranded on an island the Americans had bypassed fed themselves and kept good order, far better than the Allies had expected, and theirs was not the only cut-off garrison to do so. How did those garrisons feed themselves?
answer: They grew gardens from submarine-delivered seeds
choices: They grew gardens from submarine-delivered seeds
They raided Allied supply ships at night
They fished the lagoons with stolen nets
They bartered gold for rice from traders
context: Some bypassed garrisons planted gardens from seeds shipped in by submarine and worked with local labor, surviving better than expected. The strategy still worked: the men were useless to Japan's war effort even when they lived. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leapfrogging_(strategy)

question: Giuseppe Garibaldi set out in 1860 to unite Italy. He took about a thousand volunteers, later known as the Thousand, south to invade Sicily. Every one of them wore the same eye-catching piece of clothing, and it gave them their nickname. What were they called?
answer: the Redshirts
choices: the Redshirts
the Ironsides
the Blackcaps
the Greycloaks
context: Garibaldi's volunteers were the Redshirts (Camicie Rosse). The red shirts traced back to his years in South America — reportedly from a Montevideo factory that had meant to export them to the slaughterhouses of Argentina. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Garibaldi

question: Long before he fought for Italy, Giuseppe Garibaldi spent twelve years soldiering in South America with rebel armies in Brazil and Uruguay. Back home he became the most famous fighter of the Risorgimento, the movement that united Italy. Because he had fought on two continents, Italians gave him a grand nickname. What was it?
answer: the Hero of the Two Worlds
choices: the Hero of the Two Worlds
the Lion of the North
the Sword of Italy
the Father of the People
context: Garibaldi was nicknamed 'the Hero of the Two Worlds' for fighting in both South America and Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Garibaldi

question: Giuseppe Garibaldi's thousand or so volunteers needed ships to cross to Sicily in May 1860, and they had none. His lieutenant Nino Bixio solved the problem the night the expedition left from near Genoa. How did they come by their two steamships, the Piemonte and the Lombardo?
answer: Bixio seized them from a private shipping company
choices: Bixio seized them from a private shipping company
the king of Piedmont lent them from his navy
British merchants donated them to the cause
the volunteers bought them with pooled savings
context: Nino Bixio seized the two steamships Il Piemonte and Il Lombardo from the Rubattino shipping company to carry the roughly 1,089 volunteers. They slipped away by night on 5 May 1860 from the rocky beach of Quarto, near Genoa. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_of_the_Thousand

question: Garibaldi's volunteers charged uphill at Calatafimi in Sicily on 15 May 1860, about a thousand of them against King Francis II's Bourbon soldiers, who were dug in on the hilltop and firing down. The attack began to break apart. By tradition, Garibaldi turned to his lieutenant Nino Bixio and spoke words Italians have quoted ever since. What did he say?
answer: 'Here we make Italy, or we die'
choices: 'Here we make Italy, or we die'
'God will know His own'
'Not one step backward'
'Victory or the grave'
context: By tradition (legend), at Calatafimi, attacking uphill against entrenched Bourbon troops on the Pianto dei Romani hill, Garibaldi told Nino Bixio: 'Qui si fa l'Italia o si muore' — 'Here we make Italy, or we die.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Calatafimi

question: Giuseppe Garibaldi had conquered Sicily and Naples by October 1860, a whole kingdom won by his own sword and his band of volunteers. On 26 October he met King Victor Emmanuel II at Teano. What did the romantic hero do with everything he had conquered?
answer: he handed it all to the king and took no crown
choices: he handed it all to the king and took no crown
he had himself crowned king of the south
he split the conquered land among his officers
he demanded a great fortune as his reward
context: At Teano on 26 October 1860, Garibaldi greeted Victor Emmanuel II as 'King of Italy' and handed over his entire conquest. He then retired to the rocky island of Caprera, refusing any reward, title, or pay — the romantic hero who took no crown. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Garibaldi

question: Count Camillo di Cavour built Italy's unity through careful diplomacy rather than battle, and in 1861 he became the new kingdom's first prime minister. That June, only months into the job, he died of malaria. On his deathbed he is said to have whispered one last line about his young country. What did he whisper?
answer: 'Italy is made. All is safe'
choices: 'Italy is made. All is safe'
'I have done my duty'
'Let the work go on without me'
'The peninsula is whole at last'
context: Cavour engineered unification by diplomacy — at the secret Plombières meeting (July 1858) he and Napoleon III agreed France would help Piedmont fight Austria in exchange for Nice and Savoy. He became united Italy's first prime minister but died of malaria on 6 June 1861 after about three months; on his deathbed he is said (legend) to have murmured 'Italy is made. All is safe.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camillo_Benso,_Count_of_Cavour

question: Victor Emmanuel II had been king of Piedmont-Sardinia, and in March 1861 he became the first king of a united Italy. He could have started afresh as Victor Emmanuel I; instead he kept his old number. What did historians read into that choice about the new kingdom?
answer: that Piedmont had taken over the peninsula rather than truly merging into it
choices: that Piedmont had taken over the peninsula rather than truly merging into it
that he wished to honor a beloved earlier king of the same name
that he meant to rule only as a temporary caretaker
that he expected a third Victor Emmanuel to complete the work
context: Victor Emmanuel II kept the 'II' from his Sardinian title instead of becoming Victor Emmanuel I of Italy — a choice that hinted Piedmont had taken over the peninsula rather than truly merging into it. He became the first king of a united Italy since the 6th century when the kingdom was proclaimed on 17 March 1861. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Emmanuel_II

question: Jean-Paul Marat, the revolutionary leader, died of a stab wound in his bath in 1793, and Jacques-Louis David painted the dead man still in the tub, one arm hanging limp over its edge. David borrowed that drooping arm from an older work showing a sacred body. Which work did he copy it from?
answer: Michelangelo's 'Pietà', the dead Christ across Mary's lap
choices: Michelangelo's 'Pietà', the dead Christ across Mary's lap
Leonardo da Vinci's 'Last Supper', painted on a wall
Donatello's 'David', a young bronze warrior boy
Botticelli's 'Birth of Venus', a goddess on a shell
context: David borrowed the limp, hanging arm from Michelangelo's 'Pietà' (and Caravaggio's 'Entombment of Christ'), turning a real political murder into a secular pietà — a martyr's image for the Revolution. He even idealized the body: the real Marat had a chronic skin disease that forced him to soak for hours, but David painted his skin smooth and unblemished. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Death_of_Marat

question: Jacques-Louis David painted the Oath of the Horatii for the French crown in 1784: three Roman brothers raising their arms toward three swords and swearing to die for their country, a picture of loyalty meant to serve the king. After the Revolution came, David sat in the National Convention as one of its deputies. What did he do to the king who had once been his patron?
answer: He voted to execute King Louis XVI
choices: He voted to execute King Louis XVI
He painted a flattering new portrait of the king
He fled France to go on painting for the king
He hid the king's family inside his Paris studio
context: David voted for the king's death in January 1793 and signed the death warrant. The same man who painted a royal loyalty-allegory became the Revolution's image-maker, then later switched again to serve Napoleon — spending three years on 'The Coronation of Napoleon' as First Painter to the Emperor. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jacques-Louis-David-French-painter and https://www.biography.com/artist/jacques-louis-david

question: A strict Jain monk sets off down a path, and before nearly every step he does one small thing, again and again. He holds ahimsa, harming no living thing, to be 'the pure, unchangeable, eternal law.' What does he do?
answer: He gently sweeps the ground ahead with a soft broom so he won't crush an ant
choices: He gently sweeps the ground ahead with a soft broom so he won't crush an ant
He scatters a handful of grain to feed any hungry creatures
He rings a small bell to warn animals that a person is coming
He bows toward the rising sun and whispers a short prayer
context: Devout Jains carry ahimsa to its limit: monks sweep the path before each step with a soft broom so as not to crush an ant, wear a small cloth over the mouth (the muhpatti) to avoid inhaling an insect, and strain their drinking water to spare the tiniest lives in it. The strictest will not even swat a mosquito. Sources: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/jainism/ ; https://www.thecollector.com/who-was-mahavira/

question: Mahavira, the 'Great Hero' of the Jains, gave up his throne and at last his clothing too, and spent twelve and a half years wandering without clothes. Long after him, Jains split into two branches. The Digambara, whose name means 'sky-clad', keep their monks naked as Mahavira was. How does the rival Svetambara branch differ?
answer: Their monks and nuns wear simple white robes
choices: Their monks and nuns wear simple white robes
Their monks shave their heads but keep beards
Their monks live in temples rather than wandering
Their monks may marry and keep a household
context: The names say it: Digambara means 'sky-clad' (naked, as Mahavira lived) and Svetambara means 'white-clad.' The two branches divided largely over whether a monk must renounce clothing entirely. Mahavira, born Vardhamana around 599 BCE into a royal family, is counted as the 24th and last Tirthankara ('ford-maker'), a Jina or 'conqueror' over the self. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/who-was-mahavira/

question: Thomas Jefferson, in Paris, sent his friend James Madison two trunkfuls of books about leagues of states, ancient and modern, so that Madison could see why earlier republics had failed. When the books arrived, what did Madison call them in his letter of thanks?
answer: The literary cargo
choices: The literary cargo
The borrowed library
The Paris parcels
The scholar's bounty
context: Madison thanked Jefferson for the 'literary cargo' — two trunkfuls of books on ancient and modern confederacies that Jefferson bought for him in Europe. Madison's homework on why earlier republics collapsed became the backbone of his plan for the convention. Source: monticello.org/encyclopedia/james-madison; Madison-to-Jefferson letters, founders.archives.gov.

question: James Madison reached Philadelphia in 1787 before most delegates had arrived, carrying a complete plan for a new national government that divided power among three branches. Edmund Randolph laid it before the convention on 29 May, and the delegates argued out the whole Constitution from it. What was the plan called?
answer: The Virginia Plan
choices: The Virginia Plan
The Randolph Charter
The Philadelphia Frame
The Federal Compact
context: Madison's draft was the Virginia Plan, proposing a strong central government split into three branches that would check and balance one another. Because the whole convention debated from it, Madison earned the nickname 'Father of the Constitution.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Plan; montpelier.org/learn/the-life-of-james-madison.

question: James Madison, writing as Publius, defended the new Constitution in essays meant to win over the states, and in Federalist No. 51 he answered the fear of tyranny with a line about human nature that is still quoted. What did he write?
answer: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary"
choices: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary"
"All men are created equal"
"Power tends to corrupt"
"Government of the people, by the people"
context: Madison's line from Federalist No. 51 — paired with 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition' — became his classic argument for checks and balances: because people aren't angels, government must be designed to check itself. Source: avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/fed51.asp; founders.archives.gov.

question: A Glasgow professor handed James Watt a little machine that would not run properly in 1763, while the young instrument maker was mending scientific tools for the university. Working on it set Watt on the path to his greatest invention. What was the broken machine?
answer: a small working model of an early steam engine
choices: a small working model of an early steam engine
a brass telescope with a cracked lens
a ship's compass that pointed the wrong way
a church clock that kept losing time
context: The model was of Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine. It ran so poorly that fixing it exposed to Watt how much heat the design wasted, pointing him toward his great improvement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt.

question: James Watt's cousin Marion Campbell spread a tale about how his great idea began. As a boy, the story goes, he watched his aunt's kettle boil by her fire, and the steam kept making one thing jump up and drop back. What was it?
answer: the kettle's lid
choices: the kettle's lid
a spoon in a teacup
the iron poker
a candle flame
context: Watt's cousin Marion Campbell told this tale, and his son helped polish it, but it is almost certainly a charming myth. Watt himself said a Dr. John Robison first turned his attention to steam engines in 1759. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt; David Philip Miller, 'True Myths: James Watt's Kettle' (2004).  (Legend.)

question: James Boswell, the writer, toured Matthew Boulton's Soho works near Birmingham in 1776, where Boulton sold the engines his partner James Watt built. Boulton boasted to his visitor that he sold there the one thing the whole world wanted. What was it?
answer: power
choices: power
gold
glory
weapons
context: Boulton's full line: 'I sell here, sir, what all the world desires to have - POWER.' He meant the work his steam engines could do for mines and mills. Source: britannica.com/biography/Matthew-Boulton; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Boulton.

question: Matthew Boulton and James Watt fired up the first engine they ever sold to a paying customer at Tipton's Bloomfield Colliery, a coal mine, in March 1776. The mine had a problem that grew worse the deeper its miners dug. What did the engine do for it?
answer: it pumped the water up out of the mine
choices: it pumped the water up out of the mine
it wound the coal cages up the shaft
it pumped fresh air down into the tunnels
it hauled loaded wagons along the surface
context: Deep mines filled with water, and pumping them dry by hand or horse was brutal, so the engine was built to drain the floodwater. A month later a second engine started at John Wilkinson's ironworks. Between 1775 and 1800 the partnership built roughly 450 to 500 engines. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt_steam_engine; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulton_and_Watt.

question: Scientists honoured James Watt in 1882, more than sixty years after his death, by giving his name to a unit of measurement, and today every light bulb carries it. What does the watt measure?
answer: power - the rate at which work is done
choices: power - the rate at which work is done
distance - how far apart two places are
temperature - how hot something is
weight - how heavy an object is
context: One watt equals one joule of work every second. C. William Siemens proposed the name in 1882, over sixty years after Watt's death in 1819. The bulbs and appliances rated in watts all carry his name. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt.

question: James Watt studied the waste in Thomas Newcomen's older engine. On every stroke it sprayed cold water into its cylinder to make the piston drop, then had to heat the whole chilled cylinder again for the next one, burning about three-quarters of its coal that way. Watt's fix let the same coal do roughly twice the work. What was his idea?
answer: let the steam rush into a separate vessel to be condensed there, so the working cylinder never had to be chilled
choices: let the steam rush into a separate vessel to be condensed there, so the working cylinder never had to be chilled
add a second cylinder that took over the work while the first one cooled down
build a much hotter fire so the cylinder could be reheated twice as fast
line the inside of the cylinder with copper so it shed and regained heat faster
context: This is the 'separate condenser,' patented in 1769 - the single insight that made steam power efficient enough to remake the world. Watt also wrapped the cylinder in an outer 'steam jacket' to keep it hot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt; thenewatlantis.com/publications/the-most-useful-man-who-ever-lived.

question: James Watt went for a Sunday walk in Glasgow in May 1765 and came home with the cure for the old engine's waste. By his own later account, he had the whole engine worked out in his mind before the walk was over. Across what Glasgow place was he walking?
answer: Glasgow Green, the city's common
choices: Glasgow Green, the city's common
the deck of a Clyde river ferry
the floor of his own workshop
the nave of Glasgow Cathedral
context: By his own much-later account: 'I had not walked further than the Golf-house when the whole thing was arranged in my mind.' He recalled this about fifty years afterward, recorded by the Hart brothers, so it is vivid memory rather than a contemporaneous record. Source: thenewatlantis.com/publications/the-most-useful-man-who-ever-lived; Robert Hart, 1859.

question: James Watt set out to show mill owners, who drove their machines with teams of animals, what a clanking engine was really worth. He invented a unit equal to the work one animal could do in a minute, and he set each engine's price by how many animals it replaced. What did he call his unit?
answer: horsepower
choices: horsepower
the foot-pound
the kilowatt
the joule
context: Watt set one horsepower at 33,000 foot-pounds per minute - lifting 33,000 pounds one foot in one minute. He got the figure in 1782 from watching draft horses walk a mill wheel and rounded it to a clean number the next year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horsepower; britannica.com/science/horsepower.

question: John Wilkinson, an ironmaster, rescued James Watt's engine when no workshop could make its cylinder truly round and steam hissed past the loose piston. Wilkinson turned one of his own boring machines onto Watt's cylinders, and it cut them true. What did that machine normally bore out?
answer: the barrels of cannon
choices: the barrels of cannon
the pipes for city wells
the links of anchor chain
the rims of carriage wheels
context: Wilkinson's cannon-boring machine (1774) bored Watt's cylinders so accurately that Boulton marveled a 50-inch cylinder 'does not err the thickness of an old shilling in any part.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt_steam_engine; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilkinson_(industrialist).

question: Joseph Black, a Glasgow professor and James Watt's friend, found the reason that chilling steam inside the cylinder wasted so much coal. Turning water into steam, Black showed, swallows a great store of heat, and the steam releases all of it again the instant it condenses. What did Black name that heat?
answer: latent heat
choices: latent heat
specific heat
radiant heat
sensible heat
context: Latent heat is exactly why condensing steam inside the cylinder threw away so much fuel - and why moving the condensing into a separate vessel saved it. Black's science underpinned Watt's engineering. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt.

question: James Watt made his engine look after itself in 1788. He fitted it with a pair of metal balls spinning on a spindle: when the engine sped up, the balls flew outward and climbed, and their climb choked off the steam until the engine slowed. He had borrowed the idea from windmills. What was the device called?
answer: the centrifugal governor
choices: the centrifugal governor
the connecting rod
the boiler gauge
the drive piston
context: Watt borrowed the idea from devices that regulated the speed of windmills. The spinning balls form an early feedback loop - the engine sensing and correcting its own speed. Source: britannica.com/biography/James-Watt; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt.

question: James Watt, who could master any machine, owned up to a weakness in a letter he wrote in 1772: he dreaded haggling. He would sooner face one particular danger, he wrote, than settle an account or strike a bargain, and so he left the selling to the confident Matthew Boulton. What danger did Watt name?
answer: a loaded cannon
choices: a loaded cannon
a winter at sea
an angry mob
a long illness
context: His words: he 'would rather face a loaded cannon than settle an account or make a bargain.' The perfectionist inventor and the confident salesman made an ideal pair - Watt built the engines, Boulton sold them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt (1772 letter to William Small).

question: Colonists sent by the Virginia Company of London sailed down the Thames in three small ships in December 1606, bound across the winter Atlantic for Virginia. The next May they founded Jamestown, the first English settlement in America that lasted. What were the ships called?
answer: the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery
choices: the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery
the Mayflower, the Speedwell, and the Fortune
the Golden Hind, the Pelican, and the Squirrel
the Matthew, the Trinity, and the Christopher
context: The Susan Constant was the largest (about 71 aboard), the Godspeed mid-sized, and the Discovery a tiny pinnace of about 21. They were funded not by the king but by the Virginia Company of London, a for-profit business hoping to strike gold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Constant

question: Captain John Smith found that many of Jamestown's settlers were gentlemen who thought digging beneath them, and they would not work even while their neighbours starved. Smith laid down one blunt rule to make them help. What was it?
answer: "He that will not work shall not eat."
choices: "He that will not work shall not eat."
"Idle hands invite the enemy in."
"A gentleman digs, or a gentleman dies."
"No man rests until the fort is raised."
context: Smith's full order was that the labor of thirty or forty honest men should not be spent to feed 150 idle loiterers. The line echoes the New Testament (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/John_Smith_(explorer)

question: Powhatan warriors penned the Jamestown settlers inside their fort in the winter of 1609, and the Starving Time began. The colonists ate snakes, rats, mice, cats, dogs, even their horses. When those were gone, what did they boil and eat?
answer: their own leather boots and shoes
choices: their own leather boots and shoes
the bark stripped from pine trees
sawdust ground up into bread
candle wax melted in water
context: That winter is remembered as 'the Starving Time.' Of the roughly 240 to 500 colonists alive when winter began, only about 60 were left by spring. Source: https://encyclopediavirginia.org/entries/starving-time-the/

question: Wahunsenaca, the chief the English called Powhatan, had a young daughter named Amonute when the colonists landed at Jamestown in 1607. The English wrote down her family nickname instead, and the world remembers her by it: Pocahontas. What did the nickname mean?
answer: the playful or mischievous one
choices: the playful or mischievous one
the bright morning star at dawn
the laughing daughter of the river
the small and fearless feather
context: She was a daughter of Wahunsenaca, the paramount chief the English called Powhatan, who ruled a chiefdom of more than 30 tribes. Source: https://www.nps.gov/jame/learn/historyculture/pocahontas-her-life-and-legend.htm

question: A Jamestown settler sowed a sweeter Spanish strain from the Caribbean in 1612 and named it Orinoco, because the leaf that grew in Virginia was too harsh to sell. The new crop sold for high prices in London, and soon colonists were planting it in the very streets. What crop finally made the colony pay?
answer: tobacco
choices: tobacco
cotton
sugarcane
indigo
context: The first four barrels shipped to England in 1614, and within a few years tobacco was Virginia's cash crop. Demand was so high that colonists planted it in the streets of Jamestown. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rolfe

question: The last starving survivors of Jamestown gave up on Virginia in June 1610. They loaded their boats and started down the river, bound for the Atlantic and home to England for good. A few miles downstream, what happened that kept the colony alive?
answer: they met an incoming relief fleet that turned them back
choices: they met an incoming relief fleet that turned them back
a sudden storm wrecked their boats on the shore
the Powhatan ambushed the boats from the riverbank
their leaking ships ran aground on a sandbar
context: The fleet carried the new governor, Lord De La Warr, who ordered the colonists back to Jamestown and refused to let them leave. The settlement survived almost by accident. Source: https://historicjamestowne.org/history/history-of-jamestown/the-starving-time/

question: Men from every one of Virginia's eleven settlements, two from each, met in the Jamestown church in July 1619 to debate and vote on laws that would bind the whole colony. What was this gathering, the first of its kind in English America?
answer: the first elected representative assembly
choices: the first elected representative assembly
the first royal court of colonial justice
the first gathering of company shareholders
the first open town hall meeting
context: It was called the House of Burgesses, the first elected lawmaking body in English America and a direct ancestor of later American self-government. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/jamestown-colony-settlement-facts

question: John Smith told a story of his early life that read like an adventure novel. Fighting the Turks in Hungary, he said, he was wounded, taken prisoner and sold as a slave, long before he ever saw Jamestown. How did Smith claim he won his freedom?
answer: he killed his master and fled on foot across Russia and Poland
choices: he killed his master and fled on foot across Russia and Poland
he was ransomed by an English merchant trading in Constantinople
he was freed by a Tartar princess who had fallen for him
he stowed away on a galley sailing for Venice and Italy
context: Smith's whole life read like fiction, which is part of why later historians question some of the dramatic stories he told about himself. Source: https://www.livescience.com/40898-captain-john-smith.html

question: The crew of the White Lion, an English ship, put in at Point Comfort near Jamestown in August 1619 with '20 and odd' captive Angolans aboard. Those captives were the first enslaved Africans landed in English North America. How had the White Lion come to be carrying them?
answer: English privateers had seized them from a Portuguese slave ship
choices: English privateers had seized them from a Portuguese slave ship
the Virginia Company had bought them directly in Angola
a Dutch trading post had sold them as indentured servants
they had been captured in a war between Powhatan tribes
context: These men and women had been taken from a Portuguese vessel by privateers and brought to Virginia. The same year that English America got its first elected assembly, it also got its first enslaved Africans. Source: https://blackpast.org/african-american-history/first-africans-in-the-jamestown-colony-1619/

question: Smithsonian scientists in 2013 examined the skull and shin bone of an English girl of fourteen from Jamestown's Starving Time, and they named her Jane. Four hatchet chops across her forehead and fine cut marks on the bones proved something about the colony for the first time. What did they prove?
answer: that the dead were eaten by starving colonists
choices: that the dead were eaten by starving colonists
that a settler was murdered by another colonist
that the Powhatan raided inside the Jamestown fort
that a deadly plague had swept through the colony
context: The forehead chops were tentative, then deeper blows struck the back of her head; knife marks on the jaw showed flesh being removed. It is the first hard physical evidence that desperate colonists ate the dead. Source: https://www.si.edu/stories/survival-cannibalism-historic-jamestown

question: English colonists seized Pocahontas, Powhatan's daughter, in 1613 and held her hostage. In captivity she was baptized a Christian and named Rebecca, and in April 1614 she married an English colonist; the marriage bought a few calm years, remembered as the Peace of Pocahontas. Whom did she marry?
answer: John Rolfe
choices: John Rolfe
John Smith
Christopher Newport
Lord De La Warr
context: John Rolfe was the planter whose 'Orinoco' tobacco had begun to save the colony. His marriage to Pocahontas linked the English and the Powhatan and bought a fragile peace. Source: https://historicjamestowne.org/history/pocahontas/john-rolfe/

question: John Smith wrote afterwards that the child Pocahontas, daughter of the great chief Powhatan, threw herself over him to stop his execution. Many historians doubt his tale of a near-execution. What do many of them think the ceremony really was?
answer: an adoption ritual that 'killed' Smith and reborn him as a chief
choices: an adoption ritual that 'killed' Smith and reborn him as a chief
a staged feast meant to frighten Smith into serving Powhatan
a war dance that Smith wrongly took to be his own execution
a weapons trade that Smith later dressed up as a brush with death
context: In this view Smith was ceremonially 'killed' and 'reborn' as a weroance under Powhatan. Smith may have written the dramatic rescue version years later, only after Pocahontas was famous, to boost his own legend. At the time she was a child and Smith was 27; there was no romance. Source: https://www.nps.gov/jame/learn/historyculture/pocahontas-her-life-and-legend.htm

question: Pocahontas sailed to England in 1616 as Lady Rebecca and there found John Smith alive, after years of being told he was dead. By Smith's own account, she reminded him that her father had called him 'father,' then said something sharp about the English. What did she say of his countrymen?
answer: that "your Countriemen will lie much"
choices: that "your Countriemen will lie much"
that "your God has not kept his word"
that "your king is no king of mine"
that "your ships bring only sorrow"
context: She told Smith, 'you shall call mee childe, and so I will bee for ever and ever your Countrieman.' Pocahontas never made it home: she fell ill as the return voyage began, was taken ashore at Gravesend, and died there in March 1617, around age 21. Source: https://encyclopediavirginia.org/primary-documents/john-smith-and-pocahontas-in-england-an-excerpt-from-the-generall-historie-of-virginia-new-england-and-the-summer-isles-by-john-smith-1624/

question: Jan van Eyck painted a wealthy merchant and his wife standing together in their bedroom in 1434, in the Arnolfini Portrait. On the wall behind them he painted a little round mirror that bulges outward, and in it he showed what the couple's bodies would otherwise hide. What did he show in the mirror?
answer: The whole room seen from behind, including two figures who have just stepped into the doorway
choices: The whole room seen from behind, including two figures who have just stepped into the doorway
A second couple posing in an identical room next door
A burning candle multiplied into a ring of tiny flames
The street and rooftops of Bruges through an open window
context: The convex mirror reflects the entire room from the far side — you see the backs of the couple plus two extra people standing in the doorway facing them. One, dressed in red, may be van Eyck himself arriving as a visitor or witness. Source: nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/jan-van-eyck-the-arnolfini-portrait ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnolfini_Portrait

question: Jan van Eyck made his colours glow like jewels lit from within, and for centuries followers of the biographer Giorgio Vasari credited it to oil paint, which they said he had invented. Painters were in fact using oil before him. What did van Eyck really do to make his colours shine from inside the panel?
answer: He built the picture from many thin see-through layers of oil so light sinks in, bounces off the panel, and shines back out
choices: He built the picture from many thin see-through layers of oil so light sinks in, bounces off the panel, and shines back out
He mixed crushed gemstones into every color to make them sparkle
He coated the finished panel in a thick varnish of melted amber
He painted onto a sheet of polished silver that mirrored light through the paint
context: Van Eyck perfected — did not invent — the oil medium, tinkering with his recipes for life. He stacked translucent glazes over a careful underdrawing; light passes through the layers, reflects off the panel, and seems to light the picture from inside, something fast-drying egg tempera could never do. Vasari's invention claim in his 'Lives of the Artists' stuck around into the 1800s. Source: vaia.com/en-us/explanations/art-and-design/art-and-design-theory/jan-van-eyck/ ; theartstory.org/artist/van-eyck-jan/ ; news.artnet.com/art-world/art-bites-jan-van-eyck-oil-paint-2631103

question: Soldiers gave Japanese-American families on the West Coast as little as 48 hours to leave their homes in the spring of 1942, then tagged them with numbers like baggage and sent them off to fairgrounds and racetracks. How much of their belongings could each family bring?
answer: Only what they could carry in their own hands
choices: Only what they could carry in their own hands
One steamer trunk for each family
Whatever would fit inside a single car
Everything, shipped ahead of them by the Army
context: Families lost homes, farms, and businesses in a weekend. They were first held at hastily fenced 'assembly centers' -- some in horse stalls at racetracks -- before being shipped to ten remote camps. Source: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/education/lessons/japanese-relocation

question: Tatsuro Masuda, an Oakland grocer, hung a huge banner over his store the day after Pearl Harbor. When he was forced to close the shop in March 1942, the photographer Dorothea Lange took its picture. What four words did the banner say?
answer: "I AM AN AMERICAN"
choices: "I AM AN AMERICAN"
"GOD BLESS THIS COUNTRY"
"WE ARE LOYAL CITIZENS"
"CLOSED BY GOVERNMENT ORDER"
context: Lange's photograph of the shuttered Wanto Co. store became one of the most famous images of the incarceration -- a citizen declaring his loyalty on the very day his country imprisoned him for his ancestry. Source: Library of Congress, https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2004665381/

question: Young men from the imprisoned Japanese-American families volunteered to fight for the very country that had locked up their parents, and they came by the thousands. They served in the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, whose motto came from gamblers' slang for betting it all on one roll. What was the motto?
answer: "Go For Broke"
choices: "Go For Broke"
"Double or Nothing"
"All or Nothing"
"Win or Die"
context: For its size and length of service the 442nd became the most decorated unit in U.S. military history -- earned by men whose families remained imprisoned at home. Source: National WWII Museum, https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/442nd-regimental-combat-team

question: Fred Korematsu, a young welder and an American citizen, refused to report to the camps because he wanted to stay with his girlfriend. He changed his looks and his name to pass as someone else, until the FBI caught him in May 1942. What had he done?
answer: He had minor plastic surgery and called himself 'Clyde Sarah'
choices: He had minor plastic surgery and called himself 'Clyde Sarah'
He slipped across the border and posed as a Canadian
He shaved his head and posed as a wandering monk
He forged papers naming him a Filipino merchant sailor
context: Under the alias Clyde Sarah, Korematsu claimed Spanish-Hawaiian descent. His arrest set up the most infamous Supreme Court case of the whole episode. Source: Korematsu Institute, https://korematsuinstitute.org/freds-story/

question: President Franklin Roosevelt signed an order on 19 February 1942 under which the Army locked away about 120,000 people of Japanese descent, with no charges and no trials. What was true of most of those prisoners?
answer: About two-thirds were American citizens
choices: About two-thirds were American citizens
Nearly all were citizens of Japan
About half had been born in Japan
Hardly any had any U.S. citizenship
context: Roughly two-thirds were U.S. citizens, most born on American soil, never charged with any crime. Not one Japanese American was ever found guilty of sabotage or espionage. Source: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/executive-order-9066

question: Daniel Inouye, a lieutenant of the 442nd, had already been shot through the stomach near San Terenzo, Italy, in April 1945 when a German rifle grenade smashed his right arm. His own live grenade was still clenched in that ruined hand. What did Inouye do next?
