answer: He pried the grenade loose with his left hand and threw it into the German bunker
choices: He pried the grenade loose with his left hand and threw it into the German bunker
He smothered the grenade against the trench wall to shield his men
He ordered his squad back and lost consciousness in the mud
He rolled into a shell hole and signaled frantically for a medic
context: Inouye kept firing one-handed, telling his men only, 'Nobody called off the war!' He lost the arm and later served 50 years as a U.S. Senator from Hawaii. Source: National Park Service, https://www.nps.gov/articles/inouyeww2.htm

question: Six justices of the Supreme Court voted in December 1944 to uphold the conviction of Fred Korematsu, the welder who had refused to go to the camps, and three dissented. The majority accepted at face value the Army's own two-word reason for the camps. What was it?
answer: "Military necessity"
choices: "Military necessity"
"National emergency"
"Public safety"
"Wartime loyalty"
context: Korematsu v. United States (December 18, 1944) accepted the Army's claim of 'military necessity' at face value. The ruling has never been formally praised since, and the Court repudiated it only in 2018. Source: U.S. Courts, https://www.uscourts.gov/about-federal-courts/educational-resources/educational-activities/facts-and-case-summary-korematsu-v-us

question: Federal commissioners looked back at the wartime camps in 1982 and found that they had served no military purpose: not one Japanese American had been convicted of spying or sabotage. The commission blamed the camps on three other things instead. What were they?
answer: Race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership
choices: Race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership
Naval weakness, coastal raids, and pressure from foreign allies
Supply shortages, faulty maps, and slow battlefield communication
Port congestion, fuel rationing, and confused chains of command
context: The Commission's verdict -- 'race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership' -- became the official judgment that the imprisonment was never justified by military necessity. Source: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/executive-order-9066

question: Soldiers of the 442nd fought through the forests of France's Vosges Mountains for five days in October 1944 to rescue the Lost Battalion, some 200 Texas soldiers surrounded by German forces. They broke through at last. How did their own losses compare with the number of men they saved?
answer: Their casualties outnumbered the men they rescued
choices: Their casualties outnumbered the men they rescued
Their losses were far lighter than anyone expected
They freed every man without losing a single soldier
They lost almost exactly as many as they saved
context: The 442nd saved over 200 men of the Texas 36th Division's 1st Battalion, 141st Regiment -- and took several times that many casualties doing it. The unit earned 21 Medals of Honor and over 4,000 Purple Hearts. Source: Densho Encyclopedia, https://encyclopedia.densho.org/442nd_Regimental_Combat_Team/

question: Scouts of the 522nd Field Artillery, a Japanese-American unit, reached a sub-camp of Dachau near Hurlach in Bavaria on 29 April 1945, broke its barbed-wire gates open and helped free about 3,000 prisoners. Where had some of those soldiers come from only months before?
answer: America's own internment camps for Japanese families
choices: America's own internment camps for Japanese families
A prisoner-of-war swap with the surrendering Japanese army
Segregated training bases deep in the American South
Merchant ships interned at the start of the war
context: Some of the men who broke open the gates of a Nazi camp had themselves enlisted straight out of America's barbed-wire camps -- soldiers who freed prisoners abroad while their own families were imprisoned at home. Source: Densho Encyclopedia, https://encyclopedia.densho.org/522nd_Field_Artillery_Battalion/

question: Justice Robert Jackson refused to join the Supreme Court majority that upheld the imprisonment of Japanese Americans in 1944, and he wrote a famous warning in dissent. The ruling, he said, would now lie waiting, ready for the hand of any future leader who could claim an urgent need. Lie waiting like what?
answer: A loaded weapon
choices: A loaded weapon
A sleeping fire
An unlocked door
A poisoned well
context: Jackson warned the decision would lie 'about like a loaded weapon, ready for the hand of any authority that can bring forward a plausible claim of an urgent need.' Justice Frank Murphy, also dissenting, said the exclusion fell 'into the ugly abyss of racism.' Source: dissents in Korematsu v. United States (1944).

question: Government officials made every camp prisoner over seventeen fill out a loyalty questionnaire in 1943, and its Question 28 demanded that each one give up any loyalty to the Emperor of Japan. American law already barred the older immigrants, the Issei, from ever becoming citizens. What trap did a 'yes' spring on them?
answer: Renouncing Japan would leave them citizens of no country at all
choices: Renouncing Japan would leave them citizens of no country at all
It would have drafted them straight into combat overseas
It would have stripped their American-born children of citizenship
It would have sent the whole family to a harsher camp
context: Since U.S. law forbade the Issei from naturalizing, swearing off Japan would have made them stateless. Meanwhile the American-born Nisei had never owed the Emperor any allegiance to renounce. About 12,000 of 78,000 answered 'no-no' and were segregated at the Tule Lake camp. Source: Densho Encyclopedia, https://encyclopedia.densho.org/Questions_27_and_28/

question: A lawyer and a researcher dug through the National Archives in 1981, decades after the nation's highest court ruled against Fred Korematsu and let the camps stand. They found the Navy's own report, which said almost no Japanese Americans were a threat. What did they prove the government had done with that report and the Army's case before the justices?
answer: Hidden and altered them to win the case before the Supreme Court
choices: Hidden and altered them to win the case before the Supreme Court
Lost them in a wartime filing error and never recovered them
Destroyed every copy shortly after the war ended
Published them openly but simply chosen to ignore them
context: The suppressed Ringle Report contradicted the Army's claims. On November 10, 1983, Judge Marilyn Hall Patel erased Korematsu's conviction in the same San Francisco courthouse where he was convicted 40 years earlier. Korematsu's words: 'One person can make a difference, even if it takes forty years.' In 1988 Congress apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving prisoner. Source: Densho Encyclopedia, https://encyclopedia.densho.org/Coram_nobis_cases/

question: Katsushika Hokusai drew a monstrous wave curling over three little fishing boats in his most famous print. Far off in the hollow beneath its crest, he placed one small, calm shape, dwarfed by the wave. What did he put there?
answer: Tiny Mount Fuji
choices: Tiny Mount Fuji
A passing sailing ship
A small shore temple
A second snowy peak
context: The towering wave is the foreground, but framed inside its curl sits Mount Fuji — the highest mountain in Japan — made tiny and serene in the far distance. The whole print is really about Fuji. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Wave_off_Kanagawa

question: Katsushika Hokusai, the self-styled Old Man Mad About Drawing, designed The Great Wave off Kanagawa around 1831, at an age when most artists' best years were behind them. He was sure his best work still lay ahead. Roughly how old was he?
answer: About 70
choices: About 30
About 50
About 70
About 90
context: Hokusai was around 70 when he made his masterpiece, signing it 'Hokusai, who changed his name to Iitsu.' He called himself the Old Man Mad About Drawing and believed his best work was still ahead of him. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Wave_off_Kanagawa

question: Carvers and printers in Edo cranked out thousands of copies of Hokusai's Great Wave and sold them to ordinary townspeople as cheap street art. People used them up, so only about 113 early copies survive today. About how much did one print cost back then?
answer: About the price of a bowl of soba noodles
choices: About the price of a bowl of soba noodles
About the price of a folding paper fan
About the price of a few grilled-chicken skewers
About the price of a cup of sake
context: The Great Wave sold for roughly the price of a bowl of soba noodles — pocket-change street art for commoners. So many were used up that of the estimated 8,000 printed, only about 113 first-edition impressions are known to survive today. nippon.com/en/japan-topics/g02414

question: Felix Bracquemond, a French artist, came upon some of Hokusai's prints around 1856, soon after Japan opened up to foreign trade, and he was electrified. The prints had not reached Europe as treasures for a gallery wall. How had they arrived?
answer: Stuffed in as packing paper around crates of porcelain
choices: Stuffed in as packing paper around crates of porcelain
Lining the inside of imported tea chests
Wrapped around bundles of fine Japanese silk
Pasted onto folding screens sold to tourists
context: The prints showed up crumpled around shipments of Japanese porcelain as cheap packing paper. Around 1856 the French artist Felix Bracquemond found Hokusai prints used as packaging and was electrified — helping spark the 'Japonisme' craze that reshaped European art. nippon.com/en/column/g00284

question: Vincent van Gogh marvelled, in a letter to his brother Theo, at Hokusai's Great Wave, with its monstrous wave curling over three little fishing boats. The boat, he wrote, was caught in the waves. What did he say the waves were?
answer: Claws
choices: Claws
Mountains
Dragons
Smoke
context: Van Gogh wrote: 'these waves are claws, the boat is caught in them, you can feel it.' The wave's crest really does break into spreading white fingers that reach down toward the boats like grasping hands. theartnewspaper.com / dailyartmagazine.com/great-wave-hokusai

question: Joan of Arc, a farm girl of about thirteen in Domremy, began to hear voices in her father's garden, often just after the church bell had rung. The voices told her to drive the English out of France. Whose voices did Joan say they were?
answer: Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret
choices: Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret
Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Andrew
Saint George, Saint Denis, and Saint Martin
Saint Anne, Saint Agnes, and Saint Cecilia
context: Joan testified that the archangel Michael came first, followed by the virgin-martyrs Catherine and Margaret, guiding her for years. Source: Wikipedia 'Joan of Arc'; SparkNotes 'Joan of Arc: Voices'; saint-joan-of-arc.com 'Her Voices'.

question: A friar named Isambart held a crucifix high before Joan of Arc as she burned in the Old Market at Rouen, so that she could keep her eyes on it. She was about nineteen. She died calling out one name, three times. What was it?
answer: "Jesus! Jesus! Jesus!"
choices: "Jesus! Jesus! Jesus!"
"France! France! France!"
"Michael! Michael! Michael!"
"Charles! Charles! Charles!"
context: An English soldier was so moved he broke a stick in two, tied the pieces into a little cross, and handed it to her before the fire took her. She died on 30 May 1431; the Catholic Church canonized her as a saint in 1920. Source: famous-trials.com Joan of Arc account; thecatholicthing.org 'The Martyrdom of Joan of Arc'.

question: Charles, the uncrowned prince of France, decided to test Joan of Arc when she reached his court at Chinon in 1429. By the old story, he put on plain clothes, hid among his courtiers and set another man on the throne in his place. What did Joan do?
answer: She walked past the throne and picked the hidden prince out of the crowd
choices: She walked past the throne and picked the hidden prince out of the crowd
She knelt before the false king on the throne and called him her lord
She demanded the whole court remove their hats so she could choose
She refused to enter until the real prince was announced by name
context: Called 'La Reconnaissance' — the Recognition. The story is told in the early accounts but cannot be proven from the trial record, so it is remembered as legend rather than certain fact. Source: jeanne-darc.info 'Chinon'; maidofheaven.com 'Charles VII First Meeting'.

question: Joan of Arc stood in a trench at the siege of Orleans in May 1429, holding her white banner high to rally the French. An English arrow buried itself between her neck and her shoulder. What did she do that same day?
answer: She went back and led the final assault that broke the siege
choices: She went back and led the final assault that broke the siege
She was carried off the field and did not fight again for a week
She handed her banner to a knight and prayed in her tent
She ordered a retreat to spare her exhausted soldiers
context: The English abandoned the siege of Orleans on 8 May 1429 — only about nine days after Joan arrived. Source: Wikipedia 'Joan of Arc'; warfarehistorynetwork.com 'Joan of Arc, Siege of Orleans'.

question: Joan of Arc's men went to fetch a sword she had never laid eyes on, on her word alone. She told them exactly where it lay hidden in the church of Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, and there they found the rusty blade waiting. Where in the church was it?
answer: Behind the altar, beneath the floor
choices: Behind the altar, beneath the floor
Inside the bishop's locked treasure chest
Walled up in the bell tower
Wrapped in cloth under a saint's statue
context: When her men dug exactly where Joan described, the rusted sword was there — and she had never seen the church. Source: Wikipedia 'Joan of Arc'; jeanne-darc.info 'Sword' page.

question: The people of Reims threw open their gates to Charles VII, and on 17 July 1429 he was crowned king there with Joan of Arc beside him, her white banner in her hand. Someone asked her why the banner had earned a place of honour. What was her answer?
answer: That it had borne the burden, so it deserved the honor
choices: That it had borne the burden, so it deserved the honor
That it was painted by the finest Scotsman in France
That the king himself had commanded her to raise it
That the saints had woven it for her in a dream
context: Joan had carried the banner herself through every battle. Her white silk banner, painted at Tours, showed Christ holding the world between two angels and bore the words 'JHESUS MARIA.' Source: Wikipedia 'Joan of Arc'; jeanne-darc.info 'Banner' page.

question: Joan of Arc, who could neither read nor write, dictated a letter to the English army before the fighting at Orleans, signing herself the Maid and ordering them in God's name to leave France. If they stayed, she warned, something was coming. What did she promise?
answer: A clash of arms so great France had not seen one like it in a thousand years
choices: A clash of arms so great France had not seen one like it in a thousand years
A plague sent by the saints to empty every English camp
A flood of soldiers from every corner of Christendom
A fire from heaven that would burn their siege towers
context: She dictated the letter during Holy Week, March 1429, and could neither read nor write it herself. Source: archive.joan-of-arc.org 'Letter to the English, 22 March 1429' (primary-source transcript).

question: Burgundian soldiers dragged Joan of Arc off her horse at Compiegne in May 1430 and later sold her to the English for money. Held prisoner in Beaurevoir castle's tower, she made a desperate bid to escape. What did she do?
answer: She leapt from the top of the tower and survived the fall
choices: She leapt from the top of the tower and survived the fall
She set fire to the castle gate and fled in the smoke
She bribed a guard with her banner to unlock her cell
She starved herself until the lord agreed to free her
context: Joan jumped trying to escape and lived; she was handed over to the English that November. Source: Wikipedia 'Joan of Arc' (jumps from tower in escape attempt).

question: Geoffroy Therage, the executioner at Rouen, gathered up Joan of Arc's ashes after she died at the stake. The English had ordered him to make sure no follower could ever keep a scrap of her as a holy relic. What did Therage do with the ashes?
answer: He threw them into the river Seine
choices: He threw them into the river Seine
He sealed them inside the cathedral wall
He scattered them across an unmarked field
He buried them secretly at the city gate
context: By throwing the ashes into the river, the English meant to erase her forever — instead her legend only grew. Source: famous-trials.com Joan of Arc account ('ashes tossed into the Seine').

question: Two friars, Martin Ladvenu and Isambart de la Pierre, had a shaken visitor soon after Joan of Arc died at the stake in Rouen: the executioner who had burned her, still troubled by what he had done that day. What did he confess to them?
answer: That he greatly feared damnation, for he had burned a saint
choices: That he greatly feared damnation, for he had burned a saint
That the English had forced his hand against his will
That he would never light another execution fire
That Joan had forgiven him with her dying breath
context: The man paid to kill her walked away convinced he had murdered a holy woman. Source: thecatholicthing.org 'The Martyrdom of Joan of Arc'; historyweblog.com (consistent across multiple accounts).

question: By a legend that grew with Joan of Arc's fame, her executioner, Geoffroy Therage, swore that one part of her body would not burn, no matter how the fire raged, and was found whole among the ashes. What part of her was it?
answer: Her heart
choices: Her heart
Her right hand
Her face
Her feet
context: This is told as legend — the executioner's later claim as Joan's fame grew — not as a proven fact. Source: historysphere.com 'Joan of Arc death'; thecatholicthing.org martyrdom account (reported as the executioner's claim).

question: Joan of Arc's judges at Rouen set her a trap in 1431: was she in God's grace? A yes would sound like the sin of presumption, and a no would condemn her out of her own mouth. The court notary said her answer left the judges stupefied. What did the unlettered girl say?
answer: "If I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me in it."
choices: "If I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me in it."
"Only God may judge that, and no man in this room."
"I am, and you cannot prove otherwise before God."
"That is a question for the saints, not for me to answer."
context: The notary Boisguillaume testified the judges were stunned that a farm girl had slipped their theological trap. Source: famous-trials.com Joan of Arc account; Wikipedia 'Trial of Joan of Arc'.

question: Joan of Arc signed a recantation and promised to wear a dress, which should have spared her life. She was condemned all the same, as a relapsed heretic. What had her jailers done while she slept?
answer: They took her dress away and left her only the forbidden men's clothes
choices: They took her dress away and left her only the forbidden men's clothes
They forged her name on a fresh confession of heresy
They told the judges she had cursed the king of England
They burned the pardon that the bishop had already signed
context: Forced to choose between nakedness and the banned clothing, Joan put the men's clothes back on — and was condemned. She said of the pardon she had signed, 'What was in the schedule of abjuration I did not understand.' Source: famous-trials.com 'Joan's Relapse and Final Adjudication'; rehabilitation testimony of Massieu and Manchon.

question: Isabelle Romee, Joan of Arc's aged mother, pleaded for her daughter in person at Notre-Dame when the Church reopened the case twenty-five years after the burning. The new court ruled the old verdict 'null, invalid, worthless, and annihilated.' What did Rouen's public executioner then do?
answer: He tore out the pages of her death sentence and burned them
choices: He tore out the pages of her death sentence and burned them
He carved her innocence into the courthouse door
He returned her ashes to her family for burial
He paraded the guilty bishop's body through the streets
context: The dead judge, Bishop Cauchon, was branded the real heretic, and Joan's mother lived to hear her daughter cleared. Source: Wikipedia 'Rehabilitation trial of Joan of Arc'; archive.joan-of-arc.org 'Declaration of Innocence, July 7th 1456'.

question: Redcoats fired into an angry Boston crowd in 1770 and killed five colonists in the Boston Massacre. When the redcoats stood trial for murder, John Adams, a patriot lawyer, stunned his neighbours by taking on a job none of them would touch. What did Adams do?
answer: He served as the defense lawyer for the accused British soldiers
choices: He served as the defense lawyer for the accused British soldiers
He signed up as a witness for the grieving Boston families
He printed pamphlets demanding the soldiers be hanged at once
He sailed to London to argue the case before the king
context: John Adams believed even hated enemies deserved a fair trial. He won acquittals for six of the eight soldiers; the jury convicted only two, of manslaughter. Adams later called it 'one of the best pieces of service I ever rendered my country.' Source: U.S. National Park Service, nps.gov/articles/000/boston-massacre-trial.htm; Adams' autobiography.

question: John Adams signed the Sedition Act in 1798, making it a federal crime to print 'false, scandalous and malicious' writing against the government or the president. The first man tried under it, the Vermont congressman Matthew Lyon, went to jail for four months for mocking Adams's 'unbounded thirst for ridiculous pomp.' What did Lyon do from behind bars?
answer: He ran his re-election campaign from his cell and won in a landslide
choices: He ran his re-election campaign from his cell and won in a landslide
He smuggled out a confession admitting his writings were false
He begged the president for a pardon and was quietly released
He fled across the border into Canada before his sentence ended
context: The Alien and Sedition Acts criminalized criticism of the government Adams led — a real assault on the free-speech principle the founding professed. Federal courts prosecuted at least 26 people, mostly Jeffersonian newspaper editors. Matthew Lyon's jailhouse landslide made him a symbol of the backlash that helped sink Adams in 1800. Source: Bill of Rights Institute, billofrightsinstitute.org/essays/the-alien-and-sedition-acts; Britannica, britannica.com/event/Alien-and-Sedition-Acts.

question: John Cabot sailed west from Bristol in 1497 in a small ship called the Matthew, hunting a shortcut to Asia for King Henry VII of England. He never reached Asia, but his crew came home raving about the fish off the new land. How thick were the cod, they boasted?
answer: So thick they could scoop them up in baskets lowered over the side
choices: So thick they could scoop them up in baskets lowered over the side
So thick the ship could barely push through the water
So thick they leapt onto the deck on their own
So thick the sea looked silver from the masthead
context: Cabot's men said the cod on the Grand Banks were so plentiful they only had to lower baskets weighted with stones into the water — and boasted England would have 'no further need of Iceland' for fish. Source: https://www.heritage.nf.ca/articles/exploration/cabot-1497.php ; https://www.worldhistory.org/John_Cabot/

question: John Cabot stepped ashore for England on 24 June 1497, somewhere on the coast of what is now Canada. He saw plain signs that people lived there: old fire pits, snares and trees that had been cut. What was true of his brief landing?
answer: He never met a single person face to face
choices: He never met a single person face to face
He could not find any fresh water
He never went more than a few steps from his boat
He left without planting a flag
context: Cabot saw fire pits, snares, and carved or cut trees, but in his brief landing he encountered no people at all. He planted a cross and flew three banners: King Henry VII of England, the Pope, and Saint Mark of Venice. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/John_Cabot/

question: Martin Frobisher, the first Englishman to hunt for the Northwest Passage, brought home a heavy black stone in 1576, certain it was rich with gold. Three experts called it worthless, but a fourth swore it was real, so English fleets went back for about 1,225 tons of ore in all. What was the 'gold' really worth?
answer: Nothing — it was fool's gold, and some was dumped to pave streets
choices: Nothing — it was fool's gold, and some was dumped to pave streets
A fortune, but pirates stole it before it could be melted
Enough to fund one more voyage, then it ran out
Less than the cost of the ships sent to fetch it
context: Frobisher's ore was iron pyrite — fool's gold — worth nothing. After years trying to melt gold out of it, England gave up; some of the worthless rock was reportedly dumped as gravel to pave streets and patch walls. Source: https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/topics/martin-frobisher-north-west-passage-expedition-1576-78

question: Sir John Franklin sailed into the Arctic in the 1840s with two warships, Erebus and Terror, and every one of his 128 men died. British officials brushed off Inuit accounts of where the ships went down for more than a century, until searchers found the wrecks in 2014 and 2016, exactly where the Inuit had said. How well had Terror survived on the sea floor?
answer: So well its drawers were still shut and cabins intact
choices: So well its drawers were still shut and cabins intact
Crushed flat, with only the keel recognizable
Buried so deep in silt that divers nearly missed it
Scattered in pieces across miles of seabed
context: The Inuit were right all along. HMS Erebus was found in 2014 and HMS Terror in 2016, the Terror so well preserved that drawers were still closed and cabins intact underwater. Franklin's 128 men had all died after their ships froze fast near King William Island. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-shipwrecks-from-john-franklins-doomed-arctic-expedition-were-exactly-where-the-inuit-said-they-would-be-180986627/

question: Jehan Cauvin, the young Frenchman later known as John Calvin, studied at Orleans before he joined the Reformation or ever led the church in Geneva. What had he been training to become?
answer: A lawyer
choices: A lawyer
A sea captain
A blacksmith
A painter
context: Born Jehan Cauvin on July 10, 1509 in Noyon, Picardy, Calvin studied law at Orleans before joining the Reformation. He was French; Geneva was only his adopted city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin; Britannica 'John Calvin'.

question: Worn out by his work, John Calvin died in Geneva in 1564, aged 54. He asked to be laid in a grave with no marker of any kind, and the place is unknown to this day. Why did Calvin want no stone over his grave?
answer: So no one could turn his tomb into a shrine
choices: So no one could turn his tomb into a shrine
So his enemies could not find his body
So the city would not have to pay for a stone
So he could be moved back to France later
context: Calvin worked himself to death in poor health and died at age 54. At his own request he was buried in the Cimetiere des Rois with no marker, so no one could make his tomb a place of pilgrimage; the spot is unknown today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin.

question: Guillaume Farel, a fiery preacher, begged John Calvin to stay and reform Geneva in 1536, when Calvin was only passing through on his way to a quiet life of study. Calvin said no. Then Farel made a threat that changed his mind. What did Farel threaten?
answer: That God would curse Calvin's quiet scholar's life
choices: That God would curse Calvin's quiet scholar's life
That he would have Calvin thrown out of the city
That he would burn Calvin's unfinished books
That France would put a price on Calvin's head
context: Farel warned that God would curse his studies if he refused to help. Calvin later wrote he would 'rather submit to death a hundred times than to that cross' — but he stayed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin; museeprotestant.org.

question: John Calvin urged Geneva's council to behead the Spanish doctor Michael Servetus, a quicker death, after the city condemned him in 1553 for denying the Trinity. The council refused and sent him to the stake, and the executioners built the fire of green oak boughs with their leaves still on. What did the green wood do?
answer: It made the fire slow, so he took about half an hour to die
choices: It made the fire slow, so he took about half an hour to die
It made the fire smother him almost instantly
It refused to catch, so he was strangled instead
It burned so hot the crowd had to flee
context: Servetus was chained to a stake and burned with green, leafy oak; the slow fire meant about half an hour of dying. His last words — 'Jesus, Son of the Eternal God, have mercy on me,' pointedly NOT 'eternal Son of God' — kept his anti-Trinity belief to the end. Source: christianhistoryinstitute.org; historyofinformation.com.

question: Michael Servetus, burned at the stake in Calvin's Geneva, had worked out something true about the body: blood flows from the heart through the lungs and back. Yet his discovery was very nearly lost along with him. Where had Servetus recorded it?
answer: Inside his banned theology book, Christianismi Restitutio
choices: Inside his banned theology book, Christianismi Restitutio
In a letter to the Pope that was never opened
In a Geneva sermon he was forbidden to preach
Carved on the back of an anatomy drawing
context: Servetus buried his account of pulmonary circulation inside Christianismi Restitutio (1553) because he believed the soul lived in the blood. Almost every copy was burned with him, nearly losing the discovery. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianismi_Restitutio; hekint.org.

question: John Calvin taught and wrote in Geneva until his death in 1564. Today his name is tied to five points spelled TULIP: Total depravity, Unconditional election, Limited atonement, Irresistible grace and Perseverance of the saints. Where did those five points first come from?
answer: A Dutch synod held more than 50 years after Calvin died
choices: A Dutch synod held more than 50 years after Calvin died
Calvin's own deathbed confession in Geneva
John Knox's sermons in the Scottish Kirk
The opening pages of Calvin's Institutes
context: The five points were hammered out at the Synod of Dort (1618-1619) in the Netherlands, answering the followers of Jacob Arminius — over 50 years after Calvin's 1564 death. Calvin himself never wrote 'TULIP.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Points_of_Calvinism.

question: John Locke published a second great book in 1689, about how people come to know things. A newborn baby, he said, has no ideas in its mind; only what it sees, hears, touches and feels fills it later. What did Locke compare that mind to?
answer: A sheet of white paper
choices: A sheet of white paper
A locked treasure chest
A garden of planted seeds
A mirror facing the sky
context: Locke called the mind 'white paper, void of all characters' — the famous idea later nicknamed the 'tabula rasa' (Latin for 'blank slate'). All knowledge, he said, gets written onto it by experience, not stamped in at birth. Source: britannica.com/topic/tabula-rasa; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabula_rasa.

question: Lord Ashley had a huge cyst on his liver in 1668, and his doctor was John Locke, not yet a famous philosopher. Locke led a risky operation to remove it and left something in Ashley's side to keep the wound draining. What did Locke leave?
answer: A silver tube
choices: A silver tube
A cloth bandage roll
A bundle of dried herbs
A small iron clamp
context: Locke left a silver tap (a silver drainage tube) in Lord Ashley's side. Ashley — the future Earl of Shaftesbury — credited Locke with saving his life, and wits joked his liver would need a silver tap forever. Source: journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00031348221093528 (Nakayama 2022); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke.

question: John Locke argued in his Two Treatises of Government that a people have the right to overthrow their king, an idea so dangerous that a man could be tried and executed for it. To protect himself from the gallows when the book came out in 1689, Locke took one careful step. What did he do?
answer: Published it anonymously, with no author named
choices: Published it anonymously, with no author named
Dedicated it to the king, begging for mercy
Wrote it in cipher, hiding it from all readers
Burned every draft, keeping only his memory
context: Locke published the 'Two Treatises' anonymously in late 1689 (the title page was dated 1690), and he refused to admit he wrote it for the rest of his life — arguing for the right to depose a king was enough to get a man executed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Treatises_of_Government.

question: The king's agents hunted John Locke after he fled England, meaning to drag him home for trial and likely execution, so he lived abroad under false names. One of his aliases was a made-up doctor's name. What name did Locke hide behind?
answer: Dr. van der Linden
choices: Dr. van der Linden
Dr. Cornelis Bakker
Dr. Hendrik de Vries
Dr. Joost van Damme
context: To dodge the king's agents, Locke called himself 'Dr. van der Linden' and also 'Lamy.' He was a wanted man for his ties to the radical Earl of Shaftesbury. Source: fee.org/resources/john-locke-natural-rights-to-life-liberty-and-property/.

question: Saying he was leaving 'for his health,' John Locke suddenly slipped out of England around 1683, just after a conspiracy to kill King Charles II had come to light. His ties to radical enemies of the crown had made him a suspect. Where did Locke flee to?
answer: Holland
choices: Holland
France
Ireland
Scotland
context: The Rye House Plot (1683) was an alleged scheme to ambush and kill Charles II. Locke had no proven part in it, but his Shaftesbury connection made staying in England too dangerous, so he fled into exile in the Netherlands. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Treatises_of_Government.

question: John Locke denied for the rest of his life that he had written the Two Treatises of Government, and he owned up only weeks before he died in 1704. Even then he tucked the admission into a place no one would read until after his death. Where did Locke finally confess he was the author?
answer: In a codicil added to his will
choices: In a codicil added to his will
In a letter to King William
In the book's second printing
On a plaque above his grave
context: Locke admitted authorship only in a codicil (a last-minute addition) to his will. He died on October 28, 1704, in his study at Oates in Essex, while his friend Lady Masham read scripture aloud to him. Source: philosophynow.org/issues/156/Will_the_Real_John_Locke_Please_Step_Forward; plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke/.

question: Wild apples and open fields belong to everyone in common, John Locke said, for that is how nature leaves them. Yet some of them become private property. How, in Locke's account, does a thing ever stop being everyone's and become one person's own?
answer: His own labour
choices: His own labour
His claim of ownership
His payment of money
His grant from a king
context: Locke's answer was labour: when you 'mix your labour' with something nature left common, you 'joined to it something that is his own, and thereby makes it his property' (Second Treatise, Sec. 27). Picking, plowing, building — the work makes it yours. Source: gutenberg.org/files/7370/7370-h/7370-h.htm (Sec. 27).

question: Robert Filmer claimed in his book Patriarcha that kings had a God-given right to rule, because their power ran down in an unbroken line from one figure of the Bible. John Locke ridiculed the idea in his First Treatise. Which Biblical figure did Filmer say every rightful king descends from?
answer: Adam
choices: Adam
Noah
Abraham
David
context: Filmer traced all royal authority back to Adam, the first man — so every true king supposedly inherited Adam's fatherly power. Locke argued God gave Adam no such kingship, and that even if He had, no living man could prove he was Adam's rightful heir. Source: iep.utm.edu/locke-po/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Treatises_of_Government.

question: Suppose you are a poor beggar and your neighbor is a wealthy lord. John Locke argued that each of you can hold every one of the natural rights he named in full, at the very same time, without either of you taking anything from the other. According to Locke, what is the one thing these rights ask of other people?
answer: That they leave you alone
choices: That they leave you alone
That they provide for your needs
That they share their wealth
That they obey your wishes
context: Locke wrote that the law of nature — which is reason itself — teaches that 'no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions' (Second Treatise, Sec. 6). He framed natural rights as freedoms protected from interference: each one asks only that others NOT harm you, never that they give you anything. That is why rich and poor can hold them all at once. Source: gutenberg.org/files/7370/7370-h/7370-h.htm (Sec. 6).

question: John Locke asked a basic question in his Second Treatise of Government in 1689: why do people leave the wild 'state of nature,' where each person must defend himself alone, and bind themselves together under a government at all? His answer pointed to one chief purpose. According to Locke, what is that one job of government?
answer: To protect what is already theirs
choices: To protect what is already theirs
To provide for everyone's needs
To make the nation powerful
To teach people to be good
context: Locke wrote that 'the great and chief end... of Mens uniting into Commonwealths... is the Preservation of their Property' — by which he meant their lives, liberties, and estates. In his view government exists to protect what is yours, not to provide for you. Source: fee.org/resources/john-locke-natural-rights-to-life-liberty-and-property/; iep.utm.edu/locke-po/.

question: John Locke called government a trust that a ruler can break. When a ruler turns tyrant, trying 'to take away, and destroy the property of the people, or to reduce them to slavery,' Locke said, the people are no longer bound to obey him. According to Locke, what may the people rightfully do to such a government?
answer: Rebel and dissolve it entirely
choices: Rebel and dissolve it entirely
Petition the king for mercy
Wait for God to judge it
Flee to a foreign land
context: Locke's right of revolution (Second Treatise, Ch. 19): a government that destroys the people's rights forfeits its authority, and the people may overthrow it and start anew. This idea fed straight into the American Revolution a century later. Source: battlefields.org/learn/primary-sources/john-locke-excerpts-second-treatise-government (Sec. 222).

question: John Paul II, the Polish pope and the first pope ever to visit a Soviet-bloc country, said Mass before about a million people in Warsaw's Victory Square in June 1979, under rulers who called the state officially atheist. As he preached, the crowd broke in with a chant that one writer said swelled to thunder. What did the Poles chant?
answer: We want God!
choices: We want God!
Let your Spirit descend!
Christ conquers, Christ reigns!
Open wide the doors to Christ!
context: Peggy Noonan described the roar of 'We want God! We want God!' turning 'to thunder' — a public rejection of the officially atheist state's claim on Polish life. (The other three cries are real too: 'Let your Spirit descend' closed this Warsaw homily, 'Christus vincit, Christus regnat' was sung in a 14-minute ovation, and 'Be not afraid! Open wide the doors to Christ!' was John Paul II's 1978 inauguration motto.) Source: https://patriotpost.us/opinion/50202

question: Poland's Communist rulers, fearing what the crowds would look like on screen, ordered the state television crews to point their cameras away from the multitudes when John Paul II came home on pilgrimage in 1979. What did the broadcasts dwell on in close-up instead?
answer: A bare brick wall and elderly faces
choices: A bare brick wall and elderly faces
Empty chairs and idle soldiers
Closed shops and quiet streets
Distant rooftops and grey sky
context: State TV held shots on a brick wall and elderly people to fake the impression that young Poles weren't interested. Viewers saw through the lie, and the clumsy censorship became a symbol of the regime's dishonesty — its monopoly on public life visibly evaporating. Source: https://www.wilsoncenter.org/publication/146-one-more-reason-for-communisms-collapse-television-poland-1951-1989

question: Joseph Lister watched nearly half his surgical patients in Glasgow live through their operations in the 1860s, then die within days as their wounds rotted. He had read that tiny living germs caused rotting, so he soaked his dressings in a chemical that Carlisle used on the stench of its sewage. What was the chemical?
answer: Carbolic acid
choices: Carbolic acid
Chlorine bleach
Lime powder
Wood alcohol
context: Lister chose carbolic acid (phenol) because he had heard it was being used to deodorize and purify the foul sewage works in the town of Carlisle, England — the same 5% carbolic solution that cleaned sewage became his weapon against wound germs. His first antiseptic patient was 11-year-old James Greenlees (admitted 12 August 1865) with a leg crushed by a cart wheel; the open fracture healed without deep infection and the boy kept his leg. Source: Hektoen International, 'Joseph Lister and the story of antiseptic surgery'; History Today / Royal Society.

question: Joseph Lister told the surgeons of London that germs too small to see were getting into wounds and killing their patients. Many refused to believe in anything they could not see and kept operating with dirty hands and tools. One surgeon mocked Lister openly in front of his nurses. What did he tell them to do?
answer: Close the door so Mr. Lister's germs can't get in
choices: Close the door so Mr. Lister's germs can't get in
Boil the bandages to please Mr. Lister
Pray that Mr. Lister's germs spare the patient
Open the windows to let Mr. Lister's germs out
context: The resistance was aimed at Lister's germ theory more than at the carbolic treatment itself — surgeons couldn't accept that invisible organisms caused infection, so they ridiculed the idea. Lister had taken the germ idea from Louis Pasteur, who had shown that rotting and fermentation were caused by tiny living organisms floating in the air, not by 'bad air' itself. Source: Hektoen International, 'Joseph Lister and the story of antiseptic surgery'.

question: Julius Caesar halted his army at the Rubicon early in 49 BC. Leading troops across that river meant war on Rome. As his men crossed, tradition says, he spoke a phrase that still means a choice that cannot be undone. What did he say?
answer: The die is cast
choices: The die is cast
Render unto Caesar
I came, I saw, I conquered
Let them eat cake
context: 'Alea iacta est' (or 'iacta alea est') -- 'the die is cast.' A die is a single dice; once thrown, the gambler cannot take it back. The phrase has been the idiom for the point of no return for over 2,000 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alea_iacta_est

question: Soldiers marching with Julius Caesar came in 49 BC to the Rubicon, one of the most famous rivers in history, for their crossing started the civil war that destroyed the Roman Republic. What sort of river did they find there?
answer: A shallow brook a man could wade across
choices: A shallow brook a man could wade across
A wide flood far too deep for a man to swim
A frozen river that had to be crossed by sledge
A deep gorge spanned by a single stone bridge
context: Ancient and modern writers agree the Rubicon was 'little more than a stream.' The drama was entirely legal and symbolic -- the line that changed the world was crossed over a brook. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/julius-caesar-crossing-rubicon-rome

question: Julius Caesar was about to make war on Pompey and the whole Roman Senate when he led soldiers across the Rubicon in January 49 BC, betting everything on speed and surprise rather than numbers. How large a force did he bring over the river?
answer: One legion, about 5,000 men
choices: One legion, about 5,000 men
Ten legions, about 50,000 men
Four legions, about 20,000 men
Two legions, about 10,000 men
context: Caesar crossed with a single legion -- the Thirteenth (Legio XIII), roughly 5,000 legionaries plus about 300 cavalry. The tiny size is exactly why he relied on shock and speed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_the_Rubicon

question: Julius Caesar watched the gladiators at Ravenna on the evening he meant to cross the Rubicon, so that no one would guess his plan. After dark he slipped away toward the river on a roundabout road. How did he travel there that night?
answer: In a hired carriage pulled by mules borrowed from a bakery
choices: In a hired carriage pulled by mules borrowed from a bakery
On a warhorse riding openly at the head of his cavalry
In a covered litter carried on the shoulders of his bodyguards
Down the coast aboard a swift galley rowed through the night
context: Suetonius reports Caesar left the show, took a hired carriage drawn by mules borrowed from a nearby bakery, and went by a roundabout road to keep the move secret. Source: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Suetonius/12Caesars/Julius*.html

question: Julius Caesar led his army over the Rubicon in 49 BC, the river that marked where Italy itself began. Roman law forbade any general coming home from the provinces to bring his troops across it. By that law, what had Caesar just done?
answer: Committed treason, a crime punishable by death
choices: Committed treason, a crime punishable by death
Broken a religious fast owed to the gods
Forfeited his share of the army's plunder
Lost his right to celebrate a triumph
context: Leading an army across the Rubicon into Italy was treason, a capital offense -- and even the soldiers who obeyed Caesar faced death for it. That is why the crossing was an act of war, not just travel. Source: https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/rubico-49-bce/

question: Terrified refugees fled ahead of Julius Caesar after he crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC, seized the town of Ariminum at dawn and pushed south at speed. When the news reached Rome, what had rumour done to his small force?
answer: Swelled it into an immense army
choices: Swelled it into an immense army
Shrunk it to a band of deserters
Scattered it across the mountains
Trapped it behind a flooded river
context: Appian says Caesar moved so quickly that panic outran him and rumor inflated his one legion into an 'immense army,' which is why Pompey, the consuls, and much of the Senate fled Rome. Source: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/e/roman/texts/appian/civil_wars/2*.html

question: Suetonius tells how a sign came to Julius Caesar as he hesitated at the Rubicon: a figure of wondrous size and beauty sat on the bank, playing a reed pipe. Caesar took what the piper did next as a signal to cross. By the legend, what did the piper do?
answer: Snatched a soldier's trumpet, sounded the war-blast, and crossed the river
choices: Snatched a soldier's trumpet, sounded the war-blast, and crossed the river
Drew a flaming sword, pointed it toward Rome, and vanished into the mist
Wept three drops of blood, stilled the current, and turned the water red
Spoke the names of Caesar's enemies, laughed aloud, and sank beneath the bank
context: In Suetonius's telling, the piper grabbed a trumpet from a soldier, blew the call to advance, and crossed to the far bank -- and Caesar declared, 'Let us go where the omens of the gods and the crime of our enemies summon us.' Told as legend, not verified fact. Source: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Suetonius/12Caesars/Julius*.html

question: Pompey stood behind the Senate when it sent Julius Caesar, fresh from eight years of conquest in Gaul, an order that Caesar feared would leave him powerless and open to prosecution. He crossed the Rubicon instead of obeying. What had the Senate ordered him to do?
answer: Disband his army and return to Rome as a private citizen
choices: Disband his army and return to Rome as a private citizen
Hand his legions over to Pompey and serve under his command
Stay in Gaul and rule the conquered province for the rest of his life
Surrender to the treasury all the spoils he had won in the Gallic wars
context: The Senate ordered Caesar to give up his army and come home as an ordinary citizen. Stripped of his troops and office, he feared his enemies would prosecute him -- so he chose war, forcing Pompey and the consuls to flee. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_the_Rubicon

question: Appian tells how Julius Caesar stood at the edge of the Rubicon and weighed the choice aloud to his friends. Holding back, he said, would cause great distress to himself, but crossing would cause it to others, and then he plunged across 'like one inspired.' On whom did he say the crossing would bring distress?
answer: All mankind
choices: All mankind
The Senate
His soldiers
The Gauls
context: Appian gives the line: 'to leave this stream uncrossed will breed manifold distress for me; to cross it, for all mankind.' Caesar names the world-wide stakes of his choice, then crosses. Source: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/e/roman/texts/appian/civil_wars/2*.html

question: Plutarch says Julius Caesar spoke Greek, not Latin, as he crossed the Rubicon, and that the famous words he called out were not his own. He was quoting a writer, at the most fateful moment of his life. What kind of writer was it?
answer: A Greek comic playwright
choices: A Greek comic playwright
A Greek battle historian
A Greek temple oracle
A Greek heroic poet
context: Plutarch says Caesar quoted 'anerriphtho kybos' -- 'let the die be flung' -- a line from the comedy writer Menander. The Greek means a daring 'let the game be played'; Suetonius's Latin shifted it to the fatalist 'the die HAS been cast.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alea_iacta_est

question: Cicero wrote letters in the winter that Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon, and Caesar told the story of his civil war in his own memoir, yet neither records the famous words Caesar is said to have spoken at the river. Two later writers set the scene down more than 150 years afterwards. Which pair?
answer: Plutarch and Suetonius
choices: Plutarch and Suetonius
Sallust and Polybius
Homer and Virgil
Livy and Tacitus
context: Because Caesar's Bellum Civile and Cicero's contemporary letters say nothing about it, the 'die is cast' rests on Plutarch and Suetonius, both writing 150+ years later -- famous tradition more than verified transcript. Source: https://talesoftimesforgotten.com/2024/05/08/did-julius-caesar-really-say-the-die-is-cast/  (Legend.)

question: One of the most powerful men in Italy settled an old quarrel in 1933: which of three Italian streams was the real Rubicon that Julius Caesar crossed. He renamed a riverside town Rubicone by decree, and in 1991 scholars agreed with him, though the matter is still argued. Who made the ruling?
answer: Benito Mussolini
choices: Benito Mussolini
Marshal Pietro Badoglio
King Victor Emmanuel III
Pope Pius XI
context: Mussolini settled the question by decree in 1933, renaming the town on the Fiumicino 'Rubicone'; scholars only corroborated the choice in 1991 using the Peutinger Map's '12 miles from Rimini,' and it is still debated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubicon

question: Constantine the Great dedicated a new eastern capital on the Bosphorus in May 330 and named it Constantinople after himself, a city that would rule the eastern empire for a thousand years. Its people gave it a proud title. What did they call it?
answer: New Rome
choices: New Rome
Second Athens
Little Jerusalem
Eternal Carthage
context: The Romans hailed the city as 'New Rome,' and Constantine also named it after himself — Constantinople. It was dedicated on 11 May 330, and for a thousand years its people called themselves Romans, ruling the eastern half of the Roman Empire long after the West was gone. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Byzantine Empire' (worldhistory.org/Byzantine_Empire/).

question: Rioters set the old church of Hagia Sophia ablaze in 532, and Justinian put more than ten thousand builders to work on a new one. In Europe, cathedrals of that size often took a hundred years or more to build. About how long did Justinian's church take to finish?
answer: About six years
choices: About six years
About thirty years
About sixty years
About a hundred years
context: Hagia Sophia was completed in only about 5 years and 10 months (532-537) and was dedicated on 27 December 537 — a breathtaking pace for the biggest building on earth, with over ten thousand workers on it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hagia Sophia' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia).

question: A worshipper walking around the high altar of Justinian's Hagia Sophia saw it change colour, the legend says. The altar, of gold fused with pearls and crushed gems, gleamed like gold from one side. What colours did it show from the other sides?
answer: Silver, then deep sapphire
choices: Silver, then deep sapphire
Copper, then bright emerald
Bronze, then dark ruby
Iron, then pale amber
context: A later legendary account, the Narratio de S. Sophia, says the altar 'appears sometimes as gold, in other places as silver, elsewhere gleaming with sapphire' depending on where you stood. Told as legend. Source: CNN Travel, 'Hagia Sophia: Secrets of the 1,600-year-old megastructure' (cnn.com/travel/hagia-sophia-istanbul-history-secrets), quoting the Narratio de S. Sophia.

question: Procopius walked through Hagia Sophia when it was brand new and tried to describe its light. The church was flooded with such brightness, he wrote, that no one would believe the daylight came in from outside. Where did Procopius say the light seemed to come from instead?
answer: From the building itself
choices: From the building itself
From the hanging lamps
From the golden mosaics
From the marble columns
context: Procopius wrote that the interior glowed as though 'the rays are produced within itself,' not lit by the sun outside. The effect came from a ring of 40 windows pierced around the foot of the dome, which makes the dome look like it floats on a band of light. Source: Procopius, De Aedificiis (On Buildings) Book I (sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/procop-deaed1.asp).

question: Justinian finished the great domed church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople in 537, and no cathedral on Earth was bigger. Its enormous dome would inspire builders for centuries. For how long did no larger cathedral stand anywhere in the world?
answer: Almost 1000 years
choices: Almost 1000 years
About 100 years
About 300 years
Almost 2000 years
context: Hagia Sophia stayed the largest cathedral in the world for nearly a thousand years — not surpassed until Seville Cathedral was completed in 1520. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hagia Sophia' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia); Wikipedia, 'Seville Cathedral'.

question: Justinian meant his new Hagia Sophia, sheathed in marble and silver, to outshine every church on Earth. One Byzantine account tells that partway through the building the emperor sat down in despair, his great project suddenly in doubt. What had gone wrong?
answer: He had run out of gold to finish it
choices: He had run out of gold to finish it
He had lost his chief architect to plague
He had watched the half-built dome crack
He had turned the city's bishops against him
context: Hagia Sophia nearly emptied the imperial treasury — the historian Peter Heather estimates it cost on the order of 15,000-20,000 pounds of gold, and a Byzantine account says Justinian grew 'dispirited' mid-build because he had run short of gold. Source: CNN Travel, 'Hagia Sophia: Secrets of the 1,600-year-old megastructure' (cnn.com/travel/hagia-sophia-istanbul-history-secrets); New World Encyclopedia, 'Hagia Sophia'.

question: Belisarius, the finest general Justinian had, spent 533 and 534 smashing the Vandals in North Africa, part of his emperor's dream of winning back the Roman lands lost in the West. In 536 he won back a prize few had thought possible. What did he win back?
answer: The city of Rome itself
choices: The city of Rome itself
The whole of Roman Gaul
The Rhine frontier forts
The island of Britain
context: Justinian's dream of renovatio imperii — restoring the empire. Belisarius crushed the Vandal kingdom in North Africa in a lightning 533-534 campaign, then invaded Italy and retook the city of Rome itself in 536-537 from the Ostrogoths. Source: Wikipedia, 'Byzantine Empire under the Justinian dynasty' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire_under_the_Justinian_dynasty); Wikipedia, 'Vandalic War'.

question: Justinian's lawyers wrote a textbook for law students called the Institutes, and they opened it with one of the most quoted definitions of justice ever written. Justice, they declared, is the 'constant and perpetual will' to do one thing for every person. What is that one thing?
answer: Give each what is owed
choices: Give each what is owed
Show each the same mercy
Judge each by deeds alone
Forgive each all debts
context: The Institutes (533) opens: 'Justice is the constant and perpetual will to render to every man his due.' This little textbook, and the whole body of law Justinian's commission produced, became the foundation of European civil law. Source: Justinian, Institutes 1.1; The Latin Library, 'Institutes of Justinian' (thelatinlibrary.com/law/institutes.html).

question: Acacius worked at the Hippodrome, the great stadium of Constantinople where the whole city watched the chariot races, for the Green racing faction. His little daughter Theodora, who would one day marry the emperor Justinian, grew up backstage there. What was Acacius's job?
answer: He kept and trained the bears.
choices: He kept and trained the bears.
He drove a racing chariot.
He bred the racing horses.
He guarded the stadium gates.
context: Acacius was a bear-keeper for the Green racing faction. When he died, Theodora was still a child and the family was left destitute.

question: The rival Blue and Green chariot fans of Constantinople, who normally hated each other, joined forces in a rebellion against the emperor Justinian in January 532, and the cry they roared through the streets was a single Greek word: "Nika!" What does the word mean?
answer: Win!
choices: Win!
Burn!
Freedom!
Justice!
context: 'Nika' is Greek for 'Win!' or 'Conquer!' -- the cry fans roared to drive on their favorite racers, now turned into a battle chant against the emperor. The race-day cheer gave the Nika riot its name; the riot burned half the city.

question: Justinian's courtiers watched in awe as he drove himself relentlessly at new laws, foreign wars and grand buildings. He was a peasant's son from the Balkans whose mother tongue was Latin, raised to the throne by his uncle, Justin I. What did the courtiers call him?
answer: The emperor who never sleeps
choices: The emperor who never sleeps
The emperor of a hundred battles
The emperor born to the purple
The emperor of the golden tongue
context: Born Petrus Sabbatius near Tauresium around 482, he was raised to power by his uncle Justin I and was famous for working through the night. He reigned 527-565. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I

question: The Nika rioters had set Constantinople ablaze and proclaimed a rival emperor, and Justinian had ships waiting in the harbor to carry him to safety. His wife Theodora refused to run, and the historian Procopius records the famous line she used to stiffen his nerve. What did she tell him?
answer: That the royal purple makes a fine burial-shroud.
choices: That the royal purple makes a fine burial-shroud.
That a coward dies a thousand deaths in his fear.
That God always favors the bold in open battle.
That a throne can only be won back with blood.
context: As told by Procopius, Theodora said royalty 'is a good burial-shroud': better to die an emperor than live a fugitive. Purple was the color reserved for emperors. Justinian stayed and the riot was crushed; the speech is likely a polished set-piece by Procopius, not a word-for-word record.

question: Belisarius, Justinian's great general, had marched into Italy to win it back from the Ostrogoths. Cornered in their capital, Ravenna, in 540, the Goths made him a stunning offer: they would crown him their own Western Roman emperor. What did Belisarius do?
answer: He faked acceptance, then took the city in Justinian's name.
choices: He faked acceptance, then took the city in Justinian's name.
He refused them, and stormed Ravenna by brute force.
He accepted them, and ruled Italy as a rebel king.
He withdrew his army, and left the Goths in power.
context: Belisarius pretended to accept the crown, entered Ravenna, then seized it for Justinian. His string of reconquests earned him the title 'the Last of the Romans.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belisarius

question: When Belisarius crushed the Vandal kingdom in North Africa, he shipped its treasure home for a victory parade through Constantinople in 534. Among the gold gleamed sacred objects with a wild past: Rome had looted them from Jerusalem, and then the Vandals stole them from Rome. What was the most famous piece?
answer: the golden menorah
choices: the golden menorah
the Ark of the Covenant
the Holy Grail
the crown of thorns
context: The Temple vessels the Vandals had carried off from Rome — which Rome had earlier taken from Jerusalem — were paraded in Belisarius's triumph, the gold menorah among them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelimer

question: Theodora, Justinian's empress, never forgot her own hard girlhood on the stage in Constantinople. She founded a convent on the Bosphorus called Metanoia, Repentance, for enslaved women who had been forced into prostitution. What did she do for them?
answer: She paid their owners to set every woman free.
choices: She paid their owners to set every woman free.
She drafted them into her own palace guard.
She married them off to Roman senators by decree.
She shipped them back to their distant home villages.
context: Theodora founded the Metanoia ('Repentance') convent, buying enslaved prostitutes out of bondage, repaying their owners, and giving each woman clothing and coin. A devout Miaphysite, she also hid persecuted clergy in her own palace. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodora_(wife_of_Justinian_I)

question: Justin I, the emperor, issued a new law around 524 so that his nephew Justinian could marry Theodora. Without it, a strict old Roman law would have blocked the wedding outright. What had the old law forbidden?
answer: A high-ranking senator marrying a former actress.
choices: A high-ranking senator marrying a former actress.
An emperor marrying anyone born outside of Rome.
A Christian marrying outside the imperial church.
A soldier marrying before his term of service ended.
context: Roman law barred senators from marrying actresses, so Justin I issued a new law letting reformed actresses marry men of high rank. Theodora became Augusta — empress — on 1 April 527. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodora_(wife_of_Justinian_I)

question: Justinian and Theodora face each other across the altar of Ravenna's church of San Vitale, each pictured in glittering gold mosaic, each presenting a holy gift for the Mass. One shining detail in both portraits makes a bold claim about the couple's power. What is it?
answer: Both wear a halo, marking them as God's chosen rulers.
choices: Both wear a halo, marking them as God's chosen rulers.
Both grip a drawn sword, marking them as conquerors.
Both stand barefoot, marking them as humble pilgrims.
Both wear an iron crown, marking them as warlords.
context: In the San Vitale mosaics (c. 547), Justinian carries a golden paten and Theodora a jeweled chalice, and both are haloed — presenting the imperial couple as rulers chosen by God. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_of_San_Vitale

question: Justinian dreamed of restoring the whole old Roman Empire, renovatio imperii, and his armies had already won back North Africa and Italy. Then in 541 a catastrophe reached Constantinople that emptied his treasury, thinned his armies and wrecked the dream. What was it?
answer: A bubonic plague that killed a huge share of the people.
choices: A bubonic plague that killed a huge share of the people.
A Persian army that broke in and sacked the capital.
An earthquake that flattened the heart of the city.
A famine that emptied the surrounding countryside.
context: The Plague of Justinian (541-542), an early bubonic-plague pandemic, killed a catastrophic share of Constantinople's population and helped stall the reconquest of the Roman world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I

question: Tribonian, Justinian's brilliant lawyer, faced a jungle of Roman law: more than two thousand books, about three million lines of statutes and opinions, often contradicting one another. His team was even allowed to cut and rewrite the old texts to settle the clashes. Into how many books did they boil it all down?
answer: Fifty books
choices: Fifty books
Five hundred books
Five thousand books
Fifty thousand books
context: Tribonian's commission compressed roughly three million lines of contradictory Roman legal writing into a single usable 50-book work, the Digest (Pandects), with explicit power to cut, alter, and harmonize the old texts to remove the contradictions. Emperor Justinian I ordered the project; Tribonian, his top legal official, directed it. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/Corpus_Juris_Civilis/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digest_(Roman_law)

question: Irnerius, a teacher at Bologna, began lecturing around 1088 on Justinian's law books, which had resurfaced in northern Italy some five centuries after the emperor's day. His school helped launch Europe's first universities. What Latin nickname did his grateful students give him?
answer: The lantern of the law
choices: The lantern of the law
The father of the courts
The hammer of heretics
The sword of justice
context: Irnerius (c.1050-after 1125) was nicknamed 'lucerna juris,' the lantern of the law. Around 1084-1088 he founded the School of Glossators at Bologna, helping launch the first true European universities -- the channel through which Justinian's law became the seedbed of modern continental 'civil law.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irnerius ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Irnerius

question: Yukio Seki, a lieutenant, led five planes against American carriers in October 1944, the first organised kamikaze attack. Japan's propaganda pictured such pilots as happy to die for the Emperor and the empire, but Seki told a reporter before the mission whom he was really giving his life for. What did he say?
answer: "I'm going for my beloved wife"
choices: "I'm going for my beloved wife"
"I'm going for the honor of the Emperor"
"I'm going for the glory of the empire"
"I'm going for the comrades I have lost"
context: Seki, who led the five-plane Shikishima Squadron in the first organized attack, flatly rejected the propaganda image — he said he was dying not for Emperor or empire but for his wife. He also argued the whole tactic was a waste of skilled flyers, insisting he could drop a 500-kilogram bomb on a carrier deck 'without going in for body-crashing.' His words cut against the regime's myth of eager martyrs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yukio_Seki

question: Nikolai Burdenko headed the commission Moscow set up after German soldiers uncovered mass graves of Polish officers, police and professors in the Katyn forest in April 1943. His commission duly declared the Germans guilty. How long did the Soviet Union keep up that lie?
answer: Forty-seven years
choices: Forty-seven years
Twenty-two years
Thirty-five years
Sixty-three years
context: The mandated cool-fact is the sheer length of the lie: rather than confess, the USSR denied the killings for nearly half a century and even faked an investigation to frame its enemy. After the Soviets took eastern Poland under the secret Nazi-Soviet Pact, the NKVD murdered about 21,857 Polish prisoners (including 14 generals) in spring 1940 to behead the nation by killing its educated class. German troops found the graves and announced them on 13 April 1943; Moscow blamed the Nazis and convened the Burdenko Commission -- led by Nikolai Burdenko, head of the USSR Academy of Medical Sciences -- which duly 'proved' the Germans did it. The USSR finally confessed its own guilt on 13 April 1990 -- exactly forty-seven years to the day after the discovery -- and Beria's signed kill-order was released in 1992. Stated as established fact, with no laundering of the Soviet record. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katyn_massacre (1943 discovery, Burdenko Commission, 1990 admission, 1992 'Package No.1' release; 21,857 total, 14 generals); britannica.com/event/Katyn-Massacre.

question: Vasily Blokhin, chief executioner of Stalin's secret police, personally shot about 7,000 prisoners over twenty-eight nights in April 1940. Soviet revolvers kicked so hard that his hand ached after a dozen shots, so he brought a briefcase of other pistols for the work. Which guns did he choose?
answer: German-made Walther pistols
choices: German-made Walther pistols
Belgian-made Browning pistols
Italian-made Beretta pistols
Austrian-made Steyr pistols
context: Blokhin is recorded as the most prolific executioner in history by his own hand, with a quota of roughly 250 prisoners a night. He used German-made Walther pistols rather than Soviet ones because the standard Soviet revolvers had too much recoil and grew painful to fire after the first dozen executions; using German pistols also helped the cover-up the Soviets maintained for decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katyn_massacre; allthatsinteresting.com/vasily-blokhin ('briefcase full of his own Walther pistols').

question: Johannes Kepler took charge of a treasure two days after his Danish employer died without warning in Prague in 1601: a lifetime of sky measurements, taken with the naked eye from an island observatory in the Baltic, more exact than any made before the telescope. Whose records did Kepler inherit?
answer: Tycho Brahe
choices: Tycho Brahe
Galileo Galilei
Nicolaus Copernicus
Claudius Ptolemy
context: Tycho Brahe died in 1601; two days later Kepler was named Imperial Mathematician and got the data. He used Tycho's naked-eye records of Mars, the finest before telescopes, to crack the orbit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Kepler

question: Johannes Kepler saw that a planet hurries near the Sun and crawls far from it, and he set out to capture exactly how its speed changes. He found his rule in an imaginary line drawn from the Sun to the planet. In equal spans of time, what does that line do?
answer: Sweeps out equal areas
choices: Sweeps out equal areas
Covers equal distances
Turns through equal angles
Crosses equal numbers of stars
context: This is Kepler's second law, the equal-areas law: the Sun-to-planet line sweeps equal areas in equal times, which is exactly why a planet speeds up when close to the Sun and slows when far. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomia_nova

question: Johannes Kepler spent years on a clumsy model of wobbling little circles for the path of Mars, then saw that it had been describing one far simpler curve all along. What cry did he scold himself with in print?
answer: Ah, what a foolish bird I have been!
choices: Ah, what a foolish bird I have been!
Oh, what a blind mole I have been!
Alas, what a stubborn ox I have been!
Ah, what a sleepy owl I have been!
context: Kepler wrote 'Ah, what a foolish bird I have been!' in Astronomia nova when he saw his oscillating-epicycle model had just been a plain ellipse the whole time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomia_nova

question: In Harmonices Mundi, his book of 1619, Johannes Kepler argued that each planet, quickening near the Sun and slowing far from it, is like a voice singing its note in a cosmic choir. What did Kepler say the planets were literally doing as they moved?
answer: Making music
choices: Making music
Casting spells
Painting pictures
Ringing bells
context: Kepler made a grim pun on it: 'The Earth sings Mi, Fa, Mi: you may infer even from the syllables that in this our home MIsery and FAmine hold sway.' In his cosmic choir Mercury was the soprano and Mars the tenor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonice_Mundi

question: Surrendering to what he called a sacred frenzy, Johannes Kepler, a devout Lutheran, wrote of the moment his third law came to him, the one that ties how long a planet takes to circle the Sun to how far away it is. He had stolen something, he said, to raise a tabernacle to his God. What had he stolen?
answer: The golden vessels of the Egyptians
choices: The golden vessels of the Egyptians
The cedar timbers of Lebanon
The sacred fire of the Greeks
The hidden treasures of Babylon
context: Kepler wrote: 'I can give myself up to the sacred frenzy... I have stolen the golden vessels of the Egyptians to build a tabernacle to my God far from the bounds of Egypt.' For Kepler, uncovering the cosmos's mathematical harmony was an act of worship. Source: https://libquotes.com/johannes-kepler/works/harmonices-mundi

question: Knights strained in vain at a sword stuck through an anvil on a stone in a London churchyard, by the legend, for golden letters promised the crown to whoever pulled it free. A boy fetching his brother Sir Kay a sword drew it out easily. Who was he?
answer: The future King Arthur
choices: The future King Arthur
The young knight Sir Galahad
The squire Sir Percival
The boy Sir Bedivere
context: Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur tells it this way: Arthur drew the sword as a careless errand for Kay, not knowing the golden letters named the pulling as proof of the true-born king of all England. Galahad, Percival, and Bedivere are all later Round Table knights, not the boy of the stone. (Legend.) Source: en.wikiquote.org Thomas Malory / Le Morte d'Arthur + WebSearch.

question: King Arthur called the best knights to Camelot, Lancelot, Gawain and Percival among them. Instead of a long table with a lord at the head and lesser men at the foot, the tales say, he had a round one built. Why was it round?
answer: So no knight could claim a seat higher than any other
choices: So no knight could claim a seat higher than any other
So Arthur could see every knight's face at once during prayers
So the wizard Merlin could spin it to choose who spoke
So more knights could be squeezed around its edge
context: The poet Wace first described the Round Table in 1155, writing that Arthur made it round 'to prevent quarrels among his barons, none of whom would accept a lower place.' A round table has no head, so no seat outranks another. Layamon later added that a deadly brawl at a Yuletide feast had prompted a Cornish carpenter to build it. (Legend.) Source: en.wikipedia.org Round_Table + WebSearch.

question: An arm clad in white silk rose out of a still, magic lake, holding up a sword by the hilt, when Merlin brought the young King Arthur there to win a new blade. Arthur rowed out to claim it. What was the sword called?
answer: Excalibur
choices: Excalibur
Durendal
Caliburn's anvil
The Siege Perilous
context: In Malory's telling the arm is 'clad in white samite' (rich silk) and belongs to the Lady of the Lake, who gives Arthur the sword Excalibur. Durendal is the sword of a different legend (Roland); the Siege Perilous is a chair, not a sword. (Legend.) Source: worldhistory.org Excalibur + WebSearch.

question: Young Arthur lost the very first sword he owned, the blade that had proved him the rightful king, early in his reign, the legend says, and Merlin had to find him another. What became of that first sword?
answer: It shattered in a duel with King Pellinore
choices: It shattered in a duel with King Pellinore
It was stolen in the night by Morgan le Fay
It rusted away after he left it back in the stone
It was snapped over the knee of a giant
context: The stone-sword and Excalibur are separate weapons. Arthur's first blade — the one from the anvil — broke in a hard fight with King Pellinore, and only afterward did Merlin bring him to the lake to win Excalibur. The sword-in-the-stone proved his right to rule; once it shattered, he needed the lake-gift. (Legend.) Source: worldhistory.org Excalibur + WebSearch.

question: King Ban died and left a baby son, Lancelot, who would grow up to be the greatest knight of Arthur's court. A magical woman snatched the orphan away, the tales say, and raised him in secret, far from any court, until he was eighteen. Who was she?
answer: The Lady of the Lake
choices: The Lady of the Lake
The sorceress Morgan le Fay
Queen Guinevere of Camelot
The enchantress of Tintagel
context: The same lake-spirit who gave Arthur Excalibur raised the orphaned Lancelot beneath the water, which is why he is known as 'Lancelot du Lac' — Lancelot of the Lake. His son Galahad would later achieve the Holy Grail that Lancelot himself never could. (Legend.) Source: worldhistory.org Lancelot + WebSearch.

question: Sir Bedivere carried his dying king's sword to the lake, as King Arthur had ordered after his last battle, but twice he could not bear to lose so fine a blade, so he hid it and lied. On the third try he hurled it out over the water. What happened the moment it fell?
answer: A hand rose from the lake, caught it, and drew it under
choices: A hand rose from the lake, caught it, and drew it under
The lake froze solid around the sunken blade
The Lady of the Lake walked out across the water to fetch it
The sword burst into flame and sank as ash
context: In Malory, a hand rose from the water, caught Excalibur, brandished it three times, and drew it under — the proof Arthur had been waiting for that the sword was truly returned. Bedivere's two lies are why Arthur sent him back a third time. (Legend.) Source: en.wikipedia.org Bedivere + WebSearch of Malory.

question: Merlin warned the young King Arthur, the tales say, that the scabbard of his magic sword, the sheath the blade sat in, was worth ten of the blade itself, and that he must guard it above all. What did wearing that scabbard do for Arthur?
answer: He could be wounded but would never lose any blood
choices: He could be wounded but would never lose any blood
His blade would cut through any armor ever forged
He could not be seen by an enemy's eyes
He would always know when a man was lying to him
context: Merlin's words in Malory: 'While ye have the scabbard upon you, ye shall never lose any blood, be ye ever so sorely wounded.' The sheath, not the sword, was Arthur's true protection — which is what made its theft so deadly. (Legend.) Source: worldhistory.org Excalibur quoting Malory.
