question: Morgan le Fay, the sorceress who was Arthur's own half-sister, crept in while he slept and stole his magic scabbard, though she could not take the sword he slept clutching. Arthur rode after her. What did she do so that he could never get the scabbard back?
answer: She hurled it into a deep lake and turned herself to stone to escape
choices: She hurled it into a deep lake and turned herself to stone to escape
She melted it into a crown and wore it to taunt him
She sealed it inside an ancient oak and set a curse on the tree
She handed it to the traitor Mordred and named him her heir
context: Morgan threw the scabbard into a deep lake — dooming Arthur to bleed at his final battle — then turned herself and all her men into standing stones so the pursuing king rode right past them. The lost sheath is why his last wound was mortal. (Legend.) Source: worldhistory.org Excalibur + Nightbringer.se Morgan le Fay via WebSearch.

question: The knights of the Round Table left one seat empty, the Siege Perilous, because it would destroy any knight unworthy of it. Then golden letters appeared on it naming the one knight pure enough to sit there, and his coming began the quest for the Holy Grail. Whose name did the letters spell?
answer: Sir Galahad
choices: Sir Galahad
Sir Lancelot
Sir Gawain
Sir Kay
context: The golden letters read 'This is the Siege of Galahad.' Only Galahad, the pure son of Lancelot, could sit the death-seat unharmed, and the moment he did the Grail quest began. Lancelot, Gawain, and Kay were great knights but not pure enough for that chair. (Legend.) Source: en.wikipedia.org Round_Table + en.wikipedia.org Galahad + WebSearch.

question: Uther Pendragon burned with desire for Igraine, the wife of Duke Gorlois, the legend tells, but Gorlois shut her away in his clifftop castle of Tintagel. Uther begged Merlin for help, and that night Arthur was conceived. What magic did Merlin work to get Uther inside?
answer: He disguised Uther as her husband Gorlois, look and voice and all
choices: He disguised Uther as her husband Gorlois, look and voice and all
He cloaked Uther in fog so the guards saw no one pass
He raised a hidden bridge from the cliff to her tower window
He cast every guard and servant into an enchanted sleep
context: Merlin transformed Uther into the exact likeness of Duke Gorlois so Igraine welcomed him as her own husband; Arthur was conceived that night, and the real Gorlois was killed in battle at the very same hour. So the legend's great king begins with a magical deception. (Legend.) Source: en.wikipedia.org Uther_Pendragon + WebSearch of Geoffrey of Monmouth.

question: Scientists counted the tree rings in the great round table on the wall of Winchester's Great Hall, a table painted with King Arthur and 24 knights. For centuries people had taken it for the real table of Camelot. What did the wood reveal?
answer: The table was built around 1250–1280, far too late to be Arthur's
choices: The table was built around 1250–1280, far too late to be Arthur's
The oak came from a forest in the Holy Land
The planks were younger at the rim than at the center
The table had been repaired with timber from a Viking ship
context: Tree-ring dating placed the Winchester table around 1250–1280, built for King Edward I, who staged Arthurian 'Round Table' tournaments. It is a genuine medieval object — just centuries too young to have seated Arthur's knights. Science settled what legend could not. Source: en.wikipedia.org Round_Table + medievalchronicles.com via WebSearch.

question: Chretien de Troyes put a grail into a poem around 1190, and in his telling it was a plain serving dish carried in a procession. A later writer, Robert de Boron, made it holy. What did Robert de Boron say the Grail had been?
answer: The cup Jesus used at the Last Supper
choices: The cup Jesus used at the Last Supper
The crown worn by the first Christian king
A platter from King Solomon's temple
The spear that pierced Christ's side
context: Chrétien's 'grail' was just a platter; Robert de Boron reimagined it as the cup of the Last Supper, the same vessel Joseph of Arimathea used to catch Christ's blood at the crucifixion — which is why it became the HOLY Grail. The most famous holy relic in legend began as a serving dish. (Legend, on the story's origin.) Source: worldhistory.org Grail_Legend + WebSearch.

question: One writer launched the whole legend of King Arthur around 1136, in a book where Merlin and Guinevere first appear. Historians treat it as mostly folklore, but scholars still divide all the Arthur stories into those before it and those after. What is the book?
answer: Geoffrey of Monmouth's History of the Kings of Britain
choices: Geoffrey of Monmouth's History of the Kings of Britain
Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur
Chrétien de Troyes's Perceval
Wace's Roman de Brut
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136) gave the legend Merlin, Guinevere, and Caliburn/Excalibur, and was so dominant that scholars label Arthur tales 'pre-Geoffrey' or 'post-Geoffrey.' Malory, Chrétien, and Wace all wrote later and built on what Geoffrey began. Source: en.wikipedia.org Geoffrey_of_Monmouth + britannica.com via WebSearch.

question: British soldiers sacked the royal city of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria, in 1897 and carried off thousands of its cast-metal heads and plaques. The world came to know them as the Benin Bronzes, though most were not bronze at all. What metal were most of them cast from?
answer: Brass
choices: Brass
Copper
Tin
Iron
context: They are brass, made by the lost-wax method: an artist sculpts the figure in beeswax over a clay core, wraps it in a clay mould, melts the wax out through a hole, then pours in molten metal to fill the space the wax left behind. Source: Wikipedia, 'Benin Bronzes'; RISD Museum, 'Head in Focus' (risdmuseum.org).

question: Students at Jesus College, Cambridge, campaigned to take a looted Benin Bronze off their dining-hall wall, and in 2021 the college handed it back to Nigeria, the first in Britain to give one back. What animal did the brass sculpture show?
answer: A cockerel
choices: A cockerel
A leopard
An elephant
A python
context: The brass cockerel was named 'Okukur'. Students argued it had no place on the college wall, and the college handed it back to Nigeria in 2021 — the first Benin Bronze a UK institution returned. Source: The Art Newspaper, 28 Oct 2021; Wikipedia, 'Benin Bronzes'.

question: Craftsmen of Benin cast some 900 brass plaques, mostly under Oba Esigie in the 1500s, and nailed them onto the tall wooden pillars of the oba's palace. Taken together, what did all those plaques make for the kingdom?
answer: A picture-record of its history and ceremonies
choices: A picture-record of its history and ceremonies
A map of its trade routes and rivers
A calendar of its festivals and seasons
A code of its laws and punishments
context: The roughly 900 relief plaques, nailed to the palace pillars, formed a kind of picture-record of the kingdom — its kings, court and ceremonies — mostly cast during the reign of the great 16th-century Oba Esigie. Source: Wikipedia, 'Benin Bronzes'; smarthistory.org.

question: Patrick Darling, an archaeologist, worked out in 1999 the total length of Benin's iya, the walls and ditches its people had dug by hand around their city. Its ditches dropped as much as 17 metres below the tops of its ramparts. Laid end to end, how did the iya compare with the Great Wall of China?
answer: About four times as long
choices: About four times as long
About twice as long
About half as long
About a tenth as long
context: Darling's survey put Benin's network of earthworks at some 16,000 km — about four times longer than the Great Wall of China, and built from roughly a hundred times more material than the Great Pyramid of Cheops. In places the drop from the ditch floor to the top of the rampart reached 17 metres, the height of a six-storey building. Source: Fred Pearce, New Scientist, 11 Sept 1999; Wikipedia, 'Benin Moat'.

question: A single granite block rose about 24 metres in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, its sides carved like a building many storeys high, with fake windows and a fake door at the base. What is this towering stone called?
answer: The Obelisk of Axum
choices: The Obelisk of Axum
The Pillar of Adulis
The Tower of Zula
The Column of Ezana
context: The standing Obelisk (or Stele) of Axum is a single 160-tonne block of stone, carved so its sides mimic the floors and windows of a tall building. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: Giant carved stone pillars called stelae, some over 20 metres tall, rose over the Aksumite highlands, in today's northern Ethiopia, around the 4th century AD. Each towering pillar stood over a chamber dug into the ground beneath it. What lay buried under each one?
answer: The tomb of an Aksumite king
choices: The tomb of an Aksumite king
A vault of gold coins
A temple to the war god
A spring of holy water
context: The carved stelae were grave markers standing over underground royal burial chambers, so each towering obelisk marked the tomb of an Aksumite king beneath it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: Benito Mussolini, Italy's fascist dictator, had his soldiers seize the most famous of Aksum's carved stone pillars in 1937, a single granite block some 24 metres tall, and carry it off to stand in Rome as a war trophy. A pillar that size was far too heavy to ship as it stood. What did Mussolini's men do to it first?
answer: Cut it into three pieces
choices: Cut it into three pieces
Hollowed out its center
Coated it in bronze
Floated it on a barge
context: Italian troops looted the obelisk in 1937, cut it into three pieces, shipped it to Rome, and re-erected it at Porta Capena square, unveiling it on October 28, 1937. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: Ethiopians won their great carved granite pillar back from Italy in 2005, the one Mussolini's soldiers had carried off to Rome, and they flew it home. The first flight, aboard a giant Antonov An-124 cargo plane, set a world record. What record did the stone it carried set?
answer: The heaviest air freight ever flown
choices: The heaviest air freight ever flown
The longest nonstop cargo flight
The most valuable object ever shipped
The widest load ever moved by road
context: The first piece, flown home April 19, 2005 aboard an Antonov An-124, was called the largest and heaviest piece of air freight ever carried; the reassembled obelisk was re-erected in Axum and unveiled September 4, 2008. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: Mani, a Persian prophet of the third century, founded a new religion, Manichaeism, that spread from Rome to China. He wrote that only four kingdoms on earth were truly great. He named Babylon-and-Persia, Rome and China. Which African kingdom did Mani place beside them as the fourth?
answer: The kingdom of the Aksumites
choices: The kingdom of the Aksumites
The kingdom of the Nubians
The kingdom of the Carthaginians
The kingdom of the Phoenicians
context: Mani wrote: 'There are four great kingdoms on earth: the first is the Kingdom of Babylon and Persia; the second is the Kingdom of Rome; the third is the Kingdom of the Aksumites; the fourth is the kingdom of the Chinese.' Source: https://warhistory.org/article/aksum

question: Afonso I, the baptized king of Kongo, wrote in 1526 to Portugal's King Joao III, begging his Christian ally to stop the Portuguese slavers raiding his lands. Every day, he complained, the traders were taking something from his kingdom. What did Afonso say they were taking?
answer: His children, nobles, and even his own kin
choices: His own gold, copper, and ivory
His soldiers and palace guards
His children, nobles, and even his own kin
His harvests and cattle herds
context: Afonso wrote: 'Each day the traders are kidnapping our people -- children of this country, sons of our nobles and vassals, even people of our own family.' A baptized king pleading with Europe to stop carrying off his own subjects. Source: Afonso I's 1526 letter to King Joao III (worldhistorycommons.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_I_of_Kongo).

question: Mpanzu a Kitima had the bigger army when he fought his half-brother Afonso for the crown of Kongo around 1509. Yet Afonso's outnumbered men won, his court chroniclers said, because a sight in the sky put the foe to flight, and the scene was later painted onto the royal coat of arms. What did the chroniclers say appeared?
answer: Saint James and five heavenly horsemen
choices: A blazing comet that split into two
Saint James and five heavenly horsemen
A storm of fire-tipped arrows
An eagle clutching a golden cross
context: Legend / chronicle testimony, not forensic fact. The vision of Saint James the Great and five heavenly horsemen routing Afonso's foes became part of the Kongo royal arms -- a Christian war-miracle story told by his own court. Source: thecollector.com/kingdom-of-kongo-great-catholic-state; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_I_of_Kongo.

question: Piye, a king of Nubia, the land up the Nile south of Egypt, marched his army downriver around 728 BC. He was about to do something no Nubian king had done before. What did Piye do?
answer: Conquered Egypt and founded its 25th Dynasty
choices: Conquered Egypt and founded its 25th Dynasty
Raided Egypt's temples and then retreated home
Married an Egyptian princess to keep the peace
Built a great fort along Egypt's southern border
context: For roughly a century, Black kings from Nubia ruled over Egypt itself — the line nicknamed the 'Black Pharaohs.' It reversed the usual story of Egypt dominating Nubia. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/nubian-pharaohs-kushite-ancient-egypt

question: Royal tomb-builders of an old kingdom raised so many pyramids over their kings and queens that one modern country now holds between 200 and 255, over twice as many as Egypt has. Which country holds the most pyramids on Earth?
answer: Sudan (ancient Nubia)
choices: Sudan (ancient Nubia)
Mexico
Iraq
Peru
context: Nubia has roughly 200 to 255 pyramids — more than twice Egypt's ~138. The single royal field at Meroë holds over 200 pyramids, the largest cluster of pyramids in the world. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/sudan-archaeology-pyramdis-kush-nubia

question: The Egyptians named the land to their south after the one weapon its warriors were feared for across the ancient world: Ta-Seti. Nubian fighters called the Medjay served as Egypt's elite police. What does the name mean?
answer: the Land of the Bow
choices: the Land of the Bow
the Land of the Spear
the Land of the Sword
the Land of the Chariot
context: Nubian archers were prized abroad; fighters called the Medjay became the elite paramilitary police force of New Kingdom Egypt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta-Seti

question: Nubian builders raised pyramids over the graves of their own kings and queens, and those pyramids looked quite different from the famous ones at Giza. What shape did a Nubian pyramid have?
answer: Small, narrow, and steeply pointed
choices: Small, narrow, and steeply pointed
Wide, low, and gently sloped
Tall, stepped, and flat-topped
Broad, round, and dome-capped
context: Nubian pyramids rise at about a 70-degree angle, far sharper than the gentle 40-to-50-degree slope of the Egyptian pyramids at Giza. Source: https://www.slate.com/blogs/atlas_obscura/2014/08/29/the_nubian_meroe_pyramids_in_sudan.html

question: Taharqa, the warrior king of Kush, wore a crown with a difference at the brow, one that set him and his line apart at a glance. Egyptian kings wore a single rearing cobra there. What did Taharqa and the other Kushite kings wear instead?
answer: Two cobras, side by side
choices: Two cobras, side by side
A golden falcon
A pair of ram's horns
A single white feather
context: The two cobras stood for the Kushite king's rule over BOTH Nubia and Egypt — one snake for each land. Source: https://www.brooklynmuseum.org/opencollection/objects/3889

question: Scribes at Meroe, the Kushite capital, invented their own alphabet, the oldest known writing south of the Sahara, and carved it into their inscriptions. Scholars today can read each of its 23 letters aloud. What can they still not do?
answer: Translate what most of the inscriptions actually say
choices: Translate what most of the inscriptions actually say
Tell which direction the signs were meant to be read
Identify which kingdom carved the script
Match its words to a related known language
context: This is the Meroitic script, used with 23 signs from about 200 BC. We can read the words aloud without knowing what most of them mean — the language itself remains mostly a mystery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meroitic_script

question: British explorers came upon Meroe, the Kushite capital, ringed by black heaps of slag, for its furnaces had smelted iron on a vast scale. They nicknamed the place after an iron-making city of their own. What did they call it?
answer: the Birmingham of Africa
choices: the Birmingham of Africa
the Sheffield of the Sands
the Manchester of the South
the London of the Nile
context: Birmingham was Britain's industrial iron city, so the nickname captured just how busy Meroë's furnaces were. Source: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/antiquity/article/abs/ironworking-remains-in-the-royal-city-of-meroe-new-insights-on-the-nile-corridor-and-the-kingdom-of-kush/B44821E549BB735D365EBFFB974F7F58

question: Queen Amanirenas of Kush led an army of some 30,000 against the Romans in Egypt around 25 BC, in the reign of the emperor Augustus. Strabo, the Greek geographer, left a striking description of the warrior queen. What did Strabo say about her?
answer: She was blind in one eye
choices: She was blind in one eye
She stood a full head taller than her guards
She had hair dyed bright red
She wore a lion's skin into battle
context: Strabo called her 'a masculine sort of woman, and blind in one eye.' She struck Roman Egypt at Syene (Aswan). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanirenas

question: Warriors of Queen Amanirenas of Kush raided a Roman frontier fort, toppled the emperor Augustus's bronze statue and sawed off its head. They carried the head all the way home to their capital, Meroe. What did they do with it there?
answer: Buried it beneath a temple's front steps so everyone entering would tread on his face
choices: Buried it beneath a temple's front steps so everyone entering would tread on his face
Mounted it on a spike above the city gate so travelers would see Rome had failed
Melted it down so its bronze could be recast into Kushite weapons
Threw it into the Nile as an offering to the river god
context: Archaeologist John Garstang dug up this 'Meroë Head' in 1910, 2.5 meters down under the staircase — still keeping its eerie original eyes after 1,900 years. It is now in the British Museum. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mero%C3%AB_Head

question: Sennacherib, king of the mighty Assyrian Empire, found an army from Kush marching north against him around 701 BC, led by the warrior king Taharqa. Long centuries later, a reader could come upon Taharqa named in one particular place. Where?
answer: In the Hebrew Bible
choices: In the Hebrew Bible
On the Rosetta Stone
In Homer's Iliad
On Trajan's Column
context: He appears in 2 Kings 19:9 as 'Tirhakah, king of Cush,' marching to fight the Assyrian king Sennacherib, who was besieging Jerusalem. Source: https://www.biblicalarchaeology.org/magazine/representing-cush-in-the-hebrew-bible/

question: Nimlot lost the city of Hermopolis to the Nubian king Piye, who had his victory carved on a stela. Piye was furious with the beaten prince, but the stela says one thing pained his heart more than any of Nimlot's other crimes. What pained Piye most?
answer: That Nimlot had let his horses go hungry
choices: That Nimlot had let his horses go hungry
That Nimlot had looted a temple of Amun
That Nimlot had broken a sworn oath
That Nimlot had burned the city's grain
context: Piye's stela quotes him: 'it is more painful in my heart that my horses have been starved than any other crime you have committed.' He loved horses so much that four favorites were buried standing near his own pyramid at El-Kurru. Source: https://www.attalus.org/egypt/piye.html

question: Giuseppe Ferlini, an Italian treasure-hunter, went to the royal pyramids of Meroe in 1834 looking for gold, and he found it in Queen Amanishakheto's gold jewellery. How had Ferlini broken into those sealed royal pyramids, opening one tomb after another?
answer: He blew their tops off with explosives
choices: He blew their tops off with explosives
He dug long tunnels under their bases
He paid local villagers to break them open
He lowered himself inside on ropes
context: Ferlini wrecked around 40 pyramids and found the gold of Queen Amanishakheto — but when he tried to sell it, Europeans refused to believe such fine work could have been made in sub-Saharan Africa. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Ferlini

question: A boy meant for knighthood in medieval Europe went to a lord's household as a page at about seven. At about fourteen he moved up, carrying a knight's shield and lances and tending his armour and horses. What was he called then?
answer: A squire
choices: A squire
A herald
A marshal
A varlet
context: The path ran page (about 7) to squire (about 14) to knight (about 18-21). A squire was a knight's working apprentice on and off the battlefield. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Medieval Knight (worldhistory.org/Medieval_Knight/).

question: Two knights on horseback galloped head-on at each other down a fenced course called the lists, each trying to splinter his lance on the other or unhorse him. It was the most glamorous event of a medieval European tournament. What was it called?
answer: The joust
choices: The joust
The melee
The pas d'armes
The tilt
context: Galloping head-on, the two knights closed at a combined speed near 30 mph. A later wooden barrier between them, the tilt, kept the horses from colliding. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Medieval Tournament (worldhistory.org/Medieval_Tournament/).

question: A noble lady watching a tournament in the Middle Ages singled out her champion and handed him a ribbon, a sleeve or a veil of her own, and he tied it on and wore it into the contest for her. What was such a token called?
answer: A favour
choices: A favour
A pennon
A garland
A streamer
context: Carrying a lady's favour, a knight fought in her honor. Winners might be awarded a gold crown, a jewel, a falcon, a fine horse, or a lady's kiss. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Medieval Tournament (worldhistory.org/Medieval_Tournament/).

question: A newly made knight of medieval Europe put on the true badge of his rank, gilded where a younger trainee's was only silver or tin. Earning knighthood was even called 'winning' this gear. What was the badge?
answer: His spurs
choices: His spurs
His helm
His banner
His belt
context: Knights and royalty wore golden (gilded) spurs, squires wore silver, and pages wore tinned ones, which is why earning the rank was called 'winning your spurs.' Source: royalspurs.com, History of Spurs.

question: A young man kneeling to be knighted in the Middle Ages received the accolade, a light stroke from the flat of a sword across his neck or shoulders. Tradition gave that stroke a famous meaning. What did tradition say of it?
answer: It was the last blow he should ever take without striking back.
choices: It was the last blow he should ever take without striking back.
It was the only blow a knight could ever give to a king.
It had to be struck hard enough to leave a lifelong scar.
It needed to be returned threefold before the next dawn.
context: The accolade (also called the colee or the dubbing) made the knight. From that day a knight was a fighting man who answered a blow with a blow. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Medieval Knight; Wikipedia, Medieval accolade.

question: A knight-to-be bathed on the night before his knighting to wash away his sins, then spent the hours until dawn on his knees in a dark church, keeping guard over his weapons laid on the altar. What was this all-night rite called?
answer: The vigil of arms
choices: The vigil of arms
The investiture
The girding
The blessing of arms
context: Bath then vigil readied the squire body and soul. He knelt watching his arms on the altar until first light, when the dubbing followed. Source: English Heritage, '5 Things You Might Not Know About Knights'; Wikipedia, Vigil of arms.

question: A young rider training for knighthood in medieval Europe charged with his lance at the quintain: a post that swung on a pivot, with a shield on one arm and a heavy sandbag hanging from the other. He had to strike the shield dead-centre. What happened to him if he hit it off-centre?
answer: The sandbag whipped around and knocked him off his horse.
choices: The sandbag whipped around and knocked him off his horse.
The shield sprang open and showered him with blunt arrows.
The post toppled over and pinned his horse to the ground.
The swinging arm snapped off and the splinters cut his hands.
context: A bad hit spun the bag around to clout the rider, so a squire had to strike true AND keep riding past it. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'How to Become a Medieval Knight'; Wikipedia, Quintain (jousting).

question: A knight of the Middle Ages rode a lesser horse to the battlefield while a groom led his great warhorse, a huge trained stallion, along by hand. He mounted the warhorse only when the fighting began. What was such a horse called?
answer: The destrier
choices: The destrier
The palfrey
The courser
The rouncey
context: The destrier was the 'great horse,' saved for combat alone. A knight rode a lesser horse to the field and switched mounts to fight. Source: horsesandpeople.com.au, The Great Horse of the Middle Ages.

question: A priest of medieval Europe laid his blessing on a new knight's sword in church and charged him with one duty above all the rest, though chivalry also asked him to be loyal, honest, merciful, courteous and generous. What was a knight charged to always do?
answer: Protect the poor and the weak.
choices: Protect the poor and the weak.
Obey his king before his God.
Avenge every insult to his honor.
Win glory in every tournament.
context: The blessing of the sword charged the knight to 'always protect the poor and the weak.' Defending those who could not defend themselves was the beating heart of the chivalric ideal. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Medieval Knight; medievalchronicles.com, Code of Chivalry.

question: William Marshal, 'the greatest knight that ever lived' in an Archbishop of Canterbury's words, took so many blows at one tournament that his helmet was bent out of shape and jammed fast on his head. How did he finally get the wrecked helmet off?
answer: He knelt at a blacksmith's anvil and had it hammered and pried off.
choices: He knelt at a blacksmith's anvil and had it hammered and pried off.
He soaked his head in a horse-trough until the dented metal slipped free.
He had two squires haul on it with a rope rigged to a pulley.
He cut the leather straps and split the helmet open with an axe.
context: The greatest knight of his age had to kneel at a smith's anvil to be freed from his own helmet. He claimed he never lost and captured 500 knights for ransom over his career. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Sir William Marshal (worldhistory.org/Sir_William_Marshal/).

question: King Henry II of France rode against an opponent at a celebration tournament in 1559, safe, as he thought, inside his full armour. His opponent's lance shattered, and one splinter slipped through the narrow slit of the king's visor. What did that splinter do?
answer: It pierced his eye and drove on into his brain.
choices: It pierced his eye and drove on into his brain.
It tore open his throat just below the chin-guard.
It snapped his neck with the force of the strike.
It punched through his breastplate and into his heart.
context: King Henry II lingered in agony for ten days before he died. The horror of it helped push France to give up jousting for good. Source: historytoday.com, 'Henry II of France Dies of Tournament Wounds'; Wikipedia, Gabriel de Lorges, Count of Montgomery.

question: Suero de Quinones of Spain, a self-styled 'prisoner of love,' held a bridge against all challengers for a whole month in 1434. To prove his devotion to his lady, he vowed to wear one heavy thing around his neck every Thursday until he had broken 300 lances. What did he wear?
answer: An iron collar
choices: An iron collar
A silken blindfold
A golden chain
A black veil
context: This bridge-defense was a 'pas d'armes,' where a knight held a spot against all comers. Suero de Quinones wore a real iron collar every Thursday as a token of love until his 300 lances were spent. Source: Wikipedia, Suero de Quinones; fascinatingspain.com, 'The Passage of Arms by Suero de Quinones'.

question: King Henry V of England gave a brutal order at Agincourt in 1415, while the battle still hung in the balance, about the French knights his men had already taken alive. Knights captured in battle were usually ransomed for profit. What did Henry command his men to do?
answer: Kill the helpless prisoners.
choices: Kill the helpless prisoners.
Ransom them back for gold.
March them home in chains.
Set them all free unharmed.
context: Ransoming captured knights was the normal, profitable custom, which is what makes the order so shocking. Men spoke of honor even as they burned villages, showing the code was a goal to aim at, not a guarantee. Source: historyskills.com, Code of Chivalry; English Heritage.

question: Buddhist monks of Heungdeok Temple, in the Korean city of Cheongju, printed a book called the Jikji in July 1377. Among all the world's books, what record does the Jikji hold?
answer: The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type
choices: The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type
The longest book ever copied by hand in one monastery
The first book translated into a hundred languages
The heaviest religious book ever bound in one volume
context: The Jikji was printed at Heungdeok Temple in the city of Cheongju in July 1377, predating Gutenberg's Bible by 78 years. It is the oldest surviving book in the world made with movable metal type. Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/689333-oldest-book-printed-using-movable-metal-type

question: Sejong the Great, king of Joseon, gave his people something new in 1443 and called it 'The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People.' He made it so that ordinary commoners, not just trained scholars, could learn to read. What had Sejong made?
answer: Korea's alphabet, Hangul
choices: Korea's alphabet, Hangul
A new tax law for farmers
A royal library in the capital
A network of mountain temples
context: King Sejong the Great invented Hangul in 1443, naming it Hunminjeongeum, 'The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People.' He built it so commoners could learn to read, not only scholars. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul

question: King Sejong built a clever trick into the shapes of the letters he designed. The letter for the 'm' sound is drawn as a square, and the letter for the 'k' sound traces a curve that bends up to shut off the throat. What do the shapes of the letters show?
answer: The position of the mouth and tongue making each sound
choices: The position of the mouth and tongue making each sound
The phases of the moon over a single month
The strokes used to paint each Chinese character
The footprints of animals from a royal hunt
context: Hangul's consonant letters are shaped like the mouth making the sound: the 'm' letter is a square like closed lips; the 'k/g' letter shows the back of the tongue blocking the throat. The letters are pictures of how you say them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul

question: Victor Collin de Plancy, a French diplomat, bought the second volume of the Jikji in Seoul around 1900, the only part of that Korean book that still exists, and carried it home with him to Europe. Where is the surviving Jikji today?
answer: In the National Library of France in Paris
choices: In the National Library of France in Paris
Back at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju
In a sealed vault beneath Seoul's palace
On a touring exhibit that never stops moving
context: The surviving second volume of the Jikji sits in the National Library of France in Paris. Victor Collin de Plancy, a French diplomat, bought it in Seoul around 1900 and took it to France. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jikji

question: Jang Yeong-sil rose from palace slave to a place among King Sejong's scientists, lifted by his talent alone, and he built water clocks and sundials. In 1441 Jang made the world's first standard version of one weather instrument. What did he make?
answer: The first standardized rain gauge
choices: The first standardized rain gauge
The first compass for sea voyages
The first telescope for the stars
The first thermometer for cold winters
context: Jang Yeong-sil, born a palace slave, was raised into King Sejong's court of scientists on talent alone. In 1441 he invented the world's first standardized rain gauge, the cheugugi, along with water clocks and sun clocks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jang_Yeong-sil

question: Choe Manri, a Confucian scholar, and six others sent King Sejong an angry petition in 1444 against his new letters. A country that made its own script was acting like barbarians, they argued, and it would bring Ming China's ridicule down on Korea. How did Sejong answer them?
answer: He kept the alphabet and spread it anyway
choices: He kept the alphabet and spread it anyway
He burned the alphabet to please the scholars
He fled the capital to avoid the dispute
He handed the throne to Choe Manri
context: Choe Manri and six other Confucian scholars petitioned King Sejong in 1444, calling an independent script the mark of 'barbarians' that would invite Ming China's ridicule. Sejong made and spread the alphabet anyway. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choe_Malli

question: A Brooklyn newsboy dropped something on the pavement in June 1953, and it split in two. Inside lay a tiny photograph of coded numbers, the clue that years later led the FBI to a Soviet spy. What had the boy dropped?
answer: A hollowed-out nickel
choices: A hollowed-out nickel
A rolled newspaper
A leather coin purse
A folded delivery receipt
context: The 'Hollow Nickel Case': the coin held a microphotograph of a coded cipher. The FBI cracked it years later with help from Abel's defecting partner Reino Hayhanen, unravelling the spy ring. Source: FBI history 'Hollow Nickel / Rudolph Abel'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollow_Nickel_Case

question: Each side of the Cold War sent one prisoner walking across the Glienicke Bridge, between West Berlin and Potsdam, on 10 February 1962. Francis Gary Powers, the American U-2 pilot the Soviets had shot down, walked west. Who walked east?
answer: KGB colonel Rudolf Abel
choices: KGB colonel Rudolf Abel
Physicist Klaus Fuchs
Defector Reino Hayhanen
Courier Harry Gold
context: The exchange gave the Glienicke crossing its nickname, the 'Bridge of Spies.' Powers had been freed after the swap; Abel was the Soviet spy whose ring the hollow nickel had helped expose. Source: history.com 'Spies Swapped'; biography.com 'Rudolf Abel'

question: Francis Gary Powers carried a hollowed-out silver dollar the CIA had given him, with a tiny needle hidden inside, when the Soviets shot down his U-2 in May 1960. Powers never used it, and he was taken alive. What had the CIA put on that needle?
answer: A dose of deadly shellfish poison
choices: A dose of deadly shellfish poison
A microfilm of his orders
A miniature lock-pick
A radio homing beacon
context: The needle was tipped with saxitoxin, a poison drawn from Alaskan shellfish — a suicide weapon Powers refused to use. He was captured and later traded on the Glienicke Bridge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_U-2_incident; historynet.com 'CIA Poisoner in Chief'

question: Kim Philby climbed high in Britain's spy service, MI6, while working for the Soviets all along. In 1951 he learned that two Soviet agents he had been recruited with at Cambridge, Donald Maclean and Guy Burgess, were about to be arrested. What did Philby do that let them slip away to Moscow?
answer: He tipped them off to flee before arrest
choices: He tipped them off to flee before arrest
He forged their exit visas himself
He hid them inside the Soviet embassy
He bribed the officers tailing them
context: Warned by Philby, Maclean and Burgess fled to Moscow on May 25, 1951. Philby escaped prosecution, was publicly cleared in 1955, and finally defected to Moscow himself in 1963. They were part of the 'Cambridge Five.' Source: history.co.uk 'Who Were the Cambridge Five'; historyhit.com 'Facts About Kim Philby'

question: Julius Rosenberg went to his death in 1953, and his supporters insisted for decades afterwards that he had been framed as a spy. Then in 1995 the American government made public the Venona cables, Soviet wartime messages it had intercepted and decoded. What did they reveal about Julius Rosenberg?
answer: His Soviet codename, 'LIBERAL,' running a spy ring
choices: His Soviet codename, 'LIBERAL,' running a spy ring
A signed confession he had recanted
A Soviet payment ledger in his name
His fingerprints on stolen bomb plans
context: The Venona decrypts named Julius as 'LIBERAL' and documented the espionage ring he ran — confirming the spying was real, even as scholars still debate how much his wife Ethel was involved. Source: ahf.nuclearmuseum.org 'Rosenberg Trial'; commentary.org 'The Venona Men'

question: Dean Rusk and another young American colonel had about thirty minutes in August 1945 to split Korea, Japan's former colony, between the Soviets and the Americans. With no time to study, they grabbed the handiest thing in the room and chose the 38th parallel. What did they pull out to draw the line?
answer: A National Geographic map
choices: A National Geographic map
A captured Japanese battle plan
An old Russian railway chart
A British naval atlas
context: One of the colonels was Dean Rusk, a future U.S. Secretary of State. The 38th parallel was meant to be a temporary line just for accepting the Japanese surrender. (National Geographic, 'National Geographic, Korea, and the 38th Parallel'; NEH, 'Korea and the Thirty-Eighth Parallel')

question: North Korean troops stormed south across the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950, before first light, some 135,000 men in a surprise attack. A Soviet-built weapon led the assault, and the South had little that could stop it. What spearheaded the invasion?
answer: T-34 tanks
choices: T-34 tanks
Heavy siege cannons
Armored gunboats
Cavalry squadrons
context: The attack began at 4 a.m. The Soviet-built T-34 had been a war-winning tank for the USSR in World War II, and South Korea had almost nothing that could knock it out. (U.S. National Archives, 'US Enters the Korean Conflict'; U.S. Army, 'North Korea attacks across 38th parallel')

question: Syngman Rhee's South Korean army fell back for weeks after the North invaded in June 1950. By late summer it held only a corner of the peninsula around the port of Pusan, with the sea at its back. Which world body voted to send soldiers to defend South Korea?
answer: The United Nations
choices: The United Nations
The Warsaw Pact
The League of Nations
NATO
context: Holding the Pusan Perimeter kept the war alive until MacArthur's Inchon landing in September 1950 broke the siege from behind. (Military.com, 'Task Force Smith...Pusan Perimeter'; TheCollector, 'The American Defeat at Taejon That Saved South Korea')

question: Task Force Smith, the first American troops sent into battle in Korea, dug in at Osan in July 1950 with just 540 lightly armed men. A North Korean column of about 5,000 soldiers and 36 tanks struck them, and in the end the Americans were overrun. What had the 540 managed to do before they broke?

Knocked out every one of the 36 enemy tanks
Captured the North Korean column's commanding general
Forced the entire enemy column to turn back north
context: Task Force Smith took 181 casualties and was overrun, but its desperate seven-hour delaying action bought time that helped save the South. (Military.com, 'Task Force Smith: How the 24th Infantry Division Saved South Korea'; johnsmilitaryhistory.com)

question: Douglas MacArthur gambled in September 1950 on landing his troops at Inchon, far behind the enemy's lines, and his own planners thought it close to impossible. Their biggest worry lay in Inchon's harbor itself, a danger that could leave the whole fleet helpless. What was the danger?

Its drifting mines
Its blinding fog
Its hidden reefs
context: Inchon's tidal range was so huge that ships could only land during a few hours at high tide before being stranded in the mud. MacArthur gambled anyway, landed behind enemy lines, broke the war wide open, and lost only about 225 men killed. (Naval History Magazine, 'Operation Chromite: Target INCHON'; Britannica, 'Inchon landing')

question: Lewis 'Chesty' Puller, a Marine colonel, was holding his men at the frozen Chosin Reservoir in November 1950 when word came that the Chinese had closed in on every side. Puller did not panic, and his reply became famous among Marines. What did he say?

choices: 'We're surrounded. That simplifies the problem.'

'Hold the line at any cost.'
context: His full reply: 'We've been looking for the enemy for some time now. We've finally found him. We're surrounded. That simplifies the problem.' Surrounded, the Marines could attack the enemy in any direction. (19FortyFive, "'We're Surrounded. That Simplifies the Problem.'"; military-quotes.com)

question: Korean refugees crowded aboard the cargo ship SS Meredith Victory at the port of Hungnam in December 1950. She had been built to carry just 12 passengers. She reached safety after three days at sea with every soul aboard alive, and five babies were born on the way. How many refugees did she carry?

About 3,500
About 7,000
context: It set the Guinness record for the largest sea rescue ever by a single ship, earning the name 'Ship of Miracles.' (Korean War Memorial Foundation, 'SS Meredith Victory: The Ship of Miracles'; Washington Post, 'Korean War Christmas miracle')

question: Chinese armies closed around some 30,000 UN troops at the Chosin Reservoir on 27 November 1950, and most of the trapped men were Marines of the 1st Division. The cold sank to near 30 below zero; rifles jammed and blood plasma froze solid. How many Chinese soldiers had closed the ring?
answer: About 120,000

About 45,000
About 60,000
context: The survivors proudly call themselves 'The Frozen Chosin.' In the brutal cold the dead were stacked like cordwood. (Britannica, 'Battle of the Chosin Reservoir'; Bill of Rights Institute, 'The Korean War and the Battle of Chosin Reservoir')

question: Oliver P. Smith led his 1st Marine Division out from the Chosin Reservoir in the winter of 1950, fighting some 70 miles through the mountains to the sea. A reporter asked the general whether his Marines were retreating. Smith rejected the word with one defiant line. What did he snap back?

context: Smith's division then fought about 70 miles through the mountain passes to the sea at Hungnam. The line is often misquoted as 'advancing in a different direction.' (Wikipedia, 'Oliver P. Smith'; U.S. Marine Corps Museum, 'O.P. Smith – Savior of Chosin')

question: Commanders met at the village of Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 and signed the paper that stopped the shooting in Korea, after three years of war that had killed millions of people. Where did that signing leave North and South Korea?
answer: They are technically still at war, never having made peace

They reunited into a single country a few years afterward
They agreed the North would slowly absorb the South
context: What was signed at Panmunjom was only an armistice — a cease-fire — not a peace treaty, so the two Koreas remain officially at war, divided by the heavily-mined DMZ. (Britannica, 'Korean War – Armistice'; USFK, official Armistice Agreement text, Panmunjom, 1953)

question: Kim Il-sung ruled a communist North that still out-produced the South per head into the early 1970s, though the war had left both halves of Korea in ruins. question: Joseph Goebbels, the Nazi propaganda minister, directed stormtroopers and mobs against the Jews of Germany and annexed Austria through the night of 9 and 10 November 1938. They set fire to more than 1,400 synagogues. German firefighters came. What were their orders?
answer: Protect only the neighboring non-Jewish buildings
choices: Protect only the neighboring non-Jewish buildings
Protect the synagogues and arrest the arsonists
Protect the worshippers trapped inside the synagogues
Protect the fire crews from the rampaging mob
context: The firefighters stood by and let the synagogues burn to the ground; their orders were only to keep the flames from spreading to nearby 'Aryan' (non-Jewish) property. Around 7,500 Jewish-owned businesses were also smashed and looted that night. Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-night-of-broken-glass

question: Hermann Goring decided who would pay for the wreckage of Kristallnacht in November 1938. Jewish shopkeepers across Germany had seen their shops smashed and looted, and insurance companies owed them for the damage. Who did Goring's government force to pay for it all?
answer: The Jewish community, made to pay for all of it
choices: The Jewish community, made to pay for all of it
The insurance companies that owed the claims
The mobs and rioters who smashed the shops
The Nazi Party that had ordered the attack
context: The Nazis fined the entire Jewish community one billion Reichsmarks as an 'atonement payment' (Suhnezahlung) for the death of diplomat Ernst vom Rath, forced Jewish owners to pay for their own repairs, and confiscated the insurance money they were owed, handing it to the Reich. The victims were punished for the crime committed against them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristallnacht

question: Marco Polo told his readers that shoppers in Kublai Khan's China bought whatever they needed without handing over a single coin of gold or silver. Back home in Europe, people still lugged heavy metal coins about. What did the Chinese pay with instead?
answer: Paper money
choices: Paper money
Strings of shells
Carved jade tokens
Bars of salt
context: The Yuan paper note was called the chao, one of the first nationwide paper currencies in the world. Source: https://historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=243

question: At Xanadu, where he spent his summers, Kublai Khan kept a second palace of gilded cane and bamboo, held steady by over 200 silk cords and painted all over with beasts and birds. Marco Polo marvelled most at one thing that could be done with the whole building. What was it?

The entire palace slowly turned to follow the sun across the sky
The entire palace was burned and rebuilt fresh every single spring
context: The cane palace was braced against the wind by more than 200 silk cords and could be dismantled and moved at the Khan's command. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Xanadu/

question: Kublai Khan sorted the people he ruled into four classes before the law. Mongols stood at the top, and at the very bottom were the Southerners, Chinese from the old Song lands he had conquered. The two lowest classes were punished more harshly for the same crime. What else were they forbidden to do?

context: Under the Yuan four-class system, northern Han and Southerners could not own weapons or keep dogs or hunting eagles — an honest record of foreign rule ranking native Chinese lowest. Source: https://www.travelchinaguide.com/intro/history/yuan/four-class-system.htm

question: Frances Wood, a historian, argued that Marco Polo may never have set foot in China at all. His fellow Venetians had already mocked his book as Il Milione, The Million, for all its marvels. Wood pointed to famous Chinese things missing from its pages. Which three did Polo leave out?

context: Frances Wood ('Did Marco Polo Go to China?') notes Polo never mentions the Great Wall, tea, chopsticks, or foot-binding, and suggests he may have compiled his account from Persian guidebooks and other travelers. Source: https://www.asianstudies.org/publications/eaa/archives/debunking-the-myth-did-marco-polo-go-to-china/

question: Kublai Khan paid his suppliers and workmen in paper banknotes instead of gold or silver coins, Marco Polo reported. Every one of the Khan's notes, Polo said, was made from one material, taken from a single kind of tree. What was it?

question: Marco Polo described a cloth called salamander that would not burn. When it got dirty, its owners threw it into the fire, and it came out clean and white. Europeans took it for the hide of a lizard that lived in fire, but Polo reported something else. Where did he say the cloth really came from?

question: The last Song fighters went down before Kublai Khan's navy at Yamen in 1279, and all of China was his, the first time a foreigner had ruled the whole country. He had chosen his new dynasty's name in 1271: one word from China's ancient book of wisdom, the I Ching. What did that word, Yuan, mean?

Conqueror of the four seas

question: Six farm workers of Tolpuddle, a village in Dorset, formed a union in 1833 to seek better pay; legend says they gathered beneath a great sycamore on the green. The British government, which feared unions, struck back. What did it do to the six?

Court testimony shows the men's secret oath was actually sworn inside Thomas Standfield's cottage, not under the tree, but the sycamore became the movement's emblem. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolpuddle_Martyrs_Tree)  (Legend.)

question: George Loveless, a plowman and Methodist preacher, led five other Dorset farm laborers in forming a society in 1833 to stop the cuts to their pay. Farmers were pushing their wages down toward six shillings a week, so the men vowed to refuse any work paid below one exact figure. What weekly wage did they hold out for?

question: Prosecutors brought the six Tolpuddle laborers to trial in March 1834, but forming a union was not the charge against them. They reached instead for a 1797 law first written to punish mutinous sailors. Of what did the court convict the six men?

Burning a landlord's hay ricks

Marching armed on the county jail
context: In March 1834 the six men were sentenced to seven years' transportation to Australia — not for organizing, but for the secret oath of loyalty they had sworn, prosecuted under a 1797 law aimed at mutineers. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolpuddle_Martyrs)

question: James Brine, one of the six Tolpuddle men, was put to brutal labor after his conviction. He later remembered digging post-holes barefoot until his feet were too cut to press on the spade. question: William Lovett wrote out six demands for reforming Parliament in 1838, and they became the People's Charter. context: The Charter's six points became the program of the Chartist movement. Five eventually became law; only annual parliaments was never adopted. (newportrising.co.uk/sixpoints ; parliament.uk Chartists overview)

question: Feargus O'Connor, a Chartist leader, brought Parliament a petition in 1848 that he claimed carried 5,736,000 names. question: Richard Oastler, a Tory reformer, opened the fight for a ten-hour working day in 1830 with an angry letter to a Leeds newspaper. Small children working the Bradford mills, he charged, were treated worse than West Indian slaves. What title did Oastler give his letter?

'Bradford's Shame'
context: Oastler's 1830 'Yorkshire Slavery' letter launched the ten-hours movement; he himself became known as 'the Factory King.' The Ten Hours Act of 1847, steered by Lord Ashley and the mill-owner John Fielden, finally capped women and young workers at ten hours a day. (britannica.com/biography/Richard-Oastler)

question: Working men in Britain saw their real pay about double in the four decades from 1810, while their hours fell. According to those historians, what began to grow after 1830 that let pay catch up?

The harshness of the factory laws
The size of the protest marches
context: Historians call the early gap 'Engels' pause' — wages rose only ~12% from 1780-1840 while output per worker climbed 46%. The gap closed after 1830 as capital per worker grew, suggesting rising wages and shorter hours came chiefly from capital accumulation and productivity, not from agitation alone. (econlib.org Industrial Revolution and the Standard of Living ; nuff.ox.ac.uk Allen, engelspause.pdf)

question: King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela wanted a New Jerusalem for Ethiopia's Christians around 1200, when Muslim conquests made the road to the real one hard. His workmen gave him eleven churches in the northern highlands without laying one stone block on another. Each began as a single mass of volcanic bedrock. How did they turn the rock into a church?

They quarried the rock into bricks elsewhere and hauled them back to stack on the site
They tunneled sideways into a cliff face and propped the long hall up with stone pillars
context: Each church was carved DOWNWARD into living volcanic rock: chisel a deep trench all the way around a block, freeing it from the mountain, then hollow the freed block into a finished church roof-first, top to bottom. No stacking, no mortar — a whole church carved out of one piece of the ground, still in use for Ethiopian Orthodox worship ~800 years later. Source: metmuseum.org/essays/the-rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock-Hewn_Churches,_Lalibela.

question: The builders of King Lalibela cut the last of his eleven churches, Bete Giyorgis, named for Saint George, down into the ground from one enormous block of volcanic rock. A square keep
context: Bete Giyorgis ('House of St. George') is carved as a perfect Greek cross sunk into the earth, sitting in a courtyard roughly 72 by 72 feet and 36 feet deep — so from the rim it looks like a giant cross cut into the ground, its roof carved with a pattern of nested crosses, all from the one solid block. It was the last of the eleven built. Source: biblicalarchaeology.org/daily/ancient-cultures/ancient-near-eastern-world/rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela/.

question: Unarmed friars led by Bartolomé de las Casas walked into a region of Guatemala that soldiers called Tuzulutlán, the Land of War, to prove that preaching alone, with no soldiers at all, could win Native peoples over. question: Cisneros, the cardinal who ruled Spain as regent, gave Bartolome de las Casas a brand-new royal office in 1516, with a salary of 100 pesos a year, which gave his campaign for Native peoples official standing. What was the title of the office?

Decades later, as Bishop of Chiapas in 1545, he refused absolution to colonists who would not free their slaves; they fired shots at him and he left, never to return. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomé_de_las_Casas

question: Antonio de Montesinos, a Dominican friar, climbed into the pulpit on Hispaniola one Sunday in Advent 1511 and told the stunned Spanish settlers that their cruelty to the Taíno had put them in mortal sin. Then he hit them with one burning question about the people they were working to death. What did he thunder at them?

He refused, and the sermon helped set the young Las Casas on the path that defined his life. Source: summitdominicans.org, '500th Anniversary of the Sermon of Friar Montesinos'

question: Hatuey, a Taíno chief, had led the resistance against the Spanish in Cuba, and in 1512 they condemned him to be burned at the stake. As the fire was readied, a friar offered him heaven if he would first be baptized. Hatuey asked whether Spaniards went to heaven too. context: By Las Casas's account, Hatuey chose hell over an eternity beside the Spaniards. He became Cuba's first national hero. This comes down to us as Las Casas's recorded testimony rather than a verified transcript, so it is remembered as legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatuey

question: A single line of Scripture struck Bartolomé de las Casas in 1514 as he prepared a sermon, while he still held Native laborers himself, and it changed his life: he gave up his laborers for good. context: The line was from Sirach 34: an offering 'from what has been wrongfully obtained' is blemished, for 'the bread of the needy is the life of the poor.' Las Casas read it as God Himself condemning the encomienda, gave up his own laborers, and never turned back. Source: uscatholic.org, 'The conversion of Bartolomé de las Casas'

question: Early in his crusade, Bartolomé de las Casas made one suggestion he would spend the rest of his life regretting. That he condemned his own worst idea in writing is part of why historians read him as honest rather than self-serving. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomé_de_las_Casas (Historia de las Indias, Vol. II)

question: To shock Prince Philip, Bartolomé de las Casas set down the horrors he had witnessed in 'A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies' in 1552. context: Las Casas recorded that they hanged the Taíno thirteen at a time — 'in honour and reverence (as they said blasphemously) of our Redeemer and his Twelve Apostles' — then lit fires beneath them. Dressing mass murder in the language of devotion was, to Las Casas, the deepest horror of all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Short_Account_of_the_Destruction_of_the_Indies

question: Charles V called a public hearing at Valladolid in 1550, the first time in European history that an assembly met to judge whether a conquered people had any rights at all. Oddly, the two men never argued face to face — they addressed the judges in separate sessions. The Dominican Domingo de Soto wrote a neutral summary, and the panel deliberated privately but never issued a verdict, so both sides claimed they had won. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valladolid_debate

question: Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda laid out his case for conquering the Native Americans in a book called 'Democrates Alter,' arguing that they were natural slaves, born to be ruled, and that conquering them was therefore just. Las Casas's reply was that even if a few simple people fit Aristotle's 'natural slave,' such people existed in Spain too, so it could never justify enslaving whole nations — and Domingo de Soto, summarizing, sided against the natural-slavery doctrine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Ginés_de_Sepúlveda

question: Marcel Ravidat, eighteen, was the first of four teenage boys to squeeze into a hole beneath a fallen tree in southwestern France on 12 September 1940. Below lay Lascaux, a cave whose painted animals were some 17,000 years old. What led the boys there?

question: Maria Sanz de Sautuola, eight years old, looked up at the roof of the Altamira cave in Spain in 1879 and saw a herd of painted bison. A local painter confessed to sketching them for money
The pigments smelled of fresh oil paint still drying
context: Sautuola's eight-year-old daughter María, small enough to look straight up, first spotted the bison overhead in 1879. Scholars ridiculed him at the 1880 Lisbon Prehistoric Congress — the work was simply too good to be 'primitive,' and Sautuola couldn't explain the lack of soot on the walls. He died in 1888 still disbelieved; in 1902 his loudest doubter, Emile Cartailhac, publicly confessed his error. The ceiling is now called the 'Sistine Chapel of Paleolithic Art.' Source: en.wikipedia.org, Cave of Altamira; britannica.com.

question: Enrico Dandolo, the blind old Doge of Venice, shipped one prize home after the Fourth Crusade's knights looted a great Christian city in April 1204. It was life-size, cast in gilded bronze and torn from the city's Hippodrome, and the Venetians set it up over the door of St Mark's Basilica. What was it?
answer: A team of four bronze horses
choices: A team of four bronze horses
A pair of bronze temple doors
A golden bronze sun-disc
A bronze statue of an emperor
context: The Horses of Saint Mark are the only surviving four-horse chariot team (quadriga) in bronze from the ancient world. Crusaders looted them from the Hippodrome, Constantinople's chariot-racing stadium, in 1204. To ship them, workers severed the heads -- then hid the cuts by fastening collars around the horses' necks, collars you can still see. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horses_of_Saint_Mark

question: Knights of the Fourth Crusade boarded Venetian ships meaning to strike Muslim-held Egypt first and then win back Jerusalem, and they owed Venice a fortune for the fleet. Not one Muslim army ever met them in battle. In April 1204 they stormed the largest and wealthiest Christian city on earth instead, and looted and killed for three days. Which city was it?
answer: Constantinople
choices: Constantinople
Jerusalem
Antioch
Alexandria
context: Constantinople, capital of the Christian Byzantine Empire, fell to fellow Christians on April 12-15, 1204. The Crusaders then crowned one of their own, Baldwin of Flanders, as emperor rather than restoring a Byzantine ruler. Pope John Paul II formally apologized for the sack 800 years later, in 2004. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Constantinople_(1204)

question: Simon Bolivar fought the Spanish across South America in the early 1800s, and his wars made new nations of Bolivia, which took his name, and of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Panama. The people he had fought for gave him one sweeping title, and he carried it to his grave. What was it?
answer: The Liberator
choices: The Liberator
The Conqueror
The Protector
The Emperor
context: Bolivar earned the title 'the Liberator' for leading the fight that freed six future nations from Spanish rule: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Panama, and Bolivia. Bolivia is named after him. https://www.britannica.com/event/Guayaquil-Conference

question: Jose de San Martin led his Army of the Andes some 500 kilometres across icy mountain passes in 1817 to take the Spanish in Chile by surprise. Historians compare the march to one ancient general's famous crossing. Which crossing is it compared to?
answer: Hannibal crossing the Alps
choices: Hannibal crossing the Alps
Caesar crossing the Rubicon
Xerxes bridging the Hellespont
Alexander crossing the Hydaspes
context: San Martin's Army of the Andes departed the El Plumerillo camp near Mendoza on January 19, 1817 and entered Santiago on February 13 -- a 21-day crossing at elevations averaging 3,000 meters, compared to Hannibal's Alpine march. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_of_the_Andes

question: San Martin's soldiers hauled their cannon and stores over the high passes of the Andes in 1817 to strike the Spanish in Chile. For the heavy work he relied on one kind of pack animal, about 9,000 of them, far outnumbering his 1,600 horses. Which animal carried the army over?
answer: Mules
choices: Mules
Camels
Oxen
Elephants
context: The crossing needed roughly 9,000 mules, about 1,600 horses, and hundreds of cattle; the army even learned to cast its own cannons. Roughly a third of the 4,000 soldiers were lost on the crossing. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Andes

question: Simon Bolivar led about 2,400 men in 1819 through flooded lowlands and over a frozen pass that the royalists thought no army could cross. On 7 August he fell on the royalist army and destroyed it, capturing some 1,800 men, their commander too, and he entered Bogota three days afterwards. What was the decisive battle?
answer: The Battle of Boyaca
choices: The Battle of Boyaca
The Battle of Carabobo
The Battle of Ayacucho
The Battle of Junin
context: After crossing the Paramo de Pisba, Bolivar's victory at Boyaca captured about 1,800 prisoners including the Spanish commander; three days later he marched into Bogota and was hailed as the Liberator of New Granada. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Boyac%C3%A1

question: Alone, with no witness present and nothing written down, Simon Bolivar and Jose de San Martin met in secret at Guayaquil in July 1822. They quarrelled over what kind of government the new nations should have. Bolivar wanted republics like the United States. What did San Martin want?
answer: Constitutional monarchies under a European prince
choices: Constitutional monarchies under a European prince
Direct democracies run by town assemblies
A single empire ruled by Bolivar
Military councils of the liberating generals
context: San Martin even proposed bringing a European prince to be King of Peru. Soon after the secret Guayaquil Conference of July 26-27, 1822 -- held with no witnesses and a vow that no record be kept -- San Martin quietly handed everything over to Bolivar and left South America for good. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guayaquil_Conference

question: Simon Bolivar dreamed of one great state, Gran Colombia, and region after region broke away from it. Weeks before tuberculosis killed him in December 1830, he wrote in bitterness that America could not be governed. What famous line did he add about his life's work?
answer: 'He who serves a revolution is plowing the sea'
choices: 'He who serves a revolution is plowing the sea'
'I die without seeing the dawn I fought for'
'A king's crown was always within my reach'
'The mountains alone were honest with me'
context: Weeks before his death on December 17, 1830, the disillusioned Bolivar wrote that 'America is ungovernable' and that 'he who serves a revolution is plowing the sea.' https://www.history.com/articles/simon-bolivar-liberator-south-america-venezuela

question: Antoine Lavoisier set out to test the top theory of his day: phlogiston, an unseen 'fire-stuff' said to escape from anything as it burned. If that were true, a burned thing should end up lighter. Lavoisier sealed a metal in a vessel, weighed it, burned it, and weighed it again. What did his balance show happened to the metal's weight?
answer: It weighed more than before it burned.
choices: It weighed more than before it burned.
It weighed less than before it burned.
It weighed the same as before it burned.
It weighed almost nothing after it burned.
context: The metal GAINED weight because burning is the metal combining with oxygen from the air, not losing a fire-stuff. That weight increase was the death blow to phlogiston theory and helped Lavoisier establish that in a chemical change matter is neither created nor destroyed. Source: https://study.com/academy/lesson/antoine-lavoisier-atomic-theory-contribution.html

question: Joseph-Louis Lagrange, the mathematician, mourned Antoine Lavoisier in one line on the day after the guillotine took him. The revolutionary tribunal had sent Lavoisier to the blade on 8 May 1794, in the Reign of Terror, for once collecting the king's taxes, though he had brought the balance into chemistry. What did Lagrange say?
answer: It took them only an instant to cut off that head, but a hundred years may not produce another like it.
choices: It took them only an instant to cut off that head, but a hundred years may not produce another like it.
France has murdered her finest mind today, and history itself will never forgive this blade.
They have silenced the one balance that weighed the whole world; let no man call this justice.
A nation that beheads its own scholars has surely signed the warrant for its own ruin.
context: Lagrange's actual words: 'It took them only an instant to cut off that head, and a hundred years may not suffice to reproduce its like' ('Il ne leur a fallu qu'un moment pour faire tomber cette tête, et cent années peut-être ne suffiront pas pour en reproduire une semblable'). Lavoisier was 50; his father-in-law Jacques Paulze went to the same blade just ahead of him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Lavoisier

question: T. E. Lawrence and Auda abu Tayi, a chieftain of the Howeitat, took the Red Sea port of Aqaba from the Ottoman Turks in July 1917. The port's big guns all pointed out to sea, ready to blast any ship that came near. How did the two men beat those guns?
answer: They crossed hundreds of miles of open desert and stormed the port from its undefended landward side
choices: They crossed hundreds of miles of open desert and stormed the port from its undefended landward side
They smuggled men aboard fishing boats and seized the harbor guns at dawn
They shelled the fortress from warships until the garrison ran out of water
They tunneled beneath the walls and blew open the seaward gate with mines
context: The march began on 9 May 1917 with about 45 Howeitat and Ageyl camel men and swelled to roughly 1,000 as desert tribes joined; Aqaba surrendered on 6 July 1917. The decisive fight was inland at Aba el Lissan, where Auda's charge wiped out the Ottoman force for the loss of only two Arab dead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Aqaba ; smithsonianmag.com/history/true-story-lawrence-arabia-180951857

question: Hussein bin Ali, Sharif of Mecca, raised the Arabs against the Ottoman Turks in June 1916, trusting Britain's promise of an independent Arab kingdom once the war was won, and T. E. Lawrence fought at their side. Britain's Mark Sykes and France's Francois Georges-Picot had already drawn up a secret agreement that May. What did their deal do to the lands the Arabs were fighting to free?
answer: It divided the Ottoman Arab lands between Britain and France as their own spheres
choices: It divided the Ottoman Arab lands between Britain and France as their own spheres
It promised the same territory twice over to both the Arabs and the Russians
It handed every Ottoman province to a new League of Nations to govern jointly
It pledged the entire region to a single independent Arab kingdom under Hussein
context: The Arabs only learned of the carve-up when the new Soviet government published the secret text in late 1917. The lines drawn by Mark Sykes and Francois Georges-Picot helped seed the borders and grievances of the modern Middle East, contradicting the independence promised in the McMahon-Hussein letters. Source: britannica.com/event/Sykes-Picot-Agreement ; theconversation.com/what-was-the-sykes-picot-agreement-246332

question: Georges Lemaitre worked out from Einstein's own equations in 1927 that the whole universe is expanding. At a conference in Brussels that year he met Albert Einstein and explained the idea. Einstein agreed that the mathematics was correct. What did he say about the physics?
answer: That his physics was 'abominable.'
choices: That his physics was 'abominable.'
That his physics was 'preposterous.'
That his physics was 'unconvincing.'
That his physics was 'muddled.'
context: Einstein's full reply in 1927 was 'Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable' (French: 'Vos calculs sont corrects, mais votre physique est abominable'). He came around: in 1933, after hearing Lemaitre present the theory in California, Einstein stood up and applauded, calling it 'the most beautiful and satisfactory explanation of creation to which I have ever listened.' The father of the Big Bang was a priest. Sources: catholiceducation.org 'A Day Without Yesterday'; bigthink.com/13-8/lemaitre-priest-proved-einstein-wrong.

question: Pope Pius XII announced in 1951 that the new Big Bang theory seemed to prove the creation story in the book of Genesis. The theory's first author, Georges Lemaitre, was himself a Catholic priest. What did Lemaitre do about the Pope's announcement?
answer: He quietly persuaded the Pope to drop the claim.
choices: He quietly persuaded the Pope to drop the claim.
He publicly thanked the Pope for his support.
He pushed the Pope to make it Church doctrine.
He resigned his priesthood in open protest.
context: Lemaitre, the priest, argued that a scientific theory must never be used to prove -- or disprove -- a matter of faith, and he privately convinced Pius XII to stop making the claim. He had imagined the universe beginning as a single super-dense 'primeval atom' that shattered and expanded; shortly before he died in 1966 he learned that Penzias and Wilson had detected the cosmic microwave background, the leftover glow that confirmed his idea. Sources: inters.org/pius-xii-lemaitre; vaticanobservatory.org 'Priests in Science: Georges Lemaitre.'

question: Prisoners began arriving in 1923 at the first big camp of the Soviet secret police, an old monastery on the freezing Solovetsky Islands. Its name in Russian, the Solovki Special Purpose Camps (SLON), shrank to four initials. What animal does SLON name in everyday Russian?
answer: An elephant
choices: An elephant
A bear
A wolf
A fox
context: SLON stood for the Solovetsky Camp of Special Purpose, built inside an ancient Russian Orthodox monastery on the Solovetsky Islands; the acronym just happens to spell the Russian word for 'elephant.' Source: Anne Applebaum, Gulag: A History (erenow.org/modern/gulagahistoryanneapplebaum/4.php).

question: Vladimir Lenin founded a political police force in December 1917, six weeks after the Bolsheviks seized power, and put Felix Dzerzhinsky at its head. The KGB and the other later Soviet secret police grew from it. What was Lenin's force called?
answer: The Cheka
choices: The Cheka
The Gestapo
The Praetorian Guard
The Inquisition
context: The Cheka's full name was the All-Russian Extraordinary Commission for Combating Counter-Revolution and Sabotage; 'Iron Felix' Dzerzhinsky headed it from the Lubyanka. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheka.

question: Fanny Kaplan waited outside a Moscow factory late in August 1918 and shot Vladimir Lenin as he came out. She was no supporter of the old Tsar; she belonged to the Socialist Revolutionaries, a rival socialist party. When Lenin's secret police asked her why she had done it, what did she tell them?
answer: I shot Lenin because I consider him a traitor to the Revolution
choices: I shot Lenin because I consider him a traitor to the Revolution
I shot Lenin because he made a shameful peace with the Germans
I shot Lenin to avenge the murdered Tsar and his children
I shot Lenin on the orders of the British and their spies
context: Fanny Kaplan was a Socialist Revolutionary; she told interrogators 'I shot Lenin... I consider him a traitor to the Revolution' and was executed days later. The same day, Petrograd's Cheka chief Moisei Uritsky was assassinated. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Terror.

question: Felix Dzerzhinsky ran the political police Lenin had built to hunt down 'enemies of the revolution.' A Moscow newspaper asked him in July 1918 what his force was really for. How did he answer?
answer: We stand for organized terror -- it is absolutely necessary in revolution
choices: We stand for organized terror -- it is absolutely necessary in revolution
We act only on solid proof and only against the truly guilty
We guard the people against ordinary criminals and foreign spies
We serve as the sword and shield of the honest workers' state
context: In an interview in Novaya Zhizn (14 July 1918) Dzerzhinsky said: 'We stand for organized terror -- this should be frankly admitted. Terror is an absolute necessity during times of revolution.' Source: spartacus-educational.com/RUSterror.htm.

question: The commander of the Solovki camp stood on the shore to meet each boatload of new prisoners stumbling onto the islands of the icy White Sea. He greeted them with one chilling sentence, meant to strip away every right they thought they still had. What did he tell them?
answer: Here there is no Soviet power -- only Solovetsky power
choices: Here there is no Soviet power -- only Solovetsky power
Here the law of the old Tsar no longer protects you
Here you will work hard and one day return to your home
Here every man stands equal before the revolution
context: The camp was Solovki; the greeting -- that even Soviet law did not reach here, only the camp's own authority -- became its grim motto. Source: Anne Applebaum, Gulag: A History (erenow.org/modern/gulagahistoryanneapplebaum/4.php).

question: Guards at the Solovki camp sent prisoners for the harshest punishment up 365 wooden steps to Sekirka, an old hilltop church. Survivors remembered one torment above all, and the guards made prisoners endure it for as long as 18 hours at a stretch. What did the guards make them do?
answer: Sit dead still on a thin pole with their feet off the floor
choices: Sit dead still on a thin pole with their feet off the floor
Stand at rigid attention facing a bare stone wall
Kneel on the freezing stone with both arms held up
Lie face-down and motionless on the cold church floor
context: At Sekirka prisoners were also left tied and stripped in unheated bell towers in the Arctic winter, and some were thrown down the 365 steps as staged 'accidents.' Source: Anne Applebaum, Gulag: A History (erenow.org/modern/gulagahistoryanneapplebaum/4.php).

question: Bolshevik soldiers dragged the beaten Metropolitan Vladimir of Kiev out of the Monastery of the Caves on 25 January 1918 to shoot him, the first bishop they killed. As they marched him off, he did something people would tell of ever after. What did he do?
answer: Prayed for his killers to be forgiven
choices: Prayed for his killers to be forgiven
Called down God's judgment upon them
Sang a psalm as they dragged him out
Shouted out the names of his killers
context: Vladimir was beaten and shot on 25 January 1918, praying for his killers to be forgiven before he died. Between mid-1918 and early 1919, Bolshevik forces killed 1 metropolitan, 18 bishops, and over 100 priests. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-religious_campaign_during_the_Russian_Civil_War_(1917-1921).

question: Officials in Penza received a telegram from Vladimir Lenin in August 1918. They were to hang no fewer than one hundred kulaks, as the better-off peasants were called, where everyone could watch, 'so that the people might see and tremble,' and to publish the names. Then Lenin added a postscript. What did it say?
answer: Find some tougher people
choices: Find some tougher people
Spare the women and the children
Send me word when it is done
Burn their farms to the ground
context: Lenin's order said to hang 'no fewer than one hundred known kulaks, fatcats, bloodsuckers' in full view 'so that for hundreds of miles around the people might see and tremble,' and closed: 'Yours, Lenin. P.S. Find some tougher people.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenin's_hanging_order (U.S. Library of Congress translation).

question: Lenin's secret police agents received their orders on 5 September 1918 in a government decree called 'On Red Terror.' It called for mass shooting, and it spelled out in plain words what must be done with 'class enemies' to protect the republic. What did the decree order?
answer: Isolate them in concentration camps
choices: Isolate them in concentration camps
Deport them to the Siberian prison colonies
Confine them in old fortress dungeons
Hold them in the army's stockades
context: The decree prescribed 'mass shooting' and ordered the Cheka to secure the republic 'by isolating them in concentration camps' -- the document names the camps, proving the system began under Lenin in 1918, not Stalin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Terror.

question: Mikhail Tukhachevsky led the Red Army into Tambov province in 1921 to crush a peasant revolt against the Bolshevik grain seizures that were emptying the villages' barns. The rebels had taken to the deep forests. What weapon was Tukhachevsky cleared to use on his own countrymen there?
