answer: Poison gas, to seep through the trees
choices: Poison gas, to seep through the trees
Heavy artillery, to flatten the whole forest
Burning oil, to set the forest alight
Cavalry sweeps, to ride down the hidden men
context: The 12 June 1921 order said the gas 'must be carefully calculated, so that the layer of gas penetrates the forests and kills everyone hiding there.' To break the revolt the Bolsheviks also interned 50,000-100,000 villagers, including about 1,000 children, as hostages. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambov_Rebellion.

question: Martin Latsis, a senior official of Lenin's secret police, told his agents in 1918 how to decide a prisoner's fate. They were not to look for proof of anything the man had done. One question about him, Latsis said, mattered more than any deed, and its answer alone should decide whether he lived or died. What was that question?
answer: What social class do you come from?
choices: What social class do you come from?
What is it you are accused of doing?
Who was it that gave you your orders?
Where were you on the night in question?
context: Latsis published in the newspaper Krasny Terror: do not look for evidence the accused acted against the Soviets -- 'The first question you should ask him is what class he belongs to... These questions should determine his fate.' Guilt was decided by birth, not by any deed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Latsis.

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn followed the Soviet labour camps, the Gulag, back to their beginnings in his history The Gulag Archipelago, and he argued that Stalin had only made the system bigger. What did Solzhenitsyn point to as the real origin of the Gulag?
answer: Lenin's decrees from the revolution's first months
choices: Lenin's decrees from the revolution's first months
The old Tsar's Siberian exile system
The chaos of the Civil War years
Local Cheka bosses acting on their own
context: Solzhenitsyn traced the camp system 'from Lenin's decrees' onward and titled his chapter on how the camps filled up 'The History of Our Sewage Disposal System' -- arguing the Gulag was a core feature of the Soviet state from its birth, which Stalin merely scaled up. Source: voegelinview.com/judging-communism-works-solzhenitsyns-gulag-archipelago-reconsidered.

question: Pope Julius II wanted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel painted, and around 1508 he gave the job to Michelangelo. Michelangelo did not want it; he had not painted a fresco, and painting, he said, was not his trade. What did he insist he was?
answer: a sculptor
choices: a sculptor
an architect
a poet
a soldier
context: Michelangelo told the Pope that painting 'is not my art' and wrote to his father that it 'is not my profession.' He took the four-year job reluctantly, having never painted a fresco before. (National Catholic Reporter)

question: Michelangelo carved his David from a single tall block of Carrara marble that had lain unused for some 35 years. Two earlier sculptors had cut into it and walked away. Why had they given up on it?
answer: they judged it too flawed to carve
choices: they judged it too flawed to carve
they ran out of money to buy it
the cathedral told them to stop
they were called away to other work
context: From a single ~17-foot, 8.5-ton block that others had rejected as ruined, Michelangelo carved the David. He began on September 13, 1501 and finished in 1504. (Wikipedia: David)

question: Vincenzo Peruggia knew the Louvre well; he had worked on the glass case that protected the Mona Lisa. In 1911 he hid inside the museum overnight and lifted the painting off the wall on a Monday, when the Louvre was closed. How did he carry it out the door?
answer: wrapped in his white worker's smock
choices: wrapped in his white worker's smock
hidden inside a hollowed-out book
rolled up within a long umbrella
stuffed into a large violin case
context: Peruggia hid in the Louvre overnight, took the painting on a Monday when it was closed, wrapped it in his smock, and walked out. The theft -- not just the smile -- is what made the Mona Lisa the most famous painting in the world. (Wikipedia: Vincenzo Peruggia)

question: All his life Leonardo da Vinci longed for people to fly. He filled a notebook in 1505 with studies of how birds and bats stay in the air, and sketched hundreds of flying machines with flapping wings modelled on theirs. What were those machines called?
answer: ornithopters
choices: ornithopters
gliders
zeppelins
biplanes
context: Across his life Leonardo made an estimated 500 sketches and 35,000 words on flight. He never built a working ornithopter, but modern engineers have tested some of his designs. (V&A: Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks)

question: Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, received a letter from the young Leonardo da Vinci, who wanted work. Page after page boasted of what Leonardo could build: portable bridges, cannons, war machines and secret tunnels. Where in the letter did he say he could paint as well?
answer: at the very end, as an afterthought
choices: at the very end, as an afterthought
in the very first line, most proudly
in the middle, between two cannons
right under the bridge designs, boldly
context: Leonardo sold himself to the duke almost entirely as a military engineer, slipping in only at the very end -- almost as an afterthought -- that he could also paint and sculpt. (Britannica: Leonardo da Vinci)

question: Working by candlelight, Leonardo da Vinci cut open about thirty dead bodies so that he could paint the human body perfectly, a task most people of his time found horrifying. From that work came the first true drawing of one subject. What was it?
answer: a baby curled up inside the womb
choices: a baby curled up inside the womb
the muscles of a human arm
the bones inside a human foot
the veins running up the neck
context: Leonardo's corpses included a man he said was over 100, a 2-year-old, and a 4-month-old fetus. He also correctly described the heart as a four-chambered muscle, centuries ahead of his time. (nicofranz.art: Leonardo's anatomical studies)

question: Rather than paint a true fresco into wet plaster, Leonardo da Vinci laid an untested mix of paints on the dry plaster of the Last Supper. Decay set in by 1517, within twenty years of the finished work. About how much of his original paint survives today?
answer: fewer than half
choices: fewer than half
almost all of it
around three-quarters
barely a tenth
context: Decay was noted by 1517, and today only roughly 42-50% of Leonardo's original paint survives. He gambled on a new technique for richer detail and lost. (Britannica: Last Supper)

question: A British bomb struck the building in Milan that held Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper during a night raid on 15 August 1943, landing about 80 feet from the painting. The roof and two of the walls came down. What happened to the wall that carried the painting?
answer: it survived, shielded by sandbags piled there beforehand
choices: it survived, shielded by sandbags piled there beforehand
it crumbled into the rubble along with the rest
it stood, but the paint was scraped off just in time
it caught fire and the painting was badly scorched
context: Staff had protected the wall in advance with sandbags and scaffolding. When everything around it fell, that one wall stood -- and many called it a miracle. (Aleteia: How the Last Supper survived WWII)

question: Giorgio Vasari told how the young Michelangelo overheard visitors give the credit for his Pieta of Mary holding the dead Jesus to a rival. In a rage, by Vasari's account, he cut his own name into the marble. Ashamed of that outburst afterward, what did he vow?
answer: never to sign another work again
choices: never to sign another work again
never to carve in marble again
never to show his work in public
never to speak the rival's name
context: He had cut MICHAELANGELVS BONAROTVS FLORENTINVS FACIEBAT ('Michelangelo Buonarroti, the Florentine, made this') into the band. True to the vow, the Pietà -- finished in 1499, when he was just 24 -- is the only work he ever signed. (Wikipedia: Pietà)  (Legend.)

question: Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo could not stand each other, and around 1504 Florence hired both of them to cover walls of the Palazzo Vecchio with huge battle scenes: Leonardo the Battle of Anghiari, Michelangelo the Battle of Cascina. The city had set the two rivals against each other. How did the contest end?
answer: neither mural was ever finished
choices: neither mural was ever finished
Leonardo's mural clearly won out
Michelangelo refused and walked off
both murals still hang there today
context: Leonardo (born 1452) was about 23 years older than Michelangelo (born 1475). Leonardo's 'Battle of Anghiari' and Michelangelo's 'Battle of Cascina' were both abandoned, and neither was ever completed. (Artnet: Why did Leonardo and Michelangelo have beef?)

question: Leonardo da Vinci filled notebook after notebook, and more than 7,000 of their pages survive. He was left-handed, and the handwriting in them looked like nobody else's. What was odd about the way he wrote?
answer: He wrote backwards, every letter flipped as in a mirror
choices: He wrote backwards, every letter flipped as in a mirror
He wrote in a private code of numbers and symbols
He wrote in an alphabet he invented himself
He wrote in an old scholarly Latin shorthand
context: Leonardo's notebooks are written right-to-left with every letter reversed, readable only by holding the page up to a mirror. Being left-handed, pulling the pen leftward kept his hand from smudging the wet ink. Source: https://news.artnet.com/art-world/art-bites-leonardo-mirror-writing-2473530

question: The twelve apostles in Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, painted around 1495 on a monastery wall in Milan, burst into shock and argument. Painters before him had shown the apostles seated calmly at the table. Leonardo froze the instant just after Jesus spoke. What had Jesus said?
answer: "One of you will betray me"
choices: "One of you will betray me"
"This is my body, broken for you"
"Tonight you will all abandon me"
"Let the one without sin speak"
context: Leonardo's Last Supper captures the instant just after Jesus says one of them will betray him, with each apostle recoiling or arguing in shock, a sharp break from earlier calm, formal versions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Supper_(Leonardo)

question: Vincenzo Peruggia walked out of the Louvre in 1911 with Leonardo da Vinci's smiling Florentine lady and hid her for more than two years. Until then the picture had been one more painting in the museum's halls. What did the theft end up doing for it?
answer: It made the Mona Lisa the most famous painting in the world
choices: It made the Mona Lisa the most famous painting in the world
It forced the Louvre to close its doors for good
It convinced France to lock all art behind glass
It started a shooting war between France and Italy
context: Peruggia stole the Mona Lisa on 21 August 1911 and was caught in 1913 trying to sell it in Florence. The worldwide newspaper frenzy over the theft is largely what turned it into the most famous painting on Earth. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/how-did-vincenzo-peruggia-steal-the-mona-lisa/

question: A tourist worked her way through the crowd at the Louvre in Paris and stood at last before Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa. His Last Supper, back in Milan, filled a wall about 15 feet high and 29 feet wide. Like many visitors, she got a shock. What surprised her about the Mona Lisa?
answer: It is surprisingly tiny, smaller than a poster
choices: It is surprisingly tiny, smaller than a poster
It is painted on a sheet of solid gold
It is actually two paintings layered together
It is far larger and bolder than photos show
context: The Mona Lisa is a poplar panel only about 30 by 21 inches (77 x 53 cm), while the Last Supper covers most of a dining-hall wall at roughly 460 x 880 cm. Many visitors expect the world's most famous painting to be huge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Supper_(Leonardo)

question: To paint the Mona Lisa's face, Leonardo da Vinci softened every edge until no hard line remained anywhere, and her expression seemed to shift as people looked at her. The method's name, sfumato, comes from a shorter Italian word, fumo. What does fumo mean?
answer: Smoke
choices: Smoke
Shadow
Silk
Mist
context: Sfumato comes from the Italian fumo, meaning smoke. Leonardo described it as blending colors 'without lines or borders, in the manner of smoke,' which is what makes the Mona Lisa's smile seem to shimmer. Source: https://www.jerrypoon.com/post/sfumato-leonardo-da-vinci-painting-technique-1

question: Judas sat apart in shadow in Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, leaning back from the other apostles and gripping something tight in one hand. He was the apostle who would hand Jesus over before the night was out. What did Leonardo put in his hand?
answer: A small bag of silver coins
choices: A small bag of silver coins
A knife hidden against his side
A scrap of bread he won't share
A wine cup he has just spilled
context: Judas is the only apostle shown holding a small money bag, the payment he took to betray Jesus, and Leonardo sets him apart by leaning him back from the others. Source: https://www.italian-renaissance-art.com/Last-Supper.html

question: Sketching in the 1490s, Leonardo da Vinci drew a machine with a giant spiral meant to corkscrew its way straight up through the air, the way a screw bites into wood. A real flying machine later rose on much the same idea. What invention did his 'aerial screw' foreshadow?
answer: The helicopter
choices: The helicopter
The hot-air balloon
The glider plane
The rocket
context: Leonardo's 'aerial screw' was a spiral designed to lift straight up through the air, sketched roughly 450 years before working helicopters, whose rotors spin much the same way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo's_aerial_screw

question: Working slowly and changing his mind as he went, Leonardo da Vinci would not paint the Last Supper as a true fresco, with its colour laid into wet plaster. He put tempera and oil paint on the dry wall of the monks' dining hall instead. What did that choice cost him?
answer: The paint began flaking off within his own lifetime
choices: The paint began flaking off within his own lifetime
The colors turned black after a single winter
The wall cracked in half during an earthquake
The monks painted over it within a few years
context: Because Leonardo used tempera and oil on a dry wall instead of true fresco, the paint never bonded and began peeling within about two decades, while he was still alive, with deterioration noted by 1517. Source: https://www.walksofitaly.com/blog/art-culture/facts-about-da-vincis-last-supper

question: The monks of the monastery in Milan did something drastic in 1652 at the bottom of Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, already fading on their dining-hall wall. What did they do?
answer: They cut a doorway through it, erasing Jesus' feet
choices: They cut a doorway through it, erasing Jesus' feet
They whitewashed the lower half of the scene
They hung a heavy tapestry over the bottom
They scrubbed the wall down to bare stone
context: In 1652 the monks cut a doorway straight through the bottom of the Last Supper wall, destroying the painted feet of Jesus, simply to reach the kitchen faster. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Supper_(Leonardo)

question: Dissecting some 30 corpses, Leonardo da Vinci drew the heart so precisely that he worked out how small whirls in the blood help close one of its valves. Scientists confirmed he was right only in the late 1960s. How long had his discovery waited?
answer: About 450 years
choices: About 450 years
About 50 years
About 150 years
About 1,000 years
context: Leonardo correctly worked out that small blood-vortices help close the aortic valve, a mechanism modern science did not confirm until the late 1960s, roughly 450 years after he drew it. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3361109/

question: Leonardo da Vinci wrote nearly all his private notebooks backward. Every letter was flipped and the lines ran the wrong way. People have made up secret-code stories, but historians agree on a much simpler reason. What is the most widely accepted reason he wrote this way?
answer: He was left-handed, and writing backward kept his hand from smudging the wet ink.
choices: He was left-handed, and writing backward kept his hand from smudging the wet ink.
He was hiding his discoveries in code from rival inventors who might steal them.
He had taught himself to write and never learned the normal direction at all.
He believed that words written toward the heart somehow held greater power.
context: The most accepted reason is the simplest: as a lefty, writing right-to-left kept his hand out of the wet ink he had just laid down. Source: https://news.artnet.com/art-world/art-bites-leonardo-mirror-writing-2473530 ; https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/leonardo-da-vincis-notebooks

question: Ser Piero, a rich Florentine notary, might have opened almost any door for his son Leonardo da Vinci, a boy who could draw and reason better than grown men. Yet Leonardo could not follow his father into that respected trade, and no university would take him. What blocked his path?
answer: He was born out of wedlock.
choices: He was born out of wedlock.
He could not read or write Latin.
He had quarreled bitterly with his father.
He was promised to the Church as a boy.
context: Leonardo was the illegitimate son of Ser Piero and a young peasant woman, Caterina. Being born out of wedlock barred him from his father's profession and from university -- which freed him to teach himself by direct observation instead. He ended up with 12 half-siblings. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Leonardo-da-Vinci

question: Andrea del Verrocchio let his teenage apprentice, Leonardo da Vinci, paint a single small angel, kneeling, in his Baptism of Christ in the 1470s. Giorgio Vasari, a later biographer, claimed the angel outshone anything Verrocchio had ever painted, and that the master then did something drastic. What did Verrocchio do, by Vasari's story?
answer: He set down his brush and never painted again.
choices: He set down his brush and never painted again.
He painted over the angel in a jealous rage.
He sold his workshop and moved away to Rome.
He took Leonardo on as a full partner that day.
context: Vasari tells it as legend, but Verrocchio's painting output really does seem to stop around this time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Baptism_of_Christ_(Verrocchio_and_Leonardo)

question: 'Buy boots and shoelaces,' Leonardo da Vinci reminded himself in a notebook, and ordinary errands like that sat right beside strange research jobs he set himself. Around 1510 he scribbled an order to go and study one very particular animal part. What did he write?
answer: Describe the tongue of the woodpecker.
choices: Describe the tongue of the woodpecker.
Count the teeth of the river pike.
Measure the wingspan of the eagle.
Weigh the brain of the ox.
context: Real entries around 1510 include 'Describe the tongue of the woodpecker and the jaw of a crocodile' and 'Get hold of a skull' -- jotted between reminders to buy boots and stockings. He simply could not stop asking questions about everything. Source: https://flashbak.com/leonardo-da-vincis-to-do-lists-from-his-inspried-notebooks-464938/

question: Leonardo da Vinci built up the Mona Lisa's shadows from as many as thirty see-through glazes, each one thinner than a human hair. The result was the hazy softness called sfumato. How did Leonardo blend such delicate layers?
answer: With his bare fingers.
choices: With his bare fingers.
With a fan of fine sable brushes.
With a heated metal blade.
With a soft folded cloth.
context: Louvre X-ray analysis shows the sfumato shadows were built from up to 30 translucent glaze layers, each thinner than a human hair -- and he often blended the paint with his bare fingers. Source: https://www.chemistryviews.org/details/ezine/763413/Mona_Lisas_Secret/ ; https://www.leonardodavincisinventions.com/sfumato-technique/

question: Inside both a circle and a square, Leonardo da Vinci set the naked figure of his Vitruvian Man, drawn around 1490 to show the proportions of the human body. He also noted a simple rule. Suppose you stretch your arms out as wide as they go. By Leonardo's rule, what does their span equal?
answer: Your own height.
choices: Your own height.
Your shoulder width.
Your forearm length.
Your face, doubled.
context: Leonardo noted the body's rule that 'the span of a man's outstretched arms is equal to his height.' He also corrected the ancient architect Vitruvius -- the navel is the true center of the circle, the groin the center of the square. The fragile drawing is locked away in Venice and almost never shown. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitruvian_Man

question: When he planned the painted hall of the Last Supper, Leonardo da Vinci wanted every line of it to aim at a single point. He drove one nail into the wet plaster and stretched strings out from it like rays of light. Where did he drive that nail?
answer: Into Christ's right temple.
choices: Into Christ's right temple.
Into the center of the table.
Into the doorway behind the apostles.
Into Judas's clenched hand.
context: Every line of the painted room points back to Christ's head. The tiny nail-hole is still in the plaster today, found during restoration. Source: https://discoveringdavinci.com/works/paintings/last-supper/composition-and-perspective.html ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Last-Supper-fresco-by-Leonardo-da-Vinci

question: Adrian Nicholas, a skydiver, built a pyramid-shaped linen parachute in 2000 exactly to a design Leonardo da Vinci had sketched around 1485. Leonardo had written that with it a man could throw himself down from any great height unharmed. Nicholas jumped with it from 10,000 feet. How did the jump turn out?
answer: It held, and he floated gently to the ground.
choices: It held, and he floated gently to the ground.
It collapsed, and his backup chute saved him.
It spun hard, and he was badly hurt landing.
It tore open, and he had to cut it away.
context: Adrian Nicholas built Leonardo's parachute to his exact specs, jumped from 10,000 feet, and floated safely down -- 500 years later, it worked. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Nicholas ; https://editions.covecollective.org/content/parachute-design-da-vinci

question: Mark Rosheim rebuilt a mechanical knight in 2002 from sketches Leonardo da Vinci had made around 1495, and it moved. Leonardo's full-size knight in armour ran on hidden gears, cables and pulleys; it could sit down, stand up, turn its head and lift its visor. What is the knight often called?
answer: The first humanoid robot in the West.
choices: The first humanoid robot in the West.
The first wind-up clock in Europe.
The first suit of bulletproof armor.
The first self-moving war machine.
context: Leonardo's robot is often called the first humanoid robot in Western history. NASA roboticist Mark Rosheim rebuilt it from the sketches in 2002, and it actually moved. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo's_robot

question: To see exactly how the valves inside the heart snapped shut with each beat, Leonardo da Vinci poured molten wax into a real ox heart to make a cast, blew a clear glass model from it, and sent water packed with grass seeds through the model. Why did he fill the water with seeds?
answer: So he could watch the way the flow swirled.
choices: So he could watch the way the flow swirled.
So the glass would not crack under the pressure.
So the water would move through it more slowly.
So he could weigh how much water passed through.
context: Watching the seeds, Leonardo concluded that little vortexes snap the valve shut each beat. He was proved right -- in 1968 by dye and X-ray, and again in 2014 by MRI. Source: https://www.ajconline.org/article/S0002-9149%2812%2902610-0/fulltext ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3361109/

question: High in the mountains, far from any sea, Leonardo da Vinci kept finding fossil seashells locked in the rock. Most people of his day explained them by Noah's Flood. Leonardo studied how the shells lay in their layers and reached a very different conclusion. What did he decide?
answer: They had once been the floor of the sea.
choices: They had once been the floor of the sea.
Birds had carried the shells up the slopes.
The shells had grown inside the rock itself.
A great storm had flung them from the coast.
context: Leonardo reasoned the mountains had once been seabeds slowly pushed up over ages -- a startlingly modern idea of deep geological time, written in the Codex Leicester centuries before the science existed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codex_Leicester

question: Meriwether Lewis paid $20 for one companion on the long trek to the Pacific. On the way it hunted squirrels, fished a deer out of a river, and woke the camp whenever a grizzly or a buffalo came close. Who was this loyal companion?
answer: A Newfoundland dog named Seaman
choices: A Newfoundland dog named Seaman
A packhorse named Traveler
A tame raven named Sergeant
A mule named Pilot
context: Seaman, a big black Newfoundland, was the only non-human permanent member of the Corps. Near the journey's end (April 11, 1806) some Watlala men stole him; Lewis sent three armed men with orders to shoot, and the thieves let the dog go and fled. Source: nps.gov/articles/000/seaman-s-contributions-to-the-lewis-and-clark-expedition.htm ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaman_(dog)

question: Sure the expedition had reached the Pacific at last, William Clark scrawled the most famous line of the whole journey in his field notebook on 7 November 1805. The roaring waves of the wide Columbia River mouth had fooled him; the open sea was still some twenty miles off. What did he write?
answer: "Ocian in view! O! the joy"
choices: "Ocian in view! O! the joy"
"The great water! Our long road ends"
"We have reached the western sea!"
"The Pacific at last! God be praised"
context: Clark's spelling was famously rough. The estuary's tide-tossed waves fooled him into thinking the ocean was right there. Source: lewis-clark.org/the-trail/down-the-columbia/ocean-in-view/ ; historylink.org/File/5360

question: William Clark adored Sacagawea's baby son, Jean-Baptiste, and called him Pomp. Heading home in July 1806, Clark named a tall sandstone rock above the Yellowstone River Pompy's Tower after the boy, then climbed it and left something there that survives to this day. What did he do to the rock?
answer: Carved his name and the date into it
choices: Carved his name and the date into it
Painted a giant American flag on it
Buried a time capsule at the top
Planted a tree at the summit
context: Clark nicknamed the baby, Jean-Baptiste Charbonneau, 'Pomp' (or 'Pompy'), and named the pillar Pompy's Tower (July 25, 1806) in his honor. His carved signature survives on the rock to this day. Source: lewis-clark.org/people/sacagawea/sacagaweas-story/ ; history.com/this-day-in-history/february-11/sacagawea-gives-birth-to-pompey

question: The Corps of Discovery met a band of Shoshone in August 1805, needing their horses to cross the Rockies, and Sacagawea, stolen from her people as a girl, came to interpret. When she saw their chief, Cameahwait, she leapt up and danced for joy. Who was he?
answer: Her own brother
choices: Her own brother
Her father
The man who had captured her
A boy she grew up with
context: Clark recorded that she 'danced for the joyful Sight' and Lewis called the reunion 'really affecting.' Her family tie to Cameahwait helped secure the horses the Corps needed to get over the Rockies. Source: lewis-clark.org/people/sacagawea/sacagaweas-story/

question: Toussaint Charbonneau panicked at the rudder when a sudden squall struck the boat he was steering on 14 May 1805, and it began to fill with water. His wife, Sacagawea, stayed calm with her baby on her back and reached far out over the river. What did she rescue that the expedition could never have replaced?
answer: The instruments, journals, and medicine
choices: The instruments, journals, and medicine
The rifles, powder, and lead shot
The salt, dried meat, and water
The blankets, tools, and trade goods
context: Lewis wrote that Sacagawea showed 'equal fortitude and resolution, with any person on board.' Five days later (May 19) the captains named a river after her, 'the Sah-ca-gah-we-ah or bird woman's River.' Source: lewis-clark.org/people/sacagawea/sacagaweas-story/ ; sparknotes.com/biography/sacajawea/section3/

question: Dwight Eisenhower let the Free French armoured division of Jacques Leclerc race into Paris in August 1944, and on the night of the 24th one of its companies reached the heart of the city first. About 146 of that company's roughly 160 men were not French. They were exiles who had already fought one war against fascism and lost. Who were they?
answer: Spanish Republicans who had fled Franco's Spain
choices: Spanish Republicans who had fled Franco's Spain
Polish cavalrymen who had escaped the 1939 invasion
Italian partisans who had deserted Mussolini's army
Russian deserters who had abandoned the Tsar's army
context: About 146 of La Nueve's roughly 160 men were Spanish Republicans — they had lost the Spanish Civil War to Franco, fled into exile, and joined the Free French to fight fascism again. They named their half-tracks after the battles they had lost back home: 'Guadalajara,' 'Teruel,' 'Ebro,' 'Brunete,' and 'España Cañí.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Nueve

question: Adolf Hitler told Dietrich von Choltitz, the general holding Paris in August 1944, to leave the city a 'field of ruins.' Choltitz had his men lay explosives under the bridges over the Seine. What did he then do with the charges?
answer: He refused to set them off, and the city stood
choices: He refused to set them off, and the city stood
He blew the bridges but spared the cathedrals
He waited for Hitler's personal signal that never came
He handed them to the Resistance to use on the Germans
context: Choltitz disobeyed the order and surrendered the garrison intact on 25 August. The famous legend — from Choltitz's own 1951 memoir — is that Hitler screamed down the phone, 'Is Paris burning?'; that line rests largely on Choltitz's own account. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/during-world-war-ii-the-liberation-of-paris-saved-the-french-capital-from-destruction-180984943/

question: Charles de Gaulle, who had fled Paris in June 1940, stood at the Hotel de Ville on 25 August 1944 and spoke without notes. He built from suffering toward triumph: 'Paris outraged! Paris broken! Paris martyred!' How did the line end?
answer: 'But Paris liberated!'
choices: 'But Paris liberated!'
'Yet France endures forever!'
'And the enemy shall pay!'
'So let the bells ring out!'
context: De Gaulle's improvised line — 'Paris! Paris outragé! Paris brisé! Paris martyrisé! Mais Paris libéré!' — became the most quoted moment of the Liberation. He had last left the city on 10 June 1940, fleeing the German advance. Source: https://www.sortiraparis.com/en/what-to-visit-in-paris/history-heritage/articles/252962-ephemeris-of-august-25-in-paris-general-de-gaulle-s-speech-at-the-hotel-de-ville

question: George Patton toured Ohrdruf with Dwight Eisenhower and Omar Bradley on 12 April 1945; it was the first Nazi camp the Americans had reached. About thirty bodies dusted with white lime lay inside one shed, and just outside stood a half-burned pyre of corpses. What did the sight and the smell do to the famously tough general?
answer: He vomited against the side of a building
choices: He vomited against the side of a building
He saluted the dead and ordered taps played
He wept openly and took off his helmet
He drew his pistol and fired into the pyre
context: Patton — known for slapping a soldier he thought was a coward — was so sickened at Ohrdruf that he threw up against a building and would not enter the shed. He, Eisenhower, and General Omar Bradley toured the camp together on April 12, 1945. Source: National WWII Museum, 'What We Fought Against: Ohrdruf.'

question: Dwight Eisenhower walked through every corner of the Ohrdruf camp in April 1945. Afterward he wrote to George Marshall that he had gone through it on purpose, though no one had ordered him to. Why had he made himself see it all?
answer: So he could personally testify it was real if anyone later called it propaganda
choices: So he could personally testify it was real if anyone later called it propaganda
So he could order the entire camp burned down to ashes the next morning
So he could choose which nearby German towns to punish for the crime
So he could gather material for the war memoir he planned to write
context: Eisenhower's April 15, 1945 letter to Marshall: he made the visit 'deliberately in order to be in a position to give firsthand evidence of these things if ever, in the future, there develops a tendency to charge these allegations merely to propaganda.' He documented it on purpose so no one could ever deny it. (Note: the widely quoted 'some bastard will say this never happened' line attributed to Eisenhower is apocryphal — this letter is the real, documented version.) Source: USHMM / NPS, 'Eisenhower and the Holocaust'; letter to Marshall, April 15, 1945.

question: Inside Ford's Theatre on the night of April 14, 1865, John Wilkes Booth crept into President Abraham Lincoln's box and shot him in the back of the head. Then he leapt down onto the stage, turned to face the horrified audience and shouted a Latin phrase before he fled. What did he shout?
answer: "Sic semper tyrannis!" — "Thus always to tyrants!"
choices: "Sic semper tyrannis!" — "Thus always to tyrants!"
"Veni, vidi, vici!" — "I came, I saw, I conquered!"
"E pluribus unum!" — "Out of many, one!"
"Et tu, Brute!" — "And you, Brutus!"
context: 'Sic semper tyrannis!' means 'Thus always to tyrants!' and is the state motto of Virginia. Booth, a Confederate sympathizer, cast the killing as tyrant-slaying; his spur caught the Treasury Guard flag draped on the box railing as he jumped. Lincoln never woke; he died the next morning, April 15, at 7:22 a.m. in the Petersen House across the street. Source: https://fords.org/lincolns-assassination/

question: To kill President Abraham Lincoln inside a crowded box at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865, John Wilkes Booth needed a gun small enough to hide in his coat. It had to be deadly from a hand's reach, fired into the back of Lincoln's head. What kind of gun did Booth carry into the theatre?
answer: A small single-shot Philadelphia Deringer pistol
choices: A small single-shot Philadelphia Deringer pistol
A six-shooter Colt revolver
A double-barreled hunting shotgun
A long-barreled cavalry carbine rifle
context: The Deringer held just one ball — Booth had exactly one chance and made it count, firing behind Lincoln's left ear at about 10:14 p.m. He carried a large hunting knife as his backup weapon. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Abraham_Lincoln

question: A man slipped into the presidential box behind Abraham Lincoln at a Washington theatre on the night of April 14, 1865, and shot him. The killer, John Wilkes Booth, was no unknown drifter. Before that night, what was he known as across America?
answer: One of the country's most famous and admired stage actors
choices: One of the country's most famous and admired stage actors
A decorated Confederate cavalry general
A United States senator from Virginia
A wealthy Northern railroad tycoon
context: Booth, 26, came from the celebrated Booth theatrical dynasty — lean, athletic, with jet-black hair. His fame is exactly how he knew Ford's Theatre so well and could move through it unquestioned. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilkes_Booth

question: Abraham Lincoln sat watching a comedy at Ford's Theatre on Good Friday, April 14, 1865, when John Wilkes Booth shot him. The long Civil War between the Union and the Confederacy was already ending. Five days earlier, one event had shown the war was basically over. What was it?
answer: General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Grant at Appomattox
choices: General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Grant at Appomattox
The Confederate capital of Richmond was first captured
The Emancipation Proclamation was first issued
The Confederate states first voted to secede
context: Lee surrendered on April 9, 1865; Booth struck on April 14. By killing Lincoln at the instant of victory, Booth martyred the very man who had held the Union together through four years of war. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/abraham-lincoln-assassination

question: Other Confederate sympathizers had orders of their own on the night John Wilkes Booth shot Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre, April 14, 1865. Booth had set the whole plan for about 10 p.m., so that his men would strike other Union leaders in the same hour. What was the plot's larger goal?
answer: To kill Lincoln, the Secretary of State, and the Vice President all at once
choices: To kill Lincoln, the Secretary of State, and the Vice President all at once
To kidnap Lincoln and trade him for Confederate prisoners
To burn down the Capitol building while Congress met
To seize the federal gold reserves in Washington
context: Booth assigned Lewis Powell to kill Secretary of State William Seward and George Atzerodt to kill Vice President Andrew Johnson — a plan to behead the U.S. government in a single hour. Only Booth succeeded. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/assassination-of-Abraham-Lincoln

question: Mary Surratt kept the Washington boardinghouse where John Wilkes Booth's fellow plotters met. After Booth shot Abraham Lincoln in April 1865, a military court tried the plotters, and on July 7, 1865, Mary Surratt and three other conspirators went to the gallows together. Her hanging marked a grim first in American history. What was it?
answer: She was the first woman ever executed by the U.S. federal government
choices: She was the first woman ever executed by the U.S. federal government
She was the first person executed without any trial
She was the first prisoner hanged inside the White House grounds
She was the first conspirator to confess before the hanging
context: Hanged alongside her were Lewis Powell, David Herold, and George Atzerodt. Her guilt was argued bitterly then and since, but the execution itself was unprecedented. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/july-7/mary-surratt-is-first-woman-executed-by-u-s-federal-government

question: The audience at Ford's Theatre was watching the comedy 'Our American Cousin' on the night of April 14, 1865, while John Wilkes Booth waited to shoot President Abraham Lincoln in his box above the stage. Booth knew every line by heart. He picked one exact moment in the show for his shot. What moment did he wait for?
answer: The play's biggest laugh line, so the roar would cover the gunshot
choices: The play's biggest laugh line, so the roar would cover the gunshot
The intermission, when the lights came up
The final bow, when the audience stood to leave
A loud thunderstorm sound effect in the script
context: The actor Harry Hawk delivered the line '...you sockdologizing old man-trap!' — the show's guaranteed laugh. As the audience roared, Booth fired. Source: https://fords.org/lincolns-assassination/

question: Lewis Powell, one of John Wilkes Booth's fellow plotters, forced his way into Secretary of State William Seward's home in Washington in April 1865 and stabbed him repeatedly in his own bed. Yet Seward lived. By strange luck, what saved his life?
answer: A metal jaw brace from an earlier injury deflected the knife
choices: A metal jaw brace from an earlier injury deflected the knife
A thick family Bible in his coat stopped the blade
His son's pet dog dragged the attacker off him
A loaded pistol under his pillow scared the attacker away
context: Days earlier Seward had broken his jaw in a carriage accident; the metal-and-canvas splint turned Powell's blade. Powell fled shouting 'I'm mad! I'm mad!' after wounding five people in the house. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Powell_(conspirator)

question: Edwin Booth, brother of the man who would kill Abraham Lincoln, saved a life on a crowded Jersey City train platform about a year before the assassination. A young man was slipping toward a moving train when Edwin seized his coat collar and pulled him back. Who was the young man?
answer: Robert Todd Lincoln, the president's own son
choices: Robert Todd Lincoln, the president's own son
Ulysses S. Grant Jr., the general's son
A young Mark Twain, before he was famous
Edwin Stanton, the future Secretary of War
context: Edwin Booth yanked Robert Todd Lincoln up by the coat collar on a Jersey City platform — saving the son of the very man his brother would later kill. Source: https://historynet.com/edwin-booth-saved-robert-todd-lincolns-life-2/

question: Sergeant Boston Corbett had orders to take John Wilkes Booth alive when soldiers trapped the assassin in a burning Virginia tobacco barn after a twelve-day manhunt. Instead Corbett shot him in the neck, and the paralyzed Booth was carried to a farmhouse porch. Staring at his hands, what did he whisper as he died?
answer: "Useless, useless."
choices: "Useless, useless."
"Tell my mother I died for my country."
"I have done the state some service."
"The South is avenged."
context: Booth, who had cast himself as a hero in his pocket diary, died at age 26 staring at the hands that could no longer move. Corbett had been ordered to take him alive but fired through a gap in the burning barn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilkes_Booth

question: John Wilkes Booth strolled right up to the door of Abraham Lincoln's box at Ford's Theatre on the night of April 14, 1865, and walked in. The one man whose job was to guard that door was not there. Why was the box left unguarded?
answer: The policeman assigned to guard it had wandered off to a tavern
choices: The policeman assigned to guard it had wandered off to a tavern
A fire alarm had pulled all the guards outside
Lincoln had personally dismissed his guards that night
The guard had been bribed by Booth in advance
context: Lincoln's bodyguard that night was policeman John Frederick Parker, who left his post outside the presidential box. With no one there, Booth simply walked in. Source: https://fords.org/lincolns-assassination/

question: Soldiers carried the dying Abraham Lincoln across the street to a boardinghouse and laid him on a bed too short for his 6-foot-4 frame. He died the next morning without ever waking. As he drew his last breath, Edwin Stanton, his Secretary of War, is famously said to have spoken one sentence over him. What is that traditional line?
answer: "Now he belongs to the ages."
choices: "Now he belongs to the ages."
"The Union is saved at last."
"God has taken our best man."
"Let us bury him with honor."
context: LEGEND/disputed: the exact wording is uncertain — some present heard 'angels' rather than 'ages' — but this is the line history remembers. Lincoln died at 7:22 a.m. on April 15, 1865. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Abraham_Lincoln

question: A Florentine painter of the early 1400s laid out a tiled floor running away from the viewer, its rows shrinking and their edges rushing together, the way the two rails of a railway line seem to join far off. He aimed every one of those receding lines at a single spot on the horizon. What is that spot called?
answer: The vanishing point
choices: The vanishing point
The golden section
The picture plane
The horizon arc
context: In linear perspective, every set of parallel lines running away from the viewer (the orthogonals) appears to converge at one spot on the horizon — the vanishing point. Floor tiles shrinking toward it is the classic way painters fake real depth on a flat panel. Source: https://www.britannica.com/art/linear-perspective ; https://thevirtualinstructor.com/onepointperspective.html

question: Antonio Manetti, who wrote Filippo Brunelleschi's life, described a small picture of Florence's eight-sided Baptistery that Brunelleschi painted around 1413 to show off his new method of perspective. Where the sky belonged, the artist laid down no blue paint but burnished silver. By Manetti's account, what did the silver let the little picture do?
answer: Show real clouds and birds drifting across it
choices: Show real clouds and birds drifting across it
Glow faintly in a darkened cathedral
Stay bright for hundreds of years
Cost more than gold leaf paint
context: Brunelleschi's friend and biographer Antonio Manetti wrote that the burnished silver reflected 'the real air and atmosphere,' so 'the clouds seen in the silver are carried along by the wind as it blows' — actual drifting clouds and passing birds appeared inside the painting. Source: Antonio Manetti, Life of Brunelleschi, quoted at academia.edu and guidemeflorence.com/linear-perspective-florence/

question: Filippo Brunelleschi proved his perspective panel was perfect with a strange viewing rig. He drilled a tiny peephole through the back of the panel, and the viewer peered through the hole while holding an object out in front. Looking at that object through the hole, the viewer saw the painted Baptistery appear exactly like the real Baptistery across the square. What was the object held out in front?
answer: A flat mirror
choices: A flat mirror
A glass lens
A candle flame
A silk veil
context: The peephole was 'as small as a lentil' on the painted front and flared open on the back 'to the size of a ducat.' The viewer peered through the back while holding a mirror in front, so the painting bounced back into the eye and matched the real Baptistery exactly. Source: https://www.webexhibits.org/arrowintheeye/brunelleschi1.html (quoting Antonio Manetti's biography of Brunelleschi)

question: Carl Linnaeus gave every plant and animal a two-word Latin name, and he did something no naturalist before him had dared: he put humans right inside the animal kingdom, grouped with the apes and monkeys. What two-word name did he give the human species?
answer: Homo sapiens
choices: Homo sapiens
Canis lupus
Felis catus
Equus ferus
context: Linnaeus classified humans as Homo sapiens ('wise man') and placed us in his group Anthropomorpha, boldly among the apes and monkeys, where no naturalist before him had dared put humans so plainly. Source: https://www.sdnhm.org/blog/blog_details/carl-linnaeus-the-man-who-classified-us-homo-sapiens/121/

question: Johann Siegesbeck, a critic in St. Petersburg, damned as 'loathsome harlotry' Carl Linnaeus's system for sorting flowers, which counted their stamens and pistils and likened them to husbands and wives. Linnaeus took his revenge on the man. What did he do?
answer: Named an ugly weed after him forever
choices: Named an ugly weed after him forever
Refused to speak with him ever again
Wrote a book calling him a fool
Sent a fake plant specimen to trick him
context: Per BBC Science Focus and Wikipedia (Sigesbeckia), Linnaeus named Siegesbeckia -- a small, sticky, unattractive weed -- for his critic Johann Siegesbeck; the other choices are also real eponymous genera of his era (Buffonia/Buffon, Dillenia/Dillenius, Gardenia/Garden).

question: Lise Meitner tramped through the snow at Kungalv in Sweden at Christmas 1938 beside her nephew Otto Frisch, puzzling over a letter: uranium hit with neutrons seemed to have turned into barium. Resting on a log, the two worked out that the uranium atom had split, and they needed a name for it. What word did Frisch borrow?
answer: The biologist's word for a living cell dividing in two
choices: The biologist's word for a living cell dividing in two
The Latin word physicists used for breaking metal
The German word for the bursting of a shell
The Greek word for the releasing of trapped heat
context: Frisch asked a biologist at Bohr's institute what the splitting of a living cell was called, learned it was 'fission,' and borrowed the word for the splitting atom. Meitner and Frisch published the interpretation in Nature in early 1939 — they were the first to explain and name nuclear fission. Source: https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/key-documents/meitner-frisch-nuclear-fission/

question: Lise Meitner fled Nazi Germany for Sweden in 1938, and that winter she and her nephew explained how the uranium atom splits and gave the process its name, fission. The Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 1944 honored the discovery of fission. Who received it?
answer: Otto Hahn alone, with Meitner left out entirely
choices: Otto Hahn alone, with Meitner left out entirely
Otto Frisch alone, the nephew who walked with her
Dirk Coster alone, who had helped her escape
Niels Bohr alone, the famous Danish physicist
context: Hahn, Meitner's chemistry partner of about thirty years, received the 1944 Chemistry Nobel by himself; Meitner, who had explained and named the process, was completely omitted, an exclusion many called grossly unfair. In 1982 element 109, made at Darmstadt, was named meitnerium in her honor — the first element named solely after a non-mythological woman. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2007/12/december-1938-discovery-nuclear-fission

question: John Locke held that a government may rule a man only if he has agreed to it, and he split that agreement in two. Express consent is a clear act, such as swearing an oath, that makes a man a full citizen. The other kind a man gives without a word, simply by living under a government and travelling its roads. What did Locke call that silent kind?
answer: Tacit consent
choices: Tacit consent
Royal consent
Lawful consent
Public consent
context: Locke argued that 'simply by walking along the highways of a country a person gives tacit consent to the government' and agrees to obey its laws (Two Treatises 2.122). Express consent (an oath, an act of membership) makes you a full citizen; tacit consent binds anyone who merely enjoys a country's protection. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-political/ (citing Two Treatises 2.122).

question: John Locke likened a ruler to a man hired to do a job for others: he holds his power in trust and never owns it. When a quarrel broke out over whether a ruler had betrayed that trust, Locke asked who should settle it. Whom did he name as the rightful judge?
answer: The people
choices: The people
The church
The courts
The army
context: Locke wrote: 'The people shall be judge; for who shall be judge whether his trustee or deputy acts well... but he who deputes him?' (Second Treatise 240). A ruler holds power like an employee answering to an employer -- the people who entrusted him -- not like an owner answering to no one. Source: press-pubs.uchicago.edu/founders/documents/v1ch3s2.html (Second Treatise 240).

question: John Locke flipped the meaning of the word rebel. When a ruler tramples his own subjects' rights, Locke said, the true rebel is the ruler, not the subjects who resist him. By Locke's reasoning, what has such a ruler really done?
answer: Brought back the state of war
choices: Brought back the state of war
Forfeited his right to the throne
Broken his coronation oath
Lost the love of his subjects
context: Locke's striking reversal (226): those 'who set up force again in opposition to the laws' are the ones who 'bring back again the state of war, and are properly rebels.' A ruler who invades his people's rights is the one breaking the peace -- so resisting him is not rebellion but self-defense. Source: marxists.org/reference/subject/politics/locke/ch19.htm (Second Treatise 226).

question: John Locke pinned down what political power is in his Two Treatises of Government of 1689: a right to make laws, including laws that can send a man to his death. Even such a law, he wrote, is justified only when it serves one purpose. What did Locke say all political power exists for?
answer: The public good
choices: The public good
The royal line
The state's glory
The ruler's honor
context: Locke's opening definition (Second Treatise 3): 'Political power, then, I take to be a RIGHT of making laws with penalties of death, and consequently all less penalties... and all this only for the public good.' Power is a trust for the public, never a possession for the ruler. Source: gutenberg.org/files/7370/7370-h/7370-h.htm (Second Treatise 3).

question: John Locke taught that every man holds rights to life, liberty and possessions, and that the law of nature itself teaches that 'no one ought to harm another' in these things. A defender of kings would call such rights a gift the crown hands down to its subjects. Locke flatly denied it. In Locke's view, what is the true status of these rights?
answer: They exist before any government
choices: They exist before any government
A king grants them to his subjects
The first written laws created them
The strongest tribe seizes them
context: Locke's foundation (Second Treatise 6): the law of nature teaches that 'no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions.' These rights are NOT gifts from a ruler -- they exist first, in the state of nature, and government is invented later to protect them. This is the idea the American founding rests on. Source: gutenberg.org/files/7370/7370-h/7370-h.htm (Second Treatise 6).

question: Thomas Jefferson leaned so hard on John Locke that parts of the Declaration of Independence read like Locke cut short. Jefferson wrote that governments draw their 'just powers' from one source, the same one Locke had pointed to about a century before. Where did the Declaration say a government's just powers come from?
answer: The consent of the governed
choices: The consent of the governed
The blessing of the church
The strength of its armies
The wisdom of its rulers
context: The Declaration (1776): governments derive 'their just powers from the consent of the governed,' and when one becomes destructive 'it is the Right of the People to alter or to abolish it.' That is Locke's exact pairing -- consent as the source of authority, and the right of revolution when it fails. Source: archives.gov/founding-docs/declaration-transcript.

question: Peter Laslett, a historian, pinned down when John Locke had actually written his Two Treatises of Government, and the date overturned an old picture. Readers had long taken the book for a tidy defence of England's Glorious Revolution of 1688, a revolution already won. What did Laslett find?
answer: He wrote it years before the revolution
choices: He wrote it years before the revolution
He wrote it on his deathbed in 1704
He took the argument from Filmer
A friend wrote half of it for him
context: Peter Laslett showed Locke wrote the bulk around 1679-1681, BEFORE the 1688 revolution -- making the book a CALL to revolution, not a polite defense of one already over. That is far more radical: Locke was urging people to overthrow a still-sitting king, which is why he published it anonymously and never admitted authorship in his lifetime. Source: iep.utm.edu/locke/; plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke/.

question: 'So vile and miserable an estate of man': so John Locke described one practice in the opening line of his First Treatise, saying he could scarcely believe an Englishman would speak up for it. Scholars still debate how those words square with Locke's own investments. What was he attacking?
answer: Slavery
choices: Slavery
Taxation
Censorship
Dueling
context: Locke's First Treatise opens: 'Slavery is so vile and miserable an estate of man... that 'tis hardly to be conceived that an Englishman, much less a gentleman, should plead for't.' The teachable tension: Locke held investments tied to the slave trade, a complication scholars still debate -- a thinker who wrote these words against an evil he was also entangled in. Source: bartleby.com/lit-hub/two-treatises-on-government/chapter-i-the-introduction/; aeon.co/essays/does-lockes-entanglement-with-slavery-undermine-his-philosophy.

question: Thomas Jefferson, like John Locke before him, held that one bad law is no reason to overthrow a government; subjects ought to put up with small wrongs. Revolution was justified, each argued, only when wrongs piled up one after another and revealed a design of tyranny. What phrase did the Declaration use for that pile-up?
answer: A long train of abuses
choices: A long train of abuses
A chain of usurpations
A course of repeated injuries
A series of broken laws
context: The Declaration says a people may abolish a government only 'when a long train of abuses and usurpations, pursuing invariably the same Object' reveals a design of tyranny -- echoing Locke 210, 'if a long train of actings show the councils all tending that way.' Not one grievance, but a sustained pattern, is the trigger. Source: archives.gov/founding-docs/declaration-transcript; press-pubs.uchicago.edu/founders/documents/v1ch3s2.html.

question: Louis Pasteur found that stray germs, not age, were souring a French product, and he saved it with gentle heating, short of boiling, that killed the germs without spoiling the taste. The process still bears his name. What did pasteurization first save for France?
answer: Its wine and beer
choices: Its wine and beer
Its bread and cheese
Its butter and cream
Its vinegar and oil
context: Pasteurization (patented 1865) was born to save France's souring wine and beer; gently heating to about 55–60°C — not boiling — killed the microbes without ruining the flavor. The same trick was later used to make milk safe. Source: sciencehistory.org / britannica.com Louis Pasteur.

question: Louis Pasteur meant to finish off the old idea that living things could spring up on their own out of dead broth. He boiled the broth in a glass flask and gave the flask's long neck a clever shape, and for months the broth stayed clear. What shape did he give the neck?
answer: Bent into a long S-shaped curve
choices: Bent into a long S-shaped curve
Sealed shut with melted glass
Coiled into a tight spiral
Narrowed down to a pinhole
context: In Pasteur's 1859 swan-neck flask, air could still reach the broth, but dust and microbes settled in the bend and never got in — so it stayed clear. Tip the flask so liquid touched the dusty bend, and within days it teemed with life. The experiment won the Academy's Alhumbert Prize in 1862. Source: britannica.com; bio.libretexts.org.

question: A rabid dog bit Joseph Meister, a nine-year-old boy from Alsace, fourteen times in July 1885, and rabies had always killed. His mother carried him to Louis Pasteur in Paris as their only hope, and Pasteur risked a new, untried treatment on him. What place in medical history did Joseph win?
answer: The first human ever saved from rabies
choices: The first human ever saved from rabies
The first child ever given anesthesia
The first patient ever cured of plague
The first person ever given a transfusion
context: On July 6, 1885, Pasteur — a chemist, not a physician — treated Joseph Meister, bitten two days earlier by a rabid dog. Meister survived and became the first human ever saved from rabies by vaccination, beginning about 60 hours after the bite. Source: pasteur.fr, history of the first rabies vaccination.

question: Louis Pasteur had tried his new rabies vaccine only on animals when nine-year-old Joseph Meister was carried into his Paris laboratory in 1885, bitten by a mad dog. Pasteur was no medical doctor at all, and injecting a sick child staked his whole reputation. What kind of scientist was he?
answer: A chemist
choices: A chemist
A biologist
A physicist
A geologist
context: Pasteur was a chemist by training, not a medical doctor — part of what made treating Joseph Meister so daring. Born 1822 in Dole, the son of a leather tanner who had soldiered under Napoleon, he was entombed in 1895 in a special crypt beneath the Institut Pasteur. Source: sciencehistory.org / pasteur.fr.

question: Theodore Vone, a grocer, owned the dog that savaged nine-year-old Joseph Meister in July 1885. Villagers killed it and cut it open to make sure the dog was rabid, and its stomach showed how the disease had warped its hunger. What did they find packed inside?
answer: Grass, straw, and bits of wood
choices: Grass, straw, and bits of wood
Coins, nails, and shards of glass
Bones, fur, and scraps of leather
Stones, sand, and lumps of clay
context: When the rabid dog was killed and opened, its stomach was full of grass, straw, and pieces of wood — the deranged appetite of a rabid animal. Its owner, grocer Theodore Vone, had himself been bitten on the arm by the dog. Source: en.wikipedia.org Joseph Meister; awesomestories.com.

question: Louis Pasteur staked his reputation on a public test at Pouilly-le-Fort in May 1881. He vaccinated dozens of sheep against anthrax, left a matching group unprotected, and then injected every animal with deadly anthrax. More than 200 people came to look two days later. What did they see?
answer: Every vaccinated sheep grazing, the rest lying dead
choices: Every vaccinated sheep grazing, the rest lying dead
Every animal in both groups dead by morning
Every animal in both groups alive and grazing
Only the unvaccinated sheep left grazing
context: Pasteur vaccinated 24 sheep, 1 goat, and 6 cows on May 5, 1881, challenged all the animals with anthrax on May 31, and two days later every vaccinated sheep was alive and grazing while the unvaccinated ones lay dead or dying — to rave reviews. Source: surgeonshallmuseums.wordpress.com; britannica.com.

question: Jean-Baptiste Jupille, a shepherd of fifteen, fought off a rabid dog with his bare hands in 1885 to shield five younger children, and he became the second person Louis Pasteur treated for rabies. How is his courage honored today in the garden of the Institut Pasteur?
answer: A bronze statue of him grappling the dog
choices: A bronze statue of him grappling the dog
A marble fountain carved with his name
A stained-glass window of the rescue
A granite obelisk listing the children
context: Jean-Baptiste Jupille, treated in October 1885, was bitten while beating off a rabid dog to protect five younger children. A bronze statue of Jupille wrestling the dog still stands in the garden of the Institut Pasteur. Source: himetop.wikidot.com; fr.wikipedia.org Jean-Baptiste Jupille.

question: Louis Pasteur set out in the 1880s to make a vaccine against rabies, when a bite from a rabid dog almost always meant death. He used rabbits that rabies had killed, cut out one part of each and hung it to dry in a flask for up to two weeks; the longer it dried, the weaker it grew. Which part did he dry and inject?
answer: Their spinal cords
choices: Their spinal cords
Their brains
Their livers
Their windpipes
context: Pasteur dried the spinal cords of rabbits dead of rabies, hung in flasks over potassium hydroxide for up to 14 days; the longest-dried cord was the weakest. Joseph Meister received 13 injections, starting with the weakest cord and ending with fresh, fully virulent material. Source: PMC3342039, NIH.

question: Charles Chamberland, Louis Pasteur's assistant, left a flask of chicken-cholera germs standing through the long summer holiday around 1879. The stale culture barely sickened the hens it was given to, and afterward no dose of fresh, deadly cholera could kill those birds. What had the forgotten flask produced?
answer: The first vaccine ever made in a laboratory
choices: The first vaccine ever made in a laboratory
The first germ ever seen under a microscope
The first antibiotic ever grown from mold
The first painkiller ever brewed for surgery
context: Chamberland's forgotten chicken-cholera flask had weakened (attenuated) the germ; the mildly-sickened birds then survived fresh, deadly culture. This accident created the first lab-made vaccine and revealed the weakening method Pasteur went on to use for anthrax and rabies. Source: norkinvirology.wordpress.com; nature.com.

question: A chained, maddened dog snapped as Louis Pasteur leaned over it to capture the rabies germ itself. Through a thin glass tube held in his own mouth, Pasteur drew up drops of one of the dog's fluids. Which fluid did he collect?
answer: Its saliva
choices: Its saliva
Its blood
Its sweat
Its tears
context: Rabies is carried in saliva, so Pasteur drew up drops of a rabid dog's saliva by mouth-pipette from its foaming muzzle. A pipette he used in this rabies work survives in the Science Museum, London. Source: collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk; libquotes.com (Axel Munthe).

question: Joseph Meister, the boy Louis Pasteur had saved from rabies, became the gatekeeper of the Institut Pasteur. German troops took Paris in June 1940, and a popular legend grew up about what Meister did then, though his granddaughter and historians tell it differently. What does the legend say he did?
answer: Killed himself rather than let Germans open Pasteur's tomb
choices: Killed himself rather than let Germans open Pasteur's tomb
Fled the city carrying Pasteur's heart in a jar
Burned the Institut's secret vaccine records
Walled up the crypt entrance with his own hands
context: LEGEND, not forensic fact. The popular story says Meister killed himself rather than open Pasteur's tomb for German soldiers; historians and his own granddaughter say he despaired believing his family had been captured fleeing Paris — in fact they returned safely hours after his death on June 24, 1940. Source: en.wikipedia.org Joseph Meister.

question: Thomas Jefferson's envoys had gone to Paris to buy a single port city. Instead, in 1803, they agreed to pay Napoleon's France about 15 million dollars for some 828,000 square miles, or about three cents an acre. What did that purchase do for the young country?
answer: It doubled the size of the United States overnight
choices: It doubled the size of the United States overnight
It added a thin strip along the Gulf coast
It traded one river port for another
It shrank the frontier the government had to defend
context: For roughly $15 million the U.S. bought about 828,000 square miles west of the Mississippi -- an average of about three cents an acre -- doubling the country in a single deal. Sources: worldhistory.org/Louisiana_Purchase/ ; monticello.org/thomas-jefferson/louisiana-lewis-clark/the-louisiana-purchase/

question: Robert Livingston and James Monroe carried Thomas Jefferson's orders to Paris in 1803: buy the city of New Orleans and nothing more. Across the table, Napoleon's finance minister, Francois Barbe-Marbois, made an offer far beyond anything the two men had authority to buy. What did he put on the table?
answer: The entire Louisiana Territory, all of it
choices: The entire Louisiana Territory, all of it
The single city of New Orleans plus its docks
A long-term lease on the Mississippi River
France's sugar islands in the Caribbean
context: Barbe-Marbois offered the whole colony, not just the port. Napoleon's own words: 'I renounce Louisiana... it is the whole colony, without reserve.' The envoys had no authority to buy that much land but signed anyway before he could change his mind. Sources: worldhistory.org/Louisiana_Purchase/ ; archives.gov/publications/prologue/2003/spring/louisiana-purchase.html

question: Napoleon Bonaparte had dreamed of a French empire in America anchored on the rich sugar island of Saint-Domingue (Haiti), and he sent a large army under his own brother-in-law, General Charles Leclerc, to hold it. By 1803 he was ready to sell off Louisiana instead. What had happened to the army he sent to Haiti?
answer: A slave revolt and yellow fever wiped it out, killing Leclerc himself
choices: A slave revolt and yellow fever wiped it out, killing Leclerc himself
It mutinied and sailed home without firing a shot
A British fleet sank it before it reached the island
It froze and starved through a brutal winter
context: The Haitian slave revolt plus yellow fever destroyed Leclerc's army, and Leclerc died of the fever. Without Haiti's sugar islands, Louisiana was worthless to Napoleon, so he let it go. He reportedly boasted that selling to the U.S. handed Britain 'a maritime rival that will sooner or later humble her pride.' Source: worldhistory.org/Louisiana_Purchase/

question: Martin Luther began turning the Bible into German while he hid in the Wartburg in 1521, and before he died in 1546 his Bible had run to hundreds of editions, some 200,000 copies in all. Jacob Grimm, one of the brothers who collected fairy tales, later praised its 'almost miraculous purity.' What did Grimm say Luther's Bible was the 'kernel and foundation' of?
answer: The modern German language
choices: The modern German language
The modern German nation-state
The German national church
The modern German university system
context: Jacob Grimm called Luther's German 'the kernel and foundation of modern High German.' By Luther's death in 1546 the Bible had spread on the order of 200,000 copies in hundreds of editions, helping standardize the German language. Source: bible-researcher.com/luther02.html (citing Jakob Grimm); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luther_Bible.

question: Lorenzo, the young Medici ruler of Florence, received a copy of The Prince from Niccolo Machiavelli, who hoped it would win back the post the Medici had taken from him. The story goes that Lorenzo barely looked at it, for another visitor had brought him a gift that same day. What was that gift?
answer: A pair of hunting dogs
choices: A pair of hunting dogs
A chest of Venetian gold
A set of jeweled falcons
A finely bound rival book
context: The story is a tradition (legend), not a documented fact, but it captures the bitter irony of Machiavelli's life: he wrote the most famous book on power to claw his way back into office, and the man he gave it to was too busy admiring dogs to read it. Machiavelli died in 1527 without ever regaining the post he longed for. Source: Gulf News, 'Poem reveals Machiavelli as pet lover'; CliffsNotes, The Prince Dedication; History Today, 'Fortune's Favours.'

question: Niccolo Machiavelli wrote in The Prince that a ruler must act as two beasts at once. One must be sly enough to spot hidden traps; the other must be strong enough to scare off his enemies. Which two animals did Machiavelli name?
answer: The fox and the lion
choices: The fox and the lion
The serpent and the eagle
The wolf and the bear
The hawk and the boar
context: Machiavelli's line (Chapter 18): a prince must 'be the fox to recognize the snares, and the lion to frighten the wolves.' Being only one or the other, he warned, is fatal: pure force gets you trapped, pure cunning gets you mauled. Source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 18; Wikipedia, Niccolo Machiavelli.

question: The Medici jailed Niccolo Machiavelli for 22 days early in 1513, suspecting him of a plot against them. His jailers gave him the strappado: they bound his wrists behind his back, hoisted him by a rope and dropped him six times. What did Machiavelli do through all of it?
answer: He confessed to nothing
choices: He confessed to nothing
He named three conspirators
He signed a false confession
He begged the Medici for pardon
context: Machiavelli endured all six drops without breaking. He was freed in March 1513 only because a celebratory amnesty followed the election of the Medici pope Leo X, not because of anything he said. Source: IEP, Machiavelli (iep.utm.edu/machiave/); Storia di Firenze, Connell on the Vettori letter.

question: Niccolo Machiavelli passed his days of exile on his farm trapping birds and squabbling with villagers over cards. Every night, he wrote to his friend Francesco Vettori, he shed his muddy clothes and put on fine robes. Then, before he sat down to write, what did he do?
answer: Entered the courts of ancient men to question the great dead writers
choices: Entered the courts of ancient men to question the great dead writers
Knelt in the village chapel to pray for his lost office
Drilled by torchlight the citizen militia he once led
Composed letters pleading with the Medici to restore him
context: From Machiavelli's letter to Francesco Vettori, 10 Dec 1513: dressed in 'garments regal and courtly,' he 'enters the ancient courts of ancient men' to ask the dead writers why they acted as they did, and 'for four hours of time I do not feel boredom... I am not frightened by death.' In this same letter he reveals he has written 'a little work On Princedoms', The Prince itself. Source: Machiavelli's letter to Vettori (dhspriory.org).

question: Cesare Borgia sent a brutal deputy, Remirro de Orco, to bring the lawless Romagna to heel, and Niccolo Machiavelli held Borgia up in The Prince as the model of a new ruler. Once the people hated Remirro for the bloodshed, Borgia turned on him and made a show of it for the town of Cesena. What became of Remirro?
answer: Cut in two, a bloody knife laid beside him
choices: Cut in two, a bloody knife laid beside him
Hanged from the fortress wall as a warning
Driven into exile with his lands seized
Locked in the tower for the rest of his life
context: Machiavelli (The Prince, ch. 7) wrote that the ferocity of the spectacle left the people 'at once satisfied and stupefied': Borgia got the brutal cleanup done, then made sure the blame for it fell on the dead minister rather than on himself. Machiavelli admired the cold calculation. Source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 7; ExecutedToday on Ramiro d'Orco; Wikipedia, Ramiro de Lorca.

question: Niccolo Machiavelli finished The Prince, a blunt manual for rulers who meant to seize power and hold it, in 1513. The line most often tied to the book is 'the ends justify the means,' a phrase used to defend ruthless tactics. What do scholars who have read the whole book point out about that line?
answer: Those exact words never appear in the book
choices: Those exact words never appear in the book
He copied the phrase from an ancient Roman
He wrote it as a warning, not as advice
It appears only in a private letter
context: The crude slogan was pinned on Machiavelli by later readers. The closest he actually wrote is 'si guarda al fine': in the actions of princes, one judges by the result. The misquote helped turn his name into 'Machiavellian', a byword for cold, scheming politics, and in 1559 the Church banned all his works on the Index of Prohibited Books. Source: Wikipedia, Niccolo Machiavelli; Britannica.

question: Spanish conquerors looted and smashed Inca cities all across Peru in the 1530s. High on a cloud-wrapped ridge in the Andes, the stone city of Machu Picchu kept its temples and houses whole. What spared it?
answer: The Spanish never found it
choices: The Spanish never found it
The Inca defended it to the last man
A peace treaty placed it off-limits
Local priests bribed the conquistadors
context: Because the conquistadors never reached Machu Picchu, its temples and houses were never looted or destroyed, and the site sat quietly on its ridge for centuries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machu_Picchu

question: Hiram Bingham, a Yale historian, climbed a steep Andes ridge in 1911 and became famous for 'finding' the lost Inca city of Machu Picchu. When he reached the site, he met something that proved the city was never truly lost. What did he find there?
answer: Local families farming and living on the terraces
choices: Local families farming and living on the terraces
Spanish treasure still hidden in the temples
Nothing but collapsed rubble and thick jungle
A band of rival explorers already digging
context: Local Quechua families had been farming Machu Picchu's terraces and living there the whole time, and explorer Agustin Lizarraga had already reached the site in 1902 — nine years before Bingham. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machu_Picchu

question: Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese captain in the service of Spain's king, left Spain in September 1519 with five ships: the Trinidad, San Antonio, Concepcion, Santiago and Victoria. He meant to reach the rich Spice Islands by sailing west. Three years later only one of the five came home to Spain. Which ship was it?
answer: The Victoria
choices: The Victoria
The Trinidad
The Concepcion
The Santiago
context: Of the five ships that set out on 20 September 1519, only the Victoria completed the voyage and returned to Spain. The flagship Trinidad never made it home. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magellan_expedition

question: Ferdinand Magellan led his ships out of the storm-lashed strait at the bottom of South America in November 1520 into a huge, calm ocean no European had yet crossed. No one aboard guessed how vast it truly was. What did Magellan name the new ocean?
answer: The Pacific
choices: The Pacific
The Atlantic
The Indian Ocean
The Arctic
context: Magellan named it the Pacific (meaning peaceful) because his ships met no storms there. The crew's diarist Antonio Pigafetta wrote, 'we entered into the Pacific sea... well named Pacific, for during this same time we met with no storm.' Yet crossing it took about 98 days of slow starvation. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_First_Voyage_Round_the_World/Pigafetta's_Account_of_Magellan's_Voyage

question: A crowd gathered at Seville in September 1522 to greet the heroes home from their voyage around the world. About 270 men had sailed with Ferdinand Magellan three years before, but the crowd found only starving survivors. How many came home?
context: Only 18 starving survivors aboard the Victoria reached Seville on 8 September 1522 — a death rate of roughly 92 percent. (Another 13 crew held captive at Cape Verde straggled home later.) Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/240-men-started-magellan-voyage-around-world-only-18-finished-it

question: Ferdinand Magellan's men wintered at Port San Julian, in southern South America, in 1520 and were amazed by the tall people they met there. Magellan called them 'Patagao,' and from his word the whole region took the name it still bears. By legend, what does 'Patagonia' mean?
answer: Land of the big-feet
choices: Land of the big-feet
Land of the giants' bones
Land of endless winter
Land at the world's end
context: The name Patagonia is often read as 'land of the big-feet,' from Magellan's word 'Patagao' for the tall people his crew met at Port San Julian. His men captured two by piling presents into their arms, then clapping iron shackles on their legs while their hands were full. The exact meaning is a matter of legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patagons

question: Ferdinand Magellan led the first trip around the world but never finished it: he was killed in a battle in the Philippines in April 1521, partway through. Another captain brought the last surviving ship home to Spain in September 1522. Who was that captain?
answer: Juan Sebastian Elcano
choices: Juan Sebastian Elcano
Antonio Pigafetta
Duarte Barbosa
Juan de Cartagena
context: The Basque captain Juan Sebastian Elcano brought the Victoria home, completing the first voyage around the world even though Magellan, whose name the feat carries, had died months earlier in the Philippines. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/september-6/magellans-expedition-circumnavigates-globe

question: Ferdinand Magellan never set out to circle the globe when he left Spain in 1519. He meant to reach the far East by sailing west, so Spain could break the Portuguese monopoly and buy one precious cargo at its source. What was Magellan really after?
answer: Cloves from the Spice Islands
choices: Cloves from the Spice Islands
Gold from the New World
A passage to India by land
Silk from the court of China
