context: Magellan was Portuguese, but Portugal's king refused to fund him, so he sailed for Spain's young King Charles I. His aim was a westward route to the Spice Islands (the Moluccas) to buy cloves — not to circle the Earth. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ferdinand-Magellan/Allegiance-to-Spain

question: Ferdinand Magellan's fleet found the 350-mile passage at the tip of South America on 21 October 1520, the strait that now bears his name. While the ships were still struggling through it, the San Antonio's crew mutinied. What did the mutineers then do with their ship?
answer: Secretly sailed back to Spain, abandoning the expedition
choices: Secretly sailed back to Spain, abandoning the expedition
Turned north and searched for the Northwest Passage
Founded a small colony on the Chilean coast
Attacked the other ships and burned them
context: The San Antonio's crew mutinied inside the strait and slipped away home, abandoning Magellan and taking a large share of the fleet's food stores with them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magellan_expedition

question: Ferdinand Magellan waded ashore at Mactan, a small island in the Philippines, on 27 April 1521, in armor, with about fifty of his men, against Chief Lapulapu and some 1,500 warriors. He stood his ground in the shallows until one blow brought him down. What killed him?
answer: A spear through his unarmored leg
choices: A spear through his unarmored leg
A poisoned arrow to the throat
A war club to the back of the skull
A blade between his shoulders
context: Speared in the unarmored leg, Magellan fell face-down in the surf and was overwhelmed by Lapulapu's warriors. His body was never returned to his men. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mactan

question: Ferdinand Magellan's sailors crawled across an empty ocean for month after month early in 1521, until the ship's biscuit was gone and the drinking water had turned rotten. Men were dying of hunger by the day. To stay alive, they tore something off the ship itself, soaked it in the sea, heated it over the embers and ate it. What did they eat?
answer: The ox-hides off the rigging
choices: The ox-hides off the rigging
The wax candles from the hold
The pages of the ship's books
The tar caulking the deck
context: When the biscuit ran out the crew gnawed the ox-hides that protected the rigging. Pigafetta wrote they soaked them in the sea for days, heated them on the embers, and ate them — along with sawdust and rats, which sold for half a crown each. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_First_Voyage_Round_the_World/Pigafetta's_Account_of_Magellan's_Voyage

question: Antonio Pigafetta, the diarist on Ferdinand Magellan's voyage, watched a sickness strike the crew on the long ocean crossing of 1521, after months without fresh food. It was the disease now called scurvy. So many men fell ill that they could no longer eat, and nineteen died. What did the disease do to the sailors' mouths?
answer: Their gums swelled up over their teeth
choices: Their gums swelled up over their teeth
Their tongues turned black and split
Their teeth dropped out in their food
Their lips cracked and bled white foam
context: The disease was scurvy, caused by the lack of fresh food. Pigafetta wrote that 'the upper and lower gums of most of our men grew so much that they could not eat,' and nineteen men died of it. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_First_Voyage_Round_the_World/Pigafetta's_Account_of_Magellan's_Voyage

question: The last of Magellan's sailors put in at the Cape Verde islands in July 1522 and got a shock. Their logbook, written up daily for three years, read Wednesday, but the people of the islands said it was Thursday. The sailors had stumbled on the first real proof of an idea still in use. What had happened?
answer: By always sailing west they had gained a whole day
choices: By always sailing west they had gained a whole day
Their calendar had skipped a leap year at sea
A storm had knocked out two days of records
They had crossed the equator one time too many
context: By sailing west around the entire globe, the crew had gained 24 hours their logbook never recorded — the first real-world demonstration of what became the International Date Line. Source: https://webspace.science.uu.nl/~gent0113/idl/idl_discovery.htm

question: Enrique of Malacca, Ferdinand Magellan's enslaved Malay interpreter, may have been the first person to circle the whole Earth. He had been carried east from Malacca to Europe years before, and now he sailed west with Magellan. At one Philippine island in 1521, what proved he had come all the way round?
answer: The local people understood his own Malay language
choices: The local people understood his own Malay language
He recognized the harbor where he was born
He found relatives waiting among the islanders
He saw the same stars he had known as a boy
context: At Limasawa on 28 March 1521, locals understood Enrique's Malay — meaning he had sailed west all the way back to a place where his native tongue was spoken, possibly making him the true first person to circle the globe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_of_Malacca

question: King John came to terms with England's rebel barons in June 1215 and agreed to limits on his royal power. The two sides met to settle the charter at a spot that Magna Carta itself names. Where did they meet?
answer: A riverside meadow called Runnymede
choices: A riverside meadow called Runnymede
A great hall inside the Tower of London
The high altar of Canterbury Cathedral
A war camp on the cliffs of Dover
context: Magna Carta's own dating clause names the spot: 'the meadow that is called Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines,' a grassy field beside the River Thames. The barons chose neutral open ground where neither side could spring a trap. Source: Britannica Key Facts / National Archives education resource.

question: The rebel barons of England saw King John accept their great charter of liberties in June 1215. Many people picture him bent over the parchment with a quill, signing his name, yet no medieval king made a document binding by writing on it. How did John make Magna Carta official?
answer: He pressed his great wax seal into it
choices: He pressed his great wax seal into it
He signed his name in red ink
He swore the oath aloud and touched the parchment
He cut his thumb and marked it in blood
context: A king authenticated a document by stamping his great seal in wax, the standard medieval way to make it binding, so 'King John signs Magna Carta' pictures are wrong on the basic act. Source: Wikipedia, Magna Carta; National Archives education resource.

question: England's barons rose in armed revolt against King John and needed a bold stroke to force the stubborn king to bargain over their demands for written rights. On 17 May 1215, while John was away, they seized a prize that left him little choice but to negotiate. What did the rebels seize?
answer: London, the capital
choices: London, the capital
The king's crown and jewels
The royal fleet at Portsmouth
The bridges across the Thames
context: With the king away, the rebels took London on 17 May 1215. Losing his capital broke John's position and pushed him to terms within weeks, at Runnymede. Source: Wikipedia, Magna Carta.

question: King John lost Normandy, and with it his family's lands in France, to one rival in 1204. He then squeezed his barons with crushing taxes to win the lands back, and their fury grew into the revolt of 1215. Who took those French lands from John?
answer: King Philip II of France
choices: King Philip II of France
Emperor Frederick of Germany
Pope Innocent III
King Louis the Lion
context: John lost Normandy to Philip II of France in 1204. The brutal taxes he squeezed from his barons to fund a failed reconquest fed the resentment that exploded into the revolt of 1215. Source: Wikipedia, Magna Carta; Britannica Key Facts.

question: Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, read the English barons a long-forgotten charter at a church meeting in London in August 1213: the promises King Henry I had made at his crowning in 1100. Langton urged them to make King John renew those promises. Why did his reading matter for Magna Carta two years later?
answer: It gave the barons a written precedent to base their demands on
choices: It gave the barons a written precedent to base their demands on
It made the pope declare the barons a holy army
It gave King John a legal way to escape signing anything
It turned the barons against their own knights and tenants
context: Archbishop Stephen Langton read out Henry I's century-old coronation charter to the barons in 1213, handing them a model for written limits on the king. He then helped broker the Runnymede settlement. Source: Wikipedia, Stephen Langton; Britannica.

question: King John accepted a long charter of 63 provisions in June 1215. People now quote its parts by number, as 'clause 39' or 'clause 40', as though it had come labelled that way. Who gave the clauses of Magna Carta those numbers?
answer: Editors writing long after John's reign
choices: Editors writing long after John's reign
The royal clerks who wrote out the charter
The barons, as they argued at Runnymede
The monks who first copied the charter
context: The 1215 charter ran as one continuous block of 63 provisions with no numbers. The familiar clause numbers were assigned by much later editors for easy reference. Source: Wikipedia, Magna Carta; Britannica Key Facts.

question: King John bound himself in clause 39 of Magna Carta: no free man would be arrested, imprisoned, stripped of his lands or exiled except by the lawful judgment of his equals. The promise ran down into English and American law. That judgment by one's equals grew into which protection?
answer: Trial by jury
choices: Trial by jury
The right to bear arms
Freedom of the press
The secret ballot
context: This is clause 39, the taproot of due process. Its 'judgment of his peers' grows into trial by jury, and the 'law of the land' idea flows down centuries later into the Fifth Amendment's due-process guarantee. Source: Magna Carta Project, Clause 39.

question: King John's rebel barons forced him to accept clause 40 of Magna Carta. In his royal courts a case could turn on who a man was and how the king felt, rather than on the law. In one ringing sentence the clause bound the crown for good. What did it promise the king would never do?
answer: Sell, deny, or delay a man's day in court
choices: Sell, deny, or delay a man's day in court
Judge a case in secret, with no jury or record
Take a man's land before any trial is held
Sell royal offices to the highest bidder
context: Clause 40 reads 'Nulli vendemus, nulli negabimus, aut differemus, rectum aut justiciam,' that is, 'To no one will we sell, to no one will we deny or delay, right or justice.' It is one of only a handful of clauses still on the UK statute book today. Source: Magna Carta Project, Clause 40; UK Parliament.

question: King John had accepted Magna Carta only about ten weeks before a decree branded it 'shameful' and 'illegal' and declared it 'null, and void of all validity for ever,' on the ground that John had been forced into it. Who struck the charter down?
answer: Pope Innocent III
choices: Pope Innocent III
King Philip II of France
Archbishop Stephen Langton
The council of 25 barons
context: John had made himself the pope's vassal, so Innocent III sided with the king and voided the charter within weeks of its sealing. His papal bull called it null and void 'for ever,' yet Magna Carta outlived that judgment. Source: Wikipedia, Magna Carta.

question: Fleeing a French invasion in October 1216, King John reached Newark Castle little more than a year after his barons had forced Magna Carta on him. He died there, not on a battlefield but in bed. What killed him?
answer: Dysentery
choices: Dysentery
A crossbow wound
A sudden fever
Drowning in the Thames
context: John died of dysentery at Newark Castle on the night of 18-19 October 1216, aged about 49. His 9-year-old son became Henry III, and Henry's regency reissued Magna Carta to win back the barons. Source: Wikipedia, Magna Carta; History Hit.

question: By tradition, the incoming sea swallowed part of King John's baggage train as he attempted the Wash, a broad sweep of tidal sand and quicksand along England's east coast, in October 1216, days before his death. What is John said to have lost there, never found to this day?
answer: The crown jewels
choices: The crown jewels
His royal seal
His war horses
A copy of Magna Carta
context: By tradition John lost part of his treasure, including the crown jewels, to the tide while crossing the Wash on 12 October 1216. No trace was ever found and treasure hunters still search, though the loss is legend rather than proven fact. Source: Wikipedia, Lost jewels of John, King of England; History Hit.

question: King John's barons won a sweeping-sounding promise in clause 39: no free man, 'nullus liber homo' in the Latin, would be seized or imprisoned except by lawful judgment. Yet only a thin top slice of England, mostly nobles and small landholders, counted as free. Most peasants were bound to their lords' land, could not leave without permission, and fell outside the clause. What was this unfree majority called?
answer: Villeins
choices: Villeins
Yeomen
Burgesses
Freeholders
context: 'Liber homo' meant the free, mainly nobles and landholders, perhaps only 2-3% of England's people. The unfree peasants and serfs who made up most of the population fell outside it. The promise was real but narrow at the start. Source: Magna Carta Project, Clause 39.

question: King John accepted a leash on his own power in clause 61, the most radical in the charter of 1215. It created a council of 25 barons; if John broke the charter and failed to fix the breach within 40 days, the 25 could seize his castles, lands and goods until he made it right. What did clause 61 in effect make legal?
answer: Armed rebellion against the king
choices: Armed rebellion against the king
Taxation without the king's consent
Trial of the king by the church
Dividing England among the barons
context: By licensing 25 barons to make war on the king to enforce the charter, clause 61 legalized rebellion, an idea so extreme it was cut from the very first reissue in 1216 and never restored. Source: Wikipedia, Magna Carta.

question: An English king reissued a settled Magna Carta in 1225, and in 1297 another king confirmed it as statute, the form that truly entered English law. King John's own charter of 1215 had not lasted. Which king's confirmation of 1297 made Magna Carta binding statute?
answer: Edward I
choices: Edward I
Henry III
Edward II
Edward III
context: Henry III reissued the definitive charter in 1225, and Edward I confirmed it as statute law in 1297. That 1297 version, not the doomed 1215 one, is the Magna Carta that lived on in English law. Source: Wikipedia, Magna Carta; legislation.gov.uk Magna Carta (1297).

question: King John ordered in clause 33 of Magna Carta that 'all fish-weirs,' the traps silting up England's rivers, be torn out of the Thames, the Medway and all England except the sea coast. That humble rule outlasted nearly all of the charter's grand promises. Into which decade did it survive as law?
answer: The 1960s
choices: The 1960s
The 1860s
The 1990s
The 1480s
context: The fish-weir clause addressed a real grievance: traps were silting up the trade rivers. This down-to-earth rule survived on the statute book until the 1960s, long after almost all the grand clauses had been repealed. Source: Magna Carta Project / British Library, Clause 33.

question: In the Ramayana, the demon king Ravana has stolen Princess Sita away to Lanka, his fortress across the sea, where Prince Rama's monkey army cannot follow. Hanuman, the mighty monkey whose father is Vayu, the wind god, prays and grows to an immense size. What does he do to reach Lanka?
answer: He leaps the entire ocean in one jump
choices: He leaps the entire ocean in one jump
He sails across on a wooden raft
He digs a tunnel beneath the seabed
He summons a giant eagle to fly him over
context: Hanuman launches from the summit of Mount Mahendra and clears the whole ocean to Lanka in a single leap — one of the most beloved images in the epic. (artsandculture.google.com; vedantu.com)

question: In the Ramayana, Ravana's demons catch the monkey hero Hanuman spying in Lanka for Prince Rama. To shame him, they soak his long tail in oil and set it alight, but Hanuman turns the burning tail into a weapon. What does he do with it?
answer: He sets the entire city of Lanka ablaze
choices: He sets the entire city of Lanka ablaze
He signals Rama's army waiting on the shore
He frightens Ravana into freeing Sita
He scorches a warning into the palace gates
context: This episode is the Lanka Dahan, the 'Burning of Lanka' — Hanuman torches the whole city rooftop by rooftop, sparing only the Ashoka grove where Sita was held. (hindustory.com; saispeaks.sathyasai.org)

question: In the Mahabharata, King Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava brother, is drawn by his Kaurava cousins into a crooked dice game and loses all he has, at last even his wife, Queen Draupadi. Prince Dushasana hauls her into the court and pulls at her sari to strip her in shame, and the god Krishna steps in. What happens to the sari?
answer: The cloth becomes endless and never runs out
choices: The cloth becomes endless and never runs out
The cloth turns to iron and cannot be grasped
The cloth bursts into flames in Dushasana's hands
The cloth vanishes, leaving Draupadi in golden armor
context: As Dushasana pulls and pulls, Krishna makes Draupadi's sari endless — the cloth keeps unwinding without end until Dushasana collapses exhausted. (hindupad.com; mythologicalstories.net)

question: In the Ramayana, the ten-headed demon king Ravana wins a great boon from Brahma, the creator: no god and no demon can ever kill him. Ravana thinks himself untouchable, yet in the end the exiled Prince Rama, a mortal man, kills him. What gap in the boon lets a man defeat him?
answer: In his pride, he never asked protection from mere humans
choices: In his pride, he never asked protection from mere humans
He demanded the boon last only a thousand years
He left one of his ten heads outside the blessing
He traded the boon away for the kingdom of Lanka
context: Ravana, master of all the Vedas, thought gods and demons the only threats worth guarding against — so he never sought protection from humans, which is exactly why Rama, a man, can slay him. (britannica.com; kidsgen.com)

question: In the Mahabharata, the patriarch Bhishma holds a boon that lets him choose the moment of his own death. Arjuna's arrows bring him down at Kurukshetra, and he refuses to die until the sacred time of Uttarayana comes. How does Bhishma lie as he waits?
answer: Suspended on a bed made of arrows
choices: Suspended on a bed made of arrows
Floating on the sacred river Ganga
Resting on the lap of his charioteer
Standing upright, propped on his bow
context: Pierced by so many arrows that they held him aloft, Bhishma lay on his 'bed of arrows' for weeks, teaching dharma and statecraft to Yudhishthira before choosing to die at Uttarayana. (isha.sadhguru.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svecchamrityu)

question: The royal cousins of the Mahabharata, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, feud their way to a vast war across about 1.8 million words. That makes the epic the longest poem ever composed and some four times as long as the Ramayana. How does it compare with the Iliad and the Odyssey of Homer combined?
answer: About ten times their combined length
choices: About ten times their combined length
About twice their combined length
About the same combined length
About half their combined length
context: At roughly 100,000 shlokas and 1.8 million words, the Mahabharata dwarfs Homer — about ten times the Iliad and Odyssey combined, and about four times the Ramayana's ~24,000 shlokas. (exoticindiaart.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_poem)

question: The Duke of Zhou taught, after King Wu crushed the Shang in 1046 BCE, that the right to rule is granted to a virtuous king and taken from a cruel one, so toppling a cruel king could be right. What was this grant called?
answer: The Mandate of Heaven
choices: The Mandate of Heaven
The Pool of Wine
The Forest of Meat
The Three Guards
context: Tianming, the Mandate of Heaven. The Duke of Zhou's answer turned a conquest into a kind of cosmic performance review: the Shang were told plainly, 'Heaven has rejected and ended the Mandate of this great state of Shang.' Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Mandate_of_Heaven/

question: King Wu crushed the Shang in 1046 BCE and founded a line of kings that outlasted every other dynasty in China, though its grip on real power slipped long before the end. About how long did the Zhou rule?
answer: About 800 years
choices: About 800 years
About 80 years
About 200 years
About 400 years
context: Roughly 789 years, 1046–256 BCE — far outlasting any later dynasty. The doctrine the Zhou founders invented to excuse one conquest ended up justifying every conquest that came after them. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Zhou_Dynasty/

question: The last Shang king fell to the Zhou in 1046 BCE, and the victors gave him a new name, Zhou, written with a character of their choosing. What did that character mean?
answer: The dirtiest strap on a horse's saddle
choices: The dirtiest strap on a horse's saddle
The bravest general of the army
A jewel worn only by emperors
The first month of the new year
context: A deliberate insult. They also accused him of building a 'Pool of Wine' you could canoe across, ringed by a 'Forest of Meat' hung with roasted flesh — tales modern archaeologists doubt. The Han scholar Wang Chong already called them unreliable victor's propaganda. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yin_Zhou  (Legend.)

question: The king of Qi put a sharp question to the philosopher Mencius, centuries after the Zhou conquest: when a subject killed the cruel tyrant Zhou of Shang, was that not the murder of a king? What did Mencius tell the king?
answer: He called it the execution of 'a mere fellow,' not a king
choices: He called it the execution of 'a mere fellow,' not a king
He claimed the killer had been the rightful heir all along
He said Heaven itself had struck the king down, not any man
He insisted the tyrant had secretly died of illness first
context: 'I have heard of the execution of the mere fellow Zhou, but I have not heard of the assassinating of a ruler.' By severing the crown from the wicked man wearing it, Mencius made overthrowing a tyrant legal, not murder. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mencius

question: Mencius quoted an old line from the Book of Documents to show how Heaven judges a king. In the Zhou way of thinking, a flood, a famine or a revolt might be read as Heaven's verdict on a ruler. What did the line claim?
answer: 'Heaven sees according as my people see; Heaven hears according as my people hear'
choices: 'Heaven sees according as my people see; Heaven hears according as my people hear'
'The king alone speaks with Heaven, and the people must obey him'
'Heaven keeps its counsel hidden from kings and commoners alike'
'Only the priests may read what Heaven has written in the stars'
context: This tied Heaven's judgment to popular support: a king who lost his people's hearts had lost Heaven, so flood, famine, and revolt could be read as Heaven's verdict spoken aloud. Mencius pushed it furthest: 'the people are the most precious, the state is next, and the ruler is the least precious.' Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Mandate_of_Heaven/

question: Manhattan Project scientists watched the first atomic fireball rise over the New Mexico desert early on 16 July 1945. Its heat melted the desert sand beneath it into a thin crust of glass, faintly radioactive. What color was that glass?
answer: Light green
choices: Light green
Jet black
Deep red
Pure white
context: The heat fused desert sand into a glassy light-green crust still found at the site today; it was named trinitite after the Trinity test. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_(nuclear_test); DOE energy.gov/lm/trinity-site.

question: A crew hoisted the Manhattan Project's first atomic bomb, a steel ball packed with explosives and plutonium that the scientists called the Gadget, to the top of a 100-foot steel tower in the New Mexico desert. They set it off early on 16 July 1945. What did the blast do to the tower?
answer: The blast vaporized it, leaving only stubs of its legs.
choices: The blast vaporized it, leaving only stubs of its legs.
The blast toppled it sideways across the sand.
The blast scorched it but left it standing.
The blast buried it under a crater of rubble.
context: The 100-foot steel tower was completely vaporized by the blast, leaving only stumps of its legs. The Trinity device was nicknamed 'the Gadget.' Source: lanl.gov national-security-science 0720 Trinity Test; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_(nuclear_test).

question: Leo Szilard, a Hungarian physicist, wrote a warning letter to President Franklin Roosevelt in August 1939, as the world stood on the edge of war, and he got Albert Einstein, the most famous physicist alive, to sign it. What did the letter warn might happen?
answer: Nazi Germany might build an atomic bomb first.
choices: Nazi Germany might build an atomic bomb first.
Japan might attack the American mainland soon.
Britain might run out of uranium for its labs.
Italy might seize the world's last radium mines.
context: Einstein signed the letter, but physicist Leo Szilard actually wrote it. It warned Roosevelt that Nazi Germany might develop an atomic bomb. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein-Szilard_letter; ahf.nuclearmuseum.org Einstein-Szilard letter 1939.

question: J. Robert Oppenheimer, head of the Manhattan Project, watched the first atomic fireball rise over the New Mexico desert in July 1945. Afterward he said a line from the Hindu scripture the Bhagavad Gita had come into his mind, and in 1965 he spoke it again on film. What was the line?
answer: Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.
choices: Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.
I am the light that shines in all the darkness.
Behold, I now make all things new again.
I am the beginning, the middle, and the end.
context: Oppenheimer said this Bhagavad Gita line came to him as he watched the Trinity fireball; it became the most famous quote of the atomic age. Source: blog.nuclearsecrecy.com 2014/05/23 oppenheimer-gita; theconversation.com 'Now I am become Death' explained.

question: Robert Oppenheimer code-named the first atomic bomb test Trinity and held it on a bare stretch of the New Mexico desert in July 1945. Old travellers had given that ground a grim Spanish name, Jornada del Muerto. What does the name mean in English?
answer: Journey of the Dead Man
choices: Journey of the Dead Man
Valley of the Burning Sky
Pass of the Hanged Men
Plain of the Black Wind
context: Jornada del Muerto -- 'Journey of the Dead Man' (or 'Journey of Death') -- was the old name for the desolate basin where the bomb was tested at 5:29 a.m. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_(nuclear_test); DOE energy.gov/lm/trinity-site.

question: I. I. Rabi came last to the pool his fellow scientists ran at the Trinity test in July 1945, each of them betting on how big the blast would be, and he had to take the only number left. When the bomb went off, how did that guess do?
answer: His leftover guess was almost exact, and he won.
choices: His leftover guess was almost exact, and he won.
His leftover guess was far too low, and he lost.
His leftover guess was far too high, and he lost.
His leftover guess missed by half, and he lost.
context: Rabi arrived last and took the only number left -- 18 kilotons of TNT -- which turned out closest, so he won the pool. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_(nuclear_test).

question: Richard Feynman, a young physicist at the secret Los Alamos laboratory in New Mexico, grew bored and taught himself to open the safes that held the atomic bomb's most guarded secrets. The combination of one safe was 27-18-28. Those are the first digits of which famous number?
answer: The math constant e (2.71828)
choices: The math constant e (2.71828)
The constant pi (3.14159)
The golden ratio (1.61803)
The speed of light (299,792)
context: The combination 27-18-28 matched the first digits of the mathematical constant e (2.71828). Feynman later left a teasing note inside a locked cabinet signed 'Feynman the safecracker.' Source: openculture.com Feynman cracked the safes; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Feynman.

question: Kenneth Bainbridge, the physicist who directed the Trinity test, watched the first atomic bomb explode in the New Mexico desert in July 1945. Then he turned to J. Robert Oppenheimer and summed up the moment in seven blunt words. What did Bainbridge say?
answer: Now we are all sons of bitches.
choices: Now we are all sons of bitches.
God help us for what we've done.
There is no going back from this.
We have opened the gates of hell.
context: Bainbridge's blunt line captured the dread many scientists felt at what they had created. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_(nuclear_test); blog.nuclearsecrecy.com 2014/05/23 oppenheimer-gita.

question: Klaus Fuchs, a brilliant German-born refugee physicist, worked at Los Alamos on one of the hardest problems of the plutonium bomb. But Fuchs kept a secret of his own the whole time he worked there. What was he secretly doing?
answer: Handing the bomb's secrets to the Soviet Union.
choices: Handing the bomb's secrets to the Soviet Union.
Selling lab equipment on the black market.
Sabotaging the bomb's design to slow it down.
Reporting his coworkers to the FBI for disloyalty.
context: Fuchs passed atomic secrets to the USSR through a courier named Harry Gold; he was not caught until 1949, when the secret Venona project decrypted Soviet cables. He admitted his leaks may have sped up the Soviet bomb by at least a year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klaus_Fuchs; britannica.com Klaus Fuchs.

question: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg went to the electric chair in June 1953 at Sing Sing prison. A court had found them guilty of passing atomic secrets to the Soviet Union. What grim distinction do the Rosenbergs still hold in American history?
answer: The only U.S. civilians ever executed for peacetime spying.
choices: The only U.S. civilians ever executed for peacetime spying.
The first married couple ever tried in a federal court.
The last prisoners ever put to death at Sing Sing.
The youngest spies the FBI had ever arrested.
context: The Rosenbergs were executed June 19, 1953 -- the only U.S. civilians ever put to death for peacetime espionage. Years later Ethel's brother David Greenglass admitted he had lied on the stand about her typing the spy notes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_and_Ethel_Rosenberg; fbi.gov Atom Spy Case Rosenbergs.

question: Frank Oppenheimer stood beside his brother Robert at the Trinity test in July 1945. Twenty years later Robert gave the world a haunting line from the Bhagavad Gita about that moment, but Frank remembered his brother's words at the time as far plainer. What did Frank say Robert really said?
answer: It worked.
choices: It worked.
It's done.
It's over.
Good God.
context: Frank Oppenheimer recalled his brother's real words at Trinity were simply 'It worked.' The famous 'Now I am become Death' line came from a haggard 1965 NBC interview, two decades later. Source: blog.nuclearsecrecy.com 2014/05/23 oppenheimer-gita (Restricted Data / Alex Wellerstein).

question: A peasant family on a northern European manor led its two oxen out to plough, but the great iron-shod plough that broke the heavy, wet clay was far too much for two beasts to drag. How many oxen did the plough need?
answer: Eight oxen
choices: Eight oxen
Two oxen
Four oxen
Six oxen
context: The team of eight meant neighbors had to pool their oxen together just to plough at all -- a single family literally could not break the ground alone, which is one reason peasant farming was so communal. Source: https://spartacus-educational.com/MEDfarming.htm

question: A serf on a manor in medieval Europe walked past his own strips of land to labour without pay on the demesne, his lord's own share of the manor. His own crops had to wait until the lord's work was done. How much of this unpaid work did the lord claim from him?
answer: Two or three days, every week
choices: Two or three days, every week
One afternoon each fortnight
A single day at harvest time
One full month each autumn
context: This was called week-work: two or three days every week (and even more during harvest) had to be spent working the lord's own land -- the demesne, the slice the lord kept for himself, about 35-40% of the manor -- before the serf could touch his own crops. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Manorialism/

question: A serf's family buried him on a manor in medieval Europe and then owed the lord a death-tax, the heriot, paid with one particular thing the dead man had owned. The church often claimed a second one as well. What did the heriot take?
answer: His single best ox or cow
choices: His single best ox or cow
A year of his stored grain
His cottage and garden plot
A fixed sum of silver pennies
context: The lord took the best beast as heriot and the church frequently took the second-best on top of it -- so the family lost its two best animals just because the head of the house had died. Source: https://historicalbritainblog.com/the-english-manor-part-3-the-burden-of-the-serf/

question: Abbot Richard of St Albans seized about eighty hand-mills that the townspeople had hidden around 1331, for they were bound to grind their grain at his mill and hand over part of the flour. Then he did something to the captured millstones to humble the whole town for good. What did he do with them?
answer: Cemented them into the abbey parlour floor
choices: Cemented them into the abbey parlour floor
Paraded them through the market square
Walled them up inside the gatehouse
Hung them on chains above the mill door
context: Abbot Richard had the eighty millstones cemented into the floor of the abbey parlour as a permanent humiliation -- a paved declaration that no one in St Albans could grind corn anywhere except at his mill. Source: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13642529.2025.2473858

question: The townsfolk of St Albans rose with the Peasants' Revolt when it reached their town on 12 July 1381, and they came for the millstones their abbot had taken from them fifty years before. What did they do with the stones?
answer: Smashed them to bits and passed the fragments round as trophies
choices: Smashed them to bits and passed the fragments round as trophies
Carried them home to grind their own grain again
Hurled them through the abbey's stained-glass windows
Stacked them into a monument outside the abbey gate
context: The townsfolk tore the millstones back up out of the abbey floor, smashed them into small pieces, and passed the fragments around like trophies of their lost right to grind their own grain. Source: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13642529.2025.2473858

question: A village in medieval Europe sowed winter grain in one field, beans and peas in the next, and left the third to rest. Knowing no chemistry, the villagers had stumbled onto real agricultural science. What was the bean-and-pea field doing for the soil the grain had worn out?
answer: Putting nitrogen back into the soil
choices: Putting nitrogen back into the soil
Killing the weeds left by the grain
Draining the standing rainwater away
Loosening the soil for deeper roots
context: Legume crops like beans and peas return nitrogen to the soil that grain crops strip out, while the resting fallow field got grazed and manured by livestock -- so planting beans wasn't just for food, it healed the dirt. This three-field rotation and the heavy plough spread across northern Europe in the 9th-11th centuries, and the extra food lines up with a measurable jump in population and the growth of towns around AD 900-1000. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-field_system

question: An old griot sat in a Mande village and sang a family's history from memory, line by line: its births, its deaths, its wars. As he sang, he plucked a 21-string harp-lute whose body was half a gourd covered in cowhide. What was the instrument called?
answer: The kora
choices: The kora
The sitar
The lyre
The dulcimer
context: The kora's 21 strings were traditionally made from fishing line, strung over a calabash-gourd body covered with cow skin. A griot (called jeli or jali in Mandinka) is a living library who carries unwritten history line by line. Source: Britannica, 'griot'; web.cocc.edu, Mali Empire & Griot Traditions.

question: Amadou Hampate Ba, the Malian writer, told a conference in 1960 what is lost when an old griot dies, for the history he carries lives only in his memory. A famous Mandinka saying puts the loss in one image. When a griot dies, the saying goes, it is as if what has happened?
answer: A library has burned to the ground
choices: A library has burned to the ground
A bridge has been swept away
A well has run dry
A king has lost his crown
context: The Malian writer Amadou Hampate Ba gave the most famous version of the idea to the UNESCO General Conference on 1 December 1960: 'In Africa, when an old man dies, it's a library burning.' Because the history was never written down, it dies with the man who carried it. Source: our-ancestories.com, 'Griots: Living Historians and Musicians of West Africa'; UNESCO Courier, 'Missive to Youth.'

question: Mansa Musa crossed the Sahara in 1324 at the head of a pilgrimage caravan that may have numbered 60,000 people and stretched for miles. Behind the king plodded a train of 80 to 100 camels, and each animal bore some 300 pounds of a single cargo. What was it?
answer: Gold dust
choices: Gold dust
Sacks of salt
Rolls of silk
Jars of honey
context: Each of the roughly 80 to 100 camels carried about 300 pounds (135 kg) of gold dust. The whole caravan numbered around 60,000 people. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansa_Musa and worldhistory.org/Mansa_Musa_I.

question: Abraham Cresques, a mapmaker on Majorca, painted Mansa Musa on the great Catalan Atlas of 1375, crowned and enthroned at the heart of West Africa, a scepter in one hand and the other held out toward a rider on a camel. What did that hand hold out?
answer: A large nugget of gold
choices: A large nugget of gold
A jeweled silver chalice
A rolled-up treaty scroll
A small caged songbird
context: The 1375 Catalan Atlas shows Musa enthroned with crown, scepter and orb, holding out a big gold nugget toward a turbaned camel-rider crossing the Sahara. The caption calls him 'the richest and noblest of all these lands.' This put Mali on the European map fifty years after his hajj. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_Atlas.

question: The emirs and officials of the sultan's court in Cairo each received a load of gold from Mansa Musa of Mali when he passed through on his pilgrimage of 1324. He gave so freely that his gifts did what a single traveller almost never does: they shook a whole region's economy. What did his giving do?
answer: It crashed the price of gold across Egypt
choices: It crashed the price of gold across Egypt
It emptied the city's grain warehouses
It started a war between two emirs
It doubled the wages of every soldier
context: The scholar al-Umari wrote that Musa 'flooded Cairo with his benefactions,' leaving 'no court emir nor holder of a royal office without the gift of a load of gold.' So much gold poured in that its value collapsed -- one of the rare times one man's giving moved a regional economy. Source: worldhistorycommons.org/al-umaris-account-mansa-musas-visit-cairo (al-Umari).

question: Builders in Timbuktu raised a great mosque, the Djinguereber, for Mansa Musa after he came home from his pilgrimage around 1325. They had no stone quarries anywhere near the city on the southern edge of the Sahara. What did they build the mosque from?
answer: Mud brick
choices: Mud brick
White marble
Cedar timber shipped from Lebanon
Cut sandstone blocks
context: Musa is credited with commissioning the Djinguereber Mosque at Timbuktu around 1325-1327, built in mud brick. His mosque at Gao was said to use burnt bricks -- a building material not used in West Africa before. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djinguereber_Mosque.

question: Mansa Musa, by a later legend, marked every Friday of his long pilgrimage across the Sahara in the same way, wherever on the road the day found him. Storytellers passed the tale down; no record proves it. What does the legend say he did?
answer: Had a brand-new mosque built on the spot
choices: Had a brand-new mosque built on the spot
Freed one prisoner from his caravan
Wrote a verse of the Quran by hand
Fed every beggar in the nearest town
context: Legend (not forensic fact) holds that Musa had a new mosque built every Friday of his pilgrimage, wherever he happened to be -- a tale showing how grandly his journey was remembered. Source: britannica.com on Musa I of Mali and ebsco.com research-starters on his pilgrimage.

question: The officials of al-Nasir Muhammad, the Mamluk sultan, told Mansa Musa to kneel and kiss the ground before their master when he reached Cairo in 1324. Musa refused at first. Then, on a companion's whispered advice, he bowed, but he declared aloud that he was bowing to someone else entirely. What did he say?
answer: 'I make obeisance to God who created me!'
choices: 'I make obeisance to God who created me!'
'I bow only to the mansa of Mali!'
'Let the sultan kneel first before me!'
'I kneel for the gold I have given!'
context: After a companion whispered to him, Musa bowed but proclaimed 'I make obeisance to God who created me!' -- making clear his reverence was for God, not the sultan. Source: worldhistorycommons.org/al-umaris-account-mansa-musas-visit-cairo (al-Umari).

question: Mansa Musa showered Cairo's officials with gold on his pilgrimage of 1324. On the way back across the desert, the great king himself ran short of cash, and the way he found the money helped lift the price of gold in Egypt. What did he do?
answer: He borrowed gold back from Cairo's merchants at steep interest
choices: He borrowed gold back from Cairo's merchants at steep interest
He sold off half the camels in his caravan
He melted down the golden staffs of his guards
He demanded tribute from every town he passed
context: Al-Umari, Ibn Battuta and Ibn al-Dawadari all report that a cash-short Musa borrowed gold back at a high rate on the return -- pulling gold out of Cairo's market, which the sources say helped its value recover. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansa_Musa.

question: Al-Umari collected stories in Cairo around 1340 about Mansa Musa's earlier visit. Before Musa came, he learned, a mithqal of gold, a standard weight, had never sold for less than 25 silver dirhams. What had become of that price since Musa's visit?
answer: It dropped to 22 dirhams or below and stayed cheap for about twelve years
choices: It dropped to 22 dirhams or below and stayed cheap for about twelve years
It bounced back above 25 dirhams within a single week
It was fixed by the sultan at exactly 30 dirhams
It vanished from the records and was never quoted again
context: Al-Umari recorded the exact collapse: the mithqal, never below 25 dirhams before, fell to 22 or lower and stayed cheap 'for about twelve years' from all the gold Musa poured into Egypt. Source: worldhistorycommons.org/al-umaris-account-mansa-musas-visit-cairo (al-Umari).

question: Mansa Musa explained to the Egyptians how he had become king, and al-Umari, a scholar, later wrote the tale down. The king before him, Musa said, would not believe the ocean to the west had no end, and he launched 200 ships to seek its far side. Just one returned. What did its captain say had swallowed the rest?
answer: A river with a powerful current
choices: A river with a powerful current
A wall of black storm clouds
An island of living fire
A serpent longer than the fleet
context: By Musa's testimony (recorded by al-Umari, and treated as legend), the lone returning captain described 'a river with a powerful current' in the open ocean that swallowed the rest. The king then sailed off himself with 2,000 ships and was never seen again -- 'and so I became king in my own right.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_voyage_of_the_predecessor_of_Mansa_Musa (al-Umari).

question: Musa of Mali crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage in 1324 with thousands of followers and a train of camels laden with gold. Before his own name he carried a title in the Mandinka language: mansa. What did the word mean?
answer: King or emperor
choices: King or emperor
Holy pilgrim
Keeper of the gold mines
Master merchant
context: 'Mansa' meant king or emperor in the Mandinka language, so 'Mansa Musa' simply means 'King Musa.' He ruled Mali at the height of its wealth and reach. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansa_Musa

question: A huge caravan set out across the Sahara Desert in 1324 behind Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, on the hajj, the pilgrimage every Muslim hopes to make at least once. To which holy city was he bound?
answer: Mecca
choices: Mecca
Cairo
Timbuktu
Baghdad
context: The Hajj is the journey to Mecca in Arabia. Musa's roughly 2,700-mile trek made him the first ruler from sub-Saharan Africa to become widely known across Europe and the Middle East. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansa_Musa

question: Horsemen waving red-and-gold royal banners rode behind the men who led Mansa Musa's pilgrimage caravan into each city on the road in 1324. Five hundred men walked ahead of the king, and every one of them carried the same thing. What was it?
answer: A gold staff
choices: A gold staff
A silver trumpet
A sack of grain
A clay water jug
context: By one account each of the 500 carried a gold staff weighing about 6 pounds (2.7 kg) -- a slow-moving wall of gold announcing the king's approach. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Mansa_Musa_I/

question: Mansa Musa ordered the Djinguereber Mosque raised at Timbuktu after his pilgrimage of 1324, built not of stone but of earth. Nearly seven centuries have passed since then. What has become of the mosque?
answer: It still stands today
choices: It still stands today
It melted away in the rains
It was replaced by a stone one
Only its foundations remain
context: The Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu, built of mud-brick called 'banco,' has been standing for nearly seven centuries. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Mansa_Musa_I/

question: Mansa Musa guarded the secret of his real gold mines, at Bambuk and Bure, though West Africa supplied some two-thirds of the medieval Mediterranean's gold. To keep outsiders away from the mines, he spread a wild rumor about where Mali's gold came from. What did he claim?
answer: That gold grew like a plant in his land
choices: That gold grew like a plant in his land
That a dragon guarded a golden lake
That gold rained from the desert sky
That his ancestors forged it by magic
context: Mali's real gold was panned and mined in the regions of Bambuk and Bure; roughly two-thirds of the gold circulating in the medieval Mediterranean came from West Africa. Musa's 'gold grows like a plant' rumor helped keep the mines secret. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansa_Musa

question: Hadrien Collet, a historian, has pushed back on the claim that Mansa Musa was the richest person who ever lived. The old maps and writers, Collet and others point out, called Musa the richest only of his own part of the world. What do these historians say is the truth about his fortune?
answer: It is impossible to calculate
choices: It is impossible to calculate
He was poorer than most kings
His gold all belonged to Egypt
He invented his own fortune
context: The Catalan Atlas called Musa richest in 'these lands' -- a regional claim. The modern 'richest in history' headline is a later exaggeration; scholars say his true wealth cannot be measured. The point isn't that he wasn't staggeringly rich, but that the viral number is made up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_Atlas

question: Mansa Musa told the Egyptians how he had come to the throne, and the story survives as legend. The king before him, Musa said, refused to believe the Atlantic Ocean had no end, so he gave up his crown and set out across the open ocean with some 2,000 ships. What became of that king and his fleet, by Musa's account?
answer: They sailed west and never returned
choices: They sailed west and never returned
They reached a new land and sent gold home
They were wrecked in a storm near shore
They turned back at the desert's edge
context: Musa said his predecessor (often called Abu Bakr II) vanished into the Atlantic, which is how Musa took the throne. Modern historians doubt the legend and suspect Musa may instead have deposed him -- so it is told as a story, not proven fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansa_Musa

question: Mao Zedong ordered all of China in 1958 to wipe out sparrows, because the birds ate grain seed. Whole cities turned on the sparrows with one weapon that left them falling dead from the sky. What did the people do?
answer: They banged pots, pans and gongs for hours so the birds could never land and rest
choices: They banged pots, pans and gongs for hours so the birds could never land and rest
They poisoned every grain field across the countryside with deadly bait
They burned down the forests where the sparrows built their nests each spring
They released thousands of trained hawks to hunt the sparrows from above
context: This was the Four Pests campaign, launched 12 February 1958. Across whole cities people hammered pots, pans, gongs, drums and washbasins so no sparrow could ever land; the exhausted birds dropped dead from sheer fatigue. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Pests_campaign

question: Mao Zedong launched the Great Leap Forward in 1958 to make China outproduce Britain in steel, and he told peasants to build small backyard furnaces right in their fields. The peasants had no real scrap iron on hand. What did they feed into the fires to melt down?
answer: Their own cooking woks, pots, knives and iron farm tools
choices: Their own cooking woks, pots, knives and iron farm tools
Old coins and gold jewelry collected from every household
Iron rails pulled up from the abandoned railway lines
Scrap armour and cannon left over from China's old wars
context: Families even fed their wooden furniture into the fires for fuel. What came out was brittle, useless pig-iron slag that no factory could use, while the melted-down tools meant nobody could farm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backyard_furnace

question: Insects swarmed over China's fields once Mao Zedong's campaign of 1958 had wiped out the sparrows, and they devoured far more of the crops than the birds ever had. What did China's Communist leaders have to do around 1960 to undo the disaster?
answer: Imported crates of live sparrows from the Soviet Union
choices: Imported crates of live sparrows from the Soviet Union
Sprayed the fields with insecticide bought from America
Ordered every commune to breed frogs and toads in its ponds
Paid peasants a cash bounty for each locust they caught
context: The ornithologist Tso-hsin Cheng convinced Party leaders that sparrows eat insects as well as grain. China then had to import about 250,000 live sparrows from the Soviet Union to restock the skies. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Pests_campaign

question: Mao Zedong expected almost everyone in China to carry one small book everywhere and recite from it daily. Misquoting it could bring punishment, and around a billion copies were printed. What was this book?
answer: The Little Red Book of quotations from Chairman Mao
choices: The Little Red Book of quotations from Chairman Mao
A pocket Bible handed out by the Communist Party
A book of war poems written by Chairman Mao
A handbook of farming rules for the people's communes
context: Quotations from Chairman Mao, the 'Little Red Book,' hit roughly a billion copies by 1966, with total printings estimated up to 5 billion in 500 editions and 50 languages, making it one of the most-printed books in history. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Quotations-from-Chairman-Mao-Tse-tung

question: Communist Party officials all over China faked giant harvests to please Mao Zedong during his Great Leap Forward. One propaganda photo showed a young boy standing on top of a wheat field, the stalks supposedly grown so thick that they held up his whole weight. How was the photo really faked?
answer: The boy was standing on a table hidden under the wheat
choices: The boy was standing on a table hidden under the wheat
The wheat had been glued upright onto wooden boards
The boy was a painted cutout added into the picture
The stalks were giant fakes made of bamboo and paper
context: Communes inflated each other's harvest numbers to hit Mao's quotas, and propaganda images like this 'proved' the lie. It was later revealed the boy was simply standing on a hidden table. Source: https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/sub6/item69.html

question: Peng Dehuai, China's defence minister, was the one man at a Party conference at Lushan in July 1959 who dared tell Mao Zedong that the Great Leap Forward was starving the countryside. Instead of easing the famine, how did Mao answer Peng's honesty?
answer: Mao purged him and branded him a 'right-opportunist'
choices: Mao purged him and branded him a 'right-opportunist'
Mao thanked him and quietly slowed the campaign down
Mao promoted him to keep him close and keep him silent
Mao ignored him and let the meeting move along
context: Mao struck Peng down at the July 1959 Lushan Conference. It was a warning to every other official that telling the truth about the famine was career suicide, or worse, so the lies kept flowing. Source: https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/sub6/item69.html

question: Mao Zedong told a secret meeting of officials in Shanghai in March 1959, as the famine spread, that the state should take as much as a third of all the grain. According to Party archives quoted by the historian Frank Dikotter, what did Mao say about the deaths that would follow?
answer: 'It is better to let half of the people die so the other half can eat their fill'
choices: 'It is better to let half of the people die so the other half can eat their fill'
'A revolution can never be made without breaking a few of the eggs'
'The grain belongs to the state before it belongs to any one man'
'A little hunger today will make all the people strong tomorrow'
context: Mao said this at a secret meeting in Shanghai on 25 March 1959, quoted from Party archives by Frank Dikotter in 'Mao's Great Famine.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao's_Great_Famine

question: Mao Zedong drove China into the deadliest famine ever recorded with his Great Leap Forward, and roughly 30 to 45 million Chinese starved to death. Even as they died, his government had millions of tons of grain in hand. What happened to that grain in 1959 and 1960?
answer: It was shipped abroad and sold or given away as foreign aid
choices: It was shipped abroad and sold or given away as foreign aid
It was locked inside army warehouses for a coming war
It was left to rot because there were no trains to move it
It was burned to keep the price high inside of China
context: China exported roughly 7 million tons of grain in 1959-60, sold for hard currency and sent as foreign aid, while its own people died. By one estimate that grain could have saved as many as 16 million lives. Source: https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/sub6/item69.html

question: Peasants of Xinyang, in Henan province, died at the very doors of the local Communist Party granaries around 1960, at the height of Mao Zedong's Great Leap famine. About one in eight of the region's people starved. What was inside those granaries?
answer: They were full of grain that officials were forbidden to hand out
choices: They were full of grain that officials were forbidden to hand out
They were completely empty and had been for many months
They held only the seed grain saved for the next planting
They were full of grain set aside for the city officials
context: About 1 million of Xinyang's 8.5 million people died. Officials faced death for opening the full granaries, so peasants starved at the very doors; survivors said the dying cried out, 'Communist Party, Chairman Mao, save us.' Source: https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/sub6/entry-7457.html

question: Mao Zedong turned gangs of teenage Red Guards loose in the streets in 1966, when he launched the Cultural Revolution, with orders to smash the 'Four Olds.' What four things were the Red Guards told to destroy?
answer: Old ideas, old culture, old customs and old habits
choices: Old ideas, old culture, old customs and old habits
Old temples, old books, old paintings and old coins
Old landlords, old priests, old teachers and old officers
Old laws, old taxes, old armies and old borders
context: Mao and Lin Biao set the Red Guards, mostly students aged 14 to 25, loose to attack anything tied to China's past. In one Shanghai district they tore down about 93 percent of the shop signs alone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Olds

question: Victims knelt before screaming crowds at the Red Guards' struggle sessions, wearing high paper dunce caps, and were made to hold one agonizing pose for hours, arms wrenched up and back while their heads were shoved down. What did the Red Guards call that pose?
answer: The 'jet plane'
choices: The 'jet plane'
The 'iron chair'
The 'praying monk'
The 'broken bow'
context: Victims at struggle sessions were also forced to hang a placard with their own name crossed out. Even the President of China would be 'jet-planed' at these sessions before being left to die. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Struggle_session

question: One victim of the Cultural Revolution died untreated in a Kaifeng prison cell in 1969, after he had been branded China's chief 'capitalist roader' and battered at struggle sessions. Only a year earlier this man had held the highest office in the land. Who was he?
answer: Liu Shaoqi, the president of China
choices: Liu Shaoqi, the president of China
Zhou Enlai, the premier of China
Lin Biao, the marshal of the army
Deng Xiaoping, a later leader of China
context: Liu Shaoqi was President of the People's Republic and once Mao's chosen successor. He died of untreated diabetes and pneumonia on 12 November 1969; the order from Beijing was to 'maintain life, await further struggle.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Shaoqi

question: One city teenager sent 'Down to the Countryside' by Mao Zedong's Party dug and hauled for years in a poor village, one of some 17 million young people uprooted from 1968 at the cost of their schooling. Decades later he rose to rule China. Who was he?
answer: Xi Jinping
choices: Xi Jinping
Deng Xiaoping
Jiang Zemin
Hu Jintao
context: Roughly 17 million 'sent-down youth' were uprooted between 1968 and 1978, losing their educations to farm labour. Among them was a teenage Xi Jinping, who decades later became the ruler of China. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_to_the_Countryside_Movement

question: William Marbury sued when his signed commission as a justice of the peace never reached him. The chief justice who decided Marbury v. Madison in 1803 had a hidden tie to the case from his days in the outgoing government. Who was he?
answer: John Marshall, the outgoing Secretary of State who had failed to deliver it
choices: John Marshall, the outgoing Secretary of State who had failed to deliver it
James Madison, the new Secretary of State sworn to enforce it
Thomas Jefferson, the incoming President who opposed it
John Adams, the outgoing President who had signed it
context: John Marshall had been Adams's Secretary of State and never got Marbury's commission delivered before Jefferson's people took over. Then, as the new Chief Justice, Marshall sat in judgment on the lawsuit over his own undelivered paperwork. Source: https://www.fjc.gov/history/cases/cases-that-shaped-the-federal-courts/marbury-v-madison

question: The chief justice who heard Marbury v. Madison in 1803 ruled that William Marbury truly deserved his commission and had been wronged. Yet he held that the Court could not order it delivered, because the law letting Marbury sue there clashed with the Constitution. In giving up that small power, what far greater one did the Court claim?
answer: To strike down an act of Congress as void
choices: To strike down an act of Congress as void
To order the President to appoint new judges
To remove a sitting Secretary of State from office
To rewrite a law that Congress had passed badly
context: This is judicial review — the authority of the Supreme Court to declare a law passed by Congress unconstitutional and refuse to enforce it. Marbury v. Madison was the first time the Court struck down an act of Congress (Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789) as void. Marshall: 'No legislative act... contrary to the Constitution, can be valid.' Source: https://www.fjc.gov/history/cases/cases-that-shaped-the-federal-courts/marbury-v-madison

question: Friends gathered at Marco Polo's bedside in Venice in 1324 as the old traveller lay dying. For his soul's sake, they begged him to confess that his book of wonders about China was full of lies. By tradition, what did he answer?
answer: "I have not told half of what I saw."
choices: "I have not told half of what I saw."
"Forgive me, for I have deceived you all."
"Burn the book and forget my name."
"The Khan himself will avenge these words."
context: On his deathbed (he died Jan 8, 1324), friends urged Marco Polo to confess his book was full of lies; he refused with this line. Recorded as tradition, so it is told as legend, not a verified quote. Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Marco_Polo ; 'The Travels of Marco Polo, the Venetian' (J.M. Dent, 1926).

question: Marco Polo watched the people of Cathay dig lumps of black stone out of beds in the mountains and burn them to heat their homes, and the lumps stayed alight all night. Polo had grown up knowing only firewood. What were the black stones?
answer: Coal
choices: Coal
Peat
Amber
Sulfur
context: Polo amazed Europe by describing coal, then unknown to most Europeans. His chapter was titled 'Concerning the Black Stones That Are Dug in Cathay, and Are Burnt for Fuel,' and he marveled that lumps kindled at night were 'still alight in the morning.' Source: https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/4sub8/entry-5456.html

question: Captured when Venice lost a sea battle to Genoa, Marco Polo sat in a Genoese prison in 1298. He never wrote down his own famous book. He told his adventures aloud, and another man put them on paper. Who was that writer?
answer: A fellow prisoner, the romance-writer Rustichello of Pisa
choices: A fellow prisoner, the romance-writer Rustichello of Pisa
A monk sent by the Pope to record him
His own father, Niccolo Polo
A scribe in the service of Kublai Khan
context: Captured after the naval defeat, Marco Polo dictated his travels to his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa, a writer of Arthurian romances, who wrote it all down (Genoa prison, 1298-1299). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Travels_of_Marco_Polo ; https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/polo-marco/

question: Kublai Khan bought what he wanted across his empire with flat sheets of mulberry bark that bore his red seal, and anyone who refused them faced execution. Marco Polo had a striking way to explain how the Khan could spend bark as if it were treasure. What did Polo say the Khan possessed?
answer: The secret of the alchemists
choices: The secret of the alchemists
The blessing of the eternal Heaven
A mountain of buried gold
The loyalty of every merchant
context: Polo described Kublai Khan's paper money, made from mulberry bark stamped in red vermilion, and said the Khan thereby 'possessed the secret of the alchemists' because he could make money out of tree bark. Source: https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/4sub8/entry-5456.html ; https://fee.org/articles/marco-polo-on-money/

question: Guglielmo Marconi and his helper, George Kemp, stood on Signal Hill in Newfoundland on 12 December 1901, flying a kite that held their wire aloft. They listened for a signal sent some 2,000 miles across the Atlantic from Cornwall. Faint taps spelled one Morse letter, over and over. Which letter was it?
answer: S
choices: S
E
T
A
context: Marconi heard the letter 'S' — three faint dots in Morse. They chose 'S' on purpose: three quick dots were the easiest pattern to pick out of the Atlantic static at extreme range. (An earlier balloon antenna had blown away in the gale, so the kite was the improvised fix to get the wire high.) Some later scientists doubted the 1901 reception was even physically possible at that wavelength and wondered if Marconi heard lightning static instead of the real signal — an honest doubt, while the milestone still stands. Source: https://ethw.org/Milestones:Reception_of_Transatlantic_Radio_Signals,_1901

question: Wireless operators on ships far out at sea sat at their sets on Christmas Eve 1906, expecting nothing but the clicking Morse code that was all radio had ever carried. Then something none of them had heard before came through their headphones from Reginald Fessenden's station at Brant Rock, Massachusetts. What did they hear?
answer: A human voice and a violin
choices: A human voice and a violin
A faster string of Morse code
A ship's bell ringing the hour
A burst of crackling static
context: Fessenden made the leap from code to sound: he played Handel's 'Largo' on a phonograph, played 'O Holy Night' on his own violin and sang, and read from the Bible — the first broadcast of voice and music. Men used to hearing only clicks suddenly had a human voice in their ears, hundreds of miles out at sea. Source: https://ethw.org/Milestones:First_Wireless_Radio_Broadcast_by_Reginald_A._Fessenden,_1906

question: Hadrian, the old emperor, was charmed by the seriousness of a boy named Marcus Annius Verus, the future Marcus Aurelius, whose family name meant true. Hadrian gave the boy a nickname that stuck. What did he call him?
answer: Verissimus, 'the truest'
choices: Verissimus, 'the truest'
Optimus, 'the best'
Probus, 'the upright'
Pius, 'the dutiful'
context: Hadrian punned on the boy's family name Verus ('true') to call him Verissimus, 'the truest' or 'most truthful' - a sign of how seriously honest the young Marcus already seemed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius

question: Copyists added a two-word heading, 'Ta eis heauton,' to the notebook Marcus Aurelius had left without a title. He had written its reflections in private, never meaning anyone else to read them. What does the heading mean?
answer: 'To Himself'
choices: 'To Himself'
'Notes by Night'
'A Soldier's Diary'
'The Emperor's Book'
context: 'Ta eis heauton' (the Greek heading later added by copyists) literally means 'Things to Himself' or 'To Himself.' Marcus wrote it as a private notebook with no real title, never meaning anyone else to read it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations

question: Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor whose native tongue was Latin, kept a private notebook of reflections on his long campaigns, writing only for himself. It survived to become the Meditations, one of the most famous works of philosophy, yet he did not write it in his everyday tongue. In which language did he write it?
answer: Greek
choices: Greek
Latin
Egyptian
Aramaic
context: Though he was Rome's emperor and a native Latin speaker, Marcus wrote the Meditations in Greek - the language of philosophy in the ancient world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations

question: On Rome's northern frontier around AD 170, Marcus Aurelius was fighting a long war against Germanic tribes when he wrote part of his private notebook, the Meditations. A note in Book 1 records the spot: 'in the country of the Quadi, at the Granua,' a river on the empire's edge. Where was the ruler of the Roman world when he wrote it?
answer: An army tent at the front
choices: An army tent at the front
A captured enemy hill-fort
A torch-lit riverside barge
A frontier supply depot
context: A note in Book 1 records that Marcus wrote 'in the country of the Quadi, at the Granua' - a war tent on the Hron river in modern Slovakia; Book 2 was written at Carnuntum, a fort on the Danube frontier. The most powerful man alive wrote his philosophy on campaign. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations

question: Rusticus, a philosopher, lent Marcus Aurelius the teachings of Epictetus, a teacher who had been born a slave, and Marcus counted it the finest gift he ever received. That loaned book carried one school of philosophy from a man once enslaved to the master of the Roman world. Which school was it?
answer: Stoicism
choices: Stoicism
Epicureanism
Cynicism
Platonism
context: Marcus calls Rusticus's loan of Epictetus's discourses the most important gift of his life. Epictetus, born a slave, was a great teacher of Stoicism; that loaned book carried Stoicism from a slave to the emperor - the Athens-to-Rome line of the tradition. Source: iep.utm.edu/marcus-aurelius

question: Marcus Aurelius had come to the throne as an adopted heir, the last of Rome's Five Good Emperors, each chosen on merit rather than by blood. He broke the custom by handing the empire to his own son instead, who became one of Rome's worst emperors. Who was the son?
answer: Commodus
choices: Commodus
Lucius Verus
Avidius Cassius
Hadrian
context: Marcus ended the merit-by-adoption streak of the Five Good Emperors by leaving the throne to his own son, Commodus, remembered as one of Rome's worst rulers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius

question: Marcus Aurelius faced an empty treasury, drained by plague and endless war, and he would not squeeze his suffering people with new taxes. Instead he sold palace treasures at auction in Trajan's Forum to pay his soldiers. What did he put up for sale?
answer: His own wife's silk-and-gold robes
choices: His own wife's silk-and-gold robes
Old Hadrian's marble garden statues
The crown jewels of conquered kings
Slaves taken in the German wars
context: Rather than tax his plague-stricken people harder, Marcus auctioned off imperial treasures in Trajan's Forum - gold and crystal vessels, jewels from Hadrian's private sanctum, and even his own wife's silk-and-gold robes - to fund his army for the German wars. An imperial yard sale. Source: medium.com/of-pasta-and-plagues

question: The soldiers of the Thundering Legion stood parched and trapped in Marcus Aurelius's war against the Quadi when rain suddenly poured down on them. The historian Cassius Dio describes what the men did as it fell. What was it?
answer: They drank and fought at the same time
choices: They drank and fought at the same time
They threw down their shields to surrender
They built a dam to trap the floodwater
They fled the field under cover of the storm
context: Cassius Dio writes that the parched soldiers 'turned their faces upwards and received the water in their mouths,' caught rain in their shields and helmets, and 'drank and fought at the same time' - some gulping rainwater mixed with blood from their own wounds - while hail and thunderbolts struck the enemy. Source: livius.org - Cassius Dio on the Rain Miracle

question: Cassius Dio, the historian, put the rain that saved Marcus Aurelius's trapped legion down to an Egyptian magician in the camp, Harnouphis. Tertullian, a North African writer, told the story differently. What did Tertullian say brought the rain?
answer: The prayers of the legion's Christian soldiers
choices: The prayers of the legion's Christian soldiers
A sacrifice burned on the altar of Jupiter
A vow Marcus swore to the goddess Minerva
A spell cast by a captured Quadi shaman
context: Cassius Dio credited an Egyptian magician named Harnouphis, who summoned the god Mercury; Tertullian claimed the storm answered the prayers of Christian soldiers in the legion. Same storm, rival miracle stories. Source: livius.org - Cassius Dio on the Rain Miracle

question: Avidius Cassius, a Roman general, rebelled and claimed the throne on a false rumor that Marcus Aurelius had died, and his own officers soon killed him. A centurion brought the rebel's head to Marcus. How did Marcus respond?
answer: He refused to look at it and had it buried
choices: He refused to look at it and had it buried
He had it displayed on the Forum gates
He sent it back to Cassius's family in disgrace
He kept it as proof of the traitor's fate
context: Cassius's revolt lasted three months and six days before his officers killed him. When the centurion brought his head, Marcus refused even to look at it and ordered it buried; sources say he had hoped Cassius would be taken alive so he could show mercy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avidius_Cassius

question: Medieval Christians left one great bronze of Marcus Aurelius on horseback standing, while some twenty other bronze emperors were melted down for coin. They spared it only because they took the rider for a different, beloved ruler. Whom did they think it showed?
answer: Constantine, the first Christian emperor
choices: Constantine, the first Christian emperor
Julius Caesar, the first dictator
Augustus, the first Roman emperor
Charlemagne, the first Holy Roman Emperor
context: Medieval Christians spared the statue because they mistook the rider for Constantine, the first Christian emperor; more than twenty other bronze emperor-statues were melted down for coin. It is the only surviving full bronze statue of a pre-Christian Roman emperor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equestrian_statue_of_Marcus_Aurelius

question: Marcus Aurelius never wrote 'What we do in life echoes in eternity,' though posters and inspirational pictures carry the line under his name. His real lines run plainer. Where does the poster line actually come from?
answer: A blockbuster movie about a Roman general
choices: A blockbuster movie about a Roman general
A Renaissance forgery of a lost letter
A Victorian book of moral self-help
A medieval monk's collection of sayings
context: The line was written for the 2000 film Gladiator and given to the fictional general Maximus - not the real Marcus Aurelius. His genuine lines run plainer, like 'Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be. Be one.' Labeled as legend because it is a popular misattribution, not a real quote. Source: en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius

question: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered a brand-new element and got to name it. Marie chose a name to honor her homeland, a country that had been swallowed up by its neighbors and wiped right off the map of Europe. Which country did she name the element after?
answer: Poland
choices: Poland
Russia
Bohemia
Lithuania
context: They named it POLONIUM, 'after the name of the country of origin of one of us.' At the time Poland had been partitioned among Russia, Germany, and Austria and erased from the map, so naming an element for it was a defiant patriotic act. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/themes/marie-and-pierre-curie-and-the-discovery-of-polonium-and-radium/

question: Marie Curie, working in Paris in the 1890s, studied the invisible rays that pour out of elements such as uranium, and no word yet existed for what those elements were doing. So she coined one. What was her new word?
answer: Radioactivity
choices: Radioactivity
Luminescence
Phosphorescence
Fluorescence
context: Marie Curie coined the very word 'radioactivity' to describe the rays given off by elements like uranium, polonium, and radium. It is now used everywhere, but she made it up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie

question: In her workroom late at night, Marie Curie loved to look at the little tubes of radium she had made with her own hands. She wrote that the sight was one of her greatest joys. What did the tubes do that delighted her?
answer: Glowed on their own
choices: Glowed on their own
Froze solid
Floated upward
Changed color
context: Radium glows in the dark. In her biography of her husband, 'Pierre Curie,' Marie described seeing 'on all sides the feebly luminous silhouettes' of the tubes — 'the glowing tubes looked like faint, fairy lights.' Source: https://womenslegacyproject.com/iconic-f-fairy-lights-marie-curie/

question: Surgeons at the front in the First World War found bullets and shrapnel in wounded men with X-ray machines that Marie Curie had fitted into some twenty vehicles and driven to the battlefields herself. What did the soldiers nickname those vehicles?
answer: The petites Curies (Little Curies)
choices: The petites Curies (Little Curies)
The radium wagons
The bullet-finders
The iron angels
context: Soldiers called them the 'petites Curies.' Marie taught herself to drive and repair the vehicles, trained 150 women to operate them, and over one million wounded soldiers were helped. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-marie-curie-brought-x-ray-machines-to-battlefield-180965240/

question: Marie Curie worked in Paris in the early 1900s studying elements that gave off invisible rays. Hundreds of people have won a Nobel Prize and a handful have won two, yet her record still stands. What did she alone achieve?
answer: Won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences
choices: Won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences
Won Nobel Prizes in three different sciences
Won a Nobel Prize on three separate occasions
Won a Nobel Prize and refused two others
context: Marie Curie won Physics in 1903 (with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel) and Chemistry in 1911 (for discovering polonium and radium). She is the only person ever to win Nobels in two different sciences, and was also the first woman ever to win a Nobel at all. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1911/marie-curie/facts/

question: In a leaky shack in Paris, Marie Curie stirred boiling vats of pitchblende ore by hand for some four years, about seven tons of it in all, to prove that radium existed. How much pure radium did all that ore give up?
answer: About one-tenth of a gram
choices: About one-tenth of a gram
About two kilograms
About half a pound
About fifty grams
context: Seven tons of ore slag yielded just one-tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride, in 1902. Marie wrote of the labor: 'I had to spend a whole day mixing a boiling mass with a heavy iron rod nearly as large as myself.' Source: https://www.kroneckerwallis.com/four-years-in-a-shed-how-marie-curie-isolated-radium/

question: Wilhelm Ostwald, a German chemist, came to see the place in Paris where Marie and Pierre Curie had hunted for a hidden element in tons of black uranium ore: a leaky wooden shack behind their school. How did Ostwald describe it?
answer: A cross between a stable and a potato shed
choices: A cross between a stable and a potato shed
A drafty cellar fit only for storing coal
A cramped attic piled high with dusty junk
A crumbling barn with a slowly sagging roof
context: The shed had no ventilation and even let in the rain. Ostwald said that if he had not seen the worktable and apparatus, he 'would have thought I was being played a practical joke.' Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/themes/marie-and-pierre-curie-and-the-discovery-of-polonium-and-radium/
