question: Maria Sklodowska, the future Marie Curie, wanted to study science in Warsaw in the 1880s, under Russian rule, but the University of Warsaw refused to admit women. She and other young women of the city would not give up. How did they get their schooling?
answer: Joined secret night classes that kept moving from house to house
choices: Joined secret night classes that kept moving from house to house
Disguised themselves as boys at the official university
Learned only from tutors sent by the Russian government
Traveled together to Paris as young teenagers
context: The 'Flying University' constantly changed locations to evade the police. Later, Marie and her sister Bronya made a pact: Marie worked as a governess to fund Bronya's Paris medical studies, then Bronya funded Marie's turn at the Sorbonne — where Marie graduated first in her physics class. Source: https://www.openculture.com/2016/07/marie-curie-attended-a-secret-underground-flying-university-when-poland-blocked-her-other-women-from-advancing-their-education.html

question: Marie Curie kept radium in her desk drawer and slipped it into her coat pockets for years. Aplastic anemia, a disease of the bone marrow, killed her in 1934. What had made her so ill?
answer: The radiation from her own discovery
choices: The radiation from her own discovery
A sudden fever from influenza
A fall in her laboratory
A failing and weakened heart
context: She died on 4 July 1934 of aplastic anaemia, a bone-marrow disease caused by decades of radiation exposure. The very discovery that made her famous is what killed her. Source: https://www.britannica.com/question/How-did-Marie-Curie-die

question: Marie Curie worked out a method of isolating pure radium that laboratories, hospitals and factories all over the world wanted. A patent could have made her and her husband Pierre extremely rich. What did she decide to do with her method?
answer: Refused to patent it so all could use it free
choices: Refused to patent it so all could use it free
Sold it to the highest bidder for a fortune
Patented it and licensed it to companies
Hid it and let the secret die with her
context: Marie deliberately refused to patent the radium-isolation process so the entire scientific and medical community could use it freely. She gave away the secret rather than get rich from it — even though it left her too poor to afford radium herself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie

question: Marie Curie had been dead for more than sixty years when France carried her remains into the Pantheon in Paris in 1995, to rest among the nation's greatest minds. Her body turned out to be still dangerously radioactive, and an unusual precaution had been taken at her burial. What had she been buried in?
answer: A lead-lined coffin
choices: A lead-lined coffin
A sealed glass case
A solid gold casket
An unmarked wooden box
context: Her remains were still radioactive, so she had been buried in a lead-lined coffin. She was the first woman entombed in the Panthéon on her own merits. Source: https://www.iflscience.com/marie-curies-body-was-so-radioactive-she-was-buried-in-a-lead-lined-coffin-69080

question: Pierre and Marie Curie tested a rock called pitchblende and got a baffling result: the whole rock gave off stronger rays than the pure uranium they could pull out of it. The uranium alone could not account for all that energy. What did the Curies reason must be true?
answer: Hidden, more powerful new elements were inside the rock
choices: Hidden, more powerful new elements were inside the rock
The instruments measuring the rays were broken
The uranium itself was somehow impure and weak
Sunlight was charging the rock with extra energy
context: This reasoning — that something more radioactive than uranium was hidden in the ore — led them to announce polonium and then radium in December 1898. Source: https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200412/history.cfm

question: Lucius Clay, an American general, warned Ludwig Erhard that the general's own advisers called his move a terrible mistake. Erhard had scrapped Germany's price controls on his own authority one Sunday, while Allied generals still governed. How did Erhard answer?
answer: "Don't listen to them, General. My advisers tell me the same thing."
choices: "Don't listen to them, General. My advisers tell me the same thing."
"Then your advisers have never gone hungry, General."
"You may court-martial me, but the order stands."
"History will decide which of us was mistaken."
context: Erhard freed prices and gutted Nazi-era controls on a Sunday in June 1948 on his own authority. His quip to General Lucius Clay became famous because he was admitting his own experts opposed him too -- and pressing on anyway. The gamble launched West Germany's Wirtschaftswunder (economic miracle). Source: fee.org, 'The German Economic Miracle and the Social Market Economy.'

question: Ludwig Erhard abolished West Germany's price controls on a Sunday in June 1948 and let prices float free. For years under those controls, shopkeepers had kept their stock out of sight rather than part with it at the official prices, and an underground trade had thrived. What happened across West Germany the very next morning?
answer: Hoarded goods reappeared on the store shelves and the black market collapsed.
choices: Hoarded goods reappeared on the store shelves and the black market collapsed.
Riots broke out as prices on bread and coal shot far out of reach.
The Allied generals jailed Erhard and reinstated the old controls.
Shopkeepers kept their goods hidden, distrusting the sudden change.
context: Once merchants could sell at real prices, goods hoarded for years filled the shelves by Monday, June 21, 1948, and the black market vanished almost overnight -- the seen-vs-unseen verdict made visible. West German industrial output jumped from 51% of its 1936 level in May 1948 to 78% by December. Source: econlib.org, 'German Economic Miracle.'

question: George Marshall, the American Secretary of State, first laid out his plan to rebuild war-shattered Europe on 5 June 1947. He gave the press no warning that anything great was coming. Where did Marshall unveil one of the century's most consequential ideas?
answer: In a brief 11-minute commencement speech at Harvard
choices: In a brief 11-minute commencement speech at Harvard
In a televised address from the White House lawn
In a special joint session of the U.S. Congress
In a worldwide radio broadcast carried across Europe
context: Marshall buried it in an unadorned 11-minute graduation talk that nobody expected to matter. One of history's most consequential speeches was almost a throwaway. Source: https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2017/05/70-years-ago-a-harvard-commencement-speech-outlined-the-marshall-plan-and-calmed-a-continent/

question: Lawmakers in Washington ordered a red, white and blue shield stamped on every crate of Marshall aid bound for Europe, on every sack of flour, drum of fuel and machine, so that nobody across the ocean could mistake who had sent it. What did the shield say?
answer: Supplied by the United States of America
choices: Supplied by the United States of America
A Gift from the Free Peoples of the World
Property of the United Nations Relief Fund
Donated by the Allied Powers of Europe
context: The full label read 'For European Recovery -- Supplied by the United States of America.' Congress wanted the credit visible on every shipment. Source: https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/marshall/marsh-exhibition.html

question: Ordinary Americans filled a Friendship Train in Hollywood with food for hungry people in France and Italy in 1947, before Washington's own aid began. It pulled out with eight freight cars, and town after town along the way loaded it up. How many boxcars reached New York?
answer: 270 boxcars
choices: 45 boxcars
130 boxcars
270 boxcars
540 boxcars
context: Eight cars in Hollywood snowballed into 270 boxcars of supplies by New York -- a grassroots wave of generosity ahead of the government program. Source: https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/in-1947-friendship-train-crossed-us-gathering-food-for-hungry-europe/2019/05/18/95d9aa66-77f9-11e9-b7ae-390de4259661_story.html

question: Much of Europe still lay in ruins in June 1947 when George Marshall told an audience that the United States would pay to rebuild it. American policy, he said, was aimed 'not against any country or doctrine, but against' four enemies. Which four did he name?
answer: Hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos
choices: Hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos
Fascism, hatred, ruin and despair
Tyranny, famine, ignorance and fear
War, plague, want and disorder
context: That one sentence framed the whole program as a fight against suffering itself, not against an enemy nation -- the line most quoted from the speech ever since. Source: https://www.marshallfoundation.org/the-marshall-plan/speech/

question: Harry Truman wanted the United States to pay for rebuilding Europe in 1947, yet he handed the credit to his Secretary of State, the wartime hero General George Marshall. What did Truman expect the general's name to buy him?
answer: The votes of even the worst Republicans in Congress
choices: The votes of even the worst Republicans in Congress
The lasting gratitude of the European public
A guaranteed second term in the White House
The Soviet Union's agreement to take part
context: Truman told an aide that anything bearing his name would 'quiver a couple of times, turn belly up and die,' but 'the worst Republican on the Hill can vote for it if we name it after the General.' Source: https://www.marshallfoundation.org/articles-and-features/the-marshall-plan-in-10-minutes/

question: George Marshall, the army general who had helped win the Second World War, received an honour in 1953 that no other career army general has ever won. As Secretary of State he had given his name to the plan that rebuilt Europe with about 13 billion dollars of American aid. Which honour was it?
answer: The Nobel Peace Prize
choices: The Nobel Peace Prize
The Presidential Medal of Freedom
The Pulitzer Prize for History
The Nobel Prize in Literature
context: A lifelong soldier won the Nobel PEACE Prize -- the only professional general ever to do so. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/peace/1953/marshall/facts/

question: Paul Hoffman had never served as a diplomat when Harry Truman chose him to run the Marshall Plan, which shipped some 13 billion dollars of food, fuel and machines to rebuild Europe. Before he took on the rescue of a continent, what American company had Hoffman led?
answer: The Studebaker automobile company
choices: The Studebaker automobile company
The Chase National Bank
The U.S. Steel Corporation
The Pennsylvania Railroad
context: A carmaker ran the rescue of Europe: Hoffman, the former Studebaker chief, headed the Economic Cooperation Administration that delivered the aid. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Cooperation_Administration

question: American officials shared out the Marshall Plan's aid between 1948 and 1952, about 13 billion dollars of food, fuel and machines for sixteen Western European nations rebuilding after the Second World War. One country received more than any other, about a quarter of the whole program. Which country was it?
answer: Britain
choices: Britain
France
West Germany
Italy
context: Britain took about $3.3 billion, ahead of France (~$2.3B), West Germany (~$1.4B), and Italy (~$1.2B). The biggest industrial powers got the most, because reviving them was seen as the key to all of Europe. Source: https://www.statista.com/statistics/1227834/distribution-marshall-plan-by-country/

question: George Marshall offered a ruined Europe American dollars in 1947, and the generosity had a hard strategic edge. Above all, what was the plan racing to do?
answer: Revive prosperity before Communists could win power at the ballot box
choices: Revive prosperity before Communists could win power at the ballot box
Keep the defeated Axis nations poor and disarmed for good
Repay America's wartime loans out of European treasuries
Merge Western Europe into one federal state under Washington
context: The deeper fear was political: aid was meant to revive prosperity before communism could win the vote in Western democracies. The free West was, in effect, inoculated against it. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/marshall-plan

question: Vyacheslav Molotov, Joseph Stalin's foreign minister, came to Paris in the summer of 1947 with nearly a hundred economic experts to hear the terms of the American plan to rebuild Europe, which was offered to the Soviet bloc as well. What did Molotov do?
answer: He stormed out and rejected the plan outright
choices: He stormed out and rejected the plan outright
He signed on and brought the USSR into the program
He demanded the aid be doubled for the East
He stalled for months without ever giving an answer
context: On July 2, 1947, Molotov walked out, calling the plan 'totally unsatisfactory' and fearing it would let Eastern Europe slip out of Soviet control. Stalin turned down free money to keep his grip on the East. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/july-2/soviet-union-rejects-marshall-plan-assistance

question: Joseph Stalin forbade the Soviet satellite states of Eastern Europe to take a single dollar of the American aid offered in 1947. Two years later he answered with a rival economic bloc of his own, Comecon, and brought those states into it. What did Comecon do to them?
answer: Locked them into Soviet-controlled trade, cut off from Western technology
choices: Locked them into Soviet-controlled trade, cut off from Western technology
Gave them full freedom to trade with America and Britain
Sent them huge yearly cash gifts to rebuild their cities
Forced them to trade only with communist China
context: Comecon (the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance), founded in January 1949, was Stalin's mirror-image answer to the Marshall Plan -- binding the East to Moscow instead of opening it to the West. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov_Plan

question: Ludwig Erhard set West Germany on a free-market course, and with Marshall aid behind it, factories, houses and whole cities rose out of the rubble in just a few years. West Germans gave the boom a single name, the Wirtschaftswunder. What does the word mean?
answer: The economic miracle
choices: The economic miracle
The iron curtain
The people's car
The year zero
context: Aided West Germany's 'economic miracle' outpaced France and Britain within a decade. Meanwhile command-economy East Germany stagnated -- four decades later the East still had not reached the prosperity the West hit by the early 1960s. The contrast made the case for free markets visible across one divided country. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Wirtschaftswunder

question: A violent thunderstorm caught Martin Luther, then a young law student, crossing open country in July 1505, and lightning hit the ground right next to him. Terrified that he might die on the spot, he cried out a promise. What did he vow?
answer: 'Help! Saint Anna, I will become a monk!'
choices: 'Help! Saint Anna, I will become a monk!'
'Spare me, Lord, and I will sail for Rome!'
'Save me, and I will give all I own away!'
'Mercy! I will build a church on this spot!'
context: The storm struck on July 2, 1505. True to his terrified vow, Luther sold his books and entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt -- the decision that set the whole story in motion. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther ; https://www.ligonier.org/posts/luther-and-thunderstorm

question: Martin Luther wrote his Ninety-five Theses in Latin in 1517, for the professors of Wittenberg to argue over. Within weeks they had been translated into German and were racing across the country, far beyond any lecture hall. What carried them so far, so fast?
answer: The new printing press
choices: The new printing press
Friars traveling on foot
Merchants' private letters
Criers in the town square
context: The recently invented printing press spread the Theses faster and farther than Luther ever intended -- copies were soon being printed in Basel, Leipzig, and Nuremberg. A debate meant for scholars became a movement for everyone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses ; https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/october-31/martin-luther-posts-95-theses

question: Pope Leo X gave Martin Luther sixty days to take back his writings or be thrown out of the Church. On 10 December 1520, with his students cheering around him at Wittenberg's Elster Gate, Luther answered the pope's order with one public act. What did he do with it?
answer: Threw it into a bonfire and burned it
choices: Threw it into a bonfire and burned it
Nailed it shut across the church doors
Mailed it back to Rome unopened
Read it aloud and then signed it
context: 'Exsurge Domine' was the papal bull that demanded Luther recant. Instead, with students and faculty cheering, Luther burned it in a bonfire at the Elster Gate -- an open declaration that he would not bow to Rome. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exsurge_Domine ; https://lutheranreformation.org/history/burning-papal-bull/

question: Martin Luther stood before Emperor Charles V, the most powerful ruler in Europe, at Worms in April 1521, and the emperor ordered him to take back everything he had written against the Church. Luther refused. What reason did he give for refusing?
answer: He could not, in good conscience, speak against his own conscience
choices: He could not, in good conscience, speak against his own conscience
He had already sworn a public oath never to recant
He feared the German princes would rebel if he did
He believed an emperor had no power over a monk
context: Luther's recorded words: 'I neither can nor will retract anything, for it cannot be either safe or honest for a Christian to speak against his conscience.' Standing alone before the most powerful ruler in Europe, he made conscience itself the final authority. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1900/luthers-speech-at-the-diet-of-worms/ ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Martin-Luther/Diet-of-Worms

question: Emperor Charles V promised Martin Luther a safe-conduct for his journey to Worms in 1521, a sworn guarantee that he could come and go unharmed. Yet everyone remembered that a reformer named Jan Hus had been given the very same guarantee at Constance in 1415. What had happened to Hus?
answer: He was burned at the stake despite the promise
choices: He was burned at the stake despite the promise
He was locked in a dungeon for life despite the promise
He was banished from every Christian land despite the promise
He was forced to recant on his knees despite the promise
context: A 'safe-conduct' was a ruler's sworn guarantee of safe passage. A century earlier, Jan Hus had trusted exactly such a promise at Constance and was burned at the stake regardless. Every person at Worms knew Luther might be walking into the same trap. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diet_of_Worms ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Diet_of_Worms/

question: Jesus told his hearers to repent, and Martin Luther built the first of his Ninety-five Theses on that one command in 1517, as he attacked the Church's sale of indulgences. What did Luther's first thesis say Jesus had meant repentance to be?
answer: A task lasting a believer's entire life
choices: A task lasting a believer's entire life
A duty owed only to an ordained priest
A burden that faith alone removes
A matter for the pope alone to settle
context: Thesis 1 reads: 'When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said, Repent, he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance.' Repentance as a whole life turned toward God -- not a payment dropped in Tetzel's coffer -- struck at the very heart of the indulgence trade. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses

question: Philip Melanchthon told how Martin Luther hammered his Ninety-five Theses to a church door, but Melanchthon was not yet living in Wittenberg in 1517, and the hammering may be only a legend. By Luther's own account, how did he first send the Theses out?
answer: He mailed them in a letter to Archbishop Albert
choices: He mailed them in a letter to Archbishop Albert
He read them aloud from the cathedral pulpit
He pinned them to the town hall notice board
He handed them straight to a printer to publish
context: Legend, not forensic fact: the dramatic hammer-and-nail scene comes from Melanchthon, who wasn't present in 1517. Luther's own surviving account says he sent the Theses by letter to Archbishop Albert of Mainz. The image may capture the spirit of the moment without being literally true. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses ; https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/justin-taylor/what-was-luther-doing-when-he-nailed-his-95-theses-to-the-wittenberg-door/

question: Martin Luther finished a list of ninety-five points attacking the sale of indulgences on 31 October 1517, in the university town where he taught the Bible. By tradition, what did he do with his list that very day?
answer: Nailed it to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg
choices: Nailed it to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg
Read it aloud from the steps of Saint Peter's in Rome
Buried it beneath the altar of the cathedral at Mainz
Tossed it from the bell tower over the crowd in Leipzig
context: The list was his Ninety-five Theses, written in Latin as 'Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences' — meant as points for an academic debate, not a public revolt. The church door served as the university's bulletin board. That same day he also mailed a copy to Archbishop Albert of Brandenburg, the man in charge of the sales he was protesting. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ninety-five Theses'.

question: Katharina von Bora was one of twelve nuns who fled the convent at Nimbschen in 1523, in an escape Martin Luther had plotted. On the night before Easter they left in a merchant's covered wagon. What were the nuns hidden among as they slipped past the convent gates?
answer: Empty herring barrels
choices: Empty herring barrels
Bolts of dyed wool
Sacks of milled grain
Crates of clay jugs
context: One of the twelve smuggled-out nuns was Katharina von Bora, who married Luther on June 13, 1525 — the runaway nun and the renegade monk. The union scandalized Europe but became a genuine partnership. Source: Wikipedia, 'Katharina von Bora'.

question: Johann Tetzel, a friar, went from town to town across Germany in 1517 selling paper certificates called indulgences, and the trade enraged Martin Luther. What did the Church claim buyers got for their money?
answer: A reduction in the punishment owed for their sins
choices: A reduction in the punishment owed for their sins
A guaranteed seat at the next Church council
A blessing on their crops for the coming harvest
A pardon from taxes owed to the local bishop
context: Tetzel's sales were partly meant to fund the rebuilding of Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome — and secretly to pay off Archbishop Albert's debts to the Fugger bankers for buying his church office. Promising forgiveness for cash is exactly what Luther attacked. Source: Wikipedia, 'Johann Tetzel'.

question: Frederick the Wise hid Martin Luther in Wartburg Castle in 1521, and Luther spent about eleven weeks there on one huge project. Where German had no word for an idea, he made one up. What did he produce in those weeks?
answer: A German translation of the entire New Testament
choices: A German translation of the entire New Testament
A new hymn book for German village churches
A complete history of the German monasteries
A German dictionary of Latin Church terms
context: He translated it straight from the original Greek into everyday German. Legend says he once hurled an inkwell at the devil there — but the phrase really meant he 'fought the devil with ink,' that is, by translating; caretakers re-painted an 'ink stain' on the wall for centuries of tourists anyway. Source: Wikipedia, 'Luther Bible'; luther.de.

question: Martin Luther faced Emperor Charles V at the imperial Diet held in Worms in 1521, beside a table heaped with his own books, and was ordered to take back everything he had written. Luther refused, saying that to act against his conscience was neither safe nor right. What did he say held his conscience captive?
answer: The Word of God
choices: The Word of God
The will of the emperor
The judgment of Rome
The laws of the empire
context: His full line was that his conscience was 'captive to the Word of God.' To recant against his own conscience, he said, would be neither safe nor right. Refusing the emperor to his face was an act of staggering nerve. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Luther's Speech at the Diet of Worms'.

question: Emperor Charles V heard Martin Luther refuse to recant at Worms in 1521, and the speech came down in print with a famous closing line. Those words were probably sharpened in the first printed version rather than spoken exactly so. Which words are they?
answer: "Here I stand. I can do no other. God help me. Amen."
choices: "Here I stand. I can do no other. God help me. Amen."
"Let the world burn before I yield a single page."
"No crown nor mitre shall command my soul."
"I answer to Heaven alone, and to no man here."
context: Treat this as legend rather than a perfect transcript: the dramatic 'Here I stand' may have been sharpened by the first printers, but it captures the spirit of a lone monk refusing to back down before an emperor. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Luther's Speech at the Diet of Worms'; Crossway, 'Luther at the Diet of Worms'.

question: Martin Luther's German printers ran his thirty pamphlets through some 370 editions between 1517 and 1520, while his Theses crossed Europe within two months. In those years, how large a share of all German printing came from Luther's own pen?
answer: About half of everything printed
choices: About half of everything printed
About a tenth of everything printed
About a fifth of everything printed
Nearly all of everything printed
context: Between 1517 and 1520, thirty of his pamphlets ran through 370 editions — roughly 400,000 copies — making him the era's runaway bestseller. He claimed he had 'no wish or plan to publicize these Theses,' but the presses spread them anyway. Source: Christian History Institute, 'Preaching From the Print Shop'.

question: Johann Cochlaeus, who hated Martin Luther, grumbled that even the humblest working Germans were now reading the Bible for themselves, holding it 'as if it were a fountain of all truth.' Which workers did he name as devouring it?
answer: Tailors and shoemakers
choices: Tailors and shoemakers
Bakers and butchers
Farmers and shepherds
Miners and blacksmiths
context: Cochlaeus meant it as an insult — that uneducated commoners had no business reading Scripture for themselves — but it stands as vivid eyewitness proof of how hungrily ordinary Germans took up the printed Bible. Source: Christian History Institute, 'Preaching From the Print Shop'.

question: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote down the beliefs of a little club of revolutionaries in London, and their pamphlet was printed there in late February 1848. Its first line became one of the most famous in politics. What did it say was haunting Europe?
answer: A spectre — the spectre of communism
choices: A spectre — the spectre of communism
A hunger that no king could feed
A fire lit in the heart of Paris
A storm gathering over the factories
context: The Communist Manifesto (Manifest der kommunistischen Partei) opened: 'A spectre is haunting Europe — the spectre of communism.' Published anonymously around February 21, 1848, as a 23-page pamphlet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto ; https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-21/marx-publishes-manifesto

question: Karl Marx's three daughters never called their father Karl, even in the hard years of his exile in London. At university his dark skin and jet-black hair had won him a nickname, and the family used it ever after. What did his daughters call him?
answer: Moor
choices: Moor
Bear
Professor
Raven
context: His daughters called him 'Moor' for his dark hair and complexion. His close friend Friedrich Engels carried a nickname too — 'the General.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx ; https://mhoefert.blogspot.com/2018/05/happy-birthday-moore.html

question: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels ended their Communist Manifesto of 1848, a call to abolish private property, with a rallying cry. That one short line became among the most quoted political slogans on Earth. What was that closing call?
answer: Workers of all lands, unite!
choices: Workers of all lands, unite!
Down with every crown in Europe!
Take the factories, and take them now!
Let no man labour for another!
context: The Manifesto closes 'Working Men of All Countries, Unite!' (often rendered 'Workers of all lands, unite!'). The sentence just before it: 'The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.' 'Proletarians' is Marx's own term for the working class. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-21/marx-publishes-manifesto

question: Friedrich Engels drafted the program for his and Karl Marx's famous pamphlet of 1848 months ahead, in an odd schoolroom style: twenty-five questions, each with a short reply. Marx reworked the draft into flowing prose. What title had Engels given his question-and-answer draft?
answer: Principles of Communism
choices: Principles of Communism
The Workers' Catechism
A Confession of Faith
Letters to the League
context: Engels' 'Principles of Communism' laid out the program as 25 questions each with an answer. Marx reworked it into the Manifesto. The first edition had a dark-green cover and was printed at 46 Liverpool Street in London. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto

question: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels put their pamphlet on sale late in February 1848, and at first hardly anyone read it. Then, within a single day of its appearance, an event broke out in one European capital and set off upheavals across the whole continent. What happened?
answer: Revolution erupted in France
choices: Revolution erupted in France
A general strike shut down London
The King of Prussia abdicated
Workers seized the Vienna mint
context: Revolution broke out in France on February 22, 1848 — within a day of the Manifesto's publication — then spread in the wave known as the Revolutions of 1848. The pamphlet nobody read landed exactly as Europe caught fire. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-21/marx-publishes-manifesto

question: Friedrich Engels rode to hounds with the Manchester gentry by day, a rich executive of his family's cotton mill earning over a thousand pounds a year. In secret he passed the struggling Marx household in London thousands of pounds. What did that mill money pay for?
answer: The research and writing of Das Kapital
choices: The research and writing of Das Kapital
A printing press hidden in Brussels
Marx's escape from the Prussian police
A network of couriers across Europe
context: Engels, an executive at the Ermen & Engels mill, funneled roughly £3,000–£4,000 over about twenty years to Marx — the money behind Das Kapital, the book attacking the very capitalism that earned it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Engels

question: Friedrich Engels came to Manchester in 1842 to work in his family's cotton mill, and he began gathering evidence for a book on how the English working class really lived. He needed to walk through the city's worst slum, a district called Little Ireland, where a well-dressed German alone risked robbery or worse. Who guided him safely through it?
answer: A spirited Irish factory worker who knew the slum
choices: A spirited Irish factory worker who knew the slum
A retired constable from the Manchester police
A Catholic parish priest from the local church
A wealthy mill owner's grown son
context: Mary Burns, an Irish factory worker, led Engels through Manchester's 'Little Ireland,' giving him the material for 'The Condition of the Working Class in England' (1845). He called his own years as a cotton merchant 'purgatory' and wrote, 'Huckstering is too beastly.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Engels

question: Karl Marx finished the first volume of Das Kapital standing at his desk, because a painful condition had made sitting unbearable. He cursed his enemies over it and hoped the bourgeoisie would remember it until their dying day. What condition forced him to his feet?
answer: An eruption of boils on his rear
choices: An eruption of boils on his rear
A broken hip from a bad fall
Gout swelling both his knees
A wound that would not heal
context: Marx finished Volume 1 standing, driven up by carbuncles (boils) on his rear, cursing: 'What a swine they are!' He drafted much of it at desk G7 in the British Museum's Round Reading Room. Source: https://www.marxists.org/history/etol/newspape/isj2/1999/isj2-085/morgan.htm ; https://opinion.inquirer.net/115074/warming-seat-marx-wrote-das-kapital

question: Helen Macfarlane, a Scottish writer, put Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels's Communist Manifesto into English for the first time in 1850, two years after it appeared in German. She chose her own creature for its opening line, one that 'stalks throughout Europe.' What did she call it?
answer: A frightful hobgoblin
choices: A frightful hobgoblin
A pale wandering ghost
A hungry grey wolf
A nameless dread
context: Helen Macfarlane's 1850 translation opened: 'A frightful hobgoblin stalks throughout Europe.' It ran in George Julian Harney's paper The Red Republican in November 1850. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto

question: Edgar Marx, a bright boy, loved to belt out the French anthem 'La Marseillaise' at the top of his voice, though his family was poor in London's Soho. Several of Karl Marx's children died young, and Edgar died on 6 April 1855. Where was the boy when he died?
answer: In his father's arms
choices: In his father's arms
In a charity hospital ward
On the boat to England
Alone in the night
context: Edgar died in Marx's arms; Marx wrote to Engels, 'I feel broken down.' Only three of the seven children Jenny Marx bore survived to adulthood. The family at 28 Dean Street sometimes lived on bread and potatoes. Source: https://www.marxists.org/history/etol/newspape/isj2/1999/isj2-085/morgan.htm ; https://buddhistsocialism.weebly.com/karl-marx-ndash-life-at-28-dean-street-ndash-soho-london-w1-2016.html

question: Friedrich Engels stood at Karl Marx's grave at Highgate in 1883 before only about eleven mourners. In his speech he measured his friend against the grandest scientist of the age: Marx, he said, had discovered how human history develops, just as this man had discovered it for nature. Whom did Engels name?
answer: Charles Darwin
choices: Charles Darwin
Isaac Newton
Galileo Galilei
Michael Faraday
context: Engels said: 'Just as Darwin discovered the law of development of organic nature, so Marx discovered the law of development of human history.' He opened, 'the greatest living thinker ceased to think,' and closed, 'His name will endure through the ages.' Source: https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1883/death/burial.htm

question: 'The sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world,' Karl Marx called religion in 1844. He went on to the phrase everyone remembers, often clipped into a sneer though the full passage is gentler. How did Marx finish the thought?
answer: It is the opium of the people
choices: It is the opium of the people
It is a chain forged by kings
It is the dream of the defeated
It is a lie sold to the poor
context: Marx wrote that religion 'is the opium of the people' — meaning partly with sympathy, as a real cry of suffering and a painkiller for a hard life, not only as a sneer. From his journal the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium_of_the_people ; https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1843/critique-hpr/intro.htm

question: Karl Marx claimed to have found the single engine that drove all of human history, and he set it down in the Communist Manifesto of 1848: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of...' By Marx's argument, what moves history forward?
answer: The struggle between economic classes
choices: The struggle between economic classes
The will of great men and kings
The march of reason and ideas
The hand of God over the nations
context: Marx argued history is driven by class struggle — part of his theory of historical materialism, that how a society produces and trades its goods shapes its politics, law, and ideas. This is Marx's claim, a serious idea in the philosophy of history, not a settled fact. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-21/marx-publishes-manifesto ; https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/marx/

question: 'The philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways,' Karl Marx declared in his 'Theses on Feuerbach' of 1845, jabbing at the thinkers who came before him, and the line was later carved on his tomb at Highgate. What, he said, was the real point?
answer: The point is to change it
choices: The point is to change it
The point is to understand it
The point is to record it
The point is to endure it
context: The 11th Thesis on Feuerbach: 'The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point, however, is to change it.' Marx never published the theses; Engels printed them in 1888, five years after Marx's death. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theses_on_Feuerbach ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Karl_Marx

question: A woman stood under an elm tree at Lyme Regis in August 1800, holding the fifteen-month-old Mary Anning as she watched a horse show. Lightning struck the tree and killed three women beneath it, yet the baby lived. Carried home limp and lifeless, how was she brought back to life?
answer: She was bathed in a tub of hot water
choices: She was bathed in a tub of hot water
She was carried up to the church altar
She was wrapped in the skin of a lamb
She was rowed straight out to sea
context: Mary Anning (born 21 May 1799) was the only survivor; her family said the sickly baby afterward 'seemed to blossom,' and for years Lyme Regis credited her sharp curiosity to that lightning bolt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Joseph Anning dug a strange skull four feet long out of the crumbling sea-cliffs of Lyme Regis in 1811; it looked like a crocodile's. A few months later his twelve-year-old sister Mary went back to the same cliffs. What did she pull out of the rock?
answer: The whole 17-foot skeleton of the beast
choices: The whole 17-foot skeleton of the beast
A chest of gold the tide had buried
The bones of a drowned sailor
A nest of giant speckled eggs
context: It was the first ichthyosaur ever recognised. The British Museum bought it, and people argued for years over what kind of animal it even was. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Charles Konig of the British Museum needed a name for the dolphin-shaped sea reptile Mary Anning had freed from the Dorset cliffs, with its enormous eyes and rows of pointed teeth. He coined the word 'ichthyosaur.' What does the name mean?
answer: Fish-lizard
choices: Fish-lizard
Storm-runner
Dragon-king
Sea-ghost
context: The creature swam like a fish but was a reptile that breathed air, so 'fish-lizard' captured the puzzle of it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Tray, Mary Anning's little black-and-white terrier, worked the cliffs of Lyme Regis at her side for years. One stormy October day in 1833 a landslide came thundering down the rocks, and Mary escaped it by a moment. What happened to Tray?
answer: The falling cliff crushed him in an instant
choices: The falling cliff crushed him in an instant
He swam out to a fishing boat and was saved
He ran off and was never seen again
He dug Mary free from the rubble
context: Mary wrote to her friend Charlotte Murchison: 'the cliff that fell upon him and killed him in a moment before my eyes... it was but a moment between me and the same fate.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: The Annings of Lyme Regis had dug the first complete ichthyosaur ever recognized out of their cliffs, and scholars across England would soon argue over it. But Mary's father was dead, and the family was close to starving. What did they do with their great find?
answer: Sold it for about 23 pounds to a local gentleman
choices: Sold it for about 23 pounds to a local gentleman
Donated it free to the British Museum in London
Kept it on display in their tiny seaside shop
Reburied it in the cliffs to protect it from thieves
context: They sold it to Henry Hoste Henley, lord of the manor of Colway near Lyme Regis, for roughly 23 pounds; he then resold it to the collector William Bullock, who displayed it in London. The Annings hunted fossils not for science but to keep from starving. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Mary Anning prised her most startling monster out of the rock at Lyme Regis on 10 December 1823, a brand-new kind of creature that people would soon nickname a sea-dragon. Scientists named it Plesiosaurus. What made it look so impossible?
answer: An enormously long neck of about 35 vertebrae
choices: An enormously long neck of about 35 vertebrae
A single eye set in the middle of its skull
A shell as wide across as a cartwheel
A double row of leathery bat-like wings
context: The four-flippered Plesiosaurus had a neck so long that experts who only saw drawings refused to believe it was real. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Mary Anning dug out of the Dorset cliffs, in December 1828, a creature never before seen in Britain, and it caused a great stir among the naturalists. William Buckland of Oxford gave it its scientific name. What kind of animal had she uncovered?
answer: The first pterosaur known outside Germany
choices: The first pterosaur known outside Germany
The first woolly mammoth found in Britain
The first giant turtle of the Dorset coast
The first armoured fish of the deep past
context: Buckland named it Pterodactylus macronyx; Richard Owen later renamed it Dimorphodon macronyx. A reptile from the deep past stunned the public. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Mary Anning kept finding odd polished lumps, bezoar stones as the scholars called them, inside the ichthyosaur skeletons she dug from the Dorset cliffs. She cracked them open, studied what lay inside and worked out what they truly were. What had the lumps been while the animal lived?
answer: Its fossilised droppings
choices: Its fossilised droppings
Its swallowed eyeballs
Eggs it had been carrying
Pearls it had eaten from the sea floor
context: Anning saw they were packed with fish bones and scales. William Buckland named them 'coprolites' and, in a rare act of fairness, credited 'Miss Mary Anning' by name in his paper. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: William Conybeare stood before London's Geological Society in 1824 and showed the scientific world the plesiosaur that Mary Anning had found in the cliffs of Lyme Regis. She had dug the skeleton from the rock herself and drawn it by hand, and he used her drawing. How did Conybeare treat Anning in his talk?
answer: He left her name out of it entirely
choices: He left her name out of it entirely
He named her as his equal partner
He brought her on stage to speak
He gave her half of the prize money
context: Anning found the fossil and drew the sketch Conybeare used, yet the gentleman geologist presented it as his own triumph and never mentioned her. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Henry De la Beche, a geologist, came to the aid of his friend Mary Anning when she faced financial ruin in 1830. He painted an ancient Dorset swarming with the reptiles she had found, called it 'Duria Antiquior,' and sold prints of it and gave her the proceeds. Beyond the money, why did the painting matter to the wider world?
answer: It was the first widely circulated picture of 'deep time'
choices: It was the first widely circulated picture of 'deep time'
It was the first map ever drawn of the Jurassic Coast
It was the first life-size model of an ichthyosaur
It was the first museum guidebook to ancient reptiles
context: 'Duria Antiquior' let ordinary people picture a vanished world of ancient monsters for the first time — prehistory made visible, paid for to rescue the woman who found the bones. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Georges Cuvier, the most powerful naturalist in Europe in the 1820s, first saw drawings of the plesiosaur that Mary Anning had pulled from the cliffs of Lyme Regis. He answered with a stinging public charge against her. What did Cuvier accuse Anning of doing?
answer: Gluing bones from different animals into a fake
choices: Gluing bones from different animals into a fake
Smuggling the fossil out of a French collection
Inventing a Latin name she had no right to
Hiding the skull to drive up the price
context: Cuvier called the long neck impossible and branded the specimen a forgery — until a Geological Society meeting examined it in 1824 and he admitted he was wrong: the skeleton was real. A poor self-taught woman had out-observed the greatest anatomist alive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Anna Pinney wrote down how her friend Mary Anning spoke of the gentleman geologists who published her fossils and observations under their own names. Anning felt the sting of it. In her bitter complaint, as Pinney recorded it, what had those men of learning done?
answer: 'These men of learning have sucked her brains'
choices: 'These men of learning have sucked her brains'
'These men of learning have stolen my gold'
'These men of learning have burned my letters'
'These men of learning have barred my door'
context: The full quote: the world 'has used her ill... these men of learning have sucked her brains, and made a great deal of publishing works, of which she furnished the contents, while she derived none of the advantages.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anning

question: Stephen Winick, a Library of Congress folklorist, traced the tongue-twister 'She sells seashells by the seashore' back to its roots. Many people say it was written about Mary Anning, who sold fossils on the Dorset coast. What did Winick find?
answer: The song came long after her and never names Anning
choices: The song came long after her and never names Anning
A Lyme Regis fishmonger first shouted it as her cry
Anning's own brother Joseph composed it for her shop
Anning painted it as the slogan on her shop window
context: Winick showed the phrase was already common folklore before Terry Sullivan's 1908 song — written more than 60 years after Anning's birth — and that song never even mentions her. A charming legend, but not history. Source: https://blogs.loc.gov/folklife/2017/07/she-sells-seashells-and-mary-anning-metafolklore-with-a-twist/

question: Mary Wollstonecraft argued in her Vindication of the Rights of Woman, published in 1792, that women only seemed inferior because they were denied the education men received. Her most-quoted line begins, 'I do not wish them to have power over men; but...' Over what did she want women to have power?
answer: over themselves
choices: over the home
over the law
over themselves
over the purse
context: Wollstonecraft's goal was self-mastery through education, not dominance over men: '...but over themselves.' She wanted women equipped to reason and govern their own lives. Source: https://digitalcommons.chapman.edu/vocesnovae/vol5/iss1/4/

question: Mary Wollstonecraft took on Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the most celebrated writer of his day. In his book Emile, the ideal girl, Sophie, was brought up for one purpose: to please a man. Wollstonecraft quoted one of his lines and cut it down in a single sharp phrase. She called it the philosophy of what?
answer: the philosophy of lasciviousness
choices: the philosophy of tyranny
the philosophy of lasciviousness
the philosophy of cowardice
the philosophy of idleness
context: Wollstonecraft's argument was that reason is not sexed: if rights rest on rational nature, denying women the same education is incoherent. Rousseau's vision of training a girl purely for a man's pleasure she branded 'the philosophy of lasciviousness.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Vindication_of_the_Rights_of_Woman

question: Ashoka crowned one of his stone pillars at Sarnath with four lions carved back to back, each facing outward. More than two thousand years later, the modern nation of India adopted that carving for an official role it still holds. What did the four-lion capital become?
answer: The national emblem of India
choices: The national emblem of India
The national flag of India
The national anthem of India
The national tree of India
context: The Lion Capital of Ashoka, four life-sized lions back-to-back, is the official National Emblem of India. The pillar marked the spot at Sarnath where the Buddha is said to have preached his first sermon, roughly two centuries before Ashoka. Source: Wikipedia, Lion Capital of Ashoka; Smarthistory; World History Encyclopedia.

question: The Buddha had first preached at Sarnath, and there Ashoka raised a stone pillar crowned with four lions standing back to back, all cut from a single block of sandstone about 2,300 years ago. What on the lions' surface still survives today?
answer: A mirror-like polish that still shines
choices: A mirror-like polish that still shines
Painted colors that still glow
Carved words that still read clearly
Gold leaf that still glints
context: The capital is carved from a single block of Chunar sandstone and given the famous 'Mauryan polish,' a mirror-like shine that still gleams after about 2,300 years. The whole capital stands roughly 2.1 metres (7 feet) tall. Source: Wikipedia, Lion Capital of Ashoka; GKToday; Smarthistory.

question: The cooks of Ashoka's royal kitchen had once killed many thousands of animals every day for the king's table. In Rock Edict 1, carved in stone, Ashoka boasted that now they killed only three. Which three animals were still killed?
answer: Two peacocks and a deer
choices: Two peacocks and a deer
Two pheasants and a goat
Two swans and a boar
Two cranes and a hare
context: Rock Edict 1 boasts that where thousands of animals were once slaughtered daily for the royal table, now 'only three creatures, two peacocks and a deer, are killed, and the deer not always' -- and even those killings would stop. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Edicts of Ashoka (Rock Edict 1).

question: Chanakya, the royal adviser, slipped tiny doses of poison into the emperor Chandragupta's food, the legend says, until no killer could poison him. In the same tale the pregnant queen ate from the king's plate and died, but her unborn son was saved. He became Ashoka's father, Bindusara. What does that name mean?
answer: Drop of poison
choices: Drop of poison
Gift of the gods
Son of the serpent
Born in sorrow
context: In this tradition Chanakya laced the king's food in tiny doses to build immunity; the unborn child was saved as the queen died and was named Bindusara, 'drop of poison.' He became the next emperor and Ashoka's father. The story is legend, not documented fact. Source: Sankalp India Foundation, Poisoning the King; Medium, Bindusara (Stories of Aryavarta).

question: Ashoka conquered the kingdom of Kalinga in a war whose slaughter was later counted in stone on Rock Edict 13: 100,000 slain, 150,000 dragged away and many more dead after. Historians call that edict nearly one of a kind in the ancient world, and not for the size of the toll. What makes it so rare?
answer: He recorded the death toll of his own victory in stone
choices: He recorded the death toll of his own victory in stone
He blamed the entire slaughter on his defeated enemy
He demanded a matching toll of prisoners every year
He ordered the dead counted to set the size of his reward
context: Edict 13 states that in the Kalinga conquest 150,000 were deported, 100,000 were slain, and 'many times as many' died afterward. A king carving the body count of his OWN victory into a monument -- rather than only his glory -- is almost unique in ancient history. Source: Wikipedia, Major Rock Edicts (E. Hultzsch translation, 1925); World History Encyclopedia.

question: Ashoka had the Wheel of Law carved beneath the four lions on his pillar at Sarnath. When India became independent, its people placed a 24-spoke version of that wheel on one national object, where it still appears. Where is the Ashoka Chakra found today?
answer: India's national flag
choices: India's national flag
India's highest war medal
Every Indian coin
India's parliament building
context: The 24-spoke Ashoka Chakra sits at the centre of India's national flag -- a Mauryan emperor's symbol flying over a modern nation. The wheel beneath the Sarnath lions is the Wheel of Law. Source: Wikipedia, Lion Capital of Ashoka; Wikipedia, State Emblem of India.

question: Sanghamitta, Ashoka's daughter and a Buddhist nun, sailed to Sri Lanka with a sapling of the very tree the Buddha had sat beneath, carried in a golden vase. She put it in the ground at Anuradhapura, where it still grows. Among all the trees on Earth, what record does it hold?
answer: The oldest planted tree on record anywhere
choices: The oldest planted tree on record anywhere
The tallest living tree in all of Asia
The only tree with its own armed guard
The widest tree trunk ever measured
context: That tree, the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura, still lives and is the oldest historically authenticated planted tree in the world -- a tree whose exact planting was recorded. Sanghamitta carried it across the sea in a golden vase. Source: Tricycle, Sanghamitta; AmazingLanka, Sri Maha Bodhi.

question: Chandragupta Maurya defeated the Nanda dynasty's last king in 321 BC and founded the empire his grandson Ashoka would rule, yet even as emperor he lived in terror of assassins. Greek travellers and later Indian writers say he took one strange step every night to stay alive. What was it?
answer: He slept in a different bedroom every night
choices: He slept in a different bedroom every night
He burned every letter he read that day
He wore heavy armor to bed each night
He had a new cook prepare every meal
context: Tradition holds that Chandragupta never slept in the same bedroom two nights running, was guarded inside his palace by armed women, and had every dish tasted before he ate -- fear so deep it became legend. Source: Oxford History of India; HistoryDiscussion, Administration of Chandragupta Maurya.

question: Chandragupta defeated Seleucus, a Greek king who had once been one of Alexander the Great's own generals, around 305 BC. He sealed the peace with a gift of war animals, and Seleucus later used them to win at Ipsus. What did Chandragupta give him?
answer: Five hundred war elephants
choices: Five hundred war elephants
One thousand war horses
Three hundred war chariots
Two hundred war camels
context: The treaty handed the Mauryans huge lands including Kandahar and eastern Afghanistan and sealed a marriage alliance; in return Chandragupta gave Seleucus 500 war elephants -- which Seleucus used to win the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE. Source: Wikipedia, Seleucid-Mauryan War.

question: Ashoka had his own feelings about the Kalinga war carved into Rock Edict 13 once the kingdom was conquered, the war won and his enemy crushed. What did Ashoka express there?
answer: Deep remorse and grief over the slaughter
choices: Deep remorse and grief over the slaughter
Fierce pride in his crushing victory
Eager plans to conquer the next land
Warm thanks to the gods for the win
context: Edict 13 reads, 'This is the repentance of Beloved of the Gods on account of his conquest,' and declares that even 'the hundredth part or the thousandth part' of those killed would now be deeply deplorable to him. The conqueror publicly grieved the war he himself had won. Source: Wikipedia, Major Rock Edicts (Hultzsch translation, 1925).

question: Ashoka swore off armed conquest for good after the Kalinga war. The only victory he would seek from then on, he said, would be won not with armies but by teaching people to live rightly, and it 'bears fruit in this world and the other world.' What did he call this new kind of conquest?
answer: Conquest by Dhamma
choices: Conquest by Dhamma
Conquest by Wisdom
Conquest by Faith
Conquest by Virtue
context: Ashoka renounced war for what he called 'conquest by Dhamma' -- conquest by morality -- which he said 'bears fruit in this world and the other world.' Dhamma was his word for living and ruling rightly, and it is the line that turns a war monument into a peace manifesto. Source: Wikipedia, Major Rock Edicts; World History Encyclopedia, Edicts of Ashoka.

question: Ashoka ruled a vast Indian empire in the 200s BC, yet in all the inscriptions he had carved across his lands he never once used the name Ashoka. He called himself only Devanampiya Piyadasi, 'Beloved of the Gods.' After his empire fell, no one could match that title to a known king. For roughly how long did his identity stay lost?
answer: About two thousand years
choices: About two thousand years
About two hundred years
About five hundred years
About fifty years
context: Because he called himself only Devanampiya Piyadasi, 'Beloved of the Gods, of gracious gaze,' Ashoka's real identity was lost for almost two thousand years. His empire had collapsed within about 50 years of his death, and even the script of his edicts became unreadable. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Edicts of Ashoka; Wikipedia, Devanampriya / Priyadasi.

question: James Prinsep, a British scholar, cracked the long-unreadable Brahmi script of Ashoka's pillars in 1837. Yet the carvings named only a mystery king, 'Beloved of the Gods,' and never Ashoka. What let Prinsep prove the two were the same man?
answer: An old Sri Lankan chronicle that named the same king
choices: An old Sri Lankan chronicle that named the same king
A row of coins stamped with Ashoka's portrait
A Greek letter describing Ashoka by name
A family tree carved on the Sarnath lions
context: James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837; pointed by George Turnour to a Sri Lankan Pali chronicle, he realized the mysterious 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' of the pillars was the lost emperor Ashoka, who had been forgotten for nearly two thousand years. Source: World History Encyclopedia, Edicts of Ashoka; GKToday; Scroll.in (James Prinsep).

question: A Maya priest-astronomer wrote out a count of days using only three marks: a dot, a bar, and one more sign the Maya had invented to stand for nothing at all, the number zero. What was that third mark?
answer: A drawing of a shell
choices: A drawing of a shell
A drawing of a feather
A drawing of an eye
A drawing of a hand
context: A dot meant one, a bar meant five, and the shell stood for zero. With just those three symbols the Maya could write any number. The shell-zero is one of the few zero symbols ever invented from scratch. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_numerals

question: Maya priest-astronomers, watching the Sun, the Moon and Venus by naked eye, invented a sign for zero entirely on their own, treating nothing as a number. Europe learned the idea from India, by way of the Arabic numerals. Roughly how far ahead of Europe were the Maya?
answer: More than a thousand years
choices: More than a thousand years
About fifty years
About one century
A few decades
context: The Maya invented their shell-shaped zero independently, more than a thousand years before zero reached Europe through Arabic numerals. Inventing zero from scratch happened only a handful of times in all of human history. Source: https://www.mexicolore.co.uk/maya/home/the-maya-and-zero

question: Maya scribes had written thousands of books on folded bark paper by the time Spain conquered their lands. The Spanish bishop Diego de Landa burned every one he could seize on a single great bonfire at Mani in the Yucatan in 1562. After the whole Spanish conquest, how many Maya books were left in the world?
answer: Only four
choices: Only four
Roughly one hundred
Around three thousand
None at all
context: Bishop Diego de Landa burned thousands of codices at Mani in 1562. Just four Maya bark-paper books survived, and the Dresden Codex is the finest of them. It later turned up in a library in Dresden, Germany, which gave it its name. Source: https://mayan.org/civilization/dresden-codex/

question: Diego de Landa, the Spanish bishop, burned nearly every Maya book he could find in the Yucatan in 1562. The finest of the few survivors came to rest in a Dresden library, in Germany, and took the city's name. Centuries later the book came close to being lost a second time. What nearly destroyed the Dresden Codex then?
answer: The Allied firebombing of Dresden in 1945
choices: The Allied firebombing of Dresden in 1945
A flood of the river Elbe in 1845
A library lamp fire in 1745
A lightning strike in 1645
context: During the Allied firebombing of Dresden in February 1945 the codex took water damage but stayed readable. A Maya astronomy book had survived both a Spanish bishop's fire and a 20th-century war. Source: https://mayan.org/civilization/dresden-codex/

question: Maya astronomers tracked Venus by naked eye alone, and the tables of the Dresden Codex give its cycle as 583.92 days. They even added a leap-year-style correction so their count would not drift. Measured against the true cycle, how far off were the Maya?
answer: By about one hundredth of a day
choices: By about one hundredth of a day
By about three days
By nearly a week
By roughly a month
context: The Maya value of 583.92 days misses the modern 583.93 days by only about one hundredth of a day. They tracked Venus this precisely with the naked eye, and even built in a leap-year-style correction so the count would not drift. Source: https://www.sci.news/astronomy/dresden-codex-venus-table-discovery-04110.html

question: Diego de Landa, a Spanish friar, fed almost every Maya book he could find to the flames in 1562. No European could read their script. Yet in his own account of the Yucatan he left behind the very thing that would one day help scholars crack it. What did he write down?
answer: A list matching Maya glyphs to the letters of the Spanish alphabet
choices: A list matching Maya glyphs to the letters of the Spanish alphabet
A grammar book teaching Spanish friars to speak the Maya language
A confession admitting he had burned the books out of fear
A map showing where the surviving Maya books were hidden
context: In his 'Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan,' the man who burned the books recorded a list of Maya glyphs paired with Spanish letters — the so-called 'de Landa alphabet,' which became the key that eventually helped decipher Maya writing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Landa_alphabet

question: Yuri Knorozov, a young Soviet scholar, studied Maya glyphs from photographs in Moscow in 1952 and spotted a centuries-old mistake in Diego de Landa's list. What kind of writing system did Knorozov realize the Maya script was?
answer: A syllabary, where each glyph stands for a spoken syllable like 'be'
choices: A syllabary, where each glyph stands for a spoken syllable like 'be'
A picture-writing of symbols that each stand for a whole idea
A counting system of dots and bars with no link to speech
An alphabet borrowed directly from the Spanish friars
context: Knorozov realized de Landa's 'alphabet' was really a syllabary: asked for 'b,' the scribe wrote the glyph for the syllable 'be.' That insight turned de Landa's list into the 'Rosetta Stone' of Maya writing — and Knorozov cracked it from photographs in Moscow, not seeing a Maya ruin until 1990. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Knorozov

question: Joseph Welch, the Army's counsel, sat in the televised hearings of 1954 as Joseph McCarthy attacked Fred Fisher, a young lawyer from Welch's own law firm. Welch, his voice shaking, stopped McCarthy cold with one question that turned the room against him. What did Welch ask?
answer: "Have you no sense of decency, sir?"
choices: "Have you no sense of decency, sir?"
"Where is the list you promised us?"
"Will you swear that under oath?"
"Do you speak for the Republican Party?"
context: Welch said: 'Let us not assassinate this lad further, Senator. You've done enough. Have you no sense of decency, sir? At long last, have you left no sense of decency?' The gallery burst into applause and McCarthy's popularity collapsed. Source: U.S. Senate, 'Have You No Sense of Decency?' senate.gov.

question: Whittaker Chambers, a former communist, led congressional investigators onto his Maryland farm in December 1948 to back his charge that Alger Hiss of the State Department had passed secrets to the Soviets. There he pulled rolls of spy film from a bizarre hiding place. Where had Chambers hidden the film?
answer: Inside a hollowed-out pumpkin
choices: Inside a hollowed-out pumpkin
Under a loose floorboard
Sewn into a scarecrow
Buried beneath the barn
context: The film, wrapped in waxed paper inside a pumpkin, became known as the 'Pumpkin Papers.' Prosecutors also matched documents to Hiss's own Woodstock typewriter (No. N230099), and Hiss was convicted of perjury in 1950. Source: Wikipedia 'Pumpkin Papers'; famous-trials.com/algerhiss.

question: Harry Gold, a Soviet courier, had to be sure that David Greenglass, the spy he was meeting to trade atomic secrets at Los Alamos, was his real contact and not a trap. Gold held one jagged half of a torn object; Greenglass took the matching half from his wife's purse, and the edges fit. What was the torn object?
answer: A Jell-O box top
choices: A Jell-O box top
A dollar bill
A playing card
A train ticket
context: The jagged halves of a Jell-O box top matched, proving each man was who he claimed. Greenglass then handed over sketches of the plutonium bomb's high-explosive lenses, one of its most crucial secrets. Source: Science History Institute 'Harry Gold: Spy in the Lab'; National Archives 'Fat Man, Little Boy, A Packet of Jell-O.'

question: Dalton Trumbo and nine other Hollywood writers and directors faced a committee of the House of Representatives in October 1947. Each was asked, 'Are you now or have you ever been a member of the Communist Party?' and the Hollywood Ten refused to answer. What happened to them for refusing?
answer: They were jailed and blacklisted from films
choices: They were jailed and blacklisted from films
They were fined and quietly let go
They were deported from the country
They were cleared and praised as heroes
context: The Hollywood Ten were cited for contempt of Congress, sent to federal prison, and blacklisted by the studios. Many never worked under their own names again. Source: History.com 'Who Were the Hollywood 10?'; todayinclh.com on Dalton Trumbo.

question: Hedda Hopper, a gossip columnist, blurted out a question that laid bare a Hollywood sham. The Brave One had won the Oscar for best story in 1956 under the name of a writer nobody knew, and no one walked up to accept it. Its real author was Dalton Trumbo, writing under false names for a fraction of his former pay. What did Hopper ask?
answer: "Who the hell is Robert Rich?"
choices: "Who the hell is Robert Rich?"
"Where did the studio find him?"
"Why won't the winner stand up?"
"Has anyone read this man's contract?"
context: 'Robert Rich' was a front name for the blacklisted Trumbo, who also secretly wrote 'Spartacus' and 'Exodus.' His real name was restored to those films in 1960 and the Oscar reissued to him in 1975. Source: Hollywood Reporter on 'The Brave One'; Britannica 'Dalton Trumbo.'

question: Joseph McCarthy stood before a women's Republican club in Wheeling, West Virginia, on 9 February 1950 and waved a paper he said held the names of communists hiding in the State Department. Over the following weeks the number he cited shifted from 205 to 57, then 81, then 10. What never happened with that piece of paper?
answer: He never showed the list or proved one name
choices: He never showed the list or proved one name
He never repeated the charge in public again
He never named the State Department again
He never spoke to reporters about it
context: McCarthy waved the paper but never made the list public, and the number on it kept changing. He never produced solid evidence against even one person, yet the speech launched his crusade. Source: McCarthy's Wheeling speech text (uoregon.edu); History.com 'This Day in History: Feb 9, 1950.'

question: Edward R. Murrow used Joseph McCarthy's own filmed words to expose him on his program See It Now in March 1954. He closed by looking straight into the camera and refusing to let Americans be ruled by fear. How did Murrow finish?
answer: "We are not descended from fearful men."
choices: "We are not descended from fearful men."
"The fault lies not in our stars."
"Fear is the enemy of a free press."
"Good night, and trust your neighbors."
context: Murrow said: 'We will not walk in fear, one of another... we are not descended from fearful men.' The broadcast was a turning point that helped move the public against McCarthy. Source: CBS News on Murrow's McCarthy report; plosin.com 'See It Now' transcript, March 9, 1954.

question: Millard Tydings, a senator, called Joseph McCarthy's charges of communists in government 'a fraud and a hoax,' and McCarthy's staff set out to ruin him before his re-election in 1950. They spread hundreds of thousands of copies of a single faked photo. What did the photo show?
answer: Tydings chatting with a U.S. Communist leader
choices: Tydings chatting with a U.S. Communist leader
Tydings burning an American flag
Tydings asleep during a Senate vote
Tydings shaking hands with Stalin
context: The doctored composite spliced a 1938 photo of Tydings with a 1940 photo of Communist leader Earl Browder to fake a friendly chat; 300,000-500,000 copies circulated. Tydings lost, and a Senate panel called the campaign 'despicable, back-street.' Source: Time.com on the doctored photo; Wikipedia 'Tydings Committee.'

question: Klaus Fuchs, a German-born physicist, faced arrest in Britain early in 1950 after decoded Soviet cables unmasked him. He had worked at Los Alamos on the Manhattan Project from 1944 to 1946. According to experts, what did his spying buy the Soviet Union?
answer: Its first atomic bomb one to two years sooner
choices: Its first atomic bomb one to two years sooner
Its first atomic bomb three to four years sooner
Working plans for the U.S. hydrogen bomb
A head start on a Soviet jet bomber
context: Experts estimate Fuchs's intelligence let the USSR build and test its first atomic bomb one to two years earlier than it otherwise could have. He proved the spies in the Red Scare were not all imaginary. Source: Atomic Heritage Foundation 'Klaus Fuchs'; Smithsonian 'Spies Who Spilled Atomic Bomb Secrets.'

question: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg went to the electric chair at Sing Sing prison in June 1953. Julius died after three jolts of 2,000 volts, but Ethel survived the first jolts sent through her. How many jolts did it take in the end to kill Ethel Rosenberg?
answer: Five jolts
choices: Five jolts
Three jolts
Four jolts
Six jolts
context: Ethel survived the first jolts, and a fifth had to be ordered to kill her. Both Rosenbergs proclaimed their innocence to the end. Source: History.com 'Julius and Ethel Rosenberg executed, June 19, 1953'; UPI Archives 1953.

question: Roy Cohn, Joseph McCarthy's chief counsel, spent six months from July 1953 leaning on the Army over a single drafted private, and even threatened to 'expose the Army in its worst light' when it refused him. That quarrel led to the televised hearings that finished McCarthy. What was Cohn demanding?
answer: A cushy posting for his friend Schine
choices: A cushy posting for his friend Schine
A weekend pass for a young aide
A fast promotion for a former staffer
An early discharge for a buddy
context: Cohn pressured the Army to give cushy treatment to his friend G. David Schine, a former McCarthy aide drafted as a private. The Army's counter-charge triggered the televised hearings that ended McCarthy. Source: Wikipedia 'Army-McCarthy hearings.'

question: Prosecutors built their spy case against Julius Rosenberg without a single one of the Soviet cables that code-breakers in the secret Venona project had decoded, though those cables named him as a spy. Why were the cables kept out of his trial?
answer: The cables were still classified secrets
choices: The cables were still classified secrets
Revealing them would expose the broken codes
The cables named only his codename
The code-breakers refused to testify
context: Venona stayed classified until July 1995, so the public, and the courtroom, never saw the cables proving Julius passed the proximity fuze and P-80 jet data. The case shows the witch-hunt and real spying tangled together: Julius truly spied. Source: NSA 'The Venona Story'; Wikipedia 'Venona project.'

question: David Greenglass testified that he had watched his sister, Ethel Rosenberg, type up atomic secrets, and his word did much to send her to the electric chair. In 2001 he made a confession to the author Sam Roberts and on 60 Minutes that cast doubt on her execution. What did he admit?
answer: He had lied and never saw her type anything
choices: He had lied and never saw her type anything
He had been a Soviet agent himself all along
He had forged her signature on the documents
He had been paid by the FBI to accuse her
context: Greenglass admitted he never actually saw Ethel type and had lied to spare his own wife, Ruth, from prison so she could raise their children. So Julius truly spied, yet his wife may have gone to the chair on her brother's perjury. Source: Sam Roberts, 'The Brother'; CBS '60 Minutes' 2001.

question: Joseph McCarthy kept his Senate seat after his fellow senators voted 67 to 22 to condemn him on 2 December 1954, but he lost his chairmanship and his power. Less than three years later he was dead at 48. His death certificate named another cause, but friends knew the real one. What was it?
answer: Alcoholic liver failure
choices: Alcoholic liver failure
Heart disease from years of strain
Untreated diabetes
Long-term kidney failure
context: After the censure, McCarthy declined steeply into drink and died on May 2, 1957, of alcoholic liver failure, though his death certificate said acute hepatitis. Source: constitutioncenter.org 'The Senate censures Joseph McCarthy'; History.com 'May 2, 1957.'

question: A pilgrim on the hajj circles a black-draped stone shrine shaped like a cube, seven times round, at the heart of the Grand Mosque in Mecca. Muslims everywhere turn toward it to pray. What is the shrine called?
answer: The Kaaba
choices: The Kaaba
The minaret
The basilica
The ziggurat
context: The Kaaba is a cube about 15 metres (50 feet) tall at the centre of the Grand Mosque in Mecca; the Arabic word ka'bah literally means 'cube.' Muslims everywhere face its direction, the qibla, when they pray. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Kaaba-shrine-Mecca-Saudi-Arabia

question: A pilgrim arriving at Mecca for the hajj lays by his everyday clothes and dresses in the ihram instead: two plain white sheets, one wound at the waist and one thrown over the shoulder. Millions of other men dress exactly as he does. What striking thing happens in that crowd?
answer: You cannot tell a king from a beggar
choices: You cannot tell a king from a beggar
Each tribe forms its own line
The wealthy lead the procession
Pilgrims are sorted by their age
context: Because rich and poor, prince and pauper all wear the same simple white cloth, no one can tell who is powerful and who is poor, all standing equal before God. Source: https://hisartravel.com.au/symbolism-of-white-ihram-all-you-need-to-know-before-hajj-2026/

question: Raiders of the Qarmatian sect stormed Mecca in January 930 and carried off the Black Stone, set in a corner of the great shrine at the heart of the Grand Mosque, to eastern Arabia. It was returned about 22 years later, changed in a way that left a permanent mark. How did it come back?
answer: Broken into seven pieces
choices: Broken into seven pieces
Painted a deep gold
Wrapped in royal silk
Sealed inside a clay jar
context: The Black Stone returned around 952 CE shattered into seven fragments, which is why to this day it is cemented together and bound inside a silver frame, with a visible face only about 20 cm by 16 cm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone

question: A guard of the Venetian city council locked the gates of a small island from the outside one night in 1516, shutting in the Jews the council had forced to live there until St Mark's great bell rang at dawn. The island had once held a foundry, and the Venetian word for a foundry gave the walled quarter a name the world still uses. What is it?
answer: ghetto
choices: ghetto
bazaar
commune
quarantine
context: The Venetian word for a foundry or casting-works was 'geto' (or 'getto'). Each evening the gates of the island were locked from the outside, and each morning they were reopened only when the marangona — the great bell of St Mark's Campanile — rang. Source: britannica.com/place/Venetian-Ghetto; myjewishlearning.com/article/a-brief-history-of-the-venice-ghetto/

question: Moses Maimonides fled Cordoba as a boy when its conquerors ordered the Jews to convert, leave or die. He rose to be a physician at Saladin's court and wrote the Guide for the Perplexed, joining Aristotle's philosophy to the Torah. Later generations carved one line on his tomb at Tiberias to honour him. What does it say?
answer: "From Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses."
choices: "From Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses."
"Here lies the physician who healed both body and soul."
"He brought the wisdom of Greece into the house of Israel."
"The light of Cordoba, extinguished but never darkened."
context: The first 'Moses' is Moses the prophet, the last is Maimonides; the line ranks him as the greatest Jewish mind since the Torah's own lawgiver. Born in Cordoba in 1138, he fled when the Almohads conquered the city in 1148, settled in Fustat, Egypt, served Saladin's court as a physician, and wrote the 'Guide for the Perplexed.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maimonides

question: A knight of medieval Europe rode out in full plate, each piece bearing a name of its own: the helm for his head, the gauntlet for his hand, the greave for his shin, and the sabaton, shaped to a long point at the front. What was the sabaton?
answer: The steel shoe that covered his foot
choices: The steel shoe that covered his foot
The steel collar that guarded his neck
The steel cap that covered his knee
The steel glove that covered his hand
context: The sabaton was the pointed steel shoe. Plate armour had a whole vocabulary of named parts: the gauntlet (hand), gorget (neck), poleyn (knee), greave (shin), pauldron (shoulder), and the fauld (the skirt of overlapping steel hoops at the waist). Source: worldhistory.org/article/1244/the-armour-of-an-english-medieval-knight/
