question: Roland, the hero of French legend, carried a sword called Durendal. For hundreds of years the people of Rocamadour, a cliffside village in France, said it was the rusty blade wedged in the rock above their chapel. What happened to the sword in June 2024?
answer: Someone stole it out of the rock
choices: Someone stole it out of the rock
Lightning shattered it in a storm
The cliff crumbled and buried it
A flood swept it down the river
context: The blade that vanished was a replica; the legend it honoured says Durendal belonged to the knight Roland. In June 2024 it was stolen straight out of the cliff. Source: smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/fabled-sword-from-medieval-french-folklore-disappears-180984682/

question: The dying Roland lay in the mountain pass of Roncevaux after a bloody ambush, in the medieval French poem the Song of Roland. To keep his sword Durendal from his enemies forever, he smashed the blade against a rock. According to the poem, what happened when blade met stone?
answer: The rock split apart, but the blade stayed whole
choices: The rock split apart, but the blade stayed whole
Both the sword and the rock shattered to pieces
The sword bent double but would not break
Sparks set the dry grass around him ablaze
context: Legend, not fact. Durendal was said to be unbreakable because its golden hilt held holy relics: a tooth of Saint Peter, the blood of Saint Basil, the hair of Saint Denis, and a scrap of the Virgin Mary's robe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durendal

question: A knight in full plate armour walked up to his horse carrying some twenty to twenty-five kilograms of steel spread across his whole body. The old tale of a crane hoisting him into the saddle is a myth, born of a joke in the magazine Punch in 1843. How did the knight get into the saddle?
answer: He climbed up himself using just the stirrup
choices: He climbed up himself using just the stirrup
A team of squires lifted him by the arms
A wooden ramp was built up to the horse
He was strapped on while the horse knelt
context: A full suit of plate weighed only about 20-25 kg (45-55 lbs) spread evenly over the whole body, not piled in one spot. The crane was a myth: its first known version appeared in the magazine Punch in 1843 and was cemented by a 1944 Henry V film scene that horrified the Master of the Armouries at the Tower of London. Source: worldhistory.org/article/1244/the-armour-of-an-english-medieval-knight/

question: A knight of medieval Europe rode into a fight with his family's symbols painted on his shield so that others could tell him apart from the rest. Heraldry bound such designs with a strict rule of tincture: never metal on metal or colour on colour, such as a gold shape on a silver field. What was the rule really for?
answer: So the design stayed readable across a battlefield
choices: So the design stayed readable across a battlefield
So no two families could ever share a shield
So the paint would not flake off in the rain
So only the richest knights could afford one
context: A coat of arms had to be recognised instantly from far away, so the design needed strong contrast — that is why the rule (stated by Humphrey Llwyd in 1568) banned metal on metal or colour on colour. Heraldry even had its own colour names: red is gules, blue is azure, black is sable, gold is or, silver is argent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_tincture

question: A barber of the Middle Ages bled the sick into bowls, pulled teeth and lanced boils, and he marked his shop with a striped red-and-white pole. The pole still stands outside barbershops today. What did its two colours first stand for?
answer: Red for blood, white for the bandages
choices: Red for blood, white for the bandages
Red for fire, white for ice water
Red for wine, white for clean linen
Red for the king, white for the church
context: Medieval barber-surgeons let blood, pulled teeth, and lanced boils. By legend the very first poles were the used bloody bandages themselves, hung outside to dry and twisting in the wind into a red-and-white spiral that was later just painted on. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/why-are-barber-poles-red-white-and-blue

question: A peasant in medieval England finished his harvest at Michaelmas, the feast of the archangel Michael on 29 September, and stored his grain safely away. The Church's feast days set his whole farming year. What else fell on that same day?
answer: The rents owed to the lord
choices: The rents owed to the lord
The first snowfall blessing
The spring ploughing
The midsummer bonfire
context: The whole farming calendar ran on feast days: Candlemas (Feb 2) was when ploughing could begin, and Lammas (Aug 1) was the first-loaf harvest festival when bread from the first wheat went to the lord and the priest. Michaelmas closed the harvest and was rent day. Source: https://nicolaa5.tripod.com/articles/feast.html

question: A medieval doctor sized up a cheerful, rosy patient by the theory of the four humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, the body's fluids that had to stay in balance. English still names such a person with a word from that theory. Which humour did the doctor think he had most of?
answer: Blood
choices: Blood
Phlegm
Yellow bile
Black bile
context: A cheerful, ruddy person was 'sanguine,' from the Latin for blood. The others gave us 'phlegmatic' (sluggish, pale), 'choleric' (angry, from yellow bile), and 'melancholic' (sad and creative, from black bile). It was a coherent system reasoned from observation, not foolishness. Source: https://becker.wustl.edu/news/humors-and-you/

question: Ambroise Pare, a barber-surgeon of France, ran out, during a battle in 1537, of the boiling oil that surgeons used to seal gunshot wounds. For the rest of the wounded he made do with an improvised salve of egg yolk, oil of roses and turpentine. What did he find the next morning?
answer: The salve men were resting comfortably while the boiled men were in agony
choices: The salve men were resting comfortably while the boiled men were in agony
Both groups had died of their wounds overnight
The salve had hardened into a useless crust
The boiled men had recovered far faster
context: The accident taught Pare that the gentle dressing beat the brutal cautery. He summed up his humble view of medicine in a famous line: 'Je le pansai, Dieu le guerit' — 'I bandaged him, and God healed him.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambroise_Par%C3%A9

question: A team at Nottingham University brewed an eye salve in 2015 exactly as Bald's Leechbook, a book of Anglo-Saxon medical recipes written about a thousand years ago, set it down: garlic, another onion-family plant, English wine and cow bile, aged nine nights in a brass vessel. Then they tested it in the lab. What did it do?
answer: It killed MRSA, a modern antibiotic-resistant superbug
choices: It killed MRSA, a modern antibiotic-resistant superbug
It dissolved harmlessly with no effect at all
It turned out to be mildly poisonous
It only worked once the wine was removed
context: Strikingly, only the full mixture worked — none of the single ingredients killed the bacteria on their own, which suggests the medieval recipe-maker had genuinely tuned the combination. Medieval willow-bark tea for headaches was another real hit: willow contains salicin, the compound aspirin is made from. Source: https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/mbio.01129-15

question: Students at Bologna ran their whole university themselves in the Middle Ages, through a guild of their own, with an elected student Rector to give the orders. What power did they hold over the men who taught them?
answer: They hired the professors and paid their wages
choices: They hired the professors and paid their wages
They wrote the professors' lectures for them
They chose which subjects the city could teach
They granted the professors their final degrees
context: At Bologna the students WERE the university — a 'universitas scholarium,' a guild of scholars who hired and paid the masters out of their own pockets and elected a student Rector with authority over them. The professors worked for the students, not the other way around. Source: Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org/cathen/02641b.htm); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_university.

question: A master at Bologna who began his morning lecture late, or turned up unready for it, could expect his own students to report him through denouncers they had elected for the job. They would not put up with a teacher who slacked off. What did they do to him?
answer: Fined him a sum of money out of his pay
choices: Fined him a sum of money out of his pay
Locked him out of the lecture hall
Forced him to teach an extra year free
Reported him to the bishop for trial
context: Bologna's students fined their own professors — a master who failed to start a lecture promptly was docked nine Bolognese pounds. They even elected official 'denouncers' to report a professor's misdeeds, and masters had to leave a cash deposit the students could seize for bad behavior. Source: History of Education Society, 'Puncta for Professors' (historyofeducation.org.uk/puncta-for-professors); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bologna.

question: Masters and students crowded into Paris, Bologna and Oxford in the 1100s and 1200s, and the Latin word they used for their schools, universitas, became the English word university. It sounds as if it should mean a place of all-embracing learning, but it was ordinary Latin first. What did a universitas originally name?
answer: A guild or corporation of people
choices: A guild or corporation of people
A library holding all knowledge
A walled town with its own laws
A grand hall built for teaching
context: 'Universitas' simply meant a guild or corporation — the same word used for tradesmen. A medieval university was a 'universitas magistrorum et scholarium,' a guild of masters and scholars; the word named the PEOPLE, not the buildings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_university; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris.

question: Peter Abelard drew crowds of students in early Paris by out-arguing every rival, and his fame helped turn Paris into a university city. He fell in love with his brilliant pupil Heloise. When they had a son, they gave the boy a startling name borrowed from an astronomical instrument. What did they name him?
answer: Astrolabe
choices: Astrolabe
Quadrant
Lodestar
Meridian
context: Peter Abelard (1079–1142) and Héloïse named their son 'Astrolabe,' after the instrument used to measure the stars. Abelard's dazzling skill in logic drew crowds to Paris and helped make it a great university. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Abelard; Britannica (britannica.com/biography/Peter-Abelard).

question: Scholars at Oxford clashed with the townspeople in 1209 in a fight that turned deadly, and a frightened band of masters and students packed up and fled for good. They settled in another town and began to teach there. Which famous university grew from that flight out of Oxford?
answer: Cambridge
choices: Cambridge
Durham
Winchester
Canterbury
context: A town-and-gown riot drove Oxford scholars to flee in 1209; they regrouped and founded Cambridge. (Oxford itself had surged in 1167 when Henry II, feuding with Thomas Becket, barred English students from Paris and sent them home.) A riot literally created Cambridge. Source: University of Oxford, 'Our history' (ox.ac.uk/about/organisation/history); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford.

question: A master in a medieval university classroom had almost no books to share, because every one was copied by hand and cost a fortune. So a lecture meant something very literal: he sat before the class, performed one action, and then added his own commentary. What did he do that gave the lecture its name?
answer: Read the text aloud word for word
choices: Read the text aloud word for word
Wrote the whole text on a great board
Recited the entire text from memory
Acted out the story in the text
context: The master read the set text aloud while students copied it down, then gave his commentary — the birth of the lecture itself. The word comes from Latin 'lectio,' a reading. 'Ordinary' lectures by master teachers ran from about 6 a.m. to 9 a.m. Source: Serious Science, 'Student Life in the Medieval Universities' (serious-science.org/...10575); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_university.

question: A medieval scholar at Paris, Bologna or Oxford climbed from student to bachelor to master, and the key step was earning the licentia docendi, his license to teach. The university itself did not grant that license. Who actually granted a scholar the right to teach?
answer: The Church, through the local chancellor
choices: The Church, through the local chancellor
The king, through his royal court
The city, through its town council
The students, by their own vote
context: The 'licentia docendi' was granted by the Church — the chancellor of the diocese — so a medieval degree was literally a license to teach in the Church's name. Our words 'license' and 'licentiate' come straight from it. The Third Lateran Council of 1179 ordered the license given FREE to every qualified applicant. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licentia_docendi; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Master of Arts'.

question: Paris erupted in 1229 in history's first great student strike, and the spark was something petty. During the carnival before Lent, a band of students got into a furious quarrel that turned into a riot, and then into a deadly crackdown by the queen's guards. What small dispute set it all off?
answer: An argument over a tavern bill
choices: An argument over a tavern bill
A fight about a stolen cloak
A quarrel over a girl at a dance
A row about the price of bread
context: Students brawled with a tavern keeper over the bill for sweet wine, returned with clubs and wrecked the place; guards under regent Blanche of Castile then killed several students. The masters suspended all lectures and scattered for over two years — winning the 1231 bull 'Parens Scientiarum' (Mother of Sciences), the university's 'Magna Carta.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1229_University_of_Paris_strike.

question: Étienne Tempier, the Bishop of Paris, struck back in 1277 at the boldest philosophers of the university and condemned a long list of forbidden ideas drawn from Aristotle and his Arab commentators. One of them denied that each person has a distinct soul. Which idea did the bishop forbid Christians to hold?
answer: That all humans share one single intellect
choices: That all humans share one single intellect
That the soul dies with the body's blood
That the stars decide every human choice
That only priests possess a true soul
context: Tempier condemned 219 propositions, the most dramatic faith-and-reason clash of the medieval university. Among the 'Latin Averroist' claims he forbade: that the world is eternal, that philosophy is the highest life, and that there is one shared intellect for all humanity — which denied personal immortality and free will. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/condemnation/); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condemnations_of_1210%E2%80%931277.

question: Eleanor of Aquitaine inherited a vast wine-country duchy in southern France and first wore the French crown at the side of King Louis VII. The pope set that marriage aside, and she then married Henry II and became queen of a second kingdom. Which one?
answer: England
choices: England
Spain
Scotland
Sicily
context: Her marriage to Louis was annulled in March 1152, and she married Henry just two months later, on 18 May 1152 — making her the wife of two kings and queen of both France and England. Source: Britannica, Eleanor of Aquitaine; World History Encyclopedia.

question: A peasant woman in medieval Europe brewed more beer at home than her household could drink and sold the extra from her own front door, earning money of her own. Most trades were closed to women, but brewing at home was women's work. What were such women called?
answer: Alewives
choices: Alewives
Goodwives
Midwives
Fishwives
context: Selling ale gave ordinary women rare financial independence at a time when most trades were closed to them. Source: Medievalists.net, 'The Village Ale-Wife'; JSTOR Daily, 'A Pint for the Alewives'.

question: King Louis VII of France marched east on the Second Crusade in 1147 to defend the Christian kingdoms beyond the sea, and his queen, Eleanor of Aquitaine, did not stay home to rule. How did she travel with the crusade?
answer: She rode toward the Holy Land with her own entourage of Aquitanian ladies
choices: She rode toward the Holy Land with her own entourage of Aquitanian ladies
She sailed ahead with a fleet and seized a port to await the army
She rode in the armored vanguard alongside the Knights Templar
She marched at the rear commanding the baggage train and its guards
context: Eleanor travelled through Constantinople with her own company of Aquitanian ladies; her conduct at her uncle Raymond's court in Antioch later sparked her husband Louis VII's jealousy. Source: National Geographic, 'Life of the Lioness'; Britannica.

question: Christine de Pizan lost her husband to the plague in 1389, while she was in her mid-twenties, and was left with her mother, a niece and three young children to support. Rather than remarry, she did something almost no one in Europe had done before. What did she do?
answer: She earned her living as a professional writer
choices: She earned her living as a professional writer
She joined a convent and took vows
She ran her late husband's law practice
She became a lady-in-waiting at court
context: Christine de Pizan (c.1364–c.1430) is considered the first person in Europe to make a living by her pen. Source: National Geographic, 'France's first woman of letters'; World History Encyclopedia.

question: Hildegard of Bingen, an abbess of about sixty, made four journeys between 1158 and 1170 to cities such as Cologne and Trier. Before crowds of men she stood up and did something usually forbidden to women. What did Hildegard do on those journeys?
answer: She preached sermons to male audiences
choices: She preached sermons to male audiences
She heard the confessions of monks
She crowned local bishops
She led armies of pilgrims into battle
context: Hildegard also corresponded with popes, with Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, with St. Bernard of Clairvaux, and with King Henry II of England. Source: Encyclopedia.com; World History Encyclopedia, Hildegard of Bingen.

question: King Oswiu of Northumbria picked Hilda of Whitby's abbey in 664 to host a great meeting of churchmen, who would settle whether the English Church followed Roman or Irish custom. Hilda ran a great double monastery and held nearly the power of a bishop. Which practice were they meeting to settle?
answer: The proper date for Easter
choices: The proper date for Easter
The language of the Mass
The age for baptizing infants
The number of feast days a year
context: The synod settled how to date Easter, in favor of Roman over Irish custom; the king choosing Hilda's abbey to host it was a mark of the prestige of her position. Five future bishops trained at her abbey, and people of every class called her 'mother.' Source: World History Encyclopedia, Hilda of Whitby; Wikipedia, Synod of Whitby.

question: Jean de Meun and other poets painted women as 'vile temptresses,' and Christine de Pizan answered them in 1405 with a book. Page by page she built in it a walled refuge and filled it with great and virtuous women from history. What is the book called?
answer: The Book of the City of Ladies
choices: The Book of the City of Ladies
The Romance of the Rose
The Mirror of Princes
The Garden of Earthly Delights
context: She also publicly debated The Romance of the Rose, attacking its portrayal of women. The wrong choice 'Romance of the Rose' is the very poem she was arguing against. Source: World History Encyclopedia; Open University, 'World-Changing Women: Christine de Pizan'.

question: Hildegard of Bingen wrote music, medical books and a record of 26 mystical visions, and around 1150 she made a bold move to free her nuns from the abbot whose monastery had housed them. What did she do?
answer: She founded her own monastery at Rupertsberg
choices: She founded her own monastery at Rupertsberg
She petitioned the king to grant her a title
She sold the abbey's lands to fund a hospital
She left religious life to marry a nobleman
context: Hildegard broke from the abbot Kuno's authority so her community of nuns could flourish independently, and later founded another house at Eibingen in 1165. Source: Encyclopedia.com; World History Encyclopedia, Hildegard of Bingen.

question: Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, spent eight years crossbreeding and counting about 28,000 plants in the garden of his monastery in Brno to find the hidden rules of heredity. What humble crop did he grow and cross by the tens of thousands?
answer: Pea plants
choices: Pea plants
Grape vines
Wheat stalks
Apple trees
context: From 1856 to 1863 Mendel grew and crossbred about 28,000 plants, mostly peas, in the garden of St. Thomas Monastery in Brno. He chose peas because they were cheap, bred quickly and abundantly, and produced hundreds of observable peas per plant; he tracked seven clear traits including seed shape, seed color, pod shape, and stem length. Born Johann Mendel in 1822 to peasant farmers, he took the name Gregor when he entered the monastery. Sources: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/gregor-mendel-genetics ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregor_Mendel

question: Gregor Mendel laid out the hidden mathematics of heredity before about forty people at Brno's natural history society in 1865, and scientists paid it no attention for some thirty-five years. By his death in 1884 he was an abbot, almost unknown as a scientist. The story goes that late in life he said one thing about his work to a colleague. What did he say?
answer: "My time will come"
choices: "My time will come"
"The peas never lie"
"Let the monks judge me"
"Count, and you will see"
context: The line ('Meine Zeit wird schon kommen') is reported testimony, framed as legend. Sixteen years later it came true: in 1900 three botanists — Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak — independently rediscovered Mendel's laws and finally gave him credit, a generation after he published in 1866. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregor_Mendel ; https://www.vaticanobservatory.org/education/gregor-mendel-planting-seeds-genetics/ ; https://www.genome.gov/25520238/online-education-kit-1900-rediscovery-of-mendels-work

question: Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, spent years crossing pea plants in his monastery garden in Brno. When he bred a round-seeded pea with a wrinkled-seeded pea, every single offspring came out round and the wrinkled seeds vanished completely. Then he let those round hybrid plants pollinate themselves. What happened to the wrinkled seeds in that next generation?
answer: The wrinkled form reappeared in about a quarter of the plants
choices: The wrinkled form reappeared in about a quarter of the plants
The wrinkled form stayed gone for good
Every plant produced seeds that were half-round, half-wrinkled
The plants grew wrinkled pods instead of wrinkled seeds
context: The wrinkled trait had been hidden, not erased. Mendel called the form that shows up 'dominant' (round) and the one that hides 'recessive' (wrinkled), and the recessive form returned in a roughly 3-to-1 ratio. Proving the trait was hidden, not blended away, is Mendel's signature result. Sources: https://www.sciencelearn.org.nz/resources/2000-mendel-s-principles-of-inheritance ; https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/heredity/mendelian-genetics-ap/a/mendel-and-his-peas

question: Erich von Tschermak, Carl Correns and Hugo de Vries, three botanists working on the puzzle of heredity, came upon a forgotten paper in 1900. Gregor Mendel, a friar, had read his eight years of pea-breeding results to a small science society and died in 1884 with his work still ignored. What did the botanists find in his paper?
answer: Mendel had reached the same laws 35 years before them
choices: Mendel had reached the same laws 35 years before them
Mendel had reached the opposite conclusion entirely
Mendel had studied roses, not the question they were solving
Mendel had given up and never finished the work
context: Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak each independently re-derived Mendel's laws in 1900 and discovered he had beaten them by decades. The patient, honest pea-counting of a monastery friar, unrewarded in his own lifetime, had quietly founded the science of genetics. Sources: https://www.genome.gov/25520238/online-education-kit-1900-rediscovery-of-mendels-work ; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/gregor-mendel-genetics

question: Miguel Hidalgo, a village priest in Spanish-ruled Mexico, rang his church bell on 16 September 1810, before dawn, to wake his parish. He stood before his people and called on them to rise up and throw off Spanish rule, and his call launched Mexico's war for independence. By what name is it remembered?
answer: The Grito de Dolores, the Cry of Dolores
choices: The Grito de Dolores, the Cry of Dolores
The Reconquista, the reconquest of Spain
The Cortes of Cadiz, the Spanish assembly
The Edict of Nantes, a royal decree
context: The 'Grito de Dolores' (Cry of Dolores) is Hidalgo's call to arms on Sept. 16, 1810. Mexico still celebrates Independence Day on Sept. 16 to mark it, even though independence was not actually won until 1821. Every year the President re-rings Hidalgo's bell from the National Palace balcony and shouts 'Viva Mexico!' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grito_de_Dolores ; https://www.britannica.com/event/Grito-de-Dolores

question: Miguel Hidalgo's ragtag army stopped at the church in Atotonilco in 1810, the day after he called his parish to rise against Spain. There he took a banner down from the wall and raised it as his army's standard, and his fighters marched and fought beneath it. Whose image was on the banner?
answer: The Virgin of Guadalupe, patron saint of Mexico
choices: The Virgin of Guadalupe, patron saint of Mexico
King Ferdinand VII, the Spanish monarch
Saint James, the warrior patron of Spain
Hernan Cortes, the Spanish conqueror
context: Hidalgo seized a banner of the dark-skinned Virgin of Guadalupe (the 'virgen morena') and made it his army's standard; the insurgents' battle cry was roughly 'Long live the Virgin of Guadalupe! Death to bad government!' The image rallied thousands of Indian and mestizo fighters to his side. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banner_of_the_Virgin_of_Guadalupe ; https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/september-16/mexican-war-of-independence-begins

question: Michelangelo unveiled his David, the biblical hero carved whole from a single block of marble, in Florence in 1504. The finished figure stood far taller than any grown man who came to see it. About how tall does the statue rise?
answer: About 17 feet
choices: About 17 feet
About 5 feet
About 9 feet
About 40 feet
context: The David stands roughly 17 feet (5.17 m) tall and weighs around 6 tons, all from a single block of Carrara marble. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: Piero Cannata walked up to Michelangelo's David in Florence's Accademia museum in 1991 with a weapon hidden under his jacket, and he damaged the statue before he was stopped. What did he carry, and what did he break?
answer: A hammer, and he smashed off part of a toe
choices: A hammer, and he smashed off part of a toe
A knife, and he scratched the face
A torch, and he scorched the marble
A rope, and he toppled it over
context: Cannata hid a hammer under his jacket and broke off part of the second toe on David's left foot before bystanders stopped him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: God floats through the sky and stretches a hand down toward the first man, Adam, who reaches up in return, in the Creation of Adam that Michelangelo painted on the Sistine Chapel ceiling. What is true of their two outstretched fingers?
answer: They do not touch; a small gap holds them apart
choices: They do not touch; a small gap holds them apart
They are firmly clasped together
Adam's hand covers God's entirely
God touches Adam's shoulder, not his hand
context: The fingers come within a few centimeters but never meet, holding the scene in suspense. In 1990 physician Frank Meshberger argued the shapes around God form the outline of a human brain. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/michelangelo-creation-of-adam-meaning/

question: Workers in Florence tore down an archway to get Michelangelo's finished David, a statue of some six tons, out of the workshop, and more than forty men set off with it across the city toward the town hall. How did they haul it through the streets?
answer: Rolling it on fourteen greased logs
choices: Rolling it on fourteen greased logs
Floating it down the river on a barge
Lifting it with a giant crane
Dragging it on an iron sledge with oxen
context: More than 40 men took four days to roll the David on fourteen greased logs to the Palazzo della Signoria, unveiled on 8 September 1504. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: Pope Julius II ordered Michelangelo to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in 1508, and the pope's architect, Donato Bramante, drew up a scaffold to hang from the vault on ropes. Michelangelo threw the plan out and built his own wooden bridge instead. What was wrong with Bramante's scaffold?
answer: The rope anchors would leave holes in the surface he had to paint
choices: The rope anchors would leave holes in the surface he had to paint
The ropes would block the light he needed
It could not hold the weight of his assistants
It would take too many years to build
context: Bramante's hanging scaffold needed anchor points in the vault itself; Michelangelo refused to scar the painting surface and braced his own bridge against the side walls. Source: https://www.archeoroma.org/sites/sistine-chapel/ceiling/

question: Michelangelo had to chip his first big Sistine scene, the Flood, off the vault and start again. His Florentine plaster mix did not suit Rome's damp air, and something spread across the fresh paint. What ruined the Flood?
answer: A bloom of mold growing across the plaster
choices: A bloom of mold growing across the plaster
A crack splitting the wall in two
Soot from the chapel's candles
Rainwater leaking through the roof
context: A lime-mold fungus bloomed because the plaster mix was wrong for Rome's humidity; Michelangelo chipped the panel back to bare wall and started over. Source: https://stephaniestorey.com/blog/top-10-little-known-facts-about-the-sistine-ceiling

question: Michelangelo carved his marble David's head and right hand a little too big for the body, and he did it on purpose. The size suited the spot where the statue was first meant to stand. Where was David originally going to be placed?
answer: High up on the roofline of Florence Cathedral
choices: High up on the roofline of Florence Cathedral
Deep inside a dark chapel
At the bottom of a well-lit staircase
On a barge floating in the river
context: The David was meant for the cathedral roofline, so the upper body was enlarged to read correctly from far below. Once finished, Florence judged it too magnificent to hoist up and set it at ground level by the town hall. Source: https://selectitaly.com/blog/florence/11-things-you-didnt-know-about-michelangelos-david/

question: Donatello and Verrocchio had both shown the young David standing in triumph over Goliath's severed head. When Michelangelo carved his own David in Florence, he broke with them and chose a different moment. Which moment did he freeze in marble?
answer: The tense instant before the fight, sling on his shoulder
choices: The tense instant before the fight, sling on his shoulder
The throw of the stone in mid-air
The beheading of Goliath
Kneeling in prayer the night before the battle
context: Michelangelo shows the moment of decision: brow drawn, neck tense, veins bulging in the lowered right hand, the sling over the shoulder. He chose the instant before the battle rather than the victory his predecessors carved. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: Michelangelo painted the Sistine ceiling's nine Genesis scenes out of order, in fact backwards. The first panel he painted was the Drunkenness of Noah, over the door, and he worked toward the altar. As he painted scene after scene in this reverse sequence, how did his figures change?
answer: They grew larger and bolder
choices: They grew larger and bolder
They grew smaller and fainter
They became dull and identical
They lost all their color
context: Working backward from the Drunkenness of Noah to the Creation, Michelangelo's figures grew larger and more confident as his skill on the vault deepened. Source: https://library.biblicalarchaeology.org/sidebar/genesis-in-reverse-the-hidden-meaning-of-the-sistine-chapel-ceiling/

question: Pope Julius II once took a stick to Michelangelo, and some scholars think the painter gave the prophet Zechariah on the Sistine ceiling the pope's face. By that reading, which is tradition rather than proven fact, Michelangelo hid a small revenge in the picture. What is the boy behind Zechariah said to be doing?
answer: Making an obscene 'fig' gesture at the pope's figure
choices: Making an obscene 'fig' gesture at the pope's figure
Sticking out his tongue at the viewer
Holding a tiny portrait of the artist
Pointing toward the chapel door
context: Legend holds that a boy behind Zechariah pokes his thumb between his fingers in the 'fig,' an insult aimed at Julius II, whom the figure is said to resemble. This is interpretive tradition, not proven fact. Source: https://stephaniestorey.com/blog/top-10-little-known-facts-about-the-sistine-ceiling

question: Michelangelo carved and painted with such awesome power, the 'terribilita' Italians spoke of, that people who saw his work gave the man himself an awe-struck nickname. What was the Italian name they called him?
answer: Il Divino, the Divine One
choices: Il Divino, the Divine One
Il Maestro, the Master
Il Gigante, the Giant
Il Vecchio, the Old One
context: Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni (born March 6, 1475; died Feb 18, 1564, age 88) was called 'Il Divino' while still alive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo

question: Agostino di Duccio and Antonio Rossellino both cut into a huge block of Carrara marble in Florence and gave up on it, and it lay out in the cathedral yard for about twenty-five years. In 1501 the 26-year-old Michelangelo claimed the block for his David. What had Florentines called it?
answer: Il Gigante, the Giant
choices: Il Gigante, the Giant
La Pietra, the Stone
Il Mostro, the Monster
La Rovina, the Ruin
context: Agostino di Duccio began on it in 1464 and Rossellino tried in 1476; both gave up. Michelangelo, age 26, was awarded the block on Aug 16, 1501. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling in Rome from 1508 to 1512, and a famous legend says he lay on his back to do it. The legend is false. How did he paint it?
answer: He stood upright on his own scaffolding, head craned back, paint dripping onto his face
choices: He stood upright on his own scaffolding, head craned back, paint dripping onto his face
He lay flat on his back on a wheeled platform pushed close beneath the ceiling
He was hoisted aloft in a swaying basket on ropes at the start of each morning
He reached up from a tall ladder propped against the great wall behind the altar
context: His custom scaffold rested on brackets jutting from holes high in the walls, leaving the floor below clear. He painted over 5,000 square feet and more than 300 figures from 1508 to 1512. Source: https://www.britannica.com/question/How-did-Michelangelo-paint-the-ceiling-of-the-Sistine-Chapel

question: Pietro Torrigiano, a jealous fellow student, quarrelled with the teenage Michelangelo over a sketch in the Medici garden in Florence, where both were training as young artists. He left a mark that stayed with Michelangelo for the rest of his life. What did Torrigiano do?
answer: Shattered his nose with a punch
choices: Shattered his nose with a punch
Slashed his hand with a chisel
Burned his sketches in a fire
Smashed his first marble carving
context: Torrigiano hit him so hard he broke the bone; Michelangelo's crooked nose is visible in every portrait. Lorenzo de' Medici was enraged, and Torrigiano fled Florence. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Torrigiano

question: Michelangelo overheard pilgrims in Rome crediting his new Pieta, a marble Mary cradling the dead Christ across her lap, to a rival sculptor in 1499, as Giorgio Vasari tells it. He added his name to the statue, the only one of his works he would ever sign. How did he do it?
answer: He crept into the chapel at night and chiseled his name across the sash on Mary's chest
choices: He crept into the chapel at night and chiseled his name across the sash on Mary's chest
He returned the next morning and carved his name into the base where pilgrims would kneel
He sent a goldsmith to inlay his name in gold letters along the lower edge of the statue
He quietly scratched his name into the marble behind the figures where no one would look
context: The carved Latin reads MICHELANGELUS BONAROTUS FLORENTIN[US] FACIEBAT -- 'Michelangelo Buonarroti the Florentine made this.' He finished the Pieta about 1498-99, age 24. It remained the only work he ever signed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pieta_(Michelangelo)

question: Florence's workmen slung Michelangelo's finished David, some six tonnes of marble, in a wooden frame, and more than forty men rolled it half a mile from the cathedral workshop to the Piazza della Signoria. How long did that half-mile journey take?
answer: Four days
choices: Four days
Four hours
Two weeks
One month
context: The fragile marble could not be hurried. Centuries later, in 1991, a man named Piero Cannata attacked the David with a hidden hammer and broke off the tip of a toe before he was stopped. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo)

question: Condivi, Michelangelo's biographer, told a story about a rival, the architect Bramante. Bramante, he claimed, schemed to push the commission to paint the vast Sistine Chapel ceiling onto Michelangelo, who resisted the job. What was Bramante secretly hoping would happen?
answer: That Michelangelo would fail at a painter's task he was unsuited for
choices: That Michelangelo would fail at a painter's task he was unsuited for
That Michelangelo would run out of money mid-project
That the Pope would tire of Michelangelo and banish him
That Michelangelo would be forced to share the credit with him
context: Per Condivi, Bramante pushed the painting commission onto a man who considered himself a sculptor, expecting humiliation. Instead Michelangelo produced one of the greatest paintings in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo

question: Giovanni da Pistoia received a comic sonnet from his friend Michelangelo in 1509, after months of painting the Sistine ceiling over his head. Michelangelo wrote of a swelling in his throat, a beard pointing at heaven and paint dripping on his face. How did he end the poem?
answer: 'I am not in the right place -- I am no painter.'
choices: 'I am not in the right place -- I am no painter.'
'Yet still my hand obeys the Pope's command.'
'And so this ceiling shall outlast my bones.'
'Pray for me, friend, that I may see it done.'
context: He even sketched a little caricature of himself painting in the margin. The man who declared himself 'no painter' was creating the most famous ceiling in history. Source: https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/57328/michaelangelo-to-giovanni-da-pistoia-when-the-author-was-painting-the-vault-of-the-sistine-chapel

question: Biagio da Cesena, the pope's master of ceremonies, sneered that the nudes in Michelangelo's Last Judgment belonged 'in a bathhouse, not a chapel.' Michelangelo took his revenge by painting Biagio's face into the fresco. As whom did he paint him?
answer: Minos, the judge of hell, given donkey ears and a snake biting at his groin
choices: Minos, the judge of hell, given donkey ears and a snake biting at his groin
A blind beggar crawling forgotten before the shining gates of heaven
A horned demon dragging a chained line of sinners down into the fire
A crushed skeleton trampled beneath the marching feet of the saved
context: When Biagio begged Pope Paul III to remove it, the Pope joked that his authority did not reach into hell -- so it stayed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Judgment_(Michelangelo)

question: Lionardo, Michelangelo's nephew, had his uncle's corpse carried out of Rome past the guards in a clever disguise. Michelangelo had longed to be buried in Florence, but he died in Rome, where the Church wanted to keep his body. How was the body smuggled out?
answer: Wrapped in a bale and labeled ordinary merchandise
choices: Wrapped in a bale and labeled ordinary merchandise
Sealed inside a coffin marked for another man
Hidden in a hay cart leaving the city at night
Disguised among the baggage of a departing cardinal
context: It reached Florence and was buried at the Basilica of Santa Croce, in a tomb later designed by Giorgio Vasari. Source: https://www.dailyartmagazine.com/the-theft-of-michelangelo-the-story-of-his-stolen-body/

question: Michelangelo wrote a sonnet for his friend Vittoria Colonna about what carving does to a block of stone, and set down a short line of his own. The far more famous 'I saw the angel in the marble and carved until I set him free' is almost certainly not his. How did Michelangelo himself put it?
answer: "The more the marble wastes, the more the statue grows"
choices: "The more the marble wastes, the more the statue grows"
"The angel sleeps in the stone until the chisel wakes him"
"Every block of marble hides a prisoner waiting to be freed"
"The hand that holds the chisel must obey the marble's will"
context: From Michelangelo's sonnet to Vittoria Colonna, tr. Roscoe 1868: 'The more the marble wastes, the more the statue grows'; the popular 'angel in the marble' line is disputed/apocryphal.  (Legend.)

question: The Yongle Emperor received a live giraffe from Africa in 1414, brought home by Zheng He's fleet, and no one at his court had ever seen such a beast. His courtiers declared it a creature of legend whose coming marked a wise ruler. Which creature did they say it was?
answer: The qilin, a gentle Chinese unicorn
choices: The qilin, a gentle Chinese unicorn
The dragon, lord of rain and rivers
The phoenix, reborn from its own ashes
The turtle that carries the world
context: By Confucian tradition the qilin appeared only when a wise and benevolent ruler held power, so the giraffe was hailed as proof of Emperor Yongle's good government. Yongle had a court artist paint it — the only animal in his menagerie so honored — yet publicly insisted it was 'more important to maintain good government than to be concerned with supernatural signs.' Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/peculiar-story-giraffes-medieval-china-180963737/

question: Zheng He commanded seven huge voyages for the Ming emperors in the early 1400s, with hundreds of ships sailing as far as East Africa, decades before Columbus crossed the far smaller Atlantic in 1492. China stood poised to rule the oceans. Then, after the seventh voyage ended in 1433, the Ming court made a stunning choice. What did it do?
answer: Abandoned the fleet, banned ocean voyages, and destroyed the records
choices: Abandoned the fleet, banned ocean voyages, and destroyed the records
Doubled the fleet and sailed on to map the whole African coast
Sold the treasure ships to Arab and Indian merchants for gold
Sent the fleet west to seek a sea route around to Europe
context: After 1433 the Ming court abandoned the treasure fleets, passed Haijin (sea-ban) laws forbidding private maritime trade and restricting shipbuilding to small coastal vessels, and Confucian officials set about destroying the records of the voyages. Having reached Africa first, China deliberately turned inward — the Yongle Emperor's cosmopolitan vision replaced by the Confucian ideal of a self-sufficient agrarian realm. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/zheng-he-closing-ming-china/

question: Zhu Yuanzhang lost his father, his mother and his elder brother to plague within a few weeks when he was sixteen, and the poor peasant boy was left with nothing. He would one day found the Ming dynasty. How did the future emperor keep himself alive?
answer: He entered a Buddhist monastery and begged in the streets for food
choices: He entered a Buddhist monastery and begged in the streets for food
He sailed as a deckhand on a merchant junk to foreign ports
He inherited his family's rice fields and farmed them alone
He trained from boyhood as an officer in the Mongol army
context: From that beggar's bowl Zhu Yuanzhang rose to found the Ming dynasty in 1368, one of history's steepest rags-to-throne climbs. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hongwu_Emperor/

question: The Yongle Emperor built a vast walled palace at the heart of Beijing, a small city sealed inside the big one, and Ming and later Qing emperors lived there for nearly 500 years. It was called the Forbidden City. What could happen to an ordinary person who walked in or out without the emperor's clear permission?
answer: He could be put to death
choices: He could be put to death
He were fined a month's wages
He were turned away politely at the gate
He had to bow and leave a gift
context: That deadly rule is exactly what made the city 'forbidden' to everyone but the emperor's household and court. Source: https://www.travelchinaguide.com/why-is-it-called-forbidden-city.htm

question: Builders of the Forbidden City, the Ming emperors' palace in Beijing, took care, the legend says, not to match the Heavenly Emperor's palace above, which had 10,000 rooms, since an earthly emperor's home must never equal heaven's. How many rooms did they build instead?
answer: 9,999 and a half
choices: 9,999 and a half
exactly 9,000
context: That is the legend; a 1973 survey counted the real total at 980 buildings and 8,707 rooms across 90 courtyards. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City

question: The Yongle Emperor raised his palace in Beijing between 1406 and 1420, and its Chinese name, Zijincheng or Purple Forbidden City, pointed to the star that Chinese astronomers tied to the heavenly home of the celestial emperor, though its walls are red, not purple. Which star was it?
answer: The North Star, Polaris
choices: The North Star, Polaris
The Dog Star, Sirius
The bright blue Vega
The red giant Antares
context: The sky seems to wheel around Polaris, the still center of the heavens, so the palace cast the earthly emperor as its mirror at the center of the world. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/emperors-ruled-from-chinas-forbidden-city-for-nearly-5-centuries

question: The Ming emperors paved the throne halls of the Forbidden City with 'golden bricks,' clay tiles baked for months in special kilns near Suzhou and hauled about 1,000 miles north up the Grand Canal to Beijing. They were not made of gold. What earned them the name?
answer: Struck, they ring like metal
choices: Struck, they ring like metal
They glitter with real gold dust
They stay warm even in winter
They never crack under any weight
context: They are special clay tiles fired for months in the imperial kilns; the dense bake gives them their metallic ring. Source: https://www.chinahighlights.com/beijing/forbidden-city/

question: Yongle (Zhu Di) seized the Ming throne by waging civil war against his own nephew, the Jianwen Emperor. When Yongle's army took Nanjing in 1402, the palace caught fire and Jianwen vanished, his body never confirmed. What does legend say became of him?
answer: He escaped disguised as a wandering monk and lived nearly 40 more years
choices: He escaped disguised as a wandering monk and lived nearly 40 more years
He drowned trying to cross the Yangtze that same night
He fled north and raised a second army against Yongle
He was captured at sea aboard one of Zheng He's ships
context: This is the enduring legend; no body was ever confirmed, and the vanished Jianwen became one of China's great unsolved royal mysteries. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Yongle_Emperor/

question: An empress passed through the central doorway of the Forbidden City's Meridian Gate exactly once, on her wedding day, for that door was the emperor's alone. One other group earned the right to walk through it, just once each. Who were they?
answer: The top three scholars in the empire-wide civil-service exam
choices: The top three scholars in the empire-wide civil-service exam
Foreign kings arriving to pay tribute
The emperor's eldest son and heir
Generals returning from a great victory
context: In a society that prized learning above almost all else, scoring at the very top of the grueling imperial exam bought you a walk through the emperor's own door. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/emperors-ruled-from-chinas-forbidden-city-for-nearly-5-centuries

question: Hongwu, the first Ming emperor, charged his chancellor Hu Weiyong with treason in 1380 and had more than 15,000 officials put to death along with their families. Which line is Hongwu himself said to have spoken about the endless plotting around him?
answer: In the morning I punish a few; by evening others commit the same crime
choices: In the morning I punish a few; by evening others commit the same crime
Trust no minister, for every smile at court hides a knife
Spies whisper in my walls, and sleep has become my enemy
Cut down one traitor and ten more sprout in his place
context: The full line ends 'Day and night I cannot rest,' a chilling glimpse of a ruler who trusted almost no one. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Hongwu_Emperor/

question: The Yongle Emperor set about 2,000 scholars to work on an encyclopedia, and by 1408 it had grown to some 22,937 chapters in 11,095 volumes, too huge ever to be printed. No larger encyclopedia existed anywhere for almost 600 years. What finally passed it in 2007?
answer: Wikipedia
choices: Wikipedia
Encyclopaedia Britannica
The Library of Congress catalog
The complete works of the Qing court
context: A web project written by volunteers finally outgrew the handwritten masterpiece of 2,000 imperial scholars. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Yongle_Encyclopedia

question: Christopher Columbus sailed to the Americas in a flagship, the Santa Maria, only about 85 feet long. Beside one of the treasure ships that Zheng He led across the Indian Ocean for the Ming emperor Yongle, it would have looked like a rowboat. By the old Ming records, how big was one of Zheng He's greatest ships?
answer: Every ship of Columbus and Vasco da Gama combined could fit on its deck
choices: Every ship of Columbus and Vasco da Gama combined could fit on its deck
Its anchor alone weighed more than the entire Santa Maria
It took a full week just to sail all the way around a small island
A thousand horses could gallop across its open deck at once
context: By the traditional dimensions in Ming sources, Zheng He's longest ships ran about 400 feet, carrying nine masts and twelve sails. When archaeologists dug at the Longjiang shipyard in Nanjing in 1957 they unearthed a single rudder post about 36 feet long, longer than half of Columbus's whole ship, hinting at just how enormous the real vessels were. (Association for Asian Studies / National Geographic, 'Seven Voyages of Zheng He'; TheCollector, 'Admiral Zheng He.')

question: Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, and Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, yet Zheng He's treasure fleets had already crossed the Indian Ocean as far as Arabia and East Africa. How long before Columbus's crossing did Zheng He's fleets sail?
answer: Roughly 60 to 90 years earlier
choices: Roughly 60 to 90 years earlier
Roughly 5 to 10 years earlier
About the same time, give or take a year
Only a few months earlier
context: Zheng He's seven voyages ran from 1405 to 1433, about 60 years before Columbus crossed the Atlantic and roughly 80 years before da Gama reached India. China explored the Indian Ocean first, on a scale Europe would not match for generations, and then stopped. (Crash Course World History #21; TheCollector, 'Admiral Zheng He.')

question: Zheng He had a stone tablet set up at Galle, on the island of Ceylon, in 1409. It carries one inscription in three different languages, each part giving thanks and gifts to a different god. Which three gods did the stone honour side by side?
answer: The Buddha, the Hindu god Vishnu, and Allah
choices: The Buddha, the Hindu god Vishnu, and Allah
The Buddha, the Hindu god Shiva, and Allah
The Buddha, the Hindu god Vishnu, and the Jade Emperor
Confucius, the Hindu god Vishnu, and Allah
context: The Galle Trilingual Inscription praises the Buddha in Chinese, the Tamil-Hindu god Tenavarai Nayanar (Vishnu) in Tamil, and Allah in Persian, the only known inscription in those three languages together, and it promised offerings of 1,000 pieces of gold, 5,000 of silver, and tons of scented oil. The stone vanished for centuries and was rediscovered in 1911 lying face down, being used as a cover for a roadside drain in Galle; it now sits in the Colombo National Museum and is on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register. (Wikipedia, 'Galle Trilingual Inscription'; UNESCO Memory of the World.)

question: Moctezuma II reigned over the Aztec Empire from its island capital, Tenochtitlan, when the Spanish arrived. Before he took the throne he had led armies in battle and served Huitzilopochtli, the war god, as his high priest. What does the name Moctezuma roughly mean?
answer: he frowns like a lord
choices: he frowns like a lord
he speaks for the sun
he walks among eagles
he holds the obsidian
context: Roughly 'he frowns like a lord' or 'he who is angry in a noble manner.' Before taking the throne he served as a tlacatecuhtli (war-leader) and as high priest of Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec war-god. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moctezuma_II

question: Moctezuma II met Hernan Cortes on the great causeway into Tenochtitlan in November 1519, and the two men traded necklaces. Cortes gave a collar of pearls and cut glass. Moctezuma gave back collars of red snail shells, and from each hung eight gold figures, each about a foot and a half long. What were the gold figures shaped like?
answer: golden shrimp
choices: golden shrimp
golden eagles
golden skulls
golden serpents
context: By Cortes's own account (his Second Letter), Moctezuma gave two collars of red snail-shells, from each of which hung eight golden prawns/shrimp 'finished in a very perfect manner, about a foot and a half in length.' Source: https://www.historians.org/resource/cortes-on-meeting-moctezuma/

question: Cuauhtemoc, the last Aztec emperor, led the desperate defence of Tenochtitlan right to the very end, and he was taken alive when Hernan Cortes captured the city in August 1521. What does the name Cuauhtemoc mean in Nahuatl, the Aztec language?
answer: Descending Eagle
choices: Descending Eagle
Smoking Mirror
Speaking Stone
Obsidian Serpent
context: 'Cuauhtemoc' means 'Descending Eagle.' He led the defense of Tenochtitlan to the very end before the city fell on 13 August 1521. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cuauhtemoc

question: Hernan Cortes leaned on La Malinche, a Nahua noblewoman who had been sold into slavery, as his interpreter. Bernal Diaz said that without her the Spanish could not have understood the Aztecs at all. Yet she did not speak Spanish. How did Cortes's words reach the Aztecs?
answer: a relay through two interpreters and three tongues
choices: a relay through two interpreters and three tongues
a priest who had mastered the Nahuatl language
hand signs the two sides agreed in advance
letters drafted and read aloud in Latin
context: The chain ran: Cortes spoke Spanish to the shipwreck survivor Geronimo de Aguilar, who rendered it into Maya for Malinche, who then spoke Nahuatl (including the elite court register) to the Aztecs, and back again. Bernal Diaz: 'Without Dona Marina we could not have understood the language of New Spain and Mexico.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Malinche

question: Pedro de Alvarado, the captain Cortes left in Tenochtitlan, feared a revolt while his commander was away. In May 1520 he attacked the unarmed Aztec nobles dancing at the festival of Tezcatlipoca, and Aztec accounts say the killing began with one man. What did the Spanish do first?
answer: cut the arms off the man beating the great drum
choices: cut the arms off the man beating the great drum
set fire to the wooden steps of the temple
shot the high priest down from the gateway
seized the gold piled on the temple altar
context: The Toxcatl Massacre (22 May 1520). Aztec sources (Florentine Codex Book 12, Codex Aubin) say the Spanish first cut off the arms/hands of the man playing the great drum, then beheaded him, then slaughtered the dancers, having blocked the temple exits. Two drums appear in the codex images: the upright huehuetl and the horizontal teponaztli. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_in_the_Great_Temple_of_Tenochtitlan

question: Hernan Cortes took Tenochtitlan on 13 August 1521, and the last Aztec emperor, Cuauhtemoc, was brought before him as a captive. Cuauhtemoc had done all he could to defend his city. What did he reportedly do in front of Cortes?
answer: asked Cortes to kill him with his own dagger
choices: asked Cortes to kill him with his own dagger
begged Cortes to spare his wife and children
cursed Cortes and the Spanish in open court
offered Cortes the city's last hidden gold
context: Cuauhtemoc was intercepted by a brigantine under Garcia Holguin/Sandoval. Brought before Cortes, he reportedly touched the dagger at Cortes's belt and said, 'Take that dagger... and kill me with it,' having done all he could to defend Tenochtitlan. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cuauhtemoc

question: Hunters brought Moctezuma II an ashen-grey bird with a small round mirror set in the top of its head, say Aztec accounts written down decades after the conquest. It was one of eight omens of doom, which historians regard as mostly a tale told later. When Moctezuma looked into the mirror, what did he reportedly see?
answer: warriors riding strange deer
choices: warriors riding strange deer
the city of Tenochtitlan in flames
two suns rising over the lake
a serpent swallowing the moon
context: In the omen, Moctezuma saw warriors riding 'deer', that is, men on horses, animals the Aztecs had never seen. These 'eight omens' survive mainly in the Florentine Codex, compiled by friar Bernardino de Sahagun about 50 years after the conquest; historians treat them, and the famous claim that Moctezuma thought Cortes was the returning god Quetzalcoatl, as largely a post-conquest construction rather than reliable contemporary evidence. Source: https://mexicounexplained.com/8-omens-montezuma-end-aztec-empire/  (Legend.)

question: Moctezuma II died in Spanish custody in June 1520, and exactly how he died is still disputed. Bernal Diaz, a Spanish soldier, wrote that three stones struck Moctezuma on the head, arm and leg as he was brought out before the city. By Diaz's telling, who had thrown those stones?
answer: his own Aztec people
choices: his own Aztec people
the Spanish soldiers
Pedro de Alvarado
the Tlaxcalan warriors
context: By Bernal Diaz's Spanish account, Moctezuma was struck by stones thrown by his own people and then refused food and treatment and died of the wounds. But the death is genuinely contested: some Indigenous sources (e.g. Chimalpahin) say the Spanish killed him, and report that his body bore sword wounds. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moctezuma_II ; https://www.mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/ask-us/moctezumas-death

question: Yesugei, a clan chieftain on the Mongolian steppe, named his newborn son around 1162 after a Tatar warrior he had just captured in battle. The boy would one day be called Genghis Khan, but his birth name was Temujin. What did Temujin mean?
answer: Of iron, or blacksmith
choices: Of iron, or blacksmith
Son of the open sky
Wolf of the cold steppe
Lord of a thousand horses
context: Temujin meant 'of iron' or 'blacksmith.' 'Genghis Khan,' likely meaning 'universal ruler,' was a title given to him only in 1206. Sources: worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genghis_Khan

question: A Mongol horseman charged at full gallop out of the grass steppes of Central Asia, carrying the deadly weapon that Genghis Khan's warriors rode with. At that speed he could still hit a target hundreds of yards away with it. What was it?
answer: A composite bow of horn and sinew
choices: A composite bow of horn and sinew
A long iron-tipped cavalry lance
A curved single-edged saber
A heavy wooden siege crossbow
context: The Mongol composite bow was built from layers of sinew, horn, and wood; it could exceed 100-pound draw weights and strike at roughly 350 yards. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_bow; coldsiberia.org/monbow.htm

question: The Great Khan sent an urgent message across his empire, which ran from China to Persia, and it could travel 200 miles in a single day. It moved along a chain of posts set every 20 to 40 miles. What did each post keep ready for the next stage of the journey?
answer: A relay of fresh horses and riders
choices: A relay of fresh horses and riders
A chain of signal fires on hills
A fleet of fast river boats
A line of trained carrier pigeons
context: This postal relay was called the yam (or ortoo): a rider handed off his message and rested while a fresh rider raced on, like a pony express spanning a continent. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yam_(route); warriorsandlegends.com

question: A messenger rode into a station on the Great Khan's business, carrying the one object that won him food and a bed at every stop. Its writing began 'By the power of eternal Heaven' and warned that anyone who disrespected the bearer 'shall die.' What was the object?
answer: A metal passport tablet
choices: A metal passport tablet
A sealed wax letter
A painted silk banner
A carved bone whistle
context: The paiza (gerege): rank showed in the metal, from wood and bronze up to silver and gold for the highest. It opened 'By the power of eternal Heaven.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paiza; rubinmuseum.org

question: Marco Polo crossed the Silk Road between China and Europe under the Pax Mongolica, the peace the Mongols enforced, when its roads were safe and orderly. People summed up that order in a famous saying. What did the saying claim could be done on those roads?
answer: A maiden could carry gold across it unharmed
choices: A maiden could carry gold across it unharmed
A lone child could cross it without any fear
A merchant could sleep in the open and wake untouched
A pilgrim could walk it for a year and meet no thief
context: It was said 'a maiden bearing a nugget of gold on her head could wander safely throughout the realm.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Mongolica; education.nationalgeographic.org

question: A courier with the Great Khan's most urgent mail galloped toward the next relay post. He carried something the post could hear from far off, so that it was ready for him the moment he rode in. What did the rider use to announce himself from a distance?
answer: A belt of jingling bells
choices: A belt of jingling bells
A horn he sounded as he rode
A drum strapped to his saddle
A whistle carved from bone
context: These 'arrow messengers' rode with head and torso bandaged against the pace; for top-priority mail a rider wore a belt of bells whose jingling warned the next station from far off. Sources: warriorsandlegends.com; tldrhistory.com

question: Subutai joined Genghis Khan's army at about fourteen, though he had no family tie to the Khan at all. He rose to supreme command as the Khan's greatest general, credited with conquering 32 nations and winning 65 pitched battles. What was he when he started out?
answer: A blacksmith’s son with no royal blood
choices: A blacksmith’s son with no royal blood
A captured prince of a rival clan
A cousin born into the Khan’s family
A hired captain from a foreign land
context: Subutai was the son of a blacksmith from the Uriankhai tribe near Lake Baikal, with no blood tie to the Khan, and ended his life as a herdsman, living proof the Mongol army rewarded merit. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subutai; historyfacts.com

question: Genghis Khan sent a trading caravan of about 450 merchants to the Khwarezmian city of Otrar in 1218, expecting peaceful trade. Revenge for what happened there drove his great war in the west. What did the city's governor, Inalchuq, do to the caravan?
answer: He killed every merchant and seized the goods
choices: He killed every merchant and seized the goods
He let them pass but taxed them into ruin
He jailed the merchants and held them for ransom
He turned the caravan back at the city gate
context: Inalchuq accused the merchants of spying, killed them all, and seized their goods; when Genghis sent envoys for justice, the Shah beheaded the lead ambassador, so Genghis invaded. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otrar_Catastrophe; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inalchuq

question: Genghis Khan's followers laid him to rest in 1227 and hid the place so well that it has never been found. By tradition, they made sure that no trace of it would remain. What did they do at the grave itself?
answer: Riders trampled the grave flat to hide it
choices: Riders trampled the grave flat to hide it
He was buried at sea in a stone coffin
His tomb was filled with molten gold
His body was burned on a great pyre
context: Tradition holds that the escort had horses trample the grave flat so no mound or marker remained. The tomb has never been located. Sources: worldhistory.org/Genghis_Khan; history.com/topics/asian-history/genghis-khan  (Legend.)

question: Tolui, a son of Genghis Khan, stormed the Persian city of Nishapur in April 1221 after an arrow from its walls killed Genghis Khan's son-in-law, Toquchar. Tolui ordered every inhabitant put to the sword, the poet Attar among them. What did the Mongols leave there as a warning to anyone who might resist?
answer: Three pyramids stacked from the severed heads
choices: Three pyramids stacked from the severed heads
Fields sown with salt so nothing would grow
The great mosque burned down to bare stone
A pillar carved with the Khan's victories
context: The severed heads were reportedly built into three separate pyramids, one of men, one of women, one of children, as a warning. The poet Attar, about 78, was among the dead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Nishapur_(1221)

question: Subutai, the Mongol general, sent two armies hundreds of miles apart to smash the Poles at Legnica on 9 April 1241 and the Hungarians at Mohi two days later. Both times his light horse-archers used one trick against the heavy-armoured European knights. What was the trick?
answer: They pretended to flee, luring the knights into a hidden ambush
choices: They pretended to flee, luring the knights into a hidden ambush
They dug a deep trench across the front of the battlefield
They poisoned the rivers the knights drank from before the fight
They bribed the knights' own commanders to switch sides
context: The 'feigned retreat' was the Mongol signature: horse-archers would attack, then turn and gallop away, baiting the European knights into breaking formation and charging straight into a pre-set ambush. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Legnica-1241

question: Vienna lay in the Mongols' path at the end of 1241: Subutai's armies had smashed every force sent against them and meant to ride all the way to the 'Great Sea,' the Atlantic. No European army had stopped them, yet that winter they turned around and rode east, never to return. What turned the Mongols back?
answer: The Great Khan Ogedei died far away in Mongolia, recalling the princes
choices: The Great Khan Ogedei died far away in Mongolia, recalling the princes
A massive blizzard froze and starved the Mongol horses in the passes
The Pope's crusading army finally united and met them outside Vienna
The Mongol princes caught a plague sweeping through their camp
context: Ogedei Khan died on December 11, 1241, after a night of heavy drinking. By Mongol custom his death summoned the princes and their armies thousands of miles back to Karakorum for the kurultai - the assembly to choose the next Great Khan. Europe was saved not by a victory but by the timing of a drinking bout an empire away; it was the farthest west the Mongols ever reached. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/history-famous-people/ogedei-khan-0010837

question: John Ericsson, a Swedish engineer, designed the Union's strange new ironclad, the USS Monitor: a flat iron deck riding almost level with the water, with one fat round gun-tower in the middle of it and nothing else on top. What did sailors nickname the odd vessel?
answer: A cheesebox on a raft
choices: A cheesebox on a raft
A floating barn roof
An iron coffin afloat
A turtle in armor
context: The Monitor's single 20-foot cylindrical turret rising from a nearly flat deck gave it that look. The turret could rotate to fire its two 11-inch Dahlgren guns in any direction without the whole ship turning. (battlefields.org/learn/articles/uss-monitor-cheesebox-raft)

question: The crew of the Confederate ironclad Virginia drove her 1,500-pound iron ram into the side of the wooden Union sloop Cumberland at Hampton Roads on 8 March 1862, tearing a hole one officer said was wide enough to drive in a horse and cart. As the Cumberland sank, what happened to the Virginia's ram?
answer: It snapped off and stuck inside the sinking Cumberland
choices: It snapped off and stuck inside the sinking Cumberland
It bent backward and jammed the Virginia's own bow
It glanced off the hull and shattered into pieces
It dragged the Virginia down with the Cumberland
context: Virginia's chief engineer Ashton Ramsay compared his ship to 'a wasp we could sting but once, leaving the sting in the wound.' The Cumberland's crew kept firing as she went down with her flag still flying; about 121-123 sailors went down with her. (marinersmuseum.org/2021/10/uss-cumberland-sink-before-surrender)

question: The Baron de Montesquieu came up with the idea of splitting government into three branches so that no one person could grab all the power. Yet at home on his moated estate near Bordeaux he was a country nobleman with a very plain trade that he loved. Besides writing, how did he make his living?
answer: He grew and sold wine
choices: He grew and sold wine
He bred warhorses
He sailed trading ships
He minted the king's coins
context: Montesquieu was a real wine-grower at the moated Chateau de La Brede, where he wrote most of his great books. He fussed over his grape harvests and the sales of his renowned Graves wine. The man who engineered the separation of powers was, day to day, a merchant-winemaker. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/montesquieu); Chateau de la Brede official site.

question: America's framers built three separate branches into their Constitution, taking the plan from The Spirit of the Laws, Montesquieu's book of 1748. Freedom survives, he argued there, only if no one person or group ever holds all three kinds of a government's power at once. Which three powers did he say must be kept apart?
answer: The lawmaking, the law-enforcing, and the law-judging powers
choices: The lawmaking, the law-enforcing, and the law-judging powers
The military, the religious, and the merchant powers
The royal, the noble, and the common powers
The tax, the trade, and the treaty powers
context: In Book XI Montesquieu names them the legislative (which enacts laws), the executive (which carries out public resolutions), and the judicial (which tries the causes of individuals). Keep them in separate hands and liberty lives; merge them and it dies. This is the blueprint the Framers wired into the U.S. Constitution. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Montesquieu and the Separation of Powers' (Spirit of the Laws Bk XI Ch 6).

question: Montesquieu published a sly bestselling novel in 1721, told entirely in the letters two foreign travellers wrote home from Paris about how strange the French seemed. Through their eyes he poked fun at French kings, priests and courtiers without being punished for it. Who did he make his two letter-writers?
answer: Two Persian visitors
choices: Two Persian visitors
Two shipwrecked sailors
Two country priests
Two runaway princes
context: The book is the Persian Letters. Two Persians, Usbek and Rica, roam Paris and mock French and Christian customs in letters home, while back east Usbek's seraglio of five wives slowly falls into revolt. It ran through about ten editions in a single year. Source: Wikipedia, 'Persian Letters'.

question: Montesquieu, author of The Spirit of the Laws, went nearly blind from cataracts in the last years of his life, yet he refused to stop working on his books. To keep writing once he could no longer see the page, what did he do?
answer: He dictated his words to secretaries
choices: He dictated his words to secretaries
He learned to write with his eyes shut
He had the text read back to him in court
He carved the words into wax by feel
context: Going nearly blind, Montesquieu dictated to scribes until he died of a fever in Paris on 10 February 1755. Some of his surviving manuscripts are partly in the handwriting of the secretaries who wrote for him during his blindness. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/montesquieu).

question: Montesquieu did not trust rulers to behave themselves. In The Spirit of the Laws he warned that 'every man invested with power is apt to abuse it, and to carry his authority as far as it will go.' So instead of hoping for good rulers, what did Montesquieu say was needed 'from the very nature of things'?
answer: That power should be a check to power
choices: That power should be a check to power
That kings should be chosen by lottery
That the people should rise up and revolt
That rulers should swear a sacred oath
context: Montesquieu's remedy was not better men but a better machine: 'it is necessary from the very nature of things that power should be a check to power.' Don't trust rulers to be good; arrange the branches so each one blocks the others. Source: Founders' Constitution, Univ. of Chicago Press (Spirit of Laws Bk XI).

question: Montesquieu argued that the power to judge must be kept apart from the rest of the government. He inherited a post in Bordeaux in 1716 and held it for about eleven years. Before he became a writer, what had Montesquieu been?
answer: A judge over criminal trials
choices: A judge over criminal trials
A general of the king's army
A bishop of Bordeaux
A tax collector for the crown
context: As President a Mortier in the Parlement of Bordeaux, Montesquieu presided over the Tournelle, its criminal court, for about eleven years. The man who designed the separation of judicial power had actually been a judge. He sold the office in 1726 to devote himself to writing. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/montesquieu).

question: The Catholic Church struck back at Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws in 1751. The book had spread fast across Europe since 1748, and it boldly attacked the power of kings and priests by insisting that no one should ever hold all three branches of government at once. How did the Church punish the book?
answer: It placed the book on the list of forbidden books
choices: It placed the book on the list of forbidden books
It excommunicated everyone who read it
It ordered every copy publicly burned
It fined the printers who had sold it
context: In 1751 the Church added The Spirit of the Laws to the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, its official list of forbidden books. Montesquieu fired back with a 'Defense of the Spirit of the Laws.' Being banned only helped the book's fame spread further. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Spirit of Law'.

question: Montesquieu sorted governments into three kinds, each kept alive by a different driving passion in its people. A republic, he said, runs on virtue and a monarchy on honor, while the third and darkest kind, where 'a single person directs everything by his own will and caprice,' runs on a single emotion. What did Montesquieu say a despotism runs on?
answer: Fear
choices: Fear
Greed
Pride
Faith
context: Montesquieu paired each government with its animating principle: republic with virtue (love of country and the laws), monarchy with honor, despotism with fear. A government dies, he warned, when it loses its animating principle. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/montesquieu).

question: Montesquieu won a single grand title from James Madison, who leaned on the Frenchman heavily in Federalist No. 47 in 1788 while defending the new Constitution. What did Madison call Montesquieu?
answer: The oracle always consulted on this subject
choices: The oracle always consulted on this subject
The father of the American republic
The first true friend of liberty
The wisest king's counselor in Europe
context: Madison wrote: 'The oracle who is always consulted and cited on this subject is the celebrated Montesquieu.' Madison reported that Montesquieu treated England's constitution as the very 'mirror of political liberty,' and credited him with displaying the principle of separated powers to mankind 'most effectually.' The line from 1748 Paris to the 1787 Convention runs straight through this one Frenchman. Source: Avalon Project, Yale Law School, Federalist No. 47.

question: Donald Lutz, a scholar, counted every author the American founders quoted in their political writing from 1760 to 1805. Among all named human authors, Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws came out on top, ahead even of the famous legal scholar William Blackstone. Only one source was quoted more. What was it?
answer: The Bible
choices: The Bible
The Magna Carta
The works of Aristotle
The English common law
context: In Lutz's famous citation survey, The Spirit of the Laws was the single most-cited secular source on government in American founding-era writing. The founders quoted Montesquieu more than any author except the Bible itself. Source: Wikipedia, 'Montesquieu' (citing Donald Lutz's citation survey).

question: James Madison turned Montesquieu's warning into one of the most quoted sentences in American government. In Federalist No. 47 he wrote that piling all the lawmaking, law-enforcing and judging power into one set of hands 'may justly be pronounced' one terrible thing. What did Madison say that piling-up of power was?
answer: The very definition of tyranny
choices: The very definition of tyranny
The seed of every civil war
The death of all commerce
The end of religion itself
