context: Madison wrote that 'the accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands... may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.' It is the American restatement of Montesquieu's warning that liberty cannot survive when the branches merge. Source: Avalon Project, Yale Law School, Federalist No. 47.

question: Montesquieu insisted that judges should never get to soften or stiffen a law to suit themselves; their job was only to apply it exactly as written. To drive this home he gave judges a haunting image, saying they should be no more than one plain thing. What did Montesquieu say a judge should be no more than?
answer: The mouth that speaks the law
choices: The mouth that speaks the law
The shield that guards the law
The sword that enforces the law
The scale that weighs the law
context: Montesquieu's image (Spirit of the Laws Bk XI Ch 6): judges should be 'no more than the mouth that pronounces the words of the law, mere passive beings, incapable of moderating either its force or rigour.' The judicial branch applies the law; it does not make or bend it. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Montesquieu and the Separation of Powers'.

question: Claudio Monteverdi staged L'Orfeo in 1607, retelling the Greek myth of Orpheus, who goes down to the land of the dead to win back his bride. Orpheus must get past Charon, the grim ferryman of the river into Hades. In the aria 'Possente spirto,' what does he use to cross?
answer: His own singing, so beautiful it charms the ferryman into rowing him over
choices: His own singing, so beautiful it charms the ferryman into rowing him over
A golden coin pressed into the ferryman's hand as payment for the crossing
A sword drawn against the ferryman to force him back from the oars
A secret password the gods had taught him to speak at the river's edge
context: In 'Possente spirto,' Monteverdi piled on chitarrone, organ, two violins, two cornetts and a double-harp to make the singing itself the magic that opens the underworld. L'Orfeo, premiered 24 February 1607 for the Gonzaga court in Mantua, is the earliest opera still regularly staged today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Orfeo

question: Churchmen at the Council of Trent argued over the music of worship, and some wanted to ban polyphony, where many voices sing different lines at once, since it buried the holy words. A beloved legend, written down decades later, tells of one Mass by Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, the Missa Papae Marcelli. What does the legend say it did?
answer: Proved polyphony could be holy and clear, saving the whole tradition from the ban
choices: Proved polyphony could be holy and clear, saving the whole tradition from the ban
Was the first music ever sung in the new Sistine Chapel before the assembled cardinals
Converted a Protestant prince who heard it and returned his lands to the Church
Was composed overnight on a dare and performed for the pope the very next morning
context: This is a beloved legend, not fact: it was first claimed by the theorist Agostino Agazzari in 1607 and dramatized by biographer Giuseppe Baini in 1828; modern scholars say Palestrina's name probably never even came up in the Council's debates. The Mass is written for six voice parts, but its trick was clarity: he often had the voices move together in chords so every word could be understood. Source: ebsco.com/research-starters/music/pope-marcellus-mass

question: A worshipper knelt in a mosque in Cairo facing a small niche in its wall, the mihrab, and a worshipper in Jakarta knelt facing another. Each niche marked the one direction every Muslim faced in the five daily prayers. Toward what place did the mihrab point?
answer: The Kaaba in Mecca
choices: The Kaaba in Mecca
The grave of the local imam
The spring of Zamzam
The rising sun at dawn
context: The mihrab is a niche cut into the qibla wall, and its only purpose is to show the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, so the whole congregation faces the same way. Salah, the second pillar of Islam, is prayer five times a day, standing, bowing, kneeling and pressing the forehead to the ground while facing the Kaaba. The earliest mosques had no niche at all, just a painted line or a wooden staff in the ground to mark the way.

question: Muhammad marched into Mecca with his followers in 630 and took the city. He chose Bilal, a freed African slave famous for his beautiful voice, to give the first Muslim call to prayer over the conquered city, and he picked a dramatic spot for it. Where did Muhammad have Bilal climb?
answer: To the top of the Kaaba
choices: To the top of the Kaaba
To the gate of the city
To a hill outside Mecca
To the roof of his own house
context: Bilal ibn Rabah, an Ethiopian-descended freed slave, was the very first muezzin. Before towers existed the muezzin simply climbed onto the highest nearby rooftop to be seen and heard; the minaret tower came later. Muhammad had Bilal climb the Kaaba itself to give the call there for the first time. Source: https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/the-history-of-the-muezzin--74007 (Hurriyet); https://archive.mpac.org/article/bilal-ibn-rabah-the-voice-of-resilience/ (MPAC). Confidence: medium.

question: European ships carried cloth, brass, knives, guns, gunpowder and drink south to the coast of West Africa. On the last leg of the voyage they brought sugar, tobacco, cotton and rum from the Americas home to Europe. What did they carry on the long middle leg of the triangle, west across the ocean?
answer: Captive Africans
choices: Captive Africans
Ivory and gold dust
Salt and dried fish
Copper and palm oil
context: That middle leg was called the Middle Passage. The cycle fed itself: the guns sold in Africa were used to take more captives, and the crops the captives grew were sold for money to buy more guns. Between about 1517 and 1867 roughly 12.5 million Africans were forced onto these ships. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangular_trade ; Britannica 'Triangular trade')

question: Thomas Clarkson printed a diagram of the slave ship Brookes in 1788. It showed more than 400 people drawn lying side by side across the lower deck, packed like rows of goods. The picture's power came from one number: the width of deck each grown person was given. About how wide was that space?
answer: Sixteen inches
choices: Sixteen inches
Thirty inches
Forty inches
Sixty inches
context: Each person had about sixteen inches (40 cm) of width and roughly two and a half feet of headroom — too little to sit up or stand. The Quaker printer James Phillips ran off 7,000 copies in 1789. Clarkson called the diagram's effect 'intelligible and irresistible' and carried it on his lecture tours. (abolitionseminar.org 'Brookes')

question: African kingdoms such as Dahomey seized captives in raids and wars and sold them at the coast for guns and cloth. European slavers waited there to buy; they rarely marched inland to catch anyone themselves. Why did the Europeans leave the catching to the African kingdoms?
answer: They thought raiding inland too dangerous
choices: They thought raiding inland too dangerous
They lacked the men to march inland
Their own kings had forbidden it
They had promised the chiefs they would not
context: This is the part of the story often left untaught: the internal African slave trade came first and fed the Atlantic one. Coastal kingdoms did the capturing and sold the captives to waiting European ships, who judged the interior too deadly to enter themselves. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey ; africanhistoryextra.com 'Kingdom of Dahomey and the Atlantic')

question: Below deck on the Middle Passage, the young Olaudah Equiano found a hold so foul and crowded that each chained captive had 'scarcely room to turn himself.' In his book he recorded the most desperate act he saw there: two men, chained together, choosing death over the voyage. What did they do?
answer: Jumped through the netting into the sea
choices: Jumped through the netting into the sea
Refused all food until they died
Broke their chains and fought the crew
Begged the captain to turn the ship back
context: Equiano wrote that the two men, 'preferring death to such a life of misery, somehow made through the nettings and jumped into the sea' to drown rather than continue — a documented act of suicide-resistance on the Middle Passage. Crews strung netting along the rails precisely to stop such escapes. (https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2672/olaudah-equianos-account-of-the-middle-passage/)

question: Afonso I, the Christian king of Kongo, watched Portuguese merchants go behind his back and buy captives straight from his own nobles. In 1526 he wrote to King Joao III of Portugal to protest the trade, and he described one cruelty the slavers did to his stolen people. What did Afonso say was being done to them?
answer: Branded with a red-hot iron
choices: Branded with a red-hot iron
Sold to lands across the sea
Worked until they dropped dead
Torn from their mothers at birth
context: Afonso (born Nzinga Mbemba) wrote that traders were 'kidnapping our people — children of this country, sons of our nobles and vassals, even people of our own family,' who were then 'branded with a red-hot iron.' He is a rare example of an African ruler protesting the trade from inside it — and being ignored. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_I_of_Kongo ; worldhistorycommons.org)

question: Leopold Mozart and his wife wrote one of their baby son's names in Greek, Theophilus, when the boy was baptized in Salzburg in January 1756. In Latin the same name became Amadeus, as in Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. What does the name mean?
answer: "Beloved of God"
choices: "Beloved of God"
"Born in winter"
"Son of the court"
"Master of the keys"
context: Theophilus is Greek for 'lover of God' / 'beloved of God'; its Latin equivalent is Amadeus, the name history remembers him by. Source: mozartproject.org/the-many-names-of-wolfgang-amadeus-mozart/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozart's_name

question: Wolfgang Mozart was writing music before he was old enough to read well, and his father, Leopold, a music teacher in Salzburg, copied the boy's earliest tunes into the notebook of his older sister, Nannerl. What kind of piece was the very first, written when Wolfgang was about five?
answer: A short minuet
choices: A short minuet
A church hymn
A drum march
A sea shanty
context: His first surviving piece is a tiny Minuet in G, later catalogued as K.1, written when he was five. Source: mozartproject.org/mozarts-first-composition-a-minuet-and-trio/ ; classicfm.com/composers/mozart/first-piano-music-minuet/

question: At three, little Wolfgang Mozart was already picking out full tunes on a keyboard, before many children could even tie their shoes. His father, Leopold, taught music in Salzburg. Which keyboard instrument was the small boy playing?
answer: The harpsichord
choices: The harpsichord
The church organ
The clavichord
The fortepiano
context: Mozart could play the harpsichord by age 3 and was composing by 4-5. Source: britannica.com/biography/Wolfgang-Amadeus-Mozart

question: When Wolfgang Mozart was six, his father Leopold packed the family into a coach and set off with the boy and his older sister Nannerl on a grand tour through Munich, Vienna, Paris and London. Crowds everywhere were amazed at what the small child could do. What was young Mozart doing on the tour?
answer: Performing for kings and queens at the grandest courts
choices: Performing for kings and queens at the grandest courts
Conducting full armies on the battlefield
Painting royal portraits from memory
Sailing trading ships between cities
context: As a child he played at Versailles for the French king and in London for King George III and Queen Charlotte, where he met Johann Christian Bach. Source: britannica.com/biography/Wolfgang-Amadeus-Mozart ; ebsco.com/research-starters/history/mozart-tours-europe-child-prodigy

question: Daines Barrington, a scientist, tested eight-year-old Mozart in London for the Royal Society. The boy sight-read a hidden manuscript without a mistake and made up songs on the spot. Then, partway through, he did something that reminded everyone he was only eight. What did he do?
answer: He wandered off to play with his pet cat
choices: He wandered off to play with his pet cat
He fell asleep at the keyboard
He demanded a bag of sweets
He started crying for his mother
context: Barrington recorded that the child would sometimes abandon the harpsichord to play with his favourite cat. Source: royalsociety.org/blog/2015/03/meeting-mozart-in-london/ ; publicdomainreview.org/collection/account-of-a-very-remarkable-young-musician-1769/

question: At fourteen, Mozart sat in the Sistine Chapel in Rome during Holy Week of 1770 and heard a nine-voice choral work the Vatican guarded so closely that anyone who copied it could be thrown out of the Church. He went back to his room and wrote out the whole piece from that one hearing. Which work was it?
answer: Allegri's 'Miserere'
choices: Allegri's 'Miserere'
Bach's 'Mass in B Minor'
Handel's 'Messiah'
Vivaldi's 'Four Seasons'
context: Mozart transcribed Gregorio Allegri's 'Miserere' from memory after a single hearing during Holy Week 1770. Source: classicfm.com/composers/mozart/transcribed-allegri-miserere-sistine-chapel/ ; mymodernmet.com/mozart-miserere-gregorio-allegri/

question: Don Giovanni, the villain of Mozart's opera, jokingly invites a stone statue of the man he murdered to come to supper, and the statue comes. It knocks at the door, grips his hand and tells him to repent. When the Don refuses, how does the opera end for him?
answer: The statue drags him down to hell through the burning floor
choices: The statue drags him down to hell through the burning floor
He flees toward the harbour but drowns in the escape
He repents in terror and the statue spares his life
Soldiers seize him and wall him up alive in a tower
context: The murdered Commendatore returns as a stone statue; when Don Giovanni refuses to repent, the floor opens and flames and demons drag him down to hell. Source: metopera.org/discover/education/educator-guides/don-giovanni/the-operas-plot-creation/ ; thelistenersclub.com/2020/10/30/ghostly-mozart-the-commendatore-scene-from-don-giovanni/

question: Mozart, the story goes, came to the night before the Prague premiere of his opera Don Giovanni in 1787 without having written its overture, the burst of orchestra music that begins the show. The players needed their parts by morning, or the premiere would collapse. How did Mozart get the overture done in time?
answer: He composed the whole overture overnight in about three hours
choices: He composed the whole overture overnight in about three hours
He borrowed the overture from an older opera
He told the orchestra to make it up on the spot
He delayed the premiere by a week
context: Legend says Mozart wrote the overture in roughly three hours the night before, his wife Constanze keeping him awake with stories; copyists barely finished and the orchestra sight-read it cold. (Famous but unverified.) Source: cmuse.org/mozart-midnight-masterpiece-don-giovanni-overture/ ; classicalwonders.com/2024/10/22/mozarts-last-minute-overture-for-don-giovanni/

question: Emperor Joseph II sat through one of Mozart's new operas in Vienna and, as the story goes, told the composer to his face that it had 'too many notes.' Mozart, then in his late twenties, did not grovel. How is he said to have answered the emperor?
answer: "Exactly as many as are necessary, Your Majesty"
choices: "Exactly as many as are necessary, Your Majesty"
"Then I shall compose for the French instead"
"Your Majesty's ears are simply too small"
"I will gladly return your payment"
context: The retort is famous but unverified, popularized by the film Amadeus, tied to The Abduction from the Seraglio (1782). Source: flowingprose.com/2015/08/too-many-notes-my-dear-mozart/ ; interlude.hk/mozart-die-entfuhrung-aus-dem-serail-k-384-premiered-today-1782/  (Legend.)

question: A stranger dressed all in black came to Mozart in 1791 with an anonymous commission: a Requiem, a Mass to be sung for the dead. Mozart was sick and worn out, and the secrecy unnerved him deeply. What did he come to believe he was writing?
answer: A requiem for his own death
choices: A requiem for his own death
A secret coded message to the emperor
Music that would make him immortal
An opera disguised as a mass
context: The Requiem was secretly commissioned by Count Franz von Walsegg (who meant to pass it off as his own) via a black-clad messenger; the ailing Mozart came to believe he was composing a requiem for himself. Source: classical-music.com/features/works/requiem-mozart ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_von_Walsegg

question: Franz Xaver Sussmayr, Mozart's pupil, had to complete the Requiem that Mozart left unfinished at his death at thirty-five. The last notes in Mozart's own hand run just eight bars into one movement, where his pen stopped for good. Which movement was it?
answer: The 'Lacrimosa'
choices: The 'Lacrimosa'
The 'Hallelujah'
The 'Gloria'
The 'Magnificat'
context: The last music in Mozart's own hand is the first eight bars of the 'Lacrimosa'; his pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed the Requiem. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacrimosa ; classicfm.com/composers/mozart/music/requiem/

question: Mozart poured out symphonies, operas, concertos and church music in barely thirty-five years. To keep them straight, scholars give each of his works its own number in one catalogue, from the first piece he wrote at about five to the Requiem he never finished. What is that numbering system called?
answer: The Köchel (K.) number
choices: The Köchel (K.) number
The Salzburg index
The Vienna stamp
The Amadeus code
context: Ludwig von Köchel catalogued Mozart's works; the numbers run from K.1 (the minuet he wrote at five) to K.626 (the Requiem). A 2024 revision pushed his documented output past 700 pieces. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Köchel_catalogue ; mozarteum.at/en/presentation-of-the-new-koechel-catalogue

question: Alexander Pushkin wrote a verse play spreading the legend that Antonio Salieri, Vienna's court composer, poisoned Mozart out of jealousy, and the film Amadeus stamped it on everyone's memory. Historians have turned up no evidence for it. What did Salieri, Mozart and a third musician do together in 1785?
answer: Jointly composed a cantata to celebrate a singer recovering her voice
choices: Jointly composed a cantata to celebrate a singer recovering her voice
Co-conducted a full opera season at the Vienna court theater
Shared one apartment near the cathedral through a hard winter
Traded their best pupils back and forth between their classes
context: The 1785 cantata 'Per la ricuperata salute di Ofelia' was co-written by Salieri, Mozart, and a man named Cornetti, to a text by Lorenzo Da Ponte, to celebrate the singer Nancy Storace getting her voice back. Salieri wrote the outer parts, Mozart the middle. The score was thought lost until musicologist Timo Jouko Herrmann found it in a Prague archive in 2015-2016. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_la_ricuperata_salute_di_Ofelia

question: Antonio Salieri directed the emperor's music in Vienna for thirty-six years, and he often took pupils without charging a fee, nothing like the jealous nobody of the poisoning legend. Among the pupils he taught were three who became giants of music. Who were they?
answer: Beethoven, Schubert, and Carl Czerny
choices: Beethoven, Schubert, and Carl Czerny
Bach, Handel, and Antonio Vivaldi
Chopin, Liszt, and Johannes Brahms
Haydn, Gluck, and Niccolo Paganini
context: Salieri's pupils read like a who's-who of music: Beethoven, Schubert, Carl Czerny, Giacomo Meyerbeer, and Mozart's own son Franz Xaver Wolfgang Mozart. Beethoven dedicated his three Violin Sonatas, Op. 12, to Salieri. An orphan from Legnago, Italy, Salieri often taught for free. Historians find no evidence anyone poisoned Mozart, whose 1791 death certificate listed 'severe miliary fever.' Source: https://www.thecollector.com/antonio-salieri-misjudged-italian-composer/ ; https://www.classicfm.com/composers/mozart/guides/did-salieri-murder-mozart-mythbuster/

question: Muhammad drove trading caravans across the burning desert between Mecca and Syria as a young man, long before he was ever called a prophet. The way he dealt with the merchants of Mecca won him a proud nickname from them: al-Amin. What does al-Amin mean?
answer: The Trustworthy
choices: The Trustworthy
The Wanderer
The Merchant
The Fearless
context: Muhammad's reputation for honesty on the Syria caravan routes earned him the title 'al-Amin' -- the Trustworthy. People reportedly cried 'There he is, al-Amin! There is Muhammad!' when he arrived to settle a quarrel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad and https://lastprophet.info/6-the-ka-ba-arbitration

question: Abu Bakr slipped out of Mecca with Muhammad in 622, ahead of enemies who wanted the Prophet dead, and the two made for the oasis of Yathrib, about two hundred miles north. Its people loved Muhammad so much that they renamed the town the City of the Prophet. What is it called today?
answer: Medina
choices: Medina
Mecca
Baghdad
Damascus
context: Yathrib was renamed Madinat al-Nabi, 'the City of the Prophet,' shortened to Medina ('the City'). The caliph Umar later made the flight of 622 Year 1 of the Islamic calendar. Medina became the base from which Islam grew into an organized community and an Arabian power.

question: Refugees from Mecca, Muhammad among them, made their way to the oasis of Yathrib in 622. Later Muslims held that journey so important that they made its year Year One of their calendar, and to this day Muslims count their years from it. What is the journey called?
answer: The Hijra
choices: The Hijra
The Hajj
The Jihad
The Sunna
context: The Hijra (the word means to depart or break ties and move away) became Year One of the Islamic calendar. The caliph Umar fixed the count in 639, starting from the first day of the month Muharram -- corresponding to 16 July 622. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah

question: Khadija, a wealthy widow of Mecca of about forty, put the twenty-five-year-old Muhammad in charge of her trading caravans around 595. She watched him bring back honest profits from every trip and came to admire his character. Then she made a bold move. What did Khadija do?
answer: She proposed marriage to him
choices: She proposed marriage to him
She made him head of her household guards
She gave him half of her caravans
She sent him to study in Syria
context: Khadija bint Khuwaylid, impressed by his competence, proposed marriage to Muhammad. He stayed married only to her until she died, and she became the very first person to believe him when revelation came. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad

question: The leaders of Mecca rebuilt the Kaaba in Muhammad's day and almost came to blows over which clan would have the honour of setting the sacred Black Stone back in place. Muhammad settled the quarrel without a fight. What did he do?
answer: He laid the stone on a cloak and had each clan lift a corner together
choices: He laid the stone on a cloak and had each clan lift a corner together
He drew lots and let blind chance choose the one winning clan
He simply gave the honor to the oldest and most senior clan
He marched the stone to the wall and set it there single-handed
context: Around 605, Muhammad laid the Black Stone on a cloak and had an elder of each clan lift a corner together to carry it to the wall, then set it into place with his own hands -- so no clan was slighted. Reported in Ibn Ishaq's biography. Source: https://lastprophet.info/6-the-ka-ba-arbitration

question: Muhammad said that the angel Gabriel seized him around 610, while he was alone in the cave of Hira on a mountain near Mecca, and gave him a one-word command. Muhammad protested that he could not read, but in his account the angel repeated the word three times. What was the command?
answer: 'Recite!'
choices: 'Recite!'
'Kneel!'
'Believe!'
'Write!'
context: In the Cave of Hira the command was 'Iqra!' -- 'Recite!' Muhammad answered that he could not read; the first words of the Quran followed: 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created... who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know' (Surah Al-Alaq, 96:1-5). This account is preserved as Muslim tradition.

question: Bilal ibn Rabah's master dragged him, an enslaved convert to the new faith, onto the burning sand of Mecca and pinned him under a heavy boulder to make him give it up. Through the torture Bilal answered with only the same word, repeated again and again. What did he keep saying?
answer: 'One, One' (God is One)
choices: 'One, One' (God is One)
'Mercy, Mercy'
'Never, Never'
'Free me, free me'
context: Bilal repeated only 'Ahad, Ahad' -- 'One, One.' Abu Bakr bought his freedom, and Bilal later became Islam's first muezzin, the caller to prayer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilal_ibn_Rabah

question: Muhammad went on preaching in Mecca, though the city's leaders leaned on his uncle and protector, Abu Talib, to stop him. Muhammad answered with a vow that he would not abandon his mission even for the greatest bribe imaginable. What did he say they could offer him and still not stop him?
answer: The sun in his right hand and the moon in his left
choices: The sun in his right hand and the moon in his left
Every last camel and caravan in the whole of Arabia
The crown and kingship of Mecca and of its temple
A high throne set above all the clans of the Quraysh
context: 'By God, if they put the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left on condition that I abandon this course, I would not abandon it until God makes it victorious or I perish.' Reported in Ibn Ishaq's Sira. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_and_third_deputation_with_Abu_Talib

question: Mecca's clans agreed to surround Muhammad's house one night in 622 and kill him in his bed. To buy time and slip away unseen, Muhammad asked someone close to him to lie down in his place. Who took his bed as a decoy that night?
answer: Ali ibn Abi Talib
choices: Ali ibn Abi Talib
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq
Bilal ibn Rabah
Ja'far ibn Abi Talib
context: Muhammad's young cousin Ali ibn Abi Talib slept in his bed as a decoy while he slipped out. Ali also stayed behind to return the goods people had entrusted to Muhammad for safekeeping. The plotters had planned one man from each clan to strike together, so blood-guilt would be shared. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah

question: Fleeing Mecca, Muhammad and his companion Abu Bakr hid in the Cave of Thawr while search parties hunted them. When pursuers came so close that Abu Bakr feared they would look down and see the two of them, Muhammad calmed him with a few words, later set into the Quran. What did Muhammad tell him?
answer: 'Do not grieve, for God is with us'
choices: 'Do not grieve, for God is with us'
'Be still, and God will turn their eyes'
'Fear not, for God has hidden our path'
'Take heart, for God will not forsake us'
context: Muhammad said, 'Do not grieve, for God is with us' -- words later set in the Quran (9:40). They hid three days in the Cave of Thawr, about an hour's walk south of Mecca, while the Quraysh searched. Source: https://www.islamweb.net/en/article/154942/the-cave-of-thawr

question: Ja'far, Muhammad's cousin, was among the persecuted followers Muhammad sent across the Red Sea to seek refuge with the Negus, the Christian king of Aksum. When envoys from Mecca demanded the refugees back, Ja'far recited to the king the Quran's verses about Mary and Jesus. How did the king respond?
answer: He wept until his beard was wet and refused to surrender them
choices: He wept until his beard was wet and refused to surrender them
He sent the refugees home again to keep his peace with Mecca
He demanded that they convert to his own Christian faith first
He locked the refugees away until Mecca should pay him a ransom
context: The Negus 'wept until his beard was wet and the bishops wept until their scrolls were wet,' then said Jesus was no more than what Ja'far had said by even the width of a stick he picked up -- and refused to hand the refugees over. Reported by Ibn Ishaq. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ja'far_ibn_Abi_Talib

question: Suraqa ibn Malik, a tracker, chased the fleeing Muhammad for the Quraysh's bounty of 100 camels and nearly caught him, until his horse stumbled and its legs sank deep into the sand. Suraqa took it as a sign and let him go, and Muhammad promised that one day Suraqa would wear the bracelets of the emperor of Persia. What became of the promise?
answer: When Persia fell, Caliph Umar made him wear the captured bracelets
choices: When Persia fell, Caliph Umar made him wear the captured bracelets
He was buried in honor wearing a pair of plain golden bracelets
He wore the bracelets a single time and then gave them all away
The prophecy went unfulfilled to the very end of Suraqa's life
context: 'How will it be, Suraqa, when you wear the bracelets of Kisra?' Years later, after Muslims conquered Persia, Caliph Umar made Suraqa wear the captured bracelets of the Persian emperor (Sahih al-Bukhari 3906). Suraqa's horse had sunk into the sand 'up to its belly.' Source: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3906 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suraqa_bin_Malik

question: The emigrants who followed Muhammad from Mecca reached his new city with nothing, while the local 'helpers' there had homes and trade of their own. Muhammad found a way to bind the two groups into one community. What did he set up between them?
answer: A bond of 'brotherhood' pairing each emigrant with a local helper
choices: A bond of 'brotherhood' pairing each emigrant with a local helper
A standing tax on the local helpers to feed the new arrivals
A lottery to share out the emigrants' future spoils of war
A ruling council in which only the Meccan emigrants could vote
context: Muhammad paired the Meccan emigrants (the Muhajirun) one-to-one with local helpers (the Ansar), who shared their homes, trade, and wealth -- welding two groups into one. He also drew up the Constitution of Medina, often called one of the earliest written constitutions, binding emigrants, helpers, and the city's Jewish tribes into a single umma. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Medina

question: Search parties hunting Muhammad walked right up to the Cave of Thawr where he lay hidden, a pious legend says, yet never looked inside. In the story, two quiet signs at its mouth made it seem that no one could have gone in. What were the two signs?
answer: A spider's web across the entrance and a dove nesting on its eggs
choices: A spider's web across the entrance and a dove nesting on its eggs
A serpent coiled on the threshold and a hornet's nest overhead
A thornbush grown over the gap and wild bees humming inside
A swallow's nest under the lip and an ants' trail across the floor
context: LEGEND. By pious tradition a spider had spun a web across the entrance and a dove had laid eggs in a nest there, so the pursuers assumed no one had passed. The hadith scholar al-Albani stated there is no authentic (sahih) hadith for the spider-and-dove detail. Source: https://islamqa.info/en/answers/27224

question: Embalmers along the Nile emptied a dead person's body, dried it, wrapped it in linen and laid it in coffins one inside another, because they believed the soul would need its body in the next world. What did the embalmers do with the brain?
answer: Pushed a hook up the nose, churned the brain to liquid, and threw it away
choices: Pushed a hook up the nose, churned the brain to liquid, and threw it away
Lifted off the top of the skull, studied the brain, and wrapped it in linen
Soaked the brain in honey and sealed it in a jar beside the body
Burned the brain on an altar as an offering to the gods
context: A long crooked iron hook went up the nostrils and broke through the thin ethmoid bone behind the nose; the brain was churned to liquid, poured out, and discarded as worthless. Source: worldhistory.org/article/44/mummification-in-ancient-egypt + sciencefocus.com/nature/egyptians-octopuses-brain

question: The priests who embalmed Egypt's dead buried each body for weeks in a drying powder scraped from dry desert lakebeds, to pull out every drop of moisture before the body could rot. They called the powder netjry. What was it?
answer: Natron
choices: Natron
Sawdust
Chalk
Sand
context: Natron is a natural mix of sodium carbonate and bicarbonate, scraped from the dried lakebeds of the Wadi Natrun. The Egyptians called it netjry, 'divine salt'; it sucked the body completely dry. This was sophisticated applied chemistry, not superstition. Source: worldhistory.org/article/44/mummification-in-ancient-egypt

question: The Egyptians believed one organ was the seat of a person's thought, feeling, memory and character, and that the gods would need it at the final judgment of the soul. So their embalmers took care to leave it inside the body. Which organ did they leave in place?
answer: The heart
choices: The heart
The liver
The stomach
The lungs
context: The Egyptians believed the heart (the 'Ab'), not the brain, held thought and character, and the dead needed it for judgment. Centuries later Aristotle agreed, calling the heart the seat of intelligence and the brain merely a cooling organ. Source: worldhistory.org/article/44/mummification-in-ancient-egypt + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiocentric_hypothesis

question: Four guardian gods, the sons of Horus, watched over a mummy's organs in Egyptian belief, each one carved on the lid of one of four jars: a human, a baboon, a jackal and a falcon. The embalmers sealed the organs they took out inside those jars. What are these organ jars called?
answer: Canopic jars
choices: Canopic jars
Reliquary urns
Funeral amphorae
Burial cauldrons
context: Four canopic jars held the organs, each guarded by a Son of Horus: human-headed Imsety (liver), baboon-headed Hapy (lungs), jackal-headed Duamutef (stomach), and falcon-headed Qebehsenuef (intestines). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_sons_of_Horus + metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/550773

question: In an Egyptian embalming tent, the chief embalmer cut open the body of the dead with an animal mask over his own face, so that for as long as he worked he would be the god of the dead himself. Whose animal head did the mask copy?
answer: The jackal-headed god Anubis
choices: The jackal-headed god Anubis
The falcon-headed god Horus
The ibis-headed god Thoth
The ram-headed god Khnum
context: The chief embalmer, the hery-seshta ('He Who Is Over the Mystery'), wore a jackal-headed Anubis mask to embody the god of the dead during the cutting. A real cartonnage Anubis mask survives in the Roemer-Pelizaeus Museum in Hildesheim. Source: egyptfuntours.com/blog/the-ancient-egyptian-embalmer + mylearning.org/resources/anubis-mask

question: Herodotus, a Greek traveller, visited Egypt around 440 BC and wrote down what the priests told him about preserving a body. They packed it in a drying salt, he said, for a fixed number of days, and 'for a longer time than this it is not permitted to embalm it.' How many days did Herodotus give?
answer: 70 days
choices: 70 days
40 days
100 days
365 days
context: Herodotus recorded that mummification took exactly 70 days, with the body packed in natron, and that embalming longer than that was forbidden. Seventy days was the rule, never more. Source: worldhistory.org/article/89/herodotus-on-burial-in-egypt

question: Over a mummy's chest the Egyptians laid a green stone charm, inscribed with a spell addressed to the organ beneath it. They feared what that organ might do at the weighing. What was the charm meant to do?
answer: Bribe the heart into staying silent at the scales
choices: Bribe the heart into staying silent at the scales
Make the heart beat one last time before judgment
Replace the heart if it had been damaged
Weigh the heart down so it sank on the scale
context: The green heart scarab, carved over the chest and inscribed with Spell 30B of the Book of the Dead, was a magical bribe to keep the heart from confessing sins to the Lord of Things at the scales. Source: ancientegyptonline.co.uk/heartscarab + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_scarab

question: The Egyptians never called the four organ jars of their mummies, with lids carved as the heads of guardian gods, by the name every museum gives them today. Historians say that name is a European mistake with no ancient Egyptian root at all. How did the jars get it?
answer: Early European travelers confused them with a Greek legend about a helmsman worshipped as a jar
choices: Early European travelers confused them with a Greek legend about a helmsman worshipped as a jar
Egyptians themselves later forgot the original word and guessed at a new one
A famous translator misread the hieroglyph for 'organ' as a place-name
The jars were first dug up in a Greek town and named after its founder
context: Early travelers mixed up the human-headed organ jars with a Greek legend about Canopus, the helmsman of Menelaus, supposedly worshipped at the Egyptian town of Canopus in the shape of a jar. The wrong name stuck. Source: etymonline.com/word/Canopic + encyclopedia.com/humanities/.../canopic-jar

question: Benito Mussolini named his movement in 1919 after an emblem of power from ancient Rome, the fasces. Attendants called lictors carried it on their shoulders ahead of Roman judges, a sign of the power to punish and even to execute. What did the fasces look like?
answer: a bundle of wooden rods strapped around an axe
choices: a bundle of wooden rods strapped around an axe
a bronze eagle clutching a thunderbolt
a laurel wreath set with a gold spike
a short sword crossed over a round shield
context: The bundle meant 'strength through unity': one rod snaps easily, but a whole bundle bound together cannot be broken. The rods stood for the power to flog, the axe for the power to behead. Mussolini took both the name and the emblem straight from ancient Rome; 'fascism' takes its name from it.

question: Benito Mussolini started out as a star of the Socialist Party, editing its newspaper in Milan and lifting its readers from 20,000 to 100,000. In 1914 his own party threw him out. What had Mussolini done to get thrown out?
answer: demanded that Italy enter World War I
choices: demanded that Italy enter World War I
converted to the Catholic Church
fled the country with party funds
called for the king to be crowned emperor
context: The socialists wanted Italy to stay neutral; Mussolini broke ranks and pushed for war, so they cast him out. He then built fascism as a rival movement of his own. Source: Britannica 'Benito Mussolini'; Encyclopedia.com 'Benito Mussolini'.

question: Painters put the boast 'Mussolini is always right' on walls across Italy, part of the propaganda that turned the dictator into an almost godlike leader. His staff also played a trick every night with the windows of his office. What did they do?
answer: left the office lights burning all night long
choices: left the office lights burning all night long
projected his face onto the windows in light
kept the shutters bolted tight day and night
draped a huge portrait banner across them
context: With the lights left on, passers-by would believe Il Duce was still hard at work at 4 a.m. The whole cult was manufactured, right down to the slogan that he was never wrong. Source: Granger Historical Picture Archive; History of the Twentieth Century podcast ep. 255; Study.com 'Italian Fascist Propaganda'.

question: Blackshirts, about 25,000 strong, tramped through pouring rain toward Rome in October 1922, and their march swept the Fascists into power. Their leader, Benito Mussolini, was not among them; he waited close to the Swiss border, ready to slip abroad if his bluff collapsed. Where was Mussolini while his men marched?
answer: relaxing at the opera in Milan
choices: relaxing at the opera in Milan
hiding in a monastery near Rome
rallying a crowd in Naples
waiting aboard a warship off Genoa
context: Mussolini stayed in Milan and went to the opera two nights running, positioned near the Swiss border so he could bolt abroad if the bluff collapsed. The march itself was mostly theater. Source: Wikipedia 'March on Rome'; Britannica 'March on Rome'; World Socialist Web Site retrospective.

question: Mussolini tried to slip into Switzerland in April 1945 hidden in a German army convoy, wearing a German coat and helmet. Partisans stopped the convoy at Dongo on Lake Como and picked him out anyway. What gave him away?
answer: his bald head and heavy jaw from the posters
choices: his bald head and heavy jaw from the posters
a diary of state secrets in his pocket
his thick country accent from Predappio
a fasces ring worn on his finger
context: Decades of propaganda posters had made his shaved bald head and heavy jaw too famous to hide; he was even still wearing general's riding pants with a red stripe. He was shot the next day at Giulino di Mezzegra. Source: History.com 'Mussolini's Final Hours'; War History Online 'Benito Mussolini Execution'.

question: Benito Mussolini spelled out what fascism actually stood for in 1932, writing The Doctrine of Fascism together with the philosopher Giovanni Gentile. At its heart lay one claim about the individual person and the State. What did the Doctrine declare?
answer: the State stands above the individual, who exists to serve it
choices: the State stands above the individual, who exists to serve it
the individual holds rights the State may never touch
the State should wither away once the workers rule
the individual and the State are equal partners by contract
context: The Doctrine made the State the highest good and reorganized the economy into 'corporazioni' (state-controlled guilds) meant to fuse workers and bosses under government command: ultranationalist, anti-liberal, and anti-communist. Knowing this real creed is how you recognize fascism, rather than treating the word as a vague insult. Source: Wikipedia 'The Doctrine of Fascism'; Political Research Associates 'Mussolini on the Corporate State'.

question: The Soviet leaders in Moscow waited six years to answer NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which free Western nations had founded in April 1949. They did not set up the Warsaw Pact until 1955, and then they placed every member's army under a single Soviet commander. What finally prompted them to form it?
answer: West Germany was allowed to join NATO
choices: West Germany was allowed to join NATO
The United States tested its first hydrogen bomb
Britain and France invaded Egypt over the Suez Canal
Stalin died and a new leader took power in Moscow
context: West Germany joined NATO on May 9, 1955; just five days later, on May 14, eight Eastern-bloc states signed the Warsaw Pact — all placed under a single Soviet commander. It was a reaction, not a partnership of equals. Source: kafkadesk.org, 'On this day in 1955.'

question: Lord Hastings 'Pug' Ismay, a British general, became the first head of NATO, the alliance twelve Western countries founded in 1949 to stand together against the Soviet Union. He once summed up its whole point in a blunt joke. NATO existed, he said, to do what?
answer: keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down
choices: keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down
outspend the Soviets until their whole economy collapsed
guard the iron curtain from Berlin all the way to the sea
unite the kings of Europe under one crown against Moscow
context: Ismay's quip captured NATO's threefold purpose: block Soviet expansion, anchor America to Europe's defense, and prevent a militarized Germany from rising again. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hastings Ismay, 1st Baron Ismay.'

question: Lord Ismay, the first head of NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, led an alliance bound by one pledge in Article 5: an armed attack on one member would count as an attack on all. Its members have called on that pledge only once. What attack set it off?
answer: the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States
choices: the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States
the Soviet shooting-down of a Korean airliner in 1983
the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979
the Berlin Wall going up overnight in August 1961
context: The one time NATO's collective-defense clause was ever invoked, it was Europe coming to America's aid after 9/11 — not the other way around. Source: nato.int, 'Collective defence and Article 5.'

question: A Navajo Code Talker radioing for the Marines in the Second World War hid war machines behind an animal word. A battleship was a whale, a fighter plane a hummingbird, a tank a tortoise. What did he call a submarine?
answer: The iron fish
choices: The iron fish
The thunder eagle
The river snake
The mud crab
context: Submarine was 'besh-lo' — 'iron fish.' A dive-bomber was a 'chicken hawk.' Each English letter also had its own cover word (A = 'ant,' B = 'bear'), so a speller could shuffle words to hide common letters. (National WWII Museum; encyclopedia.com; Multo (Ghost) blog 'Turtles, Pregnant Airplanes, and Iron Fish')

question: Japanese soldiers took Sergeant Joe Kieyoomia, a Navajo, prisoner on Bataan, and when they learned he spoke Navajo, they tortured him to make him translate the Marines' coded radio messages. Kieyoomia was a native speaker of the language, yet he could not tell them what the messages said. Why not?
answer: The coded words were nonsense to him because he had never been trained in the secret code
choices: The coded words were nonsense to him because he had never been trained in the secret code
The messages were transmitted too fast for any human ear to follow
He had forgotten his Navajo after years away at an English-only school
The Marines were actually speaking a different, unrelated tribal language
context: The code wasn't just Navajo — it was Navajo words standing in for other meanings, memorized only by the trained Code Talkers. A fluent speaker who didn't know the code heard only gibberish. The Japanese never broke it. (Deseret News, 'Neither Navajo Captive Nor Code Was Broken,' 1995; encyclopedia.com)

question: Six Navajo Code Talkers worked around the clock through the first 48 hours of the battle for Iwo Jima, sending and receiving more than 800 messages. Major Howard Connor, the signal officer, marvelled at one thing about all of them. What was it?
answer: Not a single one contained an error
choices: Not a single one contained an error
Every one was sent in under ten seconds
Each was written down in a secret codebook
All were relayed by a single exhausted man
context: More than 800 messages in 48 hours without one mistake. Connor said, 'Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima.' There were no codebooks in the field — every one of the 400-plus code terms had to be memorized. (history.navy.mil Navajo Code Talkers Fact Sheet; soledadmemorial.org)

question: Dr. Janusz Korczak ran a Warsaw ghetto orphanage of nearly 200 children. In August 1942, as the Germans were rounding up the ghetto's Jews for the death trains, Polish friends on the outside got him forged papers and offered to smuggle him to safety. What did Korczak do?
answer: led the children onto the train and died with them
choices: accepted the papers and slipped out of the ghetto alone
led the children onto the train and died with them
hid the children in the orphanage cellar for the night
bribed a guard to spare the youngest orphans
context: Korczak refused to abandon his orphans. He lined them up in orderly rows and walked with them to the cattle cars bound for the Treblinka killing center, and died there with them. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Janusz Korczak'; National WWII Museum, 'Defiance in the Face of Death')

question: German soldiers marched into the Warsaw ghetto on 18 January 1943 to round up more people for the death camps, and Jewish fighters met them with gunfire from a few smuggled weapons. The fighting went on for several days. What happened then?
answer: the German troops pulled back out of the ghetto
choices: the German troops pulled back out of the ghetto
the wall around the ghetto was rebuilt overnight
the orphanage was reopened for the children
the deportation trains switched to a new schedule
context: That small success was the turning point: it convinced the ghetto that armed defense was actually possible, and the fighters spent the next months preparing for the bigger fight to come. (Jewish Virtual Library, 'The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising'; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia)

question: SS troops marched into the Warsaw ghetto on 19 April 1943 to destroy it, and the main Jewish fighting force inside, the Jewish Combat Organization, met them under the command of Mordecai Anielewicz, a poet and youth leader. He was much younger than the German generals sent to crush him. How old was he?
answer: 24 years old
choices: 24 years old
19 years old
35 years old
45 years old
context: Anielewicz was just 24 when he commanded the uprising. A second group, the Jewish Military Union (ZZW), founded by Revisionist Zionists, fought alongside the ZOB. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Britannica, 'Mordecai Anielewicz')

question: Fighters of the Jewish Military Union took a stronghold on Muranowski Square in the Warsaw ghetto on 19 April 1943 and raised two flags over it side by side. The flags flew for about four days in sight of the city, and even the SS commander Jurgen Stroop noted them in his report. Which two flags were they?
answer: the Zionist flag and the Polish flag
choices: the Zionist flag and the Polish flag
the Polish flag and a red Soviet flag
a white truce flag and the Zionist flag
the German war flag flown upside down
context: The blue-and-white Zionist flag flew beside the red-and-white Polish flag over the burning ghetto — a deliberate act of defiance and of solidarity with Poland, plainly visible to the city below. (Israel Forever Foundation; Warsaw Ghetto Museum, 1943.pl)

question: One fighter of the Jewish Combat Organization recalled what a typical member carried into battle in the Warsaw ghetto in April 1943, facing over 2,000 German soldiers backed by tanks and cannon. By his account, each went in armed with almost nothing. What did a typical fighter carry?
answer: one pistol, five grenades, and five Molotov cocktails
choices: one pistol, five grenades, and five Molotov cocktails
one rifle, two pistols, and a box of bullets
three grenades, a knife, and a smoke bomb
two pistols, one grenade, and a length of pipe
context: Pistols, homemade grenades, and Molotov cocktails against tanks and artillery — yet on the first day this handful of fighters drove the German column back out of the ghetto. (National WWII Museum, 'The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising')

question: Jurgen Stroop, the SS commander, could not beat the lightly armed fighters of the Warsaw ghetto in a straight gunfight in April 1943, so he changed his plan. How did his men finally drive out the fighters and the people hiding with them?
answer: they burned the ghetto down around the fighters
choices: they burned the ghetto down around the fighters
they poisoned the ghetto wells over many weeks
they starved the fighters by cutting off all food
they shelled the ghetto from across the river
context: The Germans torched the ghetto block by block and pumped gas into the sewers to seal the escape routes. The ZOB's deputy commander Marek Edelman later said simply: 'We were beaten by the flames, not the Germans.' (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Marek Edelman via Holocaust Historical Society)

question: Jurgen Stroop, the SS commander, expected to clear the Warsaw ghetto in three days. Families sheltering in bunkers held on beside the ghetto's fighters against his far larger, better-armed force. How long did they hold out?
answer: nearly a month
choices: nearly a month
three days
a single afternoon
an entire year
context: About 27 days. A few hundred starving, near-unarmed fighters paralyzed thousands of German troops for almost a month — far longer than several national armies had lasted against the Wehrmacht in 1939-1940. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Holocaust Memorial Day Trust)

question: Yitzhak Zuckerman received a last letter from his commander, Mordecai Anielewicz, on 23 April 1943, with the end of the Warsaw ghetto near. Anielewicz did not write of defeat. What did he tell Zuckerman?
answer: his lifelong dream of armed Jewish self-defense had come true
choices: his lifelong dream of armed Jewish self-defense had come true
word had arrived that the Allies were sending them weapons
a secret tunnel out of the ghetto had finally been finished
the German commander had quietly agreed to a ceasefire
context: Anielewicz wrote that he had lived to see Jewish armed self-defense in the ghetto 'in all its greatness and glory.' Days later he was dead, but he died believing the fight itself was the victory. (Jewish Virtual Library, 'The Last Letter from Mordechai Anielewicz')

question: Heinrich Himmler received a proud, illustrated report from Jurgen Stroop, his SS commander in Warsaw, once Stroop had crushed the ghetto uprising in May 1943. It told Himmler the job was done. What title did Stroop give it?
answer: 'The Jewish Quarter of Warsaw Is No More!'
choices: 'The Jewish Quarter of Warsaw Is No More!'
'Order Restored in the Eastern District'
'A Brief Disturbance, Now Ended'
'The Cleansing of the City Is Complete'
context: Stroop's report survived the war and became evidence of the crime he was bragging about — including the famous photograph of a small boy raising his hands at gunpoint. Stroop was later tried and hanged in Warsaw. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Library of Congress; Wikipedia, 'Stroop Report')

question: Jurgen Stroop's men had crushed the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising by 16 May 1943, and Stroop wanted one last grand symbol of his triumph over the Jews of the city. That evening he chose a single act of destruction outside the ghetto walls. What did he do?
answer: dynamited Warsaw's Great Synagogue
choices: dynamited Warsaw's Great Synagogue
renamed the city's main street after Hitler
melted down the synagogue's bells for scrap
paraded the captured fighters through the square
context: Stroop personally gave the order and blew up the Great Synagogue of Warsaw as his finishing flourish — turning a place of worship into rubble to crown his report that 'The Jewish Quarter of Warsaw Is No More!' (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Wikipedia, 'Stroop Report')

question: Marek Edelman, a deputy commander of the Jewish Combat Organization, knew that he and a few hundred starving fighters could not beat the SS. Yet they took up arms, and he said they were not fighting to survive. Why, in his words, did they fight?
answer: so the Germans could not pick the time and place of their deaths
choices: so the Germans could not pick the time and place of their deaths
so that the history books would record every fighter by name
so the watching world would be shamed into finally helping
so the children still in hiding could slip away to safety
context: Edelman said: 'We knew perfectly well that we had no chance of winning. We fought simply not to allow the Germans alone to pick the time and place of our deaths.' The fight was a refusal to be murdered passively. (Marek Edelman via Holocaust Historical Society and explorethearchive.com)

question: Emanuel Ringelblum, a historian, ran a secret archive inside the Warsaw ghetto, code-named Oneg Shabbat, to record what the Germans were doing there. His team knew the ghetto would be destroyed and meant the testimony to outlast them. How did they save some 35,000 pages of records?
answer: sealed them in milk cans and buried them underground
choices: sealed them in milk cans and buried them underground
smuggled them out of the ghetto hidden inside a coffin
memorized the pages and recited them after the war
mailed them to relatives living in America
context: They packed the records into milk cans and metal boxes and buried them. Two milk cans and the boxes were dug up after the war at 68 Nowolipki Street (1946 and 1950) — so the ghetto's own people preserved the record of what was done to them. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Oneg Shabbat Archive'; Yad Vashem)

question: Mordecai Anielewicz and about 100 fighters were hiding on 8 May 1943 in the bunker at 18 Mila Street that served as their command post, when German troops found it and began pumping gas inside. What did Anielewicz and many of the fighters do?
answer: took their own lives rather than be captured
choices: took their own lives rather than be captured
surrendered once their ammunition ran out
escaped through a tunnel into the forest
were marched out and sent to Treblinka
context: Anielewicz and roughly 100 fighters died at 'Mila 18,' many by their own hand rather than fall into German hands. A mound still marks the spot in Warsaw today. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Jewish Virtual Library; Wikipedia, 'Mordechai Anielewicz')

question: Joseph Goebbels gave the signal on 9 November 1938, and through that night Nazi mobs across Germany burned more than 1,400 synagogues and smashed thousands of Jewish shops. Shattered glass covered the streets, and the night took its grim name from it. What was the night called?
answer: Kristallnacht -- 'Night of Broken Glass'
choices: Kristallnacht -- 'Night of Broken Glass'
Blutnacht -- 'Night of Blood'
Pogromnacht -- 'Night of the Pogrom'
Scherbennacht -- 'Night of Shards'
context: Kristallnacht was set off when 17-year-old Herschel Grynszpan shot the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath in Paris on November 7, 1938; after Rath died, Joseph Goebbels gave a Munich speech signaling Nazis to 'spontaneously' attack -- violence that was in fact ordered from the top. About 100 Jews were killed directly (roughly 400 counting suicides) and some 26,000-30,000 men were sent to Dachau, Buchenwald, and Sachsenhausen. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Kristallnacht'.

question: SA storm troopers planted themselves outside Jewish-owned shops and the offices of Jewish doctors and lawyers at 10 a.m. on 1 April 1933. It was the Nazi state's first nationwide, organized action against Germany's Jews, and the troopers held up signs to turn customers away. What did the signs say?
answer: Germans! Defend yourselves! Don't buy from Jews!
choices: Germans! Defend yourselves! Don't buy from Jews!
Germany awake! Cast out every foreigner now!
Workers, rise! Take your nation back today!
Buy German always! Keep the Reich pure!
context: This 1933 boycott came more than two years before the Nuremberg Laws and showed the regime testing how far it could go in public. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Boycott of Jewish Businesses'.

question: Julius Streicher ran Der Sturmer, a Nazi hate paper full of vicious caricatures and made-up stories, and he mounted every issue in glass display cases on street corners and outside factories, where ordinary Germans walked past it every day. Every issue carried the same slogan across it. What was the slogan?
answer: The Jews are our misfortune.
choices: The Jews are our misfortune.
The Jew is the ruin of nations.
Without the Jew, Germany is free.
Trust no Jew, in word or deed.
context: In German the slogan read 'Die Juden sind unser Unglück.' Streicher founded Der Stürmer in 1923; at Nuremberg in 1946 he was sentenced to death for his propaganda. Source: Wikipedia, 'Der Stürmer'; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Julius Streicher: Biography'.

question: Reinhard Heydrich, the SS security chief, ordered in September 1941 that every Jew in Germany aged six or older sew one visible marker onto his or her outer clothing before stepping out in public. Any passer-by could then pick them out at a glance. What did they have to wear?
answer: A yellow Star of David marked 'Jude'
choices: A yellow Star of David marked 'Jude'
A red armband stamped with 'Jude'
A blue cloth triangle on the sleeve
A black diamond patch on the chest
context: The badge was one step in a series of markings: in August 1938 Jews were forced to add the names 'Israel' or 'Sara' to their own, and in October 1938 a red letter 'J' was stamped on their passports. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Jewish Badge: During the Nazi Era'; National WWII Museum, 'The Nuremberg Race Laws'.

question: A German child opened a cartoon picture book from Julius Streicher's press in 1938, made to teach children to fear and 'spot' Jews. The whole book turned on one comparison. What did it compare a Jew to?
answer: A poisonous mushroom hidden among safe ones
choices: A poisonous mushroom hidden among safe ones
A rotten apple buried in a good barrel
A weed creeping through a flowerbed
A snake coiled in the tall grass
context: The book was 'Der Giftpilz' ('The Poisonous Mushroom'), text by Ernst Hiemer with cartoons by Philipp Rupprecht ('Fips'); about 40,000 copies were printed. One page told children, 'The Jewish nose is crooked at its tip. It looks like the number 6.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Der Giftpilz'; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Julius Streicher: Biography'.

question: Adolf Hitler had the Reichstag pass the Nuremberg Laws in September 1935, and one of them banned marriage or any romance between Jews and other Germans. The Nazis named a new crime for any such couple caught together and sent thousands to camps for it. What did they call the crime?
answer: Rassenschande -- 'race defilement'
choices: Rassenschande -- 'race defilement'
Blutschuld -- 'blood guilt'
Rassenkampf -- 'race struggle'
Volksverrat -- 'betrayal of the people'
context: The same Blood Law also forbade Jewish households from employing German women under 45 as servants, and barred Jews from flying the German flag or showing the Reich colors -- stripping them even of the symbols of their own country. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Nuremberg Laws'; Wikipedia, 'Nuremberg Laws'.

question: Adolf Hitler's Reichstag passed the Reich Citizenship Law, the first of the two Nuremberg Laws, on 15 September 1935, and it struck at the most basic legal standing of every German Jew. What did the law do to Germany's Jews?
answer: Demoted them from citizens to mere 'subjects' of the state
choices: Demoted them from citizens to mere 'subjects' of the state
Barred them from voting in any national election
Required them to register all property with the state
Banned them from holding any government job
context: Only a person 'of German or related blood' could now be a Reich citizen (Reichsbürger) with full political rights; a Jew became a mere subject (Staatsangehörige) -- no longer a citizen, though born in that country. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Nuremberg Laws'; Wikipedia, 'Nuremberg Laws'.

question: Nazi officials sorted Germans by 'race' with an official blood-purity chart used in schools, government offices and marriage courts. It split people by their grandparents into those the Nazis counted as full Germans, the 'mixed' Mischlinge and Jews, each marked with its own symbol so the eye could read a family tree at a glance. How were the full Germans and the Jews marked?
answer: White circles for 'German blood', black circles for Jews
choices: White circles for 'German blood', black circles for Jews
Gold stars for Aryans, red stars for Jews
Blue squares for Germans, yellow squares for Jews
Green checks for the pure, black crosses for Jews
context: People of mixed ancestry got shaded circles. The chart counted grandparents: three or four Jewish grandparents made you a full 'Jew' (Jude), two a 'Mischling of the first degree', one a 'Mischling of the second degree'. The regime classified about 502,200 Germans as full Jews. Source: National WWII Museum, 'The Nuremberg Race Laws'; EHRI / USHMM blood-purity teaching chart.

question: Deputies of the Reichstag, the German parliament, gathered at the giant annual Nazi Party rally in September 1935, summoned by Hitler to rubber-stamp his new race laws, whose drafts had been rushed together overnight, one of them jotted down on the reverse of a menu. In all twelve years of Nazi rule, no other sitting of the Reichstag was like it. What set it apart?
answer: It was the only one ever held outside Berlin
choices: It was the only one ever held outside Berlin
It was the only one ever held after dark
It was the only one Hitler did not attend
It was the only one opened to the public
context: It was a one-off parliament summoned to the party rally in Nuremberg for the sole purpose of passing the race laws. The laws were thrown together in a frantic rush -- officials Bernhard Loesener and Franz Albrecht Medicus were hurried to Nuremberg on September 14, and around 2:30 a.m. on the 15th Hitler was handed several drafts, one scrawled on the back of a restaurant menu, and picked one only hours before announcing it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Nuremberg Laws'; National WWII Museum, 'The Nuremberg Race Laws'.

question: Adolf Hitler and his Nazis insisted that Jews were a separate race, detectable in the blood, yet no scientist had a test that could find any such thing. To decide whether someone's grandparent had been Jewish, they fell back on one ordinary kind of record. What did they use?
answer: Whether that grandparent had belonged to the Jewish religion
choices: Whether that grandparent had belonged to the Jewish religion
Whether that grandparent had carried a Jewish surname
Whether that grandparent had lived in a Jewish quarter
Whether that grandparent had looked Jewish in photographs
context: This is the hidden absurdity at the core of the laws: a system that claimed to be about 'blood' secretly rested on religious records, not biology -- it could not define a Jew by race at all without pointing to who had practiced the Jewish faith. Source: National WWII Museum, 'The Nuremberg Race Laws'.

question: Joseph Stalin rose at a banquet in Moscow on 23 August 1939, the night the foreign ministers of Germany and the Soviet Union had signed a pact dividing eastern Europe between them. Glass of Crimean sparkling wine in hand, he toasted a man whose ideology he had spent years denouncing. Whose health did Stalin drink to?
answer: Adolf Hitler, the German Fuhrer
choices: Adolf Hitler, the German Fuhrer
Vyacheslav Molotov, his foreign minister
Vladimir Lenin, the founder of the USSR
Winston Churchill, the British leader
context: Stalin said, 'I know how much the German nation loves its Fuhrer; I should therefore like to drink to his health.' He also gave his 'word of honor that the Soviet Union would not betray its partner' Germany. The leader of world communism drank to the health of the leader of fascism: the two regimes were now partners, not opposites. The toast survives in the German Foreign Office's own memorandum of the banquet.

question: Adolf Hitler's troops poured into Poland from the west on 1 September 1939, and Joseph Stalin's Red Army crossed its eastern border on 17 September. On 28 September, with Polish cities still smoking, Hitler and Stalin signed a treaty setting their new border. What word did they put beside 'Boundary' in its title?
answer: Friendship
choices: Friendship
Conquest
Neutrality
Partition
context: The German-Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty of September 28, 1939 finalized the carve-up of Poland and traded the USSR's claim on most of Lithuania for a bigger slice of central Poland (the Lublin region and eastern Warsaw province). The two totalitarian powers were collaborators years before they were enemies; Stalin only 'switched sides' once Hitler invaded him in June 1941. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German%E2%80%93Soviet_Boundary_and_Friendship_Treaty)

question: Ribbentrop and Molotov, the foreign ministers of Germany and the Soviet Union, came together in Moscow on 23 August 1939 and pledged in public that their countries would not attack each other for ten years. A secret protocol went with the pact, and the Soviets denied it existed for fifty years. What did the secret protocol do?
answer: Secretly divided Poland and the Baltic states between the two powers
choices: Secretly divided Poland and the Baltic states between the two powers
Secretly pledged the two armies to attack Britain together
Secretly promised Soviet oil and grain to fund Germany's war
Secretly set a date for Germany to invade the Soviet Union
context: The hidden protocol carved Eastern Europe into 'spheres of influence,' splitting Poland along the Narew, Vistula, and San rivers and handing Estonia, Latvia, Finland, and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere. Within weeks both powers acted on it: Germany invaded Poland from the west on September 1, the Red Army from the east on September 17, and the USSR went on to seize the Baltics and attack Finland. Moscow denied the protocol existed until 1989. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org (German-Soviet Pact); Wilson Center Digital Archive (text of the protocol).

question: The Founders chose the wording of the Declaration's third unalienable right with care: 'the pursuit of Happiness.' Thomas Jefferson meant by it a life of purpose and virtue, more than just owning things, and people have argued ever since about what the words guarantee. What did the Declaration actually offer about happiness?
answer: a freedom to pursue it, but no promise of it
choices: a freedom to pursue it, but no promise of it
a fund to pay for it, drawn from public taxes
a right to receive it, granted by the state
a duty on government to provide it to all
context: The phrase is 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness': a right to chase happiness, not a promise that anyone will hand it to you. Jefferson had in mind a purposeful, virtuous life, but the Declaration offers only the freedom to pursue it, a negative right (freedom from interference) that asks others only to leave you alone, not an entitlement the state owes you. (John Locke's older trio had named property in that place.)

question: Frederic Bastiat made his case with a neighbor's bread in The Law, a book he published in 1850. A man who walked into his neighbor's house and carried off the bread, Bastiat pointed out, would be hauled before a judge. Then he turned to a law that took the neighbor's bread and handed it to someone else. What did Bastiat say that law had become?
answer: Theft, just done through the law instead of by hand
choices: Theft, just done through the law instead of by hand
Charity, a lawful way of helping those with less
Justice, the law evening out who has too much
Progress, society outgrowing old ideas of property
context: Bastiat's test for a fake right: 'See whether the law takes from some persons that which belongs to them, to give to others what does not belong to them... an act that this citizen cannot perform without committing a crime.' If an act would be a crime when YOU do it, passing a law to do it for you doesn't make it just — it makes it legal plunder. This is the negative-vs-positive rights line: your life, speech, and property ask only that others leave you alone (everyone can hold those at once, free of charge), but a 'right' to the baker's bread can't be filled unless someone is forced to bake. The strongest case for the other side is Franklin Roosevelt's 1944 'Second Bill of Rights' (a job, a home, medical care as rights) — argued in good faith, but it requires conscripting a provider, which is exactly what Bastiat warned against. Source: Bastiat, 'The Law' (1850), Project Gutenberg #44800.

question: Soldiers in Germanicus's army camp on the Rhine dressed his toddler son, Gaius, in a tiny copy of their own leather boot, the caliga. The troops gave the little boy a nickname from it, one he came to hate as emperor. What did they call him?
answer: Caligula, 'Little Boots'
choices: Caligula, 'Little Boots'
Brutus, 'the Heavy One'
Maximus, 'the Great'
Corvus, 'the Raven'
context: The nickname 'Caligula' means 'Little Boots,' from the caliga the soldiers fitted on him in the Rhine camp. As an adult emperor he hated the name and punished anyone who used it. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/7-things-you-may-not-know-about-caligula

question: Tacitus, the Roman historian, recorded that only four of Rome's fourteen districts came through unharmed when the Great Fire tore through the city for about six days in July of AD 64, under the emperor Nero. Three were burned flat and seven left as smoking, half-ruined shells. Where did the fire start?
answer: The shops full of flammable goods by the Circus Maximus
choices: The shops full of flammable goods by the Circus Maximus
The granaries beside the river harbor
The marble Senate house in the Forum
The aqueduct arches outside the walls
context: The fire began in shops packed with flammable goods at the foot of the Palatine and Caelian hills, by the Circus Maximus. Three of Rome's fourteen districts were destroyed utterly and seven left in scorched ruins. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_Rome

question: Nero, a famous legend says, fiddled while Rome burned in AD 64. Tacitus, the Roman historian, reported only a rumour that the emperor sang of the fall of Troy, and historians call the fiddling impossible. Why could Nero never have fiddled during the Great Fire?
answer: The fiddle had not been invented yet, by over a thousand years
choices: The fiddle had not been invented yet, by over a thousand years
Nero was away from Rome at the coast that whole week
Nero could not play any musical instrument at all
Roman law forbade music during a public disaster
context: The fiddle (violin) did not exist in the ancient world; it appeared more than a thousand years later. The phrase comes from much later writers. Tacitus reports only a RUMOR that Nero sang of the fall of Troy, and flags it as rumor; Suetonius and Cassius Dio later repeated it as fact. Source: http://kiwihellenist.blogspot.com/2017/04/the-fire-of-rome-nero-and-fiddle.html  (Legend.)

question: Suetonius preserved the dying boast of Nero, who took his own life in AD 68 after the Senate declared him a public enemy and his own Praetorian Guard abandoned him for a rebel governor. What did Nero say as he died?
answer: 'What an artist dies in me!'
choices: 'What an artist dies in me!'
'I have lived as Rome deserved.'
'Let them fear me still.'
'Bury me with the eagles.'
context: Suetonius gives Nero's last words as 'Qualis artifex pereo' — 'What an artist dies in me.' His death on 9 June, AD 68, ended the Julio-Claudian dynasty and triggered the chaotic 'Year of the Four Emperors.' Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Nero

question: German troops opened the valves on thousands of buried steel cylinders near Ypres on 22 April 1915 and let a greenish-yellow cloud drift on the wind toward the French and Algerian lines. It was the first large gas attack of the war. What gas rolled across no man's land?
answer: Chlorine
choices: Chlorine
Phosgene
Mustard gas
Tear gas
context: About 160-168 tons of chlorine drifted from roughly 6,000 cylinders; the troops in its path broke and fled, tearing a gap several kilometres wide in the line. Source: National WWI Museum and Memorial (theworldwar.org); IWM 'Second Battle of Ypres'.

question: Crews of the British army drove a secret new weapon into battle at the Somme on 15 September 1916: the diamond-shaped Mark I tank, which crushed through barbed wire and crawled across trenches that stopped every other vehicle. What carried it over a trench instead of letting it stick?
answer: Caterpillar tracks running all the way around the hull
choices: Caterpillar tracks running all the way around the hull
A pair of oversized rubber balloon tires
Folding steel bridges it dropped ahead of itself
Spinning drums of cable that winched it across
context: The Mark I's tracks looped right around its rhomboid body, letting it span the cratered, trench-cut ground. This was the first time in history tanks went into battle. Source: The Tank Museum 'Tanks at Flers'; historyofwar.org 'Battle of Flers-Courcelette'.

question: Canadian soldiers at Ypres in 1915 had no gas masks yet when the poison cloud rolled toward their trench. One officer, by report, bellowed a desperate order down the line. What did he tell the men to do with their handkerchiefs?
answer: Urinate on them and tie them over their faces
choices: Urinate on them and tie them over their faces
Soak them in rum and stuff them up their nostrils
Burn them and breathe through the smoke
Bury their faces in them against the wet ground
context: The ammonia in urine partially neutralised the chlorine. The shouted order was reportedly 'Piss on your handkerchiefs and tie them over your faces!' Source: Veterans Affairs Canada '2nd Battle of Ypres'; Warfare History Network 'Salient of Death'.

question: A British soldier climbed out to cross no man's land on the first day of the Somme, into machine guns that could fire about 600 rounds a minute. The German gunners had set them so their streams of bullets crossed the ground from the sides, not straight ahead. What did swerving to dodge one gun do to him?
answer: It walked him straight into the next gun's kill zone
choices: It walked him straight into the next gun's kill zone
It let him slip through a safe gap between the streams
It drew the gunners' aim away toward the louder gun
It bought him cover until the water jackets overheated
context: The crossing streams swept advancing men from the side (enfilade) in a continuous wall of lead with no gap. On 1 July 1916, the Somme's first day, this fire helped inflict ~57,000-60,000 British casualties, the bloodiest single day in the army's history. Source: Swampfox Optics 'The Devil's Paintbrush'; Warfare History Network.

question: Anthony Fokker, a Dutch designer, built Germany a device in 1915 that let a pilot fire his machine gun straight ahead through his own spinning propeller. Before it, a forward gun would have shredded the pilot's own blades. How did Fokker's gear let the bullets pass the blades unharmed?
answer: A cam tied to the engine stopped the gun the instant a blade crossed the muzzle
choices: A cam tied to the engine stopped the gun the instant a blade crossed the muzzle
Steel wedges on the blades simply bounced any bullet that struck them
The gun was angled to fire just outside the propeller's circle
The blades were slotted with gaps the bullets were timed to find
context: Now a pilot aimed the whole aircraft at his target. Fitted to the Fokker Eindecker, it gave such dominance from mid-1915 that Allied airmen called themselves 'Fokker Fodder' during the 'Fokker Scourge.' (The bouncing-wedge choice was a real earlier fix: Roland Garros bolted deflectors to his blades before Fokker's gear existed.) Source: Wikipedia 'Synchronization gear'; RAFA.

question: A cook in Italy before 1492 made her sauce with no tomato in it, while no Irish farmer had planted a potato and no kitchen in India or Korea had tasted a chili pepper. All three foods came from one distant part of the world. Where did they come from?
answer: the Americas
choices: the Americas
Africa
China
the Middle East
context: Every one of these foods is native to the Americas and only crossed the Atlantic after 1492 as part of what historians call the Columbian Exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange

question: Farmers of southern Mexico bred a scrawny wild grass called teosinte, over about 9,000 years, into maize with fat ears of corn. They planted the maize in one mound with beans and squash. What was that trio of crops grown together called?
answer: the Three Sisters
choices: the Three Sisters
the Golden Harvest
the Sacred Grains
the Field Brothers
