context: The corn stalk gave the beans something to climb, the beans fed the soil, and the squash leaves shaded out weeds. After 1492 maize spread so far that the world now grows more of it than wheat or rice. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Sisters_(agriculture)

question: A European family given some of the first tomatoes from the Americas set them aside uneaten, afraid of poison, and Europeans went on fearing the fruit for some two hundred years. The fear came from its family tree: the tomato is related to a killer plant, and its own leaves really are poisonous. Which plant?
answer: deadly belladonna
choices: deadly belladonna
poison hemlock
monkshood
foxglove
context: Belladonna, also called deadly nightshade, gave the whole nightshade family its scary reputation. The tomato FRUIT is perfectly safe, but its leaves are genuinely toxic, which made the suspicion stick. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-the-misrepresentation-of-tomatoes-as-stinking-poison-apples-that-provoked-vomiting-made-people-afraid-of-them-for-more-than-200-years-863735/

question: Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, an army pharmacist, wanted the French to eat potatoes, but ordinary people feared the strange tuber. Around 1785, the story goes, he planted a field of them outside Paris, posted armed guards on it all day, then quietly withdrew them each night. What did he hope the villagers would do?
answer: sneak in at night to steal the 'precious' guarded crop
choices: sneak in at night to steal the 'precious' guarded crop
march to the king to demand a share of the harvest
plant their own potato fields to copy the rich man
burn the patch down out of fear of poison
context: Parmentier bet that if a crop looked valuable enough to guard, villagers would assume it was worth stealing and growing themselves. The story is told as legend, but potatoes did catch on in France soon after. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-the-potato-changed-the-world-108470605/

question: Italians of the 1500s met a new fruit from the Americas, probably an early yellow kind, and their word for it, 'pomodoro,' first appeared in print in 1554. Italians still use the word for the tomato. What does 'pomodoro' literally mean?
answer: golden apple
choices: golden apple
red jewel
love apple
sun fruit
context: 'Pomo d'oro' means 'golden apple', a hint that the first tomatoes Italians saw may have been yellow rather than red. Centuries later, in 1889, Naples gave the world Pizza Margherita with red tomato, white cheese, and green basil. Source: https://italysegreta.com/pomi-doro-the-tomato-is-italys-golden-apple/

question: Erwin Rommel led the German Afrika Korps across the open desert of North Africa in lightning raids, striking and then vanishing before his enemies could pin him down. What nickname did those raids win him among his own countrymen?
answer: The Desert Fox
choices: The Desert Fox
The Iron Lion
The Sand Eagle
The Steel Wolf
context: Germans called him the 'Wuestenfuchs' -- the Desert Fox -- for his cunning. Even his British enemies, the 'Desert Rats' of the Eighth Army, respected him. Source: history.com, This Day in History, Oct 14.

question: German engineers buried roughly half a million mines at El Alamein in the summer of 1942, in belts up to five miles deep, to hold off a British attack. Rommel's soldiers gave the minefields a chilling nickname. What did they call them?
answer: the Devil's Gardens
choices: the Devil's Gardens
the Iron Curtain
the Dead Sea
the Gates of Dust
context: Rommel's troops nicknamed the vast minefields the 'Devil's Gardens.' Source: worldhistory.org, Second Battle of El Alamein.

question: Winston Churchill celebrated General Bernard Montgomery's victory over Rommel at El Alamein in November 1942, Britain's first great land victory over the Germans, by ordering one thing done across the country for the first time in years. What did Churchill order done to mark the win?
answer: the church bells of Britain rung out
choices: the church bells of Britain rung out
a parade through London held
a national holiday declared
the king's portrait flown everywhere
context: Churchill ordered Britain's church bells rung in celebration. He later wrote in 'The Hinge of Fate' (1951): 'Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein we never had a defeat.' Source: winstonchurchill.org.

question: Bernard Montgomery code-named the opening attack at El Alamein in October 1942 'Operation Lightfoot,' and the name was a grim joke. His infantry had to go first, on foot, through Rommel's half-million buried mines before the tanks could follow. What did the name mean for those foot soldiers?
answer: step so lightly the mines wouldn't go off
choices: step so lightly the mines wouldn't go off
march faster than the enemy could aim
carry no packs to move quickly
leave their boots behind in the sand
context: Infantry were meant to step lightly enough not to trigger the mines, leaving the heavier tanks to set them off. Source: worldhistory.org, Second Battle of El Alamein.

question: General Georg Stumme was commanding at El Alamein in Erwin Rommel's place when the battle opened in October 1942, for Rommel lay sick in Germany. On the battle's second day, near the front, Stumme met a sudden fate. What happened to him?
answer: he dropped dead of a heart attack
choices: he dropped dead of a heart attack
he was captured by a British patrol
he deserted back across the lines
he was court-martialed by Berlin
context: Stumme died of a heart attack on 24 Oct 1942 while driving near the front, forcing Rommel to fly back to a battle already going wrong. Source: worldhistory.org, Second Battle of El Alamein.

question: British troops ran Operation Bertram before El Alamein to fool Rommel, draping canvas over tanks so they passed for trucks, setting out dummy tanks and laying a fake water pipeline that crept forward a few miles each day. What did the captured German general Wilhelm von Thoma admit afterwards about the trick?
answer: he had been fooled on both timing and place
choices: he had been fooled on both timing and place
he had warned Rommel but was ignored
he had spotted the dummies from the air
he had refused to believe the pipeline
context: 772 'sunshields' disguised tanks as trucks and a fake pipeline 'grew' 5 miles a day. Von Thoma admitted he was deceived on both the timing and the location of the attack. Source: Wikipedia, Operation Bertram.

question: Two generals came to Erwin Rommel's home on 14 October 1944, after he was implicated in the July plot to kill Hitler, and offered him a choice. He could face a public treason trial with reprisals against his family, or take a quieter way out that the regime would hide behind a hero's state funeral. What was that quieter way out?
answer: a cyanide capsule
choices: a cyanide capsule
a quiet exile abroad
a transfer to the eastern front
a confession in writing
context: Rommel took the poison; his death was publicly blamed on his earlier war wounds and he was given a state funeral. Source: historynet.com, 'Rommel's Last Day.'

question: NASA cameras looking down on the Korean peninsula at night caught the South blazing with electric light and the North beside it almost black, as if no one lived there. Deep in all that darkness, one city still glowed. Which city was that single point of light?
answer: Pyongyang
choices: Pyongyang
Hamhung
Wonsan
Kaesong
context: The capital, Pyongyang, is the only place the regime keeps reliably lit. After the Soviet Union collapsed in the early 1990s, North Korea lost the subsidized fuel and spare parts that ran its power plants, and electricity generation nosedived — the blackness in the photo is a country that stopped being able to keep the lights on. Source: National Geographic, 'New Space Station Photos Show North Korea at Night, Cloaked in Darkness'; NBC News, 'Satellites document North Korea's dark ages'.

question: A North Korean family waited in the 1990s for state rations that never came, while famine killed hundreds of thousands across the country. The regime refused to call the disaster a famine. It gave it a heroic name instead, from a story of Kim Il Sung's guerrilla youth, when he led his fighters through deep snow. What name did the state give the famine?
answer: the Arduous March
choices: the Arduous March
the Great Leap
the Red Banner Trek
the Iron Harvest
context: Gonanui Haenggun, the 'Arduous March' — the regime turned mass death into propaganda about a glorious struggle. By 1997 official daily rations had fallen to about 128 grams of food per person, and the UN estimated wild foraged foods made up roughly 30 percent of the diet; a 2011 U.S. Census Bureau study put excess deaths from 1993-2000 at roughly 500,000-600,000. Source: Wikipedia, '1990s North Korean famine'.

question: Kim Il Sung is said to have declared in 1972 that the 'seed' of an enemy must be eliminated, and his state built a rule of guilt by association on that line. When the state accused one person of a political crime, it did not punish that person alone. How far across a family could it reach when it sent people to the prison camps?
answer: three generations — grandparents, parents, and children
choices: three generations — grandparents, parents, and children
only the accused person
the accused and spouse
the entire home village
context: Under the three-generations rule, grandparents, parents, and children of one accused person can all be sent to the kwan-li-so camps, in most cases for life. The 1972 line attributed to Kim Il Sung read: 'Factionalists and enemies of class, whoever they are, their seed must be eliminated through three generations.' The camp network holds an estimated 80,000 to 120,000 prisoners. Source: Wikipedia, 'Yodok concentration camp'; Freedom House, 'Concentrations of Inhumanity'.

question: American scientists set off Ivy Mike, the first true hydrogen bomb, on Elugelab, a little coral island among the Marshall Islands, on 1 November 1952. It was hundreds of times stronger than the atom bombs dropped on Japan seven years before. When the smoke and steam cleared over the lagoon, what had become of the island?
answer: It had completely vanished, leaving a mile-wide crater of ocean where the island had been
choices: It had completely vanished, leaving a mile-wide crater of ocean where the island had been
It had been split cleanly in two by the blast
It had been buried under a mountain of fallen ash
It had been pushed several miles out to sea by the shockwave
context: Ivy Mike's 10.4-megaton blast vaporized Elugelab entirely, leaving a crater about 6,300 feet wide and 160 feet deep. The 'bomb' was actually an 82-ton experimental device the size of a building, not a usable weapon — its blast was over 600 times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivy_Mike

question: A Soviet crew dropped the Tsar Bomba, the largest and most powerful bomb any nation ever built, over the Arctic island of Novaya Zemlya on 30 October 1961. Its mushroom cloud climbed so high that it dwarfed the tallest mountain on Earth. How high did the cloud rise?
answer: About 67 kilometers — nearly eight times the height of Mount Everest
choices: About 67 kilometers — nearly eight times the height of Mount Everest
About 9 kilometers — roughly the height of Mount Everest
About 20 kilometers — about twice the height of Mount Everest
About 150 kilometers — into outer space itself
context: The Tsar Bomba's mushroom cloud rose about 67 km (42 miles) high and its base spread 40 km wide. The flash was visible nearly 1,000 km away. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsar_Bomba

question: Engineers building the Tsar Bomba in 1961 found it too fat for the plane meant to carry it: the bomb, 27,000 kg and 8 meters long, would not fit inside a Tu-95 bomber. What did they have to do so the bomber could carry it?
answer: Remove the bomb-bay doors so it hung half-exposed beneath the plane
choices: Remove the bomb-bay doors so it hung half-exposed beneath the plane
Strap it to the top of the fuselage above the cockpit
Tow it behind the plane on a long steel cable
Break it into two halves and carry it in separate aircraft
context: The bomb couldn't fit inside the bomber's bay, so the bomb-bay doors and a fuel tank were removed and it hung half-exposed underneath. To give the crew a chance to escape, it was lowered on an 800-kg parachute the size of 1,600 square meters. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsar_Bomba

question: An American heard Sputnik 1 beep overhead in October 1957, lifted into orbit by the Soviet R-7 rocket, nicknamed 'Semyorka.' Americans were not just impressed but frightened, because the rocket was something the United States did not yet have. What was it?
answer: The world's first intercontinental ballistic missile
choices: The world's first intercontinental ballistic missile
The world's first reusable space rocket
The world's first nuclear-powered engine
The world's largest cargo aircraft
context: The R-7 that lofted Sputnik was the first ICBM, which meant the beeping satellite proved the USSR could now drop a nuclear warhead on any American city. The panic spawned a feared 'missile gap' — but it was largely a myth: analysts imagined the Soviets leading 16-to-1, while the real Soviet ICBM count was just four. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R-7_(rocket_family)

question: Donald Brennan, an analyst, named the Cold War rule that kept both superpowers from striking first, since either could always strike back: Mutual Assured Destruction, MAD for short. He chose those words on purpose. Why did he pick that name?
answer: To mock the idea of guaranteeing peace by promising mutual annihilation
choices: To mock the idea of guaranteeing peace by promising mutual annihilation
To honor the mathematician who first proved the theory
To stand for the three cities the doctrine was designed to protect
To disguise the policy's true purpose from the public
context: Brennan, an opponent of the policy, chose 'mad' deliberately as a jab — the acronym spelling out the English word for insanity. Defense Secretary Robert McNamara argued the logic in numbers: just 400 warheads on Soviet cities would destroy a third of the population and half of industry, enough to make any attack suicidal. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutually_assured_destruction

question: The Tsar Bomba's designers had drawn it up to release 100 megatons, yet before its test over Novaya Zemlya in October 1961 the Soviet engineers cut its power roughly in half by swapping out one part. Why did they cripple their own weapon?
answer: The full design would have doused the bomber crew and a quarter of the USSR in fallout
choices: The full design would have doused the bomber crew and a quarter of the USSR in fallout
They ran out of time to build the full-power version
International treaty had capped the legal yield at 50 megatons
The bomber could not physically lift the heavier full-power design
context: The Soviets replaced the bomb's uranium tamper with lead, roughly halving the yield to 50 megatons and cutting fallout by about 97%. Even so, pilot Andrei Durnovtsev and his crew were given only a 50% chance of surviving the test. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsar_Bomba

question: The four victorious powers had to choose a German city in 1945 in which to try the captured leaders of the Nazi regime. They chose one on purpose: the very place where the Nazis had held their huge yearly party rallies through the 1930s. Which city did they pick?
answer: Nuremberg
choices: Nuremberg
Berlin
Munich
Frankfurt
context: Nuremberg was where the Nazis had held their giant yearly rallies, so trying them there was deliberately symbolic. The city's Palace of Justice was also chosen because it had survived Allied bombing fairly intact and had a prison attached where the defendants could be held between sessions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg_trials

question: Guards found Hermann Goering, the highest-ranking Nazi put on trial at Nuremberg, dead in his cell in October 1946, only about two hours before he was due on the gallows. The court had sentenced him to hang. How had Goering cheated the hangman?
answer: He bit down on a smuggled cyanide capsule
choices: He bit down on a smuggled cyanide capsule
He hanged himself with a torn bedsheet
He starved himself to death over weeks
He provoked a guard into beating him fatally
context: Guards found crushed glass particles on Goering's lips from the poison capsule. How he obtained the cyanide stayed a mystery for decades. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/roadshow/articles/hermann-goering-whats-the-explanation-for-glass-on-the-lips/

question: The prosecutors at Nuremberg dimmed the lights on 29 November 1945 and screened an hour of film, something no courtroom had done before. When the lights came back up, the whole courtroom, defendants and judges alike, sat in stunned silence. What had the film shown them?
answer: Footage of the just-liberated Nazi concentration camps
choices: Footage of the just-liberated Nazi concentration camps
Hitler's private home movies and family scenes
Maps animating Germany's planned invasions
Recordings of the huge Nazi party rallies
context: The film, 'Nazi Concentration Camps,' was shot by Allied troops as they liberated places like Buchenwald, Dachau, and Belsen. Screened on 29 November 1945, it brought the Holocaust itself into evidence. Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/we-will-show-you-their-own-films-film-at-the-nuremberg-trial

question: Gustave Gilbert, the American prison psychologist at the Nuremberg trial, secretly gave the captured leaders of the Nazi regime intelligence tests. Many people had pictured these men as dull brutes, and the results surprised him. How did the defendants score?
answer: In the genius and near-genius range
choices: In the genius and near-genius range
Far below average, as expected
Right at average, like ordinary men
Too erratic and scattered to measure
context: The top scorer, Hjalmar Schacht, reached 143, while Goering and Karl Doenitz each scored 138. Gilbert recorded his cell-block conversations with the prisoners in his book 'Nuremberg Diary.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Gilbert

question: Rudolf Hess, once Hitler's deputy, spent the opening days of the Nuremberg trial insisting he had completely lost his memory, baffling the judges and even his own defense lawyer. Then, on 30 November 1945, Hess suddenly stood up and announced the truth about his amnesia. What did he reveal?
answer: He had faked the amnesia as a tactic, and his memory was fine
choices: He had faked the amnesia as a tactic, and his memory was fine
A war injury had genuinely wiped out his memory
Doctors had drugged him into the confusion
Hitler had ordered him to stay silent in court
context: Hess told the court: 'Henceforth my memory will again respond to the outside world. The reasons for simulating loss of memory were of a tactical nature.' He admitted he had even fooled his own lawyer. Source: https://avalon.law.yale.edu/imt/v1-29.asp

question: Robert Jackson, who led the American prosecution at Nuremberg, accused Germany of secretly planning for war. Hermann Goering fired back so sharply that Jackson lost his temper, and the court had to adjourn for the rest of the day. What was Goering's stinging reply?
answer: He didn't recall reading America's own published war-mobilization plans either
choices: He didn't recall reading America's own published war-mobilization plans either
He had never read a single military document in his life
Hitler alone had planned every campaign without him
The Allies, not Germany, had truly started the war
context: Goering's defiant comeback was broadcast across Germany and actually lifted some German spirits. It was later the British prosecutor, Sir David Maxwell Fyfe, not Jackson, who finally pinned Goering down with cold, methodical cross-examination. Source: https://www.spectator.com.au/2025/12/how-goring-almost-derailed-the-nuremberg-trials/

question: The Allies could simply have lined up Hermann Goering and the other captured Nazi leaders and shot them, but they put them on trial instead. The American prosecutor Robert Jackson opened the case by praising that choice: four nations staying the hand of vengeance was 'one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid' to one thing. What was it?
answer: Reason
choices: Reason
Mercy
Victory
Justice
context: Jackson's full opening line, delivered 21 November 1945, was: 'That four great nations, flushed with victory and stung with injury, stay the hand of vengeance and voluntarily submit their captive enemies to the judgment of the law is one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid to Reason.' Source: https://famous-trials.com/nuremberg/1897-jacksonopen

question: The judges at Nuremberg laid down a rule that has echoed through every war-crimes trial since. A soldier or official who commits an atrocity cannot wipe away the blame with one common excuse. What excuse did the Nuremberg court say could never, by itself, clear a man of a crime against humanity?
answer: That he was only following his superiors' orders
choices: That he was only following his superiors' orders
That he had not personally killed anyone
That his country had been losing the war
That he had not known the law existed
context: Article 8 of the London Charter put it this way: acting 'pursuant to order of his Government or of a superior shall not free him from responsibility, but may be considered in mitigation of punishment.' This birthed the rule that 'I was just following orders' cannot excuse such a crime. Source: https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/how-were-the-crimes-defined

question: Julius Streicher, the Nazi propagandist, shouted 'Heil Hitler!' on the gallows at Nuremberg, and then he sneered 'Purimfest 1946!' The jab pointed to the Book of Esther, in which the villain Haman is hanged together with all ten of his sons. Why did Streicher choose that taunt as he faced the rope?
answer: Exactly ten Nazis were hanged that night, matching Haman's ten sons
choices: Exactly ten Nazis were hanged that night, matching Haman's ten sons
Purim happened to be the date the trial had first opened
The Book of Esther had been his favorite story as a boy
He believed the Jews had laid a curse on him to hang
context: Streicher's final words before the hood dropped were for his wife: 'Adele, my dear wife!' The ten condemned men were hanged in the early hours of 16 October 1946. Source: https://www.thetorah.com/article/purimfest-1946-the-nuremberg-trials-and-the-ten-sons-of-haman

question: Soviet prosecutors at Nuremberg pressed the court to convict the Germans of the Katyn massacre, the murder of thousands of Polish officers, even though their own country sat as one of the four judging nations. The American and British judges quietly declined to pin Katyn on any defendant. Why did they hold back?
answer: The Soviets themselves had actually committed that massacre
choices: The Soviets themselves had actually committed that massacre
The victims' bodies had never once been found
Katyn had taken place before the war even began
No Polish witnesses had survived to testify to it
context: The killings at Katyn were carried out by the Soviet NKVD, not the Germans. After Soviet prosecutor Roman Rudenko pressed the charge, the tribunal left it unresolved rather than convict. The USSR finally admitted its own guilt in 1990. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katyn_massacre

question: Albert Speer, Hitler's architect and weapons chief, stood up in the Nuremberg courtroom and accepted a share of the blame for the regime's crimes, while most of the other defendants denied any guilt. Historians think that one move helped him do what, even though men who worked under him were hanged?
answer: Avoid a death sentence, drawing 20 years in prison instead
choices: Avoid a death sentence, drawing 20 years in prison instead
Win an early release after just five years
Have every charge against him quietly dropped
Be freed to testify openly against Goering
context: Historians later argued that Speer used vague talk of 'collective' guilt to mask his real, direct responsibility for slave labor. His admission of shared responsibility is widely credited with helping him escape the gallows. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Speer

question: Sculptors of the Olmec, on Mexico's hot Gulf Coast, carved seventeen giant stone heads, some taller than a person, and no two look alike: each has its own nose, its own cheeks, its own face. What do scholars think the heads really are?
answer: Portraits of specific real Olmec rulers
choices: Portraits of specific real Olmec rulers
Statues of the Olmec rain and storm gods
Carved guardians set to watch the city gates
Faces of the founding ancestors as a group
context: Because every head is a distinct individual face rather than a repeated divine type, scholars read them as portraits of particular Olmec rulers, not images of gods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olmec_colossal_heads

question: Olmec workers carved each colossal head from a single basalt boulder in the hot lowlands of southern Mexico around 1200 BC, and the nearest stone lay in the Tuxtla mountains, more than 100 kilometers from their cities. They had no wheels and no draft animals. How did they move boulders weighing many tons all that way?
answer: By river rafts and log rollers
choices: By river rafts and log rollers
By teams of harnessed oxen
By carving them where they fell
By dragging them on iron sledges
context: With no wheels and no beasts of burden, the Olmec floated the basalt downriver on rafts and rolled it overland on logs to cover the 100-plus kilometers from the Cerro Cintepec source. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olmec_colossal_heads

question: Axis soldiers poured across the Soviet border at dawn on Sunday, 22 June 1941, more than 3.8 million of them, along a front stretching all the way from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea. What record did the invasion set?
answer: the largest land invasion in human history
choices: the largest land invasion in human history
the largest amphibious landing in human history
the largest tank battle in human history
the largest aerial bombing in human history
context: Three German army groups attacked at once across a 1,800-mile front. No bigger ground invasion has ever been launched before or since. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/invasion-of-the-soviet-union-june-1941)

question: Adolf Hitler named his 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union after a medieval emperor, Frederick I, who had led armies on the Third Crusade. Frederick was known across Europe by an Italian nickname, Barbarossa. What does it mean?
answer: Redbeard
choices: Redbeard
Blackbeard
Greybeard
Ironbeard
context: 'Barbarossa' is Italian for 'Redbeard.' Hitler first committed Germany to the invasion with Fuhrer Directive 21 on 18 December 1940. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa)

question: One Soviet defender of the Brest Fortress, the first place the Germans struck on 22 June 1941, scratched a message into a fortress wall. He and his comrades were cut off and outgunned with no orders to retreat, yet they held out for more than a week. What did it say?
answer: I am dying, but I am not surrendering! Goodbye, Motherland.
choices: I am dying, but I am not surrendering! Goodbye, Motherland.
They shall not pass while one of us still stands here.
Avenge us, comrades; remember that we did not run.
We few will hold this gate or die here together.
context: The inscription is dated '20/VII-41.' One commander, Major Pyotr Gavrilov, was finally taken, gravely wounded, on 23 July. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_of_Brest_Fortress)

question: Joseph Stalin brushed off warnings in the spring of 1941, from his own spies and from Winston Churchill, that Hitler was about to invade. He would not believe Germany would break the 1939 pact while still at war with Britain. When the blow fell on 22 June, how did the stunned Stalin react?
answer: he withdrew to his dacha in isolation for days
choices: he withdrew to his dacha in isolation for days
he ordered an immediate counter-invasion of Germany
he went on the radio that night to rally the nation
he had the spies who warned him arrested and shot
context: The Red Army was caught completely unprepared. Reports say Stalin retreated to his country house and went silent for days before re-emerging to lead. (History.com, history.com/this-day-in-history/june-22; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa)

question: Luftwaffe pilots wiped out more than a thousand Soviet aircraft on the first day of the invasion in June 1941, roughly 40 percent of the Soviet air force's front-line strength. How were so many destroyed so fast?
answer: they were caught lined up on their airfields and bombed on the ground
choices: they were caught lined up on their airfields and bombed on the ground
they were shot down in huge dogfights over the border
they ran out of fuel and crashed behind the lines
their pilots defected and flew them away to Germany
context: At least 1,136 Soviet aircraft were destroyed on the first day alone, most of them sitting neatly parked on their airfields. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German-Soviet_air_war_22_June_1941)

question: German soldiers marched east into the Soviet Union in June 1941 still in summer uniforms, because their generals expected to win before autumn. When winter struck, about 100,000 of them suffered frostbite. How did the freezing men try to keep warm?
answer: stuffing their coats with newspaper and straw
choices: stuffing their coats with newspaper and straw
skinning local horses to wear the hides
burning their own trucks to stay warm
marching only at midday to keep moving
context: The frostbite epidemic led to about 15,000 amputations. The army had simply never been equipped for a Russian winter. (History.com, history.com/articles/operation-barbarossa; Britannica)

question: The nearest German soldiers, legend says, could see one thing on the skyline in early December 1941, when Army Group Centre had pushed to within about 15 to 20 miles of Moscow and the attack froze in place. What could they see?
answer: the spires of the Kremlin
choices: the spires of the Kremlin
the smoke of the burning capital
Soviet tanks rolling out to meet them
the frozen surface of the Volga River
context: It is told that advancing soldiers believed they could see the Kremlin's towers in the distance — the closest the Germans ever came to Moscow. This is legend, not confirmed fact. (Britannica, britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Moscow; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Moscow)

question: A German column stalled on a Soviet dirt road in the autumn rains of 1941, its tanks, trucks and horses swallowed alike by bottomless mud, and the advance slowed to a crawl. Such mud came every spring and autumn, and the Russians had a name for that season. What was it?
answer: the rasputitsa
choices: the rasputitsa
the taiga
the steppe
the tundra
context: The 'rasputitsa' strikes each spring and autumn. The taiga is northern forest, the steppe is open grassland, and the tundra is the frozen far-north plain. (History.com, history.com/articles/operation-barbarossa; Britannica)

question: Hitler's generals wanted to drive straight for Moscow in August 1941, but Hitler overruled them and turned his armies south to trap the Soviet forces around Kiev. Over 600,000 Soviet troops were lost there. What did Hitler boast the victory was?
answer: the biggest battle in the history of the world
choices: the biggest battle in the history of the world
the final death blow to the Bolshevik state
the open road to the Caucasus oil fields
the greatest act of revenge for the last war
context: The Battle of Kiev ended on 26 September 1941 with about 452,700 troops trapped and over 600,000 Soviet losses. Diverting south to win it, though, cost Hitler the time he needed to take Moscow. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kiev_(1941); Hoover Institution, hoover.org/research/great-battle-kiev-september-1941)

question: Units of the German army received an order from their high command days before they invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941: the Commissar Order. Hitler planned the invasion as a war of annihilation, not just a war for land, and even the regular army was to take part. What did the order tell the troops to do?
answer: shoot captured Soviet political officers instead of taking them prisoner
choices: shoot captured Soviet political officers instead of taking them prisoner
burn every Soviet village they marched through to the ground
ship all captured Soviet soldiers back to German war factories
execute any German soldier who retreated without written orders
context: The Commissar Order of 6 June 1941 turned the Wehrmacht itself into an instrument of ideological murder, ordering the summary shooting of captured Soviet commissars rather than treating them as prisoners of war. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissar_Order; USHMM, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/commissar-order)

question: Men of the Einsatzgruppen, four SS killing squads, followed behind the German front and in the first nine months of the invasion shot about half a million people, most of them Jews. At first they killed only men; then, on Himmler's order, women and children too. By what name is this campaign of mass shooting known?
answer: the Holocaust by bullets
choices: the Holocaust by bullets
the Night of Broken Glass
the Warsaw Uprising
the Long March
context: Unlike the later death camps, this earlier phase of the Holocaust was carried out face to face with rifles and machine guns across the occupied Soviet Union. (Imperial War Museums, iwm.org.uk/blog/partnerships/2021/09/operation-barbarossa-part-two; USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia)

question: Paul Blobel's SS unit put up an order in Kiev in late September 1941 that lured the city's Jews to a ravine outside the city called Babyn Yar. There the killers forced them to undress and machine-gunned them in small groups at the edge over two days, 29 and 30 September. Their own report gave the count. How many did they murder?
context: The exact figure comes from the killers' own report — Sonderkommando 4a of Einsatzgruppe C, under SS-Standartenfuhrer Paul Blobel. In all, about 100,000 people were murdered at Babyn Yar during the occupation. (USHMM, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/kiev-and-babi-yar; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babi_Yar)

question: English kings of the 1200s called their great lords and bishops to meetings named with a word taken from the French verb parler. Long before it named lords and commons making laws, what did 'a parliament' mean?
answer: A talking-place (a speaking)
choices: A talking-place (a speaking)
A judging-place (a court)
A praying-place (a chapel)
A trading-place (a market)
context: 'Parliament' descends from Old French 'parler', 'to speak' — so the word literally means a talking-place. It meant 'a speaking, a talk' before it ever named an assembly of representatives. Source: https://www.etymonline.com/word/parliament

question: Simon de Montfort had beaten King Henry III in war and was running England in 1265 when he did something new: he summoned two ordinary townsmen from every major town to take seats alongside the barons and bishops in his council. What were these town representatives called?
answer: Burgesses
choices: Burgesses
Knights
Aldermen
Reeves
context: The two townsmen from each town were 'burgesses' — the first time town-dwellers, not just lords and knights, were summoned to a parliament. De Montfort's 1265 assembly met at the Palace of Westminster from 20 January until mid-March. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_de_Montfort's_Parliament

question: Rebel barons under Simon de Montfort sewed one symbol onto the chests of their tunics before they fought King Henry III's army at Lewes in 1264. They went on to win the battle and capture the king. What did they sew on?
answer: White crosses
choices: White crosses
Red dragons
Golden lions
Black eagles
context: De Montfort's men sewed on white crosses as though they were crusaders, giving the army a sense of a divine, holy-war mission. They went on to win the battle and capture the king. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lewes

question: Richard of Cornwall, King Henry III's brother, had even been crowned King of the Romans in Germany, but when the rebel barons won the Battle of Lewes in 1264, he hid in a windmill. The rebels found him there. How did they jeer at him?
answer: "Come down, come down, thou wicked miller!"
choices: "Come down, come down, thou wicked miller!"
"Long live the King of the Romans!"
"God save our noble emperor!"
"Run, run, the prince is coming!"
context: A would-be emperor caught cowering in a windmill was jeered as a 'wicked miller'. Chroniclers report the taunt, so it is best treated as legend rather than certain fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lewes

question: The London militia fled before Prince Edward's charge at Lewes in 1264, and the prince, the future Edward I, galloped after them for about four miles. What did his reckless chase cost him?
answer: His father the king was beaten and captured behind him
choices: His father the king was beaten and captured behind him
His warhorse collapsed and died beneath him in the chase
His own knights deserted to go and join the rebels
The Londoners turned and ambushed his scattered men
context: By the time Edward returned from chasing the Londoners four miles, his father King Henry III had been defeated and taken prisoner. Reckless pursuit lost the whole battle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lewes

question: King Henry III faced a rebel leader who was not even English: Simon de Montfort, born in France around 1208, later remembered as a founder of England's Parliament. What tie bound de Montfort to the king he rose against?
answer: He had married Eleanor, King Henry's own sister
choices: He had married Eleanor, King Henry's own sister
He was Henry's long-lost younger brother
He had once been the young king's tutor
He was Henry's chosen heir to the throne
context: Simon de Montfort, a Frenchman born around 1208 at Montfort-l'Amaury, had married Eleanor, the sister of Henry III — the very king he would later overthrow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_de_Montfort,_6th_Earl_of_Leicester

question: Knights from the counties and townsmen from the towns sat side by side in the new council Simon de Montfort summoned in 1265, after beating King Henry III in war: two knights from each county, two townsmen from each town. That pairing grew into the larger of Parliament's two chambers. Which chamber did it become?
answer: The House of Commons
choices: The House of Commons
The House of Lords
The House of Bishops
The House of Burgesses
context: Knights of the shire plus town burgesses are the seed that grew into the House of Commons — which is why de Montfort is often called the founder of the Commons. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_de_Montfort's_Parliament

question: Simon de Montfort watched banners captured from Kenilworth Castle come toward him at Evesham in 1265, flown by Prince Edward's soldiers as they closed in to destroy him. What did the old earl believe when he saw them?
answer: That his own reinforcements had finally come to save him
choices: That his own reinforcements had finally come to save him
That the king had escaped and was leading a rescue
That Edward's army was retreating in surrender
That a truce party was riding out to make peace
context: The captured Kenilworth banners fooled de Montfort into thinking allies were arriving — when really it was Edward's army coming to kill him. The battle was fought during a thunderstorm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Evesham

question: A knight at Evesham in 1265 shouted out just in time who one man in Simon de Montfort's colours really was: King Henry III, de Montfort's captive, forced into his captor's colours for the battle. By whom was the king nearly cut down?
answer: By his own son Edward's soldiers, who mistook him for the enemy
choices: By his own son Edward's soldiers, who mistook him for the enemy
By de Montfort's bodyguards, taking revenge for their lord
By Welsh archers fighting on the rebel side that day
By looters stripping the fallen bodies after the battle
context: Wearing de Montfort's colours, Henry III was nearly killed by his own son's troops, who took him for the enemy. The knight Roger de Leybourne saved him at the last moment by crying out who he was. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Evesham

question: King Edward I summoned knights from the counties and ordinary townsmen from the towns to his Model Parliament of 1295 and made the practice the regular rule. In the writ that called them, he justified it with a ringing Latin maxim. What did the maxim declare?
answer: "What touches all should be approved by all"
choices: "What touches all should be approved by all"
"The king's will alone has the force of law"
"Render unto the crown what is the crown's"
"He who pays the tax shall make the law"
context: Edward I's 1295 writ cited 'Quod omnes tangit ab omnibus approbari debet' — 'what touches all should be approved by all' — making knights and burgesses the rule and echoing the principle of consent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_Parliament

question: Simon de Montfort called townsmen to his parliament in 1265, but a limit on the king's power to tax was already fifty years old: Magna Carta's twelfth clause, from 1215, barred the king from simply helping himself to his subjects' money. Except by what could no great tax be raised?
answer: The common counsel of the kingdom
choices: The common counsel of the kingdom
The blessing of the Pope in Rome
The sworn oath of the royal knights
The consent of the King of France
context: Magna Carta clause 12 (1215): 'No scutage or aid is to be imposed in our kingdom except by the common counsel of our kingdom' — the textual ancestor of 'no taxation without consent.' Source: https://magnacarta.cmp.uea.ac.uk/read/magna_carta_1215/Clause_12

question: England's barons forced King Henry III in 1258 to accept the Provisions of Oxford, which put him under a council and ordered Parliament to meet three times every year. A Latin chronicler found the reforms so radical that he gave that assembly a mocking nickname. What did he call it?
answer: The Mad Parliament
choices: The Mad Parliament
The Iron Parliament
The Boy Parliament
The Hungry Parliament
context: A chronicler called the 1258 Oxford assembly 'insane parliamentum' — the 'Mad Parliament' — because the Provisions of Oxford put the king under a Council of Fifteen and made Parliament meet three times a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Parliament_(1258)

question: Prince Edward's soldiers hacked Simon de Montfort apart as a traitor at Evesham in 1265, and the crown wanted him forgotten, even banning visits to his grave at Evesham Abbey. What did people do there anyway?
answer: Pilgrims secretly crept there to venerate him as a saint
choices: Pilgrims secretly crept there to venerate him as a saint
Looters dug it up hunting for buried treasure
It was washed away by a flood within a year
Monks quietly moved his bones to unmarked ground
context: Despite the ban, pilgrims crept to de Montfort's grave to honour him as a saint, and a medieval 'miracle book' recorded around 200 miracles credited to him between roughly 1266 and 1280. This cult is testimony, not proven fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_de_Montfort,_6th_Earl_of_Leicester  (Legend.)

question: Vitruvius, a Roman architect, wrote a book on building that later Renaissance masters treated almost as a bible. In it he said the Greeks modelled their oldest and plainest column, the sturdy Doric, on a real body. What did Vitruvius say it was modelled on?
answer: A strong man
choices: A strong man
A graceful woman
A tall tree
A galloping horse
context: Doric is the oldest of the three Greek orders — short, thick, no base, set right on the floor with a plain cushion-and-slab top. Vitruvius (Book IV) said its sturdy proportions copied a man's body, while the slimmer Ionic copied a woman's. Source: penelope.uchicago.edu Vitruvius Book IV; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doric_order.

question: Greek sculptors crowned the Ionic column, taller and slimmer than the heavy Doric, with a carved top shaped into a matching pair of spiral curls, one on each side. What were those curls likened to?
answer: Curled-up rams' horns
choices: Curled-up rams' horns
Rolling ocean waves
A coiled serpent
An open lotus flower
context: The paired spirals atop an Ionic column are called volutes — likened to rolled-up rams' horns or curly ringlets. Vitruvius said the whole column copied a graceful woman, the volutes her curls and the flutes the folds of her gown. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_order; Vitruvius Book IV.

question: Modern scientists scanned the Parthenon's marble sculptures, which visitors today see as pure white, and found traces of something the Greeks had done to them that time and weather later wiped away. What had the Greeks done?
answer: Painted them in bright colors
choices: Painted them in bright colors
Coated them in gold leaf
Polished them mirror-smooth
Wrapped them in fine cloth
context: Imaging found traces of vivid Egyptian blue, plus white and purple, and intricate painted patterns on the figures — the Parthenon was never bare white. Source: King's College London / Antiquity, Oct 2023; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: Xerxes, the Persian king, took Athens in 480 BC, and on the Acropolis his army reached an older temple to Athena, still unfinished, on the spot where the marble Parthenon would later rise. How did Xerxes' army wreck it?
answer: Burned it to the ground
choices: Burned it to the ground
Toppled its columns into the sea
Carted its marble back to Persia
Smashed it with siege engines
context: Xerxes burned the half-built older temple in 480 BC. The marble Parthenon we know (447-438 BC) was the rebuild, raised under Pericles by the architects Iktinos and Kallikrates with Phidias over the sculpture. Source: GreekReporter, 'When Persians Destroyed Athens'; ebsco.com, Building of the Parthenon.

question: Iktinos and Kallikrates, the Parthenon's architects, knew that a column with perfectly straight sides does not read as straight to the human eye. So they gave every column a subtle shaping, entasis, that makes the eye accept it as truly straight. What shape did they give the columns?
answer: A gentle outward bulge in the middle
choices: A gentle outward bulge in the middle
A sharp taper to a point at the top
A deep inward dent near the base
A slow twist along its whole height
context: Entasis is a swelling of only about 2 cm, peaking around a third of the way up: a deliberate trick, since a truly straight shaft reads to the eye as pinched or concave. The builders added the subtle outward swell so the columns read as flawlessly straight.

question: The Parthenon's architects tilted every outer column inward by a hair, far too slightly for the eye to see. If the lines of those columns ran on up into the sky, what would they do?
answer: Meet at a single point about a mile and a half overhead
choices: Meet at a single point about a mile and a half overhead
Stay perfectly parallel and never cross at all
Cross low, just above the temple roof
Spread apart, growing wider the higher they go
context: The inward-leaning columns, projected upward, converge at one point roughly 1.5 miles (2.4 km) above the temple. None of the building's 'straight' lines is truly straight; the invisible lean is another correction that makes the temple read as crisp and upright.

question: Phidias plated his colossal Athena in the Parthenon with robes of over a ton of gold, a fortune standing in the temple, and he built every gold panel so it could be lifted off. What did that let the Athenians do with the gold in an emergency?
answer: Strip it off and spend it to fund a war
choices: Strip it off and spend it to fund a war
Melt it down to cast more statues
Trade it to Persia in exchange for peace
Bury it in the ground beneath the temple
context: About 44 talents (~1,140 kg, over a ton) of gold made up the robes. The panels were removable on purpose — so the city could weigh the gold to prove none was stolen, and strip it for emergency wartime treasure. Source: worldhistory.org/article/785; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_Parthenos.

question: Athenians looking at the shield of Phidias's giant Athena, the story goes, spotted two real, living men carved among the Greeks fighting the Amazons, and one of them was the city's leader, Pericles. What happened to Phidias?
answer: He was put on trial for impiety
choices: He was put on trial for impiety
He was ordered to grind the faces off the shield
He was banished from Athens before any trial
He was fined and made to repay the gold
context: Sneaking real people into a sacred image was treated as a sacrilege; ancient writers say Phidias was tried for impiety and may have died in prison or exile. Told as legend (ancient testimony). Source: thearchaeologist.org, 'He Hid Pericles on Athena's Shield'; britannica.com/biography/Phidias.

question: The masons of Doric temples like the Parthenon set a band of grooved stone blocks, alternating with carved panels, along the top of the temple, a band architects nickname 'petrified woodwork.' Which part of the much older wooden temples did the grooved blocks copy in stone?
answer: The exposed ends of the wooden roof-beams
choices: The exposed ends of the wooden roof-beams
The painted doors of the inner shrine
The woven reed mats on the floor
The carved wooden idols of the gods
context: The grooved blocks are triglyphs — marble imitations of the sawn-off ends of timber roof-beams from the original wooden temples. Vitruvius says carpenters painted those beam-ends blue, which is why triglyphs were painted blue and the metope panels red. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triglyph; penelope.uchicago.edu Doric.

question: Joseph Meister was nine in 1885 when a rabid dog bit him fourteen times and he received a course of Louis Pasteur's untested rabies vaccine. The boy grew up and took a job at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, where he served as its gatekeeper. What did Meister watch over there?
answer: Pasteur's tomb in the crypt below
choices: Pasteur's tomb in the crypt below
The original swan-neck flasks on display
The laboratory where the rabies vaccine was made
The records of every patient Pasteur had treated
context: The boy whose life Pasteur saved spent his own life as gatekeeper of the institute, guarding the building and Pasteur's tomb in its crypt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Meister

question: Louis Pasteur set out to prove that germs ride in on the air rather than springing to life inside a broth. He boiled broth in glass flasks whose long necks he had stretched and bent into a swan's curve, and the broth stayed clear while a flask stood upright. When he tipped one, the broth clouded within a day. Why did tipping the flask change everything?
answer: It let trapped dust slide down the curved neck into the broth
choices: It let trapped dust slide down the curved neck into the broth
It let air rush in for the first time and feed the broth
It cooled the broth fast enough to wake the germs inside
It cracked the glass so outside water could seep in
context: The curved neck trapped airborne dust and germs in its bend, so the boiled broth stayed sterile forever — until Pasteur tipped the flask and let that trapped dust slide into the broth, which then clouded. Germs came from the air, not from the broth itself. Source: https://medicalmuseum.org.uk/medical-science-pasteurs-swan-neck-flask

question: Gerald Geison, a historian, opened Louis Pasteur's sealed private notebooks about a century after Pasteur's anthrax vaccine of 1881. Pasteur had told the public he weakened the anthrax germs for that vaccine with oxygen, and the notebooks showed the public story was false. According to them, what had Pasteur actually done?
answer: He had used a rival's chemical method and never credited the rival
choices: He had used a rival's chemical method and never credited the rival
He had bought the working vaccine from a German laboratory
He had used animals already immune and faked the results
He had never tested the vaccine on sheep at all before the trial
context: The Pouilly-le-Fort vaccine was actually made with potassium dichromate, a chemical method pioneered by the veterinarian Henri Toussaint — Pasteur's rival, whom he never credited. Geison revealed this from Pasteur's own sealed notebooks a hundred years later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthrax_vaccine

question: Boston patriots planned a secret signal in the Old North Church steeple on the night of April 18, 1775. One lantern would mean the British soldiers were leaving the city by land. How many lanterns meant they were crossing by water?
answer: Two lanterns
choices: One lantern
Two lanterns
Three lanterns
Four lanterns
context: 'One if by land, two if by sea.' Robert Newman, the church sexton, hung two lanterns in the steeple because the British regulars were rowing across the Charles River. The lanterns were lit for less than a minute so the British would not spot them. Source: https://oldnorth.com/blog/robert-newman/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Revere's_midnight_ride

question: Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote his 'Concord Hymn' in 1837 about the militia who traded fire with British troops at Concord's North Bridge in April 1775, as the Revolutionary War began. In one line he named the moment they opened fire. What did Emerson call it?
answer: The shot heard round the world
choices: The shot heard round the world
The blast that woke the world
The first fire of freedom
The volley that freed a nation
context: In the 1837 'Concord Hymn,' Emerson wrote of the militia firing 'the shot heard round the world' and called the militiamen the 'embattled farmers.' The line refers to the fight at Concord's North Bridge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shot_heard_round_the_world and https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/lexington-and-concord-shot-heard-round-world

question: In the steeple of Boston's Old North Church, the signal lanterns glowed for less than a minute on the night of April 18, 1775, so the British would not spot them. One object from that night still survives in a museum about 250 years later. What is it?
answer: One of the actual lanterns
choices: One of the actual lanterns
The original church keys
Paul Revere's leather saddle
The steeple's wooden door
context: A small tinned-iron-and-glass lantern made around 1770, one of those hung in the steeple that night, can be seen today at the Concord Museum. Source: https://concordmuseum.org/collection/paul-revere-lantern/

question: Paul Revere had to slip out of British-held Boston on the night of April 18, 1775 to raise the alarm that British troops were on the march. A horse waited for him across the water in Charlestown, past a British warship anchored in the dark. Two friends got him there. How did they move him across?
answer: They rowed him across the river in a small boat
choices: They rowed him across the river in a small boat
They smuggled him out hidden in a hay cart
They led him over the long bridge on foot
They floated him across on a wooden raft
context: Two friends rowed Revere across the Charles River in a small boat, slipping past the anchored British warship HMS Somerset, before he borrowed a horse in Charlestown. Source: https://www.paulreverehouse.org/the-real-story/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Revere's_midnight_ride

question: Paul Revere rode out on the night of April 18, 1775, and legend has him shouting 'The British are coming!' as he went. He almost surely never said it: most colonists still thought of themselves as British, and his ride was meant to be secret. What did Revere really call out?
answer: The regulars are coming out
choices: The regulars are coming out
The king's men are upon us
To arms, the soldiers march
Wake and arm, the troops ride
context: Revere's real warning was 'the regulars are coming out.' 'Regulars' meant the British army troops. Shouting it openly would also have given the secret mission away. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Revere's_midnight_ride and https://www.paulreverehouse.org/the-real-story/

question: Robert Newman, the sexton of the Old North Church, went up its steeple on the night of April 18, 1775 and hung the warning lanterns in the window. Then he had to get away before British soldiers who saw the lights could come for whoever had lit them. How did Newman slip out of the church that night?
answer: He climbed out a back window
choices: He climbed out a back window
He hid inside the great church bell
He rowed himself across the Charles
He dressed as a British soldier
context: Newman escaped through a back window. The next day the British arrested him because he held the church keys; he was released after blaming Captain John Pulling, who had already fled Boston. Source: https://oldnorth.com/blog/robert-newman/

question: Deacon John Larkin of Charlestown lent Paul Revere a horse for his ride on the night of April 18, 1775, and he described it only as 'a very good horse.' The mare later picked up a famous name, Brown Beauty. Where does that name come from?
answer: A family story written down generations later
choices: A family story written down generations later
Paul Revere's own written account of the ride
Deacon Larkin's record of the loan
A British patrol officer's report
context: Revere never named the horse. 'Brown Beauty' first appears in a family tradition written down in 1930 — 155 years after the ride — so historically the horse is anonymous. The name is testimony, not record. Source: https://www.paulreverehouse.org/frequently-asked-questions-about-the-midnight-ride-of-paul-revere/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Larkin_(Deacon_of_Charlestown)  (Legend.)

question: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's 1860 poem had Paul Revere gallop in triumph all the way from Boston to Concord on the night of April 18, 1775. The real Revere never reached Concord at all. What stopped his ride on the road?
answer: A British patrol captured him at a roadblock
choices: A British patrol captured him at a roadblock
His own horse threw him into a deep ditch
He turned back to carry word to Boston
A redcoat shot him out of his saddle
context: A British patrol stopped Revere, William Dawes, and Dr. Samuel Prescott at a roadblock in Lincoln. The British captured Revere, questioned him, and took his horse; Dawes fell off his horse and escaped on foot. Source: https://www.paulreverehouse.org/frequently-asked-questions-about-the-midnight-ride-of-paul-revere/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Prescott

question: A British sergeant at a sentry post hissed at Paul Revere to stop making so much noise as he rode past late on the night of April 18, 1775, on his way to warn the militia that British soldiers were marching. Revere later wrote down his own reply. What did he snap at the sergeant?
answer: Noise! You'll have noise enough before long
choices: Noise! You'll have noise enough before long
Quiet yourself, the king has lost this land
Stand aside, I ride for honest men
Hush now, redcoat, your time is short
context: By Revere's own deposition he answered: 'Noise! You'll have noise enough before long. The regulars are coming out!' Source: https://www.paulreverehouse.org/the-real-story/

question: On Lexington Green at dawn on April 19, 1775, about 70 militiamen, most of them local farmers, stood in line to face hundreds of British troops. One man in that line is named in the histories because he was wounded in the fight. Who was he?
answer: Prince Estabrook, a Black man who was then a slave
choices: Prince Estabrook, a Black man who was then a slave
Deacon John Larkin, who had lent out his horse
Robert Newman, the sexton from the Old North Church
Hugh Earl Percy, the British relief commander
context: Prince Estabrook, a Black man enslaved at the time, served in Captain John Parker's Lexington company and was wounded in the fight — among the very first to bleed in the Revolution. The British volley killed eight militiamen and wounded ten that morning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord

question: Samuel Prescott, a young doctor riding home from visiting a lady friend, fell in with Paul Revere and William Dawes on the road on the night of the ride. A British patrol trapped all three, and one bold move made Prescott the only rider to reach Concord and raise the alarm. What did he do?
answer: He jumped his horse over a stone wall
choices: He jumped his horse over a stone wall
He swam his horse across a cold river
He hid in a dark farmhouse cellar
He outran the whole patrol on the open road
context: Prescott jumped his horse over a stone wall to escape the patrol, rode on to Concord, and rang the town bell to sound the alarm — the one rider of the three who got through. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Prescott and https://www.nps.gov/places/paul-revere-capture-site.htm

question: A single shot cracked across Lexington Green at dawn on April 19, 1775, just as about 70 militiamen turned to go. Their captain, John Parker, badly outnumbered by the British troops marching at them, had ordered them to scatter. It was the first shot of the American Revolutionary War. What do historians today say about who fired it?
answer: No one knows which side fired it
choices: No one knows which side fired it
A British officer gave the order to fire
A Lexington farmer fired the first shot
Major Pitcairn fired his own pistol first
context: As the militia dispersed, an unknown person fired first — to this day no one knows whether it was a colonist or a British soldier. Major John Pitcairn had ridden forward shouting 'Disperse, ye rebels! Lay down your arms!' Source: https://research.colonialwilliamsburg.org/Foundation/journal/Summer06/lex.cfm and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord

question: Captain John Parker drew up his small Lexington militia to face the British column at dawn on April 19, 1775. Tradition holds that he steadied his men with one line, now carved on a plaque at Lexington Battle Green. According to that tradition, what did Parker tell them?
answer: If they mean to have a war, let it begin here
choices: If they mean to have a war, let it begin here
Hold the green or die where you stand
Fire first and fire fast, my friends
God and liberty, follow me forward
context: By tradition Parker said: 'Stand your ground. Don't fire unless fired upon, but if they mean to have a war, let it begin here.' Historians dispute the exact words, but the line is carved at Lexington Battle Green. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Parker_(captain) and https://emergingcivilwar.com/2015/02/18/and-if-they-mean-to-have-a-war-let-it-begin-here-the-real-words-of-captain-john-parker/  (Legend.)

question: Major John Buttrick of Concord stood with some 400 militia at Concord's North Bridge, facing about 90 British soldiers. When the British fired into them and killed a man, Buttrick roared an order, and for the first time Americans volleyed back in formation and drove the redcoats back. What did Buttrick shout?
answer: Fire, for God's sake, fellow soldiers, fire
choices: Fire, for God's sake, fellow soldiers, fire
Charge them, boys, the bridge is ours
Steady now, and aim for the officers
Avenge him, men, and give no ground
context: Buttrick's cry — 'Fire, for God's sake, fellow soldiers, fire!' — opened the volley at the North Bridge, the moment Emerson later called 'the shot heard round the world.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_North_Bridge and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord

question: Franklin Roosevelt asked Congress for war on 8 December 1941, the day after Japanese planes struck Pearl Harbor. His draft said the day would live in 'world history,' but he crossed those two words out and wrote one in their place. What did he write?
answer: infamy
choices: infamy
tragedy
treachery
disgrace
context: FDR's first dictated draft read 'a date which will live in world history'; he crossed out 'world history' by hand and wrote 'infamy.' The line opened his war message asking Congress to declare war on Japan. Source: https://www.archives.gov/education/lessons/day-of-infamy ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_Infamy_speech

question: Japanese pilots sank the battleship Arizona at Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, and more than 1,100 sailors went down with her. Her wreck rests on the harbor bottom beneath a memorial, and a thin sheen of oil rises from her hull every day. What have people come to call that oil?
answer: the tears of the Arizona
choices: the tears of the Arizona
the blood of the fleet
the sorrow of Oahu
the ashes of December
context: The wreck is now a memorial built over the sunken ship, and the daily seep is one of its most haunting sights. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/USS-Arizona ; https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/fallen-crew-uss-arizona-and-operation-85

question: Mitsuo Fuchida, the lead pilot, swept in over Pearl Harbor with the first wave of Japanese planes on 7 December 1941. Below him the American ships lay still asleep, with no defenses up. He radioed three code words back to his aircraft carrier to say the surprise was total. What did he send?
answer: Tora! Tora! Tora!
choices: Tora! Tora! Tora!
Banzai! Banzai! Banzai!
Totsugeki! Totsugeki! Totsugeki!
Kogeki! Kogeki! Kogeki!
context: Fuchida sent it at 7:53 a.m. 'Tora' literally means 'tiger,' but here it stood as shorthand for the Japanese words for 'charge' and 'torpedo attack.' The 1970 film about the attack took its name from this signal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsuo_Fuchida ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tora!_Tora!_Tora!

question: The band of the battleship Nevada stood on deck at Pearl Harbor on the morning of 7 December 1941, playing 'The Star-Spangled Banner' for the 8 a.m. raising of the flag. A Japanese plane roared over and sprayed the deck with machine-gun fire, all around the musicians. What did the band do?
answer: kept playing the anthem to the very end, only faster
choices: kept playing the anthem to the very end, only faster
dropped their instruments and ran below for cover
switched to a quick march to rally the crew
scattered at once to their battle stations
context: Nevada was the only battleship to get underway during the attack. To keep from sinking and blocking the harbor channel, her crew deliberately ran her aground. Source: https://www.military.com/off-duty/history/pearl-harbor-uss-nevada-band.html ; https://www.war.gov/News/Feature-Stories/Story/Article/3879225/uss-nevada-was-the-only-battleship-to-get-underway-during-pearl-harbor-attack/

question: George Welch and Kenneth Taylor, two young Army pilots, had been up all night at a dance and a poker game when the bombs fell on Pearl Harbor. They raced by car to the Haleiwa airstrip and took off in their P-40 fighters without stopping to change. What were they still wearing?
answer: their formal tuxedo mess dress
choices: their formal tuxedo mess dress
their issued flight suits
their dress khaki uniforms
their cotton sleeping clothes
context: Between them Welch and Taylor shot down several enemy planes and both earned the Distinguished Service Cross. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Welch_(pilot) ; https://www.history.com/articles/heroes-of-pearl-harbor-george-welch-and-kenneth-taylor

question: Doris Miller, a ship's cook on the battleship West Virginia, carried his wounded captain to safety when Japanese planes struck Pearl Harbor. The Navy did not let Black sailors train on the big guns, yet Miller then ran to a heavy machine gun he had never been taught to fire and shot back at the planes. He became the first Black American to earn which honor?
answer: the Navy Cross
choices: the Navy Cross
the Medal of Honor
the Silver Star
the Purple Heart
context: Admiral Chester Nimitz pinned the Navy Cross on Miller in person on May 27, 1942. He had also been the ship's heavyweight boxing champion. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doris_Miller

question: Julio DeCastro, a shipyard worker at Pearl Harbor, heard sailors banging S-O-S on steel with their wrenches. The sound came from inside the battleship Oklahoma, which five torpedoes had rolled upside down within minutes, trapping the men alive in her hull. What did DeCastro and his crew do?
answer: cut through the hull and pulled the trapped men out
choices: cut through the hull and pulled the trapped men out
pumped fresh air inside to keep them alive
rolled the ship upright using harbor cranes
marked the spot and waited for Navy divers
context: DeCastro's crew cut through the steel and rescued 32 survivors, even as 429 men aboard Oklahoma were lost. It was the most successful rescue of the day. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-civilian-worker-who-spearheaded-pearl-harbors-most-successful-rescue-mission-180979167/ ; https://www.history.navy.mil/our-collections/photography/wars-and-events/world-war-ii/pearl-harbor-raid/

question: A Japanese plane high above Pearl Harbor dropped a single 1,800-pound armor-piercing bomb on the battleship Arizona on 7 December 1941. It was the deadliest blow of the whole attack: the bomb punched clean through her armored deck and went off deep inside the ship. What happened next?
answer: her forward ammunition magazine went up and the ship blew apart
choices: her forward ammunition magazine went up and the ship blew apart
her engines flooded and she slowly capsized
she caught fire but was towed to safety
her hull split and she settled upright on the bottom
context: Arizona sank with 1,177 of her crew killed -- nearly half of all the Americans who died that day. Aboard her, 23 sets of brothers died together, along with the only father-and-son pair, Thomas Free and his son William. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/USS-Arizona ; https://www.nps.gov/perl/learn/historyculture/brothersassignedarizona.htm

question: Joseph Lockard and George Elliott, two privates at the new Opana radar station on Oahu, spotted a huge blip of planes 132 miles out about an hour before the attack on Pearl Harbor, and they phoned it in. Kermit Tyler, the lieutenant on duty, told them not to worry about it. What did Tyler believe the blip was?
answer: a flight of American B-17 bombers due that morning
choices: a flight of American B-17 bombers due that morning
a flock of seabirds confusing the new radar
a Navy patrol returning toward Pearl Harbor
a thunderstorm building out over the ocean
context: The privates were Joseph Lockard and George Elliott; the blip was the incoming Japanese first wave. A flight of B-17s really was expected from California that morning, which is why Tyler waved it off. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar_warning_of_Pearl_Harbor_attack ; https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/kermit-tyler-call-would-live-infamy

question: Japan's diplomats at their embassy in Washington were to hand the United States a long, 14-part note ending the peace talks, 30 minutes before the attack on Pearl Harbor began. Japan meant the note as a last warning. When did the Americans receive it?
answer: only after the bombs had already fallen
choices: only after the bombs had already fallen
a full hour before the first plane arrived
exactly 30 minutes ahead, as planned
the day before the attack began
context: Because the envoy did not deliver it until after the strike, the attack came with no warning at all -- which fixed it in American memory as a sneak attack. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor ; https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/what-happened-at-pearl-harbor

question: Isoroku Yamamoto, the Japanese admiral, wanted the American aircraft carriers above all at Pearl Harbor, but the Enterprise, the Lexington and the Saratoga were all away from the harbor that Sunday morning. The Japanese planes sank or damaged all eight battleships and never touched a carrier. What would the three carriers go on to do?
answer: carry the war back across the Pacific to Japan
choices: carry the war back across the Pacific to Japan
guard the U.S. West Coast against invasion
ferry fighter planes to help defend Australia
escort supply convoys across the Atlantic
context: Battleships were the old measure of naval power, but the war in the Pacific would be won by carriers -- the very weapon the raid failed to touch. America's shipyards and factories then poured out the planes, ships, and supplies that became the 'arsenal of democracy.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor

question: Isoroku Yamamoto, the Japanese admiral, left diaries, letters and speeches behind him. Historians searched them for one of the most quoted lines of the war, said to be his: 'I fear all we have done is to awaken a sleeping giant and fill him with a terrible resolve.' They found it in none of them. Where does the famous line come from?
answer: the 1970 film Tora! Tora! Tora!
choices: the 1970 film Tora! Tora! Tora!
a 1943 American wartime newsreel
a popular postwar biography of Yamamoto
a Tokyo radio broadcast during the war
context: Because there is no record of him ever saying it, historians treat the 'sleeping giant' line as words the movie put in Yamamoto's mouth -- powerful, fitting, but legend rather than documented fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isoroku_Yamamoto's_sleeping_giant_quote

question: Pericles led Athens through its Golden Age in the middle of the 400s BC, and when he spoke he seemed to thunder and flash lightning. The city's comic poets joked that he had 'a thunderbolt in his tongue,' and they gave him a grand nickname that stuck. What did they call him?
answer: the Olympian
choices: the Olympian
the Golden Tongue
the Lion of the Pnyx
the Voice of Athens
context: The comic playwrights' jab stuck: 'the Olympian' likened Pericles to Zeus himself, ruling Athens from on high with words instead of lightning. Source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles (penelope.uchicago.edu); Wikipedia 'Pericles'.

question: Athens's comic poets mocked Pericles without mercy and called him 'Squill-head,' after a knobbly sea-onion. Sculptors got around the problem by almost always carving him in a Corinthian helmet pushed back on his head. What were the sculptors politely hiding?
answer: the unusual, elongated shape of his skull
choices: the unusual, elongated shape of his skull
a deep battle scar across his brow
that he had gone completely bald
a birthmark covering one cheek
context: Pericles really is shown helmeted in nearly every surviving portrait, the artists' tactful fix for a head the comedians wouldn't stop teasing. Source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles (penelope.uchicago.edu); Wikipedia 'Pericles'.

question: On the Acropolis, the sacred rocky hill above Athens, Pericles began a great rebuilding around 447 BC. Its crown was a brilliant temple of white marble to Athena, the warrior goddess who protected the city, and its ruins still stand on the hill. What is that temple called?
answer: the Parthenon
choices: the Parthenon
the Erechtheion
the Pantheon
the Temple of Olympian Zeus
context: The Parthenon (built 447-432 BC) was designed by the architects Ictinus and Callicrates, with the sculptor Phidias directing all of its art. Source: worldhistory.org/Phidias; Perseus (Martin, Overview of Classical Greek History); thecollector.com/pericles-athenian-golden-age.

question: Phidias sheathed his statue of Athena in ivory and over a ton of gold, and she towered about forty feet high inside her great temple in Athens. On the floor right in front of her he kept a shallow pool of one liquid, both to protect the ivory and to mirror her image. What filled the pool?
answer: olive oil
choices: olive oil
fresh spring water
sweet wine
scented perfume
context: The statue was Athena Parthenos ('Athena the Virgin'), dedicated in 438 BC, holding a small winged Victory (Nike) in her hand; the oil kept the ivory from cracking and threw her golden reflection back up at her. Source: worldhistory.org/Phidias.

question: Pericles governed Athens while it headed the Delian League, an alliance of Greek cities that paid yearly tribute into a common war-fund, kept on the sacred island of Delos, to defend against Persia. In 454 BC Athens moved that fund home and began spending the allies' money on temples for itself. What had the alliance quietly turned into?
answer: an empire ruled by Athens
choices: an empire ruled by Athens
a free league of equals
a religious brotherhood
a trading partnership
context: Moving the treasury from Delos to Athens 'for safekeeping' let Pericles fund the Acropolis with the allies' tribute, converting allies into subjects. Source: Wikipedia 'Delian League'; pbs.org/empires/thegreeks/keyevents/454_c.html; Britannica 'Delian League'.

question: Pericles' rivals charged that he was decking out Athens with the allies' gold 'like a vain woman, hung round with precious stones.' He offered to pay for every building himself, on one condition, and the assembly instantly shouted for him to spend public money instead. What was his condition?
answer: that his own name be carved on the temples
choices: that his own name be carved on the temples
that he be given command of the army for life
that he receive a share of all future tolls
that a statue of him stand in the marketplace
context: Rather than let Pericles claim the glory, the assembly told him to spend freely from the public treasury, exactly as he had wanted. Source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles (classics.mit.edu/Plutarch/pericles.html).

question: Thucydides the historian heard Pericles give a funeral speech for the war dead of Athens in 431 BC, and he wrote it down. Pericles said of the city's government: 'Its administration favours the many instead of the few; this is why it is called ___.' What word filled the gap?
answer: a democracy
choices: a democracy
a republic
an oligarchy
a commonwealth
context: This line from the Funeral Oration is a founding statement of the Western idea that government should rest with the many citizens, not a privileged few. Source: Thucydides 2.37, Crawley translation (en.wikisource.org/wiki/History_of_the_Peloponnesian_War/Book_2).

question: A rude Athenian once trailed Pericles around the marketplace all day long, cursing him for every deed, and Pericles said nothing back. At nightfall Pericles went home to supper and called a servant. What did he order the servant to do for the man who had been abusing him?
answer: take a torch and walk him safely home
choices: take a torch and walk him safely home
throw him out of the city gates
fetch him a fine dinner as a joke
write down every insult he had shouted
context: Plutarch's best-loved Pericles story shows the self-control that fit his nickname 'the Olympian.' Told as a famous anecdote rather than a documented event. Source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles (penelope.uchicago.edu).  (Legend.)
