question: Pericles passed a strict law in 451 BC: only a child of two Athenian parents could be a citizen. Years later a plague killed both his lawful sons, leaving only his son by Aspasia of Miletus, a foreign woman. To make that boy a citizen, what did Pericles have to do before the assembly?
answer: beg them to set aside his own law
choices: beg them to set aside his own law
pay a huge fine from his fortune
marry an Athenian wife in old age
adopt a full citizen as his heir
context: In a bitter irony, the assembly took pity and suspended the very citizenship law Pericles himself had written. Source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles (penelope.uchicago.edu); thecollector.com/pericles-athenian-golden-age.

question: Pericles packed everyone from the countryside inside the walls of Athens at the start of the long war with Sparta, and let the navy do the fighting. Cramming people in helped a plague spread through the city in 430 BC, and it killed about a quarter of Athens. Whom did it kill in 429 BC?
answer: Pericles himself
choices: Pericles himself
the king of Sparta
most of the Athenian navy
his rival Cleon
context: Pericles' own strategy backfired tragically, the plague it worsened took his life along with so many others. Source: Britannica 'Pericles'; ebsco.com 'Plague of Athens'; thecollector.com/pericles-athenian-golden-age.

question: A frail African girl of about seven was sold in Boston in July 1761, and a merchant family named the Wheatleys bought her. They gave her the first name Phillis, and they took it from a source no one expected. What did the Wheatley family name Phillis Wheatley after?
answer: The slave ship that had carried her
choices: The slave ship that had carried her
The auctioneer who sold her
A daughter of the Wheatley family
The Boston church the family attended
context: The schooner that delivered her to Boston in July 1761 was itself named Phillis, and the Wheatleys gave her the vessel's own name. They guessed she was about seven because she was shedding her front teeth. Source: worldhistory.org/Phillis_Wheatley/ ; massmoments.org (John Wheatley Purchases a Slave Child).

question: John Hancock and seventeen other leading men of Boston tested Phillis Wheatley, a young enslaved girl, because so many refused to believe she could have written her own poems. They put their names to a note saying the poems were hers. When her book came out in London in 1773, what milestone did she reach?
answer: The first African American to publish a book of poetry
choices: The first African American to publish a book of poetry
The first woman admitted to Harvard College
The first slave to win her freedom in a Boston court
The first colonist to be printed in three languages
context: 'Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral' came out in London in 1773 — no colonial printer would take it. The eighteen signers attested the poems were genuinely 'written by PHILLIS, a young Negro Girl.' Source: britannica.com/biography/Phillis-Wheatley ; smithsonianmag.com ; massmoments.org.

question: Phillis Wheatley, brought to Boston as an enslaved child, wrote a poem to General George Washington late in 1775, as the American Revolution began. In it she dreamed up a goddess figure for the young nation, and poets later took the name she gave her for America itself. What did Wheatley call her nation-goddess?
answer: Columbia
choices: Columbia
Liberty
Britannia
Minerva
context: Wheatley wrote 'Columbia's scenes of glorious toils I write.' Washington wrote back from Cambridge on Feb 28, 1776, praising her 'great poetical Talents' and inviting her to visit — which she did, meeting him in person in March 1776. The poem ends: 'A crown, a mansion, and a throne that shine, / With gold unfading, WASHINGTON! be thine.' Source: hamilton.gilderlehrman.org ; mountvernon.org.

question: The Phoenicians of Tyre made royal purple, a dye so costly under Rome that it was worn only by kings and emperors, from a living creature they crushed by the thousands. It took about 10,000 of them to colour a single garment. What creature gave up the royal purple?
answer: The murex, a spiny sea-snail
choices: The murex, a spiny sea-snail
The squid, an inky deep-sea hunter
The sea-urchin, a spined shellfish
The whelk, a coiled tide-pool snail
context: Tyrian purple was squeezed from the crushed mucus glands of murex sea-snails. About 10,000 snails dyed a single garment, and 12,000 yielded barely 1.4 grams of dye -- only enough to trim a robe. Under Rome a pound of it cost roughly three pounds of gold, making the color literally worth more than gold by weight. Sources: worldhistory.org/Tyrian_Purple/ ; history.com/articles/purple-ancient-phoenicians

question: Phoenician sailors ranged the whole Mediterranean from their home cities on the Lebanese coast, reaching as far west as Spain and founding Carthage. The Greeks did not call these traders by their own name for themselves; they named them for their most famous product. What did phoinix, the Greek word behind 'Phoenician,' mean?
answer: Reddish-purple
choices: Reddish-purple
Far-wandering
Sea-faring
Cedar-scented
context: "Phoenician" likely comes from the Greek phoinix, meaning roughly "reddish-purple" -- so the Phoenicians were literally "the Purple People," named by the Greeks for the murex dye they carried across the sea. Tyre founded Carthage around 814 BC, the city that would later challenge Rome. Sources: nationalgeographic.com ("Purple reign"); encyclopedia.com ("the Purple People")

question: Pablo Picasso's family told of his very first word as a baby: 'piz,' his way of saying the Spanish word 'lapiz.' The boy grew up to be one of history's most famous painters, and by this family legend he started early. What was the little boy already asking for?
answer: A pencil
choices: A pencil
A paintbrush
His mother
Some bread
context: 'Piz' was baby-talk for 'lapiz,' Spanish for pencil. Told as a family legend, not documented fact. Source: cigaraficionado.com/article/saved-by-the-cigar-242

question: The priest who baptized the baby Pablo Picasso in Malaga wrote down a name that went on and on: 'Pablo Diego Jose Francisco de Paula Juan Nepomuceno ... Ruiz y Picasso.' Each name honoured a saint or a relative. About how many first names did the baptism give him?
answer: More than a dozen
choices: More than a dozen
Around half a dozen
Exactly two
Just one
context: Spanish baptismal custom piled on saints' names; Picasso's stretched past a dozen given names. Source: historyfacts.com/famous-figures/fact/pablo-picassos-full-name/

question: Pablo Picasso helped invent a new way to paint. In one of his faces a nose can sit next to a side-view ear, and all the parts of one head are jumbled across the flat canvas in no normal order. What did this new style let a single picture do?
answer: Show an object from several angles at once
choices: Show an object from several angles at once
Paint a person's emotions as bright colors
Capture one frozen instant of time
Blur shapes to suggest fast motion
context: This is the core trick of Cubism: many viewpoints fused into one image, the form broken into flat planes and reassembled. Source: metmuseum.org/essays/cubism

question: Pablo Picasso answered the bombing of Guernica, a little Basque town struck by German and Italian warplanes during the Spanish Civil War, with a huge mural of his own in 1937. He wanted it to hit viewers like a war photo on the front page of a morning paper. Which colours did he keep to for the whole painting?
answer: Only grey, black, and white
choices: Only grey, black, and white
Sepia and faded brown
A range of blues only
Charcoal grey with blood red
context: The monochrome grey-black-white palette gives Guernica the immediacy of a black-and-white newspaper photograph; his partner, photographer Dora Maar, helped push it that way. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

question: A Gestapo officer of the Nazi secret police, the story goes, forced his way into Pablo Picasso's apartment in occupied Paris during World War Two. In the tale he spotted a photograph of Picasso's 'Guernica,' the painting of the German bombing of a Spanish town, pointed at it and demanded, 'Did you do that?' How did Picasso answer, as the story tells it?
answer: 'No -- you did.'
choices: 'No -- you did.'
'Yes, and I am proud of it.'
'I have never seen it before.'
'A friend of mine painted it.'
context: Picasso meant the Nazis made the horror the painting records. Recounted as legend in a Guardian editorial. Source: openculture.com/2017/05/the-gestapo-points-to-guernica-and-asks-picasso-did-you-do-this.html

question: Pablo Picasso painted a huge mural to mourn the dead of Guernica, a small Basque town in northern Spain. German bombers sent by Hitler to help the fascist side had bombed and machine-gunned it for about three hours on market day in April 1937. Who made up most of the bodies he showed lying in the rubble?
answer: Women and children
choices: Women and children
Basque militiamen
Retreating soldiers
The town's mayors
context: Most of the town's men were away at the front, so the bombing fell on the women and children left behind -- the atrocity Guernica witnesses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

question: Pablo Picasso packed his mural 'Guernica' with horror: a screaming horse, a crying mother, a fallen soldier. On the ground the dead soldier's cut-off arm still gripped a broken sword, and from that snapped blade Picasso painted one living thing rising as a hint of hope. What was it?
answer: A flower
choices: A flower
An olive sprig
A wheat stalk
A rose
context: Amid the slaughter, a sprout of hope: a lone flower grows from the broken blade in the fallen fighter's hand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

question: Andre Salmon, a poet and a friend of Pablo Picasso, gave Picasso's 1907 picture of five women with mask-like faces the gentle title it carries today, 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon,' 'The Young Ladies of Avignon.' Picasso always hated the change. What blunt name had he given the picture himself?
answer: 'The Brothel of Avignon'
choices: 'The Brothel of Avignon'
'The Streetwalkers of Barcelona'
'The Five Sisters'
'The Dancers of Avignon'
context: Picasso named it 'Le Bordel d'Avignon' after Carrer d'Avinyo, a red-light street in Barcelona; Salmon's tamer title stuck against his wishes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Demoiselles_d'Avignon

question: Louis Vauxcelles, a French critic, looked at Georges Braque's blocky, geometric landscapes around 1908 and sneered at them with a mocking phrase. The jeer caught on and gave a name to the whole art movement that Braque and Picasso had never named themselves. What did Vauxcelles say the paintings were made of?
answer: 'Little cubes'
choices: 'Little cubes'
'Little bricks'
'Paper triangles'
'Flat playing cards'
context: The insult 'bizarreries cubiques' (cubic oddities), echoing Matisse's jab about 'little cubes,' gave Cubism its name; Picasso and Braque never chose the label. Source: metmuseum.org/essays/cubism

question: Georges Braque said that he and Pablo Picasso were 'like mountain-climbers roped together' as they built Cubism side by side from about 1908 to 1914. In 1912 the two friends invented a whole new technique that artists still use today. Which technique did Picasso and Braque invent?
answer: Collage
choices: Collage
Oil painting
Fresco
Etching
context: In 1912, during their Synthetic Cubism phase, they glued real-world scraps -- newspaper, wallpaper, and labels -- straight onto the canvas, inventing collage. Source: sothebys.com/en/articles/from-picasso-to-present-the-origins-of-cubism

question: Art critics spent decades pressing Pablo Picasso to explain what the wounded horse and the looming bull in his anti-war mural 'Guernica' secretly stood for. They wanted a tidy code for the symbols, and he refused to hand one over. How did Picasso wave the question away?
answer: 'This bull is a bull and this horse is a horse.'
choices: 'This bull is a bull and this horse is a horse.'
'Only the dead know what they mean.'
'I painted them from a dream.'
'The critics may decide for me.'
context: He resisted a fixed reading, allowing elsewhere only that the bull suggests brutality and darkness and the horse the people. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

question: Pablo Picasso swore that his 'Guernica' would not hang in Spain until 'liberty and democracy' returned there, and he named no other condition. For decades the canvas waited in a New York museum while Francisco Franco ruled Spain as its dictator. What had happened by the time the painting went home in 1981?
answer: The dictator had finally died
choices: The dictator had finally died
A new constitution outlawed all art bans
The painting had been sold abroad
A grand museum was built to house it
context: Franco died in 1975; Guernica then left New York's Museum of Modern Art and reached Spain on 10 September 1981. Source: history.com/this-day-in-history/guernica-returned-to-spain

question: Francisco Pizarro marched a tiny band of Spaniards into the Andean town of Cajamarca in 1532, meaning to seize the Inca emperor Atahualpa. On the hills all around, Atahualpa waited with an army of about 80,000 warriors. How many men did Pizarro have with him?
answer: About 168 men
choices: About 168 men
About 1,600 men
About 5,000 men
About 12,000 men
context: Pizarro had only about 168 men: 62 horsemen and 106 foot soldiers, with 4 small cannons and 12 harquebuses, against an Inca army of roughly 80,000 outside Cajamarca. The Inca thought so tiny a group of strangers was no real threat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cajamarca (and Britannica); https://www.worldhistory.org/article/704/pizarro-and-atahualpa-the-curse-of-the-lost-inca-g/

question: Atahualpa, the Inca emperor, sat captive in a stone room in Cajamarca after Francisco Pizarro took him prisoner in 1532. He saw how hungry the Spanish were for gold, and to buy his freedom he made one of the most astonishing ransom offers in history. What did he promise them?
answer: A whole room filled to a high red line with gold, then twice over with silver
choices: A whole room filled to a high red line with gold, then twice over with silver
A mountain whose veins of pure gold ran straight to the sea
A fleet of llamas loaded with every jewel in the empire
His own weight measured out three times in melted gold
context: Atahualpa drew a line about 8-9 feet up the wall, as high as he could reach, and promised to fill the room once with gold and then twice over with silver. The Ransom Room (Cuarto del Rescate) still stands in Cajamarca, Peru, with a red line marking the height. It became the richest ransom ever paid. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom_Room

question: Pizarro's men charged the packed square at Cajamarca and hacked at the eighty nobles carrying Atahualpa's litter, trying to tip the emperor to the ground. Spanish eyewitnesses, Pedro Pizarro among them, wrote about what the bearers did even after swords had cut off their hands and arms. What did those men keep doing?
answer: Holding the litter aloft with their bleeding stumps
choices: Holding the litter aloft with their bleeding stumps
Singing the emperor's name as they fell
Crawling to shield Atahualpa with their bodies
Hurling their severed arms at the horses
context: The chroniclers, among them the eyewitness Pedro Pizarro, say the maimed bearers kept holding the litter up on their stumps and shoulders and refused to let the emperor fall until they were killed. Pizarro himself took a sword cut to his own hand stopping a soldier from killing Atahualpa, who was worth far more alive. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cajamarca (citing Pedro Pizarro).

question: Pizarro's men held a sham trial for Atahualpa after his ransom was paid in full, and they sentenced him to be burned alive. To the Inca a burned body could never pass on to the next life, so Atahualpa accepted Christian baptism to escape the flames. What was done to him instead, in the same square where he had been caught?
answer: He was strangled with an iron garrote
choices: He was strangled with an iron garrote
He was beheaded with a Spanish sword
He was hanged from the town gallows
He was sent in chains to Spain
context: Baptized as 'Francisco,' after Pizarro, Atahualpa avoided the fire but was throttled with the iron collar of the garrote in 1533. The charges included ordering the murder of his brother Huascar and plotting an uprising. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atahualpa; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Inca_Empire; historyskills.com.

question: Francisco Pizarro did not topple the Inca by nerve alone. The Inca world was already broken by the time he led his small band into the Andes in 1532, and its emperor, Huayna Capac, had died of disease. What else had just happened in the empire, which Pizarro exploited?
answer: A five-year civil war in which Atahualpa's generals had just beaten and captured his brother Huascar
choices: A five-year civil war in which Atahualpa's generals had just beaten and captured his brother Huascar
A famine that had emptied the granaries across the whole empire
A revolt of the southern provinces that had cut Cuzco off from the coast
A failed harvest that had broken the empire's network of roads
context: Disease, the civil war, and the loss of the god-emperor, not any magic, let so few men topple so vast an empire. Even from his cell, Atahualpa secretly had the captive Huascar killed, fearing his brother would offer the Spanish a bigger ransom. Source: ticketmachupicchu.com; worldhistory.org/Atahualpa.

question: Francisco Pizarro, the Spanish conquistador, landed on the Pacific coast of South America around 1531, when the mighty Inca empire high in the Andes was tearing itself apart after Huayna Capac, the last strong Inca emperor, had died around 1527. What killed the emperor?
answer: Smallpox
choices: Smallpox
Starvation
A spear wound
Old age
context: Smallpox swept through the Americas ahead of the Spanish themselves. Huayna Capac's death threw the throne into a civil war between his sons Huascar and Atahualpa, gutting the empire before Pizarro arrived. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huayna_Capac

question: Vicente de Valverde, a Spanish friar, handed the Inca emperor Atahualpa a Christian holy book at Cajamarca in 1532 and told him to bow to Spain and to God. The Inca heard their gods through spoken oracles, so Atahualpa held the book to his ear and heard nothing. What did he do with it that helped set off the attack?
answer: Threw it on the ground
choices: Threw it on the ground
Tore out its pages
Handed it to a priest
Slipped it into his robe
context: Because the Inca heard their gods through spoken oracles, Atahualpa held the breviary to his ear, heard nothing, and threw it down; to him a book that did not speak was worthless. The Spanish treated it as an insult to God: Valverde shouted to attack, Pizarro waved a white scarf as the signal, and a cannon fired. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cajamarca; historyskills.com.

question: Inca llama trains hauled treasure to Cajamarca for months to pay the ransom of Atahualpa, the emperor Francisco Pizarro held captive there in 1532. Much of that gold was peeled off one holy building in Cusco, the Inca capital high in the Andes, whose walls had been covered in solid plates of gold. What kind of building was it?
answer: A temple to the Sun
choices: A temple to the Sun
A royal tomb
The emperor's palace
A military fortress
context: The Coricancha (Qorikancha) was the Temple of the Sun in Cusco, sheathed in gold. The Inca stripped its gold plating, and caravans carried golden statues and life-sized model llamas across the empire to Cajamarca over about four months. Source: https://www.cuscoperu.com/en/travel/cusco/archaeological-centers/qoricancha/

question: Hernando de Soto, the story goes, rode his warhorse straight at the Inca emperor Atahualpa before the ambush at Cajamarca and pulled up hard just feet from the emperor's face, hoping to scare him. Atahualpa had never seen a horse. How did he react, by that story?
answer: He did not flinch a muscle
choices: He did not flinch a muscle
He fell backward off his stool
He drew a ceremonial axe
He ordered his guards to fire
context: This is told as legend. Atahualpa reportedly held perfectly still; some accounts say warriors of his who DID recoil were later executed for showing fear. Source: https://heatherpringle.com/2010/03/15/the-emperor-and-the-horse/

question: Atahualpa learned Spanish, chess and cards in about twenty days as Pizarro's captive, a famous legend says. Watching Hernando de Soto in a tense game of chess, the emperor is said to have leaned over and whispered a single move that won it. According to the legend, which piece did he tell de Soto to move?
answer: The rook
choices: The rook
The queen
The king
A pawn
context: Told as legend, retold by Ricardo Palma from chronicler Juan de Betanzos. Atahualpa reportedly whispered 'No, captain - the rook,' and gave chess the Quechua name 'taptana' (surprise attack). Source: https://adventuresinhistoryland.com/2019/03/10/atahualpas-rook/

question: Manco Inca, the puppet ruler the Spanish set up three years after Atahualpa died, turned against them and raised an army to trap them in Cusco. Manco's army held the city under siege from May 1536 for nearly a year, and the Spanish sent four rescue armies up from Lima. What became of those four rescue columns?
answer: His forces wiped out all four
choices: His forces wiped out all four
They broke the siege and freed the city
They lost their way in the mountains
They switched sides and joined the rebels
context: Manco Inca besieged Cusco from May 1536 with an army said to number around 100,000. His forces destroyed all four relief columns the Spanish marched up from Lima, but the siege lasted nearly a year and ultimately failed to drive the Spanish out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Cusco

question: Francisco Pizarro did not take the Inca empire with Spaniards alone. Beyond disease and the Inca civil war, his drive on Cusco was reinforced by tens of thousands of native peoples who had been brutalized under Inca rule and saw the Spanish as a chance to throw off Cusco's grip. Which two peoples were the great native allies of the Spanish?
answer: The Canari and the Chachapoya
choices: The Canari and the Chachapoya
The Huascar and the Quito
The Aztec and the Maya
The Olmec and the Toltec
context: The Canari (led by Vilchumlay) and the Chachapoya, along with the Huanca, joined the Spanish drive on Cusco, having been brutalized under Inca rule. The conquest was a coalition, not a lone-conquistador feat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Inca_Empire

question: Diego de Almagro's followers stormed Francisco Pizarro's palace in Lima in 1541. Almagro, Pizarro's old partner, had been killed in 1538, as the conquerors fell to fighting over the loot. Pizarro had won the largest ransom in history, but he did not enjoy it long. What happened to him there?
answer: He was assassinated
choices: He was assassinated
He was shipped back to Spain in chains
He escaped into the mountains
He was crowned governor for life
context: Pizarro was assassinated in his Lima palace in 1541 by supporters of Diego de Almagro, whom Pizarro's faction had executed in 1538. The conquerors turned on each other in their own civil war. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Inca_Empire

question: Aristocles, the young man the world knows as Plato, wrestled in real contests and is said to have fought in the Isthmian Games. It was his wrestling coach who pinned the nickname 'Plato' on him. What feature of the young athlete earned him that nickname?
answer: His broad, powerful shoulders
choices: His broad, powerful shoulders
His unusually long legs
His loud booming voice
His thick curly hair
context: 'Plato' comes from the Greek 'platon,' meaning 'broad.' His coach reportedly named him for his build. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/plato/ (citing Diogenes Laertius via Britannica).

question: Plato set up his school around 387 BC in a sacred park of old olive trees just outside Athens, a spot already named for a legendary local hero. The school took its name straight from the grove, and from it comes a word every student still uses today. What word?
answer: Academy
choices: Academy
Library
Lecture
Diploma
context: The grove was named for the hero Akademos (archaic 'Hekademia'). 'Academy' and 'academic' trace directly back to that patch of olive trees outside Athens; the site lasted roughly 900 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platonic_Academy.

question: Plato wrote about 35 dialogues, conversations set down like little plays, yet in nearly all of them he never gave himself a single line. He put the leading arguments in the mouth of his own old teacher, a man who in real life never wrote anything down. Which teacher leads the talk in almost all of Plato's dialogues?
answer: Socrates
choices: Socrates
Aristotle
Pythagoras
Homer
context: The real Socrates left no writings, so most of what we 'hear' from him comes through Plato's dialogues. In the Republic, Plato even casts his own two brothers, Glaucon and Adeimantus, as the men arguing with Socrates. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/plato/.

question: A writer set down two short books around 360 BC, the Timaeus and the Critias, and in them told of Atlantis, a mighty island empire swallowed by the sea. The story has sparked films and treasure hunts, yet no older source for it has ever been found. Who first told the story of Atlantis?
answer: The philosopher Plato
choices: The philosopher Plato
The poet Homer
The historian Herodotus
Egyptian temple priests
context: Scholars generally think Plato invented Atlantis as a fictional example to dramatize his political ideas. No source older than Plato mentions it. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/atlantis/.

question: The prisoners of Plato's Cave sat chained by the neck and legs from childhood, facing a blank wall they could never turn from. Behind them a fire burned, and people carried carved figures of animals and objects along a walkway. The prisoners spent their lives naming and arguing about the only things they could see on that wall. What did they mistake for the whole of reality?
answer: Flickering shadows cast on the wall
choices: Flickering shadows cast on the wall
Paintings left by older prisoners
Carved statues set into the rock
Reflections in an underground pool
context: This is the Allegory of the Cave (Republic Book VII, 514a). The prisoners take the shadows for real things because they have never seen anything else. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegory_of_the_cave.

question: Plato argued in the Republic that war, injustice and human misery would never end in cities until political power and real understanding belonged to one and the same person, so that the one who ruled was also the one who truly knew. He gave this fused ruler a famous name. What kind of ruler did Plato insist a just city requires?
answer: A philosopher-king
choices: A philosopher-king
A conquering war-hero
A high priest of the gods
The richest man in the city
context: Republic 473c-e: 'There is no end to suffering... unless either philosophers become kings... or kings become real, true philosophers.' Plato's term for the ruler who unites power with knowledge is the philosopher-king. Source: https://jaredhenderson.substack.com/p/either-philosophers-become-kings.

question: Plato divided the people of Kallipolis, 'the beautiful city' of his Republic, into three classes: ruler-guardians, soldiers and workers. To make each accept its station as natural, he had its rulers spread a founding story he openly called a 'noble lie': that people were born from the earth with different substances mixed into their souls. What did the story say was inside each person's soul?
answer: A metal — gold, silver, or bronze
choices: A metal — gold, silver, or bronze
A color — gold, blue, or grey
A guiding animal spirit
A god's personal blessing
context: The Myth of the Metals (Republic 414b–415c): gold souls rule, silver souls soldier, bronze and iron souls work. Plato presents it as a deliberate fiction to make the class system feel divinely fixed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_lie.

question: Karl Popper, a twentieth-century philosopher, read Plato's ideal state in 'The Open Society and Its Enemies' as a warning rather than a dream. He argued that the Republic was history's first detailed blueprint of one particular kind of society, and he called Plato all the more dangerous because he was a genuinely great mind. Which kind of society did Popper argue the Republic first sketched?
answer: A closed, totalitarian society
choices: A closed, totalitarian society
A militarized, conquering empire
A pious, priest-run theocracy
A rigid, caste-bound oligarchy
context: Popper subtitled the section 'The Spell of Plato' and named Plato an originator of totalitarian thought, describing the ideal state as the first 'closed society.' Presented here as one serious modern reading of the Republic, not a final verdict on Plato. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Open_Society_and_Its_Enemies.

question: The freed prisoner in Plato's Cave stumbled up out of the darkness into daylight, and at first the glare blinded him. Only slowly could his eyes bear reflections, then real things, until at last he could look at the brightest thing of all, high in the sky. Plato said that blazing source of light stands for the highest object of knowledge. What does the Sun represent in his philosophy?
answer: The Form of the Good
choices: The Form of the Good
The soul of the world
The mind of the gods
The fire of reason
context: The escaped prisoner's painful climb toward the Sun pictures the philosopher's journey toward the Form of the Good (Republic Book VII). Brought back below, he is mocked and re-blinded by the dark. Source: https://www.sparknotes.com/philosophy/republic/section7/.

question: Plato would not let his ideal city be ruled by the young or the pushy, though in Athens a man could speak in the assembly as a youth and hold real office in his thirties. Plato's guardian first spent decades in hard study and then in lower public jobs, kept from real power until an age when most Athenian men were nearing the end of public life. At what age did a guardian finally get to rule?
context: Britannica and Plato's Republic: roughly 35 years of education plus 15 years of service in lower offices means a guardian reaches the top only at about 50 — a deliberately brutal filter for power. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/philosopher-king.

question: Scholars read a scroll in 2024 that had been charred solid when Vesuvius buried Herculaneum in 79 AD, and it told how Plato died. Dying in bed at about eighty and lucid to the very end, he spent some of his last breath on one sharp, oddly specific criticism. What was that deathbed criticism?
answer: A flute-girl's poor sense of rhythm
choices: A flute-girl's poor sense of rhythm
A student's sloppy, ill-made argument
A wrongly copied line of his own writing
A house-slave's clumsy, noisy serving
context: Deciphered via the Vesuvius Challenge, research led by Prof. Graziano Ranocchia. The scroll says Plato, dying near a shrine to the Muses, criticized a Thracian flute-girl's rhythm. Source: https://www.euronews.com/culture/2024/04/30/platos-death-revealed-from-charred-remains-of-vesuvius-eruption-scroll.

question: Roald Amundsen and Robert Falcon Scott raced for the South Pole in 1911. Scott's motor sledges broke down, and his ponies struggled in the cold and had to be shot. Amundsen's Norwegians ran on skis behind teams of sled dogs, and he had worked out a cold-blooded plan in advance. What was the plan that gave Amundsen his edge?
answer: He planned exactly which dogs to shoot along the way to feed the rest
choices: He planned exactly which dogs to shoot along the way to feed the rest
He planned to abandon any man who could not keep the pace
He planned to leave all his supplies behind and travel with nothing
He planned to wait out the worst storms inside buried snow caves
context: Amundsen took 52 dogs and scheduled in advance the exact day each dog would be shot once it had hauled its load — the dead dogs were fed to the surviving dogs and the men. He had learned dog-driving and the use of fur clothing from the Inuit in the Arctic. Scott instead relied on motor sledges that broke down and ponies that had to be shot. Source: livescience.com, science history of the South Pole race.

question: Ernest Shackleton sailed his ship Endurance toward Antarctica, and the pack ice of the Weddell Sea closed around her and held her fast. For months the trapped ship drifted with the ice, while the frozen sea pressed harder and harder on her wooden hull. What became of the Endurance in November 1915?
answer: The ice crushed it and it sank
choices: The ice crushed it and it sank
The thawing ice set it free in the spring
The crew chopped it loose and sailed on
The ice carried it gently onto solid land
context: The Endurance was crushed by the pack ice of the Weddell Sea and sank on 21 November 1915, marooning Shackleton's 28 men on the drifting ice with no ship. Source: coolantarctica.com, Shackleton Endurance Trans-Antarctic Expedition.

question: Five hand-picked men climbed with Ernest Shackleton into the James Caird in April 1916, a 22-foot open lifeboat only a little bigger than a rowboat. The whole crew of the Endurance was stranded on Elephant Island, a bleak and empty scrap of land where no rescue ship would ever find them. What was the desperate plan of the six in the lifeboat?
answer: To sail 800 miles across the stormiest ocean to reach help on South Georgia
choices: To sail 800 miles across the stormiest ocean to reach help on South Georgia
To row a few miles out and wait for a passing ship
To paddle around the island hunting seals for food
To ride out the winter sleeping aboard the boat near shore
context: Shackleton left 22 men under Frank Wild on Elephant Island and set out in the 22-foot James Caird on 24 April 1916 to cross 800 miles of the Southern Ocean to South Georgia and bring back rescue. Source: Wikipedia, 'Voyage of the James Caird'.

question: Captain Lawrence Oates, crippled by frostbite on the march back from the South Pole, knew he was slowing his starving companions down. In a blizzard he rose and stepped out of the tent on purpose, never to be seen again. What did Oates quietly say as he went out to die so the others might live?
answer: 'I am just going outside and may be some time'
choices: 'I am just going outside and may be some time'
'Tell my wife I love her dearly'
'Go on without me and save yourselves'
'I will return before the storm breaks'
context: Captain Lawrence Oates, frostbitten and unable to keep pace, walked out of the tent into a blizzard to spare his companions, saying 'I am just going outside and may be some time.' He was never seen again. Source: Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'.

question: Robert Peary announced that he had reached the North Pole on 6 April 1909, but just days before, Dr. Frederick Cook had claimed that he stood at the Pole a year earlier. The two men fought bitterly over who was first, and Cook's whole claim collapsed when investigators caught him in a separate lie. What earlier boast unraveled and destroyed Cook's credibility?
answer: His claim to be first to summit Denali (Mt. McKinley)
choices: His claim to be first to summit Denali (Mt. McKinley)
His claim to have crossed Antarctica alone
His claim to have discovered a new continent
His claim to have sailed around the world twice
context: Dr. Frederick Cook claimed he reached the North Pole in April 1908, a year before Peary. Peary denounced him as a fraud, and Cook's credibility collapsed when it emerged he had also lied about being first to summit Denali (Mt. McKinley). Peary's own claim remains disputed to this day. Source: beyondpenguins.ehe.osu.edu, 'Who Got There First: The North Pole Controversies'.

question: Adolf Hitler demanded a strip of mountain borderland in Czechoslovakia that was home to about three million ethnic Germans. At a conference in Munich, the leaders of Britain and France agreed to hand it to him without a fight. What was the border land called?
answer: The Sudetenland
choices: The Sudetenland
The Rhineland
The Saarland
East Prussia
context: The Sudetenland was Czechoslovakia's fortified mountain rim. German troops were to occupy it starting 1 October 1938 and finish by 10 October. In return Hitler 'promised peace.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Agreement; encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/timeline-event/holocaust/1933-1938/munich-agreement)

question: Neville Chamberlain went nowhere without one everyday item. He kept letting Adolf Hitler take more of Europe rather than fight, and when that soft policy came to be called appeasement, cartoonists made the item its symbol. What was it?
answer: His umbrella
choices: His umbrella
His top hat
His walking cane
His pocket watch
context: Cartoonists and Hitler alike fixed on Chamberlain's umbrella. An MI5 file even recorded Hitler's sneer that if 'that silly old man comes interfering here again with his umbrella, I'll kick him downstairs and jump on his stomach in front of the photographers.' (foreignpolicy.com/2006/10/13/the-umbrellas-shadow/; nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/resources/chamberlain-and-hitler/)

question: Londoners were digging trenches and trying on gas masks in September 1938, braced for war over Germany's demands on Czechoslovakia. On the evening of the 27th, Neville Chamberlain spoke to the nation on the radio and said how horrible it was to do all this over another country's quarrel. How did he describe Czechoslovakia?
answer: A far-away country between people of whom we know nothing
choices: A far-away country between people of whom we know nothing
A small state caught between two great and hostile empires
A loyal friend we are honour-bound to stand beside
A powder keg that could set the whole continent alight
context: Full line: 'How horrible, fantastic, incredible it is that we should be digging trenches and trying on gas-masks here because of a quarrel in a far away country between people of whom we know nothing.' (encyc.org/wiki/Chamberlain's_Radio_Broadcast,_September_27,_1938)

question: At 69, Neville Chamberlain climbed into an aeroplane three times in two weeks to bargain with Hitler in person, something new for a British prime minister. His first trip ended at Hitler's private mountain home in the Bavarian Alps. Where did Chamberlain fly first?
answer: Berchtesgaden
choices: Berchtesgaden
Nuremberg
Berlin
Hamburg
context: The three flights came in quick succession: Berchtesgaden (Hitler's mountain retreat, 15 Sept), Bad Godesberg (~22-23 Sept), then Munich (29-30 Sept). Flying to a summit was almost unheard of for a leader then. (nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/resources/chamberlain-and-hitler/; historyhit.com/neville-chamberlains-three-flying-visits-to-hitler-in-1938/)

question: While the four powers decided Czechoslovakia's fate at Munich, the two Czech envoys, Vojtech Mastny and Hubert Masarik, were made to wait in an adjoining room for hours, then summoned at 1:30 a.m. to simply be handed the verdict. Masarik wrote down how Neville Chamberlain behaved while their country was being sentenced. What did he record Chamberlain doing?
answer: Yawning openly, without trying to hide it
choices: Yawning openly, without trying to hide it
Studying his papers in tense silence
Apologizing quietly to the two envoys
Pacing the room unable to sit still
context: Masarik wrote: 'The atmosphere was oppressive; sentence was about to be passed,' and that Chamberlain 'was yawning continuously, without making any effort to conceal his yawns.' (Shirer, The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich, erenow.org/ww/risefallthirdreich/66.php; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Agreement)

question: Hermann Goring told Emil Hacha, the Czech president, that the Luftwaffe would flatten Prague from the air unless he gave in. Hitler's troops marched into Prague on 15 March 1939, less than six months after Munich, and seized what was left of Czechoslovakia. What did Hacha do when faced with Goring's threat?
answer: He collapsed, then signed his country away
choices: He collapsed, then signed his country away
He refused and was arrested that night
He fled the capital before dawn
He ordered the army to fight
context: Hacha physically collapsed under the pressure and signed at 3:55 a.m., handing the last of Czechoslovakia to Hitler and shattering the Munich promise. (history.com/this-day-in-history/march-15/nazis-take-czechoslovakia; nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/appeasement-and-peace-our-time)

question: Edouard Daladier flew home from Munich braced to be booed by an angry mob for giving way to Hitler. Instead the Paris crowd cheered him and showered him with flowers, relieved that war had been avoided, though Daladier knew what the deal really was. Watching them, he muttered bitterly to an aide. What did he say?
answer: Ah, the fools!
choices: Ah, the fools!
We are lost.
God save France.
They will learn soon enough.
context: In French: 'Ah, les cons!' Daladier knew the deal was a defeat even as the crowds celebrated it as a triumph; the cheering Parisians did not understand that Munich had bought nothing. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Daladier; Shirer, erenow.org/ww/risefallthirdreich/66.php; history.com)

question: Hugh Dowding, the Royal Air Force chief, advised buying time in the autumn of 1938, when Fighter Command had just 25 squadrons and most of them flew obsolete biplanes. Neville Chamberlain's defenders build their strongest case on what Britain made of the delay. What did it build before war came, a system later called the war's single most important force-multiplier?
answer: A coastal radar network (Chain Home)
choices: A coastal radar network (Chain Home)
A fleet of new battleships
A long-range bomber force
A fortified wall along the coast
context: The Chain Home radar chain was funded and built on Chamberlain's watch; by the 1940 Battle of Britain, Fighter Command had grown to 58 squadrons of modern Spitfires and Hurricanes. This is appeasement's strongest defense: it bought Britain time to prepare. (newstatesman.com/politics/2018/04/did-neville-chamberlain-create-conditions-raf-win-battle-britain; warhistory.org/article/chamberlain-prudent-appeasement-i)

question: Winston Churchill rose in the House of Commons on 5 October 1938, while most members sat relieved that war had been dodged. The House would vote 366 to 144 for the Munich deal, and Nancy Astor heckled him from the benches. How did Churchill brand the deal in his very first sentence?
answer: A total and unmitigated defeat
choices: A total and unmitigated defeat
A shameful surrender to threats
A betrayal of a loyal ally
A blunder we would come to rue
context: Churchill: 'we have sustained a total and unmitigated defeat, and ... France has suffered even more than we have.' MP Nancy Astor heckled 'nonsense.' He warned it was 'only the first sip... of a bitter cup.' The Commons approved Munich 366 to 144; no Conservative voted against the deal, and Churchill's group only abstained. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_total_and_unmitigated_defeat; winstonchurchill.org/resources/speeches/1930-1938-the-wilderness/the-munich-agreement/)

question: Alfred Duff Cooper, First Lord of the Admiralty, resigned from Neville Chamberlain's cabinet over the Munich deal, the only member of it who did. In his resignation speech he said he could have accepted many hard outcomes, but not the one Britain had just chosen. Where did Duff Cooper draw the line?
answer: War with dishonour — that was too much
choices: War with dishonour — that was too much
Peace at this price I cannot defend
Surrender is not a policy I will sign
Honour has been traded for a quiet sleep
context: Duff Cooper said he could accept 'War with honour or peace with dishonour... but war with dishonour — that was too much.' The famous line 'you were given the choice between war and dishonour; you chose dishonour and you will have war' is usually pinned on Churchill, but it does not appear in his verified 5 October speech — its likeliest true root is Duff Cooper's documented resignation. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duff_Cooper; winstonchurchill.hillsdale.edu/alfred-duff-cooper/)

question: Under the stars of the open Pacific, a navigator steered his double-hulled canoe toward a speck of land thousands of miles from the last. Long afterward, European scholars searched the old voyaging canoes for the tools the navigators must have steered by. What did they find?
answer: None of them — no instruments at all
choices: None of them — no instruments at all
A magnetic compass and a sandglass
A sextant for reading the sun
A rolled chart of the islands
context: No compass, no sextant, no charts — archaeologists have found no evidence of any navigational device ever carried on a Polynesian voyaging canoe. Everything was held in the navigator's memory and senses. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: Mau Piailug, on the tiny Pacific island of Satawal, started learning to navigate as a baby, before he could walk, and he grew up to cross open ocean by the stars, the waves and the birds. What did his family do to begin?
answer: Set him in tide pools to feel the pull of the sea
choices: Set him in tide pools to feel the pull of the sea
Tied him to the mast of a canoe
Read him the names of the stars at night
Floated him on a raft of coconut fronds
context: As a boy Mau then learned the stars from chunks of coral laid out in the sand. To teach, navigators drew a circle in the sand for the sky, used stones for stars, shaped coconut fronds into a canoe, and laid single fronds for the swells. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Piailug

question: A flock of white terns beat out to sea at dawn, far from any island, as a Polynesian navigator watched from his canoe. The birds roosted on land each night, flew far out to fish at dawn and streamed back at dusk. To steer toward land, which way should the navigator turn the canoe?
answer: Back along the path the birds just flew out from
choices: Back along the path the birds just flew out from
Out toward the fishing grounds, following the birds
Straight ahead, keeping the birds dead in line
Wait for dusk, then trail the birds back to land
context: White terns (manu-o-Ku) fly up to about 120 miles out to sea to fish, turning a pinpoint island into a target hundreds of miles wide. The trick is the direction depends on the time: at DAWN the birds are leaving land, so land lies BEHIND them — you sail toward where they came FROM; at DUSK they are heading home, so you follow them. https://www.tetiaroasociety.org/biosphere-tetiaroa/white-tern

question: Mau Piailug steered the double-hulled canoe Hokule'a out of Hawaii in May 1976, bound for Tahiti over 2,500 miles of open Pacific, with no compass and no charts. After 34 days at sea the canoe sailed into Tahiti's harbour. Who came out to greet it on the shore?
answer: Half the island — about 17,000 people
choices: Half the island — about 17,000 people
A handful of colonial officials
A single welcoming chief
No one, the harbour was empty
context: On the 31st day Mau predicted land was near; the next day they sighted white terns, then the atoll Mataiva, reaching Tahiti on 4 June. Roughly 17,000 people — half of Tahiti's population — came down to greet the canoe. https://archive.hokulea.com/holokai/1976/ben_finney.html

question: A Marshall Islander lashed thin coconut ribs and cowrie shells into a delicate frame, with curving sticks showing how the ocean swells bend around his islands. What did the Marshall Islanders actually do with these stick charts when they went to sea?
answer: Studied them onshore but never took them to sea
choices: Studied them onshore but never took them to sea
Lashed them to the prow to steer by
Traded them to passing European ships
Burned them after each voyage as offerings
context: The Marshall Islands stick charts were memorization aids used onshore. The curving sticks showed how ocean swells bend and meet around islands; the cowrie shells marked the islands. The chart stayed home — the knowledge went to sea in the navigator's head. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: Thick clouds blacked out the sky over the open Pacific, and Mau Piailug of Satawal held his canoe's course by the ocean swells alone. He could tell eight different swell patterns apart at once, without stars or compass. How did Mau sense the swells?
answer: By the canoe's motion against his own body as he lay in the hull
choices: By the canoe's motion against his own body as he lay in the hull
By trailing his hand over the side to feel the water
By the sound the waves made striking the bow
By the spray's taste, salty from the open sea
context: Lying flat inside the hull, Mau read the canoe's roll, pitch, and yaw through his own body. A sudden change in roll meant the canoe had drifted off course. He could distinguish eight separate swell patterns at once. https://daily.jstor.org/pius-mau-piailug-master-navigator-of-micronesia/

question: The low coral atolls of the Tuamotus lay hidden below the horizon as a Polynesian navigator sailed toward them across the South Pacific. The atolls were flat rings of coral and easy to miss, but each one gave itself away in the sky before it showed on the horizon. What did the navigator watch for in the sky?
answer: A faint green tint thrown onto the clouds by the lagoon below
choices: A faint green tint thrown onto the clouds by the lagoon below
A ring of dark storm clouds circling the island
A bright halo around the moon at night
A column of smoke from the islanders' fires
context: The shallow lagoon of an atoll reflects a greenish glow onto the underside of the clouds above it. Sailing toward the Tuamotus, navigators watched for the green tint from the lagoon of Anaa atoll before the island itself was visible. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: James Cook, the British captain, sailed the Endeavour into the South Pacific in 1769 and stopped at the island of Raiatea. There he met Tupaia, a Polynesian priest and master navigator, and asked him about the ocean around them. From memory alone, with no writing and no instruments, Tupaia produced something that astonished Cook. What was it?
answer: A chart of about 130 islands, naming 74 of them
choices: A chart of about 130 islands, naming 74 of them
A logbook of his past voyages in writing
A wooden globe carved with the islands
A list of every star in the night sky
context: Tupaia drew Cook a chart covering about 130 islands within a 2,000-mile radius, naming 74 from memory. Even after Cook's Endeavour sailed all the way around New Zealand and on toward Indonesia, Tupaia could still point accurately back toward Tahiti the whole time. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupaia_(navigator)

question: Polynesian settlers loaded their double-hulled canoes for a voyage of thousands of miles across the Pacific to an empty new island, and they did not plan to survive on whatever they happened to find there. They packed what scholars now call a 'transported landscape,' everything a colony needs to plant a whole way of life. What did that cargo consist of?
answer: Live pigs, dogs, and chickens with taro, breadfruit, and coconut
choices: Live pigs, dogs, and chickens with taro, breadfruit, and coconut
Stone tools and weapons for conquest
Gold and shells to trade with whoever they found
Timber and rope to build a fort on landing
context: Settlers carried the animals and plants of life so a barren island could be turned into home. A large Tongan double canoe was reputed to carry up to 100 people along with this living cargo. https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1586/polynesian-navigation--settlement-of-the-pacific/  (Legend.)

question: A navigator's guiding star climbed too high to steer by in the night, so he switched to the next star of a sequence he had memorized, a 'star path,' and on through the night from star to star. The greatest Polynesian navigators carried whole star paths in their heads. How much did the greatest of them carry in their heads?
answer: Over 150 stars and the exact bearing of each
choices: Over 150 stars and the exact bearing of each
The single brightest star to follow all night
A dozen constellations and their shapes
The phases of the moon for a full year
context: A 'star path' is a memorized sequence of stars: as one climbs out of position, the navigator switches to the next. The greatest navigators carried over 150 stars and their bearings entirely in memory. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: Polynesian gardeners were already growing kumara, the sweet potato, by about AD 1200, centuries before the first European ships reached the Pacific. The sweet potato is not native to the Pacific at all: it grows wild on a coast far across the sea, strong evidence that Polynesian voyagers reached that coast and sailed home again. Where did the sweet potato originally come from?
answer: South America
choices: South America
Southeast Asia
West Africa
Australia
context: The sweet potato is native to South America, yet was grown across Polynesia from around AD 1200-1300 — long before Europeans arrived. It is strong evidence that Polynesian voyagers reached the Americas and sailed all the way back. https://phys.org/news/2024-09-unexpected-discovery-early-sweet-potato.html

question: A Polynesian navigator kept alert for te lapa far out in the deep ocean, where navigators said it could appear sometimes a hundred miles from any land. They said it could point a canoe toward islands no one could yet see. How did the navigators describe te lapa?
answer: Streaks of light darting toward land from under the water
choices: Streaks of light darting toward land from under the water
A wind that always blew in from the nearest shore
A taste of fresh water rising in the open sea
A low humming that came up through the hull
context: Legend, told as the navigators' own testimony: te lapa ('the flashing') is described as underwater light-flashes that dart toward land from below the surface, used to re-orient toward unseen islands. The phenomenon is still not fully explained by science. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: A Caroline Islands navigator on a voyage of hundreds of miles, with no clock and no speedometer, still had to know at every moment how far along he was. He kept track with a mental method called etak. Instead of seeing his canoe push forward through a still ocean, he held an upside-down picture in his mind. How did he see the scene?
answer: The canoe sits still while an unseen island slides backward past the stars
choices: The canoe sits still while an unseen island slides backward past the stars
The canoe races forward while the stars stay frozen above
The whole ocean tilts and pours the canoe toward land
The island sends out ripples the canoe rides inward
context: Etak (the word means 'refuge') has the navigator imagine the canoe motionless while a reference island slides backward, passing under one star bearing after another. By tracking how far the imaginary island has 'moved,' he always knows his progress — without ever measuring his own speed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etak_(navigation)

question: Nainoa Thompson, a young Hawaiian, spent years in the 1970s relearning the 'star compass' from the Micronesian master Mau Piailug, so he could guide the canoe Hokule'a himself. Polynesian navigators had once steered by it, but the knowledge had nearly died out under colonial rule. What was the star compass?
answer: A memorized map of where each star rises and sets around the horizon
choices: A memorized map of where each star rises and sets around the horizon
A carved wooden ring notched with the positions of the stars
A wide bowl of water that mirrored the night sky back up
A bundle of pointing sticks aimed at the brightest stars
context: The star compass is a mental map, not an object. The navigator memorizes the point on the horizon where each star rises and sets; in the Hawaiian version revived by Nainoa Thompson, the horizon is divided into 32 'houses' (11.25 degrees apart), and a star that rises in one house always sets in the matching house opposite. https://hokulea.com/polynesian-wayfinding/

question: Pliny the Younger, seventeen years old, stood on the shore of the Bay of Naples in AD 79 and watched Mount Vesuvius explode into the sky across the bay. Years later he described the huge dark cloud that rose over the mountain. What did he say it looked most like?
answer: An umbrella pine tree
choices: An umbrella pine tree
A giant stone tower
A coiled black serpent
A crashing ocean wave
context: Pliny the Younger wrote that the cloud 'more closely resembled a pine-tree than anything else, for what corresponded to the trunk was of great length and height, and then spread out into a number of branches' — the tall, flat-topped Italian stone pine. Source: Pliny the Younger, Letter 6.16.

question: Giuseppe Fiorelli found a clever way in 1863 to bring back into view the people Vesuvius had buried at Pompeii in AD 79. Their bodies had slowly rotted inside the ash, leaving empty spaces shaped like people. What did Fiorelli do?
answer: He poured liquid plaster into the hollows
choices: He poured liquid plaster into the hollows
He carefully dug out their preserved bones
He photographed the bodies before they decayed
He wrapped the remains in cloth bandages
context: Fiorelli poured plaster of Paris into each cavity, let it harden, then chipped away the surrounding ash — recovering the exact final shape of the person, down to faces, folds of clothing, and dying positions. The famous 'casts' of Pompeii are plaster, not bone. Source: Giuseppe Fiorelli; historyskills.com.

question: A snarling black dog on a chain glared up from a floor mosaic at the front door of Pompeii's House of the Tragic Poet, with two Latin words tiled between its paws. What do those words, cave canem, mean?
answer: Beware of the Dog
choices: Beware of the Dog
Welcome to Our Home
Wine Sold Here
Closed for the Holiday
context: CAVE CANEM — 'Beware of the Dog' — was laid in mosaic tiles at the doorway, excavated in 1824. Source: history.com; Wikipedia, House of the Tragic Poet.

question: Its owners fled the eruption of Vesuvius and left their guard dog tied up at Pompeii's House of Orpheus. As the ash kept rising, the dog fought to climb above it, and its cast is one of the most famous ever made at Pompeii. What does the cast show the dog frozen in the act of doing?
answer: Twisting onto its back straining against its collar
choices: Twisting onto its back straining against its collar
Curled up asleep beside the front door
Leaping clear over the garden wall
Calmly guarding a bowl of food
context: Found in 1874, the dog had climbed atop the deepening ash and twisted onto its back with legs in the air, straining against the bronze ring on its collar — the cast froze it in that exact pose, and the bronze ring is still on the collar. Source: seepompeii.com; pompeiiinpictures.com.

question: Archaeologists dug into a bakery at Pompeii almost 2,000 years after Mount Vesuvius buried the city in AD 79, and found an oven sealed shut by the disaster. Inside were about 80 round loaves left mid-bake. What had Vesuvius's heat done to the bread?
answer: Baked it black and rock-hard like charcoal
choices: Baked it black and rock-hard like charcoal
Turned it to fine grey powder
Left it soft and perfectly fresh
Melted it into a sticky paste
context: The carbonized loaves survive, baked black and stone-hard. The round flat loaf (panis quadratus) was scored into 8 wedges; one surviving loaf is even stamped 'Celer, slave of Quintus Granius Verus' — the baker's mark. Source: historyandarchaeologyonline.com.

question: Romans in Pompeii crossed their streets, deep with mud and water, on tall, flat stepping stones, keeping their feet out of the muck. The stones stood with gaps between them, and the gaps let one particular thing pass straight through. What were the gaps sized to let through?
answer: The wheels of carts and chariots
choices: The wheels of carts and chariots
Herds of grazing sheep
Streams of rainwater downhill
Marching ranks of soldiers
context: The gaps were spaced so cart and chariot wheels rolled straight between the stones. Generations of wheels carved ruts five to ten inches deep into the paving, and Pompeii has about twenty times more crossing stones than any other known Roman city. Source: world-archaeology.com.

question: Tacitus, a historian, received two letters from Pliny the Younger about 25 years after Pliny had watched Vesuvius erupt from across the bay as a teenager. In them Pliny told what he had seen and what became of Pliny the Elder, his uncle. What makes those two letters so prized?
answer: They are the only eyewitness account that survives
choices: They are the only eyewitness account that survives
They are the only letters of Pliny that survive
They name every town the eruption destroyed
They were copied into Rome's imperial archive
context: Pliny the Younger's Letters 6.16 and 6.20 to Tacitus are the sole surviving eyewitness record of the disaster — the named primary source for the whole event. Source: Pliny the Younger, Letters 6.16 and 6.20; ancientworldmagazine.com.

question: Pliny the Elder was leading the Roman fleet across the bay when Vesuvius erupted, and a message reached him from a woman named Rectina, begging for rescue. Instead of fleeing, he ordered his ships to sail straight toward the burning mountain. According to his nephew, what did Pliny tell his helmsman as he gave the order?
answer: 'Fortune favours the bold'
choices: 'Fortune favours the bold'
'All is now lost'
'Let the gods decide'
'Save yourselves and run'
context: 'Fortes Fortuna iuvat' — 'Fortune favours the bold; try to reach Pomponianus.' Pliny the Elder sailed across the bay to Stabiae to rescue his trapped friend Pomponianus, where he later died. Source: Pliny the Younger, Letter 6.16.

question: Burning pumice stones were raining out of the sky onto the seaside town of Stabiae when Pliny the Elder, the Roman admiral, reached it in AD 79. He had sailed his warships across the Bay of Naples toward the eruption to rescue survivors. To shield their heads as they walked out into the falling rock, what did Pliny and his companions tie on?
answer: Pillows fastened down with cloths
choices: Pillows fastened down with cloths
Bronze army helmets
Wooden shields held overhead
Wet leather hoods
context: 'They placed pillows on their heads and secured them with cloths, as a precaution against the falling stones.' Source: Pliny the Younger, Letter 6.16.

question: A Pompeian stepped up to an L-shaped marble counter on the street, its top set with big round holes and terracotta jars sunk down into them. More than 80 shops with counters like it lined the streets of Pompeii, and they were called thermopolia. What were these shops for?
answer: Selling hot food and wine to go
choices: Selling hot food and wine to go
Storing the town's tax records
Washing and dyeing wool
Renting out chariots and horses
context: Thermopolia were ancient fast-food bars — the round counter holes held jars of hot food and wine, and Romans grabbed quick meals of stewed legumes, meat skewers, and wine standing at the counter, like a modern takeaway shop. Source: contexttravel.com.

question: A young man lay on a wooden bed at Herculaneum, near Pompeii, when a blast of gas heated his town past 500 degrees and killed him in an instant. Pier Paolo Petrone's team opened his skull in 2020 and found something never seen in any other human remains, formed from his own brain by the heat. What had the heat turned his brain into?
answer: Black glass, like obsidian
choices: Black glass, like obsidian
Solid white salt crystals
A lump of pure gold
Fine drifting ash
context: The brain was heated above roughly 510 °C, then cooled so fast it vitrified into glass — the only known case of a vitrified human brain, published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Source: NEJM 2020; CNN.

question: Luke Farritor, a 21-year-old student, pulled out the first whole word recovered from an unopened Herculaneum scroll in 2023. The eruption had charred the library's 1,800 papyrus scrolls into black lumps that crumble if anyone tries to unroll them, and for 250 years they kept their secrets, until a $1 million contest, the Vesuvius Challenge, set students to search CT scans for ink. What did his first word mean?
answer: Purple
choices: Purple
Soldier
River
Silence
context: Farritor decoded the Greek word 'porphyras' — 'purple' — from an unopened scroll using AI to detect ink traces in CT scans; a team then recovered over 2,000 letters of ancient Greek philosophy. Source: scrollprize.org; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: Diggers at Pompeii found a charcoal note scratched with an October date, a clue against the eruption's traditional date of 24 August, AD 79. That summer date comes only from a copied version of Pliny's letter. What else did they find that points to a colder season?
answer: Carbonized fruit and heavy clothing on the victims
choices: Carbonized fruit and heavy clothing on the victims
Wine jars sealed for the new vintage
Olive presses left full mid-pressing
Shutters closed against the cold
context: Carbonized autumn fruit, the heavy clothing worn by victims, and charcoal heaters set up in houses all point to a colder season — so many scholars now argue for October. The August date survives only through Pliny's letter. Source: getty.edu; National Geographic.

question: Spanish colonists minted the silver of Cerro Rico, 'the rich hill' above Potosi, high in the Bolivian Andes, into a big coin that spread onto every continent, the first truly global money. What was this famous Spanish silver coin nicknamed?
answer: Pieces of eight
choices: Pieces of eight
Crowns of Castile
Wheels of silver
Lions of Madrid
context: The eight-real Spanish dollar, minted from Potosí silver, became the first global currency. The modern dollar sign ($) probably descends from the peso symbol stamped on those very coins. Sources: sites.google.com/site/100objectsbritishmuseum (British Museum, pieces of eight); ncvgrading.com/the-piece-of-eight/.

question: Potosi's people put a proud boast into their city's coat of arms. Their boomtown grew on the freezing slopes of Cerro Rico, the richest silver hill ever found, and at its height it held up to 160,000 people. What did the coat of arms declare Potosi to be?
answer: Treasure of the world, king of the mountains, envy of kings
choices: Treasure of the world, king of the mountains, envy of kings
First daughter of Spain, jewel of the southern sea
Guardian of the Andes, shield of the Inca
Gate of the Pacific, market of two oceans
context: Potosí's coat of arms boasted in words: 'I am rich Potosí, treasure of the world, king of the mountains, envy of kings.' Sources: sldinfo.com/2020/12/potosi-and-its-silver-the-beginnings-of-globalization/; globaltrademag.com/as-rich-as-potosi/.

question: Miguel de Cervantes, the author of Don Quixote, put a Spanish saying about great wealth into his writing around 1615, and Spaniards still use it whenever something is worth a fortune. Which is the real saying Cervantes helped make famous?
answer: Vale un Potosí (worth a Potosí)
choices: Vale un Potosí (worth a Potosí)
Rico como el Perú (rich as Peru)
El oro del rey (the king's gold)
La plata del cielo (silver from heaven)
context: 'Vale un Potosí' — 'it's worth a Potosí' — still means 'worth a fortune' in Spanish, the silver mountain's name standing in for boundless wealth. Sources: thenaturalsapphirecompany.com/education/.../potosi/; context.reverso.net (vale un Potosí).

question: Francisco de Toledo, the Spanish viceroy, made native Andean men work the silver mountain of Cerro Rico in shifts from 1573. Villages across sixteen provinces of Peru had to send their share of men, and some 13,500 laboured on the mountain at any one time; many died in cave-ins and of mercury poisoning in the refineries. What was this hated forced-labour draft called?
answer: The mita
choices: The mita
The encomienda
The repartimiento
The corvée
context: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo's 1573 decree established the mita; the Spanish took the name from the Inca word mit'a, meaning 'a turn.' Source: dokumen.pub/potosi-the-silver-city... ; andeanroadperu.com/mita-system....

question: A miner climbed down into the shafts of Cerro Rico, where cave-ins and the mercury of the refineries killed Indigenous and African workers in such numbers that some estimates put the dead in the millions over the colonial centuries. The silver mountain earned a grim nickname for what it did to its workers. What was the mountain called?
answer: The mountain that eats men
choices: The mountain that eats men
The widow's hill
The graveyard peak
The devil's furnace
context: The death toll from the mines and mercury amalgamation was so staggering that Cerro Rico became known as 'the mountain that eats men.' Estimate is medium-confidence. Sources: sciencedirect.com/.../S2214790X16300764; realsafetyai.org/.../potosi-silver-mercury-mining.

question: Spanish crews sailed galleons heavy with Potosi's silver across the Pacific between Acapulco and Manila each year for two and a half centuries, pouring it into Asian markets. Scholars estimate that between a third and a half of all New World silver ended up in the taxes and trade of one country. Which country?
answer: China
choices: China
India
Persia
The Ottoman Empire
context: Carried on the Manila galleons (1565–1815), between one-third and one-half of all New World silver ended up in China, where it was absorbed for taxes and trade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_silver_trade...; bulliontradingllc.com/blog/spanish-silver-fleets/.

question: Alexander Dubcek eased censorship in Communist Czechoslovakia in 1968 and offered what he called socialism with a human face, until Soviet and Warsaw Pact tanks rolled in that August to crush his reforms. With no army fighting back, ordinary Czechs and Slovaks took on the tank columns without a single weapon. How did they hold up the columns?
answer: They repainted the road signs so the tank columns got lost
choices: They repainted the road signs so the tank columns got lost
They flooded the streets to bog the tank columns down
They blocked the bridges so the tank columns turned back
They cut the power so the tank columns drove blind
context: Czechs and Slovaks tore down house numbers and repainted road signs to confuse the invaders -- famously leaving the sign for 'Moscow' pointing the soldiers back the way they came. They argued with the troops in the streets rather than firing on them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact_invasion_of_Czechoslovakia.

question: Jan Palach, a Charles University student of twenty, walked to the top of Prague's Wenceslas Square in January 1969, poured petrol over himself and set himself on fire in protest against the Soviet occupation. He left a farewell letter. What name did he sign himself?
answer: "Torch No. 1"
choices: "Torch No. 1"
"The Last Czech"
"Free Prague"
"Student Zero"
context: Palach signed his protest letter 'Torch No. 1' and claimed a secret group of volunteers would keep burning themselves until censorship ended -- though investigators found that group never existed; the threat was meant to wake the nation. Burned over about 85% of his body, he died three days later on Jan 19, 1969. His self-immolation helped forge the dissident playwright Vaclav Havel, who would lead the 1989 Velvet Revolution. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Palach; english.radio.cz/czech-martyr-jan-palachs-enduring-legacy.

question: Archaeologists dug down around about 150 of the giant stone moai on remote Easter Island, statues the Rapa Nui people carved centuries ago. Tourists nicknamed them 'the heads,' because only the heads stuck out of the grassy slopes. What did the diggers find under the soil?
answer: Full bodies buried up to the shoulders
choices: Full bodies buried up to the shoulders
Tunnels linking the statues underground
Rows of smaller statues beneath them
The carvers' stone tools left behind
context: The Easter Island 'heads' (moai) actually have full torsos and arms, buried over centuries by erosion. From 2010 Jo Anne Van Tilburg's Easter Island Statue Project excavated the hidden bodies and found crisp carvings that had been protected underground while the exposed faces above weathered smooth. Source: https://www.livescience.com/20580-easter-island-heads-bodies.html ; https://www.eisp.org/ (Easter Island Statue Project).

question: Workers digging beneath Mexico City in 1978 struck a huge carved stone disk, and the find led archaeologists to unearth the buried Aztec Templo Mayor. The disk showed the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui at one violent moment of a myth in which her own brother, the sun god Huitzilopochtli, turned on her. What did the stone show?
answer: Her body decapitated and hacked into pieces
choices: Her body decapitated and hacked into pieces
Her body chained to the face of the moon
Her body turned to stone where she stood
Her body cast into the burning underworld
context: Coyolxauhqui ('Bells-Her-Cheeks') is shown beheaded and dismembered, her head, arms, and legs hacked off and scattered after Huitzilopochtli defeats her. The workers struck the monolith on February 21, 1978, which triggered the full excavation of the Templo Mayor at the heart of old Tenochtitlan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coyolxauhqui_Stone ; https://smarthistory.org/templo-mayor-at-tenochtitlan-the-coyolxauhqui-stone-and-an-olmec-mask/.

question: Portuguese captains turned back again and again from Cape Bojador, a low cape on the West African coast, sure that the waters beyond it boiled and hid monsters at the edge of the world. Fourteen expeditions reached the dread cape and fled home without rounding it. What finally happened in 1434?
answer: A Portuguese captain sailed past it and returned alive
choices: A Portuguese captain sailed past it and returned alive
The Pope forbade any further attempts
An earthquake destroyed the cape
Arab traders drew a map of what lay beyond
context: Cape Bojador was a low, unremarkable headland, but the legend of boiling seas and monsters beyond it stopped fourteen expeditions cold. The 'edge of the world' turned out to be just more coastline. (legend — the boiling seas and monsters were sailors' belief, not fact) Source: https://fathomsdeepbeyond.substack.com/p/beyond-the-cape-of-fear

question: Prince Henry of Portugal stayed home while his captains sailed down the coast of Africa, planning the voyages and taking a 20% cut of their profits, though the world calls him Henry the Navigator. Stories still say he ran a great navigation school at Sagres that trained Portugal's captains. What is the truth about that Sagres school?
answer: It never existed — the story was invented a century after he died
choices: It never existed — the story was invented a century after he died
It trained only mapmakers, never actual sea captains
It was secretly run by his brother, not by Henry
It burned down before a single voyage set sail
context: The famous 'navigation school at Sagres' is a myth invented in the 1600s, long after Henry's death — Sagres isn't even a usable port, and the real expeditions sailed out of Lagos. Henry organized the Age of Exploration from a chair, paying for voyages and taking his 20% cut. Source: https://kids.kiddle.co/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator

question: A Portuguese captain heading home from the African coast found that north of the equator the wind and current shoved his coast-hugging ship the wrong way; sailing out had been the easy part. The navigators beat the problem with a trick they named the volta do mar, 'the turn of the sea.' How did a captain use the volta do mar to get home?
answer: Sail boldly out into the open Atlantic, loop northwest to catch westerly winds, then turn east for home
choices: Sail boldly out into the open Atlantic, loop northwest to catch westerly winds, then turn east for home
Hug the coastline north, then cut inland and portage the ship past the worst of the contrary current
Run far south first to gather speed, then loop back along the steady coastal trade winds to the north
Wait at anchor for the seasonal winds to reverse, then ride the new tailwind straight up the coast
context: The volta do mar meant steering AWAY from home to get home: out into the open ocean, looping northwest until you hit the westerlies, then riding them east. Gil Eanes used the same out-to-sea logic to slip past Cape Bojador's reefs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_do_mar

question: Early Portuguese navigators found their latitude by the Pole Star: a captain sailed until the star stood at the same height it had at his home port, then turned and ran straight home. But as the Portuguese pushed south down Africa, the trick stopped working near the equator. What had gone wrong, forcing them to measure the sun instead?
answer: The Pole Star had sunk below the horizon and vanished from view
choices: The Pole Star had sunk below the horizon and vanished from view
The Pole Star had grown too dim to see clearly
The Pole Star had drifted to a new spot in the sky
The Pole Star had been hidden by the southern haze
context: The Pole-Star trick only works in the north. Crossing toward the equator, the star dropped below the horizon and disappeared. So in 1485 the Portuguese assembled a navigator, a mathematician and an astronomer to build the first daily tables of the sun's height — the sun became the new compass for southern seas. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner's_astrolabe

question: Gil Eanes sailed past Cape Bojador, below the Canary Islands, in 1434 and found calm water there, though sailors had sworn that the sea beyond it boiled and that no ship rounding it would ever come home. To prove to doubters that he had set foot beyond the cape, he carried something back. What did he bring home as proof?
answer: Wild roses he had picked there
choices: Wild roses he had picked there
A chunk of the cape's red rock
A jar of the strange dark seawater
A feather from an unknown bird
context: Gil Eanes, born in Lagos, beat Cape Bojador by using the volta do mar, swinging away from the coast into open sea instead of hugging the shore. He reported the water beyond was 'as easy to sail in as the waters at home' and brought back the little desert flowers the Portuguese called Rosa de Santa Maria, 'St. Mary's roses' (rosemary-like plants), as proof he had set foot on land past the cape. A fistful of flowers showed that the terrifying edge of the world was nothing but ordinary coastline. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Eanes; worldhistory.org/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator; https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/gil-eannes-passes-point-no-return-cape-bojador-and-inaugurates-new-era-exploration

question: Prince Henry's shipwrights built a small, shallow vessel, the caravel, so that his captains could get home against the winds off Africa. Going out, the wind carried a ship easily down the coast; coming back, it blew straight against her.
