answer: She refused, swearing they could pull every vein from her body before she would confess
choices: She refused, swearing they could pull every vein from her body before she would confess
She broke down at once and confessed to everything they named
She fainted at the sight and had to be carried back to her cell
She begged the judges to summon her son Johannes to save her
context: Katharina Kepler was jailed for 405 days (arrested August 7, 1620). At a July 1621 hearing the executioner used the 'territio verbalis,' showing her the instruments, and she defied them, saying they could pull every vein from her body and she would still have nothing to confess. Source: Wikipedia, 'Katharina Kepler'; APS News, 'August 1620: Kepler's Mother Imprisoned for Witchcraft.'

question: Isaac Asimov and Carl Sagan each gave a bold title to the Somnium, a tale Johannes Kepler wrote of a voyage to the Moon. Long before anyone flew, Kepler had worked out how the Earth would look hanging in the Moon's sky. What did Asimov and Sagan call the Somnium?
answer: The first work of science fiction
choices: The first work of science fiction
The first map of the Moon
The first textbook of astronomy
The first book of fairy tales
context: Somnium ('The Dream', written about 1608, published after Kepler's death in 1634) is often called the first science-fiction story. Its witch-mother character resembled Kepler's own mother Katharina, and Kepler believed a leaked draft helped spark the real witchcraft rumors against her. Source: Wikipedia, 'Somnium (novel)'; Medium, 'Somnium: The forgotten father of Science Fiction.'

question: Johannes Kepler hit on his first grand idea about the heavens in 1596, and it was beautiful and wrong. He was sure he had found the very plan God used to space the planets, by nesting five perfect solid shapes one inside another like Russian dolls. What did Kepler nest together?
answer: The five Platonic solids, like the cube and pyramid
choices: The five Platonic solids, like the cube and pyramid
The five known planets, painted on glass globes
The five rings he imagined around the Sun
The five metals the ancients tied to the planets
context: In Mysterium Cosmographicum (1596) Kepler nested the five Platonic solids to explain why there were exactly six planets and why their orbits were spaced as they are. The model was elegant but false, an early sign of his lifelong faith that God built the cosmos on geometry. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Johannes Kepler'; Wikipedia, 'Mysterium Cosmographicum.'

question: Galileo Galilei argued that true science and true faith could never really clash, because God had written two books: Scripture, and the universe itself. That second book of nature, Galileo said, was written in one particular language. In what language did Galileo say the book of nature is written?
answer: The language of mathematics
choices: The language of mathematics
The language of the angels
Plain Latin and Greek
The language of music
context: Galileo held that the 'grand book of the universe is written in the language of mathematics' (The Assayer), laying out the 'two books' idea in his Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina. Source: The Renaissance Mathematicus, 'The Book of Nature...'; Physics World, 'The book of nature'; Galileo's Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina.

question: Isaac Newton explained the motion of the planets and comets with his laws of gravity in his masterwork the Principia. Yet he chose to end the 1713 edition not with an equation but with a claim about where 'this most beautiful system of the sun, planets, and comets' came from. According to Newton, such a system could only have proceeded from what?
answer: The counsel of an intelligent and powerful Being
choices: The counsel of an intelligent and powerful Being
The blind churning of endless chance
The eternal spinning of the distant stars
A vast invisible machine slowly winding down
context: Newton ended the Principia's General Scholium (1713) arguing that the cosmos 'could only proceed from the counsel and dominion of an intelligent and powerful Being.' He spent as much effort on theology and Scripture as on physics. Source: Vatican Observatory, 'Isaac Newton, God and the Universe in the General Scholium'; Newton Project, Oxford.

question: Oskar Schindler, a German businessman in the Nazi Party for profit, took over a Krakow factory in 1939 and staffed it with Jewish workers from the ghetto. The army rated it 'war-essential,' and that shielded them from deportation. What did the factory mostly make?
answer: Enamel pots and pans for the army
choices: Enamel pots and pans for the army
Leather boots for the army
Wool uniforms for the army
Glass bottles for the army
context: Schindler's Deutsche Emailwarenfabrik, nicknamed 'Emalia,' made enamelware (pots and pans, and later munitions) for the German military. He staffed it with Jewish forced laborers and used its 'war-essential' status as the shield that let him protect them. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/oskar-schindler.

question: Nazi officials in Budapest honoured a blue-and-gold paper bearing Sweden's three crowns in 1944, so official did it look. Raoul Wallenberg, the young diplomat Sweden had posted there, had designed it, and by one account it saved about 20,000 Jews. What was it?
answer: A protective passport called the Schutzpass
choices: A protective passport called the Schutzpass
A forged German army exit visa
A Red Cross hospital release letter
A church baptismal certificate
context: Recruited by the American War Refugee Board, Wallenberg designed the 'Schutzpass' to look official enough that Nazi officials respected it; on its strength alone roughly 20,000 Jews were saved. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/raoul-wallenberg-and-the-rescue-of-jews-in-budapest.

question: Oskar Schindler's Jewish workers melted down a prisoner's gold dental crown and made it into a ring for him at the war's end, when his Nazi ties forced him to flee the Allies. They had the ring engraved in Hebrew with a single line from the Talmud. What did it say?
answer: Whoever saves one life saves the world entire
choices: Whoever saves one life saves the world entire
Blessed is the one who shelters the stranger
Let justice flow down like rivers of water
Remember the days of old, and do not forget
context: The ring, made from a survivor's own gold crown, carried the Talmudic line 'Whoever saves one life saves the world entire.' Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia + SparkNotes, sparknotes.com/film/schindlerslist/quotes/page/5.

question: Raoul Wallenberg rented some thirty-two buildings in Budapest, declared each one Swedish soil and hid nearly ten thousand people inside. What did he do outside the buildings to sell the bluff that each was a piece of neutral Sweden?
answer: Flew huge Swedish flags and hung signs like 'The Swedish Library'
choices: Flew huge Swedish flags and hung signs like 'The Swedish Library'
Stationed armed Swedish soldiers at every door
Walled off the streets around them with barbed wire
Repainted them all in Sweden's blue and yellow colors
context: Wallenberg draped the houses with giant Swedish flags and official-sounding signs ('The Swedish Library' and the like) and declared them off-limits Swedish soil; these 'safe houses' sheltered nearly 10,000 people. Source: Raoul Wallenberg, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Wallenberg.

question: German soldiers cleared out Krakow's walled ghetto by night on 13 March 1943, killing thousands on the streets and shipping the rest to the death camps. Oskar Schindler had given the Jewish workers at his factory one order beforehand, and it kept them out of reach. What had he told them to do?
answer: Stay overnight at the factory instead of going back to the ghetto
choices: Stay overnight at the factory instead of going back to the ghetto
Slip out of the city and hide in the surrounding forests
Report to the train station and wait for transfer papers
Burn their identity badges and pose as Polish gentiles
context: By keeping his workers at the factory overnight rather than letting them return to the ghetto, Schindler kept them out of reach during the lethal liquidation. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/oskar-schindler.

question: Oskar Schindler spent his whole fortune on bribes and on food for his Jewish workers, and he was poor when he died in 1974. He had asked to be buried in a place where no other one-time Nazi Party member lies in honour. Where is his grave?
answer: On Mount Zion in Jerusalem
choices: On Mount Zion in Jerusalem
On the grounds of the Auschwitz memorial
In a war-heroes cemetery in Germany
In the old Jewish cemetery of Krakow
context: Schindler asked to be buried in Jerusalem; his tomb on Mount Zion makes him the only former member of the Nazi Party laid to rest there in honor. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia + See The Holy Land, seetheholyland.net/schindlers-grave.

question: Arrow Cross gunmen fired over Raoul Wallenberg's head as he worked to stop trains crammed with Budapest's Jews from rolling toward Auschwitz. He got his protective passes into the prisoners' hands anyway, then walked dozens of them off the train. How did he deliver the passes?
answer: He climbed onto the boxcar roofs and handed them down through the doors
choices: He climbed onto the boxcar roofs and handed them down through the doors
He bribed the train guards to pass them out car by car
He hid them inside food parcels tossed onto the platform
He mailed them ahead to the camp's receiving office
context: By his driver Sandor Ardai's account, Wallenberg clambered onto the roofs of the boxcars and passed the documents down through the openings while marksmen fired over his head, then walked dozens of pass-holders off the train. Source: Raoul Wallenberg, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Wallenberg.

question: Emilie Schindler refused to let the SS send the survivors on to die when two frozen cattle cars from a sub-camp of Auschwitz reached her husband's factory at Brunnlitz in January 1945. About a dozen people inside were already dead. What did she do for the roughly 100 still alive?
answer: Had the iced-over doors cut open with a soldering iron and nursed the frostbitten survivors back to life
choices: Had the iced-over doors cut open with a soldering iron and nursed the frostbitten survivors back to life
Quietly hid them among the registered factory workers under fake names
Drove them by truck across the border to a neutral country at night
Paid the SS guards to record them as already dead and gone
context: Emilie Schindler had a factory engineer cut the ice-locked doors open with a soldering iron and personally nursed about 100 frostbitten survivors, rather than let the SS deport them to their deaths. Source: Brunnlitz labor camp, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%BCnnlitz_labor_camp + USHMM.

question: Itzhak Stern and Mietek Pemper faked the record books for Oskar Schindler after he moved his factory and workers to Brunnlitz late in 1944. On paper the plant was turning out shells for the war, which kept its workers classed as essential. What was the truth about its real output?
answer: It barely produced a single usable shell the whole time
choices: It barely produced a single usable shell the whole time
It quietly redirected its shells to anti-Nazi partisans
It met its quota but shipped the shells out defective
It produced nothing but melted the metal down for bribes
context: The faked figures hid the fact that Brunnlitz barely turned out one usable shell; the sham kept the prisoners classified as essential war workers and therefore alive. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/oskar-schindler.

question: Raoul Wallenberg got a message through to General Gerhard Schmidhuber, the German commander, by way of Pal Szalai, an officer of the Arrow Cross, in January 1945. The SS planned to dynamite the Budapest ghetto and murder the roughly 70,000 Jews trapped inside, and after Wallenberg's warning the massacre was called off. What threat did he send?
answer: That he would personally see the general hanged as a war criminal
choices: That he would personally see the general hanged as a war criminal
That Sweden would immediately declare war on Germany
That Soviet tanks were already inside the city's edge
That he would pay the general a fortune in Swedish gold
context: Through the Arrow Cross officer Pal Szalai, Wallenberg warned General Schmidhuber that he would personally ensure he was hanged as a war criminal if the ghetto was destroyed; the planned slaughter of about 70,000 people was abandoned. Source: Raoul Wallenberg, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Wallenberg.

question: Oskar Schindler kept more than a thousand Jewish workers alive through the war in his Krakow factory, and after it they raised families of their own. By the 1990s their living descendants numbered over six thousand. Whom had they come to outnumber?
answer: All the Jews still living in the whole of Poland
choices: All the Jews still living in the whole of Poland
All the Jews still living in the city of Krakow
All the survivors of the Plaszow camp combined
All of Schindler's original factory workers combined
context: By the 1990s there were more than 6,000 descendants of the Schindlerjuden alive, more than the fewer than 4,000 Jews left living in all of Poland. Source: Schindlerjuden, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schindlerjuden.

question: Soviet counter-intelligence men seized Raoul Wallenberg as a suspected spy on 17 January 1945, days after the Budapest ghetto was spared. His last recorded words named where he was going: 'I'm going to Malinovsky's... whether as a guest or prisoner I do not know yet.' What became of him after that?
answer: He vanished into the Soviet prison system and was never seen free again
choices: He vanished into the Soviet prison system and was never seen free again
He was quietly released and lived out his life back in Sweden
He was executed by the retreating SS within the week
He was traded back to Sweden in a prisoner exchange
context: The man who saved a hundred thousand people from one totalitarian regime disappeared into another. The Soviets later claimed he died in Lubyanka prison in 1947, but eyewitnesses reported seeing him alive years afterward, and Sweden did not formally declare him dead until 2016, 71 years after he vanished. Source: USHMM + Raoul Wallenberg, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Wallenberg.

question: Oskar Schindler typed out his famous list himself on screen, in the film Schindler's List. Historians say the real list was drawn up by someone else, redrawn several times, with some prisoners bribing their way onto it. Who really compiled it?
answer: A Jewish SS clerk named Marcel Goldberg
choices: A Jewish SS clerk named Marcel Goldberg
Schindler's accountant Itzhak Stern alone
The Plaszow commandant Amon Goeth
A committee of the Krakow Jewish council
context: The real list was compiled by Marcel Goldberg, a Jewish clerk working for the SS, not hand-typed by Schindler as the movie dramatizes; the lists were redrawn more than once and some names were bought. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/oskar-schindler.

question: Tariq ibn Ziyad, a Berber general, brought about seven thousand men across from Africa in the spring of 711 and landed at Spain's southern tip. His troops named the place Jabal Tariq, Tariq's Mountain, and over the centuries the Arabic name wore down into another. What is the place called today?
answer: Gibraltar
choices: Gibraltar
Granada
Constantinople
Damascus
context: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the strait with about 7,000 men in spring 711. 'Jabal Tariq' wore down over centuries into 'Gibraltar' — the rock still carries the name of the general who landed there. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariq_ibn_Ziyad

question: Khalid ibn al-Walid led an Arab army against a much bigger Byzantine army at the Yarmuk River in August 636. A blinding sandstorm blew straight into the Byzantines' faces, their line broke, and Khalid's men drove them back into the steep Wadi al-Ruqqad ravine. What happened to them there?
answer: They plunged off the cliffs onto the rocks below
choices: They plunged off the cliffs onto the rocks below
They surrendered and were marched to Damascus
They regrouped and counterattacked at dawn
They escaped across the river by boat
context: A blinding sandstorm blew into the Byzantines' faces; when they broke, they were driven into the steep Wadi al-Ruqqad ravine, where some plunged off the cliffs and others were smashed on the rocks of the river below. The defeat ended Byzantine rule in Syria forever. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Yarmuk

question: Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi crossed the Pyrenees into Gaul with his army in 732 and burned Bordeaux. Near Tours the leader of the defenders held a solid wall of foot soldiers against charge after charge of the emir's horsemen, and the emir died there. Who held that line?
answer: Charles Martel
choices: Charles Martel
Tariq ibn Ziyad
King Roderic
Khalid ibn al-Walid
context: Charles Martel held a solid infantry phalanx against repeated cavalry charges near Tours on 10 October 732. Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was killed, and the northward expansion into Europe was turned back at its very edge. Source: https://www.historyhit.com/day-battle-tours/

question: A serf fled his lord and slipped in through the gate of a chartered German town, and there he stayed for a year and a day. Germans summed up what that stay did for him in a proverb of three words. What did the proverb say?
answer: Town air makes you free
choices: Town air makes you free
Town air makes you rich
Town air makes you holy
Town air makes you wise
context: "Stadtluft macht frei" - "town air makes you free." An unfree serf who lived in a chartered town for a year and a day could no longer be reclaimed by his lord and became a free man. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadtluft_macht_frei

question: A boy of about twelve walked into a medieval smithy as an apprentice, and in time he earned wages as a journeyman. To reach the top rank of his guild, he had to make one flawless example of his trade for its senior men to judge. What was that example called?
answer: His masterpiece
choices: His masterpiece
His warrant
His indenture
His tribute
context: The French term was chef d'oeuvre. The judged trial-piece is exactly where the modern word 'masterpiece' comes from - and if the masters rejected it, the man could stay a journeyman for life. Sources: https://news.artnet.com/art-world/art-bites-medieval-masterpiece-2437859 ; https://brewminate.com/the-medieval-guild-apprentice-journeyman-and-master/

question: Bremen's townsmen set up a stone giant in their market square in 1404, more than ten metres tall, the largest free-standing statue of the German Middle Ages. He was one of Charlemagne's knights, with a drawn sword in his grip, and many German market towns raised such a figure as their boast that they were free and ran their own market. Which knight stood guard?
answer: Roland
choices: Roland
Lancelot
Siegfried
Galahad
context: Roland was a paladin of Charlemagne; a stone Roland with a drawn sword in the square signalled a town's freedom and market rights. Bremen's 10.21-metre Roland of 1404 is the largest free-standing statue of the German Middle Ages. Source: https://www.welterbe.bremen.de/discover/roland-bremen-s-symbol-of-freedom-21305

question: Older traders at Bryggen, the Hanseatic wharf in Bergen, Norway, tied a rope around a teenage trainee, threw him into the harbour three times and clubbed him with sticks each time his head came up. What was the point of an ordeal this savage?
answer: To toughen the boys for the hard life of merchant trade
choices: To toughen the boys for the hard life of merchant trade
To choose the guild's next leader
To punish debts owed to older traders
To ask blessings from the sea gods
context: The Bergen Games were the Water Games (the harbour beating described here), the Smoke Games (boys hung over a smoky fire to choke while being quizzed), and the Flogging Games (keel-hauling - dragging a boy by rope under a ship's hull). Source: https://thehiddennorth.com/the-most-haunted-places-in-bergen/

question: Each townsman of a medieval town swore one oath, and with that single act the town became a commune, a body in law that could own property and make its own laws for itself. What oath did each man swear?
answer: A sworn oath of mutual defense to each other
choices: A sworn oath of mutual defense to each other
A sworn oath of obedience to their lord
A sworn oath of fealty to the bishop
A sworn oath of homage to the king
context: The commune was born from a sworn mutual oath of defense among equals - the opposite of a vassal's oath of obedience to a lord above him. That horizontal oath made the town a legal body that could own property and make laws. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_commune

question: Merchants and craftsmen of a town in the medieval Holy Roman Empire bought themselves a charter of liberties: the right to hold their own markets, run their own courts and tax themselves. Instead of their resentful local lord, they usually paid a mightier ruler above him. Who usually received the payment?
answer: The king or emperor
choices: The king or emperor
The pope in Rome
The abbot of the nearest monastery
The richest guild in the town
context: Towns frequently purchased their charter of liberties not from the resentful local lord but from the king or emperor over his head - using the higher power to escape the lower one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_commune

question: The Kwantung Army's officers seized all of Manchuria, China's vast north-east, after September 1931 and declared it an independent country, Manchukuo, while keeping the real power in their own hands. They still needed a famous face on the throne. Whom did they install as its puppet emperor?
answer: Puyi, the last emperor of China, who had been deposed as a small child
choices: Puyi, the last emperor of China, who had been deposed as a small child
Hirohito, the reigning emperor of Japan, sent to rule from abroad
Chiang Kai-shek, the Chinese general who had unified the south
Sun Yat-sen, the founder who had led China's republican revolution
context: Puyi had been emperor of China as a toddler before the 1911 revolution removed him. Japan made him 'emperor' of Manchukuo in 1934 under the era name Kangde, but real power lay with the Kwantung Army commander, who doubled as Japan's ambassador and could veto Puyi's decisions. He was a figurehead and nothing more. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchukuo

question: Yosuke Matsuoka, Japan's chief delegate, sat in the League of Nations assembly in February 1933 as it voted 42 to 1 to brand Japan the aggressor in Manchuria. Rather than accept the verdict, he led his whole delegation out of the hall. What did Matsuoka say as he left?
answer: "We are not coming back."
choices: "We are not coming back."
"History will be our judge."
"Japan acts only in self-defense."
"The League has signed its own death warrant."
context: Japan was the lone 'no' vote against the Lytton Report. Matsuoka led his delegation out and said simply, 'We are not coming back.' Japan gave formal notice of withdrawal on March 27, 1933. Source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1933/02/24/Japan-stuns-world-withdraws-from-league/2231840119817/

question: Charlie Chaplin, the world's most famous movie star, had just landed in Japan when young naval officers murdered the prime minister on 15 May 1932. Chaplin was on their list too: they hoped his death would drag the United States into war. What happened to spare his life?
answer: He was at a sumo match with the prime minister's son when the attack came
choices: He was at a sumo match with the prime minister's son when the attack came
He had already boarded a ship and left the country that morning
He talked the officers down by performing for them at the door
He was mistaken for an ordinary tourist and waved through a checkpoint
context: The plotters had planned to kill Chaplin too, hoping to provoke war with the United States. At the moment of the assassination, the prime minister's son was at a sumo match WITH Chaplin, which likely saved both their lives. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_15_incident

question: Japanese troops drilling by the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing in July 1937 reported one of their soldiers, Private Shimura Kikujiro, missing and insisted on searching the nearby town. Shots were fired, and the dispute grew into full-scale war between Japan and China. What was false about their demand?
answer: The missing soldier had already returned to his own lines
choices: The missing soldier had already returned to his own lines
The town they named was empty and had no garrison at all
The soldier had deserted to the Chinese side days before
No soldier by that name was ever on the unit's roster
context: Even though Private Shimura had already come back, the Japanese pressed their demand to enter Wanping, shooting started, and it became the opening of the Second Sino-Japanese War. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Polo_Bridge_incident

question: Japanese officers set off a charge on Japan's own railway near Mukden after dark on 18 September 1931 and blamed it on Chinese soldiers, giving Japan its excuse to invade Manchuria. One detail soon showed that the 'attack' was staged. What gave it away?
answer: A scheduled train rolled over the very same track minutes later and arrived on time
choices: A scheduled train rolled over the very same track minutes later and arrived on time
The Chinese garrison was found unarmed and still asleep in its barracks
Japanese newspapers printed the story a full day before the blast happened
The charge had been bought from a shop whose receipts the police recovered
context: The explosion damaged only a 1.5-meter section of one rail. A train from Changchun rolled over the same track minutes later and reached Shenyang on time at 10:30 p.m. The staged 'Mukden Incident' became the pretext to seize all of Manchuria. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mukden_incident

question: Chinese soldiers held a barracks at Mukden, some seven thousand strong, when about five hundred Japanese troops stormed it on a September night in 1931. Yet only two Japanese were killed, and roughly five hundred Chinese. Why was the bigger force beaten so easily?
answer: The Chinese soldiers had been ordered not to resist
choices: The Chinese soldiers had been ordered not to resist
The Chinese soldiers had run out of ammunition weeks earlier
The Japanese had secretly poisoned the garrison's water
The Japanese attacked with tanks the defenders had never faced
context: Chinese leader Chiang Kai-shek hoped to avoid a war Japan was spoiling for, so the garrison was ordered to stand down. About 500 Chinese died against two Japanese dead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mukden_incident

question: Inukai Tsuyoshi, Japan's prime minister, faced eleven young naval officers who forced their way into his home on 15 May 1932 to kill him. The old man tried to explain himself: 'If I told you, you would understand.' How did the officers answer before they shot him?
answer: "Dialogue is useless."
choices: "Dialogue is useless."
"You have already said too much."
"We understand you all too well."
"There is nothing left to explain."
context: Inukai said 'hanaseba wakaru' ('if I told you, you would understand'); the officers answered 'mondo muyo' ('dialogue is useless') and killed him. The assassins received astonishingly light sentences, a signal that civilian rule over Japan was collapsing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_15_incident

question: Young army officers led some 1,400 rebel soldiers into the snowy heart of Tokyo on 26 February 1936 and hunted down the leaders on their list. They killed Takahashi Korekiyo, the finance minister, but Keisuke Okada, the prime minister, lived. How did Okada escape the killers?
answer: He hid in a closet while his brother-in-law was mistaken for him and killed
choices: He hid in a closet while his brother-in-law was mistaken for him and killed
He slipped out a back gate disguised in a maid's clothing
He convinced the rebels he was only a household servant
He climbed down a drainpipe and walked to a police station
context: The rebels assassinated Finance Minister Takahashi Korekiyo, former PM Saito Makoto, and General Watanabe Jotaro. Okada lived only because his brother-in-law was mistaken for him and shot. The rebels surrendered on February 29. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_26_incident

question: Japan's soldiers captured Nanjing, then China's capital, in December 1937, and for about six weeks they murdered civilians and disarmed prisoners of war in the streets and countryside, raping, killing and burning whole neighbourhoods. After the war the Tokyo war-crimes tribunal counted the dead of the Rape of Nanking. How many did it find?
answer: More than 200,000
choices: More than 200,000
About 50,000
About 8,000
About 2,000
context: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East found more than 200,000 killed; estimates commonly range from 200,000 up to 300,000. This is established historical fact, accepted by the postwar tribunals. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre

question: Minnie Vautrin, an American missionary, ran Ginling Girls College in Nanjing when Japanese troops overran the city in December 1937. She took in about 10,000 Chinese women and girls fleeing rape and murder. When Japanese soldiers arrived to carry victims off, what did Vautrin do?
answer: She stood at the gate to keep the soldiers out
choices: She stood at the gate to keep the soldiers out
She hid the girls beneath the floorboards of the chapel
She marched the girls out of the city by night
She paid the soldiers in silver to turn them away
context: Vautrin sheltered about 10,000 women and girls inside Ginling Girls College in the Nanking Safety Zone, standing at the gate to block Japanese soldiers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre

question: Iwane Matsui, the general in overall command, went to the gallows in 1948 for failing to stop the massacre at Nanjing. Prince Yasuhiko Asaka had led the troops in Nanjing itself during the killing, yet he was never put on trial. Why did Asaka escape justice?
answer: He was granted immunity as a member of the imperial family
choices: He was granted immunity as a member of the imperial family
He had died before the tribunal could be convened
No witness would testify that he had been in the city
He fled to a country that refused to extradite him
context: Matsui was hanged in 1948 for failing to prevent the atrocities, yet Prince Asaka, the emperor's uncle who held field command during the massacre, received immunity as a member of the imperial family and was never tried. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre

question: Toshiaki Mukai and Tsuyoshi Noda, two Japanese officers, ran a 'contest to kill 100 people with a sword' in 1937, by the breathless reports newspapers at home printed. Most historians do not take those reports as straight fact. What do they say the 'contest' really was?
answer: War-glorifying propaganda; Noda later said he killed only a handful in real combat
choices: War-glorifying propaganda; Noda later said he killed only a handful in real combat
A coded military order to execute exactly one hundred prisoners
A complete fabrication invented decades later by foreign critics
An accurate sporting tally the two officers kept in a private diary
context: Legend, as reported by the press, not forensic fact. The Osaka Mainichi and Tokyo Nichi Nichi (Nov 30 - Dec 13, 1937) reported a tally of 106 to 105 and proposed extending the contest to 150. Most historians treat the reports as war-glorifying propaganda; Noda himself later said he had killed only four or five in actual combat, and that prisoners, not battlefield enemies, were involved. Both officers were tried and executed at Nanjing in 1948. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contest_to_kill_100_people_using_a_sword

question: Benito Mussolini launched the world's first fascist movement, the Fasci di Combattimento, in a hall in Milan on 23 March 1919. Within three years the movement would seize control of the whole country. How many people turned up to that first meeting?
answer: About two hundred people
choices: About two hundred people
About fifty thousand people
About ten thousand people
About five hundred thousand people
context: The founding meeting in Milan's Piazza San Sepolcro drew only around 200 people, yet it became the National Fascist Party within two years -- the first fascist regime in the world. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Benito_Mussolini/

question: Alessandro Mussolini, a village blacksmith and passionate socialist in northern Italy, named his baby son in 1883 after a foreign leader he deeply admired. The boy grew up to be Benito Mussolini, Italy's fascist dictator. Who was Benito named after?
answer: A Mexican president, Benito Juarez
choices: A Mexican president, Benito Juarez
A French emperor, Napoleon Bonaparte
A Russian novelist, Leo Tolstoy
An American inventor, Thomas Edison
context: His father Alessandro named him Benito after Mexican president Benito Juarez, and added the middle names Andrea and Amilcare after two Italian agitators, Andrea Costa and Amilcare Cipriani. Mussolini was raised on revolutionary heroes. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini

question: Adolf Hitler styled himself Fuhrer, a title that meant the same as the one Benito Mussolini took once he held power in Italy, where it made him the very model of the all-powerful strongman. What was Mussolini's title?
answer: Il Duce
choices: Il Duce
El Caudillo
Der Kaiser
Le Premier
context: 'Il Duce' means 'The Leader' (from the Latin 'dux,' a military commander). It became the model for other strongmen, including Hitler's 'Fuhrer' -- which also means 'leader.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Benito_Mussolini/

question: A squad of Mussolini's Blackshirts would seize a union man, a socialist or a journalist in the street after the First World War, pin him in a chair and force his mouth open. Then they poured a whole bottle of something down his throat, to break him before the crowd. What was it?
answer: A litre of castor oil
choices: A litre of castor oil
A dose of bitter purgative salts
A flask of turpentine
A pint of sea-water brine
context: Up to a litre of castor oil -- a violent purgative -- left the victim losing control of his bowels in front of crowds. Their methods were summed up as 'truncheon and castor oil' (manganello e olio di ricino). https://historyoftotalitarianism.com/mussolini-and-his-thugs/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squadrismo

question: Mussolini faced 60,000 of his Blackshirts massed in Naples in October 1922, four days before their march on Rome. From the stage he told them plainly what the Fascists wanted. What did he say their aim was?
answer: 'Our program is simple: we want to rule Italy.'
choices: 'Our program is simple: we want to rule Italy.'
'Our purpose is simple: we want Rome to fear us.'
'Our goal is simple: we will end the old parties.'
'Our path is simple: we answer to no one.'
context: He named the aim plainly to a roaring crowd in Naples four days before the march -- raw power, openly stated. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Rome

question: Luigi Facta, the prime minister, drew up an emergency order in October 1922 as the Blackshirt columns closed on Rome. It would have put Italy under a state of siege and let the army stop the march. Why did the order never take effect?
answer: King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign it
choices: King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign it
The army generals defected to the Blackshirts
A general strike shut down the railways
Facta resigned before he could issue it
context: The King would not sign -- fearing bloodshed and possibly a rival claimant to his throne -- and instead asked Mussolini to become Prime Minister. The march 'succeeded' because the King blinked, not because the Blackshirts won a battle. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Rome ; https://www.history.com/articles/mussolini-italy-fascism

question: Giacomo Matteotti, a socialist deputy, rose in Parliament on 30 May 1924 and charged Mussolini's Fascists, to their faces, with winning that year's election by open fraud and armed violence at the polls. Eleven days later a fascist squad led by Amerigo Dumini answered him. What did they do to Matteotti?
answer: They kidnapped and murdered him
choices: They kidnapped and murdered him
They stripped him of his seat
They exiled him to an island
They fined and silenced him
context: The killing of Matteotti nearly toppled Mussolini. In protest, 123 opposition deputies walked out of Parliament -- the 'Aventine Secession.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Matteotti ; https://www.britannica.com/event/Matteotti-Crisis

question: Mussolini forced a new election law through Parliament in 1923 to lock in fascist control, drawn up by Giacomo Acerbo. Under it, the party list that came first with as little as a quarter of the vote took a fixed share of all the seats. How big a share did it take?
answer: A full two-thirds of all seats
choices: A full two-thirds of all seats
An exact one-quarter of all seats
A simple majority of one seat
A guaranteed half of all seats
context: Clearing just 25% of the vote delivered two-thirds of Parliament. The 1924 election held under this law was the last competitive election in Italy until 1946. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acerbo_Law ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Acerbo-Law

question: A huge Fascist crowd gathered in Milan in October 1925, three years to the day after the march on Rome, and heard Mussolini pack his whole creed into one formula. The regime made it its motto and carved it on its monuments. Which line was it?
answer: 'Everything in the State, nothing outside the State, nothing against the State.'
choices: 'Everything in the State, nothing outside the State, nothing against the State.'
'The State serves the people, answers to the people, and may be unmade by the people.'
'Workers control the State, abolish the State, and need no State at all.'
'A small State, a free market, and a citizen left alone.'
context: 'Tutto nello Stato, niente al di fuori dello Stato, nulla contro lo Stato.' The core of fascism: the State, not the individual, is supreme -- the structure kids should learn to recognize. https://polyarchy.org/basta/documenti/mussolini.milano.html

question: George Seldes, a journalist, kept hearing one cheerful boast about Mussolini from foreign visitors to Fascist Italy: told about the beatings, they waved them away by repeating it. Historians call the boast mostly a legend. What was it?
answer: That he made the trains run on time
choices: That he made the trains run on time
That he had wiped out all poverty
That he had ended every street crime
That he had drained the Roman marshes
context: LEGEND, mostly false: much rail repair predated the fascists, and only big tourist expresses ran punctually while smaller lines stayed late. Seldes mocked how tourists, told of oppression, always replied, 'But the trains run on time!' https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/loco-motive/ ; https://professorbuzzkill.com/2022/01/10/mussolini-didnt-make-the-trains-run-on-time/

question: Alexei Stakhanov, a Soviet coal miner, was said to have cut 102 tons of coal in one shift in 1935, fourteen times his quota, and the Party made him the face of a whole movement of record-breakers. Decades later a Soviet newspaper admitted the record had been a setup. What was the trick behind it?
answer: A support team did the hauling; he got all the credit
choices: A support team did the hauling; he got all the credit
He used a secret new German cutting machine
He had simply worked three shifts back to back
The mine's coal was unusually soft that night
context: It was staged: a support team did the loading and timbering through the 5-hour-45-minute shift while the entire tonnage was tallied to Stakhanov alone. In 1988 the Soviet paper Komsomolskaya Pravda finally admitted the feat was puffery. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexei_Stakhanov ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stakhanovite_movement

question: Joseph Stalin launched his first Five-Year Plan in 1928, and his regime fixed on raising single plants, dams and steelworks that would out-build anything in the capitalist West. Western observers mocked the craze with one coined word. What was it?
answer: Gigantomania
choices: Gigantomania
Colossalism
Stakhanovism
Maximalism
context: 'Gigantomania.' The 1928 plan demanded gigantic jumps — coal from 35 to 75 million tons, pig iron from 3.3 to 10 million, electricity from 5 to 22 billion kWh — to prove a peasant country could out-build the West in a decade. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_five-year_plan_(Soviet_Union) ; spartacus-educational.com/RUSfive.htm

question: Workers and prisoners laboured in freezing cold to raise Magnitogorsk, a whole steel city, on open ground in the Ural Mountains. Stalin wanted it as proof that the Five-Year Plan could conjure modern industry from nothing. What made that exact spot the right place for a steelworks?
answer: A nearby mountain rich in iron ore
choices: A nearby mountain rich in iron ore
A river of clean-burning coal
A vast salt plain
Ancient copper mines
context: Magnitogorsk — built from scratch as a whole steel complex in the Urals. Its twin showpiece was the Dnieper Hydroelectric Dam; together they were meant to prove a backward peasant country could out-build the capitalist West in a single decade. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_five-year_plan_(Soviet_Union) ; britannica.com/money/Five-Year-Plans

question: Nikolai Yezhov ran Stalin's secret police at the height of the Great Purge, and the terror itself took his name: the Yezhovshchina, the Yezhov era. A sinister nickname followed him and made his name a thing of dread. What was Yezhov called?
answer: The Bloody Dwarf
choices: The Bloody Dwarf
The Iron Marshal
The Red Tsar
The Steel Commissar
context: The 'Bloody Dwarf' — Yezhov stood barely five feet tall. The terror is named the 'Yezhovshchina,' literally 'the Yezhov era,' after him. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Yezhov

question: Andrei Vyshinsky prosecuted Lenin's old comrades at the Moscow show trials armed with hardly anything but beaten confessions, and he heaped abuse on them, calling them vermin. He closed one tirade with a blunt command to the judges that became infamous. What did he demand?
answer: Shoot the mad dogs!
choices: Shoot the mad dogs!
Bury the secrets forever!
Spare these broken men!
Exile the traitors east!
context: Vyshinsky called the defendants 'mad dogs of Trotskyism,' 'accursed vermin' and 'dregs of society,' and demanded the court 'shoot the mad dogs.' The three big trials (1936, 1937, 1938) destroyed Lenin's old guard — Zinoviev, Kamenev, then Bukharin — almost all shot in the Lubyanka cellars. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_trials ; spartacus-educational.com/RUSshow.htm

question: Joseph Stalin strolled side by side with Nikolai Yezhov, his secret-police chief, in a famous photograph of 1937. Stalin had Yezhov arrested in 1940 and shot, and Soviet censors then painted him out of the picture. In the doctored photo, what stands where Yezhov used to be?
answer: An empty stretch of water
choices: An empty stretch of water
A pair of armed guards
A waving red banner
A row of marble statues
context: The two had been walking beside the Moscow-Volga Canal; the retouchers replaced Yezhov with a blank patch of water. It is the most famous case of Soviet photo-faking, catalogued in David King's 1997 book 'The Commissar Vanishes.' Sources: rarehistoricalphotos.com/stalin-photo-manipulation-1922-1953/ ; grokipedia.com/page/The_Commissar_Vanishes

question: Vasily Blokhin, chief executioner of Stalin's secret police, shot tens of thousands of people with his own hands, more than any other official killer on record. Before each shift he put on a special outfit to keep his uniform clean of blood. What did he wear?
answer: A leather butcher's apron
choices: A leather butcher's apron
A grey army greatcoat
A white doctor's smock
A black canvas raincoat
context: Blokhin wore a leather butcher's apron, a leather cap, and shoulder-length leather gloves to keep the blood off. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Blokhin ; allthatsinteresting.com/vasily-blokhin

question: Prisoners of the Gulag, Stalin's whole system of slave labour, built the White Sea-Baltic Canal between 1931 and 1933 as the system's first showpiece, some 126,000 of them. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn would later expose that system in The Gulag Archipelago. What did the prisoners dig the canal with?
answer: Only primitive hand tools
choices: Only primitive hand tools
Imported American excavators
German tunneling machines
Steam-powered dredgers
context: Only picks, shovels and wheelbarrows — no real machinery. An estimated 12,000-25,000 prisoners died digging the Belomorkanal. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Sea%E2%80%93Baltic_Canal ; allthatsinteresting.com/white-sea-baltic-canal

question: Mikhail Tukhachevsky, the marshal behind the Red Army's 'deep battle' tank plan, stood before a secret court for a single day in June 1937, accused of a German plot he never joined, and he was shot within hours. Decades later investigators reopened his prison file. What did they find on the pages of his confession?
answer: His own spattered blood
choices: His own spattered blood
A forged German seal
Stalin's red signature
A faded prison stamp
context: Tukhachevsky's blood was spattered across the file — the confession had been tortured out of him. His killing began the decapitation of the Red Army on the eve of war: 3 of 5 marshals, 13 of 15 army commanders and 154 of 186 division commanders were shot or removed. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Tukhachevsky ; militaryhistorynow.com/2023/01/08/the-enemy-within-five-little-known-facts-about-stalins-purge-of-the-red-army-2/

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920, before Stalin's Five-Year Plans began, that a fully socialist economy was doomed. Once private property was gone, he said, a planning ministry like Gosplan would lack one thing it could not do without. What made real planning impossible, by Mises's account?
answer: Without market prices, planners could not know what anything was truly worth
choices: Without market prices, planners could not know what anything was truly worth
Without foreign loans, the state could not buy enough machinery to start
Without a strong army, the planners could not enforce their quotas on workers
Without good weather, the harvest targets could never realistically be met
context: Mises (1920, 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth') argued that with no private property there are no real prices, so planners cannot calculate what anything is worth. Friedrich Hayek added that the knowledge to run an economy is scattered among millions and can never be gathered in one ministry. The Plans' bottlenecks, faked reports and shortages were the prediction coming true. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem ; aier.org/article/mises-and-hayek-two-complementary-critiques-of-central-planning/

question: The men of Stalin's secret police logged the executions of the Great Purge in their own files. Those who play the purge down speak vaguely of 'about half a million' dead. What figure do the secret police's own files record for 1937 and 1938 alone?
answer: 681,692 executed
choices: 681,692 executed
504,117 executed
250,431 executed
947,206 executed
context: The NKVD's own records log 681,692 executions in 1937-38 alone (plus about 116,000 Gulag deaths), which is why the honest scholarly range is 700,000 to 1.2 million killed. The soft 'about half a million' shrinks a documented massacre — the bodies were counted. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excess_mortality_in_the_Soviet_Union_under_Joseph_Stalin

question: Robert Hooke built an air pump for Robert Boyle in 1659. It was a great glass globe over a brass cylinder that could draw out the air inside. Boyle sealed a living bird in the globe and pumped, and the bird drooped and died. Then he let air rush back in. What happened when the air returned?
answer: The bird revived and stirred back to life
choices: The bird revived and stirred back to life
The glass globe cracked from the pressure
The bird caught fire and burned up
The brass cylinder filled with water
context: Boyle's air-pump (built by Hooke, ~30-quart glass receiver over a brass cylinder, 1659) let him make a near-vacuum, which most people thought impossible. A bird died when the air was pumped out but revived if air came back quickly; a mouse went giddy, staggered, and collapsed, then revived too. The demonstrations showed dramatically that animals cannot live without air. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/full-boyle/

question: Robert Boyle wrote a book in 1661 as a sharp debate and turned it on two old authorities: the four elements of earth, water, air and fire that scholars had taught for two thousand years, and the alchemists' three secret 'principles' of salt, sulfur and mercury. Questions about matter, he said, must be settled by experiment, not by secret authority. What was the book called?
answer: The Sceptical Chymist
choices: The Sceptical Chymist
The Wealth of Nations
The Starry Messenger
The Praise of Folly
context: In 'The Sceptical Chymist' (1661) Boyle attacked both the four classical elements and the alchemists' three principles, demanding evidence over authority. He is often called a father of modern chemistry for dragging it out of secretive alchemy into public, repeatable experiment. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/robert-boyle/

question: Robert Boyle trapped a pocket of air in the short sealed end of a tall J-shaped glass tube, then poured heavy liquid metal into the long open end, more and more, crushing the air into less and less space. The rule he found became Boyle's Law. At a fixed temperature, what happens to a gas's pressure when its volume is halved?
answer: It doubles
choices: It doubles
It stays the same
It is cut in half
It drops to zero
context: Boyle's Law: pressure times volume stays constant at fixed temperature, so halving the volume doubles the pressure. Boyle proved it with a J-shaped tube, pouring in mercury to crush a trapped pocket of air and measuring the shrinkage. Published in the 1662 second edition of 'New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall, Touching the Spring of the Air.' Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Robert_Boyle/

question: In the legend, the outlaw of Sherwood Forest enters an archery contest. A rival's arrow already sits dead centre in the bullseye, yet his own arrow strikes the back of it and splits it down the middle. What do archers still call that shot?
answer: a Robin Hood
choices: a Robin Hood
a Sherwood
a Nottingham
a Little John
context: Splitting an arrow that is already buried in the target is still called 'a Robin Hood' by archers worldwide. The dramatic version of the feat was made iconic by Sir Walter Scott in his 1819 novel Ivanhoe. LEGEND. Source: https://www.worldarchery.sport/news/178452/archery-history-legend-robin-hood

question: The Prioress of Kirklees has betrayed the old outlaw and bled him to death, the legend says. Little John holds him up at her window for one last shot from his longbow. What does the outlaw ask of his men as that last arrow flies?
answer: to be buried where the arrow lands
choices: to be buried where the arrow lands
to burn Kirklees to the ground
to crown Little John as their new leader
to carry his body home to Sherwood
context: Robin asks to be buried where his last arrow falls, 'within bow-shot' of Kirklees. A mound marked as Robin Hood's Grave can still be visited there today. LEGEND. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood's_Grave

question: Auguste Rodin perched a small figure high on his giant bronze doors, where it brooded over the souls of the damned below. Foundry workers called it The Thinker, and Rodin later made it the colossus the world knows. The little figure began as a real poet. Which poet?
answer: Dante, author of the journey through Hell
choices: Dante, author of the journey through Hell
Homer, who sang of the fall of Troy
Virgil, who wrote of Rome's founding
Ovid, who told tales of the gods
context: The Thinker began as a roughly 70 cm figure called 'The Poet' — Dante Alighieri, seated on the tympanum atop Rodin's 'The Gates of Hell,' brooding over the damned in the circles of his Inferno. Foundry workers nicknamed it 'The Thinker' because it reminded them of Michelangelo's brooding statue of Lorenzo de' Medici. Rodin later enlarged it to colossal size (1904) into the standalone icon. Source: https://www.musee-rodin.fr/en/musee/collections/oeuvres/thinker

question: Six citizens of Calais walked out barefoot to King Edward III in 1347 with ropes around their necks, ready to die for their town. Auguste Rodin would not set their monument on the usual tall pedestal, and he made all six life-size. Where did he want the figures placed?
answer: Directly on the ground, at the viewer's own level
choices: Directly on the ground, at the viewer's own level
High on a column above the town square
Inside a sealed glass memorial case
Atop the city's tallest Gothic spire
context: Rodin broke every rule of the heroic monument: no pedestal, six men at life size with different emotions — resignation, defiance, despair — placed on the ground so viewers meet the condemned eye to eye. Calais first rejected this and mounted them on a tall Gothic base anyway; only in 1924 did the city honor Rodin's wish and lower the Burghers to ground level before the town hall, where they still stand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Burghers_of_Calais

question: Wilhelm Roentgen noticed a coated screen glowing across his darkened laboratory at Wurzburg late in 1895, though no light could reach it. Rays he could not see were passing through black cardboard, wood and even flesh. Why did Roentgen name them X-rays?
answer: X was the mathematical symbol for an unknown quantity
choices: X was the mathematical symbol for an unknown quantity
X marked the spot on his lab bench where they appeared
X was the first letter of the screen's glowing chemical
X stood for the experiment number in his lab notebook
context: Because he could not say what the rays were, Roentgen borrowed the algebra symbol 'X' that stands for an unknown value. The name stuck worldwide, even though others called them 'Roentgen rays' to honor him. Sources: nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1901/perspectives; time.com/3649842/x-ray.

question: Anna Bertha Roentgen looked at the picture her husband Wilhelm had made of her left hand in December 1895: her finger bones in dark shadow, her ring still circling one of them. No living person had ever looked inside his own body before. What did she cry out?
answer: "I have seen my death!"
choices: "I have seen my death!"
"Take it away from me!"
"That is not my hand!"
"It is the work of the devil!"
context: The image is called 'Hand mit Ringen' (Hand with Rings). Bertha recoiled at the ghostly bones of her living hand, the first time any human had seen inside a living body. Sources: pbs.org/newshour/health/i-have-seen-my-death-how-the-world-discovered-the-x-ray; worldhistory.org/article/2497.

question: Filippo Brunelleschi studied the Pantheon in Rome closely before he raised a dome of his own. Hadrian's builders had finished its concrete dome around AD 126, 43 metres across, and it had stayed the widest on Earth for over thirteen centuries when Brunelleschi beat it in 1436. Over which building did he raise his dome?
answer: Florence Cathedral
choices: Florence Cathedral
Cologne Cathedral
Westminster Abbey
Notre-Dame de Paris
context: Filippo Brunelleschi completed the dome on Florence Cathedral in 1436, ending the Pantheon's 1,300-year reign as the world's widest. He had studied the Pantheon closely, travelling to Rome to examine its ancient structure for himself, before designing his own.

question: Hadrian raised a building almost nineteen centuries ago that still holds a world record: the largest dome of plain concrete on Earth, with no steel bar inside it. Which building is it?
answer: The Pantheon
choices: The Pantheon
The Colosseum
The Baths of Caracalla
The Circus Maximus
context: The Pantheon's concrete dome (c. AD 113-125) has no steel rebar at all and is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome on the planet. Its inside is a perfect sphere: the height to the top and the width across are exactly equal, both 43.3 metres. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: Arcades of stone arches carried Rome's water across valleys and became the famous image of a Roman aqueduct. Yet of the roughly 780 kilometres of channel that fed the city, only about 47 rode on arches. Where did the other 94 percent of the water travel?
answer: Hidden in tunnels and trenches in the ground
choices: Hidden in tunnels and trenches in the ground
Inside hollow columns along the road
Through pipes laid on the open hillsides
Across floating wooden walkways
context: About 94% of Rome's aqueduct channel was buried. The famous arcades were the rare exception, used only to carry the water across valleys where the ground dropped away. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_aqueduct

question: A Roman arch rose over a wooden frame, wedge-shaped stone by wedge-shaped stone, until one last stone was driven in at the very top. At that moment the whole ring locked solid, so that the load pressing down became a sideways squeeze, and the frame could come away. What is that final stone called?
answer: the keystone
choices: the keystone
the capstone
the anchor stone
the crown block
context: The wedge-shaped stones of an arch (voussoirs) turn the weight on top into sideways squeezing force. The keystone locks the ring, so the load holds the whole arch together instead of pushing it apart and the arch carries it as a single block of stone, enormously strong in compression. This is why Roman arches still stand. Source: https://oldentech.com/ancient-roman-arches/ ; https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Arch

question: The builders of Hadrian's great dome left a round hole, the oculus, open to the sky and the rain at its very top. It was the building's only window, but it also solved a problem for them. How did leaving the top open help hold the dome up?
answer: It removed the heaviest, most dangerous part of the dome
choices: It removed the heaviest, most dangerous part of the dome
It let hot air escape so the stone would not crack
It made the dome lighter by drying out the concrete
It let workers lower the stones from above
context: Removing the crown of the dome got rid of its heaviest, most dangerous part and gave the ring of concrete around the opening something to push against. The 30-Roman-foot oculus is the building's only source of light. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: The Romans posted their first written law code, the Twelve Tables, on bronze in the Forum for every citizen to read. Around 387 BC a disaster destroyed the original tablets, yet Rome never repealed the laws, and they stayed the bedrock of Roman justice for centuries. What happened to the tablets?
answer: The Gauls sacked Rome and burned the tablets
choices: The Gauls sacked Rome and burned the tablets
A flood of the Tiber washed the tablets away
A fire in the Senate house melted the tablets
Rioting plebeians smashed the tablets in protest
context: When the Gauls under Brennus sacked and burned Rome (traditionally 387/390 BC), the original bronze tablets were destroyed. No original text survives -- everything we know of the Twelve Tables is reconstructed from quotations in later Roman writers. Yet the laws were never formally repealed: the CODE outlived its own monument. Source: World History Encyclopedia 'Twelve Tables' (worldhistory.org/Twelve_Tables); Wikipedia 'Twelve Tables'.

question: Roman schoolboys once had to master the whole Twelve Tables, the entire law code, Cicero recalled; that was in his grandfathers' day, and nobody bothered any more in his own time, the first century BC. What had the code been to those earlier schoolboys?
answer: A required song they chanted from memory
choices: A required song they chanted from memory
A riddle contest held in the Forum
A copying drill done on wax tablets
A series of mock trials they acted out
context: Cicero (De Legibus 2.59) says that in his grandfathers' day schoolboys learned the Twelve Tables as a 'carmen necessarium' -- a 'required song' -- chanting the entire law code from memory. By Cicero's own time the practice had died out. An entire law code memorized aloud was once simply how a Roman child was schooled. Source: Wikipedia 'Twelve Tables' (citing Cicero, De Legibus 2.59).

question: Tribonian, a brilliant jurist, took on the task Justinian I set him in the 500s: sorting out a thousand years of tangled, contradictory Roman law. His team produced one ordered collection in four parts, the Codex, the Digest, the Institutes and the Novels, and it became the foundation of European civil law for centuries. What is the whole collection called?
answer: The Corpus Juris Civilis
choices: The Corpus Juris Civilis
The Edict of Milan
The Justinianic Codex alone
The Theodosian Synthesis
context: Justinian's commission under Tribonian produced the Corpus Juris Civilis ('Body of Civil Law') in four parts: the Codex (imperial decrees, first issued 529), the Digest or Pandects (jurists' opinions, 533), the Institutes (a student textbook, 533), and the Novellae (Justinian's new laws). It became the law of the Byzantine Empire and the foundation of the civil-law systems still used across much of the world.

question: Justinian's team gathered the opinions of Rome's greatest legal minds into the Digest, yet nearly all of it reached later ages through one object made soon after the original. It was kept at Amalfi, taken as war booty to Pisa in 1155, and moved to Florence in 1406, where it still rests. What was it?
answer: A single hand-copied manuscript
choices: A single hand-copied manuscript
A single carved stone slab
A single bronze tablet of decrees
A single bound roll of scrolls
context: The manuscript is the Littera Florentina, made within a generation of Justinian's original. A 13th-century account says it was held at Amalfi, seized as war booty and taken to Pisa in 1155, then carried to Florence in 1406, where it rests in the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana. Western legal civilization hung on this one book. Source: Wikipedia 'Littera Florentina'; History of Information 'Pandectarum codex Florentinus'.

question: Rome's lawgivers gave the father, the paterfamilias, terrifying power over his household in Table IV of the Twelve Tables: he could sell his own son into bondage. Yet the same rule hid a loophole. If a father sold his son a third time, that sale carried a consequence he never intended. What did the third sale do?
answer: The son went free of his father forever
choices: The son went free of his father forever
The son could buy his way out for one as
The son inherited his father's whole estate
The son owed his father triple the price
context: Table IV: 'If a father sells his son three times, the son shall be free of the father.' Roman jurists later turned this three-sales clause into the legal ritual used to deliberately free a son from his father's power -- the origin of emancipation. The same harsh table also ordered that a 'dreadfully deformed child shall be quickly killed.' Source: Yale Avalon Project, 'The Laws of the Twelve Tables', Table IV.

question: Julius Paulus, a Roman jurist, packed one of the deepest rules of the courtroom into a Latin maxim that survives in Justinian's Digest: 'Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat.' From it descends the rule that a person is innocent until proven guilty. What does it say about who must prove a charge?
answer: The accuser must prove the case, not the accused
choices: The accuser must prove the case, not the accused
Both sides share the burden of proof equally
The judge must gather the proof himself
The accused must prove that he is innocent
context: 'Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat' -- 'the burden of proof is on the one who asserts, not on the one who denies.' Attributed to the jurist Julius Paulus (2nd-3rd c. AD) and preserved in Justinian's Digest at 22.3.2, it is the direct ancestor of the rule that the accuser, not the accused, must prove the case. Source: Wikipedia 'Presumption of innocence' (citing Digest 22.3.2, Julius Paulus); LawTimesJournal 'Ei incumbit probatio qui'.

question: Trajan, the Roman emperor, ruled that no one should ever be condemned on suspicion alone, and his ruling survives in Justinian's Digest. In it he also set down a principle that Blackstone, the English jurist, would echo centuries later. Which principle did Trajan make Roman law?
answer: Better a guilty man go free than an innocent be condemned
choices: Better a guilty man go free than an innocent be condemned
No man may be tried for the same crime twice
A confession outweighs any other evidence
Punishment must always fit the gravity of the crime
context: Trajan's rescript, preserved at Digest 48.19.5 (Ulpian): 'satius esse impunitum relinqui facinus nocentis quam innocentem damnari' -- 'it is better that the crime of a guilty man go unpunished than that an innocent be condemned' -- adding that no one should be condemned on mere suspicion. Blackstone's famous 'better that ten guilty escape than one innocent suffer' is a direct descendant. Source: UCLA Law, A. Volokh 'n Guilty Men' (law.ucla.edu/Volokh/guilty.htm), quoting Digest 48.19.5 (Ulpian, De officio proconsulis 7).

question: Justinian made his Digest the only law anyone could cite in court. His lawyers had squeezed the writings of nearly forty classical jurists, some two thousand books, into that one work, and, resolved that no one should ever twist his law again, he issued one more extraordinary command. What was it?
answer: He forbade anyone to write commentaries on it
choices: He forbade anyone to write commentaries on it
He had every older law book publicly burned
He ordered it recited aloud in every court
He let only senators keep private copies
context: Tribonian's team distilled roughly 2,000 books and millions of lines from about 38-39 jurists down to some 150,000 lines (a 50-book work). Justinian declared the Digest the SOLE source of citable law and forbade anyone to write commentaries on it, hoping to freeze the law forever -- a hope that of course failed once later scholars got hold of it. Source: Wikipedia 'Corpus Juris Civilis'.

question: Scholars in Bologna got hold of Justinian's nearly forgotten Digest some time between 1070 and 1100, and Irnerius, one of their teachers, read it aloud, squeezing short explanations between its lines and into its margins. His successors built a whole course of study on those notes and turned Bologna into Europe's first true university of law. What were the notes called?
answer: Glosses
choices: Glosses
Compurgations
Disputations
Recitations
context: Irnerius read the rediscovered Digest aloud and added explanatory notes called 'glosses'; his successors, the glossators, built a curriculum around it. This revival turned Bologna into Europe's first true university of law and re-seeded Roman law across the continent -- the bridge by which Justinian's code became the backbone of modern European civil law. Source: Wikipedia 'Corpus Juris Civilis'; Visit Bologna 'Irnerius: Founder of the School of Glossators'.

question: Cicero and the Roman jurists reached beyond the written statutes of any one city for a higher standard of justice, one binding on every people on earth whatever its own laws said. Modern thinkers see in it a root of human rights and of international law. What did the Romans call this universal justice?
answer: Natural law
choices: Natural law
Statute law
Sacred law
Common law
context: The Romans coined 'ius naturale' (natural law) -- the idea that some standards of justice are universal, binding on all peoples regardless of any state's written statutes. Alongside it stood 'ius gentium,' the 'law of nations' applied between Romans and foreigners; both are acknowledged roots of modern human-rights and international law. Source: Wikipedia 'Jus gentium'; iusromanum.eu 'Roman Law Revisited'; Ernst Levy 'Natural Law in the Roman Period' (Notre Dame).

question: 'True law is right reason in agreement with nature,' Cicero wrote in his On the Republic. Then the whole of that great dialogue was lost for centuries, and the passage should have vanished with it. How did Cicero's words survive?
answer: A Christian writer quoted it long after
choices: A Christian writer quoted it long after
A monk recopied it in a monastery
A rival senator entered it into the record
An emperor had it carved onto a column
context: Cicero's natural-law passage in De Republica Book III ('True law is right reason in agreement with nature; it is of universal application, unchanging and everlasting...') survives only because the Christian writer Lactantius quoted it after the Republic itself was lost for centuries. The idea outlived the book that contained it. Source: nlnrac.org 'On the Republic (De Republica)'; Lex Christianorum 'Natural Law in Cicero's De republica' (citing Lactantius).

question: A Roman worshipper crossed the columned porch of the Pantheon into a round temple under a vast concrete dome. The temple's name joined two Greek words, pan and theon. What was it raised to honour?
answer: All the gods of Rome at once
choices: All the gods of Rome at once
Every emperor who had ever ruled
All the heroes of the legions
All the rivers and seas of the empire
context: 'Pantheon' = Greek pan (all) + theon (gods) — a temple meant to honor every god of Rome together, not just one. Source: https://www.turismoroma.it/en/places/pantheon

question: A visitor who stood in the Pantheon in Rome and looked straight up saw no side windows at all. All the daylight poured in through a single round opening at the top of the dome, nearly nine metres wide and open to the sky. What did the Romans call it?
answer: The oculus
choices: The oculus
The atrium
The forum
The vault
context: The oculus (Latin for 'eye') is about 8.8 m (29 ft) across — the Pantheon's only window and only natural light source. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pantheon/

question: A Roman standing in the Pantheon as a storm rolled over the city watched rain fall straight through the open top of the dome onto the marble floor. Yet the floor never flooded. How did the Roman builders keep the water from pooling?
answer: A raised floor with hidden drains cut into it
choices: A raised floor with hidden drains cut into it
A glass pane stretched across the opening
Slaves posted to bail it out with buckets
A sloped dome that shed the rain outside
context: Rain falls through the open oculus, but the marble floor is gently humped in the middle and about 22 hidden drain holes carry the water away so it never pools. Source: https://thepantheonrome.com/pantheon-oculus/

question: Marcus Agrippa built an earlier temple on the site of the Pantheon, and big carved letters on the porch still credit him with the building. But his temple had burned down long before the one that stands today went up. A later emperor raised today's Pantheon and kept Agrippa's name on the front rather than carving his own. Which emperor?
answer: Emperor Hadrian
choices: Emperor Hadrian
Emperor Augustus
Emperor Constantine
Emperor Trajan
context: Today's Pantheon was finished under Hadrian around 125–128 CE, but he left Agrippa's old inscription on the front — an act of imperial modesty that confused people for centuries about who really built it. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/pantheon

question: Looters stripped most of Rome's pagan temples for their stone after the empire fell, but the Pantheon came through nearly whole. In 608 it stopped being a temple to the old gods and gained caretakers instead. What did it become?
answer: A Christian church
choices: A Christian church
A military fortress
A public marketplace
A senate meeting hall
context: In 608 CE the Pantheon was consecrated as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres (St. Mary of the Martyrs), so unlike most pagan temples it was cared for instead of quarried for stone. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pantheon/

question: The Pantheon's designers made the height from the floor up to the top of its dome, about 43 metres, exactly equal to the dome's width across. Because the two match, what shape would fit snugly inside, just touching the floor and the top of the dome?
answer: A perfect sphere
choices: A perfect sphere
A tall pyramid
A long cylinder
A wide cube
context: The interior height (about 43.3 m) equals the dome's diameter, so a giant ball would fit exactly inside, touching both the floor and the crown of the dome. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pantheon/

question: Roman craftsmen cut five rings of sunken square panels into the inside of the Pantheon's dome, twenty-eight to a ring, shrinking as they climbed toward the opening at the top. The panels are beautiful, but the Romans cut them for a hard engineering reason. What practical job do they do?
answer: They scoop dead weight out of the dome
choices: They scoop dead weight out of the dome
They let rainwater drain through the roof
They lock the marble facing in place
They channel echoes down to the floor
context: The five rings of 28 sunken panels are called coffers; they look beautiful but their real job is to remove weight from the dome so it doesn't crush itself. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pantheon/

question: A Roman builder mixed grey volcanic ash, dug from the hills near Mount Vesuvius, with lime and water for concrete like the Pantheon's. It set rock-hard through a chemical reaction, even underwater, rather than just drying out in the air. What is that volcanic ash called?
answer: Pozzolana
choices: Pozzolana
Gypsum
Quartz
Slag
context: Pozzolana — volcanic ash from Pozzuoli near Vesuvius — mixed with lime and water sets through a chemical reaction and can even harden underwater, unlike ordinary mortar. Source: https://ancientengrtech.wisc.edu/roman-concrete/

question: Pope Urban VIII, head of a powerful Roman family, tore the bronze from the Pantheon's porch in 1625 to be melted into cannons. Romans were so disgusted that they coined a biting Latin line about it. What did the line say?
answer: What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did
choices: What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did
A pope who melts bronze will answer to God
Rome was looted by friends, not enemies
The cannons of the Pope guard an empty shell
context: Pope Urban VIII was a Barberini; the looting prompted the Roman quip 'Quod non fecerunt barbari, fecerunt Barberini' — 'What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.' Most of the bronze became cannons for Castel Sant'Angelo. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter's_Baldachin

question: Frederic Chopin, dying in Paris in 1849, dreaded being buried alive, and he begged that his heart be cut out after death and sent home to Warsaw. Jean Cruveilhier, a physician, removed it. How did he preserve Chopin's heart for the long journey home?
answer: Sealed in a jar of cognac
choices: Sealed in a jar of cognac
Buried in a small lead box
Wrapped tightly in silk cloth
Set in a block of beeswax
context: The physician Jean Cruveilhier removed Chopin's heart and sealed it in a crystal jar of cognac. Chopin's dread of premature burial drove the request. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Chopin

question: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky wrote his 1812 Overture to celebrate Russia's defeat of Napoleon, and he wanted it to roar like a real battle. Beside the ringing church bells of Moscow he scored in a sound no orchestra had used before. What was it?
answer: Blasts of live cannon fire
choices: Blasts of live cannon fire
A galloping troop of horses
A booming thunder machine
A set of blaring trumpets
context: The score calls for sixteen real cannon shots in all (five during the battle, eleven in the finale), alongside the pealing church bells of Moscow, to depict Russia's victory over Napoleon. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1812_Overture

question: Ludwika, Frederic Chopin's sister, promised to carry his heart home to Warsaw after he died in exile in Paris. Her road ran through Austrian and Russian border posts where officers searched travellers' bags. How did she get his heart past them?
answer: Hidden under her own cloak
choices: Hidden under her own cloak
Packed inside a wine barrel
Sewn into a feather pillow
Bribed past with gold coins
context: Ludwika hid the cognac-preserved heart under her cloak or skirt to get it past customs officers. It now rests sealed in a pillar of the Holy Cross Church in Warsaw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Chopin

question: Richard Wagner wrote The Ride of the Valkyries for the moment his warrior sky-maidens carry dead heroes up to Valhalla. Long afterward, a war film bolted loudspeakers to its attack helicopters and blasted that galloping music over a village as they swooped in. Which film?
answer: Apocalypse Now
choices: Apocalypse Now
Full Metal Jacket
Black Hawk Down
Saving Private Ryan
context: 'Ride of the Valkyries' opens Act 3 of Die Walkure; the Valkyries are warrior maidens who carry the slain to Valhalla. The same music blares from helicopter loudspeakers during the village attack in Apocalypse Now (1979). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ride_of_the_Valkyries

question: King Ludwig II of Bavaria paid for a theatre at Bayreuth that Richard Wagner built for his own operas. Other opera houses seat the musicians out front, level with the audience, but Wagner put his whole orchestra somewhere no other house ever had. Where did Wagner put it?
answer: In a covered pit below the stage
choices: In a covered pit below the stage
On a balcony above the audience
Behind a curtain at the back
Inside a glass booth onstage
context: Wagner hid the entire orchestra in a sunken, hooded pit beneath the stage, invisible to the audience, a design he called the 'mystic gulf' so nothing would distract from the drama onstage. King Ludwig II of Bavaria paid for the Festspielhaus, dedicated solely to Wagner's works. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayreuth_Festspielhaus

question: J.M.W. Turner claimed he had himself tied to a steamboat's mast during a blizzard at sea to paint Snow Storm in 1842, rather than sketch it from the shore. Some scholars doubt the story. By his own account, how long did he stay lashed there?
answer: Four hours, not expecting to escape alive
choices: Four hours, not expecting to escape alive
One quick gust before going below
A full day and a night at sea
Just long enough to make a sketch
