context: Turner, then about 67, said: 'I got the sailors to lash me to the mast to observe it; I was lashed for four hours, and I did not expect to escape, but I felt bound to record it if I did.' The steamboat was named the Ariel. The story is his own testimony — some scholars doubt it is literally true, so it is told as legend. A critic mocked the swirling result as 'soapsuds and whitewash,' but John Ruskin in 1843 called it 'one of the very grandest statements of sea-motion, mist and light, that has ever been put on canvas.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow_Storm:_Steam-Boat_off_a_Harbour%27s_Mouth ; news.artnet.com/art-world/art-bites-turner-mast-snow-storm-2561636

question: Eugène Delacroix painted Liberty Leading the People to honour the July Revolution of 1830, which drove King Charles X from his throne, though people often mistake it for a scene of 1789. At its centre a figure charged over the bodies sprawled across the barricade, waving the French tricolour onward. Who was that figure?
answer: A bare-breasted woman in a red cap, half-goddess, half-fighter
choices: A bare-breasted woman in a red cap, half-goddess, half-fighter
An armored general on a rearing warhorse
King Charles X surrendering his crown
A robed bishop blessing the fallen
context: She is both an allegory of Liberty and a robust woman of the people — an early image of Marianne, the symbol of France. She wears a red Phrygian cap and carries a bayoneted musket in one hand and the tricolore in the other; the towers of Notre-Dame rise in the smoke behind her. The fighters span the social classes — a top-hatted gentleman with a shotgun, a worker, and a boy with two pistols who later inspired Victor Hugo's street urchin Gavroche in 'Les Misérables.' The French government bought the painting in 1831 but hid it for years, nervous about its raw revolutionary energy; it now hangs in the Louvre, and reappeared as the cover art of Coldplay's 2008 album 'Viva la Vida.' Sources: dailyartmagazine.com/liberty-leading-the-people/ ; uen.pressbooks.pub/arth2720/chapter/1004/

question: Numitor lost his throne to his cruel brother Amulius, the legend says, and Amulius had Numitor's newborn twin grandsons, Romulus and Remus, left by the River Tiber to die. Before any human found them, a wild animal kept them alive. What did it do?
answer: A she-wolf let them suckle her milk
choices: A she-wolf let them suckle her milk
A great eagle carried them to its nest
A herd of wild deer sheltered them
A serpent coiled warmly around them
context: The she-wolf (Latin lupa) nursing the twins is the single most iconic image of the Roman founding myth, told as legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Romulus_and_Remus/

question: Faustulus and his wife came upon the twins Romulus and Remus, the legend says, and brought them up as sons. Never knowing their royal blood, the boys did the same rough work as the man who raised them. What did they grow up as?
answer: As shepherds tending flocks
choices: As shepherds tending flocks
As fishermen on the river
As blacksmiths at a forge
As soldiers in the army
context: A shepherd named Faustulus and his wife Acca Larentia found the twins and raised them as their own; the boys grew up herding sheep, unaware they were royal-blooded. Told as legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Romulus_and_Remus/

question: Amulius had the baby twins Romulus and Remus set adrift on the River Tiber in a basket, the founding legend of Rome says. Instead of sinking, the basket drifted until something caught it and held it fast at the foot of the Palatine Hill. What stopped it there?
answer: The roots of a wild fig tree
choices: The roots of a wild fig tree
A fisherman's tangled net
A sandbar of pale silt
A fallen marble column
context: The basket snagged in the roots of a wild fig tree at the foot of the Palatine Hill, right by the cave (the Lupercal) where the she-wolf lived. Told as legend. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Romulus_and_Remus/

question: Romulus began building the walls of his new city on the Palatine Hill, by the legend, and his twin Remus leapt over the half-built wall to mock him. According to the Roman historian Livy, how did Romulus answer the insult?
answer: He killed his brother Remus in anger
choices: He killed his brother Remus in anger
He banished Remus from the city forever
He challenged Remus to a footrace
He tore the new wall back down
context: Livy (Book 1.7) records Romulus striking Remus down and shouting 'So perish whoever else shall leap over my walls!' The fratricide that founded Rome is told plainly as the legend has it; Plutarch preserves a rival version in which a man named Celer dealt the blow. Source: http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.02.0151:book%3D1:chapter%3D7

question: Rhea Silvia bore the twins Romulus and Remus, the legend says, though she had been forced into a Vestal Virgin's vow so that she could bear no heirs. The stories say she bore them anyway because of who had fathered them. Who was their father?
answer: Mars, the god of war
choices: Mars, the god of war
Jupiter, the king of the gods
Neptune, the god of the sea
Apollo, the god of the sun
context: The war-god Mars was said to have fathered Romulus and Remus on Rhea Silvia, making the twins half-divine. Told as legend. Source: https://www.unrv.com/culture/romulus-and-remus.php

question: Romulus and Remus quarrelled over where to found their city, the legend says, and held a contest of augury, reading the gods' will in the flight of birds. Remus looked first and counted six vultures. Then Romulus looked. How many did he count?
answer: Twelve vultures
choices: Twelve vultures
Seven vultures
Three vultures
Twenty vultures
context: Remus saw six vultures first, but Romulus then saw twelve, and each claimed victory, deepening the quarrel that ended in Remus's death. Told as legend. Source: http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.02.0151:book%3D1:chapter%3D7

question: John Chard and Gonville Bromhead, two British lieutenants, chose to stand at the mission station of Rorke's Drift on 22 January 1879. Their garrison of just over 150 men held off 3,000 to 4,000 Zulu warriors for more than twelve hours, with no time to build proper defences. What did they stack into walls to shoot from behind?
answer: Maize bags and biscuit boxes
choices: Maize bags and biscuit boxes
Tree trunks and wagon ropes
Sandbags and earth baskets
Rock slabs and timber beams
context: The garrison piled up mealie (maize) bags, biscuit boxes and tinned-meat crates from their stores, and cut loopholes in the buildings to fire through. Lieutenants John Chard and Gonville Bromhead chose to stand and fight after Commissary James Dalton warned that fleeing into open country with the wounded meant death. Source: https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/defence-rorkes-drift

question: The soldiers at Rorke's Drift, a little mission station, beat back roughly 4,000 Zulu warriors through a whole night of point-blank fighting in January 1879. There were only about 150 of them, and their stand became the most honoured single action in British army history. How many Victoria Crosses, the empire's top medal for bravery, were given for it?
answer: Eleven
choices: Eleven
Three
Five
Twenty
context: Eleven Victoria Crosses were awarded for Rorke's Drift, the most ever for a single action, plus five Distinguished Conduct Medals. Only about 17 of the roughly 150 defenders were killed against some 400 Zulu dead, yet nearly every man in the garrison was wounded. Source: https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/defence-rorkes-drift

question: A Zulu army about 20,000 strong overwhelmed the British camp at Isandlwana in January 1879 and left more than 1,300 of its 1,800 men dead, earlier on the same day as the stand at Rorke's Drift. The sky dimmed in a partial eclipse at the height of the fighting. The Zulu fought in a formation named after an animal. Which formation crushed the British?
answer: The horns and chest of the buffalo
choices: The horns and chest of the buffalo
The jaws and tail of the crocodile
The wings and beak of the eagle
The coils and head of the serpent
context: In the 'horns and chest of the buffalo' formation, the two horns swept around to encircle the enemy while the chest pressed in the centre. At Isandlwana around 20,000 Zulu overran roughly 1,800 British, colonial and native troops, killing over 1,300. A partial solar eclipse darkened the field at the height of the battle; a survivor recalled 'the camp looked dark, just as if a shadow was passing over it.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Isandlwana

question: Jean-Jacques Rousseau set out in his book of 1762, The Social Contract, to explain what could make authority legitimate. He opened with one of the most famous first lines in political thought: every person is born in one condition, he wrote, yet lives everywhere in its opposite. How did the line run after 'Man is'?
answer: born free, and everywhere he is in chains
choices: born free, and everywhere he is in chains
born equal, and everywhere he is ruled
born noble, and everywhere he is debased
born wild, and everywhere he is tamed
context: The full line runs: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' Rousseau's point was NOT that chains are natural, but that he wanted to show how authority could be made legitimate. Source: Britannica, The Social Contract; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Rousseau.

question: Rousseau published The Social Contract and Emile in 1762, and within weeks he saw both books condemned as dangerous in Paris and in Geneva. The authorities there did more than ban them. What did they do to the books in public in both cities?
answer: burned them
choices: burned them
chained them shut
stamped them counterfeit
sealed them in crates
context: Both The Social Contract and Emile were publicly burned in 1762 in Paris AND in Geneva, condemned as subversive and religiously heterodox. Source: EBSCO Research Starters, Rousseau Publishes The Social Contract; SparkNotes context.

question: Rousseau wrote Emile, a whole book on how to raise a child well, and became the great theorist of childhood's natural goodness. His own five children he sent away, each one soon after birth. Where did Rousseau send all five?
answer: to a Paris foundling hospital
choices: to a Paris foundling hospital
to a wet-nurse far from Paris
to a convent orphanage
to his mother's poor relatives
context: Rousseau handed all five of his children to a Paris foundling hospital, where in the 1700s survival was bleak -- an almost certain death sentence. The author of the era's great book on tender education abandoned his own. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Rousseau.

question: Whoever refuses to obey the general will, Rousseau wrote in The Social Contract, must be compelled to obey it by the whole community. He held that a law binds only when it expresses the general will, what the whole people wills for the common good. What striking phrase did he use for that compulsion?
answer: forced to be free
choices: forced to be free
broken to the yoke
schooled by the rod
bound to the crowd
context: Rousseau wrote that such a person may be 'forced to be free.' Revolutionaries would later seize on the line. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Rousseau.

question: Maximilien Robespierre rose in 1794 to make a speech defending the Revolution's bloodiest year. The Jacobins called Rousseau their muse, and Robespierre and Saint-Just saw themselves as building his republic of the general will. In that speech Robespierre bound two things together: one without the other, he said, is murderous, and the other without the first is powerless. Which pair did he bind?
answer: virtue and terror
choices: virtue and terror
faith and fire
duty and silence
law and exile
context: Robespierre declared 'virtue, without which terror is murderous; terror, without which virtue is powerless,' calling terror 'swift, severe, indomitable justice.' Those who resisted the general will were branded enemies and sent to the guillotine. Hegel argued Rousseau's doctrine led 'inevitably' to the Terror, though some scholars insist Rousseau himself would have condemned it. Source: Robespierre, On Political Morality, 1794; Wikipedia, General will; Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews.

question: Textile workers marched through Petrograd, the Russian capital, demanding bread on 23 February 1917. Strikers from the huge Putilov works joined them until the crowd swelled to some 200,000. The day was also a holiday kept around the world. Which holiday was it?
answer: International Women's Day
choices: International Women's Day
International Workers' Day
the Russian Orthodox New Year
the Tsar's official name-day
context: This was the start of the February Revolution. Working-class women, joined by striking workers from the giant Putilov factory, marched against bread shortages and rationing; the crowd swelled to roughly 200,000 within a day. (Petrograd was the wartime name for St. Petersburg.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_Revolution ; https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/what-was-the-february-revolution

question: Vladimir Lenin came back to Petrograd in April 1917 and squeezed his whole plan into a three-word promise, short enough for ordinary Russians to chant in the streets. What three things did he promise?
answer: Peace, Land, and Bread
choices: Peace, Land, and Bread
Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
Work, Family, Fatherland
Faith, Tsar, and Country
context: Lenin laid out this slogan, along with 'All power to the Soviets,' in his 'April Theses' right after returning from exile. It promised an end to the war, land for peasants, and food for the cities. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/politics-and-government/april-theses ; https://easy-to-read.eu/peace-land-and-bread-lenins-return-from-exile-and-the/

question: The Bolsheviks moved on the Winter Palace one night in October 1917, by which time most of its guards had drifted off, hungry and with no one to lead them. Among the last still on guard, with a few hundred young cadets, was one unit remembered ever since. Who were they?
answer: a battalion of women
choices: a battalion of women
a regiment of Cossacks
the Tsar's old palace guard
a company of foreign mercenaries
context: The 2nd Russian Women's Battalion of Death, roughly 137 to 139 women, stood among the last guards of the Winter Palace alongside a few hundred military cadets after most of the male troops had melted away. Source: https://www.thevintagenews.com/2017/01/31/the-womens-battalion-of-death-were-the-last-guards-of-the-winter-palace-during-the-bolshevik-revolution/ ; https://spartacus-educational.com/Wdeath.htm

question: Tsar Nicholas II's own generals told him in March 1917 that the army was no longer his and would not fight for him. He gave up the throne, and with him ended 300 years of Romanov rule. Where was Nicholas when he abdicated?
answer: aboard his royal train
choices: aboard his royal train
inside the Winter Palace
locked in a prison cell
on a warship at sea
context: Nicholas II abdicated on 2 March 1917 (old calendar) stranded on his imperial train at Pskov, after his generals advised him he had lost the army. His brother, Grand Duke Michael, refused the throne the next day, ending Romanov rule. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_Revolution ; https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/what-was-the-february-revolution

question: Tsar Nicholas II ordered his Petrograd garrison late in February 1917 to crush the bread riots in the capital. The Volynsky Regiment's soldiers faced that order on 27 February, and what they did next turned the tide. What did the Volynsky soldiers do?
answer: turned their guns around and joined the protesters
choices: turned their guns around and joined the protesters
opened fire and scattered the protesters
surrounded and arrested the Duma
marched out of the city to the war front
context: On 27 February (old calendar) the Volynsky Regiment mutinied and refused to fire on the crowds, pulling the Semyonovsky, Preobrazhensky, and Moskovsky regiments into the uprising. General Khabalov soon reported only about 600 infantry and 500 cavalry still loyal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_Revolution

question: Vladimir Lenin sat in exile in Zurich, Switzerland, when the Tsar fell in 1917. The Germans, eager to knock Russia out of the First World War, helped him race home to Petrograd. How did they move him across their own territory?
answer: in a sealed train
choices: in a sealed train
aboard a hospital ship
hidden on a submarine
disguised as a diplomat
context: Swiss socialist Fritz Platten brokered the deal; a chalk line on the carriage floor marked the extraterritorial 'no-man's-land' separating the Russians from their German escorts. Germany also approved millions of marks for revolutionary propaganda, much of it routed through the businessman Alexander Parvus, though historians still debate how much reached the Bolsheviks. Source: https://blog.nationalmuseum.ch/en/2017/04/by-train-to-the-revolution/ ; https://blogjamesmorris.wordpress.com/2018/11/15/german-gold-for-the-bolsheviks-an-examination/

question: Vladimir Lenin crept through Petrograd's dark streets to Bolshevik headquarters in the Smolny Institute on 24 October 1917. He wore a worker's coat, a wig that kept slipping and a dirty rag over his face to fake a toothache. What did his comrade Antonov-Ovseyenko say he looked like?
answer: a schoolmaster or a second-hand book dealer
choices: a schoolmaster or a second-hand book dealer
a soldier or a sailor home on leave
a village priest or a wandering monk
a banker or a wealthy grain merchant
context: Lenin slipped into Bolshevik HQ at the Smolny Institute in this getup to direct the coup. The Bolshevik organizer Antonov-Ovseyenko said he looked like 'a schoolmaster or a second-hand book dealer.' Source: https://lenin.shm.ru/en/v-i-lenin-in-smolny-in-makeup-october-1917/ ; https://spartacus-educational.com/RUSprovisional.htm

question: Ministers sat inside the Winter Palace on the night of 25 October 1917 as the cruiser Aurora signalled the Bolshevik attack on it. In the famous image the ship pounds the palace with its heavy guns. What did the Aurora really fire that night?
answer: a single blank shell
choices: a single blank shell
a full broadside of live rounds
a volley of signal rockets
nothing at all that night
context: At 9:40 p.m. the Aurora, crewed by mutinous sailors, fired one blank shell over the Neva River as the signal to attack. It never actually bombarded the building, contrary to the famous image. Source: https://www.historytoday.com/archive/cruiser-aurora-and-russian-revolution ; https://www.rbth.com/arts/2014/11/07/aurora_the_cruiser_that_sparked_a_revolution_or_did_it_41229.html

question: The Bolsheviks seized Petrograd's key buildings in October 1917 in a tight, planned grab, no huge people's uprising, while Vladimir Lenin kept out of sight until the last hours. Who ran the operation, as chairman of the Petrograd Soviet's Military Revolutionary Committee?
answer: Leon Trotsky
choices: Leon Trotsky
Joseph Stalin
Alexander Kerensky
Grigory Zinoviev
context: Trotsky ran the Military Revolutionary Committee that planned and directed the insurrection while Lenin stayed hidden until the last moment. The 'storming' that followed was nearly bloodless; the Provisional Government's ministers were simply arrested in the palace and jailed in the Peter and Paul Fortress. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution

question: Anatoli Zheleznyakov, an anarchist sailor, commanded the guard when Russia's Constituent Assembly, the parliament chosen in the country's first free national vote, met in January 1918. Its deputies defied the Bolsheviks through a single thirteen-hour session. Then Zheleznyakov closed the assembly for good with one short sentence. What did he say?
answer: "The guard is tired."
choices: "The guard is tired."
"By order of the Soviet, disperse."
"This session is now over."
"Long live the revolution."
context: When the assembly refused Bolshevik demands and elected the Socialist-Revolutionary Viktor Chernov as its president, Zheleznyakov ended Russia's democratic experiment with this line. The Bolsheviks then locked the doors, and the assembly never met again. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoli_Zhelezniakov ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Constituent_Assembly

question: Lenin's Bolsheviks allowed a free national election, Russia's first, in November 1917, weeks after they seized power, and some 47 million people voted. The result undercut the Bolsheviks' claim to speak for the people. Which party won the most seats?
answer: the Socialist-Revolutionaries
choices: the Socialist-Revolutionaries
the Bolsheviks
the Mensheviks
the Constitutional Democrats
context: The Socialist-Revolutionaries won with 324 seats (about 37.6%); Lenin's Bolsheviks came second with 183 seats (about 23%). The Bolsheviks were a minority faction, which is why they dissolved the elected assembly by force weeks later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1917_Russian_Constituent_Assembly_election

question: Bolshevik fighters arrested the ministers inside the Winter Palace in October 1917, at the end of a nearly bloodless night. The famous picture of that night shows surging crowds storming the palace under blazing guns. Where did that heroic image mostly come from?
answer: a 1927 movie by Sergei Eisenstein
choices: a 1927 movie by Sergei Eisenstein
a 1930 painting by Isaak Brodsky
a 1925 newsreel by Dziga Vertov
a 1928 poem by Vladimir Mayakovsky
context: The dramatic image comes largely from Sergei Eisenstein's 1927-28 film 'October' and a 1920 mass re-enactment watched by about 100,000 people, both of which used more men, more ordnance, and produced more injuries than the real 1917 event. Myth literally replaced the memory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October:_Ten_Days_That_Shook_the_World ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Storming_of_the_Winter_Palace

question: Andrei Sakharov led the design of the Soviet hydrogen bomb. A scaled-up version burst over the Arctic in October 1961 with a force of 50 megatons, and it is still the most powerful bomb ever exploded. What is that bomb called?
answer: Tsar Bomba
choices: Tsar Bomba
Fat Man
Castle Bravo
Little Boy
context: Sakharov's 'Third Idea' (using radiation to symmetrically compress the fusion fuel) was first tested as RDS-37 in 1955; the scaled-up Tsar Bomba reached 50 megatons. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Sakharov

question: A vast crowd packed Prague's Wenceslas Square at six in the evening on 25 November 1989, in the days of the Velvet Revolution in Czechoslovakia. Hundreds of thousands of people did one thing together to say goodbye to the communist regime. What did they do?
answer: Jingled their keys
choices: Jingled their keys
Lit white candles
Threw down flowers
Stood in total silence
context: The jingling keys symbolized unlocking the regime's doors and ringing it a bell to say 'Goodbye.' Source: https://www.expats.cz/czech-news/article/unlocking-freedom-why-did-czechs-jingle-their-keys-during-the-velvet-revolution

question: Andrei Sakharov won the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize as 'a spokesman for the conscience of mankind,' but the Soviet government would not let him travel to Oslo to receive it. Someone else stood up in Oslo and read his Nobel lecture for him. Who read it?
answer: His wife
choices: His wife
His daughter
A diplomat
The chairman
context: His wife was Yelena Bonner, his partner in dissent; he later staged hunger strikes to force the regime to let her travel abroad for heart surgery. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/peace/1975/sakharov/facts/

question: Vaclav Havel ended a speech in Prague on 10 December 1989 by naming the creed he said the Velvet Revolution stood on. That revolution had just ended forty years of communist rule without a shot fired, and his line is now carved on memorials across the country. What was the line?
answer: Truth and love must prevail over lies and hatred
choices: Truth and love must prevail over lies and hatred
Workers of the world must unite against their masters
Liberty and equality must be won by fraternity
Peace and bread and land must be given to the people
context: Havel made non-violence and honesty the creed of the Velvet Revolution. Source: https://www.nybooks.com/online/2009/11/24/love-and-truth-vaclav-havel-in-bratislava/

question: Vaclav Havel started out shifting scenery in a Prague theatre before he wrote absurd comedies of his own. In The Memorandum, staged in 1965, he made fun of communist office life with one invention that every clerk in the play had to master. What was it?
answer: A fake bureaucratic language no one could actually speak
choices: A fake bureaucratic language no one could actually speak
A dance every worker had to perform daily
A math test required to enter any office
A list of songs everyone sang before work
context: Havel started as a stagehand at Prague's Theatre on the Balustrade before writing The Garden Party (1963) and The Memorandum (1965). Source: https://english.radio.cz/czech-books-you-must-read-8506310/13

question: Communist deputies, the men whose regime had jailed Vaclav Havel, still packed Czechoslovakia's Federal Assembly on 29 December 1989 when they voted on whether to make him president. Havel had gone from a prison cell toward Prague Castle in a single year. How did the vote go?
answer: Unanimous, with not one vote against
choices: Unanimous, with not one vote against
A slim majority squeaked him through
A deadlocked tie the chairman broke
A first-ballot rejection, then a retry
context: Not a single vote against and no abstentions - the assembly that had imprisoned him elected him unanimously. Source: https://english.radio.cz/december-29-1989-vaclav-havel-elected-president-first-time-8838384

question: Vaclav Havel and others wrote Charter 77, a manifesto for human rights, in outrage at one trial in 1976. The regime had jailed the members of a long-haired underground rock band for 'extreme vulgarity with an antisocialist impact.' Which band was it?
answer: The Plastic People of the Universe
choices: The Plastic People of the Universe
The masked riot-punks Pussy Riot
The New York band Velvet Underground
The metal act Rage Against the Machine
context: Outrage at jailing musicians for their music galvanized intellectuals; Charter 77 was published January 6, 1977 with 242 founding signatories. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_77

question: A KGB officer and two electricians came to Andrei Sakharov's flat in Gorky one December evening in 1986 and fitted a telephone, without a word about why. The regime had banished him to that closed city for condemning the invasion of Afghanistan. The next day the phone rang. Who was on the line?
answer: Mikhail Gorbachev, ending his exile
choices: Mikhail Gorbachev, ending his exile
A KGB interrogator, with new threats
An American reporter, seeking a quote
His old bomb-lab director, pleading
context: Gorbachev personally told Sakharov he could return to Moscow; Sakharov immediately used the call to press him to free other prisoners of conscience. Source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1986/12/19/Freedom-came-with-a-phone-call/9238535352400/

question: Andrei Sakharov, by then an elected deputy, rested at home on 14 December 1989 before going back to the Congress to fight the Communist Party's monopoly on power. He died of heart failure that evening. What had he just told Yelena Bonner, his companion in dissent?
answer: Tomorrow will be a battle
choices: Tomorrow will be a battle
I have done all my duty
Let me sleep a while now
The long work is finished
context: He died still in the fight, expecting to argue against one-party rule the next day. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2002/12/death-andrei-sakharov-1989

question: Vaclav Havel sat in prison in 1979, allowed to write home to Olga just one letter of four pages a week, with no cross-outs, no quotation marks, no foreign words, no underlining and no humour. For which single act of defiance did his jailers throw him into solitary?
answer: Defending an illiterate Roma prisoner
choices: Defending an illiterate Roma prisoner
Hiding a sharpened spoon in his boot
Refusing to put on the prison uniform
Leading the inmates in a hunger strike
context: He was thrown in solitary for writing on behalf of an illiterate Roma fellow prisoner; those restricted weekly letters were later published as the book 'Letters to Olga.' Source: https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/02/06/vaclav-havel-letters-to-olga/

question: Andrei Sakharov ran past his time at the microphone at the first Congress of People's Deputies, the new Soviet parliament, in June 1989. Mikhail Gorbachev switched off his microphone and snapped, 'Time's up. Don't you respect the Congress?' How did Sakharov answer him?
answer: Yes, but I respect the country and the people more
choices: Yes, but I respect the country and the people more
Yes, but the truth will not be hurried by a clock
No, for this Congress has not yet earned my respect
No, and history will remember who silenced me here
context: The exchange captured Sakharov's stance: institutions answer to the people, not the reverse. Source: https://time.com/archive/6702744/ussr-presiding-over-a-new-soviet-congress-gorbachev-gets-a-clamorous-lesson-in-democracy/

question: Andrei Sakharov stood at the banquet after his bomb's successful test in 1955 and raised a toast of his own. A Soviet marshal cut him off with a crude parable and toasted instead to using the weapons in war. Sakharov later said the feelings of that night never left him. What had his toast shown was waking in him?
answer: A conscience about the weapon he had built
choices: A conscience about the weapon he had built
A secret wish to defect to the West
Regret that the bomb was still too small
Pride at having beaten the Americans
context: Sakharov wrote that the emotions kindled that night 'completely altered my thinking' and never diminished - the seed of the dissident he became. Source: https://blog.nuclearsecrecy.com/2014/01/31/sakharovs-turning-point-first-soviet-h-bomb-test/

question: Saladin fought the Crusaders in the late 1100s and won respect from friend and foe alike for his mercy. 'Saladin' was only the Crusaders' way of clipping Salah ad-Din, a title of honour he had earned defending Islam. What does the title mean?
answer: Righteousness of the Faith
choices: Righteousness of the Faith
Sword of the Prophet
Lion of the Desert
Shadow of the Caliph
context: His full name was al-Nasir Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub; he was an ethnic Kurd born around 1137 in Tikrit, in modern Iraq. 'Salah ad-Din' means 'Righteousness of the Faith,' which Europeans clipped to 'Saladin.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saladin

question: Saladin's army crushed the Crusaders at Hattin, in the hills above the Sea of Galilee, on 4 July 1187. The thirst-maddened Christians had carried their holiest relic at the head of their column, guarded by the bishop of Acre. Saladin's men killed the bishop and seized it. What was the relic?
answer: the True Cross
choices: the True Cross
the Spear of Longinus
the Crown of Thorns
the Ark of the Covenant
context: The relic was believed to be wood from the cross of Jesus. After Hattin it was reportedly fixed upside-down on a lance and paraded to Damascus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: Saladin's officials opened his personal treasury after his death at Damascus in 1193. He had given away so much of his wealth to the poor that his own treasurers used to hide money from him, so that he would have something left to spend. What did the officials find?
answer: one gold coin and forty-seven silver pieces
choices: one gold coin and forty-seven silver pieces
one full chest of jewels and gold bars
gold enough to ransom a hundred knights
one hidden hoard of two thousand dinars
context: His treasury held only one piece of Tyre gold and forty-seven dirhams of silver, not even enough to pay for his own funeral. His treasurers had learned to hide reserves, because he gave away anything he found out about. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Saladin/

question: Reynald of Chatillon held the desert castle of Kerak, high over the caravan roads to Mecca. In 1187 he broke a shaky truce with Saladin: he ambushed a wealthy Muslim caravan, robbed and killed its people, and refused Saladin's demand to give the goods back. How did Saladin answer the broken truce?
answer: he swore a personal oath to kill Reynald himself
choices: he swore a personal oath to kill Reynald himself
he demanded twice the caravan's value in gold
he appealed to the king of Jerusalem for justice
he ordered a blockade of the Crusader ports
context: Reynald had already enraged Saladin years earlier by raiding pilgrim ships bound for Mecca and Medina. The caravan seizure made it personal, and Saladin vowed to kill him with his own hand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynald_of_Ch%C3%A2tillon

question: Saladin trapped the Crusader army in July 1187 on dry, high ground beside the twin-peaked Horns of Hattin, after taking the springs. His warriors kept up their drumming and chanting through the night while the trapped knights burned with thirst. What did Saladin's men do at dawn?
answer: set the dry grass alight so smoke blinded them
choices: set the dry grass alight so smoke blinded them
loosed a cavalry charge straight up the slope
rolled boulders down from the twin peaks
poisoned the muddy pools left within their reach
context: Saladin's men had beaten drums and chanted through the night; at dawn they fired the dry grass so the smoke blinded and choked the thirst-maddened knights. The Crusader army was destroyed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: Saladin retook Jerusalem in October 1187 and let its Christian people buy their freedom with a ransom instead of putting them to the sword. A man's freedom cost ten dinars. How did the price change for a woman and for a child?
answer: cheaper still, five dinars and two
choices: cheaper still, five dinars and two
the same ten dinars for everyone
free for women, ten for children
double for women, triple for children
context: The ransom was 10 dinars per man, 5 per woman, and 2 per child. The deliberately low, sliding price was a contrast with what had happened when the Crusaders first took the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(1187)

question: King Guy of Lusignan sat as Saladin's prisoner in the sultan's tent after Hattin in 1187, beside Reynald of Chatillon, the lord who had broken a truce by raiding Muslim caravans. Saladin offered Guy a cup of iced rose-water. Guy drank and passed the cup to Reynald. Why did Saladin refuse to let Reynald drink from it?
answer: so the laws of hospitality would not protect Reynald from him
choices: so the laws of hospitality would not protect Reynald from him
because the cup was meant only for a crowned king
because Reynald had insulted him by reaching for it
so that Guy would be forced to watch his ally die
context: By custom, a prisoner offered food or drink by his captor could not then be killed. Saladin said, 'I did not ask this evil man to drink,' and struck Reynald down himself, fulfilling his oath. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: Saladin held about 200 captured knights and lords in his camp after his victory at Hattin in July 1187. He spared King Guy of Lusignan, ruler of the Crusader kingdom of Jerusalem, yet he ordered death for one group of his prisoners above all. Which prisoners did he have beheaded?
answer: the Templar and Hospitaller knights
choices: the Templar and Hospitaller knights
the foot-soldiers who had fled
the priests who blessed the army
the lords who had broken the truce
context: Saladin saw the military-order knights as his most implacable enemies and had them beheaded, sparing only the Templar Grand Master. King Guy he kept alive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: Saladin had the golden cross torn down from the top of the Dome of the Rock after Jerusalem surrendered to him in October 1187. Next door stood the Al-Aqsa Mosque; the Crusaders had used it as a palace for nearly ninety years, and one wing of it as stables. How did Saladin have Al-Aqsa made ready for Muslim worship again?
answer: washed with rose-water and recarpeted
choices: washed with rose-water and recarpeted
torn down and rebuilt from the foundation
sealed shut for a year of mourning
painted over with the sultan's banners
context: Saladin had Al-Aqsa ritually washed with rose-water, recarpeted, and re-decorated with Quranic verse to restore it as a mosque after decades of Crusader use. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1553/saladins-conquest-of-jerusalem-1187-ce/

question: The knights of the First Crusade stormed Jerusalem in July 1099. When Saladin took the city back in October 1187 he spared its people, and by the old accounts that set the two moments side by side, his mercy shone all the brighter. What had the knights of 1099 done?
answer: massacred Muslims and Jews across the city
choices: massacred Muslims and Jews across the city
levied a heavy yearly tribute on the city
expelled every non-Christian from the walls
burned the markets but spared the people
context: The 1099 accounts describe Crusaders killing Muslims and Jews even as they sheltered in the Al-Aqsa Mosque. Many modern historians think the toll was exaggerated, but those accounts set the contrast Saladin's restraint was measured against. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_Jerusalem_(1099)

question: Balian of Ibelin bargained for Jerusalem's surrender in September 1187 as the city's last Christian commander, with Saladin's army at the walls. Saladin, remembering what the Crusaders had done in the same city in 1099, swore to take it by the sword. Balian answered with one terrible counter-threat, and Saladin agreed to a ransom instead. What did Balian threaten?
answer: to destroy the Muslim holy places and kill the Muslim prisoners
choices: to destroy the Muslim holy places and kill the Muslim prisoners
to hold the city until a Crusader relief army arrived
to poison the wells before the gates were opened
to surrender only to Saladin's rival in Damascus
context: Balian threatened that the defenders would burn the city's treasures, kill their 5,000 Muslim prisoners, and destroy the holy places including the Dome of the Rock. Only then did Saladin agree to ransom the inhabitants. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1553/saladins-conquest-of-jerusalem-1187-ce/

question: Some of Saladin's own emirs urged him to raze the Church of the Holy Sepulchre after he took Jerusalem in October 1187. It stood over the place where Christians believed the tomb of Jesus had lain, and it was their holiest shrine on earth. Saladin refused to destroy it. What did he do with the church instead?
answer: let Christians keep visiting it for a fee
choices: let Christians keep visiting it for a fee
converted it into a second mosque
gave it to his brother as a prize
stripped its gold and sealed the doors
context: Against his generals' wishes, Saladin refused to destroy the church and let Christians keep visiting, and he permitted native Christians and Jews to go on living in the city. Source: https://www.historyhit.com/saladin-re-enters-jerusalem/

question: Minstrels sang of the reckless charges of Richard I of England before he ever sailed east on the Third Crusade. The huge, fearless king loved fighting far more than governing, and in his own lifetime he already had a nickname. What was Richard called?
answer: the Lionheart
choices: the Lionheart
the Hammer
the Unready
the Conqueror
context: Coeur de Lion. The troubadour Bertran de Born was praising Richard's lion-like valor in verse as early as the 1180s, before he ever left for the Holy Land; the name is first recorded in Ambroise's chronicle 'L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_I_of_England

question: Saladin, who ruled Egypt and Syria, sent a gift across the lines in 1191 to his enemy King Richard I of England, who lay sick with a raging fever in the desert heat outside Acre. What did Saladin send the sick king?
answer: snow from the mountains and fresh fruit
choices: snow from the mountains and fresh fruit
a flask of healing waters
warm furs and spiced wine
a chest of gold and fine silk
context: Richard's fever was severe, possibly scurvy. Saladin sent fresh fruit and snow carried down from the mountains to cool him, and is reported to have offered his own personal physician. It is the wonder-moment of honor reaching across the religious line. Source: https://templarblog.com/blogs/media-and-culture-of-knights-templar/saladin-richard-the-lionheart-meeting

question: Saladin sent for King Guy of Lusignan, his exhausted prisoner, after the battle of Hattin in July 1187, and handed him rose-water cooled with snow from Mount Hermon. As Guy drank, Saladin reassured him with one short line. What did Saladin say?
answer: Kings do not kill kings.
choices: Kings do not kill kings.
Drink, and be my servant.
Your sword is mine now.
Kneel, and keep your crown.
context: Among Saladin's people, offering a captured enemy a drink was a gesture meaning his life was safe. He reassured Guy with words recorded as 'it is not the wont of kings to kill kings.' He spared the ordinary king. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: King Richard I of England lost his horse in the thick of the fighting at Jaffa in 1192 and fought on foot among the enemy. Saladin's brother al-Adil, Saphadin to the Crusaders, watched from the enemy side. What did al-Adil send out to the king?
answer: two fine Arab warhorses
choices: two fine Arab warhorses
a flag of truce
a cup of cold water
his own bodyguard
context: Al-Adil, whom the Crusaders called Saphadin, saw Richard unhorsed and sent him two fine Arab horses in the middle of the battle. Richard accepted them as a gift between worthy enemies. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Jaffa_(1192)

question: Crusader knights marched into battle at Hattin on 4 July 1187 behind a piece of the True Cross, believed to be wood from the cross on which Jesus died. Saladin's army routed them and captured the relic on the field. What did Saladin's men do with it on the road back to Damascus?
answer: fixed it upside-down on a lance and paraded it
choices: fixed it upside-down on a lance and paraded it
locked it away inside a golden shrine in Damascus
burned it in front of the captured Christian soldiers
buried it deep beneath the great city walls
context: According to the chroniclers, the captured relic was fixed upside-down on a lance and paraded in triumph to Damascus. The Kingdom of Jerusalem never got it back. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hattin

question: Christian knights of the First Crusade killed people in Jerusalem's streets by the thousands when they took the city in 1099, Muslim, Jewish and even native Christian. Saladin took Jerusalem back in October 1187, after it surrendered to him. What did he do with the Christian people still inside the walls?
answer: he spared the city and let its people ransom their freedom
choices: he spared the city and let its people ransom their freedom
he razed the walls and sold every survivor into slavery
he put the entire garrison and clergy to the sword
he burned the Christian quarter down to its foundations
context: Saladin's recapture was nearly bloodless, a deliberate and famous contrast to the 1099 slaughter. The ransom was set at 10 dinars per man, 5 per woman, and 2 per child; when many could not pay, Saladin and his brother al-Adil let thousands of the poor go free. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(1187)

question: King Richard I of England, desperate to end the war without further slaughter, floated an astonishing plan for peace: instead of fighting on for Jerusalem, the two sides would let a married royal couple rule the city together. Whom did Richard propose should marry?
answer: his sister Joan to Saladin's brother al-Adil
choices: his sister Joan to Saladin's brother al-Adil
his niece Eleanor to the Byzantine emperor's son
his cousin Constance to a prince of Antioch
his ward Isabella to Saladin's son al-Afdal
context: Richard proposed marrying his own sister Joan to al-Adil and letting the couple rule Jerusalem together. In a letter dated 12 November 1191 he begged off, saying 'The Christian people disapprove of my giving my sister in marriage without consulting the Pope' (recorded by Roger of Hoveden). Source: https://medieval.substack.com/p/the-letters-of-richard-and-saladin

question: Richard I of England took Acre in 1191, but Saladin was slow to pay the ransom he had agreed to. His patience worn through, Richard had some 2,700 Muslim prisoners marched out to the hill of Ayyadieh. What did he do to them there?
answer: had them all beheaded in sight of Saladin's army
choices: had them all beheaded in sight of Saladin's army
sold them into slavery to recover his losses
marched them back to Acre to labor on the walls
held them all for a second, far larger ransom
context: On 20 August 1191 about 2,700 Muslim prisoners were beheaded at Ayyadieh where Saladin's men could see, and Saladin retaliated by executing his own Christian captives. The two 'chivalrous' rivals were also capable of mass slaughter. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_at_Ayyadieh

question: Delegates from the world's governments met at a radio conference in 1906 and agreed on one distress call for ships in trouble at sea: SOS, in Morse code. They chose it because its pattern was short, even and almost impossible to mistake for any other signal. What is the SOS signal in Morse?
answer: three dots, three dashes, three dots
choices: three dots, three dashes, three dots
one long dash repeated nine times
a dot and a dash, over and over
five dots followed by five dashes
context: ... --- ... — three dots, three dashes, three dots. The simple, even rhythm is what made it almost impossible to garble or confuse with ordinary message traffic. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_code

question: Alfred Vail walked into the office of a Morristown newspaper in New Jersey while he and Samuel Morse were building their code. He wanted the commonest letters in English to get the shortest signals, so he counted something the printers kept on hand. What did Vail count?
answer: how many metal type pieces they had of each letter
choices: how many metal type pieces they had of each letter
how many newspapers were printed each day
how many words fit on a single page
how many letters were in the alphabet
context: Printers stocked far more of the letters they used most, so Vail's tally told him which letters mattered. That is why E, the most common English letter, gets the shortest signal of all — a single dot. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_code

question: Tokugawa Iemitsu ran Japan's armies, taxes, roads and castles in 1635 out of his fortress city of Edo, today's Tokyo, while the emperor sat in Kyoto as a sacred figurehead. What title did Iemitsu hold as Japan's real ruler?
answer: The shogun
choices: The shogun
The emperor
The daimyo
The samurai
context: Under the Tokugawa system the emperor reigned in name from Kyoto while the shogun -- the supreme military ruler -- held the real power. The man who reigned was not the man who ruled. Source: japanesesword.net 'Life in Feudal Japan'; Britannica.

question: A samurai walked out with two swords at his belt, the long katana and the shorter wakizashi, and anyone who saw the pair knew him for a warrior. The law forbade farmers, merchants and Buddhist monks to wear both together. What was the two-sword pair called?
answer: The daisho
choices: The daisho
The tatara
The hagakure
The sankin
context: Only samurai could wear the daisho -- 'big-little' -- the matched katana and wakizashi. The two-sword pair was a badge of rank no commoner was allowed to carry. Source: Wikipedia 'Daisho'; samurai-katana-shop.nl.

question: A disgraced samurai of feudal Japan knelt in his robes for seppuku, the ritual suicide his lord had sentenced him to: he would cut open his own belly with a short sword. Behind him stood his second, a trusted swordsman called the kaishakunin. What did the kaishakunin do the moment the cut was made?
answer: Struck off the dying man's head
choices: Struck off the dying man's head
Bound the dying man's wound
Handed him the short sword
Recited the death poem aloud
context: The kaishakunin stood behind the condemned samurai and beheaded him the moment the cut was made -- a mercy stroke that demanded great skill. Seppuku spared samurai the disgrace of execution by a common headsman, and was practiced until 1873. Source: Wikipedia 'Kaishakunin'; Britannica 'seppuku'.

question: Tokugawa Iemitsu, who ruled Japan from his castle city of Edo, ordered in 1635 that every daimyo, every great warrior lord in the land, live in Edo every other year. Each lord paid for two grand homes and costly parades between them, and Iemitsu meant to keep them all too weak to rebel. What did a daimyo have to leave behind in Edo when he went home to his province?
answer: His wife and heir, as hostages
choices: His wife and heir, as hostages
His swords and armor
Half of his rice harvest
His personal bodyguard
context: Under sankin-kotai ('alternate attendance'), the daimyo's wife and heir stayed in Edo as permanent hostages while he shuttled back and forth, bankrupted by the double cost. Rebel, and your family died first. Source: Wikipedia 'Sankin-kotai'; academic.mu.edu.

question: Oishi Kuranosuke led the forty-seven samurai left lordless after their master, Asano, was forced to commit seppuku, and they swore revenge on Asano's enemy, Kira. To make Kira's spies believe he had given up, Oishi spent over a year living a lie. What was Oishi's cover?
answer: Playing a drunken wastrel in the pleasure quarters
choices: Playing a drunken wastrel in the pleasure quarters
Becoming a monk in a mountain temple
Hiring himself out as a common farmer
Fleeing Japan aboard a merchant ship
context: Oishi spent over a year acting as a drunkard in the pleasure quarters of Kyoto so Kira's spies would think the ronin had given up. Then on the snowy night of January 30, 1703, the 47 stormed Kira's Edo mansion and killed him. The shogun praised their loyalty -- then ordered all 47 to commit seppuku. Source: Britannica '47 ronin'; Wikipedia.

question: Yamamoto Tsunetomo, a retired samurai, dictated the Hagakure to a scribe around 1709, in the long peace of the Edo years. It became bushido's best-known text, and it begins: 'The Way of the Samurai is found in death.' What was true of Yamamoto himself?
answer: He had never fought in a real battle
choices: He had never fought in a real battle
He had been exiled for cowardice
He could not read or write
He was not himself a samurai
context: Bushido was largely codified and idealized during the peaceful Edo period (1600-1868), when warfare had nearly vanished -- written by administrators looking back, not men fighting wars. Tsunetomo dictated the Hagakure having never seen a real battle, and the book was then forgotten for two centuries before being revived around 1900. Source: Wikipedia 'Hagakure'; the-pamphlet.com 'bushido'.

question: John Burgoyne marched a British army south from Canada in the summer of 1777, hoping to cut the rebel colonies in two. American forces under Horatio Gates cornered him at Saratoga in New York, and on 17 October Burgoyne surrendered his entire army. Why did the news shock every royal court in Europe?
answer: No entire British field army had ever surrendered to anyone, anywhere
choices: No entire British field army had ever surrendered to anyone, anywhere
Burgoyne was the king's own cousin and heir to the throne
The British had never before lost a battle on American soil
Saratoga was the largest army Britain had ever put in the field
context: It was the first time in history a complete British field army laid down its arms — Burgoyne surrendered on October 17, 1777. Source: American Battlefield Trust, '10 Facts: The Battle of Saratoga' (battlefields.org).

question: Benjamin Franklin pressed the American cause in Paris, where France had been quietly cheering the rebels while staying out of open war. News of Burgoyne's surrender at Saratoga reached the city in December 1777, and the French moved fast. What did France do in February 1778?
answer: Signed a formal alliance and entered the war openly on America's side
choices: Signed a formal alliance and entered the war openly on America's side
Sent a private loan of gold but kept its troops and fleet at home
Demanded Canada from Britain as the price of staying neutral
Offered to mediate a peace that would keep the colonies British
context: News reached Paris on December 4, 1777; foreign minister Vergennes moved fast, and France signed the Treaty of Alliance and the Treaty of Amity and Commerce on February 6, 1778 — secured by Benjamin Franklin's diplomacy. That is what Saratoga DID: it brought France in. Source: U.S. State Dept Office of the Historian, 'French Alliance' (history.state.gov).

question: Sargon of Akkad's mother sealed her baby in a basket with tar and set it on the Euphrates, the legend on a clay tablet says, because as a priestess she dared not admit she had a son. In the story a gardener named Akki found him and raised the boy, who became the world's first emperor. Over a thousand years later, a nearly identical tale was told of which baby?
answer: Moses, drawn from the Nile
choices: Moses, drawn from the Nile
Romulus, suckled by the wolf
Cyrus, left on the mountain
Oedipus, exposed on the hillside
context: Sargon's birth legend, recorded on a clay tablet kept in the Library of Ashurbanipal, predates the story of baby Moses in the bulrushes by over a thousand years. It is told here as legend, not forensic fact. Source: worldhistory.org/Sargon_of_Akkad; The Legend of Sargon (clay tablet).

question: Sargon of Akkad made his daughter high priestess of the moon god Nanna at the city of Ur. There she composed hymns to the goddess Inanna, roughly 4,300 years ago and long before Homer. What is Sargon's daughter remembered as today?
answer: The world's first author known by name
choices: The world's first author known by name
The first queen to rule alone
The first woman to read and write
The first priestess of any temple
context: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon, signed works such as 'The Exaltation of Inanna,' making her the earliest author in history whose name we know. Her image and the words 'Enheduanna... daughter of Sargon, king of the world' survive on a carved calcite disk dug up at Ur by Sir Leonard Woolley in 1927. Source: worldhistory.org/Enheduanna; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enheduanna.

question: Scipio carried Rome's war to Africa and faced the Carthaginian general who had ravaged Italy for fifteen years, a man whose name Roman mothers used to frighten their children. Scipio beat him at Zama, near Carthage, in 202 BC. Whom did he beat?
answer: Hannibal
choices: Hannibal
Masinissa
Pyrrhus
Cato
context: Zama (202 BC) was the decisive battle of the Second Punic War. Scipio beat Hannibal on Hannibal's own home ground near Carthage. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama

question: Scipio faced eighty Carthaginian war elephants at Zama in 202 BC, lined up to smash the Roman front. He did not meet them with a solid wall: he opened wide corridors between his units and made his men sound trumpets and bang their weapons on their shields. What did the panicked elephants do?
answer: They bolted harmlessly down the empty lanes
choices: They bolted harmlessly down the empty lanes
They knelt down and refused to move
They charged straight through the Roman line
They swam back across the river
context: The noise terrified the elephants, which stampeded down the corridors Scipio had left open; some even turned and trampled Hannibal's own cavalry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama

question: Scipio brought a surprise to Zama in 202 BC: fast Numidian horsemen, the very kind the Carthaginians had once used to beat Roman armies, now rode for Rome. They swept the Carthaginian cavalry off the field and hit the foot soldiers from behind. Which Numidian king led them?
answer: King Masinissa
choices: King Masinissa
King Pyrrhus
King Polybius
King Aemilianus
context: Masinissa's Numidian cavalry turned the battle: the very kind of horsemen Hannibal had once used to destroy Roman armies now broke his own. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama

question: Cato the Elder, decades after Zama, ended every speech he made in the Roman Senate with the same line, even in a dull debate about the city's sewers. What line did Cato tack on at the end?
answer: 'Carthage must be destroyed'
choices: 'Carthage must be destroyed'
'Rome was not built in a day'
'Let the consuls decide'
'The Senate has spoken'
context: In Latin: 'Ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam.' Cato repeated it relentlessly until his side won the argument for war. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthago_delenda_est

question: Roman senators watched Cato the Elder let a ripe fig fall from the folds of his toga in the middle of a debate. He wanted them to see that Carthage was still a thriving and dangerous rival. As they admired the fig's size, what did Cato tell them about it?
answer: It had grown only three days' sail from Rome
choices: It had grown only three days' sail from Rome
It had been blessed by the gods of Carthage
It was the last fig left in all of Italy
It had been sent as a gift by Hannibal's heirs
context: The point: a country rich enough to grow such fruit, and close enough to reach in three days, was no spent force. Plutarch tells the fig story in his Life of Cato. Source: Plutarch, Cato 27, https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:2008.01.0013:chapter=27

question: Roman troops fought their way through Carthage in 146 BC, street by street, at the end of a three-year siege, under the command of Scipio Aemilianus. The city burned, and its people were sold into slavery. What was Scipio Aemilianus to the Scipio who had won at Zama?
answer: His adopted grandson
choices: His adopted grandson
His older brother
His battlefield rival
His Carthaginian hostage
context: Scipio Aemilianus was the adopted grandson of Scipio Africanus. The family that began the war's end at Zama also delivered Carthage's final destruction in 146 BC. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War , https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/scipio-aemilianus/

question: Scipio Aemilianus wept as Carthage burned in 146 BC. Standing beside his friend, the historian Polybius, he recited Homer's verses about doomed Troy: 'A day will come when sacred Troy shall perish.' He told Polybius he feared the same fate would one day fall on which city?
answer: Rome itself
choices: Rome itself
Athens
Alexandria
Jerusalem
context: Polybius was an eyewitness and recorded the moment. Scipio Aemilianus feared Rome, too, would someday meet Carthage's end. Source: Polybius, via https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/scipio-aemilianus/

question: Scipio Aemilianus razed Carthage in 146 BC, and its people were sold into slavery. Later writers added that Roman soldiers ploughed the ground and salted it so that nothing would ever grow there again. What do historians conclude about the salt story?
answer: No ancient source mentions it; it is likely a 19th-century invention
choices: No ancient source mentions it; it is likely a 19th-century invention
Roman soldiers really did spread tons of salt over the ruins
Hannibal's heirs salted the fields themselves in revenge
Cato ordered the salting in his final Senate speech
context: The salt legend appears in no ancient writer. The plain ancient record is harsh enough on its own: the city was burned and its people enslaved. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War

question: Elizabeth Cady Stanton wrote a Declaration of Sentiments for the Seneca Falls convention of July 1848, and she shaped it on Thomas Jefferson's Declaration of Independence. She took Jefferson's most famous line, 'all men are created equal,' and added two words. Which two?
answer: 'and women'
choices: 'and women'
'and equal'
'and free'
'and slaves'
context: Stanton's line read 'all men and women are created equal.' By adding two words to the most famous sentence in American politics, she claimed the founders' own natural-rights principle for women rather than rejecting it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_Sentiments

question: Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton arrived at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls on the morning of 19 July 1848 to open the first women's rights convention in America. The door was locked, and no one had a key. How did the organisers get inside?
answer: They boosted a boy through an open window to unbar the door from within
choices: They boosted a boy through an open window to unbar the door from within
They broke the lock with a stone from the road
They moved the whole convention to a nearby barn
They waited until a passing carpenter cut a new key
context: Stanton's eleven-year-old nephew, Daniel Cady Eaton, was lifted through an open window and opened the door from inside. Source: https://home.nps.gov/wori/learn/historyculture/harriet-cady-eaton.htm

question: James Mott, Lucretia Mott's husband, took the chair when the Seneca Falls convention opened in July 1848, though the women alone had planned every detail of the two-day meeting. Why did the organisers hand the chair to a man?
answer: In 1848 none of them thought it proper for a woman to run a public meeting
choices: In 1848 none of them thought it proper for a woman to run a public meeting
James Mott was the only one who had memorized the rules of order
The chapel owners required a male chairman to let them use the hall
The local sheriff would only permit the meeting under a man's name
context: James Mott presided because, even among these reformers, it was not yet considered proper in 1848 for a woman to chair a public meeting. The convention was claiming a right its own organizers had not yet fully exercised. Source: https://www.nps.gov/wori/learn/historyculture/convention-officers-and-committees.htm

question: The delegates at Seneca Falls in July 1848 passed every resolution unanimously except the one demanding the vote for women, and it nearly failed. Then one man rose and argued for it, calling the denial of the vote to women a crippling of half the moral and intellectual power of the government of the world. Who was he?
answer: Frederick Douglass, the formerly enslaved abolitionist
choices: Frederick Douglass, the formerly enslaved abolitionist
James Mott, the convention's presiding officer
Henry Stanton, Elizabeth's husband
Daniel Eaton, who had opened the chapel door
context: Douglass, a formerly enslaved man and the only Black person present, edited the abolitionist paper The North Star, whose masthead read 'Right is of no Sex — Truth is of no Color.' He made the same natural-rights case for women that he made for himself. Source: https://utahwomenshistory.org/2018/10/the-suffrage-resolution-at-seneca-falls/

question: Elizabeth Cady Stanton insisted on putting a demand for the vote into the Declaration of Sentiments in 1848. Even her ally Lucretia Mott begged her to drop it, warning, 'Why Lizzie, thee will make us ridiculous.' Stanton kept it in. What was her argument for keeping it?
answer: The ballot was the right that secured all the others
choices: The ballot was the right that secured all the others
The newspapers would ignore a convention with no bold demand
Property rights meant nothing without a man's consent
The other resolutions were too weak to stand on their own
context: Mott feared the suffrage demand would make the movement a laughingstock — and the press did mock it fiercely. But Stanton held that the vote was the right that protected every other right, so she kept it in. Source: https://utahwomenshistory.org/2018/10/the-suffrage-resolution-at-seneca-falls/

question: Charlotte Woodward, a 19-year-old glovemaker who sewed at home for pennies and wanted the right to keep her own pay, signed the Declaration of Sentiments at Seneca Falls in 1848, one of a hundred signers. The Nineteenth Amendment gave American women the vote in 1920. What was remarkable about Woodward by then?
answer: She was the only one of the 100 signers still alive
choices: She was the only one of the 100 signers still alive
She had become the first woman elected to Congress
She had personally delivered the amendment to the Senate
She had outlived every president who once opposed her
context: Woodward was the sole survivor of the 100 signers in 1920 — but too ill to cast the ballot she had waited 72 years for. She had signed because she wanted to choose her own work and keep her own wages. Source: https://www.nps.gov/wori/learn/historyculture/charlotte-woodward.htm

question: Office workers streamed down the burning stairwells of the twin towers of the World Trade Center after hijackers crashed two airliners into them on 11 September 2001. Others were climbing up those same stairs, into the smoke and fire. Who were they?
answer: New York City firefighters
choices: New York City firefighters
Television news reporters
Off-duty airline pilots
City sanitation workers
context: 343 New York City firefighters died on September 11, 2001 — the single greatest loss of life in the FDNY's history. They were climbing up the stairwells of the burning towers as office workers came down. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mychal-Judge and FDNY/9-11 Memorial reporting (343 FDNY deaths).

question: Welles Crowther, a 24-year-old equities trader, guided trapped people in the burning South Tower to a stairway on 11 September 2001, then climbed back up for others. He went back to the sky lobby on the 78th floor three times before the tower collapsed with him in it. Those he saved never saw his face, yet they all remembered him by the same name. What was it?
answer: The man in the red bandana
choices: The man in the red bandana
The voice in the dark
The runner on the stairs
The whistle on 78
context: Welles Crowther had carried a red handkerchief since boyhood and used it to cover his face against the smoke. Survivors remembered only 'the man in the red bandana' who calmly guided them to a stairwell. He made three trips up to the 78th-floor sky lobby to lead people down before the tower fell with him inside. Source: https://www.911memorial.org/connect/blog/remembering-man-red-bandana.

question: Sandra Bradshaw, a flight attendant on United Flight 93, phoned her husband on 11 September 2001 to say goodbye, as the passengers and crew got ready to fight the hijackers. She told him what she was doing in the plane's galley. What was it?
answer: Heating water to throw at the hijackers
choices: Heating water to throw at the hijackers
Stacking food carts to block the aisle
Gathering knives and forks from the trays
Wedging a fire extinguisher under a seat
context: Sandra Bradshaw told her husband she was in the galley 'heating water to throw at the hijackers.' The passengers and crew were arming themselves with whatever they had before storming the cockpit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines_Flight_93.

question: Todd Beamer was on the phone with the operator Lisa Jefferson as the passengers of United Flight 93 got ready to rush the hijackers in the cockpit on 11 September 2001. She heard him ask the other passengers if they were ready. What did Beamer say next?
answer: "Let's roll."
choices: "Let's roll."
"God help us."
"Tell them I tried."
"We're going home."
context: Before the passengers rushed the cockpit, operator Lisa Jefferson heard Todd Beamer say: 'Are you ready? Okay. Let's roll.' 'Let's roll' became one of the most remembered lines of September 11. Investigators believe Flight 93's target was the U.S. Capitol; it crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania before reaching Washington. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines_Flight_93; https://www.americanheritage.com/remembering-flight-93-okay-lets-roll.

question: Father Mychal Judge, the Franciscan chaplain of the New York City fire department, ran into the North Tower with the firefighters on 11 September 2001. He was praying over the dying when falling debris killed him. One grim record became attached to his name. What was it?
answer: The first certified death, Victim 0001
choices: The first certified death, Victim 0001
The 343rd firefighter to be lost
The only priest inside the towers
The last body to be recovered
context: Father Mychal Judge ran into the North Tower to be with the firefighters and was killed by falling debris when the South Tower collapsed, after praying and giving last rites. His body was carried out by firefighters, and he was officially recorded as Victim 0001 — the first certified death of 9/11. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mychal-Judge; https://allthatsinteresting.com/mychal-judge.

question: Workers at Ground Zero found a burned tree, half dead, in the wreckage after 11 September 2001. City parks workers tended it for years, and in 2010 they replanted it at the 9/11 Memorial. What do New Yorkers call it?
answer: The Survivor Tree
choices: The Survivor Tree
The Liberty Oak
The Remembrance Ash
The Founders' Elm
context: The burned Callery pear was nursed back to health by New York City parks workers and replanted at the 9/11 Memorial in 2010. It is known today as the 'Survivor Tree.' Source: https://www.911memorial.org/visit/memorial/survivor-tree.

question: Shaka did away with his Zulu warriors' long throwing spear and armed them with a short spear, its broad iron blade almost a foot long, so they had to get in close and fight hand to hand. What was the new stabbing spear called?
answer: The iklwa
choices: The iklwa
The katana
The trident
The halberd
context: The iklwa had a roughly 24-inch (610 mm) shaft and a sword-like blade about 12 inches (300 mm) long. It replaced the long thrown assegai so warriors had to close in and fight hand-to-hand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assegai

question: Shaka's hardened older Zulu warriors formed the chest of the bull horns, his plan of battle, and locked with the enemy face to face. What did the two horns, his bands of fast young warriors, do while the chest held?
answer: Raced around both sides to surround the enemy
choices: Raced around both sides to surround the enemy
Climbed nearby hills to throw rocks down
Retreated to lure the enemy into a swamp
Lit grass fires to blind the enemy
context: The Zulu name was 'impondo zenkomo' (the bull horns). The two 'horns' of fast young men encircled the enemy while the 'chest' pinned them, and a reserve called the 'loins' waited behind to plug any gaps. Source: https://ditsong.org.za/en/shaka-zulus-famous-impondo-zenkomo-the-bull-horns-tactical-battle-formation/

question: Zulu warriors carried a new weapon into Shaka's battles: a short, heavy stabbing spear meant for close and brutal work, in place of the long throwing spear their people had always used. They named the weapon after a sound. What sound gave the spear its name?
answer: The wet sucking noise as the blade was pulled from a wound
choices: The wet sucking noise as the blade was pulled from a wound
The whistle the spear made flying through the air
The crack of the shaft against an enemy's shield
The chant warriors shouted as they charged
context: 'Iklwa' is onomatopoeia — the word imitates the sound the broad blade made coming back out of a victim's body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assegai

question: Zwide, king of the Ndwandwe, met Shaka with an army twice the size of his on the slopes of Gqokli Hill around 1818. The Ndwandwe carried the region's old long throwing spears, meant to be hurled from a distance. How did Shaka's smaller army win?
answer: Packed too tightly to throw their long spears, they were stabbed by Shaka's short-spear men charging downhill
choices: Packed too tightly to throw their long spears, they were stabbed by Shaka's short-spear men charging downhill
A sudden rainstorm soaked the Ndwandwe gunpowder and silenced their muskets
The Ndwandwe king Zwide was captured at dawn before the fighting began
Shaka's men dug pits overnight that swallowed the front ranks
context: Crammed together, the Ndwandwe could not throw their long assegais in the crush, while Shaka's men closed in and stabbed with the new short iklwa, routing a force twice their size. Source: https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Gqokli_Hill

question: Shaka forbade anyone to plant crops or use milk after Nandi, his mother, died in 1827; his grief became a terror for his people, and thousands died at his order for mourning too little. He even had cows slaughtered. Why did he have the cows killed?
answer: So the calves would also know what losing a mother felt like
choices: So the calves would also know what losing a mother felt like
So the smoke from the meat would carry his grief to the sky
So no milk could ever be drunk in the kingdom again
So the herders would have time to mourn instead of working
context: Shaka had cows killed so their calves would feel the loss of a mother just as he had. The mourning frenzy after Nandi's death is remembered as one of the most extreme episodes of his reign. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaka

question: Moshoeshoe drew scattered clans together on a mountain stronghold in southern Africa during the Mfecane, the crushing: an age of war, famine and forced migration that Shaka's wars are linked to. From those clans he built a new nation. Which kingdom did Moshoeshoe found?
answer: Lesotho
choices: Lesotho
Egypt
Carthage
Ethiopia
context: The upheaval is the Mfecane (Zulu, 'the crushing'; Sesotho 'Difaqane'). Moshoeshoe gathered clans on a mountain stronghold to found what became Lesotho, while Shaka's renegade general Mzilikazi led the Ndebele north to found Bulawayo in present-day Zimbabwe. Modern historians argue drought, the slave trade, and other powers — not Shaka alone — drove the Mfecane, and that the old death tolls of 1-2 million were exaggerated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mfecane

question: Shakespeare wrote great heroines, Juliet, Cleopatra and Lady Macbeth among them, for a stage that English law kept women off until 1660. Who first played every one of them?
answer: Teenage boys
choices: Teenage boys
Veiled noblewomen
Older married men
Masked foreign dancers
context: Audiences watched boys and young men play the heroines, since women were forbidden on the English stage until 1660. Source: Colorado State University, 'Why weren't women allowed to act in Shakespeare's plays?'; Shakespeare's Globe.

question: William Shakespeare set down more than 1,700 words that people still use and that no earlier writer is known to have written. One of them, a word for a part of the body, appears first in Henry VI, Part 1. Which word was it?
answer: Eyeball
choices: Eyeball
Eyebrow
Eyelid
Eyelash
context: Scholars are careful to say these are the FIRST RECORDED uses — Shakespeare may have coined some and merely been the first to write others down. 'Eyeball' first appears in Henry VI, Part 1. Source: Shakespeare Birthplace Trust (shakespeare.org.uk), 'Shakespeare's Words'.

question: Three witches gathered round a steaming cauldron in Shakespeare's Macbeth to brew a spell, throwing in 'eye of newt and toe of frog, wool of bat and tongue of dog.' What two lines did they chant over and over as they stirred?
answer: Double, double toil and trouble; fire burn and cauldron bubble
choices: Double, double toil and trouble; fire burn and cauldron bubble
Round about the kettle creeping; pour the venom, set it steeping
Thrice the brindled cat hath mewed; gather darkness, fate be brewed
Smoke and shadow, bone and bramble; through the night the spirits ramble
context: It is the most famous witches' chant in all of literature, from Macbeth, Act 4, Scene 1. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library, Macbeth Act 4 Scene 1 (exact text).

question: A gravedigger turned up an old skull in the graveyard scene of Shakespeare's Hamlet. Prince Hamlet lifted it and said, 'Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio.' Who had Yorick been to Hamlet when the prince was a small child at the royal court?
answer: The court jester, who carried little Hamlet on his back a thousand times
choices: The court jester, who carried little Hamlet on his back a thousand times
The old king, his father, now murdered and turned to bare bone
The royal tutor, who first taught him to read as a boy
The king's huntsman, who first set him upon a horse
context: Holding the skull of the jester who once made him laugh and gave him piggyback rides, Hamlet sees how death reduces everyone — king or clown — to dust. Hamlet, Act 5, Scene 1. Source: SparkNotes Hamlet; nosweatshakespeare.com 'Alas Poor Yorick'.

question: Juliet stood on her balcony at night in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet and cried, 'O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?' To modern ears she seems to be calling into the dark to find him, but she was not asking where he was. What does 'wherefore' mean?
answer: Why
choices: Why
Where
When
How
context: Juliet isn't asking where Romeo is — she's despairing at WHY the boy she loves had to be a Montague, her family's sworn enemy. Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 2. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library; interestingliterature.com.

question: Shakespeare opened Romeo and Juliet with a Prologue that named the young pair 'star-crossed lovers.' In his day, people held that the stars governed human fate. What did that single phrase warn the audience, in the very first minute of the play?
answer: That fate itself was set against them, dooming their love from the start
choices: That fate itself was set against them, dooming their love from the start
That they were born under the same lucky star and meant to wed
That they would wander across many distant lands before finding peace
That their feuding families would soon be joined by the marriage
context: 'Star-crossed' means the stars — fate — were crossed against them, so the audience knows the lovers are doomed before the story even begins. Source: Wikipedia 'Star-crossed'; SparkNotes Romeo and Juliet prologue analysis.

question: Shakespeare was the first to write the phrase 'wild-goose chase,' in Romeo and Juliet, and today it means a hopeless hunt for something that can never be caught. Back then the phrase had nothing to do with hunting birds. What was a wild-goose chase in his day?
answer: A horse race where riders followed a leader in a V, like flying geese
choices: A horse race where riders followed a leader in a V, like flying geese
A village game where children chased a goose around the green
A hunt where hounds were loosed after a single wild goose
A market day when farmers raced their geese to the fair
context: A real 'wild-goose chase' was a horse race in which every rider had to follow the leader's twisting path in single file, spread out like a skein of flying geese. Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 4. Source: Merriam-Webster '10 Phrases Invented by Shakespeare'; Shakespeare Birthplace Trust.
