question: Lady Macbeth, who had helped her husband murder the sleeping King Duncan, began to walk in her sleep near the end of Shakespeare's Macbeth. She rubbed her hands and cried, 'Out, damned spot! Out, I say!' What does she believe is staining her hands?
answer: King Duncan's blood, which she imagines is still on her hands
choices: King Duncan's blood, which she imagines is still on her hands
The black soot from the castle's midnight fires
The dark ink from the letters that revealed the plot
The poison she once mixed for the king's two guards
context: Driven mad by guilt, she hallucinates the murdered king's blood on her hands — a stain her conscience can never scrub away. Macbeth, Act 5, Scene 1. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library; interestingliterature.com sleepwalking-scene analysis.

question: Prince Hamlet stood alone on the stage in Shakespeare's tragedy and began the most famous speech in all of English drama: 'To be, or not to be, that is the question.' What choice was Hamlet wrestling with as he spoke?
answer: Whether to keep enduring life's pain, or to escape it through death
choices: Whether to keep enduring life's pain, or to escape it through death
Whether to avenge his father now, or wait for stronger proof
Whether to trust Ophelia's love, or push her away forever
Whether to seize the crown himself, or let his uncle keep it
context: Hamlet is weighing whether life's suffering is worth bearing, or whether death would be a release. Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 1. Source: Wikipedia 'To be, or not to be'; SparkNotes Hamlet.

question: The Chorus stepped out at the start of Shakespeare's Henry V and apologised that one small round playhouse had to stage the vast battle of Agincourt. He begged the audience to fill the gap with their imagination. What did the Chorus call the Globe?
answer: This wooden O
choices: This wooden O
This painted box
This hollow crown
This empty ring
context: 'This wooden O' captures the round, open-roofed shape of the Globe — and the Chorus's plea that the audience imagine kingdoms and armies inside it. Henry V, Prologue. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library; interestingliterature.com 'O for a Muse of Fire' analysis.

question: Margaret Hughes, the first professional actress ever to appear on the English stage, stepped onto it on 8 December 1660, once the theatres had reopened. The part she played was one of Shakespeare's heroines. Which heroine did she play that day?
answer: Desdemona, in Othello
choices: Desdemona, in Othello
Juliet, in Romeo and Juliet
Cleopatra, in Antony and Cleopatra
Ophelia, in Hamlet
context: After decades of boys in the women's roles, the first real actress on the English stage stepped out as Desdemona in Shakespeare's Othello. Source: Wikipedia 'Margaret Hughes'; EBSCO 'Women on the 17th-Century English Stage'.

question: Ben Jonson, once Shakespeare's rival, wrote a poem in his praise for the front of the First Folio in 1623, the first book to gather his plays. In it Jonson gave him a name that tied him to his birthplace. What did Jonson call him?
answer: The Sweet Swan of Avon
choices: The Sweet Swan of Avon
The Bard of the Thames
The Bright Star of London
The Nightingale of Stratford
context: In the same poem Jonson predicted Shakespeare's fame would never fade, declaring 'He was not of an age, but for all time!' Source: Ben Jonson, 'To the Memory of My Beloved... Mr. William Shakespeare' (First Folio, 1623), via Wikisource and the University of Illinois Rare Book & Manuscript Library.

question: Playgoers stood packed in the open yard right below the stage at Shakespeare's Globe, cracking hazelnuts and peeling oranges. Each had paid a single penny, about the price of a loaf, for a place with no seat at all. What were these penny fans called?
answer: Groundlings
choices: Groundlings
Pennyfolk
Yardmen
Stinkards
context: Archaeologists digging up the old Globe yard found cracked hazelnut shells and orange peel left behind by the groundlings. Source: shakespearesglobe.com/discover/shakespeares-world/audiences/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundling

question: An eyewitness watched Shakespeare's Globe burn down on 29 June 1613, during a performance of Henry VIII. A cannon fired on stage to herald the king had set fire to the thatched roof, and within an hour the theatre was gone, yet no one died. What was the only injury he reported?
answer: A man's breeches caught fire, and he put them out with ale
choices: A man's breeches caught fire, and he put them out with ale
A man's cloak caught fire, and he smothered it in mud
An actor's wig caught fire, and he flung it in the river
A boy's sleeve caught fire, and a friend beat it out
context: The eyewitness Sir Henry Wotton wrote that the man would have been 'broyled' if he had not, by a 'provident wit,' doused his burning breeches with bottle ale. Source: ebsco.com/research-starters/history/burning-globe-theatre ; shakespearedocumented.folger.edu

question: The infant William Shakespeare received his baptism in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564, and historians set his birthday at 23 April. He died in 1616. By tradition, what was strange about the day he died?
answer: He died on 23 April, the very same date as his birthday
choices: He died on 23 April, the very same date as his birthday
He died on 23 April, but aged 80, not 52
He died on 24 April, one day after turning 52
He died in London, not in Stratford at all
context: By tradition Shakespeare was born and died on the same day of the year, 23 April — his 52nd birthday. Source: shakespeare.org.uk/explore-shakespeare/shakespedia/william-shakespeare/when-was-shakespeare-born/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare

question: Shakespeare's company flew a flag over the Globe on performance days to tell Londoners a play was on. By tradition its picture matched the theatre's name: a mighty figure from Greek myth bearing the whole round world on his shoulders. Who was shown on the flag?
answer: Hercules
choices: Hercules
Atlas
Apollo
Zeus
context: Tradition holds the Globe's flag showed Hercules carrying the world, supposedly matching a motto meaning 'all the world's a playhouse' — though some scholars doubt the motto was really used in Shakespeare's own day. Source: shakespeare.org.uk/explore-shakespeare/shakespedia/shakespeares-globe-theatre/ ; research.birmingham.ac.uk  (Legend.)

question: The actors of Shakespeare's company lost the lease on the ground under their old London playhouse, The Theatre, though they still owned the building's timber. Their landlord owned the land. What did the actors do over a few nights in December 1598?
answer: They took the building apart beam by beam and carried it across the Thames
choices: They took the building apart beam by beam and carried it across the Thames
They bought the patch of land back from the landlord overnight
They burned it down so no rival company could ever use it
They sued the landlord in court and won the whole plot
context: They ferried the recycled timber across the river by barge and rebuilt it on the south bank as the first Globe, finished in 1599. Source: shalt.dmu.ac.uk/locations/globe-1599-1642/indepth.html ; historyhit.com/locations/shakespeares-globe/

question: William Shakespeare lay dying in his hometown of Stratford-upon-Avon in 1616 and made his last will. He left his house and most of his money to his elder daughter, Susanna. For his wife, Anne Hathaway, he squeezed in one short bequest. What single item did he leave her?
answer: His second-best bed
choices: His second-best bed
His best velvet gown
His silver drinking cup
His pair of gold rings
context: Historians think the 'second-best bed' was the couple's own marriage bed — the best bed was kept for guests. Source: shakespeare.org.uk/explore-shakespeare/shakespedia/william-shakespeare/second-best-bed/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare's_will

question: An actor let the title of one of Shakespeare's darkest tragedies slip inside a theatre, and by an old superstition he had to step outside, turn round three times, spit, and beg to come back in. The play was the one with three witches on a stormy moor and a general who murdered his king in his sleep for the crown. What did superstitious actors call it instead?
answer: The Scottish Play
choices: The Scottish Play
The Cursed King
The Dark Tragedy
The Northern Play
context: If someone slips and says the real name, tradition says the culprit must leave the room, turn around three times, spit, and ask to be let back in. Source: rsc.org.uk/macbeth/about-the-play/the-scottish-play ; folger.edu/blogs/shakespeare-and-beyond/macbeth-curse-scottish-play/  (Legend.)

question: Jaques, a gloomy lord in Shakespeare's comedy 'As You Like It', compared the whole world to a theatre in one of the most quoted speeches in English. Shakespeare gave that speech to Jaques, not to the prince Hamlet. What was Jaques's speech about?
answer: How a human life passes through seven stages
choices: How a human life passes through seven stages
How love conquers all obstacles
How power corrupts every king
How dreams predict the future
context: In As You Like It the gloomy lord Jaques begins his speech 'All the world's a stage,' so the two most famous lines come from two different plays. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_the_world's_a_stage ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/To_be,_or_not_to_be

question: William Shakespeare often made new words by changing a word from one part of speech to another. By the reckoning of the Oxford English Dictionary, which quotes him more than any other author, he was the first to write down some 1,700 words. Which set of everyday words first appears in his work?
answer: Frugal, obscene, bedazzle, puppy-dog
choices: Frugal, obscene, bedazzle, puppy-dog
Galaxy, tractor, sandwich, helicopter
Telephone, jungle, robot, gravity
Pizza, soccer, cartoon, weekend
context: Shakespeare often made new words by 'functional shift' — turning a noun into a verb, like 'bedazzle' — and ordinary words such as 'frugal,' 'obscene,' 'horrid,' and 'puppy-dog' are first recorded in his work. Source: litcharts.com/content/shakespeares-literature-creating-words ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influence_of_William_Shakespeare

question: John Heminges and Henry Condell, two of Shakespeare's fellow actors, gathered thirty-six of his plays into one great book in 1623, seven years after his death: the First Folio. About eighteen of them, Macbeth, The Tempest and Twelfth Night among them, had never been printed before. Without the Folio, what would have become of those plays?
answer: They would be lost today, with no other copy surviving
choices: They would be lost today, with no other copy surviving
They would survive only in old Italian translations
They would be remembered just from their titles
They would exist only as scribbled Globe stage scripts
context: Roughly 18 plays, Macbeth and The Tempest among them, were never printed anywhere else, so they exist now only because Heminges and Condell saved them in the First Folio. Source: shakespeare.org.uk/explore-shakespeare/shakespedia/shakespeares-works/shakespeares-first-folio/ ; folger.edu/explore/shakespeare-in-print/first-folio/

question: William Shakespeare is thought to have written the four-line rhyme carved on his grave in Holy Trinity Church, Stratford-upon-Avon, where he lies. The rhyme blesses one kind of man and curses another. What does it threaten a curse for?
answer: Digging up and moving his bones
choices: Digging up and moving his bones
Speaking ill of his good name
Selling off his family's land
Copying his plays without paying
context: The stone reads, in old spelling, 'Blese be ye man yt spares thes stones, / And cvrst be he yt moves my bones' — a curse meant to stop his grave being dug up. Source: nosweatshakespeare.com/resources/life/shakespeares-grave/ ; historyhit.com/the-curse-on-shakespeares-grave/

question: William Shakespeare wrote a famous tragedy about a grief-stricken prince. Years earlier, in 1596, he had lost his only son, a boy of eleven and the twin brother of his daughter Judith, and some scholars find it haunting that the prince's name is so close to the boy's. What was the boy's name?
answer: Hamnet
choices: Hamnet
Gilbert
Edmund
Richard
context: Shakespeare's son Hamnet, a twin to his sister Judith, died at 11 in 1596; some scholars link the loss to the later tragedy Hamlet, whose hero's name is nearly the same. Source: shakespeare.org.uk/explore-shakespeare/shakespedia/william-shakespeare/william-shakespeares-family/hamnet-shakespeare/ ; smithsonianmag.com/history/the-real-history-behind-hamnet-180987733/

question: By one legend, Shakespeare himself had to hurry onto the stage at the very first performance of one of his tragedies, because the boy cast in one of its roles had suddenly died. The tale was invented to explain the play's reputation for bad luck. Which role was the dead boy meant to play?
answer: Lady Macbeth
choices: Lady Macbeth
King Duncan
One of the three witches
The ghost of Banquo
context: This tale — a boy dying on opening night so Shakespeare had to step in as Lady Macbeth — is one of several legends invented to explain the play's reputation for bad luck, not a recorded fact. Source: study.com/learn/lesson/curse-macbeth-superstition-incidents.html ; rsc.org.uk/macbeth/about-the-play/the-scottish-play

question: Daniel Shays fought at Bunker Hill, Saratoga and Stony Point, then went home unpaid in 1780 and was dragged into court for debt. The Marquis de Lafayette had honoured his service with a handsome ceremonial sword. What did Shays do with Lafayette's sword?
answer: He sold it for money
choices: He sold it for money
He buried it on his farm
He gave it to his son
He mounted it over his door
context: Lafayette had given Daniel Shays an ornamental ceremonial sword for his Revolutionary War service. Broke and in debt, Shays sold it for cash — to his fellow officers a shameful act, but the perfect emblem of how the new republic left its veterans destitute. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Shays / https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ354858

question: Daniel Shays led debt-ridden Massachusetts farmers in the winter of 1786 as they shut down the courts that were seizing their farms, and in January 1787 the rebels stormed the Springfield arsenal. The weak government of the Articles of Confederation had no power to tax or raise an army to stop them. What did the scare push George Washington and other leaders to do?
answer: Call the Constitutional Convention
choices: Call the Constitutional Convention
Disband the Massachusetts militia
Cancel all the farmers' debts
Crown a king to restore order
context: The rebellion convinced America's leaders that the Articles of Confederation were too weak to survive, giving decisive momentum to the Constitutional Convention that met in Philadelphia in May 1787. The 'what it triggered' is the whole point — the scare, not the farmers, is what frightened the founders into building a stronger government. Source: https://constitutioncenter.org/education/classroom-resource-library/classroom/3.1-topic-primer-summary-of-shays-rebellion / https://www.mountvernon.org/library/digitalhistory/digital-encyclopedia/article/shays-rebellion

question: Stalin sat in his box at the Bolshoi in January 1936 watching Dmitri Shostakovich's opera, Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk, and walked out before the end. Two days later the Party's newspaper, Pravda, printed a savage unsigned editorial tearing the opera apart. Being attacked by name in Pravda was a threat to a man's life. What was the headline over that editorial?
answer: Muddle Instead of Music
choices: Muddle Instead of Music
Clamor Instead of Music
Disorder Instead of Music
Bedlam Instead of Music
context: 'Muddle Instead of Music' ran on 28 January 1936; it warned the music was 'a game of clever ingenuity that may end very badly.' Archival research credits the Soviet propagandist David Zaslavsky as the author (the rumor that Stalin wrote it himself is now thought unlikely). When Shostakovich came out to bow after the performance Stalin walked out of, witnesses said he went 'white as a sheet.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muddle_Instead_of_Music

question: Dmitri Shostakovich lived in nightly terror after Pravda denounced him in 1936, for the secret police might come for him in the dark. His son Maxim later described one thing his father did each night to be ready. What was it?
answer: Slept fully dressed with a packed suitcase beside the bed
choices: Slept fully dressed with a packed suitcase beside the bed
Hid his finished scores inside the walls of the apartment
Kept a loaded pistol under his pillow within easy reach
Burned his letters in the stove before going to sleep
context: By his son Maxim's account, Shostakovich went to bed clothed on top of the blankets with a small packed suitcase on the floor — and some nights waited by the apartment-building lift watching the elevator doors, so that if the NKVD came they would not drag him away in his pajamas in front of his wife and children. The story traces chiefly to Maxim, so the precise details are uncertain. Source: https://www.dailyo.in/arts/julian-barnes-booker-prize-2011-the-sense-of-an-ending-the-noise-of-time-dmitri-dmitriyevich-shostakovich-stalin-ussr-8994  (Legend.)

question: Dmitri Shostakovich wrote his Fifth Symphony in 1937, while his friends were vanishing into the Gulag. It closes with a blaring major-key triumph that Soviet officials applauded as loyal celebration. Solomon Volkov's Testimony, a disputed memoir published years later, quotes Shostakovich on what that triumph really felt like. How did he describe it?
answer: Like being beaten with a stick and forced to march off cheering
choices: Like being beaten with a stick and forced to march off cheering
Like a soldier saluting a flag he had stopped believing in
Like singing a hymn whose words he no longer believed
Like cheering at a parade while the police studied his face
context: The quotation comes from Solomon Volkov's 'Testimony' (1979): 'The rejoicing is forced, created under threat... It is as if someone were beating you with a stick and saying, Your business is rejoicing... and you rise up, shaky, and go marching off muttering, Our business is rejoicing.' Testimony's authenticity is disputed, but this reading of the hollow, coerced finale took hold worldwide. How triumphant it sounds depends partly on speed — Leonard Bernstein in 1959 took the ending more than twice as fast as premiere conductor Yevgeny Mravinsky, who always kept it slow and grim. Source: https://thelistenersclub.com/2020/11/11/shostakovichs-fifth-symphony-the-unlikely-triumph-of-freedom/  (Legend.)

question: German and Finnish armies closed a ring round Leningrad in September 1941, trying to starve the city into surrender. By the end of 1941, the worst of that winter, a citizen's daily bread ration was down to about 125 grams. When the real grain in the city's warehouses ran out, what did Leningrad's bakers mix into the dough?
answer: Sawdust, cellulose, and chaff
choices: Sawdust, cellulose, and chaff
Salted fish and dried peas
Crushed acorns and honey
Powdered milk and lard
context: At the siege's nadir an ordinary Leningrader got ~125 g of 'bread' a day, padded with sawdust, cellulose, and chaff once real grain ran out. The siege lasted 872 days (Sept 8, 1941 – Jan 27, 1944) and killed roughly a million people, most of them civilians who died of starvation and cold. Source: allthatsinteresting.com/siege-of-leningrad; explorethearchive.com/siege-of-leningrad.

question: Lorry drivers carried Leningrad's lifeline over the frozen surface of Lake Ladoga, the route the city called the Road of Life. The ice was thin, and more than 300 lorries broke through and sank in two winters. What did the drivers do to give themselves a chance if the ice cracked under them?
answer: Kept the cab doors open to leap clear
choices: Kept the cab doors open to leap clear
Drove only at night with headlights off
Roped each truck to the one behind it
Strapped empty barrels to the running boards
context: The Road of Life across Lake Ladoga opened Nov 22, 1941; drivers kept cab doors open to jump free if the ice gave way. Despite losing 300+ trucks through the ice, the route evacuated roughly 1.4 million people and carried over 1.5 million tonnes of supplies into the starving city. Source: tass.com/society/985484; gw2ru.com/history/3038.

question: Tanya Savicheva, a girl of eleven, kept a small alphabet notebook in besieged Leningrad. As her family starved to death one by one, she wrote each loss on a fresh page in one flat line: her sister, her grandmother, her brother, her uncles, her mother. What do the last three pages say?
answer: 'The Savichevs are dead. Everyone is dead. Only Tanya is left.'
choices: 'The Savichevs are dead. Everyone is dead. Only Tanya is left.'
'God has forgotten this street and this house.'
'Spring is coming and no one is here to see it.'
'I will write again when the war is over.'
context: Tanya Savicheva logged each death in flat lines ('Mama on May 13th at 7:30 in the morning, 1942'), ending: 'The Savichevs are dead.' / 'Everyone is dead.' / 'Only Tanya is left.' Evacuated out, she died of intestinal tuberculosis in 1944 at age 14; her diary is displayed at the State Museum of the History of St. Petersburg. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanya_Savicheva.

question: Karl Eliasberg conducted Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony, the 'Leningrad', inside the besieged city on 9 August 1942, while loudspeakers carried it to the German lines. Of the 40-member Leningrad Radio Orchestra, only about 14 musicians were still alive in the city. How did Eliasberg fill the empty chairs?
answer: Soldiers were pulled from the front line to play
choices: Soldiers were pulled from the front line to play
Recordings were piped in behind the live players
Children from the conservatory took the open seats
Wax figures were seated to fill out the stage
context: The 252-page score was flown into the encircled city from Kuibyshev; only ~14 of 40 orchestra members were alive, so soldiers were pulled from the front to fill the seats. Three musicians died of starvation during rehearsals, and Eliasberg, weakened by 'dystrophy,' had to be hauled to rehearsals on a sledge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leningrad_première_of_Shostakovich's_Symphony_No._7.

question: Leonid Govorov, a Soviet general, would not let German guns drown out the broadcast of Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony from besieged Leningrad. He launched Operation Squall, firing about 3,000 shells onto the German artillery so the music could play on. Afterward he told the conductor Karl Eliasberg one line about his gunners. What did Govorov say?
answer: 'We played our instrument in the symphony, too.'
choices: 'We played our instrument in the symphony, too.'
'Let them remember who owns this sky.'
'The guns have earned their silence tonight.'
'Tell Shostakovich the front kept time for him.'
context: Govorov's 'Operation Squall' put ~3,000 shells onto German batteries so the symphony could be broadcast unbroken; he told Eliasberg, 'we played our instrument in the symphony, too.' Eliasberg later met German soldiers who said the concert convinced them they could never take Leningrad. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leningrad_première_of_Shostakovich's_Symphony_No._7.

question: Scientists at Leningrad's Vavilov Institute faced a choice in the siege's famine, beside the world's first seed bank: some 380,000 samples of grain, rice and nuts. Nine of them made the same choice. What happened to those nine?
answer: They starved to death surrounded by edible seeds
choices: They starved to death surrounded by edible seeds
They smuggled the seeds out across the ice
They burned the records to hide them from the Germans
They were shot for hoarding state food
context: Nine Vavilov Institute scientists starved to death rather than eat the ~380,000-sample seed bank; one died holding a packet of peanuts, refusing to consume what he saw as the future of Russia's harvests. Source: sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-tragedy-of-the-worlds-first-seed-bank.

question: Nikolai Vavilov, the botanist who built Leningrad's great seed collection, clashed with Trofim Lysenko, Stalin's favourite pseudo-scientist, who rejected real genetics. Where and how did Vavilov die in January 1943?
answer: Starved on cabbage and mouldy flour in a Soviet prison
choices: Starved on cabbage and mouldy flour in a Soviet prison
Shot by a German sniper on the city wall
Lost on the ice of the Road of Life
Killed by a shell while guarding his seeds
context: Stalin had Vavilov arrested in 1940; he was starved on mashed cabbage and mouldy flour and died in a Soviet prison in January 1943 at age 55 — a famine-fighter killed by hunger inside his own country's jail. The endurance of Leningrad's people and the cruelty of Stalin's regime are separable truths. Source: sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-tragedy-of-the-worlds-first-seed-bank.

question: Walther Schwieger, in command of the German submarine U-20, fired one torpedo into the side of the British liner Lusitania off the coast of Ireland on 7 May 1915. The ship was as long as four city blocks. How fast did the Lusitania go under?
answer: In about 18 minutes
choices: In about 18 minutes
In about 3 hours
In about 9 hours
In about 30 hours
context: The Lusitania sank in roughly 18 minutes off the Old Head of Kinsale, far faster than anyone expected. 1,198 people died and only about 763 survived; 128 of the dead were Americans, which helped turn U.S. opinion toward entering World War I. Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/18-minutes-that-shocked-the-world ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_the_RMS_Lusitania

question: 'Heels over to starboard,' Walther Schwieger wrote in his war diary as he watched the Lusitania sink after his single torpedo struck. He could not see how one torpedo had brought down so giant a liner so fast, and historians still argue over why. What happened inside the ship moments after the torpedo hit?
answer: A violent second explosion deep inside her
choices: A violent second explosion deep inside her
A jammed and useless steering rudder
A mutiny among her frightened crew
A fire racing through the dining saloon
context: A second, far bigger explosion deep inside the Lusitania is what doomed her so quickly, and its cause is still debated: coal dust igniting, a boiler bursting, a ruptured steam line, or the war munitions in her cargo hold. The ship really did carry war supplies for the Western Front, including about 4.2 million rounds of Remington rifle ammunition and 1,250 cases of shrapnel shells. Source: https://www.historyhit.com/facts-about-the-sinking-of-rms-lusitania/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Schwieger ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_the_RMS_Lusitania

question: Christopher Columbus reached the Americas in 1492, and the Europeans who followed him brought diseases the peoples there had never met. One killed far more Native Americans than any other, leaving its victims covered in agonising sores and its survivors scarred with deep pits. Which disease was the great killer?
answer: Smallpox
choices: Smallpox
Measles
Influenza
Typhus
context: Smallpox (Variola major) was the deadliest of the Old World 'crowd diseases' for Native peoples. It scarred survivors deeply (pockmarks) and could blind them. Source: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/how-smallpox-devastated-the-aztecs-and-helped-spain-conquer-an-american-civilization-500-years-ago

question: A Spanish conquistador landed in the Americas with guns, cannon and horses, yet such weapons killed only a small share of the Native peoples who died. Some estimates put the toll at up to nine in ten of them within a century of contact. What killed most of them?
answer: Old World epidemic diseases
choices: Old World epidemic diseases
Spanish guns and cannon
Starvation in the silver mines
Battles against the colonists
context: Disease, not warfare, did the overwhelming majority of the killing. One widely cited estimate is about 56 million deaths by the year 1600 out of a pre-contact population as high as ~60 million. This 'germs killed more than swords' fact is real history, not a story staged for effect. Source: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2019/feb/great-dying-americas-disturbed-earths-climate

question: The Pilgrims landed in 1620 and settled a spot they named Plymouth, where dwellings already stood and human bones lay unburied. What had Plymouth been only a few years before?
answer: A Native village emptied by an epidemic
choices: A Native village emptied by an epidemic
A Spanish fort abandoned after a mutiny
A French trading post burned in a raid
An island the Pilgrims reached by mistake
context: An epidemic of 1616-1619 (often called the 'Great Dying') killed as much as 90% of the Native people of coastal southern New England before the Pilgrims landed. They settled the abandoned Patuxet village and renamed it Plymouth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patuxet

question: The crew of the fur-trade steamboat St. Peter took smallpox up the Missouri River in 1837 without knowing it. At Fort Clark, in what is now North Dakota, the Mandan came out to trade: some 2,000 people who lived in round earth-lodge towns along the river. How many were left alive three months later?
answer: About 25
choices: About 1,000
About 500
About 200
About 25
context: The Mandan were reduced from about 2,000 to roughly 23-27 survivors in three months - a death rate of at least ~93%. More than 17,000 Indigenous people died along the Missouri. Trader Francis Chardon, watching from Fort Clark, gave up counting the dead, writing that they died too fast for it to be possible; the chief Four Bears (Mato-Tope) gave a bitter final speech before dying on July 30, 1837. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1837_Great_Plains_smallpox_epidemic

question: A European sailor carried smallpox across the Atlantic after 1492. Europeans who caught it died at a rate of about one in three, yet among Native Americans it could kill half a village or more. Why were Native Americans so much more likely to die of it?
answer: They had never been exposed, so had no acquired immunity
choices: They had never been exposed, so had no acquired immunity
They lived in larger and far more crowded cities
They had no written knowledge of medicine
They had been weakened by long ocean voyages
context: Native populations had no acquired immunity because they had never been exposed to Old World crowd diseases. Historians call these 'virgin soil' epidemics (a term popularized by historian Alfred Crosby) - outbreaks in a population with zero prior immunological resistance, which is why the death rates ran so catastrophically high. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_disease_and_epidemics

question: Tisquantum, the man the Pilgrims knew as Squanto, made his way home to his people, the Patuxet, in 1619 after years held captive in Europe. What did he find there?
answer: He was the only Patuxet left alive
choices: He was the only Patuxet left alive
His village had moved far inland
His people had all been taken as slaves
A rival tribe had seized his home
context: Squanto returned in 1619 to find he was the last surviving Patuxet - his entire people had died in the 1616-1619 epidemic. The Pilgrims later settled on the empty Patuxet village site, which they renamed Plymouth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patuxet

question: Christopher Columbus met the Taino of Hispaniola before any other people of the Americas, and a census of 1508 counted about 60,000 of them. Then came enslavement, war and, in 1518, the first smallpox epidemic to strike the New World. Roughly how many Taino were left by the mid-1500s?
answer: About 400
choices: About 4,000
About 2,000
About 900
About 400
context: The Taino count fell from about 60,000 (1508) to about 23,000 by 1518, and to fewer than 500 by the mid-1500s - effectively the extinction of a people within about two generations of Columbus's arrival. The smallpox epidemic of December 1518-1519 killed up to 90% of those who remained. Source: https://www.science.org/content/article/how-europeans-brought-sickness-new-world

question: An Aztec who lived through the epidemic of 1520 described it for the friar Bernardino de Sahagun: the sick were so covered in agonizing sores they 'could only lie on their beds like corpses.' Yet many who survived the disease itself still died soon afterward. Why did so many survivors die?
answer: No one was well enough to bring them food, so they starved
choices: No one was well enough to bring them food, so they starved
The Spanish killed them as they lay helpless
The disease returned a second time and finished them
They were driven out of the city into the cold
context: Because entire families fell sick at once, there was often no one left healthy to fetch water or food, so people who might have survived the disease died of dehydration and starvation. The eyewitness account survives in the Florentine Codex, recorded by Sahagun from Nahua elders. Source: https://www.doaks.org/resources/online-exhibits/epidemics/epidemics-english/fall-of-tenochtitlan/smallpox

question: Johannes Krause's team read DNA in 2018 from the teeth of people killed by cocoliztli, an epidemic of 1545 that took millions of lives in New Spain with high fever and bleeding from the eyes and mouth. For centuries no one had known what the disease was. What did the DNA show it to be?
answer: A Salmonella bacterium causing a typhoid-like fever
choices: A Salmonella bacterium causing a typhoid-like fever
The smallpox virus, as had long been assumed
A strain of the bubonic plague
An early and unusually deadly measles
context: Krause's team (Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2018) found Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C in the teeth of cocoliztli victims buried at Teposcolula-Yucundaa in Oaxaca - the first molecular identification of a 1545 pathogen. The Spanish physician Francisco Hernandez had described the symptoms: high fever, black tongue, dark urine, and bleeding from the nose, eyes, and mouth. The 1545-1548 outbreak killed an estimated 5 to 15 million people. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/cocoliztli-salmonella-outbreak-mexico-dna-spd

question: John Winthrop, who governed the Puritans of Massachusetts, wrote a letter in 1634 noting that smallpox had killed nearly all the Native people near the colony. He read their deaths as a sign of God's favour toward the settlers. What line did Winthrop write?
answer: "The Lord hath cleared our title to what we possess"
choices: "The Lord hath cleared our title to what we possess"
"God hath given these lands to His chosen people"
"Providence hath spared us to tame this wilderness"
"Heaven smiles upon our errand in the new world"
context: From Winthrop's letter of May 22, 1634: 'For the natives, they are near all dead of the smallpox, so the Lord hath cleared our title to what we possess.' This is real primary-source history showing how colonists understood the epidemics, presented plainly. The other three quotations are invented as decoys. Source: https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/spotlight-primary-source/john-winthrop-describes-life-boston-1634

question: British soldiers holding Fort Pitt under siege in 1763, during Pontiac's War, met two Delaware envoys and handed them a grim gift. A trader named William Trent recorded it and wrote, 'I hope it will have the desired effect.' What had the British handed the envoys?
answer: Blankets taken from their smallpox hospital
choices: Blankets taken from their smallpox hospital
Rifles that had been rigged to misfire
Food that had been deliberately spoiled
Whiskey that had been laced with poison
context: A Fort Pitt ledger records the supplies, and Trent's journal hoped they would 'have the desired effect.' General Jeffery Amherst separately urged Colonel Bouquet to 'inoculate the Indians by means of blankets' to 'extirpate this execrable race.' Historians caution that smallpox was already circulating in the area, so the blankets' actual effect is uncertain - what is documented is the intent. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/colonists-native-americans-smallpox-blankets

question: Alexander Koch and his fellow scientists made a startling argument in 2019: the deaths of tens of millions of Native Americans could have chilled the whole Earth, deepening the Little Ice Age, the cold spell of the years around 1600. The case is serious but unsettled. How, by their account, could so many deaths have cooled the Earth?
answer: Abandoned farmland regrew into forests that absorbed CO2
choices: Abandoned farmland regrew into forests that absorbed CO2
Fewer cooking fires put less smoke into the sky
Rotting bodies released gases that blocked the sun
Empty cities reflected more sunlight back into space
context: Koch's University College London study argued the 'Great Dying' depopulated so much farmland - about 56 million hectares, roughly the size of Texas - that regrowing forests pulled enough CO2 out of the air to deepen the coldest part of the Little Ice Age around 1600. This is presented as a scientific argument (confidence is moderate), not a settled fact. Source: https://eos.org/articles/european-contact-with-the-americas-may-have-triggered-global-cooling

question: Rudyard Kipling published a poem in February 1899 that urged the United States to seize and rule the Philippines. It called the people there 'sullen peoples, half-devil and half-child,' and cast empire as a thankless duty. What did Kipling title the poem?
answer: The White Man's Burden
choices: The White Man's Burden
The Conqueror's Crown
The Saxon's Charge
The Empire's Errand
context: Kipling's 'The White Man's Burden' (subtitle: 'The United States and the Philippine Islands') ran just as the Philippine-American War began, casting empire as a thankless duty owed to 'your captives' need.' Then-governor Theodore Roosevelt mailed it to Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, calling it 'rather poor poetry, but good sense from the expansionist standpoint.' Source: americanliterature.com/author/rudyard-kipling/poem/the-white-mans-burden ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_White_Man%27s_Burden

question: Herbert Spencer, a British philosopher, coined the slogan 'survival of the fittest' in 1864, and Charles Darwin only borrowed it later. Spencer offered it as another name for an idea Darwin had already named in his book On the Origin of Species. What phrase had Darwin used?
answer: Natural selection
choices: Natural selection
Ancestral inheritance
Random variation
Species drift
context: Herbert Spencer wrote that his 'survival of the fittest' was 'that which Mr. Darwin has called natural selection.' The famous catchphrase was a philosopher's gloss bolted onto biology and then stretched onto human society — Darwin only adopted it later, and as a metaphor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_of_the_fittest ; smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/herbert-spencer-survival-of-the-fittest-180974756

question: Jules Ferry, prime minister of France, rose in the Chamber of Deputies in 1884 to defend French conquests overseas. He insisted that empire was a favour to the conquered, and he packed the whole case into one sentence about the 'superior races.' What did Ferry tell the deputies?
answer: They have a right because they have a duty
choices: They have a right because they have a duty
They rule because God has chosen them
They conquer because commerce demands it
They lead because none else can
context: Ferry's full line — 'The superior races have a right because they have a duty. They have the duty to civilize the inferior races' — is the textbook statement of the 'mission civilisatrice,' the civilizing mission: empire reframed as a gift to the people it conquered. Source: web.viu.ca/davies/H479B.Imperialism.Nationalism/Ferry.Fr.imperialism.1884.htm

question: Camille Pelletan, a deputy in the French Chamber, heard Jules Ferry claim in 1884 that empire was a favour to the 'inferior races,' and he would not let it stand. Right there in the chamber he demanded to know what sort of civilisation needed cannonballs to deliver it, and whether those peoples were not masters of their own houses. What did Pelletan call the conquest?
answer: another form of barbarism
choices: another form of barbarism
a mask for plain greed
a crime dressed as charity
the rich man's adventure
context: Pelletan answered Ferry in the same room: 'What is this civilization which you impose with cannonballs? What is it but another form of barbarism? Don't these populations, these inferior races, have the same rights as you? Aren't they masters of their own houses?' The rationalization was challenged in real time, by a contemporary, to the proponent's face. Source: web.viu.ca/davies/H479B.Imperialism.Nationalism/Ferry.Fr.imperialism.1884.htm ; digfir-published.macmillanusa.com/Lauldi4e/lauldi4e_ch23_2.html

question: William Graham Sumner, the American sociologist, argued that the people and nations on top must be nature's 'fittest' and so deserved to rule. To a biologist, though, 'fitness' does not mean what it sounds like in everyday speech. What does a biologist's 'fitness' measure in an animal?
answer: how many offspring it leaves
choices: how many offspring it leaves
how strong and fierce it grows
how clever it becomes
how long it manages to live
context: In biology 'fitness' just means reproductive success — leaving more offspring — not being strongest, smartest, or morally better, and never a ranking of which people or nations 'deserve' to rule. Wikipedia calls social Darwinism 'pseudoscientific' and 'discredited'; thinkers like Steven Pinker flag it as the 'appeal to nature' fallacy — what exists in nature does not tell us what is right. The leap from biology to group moral worth was always illegitimate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_of_the_fittest ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Darwinism

question: A ploughman came through the Black Death alive as the plague swept across Europe between 1347 and 1351. Now the farms and towns around him were short of hands. What changed for surviving peasants like him?
answer: They could demand far higher pay than before
choices: They could demand far higher pay than before
They were forced to work for free as punishment
They were sent away from the farms to the cities
They had to share their wages with the dead men's families
context: With a third of Europe dead, surviving workers were scarce, and scarce things command a high price. The medieval body-count turned labor into a seller's market, and serfdom began to crack. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Labourers_1351

question: John Bampton, collecting taxes for the king, came to the village of Brentwood in Essex on 30 May 1381, backed by armed men. He meant to wring a poll tax out of the villagers, a flat charge on every head that the poor hated. What did the people of Brentwood do to him?
answer: They drove him off, and the revolt spread within days
choices: They drove him off, and the revolt spread within days
They paid the tax twice over to be left alone
They elected him as their new local lord
They marched with him to collect from the next village
context: On 30 May 1381 the men of Brentwood ran Bampton out of town over a third poll tax, and the Peasants' Revolt blazed across southeast England within days. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: John Ball, a radical priest, stood before the rebels gathered on Blackheath, just outside London, on 12 June 1381 and stirred them with a single famous line. He meant by it that nobody was born a lord. What was Ball's line?
answer: "When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?"
choices: "When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?"
"Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's"
"The meek shall inherit the earth before the proud"
"No king but the King of Heaven shall rule over us"
context: John Ball's couplet became the rallying cry of the revolt: if Adam dug and Eve spun, the noble class had no birthright over the common worker. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: Peasant rebels broke into the Tower of London, the king's own fortress, on 14 June 1381. They seized two of the most powerful men in England, Simon Sudbury, the archbishop, and Robert Hales, the treasurer. What did the rebels do to them?
answer: They beheaded them and paraded their heads on London Bridge
choices: They beheaded them and paraded their heads on London Bridge
They locked them in the Tower's deepest cell for ransom
They forced them to sign away their lands and exiled them
They put them on trial before a jury of peasants
context: The rebels dragged Sudbury and Hales out of the Tower, beheaded them, and displayed their heads on London Bridge — striking at the very top of church and treasury. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: The rebels of 1381 burned and tore down John of Gaunt's lavish Savoy Palace in London, though it held treasure worth about 10,000 pounds. They called themselves 'zealots for truth and justice.' What did they do with all that wealth?
answer: They stole almost nothing from it
choices: They stole almost nothing from it
They split the gold evenly among every rebel
They hauled the treasure back to their villages
They sold it off to pay the hated poll tax for everyone
context: To prove they fought for justice and not plunder, the rebels destroyed the Savoy's riches rather than pocket them — a point of honor declared aloud as the palace burned. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: Richard II, the fourteen-year-old king, saw the rebel leader Wat Tyler struck down at Smithfield on 15 June 1381, and the angry crowd readied their bows. The boy king rode straight out toward them. What did Richard do that defused a massacre?
answer: He told the crowd to follow him as their leader
choices: He told the crowd to follow him as their leader
He drew his own sword and challenged Tyler's men
He promised to lower the poll tax on the spot
He ordered his archers to fire the first volley
context: Chroniclers say the 14-year-old Richard II rode out and told the leaderless mob he would be their captain, turning a powder-keg into a procession. The mercy did not last — within weeks he revoked every promise. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: Richard II, the boy king, signed charters in 1381 that abolished serfdom and pardoned the rebels who had marched on London, and the peasants went home. What did Richard do to those charters on 2 July?
answer: He formally revoked every one of them weeks later
choices: He formally revoked every one of them weeks later
He had them read aloud in every parish forever
He expanded them to free serfs across all of France
He locked them in the Tower as a sacred record
context: On 2 July 1381 Richard II revoked all the freedom charters he had signed under pressure; by November at least 1,500 rebels had been executed, and John Ball was hanged, drawn and quartered on 15 July. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

question: England's rulers under Edward III made it a crime, in 1349 and again in 1351, to ask for or pay more than the old wages paid before the Black Death. By 1352 Parliament admitted that the law had failed. What were workers doing in spite of it?
answer: Demanding double and treble the old rate anyway
choices: Demanding double and treble the old rate anyway
Fleeing England to work in France instead
Refusing to work any land at all
Secretly paying the lords to keep their old wages
context: Scarcity beat the statute: with workers few, supply and demand drove pay to double and treble the old rate no matter what Parliament decreed — a real seen/unseen lesson written into law and then broken. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Labourers_1351

question: Robert of Avesbury, a chronicler, watched more than 600 men arrive in London from Flanders around Michaelmas 1349, while the plague raged. Twice a day they bared their backs and whipped them bloody with knotted whips. Why did these flagellants whip themselves?
answer: To beg God to lift the Black Death
choices: To beg God to lift the Black Death
To train their bodies for war against France
To punish the tax collectors among them
To mourn a king who had died of the plague
context: The Brethren of the Cross believed self-inflicted suffering might persuade God to spare humanity from the plague; their scourges held sharp iron nails, and each man wore a red cross front and back. Source: https://fathertheo.wordpress.com/2013/05/07/flagellants-in-london-1349/

question: The Pope issued a bull, a formal decree, on 20 October 1349 about the Brethren of the Cross, the flagellants whose numbers had grown fast across plague-stricken Europe, men who whipped their own backs bloody. What did the bull do to the Brethren?
answer: It denounced them as an impious sect and ordered them suppressed
choices: It denounced them as an impious sect and ordered them suppressed
It welcomed them into the Church as a holy order
It made their 33-day whipping marches official law
It excused all their followers from paying tithes
context: The flagellants marched town to town in 33-day cycles — one day for each year of Christ's life — until the movement grew so large that on 20 October 1349 the Pope condemned the Brethren of the Cross as an impious sect to be stamped out. Source: https://medium.com/never-stop-writing/the-black-death-part-three-faith-fear-and-the-flagellants-1ef4b2415690

question: Guillaume Cale, a well-off farmer, led France's great peasant rising of 1358, the Jacquerie. Charles II of Navarre invited him to truce talks near Mello, and Cale came to parley, but the nobles seized him, saying the rules of chivalry did not protect a peasant. What did they do to Guillaume Cale?
answer: They tortured him and cut off his head
choices: They tortured him and cut off his head
They held him for a king's ransom in gold
They made him swear loyalty and set him free
They exiled him across the sea to England
context: Lured to truce talks near Mello on 10 June 1358, Guillaume Cale was seized, tortured, and decapitated by nobles who held that chivalry's rules did not apply to a peasant. The Jacquerie was crushed with at least 20,000 peasants killed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Cale

question: A jury of 500 Athenians sat in judgment on Socrates in 399 BC. The seventy-year-old philosopher was famous for asking the powerful awkward questions in the marketplace. His accusers brought two charges. One was impiety: failing to honor the gods of the city and introducing strange new spirits. What was the other?
answer: Corrupting the young men of Athens
choices: Corrupting the young men of Athens
Stealing money from the city treasury
Spying for the enemy city of Sparta
Refusing to fight in Athens' army
context: His accusers claimed his constant questioning was teaching Athens' youth to doubt and disrespect their elders and gods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Socrates

question: Socrates, on trial for his life, told the jurors of Athens that their city was a great, noble horse, too big and sluggish to move on its own, and that the god had set him on it to sting it awake. What did he call himself?
answer: A gadfly
choices: A gadfly
A wasp
A hornet
A mosquito
context: In Plato's Apology (30e) Socrates says the city is 'a great and noble horse which was somewhat sluggish because of its size and needed to be stirred up,' and he is the gadfly sent by the god to do the stirring: I am that gadfly which God has given the state, he told the jury, arousing and persuading and reproaching you. The fly that stings the lazy horse awake became his image for the philosopher who will not let a city sleep in its assumptions. Sources: Plato, Apology 30e; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_unexamined_life_is_not_worth_living

question: Socrates stood trial in Athens in 399 BC, charged with corrupting the city's young men and mocking its gods. In his defense he told the court he would rather die than stop questioning everyone he met in the marketplace. Then he gave one short line, now among the most famous in philosophy, for why he would not be silenced. What was it?
answer: The unexamined life is not worth living
choices: The unexamined life is not worth living
A man should always obey the city's laws
Knowledge is the only true form of wealth
Death is nothing to be feared by the wise
context: Plato's Apology (38a) records the line; the original Greek is 'ho de anexetastos bios ou biotos anthropoi.' For Socrates, examining your own beliefs was the whole point of being human. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_unexamined_life_is_not_worth_living

question: The Athenian jury narrowly found Socrates guilty of impiety and corrupting the young, and then asked him to name his own punishment. Instead of begging for exile or a fine, the old philosopher joked that he deserved a reward: the same public honor Athens gave its victorious Olympic champions. What did he say he deserved?
answer: Free meals for life at public expense
choices: Free meals for life at public expense
A statue raised in the marketplace
A general's command in the army
A golden crown from the assembly
context: He suggested dining for life at the Prytaneum, the honor reserved for Olympic victors. Only when his friends Plato and Crito offered to pay did he grudgingly propose a fine of thirty minae instead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apology_(Plato)

question: Athens condemned Socrates in 399 BC for 'corrupting the youth' and doubting the city's gods. His sentence was to drink a cup of hemlock, a slow and quiet poison. Told to walk about the prison until his legs grew heavy, he at last lay down to wait. How did the poison kill him?
answer: A cold numbness crept slowly up toward his heart
choices: A cold numbness crept slowly up toward his heart
A burning fever spread through his whole body
Violent convulsions seized him within moments
A deep sleep took him before any pain began
context: Hemlock causes a slow, creeping paralysis. The executioner pressed his foot and asked if he could feel it; Socrates said no. The cold rose from his feet up his shins and abdomen, and when it reached his heart, he would be gone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaedo

question: The Thirty Tyrants, a brutal junta, ruled Athens in 404 BC and executed rich citizens to seize their property. Years before his own trial, they summoned Socrates and four other men and ordered them to arrest an innocent citizen, Leon of Salamis, so that Leon could be killed and his estate taken. The other four went and did it. What did Socrates do?
answer: He simply turned and went home
choices: He simply turned and went home
He warned Leon and helped him escape
He arrested Leon but pleaded for mercy
He fled Athens that same night
context: Disobeying the Tyrants could have cost Socrates his life, but he refused to help murder an innocent man and just walked home. He told this story at his trial as proof he had never bent to unjust power. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/socrates/

question: Athens sentenced Socrates in 399 BC to die by drinking hemlock, yet he sat condemned in his prison cell for about a month. An old religious rule forbade any execution in the city during a certain stretch of days. What caused the long delay?
answer: A sacred ship was away on a holy voyage
choices: A sacred ship was away on a holy voyage
A festival of games had filled the city
A plague had shut the prison gates
An eclipse was read as an evil omen
context: Each year a sacred ship sailed to the island of Delos to honor Apollo, and no execution was permitted until it returned. That year contrary winds stretched the usual two-week trip into a month. Source: https://law.hofstra.edu/sites/law.hofstra.edu/files/2024-08/fall-2024-jurisprudence-sinha-crito.pdf

question: Socrates lay dying in his Athenian prison, the hemlock working through his body, with his old friend Crito beside him. His very last words were not a grand speech but a small, practical instruction. What did he tell Crito with his dying breath?
answer: That they owed a rooster to the healing god
choices: That they owed a rooster to the healing god
That his children should be raised by Crito
That the jury would one day be ashamed
That his books should be given to Plato
context: 'Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius; pay it and do not neglect it.' Asclepius was the god of healing, and such an offering thanked him for a cure — as if Socrates were thanking the god for curing him of life itself. Crito then closed his eyes and mouth. Source: https://classical-inquiries.chs.harvard.edu/the-last-words-of-socrates-at-the-place-where-he-died/

question: Socrates' old friend Crito crept into the prison at dawn with an escape fully arranged: guards bribed, a hiding place ready. Socrates refused to run. In Plato's dialogue Crito, what imagined confrontation did he use to explain why he would not escape?
answer: The Laws of Athens themselves rising up to accuse him
choices: The Laws of Athens themselves rising up to accuse him
His dead father returning to shame him
The gods of Olympus weighing his soul
A future Athens cursing his cowardice
context: Socrates pictured the Laws of Athens confronting him: he had lived his whole life under them and accepted their protection, so he could not break the city's verdict just because it now harmed him. Crito had no answer and gave in. Source: https://law.hofstra.edu/sites/law.hofstra.edu/files/2024-08/fall-2024-jurisprudence-sinha-crito.pdf

question: Henri Dunant, a Swiss businessman travelling to meet Napoleon III, walked into the aftermath of the battle of Solferino in June 1859. In the town of Castiglione he watched women turn their church into a hospital, nursing French, Austrian and Italian soldiers alike. What two words did the women keep repeating as they worked?
answer: "Tutti fratelli" — all are brothers
choices: "Tutti fratelli" — all are brothers
"Veni, vidi, vici" — I came, I saw, I conquered
"Ora pro nobis" — pray for us
"Avanti, Italia" — forward, Italy
context: Henri Dunant, a 31-year-old Swiss businessman, had stumbled into the aftermath of Solferino while traveling to meet Napoleon III about an Algerian land deal. The scene of the Castiglione women caring for friend and enemy alike — 'Tutti fratelli' — became the seed of his idea for a neutral society to aid the wounded of any side, the future Red Cross. Source: nationalgeographic.com/history/article/red-cross-founder-jean-henri-dunant; ifrc.org/article/world-red-cross-and-red-crescent-day-message-our-movement

question: Delegates met in Geneva in 1864 to choose an emblem for Henri Dunant's new society for helping the wounded of all sides. They wanted to honour neutral Switzerland, whose flag is a white cross on a red field. What emblem did they choose?
answer: A red cross on a white background
choices: A red cross on a white background
A white cross on a red background
A red cross on a blue background
A gold cross on a green background
context: The red-cross-on-white emblem chosen in 1864 was deliberately the exact color-reverse of neutral Switzerland's flag, honoring the Swiss origins of the movement Henri Dunant founded. Source: ifrc.org/who-we-are/international-red-cross-and-red-crescent-movement/emblems-and-logo; nationalgeographic.com/history/article/red-cross-founder-jean-henri-dunant

question: Lech Walesa stood locked outside the gates of the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk in August 1980. The yard had fired the electrician years earlier for organizing, and now its workers had seized it in protest at food price rises and the firing of a union activist. How did Walesa get in to join their strike?
answer: He climbed over the twelve-foot perimeter fence
choices: He climbed over the twelve-foot perimeter fence
He bribed a guard to open a side gate
He swam across the harbor to the docks
He hid in the back of a delivery truck
context: Walesa scaled the roughly 12-foot fence to join the strikers, who promptly elected him head of their strike committee — the fence-climb is the iconic founding image of Solidarity. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lech-Walesa

question: Lech Walesa signed the Gdansk Agreement on 31 August 1980, winning Polish workers the right to form free trade unions, the first such right anywhere in the Soviet bloc. He marked the moment with an oversized souvenir pen. What was printed on the pen?
answer: A portrait of Pope John Paul II
choices: A portrait of Pope John Paul II
The red-and-white Polish eagle crest
The Solidarnosc logo in bold red letters
An image of the Gdansk shipyard cranes
context: Walesa signed the historic accord with a giant souvenir pen bearing the face of the Polish-born pope — fusing the workers' movement with the faith that had helped fuel it. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/august-31/polish-government-signs-accord-with-gdansk-shipyard-workers

question: A Song exam candidate carried his own food, ink, bedding and a chamber pot into a roofless brick cell barely three feet wide, as later records of China's exams describe, and stayed there alone for days. Two wooden boards were all the furniture it held. What were the two boards for?
answer: One was his desk; the other was both his seat and his bed.
choices: One was his desk; the other was both his seat and his bed.
One was his door; the other sealed the cell shut at night.
One held his lamp; the other propped up a small cooking fire.
One was a shelf for his books; the other a board to kneel on.
context: By day the candidate wrote at one board; by night he slept on the other — for days on end, sealed in alone. (The cell dimensions are best documented from the later imperial exam halls of the same continuous tradition, not from measured Song halls.) Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'Imperial Examinations (Keju)'; Wikipedia, 'Imperial examination.'

question: A scholar of Song China found his name at the very top of the yellow Golden List: of every candidate in the empire, he had come first. He was now the zhuangyuan. How was the new top scholar honoured in public?
answer: He was paraded through the streets on horseback.
choices: He was paraded through the streets on horseback.
He was carried to the palace temple to be blessed.
He was handed the keys to the city's main gate.
He was seated beside the emperor at a banquet.
context: The 'zhuangyuan' (top graduate) was a celebrity overnight: his name on the yellow 'Golden List,' then a parade on horseback through the streets. Source: Wikipedia, 'Zhuangyuan'; Baidu Baike (EN), 'Zhuangyuan, the top graduate in the imperial examination.'

question: Merchants in Sichuan were already trading in paper notes of their own when the Song state took over the idea in 1023. From an office in Chengdu it began issuing jiaozi notes, the first paper money any state ever put out. What problem in Sichuan first drove the merchants to paper?
answer: The local coins were made of iron and too heavy to carry.
choices: The local coins were made of iron and too heavy to carry.
The local mines had run completely out of copper and silver.
Bandits on the roads kept robbing every shipment of coins.
The region lay too far from the capital's official mints.
context: Sichuan used bulky IRON coins, so merchants there issued lightweight paper notes instead; the state then took it over, opening the Jiaozi office (Jiaozi wu) in Chengdu in 1023 and issuing official notes by 1024. Source: Wikipedia, 'Jiaozi (currency)'; South China Morning Post, 'how China's Song dynasty pioneered global fiat currency.'

question: Officials at the Song exams kept the compound's gates sealed until the whole exam was over, as this exam tradition demanded. Now and then a candidate died in the middle of the test, at his desk, after days shut in his cell. What did the officials do with his body?
answer: They wrapped it in a mat and threw it over the compound wall.
choices: They wrapped it in a mat and threw it over the compound wall.
They laid it in his cell until the gates opened days later.
They burned it at once in a brazier out in the courtyard.
They carried it out through a small door kept for the dead.
context: Rather than break the seal on the gates, officials wrapped the body in a mat and pitched it over the high wall. (Documented from the later halls of the same continuous exam tradition, not from Song-specific records.) Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'Imperial Examinations (Keju)'; The History Reader, 'Examination Time in Early Qing Dynasty Beijing.'

question: Emperor Taizu, the general who seized the throne and founded the Song dynasty, deliberately raised scholars above soldiers. In 973 he added a brand-new final round to the civil service exam and kept one remarkable part of it for himself. What was it?
answer: He personally tested the top candidates and ranked them himself.
choices: He personally tested the top candidates and ranked them himself.
He chose which Confucian classics every candidate would study.
He selected the graders who would mark all of the papers.
He wrote out the questions for that first exam by hand.
context: By creating the Palace Examination and presiding over it, Taizu made the emperor the final examiner of his own future officials, announcing the ranked list himself. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Emperor Taizu of Song'; Britannica, 'Taizu — Reform of the examination.'

question: Su Song, a Song official, raised a water-driven clock tower about forty feet high at the capital, Kaifeng, and finished it in 1094. A giant water wheel turned its works, and a bronze sphere on top tracked the stars. What did the clock do every hour to mark the time?
answer: Little costumed figurines popped out of doors to ring bells and beat drums.
choices: Little costumed figurines popped out of doors to ring bells and beat drums.
A bronze dragon's mouth dropped a metal ball into a bowl with a clang.
A bank of bronze bells swung out and rang across the whole city.
A painted sun and moon slid across the open face of the tower.
context: 133 little costumed figurines popped from doors to ring bells and beat drums on the hour; the wheel was 11 feet across with 36 scoops, and the bronze armillary sphere on top weighed 10 to 20 tons. Source: Wikipedia, 'Su Song'; Instituto Português de Relojoaria, 'Su Sung's Clock.'

question: Jurchen Jin soldiers took Kaifeng in 1127 and hauled Su Song's great clock tower away north in pieces, yet no one could get it working again. Su Xie, Su Song's own son, then tried to rebuild his father's machine and failed too. What did Su Xie conclude?
answer: That his father had deliberately left out essential parts.
choices: That his father had deliberately left out essential parts.
That the Jin had lost crucial pieces on the journey north.
That the design had only ever worked by sheer luck.
That the water in the north was wrong for the great wheel.
context: The Jin could never reassemble the tower; Su Song's son Su Xie failed too, and concluded his father had purposely omitted essential parts. Source: Wikipedia, 'Su Song' (Jurchen dismantling 1127; Su Xie's failed reconstruction).

question: A Song grader picked up an exam paper and found a number where the candidate's name should be: from 992 the names were covered to stamp out favouritism. Yet a grader might still recognize a candidate's handwriting, so from 1015 the Song added a second safeguard. What was it?
answer: Clerks recopied every single exam by hand before it was graded.
choices: Clerks recopied every single exam by hand before it was graded.
Graders were reassigned to a different province every year.
Candidates were forced to write in one stiff official script.
Each paper was read aloud so the grader never saw the writing.
context: A whole team of clerks recopied every paper by hand so a grader couldn't recognize the writing; two graders then scored each paper and a third broke ties. Source: Wikipedia, 'Imperial examination' (anonymity reforms 992/1007/1015/1032); SonomaSage Substack, 'The Exams of China: The Song Dynasty.'

question: A farmer's son in Song China mastered the Confucian books and sat the civil service exam. Counts of the graduates in 1148 and 1256 found about 57 percent from families that had never held official rank. Since rank now came from the exam and not from birth, what became possible for him?
answer: He could outrank a general's son who had not passed.
choices: He could outrank a general's son who had not passed.
He was given command of the army's western border.
He was guaranteed a post in his own home county.
He was excused from ever paying the imperial taxes.
context: In 1148 and 1256, about 57% of degree-holders came from families with no prior official rank — so a farmer's son who mastered the books really could outrank a general's son who hadn't. Source: Wikipedia, 'Imperial examination' (citing Hartwell/Chaffee social-mobility data for 1148 and 1256).

question: Gao, capital of the Songhai Empire, sat beside a great river in West Africa. The river fed its farms and carried its trade canoes past the Sahara's southern edge. Under Askia Muhammad the city grew to about 100,000 people. Which river was it?
answer: The Niger River
choices: The Niger River
The Nile River
The Congo River
The Zambezi River
context: Gao stood on the Niger River in West Africa, and under Askia Muhammad it swelled to about 100,000 inhabitants, one of the largest cities in the region. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Songhai_Empire/

question: On the southern edge of the Sahara, one city of the Songhai Empire drew gold traders and Muslim scholars. It grew so famous for its trade and its Islamic learning that it held around 100,000 people and roughly 150 to 180 Koranic schools. Which fabled city was it?
answer: Timbuktu
choices: Timbuktu
Cairo
Baghdad
Mecca
context: Timbuktu, on the edge of the Sahara, was Songhai's jewel of scholarship, with scholars teaching at the Sankore Mosque. Its name still means 'the ends of the earth' to many. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Songhai_Empire/

question: Askia Muhammad, ruler of the Songhai Empire, set out from his capital, Gao, in 1497 to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. He crossed the Sahara with hundreds of horsemen and a huge treasury, and gave 100,000 gold pieces to charity in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. What title did the Abbasid caliph give him there?
answer: 'Caliph of the Sudan'
choices: 'Caliph of the Sudan'
'King of the Niger'
'Lion of Gao'
'Sultan of Timbuktu'
context: In Mecca the last Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil named Askia Muhammad 'Caliph of the Sudan' (West Africa). On his way home he recruited scholars from Egypt and Morocco to teach at the Sankore Mosque in Timbuktu. Source: owlcation.com via WebSearch

question: Askia Muhammad seized the Songhai throne by beating the old king's son at the Battle of Anfao in 1493, then ruled for about 37 years. He built a professional standing army and a government of specialized ministers. Where in Gao was he finally buried?
answer: In a stepped pyramid of mud and earth
choices: In a stepped pyramid of mud and earth
In a marble mosque domed with gold
Beneath the Sankore Mosque floor
In a cave carved into a cliff
context: The Tomb of Askia is a stepped pyramid of mud and earth, just over 10 meters tall, bristling with protruding acacia-wood stakes (toron) used as permanent scaffolding for re-plastering. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Tomb_of_Askia

question: Ahmad al-Mansur, the sultan of Morocco, sent an army south over the entire Sahara in 1591 to attack Songhai. At the Battle of Tondibi the huge Songhai cavalry, armed only with spears, swords and bows, charged the smaller Moroccan force. What did the Moroccans carry that decided the battle in about two hours?
answer: Firearms — arquebuses and cannon
choices: Firearms — arquebuses and cannon
Heavier armored war-elephants
A surprise river ambush by canoe
Vastly greater numbers of horsemen
context: Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur's roughly 2,000 arquebusiers and 6 cannon, led by the Spanish-born eunuch Judar Pasha, decimated the gunless Songhai. Gunpowder ended the largest empire in West African history; the region fragmented into dozens of smaller kingdoms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tondibi

question: The Songhai met Morocco's invading army at Tondibi in 1591, in what is now Mali. The Moroccans carried Spanish-style muskets and small cannon; the Songhai had cavalry and spears. In a desperate trick the Songhai drove a herd of 1,000 cattle to stampede into the Moroccan line. What went wrong with the plan?
answer: The gunfire and cannon noise turned the herd back into the Songhai's own ranks
choices: The gunfire and cannon noise turned the herd back into the Songhai's own ranks
The cattle bogged down in the Niger's mud and never reached the line
Moroccan horsemen simply rode around the slow-moving herd
The Moroccans drove their own larger herd to meet it head-on
context: The roar of arquebuses and cannon panicked the cattle, which stampeded backward into the Songhai. Some Songhai soldiers reportedly sat on their shields rather than flee and were killed where they sat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tondibi

question: Red Army soldiers fought their way west across eastern Europe in 1944, many of them farm boys raised in poor villages. They seized one small prize with such eagerness that some ended up wearing a whole row of them. What did they seize?
answer: Wristwatches
choices: Wristwatches
Wedding rings
Fountain pens
Leather boots
context: Red Army soldiers became notorious across Eastern Europe for wearing watches up each arm. A December 1944 decree letting Soviet soldiers mail parcels home was read across the army as an open invitation to grab whatever they could carry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_plunder

question: A Soviet official summed up Moscow's plan for one of the Baltic states in a single line that became infamous among its survivors. The Red Army had occupied Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania during the Second World War, and Stalin's regime deported hundreds of thousands of their citizens to Siberian labour camps. Which line did he use?
answer: "There will be Lithuania -- but without Lithuanians"
choices: "There will be Lithuania -- but without Lithuanians"
"There will be a Latvia -- but without its bourgeoisie"
"There will be an Estonia -- but without its borders"
"There will be a Baltic -- but without its old masters"
context: Between 1940 and 1953 over 200,000 Balts were deported -- roughly a tenth of the adult population. Estonian deportee mortality has been estimated at around 60 percent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_deportation

question: Soviet secret police officers banged on doors across Soviet-held eastern Poland on the bitterly cold night of 10 February 1940. Families got minutes to pack 500 kg, then were loaded onto cattle trains for Siberia; about 139,000 people went in one night. What stands out about who was on those trains?
answer: Nearly half were children under 16
choices: Nearly half were children under 16
Most were retired army generals
Almost all were Catholic priests
Nearly all were over 70 years old
context: This was the first of four deportation waves. Settlers, foresters, and refugees were packed off to 'special settlements' in Siberia and the Arctic north. Source: https://kresy-siberia.org/museum-galleries/soviet-mass-deportations-1940-41/soviet-mass-deportations/

question: Josef Stalin turned on a whole people in May 1944: his regime branded them collaborators with the German army and packed about 183,000 of them into sealed cattle wagons in a single sweep. The trains took them to Uzbekistan, in Central Asia, and roughly a fifth of them were dead within 18 months. Which people did he uproot?
answer: The Crimean Tatars
choices: The Crimean Tatars
The Cossacks of the Don
The Karelian Finns
The Georgian Mingrelians
context: The Volga Germans, the Chechens, and others met the same fate -- whole peoples uprooted at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_transfer_in_the_Soviet_Union

question: Marta Hillers wrote a secret diary through the eight weeks of Soviet occupation in Berlin in 1945, and she published it without her name. Readers in 1950s Germany rejected it as too honest, and only after her death did it become a bestseller. What was the diary called?
answer: "A Woman in Berlin"
choices: "A Woman in Berlin"
"Diary of a Berlin Woman"
"A Berlin Woman's War"
"Notes of a Woman in Berlin"
context: Hillers published it anonymously; German readers of the 1950s rejected its honesty about what the occupation did to women, and only after her death did it find its audience. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Woman_in_Berlin

question: Lavrentiy Beria, chief of the Soviet secret police, wrote a note on 5 March 1940. It asked leave to give some 22,000 captured Polish officers, policemen and professionals 'the maximum penalty.' What did Stalin do to Beria's note that sealed the men's fate?
answer: Stalin signed his approval across the top
choices: Stalin signed his approval across the top
Stalin had it read aloud to the Politburo
Stalin ordered it backdated to look legal
Stalin passed it to Molotov to sign first
context: The men were shot one by one with a pistol to the back of the head -- some 4,400 of them in Katyn Forest -- and dumped in mass graves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katyn_massacre

question: Retreating from western Ukraine in late June 1941 as Germany invaded, Soviet secret policemen killed the political prisoners in their jails rather than free them. About 10,000 to 40,000 died in eight days, by shooting, grenades and fire in their cells. How did Nazi propaganda twist this Soviet crime to its own use?
answer: They blamed it on Jews to incite pogroms
choices: They blamed it on Jews to incite pogroms
They staged it to mimic a German victory
They blamed it on the prisoners' own riots
They credited it to advancing German troops
context: The Soviet atrocity was exploited by linking 'Jews' with 'communism' to provoke mob massacres -- a libel that cost still more innocent lives. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/1941-nkvd-prison-massacres-western-ukraine

question: Antony Beevor, the historian, called the Red Army's advance of 1944 and 1945 the greatest phenomenon of mass rape in history: at least 1.4 million women in East Prussia, Pomerania and Silesia alone. Where did Beevor draw that figure from?
answer: The Soviets' own internal reports
choices: The Soviets' own internal reports
Captured German Red Cross files
Western war correspondents' notebooks
Interrogated Wehrmacht officers
context: Of the roughly 100,000 women raped in Berlin, an estimated 10,000 died afterward. Beevor drew his numbers from the NKVD's own archive reports, not enemy claims. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape_during_the_occupation_of_Germany

question: Wladyslaw Anders, a Polish general, led over 110,000 of Poland's deportees out of the Soviet Union and into Persia, orphans among them, after Stalin granted them a brief amnesty under the Sikorski-Mayski pact of 1941. From Persia the freed Poles scattered. Where did many of them end up?
answer: As far as New Zealand, Mexico, and British Africa
choices: As far as New Zealand, Mexico, and British Africa
Mostly to France, Spain, and the United States
Chiefly to Canada, Australia, and Argentina
