Largely to Egypt, Greece, and South Africa only
context: The exodus of over 110,000 Poles -- including 36,000 women and children -- escaped through Persia (Iran) and then scattered as far as Iran, India, New Zealand, Mexico, and British Africa: a diaspora born of the Gulag. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evacuation_of_Polish_civilians_from_the_USSR_in_World_War_II

question: Soviet crews flew one fearsome machine over Afghanistan's mountains against the mujahideen guerrillas in the war of 1979 to 1989. Rifle bullets glanced off its heavy armour, and it carried rockets and a nose gun. The mujahideen had their own name for it: the flying tank. What was it?
answer: The Mi-24 'Hind' gunship
choices: The Mi-24 'Hind' gunship
The B-52 'Stratofortress' bomber
The T-72 'Ural' battle tank
The MiG-21 'Fishbed' fighter
context: The Mi-24 'Hind' was so heavily armored that small-arms fire bounced off it, earning the 'flying tank' nickname from the fighters it hunted. Breaking the Hind's dominance became the central problem of the war for the mujahideen. Source: https://smallwarsjournal.com/2023/11/25/cobra-and-mongoose-legacy-mi-24-and-stinger-missile-soviet-afghan-war/

question: General Boris Gromov led the last Soviet troops out of Afghanistan on 15 February 1989, ending a ten-year war the Soviet Union could not win. He arranged to be the very last soldier out himself, and he marked the moment with one symbolic act. What did Gromov do?
answer: He walked on foot across the Friendship Bridge into Soviet territory
choices: He walked on foot across the Friendship Bridge into Soviet territory
He signed the surrender at a table inside Kabul
He fired the war's last shot into the air
He raised the Soviet flag over the capital one last time
context: General Boris Gromov crossed the Friendship Bridge over the Amu Darya River on foot, the symbolic last man out. When TV crews asked how he felt, he swore at the camera; he later said the curses were aimed at 'those who start wars while others have to clean up the mess.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_withdrawal_from_Afghanistan

question: Soviet commandos opened the war on 27 December 1979 by storming the Tajbeg Palace in Kabul, an assault code-named Operation Storm-333 that took about forty minutes. They had one aim inside the palace. What was the point of the whole raid?
answer: To kill the Afghan leader Hafizullah Amin
choices: To kill the Afghan leader Hafizullah Amin
To capture the palace treasury intact
To rescue Soviet hostages held inside
To photograph Amin's secret war plans
context: Operation Storm-333 took only about 40 minutes and ended with Hafizullah Amin dead inside the Tajbeg Palace. Eleven days earlier the KGB had tried to poison Amin's lunch, but a Soviet doctor who knew nothing of the plot treated him and saved his life, forcing the commandos to storm the palace instead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Storm-333

question: Ghaffar, a mujahideen engineer, fired five new American shoulder-launched missiles near Jalalabad on 25 September 1986. Until then the Soviets had ruled the skies over Afghanistan, and in minutes he changed the war. What did Ghaffar do with those missiles?
answer: He downed three Mi-24 helicopters in quick succession
choices: He downed three Mi-24 helicopters in quick succession
He destroyed a column of Soviet supply trucks
He drove off a Soviet ground patrol unharmed
He scattered a formation of Soviet jet fighters
context: Ghaffar fired five FIM-92 Stinger missiles and downed three Mi-24 'Hinds' in their combat debut. The shoulder-fired, heat-seeking Stinger was light enough for one fighter to carry. The CIA had funneled the missiles to the mujahideen through Pakistan in a secret program called Operation Cyclone. Source: https://smallwarsjournal.com/2023/11/25/cobra-and-mongoose-legacy-mi-24-and-stinger-missile-soviet-afghan-war/

question: Ahmad Shah Massoud, the guerrilla commander known as the Lion of Panjshir, faced nine Soviet offensives in the Panjshir, his home valley, between 1980 and 1985. Each one aimed to drive him out. How did Massoud frustrate them each time?
answer: He returned to the valley the moment the Soviets left
choices: He returned to the valley the moment the Soviets left
He surrendered the valley and fought elsewhere
He retreated permanently across the border into Pakistan
He negotiated a lasting truce after the first offensive
context: Massoud, the 'Lion of Panjshir,' held the valley against nine Soviet offensives between 1980 and 1985. The Soviets could push him out but never hold the ground; he simply came back the instant they withdrew, making the valley a symbol of how the war could not be won. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panjshir_offensives_(Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War)

question: Mikhail Gorbachev rose before the 27th Party Congress in February 1986 and admitted in public what no Soviet leader was supposed to say: the Soviet Union was trapped in a war it could not win in Afghanistan. What two-word phrase did he use for that war?
answer: A 'bleeding wound'
choices: A 'bleeding wound'
A 'glorious duty'
A 'minor setback'
A 'foreign adventure'
context: Gorbachev called Afghanistan a 'bleeding wound' before the Party Congress, a stunning public admission of failure. Roughly 15,000 Soviet soldiers would die over the decade, which is why the conflict became known as the 'Soviet Vietnam.' Source: https://soviethistory.msu.edu/1985/afghans/afghans-texts/gorbachev-statement-on-afghanistan/

question: The last Soviet soldiers came home from Afghanistan after nearly ten years of a war that had cost some 15,000 Soviet lives, drained the treasury and ended in humiliating defeat. Historians list that war as one of the blows that brought down a superpower. How soon after the last troops left did the Soviet Union itself collapse?
answer: Less than three years later, in 1991
choices: Less than three years later, in 1991
Almost twenty years later
Within a few months
Not for another generation
context: The last troops left in February 1989, and the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, fewer than three years later. The cost was staggering on both sides: Afghan civilian dead are estimated from around 850,000 to over a million, with more than five million refugees fleeing into Pakistan and Iran. Source: https://faculty.washington.edu/aseem/afganwar.pdf

question: German and Italian airmen firebombed the Basque town of Guernica on 26 April 1937, and most of its wooden buildings burned to the ground. Beside the spared Basque assembly house, one thing came through the flames. For centuries Basque lords had sworn there to respect their people's freedoms. What survived the fire?
answer: An ancient oak tree
choices: An ancient oak tree
A carved stone cross
An old stone well
A bronze church bell
context: The Gernikako Arbola -- the sacred Tree of Gernika -- and the Casa de Juntas (the Basque assembly house) both survived the firestorm. The oak had stood for centuries as the symbol of Basque liberties, the place where lords swore to honor the people's ancient freedoms. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Guernica

question: La Pasionaria, a fiery communist speaker, gave Spain's Republicans a battle cry that became the slogan of their whole cause. About 40,000 young foreigners from 52 countries went to Spain to fight Franco, among them some 2,800 Americans, most of those students who had never fired a rifle. What was the cry?
answer: 'No pasaran!' (They shall not pass!)
choices: 'No pasaran!' (They shall not pass!)
'Viva la muerte!' (Long live death!)
'Arriba Espana!' (Up with Spain!)
'No rendirse!' (We will not yield!)
context: 'No pasaran!' became the rallying cry of the defenders of Madrid and the International Brigades. The Americans formed the Abraham Lincoln Battalion. 'Viva la muerte!' and 'Arriba Espana!' were in fact Nationalist (Franco's side) cries. Source: alba-valb.org/who-we-are/about/history-the-abraham-lincoln-brigade-and-the-spanish-civil-war/

question: Wolfram von Richthofen planned and led the bombing of Guernica in 1937, and he wrote in his diary that burning the town had been 'a complete success.' He bore one of the most famous surnames in Germany. Which relative had made the name von Richthofen legendary?
answer: His cousin, the WWI ace the Red Baron
choices: His cousin, the WWI ace the Red Baron
His brother, a famous opera singer
His father, a Prussian war minister
His uncle, a noted polar explorer
context: Wolfram von Richthofen was the younger cousin of Manfred von Richthofen, the 'Red Baron,' the top-scoring fighter ace of World War I. Wolfram ran the raid under the code name 'Operation Rugen'; the attackers dropped about 22 tonnes of bombs, including incendiaries that set the town ablaze. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Guernica

question: George Orwell came to Spain a hopeful socialist and joined the militia of the Workers' Party of Marxist Unification (POUM) to fight Franco. In the Barcelona street fighting of May 1937 he watched something done by his own side that he would later draw on for his novel 1984. What did Orwell see?
answer: Communists turning their guns on their own allies
choices: Communists turning their guns on their own allies
Fascist bombers leveling the whole city of Barcelona
Anarchists looting and torching the city's churches
Hungry militiamen deserting the front lines in droves
context: The Soviet-backed Communists fired on their fellow Republicans -- the anarchists and Orwell's own POUM -- then branded them 'Fascist traitors.' The POUM was outlawed, and Orwell and his wife had to flee Spain by train to avoid being jailed by their own side. He wrote it all in 'Homage to Catalonia.' Source: litcharts.com/lit/homage-to-catalonia/summary

question: Agents of Stalin's secret police tortured Andreu Nin to death in June 1937, after he was seized in Barcelona. Nin was a leader of Orwell's party, the Workers' Party of Marxist Unification (POUM), and had once been Leon Trotsky's secretary. The killers staged a fake escape to hide the murder. When people chalked 'Where is Nin?' on the walls, how did the regime mockingly reply?
answer: 'In Salamanca or in Berlin'
choices: 'In Salamanca or in Berlin'
'Safe in Moscow with his friends'
'At rest in a Barcelona grave'
'Free across the French border'
context: Salamanca was Franco's headquarters and Berlin was Hitler's capital, so the jeer implied Nin had run off to join the fascists -- the very lie the NKVD had planted with forged German documents. His real fate stayed hidden until Moscow's archives briefly opened in the 1990s. The order is linked to NKVD agent Alexander Orlov. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreu_Nin

question: Adolf Hitler threw a victory parade in Berlin for his Condor Legion airmen when they came home from Spain, where he had used the civil war to test his newest aircraft and tactics in combat. Barely three months later he launched the real war they had rehearsed for. What did he do?
answer: Invaded Poland to the east
choices: Invaded Poland to the east
Invaded Norway to the north
Invaded France to the west
Invaded Greece to the south
context: Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939, starting World War II -- less than three months after the Condor Legion's homecoming parade. In Spain, Hitler had combat-tested his Messerschmitt Bf 109 fighter, and pilot Werner Molders had perfected the two-plane 'Rotte' that became the worldwide 'finger-four' formation; about 19,000 German airmen rotated through to gain real combat experience. Source: airandspaceforces.com/article/0213condor/

question: Spanish crews sailed one great galleon a year between Acapulco and Manila for 250 years, taking New World silver west across the Pacific. In Manila the silver bought the cargo for the voyage home. Which good was the prize, worth about ten times more in the Americas than in Manila?
answer: Chinese silk
choices: Chinese silk
Persian carpets
African ivory
Indian pepper
context: A roll of Chinese silk fetched roughly ten times its Manila price once it reached the Americas, which is why silk was by far the most valuable thing aboard the homebound galleon (porcelain, ivory, and spices came too). The whole loop ran on silver-for-silk: as much as a third of all the silver mined in Spanish America flowed to China through Manila. Source: Met Museum essay 'The Manila Galleon Trade'; World History Encyclopedia.

question: Andres de Urdaneta, a Basque friar and navigator, took the San Pedro out across the Pacific in 1565 to find a way back east. Galleons ran west with ease on the trade winds, but for years none had found a route home. What did Urdaneta do to catch a current that would carry his ship home?
answer: Sail far north, almost to the latitude of Japan
choices: Sail far north, almost to the latitude of Japan
Hug the equator straight east the whole way
Sail south below Australia into the cold seas
Wait in port for the winds to simply reverse
context: Urdaneta sailed north from the Philippines nearly to Japan's latitude, caught the Kuroshio Current and the North Pacific westerlies, and rode them east to California and down to Acapulco. That 'tornaviaje' (return voyage) took his first crossing 129 days and opened the route for 250 years. Source: Guampedia 'Andres de Urdaneta'; Wikipedia 'Manila galleon'.

question: The Spartans, as Thucydides tells it, once offered freedom to the helots judged bravest in their wars, and some two thousand stepped forward. Wearing garlands, the chosen men went round the temples in celebration. The helots outnumbered their masters about seven to one, and a revolt was Sparta's constant fear. What did the Spartans then do to the two thousand?
answer: They made every one of them vanish, and no one ever learned how each had died
choices: They made every one of them vanish, and no one ever learned how each had died
They shipped every one of them off to colonize a distant island
They drafted every one of them into a special front-line regiment
They taxed every one of them into handing back half their land
context: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 4.80, reports the Spartans promised freedom to the ~2,000 helots judged bravest in war; the chosen men garlanded themselves and toured the temples in celebration, and soon after the Spartans made them all disappear, with 'no one ever knowing how each of them perished.' It was a deliberate trap to eliminate exactly the helots most capable of leading a rebellion. Source: Thucydides 4.80 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crypteia).

question: Sparta's ephors, its chief magistrates, opened their term each year with a formal declaration aimed at the helots. The helots were the enslaved majority who farmed Spartan land, outnumbering their masters about seven to one, and Sparta ruled them by terror. What did the incoming ephors formally declare?
answer: War on the helots, so that killing one counted as a clean act of the state
choices: War on the helots, so that killing one counted as a clean act of the state
A census of the helots, so that each could be assigned to a master
A tax on the helots, so that each owed half of his harvest
A festival for the helots, so that each could honor the gods of Sparta
context: Aristotle, preserved through Plutarch's Life of Lycurgus 28, recorded that the ephors declared war on the helots upon taking office each year, so that any Spartan could kill a helot without incurring blood-guilt or religious pollution. It turned the routine killing of slaves into a legally and ritually 'clean' act of the state. Source: Aristotle via Plutarch, Lycurgus 28 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crypteia).

question: A boy in ancient Sparta reached his seventh birthday. In Athens a boy stayed at home and learned poetry, music and philosophy, but Sparta had a harsher plan for its sons, called the agoge. What happened to the Spartan boy on his seventh birthday?
answer: The state took him from his family to be raised as a soldier
choices: The state took him from his family to be raised as a soldier
He was given his father's farm and a team of oxen to work it
He chose a trade and began an apprenticeship in the city
He sailed with the navy to learn seamanship and trade
context: At age 7 Spartan boys were taken from home and enrolled in communal 'herds' (agelai) to be raised in the agoge, the state's military upbringing. They were taught only enough reading and writing 'to serve their turn' -- the rest of the training was to make them obey orders, endure hardship, and win battles. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 16-17.

question: One hungry boy of Sparta's agoge stole food, just as his upbringing meant him to: Sparta deliberately kept its boys hungry so they would steal and grow cunning. Some boys were flogged and disgraced all the same, but not for stealing itself. What was a boy flogged for?
answer: Getting caught in the act
choices: Getting caught in the act
Stealing from another Spartan
Eating more than his share
Sharing his food with a friend
context: Theft itself was not the crime -- being caught was. A boy who was caught was 'soundly flogged, as a careless and unskilful thief.' Underfeeding the boys and forcing them to steal was meant to make them cunning and resourceful. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 17.

question: A Spartan mother, the story goes, handed her son his great round shield as he marched off to war, and sent him with a grim charge. Spartan mothers raised their sons to hold the line of battle to the last. What did she tell him?
answer: 'Either this or upon this'
choices: 'Either this or upon this'
'Strike first and strike hard'
'Bring me gold or bring me glory'
'Fight for your brothers in the line'
context: 'Either this or upon this' meant: come home carrying your shield (victorious) or be carried home dead ON it. To drop the shield was to throw it away and run -- the ultimate disgrace. The saying is attributed to Queen Gorgo. Treated as legend. Source: Plutarch, Moralia: Sayings of Spartan Women.

question: A visitor from Sybaris tasted the black broth that Spartan men ate at their common mess every night and prized as tough soldier's fare. He joked that he now saw why Spartans had no fear of dying. What was the black broth made of?
answer: Pork boiled in its own blood, with vinegar and salt
choices: Pork boiled in its own blood, with vinegar and salt
Barley and lentils simmered slowly with wild herbs
Octopus stewed in dark red wine and good olive oil
Goat's milk curdled with mountain honey and figs
context: The black broth (melas zomos) was so prized that the old men gave up their share of meat just to drink it. A visitor from Sybaris who tasted it joked that now he understood why the Spartans did not fear death -- they would sooner die than swallow a second bowl. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 12; Moralia.

question: Plutarch tells of a Spartan boy of the agoge who stole a live fox cub and hid it under his cloak. While he stood talking with a group of older Spartan men, the frightened animal began clawing and biting into his belly. What did the boy do?
answer: Let the fox tear out his insides rather than be caught with it
choices: Let the fox tear out his insides rather than be caught with it
Cried out for help and dropped the fox at the men's feet
Killed the fox through his cloak with a small hidden knife
Let the fox loose and bolted for the river to get away
context: Plutarch's words: the boy 'suffered the animal to tear out his bowels with its teeth and claws, and died rather than have his theft detected.' Told as the ultimate proof of trained Spartan endurance -- treated as legend. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 18.1.

question: King Philip II of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great, sent the Spartans a bullying letter around 346 BC: 'If I invade Laconia, I will raze your city to the ground.' The Spartans, famous across Greece for short and cutting speech, wrote back a reply just one word long. What was the word?
answer: 'If'
choices: 'If'
'Never'
'Try'
'When'
context: Their whole reply was the single word 'If.' This terse style is why we still call a few cutting words 'laconic' -- from Laconia, Sparta's region. Treated as legend. Source: Plutarch, Moralia (Sayings of Spartans); Wikiquote 'Laconic phrases.'

question: Spartan warriors drilled for battle while helots worked the land around them, enslaved people outnumbering the citizens about seven to one. Fear of a helot uprising shaped Spartan law and the training of every Spartan boy. Where had this huge enslaved population come from in the first place?
answer: A whole neighbouring people Sparta had conquered and enslaved on its own land
choices: A whole neighbouring people Sparta had conquered and enslaved on its own land
Captives shipped in and sold by Phoenician slave-traders from over the sea
Prisoners of war taken in raids on many different Greek cities
Poor men who had sold themselves into bondage to pay off their debts
context: The helots were chiefly the Messenians, conquered by Sparta in the 8th-7th century BC and held in collective serfdom on their own land. They kept their own families, gods and Messenian identity -- which is exactly why Sparta lived in permanent dread of revolt and built a terror-state to control them. Source: Helots (Wikipedia); Paul Cartledge.

question: A Spartan father carried his newborn baby before the elders of his tribe, who stripped it and inspected it, for in Sparta a child belonged first to the state. A sturdy baby would be raised as a future warrior. By the tradition Plutarch preserved, what became of one the elders judged sickly or deformed?
answer: It was left to die in a chasm at the foot of Mount Taygetus
choices: It was left to die in a chasm at the foot of Mount Taygetus
It was given to a helot family to be raised as a servant
It was sent away by ship to be raised in another city
It was kept at home but barred from ever becoming a soldier
context: The place was called the Apothetae. Plutarch reports this, but no infant remains have ever been found there, and many scholars treat the detail as part of the semi-legendary tradition around Sparta's lawgiver, Lycurgus -- so it is told here as legend, not proven fact. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 16; Bad Ancient.

question: Spartan officials picked the toughest young Spartans for a secret operation called the krypteia. They armed them with daggers and sent them out by night into a countryside worked by helots, the enslaved Greeks who farmed Spartan land. What were the young men sent to do?
answer: Murder any helots they came across, especially the strongest ones
choices: Murder any helots they came across, especially the strongest ones
Spy on neighbouring cities and report back on their armies
Guard the mountain passes against foreign invaders
Hunt wild game to stock the soldiers' common mess
context: Plutarch: 'in the night they came down into the highways and killed every Helot whom they caught,' and by day they killed the strongest helots in the fields. It was a state-run program of terror against the enslaved Messenian population. Source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 28; Crypteia (Wikipedia).

question: Queen Gorgo of Sparta was once asked why Spartan women were the only ones in Greece who 'ruled' their men. Alone among Greek women, Spartans could inherit and own land, and they trained as athletes in the open air. Gorgo answered with one cutting line. What did she say?
answer: 'Because we are the only women who give birth to real men'
choices: 'Because we are the only women who give birth to real men'
'Because we alone are taught to read and to reason'
'Because our husbands fear the gods we serve'
'Because we hold the keys to every house in Sparta'
context: Gorgo's full reply: 'Because we are the only women who are mothers of [real] men.' Spartan girls were schooled and trained athletically to bear strong children, and Spartan women were the freest in all of Greece. Source: Plutarch, Moralia: Sayings of Spartan Women; World History Encyclopedia.

question: Epaminondas, a Theban general, smashed the Spartan army at Leuctra in 371 BC with a new slanted formation of massed spearmen. Then he marched south into Messenia and did the one thing that broke Sparta as a great power for good. What did he do there?
answer: Freed the helots, destroying the slave labour Sparta depended on
choices: Freed the helots, destroying the slave labour Sparta depended on
Burned the undefended city of Sparta itself to the ground
Captured both of Sparta's two kings and held them for ransom
Cut off Sparta's grain supply and starved the city into surrender
context: After Leuctra (371 BC), Epaminondas marched into Messenia (369 BC) and freed the helots after centuries of bondage, founding the fortified city of Messene at Mount Ithome. With its enslaved workforce gone, Sparta's whole warrior system collapsed and it never recovered as a great power. Source: World History Encyclopedia; Britannica.

question: Gladiators at a fighting school in Capua, about seventy of them, plotted a breakout in 73 BC. The real swords were locked away, so before fighting past their guards the men raided one room and grabbed whatever they could swing. Which room did they raid, and what did they take?
answer: The kitchen — cooking knives and roasting spits
choices: The kitchen — cooking knives and roasting spits
The chapel — bronze idols and altar candlesticks
The stable — horse whips and iron bridle bits
The armory — wooden practice swords and shields
context: Plutarch says the gladiators seized cleavers and spits from the kitchen, fought their way out, and on the road captured a wagon of real gladiator weapons. They chose Spartacus as their leader. (Plutarch, Life of Crassus 8; worldhistory.org/article/871)

question: Marcus Licinius Crassus, the richest man in Rome, crushed Spartacus's slave army in 71 BC and took 6,000 rebels alive. He wanted every slave in Italy to see with his own eyes what rebellion cost. What did Crassus do with the 6,000 prisoners?
answer: Crucified them along the Appian Way, the whole road from Capua to Rome
choices: Crucified them along the Appian Way, the whole road from Capua to Rome
Sold them at auction in the great slave market on the island of Delos
Branded their foreheads and sent them back to their old masters
Shipped them to die in the silver mines of Spain
context: Crassus left the 6,000 crosses standing along the road as a warning to any slave who might think of rebelling. Roman slavery and crucifixion were institutions, stated here as fact. (Appian, Civil Wars 1.120; worldhistory.org/article/871)

question: Gaius Claudius Glaber led a Roman force that trapped Spartacus's men on the slopes of Mount Vesuvius early in the revolt. He blocked the only path down, meaning to starve them out. The rebels got off the mountain anyway and fell on his camp from behind. How did they escape?
answer: They wove ladders from wild grapevines and climbed down the cliff
choices: They wove ladders from wild grapevines and climbed down the cliff
They dug a tunnel through the soft volcanic rock by night
They built rafts and floated down a swollen mountain stream
They disguised themselves in dead Romans' armor and walked out
context: Having climbed down the 'impossible' cliff, they circled behind Glaber's camp and wiped out his force in a surprise attack. Vesuvius's slopes were covered in wild vines. (Plutarch, Life of Crassus 9; Third Servile War)

question: Spartacus called for his warhorse in front of his men in 71 BC, just before his last battle against the Roman general Marcus Crassus. Instead of mounting it, he drew his sword and killed the horse on the spot. By his own account, why did he do it?
answer: If he won he would take fine horses from the enemy, and if he lost he would have no need of one
choices: If he won he would take fine horses from the enemy, and if he lost he would have no need of one
To feed his starving men one last meal before the fighting began
To honor an old Thracian custom of sacrificing a horse before battle
To prove to his men that there would be no retreat and no escape
context: Plutarch records his words. In the battle Spartacus charged straight for Crassus himself, cut down two centurions who attacked him together, and was finally surrounded and killed; his body was never found. (Plutarch, Life of Crassus 11)

question: Spartacus held funeral games for his officer Crixus after Crixus was killed in battle, with about 300 captured Romans in his hands. At Rome's own games, captured enemies and slaves were made to die for the crowd. What did Spartacus make the 300 Romans do?
answer: Fight each other to the death as gladiators, while slaves watched
choices: Fight each other to the death as gladiators, while slaves watched
Dig the mass grave and then march away unarmed and free
Kneel and swear an oath of loyalty to the slave army
Carry Crixus's body in procession and sing Roman funeral songs
context: Spartacus forced Roman captives to die in the arena for slave spectators — the Roman spectacle reversed, Romans now dying for the entertainment of slaves. Crixus had been killed by the consul Gellius near Mount Garganus. (Appian, Civil Wars 1.117)

question: Xuanzang, a young Buddhist monk, left Chang'an, the Tang capital, in secret in 629. Emperor Taizong had banned all travel to the west, but Xuanzang was set on going anyway, alone. What was he setting out to do?
answer: Bring the original Buddhist sutras back from India
choices: Bring the original Buddhist sutras back from India
Map a new trade road for the emperor's merchants
Carry a peace treaty to a rival western king
Find a legendary spring that cured any sickness
context: Xuanzang defied Taizong's imperial travel ban (issued for border security) and set off alone for India to recover the original Buddhist scriptures. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/xuanzang/

question: Xuanzang really did travel to India and back in the 600s to fetch Buddhist scriptures, a journey of sixteen years. Long after he died, a Ming novel made a fantasy hero of him and gave him three magical companions as guards. Who is the most famous of the three?
answer: The Monkey King, Sun Wukong
choices: The Monkey King, Sun Wukong
The dragon-emperor of the eastern sea
The white tiger of the western mountains
The thunder-god who forges his staff
context: The Ming novel 'Journey to the West' turned the historical Xuanzang into 'Tripitaka,' guarded by the Monkey King Sun Wukong, a pig-demon, and a sand-spirit. Legendary retelling, not history. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/xuanzang/

question: Alone in the 800-li Gashun Gobi, Xuanzang spilled his water bag, and the water vanished into the sand. He went four days and five nights with no water at all, surrounded by camel dung and bones, and came close to death. What saved him?
answer: His horse, which bolted on its own to a spring
choices: His horse, which bolted on its own to a spring
A sudden rainstorm that filled the dry hollows
A cool night wind that uncovered a buried stream
Circling vultures whose path led him to a pool
context: After four days and five nights without water, with no birds or animals around him, Xuanzang's horse bolted on its own and carried the half-dead monk to a spring. Source: https://en.minghui.org/html/articles/2019/7/13/178423.html

question: Xuanzang crossed the Gobi on an illegal pilgrimage to India. Deep in the sand, out of water and dying of thirst, he was tempted to turn back, and instead he kept whispering a fierce vow to himself to keep going. What did he swear?
answer: He would not go east even one step without the true scriptures
choices: He would not go east even one step without the true scriptures
He would press south to the warmer passes before the snows came
He would reach the western kingdoms or die in the sand
He would never set foot toward home until he saw the sea
context: His vow: 'I will not go back toward the east even one step without obtaining the true Buddhist scriptures.' He would rather die pushing west than live by turning back. Source: https://en.minghui.org/html/articles/2019/7/13/178423.html

question: King Qu Wentai of Gaochang, a small oasis kingdom, grew so fond of the monk Xuanzang, passing through on his way to India, that he meant to keep him at court for good as head chaplain. Xuanzang refused to stay. How did he force the king to let him go?
answer: He refused all food in a hunger strike until the king relented
choices: He refused all food in a hunger strike until the king relented
He fled at night over the city wall on a stolen horse
He threatened to burn the sutras he already carried
He sat in silent meditation and would not speak for days
context: Xuanzang refused all food until King Qu Wentai gave in; the two then swore an oath of brotherhood, and Xuanzang promised to return and teach there for three years. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/xuanzang/ ; https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat2/4sub8/entry-5450.html

question: Xuanzang and his party spent some eight days of brutal cold crossing the high Bedel Pass, a road of ice through the Tian Shan range of Central Asia, on his way to India. How heavy was the toll the frozen pass took on his men?
answer: Three or four of every ten froze to death
choices: Three or four of every ten froze to death
One in twenty was lost in a single avalanche
Half the party turned back before the summit
Every man survived but all the horses died
context: Crossing the Bedel Pass (about 4,284 m) over roughly eight days, Xuanzang lost 30 to 40 percent of his men to the cold, along with countless horses and oxen. Source: https://nembutsu.cc/2024/06/25/the-journeys-of-xuanzang-part-two-onward-and-upward/

question: Two giant Buddhas stood carved in the sandstone cliffs of Bamiyan, in what is now central Afghanistan, when Xuanzang passed through in 630 on his way to India, and he set them down in careful detail. Why do historians prize his account of the statues so highly today?
answer: It is the earliest written record of statues the Taliban later destroyed
choices: It is the earliest written record of statues the Taliban later destroyed
It contains the only surviving map of the lost city
It proves the statues were once painted in gold
It names the sculptor who carved them into the cliff
context: Xuanzang reached Bamiyan on 30 April 630 and recorded its giant cliff Buddhas and over a thousand monks — the earliest textual evidence for the statues the Taliban dynamited in 2001. Source: https://en.bharatpedia.org/wiki/Great_Tang_Records_on_the_Western_Regions

question: King Harsha of northern India called a great assembly at his capital, Kanauj, in 643, and it lasted eighteen days. Xuanzang, the Chinese monk, had studied in India for thirteen years by then, and he came to speak for his own Mahayana school of Buddhism. What did Xuanzang reportedly accomplish there?
answer: He out-argued 500 Brahmins, Jains, and rival Buddhists
choices: He out-argued 500 Brahmins, Jains, and rival Buddhists
He converted the king himself to his school
He recited every sutra he had collected from memory
He settled a war between two Indian kingdoms
context: At King Harsha's 18-day assembly at Kanauj in early 643, Xuanzang reportedly out-argued 500 Brahmins, Jains, and rival Buddhists in open debate. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/xuanzang/

question: Emperor Taizong, who had once banned the journey, welcomed Xuanzang home to Chang'an in 645 as a national hero. The monk had been gone sixteen years and some 10,000 miles, and his twenty-two horses came laden with 657 Sanskrit texts. What was built in Chang'an in 652 to house the scriptures?
answer: The 64-meter Big Wild Goose Pagoda
choices: The 64-meter Big Wild Goose Pagoda
A walled translation college beside the palace
A new western gate named for the pilgrim
A royal tomb shaped like a desert dune
context: Xuanzang returned with 657 Sanskrit texts in 520 cases loaded onto twenty-two horses; the 64-meter Big Wild Goose Pagoda was built in 652 to house them, and he spent the rest of his life (he died in 664) translating them into Chinese. Source: https://www.visitourchina.com/xian/attraction/big-wild-goose-pagoda.html ; https://iep.utm.edu/xuanzang/

question: Francis of Assisi set up the first living nativity scene in 1223, in the little mountain village of Greccio, for villagers unable to read, who could now see the birth of Jesus with their own eyes. What did he put there to make the scene?
answer: A real ox and a real donkey beside a straw-filled manger
choices: A real ox and a real donkey beside a straw-filled manger
A painted wooden altar lit by candles
A choir of robed boys singing carols
A golden statue carried through the town
context: Francis filled a manger with straw and set it between a live ox and a live donkey at Greccio in 1223 so villagers could vividly contemplate the birth of Christ. This is the origin of the Christmas crib (presepio / creche) tradition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi

question: Pietro di Bernardone, a rich and angry cloth merchant, dragged his son Francis before the Bishop of Assisi around 1206 to get his money back. In the public square Francis took off all his fine clothes and handed them to his father. Then he gave up his whole inheritance with a single line. What did he say?
answer: From now on he would say only 'Our Father who art in heaven'
choices: From now on he would say only 'Our Father who art in heaven'
He would repay every coin within a single year
He would leave Assisi and never return
He would build a great church with his own hands
context: Naked in the square, Francis declared he would no longer call Pietro di Bernardone 'my father' but say only 'Our Father who art in heaven.' The bishop covered the young man with his own cloak. Underneath his merchant's robes Francis had been wearing a rough penitential hairshirt. Source: https://www.vaticanstate.va/en/state-and-government/general-informations/saint-of-the-day/778-4-october-saint-francis-of-assisi-patron-saint-of-italy.html

question: Donato Bramante began the new St Peter's by tearing down the church, twelve centuries old, that Emperor Constantine had built there. He knocked out the nave so fast that Mass was still being said in the ruins. What mocking nickname did the Romans give him?
answer: Master Wrecker
choices: Master Wrecker
The Stone Thief
The Church Breaker
The Roman Hammer
context: In Italian the nickname was 'Maestro Ruinante' — a pun on Bramante, twisting his name into 'Master Wrecker.' He demolished Old St. Peter's, built by Constantine, so eagerly the joke stuck. Source: worldhistory.org/Donato_Bramante + theartstory.org.

question: Michelangelo took charge of St Peter's in 1547, at the age of 71, when it was the largest building project in Christendom. He set himself one condition and kept to it until he died at 88, with his dome still unbuilt. What was the condition?
answer: He would accept no payment
choices: He would accept no payment
He would carve his own tomb there
He would answer to no pope
He would never sign the plans
context: Michelangelo refused all pay, saying he took the work on 'only for the love of God and in honour of the Apostle.' He lived to see the great drum of his dome rise, but not the dome itself. Source: basilicasanpietro.va/the-dome + thehistoryofart.org.

question: Pope Sixtus V ordered total silence, on pain of death, as 900 men and 140 horses raised a 350-ton Egyptian obelisk in St Peter's Square in 1586. As the straining ropes began to smoke, a sailor named Benedetto Bresca broke the silence with a shout. What did he shout?
answer: "Water to the ropes!"
choices: "Water to the ropes!"
"Pull for the Pope!"
"Stand clear, men!"
"Cut it loose!"
context: The story says Bresca shouted 'Acqua alle funi!' — wetting the smoking ropes tightened them and saved the obelisk. As a reward Sixtus V is said to have granted Bresca's town of Bordighera the lasting right to supply the Vatican's Palm Sunday palms. Told as a beloved legend. Source: joansrome.wordpress.com + turismoroma.it.

question: Jesus made a pun on the apostle Peter's name in a line of Matthew's Gospel, and the line now circles the inside of Michelangelo's dome at St Peter's in gold lettering taller than a man. In Greek, Peter's name is also a plain everyday word. What does the name mean?
answer: Rock
choices: Rock
Shepherd
Fisherman
Servant
context: The inscription reads 'TU ES PETRUS ET SUPER HANC PETRAM AEDIFICABO ECCLESIAM MEAM' — 'Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.' Peter (petra) means rock, so Jesus is punning on his name. Catholics read this as the source of the popes' authority. Source: stpetersbasilica.info + walksinrome.com.

question: Gian Lorenzo Bernini ringed St Peter's Square with an oval colonnade four rows deep, 248 columns topped with 140 statues of saints. He gave its curving shape a meaning in one famous image of the Church. What did Bernini say the colonnade was?
answer: The arms of the Church, embracing all who enter
choices: The arms of the Church, embracing all who enter
The crown of the Church, raised over Rome
The shield of the Church, guarding the faithful
The gateway of the Church, opened to the world
context: Bernini said the colonnade was the 'maternal arms of Mother Church,' reaching out to gather in the faithful, the heretics, and the unbelievers alike. Built 1656-1667 under Pope Alexander VII. Source: en.wikipedia.org/St._Peter's_Square + roma-nonpertutti.com.

question: A colonial clerk drawing up a will in 1765 fixed a British revenue stamp to it, as Parliament's new Stamp Act now required, and every newspaper needed one too. So did a pair of pastimes, one of them made of paper. Which two had to carry the stamp?
answer: Playing cards and dice
choices: Playing cards and dice
Marbles and spinning tops
Toy soldiers and kites
Hoops and wooden horses
context: The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed paper itself — every legal document, newspaper, pamphlet, will, marriage license, diploma, and almanac needed a stamp, and even playing cards and dice were taxed. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Stamp_Act/ and https://www.ushistory.org/us/9b.asp

question: A Boston crowd strung up a straw effigy of stamp distributor Andrew Oliver from a great elm on 14 August 1765, then beheaded and burned it and tore down his office. The elm earned a name that the colonists used for the rest of the Revolution. What did they call it?
answer: The Liberty Tree
choices: The Liberty Tree
The Charter Oak
The Treason Elm
The Gallows Tree
context: The crowd marked the effigy 'A.O.' for Andrew Oliver; the great elm became the Liberty Tree, and Oliver resigned his post three days later. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/andrew-oliver and https://www.masshist.org/beehiveblog/2024/08/the-259th-anniversary-of-bostons-liberty-tree/

question: A law student of 22 stood listening in the doorway of Virginia's House of Burgesses in May 1765 while Patrick Henry, newly elected, raged against the Stamp Act. The young man remembered that speech for the rest of his life. Who was he?
answer: Thomas Jefferson
choices: Thomas Jefferson
George Washington
John Adams
James Madison
context: Jefferson, then a 22-year-old law student, witnessed Henry forcing his Virginia Resolves through the House of Burgesses and never forgot the speech. Source: https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Jefferson/03-07-02-0369-0002 and https://tenthamendmentcenter.com/2024/05/28/patrick-henrys-virginia-resolves-bedrock-principles-of-american-liberty/

question: The Speaker of Virginia's House of Burgesses leapt to his feet in May 1765 and cried 'Treason!' Patrick Henry, attacking the Stamp Act, had just named King George III in a warning. As the famous story goes, Henry did not flinch. How did he finish his sentence?
answer: 'If this be treason, make the most of it.'
choices: 'If this be treason, make the most of it.'
'Give me liberty, or give me death.'
'I know not what course others may take.'
'We must all hang together, or hang separately.'
context: Henry had warned that George III might meet the fate of Caesar; when the Speaker cried treason, Henry reportedly finished with this defiant line. It is preserved as legend — a retold story, not a verbatim transcript. Source: https://encyclopediavirginia.org/1658hpr-9260362296ba000/ and https://cardinalnews.org/2024/02/13/dispatch-from-1765-stamp-act-protest-prompts-house-speaker-to-accuse-new-legislator-patrick-henry-of-treason/

question: Patrick Henry, raging against the Stamp Act in 1765, reminded the House of Burgesses of two rulers who had died by violence, one stabbed to death, one beheaded. George the Third, he warned, might learn from their example. Which two rulers did Henry name?
answer: Caesar and Charles the First
choices: Caesar and Charles the First
Caesar and Nero
Charles the First and Richard the Third
Henry the Eighth and Charles the First
context: By naming Caesar (assassinated by Brutus) and Charles the First (executed under Cromwell), Henry was implicitly threatening that George III could meet the same fate. The Speaker's cry of 'Treason!' came mid-sentence. Source: https://cardinalnews.org/2024/02/13/dispatch-from-1765-stamp-act-protest-prompts-house-speaker-to-accuse-new-legislator-patrick-henry-of-treason/  (Legend.)

question: Charles Townshend told Parliament that the American colonists were 'children planted by our care.' Isaac Barre fired back that they were no such thing, and the colonists resisting the Stamp Act proudly took his answer as their name. What had Barre called them?
answer: Sons of Liberty
choices: Sons of Liberty
Friends of America
Patriots of the Crown
Defenders of the Charter
context: Isaac Barre's retort in Parliament gave the resistance its name; chapters of the Sons of Liberty sprang up across the colonies to enforce the boycotts and intimidate the stamp distributors. Source: http://www.stamp-act-history.com/sons-of-liberty/ and https://www.britannica.com/event/Stamp-Act-Great-Britain-1765

question: A Boston mob stormed Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson's mansion on the night of 26 August 1765 and tore it apart room by room. Besides the furniture and the 900 pounds in cash and silver they carried off, the rioters destroyed 30 years of his collected manuscripts. What did Hutchinson lose among them?
answer: His notes for a history of Massachusetts
choices: His notes for a history of Massachusetts
His maps of the colonial coastline
His letters to the King of England
His ledgers of the colony's accounts
context: The mob cut down the cupola, beat down walls, stripped slate from the roof, slit the beds open to scatter the feathers, and destroyed three decades of Hutchinson's manuscripts, including the notes for his history of Massachusetts. Source: https://newenglandhistoricalsociety.com/1765-rebels-sack-boston-mansion-thomas-hutchinson/

question: A colonial judge picked up a court filing in 1765 that carried no British tax stamp, and under the Stamp Act no court filing, ship's clearance, land deed or marriage license was valid without one. Rather than buy the hated stamps, many courts and ports took one bold step. What did they do?
answer: They shut their doors and stopped operating
choices: They shut their doors and stopped operating
They printed their own counterfeit stamps
They paid the tax under loud protest
They petitioned the King for an exemption
context: A deed, will, or contract on un-stamped paper would not stand in any court — so courts and ports closed rather than legitimize the stamps, freezing legal and commercial life. Source: https://www.ushistory.org/us/9b.asp and https://legalclarity.org/november-1765-the-stamp-act-crisis-and-colonial-resistance/

question: Leaders from nine colonies gathered at Federal Hall in New York in October 1765 as the Stamp Act Congress, to protest the first tax Parliament had ever laid directly on the colonies. Why does that meeting stand out in American history?
answer: It was the first time the colonies acted together
choices: It was the first time the colonies acted together
It was the first colonial army ever raised
It was the first time the colonies declared independence
It was the first colonial currency ever printed
context: The Stamp Act Congress issued a Declaration of Rights and Grievances asserting the colonists could be taxed only with the consent of their own elected representatives — the first time the separate colonies acted in concert. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Stamp-Act-Congress and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamp_Act_Congress

question: Delegates at the Stamp Act Congress in New York in 1765 rested their protest on what they called a principle essential to the English constitution, a right that they said only the colonies' own assemblies could honor. Their quarrel was not with the size of the tax. Which principle did they say Parliament had broken?
answer: No subject can be taxed without his own consent
choices: No subject can be taxed without his own consent
No subject can be jailed without a trial
No subject can be forced to quarter soldiers
No subject can be denied a seat in Parliament
context: The grievance was constitutional, not about the rate: a subject could not be taxed without his consent, and the colonists held that only their elected assemblies — not a distant Parliament — could grant that consent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Considerations_on_the_Propriety_of_Imposing_Taxes_in_the_British_Colonies and https://alphahistory.com/americanrevolution/daniel-dulany-british-taxation-1765/

question: Daniel Dulany, a Maryland lawyer, tore into Parliament's doctrine of virtual representation in a pamphlet of 1765. By that doctrine every member of Parliament spoke for all British subjects, even colonists who voted for no one. What was the heart of Dulany's argument against it?
answer: No English voter would ever feel a tax laid on America
choices: No English voter would ever feel a tax laid on America
Colonists already paid more tax than Englishmen did
Parliament had never claimed such a power before
The colonies were too distant for laws to reach them
context: Dulany argued that since not a single voter in England would ever be affected by a tax on America, Parliament could not truly 'represent' the colonists' interests when taxing them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Considerations_on_the_Propriety_of_Imposing_Taxes_in_the_British_Colonies and https://alphahistory.com/americanrevolution/daniel-dulany-british-taxation-1765/

question: Angry crowds across the colonies had frightened every British stamp seller into resigning or fleeing by 1 November 1765, yet the Stamp Act still stood. In March 1766 Parliament in London repealed it at last. What pressure finally forced Parliament's hand?
answer: Colonial merchants boycotted British goods until London merchants begged for repeal
choices: Colonial merchants boycotted British goods until London merchants begged for repeal
Colonial militias threatened to seize British ships in the harbors
The colonies refused to send any food to the British army
Colonial assemblies voted to stop paying the King's salary
context: The non-importation boycott bankrupted some London merchants, who then petitioned Parliament for repeal — money, not muskets, killed the Stamp Act. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Stamp-Act-Great-Britain-1765 and https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/on-this-day-the-stamp-act-plants-seeds-of-the-revolution

question: Britain's lawmakers repealed the hated Stamp Act on 18 March 1766, and on that very same day they passed a second law that made the colonists' victory hollow. It asserted Parliament's power to make laws binding the colonies 'in all cases whatsoever.' What was the second law called?
answer: The Declaratory Act
choices: The Declaratory Act
The Townshend Act
The Quartering Act
The Sugar Act
context: The Declaratory Act asserted Parliament's authority over the colonies 'in all cases whatsoever' on the same day the Stamp Act was repealed — repeal with one hand, a fresh claim of power with the other. Source: https://www.americanhistorycentral.com/documents/stamp-act-repeal-1766-text/ and https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/on-this-day-the-stamp-act-plants-seeds-of-the-revolution

question: Francis Scott Key, a lawyer, watched from a ship in Baltimore's harbor through the night of 13 September 1814 as British warships pounded Fort McHenry with bombs and rockets. Through the smoke and rain he could not tell whether the fort had fallen. What did he see by the dawn's early light?
answer: The enormous American flag still flying over the fort
choices: The enormous American flag still flying over the fort
The British fleet sailing away in defeat
The fort's stone walls cracked and smoking
A line of American soldiers marching out
context: That single image -- the huge garrison flag still there after a night of bombardment -- is the moment that inspired the national anthem. A smaller storm flag had flown through the rainy night; the giant flag Key saw was likely raised that morning. Source: https://www.nps.gov/fomc/learn/historyculture/the-star-spangled-banner.htm ; https://www.battlefields.org/learn/war-1812/battles/fort-mchenry

question: Major George Armistead, commander of Fort McHenry, ordered a giant garrison flag for the fort in 1813, a year ahead of the British attack. It measured 30 by 42 feet, with stars and stripes two feet wide. Armistead gave one blunt reason for its size. What did he say he wanted?
answer: A flag the British would have no trouble seeing from a distance
choices: A flag the British would have no trouble seeing from a distance
A flag every soldier in the fort could salute at once
A flag that could be seen from the city of Baltimore
A flag big enough to wrap a fallen man for burial
context: On that flag, each star and each stripe measured a full two feet across. Armistead, the fort's commander, wanted no doubt about whose fort it was. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/star-spangled-garrison-banner

question: Mary Pickersgill, a Baltimore widow, spent seven weeks sewing the giant Fort McHenry flag with her young daughter, two nieces and a teenage servant named Grace Wisher. The flag was too big to lay out in her own house. Where did the women spread it at night to stitch the pieces together?
answer: On the floor of a nearby brewery
choices: On the floor of a nearby brewery
On the deck of a docked ship
Across the lawn of the fort itself
In the loft of a church meeting hall
context: The women spread the flag at night on the floor of Claggett's brewery to assemble it. Pickersgill was paid $405.90 for the work -- more than most Baltimoreans earned in a whole year. Source: https://amhistory.si.edu/starspangledbanner/making-the-flag.aspx

question: Francis Scott Key and the prisoner-agent John Skinner went out to the British fleet under a flag of truce and won the freedom of Dr. William Beanes, a captured American doctor. Yet the British held all three men until their bombardment of Fort McHenry was over. Why would they not let them go?
answer: The men had seen the fleet's strength before the attack on Baltimore
choices: The men had seen the fleet's strength before the attack on Baltimore
The men had not yet signed the formal release papers
The men were suspected of carrying secret messages
The men owed a ransom that had not been fully paid
context: Because Key and prisoner-agent John Skinner had been aboard the British flagship Tonnant as the fleet prepared to strike Baltimore, the British wouldn't let them leave until it was done -- forcing Key to watch the entire bombardment from behind enemy lines. Source: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/francis-scott-key

question: Epicurus gathered his students in a garden just outside Athens, and his name lives on in the English word 'epicure': a gourmet who chases fancy food and fine wine. Yet the philosopher's own teaching on pleasure went another way. What did Epicurus say true pleasure was?
answer: A calm mind, plain bread and water, and the company of friends
choices: A calm mind, plain bread and water, and the company of friends
A table of roasted meats, honeyed wine, and rare imported spices
A grand house, fine robes, and a name everyone in Athens knew
Endless gold, so a man would never again have to want for anything
context: Epicurus prized philosophical conversation with friends over feasts; he taught that the untroubled mind he called ataraxia, not luxury, was the goal. The modern word 'epicure' completely flips his meaning. Source: IEP Epicurus https://iep.utm.edu/epicur/ ; Stanford SEP https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/epicurus/

question: Zeno of Citium gathered students in the crowded marketplace of Athens around 300 BC. At first his followers went by the name Zenonians, but in the end they took their lasting name, the Stoics, from the place where he taught. What was that place?
answer: The Painted Porch, a colonnade lined with battle murals
choices: The Painted Porch, a colonnade lined with battle murals
The Marble Temple, where the city kept its sacred treasure
The High Tower, which looked out over the whole harbor
The Long Bridge, which carried the road into the city
context: The walkway was the Stoa Poikile, Greek for 'Painted Porch.' Zeno's followers were first called Zenonians, then 'the people of the Stoa' the Stoics. The everyday word 'stoic,' meaning someone who endures pain or bad news calmly, is literally named after a porch, and it has kept that meaning for over 2,000 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoa_Poikile ; IEP Stoicism https://iep.utm.edu/stoicism/

question: American B-29 crews, 279 planes strong, dropped over 1,665 tons of napalm on Tokyo overnight on 9 and 10 March 1945, in a raid called Operation Meetinghouse. Some 100,000 died in that single raid. How did the raid's toll compare with that of the atomic bombs dropped on Japan months later?
answer: It killed more people in one night than either atomic bomb did
choices: It killed more people in one night than either atomic bomb did
It killed about the same number as a single atomic bomb
It killed roughly a tenth as many as one atomic bomb
It killed fewer people than any other raid of the war
context: Operation Meetinghouse remains the single most destructive air raid in history -- deadlier than the bombing of either Hiroshima or Nagasaki. The U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey officially counted 87,793 killed and 40,918 injured. The raid razed 16 square miles and left over a million people homeless. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/hellfire-earth-operation-meetinghouse

question: Curtis LeMay, a cigar-chewing American general in command of bombers, planned a great night firebombing raid on Tokyo early in 1945. He gambled that Japan's defenders could do little against bombers in the dark. What did LeMay have done to his B-29s before he sent them in?
answer: He stripped off their guns and armor so they could fly low and slow
choices: He stripped off their guns and armor so they could fly low and slow
He doubled their armor and gun crews to survive the run
He fitted them with extra fuel tanks to bomb from far higher up
He sent them in daylight in a tight defensive formation
context: LeMay sent the bombers in at just 5,000 to 9,000 feet instead of the usual 32,000. Lighter and lower, each plane could blanket Tokyo's dry wooden houses with napalm. Pathfinders first burned an X across the target to aim the fleet, and 65-mph firestorm winds did the rest -- the city had only 8,000 firemen and 'exactly three' firefighting extension ladders. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/hellfire-earth-operation-meetinghouse

question: Joseph Goebbels claimed 250,000 dead when the Allies firebombed Dresden in February 1945, and David Irving, a writer, later pushed for 150,000 to 200,000. A commission of historians named by the city of Dresden studied the toll for six years. What did it conclude in 2010?
answer: That about 25,000 people had died
choices: That about 25,000 people had died
That about 100,000 people had died
That Goebbels's figure of 250,000 was accurate
That the true toll could never be estimated
context: The 2010 commission's forensic count came in roughly ten times lower than Goebbels's wartime propaganda figure. Historian Donald Miller noted that most Dresden victims did not burn -- about 70 percent suffocated on carbon monoxide as the firestorm sucked the oxygen out of the cellars where they hid. American POW Kurt Vonnegut survived in an underground meat locker -- 'Slaughterhouse-Five' -- and later turned the raid into his famous anti-war novel. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/bombing-of-Dresden

question: Fashionable Parisians filled the new Theatre des Champs-Elysees on 29 May 1913 for Igor Stravinsky's ballet The Rite of Spring, expecting graceful dancing. What they got was pounding, jarring rhythms and Vaslav Nijinsky's dancers stamping pigeon-toed across the stage. As the music hammered on, what did the audience end up doing?
answer: Breaking into a brawl, fighting each other in the seats
choices: Breaking into a brawl, fighting each other in the seats
Walking out quietly in a long, silent stream
Demanding their ticket money back at the box office
Falling asleep in the warm, crowded theatre
context: The premiere at the new Théâtre des Champs-Élysées split the crowd into two screaming camps shouting over the music — one side yelling 'Marvelous, magnificent!' and the other 'Abominable, ridiculous!' — until they came to blows. A ballet that started a fight. Source: history.com 'This Day in History — Le Sacre du printemps.'

question: Pierre Monteux conducted The Rite of Spring again in 1914, a year after its scandalous premiere in Paris, but this time as a concert with no dancers at all, only the orchestra. How did the 1914 audience react to Stravinsky's score?
answer: They cheered it rapturously, and it became a celebrated classic
choices: They cheered it rapturously, and it became a celebrated classic
They rioted again, even more violently than before
They sat in stunned, total silence the whole way through
They walked out before the first movement had finished
context: The surprise reversal: strip away Nijinsky's jarring choreography and the very music the crowd had rioted over became a beloved 20th-century masterpiece. The scandal, it turned out, was as much about the stamping dancers as the notes. Source: classical-music.com 'Stravinsky: Rite of Spring.'

question: Gamal Abdel Nasser hid a code word in a speech before a huge crowd in Alexandria on 26 July 1956. Mahmoud Yunis, an engineer, was listening for it: on that signal his team would start taking over the Suez Canal. Nasser said it some fourteen times in ten minutes. What was the code word?
answer: The name of the canal's French builder, de Lesseps
choices: The name of the canal's French builder, de Lesseps
The Arabic battle cry his soldiers chanted
The name of the dam he wanted to build, Aswan
The single word 'Egypt' shouted to the crowd
context: Ferdinand de Lesseps was the Frenchman who built the Suez Canal, opened in 1869. When engineer Mahmoud Yunis heard Nasser say 'de Lesseps,' he began the takeover. Nasser, denied US/British money for his Aswan High Dam, said the canal's tolls would pay for it instead. Source: historynewsnetwork.org 'Sixty Years After the Suez Crisis'; Wilson Center Digital Archive, Nasser's Alexandria speech, July 26 1956.

question: Dwight Eisenhower learned that Britain, France and Israel had attacked Egypt in 1956 to take back the Suez Canal without a word to him. They were winning on the ground, but he refused to back them, and his weapon against Britain was not soldiers. What did Eisenhower threaten that forced Britain to give in within days?
answer: To dump America's British pound bonds and crash the pound
choices: To dump America's British pound bonds and crash the pound
To bomb the British fleet sitting off the Egyptian coast
To recognize Nasser's Egypt as the canal's rightful owner
To expel Britain from the United Nations Security Council
context: Eisenhower blocked roughly $561 million in IMF credit and about $600 million in Export-Import Bank credit to Britain, refused the dollars Britain needed to buy oil after the canal closed, and threatened to sell US-held sterling bonds, which would have crashed the pound as Britain's reserves were already collapsing. Britain and France accepted a UN ceasefire on November 6, 1956. Suez is seen as the symbolic end of Britain as a global superpower. Source: IMF WP/00/192 'Northwest of Suez'; mises.org 'Financial Warfare and the Declining Dollar'; history.state.gov/milestones, Suez.

question: Nicolas de Ovando, governor of Hispaniola, set up the first encomiendas in 1502. On paper a colonist received a group of Native villagers to work for him, and in return he was to protect them and teach them the Christian faith. The name comes from a Spanish verb. What does that verb mean?
answer: To entrust
choices: To entrust
To conquer
To purchase
To baptize
context: The word 'encomienda' comes from 'encomendar,' to entrust. The grim joke is in the name: the colonist was supposedly being 'entrusted' with the people's care and souls, while in practice it became a license to work them to death. The first encomiendas were set up on Hispaniola in 1502 by the governor Nicolas de Ovando. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Encomienda' (worldhistory.org/Encomienda).

question: On a colonial sugar plantation, workers crushed the cane, then boiled the juice down for hours over roaring fires until it thickened. They poured the hot syrup into clay molds to cool and harden. When a mold was broken open, what shape of sugar came out?
answer: A tall cone-shaped loaf
choices: A tall cone-shaped loaf
A flat brown brick
A bag of loose crystals
A thin pressed sheet
context: The molds were cone-shaped, so the sugar hardened into 'loaves' shaped like tall cones, each weighing about 15 to 20 pounds. A colonial sugar mill was one of the most technologically complex industries of its day. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Life on a Colonial Sugar Plantation' (worldhistory.org/article/1795).

question: Colonists on Hispaniola opened the first sugar mill in the Americas in 1516, crushing cane carried across from the Canary Islands. Sugar devoured more labor than any other colonial crop, and its endless demand for workers drove the horror for which the plantation system is best remembered. What was that horror?
answer: The Atlantic slave trade
choices: The Atlantic slave trade
Feudal serfdom
Debt peonage
Child factory labor
context: The cane for that first 1516 mill was carried over from the Canary Islands, off the coast of Africa. Sugar was the most labor-hungry crop in the colonies, and its demand for workers is what drove the whole forced-labor machine. Source: HistoryAtlas, 'The Indigenous Taino Have Nearly Disappeared' (historyatlas.com).

question: A worker fed sugar cane between the three heavy rollers of a colonial mill to squeeze out its juice. If his fingers caught, the rollers would keep pulling until his whole body was crushed. Another worker was always stationed right beside the rollers. What did that second worker do to save a trapped man's life?
answer: Chop off the trapped arm with a hatchet
choices: Chop off the trapped arm with a hatchet
Wrench the worker free by main force
Cut the worker's clothes loose from the cane
Drag the worker back with a rope
context: Because the three-roller crusher could not be stopped in time, a worker stood by with a cutlass or hatchet to chop off a trapped arm before the rollers dragged the whole person in and killed them. Losing an arm was the merciful outcome. Source: 'Slaves' Work on Sugar Plantations' (runaways.gla.ac.uk).

question: A sugar-mill hand toiled in the scorching heat of the boiling house, close to rollers that could crush a man, amid disease and endless overwork. How long was such a man said to last before the work killed him?
answer: About seven years
choices: About seven years
About thirty years
A full lifetime
About fifteen years
context: The average working life of a sugar-mill hand was said to be only about seven years before overwork, heat, disease, and injury killed them. The crop that sweetened Europe's tables was among the deadliest work in the colonial world. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Life on a Colonial Sugar Plantation' (worldhistory.org/article/1795).

question: Hernan Cortes brought down the Aztec empire, and the Spanish Crown rewarded him with a single encomienda in Mexico, a grant of the forced labor of Native families. The biggest grants went to the great conquerors. How many families of Native workers did that one grant cover?
answer: Over 23,000 families
choices: Over 23,000 families
About 8,000 families
Around 15,000 families
Nearly 40,000 families
context: Cortes received a single encomienda covering well over 23,000 family units of Indigenous laborers. A grant was not a few servants; it could be the forced labor of tens of thousands of people handed to one man. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Encomienda' (worldhistory.org/Encomienda).

question: Juan Lopez de Palacios Rubios, a Spanish jurist, wrote the Requerimiento, a demand that its hearers submit to the Pope and the Spanish crown or else face war. From 1513 Spanish commanders had to read it aloud before they attacked. Where and how did soldiers often read it?
answer: To empty beaches and from the decks of ships
choices: To empty beaches and from the decks of ships
To kneeling chiefs gathered in the town square
Through an interpreter, slowly, village by village
Nailed to a post as a written proclamation
context: The Requerimiento (written 1513 by the jurist Juan Lopez de Palacios Rubios) was a pure legal fig-leaf. It was read to barren beaches and empty villages after the people had fled, to prisoners after they were captured, and even from the decks of ships once the coast was merely sighted. The 'offer' was a formality nobody was meant to accept. Source: Wikipedia, 'Spanish Requirement of 1513'.

question: Spanish soldiers read out the Requerimiento, a legal demand to submit to the Pope and the Spanish crown, in Spanish or Latin to Native listeners who could not understand a single word of it, and then they attacked. Bartolome de las Casas, a Dominican friar, saw it done. What did he say he did not know whether to do?
answer: Whether to laugh or to weep
choices: Whether to laugh or to weep
Whether to fight or to flee
Whether to pray or to curse
Whether to stay or to sail home
context: Las Casas said of the absurd Requerimiento that he 'did not know whether to laugh or to weep' at it. A document read in Latin to people who spoke neither Latin nor Spanish was the conquest's legal cover, and one of its own friars saw straight through it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Spanish Requirement of 1513'.

question: Bartolome de las Casas lived among the conquistadors in the Caribbean and Mexico in the early 1500s and wrote an eyewitness account of their cruelty. In it the Dominican friar described one animal the Spanish bred and trained as a weapon of terror against the Native peoples. Which animal was it?
answer: War-mastiffs set loose on them
choices: War-mastiffs set loose on them
Falcons flown at their faces
Bulls driven through their fields
Horses ridden into their ranks
context: Las Casas wrote that the Spanish 'hunted them with their Hounds, whom they bred up and taught to pull down and tear the Indians like beasts.' These war-mastiffs were trained specifically to hunt and savage people. Source: Bartolome de las Casas, 'A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies' (faculty.chass.ncsu.edu/slatta/hi216).

question: Hatuey, a Taino chief, saw the Spanish destroying his home island of Hispaniola and decided to warn the next island in their path. He gathered his people and set out for Cuba to raise the alarm. How did Hatuey and his people cross to Cuba?
answer: They paddled across by canoe
choices: They paddled across by canoe
They walked across a land bridge
They drifted across on rafts of reeds
They sailed a captured Spanish ship
context: Hatuey fled Hispaniola by canoe to warn Cuba, then fought the Spanish there with guerrilla raids. Tracked down with the help of war-mastiffs, he was captured and burned at the stake at Yara in 1512, becoming one of the first heroes of resistance in the Americas. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hatuey'.

question: Emperor Charles V, pressed by reformers like Bartolome de las Casas, issued the New Laws in 1542, declaring that Indigenous people were free subjects who could not be enslaved. The laws also hit the encomienda itself with the one rule its holders hated most. What did that rule say must happen to an encomienda?
answer: It could not be passed down to an heir
choices: It could not be passed down to an heir
It had to be sold to the crown for gold
It must be split evenly among the workers
It could cover only half as many workers
context: The New Laws (Leyes Nuevas), issued by Emperor Charles V on November 20, 1542, ordered that an encomienda could no longer be inherited; when its holder died, it reverted to the Crown. The idea was to let the system wither away as the current holders died off. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Laws'.

question: Gonzalo Pizarro led Peru's grant-holders in open revolt against the New Laws, which threatened to end their encomiendas, and against the first viceroy of Peru, Blasco Nunez Vela, sent to enforce them. The rebellion came to its climax in 1546. What did Pizarro's men do to the viceroy?
answer: They killed him in battle
choices: They killed him in battle
They shipped him to Spain in chains
They locked him in a mountain fortress
They forced him to sign a surrender
context: Gonzalo Pizarro's encomenderos killed the first viceroy of Peru, Blasco Nunez Vela, in 1546 rather than give up their grants. The Crown blinked first: it had already revoked the no-inheritance clause in 1545. Even a king could not simply override the colonists who profited from the system. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blasco Nunez Vela'.

question: Spain's rulers replaced the fading encomienda in the Americas with a new labor system, the repartimiento, meant as a reform. Instead of handing one colonist a body of people outright, it drew its workers another way. How did the repartimiento supply labor?
answer: Villages had to send a rotating quota of workers for set periods
choices: Villages had to send a rotating quota of workers for set periods
Colonists paid a wage to any worker who chose to come
Each village owed a yearly payment in gold instead of labor
Workers were shipped from Africa to replace the natives
context: The repartimiento (the 'mita' in Peru, the 'cuatequil' in New Spain) forced Indigenous communities to rotate a quota of laborers for set periods, rather than granting a colonist a body of people outright. It was meant to be a reform, but for the workers rotated into the silver mines it was often just as deadly. Source: Britannica, 'repartimiento' (britannica.com/topic/repartimiento).

question: Sumerians raised the world's first cities on the plain of the Tigris and Euphrates, in today's southern Iraq. Around 3100 BC one of them packed some 40,000 people behind its mud-brick walls, by archaeologists' best reckoning the largest place on Earth and the first real city anywhere. Which city was it?
answer: Uruk
choices: Uruk
Babylon
Memphis
Jericho
context: Uruk, around 3100 BCE, held perhaps 40,000 people inside its walls (80,000-90,000 in the surrounding area) and sprawled across about 6 square kilometers of temples, workshops, and packed neighborhoods - a 'mega-city' before any other existed. Source: worldhistory.org/uruk and metmuseum.org/essays/uruk-the-first-city.

question: King Ur-Nammu of Ur began his city's great stepped tower around 2100 BC, and like every Sumerian city's ruler he bore the title lugal. Other titles for a ruler were en, lord, and ensi, governor. What does lugal literally mean?
answer: Big man
choices: Big man
Bright star
High priest
Good shepherd
context: 'Lugal' literally means 'big man.' Rulers also went by 'en' (lord/priest-king) and 'ensi' (governor), and the king was usually the high priest of the city's god too - the first government in history, one person bound to the gods over the land and the people. Source: worldhistory.org/Sumerians.

question: Leonard Woolley, an archaeologist, dug up game boards made around 2600 BC, inlaid with shell and blue lapis lazuli, in the ruins of a Sumerian city. Irving Finkel, a museum curator, later worked out the rules from a Babylonian tablet, so the game can still be played. What is this oldest playable board game called?
answer: The Royal Game of Ur
choices: The Royal Game of Ur
The game of Senet
Nine Men's Morris
Snakes and Ladders
context: The Royal Game of Ur (boards from about 2600-2400 BCE, dug up at Ur by Leonard Woolley) is the oldest playable game we know - a race to get seven pieces across the board, moves set by tetrahedral dice. Curator Irving Finkel decoded its rules from a Babylonian tablet written in 177 BCE. Source: britishmuseum.org and tradgames.org.uk/games/Royal-Game-Ur.htm.

question: King Gilgamesh, his epic tells, did great works in his city, and the poem about him, one of the oldest anywhere, opens with a dare aimed straight at its listener. What does the poem dare the listener to do?
answer: Climb the walls and check that the bricks are kiln-fired
choices: Climb the walls and check that the bricks are kiln-fired
Sail downriver to find the secret of eternal life
Wrestle the wild man Enkidu in the city square
Count every soldier in the king's great army
context: The prologue dares you to inspect Uruk yourself: 'Go up, pace out the walls of Uruk... examine the brickwork. Is not its masonry of kiln-fired brick?' Tradition says Gilgamesh built the wall, which ran about 9.5 km (6 miles) around the city. Source: Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet I (Foster translation) and ancientpages.com.  (Legend.)

question: King Eannatum of Lagash defeated the rival city of Umma around 2475 BC, in the first war between states that history records well, and set up a carved stone to boast of his victory. The broken slab takes its grisly nickname from the creatures carved along its top. What are they doing?
answer: Flying off with the severed heads of the enemy dead
choices: Flying off with the severed heads of the enemy dead
Dragging a war-chariot over the trampled fallen
Tearing into the bodies left on the battlefield
Dropping heavy stones onto the fleeing soldiers
context: The Stele of the Vultures (about 2475 BCE) is the earliest war monument in the world, named for the vultures carved carrying off the heads of the defeated. The Lagash-Umma fight is history's first well-documented war between states, and it ended in one of the earliest known boundary treaties. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stele_of_the_Vultures and britannica.com.

question: A Sumerian potter pressed clay into a mold and turned out one cheap, rough bowl after another, each much the same size as the last. Excavators have since found thousands of these bevel-rim bowls, history's first mass-produced object. What were they for?
answer: Doling out a fixed daily food ration to each worker
choices: Doling out a fixed daily food ration to each worker
Mixing the paints for the temple's bright murals
Burning oil to light the city streets at night
Catching rainwater that ran off the temple roofs
context: The bevel-rim bowl was churned out in huge numbers to dole out daily grain rations to workers.
