The standardized bowl is the first evidence of organized division of labor - people specializing in jobs and being paid in measured portions of food. Source: worldhistory.org/uruk and metmuseum.org/essays/uruk-the-first-city.

question: Leonard Woolley uncovered a grave at Ur that he named the Great Death Pit: 68 women in scarlet gowns and gold headdresses laid out in neat rows, with six men holding weapons posted by the entrance. Woolley believed they had all died together for a single reason. What did he conclude they were?
answer: Servants who followed a dead royal master into the grave
choices: Servants who followed a dead royal master into the grave
Soldiers killed defending the city from invaders
Plague victims buried quickly in a single pit
Slaves who had risen up and been put to death
context: In grave PG 1237, Woolley believed the 68 attendants and six armed guards had followed a royal master into death - possibly poisoned, with some skulls showing they were struck on the head. It remains his interpretation of the evidence, not a settled fact. Source: ancient-origins.net/ancient-places-asia/death-pit-of-ur-mesopotamia-0010297.

question: Craftsmen at Uruk, in what is now southern Iraq, set a heavy disk spinning around 4000 BC. It is one of the oldest wheels known anywhere, older by centuries than any wheel set under a cart. What did they spin on this first wheel?
answer: Wet clay, to shape smoother and thinner pots
choices: Wet clay, to shape smoother and thinner pots
Heavy stones, to grind grain into flour
Raw wool, to twist it into woven cloth
Copper ore, to polish it into bright mirrors
context: The potter's wheel came centuries before anyone stood a wheel on its edge and put it under a cart. The oldest surviving potter's wheel was found at Ur, in modern Iraq, dated to about 3100 BCE. Source: thepotterywheel.com/potters-wheel-history; World History Encyclopedia.

question: Sumerian farmers hitched a pair of oxen to a new kind of plow around 2500 BC, a machine that did two farm jobs at once. While its wooden blade cut a new trench behind the oxen, one of the three-man team fed something into a funnel fixed on top. What poured down the funnel?
answer: Seeds, dropping straight into the fresh furrow
choices: Seeds, dropping straight into the fresh furrow
Water, soaking the soil before planting
Ash, fertilizing the ground as it opened
Sand, marking a straight line to follow
context: One machine plowed and sowed in a single pass. Steering it took a whole team: one farmer leading the oxen, a second gripping the plow, and a third pouring the seed. Source: 180days.blog/day-12-the-seed-plough; study.com Mesopotamian Technology.

question: Boatmen on the Tigris and Euphrates hoisted sails from around 3000 BC to drive heavy Sumerian cargoes upstream against the current. By an old folk story, the idea for the sail came from an ordinary household sight. According to that story, what sparked the invention?
answer: Wet laundry billowing and tugging in the wind as it dried
choices: Wet laundry billowing and tugging in the wind as it dried
A leaf skittering fast across the surface of a pond
Smoke from a cook-fire bending sideways in a gust
A bird gliding upstream without flapping its wings
context: People likely noticed wet cloth hung to dry caught the wind, and reasoned a bigger cloth could push a boat upriver. This origin tale is plausible but not certain. Source: timelessmyths.com/stories/sumerian-inventions; study.com.  (Legend.)

question: A Sumerian father walked his son through the whole barley year, step by step, in advice preserved on a small clay tablet from about 1700 BC. A joint dig by the Universities of Chicago and Pennsylvania turned it up in southern Iraq in 1949, and it is now called the Farmer's Almanac. How deep did it say to plant each seed?
answer: About the width of two fingers into the furrow
choices: About the width of two fingers into the furrow
About the length of a man's forearm down
About as deep as an ox's hoof sinks
About one full hand-span below the surface
context: The tablet gives nuts-and-bolts plow instructions and was found on a joint University of Chicago / University of Pennsylvania expedition. Source: en-academic.com (Sumerian Farmer's Almanac); Kramer, History Begins at Sumer.

question: Griots, the hereditary singers of the Mande peoples, still perform the epic of Sundiata Keita, founder of the Mali Empire. His epic name joins his mother Sogolon's name to jata, a Mande word. What does the name Sundiata mean?
answer: Sogolon's Lion
choices: Sogolon's Lion
Sogolon's Eagle
Sogolon's Spear
Sogolon's Shadow
context: His birth name was Sogolon Djata (Mari Djata); 'Sundiata' fuses 'Sogolon' with 'jata' (lion) — the Lion of Mali. His royal title was Mansa, meaning king or emperor in Mandinka. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundiata_Keita

question: Sassouma Berete, his father's other wife, made a mockery of young Sundiata Keita and his mother, Sogolon, the epic tells. The future founder of the Mali Empire spent his early childhood unable to do one ordinary thing. What could young Sundiata not do?
answer: Walk
choices: Walk
Speak
See
Hear
context: The boy who could not walk rising to found an empire is the heart of the story; the co-wife Sassouma Bereté mocked him and his mother Sogolon. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundiata_Keita

question: Sundiata sent for a bar of iron so heavy that six men had to carry it, after his mother, Sogolon, was shamed over some baobab leaves. As he gripped it and rose, the iron bent in his hands, so the legend says. What shape did it take?
answer: A bow
choices: A bow
A crown
A throne
A chain
context: His mother Sogolon had been insulted because no one would fetch her baobab leaves; the bending iron rod is the epic's signature image of Sundiata's hidden power awakening. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Sundiata

question: Soumaoro Kante, the sorcerer-king of the Sosso, took Sundiata's homeland while the prince was in exile, the epic tells. In a hidden chamber whose floor was laid with human skins, he kept the heads of nine kings on display. Whose heads were they?
answer: Kings Soumaoro had defeated
choices: Kings Soumaoro had defeated
Soumaoro's own ancestors
Gods the Sosso worshipped
Prophets who cursed him
context: The chamber of human skins and nine kings' heads marks Soumaoro as the terrifying villain Sundiata must overthrow. Told as legend. Source: https://www.enotes.com/topics/sundiata/part-summary/part-iv-summary-soumaoro-kante-sorcerer-king

question: Sundiata Keita led an alliance of neighbouring peoples against the sorcerer-king Soumaoro Kante at the Battle of Kirina around 1235. In the epic, Sundiata had learned the one thing that could break Soumaoro's magic, and he tipped an arrow with it. What was it?
answer: A white rooster's spur
choices: A white rooster's spur
A drop of his own blood
A buried iron mask
A stolen golden ring
context: Wounded by the cock's-spur arrow, Soumaoro's magic failed and he vanished into the Koulikoro mountains; Kirina (c. 1235) is treated as the founding moment of the Mali Empire, which ruled most of West Africa for two centuries. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kirina

question: Sundiata Keita, victorious, gathered the clan chiefs at Kouroukan Fouga, a granite clearing, around 1236 and proclaimed the Manden Charter, his new empire's constitution. For centuries it was never written down but passed on by word of mouth. Scholars hail it as one of the world's earliest declarations of what?
answer: Human rights
choices: Human rights
Trade tariffs
Royal bloodlines
Battle tactics
context: Its articles include 'To satisfy one's hunger is not robbery,' that women be associated with all governance, and a rule to check tree branches for fruit or flowers before clearing land by fire; UNESCO added it to its heritage list in 2009. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kouroukan_Fouga

question: Muhammad's followers in Medina argued over one urgent question when the Prophet died in that oasis city in 632. Their quarrel divided Islam into the Sunni and Shia branches for centuries to come. What were they arguing about?
answer: Who should lead the community after him
choices: Who should lead the community after him
Which city should become the capital
How many times a day to pray
Which language the Quran should use
context: The whole Sunni-Shia divide began as a succession dispute. At a meeting in the Saqifa (a roofed courtyard) of the Banu Sa'ida, the elder companion Abu Bakr was acclaimed as the first caliph. One faction insisted Muhammad had already chosen his cousin Ali. (World History Edu, 'Succession Following the Death of Muhammad'; detailedpedia.com 'Succession of Muhammad')

question: Muhammad took the orphaned boy Ali ibn Abi Talib into his own household to raise. Early Muslim sources say Ali became the first male to accept Islam, at about the age of eleven. Yet the two were already tied by blood. How was young Ali related to Muhammad?
answer: He was Muhammad's first cousin
choices: He was Muhammad's first cousin
He was Muhammad's older brother
He was Muhammad's uncle
He was Muhammad's grandfather
context: Ali was Muhammad's first cousin AND son-in-law, marrying the Prophet's daughter Fatima around 623-625. For Shia he is the first Imam; for Sunni he is the fourth of the 'Rightly-Guided' (Rashidun) caliphs. The faction that backed him became the 'shi'at Ali' -- the party of Ali, the Shia. (Wikipedia, 'Ali')

question: Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, a Kharijite rebel, struck Ali ibn Abi Talib on the head with a sword inside Kufa's Great Mosque in 661. Ali had been caliph since 656. What had the attacker done to the blade to make sure the wound would kill him?
answer: Its blade had been smeared with poison
choices: Its blade had been smeared with poison
Its edge had been notched like a saw
Its tip had been dipped in molten lead
Its handle had been wrapped in nettles
context: The assassin, the Kharijite Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, poisoned the blade; Ali died of the wound about two days later, around age 62. He is believed to be buried at the Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf, Iraq -- a major Shia pilgrimage site. (Wikipedia, 'Assassination of Ali' and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam')

question: Husayn, the Prophet's grandson and Ali's son, refused to swear allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid in 680. An Umayyad army thousands strong surrounded him near Karbala, in Iraq. How large a company of family and followers stood with Husayn?
answer: Only about seventy to a hundred people
choices: Only about seventy to a hundred people
Around five thousand fighters
Nearly twenty thousand troops
A force evenly matched with the enemy
context: Husayn and his roughly 70-100 followers and family were overwhelmed on 10 October 680 (10 Muharram). His head was cut off and carried to the governor Ibn Ziyad and then to Yazid in Damascus; the surviving women and children were taken captive. This is the emotional core of Shia devotion. (World History Encyclopedia, 'Battle of Karbala'; Wikipedia 'Battle of Karbala')

question: Al-Hurr ibn Yazid commanded the Umayyad horsemen who first stopped Husayn's march near Karbala in 680, trapping him and his people before the main army. On the morning of the battle, Husayn's words moved the cavalry officer deeply. What did al-Hurr do then?
answer: He rode over to Husayn's side and died fighting for him
choices: He rode over to Husayn's side and died fighting for him
He quietly slipped away from the battlefield at night
He sent a secret message begging Yazid for mercy
He ordered his men to lay down their weapons and watch
context: Al-Hurr ibn Yazid al-Tamimi defected to the man he had been sent to trap, and was killed fighting for Husayn -- one of the most retold moments of Karbala. (Wikipedia, 'Battle of Karbala')

question: Shia pilgrims walk to Husayn's tomb at Karbala every year on Arba'in, forty days after Ashura, when they mourn his death in 680, and often more than twenty million of them come at once. How does that crowd compare with the Hajj, the great pilgrimage to Mecca?
answer: Arba'in is the largest annual gathering on earth
choices: Arba'in is the largest annual gathering on earth
The two draw almost exactly the same crowds
The Hajj is several times larger than Arba'in
Arba'in is a small, local event by comparison
context: Karbala is relived every year on Ashura (10 Muharram) with mourning processions and chest-beating (matam). The Arba'in walking pilgrimage forty days later is the largest annual gathering on earth -- many times the size of the Hajj. (Wikipedia, 'Battle of Karbala' and 'Arba'in pilgrimage'; Religion Media Centre)

question: Salvador Dali filled The Persistence of Memory in 1931 with pocket watches hanging limp across a dreamscape as if they had melted. When a physicist asked whether Einstein's theory of relativity lay behind them, Dali said no. They came from something he had watched turn runny in the summer sun. What was it?
answer: A wheel of Camembert cheese
choices: A wheel of Camembert cheese
A candle on his windowsill
A block of butter on bread
A bar of soap in the bath
context: Dali called the soft watches a surrealist 'camembert of time,' inspired by watching a Camembert melt in the sun on a summer evening — not by Einstein. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Persistence_of_Memory; salvadordali.com/melting-clocks-persistence-of-memory/

question: In the lower-left corner of The Persistence of Memory, where the other watches sag and droop, Dali painted one orange pocket watch with its case shut tight, the only one that has not gone soft. He covered it with something he used again and again to stand for things rotting away. What did he paint on it?
answer: A cluster of black ants
choices: A cluster of black ants
A trail of green moss
A patch of grey mold
A web of fine cracks
context: The closed pocket watch is swarmed by black ants — Dali's recurring symbol of decay. It is the one watch in the painting that stays hard instead of melting. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Persistence_of_Memory

question: A band of Thugs fell in with travellers on an Indian road and walked beside them for days, sharing meals and easy talk to win their trust. Then, without warning, the Thugs turned on them and strangled them. What did the Thugs call the strangling-cord each of them used?
answer: The rumal
choices: The rumal
The katar
The chela
The tabar
context: The rumal was a cloth handkerchief with a knot tied in one end to give the strangler a grip. The spade the Thugs used to dig their victims' secret graves was treated as a sacred pickaxe, consecrated to the goddess the cult worshipped. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thuggee; victorianweb.org/history/empire/india/thuggee.html)

question: Lord William Bentinck, Governor-General of India, signed a regulation on 4 December 1829 making suttee illegal: the burning of a widow alive on her dead husband's funeral pyre. British rulers had left the custom alone for years, fearing a ban would spark a religious revolt. Under the new law, what crime could anyone who helped burn a widow be tried for?
answer: Murder
choices: Murder
Sedition
Blasphemy
Treason
context: Bentinck's regulation of 4 December 1829 declared that 'the practice of suttee, or of burning or burying alive the widows of Hindus, is hereby declared illegal.' The campaign behind it joined two unlikely allies: the Baptist missionary William Carey and the Hindu reformer Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who argued that suttee was not actually required by Hindu scripture. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Sati_Regulation,_1829)

question: William Carey, a Baptist missionary who doubled as the British government's official Bengali translator, received the newly signed order banning suttee on a Sunday morning in 1829. It had to be turned into Bengali. What did Carey do the moment it arrived?
answer: He handed his sermon to another preacher and raced to finish the translation that same day.
choices: He handed his sermon to another preacher and raced to finish the translation that same day.
He set it aside to translate carefully over the following week.
He read the order from the pulpit and preached on it before translating it.
He refused, saying a missionary should not do the government's paperwork.
context: Carey believed that every hour of delay might cost some widow her life, so he passed his pulpit to another preacher and had the decree translated into Bengali by that evening before any more burnings could happen. He had earlier collected statistics on sati from his mission at Serampore. (Source: christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/ministry-in-killing-fields)

question: William Sleeman, a British officer, took charge in the 1830s of breaking the Thugs, a secret brotherhood that buried its victims in hidden graves and guarded its ways from every outsider. He found his great weapon in a captured Thug. What did that prisoner agree to do?
answer: Turn informer and lead the soldiers straight to his old gang.
choices: Turn informer and lead the soldiers straight to his old gang.
Recite from memory the cult's entire secret coded language.
Convert and travel the roads preaching against his former cult.
Train a company of soldiers to fight in the Thugs' own ambush style.
context: Such a turncoat was called an 'approver.' The most important was Feringheea, arrested in 1830; in January 1831 he led Sleeman to graves outside the village of Salohda where 25 men had been buried over ten years, and his testimony helped identify 283 of 289 Thugs seized near Jhansi. By 1839 Sleeman declared Thuggee 'effectively destroyed as an organisation.' (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feringheea; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Sleeman)

question: Alicia Little set up a society against foot-binding at Shanghai in 1895 and toured China to win people over. Earlier campaigners had made their case from Christianity and changed few minds, so she took a cleverer route with audiences who were not Christian. What did Little show them?
answer: X-ray photographs of crushed feet, beside quotations from Confucius.
choices: X-ray photographs of crushed feet, beside quotations from Confucius.
Pamphlets from European doctors warning of the health dangers.
Cash rewards offered to families who left their daughters' feet natural.
A printed decree from the Emperor commanding the custom to stop.
context: Little dropped religious arguments and persuaded people on health and tradition instead. Chinese reformers worked alongside the missionaries: the Belfast-born John MacGowan had gathered 60 to 70 Chinese Christian women in Xiamen in 1874, the first such society, and Kang Youwei's Anti-Footbinding Society near Canton grew to a claimed 300,000 members. The Republic of China formally banned foot-binding in 1912, though the last lotus-shoe factory, in Harbin, did not close until 1999. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alicia_Little; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_binding)

question: Hong Xiuquan, a village schoolteacher who failed the imperial civil service exam four times, fell into a fever after one failure. He dreamed that a golden-bearded old man cut out his organs and gave him a sword to cleanse the earth of demons. Years later a pamphlet by Liang Fa convinced him the old man had been God. What did that make Hong?
answer: The younger brother of Jesus Christ
choices: The reincarnation of the first emperor of China
The younger brother of Jesus Christ
A prophet chosen to restore the old gods
The last true descendant of Confucius
context: Hong Xiuquan (1814-1864) read Liang Fa's pamphlet 'Good Words to Admonish the Age' and concluded the bearded old man in his dream was God his father and Jesus his elder brother -- making Hong the literal younger brother of Christ, sent to rid China of demons. He proclaimed himself 'Heavenly King' in 1851 and launched the Taiping Rebellion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Xiuquan; newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Hong_Xiuquan.

question: Hong Xiuquan named himself Heavenly King in 1851 and gathered peasants, miners and the poor into an army against China's Qing emperors, who fought him city after city until 1864. No war anywhere in the nineteenth century, not even the American Civil War of the same years, killed more people. Roughly how many died?
answer: Between 20 and 30 million
choices: Around 200 thousand
Around 2 million
Between 20 and 30 million
Around 500 thousand
context: Estimates run 20 to 30 million dead -- many times the toll of the American Civil War being fought in the same years, and one of the bloodiest wars in all of human history. Source: britannica.com/event/Taiping-Rebellion; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiping_Rebellion.

question: Shah Jahan, the Mughal emperor, set some 20,000 craftsmen to work beside the Yamuna at Agra in 1632, and for about twenty-two years they cut and carved white marble for the Taj Mahal. He did not build it as a palace to live in, or as a mosque to pray in. Why did he build it?
answer: As a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who had died
choices: As a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who had died
As a fortress to guard the river crossing into the city
As a treasury to lock away the gold of his empire
As a throne hall where he would receive foreign kings
context: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 giving birth to their FOURTEENTH child. The grief-stricken emperor put about 20,000 artisans to work for roughly 22 years (1632-1653) building her a tomb of white marble quarried at Makrana. The poet Rabindranath Tagore later called it 'a teardrop on the cheek of time.' Source: britannica.com/topic/Taj-Mahal; mapsofindia.com.

question: Shah Jahan planned the Taj Mahal in perfect balance, every tower and hall matched by a twin around the great central dome, and he spent his last years gazing at it across the river from Agra Fort. Only one thing in the whole monument breaks its symmetry. What is it?
answer: Shah Jahan's own tomb, added later beside his wife's
choices: Shah Jahan's own tomb, added later beside his wife's
A garden fountain dug nearer to the eastern wall
A doorway cut wider on the building's southern face
A staircase built taller on the river-facing side
context: Shah Jahan spent two decades perfecting the balance, but when he died his son Aurangzeb buried him squeezed in beside Mumtaz, slightly off-axis to the west, breaking the symmetry forever. Aurangzeb had earlier seized the throne and imprisoned his father in nearby Agra Fort, where the old emperor spent his last years (1658-1666) gazing at the Taj Mahal across the river. Source: smithsonianmag.com (Eight Secrets of the Taj Mahal); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumtaz_Mahal.

question: The Tang rulers laid out their capital, Chang'an, as a vast checkerboard of straight avenues inside walls of packed earth, and they set the palace at its northern end. Merchants, monks and envoys came there from all over Asia. In Tang belief, what did this perfect grid mirror?
answer: The order of the cosmos
choices: The order of the cosmos
The body of a sleeping dragon
The route of the Silk Road
The shape of the emperor's seal
context: The Tang saw their gridded capital as a model of heavenly order on earth, with drainage ditches between the blocks and roughly a million people inside the packed-earth walls (2-3 million counting the suburbs). Source: worldhistory.org/Chang'an and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang%27an

question: Envoys from foreign courts walked the wide, straight avenues of Chang'an, the Tang capital, and carried its checkerboard plan away with them. Back home, royal capitals rose in its image, high walls and straight streets and all. Which capitals were modeled on Chang'an?
answer: Nara and Kyoto in Japan, Gyeongju in Korea
choices: Nara and Kyoto in Japan, Gyeongju in Korea
Baghdad and Basra in Iraq, Cairo in Egypt
Athens and Sparta in Greece, Rome in Italy
Delhi and Agra in India, Kabul in Afghanistan
context: Japanese envoys studied Chang'an and brought its plan back; the Japanese capitals of Nara and Heian-kyo (Kyoto) and the Korean capital Gyeongju all copied its segregated districts and wide avenues. Source: worldhistory.org/Chang'an

question: A commoner of Chang'an heard the curfew drums roll at dusk, some 800 beats, as the gates of the city's 108 walled wards swung shut. If he was still in the streets after that, he risked arrest and a beating. What were the inner walls and gates mainly for?
answer: To keep the residents penned in at night
choices: To keep the residents penned in at night
To hide the emperor's palace from view
To block sandstorms blowing off the desert
To divide rich families from poor ones
context: Closing was announced by about 800 drumbeats and opening by about 300; the ward walls existed less to keep enemies out than to keep residents in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang%27an

question: Li Bai, a wandering poet, came to Chang'an, the Tang capital, in the 740s with his verses in his pack. He Zhizhang, an elder court poet, read Li Bai's poem The Road to Shu and was stunned by its wild imagination and thunder. He gave the newcomer a nickname that stuck for good. What did he call Li Bai?
answer: The Banished Immortal
choices: The Banished Immortal
The Drunken Sage
The River Dragon
The Mountain Hermit
context: He Zhizhang hailed Li Bai as the 'Banished Immortal' (zhexian) — an immortal exiled from heaven to earth. Li Bai, born in 701 in the Silk Road town of Suyab, was also nicknamed the 'Wine Immortal.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Bai

question: A lonely traveller woke in a strange room in Li Bai's four-line poem Quiet Night Thoughts, saw moonlight on the floor and took it for frost. Then he lifted his head to the bright moon and lowered it, thinking of home. What distinction does the poem hold in China today?
answer: It is the first poem most Chinese children memorize
choices: It is the first poem most Chinese children memorize
It is carved over the Great Wall's main gate
It must be sung at every Chinese wedding
It was banned by emperors for a thousand years
context: 'Quiet Night Thoughts' is the first poem most Chinese children learn and is quoted by adults to this day. About 1,000 of Li Bai's poems survive. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Bai and 100tangpoems.wordpress.com

question: He Zhizhang, a veteran poet of the Tang court, once stood at a tavern counter with no money for his wine. He was as fond of wine as Li Bai, so he took off a token of the high rank he held at court and passed it over for a drink. What did he give up?
answer: The golden-tortoise ornament of his office
choices: The golden-tortoise ornament of his office
A jade seal given by the emperor
His ceremonial court sword
A silk scroll of his own poems
context: He Zhizhang unfastened the golden-tortoise ornament that marked his high rank and traded it across the counter for wine. Source: daydaynews.cc 'He Zhizhang'; theworldofchinese.com 'Alcoholics in ancient times'

question: Du Fu, younger than Li Bai and a graver poet, met him in the autumn of 744, and the pair travelled together for a season. They shared a room, hunted side by side and parted as sworn friends. Yet something between the two poets ran lopsided. What was it?
answer: Du Fu wrote Li Bai a dozen poems; Li Bai sent back just one
choices: Du Fu wrote Li Bai a dozen poems; Li Bai sent back just one
Li Bai dazzled the emperor's court; Du Fu never won a post there
Du Fu outlived Li Bai by decades; Li Bai died first and young
Li Bai roamed the rivers freely; Du Fu stayed bound to the city
context: The younger Du Fu wrote about a dozen poems to or about Li Bai, who left only one in return. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Du_Fu and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Bai

question: Li Bai wrote some of his wildest verses drunk on rice wine, and when he died in 762 the true cause was lost. The Chinese have always preferred one romantic legend about his end. What does the legend say killed him?
answer: He drowned leaning from his boat to embrace the moon's reflection
choices: He drowned leaning from his boat to embrace the moon's reflection
He froze while crossing a high mountain pass in deep winter
He was poisoned by a rival's hand at a grand banquet
He fell from a cliff one night while gazing up at the stars
context: Legend says Li Bai, drunk, leaned from his boat to embrace the moon's reflection on the water and drowned. The public clings to the moon-drowning because the moon shines through so much of his poetry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Bai; sothebys.com 'Reaching For the Moon'

question: Returning home in 755, Du Fu wrote a couplet: behind the red-lacquered gates of the rich, 'wine sours and meat rots,' while out on the road 'lie the bones of the frozen and starved.' What grief met him at his own door?
answer: His own young son had died of hunger
choices: His own young son had died of hunger
His house had burned to the ground
His wife had fled with the children
His life's poems had all been stolen
context: Having just witnessed the gulf between feasting nobles and the dying poor, Du Fu reached home to learn his own young son had starved to death. He is honored as the 'Poet-Sage' and 'Poet-Historian'; about 1,500 of his poems survive. Source: live2makan.com 'Du Fu'; choubb.com

question: An Lushan, a Tang general, rose in revolt in 755 and ripped the empire apart from within. The empire's own census told the cost: the count of 754, the year before the war, found nearly 53 million people. Roughly how many did the count of 764 find?
answer: About 17 million
choices: About 17 million
About 35 million
About 45 million
About 50 million
context: The 754 census recorded about 52.9 million; the 764 census recorded only about 16.9 million. Whether from death, displacement, or the collapse of the tax-census itself, it marks one of history's most lethal upheavals and the permanent end of the High Tang. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_rebellion

question: Emperor Xuanzong fled the An Lushan rebels in 756, and at Mawei Station his own guards mutinied. They refused to march another step until he gave in to one terrible demand. What did the troops force the emperor to do?
answer: Order the death of his beloved consort Yang Guifei
choices: Order the death of his beloved consort Yang Guifei
Surrender his throne to his own eldest son
Burn the imperial treasury as they retreated
Hand his crown to the rebel general An Lushan
context: The mutinous guards blamed Yang Guifei's family for the disaster; the emperor gave in and had Gao Lishi take her to a Buddhist shrine and oversee her forced suicide by strangling. She was one of the 'Four Beauties of China.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Guifei; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_rebellion

question: Li Zhu'er, a servant, cut An Lushan down inside his tent in 757, in a plot that An's own son had backed. The rebel had crowned himself emperor, then grown bloated and half blind, and he trusted no one. What did the dying An Lushan reportedly cry out?
answer: 'A thief of my own household!'
choices: 'A thief of my own household!'
'The Tang gods have cursed me!'
'My son, seize the throne!'
'I should have stayed in the north!'
context: An Lushan had seized Luoyang and declared himself emperor of the 'Great Yan' before his son An Qingxu backed the plot that killed him; he reportedly screamed that this was 'a thief of my own household.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_rebellion

question: The Mexica spent years wandering in search of a home, and their god Huitzilopochtli told them to settle wherever they saw a certain sign. They found it, the legend says, on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco around 1325. What was the sign?
answer: An eagle perched on a prickly-pear cactus
choices: An eagle perched on a prickly-pear cactus
A serpent coiled around a desert spring
A jaguar asleep beneath a cedar tree
A heron standing in a bed of reeds
context: The Mexica found that sign on a small island in Lake Texcoco and founded Tenochtitlan there around 1325. The eagle on its cactus is now the emblem at the centre of the Mexican flag; later tradition added a snake in the eagle's beak. The founding sign is told as legend.

question: When the Mexica founded their island city in Lake Texcoco, they named it in their own language, Nahuatl, after the very thing they saw on the island the day they arrived. What does the name Tenochtitlan mean?
answer: The cactus growing on a stone
choices: The cactus growing on a stone
The island between two waters
The home of the wandering people
The place the eagle came to rest
context: From Nahuatl tetl (rock/stone) + nochtli (prickly-pear cactus) + the locative -tlan: 'the place of the prickly-pear cactus growing on a stone' — the same image as the founding sign. Source: worldhistory.org/Tenochtitlan

question: Bernal Díaz was marching with Hernán Cortés in 1519 when the Spaniards came over the pass between two volcanoes and first saw Tenochtitlan, its white towers standing up out of a mountain lake. Díaz later wrote that it looked like a scene from a knight's tale. How did he say some of the men reacted?
answer: Some asked whether it was all a dream
choices: Some asked whether it was all a dream
Some fell to their knees and wept openly
Some turned their horses and refused to go on
Some swore the towers were made of solid gold
context: Bernal Diaz wrote that the city 'was like the enchantments in the book of Amadis... and some of our soldiers even asked whether the things that we saw were not a dream.' Source: worldhistory.org/Tenochtitlan

question: The Spaniards who reached Tenochtitlan with Hernán Cortés in 1519 found an island city of two hundred thousand people or more, perhaps twice that, rising from the waters of Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico. Compared with London and Paris at the same moment, how big was Tenochtitlan?
answer: Larger than most cities in Europe
choices: Larger than most cities in Europe
About the size of a large European town
Smaller than London but larger than Paris
Roughly equal to the biggest European port
context: With 200,000-400,000 people on roughly 8-13.5 square km, Tenochtitlan was one of the largest cities in the world at the time, bigger than most contemporary European cities including London and Paris. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan

question: Shoppers in Tenochtitlan's great markets paid for small everyday things with cacao beans, since no one there used coins of any kind. For a big, costly purchase, the soldier Bernal Díaz del Castillo recorded, traders measured out something else. What did they pay with?
answer: Goose quills packed with gold dust
choices: Goose quills packed with gold dust
Polished discs of green jade
Stamped bars of hammered copper
Strings of drilled seashell beads
context: Diaz wrote that 'the gold is placed in the quills of the geese of the country, white quills, so that the gold can be seen through, and according to the length and thickness of the quills they arrange their accounts.' Source: mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/aztefacts/great-market-tlatelolco

question: Aztec engineers built three long stone causeways to join Tenochtitlan's island to the shore, and they broke each one with gaps bridged by loose wooden beams, which could be lifted right out. Canoes slipped through the gaps in peacetime. In war, what did pulling out the beams do?
answer: It turned each gap into a moat the enemy could not cross
choices: It turned each gap into a moat the enemy could not cross
It dropped attackers into pits dug beneath the planks
It signaled the city's warriors to gather at the wall
It released lake water to flood the lower streets
context: During the Noche Triste (Night of Sorrows, June 1520), the removed beams trapped Cortes's fleeing men in the canals; many drowned, some dragged down by the gold they had stuffed into their clothes. Source: mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/ask-us/how-did-the-causeway-bridges-work and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan

question: Writing to the King of Spain, Hernán Cortés reported that more than sixty thousand people came in a single day to the market at Tlatelolco, the sister city beside Tenochtitlan. It was the biggest market in the Aztec world. According to Bernal Díaz del Castillo, how was that enormous crowd organized as it bought and sold?
answer: Every kind of good had its own fixed section
choices: Every kind of good had its own fixed section
Sellers shouted prices from raised stone platforms
Buyers lined up by rank before the noble stalls
Goods were traded only at a single central scale
context: Diaz said the crowd's buzz 'could be heard more than a league off,' and every type of goods had its own section — cloth, cacao, obsidian blades, jade, feathers, jaguar skins, dyes, and food of every kind. Judges sat in the market to settle disputes. Source: mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/aztefacts/great-market-tlatelolco

question: Nezahualcoyotl, king of Texcoco, rebuilt an aqueduct after a flood wrecked it in 1449. The aqueduct brought fresh water more than four kilometres from the springs of Chapultepec hill to Tenochtitlan, an island city in a salty lake. He gave it two terracotta channels side by side instead of one. Why build a second channel?
answer: So one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
choices: So one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
So twice as much water reached the growing city
So a pipe on each side fed a different half of town
So one carried drinking water and one carried waste
context: Each channel ran over 4 km. By building two, Nezahualcoyotl made sure one pipe could be shut off for cleaning or repair while the other kept the city supplied — the aqueduct was begun in 1418 and rebuilt after a 1449 flood. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapultepec_aqueduct

question: The Aztecs and Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco built a dike about 16 km long across Lake Texcoco, completed around 1453, to shield Tenochtitlan from the lake's floods. Besides holding back floods, what did that great wall in the water let them control?
answer: How salty the water around the city stayed
choices: How salty the water around the city stayed
Which direction the canoe traffic could flow
How high the lake rose in the rainy season
Where the causeways met the open water
context: The Albarradon (Dike of Nezahualcoyotl) sealed off the brackish eastern part of Lake Texcoco from the fresh spring-fed water around Tenochtitlan, in effect controlling the lake's salinity so the city's side stayed fresh. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan and mdpi.com/2073-445X/11/4/542

question: Hernán Cortés laid siege to Tenochtitlan in 1521 knowing that the island had no drinking water of its own: every drop its people drank came along the aqueduct from Chapultepec hill. How did Cortés turn that piece of Aztec engineering against the city?
answer: He cut and destroyed the aqueduct to leave the city without water
choices: He cut and destroyed the aqueduct to leave the city without water
He poisoned the springs that fed the aqueduct uphill
He seized the aqueduct and rationed water to the defenders
He diverted the aqueduct to flood the lakeside streets
context: Because the island had no other source of drinking water, Cortes severed Tenochtitlan's fresh-water supply by destroying the Chapultepec aqueduct during the 1521 siege — turning the city's own engineering into a weakness. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapultepec_aqueduct

question: The Aztecs came upon a vast, silent city of empty stone pyramids in central Mexico, centuries after its builders had vanished, and stood awed among them. They named it in Nahuatl, their own tongue, and the name has stuck: Teotihuacan. What did that name mean?
answer: The City of the Gods
choices: The City of the Gods
The Valley of the Kings
The Field of Bones
The Harbor of the Sun
context: The Aztecs called it Teotihuacan, roughly 'the place where the gods were born' (or where men became gods). Nobody knows what the original builders called themselves or their city — the famous name is Aztec, slapped on a ruin they found empty. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan; Britannica /place/Teotihuacan.

question: Wandering the empty ruins of Teotihuacan, Aztecs followed a boulevard some forty metres wide and four kilometres long, lined with stepped platforms. They took the platforms for something they were not, and they named the road for that mistake. What did they call it?
answer: The Avenue of the Dead
choices: The Avenue of the Dead
The Road of Kings
The Path of the Sun
The Way of Serpents
context: In Nahuatl, Miccaotli — the Avenue of the Dead. The Aztecs thought the platforms lining it were tombs; they were actually ceremonial buildings, not graves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan.

question: Workers found a hidden tunnel next to the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan in 1971 and followed it some 100 metres under the pyramid to a sealed room. Many scholars think the room was a sacred 'place of birth,' where the first people came into the world. What shape was it?
answer: A four-leaf clover
choices: A four-leaf clover
A perfect circle
A tall narrow well
A long straight hall
context: The 1971 tunnel ran about 100 m under the Pyramid of the Sun and ended in a chamber shaped like a four-leaf clover, thought to be a 'place of emergence' — the womb of the earth from which the first humans came. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramid_of_the_Sun; ancient-origins.net.

question: Sculptors at Teotihuacan set some 260 carved stone heads jutting from the walls of one temple, between figures in war headdresses. They gave each head huge fangs and a mouth wide enough to hold a marker. What creature did the fanged heads show?
answer: Feathered serpents
choices: Feathered serpents
Roaring jaguars
Screaming eagles
Horned bulls
context: It is the Temple of the Feathered Serpent — the god the Aztecs would later call Quetzalcoatl, here alternating with a second war-headdress figure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_the_Feathered_Serpent,_Teotihuacan.

question: Merchants from Teotihuacan carried its goods all across Mesoamerica, and at its height, around 400 to 500 CE, the city held perhaps 125,000 people. No city anywhere in the Americas grew larger until the 1400s. Where did archaeologists rank it in the whole world of its day?
answer: Among the six biggest cities on Earth
choices: Among the six biggest cities on Earth
The single biggest city on Earth
Bigger than Rome at its peak
The largest city ever built in stone
context: With roughly 100,000-200,000 people, Teotihuacan was the largest city anywhere in the Americas before the 1400s and ranked among the six largest cities on the planet in its day. Archaeologist George Cowgill: 'the largest city anywhere in the Western Hemisphere before the 1400s.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan; National Geographic.

question: Craftsmen in Teotihuacan shaped green obsidian, a volcanic glass, into blades and masks, and no other place in Mesoamerica had a source of the green kind. Archaeologists have dug up that green glass at a Maya city over 1,000 kilometres away. Which city was it?
answer: Tikal
choices: Tikal
Palenque
Copán
Monte Albán
context: The green obsidian came from the Pachuca / Sierra de las Navajas mines and turned up at Tikal in Guatemala, roughly 1,000-1,280 km away — proof of Teotihuacan's enormous trade reach. Source: worldhistory.org/article/2060/obsidian-in-mesoamerica; Cambridge, 'Mexican Obsidian at Tikal.'

question: Teotihuacan's builders set a flat, framed panel, the tablero, over a sloping wall, the talud, on building after building, and the pairing became their signature. Archaeologists find it in ruins far from Teotihuacan. What does it tell them about those places?
answer: Teotihuacan's influence reached those places
choices: Teotihuacan's influence reached those places
Those sites were built long before Teotihuacan
Those sites were built by enemies of Teotihuacan
Those sites were rebuilt after being destroyed
context: Talud (the sloping wall) plus tablero (the framed panel). The stacked style spread across Mesoamerica and marks where Teotihuacan's reach extended. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talud-tablero.

question: Zapotecs from far-off Oaxaca filled one neighbourhood of Teotihuacan with their own pottery, and merchants from the Gulf Coast made their homes in round houses in another. How did scientists prove that many of these people had been born far from the city?
answer: By testing the chemistry of their bones
choices: By testing the chemistry of their bones
By matching their DNA to living relatives
By reading their tomb inscriptions
By tracing their family names
context: Bone-chemistry (isotope) tests showed large fractions of some neighborhoods were people born far away — the chemistry of bones and teeth records the water and food of one's childhood homeland. The Tlailotlacan barrio was Zapotec; the Barrio de los Comerciantes housed Gulf Coast merchants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan; CLACS Berkeley, 'Teotihuacan: A Multiethnic Metropolis.'

question: Excavators digging beneath one temple at Teotihuacan in the 1980s found more than 200 people buried with their hands tied behind their backs. They had been sacrificed around 150 to 200 CE, when the temple was dedicated, and many still wore necklaces. What were the necklaces strung from?
answer: Real human teeth and jawbones
choices: Real human teeth and jawbones
Polished river pebbles
Painted clay beads
Woven palm fiber
context: Over 200 sacrificed people (the count may reach 260), many warriors buried with obsidian-tipped weapons and necklaces strung from real human teeth and jawbones, marked the pyramid's dedication. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_the_Feathered_Serpent,_Teotihuacan; FAMSI Cowgill report.

question: Siyaj K'ak', a warlord sent under the authority of Spearthrower Owl, a lord of Teotihuacan, reached the Maya city of Tikal on 16 January 378. Tikal's king, Chak Tok Ich'aak, died that same day. Before a year was out, a boy who was said to be the son of Spearthrower Owl ruled Tikal. What do many scholars read in those matching dates?
answer: A foreign power staged a takeover of Tikal
choices: A foreign power staged a takeover of Tikal
The old king died of natural causes
Maya calendars are unreliable
Two unrelated events lined up by chance
context: Siyaj K'ak' — 'Fire Is Born' — arrived under the authority of a Teotihuacan lord called Spearthrower Owl; within a year a boy claimed as Spearthrower Owl's son took Tikal's throne. Many scholars call this the 'entrada,' Teotihuacan's reach into the Maya world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siyaj_K%CA%BCak%CA%BC; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spearthrower_Owl.

question: The center of Teotihuacan went up in flames around 550. Archaeologists sifting the ruins found that the fire had not struck the city evenly: one kind of building took almost all of it, while others were largely spared. Which buildings took the brunt of the burning?
answer: The rulers' palaces and temples
choices: The rulers' palaces and temples
Every home in the city equally
The outer city walls and gates
The foreign merchants' quarters
context: The systematic burning targeted mainly the palaces and temples of the ruling class, not ordinary homes — pointing many archaeologists to an internal uprising or revolt rather than a foreign army. Famine in the harsh '535-536 mystery cloud' years may have lit the fuse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan.

question: Maya carvers cut boastful portraits of their rulers into stone, and Egypt laid its god-kings in tombs of gold. Yet for all Teotihuacan's size, its ruins have yielded no royal tomb, no king's portrait and no inscription naming a single ruler. From that silence, what kind of government do many experts think the city had?
answer: A shared or collective rule by noble houses
choices: A shared or collective rule by noble houses
A single god-king on a golden throne
A line of warrior-pharaohs
A foreign Aztec overlord
context: Wikipedia notes 'evidence of a king or other authoritarian ruler is strikingly absent.' Many archaeologists now propose collective or shared government — perhaps competing noble houses — rather than one god-king, making Teotihuacan unlike Egypt or the Maya. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan; National Geographic.

question: Yang Zhifa was digging a well with his neighbours near Xi'an, in China, during a drought in March 1974. Some four metres down, a shovel hit something hard. The farmers had broken into a buried pit holding thousands of what?
answer: Life-sized soldiers made of clay
choices: Life-sized soldiers made of clay
Chests of gold and jade coins
Stone tablets carved with laws
Bones from an ancient battle
context: The farmers first thought the clay head was a 'Pottery God.' They had stumbled onto the Terracotta Army — roughly 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers buried to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor. Source: travelchinaguide.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: Qin Shi Huang crushed his rivals and became the first emperor of a united China in 221 BC. Planning to keep ruling in the afterlife, he had an army of some 8,000 soldiers made and set out in battle order to stand guard over his tomb near Xi'an. A visitor walking the ranks today, looking from one soldier to the next, sees something uncanny. What is it?
answer: Every single warrior has a different face
choices: Every single warrior has a different face
They all face away from the tomb
Each one is shorter than the last
None of them were given any weapons
context: Artisans built the heads from about ten basic molds, then hand-pressed extra clay onto each one to give every soldier unique features, hair, and expression. Rank was readable too — generals stand up to about 2 meters, taller than the footsoldiers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army; history.com

question: Archaeologists dug the soldiers of the Terracotta Army out of their pits still bright with paint: black hair, rosy skin and robes of red, green, blue and purple. The colours had lasted some 2,200 years in the sealed dark. What happened to them once the warriors were out in the open?
answer: They began flaking off within minutes of hitting the air
choices: They began flaking off within minutes of hitting the air
They glowed faintly for several nights
They slowly faded over the next ten years
They washed away in the first rainfall
context: The paint sat on a thin lacquer layer that dried and curled the instant it met dry air — colors started changing in about 15 seconds and flaked off within four minutes of being unearthed. That is why most of the warriors today look bare gray. Source: travelchinaguide.com; ecns.cn

question: Augustus heard terrible news from the forests of Germania in AD 9. The aged emperor tore his clothes, let his hair and beard grow ragged for months, and beat his head against the doorposts. What did he shout?
answer: "Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!"
choices: "Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!"
"Carthage must be destroyed at any cost!"
"You too, my child, have you betrayed me?"
"Let the dice be cast, the river is crossed!"
context: The Latin was 'Quintili Vare, legiones redde!' The commander Publius Quinctilius Varus had marched the 17th, 18th, and 19th legions to their destruction; Augustus kept the anniversary of the defeat as a personal day of mourning for the rest of his life. Source: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 23.

question: Publius Quinctilius Varus, Rome's governor in Germania, led three legions into the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 along paths narrow and boggy, and Germanic warriors cut his army to pieces over three days of fighting. The man who sprang the trap, Arminius, was no stranger to Varus. Who was Arminius to the Romans he destroyed?
answer: A trusted officer in Varus's own army, Roman-trained and secretly plotting
choices: A trusted officer in Varus's own army, Roman-trained and secretly plotting
A foreign king who had openly declared war on Rome the year before
A runaway gladiator leading an army of escaped slaves
A rival Roman senator competing with Varus for command of the legions
context: Arminius was a Cherusci chieftain raised in Rome as a hostage, trained as a Roman officer, made a citizen and equestrian, and serving as a squadron leader under Varus while secretly arranging the ambush. The disaster stopped Rome's expansion cold and made the Rhine River its permanent frontier forever after. Source: worldhistory.org/article/1010; britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Teutoburg-Forest.

question: When al-Mansur, the Abbasid caliph, founded a new capital on the Tigris in 762, he laid out its core, about two kilometres across, in a shape never before used for a capital. It was said to copy the neat geometric order he had studied in Euclid's writings. What shape was it?
answer: A perfect circle
choices: A perfect circle
A perfect square
A five-pointed star
A crescent moon
context: It became known as the Round City of Baghdad. Al-Mansur reportedly studied Euclid and laid the streets out to display geometric order. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_City_of_Baghdad

question: A Persian village called Baghdad stood beside the Tigris when al-Mansur built his new capital there in 762, and the old village name stuck to the city in everyday speech. But the caliph gave his city a hopeful official name of his own. What did he call it?
answer: Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace
choices: Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace
Dar al-Khilafa, the House of the Caliph
Madinat al-Nur, the City of Light
Bab al-Dhahab, the Gate of Gold
context: Madinat al-Salam means City of Peace. The everyday name Baghdad came from an older settlement on the site. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_City_of_Baghdad

question: Al-Mansur set four great gates into the walls of his new capital of Baghdad, one facing each direction, and placed his own palace and the main mosque at the very centre. How were the four gates named?
answer: Each was named for the far-off city its road led toward
choices: Each was named for the far-off city its road led toward
Each was named after one of the four seasons
Each was named for a son of the caliph
Each was named after a planet in the sky
context: The four gates were Bab al-Kufa, Bab al-Basra, Bab al-Sham (toward Damascus), and Bab al-Khorasan, where the Great Khorasan Road to Central Asia began. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_City_of_Baghdad

question: At the very centre of al-Mansur's Baghdad, the caliph kept an almost empty plaza around his Golden Gate Palace and the main mosque, and he pushed everyone else's houses out toward the walls. What crowned the palace, visible from far off across the city?
answer: A great green dome
choices: A great green dome
A pair of bronze lions
A spire of pure silver
A garden of palm trees
context: The central plaza was kept almost empty around the caliph's palace and mosque. The green dome made the palace visible from far across the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_City_of_Baghdad

question: Einhard, Charlemagne's biographer, wrote about the elephant that Harun al-Rashid sent all the way from Baghdad to the Frankish court, and so did the Royal Frankish Annals. Yet the record of this famous gift has one odd gap. What is missing?
answer: No surviving Abbasid record mentions the gift at all
choices: No surviving Abbasid record mentions the gift at all
No one ever wrote down the elephant's name
The Frankish texts never say where it arrived
Charlemagne's own letters deny receiving it
context: The gift is well documented on the Frankish side but absent from surviving Baghdad records, an odd one-sided memory of a famous exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abul-Abbas

question: Scholars at Baghdad's House of Wisdom turned books in Greek, Persian, Sanskrit and Syriac into Arabic, people of many faiths sharing the work. Much of the hardest Greek-to-Arabic translating, though, was done by one particular group. Who were these translators?
answer: Syriac-speaking Nestorian Christian scholars
choices: Syriac-speaking Nestorian Christian scholars
Buddhist monks traveling from India
Norse traders settled in the city
Egyptian temple priests
context: Nestorian Christians already read Syriac and Greek, making them vital translators. The so-called Islamic Golden Age drew on Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians, and others. Source: https://www.middleeasteye.net/discover/iraq-baghdad-house-wisdom-uniting-east-west

question: Harun al-Rashid ruled his capital at its shining peak, and later storytellers made a hero of him. In their tales, though in no record of his court, Harun slipped through his city's streets in disguise. Which collection holds those tales?
answer: The Thousand and One Nights
choices: The Thousand and One Nights
Aesop's Fables
The Canterbury Tales
The Tales of King Arthur
context: In the stories, Harun slips through Baghdad in disguise to see his city by night. The disguised-caliph adventures are legend, not court record. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Thousand_and_One_Nights

question: Hulagu Khan, Genghis Khan's grandson, stormed Baghdad with his Mongols in February 1258 and captured al-Musta'sim, the last Abbasid caliph. Mongol custom forbade spilling royal blood on the ground, so they killed him without shedding a drop. How did he die?
answer: He was rolled inside a carpet and trampled by horses
choices: He was rolled inside a carpet and trampled by horses
He was strangled with a silk bowstring
He was drowned in the Tigris river
He was thrown from the highest tower
context: The carpet kept his royal blood from touching the earth. Some sources say instead he was starved, so the exact manner is disputed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Musta%27sim

question: Michal Biran, a historian, tested the old legend that the Mongols wiped out Baghdad's learning in 1258, flinging the city's books into the Tigris. The historian found that tale of total ruin overblown. What did Biran show actually happened to the city's learning?
answer: Large libraries reopened for teaching within two years
choices: Large libraries reopened for teaching within two years
The books had all been moved to Maragha before the siege
Only the caliph's own palace collection was destroyed
Monasteries outside the city secretly kept every copy
context: The black-ink river is a dramatic legend; Baghdad's intellectual life was wounded but not erased, with teaching resuming within a couple of years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad

question: Al-Musta'sim, the last Abbasid caliph, still had twenty thousand horsemen when Hulagu's Mongols came against Baghdad in 1258. Yet the Mongols beat that army before the real fight began, without charging it head-on, by turning the ground itself against it. What did they do to trap the riders?
answer: They broke the dikes and flooded the ground behind the army
choices: They broke the dikes and flooded the ground behind the army
They poisoned every well outside the walls
They set the whole grain harvest on fire
They built a wall to cut off the bridges
context: By breaking the dikes of the Tigris-side canals, the Mongols turned the ground behind the cavalry to mud and water, trapping and crushing them. Engineering, not just numbers, doomed Baghdad. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad

question: Crews at Kaiser's Richmond shipyard set out in November 1942 to prove that America could build cargo ships faster than German U-boats could sink them. They snapped some 250,000 parts together into one Liberty ship. How long did the whole ship take?
answer: About 4 days
choices: About 4 days
About 4 weeks
About 4 months
About 4 hours
context: The SS Robert E. Peary was assembled in 4 days, 15 hours, and 29 minutes -- roughly 14 million pounds of steel snapped together as a deliberate message to the U-boats. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Robert_E._Peary

question: An American family received a ration booklet in 1942, full of stamps to trade for goods in short supply. The first food rationed, on 27 April, came to about a pound a person every two weeks. What was it?
answer: Sugar
choices: Sugar
Beef
Bread
Eggs
context: Families got about one pound of sugar per person every two weeks; the booklet was even nicknamed the 'Sugar Book.' Coffee followed in November 1942 when German U-boats sank the ships bringing it from Brazil. Source: https://www.nps.gov/articles/rationing-in-wwii.htm

question: Norman Rockwell painted a brawny Rosie the Riveter for the Saturday Evening Post cover of Memorial Day 1943. He posed her like a prophet from the Sistine Chapel, with a rivet gun on her lap. To make plain whom she was fighting, he painted one book crushed under her shoes. Which book was it?
answer: Hitler's Mein Kampf
choices: Hitler's Mein Kampf
A German dictionary
The factory rulebook
Her own diary
context: Rockwell stamped her lunch pail 'Rosie' and put her shoes squarely on a copy of Mein Kampf -- the cover ran on Memorial Day, May 29, 1943. Source: https://www.nrm.org/rosie-the-riveter/

question: John Jacob Loeb and Redd Evans wrote a song called Rosie the Riveter in 1942, and an African-American vocal group, the Four Vagabonds, made it a hit in 1943. It gave its name to the millions of women who took men's places in the war factories. In the song, why did Rosie work so hard?
answer: To protect her marine boyfriend Charlie by building the planes he'd fly
choices: To protect her marine boyfriend Charlie by building the planes he'd fly
To win a prize being offered at her factory that year
To earn enough money to buy a house of her own
To follow in the footsteps of her riveter father
context: The Redd Evans and John Jacob Loeb song described Rosie guarding her sweetheart Charlie 'over there' by riveting the planes he flew -- the name caught on long before any of the famous images. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosie_the_Riveter

question: Charles Sorensen, production chief at Ford's mile-long Willow Run plant, boasted that it would turn out four-engine B-24 Liberator bombers at a pace that sounded impossible. By April 1944, working two nine-hour shifts six days a week, the plant made good on his boast. What pace did it reach?
answer: A finished bomber every 63 minutes
choices: A finished bomber every 63 minutes
A finished bomber every single day
A finished bomber every working week
Ten finished bombers every single hour
context: Sorensen's boast was 'a bomber an hour,' and Willow Run rolled one out every 63 minutes. Charles Lindbergh, a Ford consultant and test pilot, called the giant factory 'the Grand Canyon of a mechanized world.' Source: https://interestingengineering.com/culture/how-fords-willow-run-factory-turned-car-assembly-lines-into-bombers-built-by-the-hour

question: J. Howard Miller painted a poster in 1942 of a woman wearing a bandana, flexing her arm beneath the words 'We Can Do It!' The Westinghouse company hung it in its factories to lift morale for a fortnight or so before it vanished for decades. What is surprising about its place today as the symbol of wartime women?
answer: It wasn't actually famous during the war itself
choices: It wasn't actually famous during the war itself
The model was paid nothing for posing
It was banned outside Westinghouse factories
Miller painted it under a fake name
context: The 1942 photo of Naomi Parker Fraley at a lathe in Alameda, California carried a caption warning she 'might catch her nose in the turret lathe she is operating.' Fraley lived to 96 before Kimble set the record straight in 2016. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/naomi-parker-fraley-real-rosie-riveter-has-died-96-180967935/

question: Hebrew families recited their central prayer, the Shema, every day, while the peoples around them gave every city, river and storm a god of its own. It begins, 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is...' What single word ends that line and sums up the whole faith?
answer: one
choices: one
mighty
holy
near
context: The Shema (Hebrew for 'Hear,' from Deuteronomy 6:4) is the heartbeat of Hebrew faith: in a world of countless gods, they insisted there was only ONE. Source: https://pluralism.org/god-biblical-monotheism ; Deuteronomy 6:4.

question: Moses climbed Mount Sinai, the Book of Exodus tells, and spent forty days with God, who gave him two stone tablets carved with the Ten Commandments. Coming back down, he found the people dancing wildly around an idol they had made from their own melted jewelry. What was the idol?
answer: a golden calf
choices: a golden calf
a bronze serpent
a silver throne
a stone eagle
context: The golden calf (Exodus 32): Moses shattered the first set of tablets and had to climb Sinai again for a second. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Ten-Commandments ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sinai-covenant ; Exodus 32. (Told as the tradition tells it.)  (Legend.)

question: Ancient Jewish readers met God's personal name in their scrolls as four Hebrew letters, Y-H-W-H, the tetragrammaton, and they would not speak it aloud, for it was too holy. They said the word Adonai, 'my Lord,' in its place. That old reverence is why English Bibles still do something special wherever the name stands. What do they do?
answer: print 'the LORD' in small capitals
choices: print 'the LORD' in small capitals
leave a blank space on the page
spell it out as four letters
translate it as 'the Nameless'
context: Because Jews said 'Adonai' rather than pronounce YHWH, translators mark the spot with small-capital LORD to this day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_that_I_Am ; https://www.biblestudytools.com/bible-study/topical-studies/why-does-god-call-himself-i-am-that-i-am.html

question: The Hebrews told their whole history as one long covenant, a binding agreement between God and a people. It begins with a promise to a single man that his descendants would become a great nation, loyal to the one God. Which figure, the start of that chain, is later called 'the father of monotheism'?
answer: Abraham
choices: Abraham
Noah
Solomon
Joshua
context: God's promise to Abraham underlies the later Sinai covenant; the Hebrew story is one continuous binding agreement. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sinai-covenant ; https://www.chapelwithoutwalls.org/sermons/2020/7/26/monotheism-and-the-jews.html. (Told as the tradition tells it.)  (Legend.)

question: David Wolpe, a rabbi, has called one idea from the Hebrew Bible Judaism's greatest gift to the world: that every human being, rich or poor, healthy or sick, carries the same infinite dignity. The idea comes from the first chapter of Genesis. What does Genesis say each person is made 'in the image' of?
answer: God
choices: God
the king
the law
the stars
context: The imago Dei (Genesis 1:27): dignity is not earned by rank or wealth but given to all alike; historians credit it as a headwater of universal human rights. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_of_God ; https://www.holypost.com/post/imago-dei-the-foundation-of-human-dignity ; Genesis 1:27.

question: Amos, the Hebrew prophet, railed against a land where the rich rigged their scales against the poor, 'selling the needy for a pair of sandals.' To Amos, mistreating the widow and the orphan was an offense against God Himself, and he demanded one thing in a single thundering line. Which words are his?
answer: Let justice roll down like waters
choices: Let justice roll down like waters
Blessed are the poor in spirit
Love your neighbor as yourself
Walk humbly with your God
context: '...and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream' (Amos 5:24). The prophets fused worship with justice. Source: https://www.ibelieve.com/christian-living/what-does-let-justice-roll-like-a-river-mean-amos.html ; Amos 5:24, Amos 2:6.

question: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, smashed Jerusalem in 586 BC and marched the Hebrew people off to exile in Babylon. Far from their ruined city, the exiles poured their grief into one of the most famous laments ever set down, vowing 'If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill.' How does that psalm, Psalm 137, open?
answer: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept
choices: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept
Out of the depths I have cried unto thee, O Lord
How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me forever
The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want
context: '...when we remembered Zion.' The grief of the Babylonian exile, set to verse. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Babylonian-Captivity ; Psalm 137.

question: Archaeologists working in a burial cave near Jerusalem in 1979 found the oldest passages of the Hebrew Bible ever discovered. They date from about 600 BC, which makes them four centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls, and they had once been worn as protective charms. What objects carried the text?
answer: two tiny silver scrolls
choices: two tiny silver scrolls
a clay prayer tablet
a painted papyrus strip
a carved cedar box
context: The scrolls (about 2.5 cm) carry the Priestly Blessing of Numbers 6: 'The LORD bless you and keep you...' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketef_Hinnom_scrolls ; https://biblearchaeology.org/research-articles/the-blessing-of-the-silver-scrolls/.

question: A runner crossed the finish line first at Olympia, the sanctuary of Zeus, and in that moment became the most celebrated athlete in all Greece. Yet he went home without gold or money. What was his only prize?
answer: A crown of wild olive leaves
choices: A crown of wild olive leaves
A purse of silver coins
A bronze statue of himself
A team of racing horses
context: The prize was the kotinos, a crown of wild olive cut with a golden sickle from one sacred tree at Olympia called the Kallistephanos ('tree of the beautiful crown'), said to have been planted by Hercules. The glory, not the goods, was the reward. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Olympic_Games/.

question: Orsippos of Megara, so the story goes, lost part of his kit mid-race at Olympia around 720 BC, kept running and won. Greek athletes then took up a new custom. From then on, how did every Olympic athlete compete?
answer: Completely naked
choices: Completely naked
In matching white tunics
Wearing painted leather masks
Barefoot but cloaked in red
context: The story goes that Orsippos of Megara lost his loincloth during a race in 720 BC; afterward Greek athletes competed nude, the body itself displayed as a tribute to Zeus. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Olympic_Games/; GreekReporter, 'Why Did Athletes in the Ancient Olympic Games Compete in the Nude?'

question: Heralds rode out from Elis, host city of the Olympic Games, before every festival to proclaim the ekecheiria across Greece. Its name meant 'the holding of hands,' and in time it stretched to three months. While it lasted, what did it demand of every Greek city?
answer: All wars stopped and no army could enter Elis
choices: All wars stopped and no army could enter Elis
Every city sent a tribute of grain to Olympia
All slaves were freed for the month of the festival
Each city closed its temples until the Games ended
context: The ekecheiria halted fighting across Greece so athletes and as many as 40,000 spectators could travel to Olympia safely; no one could carry weapons into Elis. It was eventually extended to three months. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Olympic_Games/; International Olympic Truce Centre, olympictruce.org.

question: Milon of Kroton wrestled his way to six Olympic crowns, the first among the boys in 540 BC and the next five in a row among the men. The legend says he grew so strong through one habit he kept every day for years. By that legend, what did Milon do each day?
answer: Carried a young calf until it grew into a bull
choices: Carried a young calf until it grew into a bull
Wrestled a different opponent at every dawn
Swam against the current of a mountain river
Lifted the bronze gates of his city at sunrise
context: The legend says Milon carried a calf daily until it became a full-grown bull, which he then carried around the stadium, killed, and ate in a single day. He won the boys' crown in 540 BC and then five straight men's titles, 532-516 BC. Told as legend. Source: Britannica, 'Milo of Croton'; World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Olympic_Games/.

question: The judges at Olympia slapped a heavy fine on any athlete caught bribing a rival or breaking the rules. They spent the money in a way meant to shame the cheat before the whole Greek world. What did the fines pay for?
answer: Bronze statues of Zeus that every athlete walked past
choices: Bronze statues of Zeus that every athlete walked past
A marble wall carved with the cheater's full name
A feast for the rivals the cheater had wronged
A new gate barring him from ever returning
context: The fines paid for bronze statues of Zeus called 'Zanes,' lined up along the path to the stadium so every competitor passed them on the way in. The stone bases of the Zanes are still visible at Olympia today. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Olympic_Games/; Working Classicists, 'Ancient Athletics Part Three: No Cheating!'

question: Assyria's kings raised history's first true standing army, up to 200,000 men under arms, the most fearsome force the ancient Near East had seen. They could afford so many soldiers because they armed them with one metal cheap enough to hammer out in bulk. Which metal was it?
answer: Iron
choices: Iron
Bronze
Copper
Tin
context: The Assyrians fielded history's first true iron army. Iron weapons were not only sharper than bronze but could be mass-produced, so they equipped a standing force of 150,000 to 200,000 men. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Neo-Assyrian_Empire/

question: Ashurbanipal, king of Assyria at the empire's height, bragged of a rare gift. Most kings left that work to the men who served them, but he had trained for it as a boy. What could Ashurbanipal do?
answer: He could read and write
choices: He could read and write
He could tame wild lions
He could forge iron weapons
He could speak to the gods
context: Ashurbanipal trained as an apprentice scribe and mastered the wedge-shaped cuneiform script, even learning the ancient Sumerian language — then ordered cities across his empire to send copies of every text they had. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Ashurbanipal

question: Ashurnasirpal II threw a ten-day feast for 69,574 guests to open Kalhu, his new capital, in 879 BC, and he had the whole menu carved in stone to boast of it: 14,000 sheep, 1,000 oxen and 10,000 eggs. What drink did he pour, 10,000 jars of it?
answer: Beer
choices: Beer
Wine
Mead
Milk
context: Ashurnasirpal II's Banquet Stele records 69,574 guests and a menu of 1,000 oxen, 14,000 sheep, 10,000 fish, 10,000 eggs, and 10,000 jars of beer. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ashurnasirpal_II/

question: Medes and Babylonians stormed Nineveh in 612 BC and set Ashurbanipal's palace ablaze, but the fire spared his library of clay tablets. Among them was the oldest great story people ever wrote down, in which a hero survives a world-drowning flood and sends a dove out from his ship. What is the poem called?
answer: The Epic of Gilgamesh
choices: The Epic of Gilgamesh
The Epic of Atrahasis
The Epic of Creation
The Epic of Etana
context: Among the tablets Ashurbanipal's library preserved was the Epic of Gilgamesh — the oldest great story ever written, including a flood account with a man building a boat and sending out a dove. The brutal Assyrians are the reason humanity still has this poem at all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Ashurbanipal

question: Hezekiah held out inside Jerusalem in 701 BC while Sennacherib of Assyria laid siege to the city. The Assyrian king later bragged of the siege on a six-sided clay prism, though his own words never claim the city fell. He boasted that he had shut Hezekiah up in his royal city like what?
answer: A caged bird
choices: A caged bird
A cornered rat
A chained dog
A netted fish
context: Sennacherib's prism reads: 'As for Hezekiah... I shut him up like a caged bird in his royal city of Jerusalem.' Strikingly, the inscription never claims he captured the city — the Assyrian king's own brag admits Jerusalem held out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sennacherib's_Annals

question: Sennacherib's men heaped roughly three million stones, some 20,000 tons, into a ramp against the walls of Lachish in 701 BC to bring a one-ton battering ram to bear. No other Assyrian siege ramp has ever been found, and inside this one archaeologists dug up the piece that once swung the ram. Which piece was it?
answer: An iron chain
choices: An iron chain
An iron axle
An iron blade
An iron hook
context: At Lachish in 701 BCE the Assyrians built a siege ramp of about three million stones (roughly 20,000 tons) to haul battering rams up to the walls. It is the only Assyrian siege ramp ever found, and archaeologists even recovered the iron chain that swung the ram. Source: https://phys.org/news/2021-11-siege-ramps-breached-walls-ancient.html

question: Babylon's people rose against Sennacherib in 689 BC, and the Assyrian king meant to blot their holy city out of memory, so that no one would ever know where it had stood. His own inscription tells how he did it. How did Sennacherib destroy Babylon?
answer: He flooded it with water
choices: He flooded it with water
He burned it with fire
He buried it in sand
He smashed it with rams
context: Sennacherib bragged: 'In order that the site of that city and its temples would never be remembered, I devastated it with water so that it became a mere meadow.' He dug canals and flooded the ruins flat. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/745/the-mutual-destruction-of-sennacherib--babylon/

question: Sargon II of Assyria captured Samaria, the capital of Israel's northern kingdom, and recorded leading 27,290 of its people away to distant lands, the Assyrian way of breaking rebels for good. What did the exiled northern tribes come to be called?
answer: The Ten Lost Tribes
choices: The Ten Lost Tribes
The Babylonian Exiles
The Wandering Tribes
The Forgotten Twelve
context: The Assyrians invented mass deportation as state policy to break rebellion. Sargon II recorded: 'I besieged and conquered Samaria, led away as booty 27,290 inhabitants of it.' The exiled northern tribes of Israel became known as the Ten Lost Tribes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assyrian_captivity

question: Ashurnasirpal II never hid his cruelty: he had it carved in stone as a boast, so that, read aloud, it would frighten rival cities into surrender. In his own words, what did he do to the chiefs of a city that rebelled against him?
answer: Flayed them and hung their skins on a pillar
choices: Flayed them and hung their skins on a pillar
Burned them alive inside their own temple
Hurled them down from the high city walls
Buried them alive beneath the city gate
context: Ashurnasirpal II boasted in his own inscription: 'I built a pillar over against the city gate and I flayed all the chiefs who had revolted and I covered the pillar with their skins.' The Assyrians recorded their terror as a point of pride, not shame — deliberate psychological warfare, written to be feared. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ashurnasirpal_II/

question: Ashurbanipal had a royal hunt carved into stone panels for his palace at Nineveh around 645 BC. On one of them a wounded animal, pierced by arrows, drags its paralysed hind legs, and many rank it with the greatest art of the ancient world. What animal does the panel show?
