answer: A lioness
choices: A lioness
A stag
A wild bull
A war elephant
context: The 'Dying Lioness' shows a wounded lioness roaring as she drags her paralyzed hind legs, pierced by arrows. Part of Ashurbanipal's Royal Lion Hunt reliefs (British Museum), it is praised as one of the greatest works of art from the entire ancient world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion_Hunt_of_Ashurbanipal

question: Sennacherib lined his palace at Nineveh with carvings of his conquest of Lachish, showing captives put to death before him as he sat enthroned, beneath words that named him king of the world. Long after his death, an unknown hand chiseled away one part of the king's own image. Which part did it destroy?
answer: His face
choices: His face
His hands
His feet
His crown
context: The Lachish reliefs (now in the British Museum) show captives executed before the enthroned king, beneath the caption naming him 'king of the world, king of Assyria.' Sennacherib's own face was deliberately chiseled out in antiquity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lachish_reliefs

question: Nahum, a Hebrew prophet, foretold the ruin of Nineveh in a brief book of the Bible, though for centuries the Assyrian capital seemed untouchable. In 612 BC the Medes and Babylonians besieged it, broke in and burned it. How long did they need to bring Nineveh down?
answer: Three months
choices: Three months
Seven years
A single night
Twenty years
context: In 612 BCE a coalition of Medes and Babylonians besieged Nineveh, broke in after just three months, and burned it. The Hebrew prophet Nahum had foretold the city's fall in the biblical Book of Nahum; after dominating the Near East for centuries, Assyria was gone within a few years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Nineveh

question: Raiders from African kingdoms such as Dahomey brought their prisoners in chains to the Slave Coast and sold them to European traders, who paid not with coins but with tiny white seashells. The shells came from the Maldive Islands, thousands of miles away, and crossed in ships' holds as ballast. What were they called?
answer: Cowrie shells
choices: Cowrie shells
Conch trumpets
Scallop tokens
Nautilus beads
context: Cowries were the working money of the Slave Coast: tiny shells gathered in the faraway Maldives, carried west as ship ballast, and counted out by the thousand to buy human beings. (projectmanifest.eu/cowries-the-currency-of-trading-en-fr; theconversation.com/small-seashells-tell-a-big-story-of-slavery-and-transoceanic-trade-500-years-ago-166363)

question: European merchants shipped millions of captive Africans to the mines and plantations of the New World, but not evenly. One land received about 46 percent of all who landed, almost half. Which land took in by far the most?
answer: Brazil
choices: Brazil
Jamaica
Cuba
The United States
context: About 46 percent of all enslaved Africans who reached the New World were landed in Brazil, roughly 4.9 to 5.5 million people, to work the sugar and gold colonies of Portugal. Most people wrongly assume the United States was the main destination. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade_to_Brazil)

question: A slave ship landed its captives on the North American mainland, in what is now the United States. Most Americans would guess that such ships carried the bulk of the trade, yet about 388,000 Africans came there directly, while millions went elsewhere. Of every hundred survivors of the crossing, how many came straight there?
answer: Fewer than four
choices: Fewer than four
About twenty-five
About fifty
About sixty-five
context: Only about 388,000 of the roughly 10.7 million survivors were carried directly to mainland North America, under 4 percent of the whole trade, a strikingly small share that surprises most people. (pbs.org/wnet/african-americans-many-rivers-to-cross/history/how-many-slaves-landed-in-the-us)

question: Captives in chains passed through one last doorway at Cape Coast Castle, a slave fort on the African coast, and small boats waiting beyond it rowed them out to the ships. What is that doorway remembered as today?
answer: The Door of No Return
choices: The Door of No Return
The Gate of Sorrows
The Iron Threshold
The Weeping Arch
context: Once people stepped through the Door of No Return onto the boats, they never came back. Excavators at these castles later found dungeon waste compacted up to 30 cm deep, with iron shackles and cowrie shells still in it. (thinkglobalheritage.wordpress.com/2016/11/30/dark-heritage-the-door-of-no-return-at-elmina-castle-in-ghana)

question: A European trader on the African coast paid for captives with guns, iron and cloth. The captives were sold on Caribbean plantations for sugar and molasses, ships carried the molasses north to New England, and colonists there turned it into a product that went back to Africa to buy more captives. What did they make?
answer: Rum
choices: Rum
Beer
Wine
Gin
context: The loop closed on itself: molasses from slave-grown sugar was distilled into New England rum, and the rum was shipped back to Africa to purchase more captives. The same cycle paid for itself again and again. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangular_trade)

question: The Portuguese built Elmina Castle in Ghana in 1482, the oldest European building south of the Sahara. Beneath it, in a dark stone dungeon, hundreds of enslaved men sat chained, waiting for the ships. What did the Portuguese build on the floor directly above their heads?
answer: A Christian church
choices: A Christian church
A gunpowder store
A grand ballroom
A grain warehouse
context: Worship above, chained captives below: the Portuguese held church services on the floor directly over the men's slave dungeon. (ancient-origins.net/ancient-places-africa/elmina-castle-and-its-dark-history-enslavement-torture-and-death-003450; witnesstreeinstitute.org/blog-2023/confronting-the-heartbreaking-truth-at-elmina-castle)

question: British abolitionists printed a drawing of the slave ship Brookes in 1788, showing 482 people, its legal limit, laid in rows across its decks. More than 7,000 copies went out, and it became the best-known picture of the whole movement. Yet by the ship's own records, it had once carried more people than that. How many had it carried?
answer: As many as 740
choices: As many as 740
About 560
Around 900
Over 1,100
context: The Brookes poster showed 482 people, the legal maximum, yet the ship had once crammed in as many as 740. Over 7,000 copies were printed, and it became the abolition movement's most iconic image. (abolitionseminar.org/brooks; encyclopediavirginia.org/4303hpr-7e68246b9587078)

question: A slave ship's crew packed captives into its hold off the African coast, bound for the Americas, as crews did again and again from about 1525 to 1866. Scholars have since built a database from the ships' own logbooks and records of sale. About how many Africans were forced aboard in all?
answer: About 12.5 million
choices: About 12.5 million
About 1.2 million
About 4 million
About 50 million
context: About 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard the ships; roughly 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage to step ashore alive, meaning between about 1.2 and 2.4 million died during the crossing itself, with many more dying in the raids and forced marches to the coast. (pbs.org/wnet/african-americans-many-rivers-to-cross/history/how-many-slaves-landed-in-the-us; Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, eds. Eltis & Richardson)

question: Sailors of the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron patrolled the African coast against the slavers for some fifty years after Britain outlawed its own trade in slaves in 1807, and more than 1,500 of them died on that station. People at the time summed up the cost in a single grim ratio, sailors lost against Africans set free. What was it?
answer: One sailor dead for every nine slaves freed
choices: One sailor dead for every nine slaves freed
One sailor dead for every slave freed
One sailor dead for every hundred slaves freed
One sailor dead for every thousand slaves freed
context: Suppression cost Britain dearly: over 1,500 sailors died, summed up at the time as about one sailor for every nine slaves freed, and at its height the campaign consumed roughly 2 percent of national GDP. (historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofBritain/West-Africa-Squadron)

question: A team of physicists stacked uranium and graphite bricks into a pile about 20 feet tall under the football stands of the University of Chicago. On 2 December 1942 they pulled out the control rods. Which world first did they achieve?
answer: Controlled nuclear chain reaction
choices: Controlled nuclear chain reaction
Launch of a guided rocket
Working electric battery
Long-distance radio broadcast
context: Chicago Pile-1 (CP-1), built in a converted squash court, achieved the first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. Source: https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/chicago-pile-1/

question: General Thomas Farrell saw the first atomic bomb light up the New Mexico desert in July 1945 with a glare that outshone the midday sun many times over. Its heat turned the sand at ground zero into lumps of radioactive glass, and the scientists named the new glass. What did they call it?
answer: Trinitite
choices: Trinitite
Obsidian
Quartzite
Tektite
context: General Thomas Farrell described the flash as 'a searing light with the intensity many times that of the midday sun.' The heat fused the sand into a radioactive green glass named trinitite. Source: https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/trinity-test-1945/

question: Arthur Compton picked up the telephone to tell James Conant that the Chicago pile had worked, speaking in a code he invented on the spot so no spy could follow it. 'The Italian navigator has landed in the New World,' he said. Whom did Compton mean by the Italian navigator?
answer: Enrico Fermi
choices: Enrico Fermi
Arthur Compton
Eugene Wigner
Niels Bohr
context: Fermi, like Columbus, was Italian — hence the code. Conant asked, 'How were the natives?' and Compton answered, 'Very friendly.' Source: https://www.lanl.gov/media/publications/the-vault/0822-chicago-pile

question: Eugene Wigner had come prepared when the Chicago pile went critical in December 1942. No one had a speech ready, so Wigner brought out something he had bought beforehand, and the team sipped from paper cups in silence. What had he brought?
answer: A bottle of Chianti
choices: A bottle of Chianti
A box of cigars
A folded American flag
A pot of coffee
context: Wigner had secretly bought the Chianti in advance. There were no speeches — just a silent toast from paper cups. Source: https://www.archives.gov/chicago/highlights/chianti

question: Enrico Fermi tore up a sheet of paper at the Trinity test in July 1945. As the blast wave rolled past, he let the scraps fall from about six feet and measured how far the wind pushed them. What was he working out?
answer: The bomb's explosive yield
choices: The bomb's explosive yield
The distance to the tower
The speed of the shock wave
The height of the mushroom cloud
context: The wind pushed the scraps about 2.5 meters; from that Fermi reckoned roughly ten thousand tons of TNT — within a factor of two of the real ~19-kiloton yield. Source: https://www.atomicarchive.com/resources/documents/trinity/fermi.html

question: J. Robert Oppenheimer's scientists at Los Alamos built the two bombs that fell on Japan in August 1945 in two different ways. The Hiroshima bomb was a gun: it fired one slug of uranium down a barrel at another. The Nagasaki bomb used plutonium and the design first proven at Trinity. How did it set off its core?
answer: Crushing the core inward with high explosives
choices: Crushing the core inward with high explosives
Firing two plutonium pieces together
Heating the core with an electric spark
Spinning the core at high speed
context: Fat Man was an implosion bomb: a shell of high explosives crushed the plutonium core inward, the design proven at Trinity. The two bombs used different fuels (uranium vs. plutonium) and different triggers. Source: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/bombing-nagasaki-august-9-1945

question: Karl Benz finished a three-wheeled machine in his Mannheim workshop in 1885, with a small gasoline engine mounted at the back. It was the first vehicle built from scratch to power itself, not a horse-cart with a motor bolted on. What did Benz name his invention?
answer: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen
choices: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen
The Mannheim Steam Runabout
The Benz Horseless Phaeton
The Rhineland Road Locomotive
context: Karl Benz's 1885 Patent-Motorwagen had a single-cylinder four-stroke engine of just 0.75 horsepower. On 29 January 1886 he received German patent No. 37435 for it — often called the birth certificate of the automobile, and today part of the UNESCO Memory of the World register. Source: https://group.mercedes-benz.com/company/tradition/company-history/1885-1886.html

question: Bertha Benz took her husband Karl's car one August morning in 1888 without telling him and drove her two teenage sons some 66 miles to her mother's home town, the first long-distance car trip in history. When the fuel line choked up on the road, she cleared it with something she was wearing. What did she use?
answer: Her hat pin
choices: Her hat pin
Her garter
Her hairpin
Her shoelace
context: On that same 1888 drive Bertha Benz insulated a frayed ignition wire with her garter, had a blacksmith mend the drive chain, and at a cobbler's shop had leather nailed onto the brakes — inventing the world's first brake linings. She refueled at the Stadt-Apotheke pharmacy in Wiesloch, making it the first filling station in the world. Her journey proved to a skeptical public that the car actually worked. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertha_Benz

question: Bernal Díaz marvelled at the market of Tlatelolco, Tenochtitlan's twin city, for its huge stock of goods and the order kept there. Buyers paid in cacao beans or cotton cloaks, and Hernán Cortés reported judges on hand to settle fights. On a busy day, about how many people came to trade?
answer: Up to 60,000 in a single day
choices: Up to 60,000 in a single day
Up to 600 in a single day
Up to 3,000 in a single day
Up to 9,000 in a single day
context: Diaz, who had seen the markets of Europe, called the good order and control there a marvel. Buyers used cacao beans and cotton cloaks instead of coins. (https://www.pbs.org/conquistadors/cortes/cortes_f03.html ; https://www.mexicolore.co.uk/aztecs/aztefacts/great-market-tlatelolco)

question: Eagle Warriors went into battle in helmets shaped like an eagle's beak, and Jaguar Warriors in jaguar pelts, and they were the most honoured fighters in the Aztec armies. A common-born man could rise into their ranks by doing one thing in battle. What did he have to do?
answer: Capture four enemy warriors alive
choices: Capture four enemy warriors alive
Kill four enemy warriors on the field
Lead four raids against a rival city
Survive four seasons of the wars
context: The point of Aztec battle was to take captives, not to kill — religion taught the sun would die without human blood, so live prisoners were the prize. Capturing four enemies alive earned a commoner noble standing. (https://www.historyskills.com/classroom/year-8/eagle-and-jaguar-warriors/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaguar_warrior)

question: Itzcoatl, the Mexica ruler, and his adviser Tlacaelel joined forces with Texcoco and Tlacopan in 1428 to overthrow their overlord, Maxtla, the tyrant of Azcapotzalco. The three cities then promised to share the loot and wage all their later wars side by side, and that pact, not any single emperor, made the Aztec Empire. What do historians call it?
answer: The Triple Alliance
choices: The Triple Alliance
The Triad of Anahuac
The Confederation of Anahuac
The Covenant of the Five Suns
context: Tenochtitlan's ruler Itzcoatl and his adviser Tlacaelel led the revolt against Maxtla; the three victorious cities then split the conquered Tepanec lands and pledged to wage future wars jointly. That city-pact, not one king, is what we call 'the Aztec Empire.' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec_Empire)

question: Aztec armies marched back to any conquered city that stopped paying its tribute, which officials called calpixque gathered twice a year from 38 provinces. The alliance formed in 1428 had an odd way of ruling the cities it beat. What did it leave in place in each defeated city?
answer: The defeated city's own ruler
choices: The defeated city's own ruler
An Aztec governor and his garrison
A council of priests from Tenochtitlan
A wall sealing off the city
context: At its height the alliance drew tribute from 38 provinces, gathered by officials called calpixque, with the spoils split two-fifths to Tenochtitlan, two-fifths to Texcoco, and one-fifth to Tlacopan. It was less a country than a machine for extracting tribute, held together by fear of force. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec_Empire)

question: Nezahualcoyotl, king of Texcoco from 1402 to 1472, led armies, drew up laws, laid out terraced gardens and designed a great dike to hold back the lake's salt water. Yet his name lives on, and his face is on Mexico's 100-peso note, for something else he did. What did he do?
answer: He wrote philosophical poems on life and death
choices: He wrote philosophical poems on life and death
He charted the movements of the stars
He invented a new picture-writing script
He composed the songs sung at festivals
context: Nezahualcoyotl is remembered as the 'Poet-King'; his philosophical poems on life and death still survive today. Warrior, engineer, lawmaker, gardener, and poet — he is the great cultural hero of the Alliance. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nezahualcoyotl_(tlatoani) ; https://www.ancient-origins.net/ancient-places-americas/golden-age-texcoco-powerful-city-king-nezahualcoyotl-005276)

question: Tlacaelel counselled four Aztec kings one after another and never took the throne himself. Tradition remembers him as the hidden builder of Aztec power. He lifted Huitzilopochtli over all the other gods and made human sacrifice far greater than before. He is also said to have done one thing to the empire's own records, to control how the Mexica saw their past. What did he do?
answer: Had the old painted history-books burned
choices: Had the old painted history-books burned
Carved the true history onto the temple walls

context: Tradition says he burned the old codices because they 'contained lies,' then had the Mexica past rewritten to make them a chosen people. He held the office of cihuacoatl and never took the throne himself. (Legend/tradition, confidence medium.) (https://grokipedia.com/page/Tlacaelel ; https://www.historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=3936)

question: In the myth, the war god Huitzilopochtli cut his sister Coyolxauhqui to pieces, and at the base of one of the Great Temple's stairways her broken body lay carved on a stone disc about 3.25 metres wide. Captives killed on the summit were thrown down the steps onto it. Its discovery in 1978, in the middle of Mexico City, set archaeologists digging out the whole temple. Who uncovered it?
answer: Electric-company workers digging in the street
choices: Electric-company workers digging in the street
Archaeologists searching for the temple
Treasure hunters following an old map
Builders laying a new cathedral floor
context: The carving re-enacts the myth in which the newborn war-god dismembered his sister atop Coatepec hill; captives flung down the steps were beheaded and dismembered on this stone. Electric-company crews struck it by accident on 21 February 1978. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coyolx%C4%81uhqui ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Coyolxauhqui/)

question: Aztec farmers paddled their canoes down the narrow canals between the chinampas, the long garden beds where they grew much of the food for Tenochtitlan. Five hundred years after the Aztec empire fell, what has become of these gardens?
answer: Farmers still tend them and canoes still glide between them
choices: Farmers still tend them and canoes still glide between them
Nothing is left of them but old Spanish drawings
Only their stone outlines survive inside a museum
They were drained and paved over centuries ago
context: The surviving gardens are at Xochimilco in Mexico City, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, where ahuejote willows still line the plots and visitors ride canoes between them. (mexicocity-guide.com/attractions/xochimilco_attraction)

question: Tenochtitlan's canals, causeways, temples and huge market teemed with people in the early 1500s, 200,000 to 400,000 of them on one great island in a lake. Compared with the London of Henry VIII at the very same moment, how big was the Aztec capital?
answer: About five times the size of London
choices: About the same size as London
Roughly twice the size of London
About five times the size of London
Around ten times the size of London
context: Estimates run from 200,000 to 400,000 people (a much-cited academic figure is about 212,500) packed onto 13.5 sq km, making it one of the largest cities on Earth. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan)

question: The farmers who fed Tenochtitlan worked chinampa gardens that the canals kept watered day and night, while an ordinary Mexican field of the sixteenth century gave one grain harvest a year, two if the rains were kind. How many harvests in a single year could a chinampa yield?

Up to four a year
Up to seven a year
Up to twelve a year
context: The plots were held fast by ahuejote willows planted along their edges, whose dense roots gripped the soil, while the canals gave constant water -- up to seven harvests a year fed the whole capital. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinampa; mexicocity-guide.com/attractions/xochimilco_attraction)

question: Moctezuma kept a zoo inside his palace, with jaguars, pumas and snakes, and an aviary of ten rooms whose pools of fresh and salt water served eagles, macaws and quetzals. Every creature there got its own proper food. How many keepers did Moctezuma need to run it all?
answer: About three hundred keepers

About one hundred keepers
About three hundred keepers
About a thousand keepers
context: Moctezuma II's aviary held quetzals, macaws, and golden and harpy eagles; its roughly 300 keepers each tended their animals' proper diet -- a royal menagerie unlike anything in Europe at the time. (reconditosite.wordpress.com/2017/05/21/moctezumas-aviary; worldhistory.org/Montezuma)

question: Aztec carvers cut the Sun Stone from one great block of basalt, a disk of some 24 tons and nearly twelve feet across. At its center they carved a snarling face, which most scholars name as Tonatiuh, the sun, and from its open mouth, where a tongue should be, they set one object jutting out. What did they carve there?
answer: A stone sacrificial knife
choices: A stone sacrificial knife
A forked serpent's tongue
A stream of carved flames
A single round jade bead
context: Most scholars name the central face Tonatiuh, the Aztec sun. A stone sacrificial knife juts from its mouth like a tongue, and a clawed hand grips a human heart on each side of the face. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Sun_Stone/

question: Carvers of the Aztec Sun Stone set their people's story of time into it. In Aztec belief, four worlds had come and gone before their own, ended in turn by devouring monsters, by hurricanes, by a rain of fire and by a great flood. Their own age, the Fifth Sun, would end as well, they believed. How did they believe it would be destroyed?
answer: By earthquakes shaking the world apart
choices: By earthquakes shaking the world apart
By a second world-drowning flood
By another scorching rain of fire
By beasts devouring every person
context: The Fifth Sun was marked by the glyph Nahui Ollin, '4-Movement.' The Aztecs believed this present age would end in earthquakes that tear the world apart. Source: https://www.ancientpages.com/2018/07/18/aztecs-five-suns-creation-myth-and-prophecy/  (Legend.)

question: Bantu-speaking farmers carried their languages across half of Africa, from Cameroon's forests down into the far south. Their descendants speak some 500 related languages, and the whole family is named after one word they share. In them, umuntu means one person. What does Bantu mean?
answer: People
choices: People
Farmers
Travelers
Strangers
context: Built from the root -ntu (a person) plus the plural prefix ba-, so abantu = 'people.' The family is named after its own word for the human beings who carried it across the continent. Source: Etymonline, 'Bantu'; Wikipedia, 'Wilhelm Bleek.'

question: Khoisan peoples, whose speech snapped with clicks, met the first Bantu farmers to reach Africa's far south. The newcomers took the clicks into their own languages, so Zulu and Xhosa, alone among Bantu tongues, are full of them. Where does a click sit in the name 'Xhosa' itself?
answer: In the 'Xh' that opens it
choices: In the 'Xh' that opens it
In the 's' in the middle
In the final 'a'
In the 'ho' it is built around
context: The 'Xh' in 'Xhosa' is itself a click consonant — the language wears a borrowed Khoisan click right at the front of its own name. Source: Britannica, 'Xhosa language'; langcen.cam.ac.uk.

question: Archaeologists digging at Nkang, in Cameroon, found phytoliths in old rubbish pits: tiny plant-stones left by bananas, a crop that had come all the way from Southeast Asia. The traces proved that bananas grew in central Africa far earlier than anyone expected. About how old were they?
answer: About 2,500 years old
choices: About 2,500 years old
About 500 years old
About 200 years old
About 80 years old
context: The Nkang phytoliths pushed banana farming in central Africa far earlier than anyone expected — and hinted at ancient contact across the Indian Ocean long before written records. Source: Archaeology Magazine (archive.archaeology.org), Nkang banana phytoliths.

question: Scholars traced the Bantu spread across half of Africa, some two thousand years of it, without digging up a single migrating skeleton. Their map rests above all on one kind of evidence, which shows who split from whom, and roughly when. What did they study?
answer: The words of the languages themselves
choices: The words of the languages themselves
The bones in ancient graves
The pottery left in old camps
The iron tools in the soil
context: The method is called lexicostatistics — counting how many words languages still share to date their splits and map the spread. The migration was reconstructed from speech, not skeletons. Source: worldhistory.org, 'Bantu Migration.'

question: Attila rode out of the steppes at the head of his Hun horsemen and laid waste to the Roman Empire from the Balkans all the way to northern Italy. The terrified Romans gave him a nickname that has stuck to him ever since. What did they call him?
answer: The Scourge of God
choices: The Scourge of God
The Lord of the Steppe
The Breaker of Walls
The Wolf of the East
context: In Latin, Flagellum Dei — 'the Scourge of God.' Frightened Christians across the empire believed Attila's devastation was divine punishment, so the nickname stuck to him for centuries. The Huns themselves were a real people pushing west off the steppe, not demons. Source: catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/leo-the-great-versus-attila-the-hun ; attila.org/meeting-with-pope-leo-i

question: Alaric and his Visigoths broke into Rome late on 24 August 410 and looted the city for three days, the first foreign enemy inside its walls in nearly eight centuries. Alaric, an Arian Christian, gave his men one strict order. What did he command them to do?
answer: Spare the churches and anyone who fled inside them
choices: Spare the churches and anyone who fled inside them
Burn every temple of the old Roman gods
Take no prisoners and leave the city empty
Pull down the walls so Rome could never rise again
context: Alaric ordered his men to spare the Christian churches and avoid needless bloodshed — people who fled to the basilicas of St Peter and St Paul were left unharmed. By tradition the Salarian Gate had been opened from the inside by sympathizers. It was the first time since the Gauls in 390 BC, nearly 800 years earlier, that a foreign enemy had taken the city. Source: britannica.com/event/Sack-of-Rome-410 ; touchstonemag.com/archives/article.php?id=37-04-002-a

question: Genseric, king of the Vandals, came for Rome in 455, and the city braced for an army marching down through Italy, the road every earlier conqueror had taken. Instead his men came ashore at the mouth of the Tiber. How had the Vandals reached the city?
answer: They sailed a fleet across the open Mediterranean
choices: They sailed a fleet across the open Mediterranean
They rowed up the Tiber from a base in Sicily
They crossed by ship from a port in southern Spain
They ferried over from a beachhead in Greece
context: Genseric's kingdom was centered on Carthage in North Africa. He shipped his whole army by sea across the Mediterranean and landed at the Tiber's mouth — a naval invasion of Italy. Pope Leo I went out to plead, and Genseric agreed to spare the people if the gates opened without a fight, then looted the city methodically for two weeks. Source: thecollector.com/sack-of-rome-vandals/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(455)

question: Fritigern led tens of thousands of Goths to the Danube in 376, fleeing the Huns, and begged Emperor Valens to let them shelter inside the empire. Penned in and starving, the Goths fell into the hands of Lupicinus and Maximus, Roman officers who sold them dog meat. What did each dog cost the Goths?
answer: One Gothic child sold into slavery
choices: One Gothic child sold into slavery
A year of military service to Rome
All their cattle and horses
Their weapons and shields surrendered
context: The officers Lupicinus and Maximus charged one enslaved Gothic child per dog. The outraged Goths revolted, and in 378 at Adrianople they destroyed the eastern Roman field army and killed Valens himself — whose body was never found. They did not begin as invaders; Rome's own cruelty made them enemies. Source: worldhistory.org/Fritigern/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lupicinus_(comes_per_Thracias)

question: Henri Grégoire, a French bishop, coined a new word in 1794 to shame men he had watched at work, naming them after the Vandals who had looted Rome for two weeks in 455. The word was vandalisme. What was Grégoire condemning?
answer: The destruction of art during the French Revolution
choices: The destruction of art during the French Revolution
The looting of churches in a Spanish war
The burning of a royal library in Paris
The melting of statues for cannon metal
context: Grégoire watched revolutionaries smashing artworks and coined 'vandalisme' to shame them by comparison to the Vandals — who had stripped the gilded bronze roof tiles off the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline. So a 5th-century people became a modern insult thirteen centuries later. Source: thecollector.com/sack-of-rome-vandals/ ; darkageshistory.com/how-the-word-vandalism-originated/

question: Augustine, bishop of Hippo, set to work around 413 on a great book answering pagans who laid Alaric's sack of Rome in 410 at Christianity's door. No earthly city, even Rome, lasts forever, he argued. What did he title it?
answer: The City of God
choices: The City of God
On the Fall of Empires
The Eternal Throne
Confessions of Rome
context: In The City of God, Augustine answered pagans who blamed Christianity for Rome's fall: every earthly city is mortal, he wrote, but the City of God endures. The scholar Jerome, hearing the news in Bethlehem, grieved that 'the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken.' Source: britannica.com/event/Sack-of-Rome-410

question: A servant felt something stiff sewn inside the lining of Blaise Pascal's coat after Pascal died in 1662. It was a folded parchment that Pascal had stitched into each new coat for eight years, the record of a night on which, he wrote, he met God. What word stood across its top in capital letters?
answer: FIRE
choices: FIRE
LIGHT
GRACE
GLORY
context: The note is now called Pascal's 'Memorial.' He told no one about it in his lifetime; it was found only after his death at 39, hidden in his coat. (https://www.plough.com/en/topics/faith/blaise-pascals-night-of-fire ; https://www.ccel.org/ccel/pascal/memorial.i.html)

question: Blaise Pascal's father laboured into the night, evening after evening, over stacks of paperwork, and the teenage Pascal set out to spare him the grind. The boy built a machine full of brass gears and turning dials. What could young Pascal's machine do?
answer: it worked out sums all on its own
choices: it worked out sums all on its own
it stamped wax seals onto letters
it ruled neat lines for a ledger
it weighed coins to test them
context: His father's drudgery was adding up tax accounts. The machine became known as the 'Pascaline.' The same mind that did sums by machine later wrote that 'the heart has its reasons, of which reason knows nothing.' (https://philopedia.org/philosophers/blaise-pascal/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal's_wager)

question: Johannes Kepler meant to become a Lutheran pastor until a teacher pushed him toward mathematics. To Kepler, working out the laws of the planets was not invention but the tracing of patterns set down long before him. He summed up his work in one famous line: he was thinking whose thoughts, after whom?
answer: God's thoughts, after God
choices: God's thoughts, after God
the ancients' thoughts, after the ancients
his teacher's thoughts, after his teacher
nature's thoughts, after nature
context: Kepler's exact words: 'O God, I am thinking Thy thoughts after Thee.' He saw discovering the laws of the planets as tracing patterns God had already laid down, and called his science an act of worship. (https://breakpoint.org/johannes-kepler-thinking-gods-thoughts-after-him/ ; https://www.icr.org/article/science-man-god-johann-kepler)

question: In his will, Robert Boyle, whose name lives on in Boyle's Law, paid for public talks in London, given every year, defending the Christian faith against those who doubted it; the talks still continue more than three centuries on. He bound the speakers by one strict rule. What did it forbid them to do?
answer: argue about quarrels between Christians themselves
choices: argue about quarrels between Christians themselves
name any living person in the audience
charge the public any money to attend
speak for longer than a single hour
context: Boyle wanted the lectures aimed outward at unbelievers, not turned into fights between rival Christian groups. The Boyle Lectures have continued in London for over 300 years. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyle's_Lectures ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Boyle)

question: 'A thinking reed,' Blaise Pascal called a human being: the weakest thing in all of nature, snapped by a puff of wind. Yet he argued that if the whole universe crushed a man, the man would still stand nobler than the thing that killed him. What makes the man nobler, by Pascal's argument?
answer: he knows that he is dying
choices: he knows that he is dying
he can build tools to fight back
his soul will never truly die
God made him to rule over nature
context: Pascal's point: the universe has no idea what it is doing, but the man understands his own death -- so our whole dignity rests in thought, not in strength. (https://www.uvm.edu/~lderosse/courses/intro/pascal_pensees.pdf ; https://physicsdegree.com/blaise-pascal-quotes/)

question: Robert Boyle, a founder of modern chemistry, learned Hebrew, Greek, Syriac and Aramaic by himself on top of all his science, and he brought a chemist's demand for evidence to the task. Why did Boyle learn the languages in which the Bible was first written?
answer: so no translator could fool him about what it said
choices: so no translator could fool him about what it said
so he could win debates against foreign scholars
so he could teach the languages at the university
so he could decode the secret writings of alchemy
context: Boyle wanted to read Scripture firsthand, in its original words, rather than trust someone else's version. He brought a chemist's demand for checking the evidence to his faith. (https://www.icr.org/fb/boyle ; https://www.evangelicalmagazine.com/article/the-founder-of-chemistry-who-loved-the-bible/)

question: Robert Boyle was offered the presidency of the Royal Society in 1680, the greatest honour English science could give, and he turned it down for a religious reason. What stopped Boyle from accepting?
answer: the office required an oath, and he would not swear it
choices: the office required an oath, and he would not swear it
the duties clashed with his hours set aside for prayer
he had vowed never to rank himself above other men
he felt the honor belonged to an ordained churchman
context: Boyle had deep religious scruples about swearing oaths, so he declined the presidency rather than take one. He kept doing chemistry without the title. (https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Robert_Boyle ; https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Boyle/)

question: Isaac Newton decided in secret that the doctrine of the Trinity was false, slipped into the Bible by later tampering. Yet Cambridge expected its professors to be ordained as priests of a church that taught that very doctrine. What did Newton quietly obtain from King Charles II in 1675?
answer: a royal exemption releasing him from that rule
choices: a royal exemption releasing him from that rule
a royal order letting the chair be held by a layman
a royal deputy ordained to serve the post for him
a royal command striking the rule from the statutes
context: Newton was a secret anti-Trinitarian. Rather than be ordained into a doctrine he rejected, he got a special royal dispensation from Charles II freeing the holder of his Cambridge chair from having to take holy orders. (https://www.patheos.com/blogs/kermitzarleyblog/2017/10/sir-isaac-newton-strongly-anti-trinitarian/ ; https://www.sfu.ca/~poitras/Arian_newton.pdf)

question: Blaise Pascal wrote of a night on which he met God, on a parchment he kept sewn in his coat, and he hailed that God as 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.' Then he set Him sharply apart from the God of one group. Which group was it?
answer: the philosophers and the learned
choices: the philosophers and the learned
the priests and the bishops
the kings and the mighty
the scribes and the lawyers
context: Pascal -- one of the sharpest reasoners alive -- was insisting that the God he met was a living person you encounter, not a conclusion you prove on paper like a geometry theorem. (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/pascal/memorial.i.html ; https://iep.utm.edu/pascal-b/)

question: Isaac Newton, Robert Boyle and Johannes Kepler studied a cosmos that kept such exact order that its motions could be worked out years ahead. Newton filled more pages on God than on physics, Boyle paid to have Bibles printed, and Kepler called geometry the mind of God. What did the three take that order in nature to be?
answer: the handwriting of a lawgiver who designed it
choices: the handwriting of a lawgiver who designed it
a dim copy of a perfect heavenly original
a scaffold God would tear down at the end of time
a beauty made for worship, not for studying
context: To Boyle, Newton, and Kepler, finding that nature obeyed exact, discoverable laws was not evidence AGAINST God -- it was the strongest evidence FOR one, since laws imply a lawgiver. That is why the simple 'science versus faith' story fits these particular founders so poorly. (https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/14/6/795 ; https://breakpoint.org/johannes-kepler-thinking-gods-thoughts-after-him/)

question: A lone hunter stalked a giant ground sloth, a beast the size of a car, across the gypsum flats at White Sands in New Mexico, and the mud kept their tracks. Dated to some 21,000 years ago, the footprints are among the oldest human traces in the Americas. What do they show the cornered sloth doing?
answer: Rearing up on its hind legs and spinning to face the hunter
choices: Rearing up on its hind legs and spinning to face the hunter
Galloping in a straight line toward the distant treeline
Dropping flat and lying motionless in the wet mud
Wading out into the deep water of a nearby lake
context: The White Sands footprints, dated to 21,000-23,000 years ago, are among the oldest human traces in the Americas. One trackway preserves a human stalking a giant ground sloth, which reared on its hind legs and spun to confront the threat; another set shows an adult repeatedly carrying a toddler across the mudflat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Sands_footprints

question: Tom Dillehay dug into a bog at Monte Verde in Chile and uncovered a 14,500-year-old camp, kept so well by the waterlogged ground that its wooden tent frames and bits of animal hide had lasted. One small trace in it shattered the old Clovis First timeline. What had the bog preserved?
answer: A child's footprint pressed into the clay
choices: A child's footprint pressed into the clay
A row of carved stone spear points
A painted handprint on a cave wall
A necklace of drilled seashell beads
context: Monte Verde sits at the southern end of South America, yet people were living there centuries before the inland 'ice-free corridor' between the great ice sheets was even passable — so they could not have walked that route. That puzzle pushed scientists toward coastal-travel ideas like the 'kelp highway.' How and when the first people reached the Americas remains an open, debated question. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Verde

question: Berliners woke on Sunday, 13 August 1961, to find their city cut in two. In the small hours East German soldiers had torn up the streets and strung coil after coil of fencing straight through the middle of it. What do Germans still call that Sunday?
answer: Barbed Wire Sunday
choices: Barbed Wire Sunday
Black Saturday
The Iron Sunday
The Long Night
context: About 43 km of barbed wire went up across Berlin that single night, every crew guarded by armed soldiers. Germans call the day Stacheldrahtsonntag -- 'Barbed Wire Sunday.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall; adst.org/2014/08/the-berlin-wall-is-built-august-13-1961/

question: Conrad Schumann, a 19-year-old East German border guard, stood watch where the new barrier ran low on 15 August 1961, two days after it went up. He flung away his submachine gun and sprang over into West Berlin. Peter Leibing photographed him in mid-air. What is the photograph called?
answer: Leap into Freedom
choices: Leap into Freedom
The Last Patrol
Crossing the Wire
Escape at Dawn
context: Photographer Peter Leibing caught Conrad Schumann's jump; 'Leap into Freedom' (Sprung in die Freiheit) became the iconic image of the Wall's first days. Sources: allthatsinteresting.com/conrad-schumann; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Leibing

question: A family on Bernauer Strasse stepped out of its front door in East Berlin and onto a Western pavement, for the border followed the fronts of the houses. Then the East sealed the doors. How did the people trapped inside escape to the West?
answer: They climbed out of the upper-floor windows
choices: They climbed out of the upper-floor windows
They dug under the cellar floors
They swam across the harbor canal
They cut a gap in the wire fence
context: On Bernauer Strasse the windows themselves became the border. People knotted bedsheets to climb down, or jumped into rescue nets held open by the West Berlin fire brigade while East German police tried to drag them back inside. Sources: stiftung-berliner-mauer.de/en/berlin-wall-memorial/historical-site/bernauer-strasse; the-berlin-wall.com/videos/escaping-on-bernauer-strasse-534/

question: Passengers on a West Berlin subway train rode without stopping through a bricked-up station beneath East Berlin, where sentries stood on the dim platform. A few Western lines still ran under the East, past fifteen such stops. What did Berliners call these sealed and guarded stations?
answer: Ghost stations
choices: Ghost stations
Silent stations
Buried stations
Shadow stations
context: Berliners called them Geisterbahnhoefe -- 'ghost stations.' Western trains passed through without stopping while GDR guards watched from the shadows. Sources: stiftung-berliner-mauer.de/en/berlin-wall-memorial/visit/exhibitions/border-stations-and-ghost-stations-divided-berlin; berlin.de/mauer/en/sites/museums-and-exhibitions/ghost-stations-exhibition-at-the-nordbahnhof-s-bahn-station/

question: A refugee from East Germany crossed into West Berlin on 12 August 1961, one of some 2,400 who fled that day, more than on any day before. Walter Ulbricht's regime built its Wall to stop people leaving, and some 3.5 million East Germans had already gone. Roughly what share of East Germany's people was that?
answer: One in five
choices: One in three
One in five
One in eight
One in twelve
context: Roughly one in five East Germans had fled West before the border was sealed. On August 12, 1961 alone about 2,400 crossed into West Berlin -- the most defectors ever in a single day -- and the next morning the wire went up. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall; adst.org/2014/08/the-berlin-wall-is-built-august-13-1961/

question: Walter Ulbricht, East Germany's leader, faced the press in June 1961, two months before the Wall went up, and flatly denied that any wall was coming. History never let him forget the short sentence he used. What did Ulbricht say?
answer: Nobody has the intention of building a wall.
choices: Nobody has the intention of building a wall.
No one will ever close the Berlin border.
There will be no barrier between our peoples.
We would never wall our own citizens in.
context: Ulbricht was the first official to even say the word 'wall' out loud -- to deny it. 'Niemand hat die Absicht, eine Mauer zu errichten.' He started building one on August 13, 1961. Sources: germanhistorydocs.org/en/two-germanies-1961-1989/walter-ulbricht-s-speech-on-the-quot-berlin-question-quot-june-15-1961; chronik-der-mauer.de/material/178773/

question: Armed East German soldiers stood guard over every stretch of the new border all through the first night of Operation Rose, the secret plan to seal Berlin. Their loaded guns were aimed to stop one group of East Germans from fleeing west. Whom were the soldiers guarding against?
answer: The crews building the barrier
choices: The crews building the barrier
Off-duty East German soldiers
West Berliners cutting the wire
East Berlin factory workers
context: Roughly 43 km of barbed wire went out that night, the trams stopped, and every crew was watched by armed soldiers so the workers themselves could not flee West. The builders of the Wall were prisoners too. Sources: erenow.org/modern/theberlinwallaugust131961/9.php; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbed_Wire_Sunday

question: Ida Siekmann, 58, threw her bedding down from her home on Bernauer Strasse in East Berlin on 22 August 1961, the day before her birthday, and then leapt toward the West Berlin firefighters waiting below. She leapt too soon. What had the firefighters not yet done?
answer: Open their rescue sheet beneath her
choices: Open their rescue sheet beneath her
Unlock the building's front door
Raise their ladder to her window
Clear the crowd from the street
context: Ida Siekmann died of her injuries on the way to the hospital, the day before her 59th birthday -- the first person to die at the Berlin Wall. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ida_Siekmann

question: West Berlin students dug for five months under the Wall, from a bakery cellar on their side to an outhouse on the other, 12 metres down and 145 metres long. In October 1964 the tunnel carried off the largest escape the Wall ever saw, and the number who crawled through it became its name. How many crawled through?
context: It is remembered as 'Tunnel 57' -- the most successful single escape in the Wall's 28-year history. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunnel_57; smithsonianmag.com/history/most-successful-tunnel-escape-history-berlin-wall-180953268/

question: Peter Fechter, an 18-year-old bricklayer, tried to climb the Wall near Checkpoint Charlie on 17 August 1962, and the East German guards shot at him 35 times. Wounded, he dropped back into the death strip and screamed for about fifty minutes, while the guards left him there and Western police could only throw bandages over. What did the crowd in the West scream at the guards as he bled to death?
answer: Murderers!
choices: Murderers!
Cowards!
Butchers!
Animals!
context: Four guards fired 35 shots; Peter Fechter bled to death in the 'death strip' while both sides watched and the crowd screamed 'Moerder!' -- 'Murderers!' Sources: chronik-der-mauer.de/en/victims/180502/fechter-peter; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Peter_Fechter

question: A guard dog paced the raked sand of the Berlin Wall's death strip beneath a watchtower and its floodlights. The Wall's official name, the Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart, claimed it stood there to keep Western fascists out. Which way did the guns, the lights and the dogs all face?
answer: Inward, toward its own citizens
choices: Inward, toward its own citizens
Outward, toward the West
Along the border, both ways
Upward, at the watchtowers
context: A regime that aims its guns, lights and dogs at its OWN people -- not at any enemy -- has confessed what it is. The 'Antifaschistischer Schutzwall' existed to imprison citizens, not to protect them. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall; iwm.org.uk/history/cold-war/germany/berlin-wall

question: John F. Kennedy faced an enormous crowd in West Berlin in June 1963. Democracy was far from perfect, he said, 'but we have never had to put up a wall to keep our people in.' He finished with four German words that the crowd roared back at him. What were they?
answer: Ich bin ein Berliner
choices: Ich bin ein Berliner
Wir sind ein Volk
Berlin wird frei sein
Wir bleiben fuer immer
context: 'I am a Berliner.' Kennedy stood with the trapped city and named the Wall for exactly what it was -- a barrier to keep a regime's own people in. Source: jfklibrary.org/archives/other-resources/john-f-kennedy-speeches/berlin-w-germany-rudolph-wilde-platz-19630626

question: Arjuna, the warrior at the heart of the Bhagavad Gita, has his charioteer Krishna drive him out between the two armies just before the battle. Across the field stand his grandfather Bhishma, his teacher Drona, and his cousins with their sons. His legs fail him, the great bow Gandiva falls from his grip, and he will not fight. What reason does he give Krishna?
answer: That killing his own kinsmen and teachers for a kingdom would be a sin
choices: That killing his own kinsmen and teachers for a kingdom would be a sin
That the enemy army was far too large for him to defeat
That a wound had crippled his right arm before the battle began
That the gods had forbidden any fighting on that particular day
context: Arjuna's collapse is moral, not cowardice. Seeing his family across the field, his limbs give way and his bow Gandiva slips from his hand; he tells Krishna it would be a sin to kill his own kin for a throne, invoking the idea that non-violence is the highest duty. The Gita's first chapter is even titled 'Arjuna Vishada Yoga' — 'The Yoga of Arjuna's Despondency' — treating his very despair as a spiritual stage. (Bhagavad Gita Ch.1, verses 1.28-1.31; shlokam.org/gita/chapter-1; World History Encyclopedia.)

question: Krishna answers Arjuna as the warrior stands frozen between the two armies, his great bow fallen from his hand, refusing to fight. That answer becomes the Gita's most-quoted teaching. What does Krishna say a person should do about the results of the duty he performs?
answer: Do the duty, but surrender all claim to the fruits of the action
choices: Do the duty, but surrender all claim to the fruits of the action
Refuse any duty whose outcome you cannot first guarantee
Choose only the duties that promise the greatest personal reward
Postpone every duty until the gods reveal how it will end
context: Krishna's answer is 'nishkama karma' — selfless action. In the most-quoted verse, 2.47: 'You have a right to perform your prescribed duty, but you are not entitled to the fruits of action.' Do the duty; let go of attachment to the outcome. This single idea shaped figures far beyond India — Gandhi called the Gita 'my mother' and built his nonviolent movement on acting from duty without attachment to results. (Bhagavad Gita 2.47; shlokam.org/bhagavad-gita/2-47; dharmapedia.net 'Influence of Bhagavad Gita'.)

question: Three Allied leaders met at Yalta, a resort on the Black Sea, in February 1945 to settle the shape of the peace as the Second World War neared its end. Newspapers named them the Big Three. Who were they?
answer: Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin
choices: Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin
Roosevelt, Churchill, and de Gaulle
Truman, Chamberlain, and Stalin
Roosevelt, Chamberlain, and Mussolini
context: America's Franklin Roosevelt, Britain's Winston Churchill, and the Soviet Union's Joseph Stalin. They met first at Yalta (Feb 1945) and again at Potsdam (Jul-Aug 1945) to divide up the postwar world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalta_Conference

question: Winston Churchill came to Yalta, on the Black Sea, in February 1945 for a summit under a secret code name he loved: Argonaut. The name winked at an old Greek myth. Which famous voyage did it hint at?
answer: Jason sailing for the Golden Fleece
choices: Jason sailing for the Golden Fleece
Odysseus sailing home from Troy
Theseus hunting the Minotaur in the maze
Perseus flying to behead the Gorgon
context: In the myth, Jason and his Argonauts sailed the ship Argo to the Black Sea coast to win the Golden Fleece — and Yalta itself sat on the Black Sea. Churchill cabled Roosevelt that 'Argonaut' had 'a local but not deducible association' with their own voyage there. Source: https://time.com/archive/6870223/the-yalta-story-the-argonauts/

question: Franklin Roosevelt and his party settled into the Livadia at Yalta, once the tsars' fifty-room summer palace, where Stalin had lodged them. Tired from the long trip, Roosevelt gazed at all the marble and made a joke. What did he joke the palace had?
answer: all the comforts of home
choices: all the comforts of home
more rooms than the White House
a draft in every hallway
the finest view in all Russia
context: Roosevelt stayed in the Livadia Palace, the old summer home of the Russian tsars. Of its 50 rooms he remarked, 'this place has all the comforts of home.' Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/collections/item/object/205125421

question: At Yalta in February 1945, Stalin made his Western allies a secret promise: he would turn on Japan three months after Germany was beaten. But he named a price. What did Stalin demand in return?
answer: Japanese land: South Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands, and Port Arthur
choices: Japanese land: South Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands, and Port Arthur
A free hand in Poland and all the Baltic states
Command of Manchuria, Korea, and northern China
A naval base on the Mediterranean and the Suez Canal
context: Stalin kept the bargain almost to the day, declaring war on Japan three months after Germany surrendered. South Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands are still held by Russia today and remain disputed with Japan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalta_Conference

question: Lord Moran, Churchill's doctor, saw Franklin Roosevelt, the youngest of the Big Three, at Yalta, hollow-eyed, ghastly and 30 pounds underweight. Privately, Moran gave the president a few months at most. How soon was Moran proved right?
answer: Roosevelt died about two months later, that April
choices: Roosevelt died about two months later, that April
Roosevelt recovered and served several more years
Roosevelt died the following year, in 1946
Roosevelt lived to see Germany surrender in May
context: Roosevelt died of a cerebral hemorrhage on April 12, 1945, in his cottage at Warm Springs, Georgia, less than a month before Germany surrendered. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/yalta-conference-big-three-wwii-cold-war

question: Clement Attlee sat down in Winston Churchill's place at the Potsdam talks on 26 July 1945, partway through the conference, and Churchill did not come back. The leaders had met near Berlin that summer to settle the peace. Why had Churchill gone?
answer: British voters had just turned him out of office
choices: British voters had just turned him out of office
His doctors ordered him home, gravely ill
Stalin had demanded that he be barred
He quit the talks in furious protest
context: Churchill lost the 1945 British general election while the conference was underway and was replaced at Potsdam on July 26 by the new prime minister, Clement Attlee. Source: https://history.state.gov/milestones/1937-1945/potsdam-conf

question: The Big Three argued over Poland at Yalta more than over anything else. Britain had gone to war in 1939 to defend Poland, yet Stalin's soldiers now occupied all of it, and the Western leaders had almost nothing to bargain with. What did Poland lose in the deal?
answer: Roughly half its prewar territory, on its eastern side
choices: Roughly half its prewar territory, on its eastern side
Its entire army, which was disbanded
Its capital, Warsaw, handed to the Soviets
Its seat at the new United Nations
context: The new eastern border followed the Curzon Line, costing Poland about 48% of its prewar land. The country that Britain entered the war to save came out of Yalta smaller and under Soviet domination. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalta_Conference

question: Harry Truman drew Stalin aside at Potsdam in July 1945 and remarked, almost offhand, that America had a powerful new weapon. Stalin hardly reacted; he said only that he hoped the Americans would use it well against Japan. Why was he not surprised?
answer: Soviet spies had already told him about the bomb
choices: Soviet spies had already told him about the bomb
He didn't grasp what Truman was describing
He was certain Truman was bluffing
He cared only about the fate of Germany
context: Stalin only said he was glad and hoped they would make good use of it against Japan. He already knew through Soviet espionage and reportedly told his team that same day to speed up the Soviet bomb program. Source: https://www.dannen.com/decision/potsdam.html

question: Stalin marked Churchill's half-sheet of paper with a tick of his blue pencil when the two met in Moscow in 1944. On it Churchill had jotted how they would share the Balkans: 90 percent Soviet in one country, 90 percent British in another. Fearing it might look cynical, Churchill proposed, 'Let us burn the paper.' How did Stalin answer?
answer: 'No, you keep it.'
choices: 'No, you keep it.'
'Burn it, then.'
'Let history be our judge.'
'As you wish, Prime Minister.'
context: Churchill called the half-sheet 'a naughty document' and had worried aloud it would look 'cynical' to dispose of nations 'in such an offhand manner.' Stalin had already marked it with a tick from his blue pencil and coolly told Churchill to keep the evidence. Source: https://winstonchurchill.org/the-life-of-churchill/war-leader/makes-percentages-agreement-on-spheres-of-influence/

question: Molotov, Stalin's foreign minister, fretted at Yalta that the promise of free and unfettered elections for Poland might tie their hands. Stalin brushed it off: they would do things their own way, later. How long did the Poles wait for a truly free election?
answer: Until 1989, forty-four years later
choices: Until 1989, forty-four years later
Until 1947, just two years later
Until the early 1950s, after Stalin
Until 1956, a decade after the war
context: Privately, when Molotov fretted the wording might tie Stalin's hands, Stalin replied, 'Never mind. We'll do it our own way later.' Poland did not hold a genuinely free election until 1989. Source: https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-hccc-worldhistory2/chapter/the-yalta-conference/

question: Soldiers of Britain and America drove Soviet refugees back to Stalin with rifle butts and bayonets under a clause agreed at Yalta, even those who rioted or wounded themselves sooner than return. Many of those sent back were shot or sent to the gulag. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn gave the whole affair a name. What did he call it?
answer: 'the last secret of World War II'
choices: 'the last secret of World War II'
'the betrayal of the innocents'
'Stalin's quiet harvest'
'the forgotten exodus'
context: The forced transfers were later codenamed Operation Keelhaul. British and American troops used rifle butts and bayonets against those who refused to go back to the Soviet Union. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Keelhaul

question: The victors at Potsdam moved Poland's western frontier about 200 kilometres, as far as the rivers Oder and Neisse, onto what had been German land. About 12 million Germans were driven from homes their families had held for ages. In what manner did the official agreement ask that their expulsion be carried out?
answer: 'in an orderly and humane manner'
choices: 'in an orderly and humane manner'
'with all possible speed'
'under strict military guard'
'with fair compensation for the dispossessed'
context: The new border ran along the Oder and Neisse rivers, so the whole of Poland shifted westward. The expulsion of some 12 million Germans was one of the largest forced migrations in history, yet the Potsdam wording asked only that it be done 'in an orderly and humane manner.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oder%E2%80%93Neisse_line

question: Polish airmen flew in the Battle of Britain, and over 900 Polish soldiers fell taking Monte Cassino; Poland had put the fourth-largest army in the field for the Allies. Yet when London staged its Victory Parade in 1946, Britain feared angering Stalin. What did it do to the Poles?
answer: Left them out of the parade entirely
choices: Left them out of the parade entirely
Marched them at the very back
Made them carry the Soviet flag
Banned their uniforms and medals
context: Bowing to Stalin, Britain simply did not invite the Polish forces — the RAF's 303 Squadron starred in the Battle of Britain and over 900 Poles died capturing Monte Cassino. The nation whose 1939 invasion had begun the war was shut out of the victory celebration. The Big Three never met as a trio again, and the defeat of one tyranny, Nazi Germany, had left half of Europe — including Poland — under another, Stalin's. Source: https://www.britishpoles.uk/the-1946-victory-parade-the-symbol-of-polands-betrayal/

question: The people of Messina, in Sicily, watched twelve Genoese trading galleys sail into their harbour from the Crimea in October 1347, and in horror they forced the galleys back out to sea. What was it about the sailors that horrified them?
answer: The sailors were already dead or dying of plague
choices: The sailors were already dead or dying of plague
The sailors were armed and ready to raid the town
The sailors carried chests of stolen Eastern gold
The sailors spoke a language no one could understand
context: The Sicilian chronicler Michele da Piazza recorded the ghost-fleet's arrival. Driving the ships away was too late: the plague was already loose, and it spread across the whole island within weeks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death_in_Italy

question: A village gravedigger buried his neighbours until the plague took him too, as it took priests and doctors from Sicily to Norway between 1347 and 1351. What share of all Europeans died in those four years?
answer: Between a third and a half of everyone
choices: Between a third and a half of everyone
Roughly one person in twenty
Roughly one person in a hundred
Almost everyone, nine in ten
context: A third to a half of all of Europe died in a handful of years. The historian Ole J. Benedictow, studying region after region, argues the true figure for Europe as a whole was even higher, around 60-65%. Worldwide the dead are estimated at 75 to 200 million people. Source: https://www.medievalists.net/2023/11/how-many-people-died-black-death/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death

question: A plague victim felt a lump swelling in his armpit, neck or groin, a lymph node that could balloon as big as an apple. The swelling gave this form of the disease its name. What was the swelling called?
answer: A bubo
choices: A bubo
A canker
A blister
A welt
context: The swollen lymph node is the 'bubo,' which is why it is called bubonic plague. The eyewitness Giovanni Boccaccio, watching it in Florence in 1348, called these swellings 'gavoccioli' and wrote that they grew 'to the size of a common apple' or 'the size of an egg.' Two other forms were even deadlier: septicemic plague in the blood and pneumonic plague in the lungs, which could kill in one to three days. Sources: https://www.medicinenet.com/plague_facts/article.htm ; https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1537/boccaccio-on-the-black-death-text--commentary/

question: A man who buried his family in 1348 spoke of the plague by its own name; the label Black Death turns up in English only in 1755. What did people of the 1300s call the disease?
answer: The Great Pestilence, or Great Mortality
choices: The Great Pestilence, or Great Mortality
The Black Death, or the Black Plague
The Italian Fever, or Genoa's Curse
The Devil's Pox, or the Burning
context: Contemporaries wrote of the Great Pestilence, the Great Mortality, or simply the Plague (Latin 'mortalitas'). The label 'Black Death' is first attested in English in 1755, translating a Scandinavian phrase, 'den sorte dod' — the black death. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death

question: A flea riding on a black rat kept trying to feed, but the plague germ, Yersinia pestis, had clogged its gut so that it could never fill its stomach. That blockage is what made it so deadly to people. How did the starving flea infect a person?
answer: As it bit, it vomited the plague straight into the wound
choices: As it bit, it vomited the plague straight into the wound
It laid its eggs in a sleeping person's open sores
It carried the plague on its legs and wiped it on food
Its bite injected venom that rotted the flesh black
context: The bacterium is Yersinia pestis, carried mainly by the Oriental rat flea, Xenopsylla cheopis. Because the bacteria blocked the flea's gut, the flea could never get a full meal; each time it tried to feed it threw the plague-laden blood back up into the new bite. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death

question: Giovanni Boccaccio watched the dead of Florence go by the hundreds into great trenches in 1348, once the plague had killed so many that the city ran out of blessed ground to bury them in. How, in his words, were the bodies packed into the pits?
answer: In layers with dirt between them, like a ship's cargo
choices: In layers with dirt between them, like a ship's cargo
Wrapped in fine linen and sealed with wax
Burned on great pyres outside the city walls
Sunk in weighted sacks into the river Arno
context: Boccaccio wrote that 'huge trenches were dug... and into them the new arrivals were dumped by the hundreds; and they were packed in there with dirt, one on top of another, like a ship's cargo, until the trench was filled.' Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1537/boccaccio-on-the-black-death-text--commentary/

question: Bands of flagellants in white robes marked with a red cross marched from town to town in 1349, whipping themselves morning and evening. In each town they stayed exactly thirty-three and a half days. Why that odd, exact number?
answer: It matched the years Christ lived on Earth
choices: It matched the years Christ lived on Earth
It matched the days Noah's flood rose
It matched the towns the plague had struck
It matched the apostles, doubled and halved
context: The Brotherhood of the Cross marched in groups of 200-300, whipping themselves with 'hard knotted leather with little iron spikes' that tore the flesh. The thirty-three and a half days stood for the thirty-three and a half years Christ was said to have lived. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagellant ; https://www.medievalists.net/2022/02/flagellant-songs-middle-ages/

question: The men of Strasbourg rounded up the city's Jews, some two thousand people, on 14 February 1349 and burned them alive inside a wooden house, on the charge that they had poisoned the wells. What makes the massacre especially damning?
answer: The plague had not even reached Strasbourg yet
choices: The plague had not even reached Strasbourg yet
The Jews had warned the city the plague was coming
The city's own doctors had already cured the plague
The wells were later found to be perfectly clean
context: Strasbourg massacred its Jews before the disease ever arrived there — the killing was driven purely by rumor and fear, not by anything the victims had done. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strasbourg_massacre

question: Sailors on a ship from an infected port waited in isolation off Venice before anyone aboard could enter the city, under a rule Venice made in 1448. The length of their wait gave English the word quarantine. How long was it?
answer: Forty days
choices: Forty days
Thirty days
Fourteen days
Sixty days
context: Venice required 'quaranta giorni' — forty days — and from that Italian phrase comes 'quarantine.' An earlier thirty-day rule, the 'trentino,' had been imposed at the port of Ragusa (modern Dubrovnik) in 1377. Forty was chosen partly for its biblical weight: forty days of the Flood, forty years in the desert, forty days of fasting. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3559069/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7133622/

question: Khan Jani Beg's Golden Horde, in the story told by the notary Gabriele de' Mussi, laid siege to Caffa, the Genoese fort in the Crimea, and plague broke out among the besiegers. In that same story, the dying Mongols then turned their own dead against the city. What did de' Mussi say they did?
answer: Catapulted the plague-corpses over the city walls
choices: Catapulted the plague-corpses over the city walls
Floated the corpses down the river into the harbor
Left infected blankets at the city gates as gifts
Drove plague-sick prisoners through the city streets
context: De' Mussi wrote that the Tartars 'ordered corpses to be placed in catapults and lobbed into the city in the hope that the intolerable stench would kill everyone inside,' and that fleeing Genoese then carried the plague home by ship — one of the earliest claimed acts of biological warfare. Told as legend; see another question for why historians doubt it. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2732530/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Caffa

question: Gabriele de' Mussi, a notary, told a famous story of how the plague leapt from the siege of Caffa to Europe. Historians today distrust it, and the records show why. What was wrong with de' Mussi as a witness?
answer: He was never at Caffa, but home in Italy the whole time
choices: He was never at Caffa, but home in Italy the whole time
He wrote it down two hundred years after the siege
He admitted at the end he had made the story up
He confused Caffa with a different city entirely
context: Records place de' Mussi in Piacenza, Italy, for the entire siege. Historian Hannah Barker (2021) argues the plague more likely traveled to Europe in grain shipments from the Black Sea once wartime embargoes lifted. Even Mark Wheelis, who defends the tale's plausibility, concluded the attack 'probably had no more than anecdotal importance in the spread of plague.' Sources: https://thebulletin.org/2023/08/catapulting-corpses-a-famous-case-of-medieval-biological-warfare-probably-never-happened/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2732530/

question: Pope Clement VI denounced the killers of Jews in 1348 as men 'seduced by that liar, the Devil,' while mobs across Europe blamed the Jews for poisoning the wells. He answered the charge with one plain fact. What was his argument?
answer: The plague was killing Jews just as surely as Christians
choices: The plague was killing Jews just as surely as Christians
The wells had been tested and found completely pure
No Jew had been seen anywhere near the city's wells
The same plague was striking lands that had no Jews
context: In two papal bulls (6 July and 26 September 1348) Clement VI argued that since Jews were dying of the plague too, 'by the hidden judgment of God,' they could hardly be the ones causing it. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI ; https://jewishcurrents.org/july-6-clement-vi-and-the-black-plague

question: Nestorian Christians buried their dead in one of their cemeteries in 1338 and 1339 and carved the dates on the gravestones, and the skeletons in those graves turned out to carry the plague germ, years before it touched the Mediterranean. Where did this oldest known plague graveyard turn up?
answer: In the mountains of Central Asia, in modern Kyrgyzstan
choices: In the mountains of Central Asia, in modern Kyrgyzstan
On the coast of Sicily, near the port of Messina
In the deserts of Egypt, just outside Cairo
On the steppes of southern Russia, near the Volga
context: The graves are at Kara-Djigach near Lake Issyk-Kul in modern Kyrgyzstan, a Nestorian Christian cemetery. Yersinia pestis DNA in skeletons dated 1338-1339 points to Central Asia as the likely starting place, years before the plague reached Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death

question: Steve Roud, a folklorist, called the popular belief that 'Ring around the rosie' is secretly about the plague complete nonsense. Its believers point to the rosy rash, the posies against the stench and everyone falling down dead. What gives the plague reading away as false?
answer: The rhyme only shows up in print centuries after the plague
choices: The rhyme only shows up in print centuries after the plague
The rhyme was written in Latin by medieval monks
The original version had no falling-down line at all
The rhyme names a real Italian town struck by plague
context: 'Ring around the rosie' is first recorded only in the late 1700s-1800s. The plague meaning was invented around the mid-1900s — it appears in James Leasor's 1961 book 'The Plague and the Fire.' The folklorist Steve Roud called the plague origin 'complete nonsense.' Sources: https://talesoftimesforgotten.com/2017/05/03/ring-around-the-rosie-is-not-about-the-black-death-nor-has-it-ever-been/ ; https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/ring-around-rosie/

question: A London family sheltered from the Luftwaffe's bombs in the autumn of 1940 in its own back garden, inside a curved hut of corrugated steel, half-buried and heaped with soil. The shelter took its name from a government minister. What was it called?
answer: The Anderson shelter
choices: The Anderson shelter
The Churchill shelter
The Wellington shelter
The Spitfire shelter
context: The Anderson shelter was about 6ft by 4ft 6in and cost roughly 7 pounds, dug into the garden. The alternative was the indoor Morrison shelter, a steel cage that doubled as a kitchen table you could crawl under. Source: https://www.findmypast.co.uk/blog/history/anderson-and-morrison-air-raid-shelters-and-the-british-public

question: Hitler turned his air force on London on Saturday, 7 September 1940, and some 348 bombers set the docks of the East End burning from Tower Bridge to Woolwich. Londoners remember it as Black Saturday. The bombers returned the following night, and the one after. For how many nights in a row was London bombed?
answer: 57 consecutive nights
choices: 57 consecutive nights
7 consecutive nights
12 consecutive nights
100 consecutive nights
context: That first night about 348 bombers set the docks ablaze from Tower Bridge to Woolwich, killing roughly 430 people. Then London was bombed for 57 nights in a row. Source: https://www.historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofBritain/The-Blitz/

question: Herbert Mason, a Daily Mail photographer, stood on a rooftop on the night of 29th December 1940 as German fire bombs set the old City of London ablaze around him. Through the smoke and flames he caught one great building rising unharmed, and his photograph became a symbol of defiance. Which building did it show?
answer: St Paul's Cathedral
choices: St Paul's Cathedral
Buckingham Palace
the Tower of London
Westminster Abbey
context: Mason described the moment: 'Suddenly, the shining cross, dome and towers stood out like a symbol in the inferno.' Churchill had ordered a volunteer fire-watching team, the St Paul's Watch, to save it; one incendiary burned through the lead dome but fell outward onto the Stone Gallery, where the watchers put it out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul%27s_Survives

question: Queen Elizabeth said she was glad to have been bombed when a German bomb struck Buckingham Palace on 13 September 1940, while she and King George VI were at home. London's poor docklands had taken the worst of the raids. What did she say the bombing let her do at last?
answer: look the East End in the face
choices: look the East End in the face
sleep soundly at last
forgive the German people
leave London for good
context: Her full line: 'I am glad we have been bombed. It makes me feel I can look the East End in the face.' The poor East End docklands had taken the worst of the raids; now the palace had shared in it. Source: https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/londons-blitz-a-city-at-war/

question: Richard Howard was provost of St Michael's Cathedral in Coventry, the only English cathedral the war destroyed, and he stood in its burned-out shell after the German raid of 14 November 1940. He had two words carved into the stone behind the ruined altar. What were they?
answer: Father Forgive
choices: Father Forgive
Never Again
We Shall Rebuild
Lest We Forget
context: He left it simply 'FATHER FORGIVE' - including his own nation, not just the enemy. A stonemason bound two charred roof beams into a cross, and three medieval roof nails were wired into the first 'Cross of Nails,' now a worldwide symbol of reconciliation. The Coventry raid was so total the Germans coined a verb, 'Koventrieren,' to raze a city to the ground. Source: https://www.coventry.anglican.org/the-story-of-the-cross-of-nails.php

question: Duleep Singh, the Punjab's eleven-year-old Sikh ruler, surrendered a great diamond to Queen Victoria in 1849, after the East India Company's conquest of his land. The stone's Persian name is Koh-i-Noor. What does it mean?
answer: Mountain of Light
choices: Mountain of Light
River of Stars
Eye of the Sun
Heart of the Sea
context: The Koh-i-Noor ('Mountain of Light') was recut in 1852 — the cutter Voorzanger spent 38 days shrinking it from 186 carats to 105.6. By tradition the stone brings bad luck to any MAN who wears it, so only Britain's queens do. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koh-i-Noor

question: Rebels stormed into Delhi's Red Fort in 1857 and hailed Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last of the Mughals and a frail man of 82, as emperor of all Hindustan. He accepted, but with regret. What had Zafar wished to be instead of a king?
answer: a poet
choices: a poet
a monk
a merchant
a soldier
context: Bahadur Shah Zafar was a renowned poet who never wanted a throne. After Delhi fell, Major William Hodson captured him at Humayun's Tomb (Sept 1857), shot his sons dead, and the British exiled him to Rangoon, where he died in 1862 in an unmarked grave.
