Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahadur_Shah_Zafar

question: Crowds cheered India's first passenger train on its 21-mile run from Bombay to Thane on 16 April 1853, carrying 400 riders in fourteen carriages. Three locomotives pulled it. What were their names?
answer: Sahib, Sindh, and Sultan
choices: Sahib, Sindh, and Sultan
Ganga, Indus, and Bengal
Rajah, Mogul, and Delhi
Victoria, Albert, and Crown
context: The engines Sahib, Sindh, and Sultan opened a network that grew to nearly 25,000 miles by 1900 — the fourth-largest railway system in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_India

question: Sepoys handed the new Enfield rifle in 1857 found that its greased paper cartridges had to be bitten open, and a rumour spread among them about the grease. Word went round that it came from two animals, one offending Hindus and the other Muslims. No proof was ever found. Which two fats did the rumour name?
answer: cow fat and pig fat
choices: cow fat and pig fat
horse fat and dog fat
goat fat and sheep fat
bear fat and deer fat
context: The cow is sacred to Hindus and the pig unclean to Muslims, so the rumor offended both at once. There was never proof the grease was actually tainted — but the suspicion that the British were trying to break Indian religion was enough. Source: https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/why-did-indian-mutiny-happen

question: Mangal Pandey, a sepoy, urged his comrades to rise up on the Barrackpore parade ground on 29 March 1857, then shot at a British officer and slashed him with a sword. As troops closed in to seize him, he pointed his long musket at his own chest. How did he fire it?
answer: with his foot
choices: with his foot
with his teeth
with his thumb
with a cord
context: Pandey survived the self-inflicted wound and was hanged on 8 April 1857. British troops afterward used 'Pandy' as slang for any mutineer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangal_Pandey

question: Rani Lakshmibai, the widowed queen of Jhansi, refused to hand her state to the British, who had claimed it under the Doctrine of Lapse because her husband left no natural-born son. She vowed never to surrender her Jhansi and raised an army with women in its ranks. How did she meet her end in 1858?
answer: sword in hand in battle
choices: sword in hand in battle
burned upon a pyre
executed by hanging
poisoned in her palace
context: Rani Lakshmibai's defiant cry was 'Main apni Jhansi nahi doongi!' — 'I shall not surrender my Jhansi!' She died fighting near Gwalior on 17 June 1858. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rani_of_Jhansi

question: District officers of the Indian Civil Service judged the cases, ran the police and collected the taxes of districts as big as small countries, and the whole service never had many more than 1,200 British officers. They governed over three hundred million people. What was the service nicknamed?
answer: the steel frame
choices: the steel frame
the iron net
the long arm
the white thread
context: The 'steel frame' was the skeleton the whole Raj rested on. Its companion was Macaulay's single penal code, drafted in the 1830s and enforced from 1861, imposing one rule of law across the subcontinent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Civil_Service

question: Lord Lytton, the viceroy, held a week of feasting in Delhi to hail Queen Victoria as Empress of India while the Great Famine of 1876-1878 was killing about eight million Indians, and his government sent Britain a record load of wheat, 320,000 tons. His relief paid a day of heavy labour with about 1,600 calories of grain. What did the historian Mike Davis later compare that ration to?
answer: a Buchenwald concentration-camp ration
choices: a Buchenwald concentration-camp ration
a Roman galley-slave ration
a Soviet gulag ration
a medieval prison ration
context: As Indians starved, Lytton's government exported a record 320,000 tons of wheat to Britain. Mike Davis noted the relief ration was on a par with a Buchenwald camp ration. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_of_1876%E2%80%931878

question: By Buddhist tradition, Queen Maya gave birth to Prince Siddhartha beneath a tree in the garden at Lumbini, some twenty-five centuries ago. The boy would one day become the Buddha. What, by the same tradition, became of Maya very soon afterward?
answer: She died only days after his birth
choices: She died only days after his birth
She raised him alone in the palace
She fled the kingdom in grief
She was sent away by the king
context: Queen Maya died only a few days after Siddhartha was born, so the prince was raised by her sister, Mahapajapati Gotami. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_(mother_of_the_Buddha) ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Kapilavastu/

question: Siddhartha's father shut the young prince away in palaces of luxury so he would never meet hardship. At 29 Siddhartha rode out beyond the walls, and for the first time ever he saw three sights that shook him. What were they?
answer: An old man, a sick man, and a corpse
choices: An old man, a sick man, and a corpse
A beggar, a thief, and a soldier
A widow, an orphan, and a slave
A blind man, a leper, and a ghost
context: His charioteer Channa explained that aging, disease, and death come to ALL beings alike, which troubled and sorrowed Siddhartha's mind. His father had walled him inside the palace precisely so he would never see such suffering. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_sights ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Four-Signs  (Legend.)

question: Beyond the palace walls, the young prince Siddhartha met three sights that filled him with dread, and then a fourth: a man untroubled and at peace amid all that suffering. This one gave him hope instead, hope that there could be an escape from it. What kind of man was it?
answer: A wandering holy man
choices: A wandering holy man
A victorious general
A wealthy merchant
A royal physician
context: The ascetic showed Siddhartha that there might be a way to seek liberation from suffering, and he resolved to follow that example. This hope is what led to his Great Departure from the palace. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_sights ; https://pluralism.org/prince-siddhartha-renouncing-the-world  (Legend.)

question: Asita, an old sage, came down from his mountain to see the newborn prince Siddhartha and found on the baby's body every one of the thirty-two marks of a great man. Then the old seer began to weep. Why did Asita weep?
answer: He would die before the boy grew up to teach
choices: He would die before the boy grew up to teach
He foresaw the prince would die young
He saw the boy would never find peace
He knew the child would bring war
context: Asita found the thirty-two marks of a great man on the infant. He cried not for the child but for himself: the boy would become a Buddha, but Asita was too old and would die before he could ever hear him teach. Source: https://sacred-texts.com/bud/lob/lob06.htm ; https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asita  (Legend.)

question: Kanthaka, Siddhartha's white horse, carried the prince out of the palace one night and over the Anoma River as far as the edge of the forest. There Siddhartha cut his hair short with his sword, dressed in a beggar's robes and gave his royal ornaments to his charioteer Channa to take home. What, by tradition, became of the loyal horse?
answer: His heart broke and he died
choices: His heart broke and he died
He bolted away and was lost
He returned home and was honored
He lay down and refused to eat
context: At the Anoma River, Siddhartha had cut off his hair with his sword and given his charioteer Channa his royal ornaments to carry home. Kanthaka could not bear the parting; his heart broke and he died. Tradition says the horse was reborn in a heaven and later reached enlightenment after hearing the Buddha teach. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanthaka  (Legend.)

question: Siddhartha lived as a wandering ascetic in the forests for six years, eating almost nothing, as he searched for the end of suffering. The old Buddhist account gives one image of how wasted his body became, from what he felt when he touched himself. What does it say?
answer: When he touched his belly, he felt his spine
choices: When he touched his belly, he felt his spine
When he pressed his ribs, he heard them crack
When he stood up, he fainted to the ground
When he closed his eyes, he saw only darkness
context: In the canonical account, so little was left of him that when he touched his belly he could feel his spine, and when he touched his spine he could feel the skin of his belly. This near-starvation is what convinced him extreme self-denial was a dead end. Source: https://www.hdasianart.com/blogs/news/buddha-as-a-wandering-ascetic-amp-his-path-to-enlightenment ; https://buddhasartofhealing.com/blogs/thangka/fasting-buddha

question: Mara, the demon, hurled storm, flood and an army of demons at Siddhartha as he sat in meditation beneath a sacred fig tree. When all of it failed, he sent his three daughters, each named for a pull on the human mind. What were their names?
answer: Craving, Aversion, and Desire
choices: Craving, Aversion, and Desire
Pride, Envy, and Greed
Hunger, Thirst, and Pain
Doubt, Fear, and Despair
context: Mara first attacked with storm, flood, and an army of demons, then sent his three daughters, Tanha (Craving), Arati (Aversion), and Raga (Desire), to seduce him. They failed like everything else. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mara_(demon) ; https://buddhism.net/posts/buddhism-for-all/b205-when-mara-met-siddhattha/  (Legend.)

question: Sujata, a milkmaid, came upon Siddhartha near death and fed him milk-rice from a golden bowl, and his strength returned. Then he placed the empty bowl on the water of a river and made a vow: if he was to be enlightened that very day, the bowl must give him a sign. What sign did he ask of it?
answer: To float upstream against the current
choices: To float upstream against the current
To sink straight to the riverbed
To circle three times and stop
To drift to the far shore
context: The milkmaid Sujata, from the village of Senani, had mistaken the gaunt, glowing Siddhartha for the tree-spirit who had answered her prayer for a son, and gave him a golden bowl of kheer (milk-rice). The bowl then floated against the current to the middle of the river before sinking. The Sujata Stupa marking the spot was built in the 2nd century BCE. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sujata_(milkmaid) ; https://www.wisdomlib.org/buddhism/book/the-great-chronicle-of-buddhas/d/doc364450.html  (Legend.)

question: A musician tuning the string of an instrument, the story goes, showed Siddhartha his answer after years of searching for enlightenment. In that string he saw a balance he would call the Middle Way. What did the string teach him about its tuning?
answer: Too tight it snaps, too loose it won't play
choices: Too tight it snaps, too loose it won't play
Struck too hard it cracks, struck too soft it's mute
Wound too high it sours, wound too low it drones
Pulled too far it tears, pulled too near it slacks
context: The lute string showed Siddhartha that self-torture was as futile as self-indulgence: too tight, the string snaps; too loose, it won't sound; only rightly tuned does it make music. This is the Middle Way between the two extremes. Source: https://www.exoticindiaart.com/blog/buddhas-path-to-the-middle-way/ ; https://enlightenmentthangka.com/blogs/thangka/lady-sujata-and-the-fasting-buddha  (Legend.)

question: Mara's demon host roared beneath the fig tree that it stood witness for its master, after Mara dared Siddhartha to name anyone who could vouch for his enlightenment. Siddhartha had no one to speak for him. Without a word he made one gesture that countless statues of the Buddha still show. What did he do?
answer: Touched the ground, calling the earth to witness
choices: Touched the ground, calling the earth to witness
Raised one hand, calling the sky to witness
Pointed at Mara, calling the gods to witness
Bowed his head, calling no one to witness
context: Siddhartha reached down with his right hand and called the earth itself to witness, and the earth shook in agreement. This is the famous bhumisparsha ('earth-witness') gesture. In Thai and Lao tradition, an earth-goddess then wrings out her long hair, releasing a flood of all his past good deeds that sweeps Mara and his horde away. Source: https://buddhism.net/posts/buddhism-for-all/b205-when-mara-met-siddhattha/ ; https://www.renown-travel.com/mudras/subduing-mara.html  (Legend.)

question: Beneath the sacred fig tree, Siddhartha woke to the truth in three stages through a single night. In the first watch he saw every one of his past lives, and in the second the law of karma turning the wheel of death and rebirth. What did he grasp in the third watch, the deepest, with the morning star rising?
answer: The Four Noble Truths about suffering
choices: The Four Noble Truths about suffering
The thousand names of the gods
The secret hour of his own death
The spell to escape rebirth forever
context: In the third watch he grasped the Four Noble Truths and dependent origination. As the morning star rose, at about age 35, he became the Buddha, 'the Awakened One.' Seven weeks later he taught these same Four Noble Truths to five ascetics at the Deer Park in Sarnath, founding the Sangha. Source: https://www.learnreligions.com/the-enlightenment-of-the-buddha-449789 ; https://www.buddhanet.net/e-learning/history/vesak2/  (Legend.)

question: Charlemagne set monks all over his empire to copying ancient books by hand, late in the 700s and through the 800s, and the copying peaked under him. From every century before 800 combined, fewer than 2,000 Latin books survive. About how many survive from the single century after 800?
answer: More than 7,000
choices: More than 7,000
More than 4,000
More than 12,000
More than 30,000
context: More than 7,000 from one century, versus fewer than 2,000 from every earlier century combined. That copying boom under Charlemagne is the main reason ancient authors reach us at all. (Wikipedia, 'Carolingian Renaissance', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_Renaissance)

question: Lucretius, the Roman poet, wrote a masterpiece, On the Nature of Things, that very nearly vanished. Every Renaissance copy of it descends from manuscripts written out by Carolingian monks in the 800s. How many of those Carolingian copies still survive?
answer: Just two
choices: Just two
Just four
Just seven
Just twelve
context: The poem hangs by two ninth-century Carolingian copies, nicknamed the Oblongus (from Mainz) and the Quadratus (from St. Bertin); every later Renaissance copy descends from them. (The Wrong Monkey blog summarizing standard textual history; cf. Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2014.10.21, bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2014/2014.10.21)

question: Purusha, a cosmic giant in the Rig Veda, Hinduism's oldest scripture, died as a sacrifice, and his body gave birth to the four ranks of society. The priests came from his mouth and the warriors from his arms. From which part came the lowest rank, the laborers and servants?
answer: His feet
choices: His feet
His mouth
His arms
His heart
context: In the Purusha Sukta hymn (Rig Veda 10.90), the line runs: 'The Brahman was his mouth... His thighs became the Vaishya, from his feet the Shudra was produced.' The body-part order mirrors the rank: the mouth speaks sacred words at the top, the feet do the menial work at the bottom. This is a sacred origin-story, told here as the hymn tells it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna_(Hinduism), RV 10.90.11-12; worldhistory.org/article/1152.  (Legend.)

question: A translator working through the Rig Veda comes to its word varna, the name for the four ranks of priests, warriors, traders and laborers, and writes 'caste,' as is usual today. In the Rig Veda's own Sanskrit the word had an older, literal meaning. What was it?
answer: Color
choices: Color
Rank
Duty
Birth
context: In the Rigveda, 'varna' literally meant color, appearance, or form. What that 'color' referred to is debated: many scholars read it as symbolic — each varna was traditionally linked with a color — rather than skin tone, and the idea that caste began as a skin-color racial hierarchy is largely a 19th-century colonial theory, now widely disputed. The four varnas were the Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (warriors), Vaishyas (farmers and traders), and Shudras (laborers). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna_(Hinduism).

question: A Brahmin boy received a sacred thread at his initiation and won the right to study the Vedas, as did the boys of the warrior and trader ranks, but a Shudra boy was denied both. What name did the boys of the top three ranks earn?
answer: The twice-born
choices: The twice-born
The thread-keepers
The vow-takers
The pure-handed
context: The top three varnas were 'dvija' — the twice-born — entitled to the sacred-thread initiation (upanayana) and to study the Vedas. The Shudra was not twice-born, wore no sacred thread, and was barred from officiating sacrifices. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna_(Hinduism).

question: A Shudra laborer listened to the sacred verses of the Vedas, verses the Laws of Manu kept from the lower ranks. A later code, the Gautama Dharmasutra, set a punishment for what he had done. What did it order done to him?
answer: Pour molten lead into his ears
choices: Pour molten lead into his ears
Cast him out of the village forever
Brand the mark of a dog on his arm
Forbid him to ever speak again
context: The Gautama Dharmasutra prescribed pouring molten lead into the ears of a Shudra who deliberately listened to the Vedas; Manusmriti 8.272 had earlier ordered heated oil poured into the mouth and ears of a Shudra who arrogantly instructed a Brahmin, and Katyayana ordered the tongue cut in two for uttering Vedic words. The hereditary low rank was enforced with brutal punishments. Source: angelfire.com/ak/ambedkar/BRManusmriti.html (Gautama/Katyayana, cited by Ambedkar); Manusmriti 8.272.

question: B.R. Ambedkar stood before a crowd at Mahad on Christmas Day 1927 with the ancient law-book he blamed above all others for caste's scriptural foundation. Ambedkar had been born an untouchable and later drafted much of the constitution of independent India. What did he do to the book that day?
answer: He tore and burned it page by page
choices: He tore and burned it page by page
He buried a copy beneath the Chavdar Tank
He read it aloud and refuted every line
He nailed his objections to the temple door
context: At the Mahad Satyagraha, Ambedkar — himself born untouchable — publicly tore and burned copies of the Manusmriti page by page, attacking the scriptural basis of caste. The protest grew from a campaign to let untouchables drink from the public Chavdar Tank, water they had been forbidden to touch. Source: sabrangindia.in (Dec 25, 1927).

question: Thorgeir Thorkelsson, Iceland's pagan lawspeaker, lay silent under a fur cloak for a day and a night in the year 1000, while the island's parliament split into two hostile camps, pagan and Christian. To avoid war, both sides had agreed to accept his ruling. Then he rose. What did Thorgeir declare?
answer: That all Icelanders would become Christian
choices: That all Icelanders would become Christian
That the island would split into two realms
That every household must choose for itself
That the old gods alone would be honored
context: The pagans accepted it without bloodshed. Thorgeir's peace deal came with quiet concessions: people could still worship the old gods in private and still eat horse meat. Source: Ari Thorgilsson, Islendingabok (c.1067), via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianization_of_Iceland.

question: Adam of Bremen wrote of a feast at Uppsala's great temple in Sweden, nine days long and held once every nine years, at which nine males 'of every living creature' were killed in sacrifice. What, by his account, happened to the dead men, dogs and horses?
answer: They were hung together in the sacred grove beside the temple
choices: They were hung together in the sacred grove beside the temple
They were burned on a great pyre before the temple
They were sunk in a cold lake near the temple
They were buried in a mound behind the temple
context: A Christian who had been there told Adam of Bremen he counted 72 corpses, men and animals, hanging together; every tree in the grove was held divine because of the dead bodies rotting in it. Source: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis (c.1070), via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_at_Uppsala.

question: Snorri Sturluson told in his saga how Olaf Tryggvason, the king who spread the faith through Norway by preaching and by force, strode up to the idol of Thor at Maerin, gleaming with gold and silver, an ornamented staff in his hand. What did Olaf do then, by Snorri's telling?
answer: He struck Thor off his pedestal with the staff
choices: He struck Thor off his pedestal with the staff
He set fire to the temple's wooden roof
He swore an oath of peace before the idol
He knelt and laid the staff at Thor's feet
context: His men then shoved all the other idols down. The saga also claims the chieftain Raud the Strong, who refused to convert and cursed the name of Jesus, was killed by Olaf with a snake forced down his throat. Told as saga tradition, not forensic record. Source: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raud_the_Strong.  (Legend.)

question: Oswald Tilley, a British private in the trenches of Flanders, heard German voices singing carols on Christmas Eve 1914. When the British struck up 'O Come, All Ye Faithful,' Tilley wrote, the Germans joined in at once. What were they singing?
answer: 'Adeste Fideles'
choices: 'Adeste Fideles'
'Stille Nacht'
'The First Noel'
'O Tannenbaum'
context: 'Adeste Fideles' is the Latin name for 'O Come, All Ye Faithful.' Private Oswald Tilley wrote that the British started up the carol and 'the Germans immediately joined in singing the same hymn to the Latin words.' Other carols heard that night included 'Silent Night' / 'Stille Nacht.' Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/The_Christmas_Truce/ (Pvt. Oswald Tilley quoted).

question: British and German soldiers climbed out of their trenches in Flanders on Christmas morning 1914, shook hands in no man's land and traded presents. John Ferguson, a British corporal, said they were 'soon conversing as if we had known each other for years.' Which German souvenir did the British soldiers want most?
answer: A German spiked helmet
choices: A German spiked helmet
A box of German cigars
A German sausage
A German uniform button
context: The spiked helmet was the Pickelhaube, and it was the most prized British souvenir of the truce. Soldiers also swapped cigars and cigar cases, schnapps for rum, German sausages for English corned beef, chocolate, and uniform buttons and badges. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/The_Christmas_Truce/ (Cpl. John Ferguson quoted).

question: Police in Montgomery, Alabama, arrested Rosa Parks, a seamstress of 42, on 1 December 1955 for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. People later supposed her feet had hurt, and Parks said they were wrong. In her own words, what was the only thing she was tired of?
answer: Of giving in
choices: Of giving in
Of working all day
Of riding the bus
Of being afraid
context: Parks wrote: 'People always say that I didn't give up my seat because I was tired... No, the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.' Her arrest sparked a bus boycott that lasted 381 days. Source: Rosa Parks, 'My Story', quoted via the National Portrait Gallery and the Library of Congress 'Rosa Parks: In Her Own Words' exhibition.

question: Black riders in Montgomery left the city's buses empty after Rosa Parks's arrest in December 1955, and walked or shared rides instead. After 381 days the boycott won, but the city never gave in on its own. What actually ended bus segregation in Montgomery?
answer: A federal court struck the law down
choices: A federal court struck the law down
The bus company ran out of money
The state governor repealed the law
A new federal law banned it
context: The boycott ran 381 days and ended only when the federal courts, in Browder v. Gayle, ruled Alabama's bus segregation laws unconstitutional. The protest was won in the courtroom under the Constitution -- not by force. Source: Britannica 'mother of the civil rights movement'; Stanford King Institute; National Archives.

question: John Lewis and Hosea Williams headed a march of about 600 people over the Edmund Pettus Bridge at Selma, Alabama, on 7 March 1965, Bloody Sunday, demanding the vote. Alabama state troopers beat them back with clubs on the bridge, and Lewis ended up in hospital. What injury had he suffered?
answer: A fractured skull
choices: A fractured skull
A concussion
A broken jaw
Broken ribs
context: John Lewis's skull was fractured by the troopers' blows. The televised brutality drove passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which outlawed the literacy tests used to keep black citizens from voting. Source: National Museum of African American History and Culture, '#OnThisDay: Bloody Sunday'; National Archives 'Selma Marches'.

question: The crowd at the March on Washington heard Martin Luther King speak of his four young children on 28 August 1963. He dreamed of a nation where one day they would not be judged by the color of their skin, but by something else. What did he want them judged by?
answer: The content of their character
choices: The content of their character
The strength of their convictions
The worth of their labor
The merit of their deeds
context: King dreamed his children would 'not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character,' and that 'the sons of former slaves and the sons of former slaveowners will be able to sit down together at a table of brotherhood.' His dream was America's own creed redeemed: 'all men are created equal.' Source: Martin Luther King Jr., 'I Have a Dream', Avalon Project, Yale Law School.

question: Birmingham's black schoolchildren marched two by two out of the 16th Street Baptist Church in May 1963, more than a thousand strong, in the Children's Crusade. Bull Connor, the city's police boss, ordered his men to stop them. What did Connor turn on the children?
answer: Fire hoses and attack dogs
choices: Fire hoses and attack dogs
Mounted cavalry and whips
Tear gas and rubber bullets
Mass arrests and curfews
context: Connor ordered high-pressure fire hoses and attack dogs turned on the marching children. The televised images shocked the world and pushed President Kennedy to back federal civil rights law. Source: Britannica 'Birmingham Children's Crusade'; National Museum of African American History and Culture.

question: Ku Klux Klan members planted a bomb at the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama, in September 1963, under three weeks after King's 'I Have a Dream' speech. It went off at 10:22 on a Sunday morning. Whom did the blast kill?
answer: Four girls getting ready for service
choices: Four girls getting ready for service
The pastor and two deacons
A passing police officer
Two visiting civil rights lawyers
context: The blast killed Addie Mae Collins, Carole Robertson, and Cynthia Wesley, all 14, and Denise McNair, 11, as they prepared for Sunday service. The murder of four children in a church hardened the nation's resolve for the civil rights laws to come. Source: Britannica '16th Street Baptist Church bombing'; National Park Service.

question: Homer Plessy set out in New Orleans to drag Louisiana's segregation law into court, knowing he would be arrested for it. The Supreme Court heard his case as Plessy versus Ferguson and in 1896 upheld segregation, provided the separate facilities were equal. What did Plessy deliberately do to bring the case?
answer: Sat in a whites-only railroad car
choices: Sat in a whites-only railroad car
Refused to pay a segregation fine
Registered his children at a white school
Bought a house in a white district
context: Plessy deliberately sat in a whites-only car in New Orleans to challenge Louisiana's Separate Car Act of 1890, knowing he would be arrested. The Court's ruling against him locked 'separate but equal' into American law for the next 58 years. Source: National Archives 'Plessy v. Ferguson' milestone document; Oyez.

question: Kenneth and Mamie Clark, two psychologists, set four dolls before black children in the 1940s, dolls alike in every way but skin color, and asked which one each child wanted to play with. The Supreme Court leaned on their test when it weighed Brown versus Board of Education in 1954. Which doll did most of the children choose?
answer: The white doll
choices: The white doll
The black doll
An even mix of both
No doll at all
context: About 67% chose the white doll, and many called the black doll 'bad' -- evidence the Court cited that segregation made black children feel inferior and that 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.' Source: NAACP Legal Defense Fund, 'Brown v. Board: The Significance of the Doll Test'; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: Thurgood Marshall argued the children's side in Brown versus Board of Education. In 1954 the nation's highest bench, led by Earl Warren, ruled without one dissent that segregated schools were inherently unequal, and it overturned Plessy. What did Marshall himself later become?
answer: The first black Supreme Court Justice
choices: The first black Supreme Court Justice
The first black state governor
The first black U.S. Attorney General
The first black presidential nominee
context: Thurgood Marshall, who argued Brown, became the first black Justice of the Supreme Court in 1967. The case was won not by overthrowing the system but by forcing it to honor the Constitution it already had. Source: National Archives 'Brown v. Board of Education' milestone document; Cornell LII.

question: Martin Luther King called the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence a promissory note at the March on Washington in 1963, a pledge to pay made out to every American. America, he said, had handed its black citizens a different piece of paper, one that came back stamped with two words. What was it, in King's image?
answer: A bad check marked 'insufficient funds'
choices: A bad check marked 'insufficient funds'
An unpaid bill sent 'past due'
A torn deed marked 'no claim'
A blank page stamped 'denied'
context: King said America 'has given the Negro people a bad check which has come back marked insufficient funds' on the promissory note of the founding documents, 'But we refuse to believe that the bank of justice is bankrupt.' The movement framed itself as collecting a debt the founders themselves had written. Source: Martin Luther King Jr., 'I Have a Dream', Avalon Project, Yale Law School.

question: Frederick Douglass, a runaway from slavery, faced a Fourth of July audience in Rochester, New York, in 1852 and asked, 'What, to the American slave, is your Fourth of July?' He honoured the men who signed the Declaration of Independence as brave, and he did not call their Declaration wrong. What did Douglass argue instead?
answer: That America was betraying its own founding creed
choices: That America was betraying its own founding creed
That only the courts, not protest, could end slavery
That the North was as guilty as the slaveholding South
That emancipation would have to come gradually
context: Douglass praised the signers as 'brave men... great enough to give fame to a great age' and pledged to 'honor their memory.' His charge was that slavery was an American betrayal of America's own creed, not proof the creed was wrong, and that the moment demanded 'scorching irony, not convincing argument.' Source: Frederick Douglass, 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' (1852), via BlackPast.org and americanrevolutioninstitute.org.

question: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali wrote on Islamic law, philosophy and mysticism in the 1000s, and later Muslims counted him among the greatest thinkers of their faith. They gave him a towering title. What did they call him?
answer: the Proof of Islam
choices: the Proof of Islam
the Sword of the Faith
the Lamp of the East
the Father of Scholars
context: In Arabic, Hujjat al-Islam. Al-Ghazali (born around 1058 in Tus, Persia; died 1111) was also called the mujaddid, the 'renewer' divinely sent to revive the faith for the entire 11th century. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ghazali

question: Al-Ghazali, who taught in Baghdad in the 1090s, pointed his students to a flame touching a piece of cotton and asked them what really sets the cotton alight. What was his answer?
answer: God burns the cotton directly, every single time
choices: God burns the cotton directly, every single time
The cotton holds a hidden seed of fire within it
The flame and the cotton share one fiery essence
Unseen sparks leap across the gap between them
context: This doctrine is called occasionalism: the fire is only the 'occasion,' never the true cause. Centuries later this critique of cause-and-effect anticipated the philosopher David Hume's doubt that we ever really see causation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Incoherence_of_the_Philosophers

question: Hulagu Khan's Mongols stormed Baghdad in 1258 and destroyed books from its libraries. Legend tells what became of the Tigris afterward. What does the legend say happened to the river?
answer: It ran black with the ink washing off the drowned books
choices: It ran black with the ink washing off the drowned books
It overflowed its banks and swallowed the city walls
It turned to steam under the burning of the libraries
It froze solid overnight in the depth of winter
context: The same legend says so many volumes were dumped that they formed a bridge a horseman could ride across. Historians treat the river-of-ink as a famous exaggeration, since large libraries are recorded reopening within about two years, but the mass destruction of Baghdad's books was real. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad

question: A hall full of students sat before al-Ghazali one day around 1095, when he was the star professor at the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, the most prestigious teaching chair in the Muslim world. As he stood before them, a sudden affliction struck him. What happened to him?
answer: His throat constricted and he could not speak a word
choices: His throat constricted and he could not speak a word
His memory emptied and he forgot his own argument
His hands shook so badly he dropped his notes
His sight darkened until the students blurred away
context: He lost his appetite, abandoned the chair, and left Baghdad to wander as a poor Sufi for over a decade before returning to write. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ghazali

question: Averroes, a Spanish philosopher, answered The Incoherence of the Philosophers, al-Ghazali's attack on the Greek-minded Muslim thinkers, passage by passage a century after it appeared. The reply won little favour in the Islamic world but made Averroes famous in Christian Europe. What did he title it?
answer: The Incoherence of the Incoherence
choices: The Incoherence of the Incoherence
The Defense of the Philosophers
The Triumph of Reason over Faith
A Reply to the Proof of Islam
context: In Arabic, Tahafut al-Tahafut. Averroes lost the argument in the Islamic world, where almost none of his works survived, but the same book made him a giant in Christian Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Incoherence_of_the_Philosophers

question: Al-Nawawi, a later Islamic scholar, paid al-Ghazali's masterwork, The Revival of the Religious Sciences, one of the most extravagant compliments any book has received. The book wove Islamic law, theology and mysticism together. What did al-Nawawi claim about the book?
answer: It alone would suffice if all other books of Islam were lost
choices: It alone would suffice if all other books of Islam were lost
It could be memorized whole by any devoted student
It would settle every dispute among the legal schools
It deserved to be copied in gold in every mosque
context: Al-Nawawi's exact praise: 'Were the books of Islam all to be lost, excepting only the Ihya', it would suffice.' Al-Ghazali's fusion of Sufi mysticism with orthodox theology reshaped Sunni Islam permanently. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ghazali

question: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, who rode with the Mongols when they took Baghdad in 1258, would not let the city's learning simply vanish. He rescued what manuscripts he could from the ruin and carried them off to safety. Where did he take the books?
answer: To a brand-new observatory at Maragha
choices: To a brand-new observatory at Maragha
To the old caliph's emptied palace
To a hidden monastery in the mountains
To the Mongol capital far to the east
context: Built in 1259, the Maragha observatory's library is said to have grown to hundreds of thousands of volumes salvaged from Baghdad, Damascus, Mosul and Khurasan, proof the destruction did not erase everything. Source: https://muslimheritage.com/nasir-al-din-al-tusi/

question: Al-Ghazali took aim at Ibn Sina, known in Latin as Avicenna, and at al-Farabi when he wrote The Incoherence of the Philosophers in Baghdad around 1095. He did not merely disagree with them; he condemned three of their doctrines as kufr, outright unbelief. Which three?
answer: That the world is eternal, that God knows only universals, and that there is no bodily resurrection
choices: That the world is eternal, that God knows only universals, and that there is no bodily resurrection
That prophecy has ended, that the soul dies with the body, and that scripture may be reinterpreted
That God is unknowable, that miracles are impossible, and that prayer changes nothing
That fate is fixed, that angels are symbols, and that paradise is purely spiritual
context: Al-Ghazali targeted Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and al-Farabi by name. Calling fellow Muslims unbelievers on philosophical doctrine was a thunderclap; his arguments later influenced even the Christian theologian Thomas Aquinas. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Incoherence_of_the_Philosophers

question: A theologian of the Mu'tazila, a school shaped by Greek thought, told his students that reason itself could know right from wrong and that the Qur'an was created. The rival school, the Ash'aris, won out and became Sunni orthodoxy. What did the Ash'aris hold about reason and revelation?
answer: That reason must bow to revelation
choices: That reason must bow to revelation
That reason and revelation can never truly conflict
That scripture should be read as allegory
That revelation matters only for the afterlife
context: The Mu'tazila were the rationalists; the Ash'aris held that revelation outranks human reasoning. The triumph of the Ash'ari view marked a decisive turn in how Sunni Islam weighed reason against faith. Source: https://www.rep.routledge.com/articles/thematic/ash-ariyya-and-mu-tazila/v-1

question: Muhammad Abduh blamed one turn in Islamic law for leaving Muslim lands unable to adapt while Europe had its Renaissance. Teachers from about the eleventh century held the great legal questions settled by the four founding schools. Historians say this closed the gate of ijtihad, ijtihad being a scholar's own fresh reasoning on new problems. In its place the teachers urged taqlid. What did taqlid require a believer to do?
answer: Follow established precedent without independent reasoning
choices: Follow established precedent without independent reasoning
Memorize the Qur'an completely before teaching
Submit every dispute to the ruling caliph
Abandon Greek philosophy as forbidden knowledge
context: Ijtihad means independent legal reasoning; taqlid is the blind following of precedent. The reformer Muhammad Abduh blamed this turn to taqlid for leaving the Islamic world unable to adapt while Europe ran through its Renaissance and Industrial Revolution. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ijtihad

question: Neil deGrasse Tyson blamed al-Ghazali for killing science in Islam, saying he branded the manipulation of numbers 'the work of the devil.' Researchers who checked al-Ghazali's writings found no such line, but they did find a striking sentence about mathematics and faith. What did he write?
answer: That attacking the mathematical sciences in the name of Islam is a great crime against religion
choices: That attacking the mathematical sciences in the name of Islam is a great crime against religion
That mathematics is the surest path a believer has to knowing God
That only the wisest believers should be allowed to study them
That they must always be kept subordinate to theology
context: No 'work of the devil' line exists in al-Ghazali's works. His real words: 'Great indeed is the crime against religion committed by anyone who supposes that Islam is to be championed by the denial of these mathematical sciences.' The popular accusation is a modern myth. Source: https://historyforatheists.com/2023/03/neil-degrasse-tyson-and-al-ghazali/  (Legend.)

question: Vespasian began Rome's great arena around 72 CE, and its true name was the Flavian Amphitheatre. The name Colosseum was borrowed from the Colossus, a bronze giant some hundred feet high that stood right beside it. What did the statue show?
answer: The emperor Nero as the sun god
choices: The emperor Nero as the sun god
The war-god Mars holding his spear
The she-wolf nursing Romulus and Remus
The emperor Vespasian on horseback
context: The emperor Vespasian began the amphitheatre around 72 CE on the drained site of Nero's private lake, and his son Titus opened it in 80 CE. Right next to it stood a roughly 100-foot bronze statue of Nero remade as the sun god — the Colossus. People started calling the building 'the Colosseum' after that statue, and the name only truly stuck around 1000 CE. (Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Colosseum'; Wikipedia, 'Colossus of Nero'.)

question: Men hauled the velarium, a vast linen awning, out over the Colosseum crowd on a hot day, working it from about 240 wooden masts. Who were the men given the job?
answer: Sailors from the Roman war fleet
choices: Sailors from the Roman war fleet
Slaves dragged up from the mines
Soldiers of the city night-watch
Priests serving the temple of the sun
context: The word velarium comes from the Latin for 'sail,' and handling a vast sail was sailors' work — so the crew came from the war fleet at Misenum, near Naples. That was the same fleet whose admiral, the naturalist Pliny the Elder, had sailed toward the erupting Vesuvius in 79 CE and died there, just one year before the Colosseum opened. (Source: Through Eternity Tours, 'The Velarium'; Wikipedia, 'Velarium'.)

question: Rome's emperor took his seat at the very edge of the Colosseum's sand, with the senators beside him, ringside to the killing. Knights and ordinary citizens filled the rows behind them. Who sat in the topmost tier, farthest from the sand?
answer: Women, the poor, and the enslaved
choices: Women, the poor, and the enslaved
Soldiers, sailors, and armed guards
Priests, judges, and temple scribes
Merchants, traders, and money-lenders
context: The arena held roughly 50,000 people (some estimates run far higher), and the seating was a map of who mattered in Rome: power sat ringside, while women, the poor, and the enslaved were jammed into the top tier, farthest from the spectacle they had the least say in. (Source: Britannica, 'Colosseum'; History.com, 'How the Colosseum Was Built'.)

question: A gladiator beaten in a fight at the Colosseum turned to the editor, the man who was paying for the games. He did not simply collapse and hope; he gave one set signal, a formal plea to stop the fight and be let go. What did he do?
answer: Raised a single finger to the official
choices: Raised a single finger to the official
Dropped his sword and knelt down low
Threw his helmet out into the crowd
Raised his shield up over his head
context: Raising one finger was called ad digitum, 'to the finger' — a plea for missio, release. A referee called the summa rudis enforced the rules, but the final life-or-death call belonged to the games' sponsor, the editor, who was swayed by the roar of the crowd. (Source: Archaeology Magazine, 'Gladiators: The Language of the Arena'.)

question: Titus opened the Colosseum in 80 CE, back when no tunnels yet ran under the arena, so its floor could be made watertight and the ring filled with water from the aqueducts. What did he stage on that shallow lake at the opening games, by Cassius Dio's account?
answer: A full sea-battle fought with real ships
choices: A full sea-battle fought with real ships
A chariot race around the water's edge
A swimming contest between champions
A floating market of merchant stalls
context: These flooded mock sea-fights were called naumachiae. The historian Cassius Dio records that the inaugural games re-enacted a real naval battle between the Corcyreans and the Corinthians, with men fighting on actual ships in the flooded arena. (Source: Wikipedia, 'Inaugural games of the Colosseum,' citing Cassius Dio.)

question: Teams of enslaved men hauled on the ropes of some 28 elevators in the hypogeum, the two-level maze of passages and cages under the Colosseum's floor. A lion or leopard rode up in its cage beneath the watching crowd. What could the elevators make the beast seem to do?
answer: Appear suddenly as if from nowhere
choices: Appear suddenly as if from nowhere
Be paraded slowly around the ring
Charge straight out of a side gate
Be lowered on chains from above
context: About 32 trap doors dotted the arena floor. An elevator could hoist a caged lion or leopard up a shaft and pop it onto the sand through a trap door, so the beast seemed to materialize out of thin air in front of the crowd. (Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Secrets of the Colosseum.')

question: A retiarius walked out onto the Colosseum sand almost without armour, to face the secutor, the chaser, who wore heavy armour. Gladiators fought in pairs of contrasting styles, and the weapons he carried were like no other fighter's. What did the retiarius fight with?
answer: A weighted net and a three-pronged trident
choices: A weighted net and a three-pronged trident
A long spear and a heavy round shield
Two short, sharply curved daggers
A spiked war-hammer and an iron chain
context: The lightly armed retiarius was set against the heavily armoured secutor, the 'chaser,' whose smooth, almost featureless helmet was specially shaped so the net could not snag on it. The classic heavyweight pairing was the fish-helmeted murmillo against the curved-sword Thraex. (Source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Gladiators: Types and Training.')

question: A Roman in the Colosseum's stands watched the morning's beast hunts, and the gladiator duels would follow in the late afternoon. The whole day ran to a grim, fixed timetable of shows. What filled the arena at noon, in between the two?
answer: Public executions of condemned criminals
choices: Public executions of condemned criminals
A feast shared out among the whole crowd
Mock fights with blunted wooden weapons
Chariot races looping around the arena
context: Hold the wonder and the horror together: the morning beast-hunts and midday executions were killings staged as a public show — those people and animals were meant to die, not to compete. Yet most afternoon gladiator DUELS were not fatal (perhaps one bout in ten to one in five), partly because a killed fighter could cost his sponsor up to 50 times the rental fee. (Source: History.com, '5 Bloody Spectacles'; Live Science, 'Did Roman gladiators really fight to the death?')

question: The poet Martial described the duel of Priscus and Verus at the Colosseum's opening games, the only ringside account of a single fight to survive. The two were so well matched that the worn-out crowd begged for an end. What did the emperor Titus then do?
answer: Declared them both winners and set them free
choices: Declared them both winners and set them free
Ordered the pair to fight on to the death
Sent in a third fighter to break the deadlock
Had the whole bout restarted the next day
context: Titus declared both men victors and handed each a rudis, the wooden sword that meant freedom from the arena. Martial wrote of the unheard-of result: 'Equal they fought, equal they yielded... two fought and both won.' (Source: Wikipedia, 'Priscus (gladiator)' and 'Verus (gladiator),' citing Martial, Liber Spectaculorum 29.)

question: Delicatus, a fellow gladiator, cut the record of Flamma's career into his gravestone in Sicily: thirty-four bouts, twenty-one wins, nine draws. That left four bouts Flamma lost outright, and he lived through each one to fight again. What single Latin word does the stone set beside those four?
answer: Missus -- spared by the crowd, four times
choices: Missus -- spared by the crowd, four times
Victor -- victorious, four times
Damnatus -- condemned to die, four times
Liberatus -- set free, four times
context: The epitaph reads in part 'pugnavit XXXIIII, vicit XXI, stans VIIII, missus IIII' -- fought 34, won 21, drew (stood) 9, spared 4. 'Missus' means he was granted missio, the crowd's mercy. The stone names no rudis or freedom; the popular tale that he 'refused freedom four times' is a legend the epitaph does not support. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamma

question: Anthony Corbeill, a classicist, argued that a thumbs-up at the arena may even have meant kill, the reverse of what films show. The Roman writers speak only of a turned thumb, never of which way spared a man. Where did the familiar thumbs-up, thumbs-down version come from?
answer: A Victorian oil painting
choices: A Victorian oil painting
A 1950s Hollywood epic
A medieval monk's chronicle
An ancient Renaissance fresco
context: The popular gesture comes from Jean-Leon Gerome's 1872 painting 'Pollice Verso,' not from any ancient source. The classicist Anthony Corbeill has even argued the opposite of the movie version — that thumbs-UP may have meant KILL, and a thumb tucked into a closed fist meant spare. The honest answer is that we do not know. (Source: Wikipedia, 'Pollice verso,' citing Juvenal, Prudentius, and Corbeill.)

question: The emperor Claudius staged a sea fight on Lake Fucinus in the year 52, and there he was hailed with the line everyone pins on gladiators: 'Hail Caesar, those who are about to die salute you.' It turns up only that once in all of Roman history. Who shouted it at him?
answer: Condemned prisoners forced into the fight
choices: Condemned prisoners forced into the fight
Roman sailors of the imperial fleet
Senators seated in the front row
A chorus of hired temple singers
context: Suetonius reports that when the condemned men cried the salute, Claudius joked back 'Aut non' — 'Or not' — and they thought they had been pardoned and refused to fight. The battle, on Lake Fucinus in 52 CE, was no harmless show: Tacitus describes around 100 ships and as many as 19,000 condemned men, with real wounding and drowning. (Source: Wikipedia, 'Ave Imperator, morituri te salutant,' citing Suetonius and Tacitus.)

question: Hernán Cortés carried cacao home to Spain around 1528. The Aztecs ground it into xocolatl, a bitter drink, but Spanish cooks turned it into a rich luxury. What did they add to it first?
answer: Sugar
choices: Sugar
Honey
Milk
Cinnamon
context: Chocolate began as 'xocolatl,' a bitter Aztec drink; Cortes brought cacao to Spain around 1528, where adding sugar and later vanilla turned it into a luxury. It was one of the most famous foods to travel east in the Columbian Exchange. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Columbian_Exchange/

question: An Irishman sat down to yet another meal of potatoes in the 1840s; like some four million of his countrymen, half the island, he ate almost nothing else. A grown man like him got through a huge weight of potatoes every day. About how many pounds did he eat in a day?
answer: Twelve to fourteen pounds
choices: Twelve to fourteen pounds
Two to three pounds
Six to seven pounds
Twenty to twenty-five pounds
context: The potato's calories and hardiness fueled European population growth, but heavy dependence on it set the stage for the Irish Great Famine of the 1840s, when a grown man might eat 12 to 14 pounds a day. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/Columbian_Exchange/ ; https://www.britannica.com/event/Great-Famine-Irish-history

question: Motolinia, a Franciscan friar in Mexico, wrote that the Aztecs died of smallpox in heaps, like bedbugs. Whole households perished together, and with no one left to bury them, the survivors did something desperate with their dead. What did they do?
answer: They pulled the houses down on top of them, so their homes became tombs
choices: They pulled the houses down on top of them, so their homes became tombs
They burned the bodies in great fires beyond the city walls
They floated the dead out across the lake on wooden rafts
They piled the dead in the temple courtyards for the priests
context: The friar Motolinia (Toribio de Benavente) wrote that the Aztecs 'died in heaps, like bedbugs,' and that when there were too many dead to bury, survivors pulled their houses down over the bodies so their homes became their tombs. Source: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/how-smallpox-devastated-the-aztecs-and-helped-spain-conquer-an-american-civilization-500-years-ago

question: The Pueblo peoples rose in 1680 and drove the Spaniards out of New Mexico, and the Spaniards left their herds behind as they ran. Trading carried the loose horses north and east to Plains peoples such as the Sioux and the Cheyenne. Roughly how many horses had the revolt set loose?
answer: Three to five thousand
choices: Three to five thousand
Two to three hundred
Thirty to fifty thousand
A few dozen
context: In the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out of New Mexico and freed roughly 3,000-5,000 horses, which spread north and east in trade, the first large horse dispersal across the Great Plains. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pueblo_Revolt ; https://www.history.com/articles/pueblo-revolt-1680-popay

question: Christopher Columbus set off a two-way traffic across the Atlantic when he sailed in 1492: potatoes, tomatoes and cocoa went east to the Old World, while horses, wheat and smallpox crossed west to the New. Today the whole swap is called the Columbian Exchange. Where does the phrase itself come from?
answer: A historian invented it in a 1972 book
choices: A historian invented it in a 1972 book
A 1990s American history textbook introduced it
Spanish chroniclers used it in the 1500s
It appears in Columbus's own letters
context: Historian Alfred W. Crosby coined 'the Columbian Exchange' in his 1972 book of that name. He also coined 'virgin soil epidemic' for an outbreak among people with no prior exposure, who are therefore almost defenseless. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_W._Crosby ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Columbian_Exchange

question: King Charles VIII of France was besieging Naples in 1494, soon after Columbus's sailors returned, when a savage outbreak tore through his army. Historians still argue whether the sailors brought the disease from the Americas or Europe had it all along, unrecognised. Which disease was it?
answer: Syphilis
choices: Syphilis
Smallpox
Typhus
Yellow fever
context: A virulent syphilis outbreak struck Charles VIII's army at Naples in 1494-95, soon after Columbus's crews returned. Whether his sailors brought it back, or it already existed unrecognized in Europe, remains genuinely debated. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_syphilis ; https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/science-magazines/historic-dispute-did-syphilis-originate-new-world-which-it-was-brought-europe-christopher-columbus

question: Christopher Columbus sailed across the Atlantic in 1492 and linked the Old World with the New. One starchy plant had grown nowhere but high in the Andes of South America; carried to Europe, it fed the continent's swelling towns. Which crop was it?
answer: Potatoes
choices: Potatoes
Corn
Tomatoes
Chili peppers
context: The potato. Historians credit it with an estimated 12 to 25 percent of ALL population growth in Afro-Eurasia between 1700 and 1900 — a humble Andean tuber that helped feed the Old World. (The other three choices are also American crops carried out by the Exchange.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange

question: Montezuma II, the Aztec emperor, offered Hernán Cortés a cup of gold filled with a frothy, bitter brown drink. The Spanish took it home, where it became the rage among the wealthy of Europe. What drink had Cortés been served?
answer: Chocolate
choices: Chocolate
Coffee
Tea
Cola
context: Chocolate. The Aztecs drank it unsweetened and called it 'xocolatl'; the Spanish added sugar, and Europe's love of chocolate was born. Source: https://www.history.com/topics/ancient-americas/history-of-chocolate

question: John Gerard, an English herbalist, wrote in 1597 that one plant from the Americas was rank and stinking. Many Europeans spent over two hundred years calling its fruit the poison apple, and they grew it purely for show in their gardens. Which plant was it?
answer: The tomato
choices: The tomato
The potato
The chili pepper
The avocado
context: The tomato. In his 1597 herbal the English writer John Gerard called the whole plant 'of rank and stinking savour,' an opinion that kept Britain and its colonies suspicious of tomatoes for over two centuries. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-the-misrepresentation-of-tomatoes-as-stinking-poison-apples-that-provoked-vomiting-made-people-afraid-of-them-for-more-than-200-years-863735/

question: Portuguese traders shipped one starchy American root across the Atlantic to Africa in the 1500s. Little by little it pushed aside the old grains there, sorghum and millet, and no other crop feeds as many Africans today. Which root was it?
answer: Cassava
choices: Cassava
Maize
Peanuts
Sweet potatoes
context: Cassava (also called manioc). It still feeds more Africans than any other crop. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange

question: A rich European diner ate a sour new fruit from the Americas off his pewter plate and fell ill, while a poor man who ate the same fruit from a wooden trencher stayed well. A chemist later found the reason: the sour juice was pulling a poison out of the old pewter. Which poison was it?
answer: Lead
choices: Lead
Arsenic
Mercury
Copper
context: Lead. Old pewter was a lead alloy, and acidic juice leached it out — so the tomato took the blame for what the plates were doing. (Chemist Joe Schwarcz notes the amount leached was probably too trivial to truly poison anyone; the fear outran the science.) Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-the-misrepresentation-of-tomatoes-as-stinking-poison-apples-that-provoked-vomiting-made-people-afraid-of-them-for-more-than-200-years-863735/

question: Chen Zhenlong, a merchant from Fujian, set out in 1593 to smuggle the sweet potato home to China from the Spanish-held Philippines, where the plant was closely guarded. He had to get the living plant past the guards and aboard his ship. How did Chen hide the plant?
answer: He wound the vines around a rope along the ship's hull
choices: He wound the vines around a rope along the ship's hull
He sewed the cuttings into the lining of his coat
He hid the roots inside lengths of hollow bamboo
He buried the shoots in a barrel of dried rice
context: He coiled the living vines around a rope running along the hull. Promoted in China as a 'famine relief crop' that would grow on barren hillsides, the sweet potato helped China's population nearly triple, from about 130 million in 1500 to 400 million by 1900. Source: https://www.hungyichen.com/en/insights/sweet-potato-qing

question: Po'pay and the Pueblo peoples drove the Spaniards out of Santa Fe in 1680, and thousands of the Spaniards' horses broke free and wandered north. Within fifty years one nation had become the first people of the Plains to hunt bison on horseback, and it built its wealth on horses and bison. Which nation was it?
answer: The Comanche
choices: The Comanche
The Lakota
The Cheyenne
The Kiowa
context: The Comanche. Their southern-Plains empire, Comancheria, turned oceans of grass into bison meat and a thriving horse trade. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comanche_history

question: Alexander Koch's team calculated that the dying in the Americas after Columbus reached even the world's climate. By one 2019 estimate, epidemics brought the native peoples there down from roughly 60 million to about 6 million. Abandoned farmland as big as France went back to forest, and the new trees soaked up carbon dioxide. What did that 'Great Dying' help bring on around 1610?
answer: A worldwide spell of bitter cold
choices: A worldwide spell of bitter cold
A burst of huge volcanic eruptions
A string of giant earthquakes
A century of fierce ocean storms
context: It helped trigger the Little Ice Age. Regrowing forests drew CO2 down by an estimated 7 to 10 parts per million, cooling the globe. Co-author Mark Maslin put it bluntly: 'to get the full cooling you need to have this genocide-generated drop in CO2.' Source: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2019/feb/great-dying-americas-disturbed-earths-climate

question: Ada Lovelace's mother pushed her daughter into mathematics, hoping the girl would not inherit her father's stormy temper. He had walked out while Ada was still a baby, and she never knew him. What was her father famous for?
answer: He was the poet Lord Byron
choices: He was the poet Lord Byron
He was the painter J. M. W. Turner
He was the explorer Captain Cook
He was the scientist Michael Faraday
context: Ada was the only legitimate child of the wild Romantic poet Lord Byron. Her mother steered her hard toward mathematics, hoping to keep her from inheriting Byron's stormy poetic temperament. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_Lovelace

question: Alan Turing, a mathematician and a serious marathon runner, trained in 1948 to win a spot in Britain's Olympic squad. How did his best marathon time compare with that of the man who took the Olympic silver medal in 1948?
answer: Only about 11 minutes slower
choices: Only about 11 minutes slower
A full hour slower
More than two hours slower
Faster than the gold medallist
context: Turing was a world-class long-distance runner; his marathon time was only about 11 minutes slower than that year's actual Olympic silver medallist. An injury, not lack of speed, kept him from competing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing

question: Charles Babbage wrote to Ada Lovelace in 1843, while she worked beside him on his Analytical Engine, and begged her to put the world and all its troubles out of her mind. In the same letter he gave her a nickname for her gift with figures. What did he call her?
answer: The Enchantress of Number
choices: The Enchantress of Number
The Queen of Engines
The Lady of Algebra
The Mistress of Looms
context: Babbage wrote: 'Forget this world and all its troubles... but the Enchantress of Number.' The two worked closely on his proposed calculating machines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_Lovelace

question: Ada Lovelace wanted to show that Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine could handle any kind of symbol, not just numbers. She borrowed an image from the textile trade, where stiff cards punched with holes told a machine what to do. Which machine did she point to?
answer: The Jacquard loom
choices: The Jacquard loom
The spinning jenny
The cotton gin
The water frame
context: Lovelace grasped that the Jacquard loom's punched cards could let a machine manipulate symbols, not just crunch numbers — a startling leap toward the modern idea of a programmable computer. The spinning jenny, water frame, and cotton gin were other famous textile machines of the era, but only the Jacquard loom was run by punched cards. Source: https://www.computerhistory.org/babbage/adalovelace

question: Charles Babbage faced the same question from Members of Parliament again and again: if his calculating machine were fed wrong numbers, would it still give right answers? His memoir says he could not even grasp the muddled thinking behind it. His reply is remembered as an early form of which computing rule?
answer: 'Garbage in, garbage out'
choices: 'Garbage in, garbage out'
'Move fast and break things'
'The customer is always right'
'Measure twice, cut once'
context: From Babbage's 1864 memoir Passages from the Life of a Philosopher. A machine only ever does what it is told — feed it wrong figures and it faithfully produces wrong answers. Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Babbage/quotations/

question: Ada Lovelace set out in 1843, in the last of her notes on Charles Babbage's never-built Analytical Engine, how the machine could work through a calculation step by step on its own. That Note G is honoured today as the first computer program. What did it calculate?
answer: The Bernoulli numbers
choices: The Bernoulli numbers
The phases of the moon
Compound bank interest
The digits of pi
context: Note G was the last of a series of notes (A through G) Lovelace appended to her translation of a lecture on the Analytical Engine. While working it out she even caught a bug in Babbage's own underlying math. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Note_G

question: Alan Turing designed an electromechanical machine at Bletchley Park, Britain's secret codebreaking centre, during the Second World War. It whirred through millions of possible settings at speed to break Germany's main cipher, and breaking it is believed to have cut the war short. Which cipher did Turing's machine attack?
answer: The Enigma cipher
choices: The Enigma cipher
The Caesar cipher
The Morse cipher
The Vigenère cipher
context: Turing's machine was called the Bombe; the first was installed on 18 March 1940. It improved on an earlier Polish machine, the bomba kryptologiczna, built by Marian Rejewski's team, who had first broken into Enigma before the war and shared their work with Britain. Source: https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/second-world-war/how-alan-turing-cracked-the-enigma-code

question: John von Neumann credited one paper of 1936, On Computable Numbers, with the key idea behind every modern computer. Its author pictured a stripped-down device creeping along a paper tape without end, reading and writing symbols as a table of rules told it, and proved that one such device could run any computation whatever. What is that idea now called?
answer: A universal Turing machine
choices: A universal Turing machine
A stored-program machine
A finite-state machine
A logical computing machine
context: John von Neumann said 'the central concept of the modern computer was due to Turing's paper.' One machine that can carry out any computation is exactly what every modern computer does when it runs different programs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Turing_machine

question: Alan Turing took up the question of machine intelligence in 1950 and met an old doubt head-on: that a calculating engine 'has no pretensions whatever to originate anything' and does only what people order it to do. Charles Babbage's collaborator had set that doubt down a century before. What did Turing name it?
answer: The Lovelace objection
choices: The Lovelace objection
The Babbage objection
The Byron objection
The von Neumann objection
context: Turing named the challenge after Ada Lovelace, who first raised it, and answered it when arguing that machines might one day count as intelligent — for instance in his 1950 'imitation game,' the test now called the Turing Test. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_Lovelace

question: Delegates meeting in Philadelphia drew up the United States Constitution in 1787, fresh from a long war against a king, and they feared letting any one person or body hold all the power. So they split the federal government three ways. What job did they give Congress?
answer: Making the laws
choices: Making the laws
Judging the laws
Carrying out the laws
Vetoing the laws
context: Congress (Article I) makes the laws, the President (Article II) carries them out, and the courts (Article III) judge them — three branches so no single person holds all the power, and each can 'check' the others. Source: Cornell LII, Wex, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/separation_of_powers_0

question: The framers of the Constitution gave the President a veto over any bill he disliked, but they did not leave Congress helpless: it could still make the bill law without his signature. What did the framers decide must happen for Congress to override a veto?
answer: Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote for it again
choices: Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote for it again
The President changes his mind and signs it
The Supreme Court orders the President to sign
A simple majority of the House votes for it once more
context: A veto override requires a two-thirds majority in BOTH chambers — a very high bar, which is why overrides are rare. Source: Constitution Annotated, Art. I Sec. 7, https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S7-C2-2/ALDE_00013645/

question: George Washington vetoed only two bills in his eight years as President, and only when he believed a bill broke the Constitution. His first veto came on 5 April 1792. What kind of bill did it kill?
answer: A bill dividing up House seats among the states
choices: A bill dividing up House seats among the states
A bill raising taxes on imported tea
A bill building a new national capital
A bill creating a standing army
context: Washington vetoed an apportionment bill, saying it broke the Constitution's own rule of no more than one representative per 30,000 people. He was sparing with the power — only TWO vetoes in eight years. Source: Avalon Project, Washington's Veto Message, April 5, 1792, https://avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/gwveto1.asp

question: Representatives in the House voted in 1998 to impeach President Bill Clinton, formally accusing him of wrongdoing. Both chambers of Congress had a part in removing an official. What part did the Senate have to play?
answer: Holding the trial and voting whether to remove the official
choices: Holding the trial and voting whether to remove the official
Choosing which official gets accused
Signing the accusation into law
Picking the judge who will hear the case
context: The House accuses; the Senate judges. It takes a two-thirds Senate vote to convict and remove someone. Source: Constitution Annotated, Art. I Sec. 3, https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S3-C6-5/ALDE_00000710/

question: Senator Edmund Ross of Kansas rose in a silent Senate chamber in 1868 to cast the deciding vote at the trial of President Andrew Johnson. The House had impeached Johnson after a bitter quarrel with Congress over Reconstruction, and conviction needed two-thirds of the senators. What did Ross say?
answer: "Not guilty"
choices: "Not guilty"
"Guilty"
"I abstain"
"Present"
context: Ross's vote left the count one short of the two-thirds (36) needed to convict, so Johnson stayed in office. The charge: Johnson had fired Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act. Source: U.S. Senate, https://www.senate.gov/about/powers-procedures/impeachment/impeachment-johnson.htm

question: Members of the House of Representatives impeached Donald Trump in 2019 and again in 2021. Before him the House had impeached only two presidents, Andrew Johnson in 1868 and Bill Clinton in 1998. What happened to all three in the end?
answer: None was convicted, so none was removed from office
choices: None was convicted, so none was removed from office
All three were convicted and forced to resign
Two were removed and one resigned first
All three were barred from ever holding office again
context: No U.S. president has ever been removed from office by impeachment — the two-thirds Senate bar has never been met for a president. Source: Britannica, https://www.britannica.com/topic/Which-US-Presidents-Have-Been-Impeached; History.house.gov, https://history.house.gov/Institution/Origins-Development/Impeachment/

question: Woodrow Wilson put his name to a treaty, but under the Constitution a treaty binds the nation only when two-thirds of the Senate approve it. The senators refused to approve Wilson's treaty twice, in 1919 and 1920. Which treaty was it?
answer: The Treaty of Versailles
choices: The Treaty of Versailles
The Louisiana Purchase treaty
The Treaty of Ghent
The Panama Canal treaty
context: By rejecting the Treaty of Versailles (38-53 in 1919, 49-35 in 1920), the Senate kept the United States out of the League of Nations entirely. The Senate's 'advice and consent' can override the President on foreign agreements. Source: U.S. Senate, https://www.senate.gov/about/powers-procedures/treaties/senate-rejects-treaty-of-versailles.htm

question: The men who wrote Article I of the Constitution gave Congress several checks on the President, and many call one of them the strongest of all. Which check is it?
answer: Cutting off the money for a war the President has ordered
choices: Cutting off the money for a war the President has ordered
Blocking the judges the President wants to appoint
Rejecting a treaty the President has signed
Overriding a bill the President has vetoed
context: The 'power of the purse' is Congress's control over spending: Article I forbids any money being drawn from the Treasury except by a law Congress passes. So even a war the President has ordered must be funded by Congress — one of the legislature's strongest checks on the executive. Blocking judges, rejecting treaties, and overriding vetoes are real Congressional checks too, but the 'purse' means the money. Source: Cornell LII, Constitution Annotated, https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution-conan/article-1/section-1/separation-of-powers-and-checks-and-balances

question: James Madison explained the logic of the Constitution's checks in the fifty-first of the Federalist papers, and the United States has never replaced that Constitution, amending it only 27 times. Scholars found that the typical national constitution written since 1789 survived only about 19 years before being scrapped. Roughly how long has the American one lasted?
answer: More than 230 years
choices: More than 230 years
More than 60 years
More than 110 years
More than 160 years
context: America's constitution has lasted more than 230 years — over ten times the roughly 19-year median the study found — and has been amended only 27 times. Study: Elkins, Ginsburg & Melton, 'The Endurance of National Constitutions,' https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1536925

question: Catholic bishops met in the mountain city of Trent, in northern Italy, to answer Martin Luther, and in April 1546 their council declared one Bible alone to be authentic scripture. Only the Church, they ruled, could approve new translations. Which Bible did they choose?
answer: The Latin Vulgate translated long before by Saint Jerome
choices: The Latin Vulgate translated long before by Saint Jerome
A fresh Italian translation made by the council itself
Martin Luther's recent German translation
The original Greek text owned only by the pope
context: Decreed in April 1546, Trent named the Latin Vulgate, translated centuries earlier by Saint Jerome, as the sole authentic scripture, and ruled that the Church alone could authorize new translations. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Council_of_Trent/

question: The bishops at Trent took aim at a real rot inside their own Church: many priests had little training, and some bishops drew the revenues of dioceses they had never even seen. They then told every diocese to build one new institution. What was it?
answer: A seminary to train its priests
choices: A seminary to train its priests
A printing house for Bibles
A hospital for the poor
A court to try heretics
context: Trent's biggest real reform ordered every diocese to build a seminary and required bishops to actually reside in their dioceses rather than collect income from afar. Source: https://www.saet.ac.uk/Christianity/CouncilofTrent

question: The pope's legates seized on a typhus scare in 1547 to shift the Council of Trent to Bologna, a city of the Papal States beyond Emperor Charles V's influence. Charles wanted the council where he could reach it. How did he answer the move?
answer: Forbidding his own bishops to follow it to Bologna
choices: Forbidding his own bishops to follow it to Bologna
Sending his army to occupy the city of Bologna
Declaring himself the new head of the council
Quietly agreeing and moving his court to Bologna too
context: Furious at the move, Charles V forbade his bishops to follow; the Bologna sessions produced no decrees and the council stalled for years before resuming back at Trent. Source: https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/the-persistent-council

question: Martin Luther taught that a person is saved by faith alone, sola fide. The bishops at Trent struck straight back: good works alongside faith, they decreed, preserve a believer's justice and even increase it. Decree after decree closed with one fearsome Latin word aimed at whoever denied it, meaning cursed and cut off. What was the word?
answer: Anathema
choices: Anathema
Indulgentia
Purgatorium
Transubstantio
context: Trent decreed: 'If any one saith that the justice received is not preserved and also increased before God through good works... let him be anathema.' Anathema means cursed or cut off, and it closes decree after decree. Source: https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/9-things-you-should-know-about-the-council-of-trent/

question: Gian Lorenzo Bernini carved a marble showpiece of the Baroque for a church in Rome between 1647 and 1652, as Catholic artists answered the Protestants who had smashed images. It catches a vision Teresa of Avila wrote of: an angel thrusting a golden, fire-tipped spear into her heart. The pain, she said, was so sweet that she could not wish to be rid of it. What is the sculpture called?
answer: The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa
choices: The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa
The Anathema of Saint Teresa
The Coronation of Saint Teresa
The Martyrdom of Saint Teresa
context: Bernini's marble Ecstasy of Saint Teresa (1647-1652) sits in Santa Maria della Vittoria in Rome, where the Cornaro family watches from carved marble 'opera boxes' on the side walls. Teresa called the spear-vision the transverberation: 'so surpassing was the sweetness of this excessive pain, that I could not wish to be rid of it.' Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-Ecstasy-of-Saint-Teresa

question: Hugues de Payns gathered eight companions around 1118 to guard Christian pilgrims on the perilous road to Jerusalem. They took the vows of monks, poverty and chastity, yet each of them carried a sword and wore armour. What was their brotherhood called?
answer: the Knights Templar
choices: the Knights Templar
the Black Friars
the Swiss Guard
the Round Table
context: They were headquartered on the Temple Mount — hence 'Templars.' In 1147 Pope Eugene III let them wear a red cross, said to recall the blood they shed defending the Holy Land. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_Templar

question: Stephen of Cloyes, a French shepherd boy, marched thousands of children south to the port of Marseille in 1212, by a half-legendary account that historians still debate.
