He was certain God would work a miracle at the shore to bring them to the Holy Land. What did the children believe would happen there?
answer: the sea would split open
choices: the sea would split open
an angel would carry them
ships would appear from heaven
the walls would fall flat
context: They expected the Mediterranean to part like the Red Sea. It never did; by tradition many were stranded and some were sold into slavery, though modern historians debate how much of the tale is true. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children%27s_Crusade  (Legend.)

question: Fulcher of Chartres marched with the First Crusade and wrote down the reward Pope Urban II promised when he called Christian warriors east from Clermont in 1095. Anyone who died on the journey, or in battle against the enemy, would receive it at once. What was it?
answer: remission of all his sins
choices: remission of all his sins
a lordship in the Holy Land
a chest of Byzantine gold
a seat at the king's table
context: This spiritual promise was called an indulgence — the reward was forgiveness, not loot. Historians cite the real motives as protecting pilgrims, answering the Byzantine appeal for aid after the 1071 disaster at Manzikert, and the papal call itself. Source: https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/urban2-5vers.asp ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Urban_II

question: Enrico Dandolo, the blind Doge of Venice, some ninety years old, steered the knights of the Fourth Crusade against one city first, because they could not pay the 85,000 silver marks they owed Venice for their fleet. The crusaders sacked it to work off the debt. Which city was it?
answer: the Catholic city of Zara
choices: the Catholic city of Zara
the Muslim port of Acre
the Turkish city of Nicaea
the desert fortress of Damascus
context: Zara was a fellow Catholic Christian city — the first time a crusading army ever attacked other Catholics. Pope Innocent III briefly excommunicated the whole crusade for it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Fourth_Crusade/

question: Niketas Choniates, a Byzantine writer, watched the knights of the Fourth Crusade wreck the great church of Hagia Sophia when they sacked Constantinople in April 1204. They stripped its silver and made a mockery of the patriarch's own throne. By his account, what did they set on that throne?
answer: a drunken dancing prostitute
choices: a drunken dancing prostitute
a fully armored war-horse
a chained Greek bishop
a bronze statue of the Doge
context: Choniates wrote that a drunken woman sat in the patriarch's throne 'singing an obscene song and dancing,' while crusaders led mules into the sanctuary to cart off its silver and smashed the altar to bits. Source: https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/choniates1.asp ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Constantinople

question: Pope Innocent III had launched the Fourth Crusade himself, and in July 1204 he wrote a furious letter to his legate about its sack of Constantinople. The crusaders had spared neither the young nor the old, he wrote, neither men nor women, and had turned on Christians the swords they owed to the enemies of the faith. What did he say the Greeks now did, and with reason?
answer: detest the Latins more than dogs
choices: detest the Latins more than dogs
would never trust a Latin again
cursed the Pope who sent them
vowed to take back their city
context: Innocent wrote that the crusaders, 'dripping with Christian blood... have spared neither age nor sex' — so the Greeks 'with reason, detest the Latins more than dogs.' Even the Pope who began the crusade called the sack a scandal. Source: https://apholt.com/2016/10/28/pope-innocent-iii-reprimand-of-peter-a-papal-legate-for-the-sack-of-constantinople-july-1204/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Constantinople

question: Hormuzd Rassam pulled a small object of baked clay from beneath Esagila, the temple of Marduk in Babylon, in 1879. It is about nine inches long and covered in some 45 lines of cuneiform recounting the deeds of Cyrus the Great. What is it called?
answer: The Cyrus Cylinder
choices: The Cyrus Cylinder
The Babylon Tablet
The Marduk Scroll
The Esagila Stone
context: The Cyrus Cylinder, dug up by Hormuzd Rassam in 1879 from the foundations of the Esagila (the temple of the god Marduk) in Babylon, is a baked clay barrel about 22.5 cm long carrying roughly 45 lines of cuneiform. Source: britishmuseum.org object W_1880-0617-1941; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_Cylinder.

question: Cyrus the Great took Babylon and then, by his own clay record, rounded up the peoples that kings before him had carried off as captives, along with the statues of their gods that had been seized. What does Cyrus say he did with those peoples and their gods?
answer: Returned them to their own homes and temples
choices: Returned them to their own homes and temples
Melted their statues into a victory monument
Kept them as hostages inside Babylon
Sold them to merchants across the empire
context: Line 32 of the cylinder has Cyrus declaring 'I gathered all their inhabitants and returned to them their dwellings,' restoring the carried-off divine statues to their temples. The Book of Ezra credits Cyrus with the same policy toward the exiled Jews, letting them return and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem (for them it was the sacred Temple vessels, not god-statues, that were restored), though the cylinder itself never names Jerusalem or the Jews. Source: livius.org Cyrus Cylinder translation Line 32; biblicalarchaeology.org.

question: The Shah of Iran gave the United Nations a replica of Cyrus the Great's baked-clay record of his deeds in 1971, and promoted it as the world's first declaration of human rights. Irving Finkel, a British Museum scholar who knows the object well, refuses the label. What does Finkel say it really is?
answer: Royal propaganda about restoring peace, not a rights charter
choices: Royal propaganda about restoring peace, not a rights charter
A forged copy made for the Shah's 1971 festival
A legal contract between Cyrus and the priests
An early census of every people in the empire
context: Finkel says 'There are no human rights in antiquity' and calls the cylinder royal propaganda whose 'only concern is with restoring peaceful circumstances.' Scholars like Amelie Kuhrt note the brief text contains no formal statement of rights, and Jacob Wright argues it paints Cyrus too virtuously and glosses over his bloody conquests — so historians treat it as a genuine early experiment in imperial tolerance, not a modern rights charter. Source: peabody.yale.edu/news/finkel_talk; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_Cylinder.

question: Charles V declared Martin Luther an outlaw in May 1521, one any man might kill and go unpunished, and Frederick the Wise faked an ambush to hide him in Wartburg Castle. There Luther grew a beard and lived under a new identity. Who did he pass himself off as?
answer: A knight named Junker Jorg
choices: A knight named Junker Jorg
A wandering pilgrim from Rome
A traveling wine merchant
A village priest in exile
context: At Wartburg, disguised as Junker Jorg (Knight George), Luther translated the entire New Testament from Greek into German in about three months. Source: learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/5-minutes-in-church-history-with-stephen-nichols/junker-jorg; worldhistory.org/article/1900/luthers-speech-at-the-diet-of-worms/

question: Martin Luther stood before Emperor Charles V at Worms in April 1521, ordered to take back his books, and refused: his conscience, he said, was held captive by the Word of God. Schoolbooks end his speech with 'Here I stand. I can do no other. God help me. Amen.' What do historians say about that famous ending?
answer: Those words were added later and are missing from the earliest records
choices: Those words were added later and are missing from the earliest records
He shouted it in German, then again in Latin
He wrote it as the title of his next book
He spoke it kneeling before the emperor
context: The conscience reply is documented, but the celebrated 'Here I stand' tag does not appear in the earliest accounts of what Luther actually said. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diet_of_Worms; worldhistory.org/article/1900/luthers-speech-at-the-diet-of-worms/  (Legend.)

question: William the Conqueror sent his officials across the whole of England in 1086 to write down who held every estate, field and farm animal. The English gave the result a grim nickname: the Last Judgement allowed no appeal, and neither did this book. What was it called?
answer: The Domesday Book
choices: The Domesday Book
The Conqueror's Roll
The Iron Ledger
The Winchester Writ
context: Around 1179 the royal treasurer Richard FitzNeal explained in the Dialogus de Scaccario that the survey was named for the Day of Judgement: 'from it, as from the Last Judgement, there is no further appeal.' Its word could not be denied or set aside without penalty. (Dialogus de Scaccario c.1179, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book)

question: A jury of local men swore to each entry as William the Conqueror's great survey reached their district in 1086. William fixed exactly who sat on every such jury, so that the record could not be rigged. How was each jury made up?
answer: Half English and half Norman
choices: Half English and half Norman
Entirely the king's own clerks
Only the wealthiest local lords
Only sworn churchmen and bishops
context: Splitting each jury half English, half Norman meant neither the conquered nor the conquerors could fix the record alone — an early example of England's precocious centralized administration and rule-of-law instinct. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Inquisition)

question: Oklahoma families headed outdoors on 14 April 1935 under a clear blue morning sky. At 2:49 that afternoon, something swept in from the north at as much as 60 miles an hour and made eyewitnesses think the world was ending. What was it?
answer: A black wall of dust 500 to 600 feet high
choices: A black wall of dust 500 to 600 feet high
A line of tornadoes touching down
A flash flood off the river
A swarm of locusts blotting the sun
context: This was Black Sunday, the most famous dust storm of the Dust Bowl. The rolling black 'duster' swallowed farms so completely that people groped for the walls of their own homes. Source: NWS Norman OK (weather.gov/oun/events-19350414); Wikipedia, 'Black Sunday (storm)'.

question: Robert Geiger, a reporter for the Associated Press, was caught in the great dust storm that struck the southern plains on 14 April 1935. His report the next day gave the whole stricken region a name that stuck for good. What did he call it?
answer: the Dust Bowl
choices: the Dust Bowl
the Big Blow Country
the Dead Plains
the Brown Frontier
context: Geiger's April 15, 1935 wire story coined 'the dust bowl,' and the name became permanent. Source: Wikipedia, 'Black Sunday (storm)'; mentalfloss.com/black-sunday-dust-bowl-storm.

question: One Great Plains farmer tore up 50 acres of prairie in a single day while wheat was booming in the First World War, where a team of horses could manage 3. The buffalo grass he ploughed under had roots reaching down as far as five feet that had pinned the soil in place. What machine let him do it?
answer: the gasoline tractor with a disc plow
choices: the gasoline tractor with a disc plow
the steam-powered cotton gin
the horse-drawn seed drill
the windmill water pump
context: During the WWI wheat boom, gasoline tractors with disc plows let farmers turn under millions of acres of deep-rooted sod. With nothing to anchor it, the dried topsoil blew away. Source: encyclopedia.com (Dust Bowl); PBS Ken Burns, 'The Great Plow-Up'.

question: Hugh Bennett, a soil scientist, went before Congress in the spring of 1935 to beg for money against the dust storms, and he picked his moment so that a cloud of plains dust darkened the Capitol windows while he talked. A senator looked up and remarked, 'It does look like dust.' What did Congress do soon afterward?
answer: passed the Soil Conservation Act, creating a permanent Soil Conservation Service
choices: passed the Soil Conservation Act, creating a permanent Soil Conservation Service
ordered the army to plant trees across Oklahoma
banned all tractor farming on the plains
declared a national day of prayer for rain
context: Bennett's perfectly timed testimony helped pass the Soil Conservation Act in 1935, founding the Soil Conservation Service, which eventually bought back over 10 million acres to return to grassland. Source: boundarystones.weta.org/2012/11/19/hugh-bennett-and-perfect-storm.

question: Khalid ibn al-Walid, legend says, held his ground at the battle of Mu'tah so fiercely that it earned him the name Sword of Allah, Sayf Allah. He was remembered as never once beaten in battle. What did he do at Mu'tah, by the legend?
answer: He broke eight swords in his hands
choices: He broke eight swords in his hands
He fought on after losing both eyes
He held the bridge entirely alone
He slew the enemy king in single combat
context: The legend says Khalid ibn al-Walid shattered eight swords holding the line at the Battle of Mu'tah, earning 'Sayf Allah' (the Sword of Allah); he is remembered as undefeated. Told here as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Yarmuk; studioarabiya.com/the-sword-of-allah

question: The Persians drove about 33 war elephants into the Arab ranks at al-Qadisiyyah, during four days of battle in November 636. The Muslim soldiers found a way to turn the giant beasts against their own side. What did they do to the elephants?
answer: Blinded them and cut their trunks
choices: Blinded them and cut their trunks
Set their tower-howdahs on fire
Dug pits to topple them over
Fed them poisoned river water
context: The Muslims learned to blind the elephants and sever their trunks and girths; the panicked beasts stampeded back through the Persian ranks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_al-Qadisiyyah

question: The Arab victors at al-Qadisiyyah seized the Derafsh-e Kaveyan, the jewel-studded war banner that Persia's kings had carried, the holiest prize of the whole Sasanian empire. The banner bore one great jewel at its centre. What became of that jewel?
answer: It was cut up and the pieces sold in Medina
choices: It was cut up and the pieces sold in Medina
It was set into the new ruler's crown
It was hurled into the Tigris by the last shah
It was hidden in a desert tomb and lost
context: The captured Derafsh-e Kaveyan (Flag of Kaveh) had its great jewel cut up, and the pieces were sold off in Medina — the sacred banner of Persia dismantled and scattered. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_al-Qadisiyyah

question: Muhammad bin Qasim, then a young general, marched his army through Makran in 711 and took Sindh, in the same year that Tariq ibn Ziyad led his men over the strait into Spain. In one year the conquests touched both ends of the known world. Where is Sindh?
answer: On the Indus River in India
choices: On the Indus River in India
On the Nile in Egypt
On the Danube in Europe
On the Volga in the steppe
context: Sindh sits on the Indus valley; so in one year, 711, the conquests touched both Spain and India — the Atlantic edge and the Indus edge of the known world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Muslim_conquests

question: Arab armies poured out of Arabia after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632 and struck at the two great powers of the day, Byzantium and Sasanian Persia. Historians point to one reason both gave way so fast. What state were the two empires in when the Arabs struck?
answer: Exhausted from a long war against each other
choices: Exhausted from a long war against each other
Split by a sudden outbreak of plague
Leaderless after both emperors died young
Frozen in place by an unusually harsh winter
context: Byzantium and Sasanian Persia had bled each other white in the war of 602-628, so both were spent when the Arabs struck. The resulting empire stretched from the Atlantic in Spain to the Indus — about 13 million sq km, the largest the world had yet seen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Muslim_conquests

question: Boris Yeltsin, a rising Soviet politician, walked unannounced into a Randall's grocery in Houston in 1989 and spent twenty minutes in its aisles, among some 30,000 everyday products. Nothing in the Soviet Union came close to that plenty. What did Yeltsin suspect about the store?
answer: That it had been specially staged to fool him
choices: That it had been specially staged to fool him
That the goods were reserved only for officials
That the prices were secretly subsidized
That the food on the shelves was counterfeit
context: Yeltsin could not believe an ordinary American shop stocked that much for any shopper; on the flight afterward his aide Lev Sukhanov said 'the last vestige of Bolshevism collapsed inside him,' and Yeltsin asked aloud, 'What have they done to our people?' He warned that if Russians saw such stores 'there would be a revolution.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_visit_by_Boris_Yeltsin_to_the_United_States

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that without buying and selling there were no real prices for capital, so a state owning every factory could not know whether it used its resources well. Soviet practice bore out his warning: a price agency set around 24 million prices by hand, and still each year's plan could balance only a sliver of the goods. Roughly how many goods could the plan balance?
answer: Around 2,000 goods
choices: Around 2,000 goods
Around 2 million goods
Around 200 goods
Around 20 million goods
context: Gosplan's annual plan covered material balances for only about 2,000 goods (around 200,000 once every ministry was counted) out of roughly 24 million distinct items the economy produced — so almost the entire economy ran on guesswork. Friedrich Hayek added the deeper objection: the knowledge of millions of changing local needs can never be gathered into one office. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet-type_economic_planning

question: Nikita Khrushchev once complained that planning by weight gave the country chandeliers heavy enough to bring down the ceilings. A famous Soviet parable tells of a nail factory given its quota by weight, whose managers met the plan perfectly with something useless to anyone. What did the factory make?
answer: One single gigantic nail
choices: One single gigantic nail
A pile of bent scrap nails
Thousands of identical hammers
A stack of empty crates
context: Told as a parable (a teaching story rather than a documented event), it shows the calculation problem in miniature: with no real prices, a tonnage target was met by forging one enormous useless nail — and when planners switched the quota to quantity, the factory churned out millions of tiny worthless pins instead. Khrushchev himself griped that tonnage targets produced chandeliers so heavy 'they pull the ceilings down on our heads.' Source: https://kyytpress.substack.com/p/the-parable-of-the-soviet-nail-factory  (Legend.)

question: Guy de Maupassant put his name to a protest in Le Temps in 1887 that called Gustave Eiffel's unfinished iron tower useless and monstrous. Yet a beloved legend says he later ate lunch nearly every day in the tower's own restaurant. Why there, of all places, by the story?
answer: It was the one spot in Paris from which he could not see the tower he hated
choices: It was the one spot in Paris from which he could not see the tower he hated
It was the only restaurant in Paris that would still serve a man who had insulted it
It was the cheapest meal a struggling writer could find anywhere in the city
It was the only place high enough to escape the noise of the crowded streets
context: Maupassant had signed the 14 February 1887 protest in the newspaper Le Temps alongside Alexandre Dumas fils and Charles Garnier (architect of the Paris Opera). The lunch story is a beloved legend, told to mock how the tower took over the Paris skyline. Source: thevintagenews.com / toureiffel.paris.

question: Gustave Eiffel held a permit for his iron tower that ran only twenty years, and from 1 January 1910 Paris had the right to pull it down and sell the iron as scrap. Eiffel found a way to make the tower too useful to lose. How did he save it?
answer: He turned it into a giant radio antenna
choices: He turned it into a giant radio antenna
He turned it into a giant lightning rod
He turned it into a giant water tower
He turned it into a giant clock face
context: Wireless telegraphy experiments began on the tower in 1898, and by 1908 it transmitted signals up to 3,700 miles. In World War I its radio station even intercepted a coded German message about 'Operative H-21' that helped convict the spy Mata Hari. Source: history.com 'eiffel-tower-survival' / toureiffel.paris.

question: Thomas Edison backed direct current (DC) in the War of the Currents that broke out over wiring America in the 1880s. Nikola Tesla and the businessman George Westinghouse backed alternating current (AC). AC won, and it powers the world's grid today for one big reason. What could AC do that DC could not?
answer: Travel long distances at high voltage
choices: Travel long distances at high voltage
Run completely silent, without any hum
Work without any copper wire at all
Be made far more cheaply from coal
context: AC can be stepped up to high voltage with transformers and sent for hundreds of miles; Edison's DC fizzled out after less than a single mile. That is why AC runs the whole planet's power grid. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/what-was-the-war-of-the-currents

question: Michael Faraday built the first machine that turned electricity into steady motion in 1821, the seed of every electric motor since. In his tiny device, what spun round and round?
answer: A wire circling a magnet
choices: A wire circling a magnet
A glass globe full of sparks
A wheel hung with spinning keys
A copper coil dipped in acid
context: This homopolar motor, a wire endlessly spinning around a magnet, made Faraday the inventor of the electric motor, ten years before his even greater discovery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: Nikola Tesla was strolling through a park in Budapest in 1882, reciting Goethe's poems aloud to a friend, when the whole design for an alternating-current motor came to him at once. He had no paper on him. How did he capture the design right then?
answer: He drew it in the dirt with a stick
choices: He drew it in the dirt with a stick
He scratched it onto his shirt cuff
He recited it aloud as a new verse
He carved it into a wooden park bench
context: The rotating magnetic field is what lets a motor spin on alternating current. Tesla said the whole design appeared to him complete in that instant in the park. Source: https://teslasciencecenter.org/pivotalmoments/alternating-current/

question: Humphry Davy, the chemist, gave his famous public lectures at the Royal Institution in 1812, and a young London bookbinder named Michael Faraday, hungry for a life in science, sat in the audience. Afterward Faraday sent Davy something to win his notice. What did Faraday make and send him?
answer: His own notes, bound into a handsome book
choices: His own notes, bound into a handsome book
A jar of chemicals he had mixed himself
A long letter begging for any position
A small model of one of Davy's experiments
context: Faraday took careful notes at the lectures and bound them into a beautiful 300-page volume. Davy hired him as a laboratory assistant at the Royal Institution in 1813. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: Nikola Tesla set up a strange laboratory high in Colorado Springs in 1899 to prove that electricity could be sent through the air without wires. One night he switched on his giant Tesla coil, a machine as tall as a house. What did the coil hurl out, crackling up to 135 feet across the room?
answer: Bolts of man-made lightning
choices: Bolts of man-made lightning
A churning wall of white smoke
A blinding shower of sparks
Ribbons of blue flame up the walls
context: Tesla's artificial bolts reached up to 135 feet (41 m), and the crash was reportedly heard 15 miles away, all in the service of his dream of beaming power wirelessly. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla_Experimental_Station

question: Michael Faraday wound two coils of wire on opposite sides of an iron ring in 1831, never touching. He flicked the current in the first coil on and off, and each time a pulse of electricity leapt up in the other coil. What deep rule had he uncovered, the rule behind every electric generator since?
answer: A changing magnetic field creates electric current
choices: A changing magnetic field creates electric current
Electricity always flows from hot metal to cold metal
Two magnets pushed together will store a charge
Coiled wire slowly leaks its electricity into the air
context: This is electromagnetic induction: a moving or changing magnetic field makes electric current flow. Every power station on Earth still works on the principle Faraday found that day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday

question: Falling water at Niagara Falls drove the world's first great hydroelectric plant when it opened in 1895, turning out Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse's alternating current. The power ran 26 miles down a copper line, proof that electricity made in one place could be used far away. What did it do at the far end?
answer: Light up the city of Buffalo
choices: Light up the city of Buffalo
Run the streetcars of New York City
Power the docks of Chicago's harbor
Light the lamps of Toronto across the lake
context: Power made at a waterfall lit a city 26 miles away, the proof that electricity could travel. Two years earlier AC had also lit the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, after Westinghouse underbid General Electric. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/what-was-the-war-of-the-currents

question: George Westinghouse signed a deal with Nikola Tesla in 1888 that promised Tesla $2.50 for every horsepower of alternating-current power the world would ever make. That contract could have made Tesla history's first billionaire. When Westinghouse's company nearly went broke, what did Tesla reportedly do with that contract?
answer: He tore it up to save the company
choices: He tore it up to save the company
He sold it to a rival for quick cash
He sued Westinghouse for every cent
He locked it away and bided his time
context: By reportedly tearing up the royalty contract, Tesla traded a future fortune for a lump sum so Westinghouse could survive, an act of loyalty that may have cost him a billionaire's wealth. Source: https://www.celebritynetworth.com/articles/entertainment-articles/in-1897-nikola-tesla-tore-up-a-contract-that-would-have-made-him-the-worlds-first-billionaire/

question: Thomas Edison had once spoken out publicly against the death penalty. Yet in the late 1880s, to scare the public away from his rival Nikola Tesla's alternating current, he staged gruesome traveling shows meant to prove how deadly that current could be. What did Edison electrocute in front of the crowds?
answer: Live animals
choices: Live animals
Convicted criminals
Wax dummies wired to coils
Iron statues packed with gunpowder
context: Edison publicly electrocuted animals and quietly helped develop the electric chair using an AC generator, so that execution could be nicknamed being 'Westinghoused', turning his rival's own technology into propaganda against it. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/what-was-the-war-of-the-currents

question: Abraham Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation on New Year's Day 1863, while the Civil War went on, declaring free the people held in slavery in the rebel states. He chose its most quoted words to sound permanent, not provisional. What were they?
answer: Thenceforward, and forever free
choices: Thenceforward, and forever free
Loosed from every earthly chain
Restored to their God-given liberty
Delivered out of the house of bondage
context: The exact phrase from the document is 'thenceforward, and forever free.' Lincoln chose words meant to sound permanent, not provisional. Source: Avalon Project, Yale Law School (full text), https://avalon.law.yale.edu/19th_century/emancipa.asp

question: Free and enslaved Black Americans packed churches across the country as 1862 ended, many of them gathering in secret, and prayed as midnight approached, the hour the Proclamation would take effect. People still keep that vigil each New Year's Eve. What is it called?
answer: Watch Night
choices: Watch Night
Jubilee Eve
Morning Star service
The Midnight Cry
context: Watch Night, also called Freedom's Eve, traces back to the Moravians and the Methodist preacher John Wesley, but December 31, 1862, gave it new meaning as the wait for emancipation. The tradition is still kept. Source: NMAAHC, The Historical Legacy of Watch Night, https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/stories/historical-legacy-watch-night

question: An officer read out the Proclamation beneath the live oaks at Camp Saxton to the First South Carolina Volunteers, a regiment of former slaves. As the flag passed into their hands, an old man struck up a song in a cracked old voice; two women took it up unasked, then the whole crowd. What song was it?
answer: 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee'
choices: 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee'
'Go Down, Moses'
'The Battle Hymn of the Republic'
'Roll, Jordan, Roll'
context: Colonel Thomas Wentworth Higginson, who commanded the regiment, wrote that the spontaneous singing 'seemed the choked voice of a race, at last unloosed.' Sources: NPS, Camp Saxton, https://www.nps.gov/places/camp-saxton.htm ; UChicago Press, Higginson's Civil War Journal, https://press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/333302.html

question: Gordon Granger, a Union general, rode into Galveston, Texas, in 1865 and announced that every slave was free, for news of the Proclamation had taken two and a half years to reach far-off Texas. That day became America's oldest annual celebration of the end of slavery. What is it called?
answer: Juneteenth
choices: Juneteenth
Emancipation Day
Jubilee Day
Freedom Sunday
context: On June 19, 1865, Granger's order reached the last enslaved people in Texas; the holiday's name — Juneteenth — blends 'June' and 'nineteenth.' Sources: American Battlefield Trust, General Order No. 3, https://www.battlefields.org/learn/primary-sources/general-order-no-3 ; National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/news/articles/juneteenth-original-document

question: As he took up his pen to sign the Emancipation Proclamation on New Year's Day 1863, Abraham Lincoln told those present he had never felt more certain that he was doing right. If his name ever went into history, he said, it would be for this act. How did he finish the thought?
answer: My whole soul is in it
choices: My whole soul is in it
Let the nation be cleansed
The debt of two centuries is paid
Now the war has a meaning
context: Lincoln's full line: 'I never, in my life, felt more certain that I was doing right, than I do in signing this paper... and my whole soul is in it.' He signed, looked up, and said simply, 'That will do.' Sources: American Battlefield Trust, 10 Facts; NPS, https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/10-facts-emancipation-proclamation ; https://www.nps.gov/articles/the-emancipation-proclamation.htm

question: Lincoln wrote more into the Emancipation Proclamation than a promise of freedom for those held in slavery in the rebel states. He added a clause aimed straight at winning the war. What path did that clause open to freed Black men?
answer: Enlisting as Union soldiers and sailors
choices: Enlisting as Union soldiers and sailors
Working Union supply depots for wages
Settling land seized from the plantations
Voting in Union-occupied Southern towns
context: The Proclamation declared that freed men 'will be received into the armed service of the United States to garrison forts... and to man vessels of all sorts.' Nearly 200,000 Black soldiers and sailors went on to fight for the Union. Sources: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/emancipation-proclamation ; NPS, https://www.nps.gov/articles/the-emancipation-proclamation.htm

question: Lincoln confided to his cabinet that the Proclamation's timing honoured a vow he had made to God. He had solemnly promised, he said, to answer one turn of the war by declaring the slaves free. On what condition had he made that vow?
answer: If General Lee was driven back from Pennsylvania
choices: If General Lee was driven back from Pennsylvania
If the Mississippi River fell to the Union
If Richmond surrendered before the new year
If England refused to recognize the South
context: Lincoln's words, recalled by historian James M. McPherson: 'I made a solemn vow before God, that if General Lee was driven back from Pennsylvania, I would crown the result by the declaration of freedom to the slaves.' Source: NPS, The Emancipation Proclamation, https://www.nps.gov/articles/the-emancipation-proclamation.htm

question: Frederick Douglass waited with a great crowd in Boston's Tremont Temple on 1 January 1863, while messengers hurried between the hall and the telegraph office for word of the Proclamation. Midnight came and went with no news. How did Douglass describe what they were waiting for?
answer: Like a bolt from the sky that would rend the fetters of four million slaves
choices: Like a bolt from the sky that would rend the fetters of four million slaves
Like a long-promised harvest finally ripe for the reaping
Like a single candle held against two centuries of darkness
Like a debt the whole nation had at last agreed to pay
context: Douglass wrote that they waited 'as for a bolt from the sky, which should rend the fetters of four millions of slaves... longing for the answer to the agonizing prayers of centuries.' When the news finally arrived, the hall erupted in song. Source: NPS / Frederick Douglass Papers Project, https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/douglass-emancipation-boston.htm

question: Organizers of a charity fair for wounded soldiers received Abraham Lincoln's signed original of the Emancipation Proclamation after the war, to raise money. The copy the National Archives keeps today is a neatly engrossed one he also signed. One catastrophe destroyed the original for good. What was that catastrophe?
answer: The Great Chicago Fire of 1871
choices: The Great Chicago Fire of 1871
A flood that swept the Ohio River valley
A boiler explosion aboard a Mississippi steamer
A robbery at the charity fair
context: The fair was held in Chicago, and the signed draft burned in the Great Chicago Fire of October 1871. The neatly copied, Lincoln-signed engrossed version now held by the National Archives is what survives. Source: The Legal Genealogist (cross-checked against National Archives holdings), https://www.legalgenealogist.com/2012/10/08/up-in-flames/

question: Lincoln knew a president had no power to abolish slavery with a stroke of the pen, so he rested the Proclamation on his authority as commander-in-chief. In the document itself he gave the act a name of its own. What did he call it?
answer: A fit and necessary war measure
choices: A fit and necessary war measure
A solemn act of national justice
A proclamation of universal liberty
A sacred duty owed to the enslaved
context: By calling it 'a fit and necessary war measure for suppressing said rebellion,' Lincoln anchored emancipation in his war powers — the only legal hook that let him free anyone without Congress. Source: National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/emancipation-proclamation

question: Henry V faced the French at Agincourt in October 1415 with an outnumbered English army of longbowmen and men-at-arms. For every man-at-arms in his ranks, how many longbowmen were there?
answer: About five archers to every man-at-arms
choices: About five archers to every man-at-arms
About one archer to every man-at-arms
About two crossbowmen to every archer
About three knights to every archer
context: Roughly 5,000 longbowmen stood beside only about 1,000 men-at-arms — five of every six men were archers. The common bowman, not the mounted noble, had become the heart of the English army. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt

question: A longbowman of the Hundred Years War stood his war bow on end beside him. Shaped from one length of yew, it dwarfed any sporting bow. How tall was it?
answer: About 6 feet — as tall as the man himself
choices: About 6 feet — as tall as the man himself
About 3 feet — up to his waist
About 4 feet — up to his chest
About 10 feet — twice his height
context: The longbow was cut from a single stave of yew and stood roughly six feet, as tall as or taller than the archer drawing it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: An English longbowman nocked an arrow made not to slash flesh but to drive through the mail and plate armour of a knight. Its head was a short, narrow steel spike, square in section, built for that one job. What was this arrowhead called?
answer: A bodkin point
choices: A bodkin point
A broadhead point
A barbed point
A blunt point
context: The bodkin was a thin square-section steel spike designed to pierce armour. The arrows themselves ran about 30 inches long. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: Each bowman in Henry V's line at Agincourt in 1415 drove something into the mud in front of him. Any French knight who rode at the line would impale his horse on it or see the animal shy away. What did each archer plant?
answer: A sharpened wooden stake angled toward the enemy
choices: A sharpened wooden stake angled toward the enemy
A small iron caltrop with spikes
A deep hidden pit
A tall woven wicker screen
context: The angled stakes turned the archers' position into a hedge of spikes that broke the cavalry charge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt

question: A bowyer cutting a war bow from a yew stave left the pale sapwood along the back of the bow, away from the archer, and the dark heartwood on the belly, facing him. The two woods did opposite jobs, so the one stave acted like a spring. What was the sapwood on the back good at resisting?
answer: Being stretched as the bow bends
choices: Being stretched as the bow bends
Being squashed as the bow bends
Rotting in the rain
Catching fire from a spark
context: Sapwood resists stretching (tension) on the back; heartwood resists squashing (compression) on the belly. One piece of wood works like a laminate spring. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: Henry VIII lost his warship the Mary Rose off Portsmouth in 1545, and the war bows later raised from her wreck turned out far heavier to draw than the 40 to 50 pounds a modern Olympic archer pulls. Roughly how much force did one of them take to draw?
answer: About 150 pounds
choices: About 150 pounds
About 60 pounds
About 25 pounds
About 500 pounds
context: Mary Rose bows are estimated at about 150-160 pounds, some up to ~185 — three to four times the pull of a sporting bow today. The ship sank in 1545. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: French knights in full plate armour advanced across a ploughed field at Agincourt that rain had churned into a bog, and they sank knee-deep as they came. When knights lost their footing in the crush of bodies, what became of many of them?
answer: They suffocated or drowned in the mud before rising
choices: They suffocated or drowned in the mud before rising
Their squires dragged them back to safety
They cut themselves free and escaped on foot
They lay frozen where they fell until dawn
context: Armoured knights sank to their knees; when they fell in the press of bodies, many were trampled, suffocated, or effectively drowned in the mud before they could rise. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt

question: The French paid some 6,000 crossbowmen from Genoa to fight at Crécy in 1346, and the English longbowmen badly outshot them. A trained longbowman could keep loosing arrows while a crossbowman wound his weapon for the next shot. Roughly how many arrows a minute could the longbowman send?
choices: 2 to 3
About 60
context: Without their pavise shields and spare bolts, the Genoese shot exposed and outranged, then fled — and French knights rode down their own retreating crossbowmen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy

question: English archers at Agincourt, a popular legend says, jeered at the beaten French by waving the fingers the French had vowed to hack off any bowman they took. No medieval source records the gesture. Which fingers did the archers wave, in the story?
answer: The index and middle fingers
choices: The index and middle fingers
The thumb and index finger
The three middle fingers
The ring finger and little finger
context: Legend: archers waved the two bow-fingers (index and middle) in defiance. But it is unrecorded medievally — the chronicler Jean de Wavrin says the threat was to cut off THREE fingers, and the gesture story only appears from the 1970s. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V_sign

question: Edward III ordered every fit Englishman in 1363 to spend his holidays shooting at the butts, because it took a lifetime to make an archer. His law also banned one popular game that pulled men away from the practice. Which game was it?
answer: Football
choices: Football
Chess
Singing in taverns
Horse-racing
context: The 1363 law required holiday archery practice and banned idle games like football that lured men away from the butts. A longbowman took a lifetime to make; a crossbowman, only weeks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: A messenger came to Edward III at Crécy in 1346, where the king was watching the battle from a windmill: his 16-year-old son, the Black Prince, was hard pressed, and the messenger begged him to send help. Edward refused. What did he famously say?
answer: 'Let the boy win his spurs'
choices: 'Let the boy win his spurs'
'Order the archers to fall back'
'Bring the prince to me at once'
'Sound the trumpets for retreat'
context: Froissart's fuller line: 'suffer him this day to win his spurs, for if God be pleased, I will this journey be his, and the honour thereof.' The prince held and won renown. Source: https://x.com/LandsknechtPike/status/1960608786416120295

question: Archers of Henry VIII went down with the Mary Rose in 1545, men who had hauled a heavy war bow since boyhood, and the strain had reshaped their bones. Nearly one man in five among the skeletons raised from the wreck bore the same mark. What was it?
answer: A twisted, over-built left arm and shoulder
choices: A twisted, over-built left arm and shoulder
Thickened collarbones and a curved spine
A worn, flattened right shoulder socket
Spurred and curled finger bones
context: The bones show an over-built left arm, twisted spine, bone spurs, and a flat-socketed shoulder blade (os acromiale) in about 19% of the crew — the signature of drawing a war bow since childhood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow

question: The gods of the Epic of Gilgamesh shape a hairy wild man named Enkidu to be a match for Gilgamesh, the mighty king of Uruk. Before Enkidu ever sees a city, he lives far out in the wild. Whom does he live among there?
answer: The wild animals, eating grass beside the gazelles
choices: The wild animals, eating grass beside the gazelles
A roaming band of desert shepherds
A hidden village of mountain hermits
The soldiers of a forgotten frontier fort
context: Enkidu lived covered in hair, ate grass with the gazelles, and drank at the waterhole alongside the beasts -- a man raised by animals. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh; SparkNotes Gilgamesh summary.

question: Enkidu walks into Uruk and plants himself in a doorway, square across the path of King Gilgamesh. The two giants grapple and wrestle, and Gilgamesh wins the fight. What happens between the two of them next?
answer: They become inseparable best friends
choices: They become inseparable best friends
Gilgamesh throws Enkidu into the city dungeon
Enkidu flees back into the wilderness forever
Gilgamesh makes Enkidu his lowly servant
context: Enkidu's strength so impressed Gilgamesh that the two became inseparable -- their friendship is the heart of the whole story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh; worldhistory.org/gilgamesh.

question: Gilgamesh pulls up a thorny plant from the bottom of the sea, one that can make an old man young again. He lays it aside to bathe, a snake slips up and swallows it, and Gilgamesh goes home empty-handed. The storytellers use this to explain something real snakes do. What is it?
answer: Snakes shed their old skin
choices: Snakes shed their old skin
Snakes grow a whole new set of fangs
Snakes flick their tongues to taste the air
Snakes can swallow prey bigger than their heads
context: As the snake slid away it shed its skin -- which the storytellers said is why snakes renew themselves, while Gilgamesh went home empty-handed. Told as legend, the ancient explanation for a real animal trait. Source: worldhistory.org, The Eternal Life of Gilgamesh.

question: Gilgamesh strides into the opening lines of his epic as the mightiest of kings, the man who raised the great walls of Uruk. The poem says he is part god and part man. How much of him does it call divine?
answer: Two thirds
choices: Two thirds
One half
One quarter
Nine tenths
context: The poem calls him 'two thirds divine and one third mortal.' His mother was the goddess Ninsun and his father the priest-king Lugalbanda. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh; Wikiquote Epic of Gilgamesh (Andrew George 2000).

question: Ishtar demands that Gilgamesh marry her, and when he refuses and mocks her, she unleashes the Bull of Heaven on Uruk in her rage. Enkidu grabs the bull by the tail while Gilgamesh drives an axe into its skull. Then Enkidu adds one last insult for the goddess watching from the walls. What does he do?
answer: He tears off the bull's haunch and hurls it up at Ishtar
choices: He tears off the bull's haunch and hurls it up at Ishtar
He drinks a horn of wine in front of her
He carves her name into the dead bull's hide
He drags the carcass to the temple steps
context: Enkidu flung the bull's haunch up at Ishtar as she watched from the city walls. Ishtar had threatened to smash the gates of the underworld and let the dead devour the living if refused. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh; worldhistory.org.

question: Gilgamesh and Enkidu march to the Cedar Forest to fight its giant guardian, the monster Humbaba. The sun-god Shamash sends thirteen great winds that pin the monster down and blind him. Beaten, Humbaba begs the two heroes for mercy. What do they do to him?
answer: They cut off his head
choices: They cut off his head
They spare him and take his oath
They chain him and haul him to Uruk
They leave him blinded in the forest
context: Despite Humbaba's pleas, the two heroes beheaded the forest guardian. Source: worldhistory.org; k12.hillsdale.edu abridged Gilgamesh.

question: George Smith, a British Museum scholar who was self-taught, was piecing together a broken clay tablet from Nineveh in 1872. Out of the fragments came a flood story: a boat come to rest on a mountain, and a bird sent out to look for dry land. What did Smith do right then?
answer: He leaped up and ran round the room
choices: He leaped up and ran round the room
He bolted out to telegraph the news to a rival
He locked the tablet in a drawer that night
He smashed the case glass grabbing for it
context: Smith was so overcome he ran about the room and even began tearing at his clothes. He had found a Babylonian flood story older than the Bible's, and announced it on December 3, 1872, to an audience that included prime minister William Gladstone. Source: National Geographic, 'Discovering Gilgamesh'; Smithsonian Magazine 'Epic Hero'.

question: Gilgamesh weeps over the body of his friend Enkidu for six days and seven nights and lets no one bury him, as if his grief could bring him back. What finally makes him give up the body, struck with terror that he too must die?
answer: A maggot drops from Enkidu's nose
choices: A maggot drops from Enkidu's nose
The body begins to glow at dawn
A vulture circles down over the corpse
The gods send a dream commanding it
context: Seeing the maggot, Gilgamesh accepts that death is final -- and is struck with terror of his own death, which sends him searching for immortality. Source: SparkNotes Tablets 8 & 9; learner.org, 'Experts' View: Enkidu's Death.'

question: Utnapishtim, the man who lived through the great flood, tells Gilgamesh how he found dry land. One after another he let three birds fly from his stranded boat: the dove returned to him, the swallow returned too, but the third stayed away, for the waters had gone down. Which bird was it?
answer: A raven
choices: A raven
An eagle
A falcon
A heron
context: The raven found the waters gone and never came back. Afterward Utnapishtim sacrificed, and the gods crowded around the sweet smell 'like flies.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh_flood_myth; Wikiquote Tablet XI (Andrew George 2000).

question: A god orders Utnapishtim to pull down his house and use its timber for a boat to ride out the coming flood, a boat to carry his family, his craftsmen and the animals. The vessel he builds is not shaped like any ordinary ship. What shape is it?
answer: A giant cube with seven levels inside
choices: A giant cube with seven levels inside
A long, narrow war-galley
A round basket of woven reeds
A flat raft of lashed logs
context: Each side measured 120 cubits, its floor covered the area of a whole field, and it held seven levels divided into compartments. He loaded family, craftsmen, and animals before the waters came. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh_flood_myth; shmoop.com Tablet 11.

question: George Smith read out the flood story from his Nineveh tablet in 1872, and Victorian London was stunned, for the tale sounded so familiar: a god warned one man, who built a boat for his household and the beasts; it came to rest on a mountain, and birds went out to find land. Which story does the Gilgamesh flood closely match?
answer: Noah's Ark in the Book of Genesis
choices: Noah's Ark in the Book of Genesis
Deucalion's flood in Greek myth
Manu and the fish in Hindu myth
Atlantis sinking in Plato's tale
context: The two flood stories share the boat, the rescued animals, the mountain landing, and the released birds. The Gilgamesh version was written down centuries before the Hebrew one -- a fascinating resonance between two ancient peoples. Source: biblicalarchaeology.org; National Geographic.

question: A scribe-priest shaped the standard Babylonian version of the Epic of Gilgamesh out of far older tales, and he finished it around 1200 BC. Among the stories of the ancient world, that version is unusual in one way. What sets it apart?
answer: Its author is one of the few from antiquity we can name
choices: Its author is one of the few from antiquity we can name
It was sung from memory and never written down
It was set down by a king, not by a scribe
It was pressed into gold tablets, not into clay
context: The scribe-priest Sin-leqi-unninni wove together the standard Babylonian version between roughly 1300 and 1000 BCE -- making him one of the earliest authors in all of history whose name we still know, when nearly every other ancient story comes down to us anonymous. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh; worldhistory.org/gilgamesh.

question: The freed Hebrew slaves had no roads or maps when Moses led them out of Egypt into the trackless desert. The story says God went ahead to lead the way, with a sign that looked one way by day and another by night. What guided the Israelites through the wilderness?
answer: A pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night
choices: A pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night
A great white star by day and a burning torch by night
A circling eagle by day and a golden lamp by night
A long trumpet blast by day and a steady drum by night
context: By day a pillar of cloud and by night a pillar of fire went before them so they could travel at any hour. Source: Exodus 13:21-22 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parting_of_the_Red_Sea).

question: Moses and his brother Aaron walked into the court of the Pharaoh of Egypt carrying a single demand from the God of the Hebrew slaves. Thousands of years later, that same line would become a rallying cry. What did Moses and Aaron demand of Pharaoh?
answer: Let my people go
choices: Let my people go
Lower our daily quota
Give back our stolen land
Spare our newborn sons
context: The full demand was 'Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness.' Pharaoh sneered back, 'Who is the LORD, that I should obey him? I do not know the LORD.' Source: Exodus 5:1-2 (https://www.biblestudytools.com/bible-study/topical-studies/who-hardened-pharaohs-heart-in-exodus.html).

question: Hebrew families daubed lamb's blood on their door frames on the night of the last plague. The story says the LORD struck down Egypt's firstborn sons that night, but what He did at the marked houses named a festival. What did He do there?
answer: He passed over them
choices: He passed over them
He sealed them shut
He set them aflame
He turned away from them
context: Because the LORD 'passed over' the blood-marked houses (Exodus 12) and spared everyone inside, the festival has been called Passover ever since; each family had killed a lamb and painted its blood on the door frame with hyssop.

question: Aaron, the brother of Moses, threw his shepherd's staff down on the floor of Pharaoh's court to prove the power of the God of the enslaved Israelites, and it became a snake. Pharaoh's own court magicians scoffed and threw down their staffs, and those turned into snakes too. Then one thing happened that settled whose power was greater. What did Aaron's snake do?
answer: It swallowed up all of the magicians' snakes
choices: It swallowed up all of the magicians' snakes
It spat fire across the whole throne room
It coiled itself around Pharaoh's high throne
It grew as long as the great hall itself
context: Aaron's serpent devoured all the magicians' serpents. Later, when the magicians could not even copy the plague of gnats, they admitted to Pharaoh, 'This is the finger of God.' Source: Exodus 7:10-12 (https://biblehub.com/exodus/7-12.htm).

question: Trapped against the sea with Pharaoh's chariots thundering up behind them, the Israelites watched Moses stretch out his hand. A strong east wind blew the waters back all night, and the people crossed on the dry seabed between two standing walls of water. Then the whole Egyptian army charged in after them across the seabed. What happened to the Egyptians' war-chariots as they drove?
answer: Their wheels jammed and clogged
choices: Their wheels jammed and clogged
Their wheels snapped off
Their wheels sank into the sand
Their wheels caught fire
context: God 'clogged the chariot wheels' so the Egyptians drove with difficulty; then the wind dropped, the walls of water collapsed, and the sea returned over Pharaoh's army. Source: Exodus 14:21-28 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parting_of_the_Red_Sea).

question: Moses had been gone forty days up on Mount Sinai, and the restless people below gave up waiting for him. They pressed Aaron to melt down their gold earrings into an idol, and they bowed down to it. Moses's fury when he came back is famous, but it is what he did to the idol itself that nobody forgets. What did Moses do to it?
answer: He ground it to powder and made the people drink it
choices: He ground it to powder and made the people drink it
He threw it into a fire and burned it to ash
He buried it in the sand and marked the spot
He smashed it apart and handed back the gold
context: Moses burned the calf, ground it to powder, scattered it on water, and made the Israelites drink it. The people had declared of the idol, 'This is your god, O Israel.' Source: Exodus 32 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_calf).

question: Herding sheep on Mount Horeb, Moses came upon a bush wrapped in flame that burned but never turned to ash. A voice called to him out of the fire and sent him to free the Hebrew slaves. Moses asked the voice for a name to give the people. What name did it give?
answer: I AM WHO I AM
choices: I AM WHO I AM
I am the God of your fathers
I am the First and the Last
I am the Light of the World
context: In Hebrew the name is 'ehyeh asher ehyeh' (Exodus 3:14), not a label for one god among many but a statement of the self-existent One. God told Moses, 'Say to the people: I AM has sent me to you.'

question: The Israelites woke one morning, starving in the desert, to find the ground covered in thin white flakes like frost, food they believed God had rained down from heaven. They had never seen anything like it, and the name they gave it keeps, word for word, what they first said at the sight. What does the word 'manna' mean?
answer: What is it?
choices: What is it?
Is it bread?
Where is it from?
Who sent it?
context: The name comes from the people's own startled question, 'man hu?', meaning 'What is it?' God also sent flocks of quail to them in the evenings. Source: Exodus 16 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massah_and_Meribah).

question: Moses climbed alone to the top of Mount Nebo after forty years of leading the Israelites through the wilderness, and the Promised Land, the goal of the whole journey, lay spread out below him. He was an old man by then, a hundred and twenty years old. What happened to Moses there on the mountain?
answer: He was allowed to see the land but never to enter it
choices: He was allowed to see the land but never to enter it
He led the people down into the land at last
He chose to turn back into the desert alone
He vanished from the mountaintop in a cloud
context: Moses died at 120 on Mount Nebo, permitted to see the Promised Land but not to set foot in it, after the people had been sentenced to wander forty years. Source: Deuteronomy 34:1-7 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses).

question: Ancient Greek translators, turning the Hebrew scriptures into Greek, called the waters that Moses parted the 'Red Sea,' and the label stuck for two thousand years. Every English Bible still uses it, and generations of readers have pictured that sea. The original Hebrew calls it Yam Suph. What does Yam Suph mean?
answer: Sea of Reeds
choices: Sea of Reeds
Sea of Blood
Sea of Storms
Sea of the End
context: Yam Suph literally means 'Sea of Reeds'; the familiar 'Red Sea' comes from the later Greek translation, not the Hebrew. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parting_of_the_Red_Sea.

question: Joseph, who had died in Egypt centuries before the Exodus, had made his family swear a solemn oath: they were to remember him when God at last led them out of Egypt. On the chaotic night the Israelites fled, while everyone else was loading up silver and gold, Moses kept that ancient promise. How did he keep Joseph's oath?
answer: He carried his bones out with him
choices: He carried his bones out with him
He buried an empty coffin in his honor
He built a tomb for him in Egypt
He spoke his name over the people
context: The Israelites left in such haste their bread had no time to rise, and they 'plundered the Egyptians' of silver and gold; even so, Moses carried out the bones of Joseph, just as Joseph had made them swear generations earlier. Source: Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32 (https://www.esv.org/Exodus+13:19;Joshua+24:32/).

question: Benjamin Franklin had a bold idea in 1776 for the Great Seal of the brand-new United States: a picture of Moses raising his hand over the sea to drown Pharaoh and his chariots. Beneath the picture Franklin wanted a short, defiant motto. What motto did he propose for the seal?
answer: Rebellion to Tyrants is Obedience to God
choices: Rebellion to Tyrants is Obedience to God
These are the times that try men's souls
Give me liberty, or give me death
We hold these truths to be self-evident
context: Franklin's proposed seal showed 'Moses... extending his hand over the sea,' casting the American rebels as the freed Israelites and King George as Pharaoh. Thomas Jefferson separately proposed the Israelites in the wilderness led by a cloud and a pillar of fire. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Seal_of_the_United_States.

question: James Hargreaves, a Lancashire weaver, built the spinning jenny around 1764, a machine that spun many threads at once instead of one. A charming legend, never documented, says the idea came to him by accident inside his own cottage. What did he supposedly see?
answer: A spinning wheel knocked over, its spindle still turning upright
choices: A spinning wheel knocked over, its spindle still turning upright
His wife spinning faster than any neighbour in the village
A broken loom that wove two cloths instead of one
A water mill wheel turning steadily out his window
context: The story says his daughter knocked the wheel over and Hargreaves noticed the spindle kept spinning while standing upright, which suggested several spindles could stand in a row and spin together. It is a charming legend, not a documented fact. (britannica.com/biography/James-Hargreaves)

question: An angry mob broke into James Hargreaves's house near Blackburn in 1768 and smashed his spinning jennies, afraid the machines would rob the hand spinners of their living. Yet the rioters did not wreck every machine. Which jennies did they spare?
answer: Any jenny with twenty spindles or fewer
choices: Any jenny with twenty spindles or fewer
Any jenny owned by a poor widow
Any jenny that was still half-built
Any jenny made of oak rather than iron
context: The rioters judged only the bigger machines 'mischievous' enough to threaten their livelihoods, so they spared the smaller ones. Hargreaves fled south to Nottingham. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinning_jenny)

question: Richard Arkwright took out a patent on his water frame in 1769 and went on to build great cotton mills, but he did not start out as an engineer or a mill owner. What was his trade in the town of Bolton before he turned to spinning machines?
answer: A barber and wig-maker
choices: A barber and wig-maker
A blacksmith
A weaver
A clockmaker
context: Arkwright shaved chins and made wigs before patenting the water frame in 1769. He worked out the machine with clockmaker John Kay (the third choice's near-miss). (scienceandindustrymuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/richard-arkwright)

question: Workers at Richard Arkwright's Cromford mill, the world's first water-powered cotton-spinning mill, tended its machines on two thirteen-hour shifts from 1772. Put together, how long did the mill keep running each day?
answer: Around the clock, day and night
choices: Around the clock, day and night
Eighteen hours, then closed overnight
Two ten-hour shifts, twenty hours in all
Around the clock, but closed on Sundays
context: Two thirteen-hour shifts kept the machinery turning the full twenty-four hours. Sir Robert Peel testified the machines were often 'employed for the whole four-and-twenty hours.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromford_Mill)

question: Mill hands hurrying to Richard Arkwright's Cromford mill found its gates shut on the stroke of six, morning and evening, for the mill ran by the clock. A worker who turned up even a little late faced a harsh penalty. What was it?
answer: He lost that day's pay and was fined a second day's wages
choices: He lost that day's pay and was fined a second day's wages
He was sent home with a warning the first time
He had one hour docked from his pay
He was locked out for the rest of the week
context: A latecomer lost a day's pay for the work he missed AND was fined another day's pay on top of it. Strict clock discipline like this was new to workers used to setting their own pace at home. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromford_Mill)

question: Richard Arkwright filled his Cromford mill with workers from beyond the district, most of them women and children, and around the mill he laid out cottages for them, with shops, pubs, chapels and a school. What did this make Cromford?
answer: The first purpose-built factory village in the world
choices: The first purpose-built factory village in the world
The first English town with a public library
The first village in Britain lit by gas lamps
The first mill town served by its own railway
context: Arkwright built a whole village from scratch so his imported workforce would have somewhere to live next to the mill, the first factory housing development anywhere. His workforce was mostly women and children, the youngest only seven years old. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromford_Mill)

question: Richard Arkwright built the water-powered cotton mills that helped make Britain the workshop of the world, and by his death in 1792 he was one of the richest men alive. What was he said to be at his death?
answer: The wealthiest untitled man in Britain
choices: The wealthiest untitled man in Britain
The best-paid worker in all Lancashire
The largest landowner in Derbyshire
The richest man in the whole world
context: No lord or duke, just a former wig-maker, Arkwright died richer than any other commoner in the land. His factory model had spread across Britain. (scienceandindustrymuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/richard-arkwright)

question: Samuel Crompton worked in secret in a small room upstairs at a Bolton manor house, which he called his 'conjuring room', and around 1779 he finished a new spinning machine there. He named it the mule. Why did he give it that animal's name?
answer: Because it crossed two earlier machines, the jenny and the water frame
choices: Because it crossed two earlier machines, the jenny and the water frame
Because it was as stubborn as a mule to keep running
Because a real mule turned the wheel that powered it
Because Crompton had bred mules before he built it
context: A mule is the cross of a horse and a donkey, so Crompton's machine, which brought together Hargreaves' jenny and Arkwright's water frame, got the same name. Its sliding carriage rolled back and forth 54 inches and spun thread fine enough for muslin. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Crompton)

question: Edmund Cartwright patented the first power loom in 1785, bringing machines to weaving as they had come to spinning. He had never built a machine in his life before he toured Arkwright's mills in 1784. What had Cartwright been until then?
answer: A country clergyman
choices: A country clergyman
A retired sea captain
A Manchester cotton merchant
A blacksmith's apprentice
context: Cartwright was the rector of Goadby Marwood, a parish priest with no engineering training. His first loom barely worked, but by 1789 he had coupled an improved one to a Boulton and Watt steam engine. (britannica.com/biography/Edmund-Cartwright)

question: Samuel Slater, aged 21, slipped out of England in 1789 disguised as a farmhand and sailed for America with Arkwright's machine designs, though Britain allowed neither its textile machines nor its skilled mill hands to leave the country. How did Slater carry the designs past the ban?
answer: Entirely in his memory, with no drawings at all
choices: Entirely in his memory, with no drawings at all
Sewn into the lining of his coat
Hidden inside a hollow walking stick
Locked in a false-bottomed trunk
context: Slater memorized the whole machine and carried not a single plan, so nothing could be found on him. In Rhode Island his water-powered mill began spinning on 20 December 1790; back home in Belper his old neighbours branded him 'Slater the Traitor,' while Andrew Jackson later called him the 'Father of the American Industrial Revolution.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Slater)

question: Robert Blincoe wrote a memoir in 1828 of the beatings and starvation he had suffered as a London workhouse orphan, sent to the cotton mills at seven in 1799 and ending up at the notorious Litton Mill. Many argue that his story inspired a novel by Charles Dickens. Which one?
answer: Oliver Twist
choices: Oliver Twist
Hard Times
Great Expectations
David Copperfield
context: Blincoe's account of a beaten, half-starved workhouse orphan strongly echoes Dickens's most famous orphan, Oliver Twist. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blincoe)

question: Michael Sadler and his committee questioned 89 former child workers in 1832 about the textile mills, where they had toiled 12 to 16 hours a day. Late at night, the witnesses said, worn-out children fell asleep at their machines. What did the overseers do to them?
answer: Beat them to keep them awake
choices: Beat them to keep them awake
Doused them with cold water
Pinched and shook them hard
Made them stand on one leg
context: Children too tired to stay upright were beaten awake so the machines kept running. This testimony drove the Factory Act of 1833, which limited children's hours and, for the first time, sent government inspectors into the mills. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadler_report)

question: The owners of the cotton mills at Lowell, Massachusetts, slashed their mill girls' wages by 12.5 percent in February 1834. About 800 of the young women walked out, and the strike shook two of the town's banks. What did the mill girls do that shook the banks?
answer: Withdrew all their savings at once
choices: Withdrew all their savings at once
Refused to repay their store debts
Stopped depositing their weekly pay
Demanded their wages in gold coin
context: The mill girls lived in company boardinghouses on a strict bell schedule, with just thirty minutes each to rush home for breakfast and dinner. When 800 of them emptied their savings accounts at the same time, two banks faced a run. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell_mill_girls)

question: Alaric led his Visigoths through the walls of Rome on the night of 24 August 410 and looted the city, the first foreign army inside it in nearly 800 years. In Bethlehem, Jerome laid aside his scholar's work to mourn, and he caught the shock of it in a single line. What did Jerome write?
answer: "The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken."
choices: "The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken."
"Rome has fallen; now let the heavens fall with her."
"The wolves have entered the eternal city."
"Our mother is dead, and we are left orphans."
context: The sack of 410 was a psychological earthquake — Rome had not fallen to an outside foe since the Gauls centuries before. Jerome's grief captured the disbelief of an age that thought the city eternal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410)

question: King Gaiseric led his men into Rome in June 455, and they looted the city for two full weeks, even tearing the bronze roof tiles off the Temple of Jupiter. Centuries later, in the days of the French Revolution, a bishop in France made a new word for wild destruction from the name of Gaiseric's people. Which English word comes from them?
answer: Vandalism
choices: Vandalism
Sabotage
Pillage
Mayhem
context: Gaiseric's people were the Vandals; their two-week sack (2-16 June 455) became the byword for needless wreckage, and the term 'vandalism' was coined in 1794 by a French bishop describing revolutionary destruction. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(455)

question: Diocletian split the Roman Empire in two, east and west, sometime between 285 and 293, so that it would be easier to rule. One half collapsed in 476; the other, later called the Byzantine Empire, lived on for nearly a thousand years more. Which half survived?
answer: The eastern half
choices: The eastern half
The western half
Both fell in 476
Both survived to 1500
context: Diocletian's division is why we speak of a Western Roman Empire that 'fell' while the Eastern (later Byzantine) Empire lived on until 1453. The two halves drifted apart in wealth, language, and fortune. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/8-reasons-why-rome-fell

question: Romulus Augustulus, a boy of about ten, sat on the throne in 476 as the very last emperor of the West. Greek speakers had their own name for him, Momylus. What did 'Augustulus' mean?
answer: "Little Augustus" — a sneer at a powerless boy
choices: "Little Augustus" — a sneer at a powerless boy
"Second Augustus" — a hopeful new beginning
"Augustus reborn" — a sign from the gods
"Young Caesar" — an affectionate pet name
context: In Greek the mockery went further: he was called 'Momylus,' meaning 'little disgrace.' The grandest name in Rome had been turned into a playground taunt for a child who never truly ruled. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus

question: Theodoric the Great of the Ostrogoths asked Odoacer to a banquet at Ravenna in 493 to seal a peace between them, and there struck him dead with one blow of his sword. By tradition, Theodoric then gazed down at the dead man and made a grim remark. What did he say?
answer: "The wretch can't have had any bones in his body."
choices: "The wretch can't have had any bones in his body."
"Now Ravenna is mine, and all Italy with it."
"Let no man speak to me of mercy again."
"So perish every traitor who would be king."
context: The single-stroke killing and the boast are reported by tradition rather than proven fact, so they read as legend. Theodoric went on to rule Italy for over thirty years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodoric_the_Great

question: Odoacer set the last western emperor aside in 476, and to the Romans who lived through it his coup looked like one more change at the top. The year became the great turning point only centuries later, when one British historian fixed it in everyone's mind in his 1700s work 'The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire.' Who was he?
answer: Edward Gibbon
choices: Edward Gibbon
Peter Brown
Bryan Ward-Perkins
Alexander Demandt
context: Fifth-century Romans saw Odoacer's coup as ordinary politics; almost no one thought an empire had ended. It was Edward Gibbon, writing in the 1700s, who turned 476 into the grand symbol of Rome's fall that schoolchildren learn today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire

question: Julius Nepos, a rival emperor, kept the title in exile in Dalmatia after Romulus Augustulus lost his throne, and the eastern court still recognised him as the rightful emperor of the West until Ovida and Viator, two counts, murdered him near Salona four years later. Many historians say the last Western emperor therefore died later than 476. In what year did Nepos die?
context: Julius Nepos was still treated as the legitimate Western emperor in Constantinople after 476; the counts Ovida and Viator killed him at his villa near Salona on 9 May 480. By this reckoning the empire 'ended' in 480, not 476 — proof that even Rome's final date is debated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Nepos

question: Alexander Demandt, a German scholar, set out in 1984 to count every reason anyone had ever given for the fall of Rome, and he reached 210. Some sound sensible, such as invasions and money troubles; others sound strange. Which strange theory was really on his list?
answer: Romans bathed too much
choices: Romans bathed too much
Romans ate too much bread
Romans slept too little
Romans sang the wrong hymns
context: Demandt's catalogue of 210 reasons really does include excessive bathing and over-deforestation alongside the serious theories. The sheer length of the list is the lesson: honest history admits that the 'fall of Rome' has no single tidy cause. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire

question: A farmer in ancient Iraq led water onto his field from the Tigris or the Euphrates, the two great rivers of his country. Long afterwards the Greeks named that land Mesopotamia, from their words mesos and potamos. What does the name mean?
answer: the land between the rivers
choices: the land between the rivers
the valley below the mountains
the plain beside the salt sea
the gift of the flooding river
context: 'Mesopotamia' is Greek for 'the land in the middle of rivers' (mesos, 'middle' + potamos, 'river'). The two rivers are the Tigris and the Euphrates; both rise in the mountains of eastern Turkey and run down to the Persian Gulf. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Mesopotamia

question: A farmer near Ur watched the Euphrates spill over its banks one spring and flood his fields, for almost no rain ever fell in southern Mesopotamia. When the flood drained away, it left something on the ground that made the soil rich for free. What was it?
answer: a layer of river mud
choices: a layer of river mud
a drift of fine sand
a scatter of broken shells
a mat of dead reeds
context: Each flood spread a fresh coat of silt (river mud) over the fields, working like free fertilizer left behind by the water. The Tigris and Euphrates carried several times more silt for the same amount of water than the Nile did. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/9/agriculture-in-the-fertile-crescent--mesopotamia/

question: A Sumerian worker took his pay in grain and baked the same grain into his daily bread. It tolerated the salty, sun-scorched soil of southern Mesopotamia better than any other crop, while the finer grains were saved for beer and luxuries. Which grain was it?
answer: barley
choices: barley
wheat
millet
oats
context: Barley shrugged off the salty, sun-baked southern soil, so Sumerians treated it as everyday money and baked it into flatbread. Wheat and emmer were the fancier grains, saved for beer and luxury foods. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/9/agriculture-in-the-fertile-crescent--mesopotamia/

question: A Mesopotamian farmer watering his fields from irrigation channels raised far more grain than his own household could eat. Before farming, nearly every person had spent each day searching for food. What did a surplus like his free other people to do?
answer: take up crafts and trades of their own
choices: take up crafts and trades of their own
march off to conquer distant neighbors
wander away to live as roaming herders
stop all work and live in ease
context: Once a few farmers could grow more than they ate, everyone else was freed up to become potters, weavers, priests, scribes, and rulers. That division of labor is what defines a civilization, and scholars often point to Eridu as the place it first happened. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/9/agriculture-in-the-fertile-crescent--mesopotamia/

question: Reinhard Heydrich called fifteen senior Nazi officials to order at Wannsee, outside Berlin, on 20 January 1942, and they set to work on the Final Solution, their name for the murder of all Europe's Jews. How long did the whole meeting last?
answer: About 90 minutes
choices: About 90 minutes
About three days
About eight hours
About two weeks
context: Adolf Eichmann, who took the notes, later estimated the Wannsee Conference lasted 'between an hour and an hour and a half.' Fifteen men coordinated the murder of a continent's Jews in the time of a long lunch. Source: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/wannsee-conference-1942

question: Adolf Eichmann sat taking notes on 20 January 1942 as senior Nazi officials planned the murder of Europe's Jews, in a property the SS had bought as a private retreat. The place was every bit as pleasant as their plan was monstrous. What kind of building was it?
