answer: A lakeside villa
choices: A lakeside villa
A mountain fortress
An army barracks
A railway depot
context: The Wannsee Conference was held in a villa at Am Grossen Wannsee 56-58, on a lake in southwest Berlin. The setting was as ordinary and pleasant as the plan was monstrous. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wannsee_Conference

question: Adolf Hitler had already decided at the top that Europe's Jews would be murdered. The fifteen officials who met at Wannsee on 20 January 1942 were not there to argue over whether it would happen. What had they come to do?
answer: To coordinate HOW to do it across every ministry
choices: To coordinate HOW to do it across every ministry
To draft the legal decree that would authorize it
To prepare a public announcement of the new policy
To choose which single official would run it alone
context: The extermination decision was already settled. Wannsee existed only to coordinate the machinery -- to get every government ministry pulling together on the logistics of genocide. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/wannsee-conference-and-the-final-solution

question: Reinhard Heydrich chaired the meeting at Wannsee in January 1942 where senior Nazi officials organized the Final Solution, their plan to murder all of Europe's Jews, and even his fellow Nazis feared him. Adolf Hitler himself had a name for him. What did Hitler call Heydrich?
answer: The man with the iron heart
choices: The man with the iron heart
The fox of the desert war
The wolf of the U-boat fleet
The eagle of the Luftwaffe
context: Hitler called Heydrich 'the man with the iron heart.' He ran the conference that turned the Final Solution into an administrative program. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinhard_Heydrich

question: Senior Nazi officials took their seats around one table at Wannsee on 20 January 1942 to organize the murder of Europe's Jews, and ten of the fifteen had been to university. How many of the fifteen held doctorates?
answer: Eight of the fifteen
choices: Three of the fifteen
Eight of the fifteen
Eleven of the fifteen
All fifteen of them
context: Eight of the fifteen attendees held doctorates, and ten had a university education. Educated, lettered men administered genocide as paperwork. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wannsee_Conference

question: The officials at Wannsee listened in January 1942 as Reinhard Heydrich set out whom the Final Solution would target, and his count of Jews did not stop at the lands German armies held. How far did his list reach?
answer: Into neutral nations like Sweden, Switzerland, and Ireland
choices: Into neutral nations like Sweden, Switzerland, and Ireland
Into Soviet territory as far as the Ural Mountains
Into Jewish communities across the United States
Into every nation of North and South America
context: Heydrich's eleven-million figure counted Jews in Britain, Ireland, Switzerland, Sweden, Spain, Portugal, and Turkey -- nations beyond Nazi reach. The plan was the murder of every Jew on the continent, occupied or not. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/wannsee-conference-and-the-final-solution

question: Two British-trained agents, Jozef Gabčík and Jan Kubiš, lay in wait on a sharp curve of a Prague street on 27 May 1942 as Reinhard Heydrich, the chairman of Wannsee, came toward them in his open Mercedes. Gabčík's gun jammed. What did Kubiš do?
answer: Threw a grenade at the car
choices: Threw a grenade at the car
Drew a sword on Heydrich
Set the car on fire
Fired a hidden rifle
context: In Operation Anthropoid, Jan Kubis threw a grenade when the gun jammed. Heydrich died of his infected wounds on June 4, 1942. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Reinhard_Heydrich

question: SS men at the death camps of Treblinka, Sobibor and Belzec, in occupied Poland, carried out a murder campaign named for the dead Reinhard Heydrich: Aktion Reinhard. About how many people did that campaign kill?
answer: About 1.7 million
choices: About 1.7 million
About 17,000
About 170,000
About 17 million
context: The murder operation at Belzec, Sobibor, and Treblinka was code-named Operation Reinhard (Aktion Reinhard), named in memory of the slain Wannsee chairman. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/operation-reinhard-einsatz-reinhard

question: Adolf Eichmann drew up a chart for Wannsee that listed every country's Jews like stock on a warehouse shelf; it entered Ukraine's Jews, for one, as 2,994,684. About how many people did the whole chart add up to?
answer: About 11 million
choices: About 11 million
About 1 million
About 30 million
About 100 million
context: Eichmann's table listed Ukraine's Jews at 2,994,684 -- almost three million human beings entered as a single bureaucratic figure in a spreadsheet of intended victims. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wannsee_Conference

question: Adolf Eichmann kept the minutes at Wannsee, and nowhere in them did the words murder or kill appear. Deportation became evacuation to the East, and Jews worked until they died on road-building gangs were described in words that sounded almost like accounting. What was the phrase?
answer: Dropping out through 'natural diminution'
choices: Dropping out through 'natural diminution'
Suffering 'an unavoidable accident'
Quietly 'lost to enemy action'
Becoming 'casualties of the campaign'
context: The protocol said able-bodied Jews on road-building would have 'a large number undoubtedly drop out through natural diminution.' Deportation itself was called 'evacuation to the East.' The euphemism was the point -- clean words for an unspeakable act. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wannsee_Conference

question: The men at Wannsee even planned what to do with the toughest Jews who might survive being worked to death in the labour gangs. Such survivors, their protocol said, were to be 'treated accordingly,' a phrase that meant murder. What reason did the protocol give?
answer: Freed, they could become 'the seed of a new Jewish revival'
choices: Freed, they could become 'the seed of a new Jewish revival'
Freed, they would testify against the Reich before the world
Freed, they would demand all the back wages owed to them
Freed, they could not be fed during the wartime shortages
context: The protocol reasoned that any 'remnant' surviving the labor, if freed, could become 'the germ cell of a new Jewish revival' -- and so had to be destroyed too. The logic of total extermination, written plainly. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wannsee_Conference

question: Adolf Eichmann testified at his trial in 1961 that near the end of the Wannsee meeting, while butlers went round with cognac, the men set their polite words aside. What did he say they then spoke about openly?
answer: Methods of killing, liquidation, and extermination
choices: Methods of killing, liquidation, and extermination
How to divide up the murdered Jews' property
Which ministries were dragging their feet
How to deceive the foreign press about the deportations
context: Eichmann testified that over the cognac 'they minced no words at all... they spoke about methods of killing, about liquidation, about extermination.' The written minutes buried that plain truth under euphemism. Source: holocausthistoricalsociety.org.uk/contents/naziseasternempire/wannseeconference.html

question: SS men set about burning the copies of the Wannsee minutes as the Reich fell, roughly thirty in all, to destroy every trace of the plan. How many copies survived the war?
answer: Just one
choices: Just one
About half of them
All thirty copies
None at all
context: Only a single copy survived -- copy No. 16, stamped 'Secret Reich Matter!' U.S. prosecutor Robert Kempner found it in 1947 in seized German Foreign Office files. That one document is the chief proof the conference ever happened. Source: encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/wannsee-protocol

question: Hannah Arendt, a philosopher, watched Israel try Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem in 1961, and she saw not a monster but a fussy, colourless clerk who insisted he had merely followed orders. What phrase did she coin for the crimes of such ordinary functionaries?
answer: The banality of evil
choices: The banality of evil
The triumph of the will
The cult of obedience
The machinery of hatred
context: Hannah Arendt called it 'the banality of evil' -- the chilling lesson that thoughtless, ordinary bureaucrats, not raving fanatics, administered genocide. It is the load-bearing warning of Wannsee: evil can wear an office suit. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eichmann_in_Jerusalem

question: Pope Urban II called the knights of Europe at the Council of Clermont in 1095 to march east and free Jerusalem. By the account of the chronicler Robert the Monk, the crowd roared two Latin words back at him, and Urban told them to carry the cry into battle. What did they shout?
answer: "Deus vult!" — "God wills it!"
choices: "Deus vult!" — "God wills it!"
"Memento mori!" — "Remember death!"
"Pax vobis!" — "Peace to you!"
"Veni, vidi!" — "I came, I saw!"
context: The cry became the rallying phrase of the whole crusading movement. Source: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, Urban II at Clermont, Robert the Monk version (sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/source/urban2a.asp).

question: Knights who answered Pope Urban II's call in 1095 swore a public vow to march east and win Jerusalem back from Muslim rule. Each man then wore a sign of that vow where everyone could see it. How did he show he had taken it?
answer: He sewed a cloth cross onto his outer clothing
choices: He sewed a cloth cross onto his outer clothing
He shaved the crown of his head bald
He carried a sealed letter from the Pope
He wore an iron ring on his sword hand
context: The cloth went on the right shoulder or between the shoulders, so they were called 'crucesignati' — 'those signed with the cross' — and from this came the very word 'crusade.' Source: Wikipedia, Crusades (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades); Crusading movement.

question: Godfrey of Bouillon turned down the crown of the new kingdom of Jerusalem, which the crusaders offered him after they took the city in July 1099. By legend, he gave one reason for refusing to be king. What did Godfrey say?
answer: That he would not wear a crown of gold where Christ had worn a crown of thorns
choices: That he would not wear a crown of gold where Christ had worn a crown of thorns
That only the Pope in Rome had the right to crown a king
That he had sworn never to rule a city he had not been born in
That a soldier should never become a lord while the war went on
context: Godfrey took instead the title 'Advocate (Defender) of the Holy Sepulchre.' Source: Wikipedia, Godfrey of Bouillon (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godfrey_of_Bouillon); Siege of Jerusalem (1099).

question: Peter Bartholomew, a peasant marching with the starving crusaders at Antioch in 1098, said that Saint Andrew had come to him in a vision and shown him where a holy relic lay hidden under a church floor. His comrades dug beneath St Peter's Church on 14 June and found it, and the army took heart and broke the siege. What did they find?
answer: The Holy Lance — the spear that pierced Christ's side
choices: The Holy Lance — the spear that pierced Christ's side
The Crown of Thorns from the crucifixion
A nail from the True Cross
The shroud that had wrapped Christ's body
context: The 'discovery' inside the Church of St Peter rallied the starving crusaders to break the siege. Source: Wikipedia, Peter Bartholomew (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Bartholomew); Britannica, Siege of Antioch 1097-1098.

question: Guglielmo Embriaco, a Genoese commander, faced a problem outside Jerusalem in 1099: the defenders had felled every tree around the city, and the crusaders needed timber for siege towers. Embriaco found the wood. What did he do to get it?
answer: He dismantled his own ships at the coast and hauled the wood inland
choices: He dismantled his own ships at the coast and hauled the wood inland
He sailed back to Italy to fetch a fresh supply of lumber
He bought planks from merchants in nearby Egyptian towns
He had his men dig up old timbers from abandoned ruins
context: Embriaco took his ships apart at Jaffa and carried the timber overland to build two huge siege towers. Source: Wikipedia, Guglielmo Embriaco (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guglielmo_Embriaco); Siege of Jerusalem (1099).

question: A priest in the crusader camp outside Jerusalem told the army on 8 July 1099 that Bishop Adhemar, who was dead, had come to him in a vision and given orders. About 15,000 crusaders obeyed while the defenders jeered from the walls. What did they do?
answer: They walked barefoot in procession around the city walls
choices: They walked barefoot in procession around the city walls
They knelt and fasted in total silence for three days
They burned their siege engines as an offering
They sent their swords to be blessed at the river
context: The barefoot march ended on the Mount of Olives; the final assault came a week later. Source: Wikipedia, First Crusade (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade); Warfare History Network, Battle for Jerusalem.

question: Lethold of Tournai, a Flemish knight, fought from Godfrey of Bouillon's siege tower in the final assault on Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, and he won one famous honour that day. When the defenders saw what he had done, their line broke. What had Lethold done?
answer: He was the first crusader over the city wall
choices: He was the first crusader over the city wall
He cut down the commander of the garrison
He planted the crusader banner on the gate
He opened the main gate from the inside
context: Once Lethold was atop the wall, the defenders' line broke and the city fell. Source: Wikipedia, Ludolf of Tournai; Siege of Jerusalem (1099) (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(1099)).

question: Arnulf of Chocques, the crusade's chaplain, publicly called the peasant Peter Bartholomew a fraud and his relic from Antioch a fake, and many in the army doubted it too. In April 1099 Peter agreed to an ordeal to prove the relic true. What did he do?
answer: He walked a path between two walls of fire
choices: He walked a path between two walls of fire
He drank from a cup said to hold poison
He let himself be sealed alive in a tomb
He fought a champion chosen by the legate
context: Peter Bartholomew was terribly burned and died of his injuries twelve days later, on 20 April 1099. Source: Wikipedia, Peter Bartholomew (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Bartholomew).

question: Fulcher of Chartres and Ralph of Caen, two priests who marched with the First Crusade, set down with horror what happened at Ma'arra, a Syrian town the crusaders besieged late in 1098. The siege dragged on and their food ran out. What did some of the starving crusaders do?
answer: They cooked and ate the flesh of dead bodies
choices: They cooked and ate the flesh of dead bodies
They butchered and ate all of their warhorses
They poisoned the town's wells in revenge
They burned the survivors alive in the square
context: Fulcher of Chartres wrote that Christians ate the flesh of dead Muslims; Ralph of Caen described bodies cooked in cauldrons. Source: Wikipedia, Siege of Ma'arra (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Ma%27arra).

question: Raymond of Aguilers watched the crusaders storm Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 and butcher its Muslims and Jews. He tried to show the scale of the killing at the Temple of Solomon with one grisly image. What did he write?
answer: That men rode in blood up to their knees and bridle reins
choices: That men rode in blood up to their knees and bridle reins
That the streets were piled head-high with the dead
That the fires burned for seven days and nights
That not one living soul was left in the whole city
context: His line — 'in the Temple and porch of Solomon, men rode in blood up to their knees and bridle reins' — became the most quoted account of the massacre. Source: Wikipedia, Massacre of Jerusalem (1099), quoting Raymond of Aguilers.

question: Jerusalem's crusader conquerors made churches of Muslim holy places after 1099. They renamed the al-Aqsa Mosque, which stood on the Temple Mount, Templum Salomonis, Solomon's Temple, after the Temple that was thought to have stood on the site. Around 1120 a knightly order made the building its headquarters. Which order was it?
answer: The Knights Templar
choices: The Knights Templar
The Knights Hospitaller
The Teutonic Knights
The Order of Saint Lazarus
context: The crusaders renamed al-Aqsa 'Templum Salomonis' (Solomon's Temple), and the order took its very name — 'Templars' — from that 'Temple of Solomon' headquarters. Source: Wikipedia, Siege of Jerusalem (1099) (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(1099)).

question: Peter the Hermit, a preacher, gathered a ragtag People's Crusade of farmers and townspeople who had never trained to fight, and in 1096 he led it east across Europe, ahead of the trained armies. What became of this first wave?
answer: It set out and was wiped out before the knights' armies even reached the Holy Land
choices: It set out and was wiped out before the knights' armies even reached the Holy Land
It was made up of seasoned knights sent ahead as the army's vanguard
It captured the town of Civetot and held it until the main army arrived
It turned back to Europe after Peter the Hermit lost his nerve
context: The Seljuk Turks ambushed and slaughtered them at Civetot on 21 October 1096, where the knight Walter Sans Avoir — 'Walter the Penniless' — was killed, long before the main army reached the Holy Land. Source: Wikipedia, People's Crusade (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Crusade); Battle of Civetot.

question: Fierce defenders met the crusaders on the walls of Jerusalem on 15 July 1099. The old chroniclers gave huge death tolls, which modern historians treat as exaggerations, and the attackers' own losses were smaller than anyone might expect. About how many crusaders died, by the reckoning of the scholar Conor Kostick?
answer: About 3,000
choices: About 3,000
About 1,000
About 12,000
About 40,000
context: Modern historians treat the medieval death tolls (Ibn al-Athir claimed 70,000 defenders killed in al-Aqsa alone) as large exaggerations; the scholar Conor Kostick puts crusader losses at roughly 3,000. Source: Wikipedia, Siege of Jerusalem (1099); Madden 2005, Kedar 2004 cited therein.

question: Marian Rejewski, a Polish mathematician, went to work on the German Enigma cipher machine in December 1932, a full seven years before the war. He had no captured machine to open and not one stolen page, and its rotors could be wired inside in a huge number of ways. How did he work out the secret wiring?
answer: He deduced the wiring by pure mathematics, using the algebra of permutations
choices: He deduced the wiring by pure mathematics, using the algebra of permutations
He bribed a German clerk to photograph the factory blueprints
He took apart a machine smuggled out of Berlin in a diplomat's trunk
He guessed the wiring by listening to thousands of intercepted messages
context: Working from intercepted message patterns alone, Rejewski applied permutation group theory to reconstruct Enigma's rotor wirings without ever seeing inside the machine. Bletchley Park's I. J. Good later called this 'the mathematical theorem that won World War II.' Sources: ams.org/publicoutreach/feature-column/fcarc-enigma; militaryhistorynow.com/2018/10/04/marian-rejewski-meet-the-polish-cryptographer-who-cracked-germanys-top-secret-enigma-code-seven-years-before-ww2/

question: Fighters of the Polish Home Army rose up in Warsaw on 1 August 1944; they held out against the Germans for 63 days. Across the Vistula, Stalin kept his Red Army halted and let the city burn. Britain and America asked to fly supplies in to the fighters. What did Stalin do?
answer: He refused to let the Allied supply planes even land at Soviet airfields
choices: He refused to let the Allied supply planes even land at Soviet airfields
He sent Red Army tanks across the river to break the German lines
He ordered his own air force to parachute weapons into the city
He demanded the Home Army surrender to his troops instead
context: With his army idle across the river, Stalin blocked British and American planes from landing at Soviet bases, writing that the USSR would not 'associate themselves... with the adventure in Warsaw.' The rising was crushed: about 150,000 civilians and 20,000 Home Army fighters were dead, and Himmler ordered the city razed so that 'no stone can remain standing.' Sources: nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/allied-responses-warsaw-uprising-1944; britannica.com/event/Warsaw-Uprising

question: The carvers of Notre-Dame had set 28 stone figures in a row across its front. In 1793 revolutionaries clearing the cathedral for the new Cult of Reason hauled every one down and struck off its head, sure these were the monarchs of France. Whom had the carvers really meant them to show?
answer: Kings from the Old Testament of the Bible
choices: Kings from the Old Testament of the Bible
Saints of the early Christian church
Knights who had fought in the Crusades
Emperors of ancient Rome
context: The 28 figures on Notre-Dame's west front were Old Testament kings of Judah and Israel; the mob mistook them for kings of France and beheaded all 28. Statues of 'Liberty' were then set where the Virgin Mary and the saints had stood. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/notre-dame-fire-french-revolution

question: Revolutionaries turned Notre-Dame into a Temple of Reason on 10 November 1793. They tore out the altar and built a fake mountain topped by a little Greek temple, to worship Reason in place of God. Where the altar had stood, what did they set at the centre?
answer: A living woman dressed as the Goddess of Reason
choices: A living woman dressed as the Goddess of Reason
A marble statue of the writer Voltaire
A burning torch on an empty golden throne
A great open book holding the new laws
context: An actress in Republican blue-white-red was enthroned as the living Goddess of Reason, lit by a single 'torch of Truth,' as the centerpiece of the atheistic Cult of Reason meant to replace Christianity. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Reason and http://rodama1789.blogspot.com/2019/05/the-fete-de-la-raison-at-notre-dame.html

question: Madame Roland, one of the leaders of the moderate Girondins, rode in a cart to the guillotine in Paris on 8 November 1793. As she passed the statue of Liberty next to the scaffold, tradition says, she cried out a line that became the best-remembered judgment on the Revolution. What did she cry?
answer: 'O Liberty, what crimes are committed in thy name!'
choices: 'O Liberty, what crimes are committed in thy name!'
'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity, or else death!'
'Long live the Republic and death to all tyrants!'
'Show my head to the people; it is worth seeing.'
context: Legend: the line ('O Liberte, que de crimes on commet en ton nom!') is the traditional account of Madame Roland's last words, the most famous indictment of a revolution that killed in liberty's name. (The fourth option were the real last words of Georges Danton.) Sources: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Madame_Roland and https://www.thisdayinquotes.com/2023/11/o-liberty-what-crimes-are-committed-in-thy-name/

question: Maximilien Robespierre had signed away thousands of lives in the Terror. Then the Revolution turned on him: a pistol ball smashed his jaw one night, and the next day, 28 July 1794, he was overthrown. What happened to Robespierre himself?
answer: He was beheaded on the guillotine, the machine of his own Terror
choices: He was beheaded on the guillotine, the machine of his own Terror
He escaped Paris and lived out his days in exile
He seized total power and made himself dictator of France
He was set free and faded quietly into private life
context: The night before, when soldiers stormed the Hotel de Ville, a pistol shot shattered Robespierre's jaw; at the scaffold the executioner tore off the bandage, ripping the jaw loose, and the crowd cheered. He was killed as a declared outlaw, with no trial. About 21 of his allies died with him, including Saint-Just (the 'Archangel of the Terror'), the paralyzed Georges Couthon, and his own brother Augustin. The machine its leaders built consumed the leaders too. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2119/fall-of-maximilien-robespierre/

question: Deputies of the National Convention heard Maximilien Robespierre defend the mass killings in a speech of February 1794 called On Political Morality. The Terror, he claimed, did not betray the Revolution's ideals but grew right out of them. How did he define terror?
answer: As justice itself, prompt and inflexible, an emanation of virtue
choices: As justice itself, prompt and inflexible, an emanation of virtue
As a hard medicine that heals the sick body of the nation
As the shield that guards the Republic from hidden enemies
As the price of freedom, paid now so that peace can follow
context: Robespierre's actual words: 'Terror is nothing but prompt, severe, inflexible justice; it is therefore an emanation of virtue.' He paired them: 'virtue, without which terror is fatal; terror, without which virtue is impotent' - turning mass execution into a moral duty. Source: https://revolution.chnm.org/d/413 (Robespierre, 'On Political Morality').

question: Donald Greer, a historian, worked through some 17,000 official death sentences from the Terror. The guillotine's most famous victims were King Louis XVI, Queen Marie Antoinette and a long line of proud nobles. Which group did Greer find made up about 85 percent of the condemned?
answer: Ordinary commoners: day-labourers, servants, and peasants
choices: Ordinary commoners: day-labourers, servants, and peasants
Titled aristocrats: counts, dukes, and marquises
Catholic clergy: priests, monks, and bishops
Foreign enemies: spies, traitors, and captured soldiers
context: Greer's 1935 study counted 16,594 official executions (2,639 in Paris); about 85% were commoners of the Third Estate, only ~8.5% nobility and ~6.5% clergy. Tens of thousands more died in prison or without trial, putting total deaths near 35,000-45,000. The Revolution mostly devoured ordinary people. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reign_of_Terror and https://theconversation.com/the-french-revolution-executed-royals-and-nobles-yes-but-most-people-killed-were-commoners-200455

question: Abraham Lincoln closed his two-minute speech at Gettysburg in November 1863 by naming the cause the fallen had died for: a government that must not perish. His three-part phrase for it is quoted more than any other English definition of democracy. How did he describe that government?
answer: government of the people, by the people, for the people
choices: government of the people, by the people, for the people
a government by the consent and for the welfare of the governed
liberty, equality, and justice for all who are governed
a rule of the people, for the people, and crowned by the people
context: The Bliss copy reads '...that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.' It is the most quoted line of the 272-word address and is carved on the south wall of the Lincoln Memorial. Source: Bliss copy full text, AbrahamLincolnOnline.org/lincoln/speeches/gettysburg.htm.

question: Edward Everett, America's most celebrated orator, gave the main speech at Gettysburg, and it ran two hours. Lincoln followed him with two minutes. Everett sent Lincoln a note the next morning comparing the two speeches. What did he write?
answer: that his long oration had not struck the heart of the day as Lincoln's few words did
choices: that his long oration had not struck the heart of the day as Lincoln's few words did
that the muted crowd proved the brief remarks had plainly failed
that the president ought to have spoken at far greater length
that he envied the louder cheers his own oration had drawn
context: Everett wrote: 'I should be glad, if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion, in two hours, as you did in two minutes.' Lincoln replied he was 'pleased to know that... the little that I did say was not entirely a failure.' Source: Massachusetts Historical Society / MassMoments, 'Edward Everett Gives Gettysburg Address,' massmoments.org.

question: Colonel James Anderson, a kindly man, lent his books on Saturdays to mill boys like Andrew Carnegie, a poor Scottish immigrant who tended bobbins in a Pittsburgh cotton mill at 13 for $1.20 a week. What did young Carnegie vow to do if he ever grew rich?
answer: Give other working boys the same chance to read
choices: Give other working boys the same chance to read
Build the tallest building in Pittsburgh
Buy the cotton mill where he had worked
Return to Scotland and live as a lord
context: Carnegie kept the vow, funding about 2,509 free public libraries across the English-speaking world. As a poor immigrant boy from Scotland he earned $1.20 a week for 12-hour days, six days a week. Source: Columbia University Libraries; Bill of Rights Institute.

question: Cornelius Vanderbilt borrowed a hundred dollars from his mother at sixteen, bought a small boat, and carried passengers across from Staten Island to New York. From that start he built the largest steamboat company on the Hudson. What nickname did he earn?
answer: the Commodore
choices: the Commodore
the Steel King
the Railroad Baron
the Oil Tycoon
context: 'Commodore' is a naval rank, fitting for a man who ruled the water before he ever touched the rails. He didn't switch to railroads until his late 60s. Source: Britannica.

question: John D. Rockefeller, Standard Oil's devout founder, went out walking with his pockets full of coins and pressed them on the children he met, along with a word of advice. What did he hand them, and what did he tell them?
answer: Shiny dimes, urging them to work hard and save
choices: Shiny dimes, urging them to work hard and save
Bright new pennies, telling them to give to the church
Silver half-dollars, telling them to spend on themselves
Freshly minted nickels, telling them to invest in oil stock
context: He handed out shiny dimes and nickels, telling the children to work hard and save their money. Source: New World Encyclopedia; Digital History, University of Houston.

question: Henry Clay Frick, who managed Andrew Carnegie's Homestead steelworks, shut the mill behind a fence during the strike of 1892. It ran three miles, stood twelve feet tall, wore a crest of barbed wire and had holes cut for rifles. What did the workers call it?
answer: Fort Frick
choices: Fort Frick
the Iron Curtain
the Steel Cage
Carnegie's Wall
context: On July 6, 1892, hundreds of Pinkerton guards floated up the Monongahela River on barges to seize the mill; a 13-hour gun battle left roughly seven workers and three Pinkertons dead before the Pinkertons surrendered. Source: Zinn Education Project; Britannica.

question: Andrew Carnegie argued in The Gospel of Wealth, an essay of 1889, that a fortune beyond a man's needs belongs in trust to the public good, and must be given away in his lifetime. He summed it up in one harsh line about the man who keeps his wealth to the end. How did Carnegie say such a man dies?
answer: He 'dies disgraced'
choices: He 'dies disgraced'
He dies a stranger to his own children
He dies owing more than he kept
He dies remembered only as a thief
context: His exact line: 'the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.' Carnegie lived by it, selling his steel empire and giving away the bulk of his fortune. Source: Wikipedia, citing Carnegie's 1889 essay.

question: Alexander the Great reached Gordium in 333 BC on his march against Persia and found the ancient wagon of the legendary king Gordius, tied in a knot so cunning that no end of the rope could be seen. An oracle had made a promise to whoever loosened it. Alexander searched for an end, found none, and lost his patience. What did he do?
answer: Drew his sword and sliced it in half with one stroke
choices: Drew his sword and sliced it in half with one stroke
Ordered his soldiers to burn the cart it bound
Left it untouched and marched his army onward
Carried the whole cart back to Greece as a prize
context: Arrian's Anabasis Alexandri (2.3) records the famous sword-stroke: rather than untangle the knot the slow expected way, Alexander solved it with one bold cut. He went on to conquer the Persian Empire, fulfilling the oracle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordian_Knot (Arrian, Anabasis Alexandri 2.3).

question: An oracle had spoken of the knot on the wagon of King Gordius at Gordium, and for years challenger after challenger picked at it and went away beaten. Alexander the Great came to try his luck in 333 BC. What had the oracle foretold for the man who loosened it?
answer: That he would rule over all of Asia
choices: That he would rule over all of Asia
That the gods would grant him a single immortal life
That he would never lose a battle as long as he lived
That the city's treasury would be opened to him
context: Phrygian legend (Arrian; Plutarch): the cart of Gordius was dedicated to Zeus and tied with a knot impossible to undo; an oracle foretold that whoever loosed it would rule all of Asia. Alexander cut it with his sword at Gordium in 333 BC, and 'cutting the Gordian knot' became a phrase for solving a hard problem with one bold stroke.

question: Tiberius Gracchus, a tribune of the people, proposed a law in 133 BC to give public land, in small plots, to the landless families of Rome. His fellow tribune Marcus Octavius vetoed it, and a tribune's veto was final. Tiberius answered with a move no Roman had ever made against a sitting tribune. What did he do to Octavius?
answer: Had him stripped of his office and dragged out of the tribunate
choices: Had him stripped of his office and dragged out of the tribunate
Had him exiled to a frontier province for ten years
Had him fined his family's entire fortune in silver
Had him barred from speaking in the Forum for a year
context: A tribune's person was sacrosanct and his veto absolute, so deposing one mid-term broke a core norm of the Republic and turned the Senate against Tiberius. The land law itself (lex Sempronia agraria) revived an old limit of 500 iugera per citizen and handed ~30-iugera plots to poor families. Source: worldhistory.org/article/95 and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius_Gracchus.

question: Gaius Gracchus and his followers took up arms on the Aventine Hill in 121 BC, and the Senate struck back with a new decree, the senatus consultum ultimum, as it was later called, the ultimate decree. It handed the consul Lucius Opimius a power Rome had never given before. What did it let him do to Roman citizens?
answer: Kill them with any force needed, with no trial
choices: Kill them with any force needed, with no trial
Strip them of citizenship and seize their children
Sell them into slavery to foreign buyers
Tax their estates at the full value each year
context: The senatus consultum ultimum let Opimius use lethal force against Gaius and his followers without due process; it became the emergency tool later turned on figures like Catiline. After the fighting, the bodies of Gaius, Fulvius Flaccus, and about 3,000 followers were thrown into the Tiber. Source: worldhistory.org/article/95 and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Opimius.

question: A jobless man stood in a line of hungry families that stretched down a city block, waiting for a bowl of soup, at the bottom of the Great Depression. Close to thirteen million Americans had no work. About one in how many American households had no income at all?
answer: One in four
choices: One in four
One in ten
One in twenty
One in fifty
context: At the depth of the Depression, 24.9% of the labor force — 12,830,000 people — had no job, and roughly one in four households had zero income. Even workers who kept their jobs were hammered: wage income fell 42.5% between 1929 and 1933. (FDR Presidential Library & Museum, Great Depression Facts, fdrlibrary.org/great-depression-facts)

question: A family that lost its home in the Great Depression built a shack of old crates and tar paper on an empty lot, beside many others like it, and such camps rose even in New York's Central Park. What mocking nickname did people give these shanty towns?
answer: Hoovervilles
choices: Hoovervilles
Crashtowns
Slumpvilles
Bustburgs
context: They named the camps 'Hoovervilles' — a jab at President Herbert Hoover, whom they blamed for the misery. The other great image of the era was the breadline: long rows of once-middle-class families waiting for soup or bread handed out by churches and charities. (FDR Presidential Library, fdrlibrary.org/great-depression-facts; University of Washington Great Depression Project, depts.washington.edu/depress/hooverville_seattle.shtml)

question: Customers stampeded into a bank in 1932 on a rumour that it was in trouble and emptied their accounts in a day, as runs did across the country while over nine thousand banks failed. Why did a run like that ruin a family far more completely than a bank failure would today?
answer: Back then no government agency insured deposits, so once the bank's cash ran out, your savings were simply gone
choices: Back then no government agency insured deposits, so once the bank's cash ran out, your savings were simply gone
Back then the bank had quietly lent your deposit out to others and could not call the loans back in time
Back then a failed bank was allowed to repay you in its own now-worthless company stock instead of cash
Back then the law let a shaky bank freeze your account for up to ten years before it had to pay you
context: There was no deposit insurance yet. Congress created the FDIC in 1933 precisely so a bank failure could never again swallow a family's life savings. (HISTORY, How Bank Failures Contributed to the Great Depression, history.com/articles/bank-failures-great-depression-1929-crash)

question: Families on the over-ploughed, drought-stricken Great Plains watched a dust storm sweep across them on 14 April 1935, the worst storm of the Dust Bowl years, and turn noon into night. Survivors gave that one storm a grim two-word name. What did they call it?
answer: Black Sunday
choices: Black Sunday
Black Tuesday
Black Friday
Black Easter
context: They called it 'Black Sunday' — the worst single storm of the Dust Bowl. Years of drought and over-plowed land had left the topsoil loose, and the wind simply carried the Great Plains away. ('Black Tuesday' was something else entirely — the day of the 1929 stock-market crash.) (Dust Bowl, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust_Bowl; HISTORY, Dust Bowl, history.com/articles/dust-bowl)

question: Franklin Roosevelt went on the radio on 12 March 1933 for the first of his fireside chats, to a country where frightened people had pulled their cash out of the banks and hidden it at home. What did he tell them about their money?
answer: Their money was safer in a bank than under the mattress
choices: Their money was safer in a bank than under the mattress
Their money was safest buried somewhere out in the backyard
Their money should be traded for gold and locked away at home
Their money should be kept at home in a coffee can within reach
context: The reassurance worked spectacularly: when most banks reopened on March 15, 1933, the stock market had one of its best days ever — the Dow jumped about 15% in a single session as confidence came flooding back. (National Archives, FDR's Fireside Chat, archives.gov/education/lessons/fdr-fireside; janos.nyc, FDR's Bank Holiday, 1933)

question: Investors saw the Dow Jones average stand at 381 at the start of September 1929, just before the Crash. Then it slid for almost three years, and it hit its lowest close of the century in July 1932. Down from 381, where did the Dow bottom out?
answer: About 41
choices: About 41
About 60
About 110
About 180
context: From 381 all the way down to about 41, the Dow lost almost nine-tenths of its value — a fall of about 89%, and the lowest it would close in the whole twentieth century. The collapse began on 'Black Tuesday,' October 29, 1929, when panicked investors dumped about 16 million shares in a single day and wiped out roughly $14 billion. (Federal Reserve History, Stock Market Crash of 1929, federalreservehistory.org; Britannica, Black Tuesday)

question: Thomas Lamont, a banker, was among those who pleaded with Herbert Hoover to veto the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, which Congress sent him in June 1930, lifting duties on more than twenty thousand imports. Over a thousand economists asked for a veto too. To stop the tariff, which he called asinine, what did Lamont later say he had nearly done?
answer: Got down on his knees to beg the president
choices: Got down on his knees to beg the president
Resigned from his bank in open protest
Offered the president his entire fortune
Camped out on the White House lawn
context: Lamont said he 'almost went down on my knees to beg Herbert Hoover to veto the asinine Hawley-Smoot tariff.' Henry Ford called the bill 'an economic stupidity' to Hoover's face. Hoover signed it anyway. The petition gathered over 1,250 signatures, organized by economists including Irving Fisher and Paul Douglas. (Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act)

question: Herbert Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff in 1930, and America's trading partners hit back: Canada, France, Italy, Spain and others put up steep tariffs of their own, just as the economists had warned. What happened to world trade over the next five years?
answer: It collapsed by roughly two-thirds
choices: It collapsed by roughly two-thirds
It dipped by only about a tenth
It held roughly steady
It actually doubled
context: World trade shrank by about two-thirds, deepening the global slump. U.S. exports alone fell from about $5.4 billion in 1929 to $2.1 billion in 1933. A tariff meant to protect American workers helped strangle the world economy. (Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, Wikipedia; EFG International, When Protectionism Backfired, efginternational.com)

question: General Douglas MacArthur, on Herbert Hoover's orders, drove thousands of jobless veterans of the First World War out of their camp in Washington in the summer of 1932, using bayonets, cavalry and tanks, and burned their shacks. The men had come to ask for early payment of a promised bonus. When Franklin Roosevelt saw the newspaper pictures of the fire, what did he reportedly tell an aide?
answer: "This will elect me"
choices: "This will elect me"
"God help this country"
"Hoover has lost his mind"
"Send those men some food"
context: That November, Roosevelt beat Hoover by seven million votes. The veterans' camp was a Hooverville on the Anacostia Flats, and the 'Bonus Army' of about 43,000 people was led by a former sergeant named Walter W. Waters. (Bonus Army, Wikipedia; PBS American Experience, The Bonus March, pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/macarthur-bonus-march-may-july-1932)

question: American lenders demanded their money back from Germany as the Depression spread, and by 1932 over six million Germans were jobless. One party jumped from 2.6 percent in 1928 to 37.4 percent of the vote in July 1932, and it became the biggest in the Reichstag. Which party was it?
answer: The Nazi Party
choices: The Nazi Party
The Communist Party
The Social Democratic Party
The Catholic Centre Party
context: Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party went from 2.6% of the vote in 1928 to 37.4% in July 1932 — 230 of the 608 Reichstag seats, the biggest total any party won in Weimar Germany. The economic collapse that began on Wall Street helped carry Hitler toward power. (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, encyclopedia.ushmm.org; July 1932 German federal election, Wikipedia)

question: John Maynard Keynes set out the paradox of thrift in The General Theory of 1936: if scared people all rush to save at the same moment, businesses lose their customers and the slump grows worse. What did Keynes say the government itself should do to break the cycle?
answer: Pay for public works and jobs to put money in people's hands
choices: Pay for public works and jobs to put money in people's hands
Order households to save much more until confidence slowly returned
Raise taxes steeply and cut spending to keep the budget balanced
Wait calmly for wages and prices to fall until the slump cured itself
context: Keynes's cure — government spending, public works, and deficits working through a 'multiplier' — became the most influential idea in 20th-century economics. But it is genuinely contested: monetarist and Austrian economists give very different accounts, each with serious defenders, and the debate is not settled. (Keynesian economics, Wikipedia; IMF Finance & Development, What Is Keynesian Economics?, imf.org)

question: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz laid the blame on the Federal Reserve for the Depression in their account of 1963. The Fed, they argued, stood by and let one crucial thing shrink by about a third between 1929 and 1933, which they named the Great Contraction. What did they say the Fed let collapse?
answer: The nation's money supply
choices: The nation's money supply
The government's gold reserves
The number of open factories
The total wages paid to workers
context: Friedman and Schwartz argued the Fed could have stopped the banking panics and kept the money supply from collapsing — and that its failure to act was the real catastrophe. (A Monetary History of the United States, Wikipedia; University of Chicago Harris School, harris.uchicago.edu/files/monetaryhistory_1.pdf)

question: Murray Rothbard, an economist of the Austrian school, blamed the Depression on the boom that the Federal Reserve's cheap credit had built in the 1920s, and he treated the bust as the cure. What did he argue had dragged the slump out for years?
answer: Hoover propped up wages and prices instead of letting them drop
choices: Hoover propped up wages and prices instead of letting them drop
Hoover slashed federal spending far too deeply and far too fast
Hoover pulled the dollar off gold and let its value float freely
Hoover sat back and did nothing while the slump slowly healed on its own
context: Rothbard, in the Austrian tradition of Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, argued that Hoover's interventions — propping up wages and prices, blocking the necessary liquidation — prevented the bust from clearing and so prolonged the depression. It is the mirror image of Keynes: where Keynes wanted MORE government action, Rothbard blamed government action for the delay. (America's Great Depression, Wikipedia; Mises Institute, The Great Depression, mises.org/library/book/great-depression)

question: Barry Eichengreen pinned much of the blame on the gold standard for spreading the slump around the world: the golden fetters, he said, kept central banks from creating money to rescue their failing banks. He pointed to countries that cut loose from gold in 1931, ahead of the rest, and climbed out sooner. Which were they?
answer: Britain and Scandinavia
choices: Britain and Scandinavia
France and Italy
Germany and Austria
the United States and Canada
context: The gold standard was the channel that carried the American collapse around the globe — the longer a country clung to gold, the deeper its slump. Britain and the Scandinavian countries cut loose from gold early, in 1931, and were among the first to climb out. France, by contrast, clung to gold for years and stayed mired. (Barry Eichengreen, Golden Fetters, NBER, 1992, nber.org/books-and-chapters/golden-fetters; CEPR VoxEU, The End of the Gold Standard, cepr.org)

question: The Nasrid rulers of Granada built the Court of the Lions in the Alhambra between 1362 and 1391 and set its marble fountain on the backs of twelve stone lions, each spouting water from its mouth. Scholars believe the makers set the spouts at slightly different heights, so that one lion after another began to spout until all twelve ran at once. What do they think the fountain doubled as?
answer: A clock that marked the twelve hours
choices: A clock that marked the twelve hours
A pump to cool the whole palace
A tester for the water's purity
An instrument that played music
context: The Nasrid court was built 1362-1391; the staggered tube heights meant each lion 'turned on' at its own hour, so the lions together counted out the day. This reading is a scholarly reconstruction, not certain. Source: iflscience.com 'This Incredible Islamic Fountain From The 1300s Might Have Actually Been A Clock'; ijisrt.com IJISRT22JAN498.  (Legend.)

question: Egyptian workers finished the Great Pyramid at Giza, on the desert's edge outside Cairo, around 2560 BC, piling up more than two million stone blocks for one king's tomb. Which pharaoh was it built for, the man the Greeks later called Cheops?
answer: Khufu
choices: Khufu
Ramesses
Tutankhamun
Thutmose
context: Khufu was the second king of Egypt's 4th Dynasty; the Greeks called him Cheops. The Great Pyramid was raised as his tomb around 2560 BC. (britannica.com/place/Great-Pyramid-of-Giza; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza)

question: Ancient writers drew up a famous list of the Seven Wonders of the World. Earthquakes, fires and looters brought six of them down. Only one still stands whole. Which Wonder is it?
answer: The Great Pyramid of Giza
choices: The Great Pyramid of Giza
The Colossus of Rhodes
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon
The Lighthouse of Alexandria
context: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one still substantially intact; the other six were destroyed by earthquakes, fire, or dismantling. (Britannica, Seven Wonders of the Ancient World)

question: When the builders set the last block of the Great Pyramid, it stood about 481 feet high. No one built anything taller until an English cathedral spire beat it in the 1300s AD. About how long did the Great Pyramid hold the record for tallest thing on Earth?
answer: About 3,800 years
choices: About 3,800 years
About 500 years
About 1,200 years
About 100 years
context: The Great Pyramid held the title of tallest human-made structure on Earth for roughly 3,800 years — longer than any other building in history — out-topped only around 1311 AD by the spire of Lincoln Cathedral. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza; mused.com/items/503/khufu-pyramid-or-the-great-pyramid/)

question: Khufu had the largest pyramid at Giza raised as his tomb around 2560 BC, the one the world now calls the Great Pyramid. The Egyptians never used that plain name. They called it Akhet-Khufu instead. What does the name Akhet-Khufu mean?
answer: The Horizon of Khufu
choices: The Horizon of Khufu
The Mountain of Khufu
The Throne of Khufu
The Gate of Khufu
context: The Egyptians named the Great Pyramid 'Akhet-Khufu,' meaning 'the Horizon of Khufu.' The name appears in the world's oldest papyrus, the Diary of Merer. (nationalgeographic.com/premium/article/red-sea-scrolls-pyramids-egypt; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza)

question: Sultan an-Nasir's men went to work on the Great Pyramid around 1356, after an earthquake in 1303 had loosened the 144,000 polished casing stones that once made it gleam. They stripped the casing away. What did they do with the stone?
answer: Hauled it away to build the city of Cairo
choices: Hauled it away to build the city of Cairo
Ground it into powder for medicine
Shipped it to Rome as a gift
Buried it in a pit beside the pyramid
context: Sultan an-Nasir's men stripped the loosened white Tura limestone casing around 1356 AD and carted it off to build Cairo — which is why the pyramid looks rough and stepped today instead of mirror-bright. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza; mused.com/items/503/khufu-pyramid-or-the-great-pyramid/)

question: Elon Musk, the billionaire, tweeted in 2020, 'Aliens built the pyramids obv.' Rania al-Mashat, Egypt's minister of tourism, wrote back and asked him to fly to Giza and look at one thing with his own eyes. What did she want him to see?
answer: The tombs of the pyramid builders
choices: The tombs of the pyramid builders
The workers' bakery and beer vats
The foremen's payroll records
A wall of crew-name graffiti
context: Rania al-Mashat invited Musk and SpaceX to visit the tombs of the pyramid builders — the real workers' graves at Giza — as her answer to the 'aliens built them' claim. (bbc.com/news/world-africa-53627888; thejakartapost.com)

question: Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass, two archaeologists, uncovered a whole town of the Great Pyramid's builders at Giza, along with their graves. The builders were not whipped slaves but organised crews, and the gangs had written their own names on the blocks. What did two of the gangs call themselves?
answer: 'Friends of Khufu' and 'Drunkards of Menkaure'
choices: 'Friends of Khufu' and 'Drunkards of Menkaure'
'Companions of Ra' and 'Champions of Sneferu'
'Falcons of Khafre' and 'Lions of Giza'
'Servants of the Sun' and 'Sons of the Nile'
context: Archaeologists Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass found the builders' town and tombs at Giza; the workers' graffiti shows organized crews with names like 'Friends of Khufu' and 'Drunkards of Menkaure' — not slaves. (harvardmagazine.com/2003/07/who-built-the-pyramids-html; guardians.net/hawass/buildtomb.htm)

question: The builders of the Great Pyramid lined up its four sides with true north, south, east and west, and missed by less than one-fifteenth of a degree. They had no compass. How, by one leading theory, did they find true north?
answer: By using the autumn equinox
choices: By using the autumn equinox
By following a sacred map from the temple
By copying an older pyramid's angle
By guessing and getting lucky
context: The four sides miss true north–south–east–west by only about 3 minutes 38 seconds of arc. A leading theory holds the builders used the autumn equinox to find true north. (livescience.com/61799-great-pyramid-near-perfect-alignment.html; smithsonianmag.com)

question: Explorers who reached the King's Chamber deep inside the Great Pyramid found the king's granite coffer standing there, empty. The coffer was broader than the chamber's only doorway, so it could never have been carried in. What did its size reveal about how the chamber was built?
answer: The coffer was set in place first, and the room was built up around it
choices: The coffer was set in place first, and the room was built up around it
The coffer was carved from a block already inside
The doorway was later narrowed by robbers
The coffer was lowered through a hole in the ceiling
context: The granite sarcophagus is wider than the doorway — proof it was placed first and the King's Chamber built up around it. It was found completely empty, with no mummy ever inside. (ancientegyptonline.co.uk/kingschambergp/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza)

question: Pierre Tallet, digging at the Red Sea port of Wadi al-Jarf in 2013, found the oldest papyrus ever discovered: the logbook of an inspector named Merer, written in the 27th year of the reign of the Great Pyramid's king. What job for the pyramid did Merer's diary show him doing?
answer: Shipping white limestone by boat to the pyramid
choices: Shipping white limestone by boat to the pyramid
Counting the gold buried in the king's tomb
Guarding prisoners chained at the work site
Drawing the secret plans for the burial chamber
context: The Diary of Merer — the world's oldest surviving papyrus — is the logbook of an inspector who led a 200-man crew shipping white Tura limestone by boat to 'Akhet-Khufu,' a roughly 3-day trip. One entry reads: 'Inspector Merer sets sail... laden with stone blocks, to Akhet-Khufu.' (nationalgeographic.com/premium/article/red-sea-scrolls-pyramids-egypt; history.com)

question: Physicists scanned the Great Pyramid in 2017 without drilling a single hole. They used cosmic-ray muons, tiny particles that rain down from space and pass right through stone, and they published the result in the journal Nature. What did the scan find hidden above the Grand Gallery?
answer: A mysterious empty 'Big Void' at least 100 feet long
choices: A mysterious empty 'Big Void' at least 100 feet long
A second royal coffin filled with gold
A network of flooded tunnels
A statue of Khufu sealed in stone
context: The 2017 muon scan, published in Nature, found a mysterious empty 'Big Void' at least 30 meters (100 ft) long above the Grand Gallery — the first major hidden space discovered inside the pyramid since the 1800s. (nature.com/articles/nature24647; sci.news)

question: Archaeologists digging at the Hatnub quarry found a ramp from the Great Pyramid's own time, about 4,500 years old, with a row of wooden post-holes running up each side. The pyramid's workers had no machines to lift two-tonne blocks up the growing pyramid. How did the posts help them move stone up steep slopes?
answer: They tied ropes to the posts to drag sledges up the ramp
choices: They tied ropes to the posts to drag sledges up the ramp
They rolled the stones over the posts like logs
They floated the stones up a water channel beside the posts
They balanced the stones on the posts as scaffolding
context: The 4,500-year-old Hatnub ramp is flanked by two staircases full of post-holes: workers tied ropes to the wooden posts and used them to help drag sledges loaded with stone up slopes as steep as 20%. (news.liverpool.ac.uk/2018/11/02; livescience.com/63978-great-pyramid-ramp-discovered.html)

question: Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida and two fellow envoys of Pope Leo IX strode into Constantinople's great domed cathedral, Hagia Sophia, on 16 July 1054, while the Divine Liturgy was under way. What did the envoys lay on the high altar?
answer: A written order excommunicating the patriarch
choices: A written order excommunicating the patriarch
A bag of gold coins for the church
The keys to the city of Rome
A signed treaty of friendship
context: The document was a 'bull' of excommunication, drawn up by Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, laid right on the altar during the Divine Liturgy. This dramatic scene is the famous flashpoint of the East-West split between the Catholic and Orthodox churches. Source: christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/east-west-schism ; oca.org church-history eleventh-century the-great-schism.

question: Nicephorus, the aide of Patriarch Michael Cerularius, broke into the Latin churches of Constantinople in 1053, once the patriarch had shut them. The Latins made their Communion bread flat, with no yeast, and the Greeks refused to count such bread as true Communion. What did Nicephorus do to that flat bread?
answer: Trampled it underfoot
choices: Trampled it underfoot
Sold it in the market
Locked it in a golden box
Mailed it back to Rome
context: Nicephorus burst open the Latin tabernacles and trampled the consecrated bread because, being unleavened (azyme), the Greeks did not accept it as true Communion bread. Patriarch Michael Cerularius had ordered all the Latin churches in the city closed. Source: newadvent.org/cathen/10273a.htm ; courses.lumenlearning.com great-schism-of-1054.

question: Three envoys from Rome walked out of Hagia Sophia in July 1054 and stopped on the threshold. They shook the dust of the cathedral off their feet, an old sign that they were done with the place, and shouted one sentence in Latin. What did they shout?
answer: 'Videat Deus et judicet!' — 'May God see and judge!'
choices: 'Videat Deus et judicet!' — 'May God see and judge!'
'Roma locuta, causa finita!' — 'Rome has spoken!'
'Veni, vidi, vici!' — 'I came, I saw, I conquered!'
'Pax vobiscum!' — 'Peace be with you!'
context: Cardinal Humbert led the legation; shaking the dust off the feet echoes a gesture of final rejection. The three legates were Humbert of Silva Candida, Frederick of Lorraine (later Pope Stephen IX), and Peter, Archbishop of Amalfi. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humbert_of_Silva_Candida ; greekcitytimes.com On This Day Great Schism.

question: Patriarch Michael Cerularius answered the Roman legates in July 1054. He called twenty-one bishops together in Hagia Sophia on 24 July, pronounced a solemn anathema of his own, and had the bull of the legates publicly burned. Whom did his anathema name?
answer: Only the three legates, named one by one
choices: Only the three legates, named one by one
The entire Western Church and its pope
Every Latin living in Constantinople
The emperor who had welcomed the legates
context: Cerularius convened 21 metropolitans and bishops and excommunicated the three envoys by name, not the whole Latin Church — one reason historians say the 'total' break of 1054 is overstated. The bull was then publicly burned in Constantinople. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_I_Cerularius.

question: Pope Leo IX had sent Cardinal Humbert and two other legates to Constantinople, and they struck at Patriarch Michael Cerularius in Leo's name on 16 July 1054. That act helped split Christianity into a Catholic West and an Orthodox East. Yet it carried a hidden legal flaw. What had happened to Leo by the time his legates acted?
answer: He had died three months earlier
choices: He had died three months earlier
He had secretly recalled them to Rome
He had reconciled with the patriarch
He had been deposed by the emperor
context: Leo IX died on April 19, 1054; the excommunication came on July 16. With the pope who authorized them already dead, the legates technically had no authority to excommunicate anyone — Humbert is said to have 'taken advantage of the papal vacancy to retaliate.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_I_Cerularius ; oca.org the-great-schism.

question: The Roman legates listed eleven charges against the Greeks in the bull they left in Hagia Sophia. One charged that the Greeks had dropped a phrase from the Creed: the filioque, which says the Holy Spirit proceeds 'and from the Son.' Why do historians call that charge backwards?
answer: The West had ADDED the clause; the East never accepted it
choices: The West had ADDED the clause; the East never accepted it
The Greeks had written the original Creed themselves
The clause had been removed by the emperor, not the church
Both sides had agreed to drop it centuries earlier
context: The filioque ('and the Son') was a Latin addition to the Nicene Creed; the East held the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and rejected the addition as tampering. So the bull accused the Greeks of removing something the West had in fact inserted. Tellingly, the filioque was only the SEVENTH of the eleven charges — the dispute over leavened versus unleavened bread came first. Source: mgr.org/PapalBull1054.html ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_Schism.

question: Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I took up the two curses of 1054 in December 1965, after they had stood for 911 years. They held twin ceremonies at the same hour in Rome and Istanbul. What did they agree to do with the curses?
answer: Commit them 'to oblivion' and lift them
choices: Commit them 'to oblivion' and lift them
Re-read them aloud as a warning
Carve them into the walls of both churches
Mail the original bull back to Rome
context: On December 7, 1965, the two leaders lifted the anathemas simultaneously, agreeing to 'commit these excommunications to oblivion' — 911 years after Humbert's legates first laid the bull on the altar. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic%E2%80%93Orthodox_Joint_Declaration_of_1965 ; vaticannews.va lifting-anathemas.

question: Sculptors on the Giza plateau made the Great Sphinx, a crouching giant some 73 metres from end to end and 20 metres tall. The pyramids behind it were stacked from cut blocks of stone, but the Sphinx was not built that way. How did its makers shape it?
answer: They carved the whole beast in place from one ridge of natural limestone bedrock
choices: They carved the whole beast in place from one ridge of natural limestone bedrock
They stacked thousands of quarried limestone blocks into a lion shape
They cast it in a giant mold from melted desert sand
They assembled it from cedar timber hauled in from Lebanon
context: Sculptors cut the lion-body directly out of the living rock of the Giza plateau rather than building it up from blocks, which is why the Sphinx is the oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Sphinx_of_Giza

question: By a favourite tale, Napoleon's soldiers blasted the nose off the Great Sphinx with cannon fire when France invaded Egypt in 1798. Chisel marks on the face show that someone did pry the nose away on purpose. What proves the cannon tale cannot be true?
answer: A drawing by Frederic Louis Norden, made in 1737, already shows the nose gone
choices: A drawing by Frederic Louis Norden, made in 1737, already shows the nose gone
An ancient Egyptian inscription on the Sphinx blames a desert sandstorm
Napoleon's own diary records that the nose was already missing in Paris
Cannons of that era could not be aimed high enough to reach the face
context: Norden sketched the noseless Sphinx more than 60 years before Napoleon's troops ever reached Egypt, so they cannot have been the ones who broke it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Sphinx_of_Giza

question: The builders of the Great Wall of China ran its eastern end to the coast by Shanhai Pass and out into the Bohai Gulf. To them the wall looked like a giant creature stooping to drink from the sea. What did they call that spot?
answer: Old Dragon's Head
choices: Old Dragon's Head
Tiger's Leap Gorge
The Sleeping Giant
Crane's Beak Point
context: Laolongtou, 'Old Dragon's Head,' sits near Shanhai Pass, the wall's eastern terminus on the Bohai Gulf. The pass itself was nicknamed 'the First Pass Under Heaven.' Source: chinahighlights.com; amusingplanet.com.

question: Yang Liwei, China's first astronaut, looked down on the Earth from orbit in 2003. A famous saying held that the Great Wall was the one human work anyone could see from the Moon. What did Yang say about the wall?
answer: He could not pick out the structure with the naked eye
choices: He could not pick out the structure with the naked eye
He said it was the clearest human mark on the land
He said it stood out sharply along the old Silk Road
He said rivers and snowfields hid it from view
context: National Geographic helped spread the myth in 1923; Neil Armstrong said after Apollo 11 he saw no sign of it. Yang Liwei said from orbit he 'couldn't identify the structure with the naked eye.' It is only sometimes glimpsed from LOW orbit under slanting sunlight. Source: smithsonianmag.com.

question: Peasants, soldiers and convicts laboured on the ridges of northern China to raise the Great Wall from rammed earth, stone and brick. Many people still picture it as one long wall, thrown up by a single emperor. What have historians and archaeologists actually found along the frontier?
answer: Many separate walls built across many different dynasties
choices: Many separate walls built across many different dynasties
A single wall finished by one emperor in his own lifetime
Mostly natural mountain ridges with only short stretches of masonry
One short fortress wall that guarded the capital and nothing more
context: Historians and archaeologists: the 'Great Wall' is not one continuous structure but many walls and fortifications of stone, brick, and rammed earth, raised, abandoned, and rebuilt by successive dynasties over roughly two thousand years, the best-preserved sections being Ming-era.

question: China's emperors forced peasants, soldiers and convicts onto the steep northern ridges to build the Great Wall in bitter cold, with too little food. By one common estimate, some 400,000 of them died. What grim nickname did the wall earn?
answer: The longest cemetery on Earth
choices: The longest cemetery on Earth
The wall of a thousand tears
The emperor's stone curse
The road of broken backs
context: One common estimate puts the death toll around 400,000. Bodies were buried in mass graves alongside the wall, earning it the nickname. Source: smithsonianmag.com; factretriever.com.

question: Ming engineers rebuilt long stretches of the Great Wall in brick and stone, and they needed mortar that would ride out earthquakes and centuries of weather. They stirred an everyday food into their lime mortar, and the mixture set into an early kind of composite glue. What did they stir in?
answer: Sticky rice
choices: Sticky rice
Beaten egg whites
Honey
Bean paste
context: The rice's amylopectin made an early composite mortar that helped walls resist earthquakes and weathering. Some old accounts add egg whites. Source: smithsonianmag.com; newworldencyclopedia.org.

question: Wu Sangui, a Ming general, stood guard at the gateway near the eastern end of the Great Wall, where it runs down to the Bohai Gulf. He was there to hold it, yet in 1644 one choice of his finished the Ming dynasty. What did Wu Sangui do?
answer: He swung open the gates of Shanhai Pass to the Manchu army
choices: He swung open the gates of Shanhai Pass to the Manchu army
He set fire to his own watchtowers and then fled west
He bribed the invaders to march around the wall instead
He tore down a wall section to build himself a fortress
context: Wu Sangui, a Ming general, opened the gates of Shanhai Pass to the Manchu army in 1644, ending the Ming dynasty. The wall was undone by a traitor, not a siege. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org.

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, a decorated artillery officer, was fighting in East Prussia in February 1945, and there at the front his own side seized him. The charge sent him to the labour camps for eight years. What was his crime?
answer: Private letters mocking Stalin to a school friend
choices: Private letters mocking Stalin to a school friend
Deserting his artillery battery under enemy fire
Losing a key battle on the East Prussian front
Passing secret maps to the German army
context: He criticized Stalin in private wartime letters to his school friend Nikolai Vitkevich and was sentenced under Article 58, 'counter-revolutionary activity,' to eight years. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Aleksandr-Solzhenitsyn

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn put the word GULAG into the title of his great book, though the word names no place on any map. In Russian its five letters are an abbreviation. What do they spell out the name of?
answer: A government bureau running the whole camp system
choices: A government bureau running the whole camp system
The largest prison camp in all of Siberia
The frozen wasteland the camps were built on
The secret police force that made the arrests
context: GULAG is an acronym for the Russian 'Glavnoe Upravlenie Lagerei' — the Main Directorate of Camps, the office that ran the system. Solzhenitsyn's title compares the scattered camps to a hidden 'archipelago,' a chain of islands. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago

question: Nikita Khrushchev overruled other Party bosses and personally approved a short novel by Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, and the journal Novy Mir printed it in 1962. It became the first honest look at the camps ever printed openly in the Soviet Union. How much of the prisoner Shukhov's camp life does the book cover?
answer: A single ordinary day
choices: A single ordinary day
His entire eight-year sentence
His first month behind the wire
The morning of his release
context: The book is 'One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich,' following the prisoner Ivan Denisovich Shukhov through one unremarkable day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Day_in_the_Life_of_Ivan_Denisovich

question: Prisoners of the Kolyma camps hacked a road through some 2,000 kilometres of frozen ground in Siberia's far east, starting from the port of Magadan, and so many of them died building it that the guards packed the dead into the roadbed. What is the road still called?
answer: The Road of Bones
choices: The Road of Bones
The Iron Road
The Frozen Highway
The White Road
context: Kolyma's prisoners also mined gold in lethal cold — at its height the region produced about a third of the world's gold. Source: https://factsanddetails.com/russia/Places/sub9_9e/entry-7102.html

question: A prisoner brought to the Solovetsky Islands in the White Sea entered the camp that opened there about 1923, the one that, Solzhenitsyn said, every later Soviet camp copied. It stood inside walls raised long before, for the opposite purpose. What had stood on those islands first?
answer: An ancient Orthodox monastery
choices: An ancient Orthodox monastery
A tsar's summer palace
An abandoned naval fortress
A remote fishing village
context: Solovki was a place of prayer turned into a place of death — the model, Solzhenitsyn said, from which all later camps were copied. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/literature-and-writing/gulag-archipelago-1918-1956-aleksandr-solzhenitsyn

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn stepped out of the labour camps in 1953, when his sentence finally ran out, though even then the state banished him for life to Kazakhstan. His very first day out of the camps fell on the same day as one enormous event. What was it?
answer: The day Stalin died
choices: The day Stalin died
The end of the Second World War
The launch of the first Sputnik
The outbreak of the Korean War
context: His first day free was March 5, 1953 — the day Stalin died. He was then sent to internal exile 'in perpetuity' in Kazakhstan, where he nearly died of cancer. Source: https://www.solzhenitsyncenter.org/timeline

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn won the 1970 Nobel Prize for Literature but did not dare travel to collect it, afraid he would be barred from returning home. His Nobel lecture closed on an old Russian proverb, the motto of his struggle against the state's lies. Which line was it?
answer: One word of truth shall outweigh the whole world
choices: One word of truth shall outweigh the whole world
A lie will travel the length of the earth
Truth is the patient daughter of time
The axe forgets, but the tree remembers
context: He won the Nobel in 1970 but did not dare travel to collect it, fearing he would not be let back into the USSR; he finally accepted it in person in Stockholm in 1974. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/1970/solzhenitsyn/lecture/

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn composed long poems in his head during his years in the camps, where prisoners were forbidden paper. He had to hold thousands of finished lines in memory without ever losing his place. How did he keep count of them?
answer: He broke matchsticks into beads and told them like a rosary
choices: He broke matchsticks into beads and told them like a rosary
He scratched tally marks into the prison wall each night
He tied a row of small knots along a length of thread
He carved the finished lines into a hidden bar of soap
context: He laid the matchstick pieces in rows of tens and units on his cigarette case, running them through his fingers as he recited. By this method he carried roughly 12,000 lines of verse out of the Gulag in his memory. Source: https://nevalalee.wordpress.com/2016/07/11/solzhenitsyns-rosary/

question: Officers of the KGB, the Soviet secret police, hunted through the 1960s for a manuscript that Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was writing in secret: The Gulag Archipelago, his history of the camps. A single raid could have seized the entire book. How did he make sure no raid ever could?
answer: He never kept the whole book in one place, hiding fragments with scattered friends
choices: He never kept the whole book in one place, hiding fragments with scattered friends
He wrote the entire book in one hidden night and burned his notes
He mailed each finished chapter straight out of the country
He disguised every page to look like a routine Party report
context: He worked on only fragments at a time and stashed the pieces with trusted friends around Moscow and at a secret retreat in Estonia, so no single seizure could capture the whole. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago

question: Elizaveta Voronyanskaya, Solzhenitsyn's typist, broke after days of questioning by KGB officers in 1973 and told them where one copy of The Gulag Archipelago, his secret history of the camps, was hidden. Not long after, she was found hanged. What did Solzhenitsyn do in answer?
answer: He ordered the book published at once in the West
choices: He ordered the book published at once in the West
He burned every remaining copy he still held
He fled Moscow and went into deep hiding
He wrote an open letter naming the KGB officers
context: 'The Gulag Archipelago' appeared from YMCA-Press in Paris on December 28, 1973. Months later Solzhenitsyn was arrested for treason, stripped of his citizenship, and expelled to West Germany. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn set down his most famous thought about good and evil in The Gulag Archipelago, his great history of the camps. He rejected the comfortable belief that evil belongs to other people alone. Where did he say the line between good and evil runs?
answer: Right through every human heart
choices: Right through every human heart
Between the rich and the poor
Between Russia and the West
Between the jailers and the jailed
context: The full line: the dividing line 'passes not through states, nor between classes, nor between political parties either — but right through every human heart.' He added that even in the worst heart 'one small bridgehead of good is retained.' Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago

question: Sculptors in Gandhara, in what is now Pakistan and Afghanistan, carved the first statues ever made of the Buddha in human form. Buddhist artists before them had shown only an empty throne or a pair of footprints to mark his presence. How did the Gandhara sculptors dress their new Buddha?
answer: In a Greek himation, the toga-like robe with deep folds
choices: In a Greek himation, the toga-like robe with deep folds
In the silk court robes of a Persian emperor
In the saffron rags of a wandering beggar-monk
In the jeweled armor of an Indian warrior-prince
context: Greco-Buddhist art at Gandhara produced the first human images of the Buddha, draped like a Greek in a deeply folded himation. Before this, the Buddha was shown only through symbols such as an empty throne or footprints. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Buddhist_art

question: Vajrapani walked at the Buddha's side as his bodyguard in the carvings of Gandhara, in what is now Pakistan and Afghanistan. The sculptors there had trained in the Greek style, and they modelled the guardian on a hero of Greek myth. Which Greek figure did Vajrapani become?
answer: Herakles, the muscular hero with his club
choices: Herakles, the muscular hero with his club
Zeus, the king of the gods with his thunderbolt
Hermes, the swift messenger with winged sandals
Achilles, the warrior dipped in the river Styx
context: In Gandharan art the Buddha's guardian Vajrapani is sculpted as Herakles (Hercules), a muscular strongman carrying his club — a Greek demigod reused as a Buddhist protector deity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Buddhist_art

question: Alexander the Great's armies spread a simplified form of Greek across the lands they conquered, and merchants and scholars from Egypt to India took it up as a shared tongue, Koine. Koine lasted long after his empire fell, and centuries after him it was the first language of one of history's most-read books. Which book?
answer: The New Testament
choices: The New Testament
The Iliad
The Odyssey
Aesop's Fables
