context: Koine ('the common tongue') spread from Egypt to India as the language of trade and learning. Centuries later it was the language in which the New Testament and the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) were written. Homer's epics and Aesop's fables were composed in older forms of Greek. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koine_Greek

question: Eratosthenes, the librarian of Alexandria, weighed the noon shadows of Syene and of his own city on midsummer's day around 240 BC: they differed by some seven degrees. From that one gap, what did he work out?
answer: The circumference of the whole Earth
choices: The circumference of the whole Earth
The distance from the Earth to the Sun
The exact length of one year
The height of the Great Pyramid
context: Using the 7-degree difference in shadow angle between Syene and Alexandria, Eratosthenes calculated the Earth's circumference around 240 BC — landing astonishingly close to the true figure of about 24,900 miles. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/eratosthenes-measures-earths-circumference

question: Ptolemy of Egypt banned the export of papyrus, the standard writing material of the day, meaning to starve the rival library at Pergamon of books. The people of Pergamon got very good at writing on treated animal hides instead. What material came out of Ptolemy's ban?
answer: Parchment
choices: Parchment
Papyrus
Vellum
Velvet
context: When Ptolemy banned papyrus exports to cripple the Library of Pergamon, its people developed fine animal-skin writing material — 'parchment,' from pergamenum, 'from Pergamon.' Vellum (calfskin) is named from the Latin for calf, not from the city. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Library_of_Pergamon/

question: Alexander the Great named some twenty to thirty cities after himself, Alexandrias scattered across three continents. One city he founded in India carried a different name, given in honour of a beloved companion who had just died there. Which companion did the city honour?
answer: His warhorse, Bucephalus
choices: His warhorse, Bucephalus
His mother, Olympias
His tutor, Aristotle
His friend, Hephaestion
context: Alexander founded roughly twenty to thirty cities named Alexandria across three continents. After his beloved horse Bucephalus died in India, he founded a city named for it: Bucephala. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_founded_by_Alexander_the_Great

question: Gandhara's Greek-trained carvers modelled the Buddha's serene face on the Belvedere Apollo, a Greek statue of about 330 BC, and the look they gave him spread across all of Asia. From the Apollo, the Buddha inherited one feature of his look for good. Which one?
answer: His wavy curls gathered into a topknot
choices: His wavy curls gathered into a topknot
His long, drooping earlobes
His half-closed, meditating eyes
His upraised, open right hand
context: The Buddha's iconic wavy, curly hair gathered in a topknot was copied from the curly Mediterranean hairstyle of the Belvedere Apollo (c. 330 BC); the idealized Greek face became the standard look of the Buddha across Asia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Buddhist_art

question: Klearchos set up a carved stone slab at Ai-Khanoum, a Greek city through and through, far out in Afghanistan, with a gymnasium and a theatre that seated five thousand. On it he had cut the wise sayings of Apollo's most sacred temple, back in Greece. What did Klearchos carve on the slab?
answer: The Delphic Maxims
choices: The Delphic Maxims
The maxims of the Seven Sages
The oath of Hippocrates
The laws of Solon
context: Klearchos carved the Delphic Maxims — the wisdom sayings from Apollo's temple at Delphi — onto a stele at Ai-Khanoum in Afghanistan. It is the oldest surviving copy of the maxims; none remain at Delphi itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ai-Khanoum

question: Strabo, the Greek geographer, looked back a century on Menander I, the Indo-Greek king who ruled the lands of today's Pakistan and north-west India in the 100s BC, and whom his Indian subjects called Milinda. Strabo paid him a striking compliment. According to Strabo, what had Menander done?
answer: Conquered more tribes than Alexander the Great
choices: Conquered more tribes than Alexander the Great
Lived longer than any other Greek king
Built a library larger than Alexandria's
Owned more war elephants than any rival
context: Menander I (Pali: Milinda) ruled an Indo-Greek kingdom in the 2nd century BC. Strabo wrote that Menander 'conquered more tribes than Alexander the Great.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menander_I

question: Plutarch tells how the cities of Menander's kingdom fought over his ashes when the Indo-Greek king died around 130 BC, just as cities had once quarrelled over the relics of the Buddha. By legend, how did Menander's cities settle the quarrel?
answer: They divided the ashes and raised stupas over them
choices: They divided the ashes and raised stupas over them
They scattered the ashes into the Ganges river
They sealed the ashes inside a single golden statue
They returned the ashes to his homeland in Greece
context: Plutarch recorded that Menander's cities divided his ashes among themselves and built monuments (stupas) over them — a Greek king honored exactly like the Buddha. This account is preserved as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menander_I

question: Heliodorus, a Greek ambassador sent by an Indo-Greek king, came to an Indian royal court around 113 BC and adopted the faith he found there. He raised a stone pillar at Besnagar, proclaiming himself a devotee. Whose devotee did Heliodorus declare himself?
answer: The Hindu god Vishnu, worshipped as Krishna
choices: The Hindu god Vishnu, worshipped as Krishna
The Buddha, the awakened teacher
Indra, the storm-god king of heaven
Agni, the god of sacred fire
context: Around 113 BC Heliodorus, a Greek ambassador, converted to the worship of Vishnu and erected a pillar at Besnagar topped by Garuda, calling himself a 'Bhagavata' (devotee of Vasudeva-Krishna) — one of the earliest recorded worshippers of Krishna. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliodorus_pillar

question: Divers hauled a corroded lump of bronze gears out of an ancient shipwreck, a hand-turned machine built between about 150 and 100 BC. It followed the Sun and the Moon and predicted eclipses years in advance, and nothing so intricate appeared again for over a thousand years. What is the device called?
answer: The Antikythera mechanism
choices: The Antikythera mechanism
The Archimedes screw
The Rosetta Stone
The astrolabe of Hipparchus
context: The Antikythera mechanism, a bronze geared device from c. 150-100 BC found in a shipwreck, could predict the positions of the Sun and Moon and forecast eclipses decades ahead — a Hellenistic 'analog computer' unmatched for over a thousand years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_mechanism

question: By the Letter of Aristeas, Ptolemy II gathered seventy-two Jewish scholars at Alexandria to translate the Hebrew Bible into Greek, and their work became the Septuagint. Philo went further with a legend of his own: the scholars each worked shut away in a separate cell. By Philo's account, what came of their separate work?
answer: They each produced word-for-word identical translations
choices: They each produced word-for-word identical translations
They finished the entire task in a single night
They refused to eat until the work was complete
They burned every draft that contained an error
context: By legend (the Letter of Aristeas), Ptolemy II had 72 Jewish scholars translate the Hebrew Bible into Greek, producing the Septuagint ('seventy'). Philo claimed the 72 worked in separate cells yet produced word-for-word identical translations. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septuagint

question: Sostratus built Alexandria's great lighthouse, the Pharos, which rose over a hundred metres and was counted among the Seven Wonders. Legend says the king expected the tower to bear the royal name and no other. By that legend, how did Sostratus claim lasting credit anyway?
answer: He carved his own name in the stone beneath the king's plaster
choices: He carved his own name in the stone beneath the king's plaster
He hid a portrait of himself inside the lighthouse flame
He signed each block with a secret mason's mark
He built a smaller twin tower bearing only his name
context: The Pharos of Alexandria, built under Ptolemy II, towered over 100 meters (330+ feet). Legend says its architect Sostratus secretly carved his own name into the stone under a layer of plaster bearing the king's name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse_of_Alexandria

question: Hattusili III, king of the Hittites, and the pharaoh Ramesses II of Egypt had the terms of an agreement engraved on tablets of silver around 1258 BC. Turkey later presented a copper copy to the United Nations, and it hangs in the UN's New York headquarters close to the Security Council. Of all such documents ever found, it is the oldest surviving what?
answer: peace treaty
choices: peace treaty
marriage contract
trade agreement
law code
context: The Treaty of Kadesh, sealed about 1258 BC, is the oldest surviving peace treaty in the world. Turkey gifted a copper bas-relief replica to the UN; Secretary-General U Thant accepted it on September 24, 1970, and it hangs in the second-floor delegates' corridor near the Security Council Chamber. Source: https://www.un.org/ungifts/replica-peace-treaty-between-hattusilis-and-ramses-ii

question: A foreign king wrote to Hattusili III of the Hittites asking for good iron, the metal that would later take the place of bronze. Hattusili could send him just one iron dagger-blade. In his reply, what did he admit about the iron in his own storehouse at Kizzuwatna?
answer: that he had none of it ready to give
choices: that he had none of it ready to give
that he had pledged all of it to his army
that he kept all of it locked from foreigners
that he had traded the last of it for gold
context: Hattusili III wrote: 'good iron is not at present available in my storehouse in Kizzuwatna... At present I am sending you an iron dagger-blade' -- even a king could not yet supply the iron requested. Anatolia has the earliest textual evidence of iron smelting (2nd millennium BC), but modern scholars reject the old idea that a Hittite 'state monopoly' on iron won them their wars (one of the wrong choices). Sources: https://periclespress.net/Hittites_iron.html ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-019-09129-6

question: Gareth Jones got off his train about forty miles early and crossed into the famine zone of Soviet Ukraine on foot, where foreigners were barred. He carried a knapsack and slowly emptied it as he walked from one village to the next. What did he give away to the starving people he met?
answer: His bread and chocolate
choices: His bread and chocolate
His coat and boots
His train ticket and money
His camera and notebook
context: Jones had packed the knapsack with bread and chocolate specifically to hand out as he tramped from village to village gathering testimony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)

question: Joseph Goebbels, the propagandist, flew to Frankfurt in late February 1933 with a rising German politician, and Gareth Jones, a Welsh reporter, was on the same plane. Jones wrote that a crash would have changed the history of Europe. Who was the politician?
answer: Adolf Hitler
choices: Adolf Hitler
Hermann Goering
Gregor Strasser
Ernst Roehm
context: Jones wrote that if the plane had crashed, "the history of Europe would be changed." The aircraft was named the Richthofen, and Jones flew with the British reporter Sefton Delmer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)

question: A hungry peasant in Ukraine bent in a collective farm's stubble to pick up a few stray ears of wheat, and under a decree of 7 August 1932 that handful could cost him his life or ten years in a camp. Villagers named the decree after the tiny scraps it punished. What did they call it?
answer: The Law of Spikelets
choices: The Law of Spikelets
The Bread Decree
The Iron Harvest Act
The Collective Granary Law
context: Its formal name was the Decree on the Protection of Socialist Property, and it was also called the Law of Five Ears of Grain. A few stray stalks gleaned from a collective field counted as stealing socialist property. Over 200,000 people were sentenced under it, while the man-made famine, the Holodomor, killed roughly 3.9 million Ukrainians by the most detailed studies.

question: Stalin's officials put any Ukrainian village that missed its grain quota on a list that was really a death sentence. They closed every shop, stopped all its trade and sealed the whole village in, children and teachers too, to starve. What was the list called?
answer: The black board
choices: The black board
The black book
The quota roll
The hunger register
context: In Ukrainian, chorni doshky. Hundreds of collective farms and dozens of districts were blacklisted, each one cut off to starve. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor

question: Joseph Stalin and Vyacheslav Molotov signed a directive on 22 January 1933 aimed at the starving peasants of Ukraine, whose villages Stalin's grain quotas had stripped bare. The famine was no accident of weather. What did the order do to the peasants?
answer: It sealed the borders so they could not flee for food
choices: It sealed the borders so they could not flee for food
It drafted them into labor brigades
It forgave the unpaid grain quotas
It opened state granaries to feed them
context: Combined with the internal-passport system introduced in December 1932, peasants were legally forbidden to leave the famine zone in search of food, trapping them inside to die. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causes_of_the_Holodomor ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor

question: Michael Ellman, a historian, looked hard at the grain Stalin's state sold abroad for hard currency while Ukraine starved in 1932 and 1933, almost two million tonnes of it. By his calculation, that grain alone could have kept people alive for a year. About how many people?
answer: Roughly five million people
choices: Roughly five million people
Roughly two million people
Roughly eight million people
Roughly one million people
context: The grain was sold abroad for hard currency while Ukrainian villages were blacklisted and sealed off to starve. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor

question: Eugene Lyons and the other Moscow correspondents knew Gareth Jones had told the truth, yet to guard their visas they turned on him in a session with Constantine Umansky, the Soviet censor. Later Lyons confessed it in his memoir, Assignment in Utopia. In his own words, how did they treat Jones?
answer: "Throw him down we did, unanimously"
choices: "Throw him down we did, unanimously"
We called his account Soviet-baiting
We branded his story a clever lie
We said the truth lay somewhere between
context: Lyons wrote that denouncing Jones "was as unpleasant a chore as fell to any of us, but throw him down we did, unanimously and in almost identical formulas of equivocation." After agreeing to brand Jones a liar at a meeting with the Soviet censor Constantine Umansky, the correspondents ordered vodka and celebrated with him into the early hours. Source: https://www.garethjones.org/soviet_articles/assignment_in_utopia.htm

question: Joseph Stalin's officials stripped the villages of Soviet Ukraine of grain in 1932 and 1933 and turned a shortage into a famine made on purpose, which killed millions of peasants. Ukrainians named it with a word that refuses the neutral 'famine.' What does 'Holodomor' mean?
answer: Death by hunger
choices: Death by hunger
The great hunger
The years of sorrow
The stolen harvest
context: Holodomor combines holod (hunger) and mor (death/plague) -- literally 'to kill by starvation.' The name itself insists it was deliberate, not an accident of weather. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor

question: A hungry peasant in Soviet Ukraine stooped to glean a few stalks left in a collective field after the harvest of 1932. Stalin's government had made such a handful a crime by a decree that August. What could happen to him if he was caught?
answer: Shot, or at least ten years in prison
choices: Shot, or at least ten years in prison
Stripped of all land and exiled north
Worked to death in a labor camp
Flogged, then sent home a marked thief
context: The August 7, 1932 decree let officials execute a peasant for gleaning a handful of grain, or hand down 10+ years in prison with all property seized -- punished for taking the very crop they had grown. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_Spikelets

question: Armed brigades went from house to house through the villages of Soviet Ukraine in 1932 and 1933, carrying off whatever a family could eat: potatoes, livestock, even pets. What did they take that was the cruellest loss of all?
answer: The seed grain set aside for planting
choices: The seed grain set aside for planting
The last cured ham in the cellar
The silver icons off the wall
Every coin kept in the house
context: The brigades took not only the grain meant for eating but next year's planting seed, the animals, and a family's final potatoes -- even pets -- guaranteeing the starvation would continue. The seed was the cruelest loss: it was next year's whole crop. Source: https://www.history.com/articles/ukrainian-famine-stalin

question: Gareth Jones, a young Welsh journalist, got off his train near Kharkiv in March 1933, while most foreign correspondents stayed in Moscow and passed on whatever officials told them. He meant to see the famine for himself. How did Jones do it?
answer: He walked on foot through about twenty villages, sleeping in peasants' huts
choices: He walked on foot through about twenty villages, sleeping in peasants' huts
He flew over the region in a military plane
He interviewed officials from his hotel by telephone
He read the harvest reports in the state archive
context: Jones trekked roughly 40 miles north of Kharkiv on foot through some 20 villages and a dozen collective farms, sleeping in the huts so he could witness the famine firsthand. Source: https://education.holodomor.ca/gareth-jones/

question: Joseph Stalin demanded more grain from Ukraine, the Soviet Union's breadbasket, than its villages could give. By June 1933 the famine that followed was at its height. How fast were Ukrainians dying that month?
answer: About 28,000 every day
choices: About 28,000 every day
About 28,000 every year
About 280 every day
About 2.8 million in a single week
context: Roughly 28,000 deaths a day -- about 17 every minute -- in the country that fed the USSR. The breadbasket starved while its grain was shipped out. Source: https://holodomormuseum.org.ua/en/mass-mortality/

question: Gareth Jones filled his pocket notebook as he went among the starving villages of Soviet Ukraine in March 1933. One set of words came back from the peasants again and again, and he wrote them down. What did the villagers keep telling him?
answer: 'There is no bread; we are waiting for death'
choices: 'There is no bread; we are waiting for death'
'The black earth will not feed us now'
'They left us nothing but the snow'
'Our children no longer ask for food'
context: Jones wrote down 'There is no bread; we are dying' and 'We are waiting for death,' plus the Russian 'Vse pukhli' -- 'everyone is swollen.' He saw children with swollen stomachs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)

question: Gareth Jones faced reporters in Berlin on 29 March 1933, back from the starving villages of Soviet Ukraine, and told them what he had seen there. Walter Duranty of The New York Times would answer him two days later. What did the headline over Jones's story announce?
answer: 'Famine Grips Russia, Millions Dying'
choices: 'Famine Grips Russia, Millions Dying'
'Stalin's Grain War Empties the Villages'
'Ukraine Starves as the Seed Is Seized'
'Red Famine Creeps Toward the Volga'
context: Jones told the truth -- 'Famine Grips Russia, Millions Dying' -- at the exact moment the press corps in Moscow was burying it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)

question: Walter Duranty, Moscow bureau chief of The New York Times, answered Gareth Jones in print two days after Jones spoke in Berlin, under the headline 'Russians Hungry, But Not Starving.' He brushed off Jones's account as a scare story. What did Duranty flatly tell his readers?
answer: 'There is no famine or starvation'
choices: 'There is no famine or starvation'
'Conditions are no worse than in 1921'
'The shortages are local and will soon pass'
'The peasants are merely underfed, not dying'
context: On March 31, 1933 Duranty wrote 'there is no famine or starvation' and waved Jones away. It was a direct, public denial of mass death he would later privately admit was real. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty

question: Walter Duranty, Moscow bureau chief of The New York Times, recast the peasants dying under Stalin's forced collectivization as the cost of building socialism. He packed his excuse into one line that the world still remembers him for. What was it?
answer: 'You can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'
choices: 'You can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'
'History is written by the victors'
'The ends are clouded but the cause is pure'
'A hard road builds a strong people'
context: Duranty's signature line -- 'But, to put it brutally, you can't make an omelet without breaking eggs' -- recast millions of dead Ukrainians as 'broken eggs' on the way to Stalin's project. Source: https://education.holodomor.ca/teaching-materials/quotations/suggested-quotes-to-use-with-student-activities/

question: Bandits kidnapped Gareth Jones on a journey through Inner Mongolia, then under Japanese occupation, in August 1935, and they shot him dead one day short of his thirtieth birthday. Nothing has ever been proved. Who do some historians suspect was really behind the killing?
answer: The Soviet secret police, the NKVD
choices: The Soviet secret police, the NKVD
The Japanese occupation forces
The local bandits, acting on their own
A rival Chinese warlord's troops
context: Jones was murdered on August 12, 1935, one day shy of turning 30. Some historians suspect the Soviet secret police, the NKVD, arranged it -- a suspicion, not proven fact -- as payback for exposing Stalin's famine. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist)  (Legend.)

question: William Strang, a British diplomat, talked with Walter Duranty of The New York Times around September 1933, and Duranty told him privately how many had starved in the past twelve months. It was a figure Duranty never printed. What did he concede?
answer: That perhaps ten million may have died from lack of food
choices: That perhaps ten million may have died from lack of food
That a few thousand had died in isolated villages
That the deaths could not be counted at all
That the harvest had merely been delayed
context: Duranty privately told Strang 'as many as ten million people may have died directly or indirectly from lack of food' -- the truth he hid from his own readers. A 1931 embassy memo recorded him admitting his dispatches 'always reflect the official opinion of the Soviet government.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty

question: Mark von Hagen, a historian, reviewed in 2003 the flattering 1931 reports on the Soviet Union that had won Walter Duranty a major prize. He judged them unbalanced and uncritical and called for the prize to be taken back, but its board saw no clear proof of an intent to deceive. Which prize did Duranty keep?
answer: The Pulitzer Prize
choices: The Pulitzer Prize
The George Polk Award
The Overseas Press Club award
The National Press Club medal
context: Duranty's 1932 Pulitzer still stands. Von Hagen called the work 'unbalanced and uncritical' and said the honor should be revoked; the NYT later called it 'some of the worst reporting to appear in this newspaper,' but the Pulitzer Board has never taken it back. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty

question: Walter Duranty and reporters like him helped bury the Holodomor, and for decades the accepted toll stood at only about half a million, a number that measured how well the truth was hidden. How many Ukrainian dead do serious historians count today?
answer: Roughly 3.5 to 7 million
choices: Roughly 3.5 to 7 million
Roughly 400 to 600 thousand
Roughly 30 to 60 thousand
Roughly 12 to 15 million
context: Estimates run from about 3.5 to 7 million Ukrainians, with some figures reaching 10 million for the wider Soviet famine. The 'soft' half-million number was the measure of the cover-up. Ukraine's parliament declared the Holodomor a genocide in 2006. Source: https://www.britannica.com/event/Holodomor

question: The Lakota first met the horse in the 1600s, after runaway and bartered Spanish horses spread north from Mexico onto the Great Plains. They had no word for the new animal, so they named it after the only animal that had ever hauled their tents and gear. What did the Lakota call the horse?
answer: The sacred dog
choices: The sacred dog
The great elk
The swift deer
The thunder bird
context: The Lakota called the horse 'sunka wakan' — sunka meaning dog, wakan meaning sacred or mysterious. Before the horse arrived, dogs were the only animals Plains peoples used to haul loads, so they named the newcomer after them: the 'sacred dog' or 'mystery dog.' Source: blog.nativehope.org/native-american-relative-horse; nativesunnews.today (Shunka Wakan, the Sacred Dog).

question: Christopher Columbus shipped about two dozen horses across the Atlantic on his second voyage, in 1493. They were the first horses to set hoof in the Americas in about ten thousand years. Why had there been none there for so long?
answer: Horses had once lived in the Americas but had gone extinct there
choices: Horses had once lived in the Americas but had gone extinct there
Horses had been hunted to nothing by early Spanish sailors
Horses could not survive the long ocean crossing until 1493
Horses had been kept penned in Spain and never allowed to leave
context: The horse actually EVOLVED in North America over millions of years, then died out on the continent about 10,000 years ago at the end of the last ice age. So when the Spanish brought Andalusian horses across the ocean, the animal was returning to the very land it had originally come from. Source: history.com/articles/horses-plains-indians-native-americans.

question: A later biographer wrote that the caliph paid Hunayn ibn Ishaq for every finished book in a lavish way. Hunayn, a Christian scholar, ran the translation office at Baghdad's House of Wisdom and turned Greek works of medicine, mathematics and philosophy into Arabic. How was he reportedly paid?
answer: The book's exact weight in gold
choices: The book's exact weight in gold
A fine herd of Arabian horses
A grand palace beside the river
A chest of rare silver coins
context: The 13th-century biographer Ibn Abi Usaybia wrote that Hunayn was paid the weight of each completed book in gold. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hunayn-ibn-Ishaq

question: Al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician in Baghdad, wrote a groundbreaking book around 830. Its title began with an Arabic word meaning restoration. A whole branch of mathematics is named after that one word. Which branch?
answer: Algebra
choices: Algebra
Geometry
Arithmetic
Calculus
context: Al-Khwarizmi's 'Kitab al-Jabr wa'l-Muqabala' (The Compendious Book on Calculation by Restoration and Balancing) gave us the word ALGEBRA, taken from 'al-jabr,' meaning restoration. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Jabr

question: Al-Ma'mun hunted down Greek works of science and philosophy and had them turned into Arabic at his House of Wisdom in Baghdad. His love of Greek learning, by tradition, began with a dream in which an ancient philosopher sat on a throne and urged him to gather the wisdom of the ancients. Who was the philosopher?
answer: Aristotle
choices: Aristotle
Socrates
Pythagoras
Plato
context: The dream of Aristotle is one of the famous legends behind al-Ma'mun's translation movement. Told as tradition, not fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wisdom

question: Theophilus, the Byzantine emperor, lost a war to al-Ma'mun, and the caliph, it is said, demanded of him not gold or land but Greek books. Al-Ma'mun's scholars at the House of Wisdom turned the manuscripts into Arabic. Which subjects did the books he prized most cover?
answer: Astronomy and mathematics
choices: Astronomy and mathematics
Poetry and drama
Farming and cooking
War and politics
context: The Almagest (about AD 150) was Ptolemy's great astronomy book; al-Ma'mun is said to have demanded Greek manuscripts, including it, from Emperor Theophilus. Source: https://www.middleeasteye.net/discover/iraq-baghdad-house-wisdom-uniting-east-west

question: Al-Mutawakkil, a later caliph, offered Hunayn ibn Ishaq lavish rewards to brew a poison for an enemy of the court. Hunayn, the physician who had put the Greek doctor Galen into Arabic, flatly refused and was thrown into prison for a whole year. What reason did he give?
answer: His oath as a physician bound him to heal, never to harm
choices: His oath as a physician bound him to heal, never to harm
His faith forbade him to take any human life
He had sworn that same healer's oath to the enemy too
He held that poisoning dishonored the calling of a healer
context: Hunayn answered that the physician's oath bound him to help and not to harm; al-Mutawakkil jailed him for a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunayn_ibn_Ishaq

question: Al-Ma'mun's astronomers split into two teams on the level plain of Sinjar around 830, one team marching due north and the other due south. Both counted every pace and planted arrows to mark how far they had come. What were they trying to measure?
answer: The size of the Earth
choices: The size of the Earth
The distance to the Sun
The height of the sky
The width of the desert
context: On the plain of Sinjar al-Ma'mun's astronomers measured one degree of latitude as about 56 2/3 Arabic miles, landing within a few hundred miles of the true circumference -- then crossed the desert again to double-check. Source: https://www.chalkefestival.com/history-hub/writing/power-and-curiosity-how-the-abbasid-caliph-al-mamun-pushed-the-boundaries-of-scientific-knowledge/

question: Al-Kindi, a philosopher in Baghdad, wrote the first known book on cracking secret codes around 850, a manuscript later lost for centuries. His method began with the symbol that shows up most often in a coded message. What did he match that symbol to?
answer: The most common letter of the ordinary language
choices: The most common letter of the ordinary language
The first letter the writer wrote down
The rarest letter of the ordinary language
The letter that looks most like the symbol
context: Al-Kindi's 'Manuscript on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages' invented the method now called frequency analysis -- match the commonest cipher-letter to the commonest plain-letter. The text was lost for centuries and only rediscovered in an Istanbul archive in 1987, about 800 years ahead of European cryptanalysis. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Kindi

question: Hunayn ibn Ishaq turned 129 works of the Greek doctor Galen into Arabic. For many of those books, the Greek that Galen wrote has vanished, with every copy lost. How can a scholar today still read those works at all?
answer: Only in Hunayn's Arabic translation
choices: Only in Hunayn's Arabic translation
From carvings found inside Galen's tomb
From a single Greek copy kept in Rome
Only by guessing at the missing text
context: Many of Galen's works survive only in Hunayn's Arabic, the Greek originals having been lost -- a vivid example of Baghdad preserving Greek learning the West had largely lost. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunayn_ibn_Ishaq

question: Al-Jahiz, an Iraqi writer, filled his Book of Animals with more than 350 creatures. In it he claimed that animals are locked in a struggle for existence, an idea that would not get its modern name for about a thousand years. Which later theory does his idea foreshadow?
answer: Natural selection
choices: Natural selection
Inheritance of acquired traits
Laws of heredity
Germ theory of disease
context: Al-Jahiz's 'Kitab al-Hayawan' described a struggle for existence and how environment shapes survival -- ideas that foreshadow natural selection, named in Charles Darwin's 1859 'On the Origin of Species.' The other choices point to Lamarck (acquired traits), Mendel (heredity), and Pasteur (germ theory). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Jahiz

question: Charles Myers, a Cambridge psychologist, wrote about three British soldiers who had been near exploding artillery; one had lost his taste and smell. In February 1915 he named their condition in The Lancet, and the name stuck. What did Myers call it?
answer: Shell shock
choices: Shell shock
Trench fever
Combat fatigue
Soldier's heart
context: Charles Samuel Myers, director of the Cambridge Psychological Laboratory, first used 'shell shock' in print in The Lancet on 13 February 1915, after noticing how alike the symptoms were in three men each blown up by shells. Source: https://www.psychol.cam.ac.uk/news/2015-02-13-shell-shock

question: A First World War doctor saw soldiers come in from near bursting shells with ears that rang, dizzy spells and bad dreams, and most of all a shaking that ran through the whole body. He found one vivid picture for that shaking. What did he liken it to?
answer: A jelly shaking
choices: A jelly shaking
A leaf in the wind
A plucked harp string
A drum being beaten
context: Period doctors described the shell-shocked soldier's trembling as 'rather like a jelly shaking,' alongside ringing ears, dizziness, sleepwalking, and dreams of France and 'dead Germans.' Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-shock-of-war-55376701/

question: Wilfred Owen and Siegfried Sassoon, both poets, met as patients of Dr William Rivers at Craiglockhart, an officers' hospital near Edinburgh, in 1917. Rivers treated his officers with a gentle talking cure. Which poem mourning the soldiers dying at the front did Owen write there while he recovered?
answer: Anthem for Doomed Youth
choices: Anthem for Doomed Youth
The Charge of the Light Brigade
In Flanders Fields
The Soldier
context: Owen wrote 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' during his recovery at Craiglockhart, where Rivers' talking cure had brought him together with Siegfried Sassoon. Source: https://livesofthefirstworldwar.iwm.org.uk/story/78958

question: Private Harry Farr trembled so hard that he was unable to hold a pen, yet a British court martial sentenced him to death for cowardice in 1916. On 18 October he was led out to be shot. What did Farr do before the volley?
answer: He refused the blindfold and looked the firing squad in the eye
choices: He refused the blindfold and looked the firing squad in the eye
He sang a hymn until the volley silenced him
He handed his medals to the chaplain
He saluted the officer who gave the order
context: Harry Farr, hospitalized for shell shock so severe he 'could not hold a pen,' was executed for cowardice on 18 October 1916; he refused the blindfold and faced the firing squad. In 2006 his granddaughter's campaign won a pardon for him and 305 other executed men. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Farr

question: Dr Lewis Yealland told one soldier struck dumb by the war, 'You will not leave this room until you are talking as well as you ever did.' Then he forced the man's mouth open and applied something to the back of his throat until he spoke. Yealland claimed the treatment always worked. What did he apply?
answer: A strong electric current
choices: A strong electric current
A scalding hot iron
A bitter chemical paste
A jolt of pressurized air
context: Dr. Lewis Yealland applied a strong faradic (electric) current to the back of mute soldiers' throats and claimed a 100% success rate — a violent contrast to Rivers' gentle talking cure. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3673538/

question: By tradition, the sixteen-year-old Edward, the Black Prince, walked the battlefield of Crécy after the English victory of 1346 and took the crest and motto of a fallen enemy, the blind King John of Bohemia. Every Prince of Wales has borne that badge since. What is it?
answer: Three ostrich feathers and the motto 'Ich dien' ('I serve')
choices: Three ostrich feathers and the motto 'Ich dien' ('I serve')
A red dragon and the motto 'Cymru am byth' ('Wales forever')
A golden lion and the motto 'Dieu et mon droit' ('God and my right')
A silver unicorn and the motto 'Nemo me impune' ('None provoke me')
context: At Crecy the blind King John of Bohemia had his knights tie their horses' reins to his so he could charge in; they were found dead together the next morning. The 16-year-old Black Prince took his crest of three ostrich feathers and motto 'Ich dien,' and every Prince of Wales has used the badge since. (englishmonarchs.co.uk/black_prince.htm; baldwin.co.uk/news/edward-the-black-prince)

question: English and French kings fought the Hundred Years' War in bouts broken by long truces, and the war outlived five kings on each side. It ran far longer than its name suggests. How long did it really last?
answer: 116 years
choices: 116 years
104 years
131 years
97 years
context: The war ran from 1337 to 1453 -- 116 years -- and outlasted five English kings and five French kings. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War)

question: King John of Bohemia rode with the French army at Crécy in 1346, the scene of England's first great victory of the war. He was old and completely blind and could not see the enemy in front of him, yet he meant to strike at least one blow. What did he do?
answer: He had his knights tie their horses' reins to his and charge with him into the fight
choices: He had his knights tie their horses' reins to his and charge with him into the fight
He stayed at the rear and shouted commands to his marshals by name
He surrendered his sword to the English rather than risk his knights
He climbed a hill to be carried in a litter above the battle line
context: The blind king's knights lashed their reins to his so he could ride into a battle he could not see; the whole group was found dead together the next morning. (britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/battle-of-crecy; britainuntold.co.uk)

question: Edward, the Black Prince, led the army that took King John II of France prisoner on the battlefield of Poitiers in 1356, an even rarer prize than victory. At the feast that night the prince treated his royal prisoner with startling honour. What did he do for King John?
answer: He stood and personally served the captured king his food at the table
choices: He stood and personally served the captured king his food at the table
He returned the king's sword and crown before the meal began
He freed the king on the spot and asked for nothing in return
He seated the king on his own throne and knelt at his feet
context: John II had surrendered by handing his right glove to a knight, Sir Denis de Morbecque. At the banquet the Black Prince waited on the defeated king himself, as a sign of chivalric respect for a brave enemy. (worldhistory.org/article/1511/battle-of-poitiers-1356-ce)

question: Jean Bureau massed perhaps more than two hundred French cannon at Castillon in 1453 and shattered the English attack. A cannonball brought down John Talbot's horse and pinned the great English commander beneath it, and he died there. Longbows had won the famous battles, but cannon won the war. What was left to England of its old French lands?
answer: A single port, Calais
choices: A single port, Calais
The whole region of Normandy
The wine-rich land of Gascony
The crown of France itself
context: Castillon was the first major European battle decided by massed cannon. After 116 years of war over the French crown, England was left with only the port of Calais -- the longbow had won the famous battles, but artillery won the war. (britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Castillon; britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/battle-of-castillon)

question: John of Damascus, a monk in Syria who wrote under Muslim rulers and so lay beyond the emperor's grasp, answered the image-breakers who called it idolatry to kiss a painted icon of Christ. What, by his argument, does the honour paid to an icon do?
answer: Passes through to the real person the image depicts
choices: Passes through to the real person the image depicts
Cleanses the painter of the sin of vanity
Binds an angel to guard the wooden panel
Stores up holiness inside the paint and gold
context: John of Damascus (a Syrian monk writing under Muslim rule, safe from the emperor) taught that the honor paid to an image passes through to its prototype — you do not worship the wood and paint, you honor the person it shows, the way one might kiss a portrait of a loved one. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) made this official church teaching. Source: Britannica iconoclasm article; New World Encyclopedia, Second Council of Nicaea; World History Encyclopedia, Byzantine Icons.

question: Constantine V, author of thirteen treatises against icons, argued at the church council of Hieria in 754 that every painter of Christ is trapped. Paint his humanity alone, and the painter splits it from his godhead; paint the godhead, and he blurs the two natures together. What did Constantine call Christ's only faithful image?
answer: The bread and wine of the Eucharist
choices: The bread and wine of the Eucharist
The wooden cross of the crucifixion
The empty tomb outside Jerusalem
The written words of the four Gospels
context: Constantine V was so committed he personally wrote 13 treatises against icons. His Christological dilemma — painting Christ forces you into either the Nestorian error (splitting his natures) or the Monophysite error (blurring them) — let him conclude the Eucharist was the only faithful image of Christ. The Council of Hieria condemned all icons as idols and cursed everyone who venerated them; the Second Council of Nicaea overturned it in 787. Source: Wikipedia, Council of Hieria; encyclopedia.com Iconoclasm; thecollector.com/what-was-iconoclasm-in-byzantium.

question: A band of senators struck down Julius Caesar on the Ides of March in 44 BC, and ever since the date has carried a sense of doom. To a Roman, what point in the month did the Ides mark?
answer: The middle of the month
choices: The middle of the month
The first day of the month
The last day of the month
The day of the new moon
context: The Ides was simply the middle — the 15th in March, May, July, and October, the 13th in the rest. After Caesar's murder, 'the Ides of March' became shorthand for looming doom. Source: britannica.com/topic/Ides-of-March; worldhistory.org/article/803.

question: Spurinna, a seer, had told Julius Caesar that peril would reach him by the Ides of March at the latest. On the morning itself, walking to the Senate, Caesar joked to him that the Ides had come. What did Spurinna answer?
answer: 'Yes — but they are not gone.'
choices: 'Yes — but they are not gone.'
'Then the gods have spared you.'
'The omens have all passed.'
'Your fortune holds, Caesar.'
context: 'Yes, they are come, but they are not gone.' Hours later Caesar was dead. Spurinna was a haruspex — a priest who read omens. Source: worldhistory.org/article/803; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spurinna.

question: Suetonius and Plutarch both tell how the seer Spurinna warned Julius Caesar that danger would come by the Ides of March. The famous words 'Beware the Ides of March' are another matter. Where do they come from?
answer: A play William Shakespeare wrote in 1599
choices: A play William Shakespeare wrote in 1599
A letter Caesar's wife sent that morning
A Roman law carved over the Senate door
A prophecy kept in the Temple of Vesta
context: Shakespeare invented the exact wording for his play 'Julius Caesar' (1599). Ancient writers Suetonius and Plutarch record only Spurinna's blunt warning, not that catchy line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Et_tu,_Brute; britannica.com/topic/Ides-of-March.

question: Tillius Cimber, a senator, approached Julius Caesar pretending to beg a favour for his banished brother. Then he grabbed Caesar's toga and yanked it off his neck, the signal the plotters had agreed on. What did Caesar cry out as the cloth tore away?
answer: 'Why, this is violence!'
choices: 'Why, this is violence!'
'Stand back, all of you!'
'Guards, to me at once!'
'Have you all gone mad?'
context: The toga-grab was the prearranged signal. Cimber pretended to plead for his exiled brother to get close enough to seize Caesar. Source: lexundria.com/plut_caes/66/prr (Plutarch); worldhistory.org/article/803.

question: By legend, Calpurnia, the wife of Julius Caesar, woke from a terrible dream on the night before the Ides of March and begged him not to go out. He nearly gave in, until Decimus Brutus, one of the plotters, arrived and coaxed him out of the house. What had Calpurnia dreamed?
answer: Caesar stabbed to death in her arms
choices: Caesar stabbed to death in her arms
A wolf loose inside the Senate house
Their children weeping over an empty bed
A fire sweeping through all of Rome
context: Suetonius reports Calpurnia dreamed the gable of their house collapsed and that Caesar was killed in her arms — told as an omen-legend. The conspirator Decimus Brutus arrived and coaxed Caesar into going anyway. Source: livius.org (Suetonius); worldhistory.org/article/803.

question: Artemidorus, a Greek teacher, pressed a scroll into Julius Caesar's hand at the door as Caesar arrived for the Senate's meeting on the Ides of March. The scroll named every one of the plotters, and Caesar took it. What became of that warning?
answer: He never read it before he died
choices: He never read it before he died
He passed it straight to a guard
He read it and laughed it off
He dropped it in the crowd
context: Caesar tucked the note among his other papers in his left hand, meaning to read it later — and never did. The unread scroll could have saved his life. Source: livius.org (Suetonius); worldhistory.org/article/803.

question: Brutus struck a silver coin after the killing of Julius Caesar, with his own portrait on the front. The back showed two daggers on either side of a freed slave's cap, over the letters EID MAR (for the Ides of March). What makes the coin one of the most startling objects to survive from Rome?
answer: A politician advertising a murder on money
choices: A politician advertising a murder on money
The first coin to ever show a living man
A coin secretly buried with Caesar's body
The only coin Rome made of solid gold
context: The two daggers flank a 'pileus,' the cap a freed slave wore — Brutus was bragging that the killing set Rome free. Only about 100 EID MAR denarii survive; they are among the most prized of all ancient coins. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ides_of_March_coin.

question: Servilius Casca stabbed first on the Ides of March, from behind, aiming at Julius Caesar's neck, but the wound was shallow. Caesar fought back with the only thing in his hand and drove it through Casca's arm. What did Caesar stab him with?
answer: His iron writing-stylus
choices: His iron writing-stylus
A dagger he tore loose
A bronze inkpot
A bench leg
context: Caesar seized Casca's arm and drove his stylus — a pointed metal pen — through it, shouting in Latin, 'Casca, you villain, what are you doing?' Source: livius.org (Suetonius); lexundria.com/plut_caes/66/prr (Plutarch).

question: Brutus stood among the senators who stabbed Julius Caesar to death in the Senate hall, and he and his fellow conspirators, sixty or more of them, chose a proud name for themselves. In their own minds, what were they doing by killing Caesar?
answer: Saving the Republic from a dictator
choices: Saving the Republic from a dictator
Avenging a personal family insult
Seizing his fortune for themselves
Obeying a secret order from the gods
context: They called themselves the 'Liberatores' (Liberators) and believed they were rescuing the Roman Republic from the man who had made himself dictator-for-life. The night was meant to restore liberty, not to be a crime. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Julius_Caesar; worldhistory.org/Marcus_Junius_Brutus.

question: Julius Caesar fell under twenty-three stab wounds as about twenty plotters closed in on him in the Senate hall on the Ides of March; Plutarch tells how they packed so tightly around him that he was not the only one hurt. Who else was wounded in the frenzy?
answer: Several of the conspirators themselves
choices: Several of the conspirators themselves
Two senators who tried to help Caesar
A pair of guards at the doorway
Caesar's slaves waiting outside
context: Plutarch writes that 'the conspirators themselves were many of them wounded by each other, while they all aimed their blows at the same man.' Every plotter was meant to strike so that all shared the guilt. Source: lexundria.com/plut_caes/66/prr (Plutarch).

question: Julius Caesar went to meet the Senate on the Ides of March in a hall built by the very rival he had beaten in the civil war. Stabbed again and again, he fell there. At the foot of what did he collapse and die?
answer: A towering statue of Pompey
choices: A towering statue of Pompey
The Senate's bronze doors
An altar to the war-god Mars
The empty chair of the consul
context: Caesar fell at the base of a statue of Pompey the Great, his defeated enemy; Plutarch says the pedestal was 'drenched with his blood.' Just before striking, Cassius prayed to that same statue, as if calling on Pompey's ghost. Source: lexundria.com/plut_caes/66/prr (Plutarch).

question: Antistius, a Greek doctor, studied the body of Julius Caesar after the murder on the Ides of March, in what is often counted as history's first recorded autopsy, and he announced his finding in the Forum. Of the twenty-three wounds, what did he report?
answer: Only one wound had truly been fatal
choices: Only one wound had truly been fatal
All 23 had struck at once
None alone could have killed him
The first blow was the deadly one
context: Antistius judged that only the second wound, in the chest, had actually killed Caesar — often called history's first recorded forensic autopsy. He announced it publicly in the Forum; the word 'forensic' itself comes from 'forum.' Source: livius.org (Suetonius); simplyforensic.com.

question: Octavian, the adopted son of Julius Caesar, rose to rule Rome alone within a few years of the Ides of March, after Brutus and Cassius had both died. What did Caesar's murder do to the Republic in the end?
answer: It ended the Republic for good
choices: It ended the Republic for good
It restored the Senate's full power
It split Rome into two republics
It returned Rome to electing kings
context: The murder triggered fresh civil wars and destroyed the very Republic it was meant to save; Octavian became Augustus, Rome's first emperor. The act meant to save liberty ended it forever. Source: history.com/articles/julius-caesar-assassination-fall-roman-republic.

question: High in the Peruvian Andes, an Inca emperor looked out over Cusco, the capital of the greatest empire of the Americas in its day, a city he and his people saw as the very center of everything. In their Quechua language, what does its name, Qosqo, mean?
answer: The navel of the world
choices: The navel of the world
The roof of the sky
The gate of the sun
The heart of the mountain
context: Qosqo is a Quechua word meaning 'navel' or 'center.' The Inca saw their capital as the navel of the world — the point where the empire's four quarters joined. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Cuzco

question: Pachacuti set out from Cusco to conquer the Andes. In Quechua the Inca gave his realm a name of their own, Tawantinsuyu, and never the Inca Empire. What does Tawantinsuyu mean?
answer: The Realm of the Four Parts
choices: The Realm of the Four Parts
The Children of the Sun
The Throne of the Andes
The People of the High Snows
context: Tawantinsuyu means 'the Realm (or Land) of the Four Parts.' Four quarters (suyu) radiated out from the capital, so the name itself was a map of how the empire was organized. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire

question: Manco Cápac and his sister Mama Ocllo, son and daughter of Inti, the sun god, came up out of Lake Titicaca carrying a shining rod of gold, the Inca founding legend says. Inti told them to wander until the rod did one thing, and there to build their city. What were they to watch for?
answer: The golden staff sinking into the earth
choices: The golden staff sinking into the earth
A condor circling above a peak
The staff turning warm in their hands
A spring of water bursting from the rock
context: In the legend, Inti said to settle wherever the golden staff sank into the ground — and it sank at Cusco. This is a founding legend, told as sacred story, not as recorded history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_mythology

question: Pachacuti, legend says, laid out Cusco in the shape of a single animal: the great fortress of Sacsayhuamán formed its head, the main plaza its belly, and the meeting of two rivers its tail. What animal was Cusco built to look like?
answer: A crouching puma
choices: A crouching puma
A coiled serpent
A soaring condor
A charging llama
context: Legend says Pachacuti laid out Cusco as a crouching puma — the symbol of Inca might — with Sacsayhuamán as the head and the plaza as the belly. This is a traditional account of the city's design. Source: https://smarthistory.org/city-of-cusco/

question: An Inca family high in the freezing Andes made chuño from its potatoes, a rock-hard food that would last as long as ten years in a stone storehouse as a store against famine. How did the family turn a fresh potato into chuño?
answer: Froze it on cold nights, then stomped it underfoot by day
choices: Froze it on cold nights, then stomped it underfoot by day
Buried it deep in dry desert sand
Boiled it down into a thick paste
Smoked it for days over a slow fire
context: Families left potatoes out to freeze in the bitter Andean night, let them thaw by day and trampled the water out with bare feet, again and again, until the potatoes turned rock-hard. That was freeze-drying centuries before electricity, and chuño kept for up to ten years in stone storehouses as a hedge against famine.

question: A prince of Cusco led the city's defense against an invading Chanca army and crushed it at Yahuar Pampa. Then he began the conquests that, in just three generations, would stretch his realm across the whole length of the Andes. He took a throne name for himself, Pachacuti. What does the name mean?
answer: Earth-Shaker, Reverser of the World
choices: Earth-Shaker, Reverser of the World
Lord of the Golden Sun, Child of Inti
Father of the Four Quarters, Son of the Andes
Master of the High Snows, Keeper of the Sun
context: Pachacuti (Quechua pacha kutiy) means 'Earth-Shaker' or 'Reverser/Turner-Over of the World.' He took the name after defeating the Chanca and transforming Cusco from a city into an empire. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Pachacuti_Inca_Yupanqui/

question: Spanish conquerors stripped the gold from the Qorikancha, Cusco's holiest temple, whose walls had been lined with hundreds of gold sheets and whose garden held life-size corn and llamas of gold and silver. They melted it into bars and raised a Catholic church on the temple's foundations. Earthquakes shook Cusco in 1650 and again in 1950 and wrecked the church. What happened to the Inca stonework beneath it?
answer: The Inca walls stood firm and survived
choices: The Inca walls stood firm and survived
The Inca walls crumbled to dust first
The Inca walls were swallowed by a sinkhole
The Inca walls were found to be hollow inside
context: The Spanish melted down the Qorikancha's roughly 700 gold sheets and built Santo Domingo on top — but the mortarless Inca foundations outlasted the colonial church, surviving the earthquakes that wrecked it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coricancha

question: A porter climbed an Andean trail in the 1400s with his load on his own back, the way most Inca loads were carried. Only one kind of pack animal shared the work. Which was it?
answer: The llama
choices: The llama
The horse
The ox
The camel
context: The llama was the Inca's only beast of burden, and even it could carry only about 40 kg. With no horses, oxen, or wheels, almost everything else was moved by human muscle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire.

question: Inca road builders laced their mountain empire together with two great highways, one hugging the coast and one threading the peaks, and armies and messages moved along them the length of the Andes. The Inca called this road system the Qhapaq Ñan. What does that name mean?
answer: Road of the Lord
choices: Road of the Lord
Path of the Sun
Way of the Mountains
Trail of the Four Winds
context: The Qhapaq Nan ('Road of the Lord') ran for over 40,000 km (25,000 miles) through what is now Peru, Ecuador, Chile, Bolivia, and Argentina — all built with no wheel and no iron. Source: worldhistory.org/article/757/the-inca-road-system.

question: Stonemasons raised Machu Picchu around 1450 on a mountain ridge high in the Peruvian Andes, about 80 km from Cusco, out of granite blocks fitted without mortar. It was not a fortress, and it was not a temple-city. What was Machu Picchu built to be?
answer: A mountain estate for the emperor Pachacuti
choices: A mountain estate for the emperor Pachacuti
A fortress guarding the road to Cusco
A prison for captured enemy kings
A market town for coca traders
context: Machu Picchu was a royal estate for the emperor Pachacuti, sitting at 2,430 m (7,970 ft) — a private mountain retreat for the ruler, not a city for ordinary people. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machu_Picchu.

question: At the very top of the stone city of Machu Picchu, Inca priests read one carved rock like a calendar in stone, to follow the seasons and know when each festival should begin. What name did the Inca give that rock?
answer: The Hitching Post of the Sun
choices: The Hitching Post of the Sun
The Mirror of the Moon
The Gate of the Condor
The Throne of the Stars
context: The Intihuatana, the carved 'Hitching Post of the Sun,' is aligned to the winter solstice. The Inca used it like a calendar in stone, watching the sun to know when the festivals should begin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machu_Picchu.

question: Quechua villagers still keep one Inca grass bridge hanging, the Q'eswachaka over the Apurímac River, five hundred years after the Inca wove suspension bridges wherever their royal roads crossed deep canyons. How do the villagers keep it from falling apart?
answer: They reweave it from fresh grass each year
choices: They reweave it from fresh grass each year
They reinforce it with hidden steel cables
They rebuild the cracked spans in stone
They coat its ropes in tar each spring
context: Every June the communities tear the old bridge down and rebuild it from scratch: women twist ichu grass into thin rope, the strands are braided into heavy cables, and the whole bridge is finished in just three days of work, prayer, and festival. Source: nationalgeographic.com/travel/article/inca-grass-rope-bridge-qeswachaka-unesco.

question: A knot-maker recording numbers on an Inca quipu set his knots in base-ten rows, so that a knot's place on the cord made it units, tens, hundreds or thousands, and a figure-eight knot stood for one. When a number had a zero in one of its columns, what did knot-makers like him do?
answer: They left a gap with no knot
choices: They left a gap with no knot
They tied a special black knot
They added a bright red string
They doubled the figure-eight knot
context: A missing knot meant zero — the Inca recorded 'nothing' simply by leaving an empty space on the cord, a true place-value system with no writing at all. Source: worldhistory.org/Quipu.

question: Francisco Pizarro led fewer than 170 Spaniards into the Inca empire in 1532, and at Cajamarca he came face to face with Atahualpa, the Inca emperor, who stood surrounded by thousands of his own warriors. What did Pizarro's tiny force do?
answer: Ambushed the crowd and seized the emperor
choices: Ambushed the crowd and seized the emperor
Retreated into the mountains by night
Challenged the emperor to single combat
Offered to fight as his hired soldiers
context: On 16 November 1532, Pizarro's hidden cavalry charged the gathering and grabbed Atahualpa in the middle of his own army — capturing the ruler of millions with fewer than 170 men. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom_Room.

question: An ordinary Inca family set out to pay the emperor its tax for the year, as every community in the realm had to, though the empire had no coins and no money of any kind. With no cash to hand over, how did the family pay?
answer: By giving the state a turn of labor
choices: By giving the state a turn of labor
By handing over their firstborn child
By surrendering half of their herd
By paying a yearly tax in gold
context: The mit'a was a tax paid in WORK: each community owed the state a turn of labor — building roads, terraces, and bridges, or farming state land. The yearly rebuilding of the Q'eswachaka grass bridge began as exactly this kind of mit'a duty. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queshuachaka.

question: Villagers of Huinchiri and three other Quechua communities twisted strands into six great cables, each as thick as a man's thigh, and hung the Q'eswachaka, the last Inca rope bridge, across the Apurímac River's gorge. What was the whole bridge made from?
answer: Braided grass
choices: Braided grass
Animal hide
Wooden planks
Woven vines
context: The Q'eswachaka, spanning a gorge of the Apurimac River, is woven entirely from grass — q'oya, a cousin of the tough Andean ichu grass. Over 1,000 people from four communities (Huinchiri, Chaupibanda, Choccayhua, and Ccollana) rebuild it by hand in about three days, twisting straw into six great cables as thick as a person's thigh, then dropping the old bridge into the river. UNESCO named the annual renewal an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013. Sources: ich.unesco.org/en/RL/...q-eswachaka-00594 ; nationalgeographic.com/travel/article/inca-grass-rope-bridge-qeswachaka-unesco

question: Pedro de Cieza de León, a Spanish chronicler, judged that not even the swiftest horses could have carried news faster than the chasqui runners of the Inca roads, though the Inca owned no horses of any kind. One of their loads arrived at the emperor's table in Cusco, high in the mountains, still fit to eat. What did the runners bring him?
answer: Fresh fish from the sea
choices: Fresh fish from the sea
Fruit from the warm lowlands
Snow from the mountain peaks
Honey from the forest hives
context: A fresh runner sprinted alongside each arriving one to take the message without stopping, so the relay could move news up to about 240 km (150 miles) a day — fast enough that fish caught in the Pacific reached the emperor's table in Cusco in roughly two days, still fresh. The Spanish chronicler Pedro de Cieza de Leon judged the system unbeatable, writing that 'news could not have been transmitted by greater speed than with the swiftest horses' — and the Inca had none. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasqui ; thecollector.com/chasquis-famed-inca-couriers/

question: William the Conqueror set sail to invade England in 1066. When Christ was born, the average person had got by on about $2 a day, counted in today's money. Where did that daily income stand in William's time?
answer: Still about $2 a day
choices: Still about $2 a day
Up to about $5 a day
Up to about $10 a day
Up to about $20 a day
context: For roughly 1,800 years the world's income line was essentially flat: about $2 a day (in 2011 dollars) at the time of Christ, still about $2 a day in 1066, and only crept to $2.80 a day by 1800. That long flat stretch is the 'shaft' of the hockey stick — then the line bent sharply upward around 1800. Source: Human Progress, 'The Great Miracle of Industrialization,' citing the Maddison Project's per-person-per-day figures.

question: William Blake wrote of 'dark satanic mills' in the early factory age, an age that still brings to mind child labour and choking smoke. Yet during those very years something changed that had never changed before. What began then?
answer: The death of young children began its long collapse
choices: The death of young children began its long collapse
Family sizes began shrinking sharply
Children's reading and writing began falling
Village famines began striking more often
context: Around 1800 more than one-third of all children died before their fifth birthday — in some places every second child — and a typical mother of five to seven children expected to bury two or three. Losing children was, as historians put it, 'not a rare occurrence but the norm.' The industrial era is exactly when that began its long fall; the global rate today is around 4%. The escape from death and poverty, not the misery of the mills, is the real headline of the age. Source: Our World in Data, 'How child mortality has declined in the last two centuries.'

question: HMS Black Joke, a fast Baltimore-built brig, chased slave ships off West Africa for the Royal Navy. By the late 1820s she was the squadron's most famous hunter, with eleven slavers caught in a single year. Her own past held a dark irony. What was it?
answer: She had been a captured slave ship herself.
choices: She had been a captured slave ship herself.
She had been a pirate ship the Navy hunted down.
She had been a royal yacht handed to the Navy.
She had been built in Britain as a warship.
context: Black Joke was the Baltimore-built Brazilian slaver Henriquetta, which had carried about 3,040 enslaved people to Brazil before the Royal Navy seized her in 1827, renamed her after an English song and re-armed her as a chaser. The Navy turned a slave ship into the slavers' nightmare: in one year she ran down eleven of them, before her rotten timbers forced the Navy to burn her in 1832. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Black_Joke_(1827)

question: At Ouidah, the Atlantic slave-ship port of the Kingdom of Dahomey, captives raided from the kingdom's neighbours waited to be sold to European ships. Tradition says they were first made to walk around one particular tree, circling it a set number of times. What was the ritual said to do to them?
answer: Wipe away the memory of their homes and families.
choices: Wipe away the memory of their homes and families.
Bind their spirits to serve the king forever.
Protect the slave ships from storms at sea.
Bring a good price from the waiting traders.
context: Tradition calls it the 'Tree of Forgetfulness,' meant to erase a captive's memory of homeland and kin before the ocean crossing. The detail is legend rather than documented fact, but it captures what the trade tried to do to a person. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey

question: David Livingstone walked across central Africa for years as a missionary and explorer, mapping rivers and exposing the East African slave trade to the world. He died in 1873, deep in present-day Zambia, and his African friends buried his heart there. What did they do with his body to send it home to Westminster Abbey?
answer: Dried it in the sun and carried it 930 miles overland to the coast.
choices: Dried it in the sun and carried it 930 miles overland to the coast.
Floated it down the river by canoe to the coast.
Loaded it onto a trade caravan heading for the coast.
Packed it in salt and sent it by ox-wagon to the coast.
context: Livingstone's companions dried his body and carried it on foot 930 miles to be shipped to Westminster Abbey. His last written plea, now on his Abbey memorial, begs heaven to bless anyone 'who will help to heal this open sore of the world.' Source: https://www.westminster-abbey.org/abbey-commemorations/commemorations/david-livingstone

question: The Spanish slaver El Almirante ran for thirty-one hours in February 1829 with the two-gun HMS Black Joke on her heels, and when the wind died the Black Joke's crew rowed. Then the little ship beat the slaver's fourteen guns and freed the 466 enslaved people in her hold. A naval surgeon wrote that she had done more to end the slave trade than what?
answer: Than all the other ships of the station put together.
choices: Than all the other ships of the station put together.
Than every treaty Britain had signed with Spain.
Than all the speeches ever given in Parliament.
Than the entire blockade of the African coast.
context: Black Joke had chased the slaver El Almirante for 31 hours — even rowing with oars when the wind died — then won in 80 minutes. The West Africa Squadron freed about 150,000 people at sea between 1808 and the 1860s. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Black_Joke_(1827)

question: Britain forced Sultan Barghash of Zanzibar to shut East Africa's largest slave market in June 1873, a market that had passed as many as 50,000 captives a year. On that ground Anglican missionaries raised Christ Church Cathedral, and they set one part of it deliberately over the spot of the old whipping post. Which part did they place there?
answer: The altar.
choices: The altar.
The bell tower.
The main doorway.
The baptismal font.
context: Under the 1873 Frere Treaty Britain made Sultan Barghash close Zanzibar's slave market. Christ Church Cathedral was built on the site, with its altar set deliberately over the place where the whipping post had stood, turning the cruelest spot in the market into its holiest. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church,_Zanzibar ; https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2017/01/05/zanzibar-cathedral-restoration-shows-past-can-unite-rather-than-divide-us

question: When British envoys pressed King Ghezo of Dahomey in the 1840s to stop selling captives to the slave ships, he flatly refused, calling the trade the ruling principle of his people. In his own words, what was the slave trade the source of for his people?
answer: Their glory and wealth.
choices: Their glory and wealth.
Their peace and safety.
Their faith and law.
Their freedom and pride.
context: Ghezo's refusal is part of the honest record the usual story leaves out: the trade had a large internal-African supply side, and powerful African kings defended it. It took a Royal Navy blockade in 1851 to force Dahomey into a treaty the next year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey

question: Dahomey's raiders swept into neighbouring lands for captives to sell into the Atlantic slave trade, and the West African kingdom grew rich on it. Its most feared warriors formed an elite fighting force, and European visitors were shocked to see who served in it. Who made up the unit?
answer: Women — about 6,000 in an all-female regiment
choices: Women — about 6,000 in an all-female regiment
Boys — taken from conquered villages and raised to fight
Foreigners — mercenaries hired with European guns
Priests — who fought between the kingdom's festivals
context: The Agojie — nicknamed the 'Dahomey Amazons' by Europeans — numbered about 6,000 at their 1840s peak and were Dahomey's raiders, taking captives to sell or to be sacrificed at the kingdom's Annual Customs. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahomey_Amazons

question: Zanzibar's Hamad bin Muhammad al-Murjabi started out with fewer than 100 armed men and rose to be one of the richest slave and ivory traders in history. People called him Tippu Tip, and he said the name came from a sound. What sound was it?
answer: The 'tip-tip' of his guns firing
choices: The 'tip-tip' of his guns firing
The 'tip-tip' of rain on his tent
The tapping of his cane as he walked
The clink of the coins he counted
context: Tippu Tip (born about 1832) said his nickname came from the 'tip-tip' sound of his guns. He ran the East African trade long after the Atlantic trade was dying; by 1895 he controlled seven clove plantations and around 10,000 enslaved people, and in 1887 the Belgian-run Congo Free State even made the slaver its district governor. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tippu_Tip

question: The Asante kings of the Gold Coast traded war captives to British and Dutch slavers on the shore, and in return they wanted one European good above the rest: firearms. By the mid-1700s Asante was the most powerful state on the coast. What did the Asante use the guns to do?
answer: Seize more land and capture more people
choices: Seize more land and capture more people
Defend their coast from European raiders
Hunt elephants for the ivory trade
Guard the gold mines from rival kingdoms
context: Historians call this the 'gun-slave cycle': Asante sold war captives to British and Dutch traders for guns, and the guns let the Asante conquer neighbours and take more captives to sell for still more guns. The cycle made Asante the dominant coastal power by the mid-1700s; the wars that filled the slave ships were African wars, fought with European weapons. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asante_Empire ; https://blackpast.org/global-african-history/ashanti-empire-asante-kingdom-18th-late-19th-century/

question: When European traders came to the Gold Coast to buy slaves, the Asante had long kept slaves of their own. But Akan slavery differed in one big way from the slavery Europeans set up across the Atlantic. What was true of slaves in Akan lands that was almost never true of slaves in the Americas?
answer: Could rise to become an influential figure in the community
choices: Could rise to become an influential figure in the community
Were always freed after exactly seven years
Could never be bought or sold, only inherited
Were paid wages for the work done
context: In Akan society an enslaved person could rise to real standing in the community — historians cite this as the biggest difference from European chattel slavery, which fixed a person's status for life. https://blackpast.org/global-african-history/ashanti-empire-asante-kingdom-18th-late-19th-century/

question: The riverside market at Nyangwe, on the Lualaba River, was crowded with shoppers on 15 July 1871 when the slave trader Dugumbe's men turned their guns on them, and some 400 to 500 people died. David Livingstone was standing in the market and saw it happen. What did that single day become for him?
answer: The emotional center of his campaign to end the East African slave trade
choices: The emotional center of his campaign to end the East African slave trade
The reason he finally turned back and sailed home to Britain
The day he was taken prisoner by the slavers
The moment he abandoned exploring to become a missionary
context: Livingstone witnessed Arab/Swahili slavers under Dugumbe open fire on the Nyangwe market crowd, killing 400-500; the horror became the heart of his crusade against the East African trade. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyangwe

question: Deep in the Congo in 1871, David Livingstone was set on recording what the slavers were doing when his paper and ink ran out. He brewed ink from clothing dye and found something else to write on. Where did he write his field diary?
answer: In the margins of an old newspaper
choices: In the margins of an old newspaper
On strips of bark peeled from trees
On the blank backs of his maps
On the inside covers of his Bible
context: Out of supplies, Livingstone wrote his 1871 field diary — including his account of the Nyangwe massacre — in the margins of an old copy of The Standard, in ink brewed from clothing dye. https://livingstoneonline.org/spectral-imaging/livingstones-1871-field-diary

question: David Livingstone spent his last years on foot in central Africa, exposing the East African slave trade. On 1 May 1872, a year to the day before he died, he wrote a prayer about the trade, and its words were later carved onto his tomb in Westminster Abbey. What did he call the trade?
answer: This open sore of the world
choices: This open sore of the world
This chain that girdles the earth
The great wound of Africa
The shame of all the nations
context: Livingstone wrote the prayer on 1 May 1872, a year to the day before his death, praying for 'every one, American, English, or Turk, who will help to heal this open sore of the world'; the line is engraved on his tomb in Westminster Abbey. https://blog.library.si.edu/blog/2013/10/23/david-livingstone-and-the-other-slave-trade-part-iii-the-slaver-and-the-abolitionist/

question: The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron hunted slave ships along thousands of kilometres of African coast for about fifty years after Britain banned its slave trade in 1807, from about 1808 to 1860. What did those fifty years of patrols add up to?
answer: About 1,600 slave ships seized and about 150,000 Africans freed
choices: About 1,600 slave ships seized and about 150,000 Africans freed
About 600 slave ships seized and about 40,000 Africans freed
About 3,000 slave ships seized but fewer than 10,000 Africans freed
About 250 slave ships seized and about 75,000 Africans freed
context: From about 1808 to 1860 the West Africa Squadron patrolled 5,000+ km of coast, seizing roughly 1,600 slave ships and freeing around 150,000 Africans. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa_Squadron

question: British sailors who patrolled the slave coast with the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron gave it a grim nickname. Between 1830 and 1865 about 1,600 of them died on that duty, almost all of them not in battle but from one cause. What killed nearly all of them?
answer: Tropical disease
choices: Tropical disease
Slaver cannon fire
Storms and shipwreck
Starvation at sea
context: Roughly 1,600 West Africa Squadron sailors died between 1830 and 1865, almost all from tropical disease — the patrol was so lethal the coast was nicknamed 'the white man's grave.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa_Squadron

question: Robert Pape and Chaim Kaufmann, two political scientists, put a price tag on Britain's sixty-year campaign to suppress the Atlantic slave trade. They found it had consumed about 1.8% of the nation's income, and they summed it up in one striking phrase. How did they describe what Britain had done?
answer: The most expensive case of costly international moral action in modern history
choices: The most expensive case of costly international moral action in modern history
The costliest overseas military campaign Britain waged in the whole 19th century
A vast expense that Parliament deliberately hid from the British public
A moral burden that later judges said outweighed any good it achieved
context: Pape and Kaufmann calculated the campaign cost about 1.8% of national income, calling it 'the most expensive example of costly international moral action recorded in modern history.' https://library.fes.de/libalt/journals/swetsfulltext/7064300.pdf

question: King Agaja of Dahomey sent his armies against neighbouring peoples for captives, and Dahomey sold them to European traders at the coast. Robert Harms, a historian, has explained why the kingdom could not stop: the trade bought the one thing its wars ran on. What did Dahomey get in exchange for captives?
answer: Firearms and gunpowder
choices: Firearms and gunpowder
Cloth and cowrie shells
Horses and iron bars
Rum and tobacco
