The Carthaginians poured down and killed him and thousands of Romans. What natural condition let Hannibal hide a whole army so close to them?
answer: A thick early-morning fog
choices: A thick early-morning fog
A moonless, pitch-black night
A blinding desert sandstorm
A heavy curtain of falling snow
context: Around 15,000 Romans were killed and thousands more captured — one of the largest ambushes in military history. Source: Wikipedia, Battle of Lake Trasimene; Britannica, Battle of Trasimene.

question: Phoenician settlers built Carthage around 814 BC. Legend says Queen Dido was promised only as much land as one ox-hide could cover. How did Dido turn that little scrap of leather into ground for a whole city on a hilltop?
answer: Cut it into thin strips and ringed a hilltop
choices: Cut it into thin strips and ringed a hilltop
Soaked it for weeks until it stretched huge
Traded it to the locals for far more land
Prayed to the gods to make the hide grow
context: The hill she claimed was called Byrsa. Carthage grew into the richest city in the Mediterranean, with a famous circular war-harbor (the cothon) that could shelter on the order of 170–180 warships. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Carthage.'  (Legend.)

question: Reeling from the slaughter at Cannae, Rome turned to a steady old commander, Quintus Fabius Maximus, who refused to give Hannibal the head-on battle he was hungry for. Fabius shadowed the Carthaginians through the hill country — where Hannibal's feared cavalry was useless — and wore them down instead. For this, Romans hung a one-word nickname on Fabius that history never let go of. What did they call him?
answer: Cunctator, 'the Delayer'
choices: Cunctator, 'the Delayer'
Maximus, 'the Greatest'
Cautus, 'the Careful'
Custos, 'the Guardian'
context: 'Fabian strategy' still means winning by patient avoidance — George Washington later used the same approach against the British. In the hills, Hannibal's feared cavalry was nearly useless. Source: Wikipedia, Quintus Fabius Maximus / Fabian strategy; Mount Vernon, 'Fabian Strategy.'

question: The night after Cannae, Hannibal's cavalry commander Maharbal begged him to march straight on Rome at once, promising, 'In five days you will dine on the Capitol.' When Hannibal hesitated instead, a stunned Maharbal threw a famous line back at him. What did Maharbal say to Hannibal?
answer: 'You know how to win a victory, but not how to use one.'
choices: 'You know how to win a victory, but not how to use one.'
'You have beaten Rome, but you will never hold it.'
'The gods gave you this day; do not waste the next.'
'A lion upon the field, a lamb before the gate.'
context: In Livy's Latin: 'Vincere scis, Hannibal; victoria uti nescis.' Hannibal never did march on Rome, and historians have argued about that choice ever since. Source: Livy, History of Rome (via wikiquote.org/wiki/Hannibal and libquotes.com/maharbal).

question: At Zama in 202 BC, Hannibal opened the battle the way he always loved to — with a thundering charge of war elephants. But the Roman general Scipio was ready with two tricks: he had his men blast trumpets and horns to terrify the beasts, and he had arranged his battle lines in a clever way so the charge did almost no harm. What had Scipio done with his lines?
answer: Left open lanes for the elephants to run straight through
choices: Left open lanes for the elephants to run straight through
Packed them into one tight, unbroken wall of shields
Pulled them back behind a deep water-filled ditch
Hidden them completely inside the nearby woods
context: Many elephants bolted harmlessly down the lanes, and others panicked and trampled back through Hannibal's own ranks. Scipio beat Hannibal at his own game and ended the Second Punic War. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'The Battle of Zama'; Wikipedia, Battle of Zama.

question: At Cannae, Hannibal put his weakest troops, Gauls and Spaniards, in the center on purpose. They bulged forward, then bent back as the Romans pushed in. His veteran African infantry on the wings wheeled inward. His cavalry closed off the rear. The Romans were trapped in a ring and cut down from every side. What is this move, still taught at West Point, called?
answer: The double envelopment
choices: The double envelopment
The feigned retreat
The flying wedge
The oblique advance
context: Polybius describes Hannibal arranging 'the central companies of Hispanics and Celts' into a crescent. Polybius counts about 70,000 Romans killed in a single day (Livy says about 48,200), against Carthaginian losses of only 5,700–8,000 — one of the deadliest single days in the history of warfare. Source: Wikipedia, Battle of Cannae; Britannica, Battle of Cannae.

question: Suppose you wished to become a Muslim. Islam asks one thing to begin: that you say a single short sentence, the Shahada, and mean it sincerely. What does the Shahada say?
answer: There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God
choices: There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God
Pray five times each day and give to the poor
Make the pilgrimage to Mecca at least once in your life
Fast from dawn to sunset all through Ramadan
context: The Shahada is the first of the Five Pillars of Islam. Simply saying it sincerely is how a person becomes a Muslim. Source: islamic-relief.org.uk Five Pillars of Islam.

question: A family sits at its table as the sun sets on a day of the Ramadan fast; since dawn none of them has eaten or drunk anything, not even water. Following the Prophet Muhammad's example, they break the fast with one particular food first. What do they reach for?
answer: Dates and water
choices: Dates and water
Bread and honey
Lamb and rice
Figs and milk
context: Sawm, the fourth pillar, is the Ramadan fast. Muslims rise before dawn for a meal called suhoor, then break the fast at sunset (iftar), traditionally with dates and water. Source: islamic-relief.org.uk Ramadan; iqranetwork.com iftar.

question: A pilgrim on the hajj walks seven times counter-clockwise around the Kaaba, a black cube-shaped building in Mecca, in the ritual called the tawaf. Each time he passes one corner he tries to touch or kiss something set into it, or, when the crowd holds him back, points at it. What is set into that corner?
answer: The Black Stone
choices: The Black Stone
A golden door
A bronze bell
A silver crescent
context: The black cube is the Kaaba, and the object is the Black Stone (Hajar al-Aswad), set in its corner. Pilgrims unable to reach it through the crowd point to it from a distance. Source: timesofisrael.com rituals of the hajj; asiasociety.org.

question: A reciter working through the Quran begins chapter after chapter with the same blessing, the Bismillah: 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.' All but one of the 114 chapters open with it. Which chapter is the exception?
answer: The ninth chapter, At-Tawbah
choices: The ninth chapter, At-Tawbah
The first chapter, Al-Fatiha
The longest chapter, Al-Baqarah
The shortest chapter, Al-Kawthar
context: The Bismillah opens 113 of the Quran's 114 chapters; the ninth surah, At-Tawbah, is the sole exception. Source: alislam.org Bismillah article; islamqa.info.

question: In October 1829, five machines lined up at the Rainhill Trials to prove steam engines could haul trains. Only one of the five even finished the contest. It hauled 13 tons and outran a galloping horse at 30 mph. Which engine was it?
answer: Rocket
choices: Rocket
Novelty
Sans Pareil
Cycloped
context: Stephenson's Rocket was the sole finisher at the Rainhill Trials (6-14 Oct 1829), reaching 30 mph (48 km/h) with a 13-ton load and astonishing spectators by outrunning a horse. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainhill_trials

question: In 1829, the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in England held the Rainhill Trials to pick the best steam locomotive for its new tracks. Every machine entered was supposed to run on steam. But one entry, the Cycloped, had no steam engine and no boiler at all. What actually drove the Cycloped forward down the rails?
answer: A horse walking on a moving belt
choices: A horse walking on a moving belt
A team of men cranking a wheel
A falling weight on a long chain
A coiled spring wound by hand
context: The Cycloped was powered by a horse walking on a treadmill belt. It withdrew from the trials when the horse crashed through the belt at about 5 mph. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainhill_trials

question: George Stephenson, later called the 'Father of Railways,' could not read or write until he was 18. He had started work at age 8 keeping cows off the colliery waggonways. How did he finally learn to read, write, and do arithmetic?
answer: He paid out of his own wages for night school
choices: He paid out of his own wages for night school
He was taught by a wealthy mine owner
He learned from books left by his father
He attended a free school for poor boys
context: George Stephenson was illiterate until age 18 and paid from his own colliery wages to attend night school. He rose to become the 'Father of Railways.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stephenson

question: In 1829 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway held the Rainhill Trials for a 500-pound prize. The rules were harsh. An engine had to average at least 10 mph over 70 miles of back-and-forth runs. What crushing load did a winner also have to pull?
answer: Three times its own weight
choices: Three times its own weight
Exactly one hundred tons
Twice the weight of a horse team
Its own weight in passengers
context: To win the 500-pound prize (about 47,000 pounds today), an engine had to haul three times its own weight and average at least 10 mph over a 70-mile total on a one-mile track. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainhill_trials

question: George Stephenson built his very first locomotive in 1814 at a colliery. It hauled 30 tons of coal up a hill at 4 mph and was the first engine to grip a smooth iron rail by friction alone. He named it after a Prussian general who had helped beat Napoleon. What was the engine called?
answer: Blucher
choices: Blucher
Hercules
Samson
Goliath
context: Stephenson's 1814 locomotive Blucher was named after the Prussian general Gebhard von Blucher. It was the first successful flanged-wheel locomotive to grip a smooth iron rail by friction alone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stephenson

question: On September 27, 1825, George Stephenson drove the engine that opened the Stockton and Darlington Railway. It was the first public steam railway to carry riders. It hauled 80 tons of coal and flour, with about 600 people crammed aboard. What was the engine named?
answer: Locomotion No. 1
choices: Locomotion No. 1
Blucher
Sans Pareil
Novelty
context: George Stephenson drove Locomotion No. 1 to open the Stockton & Darlington Railway on 27 Sept 1825, hauling an 80-ton load and reaching 15 mph with roughly 600 people aboard. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locomotion_No._1

question: At Rainhill in 1829, one entry briefly stole the show. The Novelty, built by John Ericsson and John Braithwaite, was actually faster than Rocket early on, hitting over 24 mph and thrilling the crowd. Why did this crowd favorite never finish the trials?
answer: Its boiler joint burst under pressure
choices: Its boiler joint burst under pressure
Its driving wheels slipped off the rail
Its firebox ran completely out of coke
Its frame snapped on a sharp curve
context: The Novelty hit over 24 mph and thrilled spectators, but its boiler/bellows joint burst under pressure and it never completed the Rainhill Trials. Source: https://www.historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofBritain/Rainhill-Trials/

question: At the 1829 Rainhill Trials in England, the winning steam engine Rocket — built by George Stephenson and his son Robert — beat its rivals because of a clever boiler design that let it raise steam far faster than any other engine. Instead of sending the fire's heat through one big flue, what did Rocket's boiler send the hot gas through?
answer: 25 narrow copper tubes running through the water
choices: 25 narrow copper tubes running through the water
One wide chamber surrounded by cold air
A coiled pipe submerged in an oil bath
Two large drums packed with hot bricks
context: Rocket's multitubular boiler ran the fire's hot gas through 25 narrow copper tubes (3 inches across) inside the water tank. The huge gain in heating surface let it raise steam far faster than its rivals. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephenson's_Rocket

question: A Liverpool newspaper struggled to describe how fast Rocket flew past the crowd at Rainhill. The Times called its speed 'almost incredible.' To capture how it raced past the crowd, the Liverpool paper compared the engine to what living thing?
answer: A swallow
choices: A swallow
A racehorse
A hawk
A hare
context: A Liverpool newspaper described Rocket 'darting past the spectators' with 'the rapidity with which the swallow darts through the air.' The Times called its speed 'almost incredible.' Source: https://www.railwaymuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/stephensons-rocket-rainhill-and-rise-locomotive

question: On 15 September 1830, the Liverpool & Manchester Railway had its grand opening. William Huskisson, a Member of Parliament, stepped down at Parkside to shake hands with the Duke of Wellington. A voice shouted a warning, 'An engine is coming!' Huskisson panicked, and a carriage door swung open into Rocket's path. What happened to him?
answer: His leg was crushed by the oncoming engine
choices: His leg was crushed by the oncoming engine
His coat was caught and dragged on the rail
His arm was broken against the carriage door
His head struck the platform as he fell
context: William Huskisson panicked as Rocket approached at Parkside; a carriage door swung open into the engine's path and crushed his leg. He became the first widely-reported railway fatality. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Huskisson

question: Before a Parliamentary committee in 1825, a member tried to make Stephenson's railway plans look foolish. Would it not be 'a most inconvenient circumstance,' he asked, if a cow strayed onto the line in front of a speeding engine? In his thick Northumbrian accent, what did Stephenson shoot back?
answer: 'Very awkward -- for the coo (cow)'
choices: 'Very awkward -- for the coo (cow)'
'Then the cow had best learn to run'
'No cow would dare stand its ground'
'We shall fence the whole line, sir'
context: By tradition (Samuel Smiles, 1857), when asked about a cow on the line, Stephenson replied in his Northumbrian accent, 'Very awkward -- for the coo,' and the questioner gave up. Recorded as anecdote, so labeled legend. Source: Samuel Smiles, 'The Life of George Stephenson' (1857), via gutenberg.org/files/46229

question: At the 1830 railway opening, William Huskisson was dying of a crushed leg. George Stephenson unhooked the locomotive Northumbrian and raced it to Eccles for help, flat-out at about 36 mph. In that mad dash to save a dying man, what did Stephenson achieve by accident?
answer: A new world speed record
choices: A new world speed record
The first nighttime rail run
The longest non-stop journey
The first crossing of a river bridge
context: Racing the Northumbrian to Eccles at about 36 mph to save Huskisson, Stephenson set a new world speed record during the rescue. Huskisson still died that evening around 9 pm. Source: https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/arts/history/ecc/archive/emforum/projects/adayinhistory/15september1830

question: In the 1820s, the English engineer George Stephenson began building the world's first steam railways in the coalfields of northern England. When he set the distance between his two rails, he did not sit down and calculate a scientific number — he simply used the same rough spacing the old horse-drawn coal wagons at his colliery had used: 4 feet 8.5 inches. That strange, oddly precise measurement is now called 'standard gauge.' What is remarkable about it today?
answer: Most of the world's railways still use it
choices: Most of the world's railways still use it
No country ever copied it again
It was banned as unsafe within a decade
Only British steam engines ever fit it
context: Stephenson's 4 feet 8.5 inches became the 'standard gauge' adopted across Britain and most of the world. The spacing of rails on most of the planet today traces back to one Northumberland enginewright. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stephenson

question: After Rocket's triumph, Britain went railway-mad. In 1830 the country had just 98 miles of railway. Through the 'Railway Mania' of the 1840s, with Parliament passing hundreds of acts for new lines, how far had the network exploded by 1849?
answer: 6,000 miles
choices: 6,000 miles
500 miles
1,200 miles
20,000 miles
context: Britain's rail network grew from 98 miles (1830) to 6,000 miles (1849). In 1846 alone Parliament passed 263 railway acts for 9,500 proposed miles before the share bubble burst. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_Mania

question: George Hudson, the 'Railway King,' controlled over a third of Britain's track by 1844 and paid fat dividends that made investors adore him. But those dividends were a fraud: he paid old investors out of new investors' money. After he was exposed, what happened to his wax figure at Madame Tussaud's?
answer: It was melted down
choices: It was melted down
It was hidden in storage
It was moved beside other swindlers
It was sold off to a collector
context: George Hudson ran his railway empire as a Ponzi scheme, paying dividends from new investors' capital. When exposed, his waxwork at Madame Tussaud's was melted down, and he died with an estate worth under 200 pounds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Hudson

question: In 1829 Rocket won the greatest locomotive contest of the age and amazed the world by outrunning a horse. Yet so many engineers rushed to improve on it that Rocket did not stay the best for long. How quickly was the winner left behind by better engines?
answer: It was obsolete within about 18 months
choices: It was obsolete within about 18 months
It stayed the fastest for fifty years
It was destroyed in a boiler blast
It was shipped off to an American line
context: Rocket (about 4.5 tons, an 0-2-2 wheel layout, a 16-foot chimney) was made obsolete by improved engines within about 18 months of winning Rainhill. The real Rocket still survives in the Science Museum collection. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephenson's_Rocket

question: Rocket's second great trick was an arrangement that shot the engine's used exhaust steam straight up the chimney. This sucked air through the fire like a giant bellows, so the coke burned hotter the faster the engine ran. What was this self-feeding device called?
answer: The blast pipe
choices: The blast pipe
The steam dome
The safety valve
The slide valve
context: Rocket's blast pipe shot exhaust steam up the chimney, drawing air through the fire like a bellows so the coke burned hotter at speed. This plus the multitube boiler became standard on nearly every steam locomotive worldwide. Source: https://www.railwaymuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/stephensons-rocket-rainhill-and-rise-locomotive

question: When Japanese forces overran Nanjing in December 1937 and began six weeks of mass killing, John Rabe, a German businessman and Nazi Party member, sheltered more than 600 Chinese refugees in his own house and garden. He gambled that pilots would never strike their ally Germany's own emblem. So he draped one giant item over his air-raid shelter. What did Rabe spread over the shelter?
answer: A giant swastika flag
choices: A giant swastika flag
A red diplomatic banner
A painted Siemens company sign
A white hospital cross
context: Rabe ran the Siemens office in Nanjing and led the International Committee that turned a 3.86-square-km neutral zone into a refuge for roughly 250,000 Chinese civilians. A survivor recalled him saying that once the Japanese saw the swastika flag they 'definitely wouldn't bomb' — and he was right. He even noted that his Nazi armband worked where the American flag failed. Source: NPR 'Shelter Under the Swastika: The John Rabe Story'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rabe.

question: General Iwane Matsui commanded the Japanese army that captured Nanjing. Troops there killed about 200,000 to 300,000 Chinese civilians and unarmed prisoners. The Tokyo war-crimes court convicted him and hanged him in 1948, but not for ordering the massacre. What did the judges hold him responsible for instead?
answer: His failure to prevent his troops' atrocities
choices: His failure to prevent his troops' atrocities
His personal beheading of prisoners
His forging of the surrender terms
His looting of the city's treasury
context: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East applied the principle of command responsibility: a commander can hang for crimes he did not order if he failed to stop troops under his command. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwane_Matsui; Britannica, Nanjing Massacre.

question: El Cid's warhorse Babieca grew into the most famous steed in all of Spain. The story goes that when young Rodrigo first picked the colt out of the herd, his godfather scoffed and blurted out the very word that stuck as the horse's name for life. What does 'Babieca' mean?
answer: Roughly 'stupid' or 'dummy'
choices: Roughly 'stupid' or 'dummy'
Roughly 'lazybones'
Roughly 'runt'
Roughly 'mule'
context: By legend the godfather thought Rodrigo had chosen a weak, clumsy colt and exclaimed 'Babieca!' The 'dumb' colt became the greatest warhorse in Spain. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Babieca'; New World Encyclopedia, 'El Cid.'

question: Boabdil, the last Muslim sultan of Granada, reined in his horse at a mountain pass to look back at the Alhambra one last time as he rode into exile in 1492, and his eyes filled with tears. By legend his mother Aixa offered him no comfort, only a stinging rebuke. What did she say?
answer: 'You weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man.'
choices: 'You weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man.'
'A crown you cannot hold is a crown you never earned.'
'Your father would never have shed these tears.'
'Tears now will not win back what your hand let slip.'
context: The pass is still called Puerto del Suspiro del Moro, the Pass of the Moor's Sigh. The famous taunt is almost certainly a later literary invention: historians trace it to Bishop Antonio de Guevara, who composed the scene around 1526 for Emperor Charles V's visit, so it is a beloved legend, not a record of Aixa's real words. Source: Andalucia.com, 'Boabdil'; Historia Magazine, 'Reinterpreting the Fall of Granada.'

question: When El Cid died defending Valencia in 1099, the Almoravid army was still surrounding the city, and his people feared the siege was lost without him. Legend says his wife Jimena hit on a daring plan to save Valencia using the dead hero himself. What did she do?
answer: Strapped his armored body upright on his horse and sent him out to lead one last charge
choices: Strapped his armored body upright on his horse and sent him out to lead one last charge
Dressed a young soldier in his armor to impersonate him before the troops
Hid news of his death and ransomed the city back to the Almoravid emir
Burned his body on the walls so the enemy would think a beacon called for aid
context: Terrified that the dead Cid had risen, the Almoravid besiegers fled to their ships, so the saying goes that 'El Cid won the battle dead on a horse.' The horse was Babieca. Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'El Cid.'  (Legend.)

question: By the late 1400s, only one Muslim kingdom was left in Spain — the emirate of Granada, in the mountains of the south. Its last sultan was Boabdil. Year by year, the armies of the Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella took his cities one by one, until in 1492 they took Granada itself. All through those years the Spaniards mocked Boabdil with the nickname 'el rey chico' — 'the little king.' It had nothing to do with how tall he was. Why did they call him 'little'?
answer: His kingdom kept shrinking around him
choices: His kingdom kept shrinking around him
He had been crowned while still a young boy
He ruled in his powerful father's shadow
He paid tribute and ruled at Ferdinand's mercy
context: He was also called 'el-Zogoibi,' 'the unfortunate' or 'unlucky one.' After surrendering he was given the mountainous Alpujarras, then crossed to Fez in Morocco, where he is said to have died decades later. Source: Andalucia.com, 'Boabdil'; Discovery UK, 'Boabdil: The Last Sultan of Granada.'

question: Spain's great Christian war-hero Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar is remembered everywhere as 'El Cid.' Yet he also fought for the pay of Muslim kings, and the title 'El Cid' came straight out of his Muslim soldiers' own language. From the Arabic 'al-sidi,' what does 'El Cid' actually mean?
answer: 'The lord' or 'the master'
choices: 'The lord' or 'the master'
'The conqueror'
'The faithful'
'The exile'
context: After King Alfonso VI exiled him, El Cid fought for the Muslim Taifa of Zaragoza before taking Valencia as his own principality. His other title, 'Campeador,' is from Latin campi doctor, 'master of the battlefield.' Source: Wikipedia, 'El Cid'; New World Encyclopedia, 'El Cid.'

question: In January 1492 the fall of Granada ended nearly eight centuries of war between Christian and Muslim Spain. Standing in Ferdinand and Isabella's camp that very season was a foreign sailor who would soon win the monarchs' backing for a voyage into the unknown. Which sailor was it?
answer: Christopher Columbus, who that same year sailed west for the Americas
choices: Christopher Columbus, who that same year sailed west for the Americas
Amerigo Vespucci, who that same year mapped the new continent
Vasco da Gama, who that same year rounded Africa to India
Ferdinand Magellan, who that same year set out to circle the globe
context: Columbus was present at Granada's surrender and received his royal commission from Ferdinand and Isabella that same year, so the end of the Reconquista and the start of the voyage to the Americas happened in the same place and the same year. Source: The Conversation, 'These are the keys of this paradise'; EBSCO Research Starters, 'Fall of Granada.'

question: The Capitulations of Granada in 1491 promised the city's Muslims they could keep their religion, their mosques, their property, and their language. Within a few years Cardinal Cisneros broke that promise outright. What did he do that he then boasted about in a letter to the Pope?
answer: Forced mass baptisms, 3,000 Muslims converted in a single day
choices: Forced mass baptisms, 3,000 Muslims converted in a single day
Forced 4,000 baptisms in the cathedral over one weekend
Burned the city's Qurans in the public square
Banned Arabic and the Muslim call to prayer
context: Cisneros boasted to the Pope of 3,000 conversions in one December day in 1499. The broken promise sparked the Alpujarras revolt and a 1501 decree ordering the Muslims of Granada to convert or leave. Source: Wikipedia, 'Treaty of Granada (1491)' and 'Rebellion of the Alpujarras (1499-1501)'; Britannica, 'Spain: The conquest of Granada.'

question: Manfred von Richthofen was the deadliest fighter pilot of World War I, shooting down 80 enemy aircraft. He also earned the most famous nickname in the war, the 'Red Baron.' What did he do that won him that name?
answer: He painted his whole fighter plane blood-red
choices: He painted his whole fighter plane blood-red
He flew only at dawn when the sky turned red
He wore a long red scarf in every battle
He fought above a town in the red hills
context: Richthofen had his fighter painted blood-red around January 1917 — that one vivid color is what earned him the name 'Red Baron.' His Albatros D.III was the first plane he painted red. Source: history.com/articles/manfred-baron-von-richthofen

question: The Red Baron, Manfred von Richthofen, flew many planes. But the one history remembers had a rare feature. Most fighters had two wings. This one stacked three wings, so it could turn and climb tight in a dogfight. What was this famous plane called?
answer: The Fokker Dr.I triplane
choices: The Fokker Dr.I triplane
The Albatros scout biplane
The Sopwith Camel fighter
The Pfalz monoplane racer
context: The Fokker Dr.I — a three-winged 'triplane,' painted all red — was Richthofen's most famous aircraft. The stacked triple wings gave it a tight turn and climb in a dogfight. Source: history.com/articles/ace-of-aces-how-the-red-baron-became-wwis-most-legendary-fighter-pilot

question: Lorenzo de' Medici survived the Pazzi plot of 1478 and took his revenge in paint. He paid Sandro Botticelli forty gold florins for a picture all of Florence would see, and it stayed up until his family was driven from the city in 1494. What did Lorenzo have Botticelli paint?
answer: Life-size figures of the hanged plotters dangling on the jail wall
choices: Life-size figures of the hanged plotters dangling on the jail wall
A triumphal mural of Lorenzo riding in glory through the city
A grand scene of the city guards executing the captured traitors
A bold proclamation of every family that had aided the plotters
context: These were 'pittura infamante' — paintings of infamy — showing the traitors hanging by their necks on the wall of the Florentine jail. They stayed there until the Medici were driven into exile in 1494. Source: smithsonianmag.com; virtualuffizi.com 'pittura d'infamia'.

question: Leonardo da Vinci drew his Vitruvian Man around 1490, a naked man in pen and ink with arms and legs outstretched, to show the ideal proportions of the human body. Earlier artists had failed to fit those limbs inside a perfect circle and a perfect square with one shared center. Leonardo's answer was to give each shape a center of its own. Where did he put the two centers?
answer: The circle on the navel, the square on the groin
choices: The circle on the navel, the square on the groin
The circle on the heart, the square on the navel
Both centered exactly on the navel together
The circle on the head, the square on the feet
context: Leonardo's Vitruvian Man (c. 1490): the circle is centered on the navel and the square on the groin; offsetting the two centers, rather than sharing one, let the figure fit both without distortion. (britannica.com; iflscience.com)

question: Sultan Mehmed II broke into the great city of Constantinople in 1453 after a siege of 53 days, and Greek scholars fled west into Italy. As they ran, they carried away the one kind of treasure they prized above all else. What did they carry out with them?
answer: Ancient Greek manuscripts saved from the city's libraries
choices: Ancient Greek manuscripts saved from the city's libraries
Chests of gold seized from the imperial palace
The sacred relics of the city's churches
Skilled crews to build a new war fleet
context: Among the rescued texts were the complete works of Plato. The scholars settled especially in Florence and Venice, pouring classical Greek knowledge back into the West and fueling the Renaissance recovery of ancient learning. Source: Wikipedia 'Greek scholars in the Renaissance'; nlm.nih.gov.

question: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, aged 23, offered in 1486 to defend 900 theses on all of human knowledge against any challenger in Rome. He opened with a speech now known as the 'Manifesto of the Renaissance.' One daring claim in it about human nature alarmed the Church so much that it banned the debate and charged him with heresy. What did Pico claim about a human being?
answer: A human being can become anything he chooses to be
choices: A human being can become anything he chooses to be
A human being shares directly in the very mind of God
A human being is born already free of every sin
A human being can reach God with no priest at all
context: Pico's speech is the 'Oration on the Dignity of Man.' The Church banned the debate and charged him with heresy, but his proclamation of human freedom became a defining cry of the Renaissance. Source: Wikipedia 'Oration on the Dignity of Man'; 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'.

question: Cosimo de' Medici set the scholar Marsilio Ficino up in a villa to translate all of Plato into Latin for the first time. Yet as Cosimo lay dying in 1464, he ordered Ficino to halt Plato and rush another bundle of writings into Latin first, writings he believed held the wisdom of a sage even older than Plato. What kind of writings did the dying man demand?
answer: A collection of ancient Egyptian magical texts
choices: A collection of ancient Egyptian magical texts
The battle diaries of Alexander the Great
The sayings of the Buddha
The love poems of Sappho
context: Ficino set Plato aside and translated the Hermetic writings so Cosimo could read them before he died. Ficino went on to give the world its first complete Latin Plato and to coin the phrase 'Platonic love.' Source: Wikipedia 'Marsilio Ficino'.

question: Marsilio Ficino looked around Florence and was sure, by 1492, that he was living through something extraordinary. He wrote that his century had brought the liberal arts, almost dead, back to light, and he gave his own age a ringing name. What did Ficino call it?
answer: A golden age
choices: A golden age
A new springtime
A second dawn
A bright rebirth
context: Ficino wrote that 'this century, like a golden age, has restored to light the liberal arts, which were almost extinct' — proof that the people of the Renaissance knew, even as they lived it, that they were inside a true rebirth of learning. Source: Wikipedia 'Marsilio Ficino'.

question: In February 1848, revolution drove King Louis Philippe of France off his throne. Rather than face the guillotine that had killed Louis XVI, he slipped out of Paris in an ordinary cab, in disguise, traveling under a false name. What name did the King of France escape under?
answer: 'Mr. Smith'
choices: 'Mr. Smith'
'Mr. Jones'
'Mr. Williams'
'Mr. Brown'
context: Louis Philippe abdicated Feb 24, 1848 and fled to England disguised, calling himself 'Mr. Smith' — terrified of sharing Louis XVI's fate. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-Philippe/The-July-Revolution

question: On March 15, 1848, in Budapest, the young poet Sándor Petőfi climbed the steps of the Hungarian National Museum. He recited verses that became the battle cry of the Hungarian revolt. The crowd then seized the printing presses to print them. By what name is that poem remembered?
answer: the 'National Song'
choices: the 'National Song'
the 'Twelve Points'
the 'Springtime Hymn'
the 'Magyar Creed'
context: Petőfi recited his 'National Song' (Nemzeti dal) — 'Talpra magyar, hí a haza!' ('Rise up, Hungarian, the homeland calls!') — and the crowd printed it alongside the revolutionaries' Twelve Points. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemzeti_dal

question: For decades after 1815, Klemens von Metternich was Austria's chancellor. He stood for the old order of Europe. On March 13, 1848, the revolution reached Vienna and forced him to quit and flee. What did Metternich reportedly say on hearing the news?
answer: 'Well, my dear, it is all over.'
choices: 'Well, my dear, it is all over.'
'Order will be restored by spring.'
'Let the rabble have their banquet.'
'The Empire has seen worse storms.'
context: Metternich reportedly said 'Eh bien, mon cher, tout est fini!' before fleeing Vienna — the symbol of the post-1815 order swept away. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1848

question: During the Five Days of Milan (March 18 to 22, 1848), the city's people threw up barricades and fired from windows and rooftops. They faced 13,000 Austrian troops under Field Marshal Radetzky. By the fifth day, what had the people of Milan done to that veteran army?
answer: they drove the entire garrison out of the city
choices: they drove the entire garrison out of the city
they forced Radetzky to sign a constitution
they captured Radetzky and held him hostage
they burned the Austrian arsenal to the ground
context: In five days of street fighting, Milan's residents expelled Radetzky's whole 13,000-man garrison — though he would return the next year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Days_of_Milan

question: In 1849 the elected Frankfurt Parliament, hoping to unite Germany, offered the imperial crown to King Frederick William IV of Prussia. He turned it down — but his reason cut to the heart of the whole liberal project. Why did Frederick William IV refuse the crown a people's assembly offered him?
answer: he scorned a crown offered up from the gutter rather than granted by his fellow princes
choices: he scorned a crown offered up from the gutter rather than granted by his fellow princes
he had secretly promised the German throne to the emperor of Austria
he believed a divided Germany was too poor to support an empire
he feared he would be assassinated by the Frankfurt delegates
context: Frederick William IV refused the Frankfurt Parliament's crown on April 3, 1849, rejecting a title from a revolutionary assembly rather than from his fellow monarchs — gutting the liberal hope of unification by consent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfurt_Parliament

question: In Paris in June 1848, the revolution that had toppled the king turned on itself: tens of thousands of workers raised barricades and fought the very republicans who had won power months earlier, until the army crushed them. The same spring, Marx and Engels put out a slim pamphlet that would echo for a century. Which two movements split apart and turned against each other in 1848?
answer: the liberal-constitutional road and the socialist road
choices: the liberal-constitutional road and the socialist road
the monarchist road and the republican road
the Catholic road and the Protestant road
the nationalist road and the imperialist road
context: 1848 saw the liberal-constitutional and socialist roads visibly diverge — the same springtime 'The Communist Manifesto' appeared. The June Days in Paris, where liberal republicans and workers fought each other on the barricades, made the split bloody and plain. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1848

question: A Turkish war chief held a little borderland around Sogut, a town in the north-west of Anatolia, around the year 1300, pushing against the crumbling Byzantine Empire. His descendants ruled an empire that stretched from Vienna to Baghdad and lasted until 1923, and his whole dynasty was named after him. What was his name?
answer: Osman
choices: Osman
Orhan
Mehmed
Suleiman
context: The Ottomans (Osmanlis) are named for Osman, who led a small band of frontier warriors in northwest Anatolia around 1300. From that tiny start grew an empire that endured until 1923. Source: https://worldhistoryedu.com/osman-i-founder-of-the-ottoman-empire/

question: Mehmed II hired a gun-founder named Urban to cast a huge cannon called the Basilica, some 27 feet in length, to smash the old walls of Constantinople. Hauling it 120 miles to the walls needed 60 oxen, 1,000 men and 42 days. What did the giant cannon fire?
answer: Stone balls weighing about 600 pounds
choices: Stone balls weighing about 600 pounds
Barrels of burning Greek fire
Iron bolts the size of tree trunks
Clay pots full of gunpowder
context: Urban's bombard, the Basilica, flung stone cannonballs of roughly 600 pounds nearly a mile. It took 60 oxen and 1,000 men 42 days to haul it ~120 miles to Constantinople. Source: https://www.historyanswers.co.uk/medieval-renaissance/ottoman-super-cannon-the-bombard-that-built-an-empire/

question: Ottoman officers walked into Christian villages in the Balkans every few years and took boys aged 8 to 20 through the devshirme, the child levy. The boys were raised as Muslims, cut off from their families and trained as soldiers for the Janissaries, the empire's elite troops. To whom were they loyal?
answer: Only to the Sultan, who paid their salary
choices: Only to the Sultan, who paid their salary
To the village elders who raised them
To the Islamic clergy who taught them
To whichever general led them in battle
context: Through the devshirme, Christian boys were levied, converted to Islam, severed from their families, and raised as salaried soldiers loyal to no one but the Sultan -- a genuinely strange institution that produced the empire's elite Janissary corps. Source: https://timelessmyths.com/stories/devshirme/

question: Joseph, a Christian boy from near Kayseri, entered the Janissary corps after the Ottoman child levy took him around 1512. A captive of the devshirme was not doomed; it could lift him all the way to the top. Under his new name, Mimar Sinan, what did Joseph become?
answer: The empire's greatest architect
choices: The empire's greatest architect
The richest merchant in Istanbul
The admiral of the whole Ottoman fleet
The personal physician to the Sultan
context: Mimar Sinan -- born the Christian boy Joseph near Kayseri and taken in the devshirme -- became the Ottoman Empire's greatest architect, designing some 374 buildings, his masterpiece the Selimiye Mosque at Edirne, finished when he was over 80. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimar_Sinan

question: Suleiman ruled the Ottomans through their golden age for 46 years, longer than any other sultan, and Europe called him the Magnificent. His own people gave him a different name. What did the Ottomans call him?
answer: Kanuni, the Lawgiver
choices: Kanuni, the Lawgiver
Fatih, the Conqueror
Gazi, the Holy Warrior
Selim, the Just
context: To his people Suleiman was 'Kanuni' -- the Lawgiver -- for codifying Ottoman law into kanuns. He reigned 1520-1566, longer than any other sultan, and was himself a poet and goldsmith. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Suleyman-the-Magnificent

question: Ottoman storytellers gave their dynasty a founding legend, recorded in the 1400s, long after the founder had died. In it the founder fell asleep at the home of Edebali, a holy man, and had a dream that was read as a sign his family would one day rule a huge empire. What grew from his navel until it spread over the whole world?
answer: A tree
choices: A tree
A river
A flame
A crescent moon
context: In the legend of 'Osman's Dream,' a tree grows from Osman's navel and shades the whole world -- a sign his line would rule a great empire. The tale was actually written down in the 1400s, long after Osman's death, to give the dynasty a founding myth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osman%27s_Dream

question: In 1923 an all-Black Broadway show called 'Runnin' Wild' had a song-and-dance number with wild flapping arms and kicking legs. It spread across America so fast it became the top dance of the whole decade. What was it called?
answer: The Charleston
choices: The Charleston
The Foxtrot
The Lindy Hop
The Tango
context: The 'Charleston' number in 'Runnin' Wild' (1923) gave the Roaring Twenties its signature dance, with its flapping arms and kicking legs. Source: https://www.summerjamboree.com/en/1940s/charleston/

question: In America in the 1920s — the Roaring Twenties, when jazz music was new and radios crackled in every home — a young woman might bob her hair short, wear a skirt above the knee, smoke cigarettes, and dance in jazz clubs until dawn. It broke every rule her mother had grown up with. Newspapers gave this bold new kind of young woman a nickname. What was she called?
answer: A flapper
choices: A flapper
A debutante
A suffragette
A bohemian
context: The 'flapper' was the icon of 1920s rebellion: bobbed hair, knee-length skirts, cigarettes, and jazz clubs. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/the-history-of-the-flapper-part-1-a-call-for-freedom-11957978/

question: Henry Ford's moving assembly line cut the time to build a Model T chassis from over twelve hours down to just 93 minutes. To keep the line moving, Ford allowed the cars to come in only one thing. Only one what?
answer: One color: black
choices: One color: black
One body shape
One engine size
One wheel size
context: By 1914 Ford's moving line built a Model T chassis in 93 minutes, and the cars came in only black to keep the line moving. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/october-7/moving-assembly-line-at-ford

question: In May 1927 Charles Lindbergh flew his single-engine plane the Spirit of St. Louis alone from New York to Paris — 33.5 hours over open ocean, navigating by dead reckoning through fog. When he landed at Le Bourget field, what greeted 'Lucky Lindy'?
answer: A crowd of over 100,000 people
choices: A crowd of over 100,000 people
A military court-martial
An empty, fog-bound runway
A telegram ordering him home
context: Lindbergh's solo Atlantic crossing in 1927 made him a global hero; over 100,000 people mobbed Le Bourget when he landed. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/may-21/lindbergh-lands-in-paris

question: On September 30, 1927, the great slugger Babe Ruth of the New York Yankees smashed his record-breaking 60th home run of the baseball season. Nobody had ever hit that many in a single year. To describe just how staggering the number was, sports writers stopped comparing him to other batters and started comparing him to whole rival teams. What did Ruth's 60 home runs outdo?
answer: More than any entire other team in the American League hit that year
choices: More than any entire other team in the American League hit that year
More than the Yankees had hit in the whole previous decade
More than every player in the World Series combined
More than the National League's top three sluggers together
context: Ruth's 60 home runs in 1927 were more than any OTHER entire AL team hit that season; the Yankees' lineup was nicknamed 'Murderers' Row.' Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/september-30/babe-ruth-hits-60th-homer-of-1927-season

question: On November 2, 1920, Pittsburgh station KDKA made the first commercial radio broadcast, reading election returns aloud. Because of that broadcast, listeners sitting at home learned one thing before the morning newspapers could even print it. What did they learn?
answer: That Warren Harding had won the presidency
choices: That Warren Harding had won the presidency
That the stock market had crashed overnight
That a war had broken out in Europe
That the World Series had been decided
context: KDKA's 1920 broadcast of the Harding-Cox returns was the first commercial radio broadcast; home listeners knew Harding had won before the papers printed it. Source: https://theconversation.com/100-years-ago-the-first-commercial-radio-broadcast-announced-the-results-of-the-1920-election-politics-would-never-be-the-same-148143

question: In 1927 Duke Ellington's orchestra became the house band at Harlem's whites-only, plantation-themed Cotton Club, where the management told him to play crude 'jungle music.' Instead of resenting the order, Ellington did something with it that helped define the Harlem Renaissance. What did he do?
answer: He turned it into a proud, signature sound of his own
choices: He turned it into a proud, signature sound of his own
He quietly walked out and refused the job
He hired white musicians to play instead
He kept the band silent in protest
context: Ordered to play 'jungle music' at the Cotton Club, Ellington transformed the assignment into his own celebrated signature style, a cornerstone of the Harlem Renaissance. Source: https://www.wgbh.org/news/2014-02-03/after-midnight-and-the-cotton-club-is-swinging-again

question: The standard close-combat weapon of the Roman legionary was the gladius. Among all the swords of the ancient world, what made the gladius unusual?
answer: It was a short stabbing sword, only about two feet long
choices: It was a short stabbing sword, only about two feet long
It was a long slashing sword built for sweeping cuts
It was a heavy chopping blade weighted at the tip
It was a curved sabre meant for fighting on horseback
context: The gladius was deliberately short (about 60-70 cm) so legionaries packed shoulder-to-shoulder could thrust it past their shields in tight formation rather than needing room to swing. Source: warfarehistorynetwork.com/article/the-roman-gladius/

question: After a long day's march into enemy land, a Roman legion did not just stop and sleep. Every evening, before resting, what did the soldiers do?
answer: Built a fully fortified camp with ditch, rampart, and stake wall from scratch
choices: Built a fully fortified camp with ditch, rampart, and stake wall from scratch
Sent scouts ahead to find a friendly village to shelter in
Drew lots to decide which men would stand guard through the night
Burned the surrounding fields so enemies could not approach unseen
context: They dug a ditch (fossa), raised an earth rampart (vallum), and planted a palisade of sharpened stakes, finishing in roughly 4-5 hours, then tore it all down the next morning and did it again. Source: imperiumromanum.pl/en/roman-army/roman-camp/

question: In a siege, Roman soldiers in the front row locked their shields into a wall. The men behind them raised shields over their heads to make a roof. The unit became a moving shell against arrows and stones. What was this formation called?
answer: The testudo, or 'tortoise'
choices: The testudo, or 'tortoise'
The phalanx, or 'finger'
The vexillum, or 'banner'
The pilum, or 'spear-line'
context: The testudo ('tortoise') was held together by nothing but disciplined positioning. It was only a shelter, not a fighting stance: the instant hand-to-hand combat began it dissolved so each man could draw his gladius. Source: unrv.com/military/testudo-formation.php

question: New rules in the late Republic made each Roman legionary carry his own gear tied to a T-shaped pole. He hauled a saw, basket, pick, axe, digging tool, stakes, and three days of food on the march. What mocking nickname did the legionaries earn?
answer: 'Marius's mules'
choices: 'Marius's mules'
'The iron wolves'
'Caesar's hounds'
'The dust eaters'
context: The reforms tied to the general Marius made each man his own pack-animal (muli Mariani). Josephus lists the load: 'a saw and a basket, a pick-axe and an axe, a thong of leather and a hook, with provisions for three days.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcina

question: The Roman pilum was a heavy javelin with a long thin iron shank tipped by a small point wider than the rod itself. When a pilum struck an enemy's shield and buried deep, the long shank was nearly impossible to yank back out. What was an enemy usually forced to do?
answer: Throw away his own shield to get free of it
choices: Throw away his own shield to get free of it
Snap the shaft off and keep fighting behind the shield
Pull it loose and hurl it straight back
Drop to the ground and crawl beneath the volley
context: The point punched a hole bigger than the rod, so the embedded shank stuck fast and the enemy had to ditch his shield. (Some ancient writers say it bent on impact; modern archaeologists debate whether the bending was by design.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilum

question: A Roman centurion carried a metre-long vine-wood staff, the vitis, and after the Porcian Laws it was the only legal way to strike a Roman citizen-soldier. The historian Tacitus records one centurion the troops nicknamed 'Cedo Alteram' ('Bring me another'). How did the centurion earn that name?
answer: He kept breaking his vine-staffs on soldiers' backs
choices: He kept breaking his vine-staffs on soldiers' backs
He kept losing his sword and demanding replacements
He kept calling for a fresh standard after each battle
He kept ordering a second helping at every meal
context: He shouted 'cedo alteram' ('gimme another') each time a staff snapped on a man's back. The soldiers killed him first in the mutiny of AD 14. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vine_staff

question: Cincinnatus was ploughing his small farm in 458 BC when Roman messengers came. They named him dictator to rescue an army trapped by the enemy. He smashed the enemy in about two weeks. With full power in his hands, what did Cincinnatus choose to do?
answer: Resigned the dictatorship and went straight back to his plough
choices: Resigned the dictatorship and went straight back to his plough
Kept the dictatorship and ruled over Rome for life
Marched his victorious army back against the Senate
Seized the conquered land as his own private estate
context: Cincinnatus gave up supreme power after only about 15-16 days, having defeated the Aequi at Mount Algidus, and became the ancient world's model of a leader who surrenders absolute power voluntarily. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Quinctius_Cincinnatus ; mountvernon.org/library/digitalhistory/digital-encyclopedia/article/cincinnatus

question: George Washington stunned the world in 1783. He did not seize the new nation he had won. He quit as commander-in-chief and went home to farm. He handed all military power back to Congress. When King George III heard Washington meant to give up power, the king said it would make Washington exactly what?
answer: The greatest man in the world
choices: The greatest man in the world
A traitor to his own soldiers
A fool who threw away a crown
The first true king of America
context: Washington resigned before the Continental Congress at Annapolis on December 23, 1783 and returned to Mount Vernon, deliberately echoing Cincinnatus turning his sword back into a plough. Source: americanrevolutioninstitute.org/the-american-cincinnatus/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington's_resignation_as_commander-in-chief

question: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay wrote 85 essays to urge Americans to back the Constitution. All three shared one pen name. Their opponents wrote back under pen names like 'Brutus' and 'Cato.' The whole fight was argued in disguise. What did all these pen names have in common?
answer: They were all names from ancient Rome's republic
choices: They were all names from ancient Rome's republic
They were all names of English kings
They were all names from the Bible
They were all names of Greek philosophers
context: The name honored Publius Valerius Publicola, who in Plutarch's 'Lives' repeatedly rescued the young Republic from would-be tyrants; with both sides using Roman pseudonyms, the entire debate over the Constitution was conducted in Roman costume. Source: federalism.org/library/american-federalism/who-was-publius/ ; csac.history.wisc.edu/2022/07/22/pseudonyms-and-the-debate-over-the-constitution/

question: Step into the U.S. House of Representatives and on each side of the Speaker stands a large bronze bundle of wooden rods strapped tightly around an axe -- copied straight from the emblem that Roman magistrates' guards carried to display their authority. The American bundle has 13 rods, one for each original state, and it teaches a lesson a single rod cannot: a thin rod snaps easily alone, but a bound bundle will not. What is this Roman bundle of rods-and-axe called?
answer: The fasces
choices: The fasces
The aquila
The labarum
The corona
context: The fasces was adopted as the emblem of the House's Sergeant at Arms in 1789; the House version carries 13 rods (one more than the Roman model) for the original 13 states, signifying strength through unity. Source: history.house.gov/Blog/Detail/15032450168 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbols_of_the_United_States_Senate

question: Roman coins, monuments, and the army's battle standards all carried four letters: SPQR. The Romans packed the two halves of their government into the city's own name for itself. What do the letters SPQR stand for?
answer: The Senate and the People of Rome
choices: The Senate and the People of Rome
The Empire and the Legions of Rome
The Kings and the Priests of Rome
The Gods and the Heroes of Rome
context: SPQR = 'Senatus Populusque Romanus.' Putting both the aristocratic Senate and the common People into Rome's own name captured the mixed government: power was shared between the few and the many. Source: Wikipedia, 'SPQR'; UNRV Roman History.

question: In 509 BC the Romans drove out their last king, Tarquin the Proud, and swore never to be ruled by one man again. To guarantee it, they replaced the king with two officials elected together for a single year — so each could cancel the other. What were these paired rulers called?
answer: Consuls
choices: Consuls
Pharaohs
Emperors
Bishops
context: Two consuls shared the old king's power, each holding office for just one year. Romans even dated their years by them — they called 59 BC 'the consulship of Caesar and Bibulus.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Roman consul'.

question: Rome's noble class was called the patricians. Tradition holds that Romulus, the city's founder, picked 100 leading men to form Rome's first Senate and called them the 'patres.' From that Latin word the patricians took their name. What does 'patres' mean?
answer: Fathers
choices: Fathers
Soldiers
Strangers
Servants
context: Legend: 'patres' is Latin for 'fathers,' and the descendants of Romulus's first senators became the patrician nobility. Everyone else — the plebeians who farmed and fought — could at first hold no high office. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patrician (ancient Rome)'.

question: Rome never let either consul rule alone. When both consuls were in the city, they took turns being in charge, switching the lead back and forth on a fixed schedule so neither man held sole command long enough to seize the state. How often did the two consuls swap who was in charge?
answer: Every month
choices: Every month
Every week
Every season
Every day
context: With both consuls in Rome, command rotated monthly, and either could veto the other's decisions. After their single year, each had to step down and account for everything he had done. Source: Wikipedia, 'Roman consul'; Polybius, Histories Book 6.

question: A Roman consul walked the city escorted by twelve attendants, each carrying the fasces — an axe bound inside a bundle of wooden rods. But inside Rome's walls one part of that bundle was always removed before the consul carried it through the streets. Which part was taken out while the consul was inside the city?
answer: The axe
choices: The axe
The rods
The leather straps
The wooden handle
context: Inside the city the axe came out of the bundle, because no citizen could be put to death without a trial: the rods were for beating, the axe for beheading. Outside the walls the axe went back in — there the consul held power of life and death over his soldiers. Source: Wikipedia, 'Roman consul'.

question: Rome's common citizens, the plebeians, had no high office and no easy way to force change — so they invented a weapon. Five times between 494 and 287 BC, in events called the Secessions of the Plebs, they pressured the patricians with one bold act that suddenly left the city helpless. What did the plebeians do?
answer: Walked out of Rome onto a nearby hill
choices: Walked out of Rome onto a nearby hill
Set fire to the Senate house
Sailed away to found a rival city
Stormed the gates of the patricians' homes
context: It was history's first general strike: the commoners simply left, camping on the Sacred Mount in 494 BC and the Aventine later. With no one to fight or farm, the patricians had to bargain — and each peaceful walkout won the plebs new rights. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Secession of the Plebs'.

question: In 494 BC the plebeians had walked out of Rome, and the patrician envoy Menenius Agrippa came to coax them back. To argue that nobles and commoners need each other, he told a fable in which one organ of the body got starved by the rest until the whole body wasted away. Which famous fable did Menenius Agrippa tell?
answer: The fable of the belly and the limbs
choices: The fable of the belly and the limbs
The fable of the tortoise and the hare
The fable of the fox and the grapes
The fable of the boy who cried wolf
context: Legend: in the Fable of the Belly, the limbs rebel and refuse to feed the lazy-looking stomach — and the whole body wastes away. The plebs took the point that patricians and plebeians need each other, returned to Rome, and won the office of tribune. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Secession of the Plebs'.

question: The tribune of the plebs was the commoners' protector, armed with a veto that could halt even a consul. To let him stand up to the powerful, Roman law made the tribune 'sacrosanct.' What did being sacrosanct grant a tribune?
answer: Anyone who laid a hand on him could be killed on the spot
choices: Anyone who laid a hand on him could be killed on the spot
His veto could overturn a verdict of the law courts
He could summon the Senate to meet at any hour
He could pardon any citizen condemned to death
context: The tribune's body was sacrosanct — harming him meant death with no trial, the shield that let him use his veto, 'intercessio' ('I forbid'), against the powerful. There were 2 tribunes at first; by 457 BC there were 10. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tribune of the plebs'.

question: Before 451 BC, Rome's laws were unwritten, and only patrician priests knew them — so commoners could be judged by rules they were never allowed to see. The plebeians forced the law to be written down and posted in the Forum for every citizen to read. What was this first written Roman law code called?
answer: The Twelve Tables
choices: The Twelve Tables
The Laws of Romulus
The Servian Code
The Edict of the Praetor
context: Ten commissioners wrote the law onto bronze tablets set up in the Forum, so all citizens could finally read the rules used against them. Cicero said Roman schoolboys still memorized the Twelve Tables centuries later. Source: Britannica, 'Law of the Twelve Tables'.

question: In 458 BC, a Roman army was trapped by the Aequi at Mount Algidus. Senators ran to a small farm across the Tiber and found Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus at his plow. They made him dictator with full power to save the army. After he beat the enemy, what did Cincinnatus do?
answer: Laid down his power after 15 days and returned to farming
choices: Laid down his power after 15 days and returned to farming
Crowned himself the new king of Rome
Marched his army into Rome to take the Senate
Demanded a lifetime appointment as dictator
context: Legend: a Roman dictator could hold total power, but only for a maximum of six months. Cincinnatus needed just 15 days — he rescued the army, made the Aequi 'pass under the yoke,' then gave up his power and went back to his plow. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus'.

question: Polybius, a Greek writer living in Rome, judged the Senate's deadliest weapon to be the way it could starve a man it had sent to war. A consul might be a brilliant general, Polybius noted, yet still be at the Senate's mercy. How could the Senate ruin a victorious commander out in the field?
answer: By withholding the grain, clothing, and pay his army needed
choices: By withholding the grain, clothing, and pay his army needed
By forbidding him to ever marry a patrician
By erasing his name from the list of consuls
By banning him from speaking in the Forum
context: Polybius wrote that the Senate controlled the treasury, and no coin could be spent 'without a decree of the senate.' A general could win every battle, but if the Senate cut off supplies, his army starved — the purse was the check that kept commanders loyal. Source: Polybius, Histories Book 6, sec. 13.

question: In 449 BC a ruler named Appius Claudius rigged a court to declare the free plebeian girl Verginia a slave, so he could seize her. Her father, a soldier, could not save her by law — and in the crowded Forum he did something so shocking it toppled Appius Claudius from power. What did Verginia's father do?
answer: Stabbed his own daughter dead rather than let her be taken
choices: Stabbed his own daughter dead rather than let her be taken
Set himself on fire before the judge's seat
Surrendered her quietly and fled the city
Paid a ransom to buy back her freedom
context: Legend: rather than hand Verginia to Appius Claudius, her father killed her in the Forum. The outrage triggered the second secession of the plebs, brought down the decemvirs who had seized power, and restored the tribunes. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Secession of the Plebs'.

question: America's founders studied Rome's mixed government and built a Senate into the U.S. Constitution. In Federalist No. 63 (1788), James Madison defended that choice by pointing to the ancient republics. What did Madison argue history proved about long-lasting republics?
answer: No long-lived republic ever existed without a senate
choices: No long-lived republic ever existed without a senate
A senate must be elected directly by the whole people
A senate should sit for life to guard against passions
A senate works only in a small republic, never a large one
context: Madison wrote that 'history informs us of no long-lived republic which had not a senate,' naming Sparta, Rome, and Carthage as proof that a lasting republic needs a stabilizing upper house. The Roman model became part of America's design. Source: James Madison, Federalist No. 63 (1788).

question: The Rosetta Stone shows one decree carved three times in three scripts, stacked top to bottom. Egyptian hieroglyphs on top. Demotic Egyptian in the middle. One more script at the bottom. Scholars in the 1800s could already read that bottom script. It became the key that unlocked the two Egyptian scripts above. Which language sat at the bottom?
answer: Ancient Greek
choices: Ancient Greek
Latin
Aramaic
Phoenician
context: The same Memphis Decree appears in all three scripts. Because scholars could read the Greek at the bottom, they could match it against the hieroglyphs and Demotic above and work out what those said. The stone is a slab of dark granodiorite about 1.13 m tall, found in 1799. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosetta_Stone; britishmuseum.org.

question: By the time the Rosetta Stone was dug up in 1799, no one on Earth had been able to read Egyptian hieroglyphs for roughly 1,400 years — the knowledge had died out completely. The Frenchman Jean-Francois Champollion cracked the silent code at last, and the story goes that in September 1822 he ran to his brother's house, cried out 'Je tiens l'affaire!' ('I've got it!'), and then did what?
answer: Collapsed in a faint from the shock
choices: Collapsed in a faint from the shock
Burned his rival's notes
Demanded the stone be returned to Egypt
Refused to publish for ten years
context: Legend holds that the excitement of reading the name 'Ramses' — and grasping that the signs were figurative, symbolic, and phonetic all at once — overwhelmed Champollion, who fainted and was bedridden for days. Days later he presented his findings in the 'Lettre a M. Dacier.' Told as legend. Source: nationalgeographic.com; rsc.byu.edu.

question: Jean-Francois Champollion's great proof that Egyptian hieroglyphs could spell out SOUNDS — not just stand for whole ideas — came from studying cartouches, the oval rings drawn around royal names. He lined up the rings holding 'Ptolemy' and 'Cleopatra' and looked for the same signs in the same spots. What let those two names crack the system open?
answer: They share the sounds p, t, o, and l, so the matching signs had to spell letters
choices: They share the sounds p, t, o, and l, so the matching signs had to spell letters
They were the only two names carved on the stone
They were both written in Greek, not hieroglyphs
They were the longest words in the whole decree
context: The shared letters appeared as the SAME hieroglyphic signs in the SAME positions across both cartouches — proof the signs stood for sounds, like an alphabet. Champollion's knowledge of Coptic, the late descendant of ancient Egyptian, then let him guess what the deciphered words MEANT, beating his English rival Thomas Young. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosetta_Stone; britannica.com.

question: In 1539 the Dominican friar Francisco de Vitoria spoke to a packed hall at Salamanca. He said Spain had no right to seize the New World just by 'finding' it. To show how silly the discovery excuse was, what did Vitoria say about the Native Americans?
answer: The Indians could have 'discovered' Spain and France, by the very same right
choices: The Indians could have 'discovered' Spain and France, by the very same right
The Indians had in fact reached Spain long before, sailing there in secret
The Indians, being pagans, could rightfully hold no land at all
The Indians owned only the coasts the Spanish ships had not yet mapped
context: Vitoria's exact line: discovering the Indians gave Spain no more title 'than the Americans would have had if they had discovered the Spaniards and the French.' Finding a land that already has people in it grants no ownership. His 1539 lecture 'On the American Indians' (De Indis) argued the Natives were 'veri domini' — the true owners of their lands before any Spaniard arrived. Source: Opinio Juris 'A Tale of Three Vitorias' (paraphrasing De Indis); plato.stanford.edu/entries/school-salamanca/.

question: Francisco Suárez, a Jesuit teacher in the Salamanca tradition, wrote a 1613 book so dangerous to crowned heads that King James I of England had it publicly burned in London, and a Paris court burned it again the next year. The book's central claim was about where a king's power truly comes from. What did Suárez argue?
answer: It flows from God to the whole people, who may depose a tyrant king
choices: It flows from God to the whole people, who may depose a tyrant king
It flows from God straight to the king, to wield however he wills
It flows from the Pope, who alone may crown and uncrown a true king
It flows from the king's own blood, handed down by birth to his heir
context: Suárez, nicknamed 'Doctor Eximius' (the Exceptional Doctor), rejected the divine right of kings in his book 'Defensio Fidei.' Power passes from God to the PEOPLE, who consent to be governed and 'in extreme cases, may depose their king.' Lord Acton later credited the Salamanca scholars' natural-rights teaching as a basis for Locke, Rousseau, and Adam Smith — an early link in the chain that reached the American Founding. Source: Acton Institute 'Francisco Suarez'; Britannica 'Defensio Fidei Catholicae by Suarez'; plato.stanford.edu/entries/suarez/.

question: In the 1700s, before phones or cheap printing, thinkers all over Europe argued by hand-written letters carried in the mail. They called this network the 'Republic of Letters.' Voltaire was its busiest writer. About how many of his letters have survived for us to read today?
answer: About 19,000 letters
choices: About 200 letters
About 2,000 letters
About 19,000 letters
About 50 letters
context: Voltaire alone left nearly 19,000 surviving letters. Stanford's 'Mapping the Republic of Letters' project plotted where they traveled and found the network ran heavily through Paris and Geneva — a kind of slow, paper internet linking thinkers who mostly never met face to face. Sources: republicofletters.stanford.edu/casestudies/voltaire.html; neh.gov 'Mapping the Republic of Letters' (2013).

question: In Paris in 1754, the blind Madame du Deffand hired a sharp young woman, Julie de Lespinasse, to help run her famous salon. It was an evening gathering where thinkers argued ideas. Ten years later du Deffand found out that Lespinasse had been quietly hosting the best guests, like the mathematician d'Alembert, for a full hour before du Deffand came down. Du Deffand fired her. What did Lespinasse do that turned the firing into du Deffand's loss?
answer: She walked out and took d'Alembert and the whole literary clique with her to start a rival salon
choices: She apologized and quietly retired from Paris society
She walked out and took d'Alembert and the whole literary clique with her to start a rival salon
She wrote a book exposing du Deffand's private letters
She married d'Alembert and left Paris for the countryside
context: When du Deffand dismissed her in 1764, Julie de Lespinasse left taking d'Alembert, Turgot and the whole literary circle with her, and opened her own salon that rivaled her former employer's. It is a striking picture of how much real power these women held over the intellectual life of the age. Sources: encyclopedia.com (du Deffand entry); britannica.com 'Julie de Lespinasse.'

question: Francis Bacon helped found modern science. He said a scientist should not be like an ant, which just collects, or a spider, which spins webs from inside itself. Which creature did Bacon call the perfect scientist? It both gathers from the world and turns what it gathers into something new.
answer: The bee
choices: The bee
The ant
The spider
The moth
context: In Novum Organum (1620), Aphorism 95, Bacon wrote that pure experimenters 'are like the ant,' pure reasoners 'resemble spiders, who make cobwebs out of their own substance,' but the bee 'gathers its material from the flowers' and then 'transforms and digests it by a power of its own.' The bee mixes real evidence with careful thinking. (Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book 1, Aphorism 95)

question: In the 1640s the French philosopher Rene Descartes set out to test what he could actually know for certain. He decided to doubt everything. He doubted his own eyes and ears, since senses can fool us. He doubted whether he was awake or dreaming. He even imagined an evil demon feeding him a whole fake world. After all that doubt, one thing was still left standing. What did Descartes conclude he knew for sure?
answer: That he was thinking, so he must exist
choices: That he was thinking, so he must exist
That the outside world was real, just as it looked
That his memories were accurate, every one of them
That God was good, so no demon could fool him
context: This is the famous 'I think, therefore I am.' Descartes reasoned that the act of doubting is itself thinking, and thinking proves there is a thinker. Even a demon faking your whole world cannot make you not exist while you are being fooled, because there has to be a 'you' there to fool. The other claims sound certain, but the cogito alone does not establish them. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes')

question: The French philosopher Rene Descartes lay in bed one morning in the 1630s and watched a fly crawl across his ceiling. He realized he could name the fly's exact spot using just two numbers — how far it was from one wall, and how far from the other wall. That simple idea grew into one of the most useful tools in all of mathematics. According to the story, what did that one idea give birth to?
answer: The graph and its x and y axes
choices: The graph and its x and y axes
The telescope
The printing press
The number zero
context: Historians treat the fly-on-the-ceiling tale as a legend, not documented fact. But Descartes really did invent coordinate geometry, marrying algebra to geometry to create the system of pinning any point down by two distances. (wild.maths.org, 'Rene Descartes and the Fly on the Ceiling')

question: Rene Descartes, the man who tried to doubt everything, also invented the graph. He joined algebra to geometry, so any point could be found by two distances. What do we still call this system of x and y axes today?
answer: Cartesian coordinates
choices: Cartesian coordinates
Euclidean coordinates
Galilean coordinates
Baconian coordinates
context: We call it 'Cartesian' because Cartesius is the Latin form of Descartes's name. He published the system in 'La Geometrie' in 1637, and he is also the reason we use x, y, and z to stand for unknowns in equations. The doubter of everything gave math one of its most useful tools. (Britannica, 'Cartesian coordinates')

question: Francis Bacon taught that you learn nature's secrets by actively prodding and testing it, not just watching. He died living out that very idea: on a freezing road in 1626, he tried an experiment to see whether cold could preserve meat, caught a chill, and died of pneumonia. What did he do to test his theory?
answer: Stuffed a chicken with snow
choices: Stuffed a chicken with snow
Buried a chicken in a snowbank
Packed a chicken in river ice
Sealed a chicken in icy water
context: Bacon believed 'the nature of things shows itself more openly under the vexations of art' - meaning you learn most by manipulating nature in a controlled test. Fittingly, the experiment that killed him was a hands-on one: packing a fowl with snow to test refrigeration. He died on 9 April 1626. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon')

question: In 1620 Francis Bacon published the book that laid out his new way of doing science. He named it to throw a direct punch at Aristotle, whose ancient logic textbooks were called the 'Organon.' Bacon titled his book 'Novum Organum,' a Latin phrase. What does that title mean?
answer: The New Instrument
choices: The New Instrument
The New Logic
The New Organ
The New Method
context: By calling his book 'the New Instrument,' Bacon was openly declaring that the ancient way of reasoning was broken and here was a new tool to replace it. The title was a deliberate shot across two thousand years of Aristotle's authority - whose own logic collection was called the 'Organon,' the instrument. (Britannica, 'Novum Organum')

question: Rene Descartes traced his life's mission to one strange night in November 1619. Serving as a young soldier, he shut himself in a small room warmed by a stove to escape the winter cold, and that night something happened that convinced him he was meant to rebuild all of human knowledge. What did he experience?
answer: Three vivid dreams
choices: Three vivid dreams
A bolt of lightning
A voice from a fire
A fever that nearly killed him
context: On the night of 10-11 November 1619, according to his biographer Adrien Baillet, Descartes had three vivid dreams that he treated as a calling for the rest of his life. The stove-heated room ('poele') and the three dreams became the origin story of his whole philosophy. (Wikipedia, 'Rene Descartes')

question: Francis Bacon warned that the human mind is haunted by four 'Idols' - mental traps that fool us before we even start thinking. He singled out one of them, born from sloppy and empty words, as 'the greatest nuisances of them all.' What did Bacon name the trap caused by confusing or meaningless language?
answer: The Idols of the Marketplace
choices: The Idols of the Marketplace
The Idols of the Tribe
The Idols of the Cave
The Idols of the Theatre
context: Bacon's four Idols: the Tribe (errors built into all humans), the Cave (your personal biases), the Marketplace (confusion from sloppy words - 'the greatest nuisances of them all'), and the Theatre (blind faith in old dogmas, like mistaking a play for reality). Naming them was an early map of how the mind deceives itself. (Wikipedia, 'Novum Organum')

question: The slogan 'knowledge is power' is famous as a Francis Bacon line - but Bacon never actually wrote those exact words. The crisp Latin form 'scientia potentia est' was printed later by a different thinker, a man who had once worked as Bacon's young secretary. Who put the famous phrase into its sharp final shape?
answer: Thomas Hobbes
choices: Thomas Hobbes
Isaac Newton
Rene Descartes
John Locke
context: Bacon's closest version was 'ipsa scientia potestas est' ('knowledge itself is power') in his 1597 Meditationes Sacrae. The punchy 'scientia potentia est' came from Thomas Hobbes, who had served as Bacon's secretary - so the world's most quoted line about knowledge is a polish of the master's words by his apprentice. (Wikipedia, 'Scientia potentia est')
