question: Francis Bacon did not just write about science - he rose to be Lord Chancellor of England, the highest legal office in the land. Then in 1621 Parliament charged him with 23 counts of taking bribes. Rather than fight, Bacon confessed to the lords and begged them for mercy, humbling himself with a vivid image. What did Bacon call himself?
answer: A broken reed
choices: A broken reed
A fallen oak
A cracked mirror
A spent candle
context: Bacon told the lords: 'It is my act, my hand, and my heart; I beseech your lordships to be merciful to a broken reed.' He was fined 40,000 pounds and briefly jailed in the Tower of London. The father of the careful method admitted he had failed his own standard of integrity. (Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Bacon, Francis')

question: In 1633 the Inquisition condemned Galileo for teaching that the Earth moves. Rene Descartes had just finished a book called 'The World' (Le Monde) that argued the very same thing. Frightened of becoming the next Galileo, what did Descartes do with his finished book?
answer: Quietly suppressed it and refused to publish it
choices: Quietly suppressed it and refused to publish it
Rewrote it to cut out the dangerous parts
Showed it only to a few trusted friends in private
Translated it into Latin to dodge the censors
context: Descartes decided it was wiser to stay quiet than risk the Church's wrath, so he shelved 'The World' rather than defend it. He was a sincere believer who saw his method as a path to truth, not an attack on faith - but Galileo's fate made him cautious. (Wikipedia, 'Rene Descartes')

question: Francis Bacon and Rene Descartes are both fathers of the scientific method, yet they pointed in opposite directions. Bacon said to start with the EVIDENCE - gather many careful observations of nature, then work up to general laws. Rene Descartes took the opposite path. Where did Descartes say real knowledge should begin?
answer: By doubting everything, then rebuilding from a few certainties by pure reason
choices: By doubting everything, then rebuilding from a few certainties by pure reason
By trusting whichever idea the mind pictures most clearly and most vividly
By accepting Aristotle and the Church as the bedrock everything rests on
By measuring the heavens with instruments until the hidden laws appear
context: This is the great split at the root of modern science: Bacon's induction (gather evidence, then generalize - the bee gathering from flowers) versus Descartes's deduction (doubt all, then rebuild from bedrock certainties like 'I think, therefore I am'). One trusted the senses tested carefully; the other trusted reason purified by doubt. The method that powered the whole Scientific Revolution grew out of both. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon' and 'Descartes')

question: In 1884 the German leader Otto von Bismarck called fourteen nations to Berlin. Their job was to split up Africa and draw borders on a huge map. Who from Africa got to sit at the table and speak for the land?
answer: Not a single African
choices: Not a single African
One chief from each region
The kings of Ethiopia and Egypt
A council of African elders
context: The Berlin Conference (Nov 1884 - Feb 1885) divided Africa among European powers with no African present; African states were not treated as legitimate parties, and the Europeans drew claims on a continent none of them ruled. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Conference

question: The Berlin Conference gave away the huge Congo region in Africa. One ruler took it as his own private land. He governed about twenty million people there but never set foot in the place. Who owned the Congo?
answer: King Leopold II of Belgium
choices: King Leopold II of Belgium
Queen Victoria of Britain
A Belgian rubber tycoon
A French explorer
context: On 1 August 1885 the territory became the 'Congo Free State', owned personally by King Leopold II rather than by Belgium. He ruled about twenty million people as private property and never once set foot in the Congo. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Conference

question: In 1870, most of Africa was still ruled by Africans, from the sultans of the Sahara to the kingdoms of the Congo. But in the 1880s the European powers — Britain, France, Belgium, Germany, Portugal, and Italy — met at the Berlin Conference and carved up the continent between them. By the time World War I began in 1914, Europe had swallowed about ninety percent of Africa. Only two states stayed free through the whole Scramble. Which two were they?
answer: Ethiopia and Liberia
choices: Ethiopia and Liberia
Egypt and Morocco
Sudan and Somalia
Kenya and Uganda
context: By 1914 roughly 90% of Africa had been colonized; only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent. Source: https://www.thecollector.com/what-was-berlin-conference/

question: King Leopold II of Belgium forced Congolese villagers to gather wild rubber. His private army made each soldier prove every bullet was fired at a person, not wasted. What grim object did a soldier bring back as proof for each bullet?
answer: A severed human right hand
choices: A severed human right hand
A spent brass cartridge
A signed work ticket
A basket of rubber
context: Soldiers of the Force Publique brought back severed right hands to account for bullets; baskets of smoked hands became a grim form of accounting and currency in the Congo Free State. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atrocities_in_the_Congo_Free_State

question: E.D. Morel, a young shipping clerk in Belgium, grew suspicious watching the cargo manifests: ships left for the Congo packed with guns, chains and ammunition but no trade goods, yet returned loaded with rubber and ivory. What did this lopsided cargo prove to him?
answer: The rubber was being seized by force, not bought
choices: The rubber was being seized by force, not bought
The Congo had run out of money to trade
Belgian merchants were smuggling weapons home
The ivory trade was secretly more profitable
context: Morel realized that cargo of only weapons going out and only rubber coming back meant the rubber was taken by force, not traded. He quit his job and founded the Congo Reform Association to expose it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._D._Morel

question: In 1904 the missionary Alice Seeley Harris took one of history's most haunting photos in the Congo. Such Kodak pictures became the reform campaign's deadliest weapon. The photo shows a father named Nsala of Wala sitting on the mission porch. He is staring down at a small bundle on the boards after his village missed its rubber quota. What was Nsala looking at?
answer: The severed hand and foot of his daughter
choices: The severed hand and foot of his daughter
An empty basket where she had slept
The torch marks of his burned hut
A soldier's discarded rifle
context: Alice Seeley Harris's 1904 photograph of Nsala contemplating the severed hand and foot of his five-year-old daughter, all the Force Publique left of her after his village missed its rubber quota, became an iconic image of the rubber terror. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atrocities_in_the_Congo_Free_State

question: The American writer Mark Twain — author of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn — joined the international outcry against Belgian atrocities in the Congo. In 1905 he wrote a bitter satire called King Leopold's Soliloquy, in which Leopold II moans alone about a new invention he could not bribe, threaten, or lie his way past. In Twain's story, what had become 'the most powerful enemy that has confronted us'?
answer: The Kodak camera
choices: The Kodak camera
The telegraph wire
The missionary's sermon
The British consul's pen
context: In Twain's satire Leopold calls the kodak 'a sore calamity... the most powerful enemy that has confronted us,' because photographs could not be denied like words. Twain donated all proceeds to Congo relief, and Arthur Conan Doyle also lent his fame to the cause. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Leopold's_Soliloquy

question: The Berlin Conference made one rule that turned the Scramble for Africa into a race across the continent. A European power could claim land only by actually holding it. To make a valid claim under this rule of 'effective occupation,' what did a power have to do on the ground?
answer: Plant its flag, sign treaties with local chiefs, and station troops
choices: Plant its flag, sign treaties with local chiefs, and station troops
Send a sealed claim, pay a fee, and await Berlin's approval
Buy the land outright, name a governor, and chart the rivers
Survey the coast, raise a fort, and pay the African king
context: 'Effective occupation' required flag, treaties with local chiefs, and police or troops to control the land - turning the Scramble into a land-grab race. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Conference

question: How many Congolese died under Leopold II from 1885 to 1908 is still argued. The British agent Roger Casement guessed about three million and called even that too low. Historians Adam Hochschild and Jan Vansina put the number much higher. What is their higher guess?
answer: About ten million, roughly half the people
choices: About ten million, roughly half the people
About six million, under a third of the people
About eight million, two in every five people
About thirteen million, nearly two-thirds of the people
context: Hochschild and Vansina estimate roughly ten million deaths - about half the Congo's population of some twenty million - from murder, starvation, exhaustion and disease, while Casement's lower figure of three million was offered as an undercount. The figures are debated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atrocities_in_the_Congo_Free_State

question: Rome began as a kingdom ruled by a line of seven kings, ending with the tyrant Lucius Tarquinius Superbus. Around 509 BC the Romans drove him out and started a republic. According to the story, what did they swear they would never again allow?
answer: To be ruled by a king
choices: To be ruled by a king
To make peace with the Etruscans
To worship the Greek gods
To build walls around the city
context: Rome's hatred of one-man rule became the bedrock of its Republic, the model the American Founders later studied when they split power so no one person could rule for life. Source: https://courses.lumenlearning.com/atd-herkimer-westerncivilization/chapter/the-seven-kings/

question: The seventh and last king of Rome, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, ruled as a tyrant. He kicked any senator who opposed him out of the Senate. The Latin word 'Superbus' stuck to his name forever as an insult. What does it mean?
answer: The Proud
choices: The Proud
The Cruel
The Foreigner
The Tall
context: 'Superbus' means 'the Proud' or 'the Arrogant.' He earned it by his overbearing rule, not by inheritance, and it has stuck to him for 2,500 years. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Tarquin-king-of-Rome-534-509-BC

question: To make sure one man could never again hold power for life, the new Roman Republic of 509 BC split its top office between two leaders. Each one served for just a single year. What were these paired rulers called?
answer: Consuls
choices: Consuls
Senators
Tribunes
Dictators
context: Two consuls, equal in power and serving one year, meant either could block the other, and both were soon replaced. It was a deliberate machine against kingship. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Lucius-Junius-Brutus-legendary-Roman

question: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus seized Rome's throne by murdering the old king, Servius Tullius, who was his own father-in-law. As the dead king lay in the road, his daughter Tullia drove her chariot straight over her father's body. Horrified Romans renamed that street for the deed. What did they call it?
answer: The Street of Crime
choices: The Street of Crime
The Street of Mourning
The Street of Kings
The Street of Blood
context: Roman tradition (Livy) named it the Vicus Sceleratus, the 'Street of Crime.' The tale is legend, written centuries later, but Romans pointed to the street as a real place. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Lucius_Tarquinius_Superbus/

question: While their army besieged the city of Ardea, Rome's young noblemen made a drunken bet over whose wife was the worthiest, then rode home by night to spy on them unannounced. The royal princes' wives were caught feasting at a lavish banquet. But one wife, Collatinus's, won the contest hands down. What was Lucretia doing when the men found her?
answer: Spinning wool by lamplight with her maids
choices: Spinning wool by lamplight with her maids
Praying alone at the family shrine
Asleep in her chamber for the night
Sewing fine clothes by candlelight
context: To Romans, a wife working wool late by lamplight was the very picture of virtue, which is why Lucretia 'won' the wager while the feasting wives lost it. The story comes from Livy and is told as legend. Source: https://pressbooks.claremont.edu/clas112pomonavalentine/chapter/livy-i-49-1-60/

question: Lucretia was the wife of the nobleman Collatinus. She was wronged by Sextus Tarquinius, a son of the king. The historian Livy says she called her father and husband, made them swear to avenge her, and said her shame must not be an excuse for any unfaithful wife after her. Then, before the men could stop her, what did Lucretia do?
answer: Drew a hidden knife and stabbed herself
choices: Drew a hidden knife and stabbed herself
Threw herself down from the high wall
Drank a cup of deadly poison
Fled into the night with her maids
context: Livy gives her dying words: she acquitted herself of sin but would not absolve herself of punishment, lest any unchaste woman ever cite Lucretia as her example. Her death, told as legend, became the spark of the Republic. Source: https://pressbooks.claremont.edu/clas112pomonavalentine/chapter/livy-i-49-1-60/

question: The exiled Tarquin talked the Etruscan king Lars Porsena into marching on Rome. One Roman soldier, Horatius Cocles, stood alone at the far end of the wooden bridge. He held off Porsena's whole army while his countrymen chopped the bridge down behind him. When the bridge fell, how did Horatius get away?
answer: Swam back across the Tiber in his armor
choices: Swam back across the Tiber in his armor
Fought his way through the enemy ranks
Was rescued by a Roman cavalry charge
Leapt onto a passing river boat
context: By holding the only bridge until it fell, Horatius stopped the Etruscans from rushing straight into Rome, then swam the river still wearing his armor. The feat is told as legend but became a byword for standing alone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatius_Cocles

question: As Lucretia lay dying, a man everyone had thought was a half-wit stunned the room. Lucius Junius Brutus pulled the bloody knife from her wound and held it up. He swore by her blood to drive out King Tarquin and his whole family 'with sword, with fire.' What did Brutus do with the knife the moment he was done?
answer: Passed it to each man to swear the same oath
choices: Passed it to each man to swear the same oath
Buried it beside Lucretia's body
Carried it to the temple as an offering
Hurled it down at the king's gate
context: By passing the blade so every man swore on Lucretia's blood, Brutus turned a private grief into a shared, binding vow against the monarchy. This oath, told as legend by Livy, is the traditional birth of the Republic. Source: https://pressbooks.claremont.edu/clas112pomonavalentine/chapter/livy-i-49-1-60/

question: Lucius Junius Brutus survived the tyrant Tarquin, who had murdered leading Romans including Brutus's own brother, by playing the harmless fool so no one would see him as a threat. He fit the act so well that the cognomen 'Brutus' clung to him. What does the name 'Brutus' actually mean?
answer: Dullard, or idiot
choices: Dullard, or idiot
Bold, or fearless
Exile, or wanderer
Avenger, or champion
context: The founder of the Republic was literally nicknamed 'idiot,' a disguise he wore on purpose to stay alive under a murderous king. The tale is legend, but the name was real and famous. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Junius_Brutus

question: At the Oracle of Delphi, the sons of King Tarquin asked who would rule Rome next. The oracle answered that 'the first to kiss his mother shall hold supreme power.' The princes thought of racing home to kiss their own mothers, but Brutus, traveling with them, saw the riddle's hidden meaning. What did Brutus do?
answer: Pretended to trip and kissed the earth
choices: Pretended to trip and kissed the earth
Hurried home to kiss his own mother
Bowed and kissed the oracle's feet
Knelt and kissed the temple altar
context: Brutus read 'mother' as the Earth, mother of all, and kissed the ground, claiming the prophecy while the princes missed it. Told as legend, it casts the 'fool' as the cleverest man in Rome. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Junius_Brutus

question: An old woman, the Cumaean Sibyl, offered King Tarquin nine books of prophecy at a steep price. He scoffed at the cost, so she burned three of them and demanded for the remaining six the exact figure she had first named for all nine. He refused again, and she burned three more. In the end, how much did Tarquin pay for the last three books?
answer: The same price first asked for nine
choices: The same price first asked for nine
Only a third of the first price
Triple the original asking price
Half of the original asking price
context: Tarquin paid the full nine-book price for just three, the prophecies now too precious to lose. The surviving Sibylline Books were stored under the Temple of Jupiter and consulted in emergencies. Told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibylline_Books

question: Soon after founding the Republic, Brutus discovered that his own two sons had joined a secret plot to bring King Tarquin back. As consul, he had to enforce the law's penalty, which was death. When his boys were led out to be executed in front of him, what did Brutus do?
answer: Sat and watched, never stopping it
choices: Sat and watched, never stopping it
Pardoned them and resigned his office
Begged the Senate to spare their lives
Sent them into exile instead
context: Livy says Brutus showed a father's anguish but never halted the execution, putting the Republic above his own sons. It is the legend's harshest lesson: the law must bind even the men who made it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarquinian_conspiracy

question: Merchant caravans between China and the West traveled the ancient Silk Road, but they had to skirt the Taklamakan Desert — a place so deadly nobody dared cross its center. So the road split into a north branch and a south branch that curled around the sands. Both branches had to string themselves from one water source to the next to stay alive. What were both branches hugging?
answer: The chains of desert oasis towns, fed by mountain meltwater
choices: The chains of desert oasis towns, fed by mountain meltwater
The banks of a single great river running west
The line of imperial fortress walls along the route
The coastline of an inland sea to the south
context: The Taklamakan was so deadly that the two famous branches of the Silk Road existed specifically to AVOID crossing its center. Travelers hugged the oasis chains along the desert's northern and southern rims, where meltwater from the surrounding mountains kept the towns alive. Source: https://eugene.kaspersky.com/2025/02/13/the-taklamakan-desert-the-dunhuang-dunes-and-the-500-buddhist-caves-of-mogao/ ; https://www.timeless-travels.co.uk/post/hidden-secrets-of-the-silk-road-1

question: Silk Road caravans traveling west from China had to skirt a huge, waterless sand sea that no one dared cross straight through. At its eastern edge stood a gateway oasis town where the road split into a northern and southern path that curled around the sand. What was the name of this brutal desert?
answer: The Taklamakan Desert
choices: The Taklamakan Desert
The Sahara Desert
The Kalahari Desert
The Atacama Desert
context: All Silk Road traffic between China and the West funneled through the oasis town of Dunhuang, where the road forked into a northern and a southern branch to skirt the Taklamakan. It was the last stock-up before crossing and the first safe haven on the way home. Source: https://thechinaproject.com/2016/12/23/dunhuang-history-travel-guide/ ; https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat15/sub103/entry-6520.html

question: China guarded the secret of silk so jealously that smuggling out silkworm eggs was punishable by death. Around 552 CE, two monks finally broke that monopoly forever, carrying live silkworm eggs west to the Byzantine emperor Justinian I. How did they sneak the eggs past China's guards?
answer: Hidden inside hollow bamboo canes
choices: Hidden inside hollow bamboo canes
Sewn into the lining of their robes
Swallowed in sealed clay capsules
Packed among bags of ordinary mulberry seeds
context: Exporting silkworms, eggs, or even mulberry seeds was a death-penalty offense in China. Around 552 CE two monks smuggled live silkworm eggs to Justinian I hidden inside hollow bamboo canes, breaking China's silk monopoly forever. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smuggling_of_silkworm_eggs_into_the_Byzantine_Empire

question: At Dunhuang, monks carved over 700 caves into a cliff face across a thousand years and painted them with murals — the Mogao Caves. These caves prove the Silk Road carried more than just goods. What did the murals show was traveling INTO China along these same routes?
answer: Buddhism, the religion the murals depict
choices: Buddhism, the religion the murals depict
The Chinese writing system, spreading outward
A new breed of war-horse from the west
Glassblowing techniques from Rome
context: Over 700 caves were carved at Dunhuang from the 4th to 14th centuries and painted with Buddhist murals — the Mogao Caves. They are physical proof the road carried IDEAS: Buddhism traveled INTO China along these trade routes. Source: https://www.kupi.com/en-ae/explore/china/dunhuang/history ; https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat15/sub103/entry-6520.html

question: In 1907, near Dunhuang, archaeologist Aurel Stein recovered an abandoned mailbag of Sogdian letters from 313 CE — never delivered. One was from a woman named Miwnay, stranded for three years by a husband who kept refusing to come fetch her. How did her furious letter to him end?
answer: 'I would rather be a dog's or a pig's wife than yours!'
choices: 'I would rather be a dog's or a pig's wife than yours!'
'May the gods grant you the death you have earned.'
'I shall walk home alone, and curse each step to you.'
'Send the silver you owe, or send nothing ever again.'
context: Stein found a mailbag of Sogdian letters from 313-314 CE that were never delivered. Miwnay (or Shayn), stranded in Dunhuang three years by a husband who kept refusing to fetch her, signed off: 'I would rather be a dog's or a pig's wife than yours!' — a 1,700-year-old furious letter. Source: https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/sogdlet.html ; https://theletters.page/2023/06/30/end-of-the-silk-road-sogdian-ancient-letters/

question: Inside a sealed library cave at Dunhuang, bricked shut for 900 years, lay the Diamond Sutra — dated 868 CE, the world's oldest dated printed book, centuries before Gutenberg. Its colophon reveals WHY a man named Wang Jie had it printed. For whom did he make it?
answer: As a gift on behalf of his two parents
choices: As a gift on behalf of his two parents
To win favor with the Tang emperor's court
To repay a debt owed to a monastery
To mark his own recovery from illness
context: The Diamond Sutra, dated 11 May 868 CE, is the world's oldest dated printed book. Its colophon reads that 'Wang Jie had this made for universal distribution on behalf of his two parents' — a printed book made as a gift of love to his mother and father, centuries before Gutenberg. Source: https://www.cabinet.ox.ac.uk/worlds-earliest-dated-printed-book-diamond-sutra-868-ce ; https://www.lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/the-diamond-sutra/

question: The traders who actually moved goods along the Silk Road were rarely Chinese or Roman — they were the Sogdians, merchants from Samarkand and Bukhara. Through sheer commercial necessity, one thing of theirs spread so far it became the shared working tongue of the whole route. What was it?
answer: Their language, the trade lingua franca
choices: Their language, the trade lingua franca
Their silver coinage, accepted everywhere
Their system of weights and measures
Their caravan-contract law
context: The Sogdians, merchants from Samarkand and Bukhara, were the Silk Road's middlemen. Their language became the route's lingua franca through commercial necessity, and educated Sogdians routinely spoke four or five languages. Source: https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/sogdlet.html ; https://sogdians.si.edu/sidebars/sogdian-language

question: Between 1508 and 1512 the Italian artist Michelangelo lay on his back on high wooden scaffolding and painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome. The most famous panel is called the Creation of Adam. God sweeps in from the right with a swirl of angels, and the first man Adam reaches up toward Him. Michelangelo did one small thing with their two reaching hands that made this picture the most copied image on the ceiling. What did he do?
answer: Their fingertips never quite meet, a sliver of air between them
choices: Their fingertips never quite meet, a sliver of air between them
Their fingertips press flat together, palm against palm
Their fingers interlock tightly, knuckle over knuckle
Their hands clasp in a firm, two-handed grip
context: The outstretched fingers of God and Adam do not touch -- a small gap of empty air separates them, frozen at the instant just before life passes across. That nearly-touching gap is the single most reproduced detail of the entire ceiling. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Creation_of_Adam

question: Everyone pictures Michelangelo lying flat on his back to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling, but that is a myth. Vasari, who knew him, wrote the work was done 'with the greatest discomfort.' How did Michelangelo actually paint the vault high above him?
answer: He stood on a scaffold, head tilted back, reaching up over his head
choices: He stood on a scaffold, head tilted back, reaching up over his head
He hung in a rope sling, lying face-up toward the vault
He sat on a high platform, painting at eye level on angled boards
He climbed a tall ladder, leaning one shoulder against the wall
context: He worked standing on a scaffold with his head cranked backward, reaching up over his head for four years (1508-1512). Vasari: the frescoes 'were done with the greatest discomfort, for he had to stand there working with his head tilted backwards.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistine_Chapel_ceiling (Vasari, Lives of the Artists); https://canvas.nma.art/2020/06/02/a-vision-of-the-heavens/ (Dr. William E. Wallace)

question: Socrates went barefoot about the marketplace of Athens asking 'What is justice?' He is remembered for teaching the West to think, yet all that survives of him was set down by his pupils Plato and Xenophon. Why is there no book in his own hand?
answer: Socrates never wrote anything down himself
choices: Socrates never wrote anything down himself
A fire destroyed all of his writings
His enemies burned his books after the trial
He wrote only in a secret code no one solved
context: Socrates taught entirely by talking and questioning in the streets and marketplace of Athens, and he wrote not one page. Everything we know of him and his method survives only because two of his pupils wrote it down after his death: the philosopher Plato and the soldier-historian Xenophon. The man who taught the world to think left no book of his own. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socrates; https://iep.utm.edu/socrates/

question: Socrates said his whole life of questioning began with a reply from a god. His friend Chaerephon traveled to Delphi, where a priestess spoke for Apollo, and asked whether any man alive was wiser than Socrates. Socrates himself was certain he knew nothing. What did the priestess answer?
answer: That no man was wiser
choices: That no man was wiser
That the gods were wisest
That Chaerephon was wiser
That wisdom could not be measured
context: The Pythia answered no: no man was wiser. Socrates felt he knew nothing, so the answer puzzled him. He set out to disprove the oracle by hunting for a wiser man, questioning poets, craftsmen and politicians, and kept finding men who only thought they knew things. The elenchus was born from that search. Sources: Plato, Apology 21a; https://www.thecollector.com/delphic-oracle-calls-socrates-wisest/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apology_(Plato)

question: In Plato's Symposium a drunken Alcibiades stood up to describe Socrates: snub-nosed, bug-eyed, ugly as a satyr, barefoot and in shabby clothes. He likened him to a cheap Silenus statuette, the kind made to be cracked open. What did Alcibiades say was packed inside?
answer: Little golden gods
choices: Little golden gods
A coil of old rope
A nest of stinging bees
A single silver coin
context: Crack the ugly Silenus open, Alcibiades says, and it is packed with little golden gods. The plain, grotesque outside hid the treasure within, his way of saying Socrates' shabby talk concealed something precious. Source: Plato, Symposium 215a-b; https://www.ancientworldmagazine.com/articles/a-portrait-of-socrates/

question: Socrates went about Athens questioning generals, priests and politicians who were certain they were wise. He took each confident answer and tried it against case after case until it gave way. The Greeks had one word for his technique: elenchos. What does that word literally mean?
answer: A cross-examination
choices: A cross-examination
A public speech
A wrestling hold
A witness's oath
context: Elenchos (Greek elenchus) literally means cross-examination, testing, scrutiny, an argument of disproof or refutation. It is not teaching; it is interrogation, letting a confident man's answers collapse under their own weight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socratic_method

question: In Plato's Meno, a rich young man named Meno was questioned to a standstill and grew angry. He complained that Socrates had left his mind frozen and his tongue helpless, and he likened Socrates to a sea creature that stops a man dead with a single touch. Which creature did he name?
answer: A torpedo fish
choices: A torpedo fish
A giant squid
A moray eel
A stinging jellyfish
context: Meno compares Socrates to the torpedo fish (the electric ray, Greek narke, named for its power to numb). Socrates turns the insult inside out: he confuses others, he says, only because he is more confused than anyone himself. Source: Plato, Meno 80a-c

question: Socrates never handed anyone an answer. He asked questions until people drew out a truth he insisted had been inside them the whole time, and then he tested whether it could stand. Socrates said this was exactly the trade his own mother Phaenarete had worked. What was her trade?
answer: She was a midwife
choices: She was a midwife
She was a weaver
She was a priestess
She was a healer
context: Phaenarete was a midwife (his father Sophroniscus a stonemason). In the Theaetetus, Socrates says he delivers ideas the way she delivered babies: I myself am barren of wisdom, he says, but he helps others give birth to thoughts and tests whether each is sound or a mere phantom. Source: Plato, Theaetetus 148e-151a; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socrates

question: Outside the Athenian court, Socrates ran into Euthyphro, who called himself an expert on religion. Euthyphro was so sure he was right that he had come to charge a relative over the death of a hired worker left tied up in a ditch. Socrates marveled that anyone could be so sure. Which relative was Euthyphro charging?
answer: His father
choices: His father
His brother
His uncle
His cousin
context: Euthyphro, a self-styled religious expert, was prosecuting his own father. Socrates, dripping with irony, begs to become the pupil of so confident a man, so Euthyphro can surely define piety. Five failed definitions later, Euthyphro suddenly remembers an appointment and flees. Source: Plato, Euthyphro

question: People often quote Socrates as saying 'I know that I know nothing,' but the words are a later paraphrase and appear nowhere in Plato. In Plato's Apology the real line is sharper. After questioning a politician everyone praised as wise, Socrates judged himself better off by one precise difference. What was it?
answer: He knows nothing but thinks he knows; I neither know nor think I know
choices: He knows nothing but thinks he knows; I neither know nor think I know
He has read many books; I have read almost none at all
He speaks beautifully in public; I can barely speak in public
He was born to wealth and rank; I was born poor and low
context: From the Apology (21d): I am better off than he is, for he knows nothing and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know. Other men think they know when they do not. The whole of Socrates' wisdom was knowing the exact size of his own ignorance. Sources: Plato, Apology 21d; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_know_that_I_know_nothing

question: In Plato's Meno, Socrates claimed that an untaught slave boy could do geometry, and he proved it by asking questions alone. Step by step the boy worked out how to draw a new square with exactly double the area of a given one, though Socrates never told him the answer. On which line of the original figure did the boy build it?
answer: On the diagonal of the old square
choices: On the diagonal of the old square
On a side made twice as long
On a side made one and a half times as long
On a line from one corner to the center
context: The boy's first instinct is to double each side, but that quadruples the area. Guided only by questions, he discovers you double a square's area by building the new square on the diagonal of the old one. Socrates told him nothing; the boy recollected it, which Socrates used to argue that learning is really remembering (anamnesis). Source: Plato, Meno 82b-85b; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meno%27s_slave

question: In Plato's Republic, Thrasymachus the sophist charged in like a wild beast, roaring that justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger. Socrates took him apart question by question until he admitted that the unjust man is the ignorant and bad one. Plato recorded a vivid physical sign of his defeat. What happened to Thrasymachus?
answer: He blushed
choices: He blushed
He stormed out
He drew a knife
He fell silent and wept
context: Plato writes that Thrasymachus gave in with prodigious sweating, it being summer, and then I beheld what I had never seen before: Thrasymachus blushing. The loud sophist, forced by his own admissions, turned red in front of the room. Source: Plato, Republic 350d

question: Euthyphro tried five times to say what piety is, failed each time, and fled. He never noticed that his own certainty hid a question philosophers still argue over 2,400 years later, the Euthyphro dilemma. Socrates did not answer it; he only brought it to light. What was the question?
answer: Is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because they love it
choices: Is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because they love it
Is a thing pious because it helps the city, or helpful because it is pious
Do all the gods agree on what is pious, or quarrel among themselves over it
Is piety a single thing, or a different thing for each of the gods
context: The Euthyphro dilemma (Euthyphro 10a): is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or is it pious because they love it? Socrates left it open. He had simply shown Euthyphro a question hiding inside the certainty he walked in with. Source: Plato, Euthyphro 10a; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euthyphro

question: In 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite. It was a shiny metal ball about the size of a beach ball, and it circled the Earth. What could ordinary people all over the world pick up on cheap radios, the first sound ever sent down from space?
answer: A steady beeping signal from the satellite overhead
choices: A steady beeping signal from the satellite overhead
A recorded speech from the Soviet leader
A burst of strange organ music
A voice counting down in Russian
context: Chief designer Sergei Korolev deliberately put a simple 1-watt transmitter on Sputnik broadcasting on easy frequencies (20.005 and 40.002 MHz) so amateur radio operators and ordinary people everywhere could pick up the 'beep... beep... beep' themselves. The batteries lasted 22 days. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1

question: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union stunned the world by launching Sputnik 1 — the first man-made satellite ever to orbit the Earth. Just one month later, on November 3, 1957, the Soviets launched a second rocket, Sputnik 2, from the Baikonur base in Kazakhstan. This time the capsule at the top carried a passenger — the first living creature ever to reach orbit around our planet. Who circled the Earth aboard Sputnik 2?
answer: A stray Moscow dog named Laika
choices: A stray Moscow dog named Laika
A pair of trained homing pigeons
A young chimpanzee from a zoo
A jar of laboratory mice
context: Laika ('Barker') was a stray picked up off the Moscow streets. There was no way to bring her home — the mission was one-way from the start — and she died of overheating within hours, on the craft's fourth orbit. Source: https://www.nasa.gov/history/60-years-ago-the-first-animal-in-orbit/

question: On April 12, 1961, at the height of the Space Race between the Soviet Union and the United States, a 27-year-old Russian air-force pilot named Yuri Gagarin climbed into the tiny capsule Vostok 1 at the Baikonur Cosmodrome. Rockets roared beneath him and he lifted off toward orbit to become the first human being ever in space. At the exact moment of liftoff, Gagarin shouted a single Russian word into his radio — a word that became famous around the world. What did he shout?
answer: 'Poyekhali!' — 'Let's go!'
choices: 'Poyekhali!' — 'Let's go!'
'Pobeda!' — 'Victory!'
'Vpered!' — 'Forward!'
'Slava!' — 'Glory!'
context: Gagarin orbited the Earth once in 108 minutes. He was picked partly because, at 5 feet 2 inches, he fit the cramped capsule. Source: https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/vostok-1

question: When Yuri Gagarin's spaceflight ended, he did not ride the Vostok 1 capsule all the way to the ground. About 7 kilometers up, over a field near Saratov, what did the first human in space actually do to reach the ground?
answer: He ejected and parachuted down separately from the capsule
choices: He ejected and parachuted down separately from the capsule
He splashed down in the sea and waited in a raft
He glided the capsule to a runway like an airplane
He was lowered slowly by a giant balloon
context: A startled farmer and his family backed away as he landed; Gagarin reassured them he was 'a Soviet citizen like you, who has descended from space.' The Soviets hid the separate ejection until 1971, because the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale required a pilot to land inside his craft to set an official record. Source: https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/vostok-1

question: The beep from Sputnik terrified Americans. The same rockets that put a satellite over their cities every 96 minutes could just as easily drop a nuclear bomb. Within months, the shock pushed the United States to do what — set up the groups that would carry open science into space?
answer: Found NASA and the research agency ARPA, later DARPA
choices: Found NASA and the research agency ARPA, later DARPA
Sign a treaty banning all rockets from space
Build a chain of giant radar towers along the coasts
Shut down its universities' physics departments
context: The same Sputnik shock also pushed Congress to pass the National Defense Education Act. America's own first satellite, Explorer 1, reached orbit January 31, 1958, and its cosmic-ray detector let James Van Allen discover the radiation belts that bear his name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1

question: The Spanish Armada lay at anchor off Calais in a close half-moon in August 1588, too solid for English guns to break. One night the English set eight old ships ablaze and let them drift into the fleet. Sure they were floating bombs about to explode, what did the panicked Spanish captains do?
answer: Cut their anchor cables and scattered into the darkness
choices: Cut their anchor cables and scattered into the darkness
Lashed their ships together to fight the fires as one
Rowed out in small boats to tow the burning hulks away
Fired every cannon at the drifting ships at once
context: On the night of 7-8 August 1588 the English floated eight fireships into the Armada at Calais. The Spanish dreaded 'hellburners' (floating bombs), so they cut their cables and scattered in panic, breaking their crescent formation for good. Not one Spanish ship actually caught fire -- the terror alone did the damage. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Armada

question: Storms smashed ship after ship of the beaten Armada on the rocks of Scotland and Ireland in 1588, as it fled the long way home because it could not sail back down the Channel against the wind. Queen Elizabeth gave God the credit for that storm on her victory medal, not her sailors. What did the English call the storm?
answer: The Protestant Wind
choices: The Protestant Wind
The King's Tempest
The Channel Gale
The Armada Squall
context: Elizabeth's medal read 'Flavit Jehovah et Dissipati Sunt' -- 'He blew with His winds, and they were scattered' (echoing Psalm 104) -- and gave us the phrase 'the Protestant Wind.' As many as 24 ships were wrecked on the Scottish and Irish coasts on that long flight home; around half the 130-ship fleet never made it back. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Armada

question: Philip II of Spain launched a fleet of about 130 ships and 30,000 men against Protestant England in 1588, meaning to depose Queen Elizabeth I and end the English raids on his treasure fleets. The fleet went down in history under a boastful name that became a bitter joke, for about half of it never returned. By what name is the fleet remembered?
answer: the Invincible Armada
choices: the Invincible Armada
the Holy Crusade Fleet
the Grand Catholic Navy
the Sword of Philip
context: The Spanish called it 'la Armada Invencible' — the Invincible Armada. About half of it never came home, making the name one of history's most famous overreaches. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Spanish_Armada/

question: Lord Howard of Effingham led the English fleet against the Armada in 1588, with a famous sea-raider serving as his vice-admiral on the Revenge. The Spanish gave that man a name meaning the Dragon, half curse and half dread, for he had plundered their treasure for years. Who was he?
answer: Francis Drake
choices: Francis Drake
Walter Raleigh
John Hawkins
Martin Frobisher
context: Francis Drake — 'El Draque,' the Dragon — had plundered Spanish treasure for years, so the name was equal parts curse and dread. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Spanish_Armada/

question: The broken Armada fled the long way home after the battle of Gravelines in 1588, round the top of Scotland and down past the Irish coast, and gales wrecked ship after ship. England struck a victory medal, and its Latin line gave the glory to God instead of the sailors. What did the medal say?
answer: God blew and they were scattered
choices: God blew and they were scattered
Thus the tempest swept the proud foe away
God defend the right and crown of England
The Lord alone is my shield and my fortress
context: The medal read 'Afflavit Deus et dissipati sunt' — 'God blew and they were scattered' — crediting the storm and the divine wind rather than the fleet. About 24 ships were lost off Ireland alone. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Spanish_Armada/

question: The 1918 flu is remembered as the 'Spanish Flu,' yet it almost certainly did not begin in Spain. Spain stayed neutral in World War I, so its newspapers printed news of the spreading sickness while the warring nations gagged their own papers to keep morale up. Why did the whole world end up blaming Spain?
answer: Spanish papers were the only ones openly reporting the outbreak
choices: Spanish papers were the only ones openly reporting the outbreak
Spanish sailors first carried the disease across the ocean
Spanish doctors were the first to give the disease a name
Spanish soldiers brought the disease home from the trenches
context: Because warring nations like Britain, France, Germany and the U.S. censored news of the epidemic to protect wartime morale, the world only read about it in Spain's free press and wrongly pinned it on Spain. Spain itself blamed France. Sources: history.com/articles/1918-pandemic-spanish-flu-censorship ; iwm.org.uk/history/spanish-flu-the-unseen-enemy

question: The Spanish flu of 1918 swept the entire planet, infecting roughly one in three people then alive and killing an estimated 50 million. To grasp how staggering that toll was, historians compare it to the event it overlapped — the Great War of 1914-1918. How did the flu's death toll compare to that trench conflict?
answer: The flu killed more people than World War I did
choices: The flu killed more people than World War I did
The flu killed about half as many as the war
The flu and the war killed roughly equal numbers
The flu killed only soldiers, never civilians
context: Estimates of the flu's dead run from 50 million to as high as 100 million, out of about 500 million infected, roughly a third of everyone on Earth. World War I's death toll, by comparison, was around 17-20 million. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_flu ; ourworldindata.org/spanish-flu-largest-influenza-pandemic-in-history

question: On September 28, 1918, with the flu already in town, the city of Philadelphia went ahead with a giant Liberty Loan war-bond parade. Over 200,000 people packed the streets shoulder to shoulder despite public warnings. Within 72 hours, every one of the city's 31 hospitals was full and the dead were piling up. What grim title did this event earn?
answer: The deadliest parade in American history
choices: The deadliest parade in American history
The first quarantine of an American city
The largest war-bond drive ever held
The end of all public gatherings nationwide
context: About 2,600 Philadelphians were dead by the end of that week, and roughly 12,000 died in the weeks that followed. St. Louis, which cancelled its own parade and shut down public gatherings, fared far better, a stark lesson in the cost of going ahead. Sources: history.com/this-day-in-history/september-28/flu-epidemic-hits-philadelphia ; smithsonianmag.com/history/philadelphia-threw-wwi-parade-gave-thousands-onlookers-flu-180970372/

question: A normal flu mostly kills the very young and the very old. The 1918 flu was eerily different: charts of its deaths showed a 'W' shape, with a third huge spike in the middle, striking healthy adults aged 25 to 35 in the prime of life. Doctors later realized what turned these strong victims against themselves. What killed them?
answer: Their own powerful immune systems overreacting and flooding their lungs
choices: Their own powerful immune systems overreacting and flooding their lungs
A second bacterial infection that only spread among young adults
The physical exhaustion of wartime work and rationing
A weakness in young adults' hearts that the virus attacked
context: The strong immune response of healthy young adults triggered a 'cytokine storm,' an overreaction that flooded the lungs with fluid and suffocated them, which is why the disease was deadliest to the people you'd expect to survive it. Sources: history.com/articles/spanish-flu-second-wave-resurgence ; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3734171/

question: In the tiny Alaska village of Brevig Mission, the flu killed 72 of the 80 villagers in just five days in 1918, and their bodies were buried in ground that stays frozen year-round. Decades later that frozen ground made Brevig Mission the key to solving the whole pandemic. How did this remote grave crack the case?
answer: Frozen lung tissue let scientists rebuild the entire 1918 virus
choices: Frozen lung tissue let scientists rebuild the entire 1918 virus
Survivors' written diaries described the disease in exact detail
Church records pinpointed the exact day the flu arrived
Old photographs revealed how the villagers were buried
context: In 1997 researcher Johan Hultin recovered virus-laden lung tissue from a woman's well-preserved grave in the permafrost; by 2005 Jeffery Taubenberger's team had reconstructed the entire 1918 virus genome from it, proving the killer had originated in birds. Sources: adn.com/alaska-news/science/2020/03/22/how-an-alaska-village-grave-led-to-a-spanish-flu-breakthrough/ ; archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/flu/pandemic-resources/reconstruction-1918-virus.html

question: In 1829 a galloping horse was the fastest thing most people in England had ever seen. Then, at the Rainhill Trials, the locomotive known as Stephenson's Rocket roared past hauling a carriage. How fast did the Rocket go?
answer: About 30 miles per hour
choices: About 30 miles per hour
About 8 miles per hour
About 70 miles per hour
About 100 miles per hour
context: The Rocket hit roughly 30 mph at the Rainhill Trials in October 1829 — faster than any machine most people had ever witnessed, in an age when a galloping horse set the speed limit. Source: scienceandindustrymuseum.org.uk/what-was-on/stephensons-rocket ; historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofBritain/Rainhill-Trials/

question: On May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit in Utah, two great steam engines were pulled up nose to nose with only a single rail tie between them. From the east came the Union Pacific's engine No. 119. From the west came the Central Pacific's engine Jupiter. For six years each company had been laying track from opposite coasts of America, racing toward the middle. Now the two lines were about to touch. What was the moment marking?
answer: The joining of the first transcontinental railroad
choices: The joining of the first transcontinental railroad
The opening of the first railway tunnel
The first train to carry the U.S. mail
The first railroad bridge over a river
context: At Promontory Summit on May 10, 1869, the Central Pacific's Jupiter and the Union Pacific's No. 119 faced each other across a single tie to mark the completion of the first transcontinental railroad. Source: nps.gov/gosp/learn/historyculture/everlasting-steam-the-story-of-jupiter-and-no-119.htm ; up.com/aboutup/community/great-race/golden-spike/

question: On May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit in Utah, America's first railroad from coast to coast was about to be finished. The last spike, made of pure gold, waited to be driven into the last rail. Central Pacific boss Leland Stanford — later founder of Stanford University — raised the silver hammer to drive it home in front of a huge crowd, with telegraph reporters ready to flash word across the nation. Stanford swung. What happened?
answer: He missed the spike entirely
choices: He missed the spike entirely
He drove it in a single blow
He bent the golden spike in half
He dropped the hammer on his foot
context: Stanford swung at the Golden Spike and missed. It didn't matter — the spike was wired to a telegraph, and the operator flashed the single word 'DONE' across the country, setting off coast-to-coast celebrations anyway. Source: nps.gov/gosp/learn/historyculture/everlasting-steam-the-story-of-jupiter-and-no-119.htm ; up.com/aboutup/community/great-race/golden-spike/

question: America's first transcontinental railroad, built in the 1860s, had to punch through hard mountain country in the American West. The Central Pacific company found few white workers willing to do it. By 1867 more than 90% of its crew — some 10,000 to 15,000 men — were Chinese immigrants, paid less than white workers and forced to buy their own food. Where on the line did these Chinese crews do their most dangerous work?
answer: Blasting tunnels through the granite of the Sierra Nevada
choices: Blasting tunnels through the granite of the Sierra Nevada
Building wooden bridges over the Mississippi River
Laying flat track across the open plains
Painting and decorating the passenger stations
context: Chinese laborers blasted the tunnels through the Sierra Nevada's granite — the deadliest work on the line. More than 1,000 are estimated to have died from avalanches, rockslides, explosions, and exposure, while the Union Pacific's eastbound crews were largely Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans. Source: history.com/articles/transcontinental-railroad-chinese-immigrants ; aflcio.org/2019/5/9/asian-pacific-american-heritage-month-profiles-chinese-railroad-laborers

question: Stephenson's Rocket was the only locomotive to finish the 1829 Rainhill Trials. Its rivals, Sans Pareil and the crowd-favorite Novelty, both broke down. Rocket's winning advantage was a hidden boiler design. What made its boiler so powerful?
answer: A boiler pierced by 25 copper tubes plus a blastpipe drawing air through the fire
choices: A boiler pierced by 25 copper tubes plus a blastpipe drawing air through the fire
A second furnace mounted on the rear of the engine
A pair of giant bellows pumped by the wheels
A reservoir of compressed air released into the cylinders
context: Rocket's secret was a multi-tube boiler — 25 copper fire-tubes — paired with a blastpipe that shot used steam up the chimney to suck air through the fire. The result was far more heat and far more power than older single-flue designs. It was built by Robert Stephenson with his father George and Henry Booth at the Forth Street Works in Newcastle in 1829, and survives today in the National Railway Museum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephenson's_Rocket

question: The Suez Canal opened in Egypt in 1869. It was dug across a narrow strip of land so ships could pass straight through. Before the canal, ships had to sail all the way around one whole continent. Which one?
answer: Africa
choices: Africa
Australia
South America
Antarctica
context: The canal joined the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, so ships traveling between Europe and Asia no longer had to go the long way around Africa's southern tip, the Cape of Good Hope. Source: https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/november-17/suez-canal-opens

question: Before the Suez Canal opened in 1869, a ship from London to Bombay had to sail thousands of extra miles around Africa. The canal cut straight through Egypt instead. About how much shorter did it make that trip?
answer: About 4,500 miles
choices: About 4,500 miles
About 45 miles
About 450 miles
About 45,000 miles
context: The new shortcut from the Mediterranean to the Red Sea slashed the Europe-to-India voyage by roughly 4,000 to 6,000 miles, letting ships skip the long and dangerous trip around the Cape of Good Hope. Source: https://www.shippingwondersoftheworld.com/suez_canal.html

question: At the grand opening of the Suez Canal in November 1869, a line of 77 ships was meant to enter in order. The French royal yacht L'Aigle, carrying Empress Eugenie, was to lead. But the night before, one rival power's warship crept to the front in the dark so it would be first through the canal. Which country pulled off the stunt?
answer: Britain
choices: Britain
Russia
The Ottoman Empire
The United States
context: By slipping ahead in the dark, the British warship HMS Newport became the first ship ever to enter the Suez Canal, beating the official lead ship L'Aigle that carried Empress Eugenie, wife of Napoleon III, at the head of the 77-ship procession. Source: https://maritimecyprus.com/2025/11/16/flashback-in-maritime-history-suez-canal-opens-to-the-world-17-november-1869/

question: In 1875 the bankrupt ruler of Egypt, Khedive Ismail, suddenly put his huge stake in the Suez Canal up for sale. British Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli wanted to grab nearly half the canal company for Britain, but Parliament was not in session to approve the money. Legend says Disraeli got the 4 million pounds he needed in a single stroke. How is the deal remembered as having been struck?
answer: On a Rothschild's word, with no contract signed
choices: On a Rothschild's word, with no contract signed
By a vote of the full Parliament
By a loan from the Bank of England
By the Queen paying out of her own purse
context: As the story is told, Disraeli borrowed the 4 million pounds from the banker Lionel de Rothschild on a gentleman's word with no contract, letting Britain snap up the Khedive's shares and turn the canal into an imperial lifeline to India. The no-contract detail is remembered as legend. Source: https://www.rothschildarchive.org/collections/archivists_choice/march_2015_suez_canal_loan_receipts_1876

question: An hour has 60 minutes and a minute has 60 seconds. So every clock on Earth counts by sixties. This way of counting was made up over 4,000 years ago by which people, whose habit we still keep every time we read the time?
answer: The Sumerians of Mesopotamia
choices: The Sumerians of Mesopotamia
The Phoenicians of the coast
The Etruscans of Italy
The Minoans of Crete
context: The Sumerians (and later the Babylonians) of Mesopotamia counted in base 60 -- the 'sexagesimal' system -- back in the 3rd millennium BC. It is the oldest counting system that still survives in everyday life: 60 minutes, 60 seconds, every single day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexagesimal

question: The Sumerians counted by 60 instead of by 10. Sixty turned out to be a smart pick for one math reason. That is why an hour splits cleanly into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, and sixths with nothing left over. What makes 60 so special?
answer: It is the smallest number that divides evenly by every number from 1 to 6
choices: It is the smallest number that divides evenly by every number from 1 to 6
It is the largest number you can count to on both hands at once
It is the only number that equals the days in a Sumerian month
It is the smallest number that is a perfect square and a cube
context: Sixty splits evenly into 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, or 30 equal parts with no leftovers -- the smallest number divisible by every value from 1 to 6. Base 10 cannot do this (10 will not split into thirds). That clean divisibility is why an hour divides so neatly into halves, thirds, and quarters. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexagesimal

question: The trading towns strung along the East African coast gave their name to a whole people and language: Swahili. That word was borrowed from the Arabic traders who sailed in, and it simply names where these towns sat. What does the Arabic word behind 'Swahili' mean?
answer: The coasts
choices: The coasts
The traders
The islands
The harbors
context: From Arabic 'sawahil,' meaning coasts. The Swahili language is Bantu at its core but absorbed Arabic and Persian words from settled traders, so the very name of the people records African and Arab cultures merging. Source: courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-hccc-worldcivilization/chapter/the-swahili-culture/ ; education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/people-coast/

question: Swahili sailors crossed the open Indian Ocean in boats called mtepe, which carried no iron at all. The coast was lined with razor-sharp coral reefs that would shatter a stiff, rigidly built hull. So how were the coconut-wood planks of a mtepe held together?
answer: Stitched edge to edge with coconut-fiber rope
choices: Stitched edge to edge with coconut-fiber rope
Bolted with bronze plates and tar
Slotted into deep wooden grooves
Riveted with hammered copper studs
context: The planks were sewn with coir (coconut-husk fiber) rope and pegged with wood, so the hull flexed instead of snapping when it scraped coral. One 19th-century mtepe reached nearly 30 metres long, and this sewn-boat method is so old it appears in the 1st-century AD Greek trade guide, the Periplus. Source: kandilivilla.wordpress.com/tag/zanzibar-tradition/ ; academia.edu/51346567/Sewn_boats_of_the_Swahili_coast

question: Kilwa was the richest of the medieval Swahili cities on the East African coast. Its sultan ruled from a coral-stone palace of over a hundred rooms, with an eight-sided pool and indoor plumbing. Kilwa grew rich by trading across one huge body of water, riding the monsoon winds to reach India and Arabia. Which one?
answer: The Indian Ocean
choices: The Indian Ocean
The Atlantic Ocean
The Mediterranean Sea
The Red Sea
context: Husuni Kubwa also had a stepped courtyard that doubled as a warehouse-and-rest-stop where merchants stored goods and reloaded them onto ships. Source: panafrocore.com/2024/03/13/husuni-kubwa-palace-a-brief-history ; nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/abandoned-east-african-city-kilwa

question: The Kilwa Chronicle tells how the Persian prince Ali ibn al-Hasan bought the island of Kilwa from its local Bantu king. The price the king named sounds simple, but it took an astonishing amount of one trade good to pay it. According to the chronicle, Ali paid in enough colored cloth to do what?
answer: Stretch all the way around the island's edge
choices: Stretch all the way around the island's edge
Fill the king's largest warehouse to the roof
Drape every house in the king's own town
Load the holds of a hundred trading dhows
context: Legend, per the Kilwa Chronicle. When the king later regretted the deal and tried to take Kilwa back, he found the Persians had dug away the narrow land bridge, so Kilwa was now a true island, cut off and no longer his. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_ibn_al-Hassan_Shirazi ; pieterderideaux.jimdofree.com/.../kilwa-chronicle/

question: In 1414, envoys from the Swahili city of Malindi brought a strange long-necked animal as a gift to the Ming court of China. They handed it to admiral Zheng He's fleet. The Chinese had never seen such a beast. They decided it was a famous mythical creature whose arrival meant a wise, good ruler sat on the throne. What did they think the giraffe was?
answer: The qilin, a unicorn-like omen-beast
choices: The qilin, a unicorn-like omen-beast
A young dragon of the eastern sea
The phoenix returned in the flesh
A guardian lion sent from heaven
context: By ancient tradition the qilin appeared only when a wise and virtuous ruler held the throne, so the giraffe became powerful propaganda for the emperor. Source: face2faceafrica.com/article/how-a-giraffe-cemented-east-africas-trade-relations-with-china-in-1414 ; smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/peculiar-story-giraffes-medieval-china

question: Kilwa minted its own copper coins around 1150-1330. In 1944 an Australian soldier, Morry Isenberg, picked some odd old coins off a beach in the Wessel Islands off northern Australia and dropped them in a tin, where they sat for 35 years. When experts finally identified them in 1979, what made the find a real mystery?
answer: They were medieval Kilwa coins, the oldest foreign object found in Australia
choices: They were medieval Kilwa coins, the oldest foreign object found in Australia
They were forged copies stamped centuries after Kilwa fell
They matched no mint and could not be dated at all
They were Portuguese coins lost in a later shipwreck
context: Nobody knows how copper coins from a medieval African city crossed the entire Indian Ocean to a beach in northern Australia. Source: australiangeographic.com.au/history-culture/2014/08/mystery-of-ancient-african-coins-found-in-australia/ ; thehistoryblog.com/archives/26800

question: The whole Indian Ocean trade ran on the monsoon winds, which for three or four months blew toward the East African coast, then reversed and blew back toward Arabia and India. Because of this rhythm, a merchant who sailed in on one wind often could not leave for months. Historians point to that forced wait as the very thing that created the Swahili. How did the stranded waiting build a blended people?
answer: Marooned traders married into local families
choices: Marooned traders married into local families
Idle crews built the coral-stone palaces
Waiting merchants taught the locals Arabic
Stuck sailors drew the first coast maps
context: With the wind against them, traders waited out the season ashore, married into Bantu families, and over generations the African and Arab worlds fused into the Swahili. Source: courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-hccc-worldcivilization/chapter/the-swahili-culture/

question: Kilwa's golden age ended with the Portuguese. In 1505 Francisco de Almeida landed about 500 troops, fought through the narrow streets, and plundered and burned the city. To hold the harbor for Portugal's ships bound for India, Almeida left a permanent mark on the conquered town. What did the Portuguese build at Kilwa?
answer: A stone fort, the Gereza, to control the harbor
choices: A stone fort, the Gereza, to control the harbor
A new cathedral over the Great Mosque
A treaty-house for the captured sultan
A shipyard to repair their war fleet
context: Three years earlier Vasco da Gama had already forced Kilwa's ruler to promise yearly tribute in gold and pearls. After taking Kilwa, the same Portuguese fleet sailed north and sacked and burned Mombasa on 13 August 1505, the second great Swahili port to fall in one voyage. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Kilwa ; zum.de/whkmla/military/16cen/kilwa1505.html

question: Samuel Morse sat at his telegraph key in a room of the Capitol in Washington on 24 May 1844, ready to send the first official message down some 40 miles of wire to his partner, Alfred Vail, in Baltimore. Seventeen-year-old Annie Ellsworth had chosen the words. What four words did Morse tap out?
answer: "What hath God wrought"
choices: "What hath God wrought"
"Come at once, Vail"
"The line is open"
"Glory to the Union"
context: The line ran from the Old Supreme Court Chamber in the Capitol to Morse's partner Alfred Vail in Baltimore. The four words are a Bible verse, Numbers 23:23, and 17-year-old Annie Ellsworth picked them — Morse had promised her the first dispatch because she rushed him the news that his funding bill had passed Congress. Sources: history.house.gov; Smithsonian National Museum of American History nmah_713485; loc.gov.

question: Henry Clay became the Whigs' choice for president on 1 May 1844, and the news left Baltimore for Washington two ways: aboard a train, and down Samuel Morse's half-built telegraph line. The line was not even finished, and its first official message was still three weeks away. What made that day historic?
answer: The wired news arrived about an hour before the train carrying it
choices: The wired news arrived about an hour before the train carrying it
The train's passengers cheered when they saw the message posted
Clay telegraphed his own thanks back down the line
Morse rode the train to confirm the wire had worked
context: The telegraphed report beat the train into Washington by roughly 64 minutes — the first time information traveled faster than the person carrying it. Distance had been annihilated: news could now outrun the messenger. Source: Boundary Stones (WETA), 'What Hath God Wrought: The Long Road to Washington's First Telegraph.'

question: When the law was given at Mount Sinai, the whole mountain was wrapped in smoke 'like the smoke of a kiln' and quaked while thunder rolled and lightning flashed. One more thing pierced the chaos and kept growing louder and louder until the people trembled. What was it?
answer: The blast of a trumpet, a ram's-horn shofar
choices: The blast of a trumpet, a ram's-horn shofar
The roar of a great waterfall below
The drumming of an unseen army
The howling of wind through the rocks
context: Exodus 19:16-19 describes the shofar (ram's-horn trumpet) sounding 'long and growing louder' as the mountain smoked and quaked. The shofar became Israel's instrument for sacred, awe-filled moments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Sinai_(Bible); bible.usccb.org/bible/exodus/19.

question: The book of Exodus says God himself produced the writing on the first two stone tablets given at Sinai — the only time the Bible describes something as inscribed personally by God. The phrase it uses for HOW they were written is famous. What is that striking phrase?
answer: Written 'by the finger of God'
choices: Written 'by the finger of God'
Carved 'with a tongue of flame'
Burned 'by the breath of heaven'
Cut 'with the sword of the word'
context: Exodus 31:18 says the tablets were 'written with the finger of God.' Nothing else in the Bible is described as inscribed directly by God. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablets_of_Stone (citing Exodus 31:18).

question: Moses came down Mount Sinai carrying the stone tablets and found the people had built a golden calf and were dancing around it. His anger 'burned.' In that fury, what did Moses do with the tablets right there at the foot of the mountain?
answer: Smashed them to pieces on the ground
choices: Smashed them to pieces on the ground
Hid them inside his cloak
Held them up to silence the crowd
Buried them beneath the altar
context: Exodus 32:19 — seeing the golden calf and the dancing, Moses 'threw the tablets out of his hands, breaking them at the foot of the mountain.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablets_of_Stone; biblehub.com/exodus/32-20.htm.

question: After confronting the golden calf at Sinai, Moses burned it, then ground the gold down to fine powder and scattered it over water. He then forced the Israelites to do one humiliating thing with that water. What did he make them do?
answer: Drink it down
choices: Drink it down
Wash their faces in it
Carry it back up the mountain
Pour it over the altar
context: Exodus 32:20 — Moses 'strewed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it,' forcing them to swallow their own false god. Source: biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/32-20.htm (KJV Exodus 32:20).

question: Aaron was the one who had actually made the golden calf out of the people's gold. When Moses demanded an explanation, Aaron dodged the blame in a famously feeble way. How did Aaron say the calf came to be?
answer: He threw the gold in the fire and 'out came this calf'
choices: He threw the gold in the fire and 'out came this calf'
A stranger had cast it while he slept
The people had forced his hand with threats
He had shaped it only as a harmless toy
context: Exodus 32:24 — Aaron claims he threw the gold into the fire 'and out came this calf,' blaming the fire rather than his own hands. Source: bibleproject.com/bible/nlt/exodus/32/; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/.

question: The Code of Hammurabi still stands, carved on a black stone slab over seven feet tall. At the top, King Hammurabi stands before a seated god. The god hands him a ring and a rod, symbols of the power to give law. Which god is shown giving Hammurabi that power?
answer: Shamash, the sun god
choices: Shamash, the sun god
Marduk, the chief god of Babylon
Enlil, the king of the gods
Ea, the god of the deep
context: The relief atop the Louvre's Hammurabi stele shows Shamash, the sun god and patron of justice, handing the king a ring and rod. Hammurabi's law thus claims a god-given mandate to a single ruler. Source: louvre.fr/en/the-code-of-hammurabi; smarthistory.org/hammurabi-2/.

question: At Sinai the people were so terrified by the fire, smoke, and the voice from the mountain that they stood far off and begged Moses to be their go-between. What did the people plead with Moses in Exodus 20:19?
answer: 'You speak to us, but do not let God speak to us, lest we die'
choices: 'You speak to us, but do not let God speak to us, lest we die'
'Lead us away from this mountain at once'
'Tell us the words later, when the fire has passed'
'Let the elders alone come near to listen'
context: Exodus 20:18-19 — the people 'stood at a distance' and begged Moses to receive the words so they would not have to hear the voice directly and die. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Sinai_(Bible) (citing Exodus 20:18-19).

question: At Mount Sinai, Moses smashed the first stone tablets of the Ten Commandments in fury after finding the Israelites worshiping a golden calf. God then provided a second set — but the renewed covenant was made by a striking split of labor between God and Moses. Exodus 34:1 describes who did what for these replacement tablets. How were the second tablets actually produced?
answer: Moses carved the blank stones, then God re-wrote the words on them
choices: Moses carved the blank stones, then God re-wrote the words on them
God produced both the stones and the writing again
Moses both carved the stones and copied the words himself
An angel cut the stones and Moses inscribed them
context: Exodus 34:1 — God tells Moses to cut two new tablets himself, and God will write the words on them. The renewed covenant is thus cut by human hands but inscribed by God. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablets_of_Stone (Exodus 34:1).

question: When God gave the Ten Commandments to Moses at Mount Sinai, the fourth one ordered a day of weekly rest called the Sabbath. It reached people no other ancient law in the world protected. In Exodus 20:10, alongside a household's sons and daughters, which group is explicitly guaranteed that same day of rest?
answer: Slaves, work animals, and the foreigner within the gates
choices: Slaves, work animals, and the foreigner within the gates
The king, the priests, and the temple guards
Travelers and merchants passing through the land
The firstborn son of every household
context: Exodus 20:10 / Deut 5:14 extend rest to son, daughter, male and female slave, the ox and donkey, and 'the foreigner within your gates' — a guaranteed day off for slaves and animals alike, unheard of in the ancient world. Source: biblehub.com/exodus/20-10.htm; biblehub.com/deuteronomy/5-14.htm.

question: In the Book of Exodus, the Hebrew people camp at the foot of Mount Sinai and Moses climbs up into the cloud to receive God's law carved on two stone tablets. English Bibles call the ten sayings on those tablets the 'Ten Commandments.' But the Hebrew Bible itself never uses the word 'commandments' for them at all. Three times it calls them 'Aseret ha-Devarim.' What does that Hebrew name literally mean?
answer: The Ten Words
choices: The Ten Words
The Ten Laws
The Ten Judgments
The Ten Decrees
context: 'Aseret ha-Devarim' means the Ten Words (or Ten Utterances). The Greek Septuagint rendered this 'deka logoi,' the source of our word 'Decalogue.' Source: jewishvirtuallibrary.org/decalogue; thetorah.com/article/the-decalogue-ten-commandments-or-ten-statements (Deut 4:13, 10:4).

question: The Ten Commandments — the Hebrew calls them the Ten Words — that Moses brought down from Mount Sinai are written as flat, absolute commands: 'You shall not steal,' full stop. Every other ancient Near Eastern law code, including the famous Code of Hammurabi carved in Babylon around 1750 BC, was written in a completely different grammar. What form did those other codes take?
answer: Case law: 'If a man does X, then Y follows'
choices: Case law: 'If a man does X, then Y follows'
Blessings and curses: 'Do this and live; do that and be cut off'
Prayers asking the gods to punish wrongdoers
Lists of rewards for the obedient
context: Scholars call the Ten Words 'apodictic' (flat command, no penalty) versus the 'casuistic' case-law of Hammurabi and other codes, framed as 'if a man does X, then Y.' Source: jewishvirtuallibrary.org/decalogue; openmedia.yale.edu Yale RLST 145 transcript 10.

question: Hammurabi's famous rule 'an eye for an eye' (Law 196) sounds like equal justice, but it did not apply equally. A noble who blinded another noble lost his own eye — but if the victim was a slave, the offender simply paid silver. How much silver was a slave's eye reckoned to be worth?
answer: Half the slave's purchase price
choices: Half the slave's purchase price
A fixed fine of sixty shekels
One-third of the slave's purchase price
Twice the slave's purchase price
context: Hammurabi's Law 196-199 graded penalties by class: destroying a noble's eye cost your own, but a slave's eye was paid off in silver, valued at half the slave's price. The Decalogue, by contrast, bound everyone equally. Source: courses.lumenlearning.com (Law 196-199); encyclopedia.com 'Class and Society in Ancient Near Eastern Law.'

question: Hammurabi's laws in Babylon around 1750 BC were handed down by a god-king and applied differently depending on a person's rank — a broken bone cost more if the victim was noble. The Ten Commandments — the Ten Words — were delivered very differently at Mount Sinai. According to the book of Exodus, how did the Israelites first receive them from God through Moses?
answer: Proclaimed aloud to the whole assembled people at once
choices: Proclaimed aloud to the whole assembled people at once
Written privately and given only to the priests
Revealed in a dream to Moses alone, who recited them later
Posted on a stone pillar for scribes to copy
context: Unlike a king's decree handed to elites, the Decalogue was spoken directly to the whole assembled nation at Sinai, making the entire people — not just rulers — party to the covenant. Source: britannica.com/topic/Sinai-covenant; crosstocrown.org Tablets of Stone ch.6.

question: At the ruined Toltec city of Tula in central Mexico, four giant figures still stand on top of Pyramid B. Each is carved from stone, about 15 feet tall, and built from four stacked drums. What does each of these tall figures show?
answer: A warrior dressed for battle
choices: A warrior dressed for battle
A seated and robed priest
A coiled feathered serpent
A kneeling captive bound with rope
context: Nicknamed the 'Atlanteans,' the four warriors each wear a tall feathered drum-headdress and a butterfly-shaped chest plate, carry an atlatl (spear-thrower), and wear a round solar-disk back-plate. They likely once stood as columns holding up the temple roof. The four are so alike that Toltec stone workshops must have mass-produced huge sculptures to a standard pattern. Source: World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Toltec_Civilization/; EBSCO Research Starters 'Toltecs Build Tula.'

question: Long after Tula fell, the Aztecs looked back on the Toltecs as a lost golden-age people, the masters of every craft. The Aztecs took the very name of that people and turned it into an everyday word in their Nahuatl language. When an Aztec called a person a 'Toltecatl,' what did the word mean?
answer: A skilled artist or craftsman
choices: A skilled artist or craftsman
A foreign tribute-payer
A wandering desert nomad
A priest of the feathered serpent
context: 'Toltecatl' came to mean artist, craftsman, or wise man, and 'toltecayotl' (Toltec-ness) meant art, culture, and civilization itself — the opposite of 'chichimecayotl,' the savage nomadic state. To say someone had a 'Toltec heart' meant that person excelled at a craft. Source: Wikipedia 'Toltecayotl'; World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org/Toltec_Civilization/.

question: In 1869 two crews finally met at Promontory Summit, Utah. The Central Pacific had built east from Sacramento. The Union Pacific had built west from Omaha.
