To mark their tracks joining into the first railroad across America, the bosses tapped in one last spike made of a very precious metal. What was that famous last spike made of?
answer: Gold
choices: Gold
Iron
Copper
Bronze
context: The golden spike was 17.6-carat gold engraved to honor the railroad's completion. It was never left in the track — it was pulled out after the ceremony and given to Stanford University, where it is still on display. (Three other ceremonial spikes were also tapped that day: a second gold one, a silver spike from Nevada, and a blended iron-silver-gold spike from Arizona, all into a polished laurelwood tie.) Source: Union Pacific official history, up.com/about-us/history/golden-spike.

question: At Promontory Summit, on the day the cross-country railroad was done, two steam engines rolled up nose to nose: the Central Pacific's 'Jupiter' and the Union Pacific's 'No. 119.' A photographer caught the rival crews leaning out to shake hands in the narrow gap. What is that famous photo called?
answer: The Wedding of the Rails
choices: The Wedding of the Rails
The Meeting of the Engines
The Last Spike
The Golden Junction
context: The journey from coast to coast dropped from four-plus months to about one week once the rails were joined. The two engines facing each other — Jupiter pointing east, No. 119 pointing west — made the photo an instant icon. Source: NPS 'Everlasting Steam: The Story of Jupiter and No. 119,' nps.gov/gosp.

question: The golden spike was wired to the telegraph so the whole nation could 'hear' each blow land. Leland Stanford, president of the Central Pacific, lifted the heavy silver maul, took aim at the spike, and swung in front of the watching crowd. What happened on that first swing?
answer: He swung and missed the spike completely
choices: He swung and missed the spike completely
He drove the spike in with one clean blow
He shattered the soft gold spike in half
He stopped and handed the maul to a worker
context: Then Union Pacific's Thomas Durant — nursing a headache from too much partying — swung and missed too, and the construction bosses had to finish the job. After the misses, the telegraph operator simply tapped out the message himself: a single word flashed across America — 'DONE.' Cannons fired in San Francisco and the Liberty Bell was rung in Philadelphia. Source: Salt Lake Magazine, saltlakemagazine.com/golden-spike.

question: On April 28, 1869, the Central Pacific raced to lay a huge amount of track in one day. They finished with 10 miles and 56 feet of rail set down by hand. No hand crew has ever beaten it. The last rails were carried by a team of eight Irishmen. Each man is thought to have lifted about 125 tons of iron that day. When lunch came and fresh workers were offered to spell them, what did the eight do?
answer: They turned down the relief and carried the rails the rest of the day
choices: They turned down the relief and carried the rails the rest of the day
They handed off to the fresh crew and finally rested
They quit early, too exhausted to keep lifting iron
They refused to work again until they were paid more
context: The eight rail handlers were named in the record: Michael Shay, Thomas Daley, George Elliott, Michael Sullivan, Edward Killeen, Patrick Joyce, Michael Kennedy, and Fred McNamara. Reporters timed cars of rail being emptied in 75-80 seconds each across the roughly 12-hour day. Source: Irish America, irishamerica.com 'April 28, 1869'; CPRR Museum 'Ten Mile Day.'

question: To carry the Central Pacific over the Sierra Nevada at Donner Pass, thousands of Chinese workers kept blasting rock tunnels straight through the winter of 1866-67. They made up about eight in ten of the western crew. Forty-four storms buried the summit under more than forty feet of snow. Where did these crews live and work for months to reach the granite?
answer: In snow tunnels they dug, living underground by lantern light
choices: In snow tunnels they dug, living underground by lantern light
In heated railcars hauled up to the summit each night
In timber bunkhouses built above the level of the snow
In caves they blasted out of the granite cliffs nearby
context: They carved snow tunnels 50 to 500 feet long with air shafts bored through the walls, almost never seeing the sky. Leland Stanford himself testified of the Chinese workers, 'Without them it would be impossible to complete the western portion of this great national enterprise.' Source: PBS American Experience 'Tunneling in the Sierra Nevada'; Stanford Chinese Railroad Workers Project FAQ, web.stanford.edu/group/chineserailroad.

question: In summer 1958 Jack Kilby was so new at Texas Instruments (TI) that he had no vacation time. While the whole company took its long summer break, he worked alone in an empty lab. There he had the idea that became the first integrated circuit. On September 12, 1958, he showed it to TI bosses. He flipped a switch, and something appeared on an oscilloscope screen. What did they see?
answer: A green wavy line rolling across the screen
choices: A green wavy line rolling across the screen
A row of numbers counting upward
A bright flash that then went dark
A steady straight line holding flat
context: Kilby's first chip was a rough patchwork of germanium holding a transistor, a capacitor, and resistors joined by fine gold 'flying-wires' on one piece of semiconductor. The green wavy line was a working oscillator. Kilby and Robert Noyce are both credited as inventors of the integrated circuit; Kilby won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics. Source: Computer History Museum, Silicon Engine; TI.com 'From idea to invention'.

question: By the 1950s engineers hit what they called the 'tyranny of numbers.' A single machine needed so many separate transistors, resistors, and capacitors that nobody could wire them all by hand. What breakthrough solved this, by fitting a whole circuit onto one small chip?
answer: The integrated circuit
choices: The integrated circuit
The vacuum tube
The copper wiring harness
The magnetic tape reel
context: Instead of soldering thousands of separate parts, the integrated circuit put the transistors, resistors, and capacitors all onto one chip. Jack Kilby built the first one in 1958; Robert Noyce at Fairchild devised a version in 1959 using the 'planar process' that printed the connecting wires right onto the chip, making mass production practical. Source: Computer History Museum, Silicon Engine: 'All Semiconductor Solid Circuit is Demonstrated'.

question: In 1971 the Intel 4004 became the first microprocessor — an entire computer's central processor squeezed onto a single chip, packing 2,300 transistors into a die about 12 square millimeters. Its designer, Federico Faggin, was so proud of the chip that he left a personal mark on it. What did he do?
answer: Etched his initials 'F.F.' onto the chip itself
choices: Etched his initials 'F.F.' onto the chip itself
Mailed the first chip to his old professor
Named the chip after his daughter
Kept the first chip locked in a safe
context: The Intel 4004 shrank a whole CPU onto one chip — the leap that led toward personal computers. Faggin's initials are etched right into the silicon. The path ran from the 1947 Bell Labs transistor, to Kilby and Noyce's integrated circuit, to the microprocessor that built the modern world. Source: Computer History Museum, Silicon Engine: 'Microprocessor Integrates CPU Function onto a Single Chip'; IEEE Spectrum 'Chip Hall of Fame: Intel 4004'.

question: Odysseus found a way into Troy after ten years of siege. The Greeks built one enormous thing, left it before the gates and pretended to sail home in defeat, and the Trojans hauled it inside. What was it, and what was its secret?
answer: A giant hollow wooden horse with Greek warriors hidden inside it
choices: A giant hollow wooden horse with Greek warriors hidden inside it
A towering bronze statue of the goddess Athena holding a spear
A huge wooden tower on wheels packed with barrels of fire
An immense heap of treasure and weapons piled before the gates
context: The Trojans dragged it inside themselves; that night the hidden men climbed out and opened the gates. This is where the phrase 'Trojan horse' comes from -- any gift or offer with an attack hidden inside (in computing, a 'Trojan' is malware disguised as something harmless). Legend, from Homer and Virgil. Source: Britannica, 'Trojan horse'; Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.

question: Laocoon, a priest of Troy, saw the danger in the gift the Greeks had left by the city and hurled his spear into its side, warning his people: 'I fear the Greeks, even those bearing gifts.' Then a sudden horror fell on him that the Trojans read as a sign from the gods to drag the gift inside. What struck Laocoon down?
answer: Two giant serpents rose from the sea and crushed him and both his sons
choices: Two giant serpents rose from the sea and crushed him and both his sons
A bolt of lightning split the sky and struck him and his sons dead
A sudden plague swept the temple and killed him and his household
The earth cracked open beneath the altar and swallowed him whole
context: So the warning that should have saved Troy is exactly what doomed it -- the Trojans took the serpents as proof the gods wanted the horse inside. The Latin line 'Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes' comes from Virgil's Aeneid; the marble statue of Laocoon and his sons in the serpents' coils was dug up in Rome in 1506 and now stands in the Vatican Museums. Legend. Source: Virgil, Aeneid Book 2 (via World History Encyclopedia, 'Laocoon').

question: Before Rome wrote down its laws around 450 BC, only a small circle of upper-class priests called the pontifices knew what the law actually said. They alone interpreted the old customs, all of it kept in their memory. Then the Romans carved the laws onto bronze tablets and did the one thing that ended the priests' secret hold on the law. What did they do with the tablets?
answer: They bolted the tablets up in the Forum, where every citizen could read the same law
choices: They bolted the tablets up in the Forum, where every citizen could read the same law
They handed the tablets to an assembly of plebeians to guard in secret
They made the priests swear a public oath to interpret the tablets honestly
They burned the old memorized customs so only the new tablets remained
context: The Twelve Tables (c. 451-450 BC) were posted in the Forum, the open square every Roman crossed, so a plebeian and a patrician could read the very same law with their own eyes. That broke the pontifices' monopoly: no one could now claim the law said something secret. Historians count it a distant ancestor of the Western ideal that the law is written down, public, and the same for everyone. Sources: worldhistory.org/Twelve_Tables; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_Tables

question: Table III of the Twelve Tables dealt with Romans who could not pay their debts. An unpaid debtor was bound in chains weighing at least fifteen pounds, and if no one paid for his release by the third market day, the law allowed his creditors to do something shocking. What could they legally do to him?
answer: Cut his body into pieces, and divide the parts among themselves
choices: Cut his body into pieces, and divide the parts among themselves
Brand his forehead with a hot iron and then set him free
Sell him across the Tiber into slavery in a foreign land
Throw him from the Tarpeian Rock onto the stones below
context: The Latin reads 'partis secanto' — let them cut the parts. The clause even added that if the creditors cut more or less than their share, it was no crime. It is the most notorious line in the Twelve Tables, a glimpse of how harsh early Roman debt law could be. Sources: thelatinlibrary.com/law/12tables.html; thecollector.com/twelve-tables-rome

question: Abd al-Rahman I, then a young Umayyad prince, escaped in 750 when the rival Abbasid family broke his dynasty's power by the river Zab, then hunted the princes down one after another. He made his way west across the full length of North Africa. Where did he found a new Umayyad state?
answer: Cordoba, in Spain
choices: Cordoba, in Spain
Cairo, in Egypt
Kairouan, in Tunisia
Tangier, in Morocco
context: Abd al-Rahman I was the sole prince to survive the Abbasid massacre. After fleeing across North Africa he founded an Umayyad state at Cordoba in Spain that became a famed center of learning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate

question: In 1550 the Spanish emperor Charles V did something almost no empire has ever done. He ordered all new conquests in the Americas to stop. He called a panel of judges to Valladolid to settle one question in public, under his own crown. What was that question?
answer: Whether it was just to wage war on the native peoples of the Americas
choices: Whether it was just to wage war on the native peoples of the Americas
Whether to share captured gold among the conquering soldiers
Whether to build a new cathedral in the conquered cities
Whether to send more ships across the Atlantic that year
context: Charles V halted new conquests and convened the Valladolid debate (1550-51) to ask whether the conquest of the Indigenous peoples was just. It is one of the only times an empire paused its own expansion to argue, openly and under its own crown, whether what it was doing was right. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valladolid_debate

question: At Valladolid, the scholar Juan Gines de Sepulveda argued for war on the native peoples. He built his case on Aristotle's idea of the 'natural slave' — people he claimed were born to be ruled by their betters. To rank the natives below the Spanish, what shocking comparison did his argument reach for?
answer: They stood to Spaniards as children to adults, as women to men, even as apes to men
choices: They stood to Spaniards as children to adults, as women to men, even as apes to men
They were a lost tribe of Israel scattered after a forgotten war
They were descended from sailors blown off course centuries earlier
They were a people cursed to wander after defying their own gods
context: Sepúlveda argued the native peoples were as inferior to Spaniards 'as children to adults, as women to men,' and even fell 'between apes and men' — so, he claimed, it was natural and right for Spain to rule them. It was a serious, learned argument of its day, not a cartoon; the point of Valladolid is that the West argued such claims out in the open. Bartolomé de las Casas answered that the native peoples had real laws, agriculture, and religion and were 'fully capable of reason.' Source: https://www.columbia.edu/acis/ets/CCREAD/sepulved.htm

question: The Thirty Years' War began in 1618 when angry Protestants in Prague threw two Catholic officials and their secretary out a castle window about 70 feet up. Astonishingly, all three men survived the fall. What had they landed in that broke their fall?
answer: A pile of dung
choices: A pile of dung
A flowing moat
A stack of timber
A market awning
context: The 23 May 1618 Defenestration of Prague: Bohemian Protestants hurled two Catholic imperial regents and their secretary from a Prague Castle window roughly 70 feet up, and all three landed on a dung heap and lived. Catholics called the survival a miracle; Protestants said it was just the manure. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defenestration ; private-prague-guide.com 'The Second Defenestration of Prague')

question: The French Wars of Religion began on 1 March 1562 when the Duke Francois de Guise and his men killed about a hundred Huguenots in the town of Wassy. The victims were not soldiers but ordinary people, caught while they were worshipping. Where had they gathered to worship?
answer: In a barn
choices: In a barn
In a cathedral
In a town hall
In a vineyard
context: The Massacre of Vassy (Wassy), 1 March 1562: the Duke Francois de Guise and his men killed roughly a hundred Huguenots who were worshipping in a barn, lighting the fuse for thirty-six years of civil war. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_Vassy ; Musee protestant, 'The eight wars of religion 1562-1598')

question: During the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 24 August 1572, Catholics in Paris hunted Huguenots house by house through the streets. To keep from killing one another in the chaos, the attackers all wore the same mark on their sleeves. What did they wear so they could tell friend from foe?
answer: White scarves
choices: White scarves
Red crosses
Black ribbons
Iron badges
context: The St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre began in the dark hours of 24 August 1572, set off by church bells tolling for matins near the Louvre. Catholic attackers wore white scarves or armbands on their sleeves to distinguish friend from foe as they hunted Huguenots house by house. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Bartholomew's_Day_massacre)

question: On St. Bartholomew's Day in 1572, men of the Duke of Guise dragged the Huguenot leader Admiral Gaspard de Coligny from his bed and killed him. A killer reportedly said he never saw anyone die more steadfastly. What did the men then do with Coligny's body?
answer: Threw it from the window
choices: Threw it from the window
Burned it in the courtyard
Sank it in the Seine
Buried it in secret
context: Gaspard de Coligny was dragged from his bed, killed by the Duke of Guise's men, and his body was thrown out the window into the street. The historian Jacques-Auguste de Thou recorded a killer saying Coligny 'never saw anyone less afraid in so great a peril, nor die more steadfastly.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Bartholomew's_Day_massacre, quoting Jacques-Auguste de Thou)

question: In 1598 King Henry IV ended the French Wars of Religion with the Edict of Nantes. Beyond letting Huguenots worship and hold public office, the edict gave them a guarantee that no mere promise of tolerance could match: it let them keep more than a hundred of one specific thing across France. What did it let them keep?
answer: Fortified towns they could garrison
choices: Fortified towns they could garrison
Seats on the royal council
Their own printing presses
Tax-free trading harbors
context: The Edict of Nantes, promulgated at Nantes on 13 April 1598, let Huguenots worship in many parts of the kingdom (not Paris), opened universities and office to them, and let them keep over a hundred fortified 'places of safety' they could garrison, including La Rochelle, Montauban, Montpellier, and Saumur. Catholicism stayed the state religion. (britannica.com/event/Edict-of-Nantes ; worldhistory.org)

question: The 1555 Peace of Augsburg tried to end Germany's religious war by letting each prince pick Catholicism or Lutheranism for his own land -- 'whose realm, his religion.' But it had a fatal flaw: it recognized only those two faiths and refused to include one fast-growing Protestant group, which helped set up the far bloodier Thirty Years' War. Which group did the peace leave out?
answer: The Calvinists
choices: The Calvinists
The Anabaptists
The Jesuits
The Orthodox
context: The Peace of Augsburg (1555) enshrined cuius regio, eius religio -- 'whose realm, his religion' -- but recognized only Catholics and Lutherans, leaving out the Calvinists. That omission helped set the stage for the much deadlier Thirty Years' War (1618-1648). (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuius_regio,_eius_religio ; encyclopedia.com 'Augsburg, Religious Peace of 1555')

question: When news of the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre reached Rome, Pope Gregory XIII did not mourn -- he celebrated, ordering a Te Deum of thanksgiving sung and striking a commemorative medal. The blunt Latin words stamped on that medal named the killing for exactly what it was. What did the medal's inscription call the event?
answer: The Slaughter of the Huguenots
choices: The Slaughter of the Huguenots
The Triumph of True Faith
The Peace of Christendom
The Deliverance of Paris
context: Pope Gregory XIII greeted the massacre with a Te Deum and a commemorative medal reading 'VGONOTTORVM STRAGES 1572' -- 'Slaughter of the Huguenots, 1572' -- its reverse showing an angel with cross and drawn sword striking down the fallen Protestants. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Bartholomew's_Day_massacre ; Carleton, 'Medal in Commemoration of the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre')

question: In 1878, long before they built anything that could fly, the Wright brothers' father came home with a small toy that he tossed into the air. It buzzed up to the ceiling, fluttered, and sank to the floor, and the two boys never forgot it. What was this toy that first set them dreaming of flight?
answer: A little helicopter of paper, bamboo and cork
choices: A little helicopter of paper, bamboo and cork
A wooden glider carved like a bird
A brass model of a hot-air balloon
A kite shaped like an eagle
context: Orville and Wilbur Wright recalled watching it 'fly across the room till it struck the ceiling, where it fluttered awhile, and finally sank to the floor.' Their father, Milton Wright, brought it home in 1878. Source: AOPA, 'What you never knew about the Wright brothers' (aopa.org).

question: The Wright brothers built the first airplane, but they were not scientists or trained engineers. Neither one even finished high school. They taught themselves by reading. What was their day job back home in Dayton, Ohio?
answer: They built and sold bicycles in their own shop
choices: They built and sold bicycles in their own shop
They were professors at a university
They worked as railroad engineers
They ran a newspaper printing press
context: The Wright Cycle Company sold bikes the brothers built themselves, including their 'Van Cleve' and 'St. Clair' models. The mechanical skill they learned fixing and building bicycles is what let them build a flying machine. Source: Wikipedia, 'Wright Cycle Company'; AOPA (aopa.org).

question: On December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright flew the first powered plane in history. He lay flat on the lower wing while Wilbur ran alongside. That short flight changed the world. How long did it last?
answer: About 12 seconds
choices: About 12 seconds
About 8 minutes
About half an hour
About two hours
context: Twelve seconds, covering 120 feet, at 10:35 a.m. into a 27-mph wind. A tiny hop, but it was the first time a powered, heavier-than-air machine carried a person under control. Source: NPS, 'First Flight' (nps.gov); Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum (airandspace.si.edu).

question: In 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first human to walk on the Moon. To honor how far flight had come in just 66 years, he carried a small relic of the very first airplane all the way to the lunar surface. What did Armstrong take with him to the Moon?
answer: A piece of wood from the 1903 Flyer's propeller and a swatch of its wing cloth
choices: A piece of wood from the 1903 Flyer's propeller and a swatch of its wing cloth
A photograph of Orville and Wilbur Wright
A bolt from the 1903 Flyer's engine
Wilbur Wright's pocket watch
context: Armstrong carried wood from the propeller and a piece of unbleached muslin from the wing, linking the first 12-second flight at Kitty Hawk to the first Moon landing. Source: AOPA (aopa.org).

question: Other inventors built wings and engines, but their planes kept crashing. Pilots could not keep them level. The Wright brothers found a fix. They could tip the plane and turn it by twisting the wingtips in opposite ways. What was this trick called?
answer: Wing-warping
choices: Wing-warping
Tail-dragging
Air-braking
Skid-steering
context: Wing-warping let the Wrights control roll, the third piece of true three-axis control (pitch, roll, and yaw). Wilbur reportedly got the idea while idly twisting an empty long cardboard bicycle inner-tube box in the shop and noticing it could twist while staying rigid. Source: Wikipedia, 'Wing warping'; wright-brothers.org.

question: The Wright brothers needed a gasoline engine light enough to fly, but no company could build one. So a machinist in their bicycle shop built one from scratch in about six weeks, working from rough sketches with no formal plans. Who built the engine that powered the first flight?
answer: Charlie Taylor, the brothers' shop machinist
choices: Charlie Taylor, the brothers' shop machinist
Henry Ford, the automobile maker
Thomas Edison, the inventor
Glenn Curtiss, a rival airplane builder
context: Charlie Taylor's engine was a 4-cylinder of about 12 horsepower. To save weight he cast its engine block from aluminum, the first time aluminum was ever used in an aircraft engine. Source: NPS, 'Wright Flyer' (nps.gov); macsmotorcitygarage.com.

question: Orville and Wilbur Wright flipped a coin to decide who would get to fly first. Wilbur won the toss and made the first attempt on December 14, 1903, but he pulled the nose up too sharply, stalled, and dove into the sand after only about three seconds. Because of that, what happened on December 17?
answer: Orville took the controls and made the famous successful flight
choices: Orville took the controls and made the famous successful flight
Wilbur flew first again and finally succeeded
They called off all flying until the spring
They flipped the coin a second time
context: Wilbur's December 14 try ended in a harmless nose-dive into the soft sand. Three days later it was Orville's turn at the controls for the first true flight. Source: Wikipedia, 'Wright brothers'; NPS, 'First Flight' (nps.gov).

question: Just after the first flight at Kitty Hawk, the Wright brothers nearly lost their plane. A sudden gust of wind tumbled the parked Flyer across the sand. It even rolled one of the helpers along inside it. What happened to the 1903 Flyer after that gust?
answer: It was damaged badly and never flew again
choices: It was damaged badly and never flew again
They repaired it and flew it for years
They flew it home to Dayton the next week
They sold it to the Smithsonian intact
context: The gust caught lifesaver John T. Daniels and rolled him in the machine; he was shaken but unhurt. The Flyer was wrecked beyond simple repair and never flew again. Source: NPS, 'First Flight' (nps.gov); Wikipedia, 'Wright brothers'.

question: The Wright brothers made four flights on December 17, 1903, each one longer than the last. The first was just a 120-foot hop. Wilbur flew the fourth and best one of the day, going far enough that the era of brief hops was clearly over. How far did that fourth flight go?
answer: 852 feet in 59 seconds
choices: 852 feet in 59 seconds
410 feet in 28 seconds
1,340 feet in 95 seconds
2,100 feet in 140 seconds
context: Orville's telegram home read 'Success four flights Thursday morning... longest 57 seconds inform Press home Christmas' - the telegraph operator garbled the 59 as 57 and even misspelled Orville's name. Source: Library of Congress original telegram (loc.gov); Wright State University Libraries.

question: When the Wright brothers needed propellers, they found there was no real science of how a propeller should be shaped, so they had to invent it. Their key insight was that a propeller is not really a kind of screw at all. So what did they realize a propeller actually is?
answer: A wing turned sideways, spinning in a vertical circle
choices: A wing turned sideways, spinning in a vertical circle
A simple paddle that pushes air backward
A screw that bites into the air like wood
A fan that only cools the engine
context: Treating the propeller as 'a wing rotating in the vertical plane,' the Wrights designed theirs from their own wind-tunnel airfoil data and computed the thrust to within about 1% of what the propellers actually delivered. Source: Wikipedia, 'Wright brothers'; Hartzell Propeller (hartzellprop.com).

question: In 1901 the Wright brothers built a wooden wind tunnel in their shop and tested tiny model wings inside it. The results shocked them: the published wing data from the world's most famous glider pioneer, the German Otto Lilienthal, simply did not match what the brothers measured. How wrong did Lilienthal's lift numbers turn out to be?
answer: Their wing made only about a third of the lift his tables predicted
choices: Their wing made only about a third of the lift his tables predicted
His numbers matched their wing almost exactly
His numbers were too small by about half
His numbers only failed in very light winds
context: The brothers threw out the accepted numbers and built their own corrected lift-and-drag tables from scratch, testing between 100 and 200 miniature wing shapes. Trusting their own data over the famous expert's is what let them succeed. Source: NASA Glenn Research Center (grc.nasa.gov).

question: While building the airplane, the Wright brothers checked a number called the Smeaton coefficient, a constant that everyone calculating lift and air pressure had trusted for more than a century. When they measured it themselves in their wind tunnel, they found the long-accepted value was badly off. By how much was this century-old constant wrong?
answer: Off by nearly a factor of two
choices: Off by nearly a factor of two
Off by less than one percent
Off by exactly ten times
Off by a factor of a thousand
context: The accepted Smeaton value was about 0.0054; the Wrights' tests showed the true figure was closer to 0.0033. A number engineers had relied on for over a hundred years was nearly off by half, and the bicycle mechanics were the ones who caught it. Source: NASA Glenn Research Center (grc.nasa.gov); Wikipedia, 'Wright brothers'.

question: Xerxes demanded that the Greeks at Thermopylae hand over their weapons. By later tradition, Leonidas of Sparta answered in just two words of Greek, a reply Plutarch recorded centuries afterwards but Herodotus never mentions. What did Leonidas say?
answer: "Come and take them."
choices: "Come and take them."
"We will never kneel."
"Sparta does not yield."
"Take them by force."
context: In Greek, 'Molon labe.' The line is recorded by Plutarch in his 'Sayings of Spartans,' some 500 years afterward, not by the historian Herodotus, so it is a celebrated later tradition rather than a verified quote.

question: Dieneces, a Spartan at Thermopylae, heard a Greek warn that the Persian archers were so many their arrows would blot out the sun. He was not frightened, and his reply made Herodotus call him the bravest man of the battle. What did Dieneces say?
answer: "Then we shall fight in the shade."
choices: "Then we shall fight in the shade."
"Then we shall die in glory."
"Then the gods will guide my spear."
"Then their arrows will find Spartan shields."
context: Herodotus singled out Dieneces as the bravest of all the Greeks at Thermopylae for this calm retort, the best of many Spartan retorts that day (7.226).

question: Leonidas of Sparta led about 7,000 Greeks to a narrow coastal pass north of Athens to slow the vast army of Xerxes. Cliffs squeezed the road there to a strip only a few paces wide, and sulphur springs steamed up from the rocks and gave the place its Greek name. What does 'Thermopylae' mean?
answer: the Hot Gates
choices: the Hot Gates
the Iron Pass
the Burning Road
the Smoking Cliffs
context: The steaming sulfur springs gave the defile its name; the cliffs and sea squeezed the road so tight that a small force could hold off a huge one. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/betrayal-crushed-spartas-last-stand-at-the-battle-of-thermopylae

question: Ephialtes, a Greek from near Thermopylae, hoped Xerxes would reward him. He showed the Persians a hidden mountain path that led around behind the pass. The Greeks never forgave him: his name is an ordinary Greek word, and it also came to mean traitor. What does the word mean?
answer: a nightmare
choices: a nightmare
a coward
a stranger
a debt
context: 'Ephialtes' became the ordinary Greek word for nightmare and, by extension, traitor. The hidden route he revealed was the Anopaea path over the mountains. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephialtes_of_Trachis

question: Hydarnes led ten thousand picked men up the hidden mountain path by night, on the orders of Xerxes, to get behind the Greeks at Thermopylae. The Greeks called these soldiers the Immortals. Why did they earn that name?
answer: Every man who fell was instantly replaced.
choices: Every man who fell was instantly replaced.
They were sworn never to retreat in battle.
They alone wore armor no arrow could pierce.
They were the king's own blood relatives.
context: The moment a soldier was killed, wounded, or sick, a waiting replacement stepped into his place, so the corps never dropped below 10,000 and seemed never to die. They were never truly deathless; that was the point of the nickname. Xerxes sent them by night under his commander Hydarnes.

question: Simonides of Ceos wrote the words for the stone the Greeks raised, long afterwards, where the Spartans fell at Thermopylae. Leonidas and his men had died there when the Persians surrounded them on the third day. The epitaph became the most famous ever written for soldiers. What does it say?
answer: "Stranger, go tell the Spartans that here we lie, obedient to their laws."
choices: "Stranger, go tell the Spartans that here we lie, obedient to their laws."
"Here sleep the sons of Sparta, who chose death over chains."
"Weep not for these, who gave their lives that Greece might live."
"Remember the three hundred who feared no king of Persia."
context: Simonides's epitaph speaks in the voice of the fallen, asking any passing traveler to carry word home that they died doing exactly what Spartan law demanded. Source: https://www.attalus.org/poetry/simonides.html

question: A Persian scout sent ahead by Xerxes returned from the Greek camp at Thermopylae puzzled. The Spartans were calmly busy at something that made no sense to him. Demaratus, a Spartan king in exile who had joined the Persians, said it was their custom before risking their lives. What were the Spartans doing?
answer: combing and dressing their long hair
choices: combing and dressing their long hair
sharpening their spears in silence
singing hymns to their war-god
feasting on their last provisions
context: Demaratus told Xerxes that grooming their hair was how Spartans prepared to die well. The sight of warriors calmly tending their hair before a hopeless fight unnerved the Persians. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/herodotus/herodotus-on-thermopylae/

question: A thousand Phocian Greeks kept watch over the secret mountain path above Thermopylae. When the Immortals climbed it by night, the Phocians did not see or hear soldiers at first; one small thing in the dark told them the enemy was upon them. What gave the Persians away?
answer: the rustling of oak leaves under their feet
choices: the rustling of oak leaves under their feet
the glint of moonlight on their spears
the smell of smoke from their torches
the distant call of a Persian horn
context: In the still night the thick carpet of fallen oak leaves crackled under the climbing Persians, and the Phocians realized too late they had been outflanked. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/herodotus/herodotus-on-thermopylae/

question: The Persians closed around the last of the Greeks with Leonidas at Thermopylae on the third day. The Greeks fought until their spears snapped, then drew their swords and fought until those broke too. Herodotus writes that even then the survivors kept fighting. What did they fight with?
answer: their hands and teeth
choices: their hands and teeth
stones torn from the ground
the broken shafts of their spears
the shields of the fallen
context: Herodotus writes that weaponless, the Greeks fought on 'with their hands and teeth' until the Persians overwhelmed them with arrows. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Thermopylae

question: The pass of Thermopylae fell to Xerxes at last, and he was furious that so few men had defied him for so long. The Greeks thought it a sacred duty to return a fallen enemy's body for an honourable burial, but Xerxes broke that custom with an order about the body of King Leonidas. What did he order?
answer: that the head be cut off and set on a stake
choices: that the head be cut off and set on a stake
that the body be burned to leave no grave
that the bones be carried back to Persia
that the body be thrown into the sea
context: Beheading a fallen foe and displaying the head violated every Greek convention of honoring the dead; Herodotus presents it as a measure of Xerxes's rage at how dearly the pass had cost him. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/betrayal-crushed-spartas-last-stand-at-the-battle-of-thermopylae

question: Eurytus and Aristodemus, two of the 300 Spartans, had a disease of the eyes and were excused before the last fight. Eurytus had a slave lead him blind back into the battle, and he died there. Aristodemus went home to Sparta alive, and his whole city punished him as a coward. How did Sparta treat him?
answer: No Spartan would speak to him or give him fire.
choices: No Spartan would speak to him or give him fire.
He was stripped of his land and exiled for life.
He was made to serve the families of the dead.
He was forbidden ever to carry arms again.
context: Aristodemus was shunned as 'the Trembler' — denied conversation and even a light for his hearth. A year later he erased the shame by fighting with reckless courage at the Battle of Plataea. Source: https://www.livius.org/sources/content/herodotus/herodotus-on-thermopylae/

question: Xerxes asked Demaratus, once king of Sparta and now in exile with the Persian army, why the tiny Spartan force at Thermopylae would stand and fight instead of running. Herodotus says Demaratus warned that the Spartans were bound to fight to the death by something stronger than any commander. What did he say held them in place?
answer: a Law they feared more than the Persians feared the king
choices: a Law they feared more than the Persians feared the king
an oath they had sworn to the gods of Greece
the shame of facing their wives if they fled
the promise of glory and reward after victory
context: Demaratus told Xerxes the Spartans' true master was the Law, which forbade them to flee and commanded them to conquer or die — and they feared it far more than Xerxes's own soldiers feared him. Source: https://classics.mit.edu/Herodotus/history.7.vii.html

question: In Albert the Great's classroom in Paris in the 1240s sat a young Italian, Thomas Aquinas, huge, heavy and so silent that most of the other students thought him dim. They mocked him with a cruel animal nickname. What did they call him?
answer: the Dumb Ox
choices: the Dumb Ox
the Silent Bear
the Sleeping Ram
the Slow Mule
context: 'Bos mutus,' the Dumb Ox. His teacher Albertus Magnus shut the mockers down: 'You call him the dumb ox, but in his teaching he will one day produce such a bellowing that it will be heard throughout the world.' The prophecy proved right: Aquinas became the towering theologian of the Middle Ages. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Thomas_Aquinas/

question: The powerful Aquino family gave their youngest son, Thomas, to the Church by custom, hoping he would one day rule the abbey of Monte Cassino as its wealthy abbot. He was a small child when they sent him to the monks there. How old was he when they gave him away?
answer: five years old
choices: five years old
nine years old
twelve years old
sixteen years old
context: He was sent at about age five to the great Benedictine monastery of Monte Cassino, where his family hoped he would grow up to become its wealthy abbot. Source: https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14663b.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas

question: At nineteen, in 1244, Thomas Aquinas wrecked his noble family's plans: instead of becoming a rich abbot, he joined the Dominicans, wandering friars who owned nothing and begged for their bread. On the road he was ambushed, carried off and locked for nearly a year in the family castle. Who ambushed him?
answer: his own brothers
choices: his own brothers
the monks of Monte Cassino
a band of hired soldiers
the local bishop's men
context: His brothers held him captive for almost a year in a tower of the family castle (Monte San Giovanni / Roccasecca), trying to force him to abandon the begging order. He refused and kept his vows. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Thomas_Aquinas/

question: Roccasecca castle held Thomas Aquinas for nearly a year because he would not give up the Dominicans, and his captors could not break his will. In the end, how did he get free to go and study in Paris?
answer: his mother had him lowered through a window at night
choices: his mother had him lowered through a window at night
the Pope ordered his noble family to release him
he overpowered the guards and fled on a stolen horse
the Dominicans paid his family a ransom in gold
context: His mother, Theodora, gave up the fight and arranged for him to be let down through a window after dark; he then went to Paris to study under Albertus Magnus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas

question: Pope John XXII made Thomas Aquinas a saint in 1323, honouring the friar who had written the Summa Theologiae, one of the greatest works of Christian thought, and in 1880 the Church made him the patron of all Catholic schools and colleges. He is honoured with a glowing title as well. What is Aquinas called?
answer: the Angelic Doctor
choices: the Angelic Doctor
the Golden Preacher
the Seraphic Father
the Universal Bishop
context: He was canonized in 1323 by Pope John XXII, declared a Doctor of the Church in 1567, and in 1880 made patron saint of all Catholic schools and universities — his nickname now the 'Angelic Doctor.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas

question: Aquinas's captors at Roccasecca tried one last trick on the teenage friar, who would not give up his vows to the begging Dominicans: they shoved a woman into his locked room, hoping she would seduce him into breaking his promise never to marry. What did Thomas do, according to the records collected for his sainthood?
answer: snatched a burning log from the fire and drove her out
choices: snatched a burning log from the fire and drove her out
knelt in the corner and prayed until she left
bribed the guards to carry her away by morning
recited Aristotle aloud until she fell asleep
context: Legend, from the canonization records: after driving her out, he is said to have used the firebrand to scorch the sign of the cross onto the wall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Thomas_Aquinas/

question: A carved figure of Christ spoke to Thomas Aquinas, the legend goes, when he had finished his account of the Eucharist, the Mass in which bread and wine are believed to become the body and blood of Christ. As he knelt before the crucifix, a voice came from it: 'You have written well of me, Thomas. What reward would you have?' How did he answer?
answer: "Nothing but you, Lord."
choices: "Nothing but you, Lord."
"Only to finish my work, Lord."
"A place in heaven, Lord."
"Wisdom above all men, Lord."
context: In the Latin of the legend: 'Non nisi te, Domine.' The abbey's sacristan was said to have witnessed the exchange. Source: https://melbournecatholic.org/news/nothing-but-you-lord-the-heart-of-st-thomas-aquinas ; https://www.regnumchristi.com/en/st-thomas-aquinas/

question: On his way to a Church council, Thomas Aquinas fell ill in 1274 and died at the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova, already whispered to be a saint. A saint's bones drew pilgrims and gifts, and the monks feared his own Dominicans would carry the body off. What did the monks do to the corpse to keep it?
answer: cut off his head and boiled the flesh from his bones
choices: cut off his head and boiled the flesh from his bones
sealed it inside the abbey's thickest stone wall
buried it secretly beneath the high altar at night
dressed it in armor and posted guards around it
context: In 1369 about 50 of his bones were finally handed to the Dominicans of Toulouse, where his tomb stands today — and two rival skulls are still each claimed as his. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonization_of_Thomas_Aquinas ; https://live.christian.expert/skull-aquinas

question: Thomas Aquinas spent his last years on a giant summary of Christian teaching, the Summa Theologica: about 3,000 pages, with thousands of short Articles under its 512 Questions, taking on every major debate of the Church in the 1200s. Yet in its opening lines he named a very simple audience. Who did he say he wrote it for?
answer: beginners in Christian doctrine
choices: beginners in Christian doctrine
the Pope and his cardinals
the masters of the University of Paris
monks preparing to become priests
context: He genuinely framed his 3,000-page colossus as a textbook to instruct beginners in the faith. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summa_Theologica ; https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/summa-and-its-parts

question: Aristotle, a pagan Greek, had been dead some sixteen centuries when Thomas Aquinas set out to wed his logic to Christian faith, arguing that faith and reason can never truly contradict. Aquinas admired him so much that he rarely troubled to write his name, and used one reverent title instead. What did Aquinas call Aristotle?
answer: "the Philosopher"
choices: "the Philosopher"
"the Teacher"
"the Sage"
"the Master"
context: Aquinas leaned on Aristotle's ideas of motion, cause, potentiality, and final ends as the scaffolding for his own arguments — and referred to him throughout simply as 'the Philosopher.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Ways_(Aquinas) ; https://www.philosophynotebook.com/intro/aquinas.shtml

question: Reginald, Thomas Aquinas's secretary, begged him to keep writing, but after a shattering vision at Mass on 6 December 1273 Aquinas never wrote another word, and the Summa stayed unfinished. Next to what had been revealed to him, he said, all of his writing now seemed like one thing. What did it seem like to him?
answer: straw
choices: straw
dust
ash
chaff
context: His exact reported words: 'I cannot, because all that I have written seems like straw to me.' He left the Summa unfinished forever and died about three months later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas ; https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14663b.htm ; christianhistoryinstitute.org, 'I can write no more'

question: "Whether...": with that word Thomas Aquinas opened the question of every Article in his great Summa, and every Article followed the same combative pattern. Before he argued for his own answer, he set something else down first. What did he set down?
answer: the strongest arguments against his own position
choices: the strongest arguments against his own position
a prayer asking God for the right answer
a quotation from Scripture to open the topic
a list of the questions he would tackle
context: Each Article states the Objections (the best arguments against him) fairly and first, then a 'Sed contra' ('On the contrary...'), then his own answer 'Respondeo' ('I answer that...'), then a point-by-point reply to every objection. Steelman the opponent first, then refute: this 'disputatio' is the engine of scholastic reasoning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summa_Theologica ; https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/summa-and-its-parts

question: Near the start of the Summa Theologica, Thomas Aquinas paused to give five short arguments, each of which, he believed, proved on its own that God exists. They drew on motion, first causes, a necessary being, degrees of perfection and the design of nature, and every one of them closed by naming God. What are the five arguments called?
answer: the Five Ways
choices: the Five Ways
the Five Pillars
the Five Proofs
the Five Mysteries
context: The 'Five Ways' (Quinque viae) appear in Part I, Question 2, Article 3 — and each one closes with the same line: 'and this everyone understands to be God.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Ways_(Aquinas) ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/the-Five-Ways

question: King Henry II had feuded for years with Thomas Becket, the Archbishop of Canterbury, over the power of the Church. One day the king flew into a rage at court and shouted about Becket. Four of his knights took it as an order to kill. They rode to Canterbury and cut the archbishop down. What is Henry said to have shouted?
answer: "Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?"
choices: "Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?"
"Bring me the head of this rebel archbishop!"
"Let the man be banished from my kingdom forever!"
"I shall ride to Canterbury and judge him myself!"
context: The line is the most famous royal outburst in English history, but it appears in no contemporary account and is almost certainly apocryphal -- chroniclers report Henry cursing the 'low-born clerks' he had raised who let one man shame him. The four knights -- Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, and Richard le Breton -- murdered Becket inside Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170. Source: historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofEngland/Thomas-Becket/  (Legend.)

question: In 1170, King Henry II's knights killed Thomas Becket inside Canterbury Cathedral. The monks stripped his body to prepare it for burial. Under his fine robes they found a hidden secret. He had worn it against his bare skin every day. It convinced people he was a true saint even more than the murder itself did. What did the monks find under his robes?
answer: A coarse goat-hair shirt crawling with lice and vermin
choices: A coarse goat-hair shirt crawling with lice and vermin
A jeweled silver cross worth a small fortune
A letter naming the four knights who hunted him
A wound from an old assassination attempt
context: The lice-ridden goat-hair shirt was a hidden penance; the monks were stunned that their archbishop had secretly mortified his own flesh. Reported miracle cures soon poured in at his tomb, and Pope Alexander III canonised Becket in 1173 -- barely three years after his death. Sources: learning.canterbury-cathedral.org/a-walk-through-time/becket/ and Cambridge, 'Dirty Laundry: Thomas Becket's Hair Shirt and the Making of a Saint'

question: Thomas Edison built a new kind of research laboratory in the 1870s. Out of it poured invention after invention: the phonograph, the carbon microphone and soon the practical electric light bulb. By 1878 newspapers everywhere had given him a magical nickname. What did they call him?
answer: The Wizard of Menlo Park
choices: The Wizard of Menlo Park
The Sorcerer of Manhattan
The Genius of New York
The Magician of Detroit
context: Edison's New Jersey lab turned out invention after invention, and the world was calling him 'The Wizard of Menlo Park' by 1878. Source: Thomas Edison Center at Menlo Park, https://www.menloparkmuseum.org/history

question: Thomas Edison shouted a nursery rhyme into a hand-cranked tinfoil cylinder in 1877, as a test: one needle scratched grooves as he spoke, and another played them back. The machine startled even Edison by saying the words right back. What words did it say?
answer: "Mary had a little lamb"
choices: "Mary had a little lamb"
"Twinkle, twinkle, little star"
"Hark, the herald angels sing"
"Hickory dickory dock"
context: Edison's first phonograph (1877) was a tinfoil cylinder with one needle to scratch the grooves and another to play them back; his mechanic John Kruesi built it in about 30 hours. Edison recited the nursery rhyme to test it, and even he was startled that it worked on the first try. Sources: ASME, https://www.asme.org/about-asme/engineering-history/landmarks/68-edison-experimental-recording-phonograph; https://ethw.org/Phonograph

question: Thomas Edison switched on his first practical electric light at Menlo Park in 1879, and it burned for more than thirteen hours. The thin thread that glowed inside the glass, called the filament, was no rare or costly stuff. It was an everyday household item, baked black and sealed in a vacuum. What was it?
answer: A loop of cotton sewing thread
choices: A loop of cotton sewing thread
A strand of fine silk thread
A length of braided horsehair
A strip of folded writing paper
context: The filament in the first successful 1879 lamp, which burned about thirteen and a half hours, was a loop of ordinary cotton sewing thread, carbonized (charred). Charring turned it into a filament that resisted the current and glowed instead of burning up. Sources: U.S. Dept. of Energy, https://www.energy.gov/articles/history-light-bulb; IEEE, https://ethw.org/Edison's_Incandescent_Lamp; https://edison.rutgers.edu/life-of-edison/biographical-essays/lighting/the-carbon-filament-lamp

question: Thomas Edison strung rows of glowing electric lamps around his Menlo Park grounds on New Year's Eve of 1879, and crowds poured off special trains of the Pennsylvania Railroad to see night turned into day. What did some of those visitors do to the bulbs?
answer: They stole eight of them as souvenirs
choices: They stole eight of them as souvenirs
They smashed several in a panic
They painted them different colors
They unscrewed them to keep warm
context: Edison explained the lamps 'in plain language and a homespun manner,' but eight of the bulbs walked off as souvenirs that night. Source: History.com, https://www.history.com/articles/when-edison-turned-night-into-day

question: Thomas Edison, a famous story says, would lean in and bite down on a piano's wooden case so the vibrations traveled up through his jaw into his skull. He was almost completely deaf, yet he still wanted to enjoy music. How did Edison describe doing this?
answer: "I hear through my teeth"
choices: "I hear through my teeth"
"I listen with my bones"
"The music lives in the wood"
"My jaw became my ear"
context: Edison was deaf in his left ear and roughly 80% deaf in the right; the bite-the-piano story ('I hear through my teeth') is told as legend, and a surviving Steinway grand bears bite marks believed to be his. Source: Mental Floss, https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/641725/thomas-edison-facts ; VOA, https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/piano-belonging-to-thomas-edison-shows-unusual-marks/6815113.html

question: Thomas Edison's scouts combed the world for plant fibers after his first bulbs burned out in about half a day, and he burned thousands of them, hunting for a filament that would last. The winner glowed for about 1,200 hours and stayed in his bulbs for nearly ten years. A scout shipped it home from a grove beside a far-off shrine. What plant gave Edison that filament?
answer: Japanese bamboo
choices: Japanese bamboo
Brazilian palm
Egyptian papyrus
Himalayan cotton
context: In 1880 Edison's scout William H. Moore sent samples from a bamboo grove by the Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine near Kyoto (Phyllostachys bambusoides); carbonized, the charred bamboo fibres made a tough filament that burned about 1,200 hours. Edison did not invent the glowing bulb from nothing, but he built the first practical, long-lasting one, plus the wires and generators to light a city. Sources: Amusing Planet, https://www.amusingplanet.com/2019/05/how-japanese-bamboo-helped-edison-make.html; Government of Japan, https://www.gov-online.go.jp/eng/publicity/book/hlj/html/202208/202208_08_en.html; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Edison

question: Thomas Edison opened Pearl Street Station in Manhattan in 1882, America's first central power plant, run by giant 27-ton generators. He named those huge machines after the most famous animal of the day, P.T. Barnum's massive circus elephant. What were the generators called?
answer: Jumbo
choices: Jumbo
Goliath
Mammoth
Titan
context: On September 4, 1882, at 3 o'clock Edison flipped the switch at Pearl Street Station; its 27-ton 'Jumbo' dynamos were named after Barnum's celebrated elephant. Source: IEEE, https://ethw.org/Pearl_Street_Station ; https://ethw.org/Milestones:Pearl_Street_Station,_1882

question: Thomas Edison tried thousands of materials in his New Jersey laboratory in the late 1870s, hunting for a thin filament that would glow steadily inside a bulb without burning up. He failed over and over. By legend, when a reporter asked him about all those failures, Edison gave a stubborn answer that refused to call them failures at all. What did he say?
answer: "I have not failed — I've found 10,000 ways that won't work"
choices: "I have not failed — I've found 10,000 ways that won't work"
"I have not lost — I've ruled out a thousand wrong roads"
"I have not quit — I've crossed off 5,000 dead ends"
"I have not stumbled — I've mapped the road around each miss"
context: The legendary '10,000 ways that won't work' line is the famous version; the earliest documented form (Dyer & Martin, 1910) is gentler: 'I have gotten a lot of results! I know several thousand things that won't work.' Source: Quote Investigator, https://quoteinvestigator.com/2012/07/31/edison-lot-results/

question: At Menlo Park, Thomas Edison filled one building with a staff of skilled workers and all their equipment, set up on purpose to turn out one new device after another. No one had ever run a laboratory that way before. What did Edison call his first-of-its-kind operation?
answer: The Invention Factory
choices: The Invention Factory
The Idea Mill
The Thinking Shop
The Genius Works
context: Menlo Park was the world's first industrial research-and-development laboratory; Edison called it the 'Invention Factory,' and while based there he applied for about 400 patents. Source: Thomas Edison Center at Menlo Park, https://www.menloparkmuseum.org/history

question: Thomas Edison knew a light bulb was useless with no power to run it, so he built the whole electrical system around it: power plants, wires into homes, sockets and switches. He also invented one more thing, so the new electric company could fairly charge each customer. What was it?
answer: An electric meter that measured each home's use
choices: An electric meter that measured each home's use
A coin slot built into every lamp
A bell that rang when a bill came due
A clock that shut the power off at night
context: Edison invented the whole system around the bulb — central power plant, distribution wires, sockets and switches — plus the first electric meter to measure each customer's use and bill for it. Source: U.S. Dept. of Energy, https://www.energy.gov/articles/history-light-bulb ; IEEE, https://ethw.org/Edison's_Electric_Light_and_Power_System

question: Joseph Swan had already shown off his own carbon-filament bulb in Britain and patented it there in 1878, before Thomas Edison's, though the common story credits Edison with inventing the light bulb. When the two men clashed over the invention in the British courts, how did the case end?
answer: Edison lost the case and took Swan in as a partner
choices: Edison lost the case and took Swan in as a partner
Edison won the case and Swan paid him royalties
Edison and Swan both quit the light-bulb business
The British court banned both men from selling bulbs
context: Edison didn't invent the bulb — he made it practical. He lost a British patent-infringement case to Swan and had to take him in as a partner, forming the Edison & Swan United Electric Light Company in 1883. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edison_and_Swan_Electric_Light_Company ; IEEE, https://ethw.org/Edison's_Incandescent_Lamp

question: Thomas Edison went the opposite way from his rivals, whose thick filaments gulped huge currents: his filament was hair-thin, with high resistance, and needed only a small current. Why did that thin, high-resistance filament matter so much for lighting a whole city?
answer: It let thin, cheap copper wires feed many bulbs at once
choices: It let thin, cheap copper wires feed many bulbs at once
It made each bulb glow ten times brighter than rivals'
It let the bulbs run with no power plant at all
It allowed bulbs to work underwater without sealing
context: High resistance and a small current meant power could travel through thin, cheap copper wires to many bulbs at once — which is what made a citywide lighting system affordable. Source: IEEE, https://ethw.org/Edison's_Incandescent_Lamp ; U.S. Dept. of Energy, https://www.energy.gov/articles/history-light-bulb

question: The English philosopher Thomas Hobbes lived through England's bloody civil war of the 1640s and hated the chaos he had seen. In his 1651 book Leviathan he argued that without a strong government, every person would be at war with every other, and human life would fall apart into fear and violence. He summed up that state-of-nature life in four grim little words. He said life without government is solitary, poor, nasty, and what?
answer: Brutish and short
choices: Brutish and short
Cruel and bitter
Savage and cold
Wretched and dark
context: The full line: in the state of nature, with no government to keep order, the life of man is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' (Leviathan, Book I, Ch. 13, 1651). It is Hobbes' single most famous sentence. Source: https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2021/07/14/hobbes-on-the-state-of-nature/

question: Thomas Hobbes named his great book about government after a monster from the Bible's Book of Job. The creature was called 'king over all the children of pride.' Hobbes wanted his ruler to strike fear the way this monster did. What creature is the book named after?
answer: The Leviathan, a sea serpent
choices: The Leviathan, a sea serpent
The Behemoth, a land beast
The Phoenix, a fire bird
The Basilisk, a serpent king
context: Hobbes named his book Leviathan after the monstrous sea serpent of the Book of Job. The sovereign, like the serpent, is a fearsome creature that must overawe everyone to keep the peace. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leviathan_(Hobbes_book)

question: Thomas Hobbes was born early on April 5, 1588, when his mother heard the Spanish Armada was sailing to attack England and the terror sent her into labor. In his autobiography he joked about the fear that surrounded his birth with a famous line. What did Hobbes say was born alongside him?
answer: His twin, Fear
choices: His twin, Fear
His enemy, War
His shadow, Doubt
His friend, Reason
context: Hobbes wrote that 'fear and I were born twins together' — his mother went into early labor on hearing the Armada was coming. Fear of violent death is the engine of his whole philosophy. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/thomas-hobbes

question: Thomas Hobbes wrote Leviathan in exile in Paris. England was in civil war, and King Charles I had just been beheaded. To Hobbes, the only escape from such chaos was one deal. Each person gives up the right to rule himself, but only if everyone else does too. All hand that power to one ruler. What do people get in return, according to Hobbes?
answer: Protection
choices: Protection
Wealth
Glory
Wisdom
context: Hobbes' social contract: each says 'I authorise and give up my right of governing myself to this man... on this condition, that thou give up thy right to him,' trading liberty to one sovereign — an 'artificial man' — for protection. Hobbes reasons from the same state of nature as Locke but lands on absolute rule, not limited government. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leviathan_(Hobbes_book)

question: The 1651 frontispiece of Leviathan, engraved by Abraham Bosse, shows a crowned giant towering over the land, gripping a sword in one hand and a bishop's crosier in the other. Look closely and the giant's body is not solid — it is built entirely out of something. What makes up the giant's body?
answer: More than 300 tiny people
choices: More than 300 tiny people
Coins stamped with crowns
Stone blocks of a fortress
Coils of an iron chain
context: The giant's body is built from more than 300 tiny human figures — the people themselves make up the sovereign. The sword stands for worldly power, the crosier for church power. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leviathan_(Hobbes_book)

question: Thomas Hobbes lived to age 91 and died at the Cavendish family's Chatsworth House on December 4, 1679. According to a long-told story, this philosopher who built his whole life's work on the fear of death faced his own end with a single calm, witty remark. What were Hobbes' reported last words?
answer: A great leap in the dark
choices: A great leap in the dark
A long sleep, well earned
The final war is won
No more fear for me
context: Hobbes' reported last words were 'a great leap in the dark.' This is traditional testimony rather than documented fact — told as legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes

question: John Adams sat with the 33-year-old Thomas Jefferson on the Committee of Five, named by Congress in June 1776 to draft a declaration of independence. The five agreed that one man should write it, and Adams pushed Jefferson to hold the pen rather than hold it himself. Why did Adams want Jefferson to write it?
answer: Adams thought Jefferson could write better than he could
choices: Adams thought Jefferson could write better than he could
Adams was too busy arguing with the other delegates
Adams was not yet a member of the Continental Congress
Adams could not write because his hand was injured
context: Adams later recalled telling Jefferson he had a far better pen — and a reputation to match. The five-man 'Committee of Five' was appointed in June 1776; the 33-year-old Jefferson was its youngest member. Source: Committee of Five — Wikipedia; Monticello / jeffersonpapers.princeton.edu drafting page.

question: British troops marched into Washington in August 1814 and destroyed the small Library of Congress in the burning Capitol. Thomas Jefferson, 71 and retired, had once told John Adams, 'I cannot live without books,' and he owned the greatest personal book collection in America. How did he help rebuild the library?
answer: He sold his own library of nearly 6,500 books to rebuild it
choices: He sold his own library of nearly 6,500 books to rebuild it
He sailed to London to buy replacement books himself
He ordered the British ambassador to pay for new books
He wrote new books from memory to refill the shelves
context: Jefferson sold the government his personal collection — nearly 6,500 volumes — for $23,950, and it became the new core of the Library of Congress. Source: Library of Congress; Wikipedia (Thomas Jefferson).

question: Thomas Jefferson had almost no idea what lay in the huge western land he bought from France in 1803. So he sent the Corps of Discovery, a small team of soldiers and scouts, up the Missouri from St. Louis in 1804, over the Rockies and on to the Pacific and back. Who led the trip?
answer: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark
choices: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark
Daniel Boone and Davy Crockett
Robert Livingston and Roger Sherman
John Adams and Benjamin Franklin
context: Lewis had been Jefferson's own personal secretary. The Corps set out up the Missouri in May 1804 and reached the Pacific. Source: National Archives — Lewis & Clark lesson; Lewis and Clark Expedition — Wikipedia.

question: The delegates in Philadelphia argued over Thomas Jefferson's draft of the Declaration of Independence for two days in the summer of 1776, trimming about a quarter of his words, a fiery passage against the slave trade among them. How did Jefferson act while they cut his words?
answer: He sat in unhappy silence while they cut his words
choices: He sat in unhappy silence while they cut his words
He stood up and read the whole draft aloud again
He stormed out and refused to sign the final text
He cheerfully helped the delegates rewrite each line
context: Congress slashed about a quarter of his text before adopting it on the afternoon of July 4, 1776. Jefferson, by accounts, sat in pained silence as delegates trimmed his prose. Source: National Archives; History.com — writing of the Declaration of Independence.

question: Thomas Jefferson wrote out his own tombstone in his own hand, with strict orders that only three achievements be carved on it: that he wrote the Declaration of Independence, that he wrote Virginia's law for religious freedom, and that he founded the University of Virginia. What did he deliberately leave off?
answer: That he had been President of the United States
choices: That he had been President of the United States
That he had drafted the Declaration of Independence
That he had founded the University of Virginia
That he had written Notes on the State of Virginia
context: He served two terms as the third president — and deliberately omitted it, choosing instead the things he had created. Source: Library of Congress — Jefferson exhibit; Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom — Wikipedia.

question: Thomas Jefferson tinkered for decades with Monticello, his Virginia home, filling it with his own inventions: a dumbwaiter that lifted wine up from the cellar, a machine that copied each letter as he wrote it. In the front hall he built a tall Great Clock, kept running by heavy weights that sank slowly on ropes. What odd objects did he use for the weights?
answer: Revolutionary-War cannonballs
choices: Revolutionary-War cannonballs
A pair of brass church bells
Buckets of Virginia river water
Iron horseshoes from his stable
context: Jefferson tinkered with Monticello for decades, calling 'putting up, and pulling down' a favorite amusement; his Great Clock was driven by cannonball weights. Source: Monticello encyclopedia; American Scientist — 'Jefferson's Old Bones.'

question: 'All men are created equal,' Thomas Jefferson wrote in the Declaration of Independence in 1776, with unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Yet at Monticello and on his other Virginia estates, the same man went sharply against those words. Over his lifetime, roughly how many people did he enslave?
answer: He enslaved more than 600 people
choices: He enslaved more than 600 people
He enslaved more than 50 people
He enslaved more than 200 people
He enslaved more than 1,000 people
context: Jefferson enslaved over 600 human beings across his lifetime, about 130 at the time he died — the founding's sharpest contradiction: the man who penned the creed of equality owned the people who served his dinner. Source: Wikipedia (Thomas Jefferson); The Henry Ford; Monticello.

question: John Adams and Jefferson, friends, then bitter political rivals, then friends again by letter, both died on the same day: July 4, 1826, exactly fifty years after the Declaration of Independence. Adams died a few hours after Jefferson but never knew that his old rival had gone first. What were Adams's reported last words?
answer: 'Thomas Jefferson survives'
choices: 'Thomas Jefferson survives'
'Independence forever, and amen'
'I have done my duty to the end'
'Let the trumpets sound for liberty'
context: Adams died believing his old rival had outlived him — but Jefferson had died hours earlier. Jefferson's own last conscious words were 'Is it the Fourth?' Source: Library of Congress blog (Headlines & Heroes, 2022); Monticello encyclopedia (John Adams); Constitution Center.

question: Buffon, a French naturalist, claimed that animals in America were smaller and weaker than those of Europe. Thomas Jefferson took the claim as an insult to his country, collected huge mastodon ('mammoth') bones to prove him wrong, and went further with a bold claim about the giant beasts. What did Jefferson argue about them?
answer: That they might still be alive, roaming the unexplored West
choices: That they might still be alive, roaming the unexplored West
That their bones proved a great flood had once drowned America
That they were the ancestors of America's modern bears
That European hunters had killed off all the largest ones
context: Jefferson's only published book, Notes on the State of Virginia, was partly a catalog of American nature meant to refute Buffon. He genuinely hoped the mammoths still walked the West. Source: American Scientist — 'Jefferson's Old Bones'; Notes on the State of Virginia — Wikipedia.

question: Napoleon offered all of Louisiana for sale in 1803, a territory stretching from the Mississippi River to the Rockies, and Thomas Jefferson seized the chance to buy it for about $15 million. Yet the purchase troubled Jefferson's own conscience. What exactly did he privately doubt about the deal he had just made?
answer: Whether the Constitution gave him any power to buy foreign land
choices: Whether the Constitution gave him any power to buy foreign land
Whether Napoleon would actually hand over the territory
Whether the $15 million price was far too high to pay
Whether the Senate would ever agree to approve it
context: Jefferson believed the federal government 'has not given it power of holding foreign territory' and thought an amendment was needed — yet told John Dickinson they must 'ratify and pay our money... and rely on the nation to sanction an act done for its great good.' Source: Constitution Center — 'Jefferson's Constitutional Gamble.'

question: A group of anxious Baptists in Danbury, Connecticut, received a famous letter from Thomas Jefferson in 1802. In it he explained what the First Amendment had done to the tie between government and religion. What phrase did Jefferson coin in that letter, words the Supreme Court would later quote?
answer: A wall of separation between Church and State
choices: A wall of separation between Church and State
A common altar for every American faith
A shield of conscience over every believer
A bridge of tolerance among all the churches
context: Jefferson's 'wall of separation' became the Court's authoritative reading of the religion clauses. His 1786 Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom — which barred forcing anyone to support or attend worship — had been the direct model for those clauses. Source: Library of Congress — Danbury letter; Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom — Wikipedia.

question: A popular myth says the Constitution's three-fifths clause was the framers declaring an enslaved person to be 'three-fifths of a human being.' The real fight at the 1787 Convention was the reverse: a battle over who got to COUNT enslaved people toward a state's House delegation. Which side pushed hardest to count them?
answer: The slave states, who wanted more seats in Congress
choices: The slave states, who wanted more seats in Congress
The antislavery states, who wanted to honor the enslaved
The small states, who feared being outvoted
The frontier territories, who wanted faster statehood
context: The counterintuitive truth: slaveholding states fought to count the very people they held as property, because more counted heads meant more seats in the House and more votes for president. Antislavery delegates resisted exactly this. Three-fifths was a grim bargain to hold the union together, not a measure of a person's humanity. (Britannica, 'Three-fifths compromise'; Constitutional Accountability Center, theusconstitution.org)

question: Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery himself, refused to call the Constitution a slaveholders' document. He pointed out that the three-fifths clause counted a FREED person as a whole person, not three-fifths — so every enslaved person a state set free made that state GAIN seats in Congress. What did Douglass argue this hidden arithmetic handed the South?
answer: A built-in reward for freeing its slaves
choices: A built-in reward for freeing its slaves
A permanent veto over all Northern laws
A secret right to expand slavery westward
A guaranteed standing majority in the Senate
context: Douglass called the clause 'a standing rebuke' to the South — a built-in bribe to free the enslaved, since each freed person became a whole person in the count and won the state more representation. Against William Lloyd Garrison, who burned the Constitution as a pro-slavery pact, Douglass insisted it was an antislavery document and 'not a word' of it needed changing to abolish slavery. (Cato Institute, 'Frederick Douglass: The US Constitution Is an Anti-Slavery Document'; Douglass, 1860 Glasgow speech)

question: Corn grew from a wild Mexican grass called teosinte. Native farmers bred it into corn over thousands of years. But teosinte looks nothing like corn. Its tiny ear held only about two rows of a few kernels. Each kernel was sealed inside something a corncob never has. What covered each teosinte kernel?
answer: A rock-hard shell, like a little acorn
choices: A rock-hard shell, like a little acorn
A papery husk you peeled away
A coat of fine silk threads
A ring of sharp green spines
context: Wild teosinte kernels were locked inside a stony 'fruitcase' shell, two rows of only 5 to 12 of them per tiny ear, nothing like the naked kernels of a modern cob. Native farmers in Mexico turned this scrawny branching grass into corn. Source: evolution.earthathome.org maize-domestication; Native Seeds Search teosinte page.

question: Wild teosinte kept its seeds locked inside stony shells, useless to eat without cracking each one open. Corn's kernels sit naked and ready to eat. Geneticists found that flipping one single gene, called teosinte glume architecture1 (tga1), made that exact change happen. What did that one gene's change do to the kernels?
answer: It popped them out of their hard cases
choices: It popped them out of their hard cases
It doubled how many rows the ear grew
It turned them from blue to golden yellow
It made the whole ear grow twice as long
context: A single mutation in tga1 freed the kernels from their armored 'fruitcases', turning teosinte's locked seeds into corn's naked, eat-anytime kernels. A second gene, tb1, collapsed the bushy grass into one upright stalk. Source: evolution.earthathome.org maize-domestication.

question: On June 5, 1989, the day after Chinese soldiers crushed the Tiananmen Square protests, a lone man in a white shirt walked into a wide Beijing avenue. He stopped right in front of a row of army tanks. What was he holding in his hands as he stood there?
answer: two shopping bags
choices: two shopping bags
a protest banner
a bicycle
a bullhorn
context: The man, known only as 'Tank Man,' stepped into Beijing's Chang'an Avenue carrying two ordinary shopping bags. When the lead tank tried to steer around him he sidestepped to block it again, and even climbed onto the hull to speak to the crew before resuming his stand. To this day nobody knows his name or what became of him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank_Man

question: The famous Tiananmen photo, of a man in a white shirt blocking tanks, almost never got out. Police were seizing film from reporters all over Beijing. An American student named Kirk Martsen offered to smuggle the roll to the Associated Press office. Where on his body did he hide it?
answer: inside his underwear
choices: inside his underwear
taped against his chest
hidden in his shoe
sewn into his hat
context: AP photographer Jeff Widener shot the Tank Man picture from a sixth-floor hotel balcony half a mile away — while sick with flu and nursing a concussion from a rock that had hit his head the day before. To get the film past police, Martsen hid the roll in his underwear. (Newsweek's Charlie Cole, facing a room raid, hid his own roll in a hotel toilet tank.) Source: https://www.wral.com/story/the-man-in-front-of-the-tank-how-journalists-smuggled-out-the-iconic-tiananmen-square-photo/21465861/

question: Ibn Battuta, the great Moroccan traveller, came in 1352 to Taghaza, a mining town deep in the Sahara where the ground itself was solid salt.
